meaning.en_short: To say, speak, utter, express verbally
meaning.en: To say, to speak, to utter, to express verbally in a deliberate, meaningful manner. Encompasses all forms of verbal expression — from the divine creative command (kun fa-yakūn) to human conversation, from revealed scripture to inner conviction voiced aloud. The root bridges interior thought and exterior articulation. Quranic usage spans: divine speech (qāla rabbuka), prophetic command (qul, ~332x), reporting human dialogue (qālū), passive receipt of revelation (qīla), and condemnation of fabricated speech (taqawwala).
meaning.ar: النُّطْقُ بِاللِّسَانِ، وَالتَّعْبِيرُ عَمَّا فِي النَّفْسِ بِالْكَلَامِ الْمَفْهُومِ، وَيَشْمَلُ الْأَمْرَ الْإِلٰهِيَّ وَالْحَدِيثَ الْبَشَرِيَّ وَالْوَحْيَ الْمُنَزَّلَ
meaning.en_detailed: The triconsonantal root ق و ل (قَوْل) — 1722 Quranic occurrences — fundamentally expresses To say, speak, utter, express verbally. The form V taqawwala (to fabricate, 69:44-46) names the deliberate invention of speech against revelation — a sin the Quran threatens with seizure by the right hand and severance of the aorta. The noun qawl (92x) extends from ethical quality (qawl sadīd, 'right saying,' 4:9) to passive reception (qīla, 'it was said'), while maqāl preserves eloquence and aqāwīl marks false sayings. Al-Rāghib distinguishes four Quranic meanings: vocal utterance, inner conviction, divine creative command, and revelation. Proto-Semitic *qawl ('voice, sound') underlies Hebrew qōl and Aramaic qālā; Arabic narrowed the sense to intentional, meaningful speech — bridging interior thought and exterior articulation, and providing the conceptual vocabulary for distinguishing sincere speech from fabricated falsehood in the Quranic worldview.
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To say, speak, utter, express verbally
meaning.ar_definition: جذر قَوْل — 1722 مرة — القول والنطق والتعبير بالكلام

etymology.semantic_evolution: Originally voice/sound in Proto-Semitic; narrowed in Arabic to articulated, intentional speech. Bridges physical utterance and meaningful expression.

derived_forms.meaning: to say, tell, speak, call, advocate
derived_forms.key_verse: 112:1 قُلْ هُوَ ٱللَّهُ أَحَدٌ (Say: He is Allah, the One)

key_nominals.meaning: saying, opinion; passive: it was said

usage_patterns.desc: Majority of Form I reports what people said

lexicographical_sources.ibn_faris: A univocal root indicating utterance of speech (النطق بالكلام). No secondary meaning. (Muʿjam Maqāyīs al-Lughah)
lexicographical_sources.al_raghib: Articulated speech (الكلام الملفوظ به). Four Quranic meanings: vocal utterance, inner conviction, divine creative command, revelation. Distinguishes from kalām as species/genus. (Al-Mufradāt)
lexicographical_sources.lane: He said — all modes of saying, aloud or in the heart. Maqāl: eloquent speech. Qīla wa-qāla = idle talk. (Lane, Vol.5, pp.2574-2579)

semantic_field.core_concept: Intentional articulated expression — bridge between consciousness and communication

near_synonyms.contrast: qawl = discrete saying; kalām = connected speech

theological_dimensions.aqidah: Vehicle of creedal declaration. Shahādah is qawl. Divine attribute of speech — debate over Quran as eternal or created divine qawl (the Miḥnah).
theological_dimensions.fiqh: Legal rulings derived from divine qawl. Imperative qul studied in uṣūl al-fiqh.
theological_dimensions.tasawwuf: Qīl wa-qāl (idle talk) as spiritual disease. Ṣamt (silence) as virtue. Dhikr as highest qawl.

hadith_evidence.ar: مَنْ كَانَ يُؤْمِنُ بِٱللَّهِ وَٱلْيَوْمِ ٱلْـَٔاخِرِ فَلْيَقُلْ خَيْرًا أَوْ لِيَصْمُتْ
hadith_evidence.en: Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him speak good or remain silent.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ ٱلْعَبْدَ لَيَتَكَلَّمُ بِٱلْكَلِمَةِ ... يَهْوِى بِهَا فِى جَهَنَّمَ
hadith_evidence.en: A servant may speak a word and ascend by it, or plummet into Hell by it.

cross_references.cultural_note: Qawwāl → Qawwali (devotional Sufi music of South Asia)

meaning.en: To be, to exist, to occur, to come into being, to become. The most fundamental ontological verb in Arabic — expressing existence, temporal state, transformation, and the transition from non-existence to existence. Central to Islamic theology as the verb through which Allah's creative power is expressed (KUN fa-yakūn). In Quranic Arabic, kāna functions uniquely as a tensed copula that can take accusative predicates. The imperative kun (Be!) appears in 8 verses as the divine creative command.
meaning.ar: الْوُجُودُ وَالْحُدُوثُ، وَالصَّيْرُورَةُ وَالِاتِّصَافُ بِالْحَالِ. أَصْلُ الْفِعْلِ فِي اللُّغَةِ الْعَرَبِيَّةِ الدَّالُّ عَلَى الْكَيْنُونَةِ وَالزَّمَانِ
meaning.en_detailed: Root ك و ن (كَوْن), attested 1390 times in the Quran, derives its core meaning of To be, exist, occur, become from Proto-Semitic sources. Its most celebrated instantiation — the formula kun fa-yakūn ('Be, and it is,' 2:117; 36:82) — encapsulates divine creative power: the imperative kun paired with fa-yakūn via the fa particle marks instantaneous actualization, with no temporal gap between divine will and instantiation. As a tensed copula unique to Semitic, kāna enters nominal sentences to mark past states (2:28: 'you were dead, then He gave you life'), transformation of state (2:34: 'he became of the disbelievers'), and past habitual action (kāna + imperfect verb). The derivative makān ('place,' 27x) preserves the root's original sense of 'established location.' Proto-Semitic *kwn ('to be firm, established') underlies Hebrew kûn ('to be firm') and Akkadian kânu ('to be firm, reliable') — the movement from concrete establishment to abstract existential copula marks Arabic's distinctive ontological grammar.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر كَوْن — 1390 مرة — الوجود والكون والحدوث

etymology.semantic_evolution: Proto-Semitic *kwn = 'to be firm, established' → Hebrew 'to be firm, prepare' → Arabic kāna generalized to existential copula 'to be'. Movement from concrete establishment to abstract existence. The Quran uses kāna as primary temporal/existential auxiliary. The derivative makān (place) preserves original spatial 'established location' sense.

usage_patterns.desc: 8 verses. Imperative kun + consequential fa + yakūn. Expresses that divine will = instant actualization. No temporal gap.
Enters nominal sentences: subject = nominative (ism kāna), predicate = accusative (khabar kāna). Unique to Semitic.
kāna + imperfect verb = used to / would do (past continuous/habitual). Common Quranic narrative technique.

lexicographical_sources.ibn_faris: Root indicates occurrence, existence, and eventuation (الحدوث والوجود والكون). A sound root: something happening or coming into existence. (Maqāyīs al-Lughah)
lexicographical_sources.al_raghib: kāna: occurrence and eventuation (الوقوع والحدوث). Allah's 'kun' is not a speech sound but an expression of His will (إرادة). Distinguishes kawn (temporal being) from wujūd (absolute being). (Al-Mufradāt)

theological_dimensions: Kun fa-yakūn (Be! and it is) — divine creative fiat. kāna as the verb of ontological reality. Divine existence as necessary being (wājib al-wujūd).

hadith_evidence.ar: كَانَ ٱللَّهُ وَلَمْ يَكُنْ شَىْءٌ قَبْلَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: Allah existed and there was nothing before Him.
hadith_evidence.relevance: Establishes Allah's pre-eternal existence via kāna

cross_references.cultural_note: al-kawn = the universe in modern Arabic. al-kawniyyāt = cosmology.

meaning.en: Lord, master, owner, sustainer, nurturer, sovereign. One who possesses authority, provides care and upbringing, manages affairs, and brings to completion. The most frequent divine title in the Quran (860x as rabb) — expressing Allah's comprehensive lordship over creation. The Arabic rabb simultaneously conveys ownership (mulk), authority (siyādah), nurturing care (tarbiyah), management (tadbīr), and bringing to completion. No exact English equivalent.
meaning.ar: الْمَالِكُ، وَالسَّيِّدُ، وَالْمُدَبِّرُ، وَالْمُرَبِّي، وَالْمُنْعِمُ، وَالْقَيِّمُ. أَشْمَلُ أَسْمَاءِ اللَّهِ دَلَالَةً عَلَى الرُّبُوبِيَّةِ الْعَامَّةِ
meaning.en_detailed: Root ر ب ب (رَبّ), attested 980 times in the Quran, derives its core meaning of Lord, master, sustainer, nurturer, sovereign from Proto-Semitic sources. Its semantic range exceeds any English equivalent, simultaneously denoting ownership (mulk), nurturing care (tarbiyah), management (tadbīr), and bringing-to-completion, as the opening declaration Rabb al-ʿĀlamīn (1:2) establishes cosmic lordship as the foundational creed. The pairing ʿabd-rabb (servant-lord) structures the entire divine-human relationship across the Quran, from 2:21's first command ('O mankind, worship your Lord') to 114:1's intimate refuge ('Lord of mankind'). The opening revelation (96:1: 'Read in the name of your Lord who created') founds knowledge in rabb-ʿālamīn lordship, while 12:39's polemic ('Are many lords better or Allah, the One, the Prevailing?') argues monotheism from the singularity of lordship. Ibn Faris's core sense — 'nurturing stage by stage to completion' — captures the divine pedagogy the root implies.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر رَبّ — 980 مرة — الربوبية والسيادة والتربية والتدبير

etymology.semantic_evolution: Proto-Semitic *kwn = 'to be firm, established' → Hebrew developed 'to be firm, prepare' → Arabic kāna generalized to existential copula 'to be'. The meaning broadened from concrete establishment to abstract existence. The Quran uses kāna as the primary temporal/existential auxiliary, often marking past habitual or completed states. The derivative makān (place) preserves the original spatial 'established location' sense.

thematic_clusters.desc: The most repeated divine epithet. Rabbaniyyah is universal lordship, not limited to believers.
The fundamental relational pair: Rabb (Lord) and ʿAbd (servant). All worship flows from this.

lexicographical_sources.ibn_faris: Three core senses: foundation, rectification/completion of a thing (إصلاح الشيء وتمامه), and tarbiyah — nurturing stage by stage to completion. (Maqāyīs)
lexicographical_sources.al_raghib: Ar-rabb = tarbiyah: bringing a thing stage by stage to completion (إنشاء الشيء حالاً فحالاً إلى حد التمام). Distinguishes al-rabb al-muṭlaq (absolute — Allah) from al-rabb al-muḍāf (restricted — rabb al-dār). (Al-Mufradāt)

theological_dimensions: Ar-Rabb as the most fundamental divine title — God's nurturing lordship over creation
The Rabb-ʿabd (Lord-servant) relationship as the core Quranic ontology of the human-divine relationship
Tarbiyah (education, nurturing) as divine pedagogy — God as the educator of humanity through revelation

hadith_evidence.ar: اللَّهُمَّ أَنْتَ رَبِّى لَا إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا أَنْتَ ... فَٱغْفِرْ لِى فَإِنَّهُ لَا يَغْفِرُ ٱلذُّنُوبَ إِلَّا أَنْتَ
hadith_evidence.en: O Allah, You are my Lord. There is no god but You... forgive me, for none forgives sins except You.
hadith_evidence.relevance: Opens with Anta Rabbī — the rabb-ʿabd relationship is the foundation of supplication

cross_references.cultural_note: The Quran's most frequent divine name. Rabbāniyyūn may be the origin of 'rabbi' in later Jewish usage.

derived_forms.meaning: to be lord/master over, to nurture

meaning.en: To be secure, safe, at peace, free from fear. To believe, have faith, trust, be faithful. To entrust something valuable to someone's care. The root bridges psychological safety and theological conviction — true faith (īmān) is the ultimate source of security (amn). The root covers three overlapping domains: personal security (amn, āmin), trust/entrustment (amānah, amīn), and faith/belief (īmān, muʾmin). The semantic bridge: to believe (āmana bi-) is to entrust oneself to someone, finding safety (amn) in that relationship.
meaning.ar: الْأَمَانُ وَالسَّلَامَةُ وَالطُّمَأْنِينَةُ — زَوَالُ الْخَوْفِ؛ وَالتَّصْدِيقُ وَالْإِذْعَانُ — الْإِيمَانُ؛ وَالْأَمَانَةُ — حِفْظُ مَا اؤْتُمِنَ عَلَيْهِ
meaning.en_detailed: Root أ م ن (أَمْن), attested 879 times in the Quran, derives its core meaning of Security, safety, faith, trust, belief from Proto-Semitic sources. The cosmic amānah offered to the heavens, earth, and mountains but borne by humanity alone (33:72) constitutes the root's most theologically dense usage, marking humans as unique bearers of moral agency in a cosmos that refused. Al-Muʾmin ('The Giver of Security') is one of the 99 Names (59:23), and divine security extends both to physical realms (106:4: 'He fed them against hunger and gave them security from fear') and to freedom of conscience (2:256, where īmān remains voluntary). Proto-Semitic *ʾmn ('to be firm, reliable') underlies the spiritualized meaning — belief is not intellectual assent but unshakable trust, as the hadith of the muʾmin ('the believer is one whom people trust with their blood and wealth') grounds ethical faith in social security.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر أَمْن — 879 مرة — الإيمان والتصديق والأمان

cognates.hebrew: עָלַם (ʿālam) — to conceal; עוֹלָם (ʿōlām) — eternity, world

etymology.semantic_evolution: Proto-Semitic *ʿlm had a dual sense: 'to know' and 'to mark/conceal'. In Arabic, the 'knowing' sense dominates (ʿalima, ʿallama, taʿallama). The noun ʿālam (world) developed from the sense of 'that by which something is known/marked' → the created world as a sign pointing to the Creator. Hebrew split: ʿālam = conceal (hide knowledge) vs ʿōlām = world/eternity (that which is hidden/unknown). The Quranic ʿālamīn (worlds) encompasses all created realms as signs pointing to divine knowledge.

derived_forms.meaning: to be safe, secure, trust, believe

thematic_clusters.desc: Classical Sunni theology: īmān = belief in heart (taṣdīq) + confession by tongue (iqrār) + action by limbs (ʿamal). All three derive from the root's semantic range.
Humanity uniquely bears the amānah that even the cosmos refused. This is moral agency, free will, and the capacity for trust.
Q 49:14 distinguishes: Bedouins claim īmān (faith) but are told to say islām (submission) because īmān has not entered their hearts. Īmān is inner; islām is outer.

lexicographical_sources.ibn_faris: الأصل الواحد: ضد الخوف — The single core: the opposite of fear. From this: āmana bihi = believed in him (was safe from his untruth), amānah = what one entrusts for safe return. (Maqāyīs)
lexicographical_sources.al_raghib: الأصل: سكون القلب — The root: tranquility of heart. Al-amn: stillness and absence of fear. Al-īmān: (1) absolute: mere affirmation (taṣdīq), (2) restricted: affirmation of all from God in detail (Islamic īmān). Īmān necessarily implies ʿamal (action) because true inner conviction produces outward compliance. (Al-Mufradāt)

theological_dimensions: Īmān as firm trust (not mere intellectual belief) — grounded in the root's semantic core of firmness
The amānah (Trust) offered to heavens, earth, mountains but accepted by humans (33:72)
Al-Mu'min (The Giver of Security) as divine name — God as the source of all safety and faith

hadith_evidence.ar: أَنْ تَعْبُدَ ٱللَّهَ كَأَنَّكَ تَرَىٰهُ، فَإِن لَّمْ تَكُن تَّرَىٰهُ فَإِنَّهُ يَرَىٰكَ
hadith_evidence.en: To worship Allah as if you see Him, for if you do not see Him, He indeed sees you.
hadith_evidence.source: Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 8 — Ḥadīth Jibrīl (definition of iḥsān)
hadith_evidence.relevance: Part of the Jibrīl hadith defining īmān, islām, and iḥsān

hadith_evidence.ar: ٱلْمُسْلِمُ مَن سَلِمَ ٱلْمُسْلِمُونَ مِن لِّسَانِهِۦ وَيَدِهِۦ، وَٱلْمُؤْمِنُ مَنْ أَمِنَهُ ٱلنَّاسُ عَلَىٰ دِمَآئِهِمْ وَأَمْوَٰلِهِمْ
hadith_evidence.en: The Muslim is one from whose tongue and hand Muslims are safe. The believer (muʾmin) is one whom people trust with their blood and wealth.
hadith_evidence.relevance: Definition of muʾmin through amn — the believer is the source of security for others

cross_references.cultural_note: The invocation 'Āmīn' (amen) after al-Fātiḥah derives from this root. Al-Amīn (the Trustworthy) was Muhammad's epithet before prophethood.

meaning.en_short: To know, have knowledge, be aware; to teach; to mark
meaning.en: To know, to have knowledge, to be aware, to perceive, to recognize; to teach, to inform, to instruct; to mark, to distinguish by a sign. The root encompasses the full spectrum of cognition — from divine omniscience to human learning, from instinctive recognition to scholarly expertise, from sensory perception to rational understanding. The root links the act of knowing (ʿalima) with the marks/signs (ʿalāmāt) by which things are known: knowledge is not passive reception but active discernment. The word ʿālam (world) derives from this root — the universe is the ʿalāmah (sign) by which the Creator is known.
meaning.ar: الْإِدْرَاكُ وَالْمَعْرِفَةُ وَالْفَهْمُ وَالتَّبَيُّنُ؛ وَالتَّعْلِيمُ وَالْإِعْلَامُ وَالْإِرْشَادُ؛ وَالْعَلَامَةُ وَالتَّمْيِيزُ وَالتَّحْدِيدُ
meaning.en_detailed: Root ع ل م (عِلْم), attested 854 times in the Quran, derives its core meaning of To know, have knowledge, be aware; to teach; to mark from Proto-Semitic sources. The first revelation (96:1-5) makes ʿallama ('He taught') the foundational divine-human act, with ʿallama repeated three times for emphasis; while 2:31 establishes ʿilm as the basis for human superiority over angels, who confess 'lā ʿilma lanā illā mā ʿallamtanā' ('we have no knowledge except what You taught us,' 2:32). Al-ʿAlīm ('All-Knowing,' 163x) and ʿAllām al-Ghuyūb ('Knower of the Unseen,' 4x) express divine omniscience, which remains exclusive to Allah (6:59: 'With Him are the keys of the unseen; none knows them except Him'). The derivative ʿālam ('world,' 73x in ʿālamīn) reveals that the cosmos itself is the ʿalāmah ('sign') by which the Creator is known — making ʿilm the cognitive bridge between creation and Creator, and Rabb al-ʿĀlamīn the natural invocation.
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To know, have knowledge, be aware; to teach; to mark

cognates.hebrew: אָמַן (ʾāman) — to confirm, support, believe; אֱמוּנָה (ʾĕmūnāh) — faith

etymology.semantic_evolution: Proto-Semitic *ʾmn = 'to be firm, reliable, trustworthy'. Arabic developed two main branches: (1) amina = to be safe/secure (passive sense), and (2) āmana = to believe/have faith (active trust). The semantic shift from physical firmness to spiritual faith is the conceptual heart of the Quranic īmān — belief is not mere intellectual assent but a firm, unshakable trust in God. The noun amānah (trust, responsibility) preserves the original sense of something entrusted to someone reliable.

thematic_clusters.desc: ʿAlīm (All-Knowing) = 163x; ʿAllām (Knower of unseen) = 4x; ʿĀlim al-Ghayb (Knower of unseen) = 18x. Often paired with Samīʿ (Hearing), Ḥakīm (Wise), Qadīr (Powerful).
Allah taught Adam names (2:31), taught the Quran (55:2), taught by the pen (96:4), taught bayān (55:4). ʿIlm originates from divine instruction.
The universe (ʿālam) derives from ʿilm — the cosmos is a sign (ʿalāmah) indicating the Creator. Rabb al-ʿĀlamīn = Lord of all worlds/signs.

lexicographical_sources.ibn_faris: Core meaning: the trace/mark by which something is known (الأثر الذي يُعرف به الشيء). From this: ʿalam = flag, ʿalāmah = sign, ʿilm = knowledge (impression of reality on mind). (Maqāyīs)
lexicographical_sources.al_raghib: ʿIlm = perception of something as it truly is (إدراك الشيء على ما هو به). Two types: (1) divine — eternal, essential; (2) acquired — through senses, reason, revelation. Distinguishes ʿilm (comprehensive knowledge) from maʿrifah (knowledge after prior ignorance). ʿĀlam = that by which the Creator is known. (Al-Mufradāt)

theological_dimensions: Īmān as firm trust (not just intellectual belief) — grounded in the root's semantic core of firmness
The amānah (Trust) offered to heavens, earth, and mountains but accepted by humans (33:72) — the ontological weight of moral responsibility
Al-Mu'min (The Giver of Security) as divine name — God as the source of all safety and faith

hadith_evidence.ar: طَلَبُ ٱلْعِلْمِ فَرِيضَةٌ عَلَىٰ كُلِّ مُسْلِمٍ
hadith_evidence.en: Seeking knowledge is an obligation upon every Muslim.

hadith_evidence.ar: مَن سَلَكَ طَرِيقًا يَلْتَمِسُ فِيهِ عِلْمًا سَهَّلَ ٱللَّهُ لَهُۥ طَرِيقًا إِلَى ٱلْجَنَّةِ
hadith_evidence.en: Whoever takes a path seeking knowledge, Allah makes easy for him a path to Paradise.
hadith_evidence.relevance: ʿIlm as spiritual path to Paradise

hadith_evidence.ar: فَضْلُ ٱلْعَالِمِ عَلَى ٱلْعَابِدِ كَفَضْلِ ٱلْقَمَرِ لَيْلَةَ ٱلْبَدْرِ عَلَىٰ سَائِرِ ٱلْكَوَاكِبِ
hadith_evidence.en: The superiority of the scholar over the worshipper is like the superiority of the full moon over all the stars.

cross_references.cultural_note: ʿĀlamīn (worlds) in al-Fātiḥah. ʿUlamāʾ as a social class in Islamic civilization. Ilm al-kalām = Islamic scholastic theology.

meaning.en_short: To stand, rise, establish; a people, nation, community
meaning.en: To stand, rise, establish, maintain; a people, nation, community. The root's core physical sense of 'standing upright' extends metaphorically to moral uprightness (istiqāmah), social organization (qawm), custodianship (qawwām/qayyim), and eschatological resurrection (qiyāmah). The root provides the language for Islam's most central ethical concept: al-ṣirāṭ al-mustaqīm (the straight/upright path). Form X istaqāma means to be perpetually upright — the command fa-staqim (11:112) represents the entire spiritual life.
meaning.ar: الْقِيَامُ وَالِانْتِصَابُ وَالثَّبَاتُ؛ وَالْجَمَاعَةُ وَالْأُمَّةُ؛ وَالِاسْتِقَامَةُ وَالْعَدْلُ؛ وَالْقِيَمُ وَالْحِفَاظُ
meaning.en_detailed: قَوْم (ق و م), a root appearing 660 times in the Quran, encodes the notion of To stand, rise, establish; a people, nation, community across its various verbal and nominal forms. Its most theologically pregnant nominal, al-Qayyūm ('Self-Subsisting,' 2:255, paired with al-Ḥayy in Āyat al-Kursī), names the divine attribute by which Allah sustains all existence without Himself requiring support. The Quranic verb istaqāma (Form X, 10x) names the spiritual life itself — 'fa-staqim kamā umirt' (11:112, 'stand firm as you are commanded'), a verse the Prophet said aged him. While qawm ('people/nation,' 383x) designates kinship-based communities and contrasts with ummah ('faith-community'), yawm al-qiyāmah ('Day of Resurrection,' 70x) gathers all humanity into the ultimate act of standing before God. Aqīmū al-ṣalāh ('establish prayer,' ~20x) names iqāmah as ongoing maintenance, not one-time performance — defining a believer as one who stands for prayer continuously.

cognates.hebrew: קָם (qām) — to rise, stand up, arise
cognates.akkadian: kâmu — to become firm, be established

etymology.semantic_evolution: Physical standing → moral uprightness → communal organization (people who 'stand together') → eschatological standing (resurrection).

derived_forms.key_verse: 95:4 فِىٓ أَحْسَنِ تَقْوِيمٍۢ (in the best of stature/form)

derived_forms.meaning: to be upright, stand firm, remain steadfast
derived_forms.key_verse: 11:112 فَٱسْتَقِمْ كَمَآ أُمِرْتَ (So stand firm as you are commanded)

key_nominals.meaning: straight, upright, correct (Form X act. part.)

usage_patterns.desc: The straight/upright path — Islam's central ethical concept. Occurs ~35x, always in context of guidance and salvation.
aqīmū al-ṣalāh (~20x). Iqāmah = ongoing establishment/maintenance, not one-time performance.
Day of Resurrection (~70x). Lit. 'Day of Standing' — all creation stands before the Creator for judgment.

lexicographical_sources.ibn_faris: Root centered on standing (قيام) and uprightness. From physical standing → moral rectitude, establishment, and communal standing-together. (Maqāyīs)
lexicographical_sources.al_raghib: Distinguishes physical standing (qiyām) from spiritual/moral standing (istiqāmah). Al-Qayyūm = the Self-Subsisting by whom all else subsists. Al-dīn al-qayyim = the upright religion. (Al-Mufradāt)

semantic_field.core_concept: Uprightness in all dimensions — physical (standing), moral (rectitude), social (community), and cosmic (divine self-subsistence)

contrast_qawm_vs_ummah.qawm: People/tribe bound by kinship, language, or territory — pre-existing group (qawm Nūḥ, qawm Mūsā)
contrast_qawm_vs_ummah.ummah: Community bound by shared faith, covenant, or divine guidance (ummah wāḥidah, the Muslim ummah)

theological_dimensions.aqidah: Istiqāmah as perpetual uprightness. Al-Qayyūm as essential divine attribute (2:255). Al-ṣirāṭ al-mustaqīm as the bridge (ṣirāṭ) over Hell — mustaqīm = upright, not crooked.
theological_dimensions.tasawwuf: Istiqāmah as the highest station. Abū ʿAlī al-Daqqāq: 'Istiqāmah is that you stand for Allah with truthfulness, not for your own ego.' Al-Qayyūm as the divine name of sustenance — the mystic is sustained (maqwūm) by al-Qayyūm.

hadith_evidence.ar: قُلْ آمَنْتُ بِٱللَّهِ ثُمَّ ٱسْتَقِمْ
hadith_evidence.en: Say: I believe in Allah, then be upright (istaqim).
hadith_evidence.relevance: The entire religion summarized in īmān + istiqāmah

cross_references.cultural_note: Al-Qayyūm is the divine name paired with al-Ḥayy (the Living) in Āyat al-Kursī. Qiyām al-layl = night vigil prayer. Qawm as the most frequent social noun in the Quran.

meaning.en_short: To come, arrive, bring, give, bestow
meaning.en: To come, to arrive, to bring, to approach, to do, to commit. Expresses motion toward a destination — physical, temporal, or metaphysical. Includes the coming of divine command, death, the Hour, revelation, and sustenance. The root has a remarkable split: Form I atā (264x) = to come/bring/do; Form IV ātā (271x) = to give/bestow/grant. This near-equal split reflects the two faces of divine action: Allah causes things to come (atā) AND gives/bestows them (ātā). Form IV is almost synonymous with aʿṭā (to give).
meaning.ar: الْمَجِيءُ وَالْإِتْيَانُ وَالْوُصُولُ، وَالْإِحْضَارُ وَالتَّقْدِيمُ. يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْحَرَكَةِ نَحْوَ غَايَةٍ مَكَانِيَّةٍ أَوْ زَمَانِيَّةٍ أَوْ مَعْنَوِيَّةٍ
meaning.en_detailed: The triconsonantal root أ ت ي (أَتْي) — 549 Quranic occurrences — fundamentally expresses To come, arrive, bring, give, bestow. Form I marks the inevitable approach of divine decree (16:1: 'atā amr Allāh'), the Quranic challenge of bringing a counter-revelation (2:23: 'fāʾtū bi-sūrah min mithlih'), and euphemistic usage for marital relations (2:222). Form IV dominates descriptions of divine bestowal — 14:34 ('He gave you of all that you asked') and 7:175 ('We gave him Our signs'). Cognates with Aramaic ʾăṯā ('to come') and Ge'ez ʾätäwä ('to go home') establish the Semitic antiquity of this motion verb, which according to al-Rāghib retains a connotation of coming with ease rather than force. The imperative ātini ('give me') recurs in prophetic prayers, as in 19:33-34.
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To come, arrive, bring, give, bestow

etymology.proto_semitic: Cognates with Aramaic אֲתָא (ʾăṯā — to come), Ge'ez አተወ (ʾätäwä — to go home), Ugaritic 𐎀𐎚𐎆 (ảtw — to come)
etymology.semantic_evolution: Core: coming with ease (Al-Raghib). Extended: to do/commit (atā bi-), to bring (atā bi-), to give/bestow (Form IV ātā), to destroy (atā ʿalā). The passive utiya = he was deceived/deluded (his senses altered).

derived_forms.meaning: to come, arrive, bring (with bi-), do, commit, destroy (with ʿalā)
derived_forms.key_verse: 16:1 أَتَىٰٓ أَمْرُ ٱللَّهِ فَلَا تَسْتَعْجِلُوهُ (The command of Allah has come)

derived_forms.meaning: to give, bestow, grant, bring to someone
derived_forms.key_verse: 7:175 وَٱتْلُ عَلَيْهِمْ نَبَأَ ٱلَّذِىٓ ءَاتَيْنَـٰهُ ءَايَـٰتِنَا (We gave him Our signs)

key_nominals.meaning: tax, tribute, bribe (from a variant root form)

quranic_analysis.distinction_from_jaa: atā implies coming with ease, deliberate approach (Al-Raghib); jāʾa implies coming with force or suddenness. atā has a much broader semantic range: to do, commit, produce, destroy, give. jāʾa is more restricted to physical/spiritual arrival.

lexicographical_sources.al_raghib: The proper signification of al-ityān is the coming with ease. (Al-Mufradāt)
lexicographical_sources.lane: He came; he came to him; he was present. Also: to do, execute, perform; to commit (a crime); to lie with (a woman, euphemistic); to destroy (with ʿalā); to bring (with bi-). Utiya = he was deceived, his senses altered. (Lane, pp.15-16)

semantic_field.core_concept: Directed motion toward — the movement of an agent toward a terminus, whether literal (arriving), temporal (coming of an appointed time), or metaphysical (coming of divine decree)

near_synonyms.nuance: To come — often with force or suddenness
near_synonyms.contrast: atā = deliberate coming; jāʾa = more sudden/dramatic

theological_dimensions.aqidah: The coming of Allah's command (atā amr Allāh) is inevitable. The Hour (al-sāʿah) comes (atā/tā).
theological_dimensions.fiqh: ityān al-marʾah = sexual intercourse with one's wife — standard fiqh term. Ītāʾ al-zakāh = giving zakah (Form IV).

hadith_evidence.ar: إِذَا جَاءَ رَمَضَانُ فُتِّحَتْ أَبْوَابُ ٱلْجَنَّةِ
hadith_evidence.en: When Ramadan comes, the gates of Paradise are opened.
hadith_evidence.relevance: Note: uses jāʾa, not atā — the sudden/special arrival of the sacred month

influenced_languages: Persian: آمدن (āmadan = to come — unrelated root, but semantic overlap with atā's meaning)

meaning.en_short: Between; to be clear, distinct, evident; to make manifest
meaning.en: Between, among; to be clear, distinct, evident; to make manifest, explain, elucidate. The root exhibits a famous semantic polarity in Arabic: spatial separation/betweenness (bayn) on one hand, and cognitive clarity/distinction (bayān) on the other. To separate (bāna) two things is to make each one distinct (bayyin) and therefore clear (bayyin). Separation creates clarity — what is set apart becomes evident. The Quran is described as mubīn (clear/manifest, 119x) and as bayyināt (clear proofs, 71x).
meaning.ar: الْبَيْنُ: الْفَصْلُ وَالْوَصْلُ — بَيْنَ الشَّيْئَيْنِ؛ وَالْبَيَانُ: الْوُضُوحُ وَالْإِيضَاحُ وَالْإِفْصَاحُ
meaning.en_detailed: Root ب ي ن (بَيْن), attested 523 times in the Quran, derives its core meaning of Between; to be clear, distinct, evident; to make manifest from Proto-Semitic sources. The Quran's most frequent self-description is mubīn ('clear,' 119x) and bayyināt ('clear proofs,' 71x), with 2:185 calling the Quran 'bayyināt min al-hudā wa-l-furqān' ('clear proofs of guidance and criterion'). The imperative fatabayyanū (49:6) establishes tabayyun as an Islamic epistemic principle — verify before acting on reports. 55:4 names al-bayān ('eloquence, clear expression') as a uniquely human gift taught by Allah, while 2:256's 'tabayyana al-rushd min al-ghayy' ('truth has become distinct from wrong') grounds religious freedom in clarity. The contrast with furqān ('criterion,' separator) sharpens bayān's sense as explanation rather than active separation.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *byn = 'to separate, divide' → 'to distinguish, discern, understand'. Arabic developed bayn (between) — a spatial preposition from the sense of separation — and bayān (clear explanation) — the act of making distinctions. The Quran calls itself bayān (55:4) and bayyināt (clear proofs).

thematic_clusters.desc: The Quran describes itself as mubīn (clear, 119x) and as bayyināt (clear proofs, 71x). Revelation is self-authenticating through its clarity.
The imperative fatabayyanū = verify! Investigate before acting on news. Foundation for Islamic epistemology of transmitted reports (khabar).
The hadith: 'The lawful is clear (bayyin) and the unlawful is clear (bayyin).' Establishes categorical clarity in divine law.

lexicographical_sources.lane: Bayn: the separation or division of a thing from another; state of being separate or distinct. Bāna: became separate, severed, cut off; hence became distinct, manifest, evident, clear. Bayān: making a thing apparent; eloquence is the faculty of making meaning manifest. (Lane)
lexicographical_sources.ibn_faris: Root centered on separation (الانفصال) and distinction (التمييز). The bridge: what is separated is distinguished; what is distinguished is clear. (Maqāyīs)

semantic_field.core_concept: Separation and clarity — the root links physical betweenness with cognitive distinction: what is 'between' is distinct; what is 'clear' is distinguished

near_synonyms.nuance: Criterion, discriminator — what separates truth from falsehood

theological_dimensions.aqidah: The Quran's self-description as mubīn is central: it is inherently clear, not obscure. Bayyināt = miracles/proofs given to prophets. Tabayyun = obligation to verify before believing — rational faith.
theological_dimensions.fiqh: The hadith of halāl wa-ḥarām bayyin (Bukhārī 52, Muslim 1599) establishes that divine rulings are categorically clear. Doubtful matters (shubuhāt) are the exception. Bayyinah as legal evidence/proof.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ ٱلْحَلَـٰلَ بَيِّنٌۭ وَإِنَّ ٱلْحَرَامَ بَيِّنٌۭ، وَبَيْنَهُمَآ أُمُورٌۭ مُّشْتَبِهَـٰتٌۭ
hadith_evidence.en: The lawful is clear and the unlawful is clear, and between them are doubtful matters.
hadith_evidence.relevance: Establishes categorical clarity of divine law

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ مِنَ ٱلْبَيَانِ لَسِحْرًۭا
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed some eloquence (bayān) is like magic.
hadith_evidence.relevance: The persuasive power of clear expression recognized — both its virtue and its danger

cross_references.cultural_note: ʿIlm al-bayān = Arabic rhetoric (one of three branches of balāghah). Bayān as official communiqué in modern Arabic.

meaning.en_short: To cover, conceal; to disbelieve, deny, be ungrateful
meaning.en: To cover, conceal, hide; to disbelieve, deny, reject, be ungrateful. The root's physical sense (covering — as a farmer covers seed with soil) extends metaphorically to the covering of truth with denial, and the covering of divine favors with ingratitude. The pre-Islamic kāfir was a farmer (one who covers seeds in earth) — preserved in Quran 57:20. The semantic trajectory: covering seeds (physical) → covering truth (spiritual) → denying God's favors/ingratitude (theological). Kufr is the antithesis of both īmān (faith) and shukr (gratitude).
meaning.ar: السَّتْرُ وَالتَّغْطِيَةُ — وَمِنْهُ كَفَرَ الزَّارِعُ الْبَذْرَ: غَطَّاهُ بِالتُّرَابِ؛ وَالْجُحُودُ وَالْإِنْكَارُ وَعَدَمُ الْإِيمَانِ؛ وَكُفْرَانُ النِّعْمَةِ: جُحُودُهَا وَسَتْرُهَا
meaning.en_detailed: The triconsonantal root ك ف ر (كُفْر) — 525 Quranic occurrences — fundamentally expresses To cover, conceal; to disbelieve, deny, be ungrateful. Surah al-Kāfirūn (109) addresses disbelievers directly, while 2:152 sets kufr over against shukr ('be grateful to Me and do not be ungrateful,' takfurūn). The derivative kaffārah ('expiation,' 4x) preserves the semantic source — covering sin with compensatory act — the Islamic parallel to Yom Kippur. Six types of major kufr (akbar) include takdhīb ('denial'), ibāʾ ('arrogant refusal,' Iblīs's), and shakk ('doubt'). The hadith 'sibāb al-muslim fusūq wa-qitāluhu kufr' demonstrates the minor kufr ('aṣghar') for grave sins, while the prohibition of reckless takfīr guards against sectarian excommunication.
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To cover, conceal; to disbelieve, deny, be ungrateful

etymology.proto_semitic: Strong Semitic root for covering/atonement: Hebrew כָּפַר (kāp̄ar — to cover, atone; Yom Kippur = Day of Atonement), Syriac ܟܦܲܪ (kəp̄ar — to cover, expiate), Akkadian kapāru (to smear, wipe, rub off)
etymology.physical_origin: Covering/concealing is the primordial meaning. Farmer = kāfir (one who covers seeds). Tar = kufr (covering substance, from Akkadian kupru). Village = kafr (covered settlement, from Aramaic). Darkness = kafr (something covered in black).
etymology.semantic_evolution: Covering seeds (physical) → covering truth (spiritual denial) → covering favors (ingratitude). The theological sense is a metaphorical extension: the kāfir 'covers' truth with denial just as the farmer 'covers' seed with soil.

thematic_clusters.desc: Major kufr (akbar): denial, defiance, doubt, turning away, hypocrisy — expels from Islam. Minor kufr (aṣghar): ingratitude, certain sins (e.g., fighting a Muslim is 'kufr' metaphorically).
The deepest Quranic meaning: kufr = refusal to acknowledge receipt of blessings — covering them as if they never came from God. Shukr = open acknowledgment.

lexicographical_sources.ibn_faris: الكاف والفاء والراء أصل واحد يدل على معنى الستر — K-F-R is a single root indicating covering. The kāfir covers truth; kuffār (farmers) cover seeds in earth. (Maqāyīs)
lexicographical_sources.lane: Primary: to cover, conceal. Theological: disbelief — covering truth with denial. Kaffārah: expiation — covering sin with compensatory act. (Lane, pp.2620-2621)

semantic_field.core_concept: Covering — physical act of concealment extended metaphorically to spiritual denial and moral ingratitude

antonyms.meaning: Faith, belief — the positive affirmation kufr conceals
Gratitude — open acknowledgment of blessings that kufr covers
Affirmation as true — the cognitive dimension of īmān

theological_dimensions.aqidah: Six types of major kufr (kufr akbar): (1) takdhīb — denial of truth, (2) ibāʾ wa-istikbār — arrogant refusal despite conviction (Iblīs), (3) shakk wa-ẓann — doubt, (4) iʿrāḍ — turning away, (5) nifāq — hypocrisy, (6) juḥūd — rejection despite inner acknowledgment.
theological_dimensions.fiqh: Takfīr (declaring a Muslim kāfir) is severely restricted. Hadith: 'Whoever calls his brother kāfir, it returns upon one of them' (Bukhārī, Muslim). Khawārij practiced unrestricted takfīr. Kaffārah = expiatory acts for specific violations.

hadith_evidence.ar: سِبَابُ ٱلْمُسْلِمِ فُسُوقٌۭ وَقِتَالُهُۥ كُفْرٌۭ
hadith_evidence.en: Abusing a Muslim is wickedness (fusūq) and fighting him is disbelief (kufr).
hadith_evidence.relevance: Kufr used metaphorically for severe sin (minor kufr)

hadith_evidence.ar: إِذَا قَالَ ٱلرَّجُلُ لِأَخِيهِ يَا كَافِرُ فَقَدْ بَآءَ بِهَآ أَحَدُهُمَآ
hadith_evidence.en: If a man says to his brother 'O kāfir,' it returns upon one of them.

cross_references.cultural_note: Yom Kippur (Day of Atonement) derives from the same Semitic root — covering/atoning for sin. Kaffārah is the Islamic parallel.

meaning.en_short: To send, dispatch; messenger, envoy, apostle
meaning.en: To send, dispatch, release; a messenger, envoy, apostle. The root encompasses the act of sending (irsāl), the one sent (rasūl), the message carried (risālah), and — in a distinct classical sense — gentleness and deliberation (rasal). Rasūl (332x) is the most frequent form, designating the chain of divine messengers from Noah to Muhammad. The dual concept: a messenger is 'sent' (arsala) with a 'message' (risālah). Every rasūl is a nabī, but not every nabī is a rasūl (22:52).
meaning.ar: الْإِرْسَالُ وَالْبَعْثُ وَالتَّوْجِيهُ؛ وَالرَّسُولُ: الْمَبْعُوثُ بِرِسَالَةٍ؛ وَالرِّسَالَةُ: مَا أُرْسِلَ بِهِ؛ وَالرَّسَلُ: التُّؤَدَةُ وَالرِّفْقُ
meaning.en_detailed: The Arabic root ر س ل (رَسْل) appears 513 times in the Quran, governing the semantic domain of To send, dispatch; messenger, envoy, apostle. The most frequent nominal rasūl ('messenger,' 332x) names the chain of divine messengers from Noah (71:1) to Muhammad (khātam al-nabiyyīn, 33:40), and obedience to the rasūl constitutes obedience to Allah itself (4:80: 'whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah'). The risālah was always universal in scope — 'We sent you only as a mercy to the worlds' (21:107) — yet also linguistically particular, since every prophet spoke the language of his people (14:4). Form IV arsala (130x) and mursal ('one sent,' 35x) preserve the dispatch model; Surah al-Mursalāt (77) names the winds sent forth as bearers of mercy. Believing in messengers (rusul) is the second article of the Jibrīl hadith's īmān.

etymology.proto_semitic: Widespread: Hebrew/Aramaic/Syriac roots for sending; Geez rasala — to send
etymology.semantic_evolution: Core: to send/dispatch. Secondary sense: gentleness/ease of movement (rasal). The messenger is one sent (mursal) on a mission (risālah).

derived_forms.meaning: to send, send forth, dispatch, commission
to go gently, at an easy pace (classical, rare in Quran)

key_nominals.meaning: things sent, winds (fem. pl. passive participle; also title of Surah 77)

thematic_clusters.desc: Allah sent a messenger to every nation (10:47, 16:36). Noah was the first; Muhammad the last. Each spoke the language of his people (14:4).
Every rasūl is nabī; not every nabī is rasūl (22:52). Rasūl brings a new sharīʿah or scripture; nabī reinforces existing law.
Allah sends (yursilu) winds as glad tidings before His mercy (7:57). The mursalāt (Surah 77) = winds or angels sent forth successively.

lexicographical_sources.ibn_faris: Root has two cores: (1) sending/dispatching, (2) gentleness/ease. Rasūl = one who carries a message; arsala = to dispatch; risālah = the message itself. (Maqāyīs)
lexicographical_sources.al_raghib: Al-Rasūl is the one sent with a message. The rasūl carries the risālah from the sender (mursil) to the recipient. Covers both angelic messengers and human messengers. (Al-Mufradāt)

semantic_field.core_concept: Directed sending — the dispatch of a message or messenger from a sender to a recipient. Carries connotations of authority (sender commissions), representation (messenger speaks for sender), and purpose (sending has intended outcome).

near_synonyms.nuance: Prophet — receives divine inspiration, may not bring new law
near_synonyms.contrast: rasūl is sent with message/law; nabī may reinforce existing law

theological_dimensions.aqidah: Belief in messengers (rusul) = 2nd article of īmān in the Jibrīl hadith. Finality of prophethood (khātam al-nabiyyīn, 33:40). Rasūl as intermediary of revelation — obedience to rasūl = obedience to Allah (4:80).
theological_dimensions.fiqh: Sunnah as second source of law — derived from the rasūl's words and actions. The risālah (message) is universal for all humanity.
theological_dimensions.tasawwuf: Rasūl as perfect human (al-insān al-kāmil). The spiritual path follows the rasūl's sunnah as the path to Allah.

hadith_evidence.ar: أَرْسَلَنِى ٱللَّهُ بِالْهُدَىٰ وَدِينِ ٱلْحَقِّ
hadith_evidence.en: Allah sent me with guidance and the religion of truth.

hadith_evidence.ar: كُلُّ نَبِىٍّۭ قَدْ أُرْسِلَ
hadith_evidence.en: Every prophet was sent.
hadith_evidence.relevance: Rasūl-nabī overlap — being sent (irsāl) is inherent to prophethood

cross_references.cultural_note: Rasūl Allāh as the second half of the shahādah — the most frequently uttered Arabic phrase worldwide. Al-Mursalāt = Surah 77.

meaning.en_short: Slave, servant; to worship, serve with humility
meaning.en: Slave, servant; to worship, to serve with humility and total submission. The root encompasses the relationship of complete devotion and obedience to Allah — ʿubūdiyyah as the highest human station, combining love, fear, hope, and absolute submission. ʿAbd (131x) is the most frequent noun — prophets are honored as ʿabd Allāh. ʿIbādah (9x) is voluntary worship. Two plurals: ʿibād = servants of God (theological), ʿabīd = chattel slaves (social).
meaning.ar: الْعُبُودِيَّةُ وَالْخُضُوعُ وَالذُّلُّ — وَالْعِبَادَةُ: غَايَةُ التَّذَلُّلِ وَالْخُشُوعِ لِلَّهِ
meaning.en_detailed: Root ع ب د (عَبْد), attested 275 times in the Quran, derives its core meaning of Slave, servant; to worship, serve with humility from Proto-Semitic sources. The pivot of al-Fātiḥah (1:5) declares iyyāka naʿbudu ('You alone we worship'), and 51:56 names ʿibādah as the purpose of creation itself ('I did not create jinn and mankind except to worship Me'). Two plurals distinguish spiritual from social servitude — ʿibād ('devoted servants of God,' theological) versus ʿabīd ('chattel slaves,' 3:182; 8:51; 22:10). The Prophet's honored title ʿabduhu wa-rasūluhu ('His servant and messenger') reveals ʿabd as paradoxical honor: true freedom through exclusive servitude to God. The Messiah, as 4:172 declares, would never disdain to be a servant of Allah — even the highest prophets bear this title as their most exalted designation. Proto-Semitic *ʿbd ('to work, serve') underlies Hebrew ʿăvōdâ, which preserves the dual work-worship sense.

cognates.aramaic: עבד (ʿbd) — to do, make; to worship
cognates.geez: ዓበደ (ʿabada) — to do, work; to serve

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *ʿbd = 'to do, make, work' → 'to serve' → 'to worship'. The concept of worship (ʿibādah) in the Quran is rooted in the idea of service — worship IS service to God. The evolution from labor/work (still seen in Hebrew ʿavodah = work and also worship) to divine service reflects the transformation of all human activity into worship when directed toward God. The ʿabd (servant) is the highest human station — a human liberated from all other servitudes through exclusive servitude to God.

quranic_analysis.contrast_plurals: ʿIbād (عباد) = servants of God (theological). ʿAbīd (عبيد) = chattel slaves (social). Quran uses ʿibād for devoted servants, ʿabīd rarely (3:182, 8:51, 22:10).

lexicographical_sources.ibn_faris: Core meaning: humility and submission (الذل والخضوع). ʿIbādah = ultimate expression of this. (Maqāyīs)
lexicographical_sources.al_raghib: ʿUbūdiyyah = universal/involuntary servitude to God. ʿIbādah = voluntary conscious worship. (Al-Mufradāt)

theological_dimensions: ʿIbādah as the purpose of creation — 'I did not create jinn and mankind except to worship Me' (51:56)
The ʿabd as the highest human station — the Prophet as ʿabduhu wa rasūluh (His servant and messenger)
Tawḥīd al-ʿibādah (unity of worship) — exclusive devotion to God as the core of monotheism

hadith_evidence.ar: أَنْ تَعْبُدَ ٱللَّهَ كَأَنَّكَ تَرَىٰهُ
hadith_evidence.en: To worship Allah as if you see Him.

cross_references.cultural_note: ʿAbd Allāh = most common Muslim name. True freedom through servitude to God alone.

meaning.en_short: To help, aid, support, grant victory
meaning.en: To help, aid, support, grant victory. Expresses active divine or human assistance that turns the tide for the oppressed against overwhelming odds. Central verse: Surah al-Naṣr (110). Theologically: victory comes only from Allah (3:126). The conditional: 'If you help Allah, He will help you' (47:7). Anṣār = the Medinan helpers. NOTE: This is ن ص ر (ṣād), NOT ن س ر (sīn — idol Nasr with 1 occurrence).
meaning.ar: الْإِعَانَةُ وَالْإِغَاثَةُ — وَالنَّصْرُ: إِتْيَانُ الْخَيْرِ مِنْ عِنْدِ اللَّهِ
meaning.en_detailed: نَصْر (ن ص ر), a root appearing 158 times in the Quran, encodes the notion of To help, aid, support, grant victory across its various verbal and nominal forms. The theological axiom 'al-naṣr illā min ʿind Allāh' (3:126, 'victory is only from Allah') establishes divine assistance as the source of all triumph, while 47:7's reciprocity ('if you help Allah, He will help you') grounds human agency within divine sovereignty. Surah al-Naṣr (110), the Prophet's final surah, signals the completion of his mission. The Anṣār of Madīnah and the divine name al-Naṣīr ('The Helper') extend the semantic field. Proto-Semitic *nṣr ('to watch, guard') underlies Hebrew nāṣar ('to watch, preserve'); the trajectory moves from watchman to guardian to helper — victory comes only from Allah.
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To help, aid, support, grant victory

derived_forms.meaning: to seek help, call for aid

quranic_analysis.data_correction: Original file had occurrence count=1 — confused with ن س ر (idol Nasr). Corrected to 158.

hadith_evidence.ar: ٱنصُرْ أَخَاكَ ظَالِمًا أَوْ مَظْلُومًا
hadith_evidence.en: Help your brother, oppressor or oppressed.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *nṣr = 'to watch over → help, protect'. The watchman → guardian → helper. Al-Naṣīr (The Helper) is a divine name. 'Victory (naṣr) is only from Allah' (3:126). The Anṣār (helpers) of Medina received the Prophet.

meaning.en_short: To make, create, place, appoint, establish, render
meaning.en: A versatile verb of causation — from divine creative action to human manufacturing. Jaʿala (340x) is distinct from khalaqa: jaʿala = making from existing material, appointing to role, assigning function, transforming. Classified as: verb of transformation (afʿāl al-taṣyīr), inchoative verb (afʿāl al-shurūʿ), and sister of ẓanna (takes two accusative objects).
meaning.ar: الصُّنْعُ وَالْإِيجَادُ وَالتَّصْيِيرُ
meaning.en_detailed: Root ج ع ل (جَعْل), attested 346 times in the Quran, derives its core meaning of To make, create, place, appoint, establish, render from Proto-Semitic sources. Al-Rāghib's distinction is precise: 'khalq is origination without precedent; jaʿl is transformation from one state to another.' The root appoints roles (2:30: 'innī jāʿilun fī al-arḍi khalīfah,' 'I am placing a vicegerent on earth'), arranges cosmic order (25:61: 'who placed constellations in the sky'), and renders states — assigning qualities, transforming conditions (juʿala), establishing (jaʿala) functions. Jaʿala (340x) functions as verb of transformation (afʿāl al-taṣyīr) and inchoative action (afʿāl al-shurūʿ), and as a sister of ẓanna takes two accusative objects, extending its structural capacity beyond most Arabic verbs.
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To make, create, place, appoint, establish, render

quranic_analysis.distinction_from_khalaqa: Khalaqa = ex nihilo creation. Jaʿala = making from existing/appointing. Al-Raghib: 'Khalq is origination without precedent; jaʿl is transformation from one state to another.'

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *ǧʿl = 'to make, place, set'. Arabic jaʿala is the primary verb of divine action — God 'makes' things happen. Distinct from khalaqa (to create from nothing), jaʿala implies arrangement, appointment, and transformation. Qāla lahu kun fa-yakūn → jaʿala: the execution of divine will.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ اللَّهَ جَعَلَ الرَّحْمَةَ مِائَةَ جُزْءٍ
hadith_evidence.en: Allah has made mercy into one hundred parts.

meaning.en_short: To trace, relate, transmit (tradition); to have an effect, mark, vestige
meaning.en: The root hamza-thāʾ-rāʾ carries two primary semantic domains in the Quran: (1) to trace, relate, or transmit a saying or tradition from a predecessor — specifically the remnant or vestige (athar) of former knowledge, and (2) to give preference or choose one thing over another (īthār). In post-Quranic Arabic, ʾathar became the standard term for Prophetic hadith (ʿilm al-ʾathar), linking this root to the very concept of Islamic tradition.
meaning.ar: نَقَلُ الْخَبَرِ عَنِ السَّلَفِ، وَبَقِيَّةُ الشَّيْءِ، وَتَفْضِيلُ الشَّيْءِ عَلَى غَيْرِهِ
meaning.en_detailed: Triliteral Arabic root hamza-thāʾ-rāʾ (أ-ث-ر), 21 Quranic occurrences, with two principal semantic domains: (1) tracing and transmitting a tradition or a remnant (ʾathar) of former knowledge — famously yielding the post-Quranic technical term ʿilm al-ʾathar (the science of hadith) — and (2) preferring or choosing one thing over another, particularly in the sense of īthār (altruistic preference). Key verses include 46:4 'or some remnant of knowledge (aw ʾathāratin min ʿilm)' concerning the earlier generations' transmitted traces of prophecy, and 79:38 'and preferred (wa-ʾāthara) the life of this world,' condemning attachment to worldly life. The Form IV verb ʾāthara (to prefer) appears 6 times in the Quran; the noun ʾathar (trace/tradition) appears 7 times; the verb ʾathara (to relate) once.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر أ ث ر — 21 مرة — To trace

etymology.semantic_evolution: Proto-Semitic 'trace/footprint' gave Arabic concrete 'vestige, mark' and abstract 'tradition (that which is traced back)'. The verb Āthara (Form IV) developed the sense 'to prefer' (to mark out one thing over another).

derived_forms.meaning: to prefer, choose one over another

usage_patterns: ʾathar as tradition vs raʾy (opinion) in Islamic methodology

lexicographical_sources: Ibn Faris: Maqayis — both 'transmission' and 'preference' senses
theological_dimensions: The concept of īthār (altruistic preference) in Sufi ethics
hadith_evidence: ʿIlm al-ʾathar as a synonym for ʿilm al-ḥadīth

meaning.en_short: To call, summon, invite; to supplicate, pray
meaning.en: To call, summon, invite; to supplicate, pray, invoke. Encompasses: divine call to faith (daʿwah), prophetic invitation (16:125), the believer's intimate supplication (duʿāʾ), and naming (duʿiya). Key distinction: daʿwah = call to others (outward, propagation); duʿāʾ = call to God (upward, petition). The hadith 'al-duʿāʾ huwa al-ʿibādah' identifies supplication as the essence of worship.
meaning.ar: النِّدَاءُ وَالطَّلَبُ — الدَّعْوَةُ إِلَى اللَّهِ، وَالدُّعَاءُ: طَلَبُ الْعَبْدِ مِنْ رَبِّهِ
meaning.en_detailed: The triconsonantal root د ع و (دَعْو) — 212 Quranic occurrences — fundamentally expresses To call, summon, invite; to supplicate, pray. The hadith 'al-duʿāʾ huwa al-ʿibādah' (Tirmidhī) identifies supplication as the essence of worship, while 40:60 promises 'udʿūnī astajib lakum' ('Call Me, I will respond to you') — divine nearness through responsiveness. 2:186 reinforces: 'I answer the call of the caller when he calls Me.' The methodology of daʿwah receives its Quranic charter in 16:125 ('Call to your Lord's way with wisdom and beautiful preaching'). Form I daʿā (170x) covers all senses; Form VIII iddaʿā (3x) signifies claiming for oneself (36:57). The divine address yā ayyuhā al-muʾminūn descends upon the community as collective summons, while iyyāka naʿbudu names God as the sole summoned-to.
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To call, summon, invite; to supplicate, pray

etymology.ibn_faris: Core meaning: sound and calling (الصوت والنداء). All derivations return to directing speech toward someone.
etymology.al_raghib: Duʿāʾ = asking/requesting directed to God. Daʿwah = invitation extended by God or humans. Iddaʿā (Form VIII) = claiming for oneself.

derived_forms.key_verse: 40:60 ٱدْعُونِىٓ أَسْتَجِبْ لَكُمْ (Call Me, I respond)

quranic_analysis.daʿwah_vs_duʿāʾ: Daʿwah (دَعْوَة) = outward call to others, propagation, invitation to faith. Duʿāʾ (دُعَاء) = upward call to God, personal petition, worship through requesting.

hadith_evidence.ar: ٱلدُّعَآءُ هُوَ ٱلْعِبَادَةُ
hadith_evidence.en: Supplication is worship itself.

meaning.en_short: Self, soul, spirit, person; breath, psyche
meaning.en: Self, soul, spirit, person. The root designates the individual human being in totality — as living consciousness, moral agent, and unique irreplaceable entity. The root's physical sense of 'breath' (nafas) anchors its psychological and spiritual meaning (nafs). Three Quranic stages of nafs: (1) al-ammārah bi-l-sūʾ — the evil-commanding soul (12:53), (2) al-lawwāmah — the self-accusing soul (75:2), (3) al-muṭmaʾinnah — the soul at peace (89:27). Cognate with Hebrew nephesh (נֶפֶשׁ). The greater jihād (al-jihād al-akbar) is the struggle against one's nafs.
meaning.ar: الذَّاتُ وَالرُّوحُ وَالشَّخْصُ — النَّفْسُ: حَقِيقَةُ الْإِنْسَانِ الْجَامِعَةُ
meaning.en_detailed: The triconsonantal root ن ف س (نَفْس) — 298 Quranic occurrences — fundamentally expresses Self, soul, spirit, person; breath, psyche. Three Quranic stages structure its spiritual psychology: al-nafs al-ammārah bi-l-sūʾ ('the evil-commanding self,' 12:53), al-nafs al-lawwāmah ('the self-reproaching,' 75:2), and al-nafs al-muṭmaʾinnah ('the soul at peace,' 89:27). The anchor verse 5:32 ('whoever kills a soul... it is as if he killed all humanity') grounds the sanctity of individual life, while 2:48 affirms that no soul shall avail another on Judgment Day. 91:7 swears 'by the soul and He who proportioned it,' with 91:8 noting 'He inspired it with its wickedness and its piety.' Proto-Semitic *napš ('breath, throat, soul') underlies Hebrew nephesh and Ugaritic npš — breath IS the life.

etymology.semantic_evolution: Nafas (breath/wind) → nafs (soul/self) — following universal metaphor: breath IS the life/soul.

three_stages.name: al-nafs al-ammārah bi-l-sūʾ
three_stages.desc: The inciting soul — primal urges, base instincts. Rūmī: 'The nafs has a rosary in its right hand and a dagger in its sleeve.'

three_stages.name: al-nafs al-lawwāmah
three_stages.desc: The self-accusing soul — awakened conscience, moral self-critique

three_stages.name: al-nafs al-muṭmaʾinnah
three_stages.desc: The soul at peace — complete spiritual equilibrium. 'Return to your Lord, well-pleased and pleasing.'

theological_dimensions: The tripartite nafs: ammārah (evil-commanding), lawwāmah (self-reproaching), muṭmaʾinnah (tranquil) — a psychology of spiritual growth
'Every nafs shall taste death' (3:185) — the universality of mortality
The nafs as the locus of moral responsibility — 'no nafs shall bear the burden of another' (6:164)

hadith_evidence.ar: أَعْدَىٰ عَدُوِّكَ نَفْسُكَ ٱلَّتِى بَيْنَ جَنْبَيْكَ
hadith_evidence.en: Your worst enemy is your nafs between your sides.
hadith_evidence.source: Bayhaqī — widely cited in Sufi literature

meaning.en_short: To go astray, be lost, err, deviate from truth
meaning.en: To go astray, be lost, deviate from the right path, err. The root encapsulates the condition of being without guidance — physically (lost), intellectually (false beliefs), or spiritually (disconnected from Allah). Ḍalāl is the opposite of hudā (guidance) — the fundamental binary of the Quran. The root distinguishes degrees: from innocent pre-revelation unawareness (93:7, 26:20) to culpable disbelief (shirk/kufr). Recited daily in al-Fātiḥa: 'wa lā al-ḍāllīn' (1:7). The hadith qudsī: 'All of you are astray except those I guide.'
meaning.ar: الذَّهَابُ عَنِ الطَّرِيقِ — وَالضَّلَالُ: ضِدُّ الْهُدَى
meaning.en_detailed: Occurring 191 times in the Quranic text, the root ض ل ل (ضَلَال) conveys the essential concept of To go astray, be lost, err, deviate from truth. The Quran's most fundamental binary, hudā versus ḍalāl, is recited daily in al-Fātiḥah (1:7, 'ghayr al-maghḍūb ʿalayhim wa lā al-ḍāllīn'). The root distinguishes non-culpable pre-revelation unawareness (93:7: 'He found you lost and guided you') from culpable disbelief, error in judgment (2:282), and deeds nullified (47:1). The hadith qudsī declares 'all of you are astray except those I guide, so seek guidance from Me' (Muslim) — making straying the human default and guidance the divine gift. Moses acknowledges his pre-prophetic ḍalāl (26:20), and 91:11's 'ka-dhahābin awwa baṣara' shows Iblīs's claim of superiority as a form of straying.
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To go astray, be lost, err, deviate from truth

quranic_analysis.contrast_with_ghalat: Ḍalāl = existential/moral/spiritual deviation. Ghalaṭ/khaṭaʾ = accidental/factual mistake (2:286).

lexicographical_sources.ibn_faris: One single root: a thing's departure from its proper/straight state (ذهاب الشيء عن استقامته). (Maqāyīs)

hadith_evidence.ar: كُلُّكُمْ ضَالٌّ إِلَّا مَنْ هَدَيْتُهُ، فَٱسْتَهْدُونِىٓ أَهْدِكُمْ
hadith_evidence.en: All of you are astray except those I guide; seek guidance from Me.
hadith_evidence.relevance: Guidance as gratuitous; straying as default

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *ḍll = 'to wander, go astray'. Arabic ḍalla = to be lost, err. The Quranic ḍalāl (error, misguidance) is the antonym of hudā (guidance). Those who go astray are ḍāllūn — wandering without a guide. Iyyāka naʿbudu wa iyyāka nastaʿīn — ihdinā al-ṣirāṭ al-mustaqīm.

meaning.en_short: To guide, direct to the right path, lead aright
meaning.en: To guide, to direct to the right path, to lead aright. The root encompasses divine guidance through revelation and inspiration, prophetic guidance through teaching and example, and the human response of being guided (ihtidāʾ). Hudā is the most central Quranic concept — the primary petition of al-Fātiḥa (1:6), the Quran's self-description (2:2), and the direct opposite of ḍalāl. Classical scholars distinguish two dimensions: (1) hudā al-irshād — guidance as showing the way (the map/revelation), universal; (2) hudā al-tawfīq — guidance as granting ability to follow (successful attainment), specific to whom Allah wills. Al-Hādī is one of the 99 Names.
meaning.ar: الْإِرْشَادُ وَالدَّلَالَةُ عَلَى الطَّرِيقِ — وَالْهُدَى: ضِدُّ الضَّلَالِ
meaning.en_detailed: هُدًى (ه د ي), a root appearing 316 times in the Quran, encodes the notion of To guide, direct to the right path, lead aright across its various verbal and nominal forms. The Quran's most central petition — 'ihdinā al-ṣirāṭ al-mustaqīm' (1:6) — asks for this gift seventeen times daily, while 2:2 names the Quran itself as 'hudan li-l-muttaqīn' ('guidance for the God-conscious'). Two dimensions are distinguished classically: hudā al-irshād ('showing the way,' universal) and hudā al-tawfīq ('granting ability to follow,' particular). 28:56's axiom ('innaka lā tahdī man aḥbabta wa-lākinna Allāha yahdī man yashāʾ,' 'you cannot guide whom you love, but Allah guides whom He wills') establishes guidance as exclusively divine. Cognates include Hebrew hāḏâ ('to stretch out, direct') and Ge'ez hadaya ('to guide').
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To guide, direct to the right path, lead aright

quranic_analysis.two_dimensions: Al-Raghib: (1) Hudā al-irshād (showing the way — universal), (2) Hudā al-tawfīq (granting success — specific). Ibn Faris: 'Gentle indication/direction (الدلالة بلطف)' — unlike forceful driving.

hadith_evidence.ar: مَن يَهْدِهِ ٱللَّهُ فَلَا مُضِلَّ لَهُۥ
hadith_evidence.en: Whoever Allah guides, none can lead astray.

hadith_evidence.ar: ٱللَّهُمَّ إِنِّىٓ أَسْـَٔلُكَ ٱلْهُدَىٰ وَٱلتُّقَىٰ
hadith_evidence.en: O Allah, I ask You for guidance and piety.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *hdy = 'to guide, lead'. The Quranic hudā (guidance) is central — it is what the Quran provides, what prophets bring, and what the believer seeks. 'Guide us (ihdinā) to the Straight Path' (1:6). Hadiyyah (gift) derives from the same root — guidance as a divine gift.

meaning.en_short: To be familiar, intimate; to perceive; human beings
meaning.en: To be familiar, intimate, at ease; to perceive, sense; human beings (insān, nās, unās). The root bridges social familiarity and humanity itself — insān (71x) is the most frequent form. Two competing etymologies: (1) from uns (familiarity/sociability) — humans are social beings; (2) from nisyān (forgetfulness) — humans are forgetful. Ibn Faris favors uns. The Quran's theological anthropology presents insān as: created from clay, carrier of the Trust, weak and hasty, capable of the highest and lowest. Istiʾnās (Form X) = seeking permission before entering (24:27) — ensuring welcome.
meaning.ar: الْأُلْفَةُ وَالطُّمَأْنِينَةُ — وَالْإِنْسَانُ مِنَ الْأُنْسِ
meaning.en_detailed: The triconsonantal root أ ن س (أُنْس) — 97 Quranic occurrences — fundamentally expresses To be familiar, intimate; to perceive; human beings. The most frequent derivative insān ('human being') is, according to Ibn Faris's preferred etymology, 'the sociable one' — from ʾuns ('familiarity, intimacy') rather than nisyān ('forgetting,' the alternative etymology). The theological anthropology it names presents humans as: created from clay (15:26), bearers of the cosmic Trust (33:72), weak (4:28: 'wa-kāna al-insānu ʿajūlan') and hasty (17:11), quarrelsome (18:54), yet in the best of stature (95:4). 24:27's istiʾnās ('seeking permission before entering') extends the root socially into etiquette. The contrast ins ('humans,' settled/civilized) versus jinn ('unseen,' wild) marks a pre-Islamic cultural polarity preserved in the Quran.

etymology.theory_a: From uns (أُنْس) — familiarity, sociability. Insān = the social/sociable being. Favored by Ibn Faris.
etymology.theory_b: From nisyān (نِسْيَان) — forgetfulness. Insān = the forgetful one. Favored by some grammarians.
etymology.consensus: Majority favor Theory A. Pre-Islamic: ins = settled/civilized vs. jinn = unseen/wild.

quranic_analysis.theological_anthropology: Insān created from clay (15:26), weak (4:28), hasty (17:11), quarrelsome (18:54), bearer of the Trust (33:72), in best stature (95:4), capable of falling to lowest (95:5).

hadith_evidence.ar: خُلِقَ الْإِنْسَانُ مِنْ عَجَلٍ
hadith_evidence.en: Man was created of haste.

meaning.en: Mercy, compassion, loving tenderness. The root's core image is the womb (raḥim) — the place of nurturing, protection, and the strongest natural bonds of love. Divine mercy (raḥmah, 114x) encompasses all creation and is the dominant divine attribute in the Quran. Al-Raḥmān (57x) = intrinsic, universal, exhaustive mercy (faʿlān pattern — for Allah only). Al-Raḥīm (116x) = active, bestowed, ongoing mercy (faʿīl pattern — for Allah and humans). The pair appears together 17 times in the basmalah and throughout. The etymological link: womb (raḥim) → kinship (arḥām) → divine mercy (raḥmah) — mercy as maternal, protective love.
meaning.ar: الرِّقَّةُ وَالشَّفَقَةُ وَالْعَطْفُ — وَالرَّحِمُ: مَوْضِعُ تَكْوِينِ الْجَنِينِ
meaning.en_detailed: The Arabic root ر ح م (رَحْم) appears 339 times in the Quran, governing the semantic domain of Mercy, compassion, loving tenderness; womb. Its dual divine names al-Raḥmān (57x, faʿlān pattern — intrinsic, universal mercy) and al-Raḥīm (115x, faʿīl pattern — active, ongoing mercy) open every surah with the basmalah, making this the most formulaically significant Quranic root. 21:107 names the Prophet's mission itself as mercy to the worlds ('raḥmatan li-l-ʿālamīn'), while 7:156 declares 'wa-raḥmatī wasiʿat kulla shayʾ' ('My Mercy encompasses all things'). 11:119 names mercy as the purpose of creation ('except those upon whom your Lord has mercy, and for that He created them'). Proto-Semitic *rḥm ('womb; to have compassion') links Hebrew reḥem and Ge'ez rəḥm — the hadith of one hundred mercies (Bukhārī 6000) grounds all earthly compassion.

cognates.hebrew: רֶחֶם (reḥem) — womb; רַחֵם (raḥēm) — to have mercy
cognates.aramaic: רחם (rḥm) — womb; to love, have mercy

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *rḥm = 'womb' → 'kinship bond' → 'compassion, mercy'. The concrete meaning 'womb' is the semantic source — from the physical organ of maternal care to the abstract quality of divine mercy. The Quran combines the intensive raḥmān (universal, all-encompassing mercy in this world) with the descriptive raḥīm (particular, enduring mercy in the Hereafter). The phrase Bismillāh al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm opens all but one surah, making this root the most formulaically significant.

raḥmān_vs_raḥīm.raḥmān: Faʿlān pattern — intrinsic, exhaustive, universal. Allah only. Scope: all creation. Analogy: the ocean of mercy.
raḥmān_vs_raḥīm.raḥīm: Faʿīl pattern — active, bestowed, ongoing. Allah and humans (48:29). Scope: believers specifically. Analogy: the waves reaching shore.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ لِلَّهِ مِا۟ئَةَ رَحْمَةٍۢ ... فَأَمْسَكَ عِندَهُۥ تِسْعَةًۭ وَتِسْعِينَ
hadith_evidence.en: Allah has one hundred mercies... He kept ninety-nine with Him and sent one to earth.
hadith_evidence.relevance: The one mercy on earth — all compassion between creatures comes from it

theological_dimensions: Al-Raḥmān and Al-Raḥīm — the two mercy names that open every surah
Raḥmah as the purpose of creation — 'except those upon whom your Lord has mercy, and for that He created them' (11:119)
The womb (raḥim) as a 'branch' of the divine name al-Raḥmān — silat al-raḥim (maintaining kinship) as religious duty

meaning.en: To see (physically), perceive, deem, hold an opinion. Ra'y = legal opinion (Ahl al-Ra'y). Ru'ya = dream/vision. Key: Moses' request (7:143), Mi'raj vision (53:11). Cognate: Hebrew ra'ah.
meaning.ar: الإبصار بالعين والعلم والاعتقاد
meaning.en_detailed: The Arabic root ر أ ي (رَأْي) appears 328 times in the Quran, governing the semantic domain of View; opinion; judgment; perception. The root's most theologically intense moment is Moses' request to see Allah (7:143: 'Rabbi arinī anẓur ilayka,' 'My Lord, show me that I may see You') and the divine refusal ('lan tarānī'), while the Prophet's Miʿrāj includes the ruʾyat al-qalb ('vision of the heart,' 53:11: 'mā kadhaba al-fuʾādu mā raʾā,' 'the heart did not lie about what it saw'). The contrast with baṣar ('physical sight') is sharp: raʾā adds intellectual perception and considered judgment — raʾy is what one 'sees' with insight. The derivative raʾy became the foundation of the Kufan juristic school (Ahl al-Raʾy), most associated with Abū Ḥanīfa. The rhetorical a-raʾayta ('Have you considered?') summons attention throughout the Quran.
meaning.ar_definition: النظر والاعتقاد والتدبر؛ الإبصار بالقلب والعقل

quranic_analysis.ra'y_in_fiqh: Ra'y = personal juristic opinion. Ahl al-Ra'y = Kufan school (Abu Hanifa).

contrast_with_basar: Basar = physical eyesight. Ra'a = sight + intellectual perception.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *rʾy = 'to see → to perceive, think'. Arabic raʾā = to see. Raʾy = opinion (what one 'sees'). The ruʾyā (vision, dream) is a mode of divine communication — Yusuf's gift (12:4-100). The Quranic 'a-raʾayta' (Have you seen?/Consider!) is a rhetorical device demanding attention.

hadith_evidence.ar: الْإِحْسَانُ أَنْ تَعْبُدَ اللَّهَ كَأَنَّكَ تَرَاهُ
hadith_evidence.en: Iḥsān is to worship Allah as if you see Him.

meaning.en: Wrong, injustice, darkness, oppression. Two meanings: darkness (zulumat) and putting in wrong place (injustice). Three types: self, others, shirk (31:13). Zalim (129x) = wrongdoer. Allah declares zulm haram upon Himself.
meaning.ar: وضع الشيء في غير موضعه — ضد العدل
meaning.en_detailed: The Arabic root ظ ل م (ظُلْم) appears 315 times in the Quran, governing the semantic domain of Injustice; oppression; wrongdoing; darkness. The hadith qudsī 'innī ḥarramtu al-ẓulm ʿalā nafsī wa-jʿaltuhu baynakum muḥarraman' (Muslim, 'I have forbidden oppression for Myself and made it forbidden among you') establishes divine justice as ontological, while 31:13 names shirk as the greatest ẓulm ('innahu shirkun kabīr') — the broadest category encompassing injustice against God. Three types are distinguished: against self, against others, and against God (shirk). The semantic bridge from ẓulumāt ('darknesses,' 23x) to ẓulm ('injustice,' 20x) is cognitively illuminating — darkness is the absence of light as injustice is the absence of justice. Hebrew ṣālam ('dark') and Akkadian ṣalāmu confirm Proto-Semitic *ẓlm.
meaning.ar_definition: وَضْعُ الشَّيْءِ فِي غَيْرِ مَوْضِعِهِ؛ الْجَوْرُ وَمُجَاوَزَةُ الْحَدِّ

quranic_analysis.three_types: (1) Self, (2) Others, (3) Shirk = greatest. Ibn Faris: constriction/deviation.

hadith_evidence.ar: يا عبادي إني حرمت الظلم على نفسي
hadith_evidence.en: O My servants, I have forbidden oppression for Myself.

cognates.hebrew: צָלַם (ṣālam) — to be dark; צֶלֶם (ṣelem) — image, shadow

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *ẓlm = 'to be dark → to do wrong'. The semantic bridge: darkness is the absence of light just as injustice (ẓulm) is the absence of justice. Ẓulumāt (darknesses, plural) vs nūr (light, singular) — darkness is manifold, light is one. The ẓālim (wrongdoer) places things in darkness rather than light.

meaning.en: Truth, reality, right, justice. Al-Haqq = Divine Name — the Real. Core opposition: haqq vs batil. Ibn Faris: permanence, necessity, truth. Al-Haqqah = the Sure Reality (Judgment). Cognate: Hebrew choq (law). Haqq as right/due in fiqh.
meaning.ar: الثبوت والوجوب والصدق — ضد الباطل
meaning.en_detailed: حَقّ (ح ق ق), a root appearing 287 times in the Quran, encodes the notion of Truth; right; reality; due; certainty across its various verbal and nominal forms. Al-Ḥaqq (22:62: 'Allāh — Huwa al-Ḥaqq al-Mubīn') names the divine Reality, the ontological ground of being. The Quran's most fundamental binary — ḥaqq versus bāṭil ('falsehood') — structures ethical discourse: 'wa-qul jāʾa al-Ḥaqq wa-zahaqa al-bāṭil' (17:81, 'truth has come and falsehood has vanished') and 'naqḍifu al-Ḥaqqa ʿalā al-bāṭili fa-yadmaḥuhu' (21:18, 'We hurl truth against falsehood and it crushes it'). In fiqh, ḥaqq names both legal right ('entitlement') and divine decree. Proto-Semitic *ḥqq ('to engrave, decree') underlies Hebrew ḥāqaq ('engrave') and ḥōq ('statute') — the semantic path moves from physical inscription to legal binding to ontological truth.
meaning.ar_definition: الثابت الذي لا يسوغ إنكاره؛ نقيض الباطل؛ الأمر الواجب

quranic_analysis.al_haqq_vs_batil: Haqq = the Real, the Established. Batil = the false, the perishing.

cognates.hebrew: חָקַק (ḥāqaq) — to engrave, decree; חֹק (ḥōq) — statute, law

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *ḥqq = 'to engrave, inscribe → decree, establish as law → be right, true, permanent'. The semantic path: physical engraving → legal decree (what is inscribed is binding) → truth (what is established/unalterable). Arabic retains both senses: ḥaqq=truth/reality and ḥaqq=right/due. The Quran's al-Ḥaqq as a divine name means 'The Truth, The Reality' — God as the ground of all being.

theological_dimensions: Al-Ḥaqq (The Truth, The Reality) — God as the ultimate ontological ground
Ḥaqq vs bāṭil (truth vs falsehood) — the fundamental Quranic binary
Ḥuqūq (rights/duties) — the ethical-legal framework of Islamic law

hadith_evidence.ar: الْحَقُّ مِنْ رَبِّكَ فَلَا تَكُونَنَّ مِنَ الْمُمْتَرِينَ
hadith_evidence.en: The truth is from your Lord, so be not among the doubters.

meaning.en: To write, prescribe, decree. Ibn Faris: core = gathering/joining. Kitab = scripture AND divine decree. Kutiba 'alaykum = it is prescribed (central legal formula). Kitab (260x) = the Quran calls itself al-Kitab (2:2).
meaning.ar: الكتابة — جمع الحروف — والفرض والإيجاب
meaning.en_detailed: Root ك ت ب (كِتَاب), attested 319 times in the Quran, derives its core meaning of Book; scripture; record; decree; obligation from Proto-Semitic sources. The Quran's central self-description — dhālika al-kitāb lā rayba fīh (2:2, 'This is the Book, no doubt in it') — names revelation as al-Kitāb, the written. The legal formula kutiba ʿalaykum ('it is prescribed for you,' 2:183 regarding fasting) extends writing to divine obligation, while 4:103 names ṣalāh as 'kitāban mawqūtan' ('a timed decree'). Ibn Faris identifies the root's deeper sense as 'gathering and joining' — letters gathered into words, deeds gathered into record, scripture gathered into revelation. The umm al-kitāb ('Mother of the Book,' 13:39) names the heavenly archetype. The most emphatic Quranic command, 2:282's 'uktubū' ('write it down'), establishes written contracts as legal foundation.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *ktb = 'to write, inscribe'. The Quranic kitāb (book/scripture) is the central metaphor for divine communication — the 'written' word of God. The concept extends to 'decree' (God 'writes' destiny) and 'prescription' (the kitāb of fasting).

hadith_evidence.ar: كَتَبَ اللَّهُ مَقَادِيرَ الْخَلَائِقِ قَبْلَ أَنْ يَخْلُقَ السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضَ
hadith_evidence.en: Allah wrote the decrees of creation before He created the heavens and earth.

meaning.en: To descend, send down, reveal. Critical: inzal (Form IV, 183x) = single act (97:1). Tanzil (Form II, 62x) = gradual over 23 years (17:106). Quran: inzal (whole to lowest heaven) then tanzil (piecemeal via Jibril). Nuzul (8x) = hospitality in Paradise.
meaning.ar: النزول — والتنزيل: إنزال الشيء شيئا بعد شيء
meaning.en_detailed: The Arabic root ن ز ل (نُزُول) appears 293 times in the Quran, governing the semantic domain of Descent; revelation; sending down; lodging. Nuzul (6x) names both the hospitality of Paradise and the descending verses. The contrast with waḥy ('revelation') clarifies: nuzul is spatial (through Jibrīl), waḥy is non-spatial. 25:32's question 'Why was the Quran not sent down all at once?' receives its answer in this distinction.
meaning.ar_definition: الهُبُوط؛ حُلُولُ الشَّيْءِ مِنْ عُلْوٍ إلَى سُفْلٍ؛ الْإِنْزَال

quranic_analysis.tanzil_vs_inzal: Inzal = single descent to lowest heaven. Tanzil = progressive over 23 years.

contrast_with_wahy: Nuzul = spatial descent (through Jibril). Wahy = non-spatial inspiration. All tanzil is wahy; not all wahy is tanzil.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *nzl = 'to descend, come down'. The Quranic tanzīl (revelation) is the 'sending down' of the Quran — a descent from the divine realm. The contrast between nazzala (intensive: repeated descent) and anzala (single event) is a subtle Quranic stylistic feature reflecting the gradual (najman najman) vs whole revelation.

hadith_evidence.ar: يَنْزِلُ رَبُّنَا تَبَارَكَ وَتَعَالَى كُلَّ لَيْلَةٍ إِلَى السَّمَاءِ الدُّنْيَا
hadith_evidence.en: Our Lord descends every night to the lowest heaven.

meaning.en: To remember, mention; male. Dual-core: (1) remembrance/mention — dhikr (76x), dhikr Allah (13:28), Quran as al-Dhikr (15:9); (2) male (dhakar). Ibn Faris: both return to prominence — male is the prominent/remembered one. Cognates: Akkadian zakarum, Hebrew zakhar.
meaning.ar: الذكر: ضد النسيان — والذكر: ضد الأنثى
meaning.en_detailed: Root ذ ك ر (ذِكْر), attested 292 times in the Quran, derives its core meaning of Remembrance; mention; reminder; renown from Proto-Semitic sources. The covenant verse 2:152 ('fa-dhkurūnī adhkurkum wa-shkurū lī wa-lā takfurūn,' 'Remember Me, I will remember you, be grateful to Me, and do not be ungrateful') establishes dhikr as both divine command and human consolation. The consolation 13:28 declares 'a-lā bi-dhikri Allāhi tatmaʾinnu al-qulūb' ('in remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest'). The Quran names itself al-Dhikr (15:9: 'innā naḥnu nazzalnā al-dhikr wa-innā lahu la-ḥāfiẓūn,' 'We sent down the Reminder, and We are its guardians'). The dual-core sense — dhikr ('remembrance') and dhakar ('male') — both derive, per Ibn Faris, from 'prominence,' since the remembered and the male are the prominent.
meaning.ar_definition: التذكار؛ حفظ الشيء في القلب؛ ذكره باللسان؛ الشرف والصيت

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *ḏkr = 'to remember → to mention (cause to remember)'. The Quranic dhikr (remembrance) is the core of worship: dhikr Allāh (remembering God) through prayer, recitation, and reflection. The Quran is itself called al-Dhikr (the Reminder). The opposite is nisyān (forgetting).

hadith_evidence.ar: لَا يَزَالُ لِسَانُكَ رَطْبًا مِنْ ذِكْرِ اللَّهِ
hadith_evidence.en: Let your tongue always be moist with the remembrance of Allah.

meaning.en: To lie, deny, reject as false. Kadhaba (Form I, 11x) = individual lie. Kadhdhaba (Form II, 176x) = systematic denial of revelation — the dominant Quranic form. 39:32 juxtaposes both. Cognates: Hebrew kazav (to lie).
meaning.ar: خلاف الخبر لما هو عليه في الحقيقة
meaning.en_detailed: Occurring 282 times in the Quranic text, the root ك ذ ب (كَذِب) conveys the essential concept of Lie; falsehood; denial; fabrication. The 39:32 juxtaposition ('faman aẓlamu mimman kadhaba ʿalā Allāh wa-kadhaba bi-l-ṣidqi idh jāʾahu,' 'who lies against Allah and denies the truth when it comes to him?') names both forms, but the theological crime is kadhdhaba — calling truth itself falsehood. The Bukhārī-Muslim hadith of the hypocrite's three signs opens with 'idhā ḥaddatha kadhaba' ('when he speaks, he lies'), making kadhib a marker of spiritual disease. The noun kadhdhāb ('frequent liar,' 32x) names a moral type, while mukadhdhib ('denier,' 21x) names a theological position.
meaning.ar_definition: نقيض الصدق؛ الإخبار عن الشيء بخلاف ما هو عليه

quranic_analysis.contrast: Kadhaba = lie about (moral). Kadhdhaba = deny/reject revelation (theological crime).

hadith_evidence.ar: إذا حدث كذب
hadith_evidence.en: When he speaks he lies.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *kṯb — possibly a variant of ktb (to write) specialized to 'falsifying what is written'. Arabic kadhaba = to lie, deny, falsify. The semantic path: writing → false writing → lying. The Quranic kidhb is the greatest sin — calling truth falsehood.

meaning.en: To take, seize; to adopt. Akhadha (Form I, 127x) = physical taking — covenant (mithaq), divine seizure. Ittakhadha (Form VIII, 124x) = to take/adopt AS — allies, gods, Ibrahim as friend (4:125). Cognates: Hebrew achaz (seize).
meaning.ar: التناول والقبض — والاتخاذ: جعل الشيء للنفس
