meaning.en_detailed: Root أ خ ذ (أَخْذ), attested 273 times in the Quran, derives its core meaning of Taking; seizing; grasping; punishment from Proto-Semitic sources. The Quran's covenant phrase 'akhadhnā mithāqakum' ('We took your covenant,' 2:63) establishes divine covenant-making as taking. Form VIII names the most damning spiritual act — 'ittakhadha ālihatan ākharīn' ('taking other gods,' 7:180) versus the highest honor, 4:125's 'wa-takhadha Allāhu Ibrāhīm khalīlan' ('Allah took Ibrāhīm as intimate friend,' khallīl). 2:255's 'lā taʾkhudhuhu sinatun wa-lā nawm' ('neither drowsiness overtakes Him nor sleep') applies the root to divine vigilance. The noun akhdh ('seizure,' 6x) names the divine punishment pattern — 'such is the akhdh of your Lord when He seizes the towns' (11:102) — marking the irresistible suddenness of judgment. Proto-Semitic *ʾḫḏ ('to seize') underlies Hebrew ʾāḥaz ('to seize, grasp, hold').

quranic_analysis.akhadha_vs_ittakhadha: Akhadha = physical seizure (covenant, punishment). Ittakhadha = taking AS (adopting beliefs, allies).

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *ʾḫḏ = 'to take, seize'. The Quranic akhadha is the primary verb of divine punishment: 'We seized (akhadhnā) them' — God's seizure of nations. The root emphasizes the suddenness and irresistibility of divine judgment: 'such is the seizing (akhdh) of your Lord' (11:102).

hadith_evidence.ar: مَا أَخَذَ اللَّهُ بِيَمِينِهِ فَهُوَ فِي قَبْضَتِهِ
hadith_evidence.en: What Allah takes with His right hand is in His grasp.

meaning.en: Action. Amila=work. Amal=deed. 2:82: those who believe and do righteous deeds (as-salihati). Faith and works inextricably linked.
meaning.en_detailed: أَمَلَ (أ م ل), a root appearing 2 times in the Quran, encodes the notion of To act; work ('amal) across its various verbal and nominal forms. The most repeated Quranic phrase — 'alladhīna āmanū wa-ʿamilū al-ṣāliḥāt' ('those who believe and do righteous deeds') — grounds Islamic soteriology in the inseparability of īmān (faith) and ʿamal (action). 2:82 names this conjunction explicitly ('wa-alladhīna āmanū wa-ʿamilū al-ṣāliḥāt ulāʾika humu al-muʾminūn ḥaqqan,' 'they are the believers in truth'), while the hadith 'innamā al-aʿmāl bi-l-niyyāt' ('deeds are by intentions,' Bukhārī 1) establishes the inner dimension of outward action. Proto-Semitic *ʿml ('to labor, toil') underlies Hebrew ʿāmal.

quranic_analysis.theme: Faith and deeds
quranic_analysis.detail: Walladhina amanu wa amilu al-salihat—those who believe and do righteous deeds.

key_nominals.meaning: deed, action (71x)—deliberate product of human effort
deeds (38x broken pl)—record weighed on Judgment Day

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *ʿml = 'to labor, toil → to do, act'. Arabic ʿamila = to work, do. The ʿamal (deed) is almost always paired with īmān (faith) — the Quranic vision of faith as inherently active. 'Those who believe and do righteous deeds (al-ṣāliḥāt)' is the most repeated Quranic phrase.

theological_dimensions: Iman = heart + tongue + action of limbs (Sunni orthodoxy)
Deeds on scales (mizan): decisive for salvation
Intention (niyya): innama al-amalu bi al-niyyat

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّمَا الْأَعْمَالُ بِالنِّيَّاتِ
hadith_evidence.en: Actions are judged by intentions.

meaning.en: To carry, bear, load; to be pregnant. Ibn Faris: bearing a weight. Haml (a-vowel) = internal burden (pregnancy, fetus). Himl (i-vowel) = external burden (load). Key: the Trust humanity bore (33:72), 'do not burden us' (2:286), carrying books like donkey (62:5), carrying the Throne (40:7).
meaning.ar: رفع الشيء — حَمْل (باطني) وحِمْل (ظاهري)
meaning.en_detailed: حَمْل (ح م ل), a root appearing 64 times in the Quran, encodes the notion of Carrying; bearing; burden; pregnancy across its various verbal and nominal forms. The root's theological climax is 33:72, where humanity bears the cosmic Trust ('wa-ḥamalāhā al-insānu innahu kāna ẓalūman jahūlan,' 'man undertook it; indeed he was unjust and ignorant') that even the heavens, earth, and mountains refused. The opposite petition — 'lā tuḥammilnā mā lā ṭāqatanā bihi' (2:286, 'do not burden us beyond what we have strength for') — captures the believer's plea against unbearable trials. 6:164 ('lā yaziru wāziratun wizra ukhrā,' 'no bearer shall bear the burden of another') grounds individual moral responsibility. The Throne-bearers (ḥāmilūn al-ʿarsh, 40:7) extend the root to angelic liturgy.
meaning.ar_definition: رَفْعُ الشَّيْءِ عَلَى الظَّهْرِ أَوِ الرَّأْسِ؛ الْوِقْر؛ الْحَبَل

quranic_analysis.haml_vs_himl: Haml (a) = internal: pregnancy, fruit. Himl (i) = external: load on back. Classical Arabic preserves this vowel distinction.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *ḥml = 'to carry, bear a load'. Ḥamala = to carry. Ḥaml = pregnancy, burden. 'No bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another' (6:164) — individual moral responsibility.

hadith_evidence.ar: مَنْ حَمَلَ عَلَيْنَا السِّلَاحَ فَلَيْسَ مِنَّا
hadith_evidence.en: Whoever bears arms against us is not of us.

meaning.en: To seal, stamp, conclude. Ibn Faris: core = reaching the end of something. A seal marks finality. Quran: sealed hearts (2:7), Seal of Prophets (33:40), mouths sealed (36:65), sealed nectar (83:25-26).
meaning.ar: بلوغ آخر الشيء
meaning.en_detailed: خَتْم (خ ت م), a root appearing 8 times in the Quran, encodes the notion of Seal; sealing; conclusion; end across its various verbal and nominal forms. The most famous usage — khātam al-nabiyyīn (33:40, 'wa-lākin rasūla Allāh wa-khātama al-nabiyyīn,' 'but the Messenger of Allah and the Seal of the Prophets') — establishes Muhammad as the final messenger, closing the prophetic chain. Allah's sealing of hearts (2:7: 'khutama Allāhu ʿalā qulūbihim wa-ʿalā samʿihim wa-ʿalā abṣārihim ghishāwah,' 'Allah sealed their hearts, their hearing, and a covering over their sight') names the divine act that prevents guidance for those who persistently reject. The eternal seal of the wine of Paradise (83:25-26: 'makhtūm, khitāmuhu misk,' 'sealed, its seal is musk') extends the root to eschatological imagery.
meaning.ar_definition: الطَّبْعُ؛ التغطية؛ البلوغ إلى آخر الشيء

key_nominals.meaning: seal, signet; the Seal of Prophets

quranic_analysis.khatm_vs_tab: Khatm = final closure/conclusion. Tab = physical impressing. Khatm carries stronger finality.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَتْم — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 8 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root xtm (خَتْم) appears 8 times in the Quran, including 33:40.

meaning.en: To be safe, sound, at peace; to submit to God. The most theologically significant root. Salam = peace, greeting; Divine Name. Islam = submission, the religion. Muslim = one who submits. Salim = sound heart. Cognate: Hebrew shalom.
meaning.ar: السلامة — ضد العيب — والإسلام: الانقياد لله
meaning.en_detailed: The Arabic root س ل م (سَلْم) appears 140 times in the Quran, governing the semantic domain of Peace; submission; safety; soundness. 3:19 names 'inn al-dīna ʿinda Allāhi al-islām' ('the religion with God is islām, submission'), while 59:23 names al-Salām as one of the 99 Names ('al-Malik al-Quddūs al-Salām'). The root's paradoxical heart: true freedom through submission (islām), wholeness through surrender (qalb salīm, 26:89). Dār al-Salām (10:25: 'Allāhu yadʿū ilā dāri al-salām,' 'Allah calls to the Abode of Peace') names Paradise. Proto-Semitic *šlm ('to be whole, complete') underlies Hebrew shālēm ('complete, at peace') and Ge'ez salāma ('safe') — the path from material wholeness to spiritual submission.
meaning.ar_definition: الصُّلْح؛ ضِدُّ الْحَرْبِ؛ الْبَرَاءَةُ مِنَ الْعُيُوبِ

cognate: Hebrew shalom — wholeness, peace. Semitic root SLM.

etymology.proto_semitic: *slm (to be safe, at peace; to submit)

cognates.hebrew: שָׁלֵם (šālēm) — to be complete, at peace

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *šlm = 'to be whole, complete → at peace'. Salima = to be safe. Islām = submission to God. Salām = peace. The root unifies safety, wholeness, peace, and submission — the holistic vision of Islamic spirituality.

hadith_evidence.ar: الْمُسْلِمُ مَنْ سَلِمَ الْمُسْلِمُونَ مِنْ لِسَانِهِ وَيَدِهِ
hadith_evidence.en: The Muslim is one from whose tongue and hand the Muslims are safe.

meaning.en: To create, form, originate with design. Ibn Faris: measuring (taqdir) then bringing into existence. Distinct from ja ala: khalq = ex nihilo. Khalq = creation. Al-Khaliq = Creator. Al-Khallaq = Supreme Creator. Khuluq = moral character (68:4).
meaning.ar: تقدير الشيء ثم إحداثه
meaning.en_detailed: Occurring 261 times in the Quranic text, the root خ ل ق (خَلْق) conveys the essential concept of Creation; creatures; making; origination. The contrast with jaʿala is sharp: khalaqa creates ex nihilo (as the first revelation 96:2 names 'khalaqa al-insāna min ʿalaq,' 'He created man from a clot'), while jaʿala makes from existing. The divine name al-Khāliq ('Creator,' 12x) names the attribute of origination, while al-Khallāq ('Supreme Creator,' 2x, in 15:86 and 36:81) intensifies it. The derivative khuluq ('moral character,' 68:4: 'wa-innaka la-ʿalā khuluqin ʿaẓīm,' 'you stand upon an immense character') names a created quality, suggesting that character itself is fashioned by the same divine hand that creates bodies. The khalq ('creation,' 52x) often pairs with qadar ('measuring'), preserving Ibn Faris's core semantic: 'measuring, then bringing into existence.'
meaning.ar_definition: إيجاد الشيء من العدم؛ تقديره؛ المخلوقات

quranic_analysis.vs_jaala: Khalaqa = ex nihilo origination. Jaala = making from existing/appointing.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *ḫlq = 'to measure, proportion → to create'. The Quranic khalq encompasses creation, formation, and the moral character (khuluq) of the created being. Al-Khāliq (The Creator) is the divine name of origination. The idea that God 'measured' before creating is preserved in qadar alongside khalq.

hadith_evidence.ar: الْمُؤْمِنُ يَأْكُلُ فِي مِعًى وَاحِدٍ وَالْكَافِرُ يَأْكُلُ فِي سَبْعَةِ أَمْعَاءٍ
hadith_evidence.en: The believer eats in one intestine and the disbeliever eats in seven intestines.

meaning.en: To face, accept, encounter; before. Ibn Faris: core = facing/encountering. Qiblah = direction of prayer (2:144). Qabila = to accept (9:104). Taqabbala = graciously accept (2:127). Qabl = before (temporal, 242x). Qabail = tribes (49:13). Hebrew cognate: q-b-l (Kabbalah).
meaning.ar: استقبال الشيء ومواجهته
meaning.en_detailed: Root ق ب ل (قُبْل), attested 294 times in the Quran, derives its core meaning of Acceptance; receiving; facing; direction from Proto-Semitic sources. Its derivatives govern three domains: qiblah ('direction of prayer,' 7x; 2:144's reorientation from Jerusalem to Makkah, 'fa-wallī wajhaka shatra al-masjidi al-ḥarām'), qabūl ('acceptance' of deeds, repentance), and qabl ('before,' 242x). The verb qabila (9x) names acceptance; taqabbala (10x) names gracious acceptance — 2:127's prayer 'Rabbanā taqabbal minnā' ('Our Lord, accept from us') uses the intensive form. The noun qabāʾil ('tribes,' 1x) in 49:13 names the human diversity God willed ('wa-jaʿalnākum shuʿūban wa-qabāʾila li-taʿārafū'). Hebrew qibbēl ('receive') and Aramaic qbl confirm Proto-Semitic *qbl — the kabbalistic tradition of 'received tradition' (Kabbalah) preserves the receiving sense across Semitic languages.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *qbl = 'to face, be in front → to receive'. Arabic qabila = to accept. Qabla = before. The Quranic qiblah (2:144) is the 'direction one faces' toward God.

hadith_evidence.ar: قُبْل — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 294 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root qbl (قُبْل) appears 294 times in the Quran, including 2:144.

meaning.en: To know, recognize. Marifah (experiential) vs ilm (comprehensive). Arrafa (20x) = recognize by marks (7:46). Itarafa (3x) = confess (9:102). Taarafa (2x) = know one another (49:13). Maruf (39x) = the known good (amr bi-l-maruf). Urf (2x) = custom (7:199). Araf (2x) = the Heights. Sufi: irfan = gnosis.
meaning.ar: المعرفة — إدراك الشيء بأثر
meaning.en_detailed: From the triliteral ʿ-r-f (عَرْف), occurring 70 times, the semantic field spans experiential recognition, communal acknowledgement, and customary approval—anchored in the verb ʿarafa ('to know by acquaintance'). The conceptual centre is maʿrūf (the known and recognised good), which the Quran positions as the positive pole of its ethical binary at 3:104, calling 'a community commanding the maʿrūf and forbidding the munkar.' The eschatological counter-image appears at 7:46 where the people of the Heights recognise their marks, while 49:13 frames human difference as a divinely ordained occasion for taʿāruf ('knowing one another'). The proper noun ʿAraf and ma'rifa in Sufi gnosis descend from this same root of acknowledged presence.
meaning.ar_definition: المعرفة والعلم بالشيء؛ الإقرار؛ الأمر المشهور المستحسن

quranic_analysis.maruf_vs_munkar: Maruf = communal good. Munkar = rejected evil. Amr bi-l-maruf = foundational Islamic ethical principle.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *ʿrp = 'to know, recognize'. Arabic ʿarafa = to know. Maʿrūf = what is known/accepted as good. ʿArafāt is the plain of divine recognition.

hadith_evidence.ar: مَنْ سَلَكَ طَرِيقًا يَلْتَمِسُ فِيهِ عِلْمًا سَهَّلَ اللَّهُ لَهُ طَرِيقًا إِلَى الْجَنَّةِ
hadith_evidence.en: Whoever travels a path seeking knowledge, Allah makes the path to Paradise easy for him.

meaning.en: To fast, abstain, stand still. Ibn Faris: core = abstention (imsak). Siyam (9x) = fasting institution (2:183). Sawm (1x) = abstention from speech (19:26 — Mary). Cognates: Hebrew tsom, Aramaic sawma — all meaning fast. Possibly Aramaic semantic loan.
meaning.ar: الإمساك عن الطعام والكلام والحركة
meaning.en_detailed: The root ṣ-w-m (صَوْم) occurs 14 times, denoting abstention in its most concentrated form—chiefly from food, drink, and (in Maryam's case) speech. Its foundational verse is 2:183, where siyām is prescribed upon the believers as the institutional fast, while 19:26 extends the root semantically when Maryam vows 'a fast (ṣawman) for the Merciful'—using the same lexeme to denote ritual silence. In 33:35 the verbal and active participial forms (ṣāʾimūn/ṣāʾimāt) frame fasting as part of the comprehensive catalogue of believers, and Ibn Faris reads the root's core as imsāk (restraint), making ṣawm a species of broader abstinence whose etymology is shared across Hebrew and Aramaic.
meaning.ar_definition: الإمساك عن الطعام والشراب والكلام؛ الكف عن الشيء

quranic_analysis.sawm_vs_imsak: Sawm = Quranic term for religious fasting/abstention. Imsak = general restraint. Ibn Faris: sawm is a species of imsak.

hadith_evidence.ar: مَنْ صَامَ رَمَضَانَ إِيمَانًا وَاحْتِسَابًا غُفِرَ لَهُ مَا تَقَدَّمَ مِنْ ذَنْبِهِ
hadith_evidence.en: Whoever fasts Ramadan with faith and seeking reward, his past sins are forgiven.

meaning.en: Truth, sincerity, charity, friendship. Ibn Faris: core = strength/rigidity in speech and action. Sadaqa = speak truth/fulfill. Saddaqa = believe/affirm. Tasaddaqa = give charity. Sidq = truthfulness. Sadaqah = charity (proof of sincerity). Siddiq = eminently truthful (Joseph, Mary). Sadiq = friend (lit. truthful one). Cognate: Hebrew tzedek.
meaning.ar: الصلابة والقوة في القول — الصدق: ضد الكذب
meaning.en_detailed: Built on the triliteral ṣ-d-q (صِدْق) and appearing 155 times, this root conflates verbal truthfulness with the rigour that backs sincere speech, branching into charity (ṣadaqah) and the superlative of truthfulness (ṣiddīq). Its central devotional thrust appears at 9:103 where the Prophet is told to 'take ṣadaqah from their wealth—it purifies them and causes them to grow,' linking financial outflow to inward sincerity. The root's honorific reaches its apex with Yūsuf called 'O ṣiddīq' (12:46), while 33:8 ('Ask the people of truth [ṣidq] about their truth') elevates ṣidq to a settled cosmic category beyond mere contrast with kadhib. Sadaqah, etymologically the proof of sidq, anchors the root in Islamic ethics.
meaning.ar_definition: ضد الكذب؛ مطابقة الكلام للواقع؛ الصدقة من تمام الصدق

quranic_analysis.sadaqah_etymology: Sadaqah from sidq — charity PROVES sincerity of faith.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *ṣdq = 'to be true, right, just'. Ṣadaqa = to speak truth. Ṣidq = truthfulness. Ṣadaqah = charity (given in truthfulness). Al-Ṣiddīq = the Truthful One (title of Abu Bakr).

hadith_evidence.ar: عَلَيْكُمْ بِالصِّدْقِ فَإِنَّ الصِّدْقَ يَهْدِي إِلَى الْبِرِّ
hadith_evidence.en: Adhere to truthfulness, for truthfulness leads to righteousness.

meaning.en: To judge, rule; wisdom, perfection. Ibn Faris: core = restraining (putting bit in horse mouth). Judgment prevents wrongdoing; wisdom restrains from error; perfection prevents flaw. Hakam (45x) = to judge. Hakim (97x) = All-Wise (Divine Name). Hikmah (20x) = wisdom. Muhkam (2x) = definitive (verses, 3:7).
meaning.ar: المنع — الحكم: منع الظلم. والحكمة: منع الخطأ
meaning.en_detailed: Spanning the triliteral ḥ-k-m (حُكْم) and tallying 210 occurrences, this root unifies judicial restraint with wisdom, since for Ibn Faris both judgment and wisdom 'prevent' (ḥ-k-m = man')—the former restraining wrong, the latter restraining error. The Quran names al-Ḥakīm as a divine attribute ~97 times, usually paired with al-ʿAlīm, as in 4:58 where God commands to 'judge between them with justice (bi'l-ʿadl)' and at 16:125 enjoins calling 'to the way of your Lord with ḥikmah.' Verses 11:1 and 3:7 use muḥkam and uḥkimat to mark the Quran's structural perfection, distinguishing decisive (muḥkamāt) verses from ambiguous (mutashābihāt) ones.
meaning.ar_definition: القضاء بالعدل؛ العلم والفقه؛ المنع من الفساد

quranic_analysis.al_hakim: Al-Hakim = ~93x as Divine Name, always paired with al-Aziz or al-Alim.

cognates.hebrew: חָכַם (ḥākam) — to be wise; חָכָם (ḥākām) — wise man

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *ḥkm = 'to be wise → to judge'. The semantic unity of wisdom and judgment is preserved: the ḥakīm judges with wisdom. In the Quran, al-Ḥakīm (The All-Wise) is always paired with al-ʿAlīm (The All-Knowing) — divine wisdom grounded in complete knowledge.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِذَا حَكَمَ الْحَاكِمُ فَاجْتَهَدَ فَأَصَابَ فَلَهُ أَجْرَانِ
hadith_evidence.en: When a judge rules and strives and is correct, he has two rewards.

meaning.en: To go, depart, perish; gold. Famous tension: dhahaba (verb) = transience vs dhahab (noun) = enduring gold. Dhahaba bi- = to take away (2:17). Adhhaba (IV) = to remove (11:114 — good deeds remove evil). Dhahab = gold. Madhhab = school of thought (lit. place one goes). Gold named from dhahaba — gold that circulates/goes from hand to hand. Cognate: Hebrew zahav.
meaning.ar: الذَّهاب والمرور — والذَّهب: سمي لأنه يذهب
meaning.en_detailed: From the letters ḏ-h-b (ذَهَب) and appearing 56 times, the root shuttles between transience and the metal that symbolises it—dhahaba as verb ('to go, pass') and dhahab as the noun 'gold' that 'goes from hand to hand.' The paradox surfaces at 3:14 ('the love of dhahab is made beautiful to mankind') and 11:114 ('good deeds remove [yudhhibna] evil deeds'), where the same root describes what is taken away and the most enduring of substances. The cosmological question at 81:26 ('Where are you going [tadhhabūn]?') and the maʿādh-style orientation toward return give the verb its eschatological weight; madhhab later abstracts the root into 'school of thought' through Jewish, Christian, and Islamic jurisprudential tradition.
meaning.ar_definition: المعدن النفيس المعروف؛ الذهاب والمضي؛ المذهب والرأي

derived_forms.meaning: to go, depart; with bi-: take away

quranic_analysis.madhhab: Madhhab = place one goes -> path -> school of thought. Hanafi, Maliki, etc.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *ḏhb = 'to go → gold'. Dhahaba = to go. Dhahab = gold. 'The love of gold (dhahab)' (3:14) — the human attraction to precious metals.

hadith_evidence.ar: ذَهَب — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 56 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root *hb (ذَهَب) appears 56 times in the Quran, including 2:17.

meaning.en: To possess, own, rule; king, sovereignty, angel. Ibn Faris: core = strength and capability. Mulk = sovereignty (48x, 67:1). Malik = king (15x, Divine Name 20:114). Mālik = owner (4x, 1:4 Master of Judgment). Malak = angel (88x — distinct root from Ge'ez). Malakūt = dominion (4x, 6:75, Aramaic loan). Hebrew: melekh.
meaning.ar: القُدْرَة والشِّدَّة — المُلك: سَعَة التَّصَرُّف
meaning.en_detailed: Traced through m-l-k (مُلْك) with 206 occurrences, the root develops three branches: mulk (sovereignty), malik (king), and malak (angel)—the latter probably via Ethiopic malʾak. The Quran concentrates sovereignty exclusively in God: at 3:26 He is 'Mālik al-Mulk' and 67:1 declares 'Blessed is He in whose hand is the mulk.' The theology of dominion reaches its visionary peak at 6:75 where Ibrāhīm is shown 'the malakūt of the heavens and earth,' contrasting the visible kingdom with its invisible architecture. 1:4's 'Mālik of yawm al-dīn' and 20:114's 'al-Malik al-Ḥaqq' close the circle, reserving all rulership for the divine king.
meaning.ar_definition: السلطان والقدرة؛ الملكوت؛ التصرف بالأمر والنهي

quranic_analysis.malak_note: Malak (angel) is NOT from mlk root — borrowed from Ge'ez malak (messenger). Malakut = Aramaic malkuta.

cognates.hebrew: מָלַךְ (mālak) — to reign, be king; מֶלֶךְ (melek) — king

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *mlk = 'to counsel, decide → to rule, reign'. Arabic developed three branches: (1) mulk = sovereignty (the abstract quality of kingship), (2) malik = king (the person), and (3) malak/malāʾikah = angel (heavenly messenger). The angel connection is debated — some see it as a loanword from Ethiopic (Ge'ez malʾak=messenger), others trace it to a separate root meaning 'to send with a message'. The Quranic malakūt (dominion) is a loan from Aramaic malkūtā.

theological_dimensions: Al-Malik (The King), Al-Mālik (The Owner), Mālik al-Mulk (Owner of Sovereignty) — triple divine royal titles
Mulk vs malakūt — the visible kingdom vs the invisible spiritual dominion shown to Abraham (6:75)
The malāʾikah (angels) as the heavenly court — qawānitūn (obedient servants, 16:49-50)

hadith_evidence.ar: مُلْك — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 206 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root mlk (مُلْك) appears 206 times in the Quran, including 1:4.

meaning.en: Evil, bad, wickedness; sparks. Ibn Faris: core = scattering/dispersion — evil scatters harmony, sparks scatter from fire. Sharr (27x) = evil/bad — opposite of khayr. Sharar (1x, 77:32) = sparks of Hellfire (the physical root meaning preserved). Ashrar = evil ones (38:62). Used intensively in al-Mu'awwidhatayn (Surah 113-114): "from the evil (sharr) of..." repeated 5x. Superlative: sharra al-dawābb = worst of creatures (8:22).
meaning.ar: الشَّرّ: خلاف الخير — كل ما يضر ويؤذي — وأصل الكلمة: النشر والتفريق
meaning.en_detailed: Rooted in sh-r-r (شَرّ), appearing 31 times, this lexeme denotes that which scatters harmony—hence Ibn Faris links it to the sharar (sparks) flung from a fire, the only physical survival of the root in 77:32 ('it throws sparks [sharar] like castles'). The moral sense is fully developed at 2:216 where believers are told 'perhaps you hate a thing, though it is good for you, and love a thing though it is evil [sharr] for you,' setting sharr against khayr in the Quran's most fundamental ethical pairing. The superlative form marks the dishonourable at 8:22 ('sharr al-dawābb'), and al-Mu'awwidhatayn's fivefold repetition of 'sharr' (113:1–5) draws on this lexical threat against all created harm.

quranic_analysis.sharr_vs_khayr: Sharr (evil) is the Quranic opposite of khayr (good). Tested with both (21:35). Allah hastens khayr but delays sharr (10:11).

dual_sense: Ibn Faris: root originally meant scattering (like sparks from fire). Moral evil is that which scatters harmony and well-being — a metaphorical extension from physical dispersion.

hadith_evidence.ar: شَرّ — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 31 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root $rr (شَرّ) appears 31 times in the Quran, including 2:216.

meaning.en: To calculate, reckon, think, suppose; sufficiency. Ibn Faris: core = enumeration/computation (al-'add wa al-ihsa'). Tripartite Quranic meaning: (1) Reckoning/account — hisāb (39x), yawm al-hisāb (Day of Account); (2) Thinking/supposing — hasiba (44x), classified among zanna and her sisters; (3) Sufficiency/enough — hasb (11x) — "Allah is sufficient for us" (3:173). Al-Hasīb = The Reckoner (Divine Name).
meaning.ar: العد والإحصاء — الحساب: المحاسبة — والحسب: الكفاية
meaning.en_detailed: The triconsonantal root ح س ب (حِسَاب) — 109 Quranic occurrences — fundamentally expresses Reckoning; account; calculation; sufficiency. The eschatological pole is fixed by 75:3 ('Does man think [ayaḥsabu] We will not gather his bones?'), while 2:281–282 frames human contracts within the same root, demanding witnesses and a scribe before debt. The third branch yields the Quran's most counter-intuitive invocation at 3:173, where the persecuted believers declare 'ḥasbunā Allāhu wa niʿma al-wakīl'—trust itself a function of calculated sufficiency. 65:3 ('He provides from where he does not expect [lā yaḥtasibu]') extends reckoning into providence.
meaning.ar_definition: العَدُّ؛ الإحصاء؛ المحاسبة على الأعمال؛ الكفاية

quranic_analysis.tripartite: One root, three Quranic domains: calculation, thinking, sufficiency. All trace to Ibn Faris core: enumeration.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *ḥšb = 'to calculate → think, consider'. Ḥasiba = to reckon, think. Ḥisāb = reckoning, accounting. Yawm al-Ḥisāb = the Day of Reckoning. 'Allah is swift in reckoning (sarīʿ al-ḥisāb)' (2:202).

hadith_evidence.ar: حَاسِبُوا أَنْفُسَكُمْ قَبْلَ أَنْ تُحَاسَبُوا
hadith_evidence.en: Take account of yourselves before you are taken to account.

meaning.en_short: Sin, crime, transgression, wrongdoing; to incur guilt
meaning.en: The root hamza-thāʾ-mīm denotes sin (ʾithm), crime, and wrongdoing in the Quran. It encompasses both the act of transgression and the state of bearing guilt. The Form I verb ʾathima means 'he committed a sin'; the nominal ʾithm appears frequently as the consequence of violating divine law. Associated with deliberate disobedience, especially in matters of oath-breaking, injustice, and prohibited acts.
meaning.ar: الذَّنْبُ وَالْمَعْصِيَةُ وَالْإِثْمُ الَّذِي يَسْتَحِقُّ عَلَيْهِ الْعِقَابُ
meaning.en_detailed: Triliteral Arabic root hamza-thāʾ-mīm (أ-ث-م), 48 Quranic occurrences, denoting sin (ʾithm), crime, and wrongdoing — both the act of transgression and the resultant state of bearing guilt before divine law. The nominal ʾithm appears 35 times and is among the most frequent Quranic terms for sin, parallel to Hebrew ʾāšām (guilt-offering in Leviticus) and Ugaritic ảṯm; al-Rāghib glosses ʾithm as 'delay from goodness.' Key verses include 2:173 wa-inna taʿtahū ʾithman fa-ʾinnahu ʾithm — affirming that what is prohibited carries ʾithm unless under duress (the principle of necessity in Islamic law); 33:58 pairing ʾithm with buhtān (slander); 2:283 declaring the heart of one who conceals testimony 'sinful' (dhanīb). The Form I verb ʾathima (to sin) occurs 4 times; the active participle ʾāthim (sinner) 9 times.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر أ ث م — 48 مرة — Sin

cognates.hebrew: אָשָׁם (ʾāšām) — guilt, guilt offering; אָשֵׁם (ʾāšēm) — guilty

etymology.semantic_evolution: Proto-Semitic 'guilt/offense' is preserved remarkably consistently across Hebrew (ʾāšām guilt-offering in Leviticus), Aramaic, and Arabic. The Arabic ʾithm directly parallels the Hebrew ʾāšām both in meaning and the legal-theological context of liability before God.

derived_forms.key_verse: 2:283 — whoever conceals testimony, his heart is sinful

usage_patterns: ʾithm often appears in legal contexts describing prohibited acts

lexicographical_sources: Raghib al-Isfahani: ʾithm is delay from goodness
theological_dimensions: ʾithm as the objective moral value of a prohibited act
hadith_evidence: Al-ʾithmu mā ḥāka fī ṣ-ṣadr

meaning.en: To return, repeat, go back, restore. Ibn Faris: core = return to a previous state. Āda (I, 18x) = to return. Aʿāda (IV, 18x) = to cause to return/repeat — almost exclusively divine: "He originates creation then repeats it" (10:4, 85:13). Maʿād = place of return, the Hereafter (28:85). ʿĪd = festival — recurring celebration (5:114). Proper noun ʿĀd (24x) = the ancient tribe.
meaning.ar: العود: رجوع الشيء إلى حاله التي كان عليها — والمعاد: المرجع
meaning.en_detailed: Built on ʿ-w-d (عَوْد) with 63 occurrences (excluding the proper noun ʿĀd), the root denotes the return of a thing to its prior state and is overwhelmingly applied to God's repeated creative act. The divine cycle appears at 10:4 ('He originates creation, then repeats it [yuʿīduhu]') and 85:13 ('Indeed He originates and repeats [yuʿīd]'), with 7:29 supplying the human counterpart ('As He originated you, so you will return [taʿūdūn]'). Eschatology gives the noun maʿād ('place of return,' 28:85) its fullest meaning, while ʿīd ('festival,' 5:114) shows the same root generating recurring celebration through Jesus's prayer for his followers.
meaning.ar_definition: الرجوع إلى الشيء بعد الانصراف عنه؛ التكرار؛ الإعادة

derived_forms.meaning: to cause to return, repeat, restore

quranic_analysis.note: 24 occurrences are the proper noun ʿĀd (tribe of Hud). Excluding proper noun: 39 verbal/derived uses.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *ʿwd = 'to return, go back'. ʿĀda = to return. ʿĪd = festival (cyclic return). Maʿād = place of return (resurrection). 'As He originated you, you will return (taʿūdūna)' (7:29) — the return to God.

hadith_evidence.ar: عَوْد — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 63 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root Ewd (عَوْد) appears 63 times in the Quran, including 7:29.

meaning.en: To seek, request, demand, search for. Ibn Faris: core = seeking/searching (ṭalab). Rare in Quran (4x) but extremely productive in Islamic vocabulary: ṭālib (student/seeker of knowledge), maṭlūb (sought/required), ṭalab (request). 22:73 has both ṭālib and maṭlūb in one verse — "the seeker and the sought are both weak." Descendants: Turkish talep, Persian/Urdu talab.
meaning.ar: التماس الشيء وطلبه — الطالب: ملتمس العلم
meaning.en_detailed: Though rare in the Quran—only 4 occurrences of the root ṭ-l-b (طَلَب)—its semantic field of pursuit and demand is foundational. The root frames cosmic alternation at 7:54, where 'the night seeks [yaṭlubuhu] the day rapidly,' and reappears as the striking pair ṭālib/maṭlūb at 22:73 ('the seeker and the sought are both weak'), a verse which became central to Ṣūfī readings of the lover and the Beloved. From 18:41 ('You would never be able to seek it [ṭalaban]') the Quran draws the moral that all seeking is finite and divinely bounded, and post-Quranic usage—ṭālib al-ʿilm, maṭlūb—constructs entire pedagogical vocabularies from this lean scriptural stem.

quranic_analysis.islamic_vocab: Despite only 4 Quranic occurrences, root is foundation for: ṭālib al-ʿilm (student of knowledge), maṭlūb (wanted/required person), ṭalab (demand/petition).

hadith_evidence.ar: طَلَب — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 4 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root Tlb (طَلَب) appears 4 times in the Quran, including 7:54.

meaning.en: To turn, revolve, circulate. Ibn Faris: core = circulation/rotation. Dāra (I, 1x) = to turn/revolve (33:19 — eyes revolving). Adāra (IV, 1x) = to cause to turn/carry out (2:282 — commerce circulation). Dār (48x) = house/dwelling — the dominant Quranic form (dār al-ākhirah = the Hereafter, dār al-salām = Paradise, dār al-bawār = ruin). Dāʾirah (3x) = turn of fortune/misfortune. Dayyār (1x) = inhabitant (71:26). NOTE: "alternating days" (3:140) and "wealth circulation" (59:7) are from root d-w-l, NOT d-w-r.
meaning.ar: الدوران — الدار: محل الإقامة — والدائرة: النائبة
meaning.en_detailed: From d-w-r (دَوْر) with 55 occurrences, the root's core is circulation, producing the dominant noun dār (abode, 48x) along with the verbal dāra ('revolve,' 33:19) and the rare but pointed dawrah. The Quran uses dār to map both earthly and eternal dwellings—dār al-salām at 6:127 ('the Home of Peace'), dār al-bawār at 14:28 (the abode of perdition)—tying location to moral outcome. 5:52 captures the verbal sense ('We fear a dāʾira may strike us'), and 71:26's prayer to leave 'no dayyār on earth' shows the root extending to inhabitants of cycles, not merely cycles themselves; the root must be distinguished from d-w-l, which carries the temporal sense of alternation.
meaning.ar_definition: الحركة الدائرية؛ تَعَاقُبُ الأيام بين الناس؛ النَّوْبَة

quranic_analysis.important_note: Root d-w-r is distinct from d-w-l. 3:140 (nudāwiluhā — We alternate) and 59:7 (dawlah — wealth circulation) use d-w-l, NOT d-w-r.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *dwr = 'to turn, revolve, circle'. Dāra = to turn, rotate. Dār = house, abode (where one 'circles' — the courtyard). Dawrah = cycle, period. Al-dunyā = the 'nearer' abode — the house of this world.

hadith_evidence.ar: دَوْر — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 55 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root dwr (دَوْر) appears 55 times in the Quran, including 33:19.

meaning.en: To be wide, spacious, encompass, have capacity. Ibn Faris: core = opposite of narrowness. Wasiʿa (6x) = to encompass — exclusively theological: Allah's knowledge/mercy/throne encompasses all (2:255, 7:156). Wusʿ (5x) = capacity — "Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity" (2:286). Wāsiʿ (9x) = All-Encompassing (Divine Name) — paired with ʿAlīm. Wāsiʿah (4x) = spacious/vast (of earth, 4:97). Mūsiʿ (2x) = wealthy, expander (2:236, 51:47 — the universe expander).
meaning.ar: الوسع: ضد الضيق — والوسع: الطاقة والقدرة
meaning.en_detailed: Built on w-s-ʿ (وَسْع), with 32 occurrences, this root names a divine attribute—the All-Encompassing (al-Wāsiʿ)—and the human condition of capacity before it. The most celebrated verse, 2:255 (Āyat al-Kursī), declares that 'His throne extends [wasiʿa] over the heavens and earth,' anchoring the cosmological claim, while 7:156 follows with 'My mercy encompasses [wasiʿat] all things.' Counterbalancing the divine vastness, 2:286's 'God does not burden a soul beyond its wusʿ' limits the demand to the capacity, and 51:47's 'We are its Expanders [mūsiʿūn]' turns the root cosmogonic—the universe itself an act of divine broadening.

quranic_analysis.al_wasi: Al-Wāsiʿ (All-Encompassing) as Divine Name: 7 of 9 times paired with ʿAlīm. Once: Wāsiʿu al-maghfirah (vast in forgiveness, 53:32).

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ الدِّينَ يُسْرٌ
hadith_evidence.en: Religion is easy.

meaning.en: To follow, succeed, obey; follower. Ibn Faris: core = following behind. Ittabaʿa (VIII, 136x) = the central Quranic concept of intentional following — of revelation (7:3), prophets (3:31), truth vs desire. Tabiʿa (I, 9x) = to follow/come after. Atbaʿa (IV, 15x) = to cause to follow/pursue. The key verse: "If you love Allah, follow me (ittabiʿūnī)" (3:31). NOTE: The root is ت ب ع (t-b-'), NOT ط ب ع (ṭ-b-' = to seal). The Buckwalter TbE gives the wrong root.
meaning.ar: الاتباع — التبع: من يتبع غيره — والاتباع: قبول ما يؤمر به
meaning.en_detailed: From the letters t-b-ʿ (تَبَع), the root appears 172 times and centres on the volitional act of following—the very grammar of religious commitment. 3:31 supplies its doctrinal hinge ('If you love God, follow me [ittabiʿūnī]'), and 7:3 universalises it ('Follow what is revealed to you from your Lord'), making ittibāʿ the privileged mode of adherence to revelation. Its negative counterpart at 47:3 ('believers follow truth; disbelievers follow falsehood') structures the ethical binary, while 4:92's muṭatābiʿayn ('two consecutive') extends the root temporally. The ṭābiʿūn, the second-generation 'Followers,' drew their foundational identity from this lexeme that distinguishes correct adherence from blind following (taqlīd).

quranic_analysis.ibn_faris: Core = following behind — physically, in rank, in obedience. The central Islamic ethical binary: ittibāʿ al-haqq (following truth) vs ittibāʿ al-hawā (following desire).

important_note: This is root ت ب ع (tbE in Buckwalter lowercase), NOT ط ب ع (TbE uppercase = to seal). The original file entry 48 listed TbE with count 11 — this was the WRONG root. Correct root tbE has 172 occurrences.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *tbʿ = 'to follow after'. The Quranic ittibāʿ (following) is the central category of religious adherence — following the Prophet, following guidance, vs following desires. The tābiʿūn (Followers/Successors) are the second generation of Islam.

hadith_evidence.ar: تَبَع — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 172 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root tbE (تَبَع) appears 172 times in the Quran, including 2:38.

meaning.en: To promise, threaten; appointed time. Ibn Faris: core = making a binding commitment — for good or evil. Context determines meaning: waʿd = promise (good) AND threat (evil). Waʿada (I, 70x) = to promise/threaten. Wāʿada (III, 4x) = to appoint a time (2:51 — forty nights with Moses). Tawāʿada (VI, 1x) = mutual appointment. Waʿd (49x) = promise. Waʿīd (6x) = threat/warning. Mīʿād (6x) = appointed time — "Allah does not break the mīʿād" (3:9). Mawʿūd (1x) = the Promised Day (85:2).
meaning.ar: الوعد: التزام أمر من الخير والشر — والميعاد: الوقت المعين
meaning.en_detailed: Occurring 151 times across w-ʿ-d (وَعْد), the root carries the Quran's most fraught ambivalence, covering both promise (good) and threat (evil)—context alone distinguishes them. The divine promise is repeatedly affirmed: 3:9 ('God does not break the mīʿād'), 4:95 ('the waʿd of truth'), and 85:2 ('by the Promised Day') show its eschatological weight; meanwhile 19:54 praises Ismāʿīl as 'ṣādiq al-waʿd' (true to his promise). Form III generates the temporal sense at 2:51 ('We appointed [wāʿadnā] with Moses forty nights'), and waʿīd specializes as warning, completing the root's twin registers of divine speech.
meaning.ar_definition: الإخبار بما سيكون من خير أو شر؛ العهد؛ الميعاد

quranic_analysis.ambivalent_root: Same root for promise and threat — context determines. Allah's waʿd to believers = Paradise. To disbelievers = Hell. Satan's waʿd = deception (4:120).

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *wʿd = 'to promise; to threaten'. Waʿada = to promise (good). Waʿīd = threat (punishment). The same root for divine promise and warning — the dual face of eschatology.

hadith_evidence.ar: الْمُؤْمِنُ يَأْكُلُ فِي مِعًى وَاحِدٍ وَالْكَافِرُ يَأْكُلُ فِي سَبْعَةِ أَمْعَاءٍ
hadith_evidence.en: The believer eats in one intestine and the disbeliever eats in seven intestines.

meaning.en: To be near, approach, draw close; relatives. Ibn Faris: core = nearness/approach — opposite of buʿd (distance). Qariba (I, 11x) = to approach (mostly prohibitive: "do not approach"). Qarraba (II, 5x) = to bring near (qurbān = sacrifice/offering, 5:27). Iqtaraba (VIII, 5x) = to draw near (54:1 — the Hour draws near). Qarīb (26x) = near/imminent — "I am near" (2:186). Aqrab (19x) = nearer — "We are nearer than his jugular vein" (50:16). Qurbā (16x) = nearness of kin. Muqarrabūn (8x) = those brought near to Allah (angels, righteous).
meaning.ar: القرب: ضد البعد — والقربان: ما يتقرب به — والقريب: الداني
meaning.en_detailed: From the triliteral q-r-b (قَرَب), occurring 96 times, this root binds spatial, temporal, spiritual, and relational nearness into one semantic axis. The most striking claim is at 50:16 ('We are nearer [aqrab] to him than his jugular vein'), with 2:186 supplying the divine declaration 'I am near [qarīb]; I answer the caller's call.' The eschatological escalation culminates at 54:1 ('The Hour has drawn near [iqtarabat]'), while the spiritual imperative is given in 96:19 ('prostrate and draw near [iqtarib]'). Through qurbān (offering, 5:27) and muqarrabūn (those brought near, 56:11), the root systematises how humans cross the distance to God.
meaning.ar_definition: ضد البعد؛ الدنو في المكان والزمان والنسب

quranic_analysis.semantic_field: Physical (approach a tree, 2:35), temporal (the Hour is near), spiritual (Allah is near, draw near to Him), relational (near kin, dhu al-qurbā), ritual (qurbān as means of nearness).

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *qrb = 'to be near, approach'. Qaruba = to be near. Qurb = nearness. Qurbān = offering (what brings one near). 'We are nearer (aqrabu) to him than his jugular vein' (50:16) — divine proximity.

hadith_evidence.ar: قَرَبَ — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 96 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root qrb (قَرَبَ) appears 96 times in the Quran, including 2:186.

meaning.en: The root k-r-h expresses hatred, dislike, aversion, and unwillingness. Appears 41 times across eight derived forms. Kariha (I, 17x) = to dislike. Karraha (II, 1x) = to make hateful (49:7). Akraha (IV, 5x) = to compel. Key distinction: karh (كَرْه, 5x) = external coerced unwillingness; kurh (كُرْه, 3x) = internal hardship/hatefulness. Ikrah (2x) = compulsion — la ikraha fi al-din (2:256). The Quran teaches divine wisdom behind human dislike: perhaps you dislike something though it is good for you (2:216).
meaning.ar: جذر ك-ر-ه: الكراهة والبغض — لا إكراه في الدين — وعسى أن تكرهوا شيئا وهو خير لكم
meaning.en_detailed: The root k-r-h (ك ر ه), with 41 occurrences, spans dislike and external compulsion—divided lexically into karh (external unwillingness), kurh (internal hardship), and ikrah (compulsion). The Quran establishes freedom of conscience at 2:256 ('la ikrāha fī al-dīn'), with 16:106 permitting forced utterance when the heart remains firm. The root's deepest meditation is at 2:216: 'Perhaps you hate [takrahū] a thing though it is good for you,' exposing divine wisdom behind human aversion. 49:7 reverses polarity ('God made faith beloved and disbelief hateful [karrahahā]'), ascribing the very love of faith to divine causation.

etymology.semantic_evolution: Proto-Semitic aversion → Arabic developed three branches: (1) subjective dislike (kariha), (2) external compulsion (karh/akraha), (3) objective detestability (makruh). Ikrah became central to Islamic legal theory on free will and duress.

derived_forms.meaning: to make hateful (49:7 — Allah made disbelief hateful)

key_nominals.meaning: External unwillingness, coercion (5x) — paired with tawan (willingly)
Internal hardship/hatefulness (3x) — fighting is hateful to you (2:216)
Compulsion (2x) — 2:256 la ikraha fi al-din; 24:33 force in exploitation
One who dislikes (7x) — of hypocrites averse to truth
Hateful/detestable (1x, 17:38) — all evil is hateful to your Lord

quranic_analysis.theme: Divine wisdom behind human dislike
quranic_analysis.detail: Perhaps you dislike something and it is good for you — establishes that divine decree transcends human preference.

quranic_analysis.theme: Freedom of conscience
quranic_analysis.detail: La ikraha fi al-din — faith cannot be coerced. Exception: forced utterance while heart remains firm in faith.

quranic_analysis.theme: Cosmic submission
quranic_analysis.detail: All creation submits to Allah willingly or unwillingly (tawan aw karhan).

quranic_analysis.theme: Divine causation of aversion
quranic_analysis.detail: Allah makes faith beloved and disbelief hateful — transformation of human inclination as divine act.

lexicographical_sources.ibn_faris: Single root: opposite of love. Karihtu al-shay = I detested it. Karh = hardship. Kurh = forcing unwillingness. Ikrah = compelling by force.
lexicographical_sources.al_raghib: Karh (external compulsion) vs Kurh (internal hardship). Subtle distinction: karh from another, kurh from the self. Ikrah = compelling another to what they dislike.
lexicographical_sources.lane: Kariha-hu = he disliked/hated it (opposite of ahabba). Karh = unwillingness from external constraint. Kurh = that from internal dislike. Karraha = made hateful. Akraha = compelled/forced.

theological_dimensions: Free will vs divine decree: 2:216 teaches what humans dislike may be divinely ordained good
Freedom of religion: 2:256 la ikraha fi al-din establishes that faith cannot be coerced
Faith under duress: 16:106 provides apostasy exception for compelled utterance with inward faith
Cosmic submission: all creation submits willingly or unwillingly (3:83, 13:15)
Divine causation of inclination: 49:7 attributes love of faith and hatred of disbelief to Allah
hadith_evidence: Allah has forgiven my ummah for what they do under compulsion (ikrah), forgetfulness, and force (Bukhari, Kitab al-Ikrah)
The Prophet sought refuge from being forced — practical application of ikrah principle
Ammar ibn Yasir: forced to utter disbelief while heart firm in faith — 16:106 revealed about him (Bukhari, Tafsir Surah al-Nahl)
cross_references: HBB (حب) — love: direct antonym of k-r-h
JBR (جبر) — compulsion/constraint: related to ikrah concept
RSHD (رشد) — right guidance: paired with ikrah in 2:256
SXT (سخط) — divine displeasure: related to divine karaha
GHFR (غفر) — forgiveness: sought for coerced actions

meaning.en_short: To witness, testify, be present; martyr
meaning.en: To witness, testify, bear witness, be present. 160 occurrences. Shahida (44x)=to testify—Allah bears witness that there is no deity except Him (3:18). Shahadah (23x)=testimony/evidence; also the creedal declaration. Shahid (56x)=witness/martyr; divine name al-Shahid. Ash-hada (7x)=to call to witness—the Covenant of Alast (7:172). Istashhada (2x)=to call for witnesses (2:282). Ummah as shuhada ala al-nas (2:143)=witnesses over humanity. Martyrdom (shahadah): those killed in Allah path are alive with their Lord (3:169). Proto-Semitic *š-h-d, Syriac sāhədā (witness/martyr—parallel to Greek martys).
meaning.ar: الشهادة: الحضور والعلم — شهد الله أنه لا إله إلا هو — لتكونوا شهداء على الناس
meaning.en_detailed: From sh-h-d (شَهِد) with 160 occurrences, this root unifies presence, observation, and truthful testimony—hence the martyr (shahīd) is one who witnesses through death. The divine Self-Witness anchors the doctrine at 3:18 ('God bears witness [shahida Allāh] that there is no god but He'), and 7:172 recalls the primordial covenant where God made all souls testify against themselves. The Quran appoints the Muslim community 'witnesses over mankind [shuhadāʾ ʿalā al-nās]' at 2:143, while 3:169–170 promises that 'those killed in God's way are alive with their Lord.' The legal ramifications span 2:282–283 (debt witnesses) to 24:4 (the liʿān process).
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To witness, testify, be present; martyr

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *šhd = 'to be present → to witness'. The root is central to Islamic legal and theological vocabulary: the shahādah (testimony of faith), the shahīd (a witness and also a martyr — one who witnesses to faith through death), and shāhid (eyewitness). The concept unifies presence, observation, and truthful testimony.

derived_forms.meaning: to call as witness, make testify

quranic_analysis.theme: God as Witness
quranic_analysis.detail: Allah bears witness: shahida Allahu annahu la ilaha illa huwa (3:18)—divine self-witnessing to tawhid, joined by angels and ulu al-ilm.

quranic_analysis.theme: Ummah as witnesses over mankind
quranic_analysis.detail: The Muslim community designated shuhada ala al-nas—witnesses over humanity; the Prophet is witness over them.

quranic_analysis.theme: Legal testimony
quranic_analysis.detail: Debt contracts: two male witnesses; adultery: four witnesses; false accusation (qadhf): 80 lashes.

quranic_analysis.theme: Martyrdom
quranic_analysis.detail: Martyrs alive with their Lord; the martyr bears ultimate witness through sacrifice.

quranic_analysis.theme: The Primordial Covenant
quranic_analysis.detail: ashhadahum ala anfusihim—God made all souls testify to His Lordship: the pre-eternal mithaq.

lexicographical_sources.ibn_faris: Single core: al-hudur wa al-ilm (presence and knowledge). All derivations return to this.
lexicographical_sources.al_raghib: shahadah = hudur (presence). Three levels: shahadat al-basar (ocular), shahadat al-ilm (knowledge), shahadat al-qalb (heart). The martyr is called such because angels witness his Paradise.
lexicographical_sources.lane: shahida=he was present; he knew; he bore witness. Shahid=witness, also martyr. The semantic shift witness→martyr is shared with Greek martys.

theological_dimensions: Shahadah as first pillar of Islam—ashhadu an la ilaha illa Allah
al-Shahid as divine name: combines omniscience, justice, self-sufficiency
Ummah as shuhada ala al-nas: communal responsibility to bear witness to truth
Martyrdom: the martyr gives ultimate testimony; alive with Lord, provided for
al-Ghayb wa al-Shahadah: Quranic epistemological merism—God encompasses unseen and seen
hadith_evidence: Islam built on five: shahadati an la ilaha illa Allah (Bukhari, Muslim)
Best testimony: la ilaha illa Allah (Ahmad)
Martyrdom expiates all sins except debt (Muslim)
The Prophet sought refuge from being forced—application of ikrah/shahadah principle
cross_references: عل م (ilm)—knowledge: shahadah combines presence + knowledge
حض ر (hDr)—presence: Ibn Faris derives shahadah from hudur

meaning.en_short: To repent, turn back; divine acceptance of repentance
meaning.en: To repent, return, turn back (to God). 87 occurrences—bidirectional: human taba ila (repent to God) and divine taba ala (God turns in mercy). Taba (63x), tawwab (12x intensive—al-Tawwab divine name, paired Rahim 11x), tawbah (7x repentance), tawbatan nasuhan (66:8 sincere repentance). Adam first repented (2:37). 9:117-118: divine tawba for Prophet and three companions left behind at Tabuk. Proto-Semitic *tūb-, Hebrew teshuvah. Ibn Faris: core = rujū (return).
meaning.ar: التوبة: الرجوع — وتوبوا إلى الله جميعا — إن الله يحب التوابين
meaning.en_detailed: Built on t-w-b (تَاب), occurring 87 times, this root is bidirectional—human repentance (tāba ilā) and divine acceptance (tāba ʿalā)—with the reciprocal made explicit at 9:118 ('He turned toward them that they might turn [li-yatūbū]'). The Divine Name al-Tawwāb (~11x) shows habitual divine action, and 2:37 records Adam's 'tābā'—the paradigm of post-fall repentance. The aspirational ideal is tawbatun naṣūḥ at 66:8, sincere repentance of three conditions (regret, cessation, resolve). The root binds every chapter of Islamic ethics: 4:146 (repentance with reform), 2:54 (Moses' intercession for his people), and 25:70 (the wish of sinners to return).
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To repent, turn back; divine acceptance of repentance

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *twb = 'to turn, return'. In Arabic, the meaning specialized to 'repentance' — turning back to God. The unique Quranic feature is that God also 'returns' (tawwāb) to the servant — a reciprocal movement of turning. Tawbah is not merely regret but a complete reorientation of the self toward God.

quranic_analysis.theme: Al-Tawwab: Divine Name
quranic_analysis.detail: 11x divine, 1x human (2:222). Fa''al pattern = habitual, repeated divine action—Allah perpetually returns to accept repentance.

quranic_analysis.theme: Structure of Repentance
quranic_analysis.detail: Three-part pattern: tabu (repented) + wa-aslahu (reformed) + faith and righteous deeds. Inner repentance must produce outward rectification.

quranic_analysis.theme: Divine Prevenience
quranic_analysis.detail: taba alayhim li-yatubu—He turned toward them so that they might turn: God's tawba precedes and enables human tawba.

quranic_analysis.theme: Tawba Nasuh
quranic_analysis.detail: The only adjectival modifier: nasuh = sincere, pure, permanent. Three conditions: regret, cessation, resolve not to return.

lexicographical_sources.ibn_faris: Core = al-ruju (return). Single root meaning: return of a thing to its previous state.
lexicographical_sources.al_raghib: Three elements: regret for past sin, immediate abandonment, resolve not to return. Distinguishes tawbah (from sin), inabah (to Allah), awbah (to God's presence).
lexicographical_sources.lane: taba ilayhi: he returned to him. taba ila Allah: he repented. taba alayhi: He accepted his repentance. Al-Tawwab: Acceptor of Repentance.

theological_dimensions: Bidirectional: divine taba ala precedes human taba ila—God's grace enables repentance
Al-Tawwab: 99 Names—God's fundamental disposition toward acceptance
Tawba nasuh (66:8): sincere, pure, permanent—the ideal of repentance
Istighfar as Prophetic Sunnah (100x daily—Muslim 2702)
Adam's tawba (2:37): first repentance sets paradigm of divine mercy
hadith_evidence: O people, turn in repentance; I turn in repentance 100 times daily (Muslim 2702)
Allah stretches out His hand by night for daytime sinner, and by day for nighttime sinner (Muslim 2759)
Were your sins to reach the clouds, then you sought My forgiveness, I would forgive you (Hadith Qudsi)
Allah rejoices more at His servant's repentance than one finding his camel in the desert (Bukhari 6309, Muslim 2744)
cross_references: غفر (gfr)—forgiveness: consequence of tawbah (40:3 qabil al-tawb + ghafir al-dhanb)

meaning.en: thing, something; to will. 519 occurrences. Shaa (236x)=to will. Shay (283x)=thing. kulli shayin qadir (~45x).
meaning.ar: المشيئة: الإرادة
meaning.en_detailed: With 519 occurrences of the root sh-y-ʾ (شَاءَ), this is one of the Quran's densest semantic axes, covering both the verb shāʾa ('to will') and the most universal noun shayʾ ('thing'). The divine formula 'kulli shayʾ qādir' ('over all things Powerful') recurs ~45 times, anchoring God as the agent over every existing thing. The verbal usage anchors conditional clauses: 'If God wills [in shāʾa Allāh]' frames human planning within divine volition, as at 18:23 ('do not say of any matter, I will do that tomorrow, without [adding] if God wills'). Ibn Faris noted two cores—willing and existence—fused here: what God wills comes into being, so shayʾ names whatever the will brings forth.

etymology.semantic_evolution: Proto-Semitic volitional → Arabic: will → thing

quranic_analysis.theme: Kulli shayin qadir
quranic_analysis.detail: Most repeated divine-epithet

lexicographical_sources.ibn_faris: Two cores: will and existent
lexicographical_sources.lane: shaa: he willed

hadith_evidence.ar: تَدَبَّرُوا الْقُرْآنَ فَإِنَّهُ حُجَّةٌ لَكُمْ أَوْ عَلَيْكُمْ
hadith_evidence.en: Reflect upon the Quran, for it is either a proof for you or against you.
hadith_evidence.source: Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim via ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb

meaning.en: Day. 405x. Yawm = day—40+ Judgment Day epithets (Yawm al-Din 1:4). Yawma'idhin (~25x). Six days creation (7:54). Proto-Semitic *yawm-, Hebrew yom. Alternation of night/day as divine sign.
meaning.en_detailed: From the simple triliteral y-w-m (يَوْم), occurring 405 times, the Quran builds its primary temporal unit from the daily daylight of 7:54 ('the night pursues the day, seeking it rapidly') to the eternal Day of Judgment. The foundational confession at 1:4—'Mālik of yawm al-dīn'—pivots the root onto the Final Hour, which receives more than 40 distinct epithets (yawm al-qiyāma, yawm al-ḥisāb, yawm al-jamʿ, yawm al-fasl). The plural ayyām (30x) preserves the root in historical time, especially the six-day creation at 7:54, 10:3, and 32:4. Yawmaʾidhin ('that Day') recurs ~70 times as the eschatological pivot of every peroration.

quranic_analysis.theme: Judgment Day
quranic_analysis.detail: Maliki yawm al-din. 40+ epithets for the Final Day.

quranic_analysis.theme: Creation in six days
quranic_analysis.detail: Khalaqa al-samawati wa al-arda fi sittati ayyam.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *ywm = 'day'. The Quranic yawm is the primary temporal unit — from creation ('six days') to judgment ('Yawm al-Dīn'). The plural ayyām (days) alternates with singular yawm in a rhythmic pattern throughout the Quran.

hadith_evidence.ar: تَدَبَّرُوا الْقُرْآنَ فَإِنَّهُ حُجَّةٌ لَكُمْ أَوْ عَلَيْكُمْ
hadith_evidence.en: Reflect upon the Quran, for it is either a proof for you or against you.
hadith_evidence.source: Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim via ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb

meaning.en: Punishment, torment; also sweet/palatable water. 373 occurrences. Adhdhaba (II, 41x) = to punish (exclusively divine subject). Adhab (322x) = punishment/torment. Adhb (2x) = sweet water (25:53, 35:12—contrasted with salty). Ibn Faris: al-man' wa al-habs (prevention and restraint)—punishment 'restrains' from one's will; sweet water is 'restrained' from saltiness. Rich taxonomy of intensifiers: alim (painful, ~65x), azim (grievous), shadid (severe), muhin (humiliating), muqim (permanent), ghaliz (harsh). Shadid al-Adhab = Severe in Punishment.
meaning.ar: العذاب: المنع والحبس — إن عذابي لشديد
meaning.en_detailed: Occurring 373 times across ʿ-ḏ-b (عَذَّبَ), the root splits into two branches linked by Ibn Faris to a single idea—prevention and restraint: punishment as that which prevents the wrongdoer from will, and sweet water as that which prevents salt from spoiling it. The punishment sense dominates (322x for ʿadhāb), with ʿadhb (sweet water) surviving only at 25:53 and 35:12. The Quran constructs a rich intensifier system—ʿadhāb alīm (painful, ~65x), shadīd (severe), muḥīn (humiliating), muqīm (permanent)—and reserves adhdhaba (Form II) for divine and human contexts: 2:201 ('whoever does evil, He gives them a taste of punishment'), and 33:33's purification of Ahl al-Bayt.

etymology.proto_semitic: *ġ-d-b — to restrain, prevent; to be bitter (metathesis)
etymology.semantic_evolution: Ibn Faris: single root = al-man' wa al-habs. Two branches: (1) punishment = preventing someone from their will; (2) sweet water = 'restrained' from saltiness. What is 'restrained' can be either painful (punishment) or pleasant (fresh water).

quranic_analysis.theme: Adhab Taxonomy
quranic_analysis.detail: Rich intensifier system: alim (~65x), azim, shadid, muhin, muqim, ghaliz, nukr. Each modifier specifies quality and severity.

quranic_analysis.theme: Punishment of the Fire
quranic_analysis.detail: Adhab al-Nar = Fire's punishment; la yukhaffaf anhum—not lightened, emphasizing perpetuity.

quranic_analysis.theme: Divine Prerogative
quranic_analysis.detail: Punishment as divine prerogative: paired with forgiveness—yuadhdhibu man yasha wa yaghfiru liman yasha.

lexicographical_sources.ibn_faris: Core = al-man' wa al-habs (prevention and restraint). Punishment prevents one from will; sweet water's saltiness is restrained.
lexicographical_sources.al_raghib: Adhab = most severe form of prevention. Adhb = pleasant water whose sweetness 'prevents' thirst.
lexicographical_sources.lane: Adhdhaba = he punished, tormented. Adhab = punishment, torture. Adhb = sweet pleasant water.

theological_dimensions: Shadid al-Adhab: divine attribute paired with Forgiver in targhib/tarhib dialectic
Adhab al-Qabr: punishment of grave—well-established in hadith
Al-Adhab al-Akbar (88:24): the greatest punishment—ultimate eschatological penalty
Punishment as just deserts: consistently framed as retribution for 'what hands sent forth'
hadith_evidence: Seek refuge from punishment of grave and punishment of Hell (Bukhari, Muslim)
Fasting is a shield from Allah's punishment (Bukhari, Muslim)
Whoever dies calling on a rival to Allah enters the Fire—punishment for shirk
cross_references: غفر (gfr)—forgiveness: constant pair in fear/hope dialectic
نار (nwr)—Fire: adhab al-nar is most frequent construct
رحم (rHm)—mercy: paired with adhab in divine attribute balance

meaning.en: All, every. 377x. Kull (359x)=all/every—kulli shay'in qadir (~45x). Kullama (15x)=whenever. Kall (1x)=burden. Kalalah (2x)=collateral inheritance. Proto-Semitic *kull-, Hebrew kol.
meaning.en_detailed: The Arabic root ك ل ل (كُلّ) appears 377 times in the Quran, governing the semantic domain of All, every, totality. Its principal deployment is in divine omnipotence formulas: 'kulli shayʾ qādir' ('over all things Powerful,' ~45x), underwriting the doctrine of unqualified divine agency. The Quranic cosmology of creation-in-six-days contrasts 'all' with 'every' in micro-modal distinctions, while kalālah (2x) names the inheritance where the deceased leaves neither parent nor child, and kall (1x) carries the sense of burden in 23:81 ('the ummī prophets'). The root reaches its logical apex in verses declaring 'all that is in the heavens and earth belongs to Him.'

quranic_analysis.theme: Divine omnipotence
quranic_analysis.detail: Kulli shay'in qadir—over all things competent.

cognates.hebrew: כָּלַל (kālal) — to complete, perfect; כֹּל (kōl) — all

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *kll = 'to be complete → all, every'. The Arabic kull (all, every) is the universal quantifier — encompassing totality. The kalālah (inheritance without parents or children) means the 'complete/encircling' heir who has no direct line. The root moved from 'being complete' to 'encompassing all'.

hadith_evidence.ar: تَدَبَّرُوا الْقُرْآنَ فَإِنَّهُ حُجَّةٌ لَكُمْ أَوْ عَلَيْكُمْ
hadith_evidence.en: Reflect upon the Quran, for it is either a proof for you or against you.
hadith_evidence.source: Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim via ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb

meaning.en: To work, do, act. 360 occurrences. Amila (276x)=to do/work. Amal (71x)=deed. Amil (12x)=doer. Formula: amanu wa-amilu al-salihat (~30x)—salvation requires faith AND action. Ibn Faris: making with mastery and intentional will—distinguished from fil (any action).
meaning.ar: العمل: صنع الشيء بإحكام وإرادة — آمنوا وعملوا الصالحات
meaning.en_detailed: From ʿ-m-l (عَمِلَ) with 360 occurrences, the root names intentional productive action—the bridge between faith and its fruits. The Quran's most characteristic collocation, āmanū wa ʿamilū al-ṣāliḥāt ('believed and did righteous deeds'), recurs ~30 times and structures the soteriology. 2:74 ('God is not unaware of what you do'), 14:18 ('their deeds are like ashes in the wind'), and 99:7–8 ('an atom's weight of good or evil') all stress that deeds are weighed precisely. Ibn Faris distinguishes ʿamal from fil by mastery (iḥkām) and intent (irāda), making ʿamal the ethically weighted branch of action whose metaphysical opposite is 'deed of another' (ʿamal ghayrih, 35:18).

etymology.semantic_evolution: Common Semitic root for intentional productive action. Arabic: central term for moral/religious deeds. Post-Quranic: grammatical sense is Latin semantic loan.

derived_forms.meaning: to work, do, act—intentional action with craftsmanship

key_nominals.meaning: deed, action (71x)—deliberate product of human effort
deeds (38x broken pl)—record weighed on Judgment Day

quranic_analysis.theme: Faith + Righteous Deeds
quranic_analysis.detail: Amanu wa-amilu al-salihat—the Quran most characteristic collocation. Salvation requires faith AND action.

quranic_analysis.theme: Deeds Nullified
quranic_analysis.detail: Disbelievers deeds like ashes blown by wind—no weight on Judgment Day.

quranic_analysis.theme: Accountability
quranic_analysis.detail: Every soul compensated. Atoms weight of good/evil will be seen.

quranic_analysis.theme: Divine observation
quranic_analysis.detail: Allah is not unaware of what you do—divine gaze creates accountability.

lexicographical_sources.ibn_faris: amal = sun with ihkam (mastery) and iradah (intent). Distinguished from random motion.
lexicographical_sources.al_raghib: Distinguishes amal (deliberate action) from fil (any action/event).
lexicographical_sources.lane: amila = he worked, did, acted. amal = deed, action.

theological_dimensions: Iman = heart + tongue + action of limbs (Sunni orthodoxy)
Deeds on scales (mizan): decisive for salvation
Intention (niyya): innama al-amalu bi al-niyyat
hadith_evidence: Innama al-amalu bi al-niyyat—Actions by intentions (Bukhari 1, Muslim 1907)
No one has eaten better than from work of own hands (Bukhari 2072)
Allah loves that when you do a work, do it with excellence (al-Bayhaqi)

meaning.en: To command, order; affair, matter. 248 occurrences. Amara (77x)=to command. Amr (166x)=command, affair, decree. Kun fa-yakun (7x): When He decrees a matter He only says Be and it is. Ulu al-amr (4:59): those in authority. Amr bi al-maruf: commanding right. Ibn Faris: dual meaning—commanding AND the thing commanded. Proto-Semitic *-m-r: Hebrew amar=to say; Arabic specialized to command.
meaning.ar: الأمر: الطلب والإلزام — أطيعوا الله وأطيعوا الرسول وأولي الأمر
meaning.en_detailed: Occurring 248 times across ʾ-m-r (أَمَرَ), the root carries a built-in duality—command and the thing commanded, command and the matter it produces. The creative formula 'kun fa-yakūn' ('Be, and it is') repeats seven times (2:117, 3:47, 16:40, 19:35, 36:82, 40:68) to anchor amr as God's sovereign decree. 4:59 extends the obedience hierarchy ('obey God, the Messenger, and ulī al-amr'), and 12:53's 'al-nafs al-ammāra bi-l-sūʾ'—the soul commanding evil—reveals the root's psychological descent. Through amr bi-l-maʿrūf (commanding right) and nahy ʿan al-munkar (forbidding wrong), the root builds Quranic public ethics.

etymology.semantic_evolution: Proto-Semitic 'to say/speak' → Arabic specialized to 'command' (directive speech act). Hebrew preserved the broader 'say' meaning. Key distinction: amr (command/matter) carries inherent dual semantics—both the act of commanding and the thing commanded.

key_nominals.meaning: command, affair, matter (166x)—divine creative decree; human affairs
those in authority (4:59)—foundational to Islamic political theology

quranic_analysis.theme: Kun fa-yakun
quranic_analysis.detail: When He decrees a matter, He says Be and it is—absolute creative sovereignty.

quranic_analysis.theme: Amr Allah
quranic_analysis.detail: Divine command as inevitable decree—kana amru Allahi maf'ulan.

quranic_analysis.theme: Ulu al-amr
quranic_analysis.detail: Obey Allah, Messenger, and those in authority—obedience hierarchy in Islam.

quranic_analysis.theme: Amr bi al-maruf
quranic_analysis.detail: Commanding right and forbidding wrong—central Quranic ethical principle.

lexicographical_sources.ibn_faris: Inherent duality: both the act of commanding AND the thing commanded.
lexicographical_sources.al_raghib: amr = command/affair. Distinguishes amr (command) from nahy (prohibition).
lexicographical_sources.lane: amara: commanded, ordered. amr: a command, order, affair, matter.

theological_dimensions: Kun fa-yakun: absolute divine creative sovereignty—no substrate needed
Ulu al-amr: Sunni (rulers), Shia (Imams), scholarly interpretations
Amr bi al-maruf: collective obligation (fard kifaya)
Nafs al-ammarah: foundation of Sufi psychology—soul predisposed to evil
hadith_evidence: Whoever sees an evil, let him change it with his hand... tongue... heart (Muslim)
No obedience to creation in disobedience of the Creator (Bukhari, Muslim)
cross_references: نهي (nhy)—forbid: direct antonym in amr bi al-maruf wa nahy an al-munkar
قضى (qDy)—decree: qada amran (He decreed a matter)

meaning.en: To forgive, pardon, cover (sin). 234 occurrences. Ghafara (65x)=to forgive. Istaghfara (40x)=to seek forgiveness. Ghafur (91x)=Oft-Forgiving—divine name paired with Rahim (~58x). Ghaffar (5x)=Ever-Forgiving. Maghfirah (28x)=forgiveness. Ibn Faris: al-satr wa al-taghtiyah (covering and concealing)—forgiveness as God covering sin. Shirk exception (4:48, 4:116): Allah does not forgive shirk but forgives what is less. 39:53: Do not despair—Allah forgives all sins. Proto-Semitic *ġpr—to cover, protect (Hebrew kopher=covering/pitch).
meaning.ar: المغفرة: الستر — استغفروا ربكم إنه كان غفارا
meaning.en_detailed: From gh-f-r (غَفَرَ) with 234 occurrences, the root's core is covering—and forgiveness is God's covering of sin from view. The Divine Names Ghafūr (91x, Oft-Forgiving) and Ghaffār (5x, Ever-Forgiving) dominate, paired with Raḥīm ~58 times (2:173, 15:49, 39:53) to seal forgiveness in mercy. The exception is the unique limit: 4:48 and 4:116 declare shirk unforgivable unless repented of, while 39:53 opens the door fully ('Do not despair—God forgives all sins'). The imperative of human reciprocity appears at 24:22 ('forgive and overlook'), making maghfirah both gift and demand; the root's primal image is the helmet (mighfar) that covers the head.

cognates.hebrew: כפר (g-p-r)—to pitch/cover; kopher=pitch; kippur (atonement via metathesis)

etymology.semantic_evolution: Proto-Semitic physical 'covering' (helmet, pitch) → metaphorical 'covering sin' = forgiveness. Shared etymological root with kaffara (to atone)—both = covering. Istighfar: seeking to have sins covered by divine mercy.

quranic_analysis.theme: Divine monopoly on forgiveness
quranic_analysis.detail: Who forgives sins except Allah?—rhetorical question establishing divine prerogative.

quranic_analysis.theme: Shirk exception
quranic_analysis.detail: Allah does not forgive shirk but forgives what is less—the single explicit limit.

quranic_analysis.theme: Universal offer
quranic_analysis.detail: Do not despair—Allah forgives ALL sins—the most expansive statement, conditional on repentance.

quranic_analysis.theme: Ghafur-Rahim pair
quranic_analysis.detail: The most frequent divine binomial—forgiveness rooted in mercy.

lexicographical_sources.ibn_faris: al-satr wa al-taghtiyah (covering). Mighfar=helmet (what covers the head). Religious sense: God covering sin from exposure.
lexicographical_sources.al_raghib: Maghfirah = covering sin by God: removing from visibility and protecting from consequence. Distinguishes from afa (effacing).
lexicographical_sources.lane: ghafara = covered, protected, forgave. ghafur = one who forgives abundantly. ghaffar = incessant forgiver.

theological_dimensions: Al-Ghafur al-Rahim: most frequent divine binomial—forgiveness rooted in mercy
Shirk exception: only unforgivable sin without repentance
39:53: universal offer—Allah forgives all sins
Istighfar as spiritual practice: Prophet 100x daily
Human forgiveness as condition: forgive others → receive divine forgiveness (24:22)
hadith_evidence: If sins reached clouds then you asked forgiveness, I would forgive you (Tirmidhi 3540)
Sayyid al-Istighfar: O Allah You are my Lord... forgive me, none forgives except You (Bukhari 6306)
Allah stretches out His hand at night for daytime sinner, in day for nighttime sinner (Muslim 2759)
Prophet sought forgiveness 100 times daily (Muslim 2702)
cross_references: توب (twb)—repentance: tawba precedes and conditions maghfirah
عفو (Efw)—effacement: total erasure vs ghafr covering

meaning.en: Guardian, protector, ally, friend; authority, governance. 232 occurrences. Waliyy (86x)=guardian/ally—Allahu waliyyu alladhina amanu (2:257). Tawalla (78x)=to turn away/reject OR take as ally—dual usage. Walla (30x)=to turn, direct. Mawla (18x)=protector/master—nima al-mawla (Excellent Protector, 8:40). Awla (11x)=more worthy, nearer. Core: proximity (al-qurb)—what is near is what one turns to or depends on. Al-Wali is among the 99 Names. Semantic polarity: wilayah = friendship/sainthood; wilayah = authority/governance.
meaning.ar: الولاية: القرب — الله ولي الذين آمنوا
meaning.en_detailed: Built on w-l-y (وَلِيَ) with 232 occurrences, the root centres on proximity—what is near is what one turns to and depends on. The protective sense anchors 2:257 ('God is the waliyy of those who believe; He brings them from darknesses into light'), and 10:62–63 promises awliyāʾ Allāh ('friends of God') fearless and grieving-free. The same root generates awlā ('more worthy,' 11x) and mawlā ('patron, master,' 18x), with 33:6 supplying the highest political claim: 'the Prophet is closer [awlā] to the believers than themselves.' Its dual polarity—turning toward (wali) and turning away (tawallā)—gives wilāya its full ethical range across sainthood and political authority.

etymology.semantic_evolution: Proto-Semitic 'proximity/closeness' → Arabic: (1) friendship/guardianship (wali), (2) authority (wilayah), (3) turning toward/away (tawalla/walla). The link: what is near is what one turns to or depends on. Semantic polarity: same root means 'turn toward' AND 'turn away'—context disambiguates.

derived_forms.meaning: to be close, adjacent, follow immediately
to turn, direct, appoint; turn back in battle
to turn away/reject OR take as ally—dual usage

key_nominals.meaning: guardian, protecting friend (86x)—divine name al-Wali; plural awliya
protector, master (18x)—nima al-mawla wa nima al-nasir (8:40)
more worthy, nearer (11x)—elative; awla bi (closer to)

quranic_analysis.theme: Allah as Guardian
quranic_analysis.detail: Allahu waliyyu alladhina amanu—Allah brings believers from darkness to light.

quranic_analysis.theme: Friends of Allah
quranic_analysis.detail: Awliya Allah la khawfun alayhim—no fear, no grief. Those who believe and have taqwa.

quranic_analysis.theme: Prohibition of disbeliever alliance
quranic_analysis.detail: Do not take Jews/Christians as awliya (in contexts of religious loyalty). Your wali is only Allah, Messenger, believers.

quranic_analysis.theme: Prophet closer than selves
quranic_analysis.detail: al-Nabiyyu awla bi al-muminin min anfusihim—prophetic authority.

lexicographical_sources.ibn_faris: Single root: proximity and closeness (al-qurb). All forms return to this.
lexicographical_sources.al_raghib: walayah = nearness; wilayah = authority/dominion; wali = one who is close.
lexicographical_sources.lane: w-l-y: being near, friend, authority; tawalla: turning toward or away.

theological_dimensions: Al-Wali: divine name—the Protecting Guardian, paired with al-Nasir
Walayah vs Wilayah: friendship/sainthood vs political authority
Tawalli: taking allies—central to Islamic loyalty concept
Awliya Allah (10:62): foundational for Sufi concepts of sainthood
Prophetic wilaya (33:6): Prophet closer to believers than their own selves
hadith_evidence: Man adha li waliyyan fa-qad adhantu bi al-harb—Whoever shows enmity to My friend, I declare war (Hadith Qudsi, Bukhari)
The believers are awliya of one another—mutual guardianship
cross_references: نصر (nSr)—help: paired nima al-mawla wa nima al-nasir
وكيل (wkA)—guardian: wakil as disposer of affairs
تولى (tawalla)—turning away: vs i'rad (also turning away)

meaning.en: Garden/Paradise; jinn (unseen beings); to cover, conceal. 201 occurrences. Jannah (147x)=Paradise—jannat tajri min tahtiha al-anhar. Jinn (22x)=unseen beings created from fire. Majnun (11x)=possessed/mad. Core: j-n-n = to cover/conceal. Jannah = garden covered by trees. Jinn = concealed from sight. Majnun = mind covered. Proto-Semitic *g-n-n, Hebrew gan (garden). 18:50: Iblis was of the jinn. 51:56: created jinn and mankind for worship.
meaning.ar: الجنة: البستان — والجن: المستترون عن الأعين — وما خلقت الجن والإنس إلا ليعبدون
meaning.en_detailed: From j-n-n (جَنَّ) with 201 occurrences, the root's single core—covering—divides into garden (jannah = trees covering the earth), unseen beings (jinn = beings hidden from sight), and madness (junūn = mind covered from reason). The Paradise branch is densest: jannah recurs 147x, with the canonical description 'jannāt tajrī min taḥtihā al-anḥār' ('gardens beneath which rivers flow'). 18:50 makes the ontology explicit ('Iblīs was of the jinn, not the angels'), explaining his capacity for refusal, and 51:56 binds creation to worship ('I created jinn and mankind only to worship Me'). The majnūn accusations at 15:6, 23:70, and 68:2 form a systematic polemic against dismissing the Prophet.

etymology.semantic_evolution: Proto-Semitic 'covering/concealing' → Arabic: (1) Paradise = place covered by trees, (2) jinn = concealed beings, (3) madness = mind concealed. The jinn sense via Syriac gne (tutelary spirit).

quranic_analysis.theme: Paradise: flowing gardens
quranic_analysis.detail: Standard description: gardens under which rivers flow as reward for amanu wa amilu al-salihat.

quranic_analysis.theme: Jinn as parallel creation
quranic_analysis.detail: Created from fire; moral agents with free will; believers among them (72:1-15).

quranic_analysis.theme: Iblis was of the jinn
quranic_analysis.detail: Kana min al-jinni—Iblis was jinn, not angel; explains his disobedience (jinn have free will).

quranic_analysis.theme: Majnun accusation
quranic_analysis.detail: Disbelievers repeatedly called Prophet mad—veiled intellect accusation.

lexicographical_sources.ibn_faris: j-n-n = al-satr (covering/concealment). All derivatives return to this single meaning.
lexicographical_sources.al_raghib: Jinn are concealed from sight. Jannah is a garden covered by trees. Junun is intellect covered.
lexicographical_sources.lane: j-n-n = covering, veiling, hiding. Jannah = garden. Jinn = unseen beings.

theological_dimensions: Jannah: ultimate reward—gardens of eternity described in vivid sensory detail
Jinn: parallel creation with free will; some believe, most disbelieve
Iblis ontology (18:50): jinn, not angel—distinct from Christian fallen angel
Majnun: systematic Quranic refutation of madness accusation
Junnah: fasting as shield (al-siyamu junnah)
hadith_evidence: Al-siyamu junnah—Fasting is a shield (Bukhari, Muslim)
The jinn came to listen to the Quran (Surah al-Jinn revelation context)
Iblis was of the jinn, not angels—clarified by Ibn Abbas
cross_references: إنس (ins)—mankind: paired with jinn throughout Quran
ملك (mlk)—angels: distinct creation; Iblis was jinn, not angel

meaning.en: With, at, near. 201x. Inda (197x)=with/near—inda Allah (~150x). Anid (4x)=obstinate. 3:19: inna al-dina inda Allahi al-Islam.
meaning.en_detailed: With 201 occurrences of the preposition ʿinda (عِنْدَ), this root names the Quran's central relational axis—what is 'with' or 'at' God versus what is with creatures. The doctrine peaks at 3:19 ('the religion with God is Islam') and 3:14 ('all that is with you is transient, but what is with God endures'). The same root generates ʿanīd ('obstinate,' 4x) and ʿunūd ('rebellion,' 3x), preserving the negative pole in 11:59 and 71:7 against its primary positive sense. Spatial proximity in 57:4 ('He is with you wherever you are') extends the preposition into divine omnipresence, the ʿindiyyah of God.

quranic_analysis.theme: What is with Allah
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa ma inda Allahi khayrun wa abqa—what is with Allah is better.

derived_forms.meaning: at, with, near, in the presence of

key_nominals.m: at, with, in the presence of

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *ʿnd = 'to be present, at hand'. In Arabic, ʿinda functions as a preposition of presence = 'at, with, near, in the possession of'. The Quranic usage ranges from spatial proximity to divine presence: 'He is with you wherever you are' (57:4) — the ʿindiyyah of God.

hadith_evidence.ar: تَدَبَّرُوا الْقُرْآنَ فَإِنَّهُ حُجَّةٌ لَكُمْ أَوْ عَلَيْكُمْ
hadith_evidence.en: Reflect upon the Quran, for it is either a proof for you or against you.
hadith_evidence.source: Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim via ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb

meaning.en: Light; fire. 194 occurrences. Nur (43x)=light—Allahu nuru al-samawati wa al-ard (24:35, Ayat al-Nur). Nar (145x)=fire—overwhelmingly Hellfire (~120x). Munir (6x)=illuminating. Proto-Semitic *nūr-. Arabic split: nur=light (guidance, revelation, divine), nar=fire (punishment, Hell). Singular nur vs plural zulumat: truth is one, falsehood is many. Nur ala nur (light upon light) in 24:35—the most sustained Quranic metaphor. 57:12: believers run by their light on Judgment Day.
meaning.ar: النور: الضوء — الله نور السماوات والأرض
meaning.en_detailed: From n-w-r (نَوَّرَ) with 194 occurrences, the root splits into nūr (light, 43x) and nār (fire, 145x)—a lexical doublet examined in Arabic linguistics as a single semantic field. The light branch reaches its mystical peak in 24:35, the Ayat al-Nur ('God is the Light of the heavens and earth'), where nūr is repeated five times in a single verse. The fire branch dominates the eschatology, with 57:12–13 promising that on the Last Day 'believers will run by their light' while hypocrites beg to share it. The root's sevenfold 'from darknesses (zulumāt, plural) into the light (nūr, singular)' (2:257, 14:1, 57:9, 65:11) encapsulates Quranic epistemology.
