etymology.semantic_evolution: Proto-Semitic root for both light and fire. Arabic preserved both: nur (guidance, revelation, divine light) and nar (punishment, Hellfire). The dual sense: fire/light illuminates (guides) but also burns (punishes). The nūr/nār lexical doublet is one of the most studied in Arabic linguistics.

quranic_analysis.theme: Ayat al-Nur
quranic_analysis.detail: Allahu nuru al-samawati wa al-ard—the most profound meditation on divine light: niche-lamp-glass-oil-star parable. Nur repeated 5x, nar 1x in single verse.

quranic_analysis.theme: From darknesses to light
quranic_analysis.detail: Yukhrijuhum min al-zulumat ila al-nur—7x. Singular nur always vs plural zulumat: truth is one.

quranic_analysis.theme: Quran as light
quranic_analysis.detail: Qad jaakum min Allahi nurun wa kitabun mubin—light and clear Book.

quranic_analysis.theme: Believers light on Judgment Day
quranic_analysis.detail: Nuruhum yasa bayna aydihim—their light streaming before them; hypocrites will beg for light.

lexicographical_sources.ibn_faris: Two meanings: illumination/radiance and fire. Nur wa nar kulluha min bab wahid—all from single root domain.
lexicographical_sources.al_raghib: Nur clarifies—used literally and metaphorically. Zulumat always plural because false paths are many; nur singular because truth is one.
lexicographical_sources.lane: Comprehensive: physical and metaphorical light; nar (fire) distinct from nur (light).

theological_dimensions: Nur as divine attribute: Allahu nur—one of the few places Allah described by cognate noun
Singular nur vs plural zulumat: truth is one, falsehood is many
Light of faith on Judgment Day: believers receive light proportionate to deeds
Nur/nar doublet: fire illuminates AND punishes—divine ambivalence
Quran as nur: revelation described as light 6x
hadith_evidence: Allahumma ij al fi qalbi nuran—O Allah place light in my heart (Prophetic supplication, Muslim)
Al-salat is nur—prayer is light (Muslim)
Allah created the angels from light (Muslim)
cross_references: ضوء (DwA)—light: nur is spiritual/metaphysical; daw is physical
نار vs جهنم (jhnm)—nar is the fire; jahannam is the place

meaning.en: Good, better. 196x. Khayr=good/better (178x). Ikhtara VIII=choose. 2:216: perhaps you dislike a thing but it is good for you. 97:3: laylat al-qadr khayrun min alfi shahr.
meaning.en_detailed: With 196 occurrences of kh-y-r (خَيْر), this root names the supreme positive value—khayr as 'good, better' and the verbal khāra/ikhtāra ('to choose') confirming that what is chosen is good. The ethical paradox appears at 2:216 ('perhaps you hate a thing though it is good for you') and 2:180 ('if someone leaves better provision behind, let it be for his parents'). 97:3 ('Laylat al-Qadr is better than a thousand months') shows the comparative form scaling value, and khayr applies equally to wealth (4:19), character (3:180), and outcome (16:30). The Quranic 'khayr' thus joins utilitarian goodness with divine choice; what God chooses for the believer exceeds their preference.

quranic_analysis.theme: Divine wisdom
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa asa an takrahu shay'an wa huwa khayrun lakum.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *ḫyr = 'to choose → to be good'. What is chosen is good; what is good is chosen. Arabic khāra = to choose. Khayr = good, goodness, better. 'Khayr' recurs 176 times — the comprehensive term for all that is beneficial.

hadith_evidence.ar: تَدَبَّرُوا الْقُرْآنَ فَإِنَّهُ حُجَّةٌ لَكُمْ أَوْ عَلَيْكُمْ
hadith_evidence.en: Reflect upon the Quran, for it is either a proof for you or against you.
hadith_evidence.source: Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim via ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb

meaning.en: To be good, beautiful, excellent. 194 occurrences. Ahsana IV (21x)=to do good/excel. Muhsin (38x)=doer of good—Allah loves al-muhsinin (5x: 2:195, 3:134, 3:148, 5:13, 5:93). Ahsan (36x)=better/best—Ahsan al-Khaliqin (23:14). Hasanah (28x)=good deed—hasanat erase sayyiat (11:114). Ihsan (12x)=excellence—reward of ihsan is ihsan (55:60). Husna (17x)=best outcome/Paradise. The Quran most ethically rich root—bridging aesthetic beauty and moral goodness.
meaning.ar: الحسن: الجمال — وأحسنوا إن الله يحب المحسنين
meaning.en_detailed: From ḥ-s-n (حَسُنَ) with 194 occurrences, the root bridges aesthetic beauty and moral goodness, generating iḥsān (excellence, 12x), muḥsin (doer of good, 38x), ḥasanāt (good deeds, 28x), and the superlative ḥusnā (17x). God 'loves the muḥsinīn' five times (2:195, 3:134, 3:148, 5:13, 5:93), and 16:90 commands 'justice and iḥsān.' 23:14 calls God 'Aḥsan al-Khāliqīn' (Best of Creators), and 11:114 ('the ḥasanāt remove the sayyiʾāt') establishes the transformative power of beautiful deeds. 55:60 ('the reward of iḥsān is iḥsān') builds a theology of divine reciprocity on this root that fuses ethics and aesthetics.

etymology.semantic_evolution: Proto-Semitic 'beauty/goodness' → Arabic: the richest ethical vocabulary—ahsana (do good), ihsan (excellence), muhsin (doer of good), hasanah (good deed). The root bridges aesthetic beauty and moral goodness.

derived_forms.meaning: to do good, excel, make beautiful

quranic_analysis.theme: Muhsinun loved by Allah
quranic_analysis.detail: 5x Allah explicitly declares His love for al-muhsinin—the surest path to divine love.

quranic_analysis.theme: Ahsan al-Khaliqin
quranic_analysis.detail: God as Best of Creators—creation most excellent, beautiful, perfected.

quranic_analysis.theme: Ihsan as ultimate virtue
quranic_analysis.detail: Kindness to parents (bi al-walidayni ihsana); Allah commands justice and ihsan (16:90).

quranic_analysis.theme: Good deeds erase bad deeds
quranic_analysis.detail: Inna al-hasanati yudhhibna al-sayyiat—transformative power of good actions.

lexicographical_sources.ibn_faris: ḥ-s-n = beauty and goodness in all manifestations.
lexicographical_sources.al_raghib: Al-husn brings about admiration. Ihsan = showing kindness. Muhsin = beautiful actions.
lexicographical_sources.lane: ḥ-s-n: good, beautiful, excellent. ahsana: did well, acted kindly.

theological_dimensions: Ihsan as highest faith: worship Allah as if you see Him (Hadith Jibril)
Al-Asma al-Husna: the Most Beautiful Names—reflecting divine perfection
Muhsinun loved by Allah (5x): ihsan as surest path to divine love
Reward of ihsan is ihsan (55:60): divine reciprocity
hadith_evidence: Ihsan: to worship Allah as if you see Him (Hadith Jibril, Muslim)
Allah has prescribed ihsan in everything—even in slaughter (Muslim)
Best of you are those best in character (ahsanukum akhlaqan) (Bukhari)
cross_references: خير (xyr)—good: khayr = objectively beneficial; hasan = subjectively beautiful
جمل (jml)—beauty: jamal = physical; husn = comprehensive beauty/goodness

meaning.en: To hear. 185x. Samia=hear. Sami'=All-Hearing (47x). 2:285: sami'na wa ata'na. Proto-Semitic *shama-, Hebrew shama.
meaning.en_detailed: From s-m-ʿ (سَمِعَ) with 185 occurrences, the root fuses auditory reception with obedience—al-Samīʿ ('the All-Hearing') is God's distinguishing name, paired ~47 times with al-ʿAlīm. The covenant formula at 2:285 ('we hear [samiʿnā] and we obey') binds the two acts inseparably, while 5:7 reminds believers that 'God's hearing is not as your hearing.' The eighth form, istamaʿa ('to listen attentively,' ~20x), governs the meditative postures at 4:46, 7:204, and the angelic gathering at 78:1 ('they listen attentively, while the angels are ranged in rows'). The repeated interrogative 'a-fa-lā tasmaʿūn' ('will you not hear?') ties spiritual receptivity to doctrinal obedience.

quranic_analysis.theme: We hear and obey
quranic_analysis.detail: Sami'na wa ata'na—hearing entails obedience.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *šmʿ = 'to hear → to obey'. The Hebrew šāmaʿ carries the same dual sense: hearing and obeying are one. Arabic samiʿa = to hear. Al-Samīʿ (the All-Hearing) is a frequent divine name. The Quran's repeated 'a-fa-lā tasmaʿūn' (Will you not hear/listen?) is a call to both auditory and spiritual receptivity.

hadith_evidence.ar: تَدَبَّرُوا الْقُرْآنَ فَإِنَّهُ حُجَّةٌ لَكُمْ أَوْ عَلَيْكُمْ
hadith_evidence.en: Reflect upon the Quran, for it is either a proof for you or against you.
hadith_evidence.source: Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim via ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb

meaning.en_short: To exit, go out; to bring forth
meaning.en: To exit, go out, leave; to bring forth, expel. 182 occurrences. Kharaja I (53x)=to go out. Akhraja IV (99x)=to bring forth—dominant form. Divine extraction theme: Allah brings vegetation from earth, living from dead, believers from darkness to light. Makhraj (1x, 65:2): whoever fears Allah—He makes a way out. From darknesses to light (2:257, 5:16, 14:1, 33:43, 57:9, 65:11) appears 7x. Those expelled from homes unjustly (22:40). Resurrection: coming out of graves (54:7, 70:43).
meaning.ar: الخروج: البروز — يخرج الحي من الميت — ومن يتق الله يجعل له مخرجا
meaning.en_detailed: From kh-r-j (خَرَجَ) with 182 occurrences, the root's transitive Form IV (akhraja, 99x) dominates over the intransitive kharaja (53x), making 'bringing forth' the divine-action default. The verb sustains the Quranic exodus theology: 'He brings forth the living from the dead' (3:27, 6:95), 'brings forth vegetation' (7:57, 30:19), and seven times 'brings them out of darknesses into the light' (2:257, 5:16, 14:1, 33:43, 57:9, 65:11). 65:2 ('whoever fears God, He makes for him a makhraj') joins the threat of taqwā to a guaranteed exit. The hijrah ('emigration') of the persecuted early community, narrated at 8:72, 9:40, and 22:40, anchors the root in Islamic political memory.
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To exit, go out; to bring forth

etymology.semantic_evolution: Proto-Semitic emergence/exit → Arabic: primary verb for exiting. Form IV (akhraja=bring out) became dominant Quranic form—used for divine acts: vegetation, life from death, guidance from darkness.

derived_forms.meaning: to bring forth, drive out, extract—causative, divine agency
to draw out, extract (request/benefit)—Yusuf cup (12:76), sea ornaments (16:14)

key_nominals.meaning: expulsion, driving out (6x)—of believers from homes, Adam from Paradise
way out (1x, 65:2)—wa man yattaqi Allaha yaj al lahu makhrajan

quranic_analysis.theme: Divine extraction: akhraja
quranic_analysis.detail: Allah brings vegetation from earth, living from dead—demonstrating creative power.

quranic_analysis.theme: From darknesses to light
quranic_analysis.detail: Yukhrijuhum min al-zulumat ila al-nur—7 verses. God brings believers from plural darknesses to singular light.

quranic_analysis.theme: Way out for the God-conscious
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa man yattaqi Allaha yaj al lahu makhrajan—divine promise of a way out for the muttaqun.

quranic_analysis.theme: Expulsion of believers
quranic_analysis.detail: Alladhina ukhriju min diyarihim—those expelled unjustly from homes; hijrah context.

lexicographical_sources.ibn_faris: kh-r-j = emergence and going out.
lexicographical_sources.al_raghib: Al-khuruj opposite of al-dukhul. Akhraja more frequent—emphasizes divine agency.
lexicographical_sources.lane: kharaja: went forth, departed. akhraja: caused to go forth, expelled, extracted.

theological_dimensions: Divine extraction: akhraja emphasizes God as agent bringing things forth
Makhraj for muttaqun (65:2-3): promise of way out for the God-conscious
Hijrah as khuruj: leaving home for God—foundational to early Islamic community
Exodus paradigm: Allah brings His servants out of oppression (Moses paradigm)
Resurrection: emergence from graves—yawma yakhrujuna min al-ajdath
hadith_evidence: Man taraka shayan li-llahi awadahu Allahu khayran minh—Whoever leaves something for Allah, Allah replaces it
Al-hijrah: leaving what Allah has forbidden (Bukhari)
The Prophet expelled from Makkah—quintessential ukhrija narrative
cross_references: بعث (bEv)—resurrect: baatha + kharaja = emergence from graves

meaning.en: Righteousness, reform. 180x. Salih=righteous. Salihat=righteous deeds. Aslaha IV=reform. amanu wa-amilu al-salihat (~60x). Tabu wa aslahu.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ص-ل-ح (ṣ-l-ḥ), from Proto-Semitic *ṣ-l-ḥ 'to be whole,' generates 180 occurrences spanning soundness, righteousness, and reconciliation. The central Quranic formula āmanū wa-ʿamilū al-ṣāliḥāt ('they believed and did righteous deeds') recurs in roughly sixty verses—2:25, 4:174, 5:93, 9:111, 11:23—forming the standard soteriology of faith plus works. The intensive IV aṣlaḥa ('to reform') names the divine-human project of restoring soundness to what is corrupt (4:35, 7:35, 11:88), while ṣāliḥ designates both the righteous servant and the Prophet Ṣāliḥ sent to Thamud (7:73-79, 11:61-68, 26:141-159). The nominal ṣulḥ (reconciliation, 2:224) and iṣlāḥ (reform, 4:35) extend the same root into social and political domains. Arabic developed the widest ethical range among the cognates (Hebrew ṣālaḥ 'to prosper,' Ge'ez ṣalaḥa 'to be righteous'), framing righteousness as the soundness of deed and being.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر صَلُحَ — 180 مرة — righteousness; to reform

quranic_analysis.theme: Faith + deeds
quranic_analysis.detail: Amanu wa-amilu al-salihat—the Quran's central soteriological formula.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *ṣlḥ = 'to be sound, whole → to be righteous'. The Arabic ṣāliḥ (righteous) is one whose deeds are 'sound'. The Quranic iṣlāḥ (reform) is making things sound again — bringing harmony to what was discordant. Ṣāliḥ is also the name of the prophet sent to Thamud.

hadith_evidence.ar: تَدَبَّرُوا الْقُرْآنَ فَإِنَّهُ حُجَّةٌ لَكُمْ أَوْ عَلَيْكُمْ
hadith_evidence.en: Reflect upon the Quran, for it is either a proof for you or against you.
hadith_evidence.source: Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim via ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb

meaning.en: To kill, fight. 170x. Qatala I=kill. Qatala III=fight. 5:32: killing one = killing all humanity. 2:216: fighting prescribed. 3:169: martyrs alive.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ق-ت-ل (q-t-l), from Proto-Semitic *q-ṭ-l 'to cut off,' generates 170 occurrences distributed between killing (Form I qatala, ~50x) and fighting (Form III qātala, ~50x) plus the verbal noun qitāl (~10x). Verse 5:32 establishes the foundational legal-moral axiom: 'man qatala nafsan... fa-ka-annamā qatala al-nāsa jamīʿan' ('whoever kills a soul... is as if he had killed mankind entirely')—the sanctity of life as one murder equals the murder of all. Verse 2:216 grounds the doctrine of defensive warfare: 'kutiba ʿalaykum al-qitāl wa-huwa kurhun lakum' ('fighting has been prescribed for you though you dislike it'); 3:169 affirms that the shuhadāʾ 'alive with their Lord'—martyrdom as transition rather than loss. The Quranic usage carefully distinguishes unjust killing (qatl al-nafs bi-ghayr al-haqq, 6:151, 17:33) from sanctioned capital punishment (al-qiṣāṣ, 2:178-179) and ritual slaughter (dhāb, 22:37).

quranic_analysis.theme: Sanctity of life
quranic_analysis.detail: Man qatala nafsan... fa-ka-annama qatala al-nasa jami'an.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *qṭl = 'to cut off → to kill'. A visceral root with stable meaning across Semitic languages. The Quranic usage spans literal killing and sacred/symbolic killing (sacrifice).

hadith_evidence.ar: أَكْثِرُوا ذِكْرَ هَادِمِ اللَّذَّاتِ — الْمَوْتِ
hadith_evidence.en: Increase remembrance of the destroyer of pleasures — death.

meaning.en: Heart; to turn, overturn, return. 168 occurrences. Qalb/qulub (132x)=heart—seat of intellect, faith, and spiritual perception in Quranic anthropology. Qalaba I (1x)=to turn. Qallaba II (6x)=to turn/alternate. Inqalaba VII (17x)=to turn back, return, apostatize. Taqallaba V (1x)=to fluctuate. 22:46: not eyes blind but hearts in breasts. Ibn Faris: two cores—(1) heart, named for constant fluctuation (taqallub), (2) turning/reversing. Proto-Semitic *libb-: Arabic qalb = q- prosthesis + *libb; cognate lubb = core/intellect.
meaning.ar: الجذر ق ل ب: القلب والتحويل — أفلا يتدبرون القرآن أم على قلوب أقفالها
meaning.en_detailed: Root ق-ل-ب (q-l-b), with the prosthetic q- attached to Proto-Semitic *libb- ('heart'), accounts for 168 occurrences that constitute Quranic anthropology's central category: the heart as seat of intellect, faith, and spiritual perception. The Form VII inqalaba ('to turn back, revert') is most frequent verbally (17x) and dominates the eschatological sense of returning—seen in 3:144 'innaka mayyitun wa-innahum mayyitun thumma innakum yawma al-qiyāmati ʿinda rabbikum takhtaṣimūn.' Verse 22:46 anchors the doctrine that spiritual blindness exceeds physical: 'fa-innaha lā taʿmā al-abṣāru wa-lakin taʿmā al-qulūbu allatī fī al-ṣudūr' ('not the eyes are blind but the hearts in the breasts'). The diseased heart (fī qulūbihim maraḍ, 2:10) marks the munāfiq (hypocrite); the qalb salīm ('sound heart,' 26:88-89, 37:84) is the sole criterion of salvation. Cognate lubb (core, intellect) names 'people of understanding' (ulū al-albāb, 16x).

cognates.hebrew: לב (lev), לבב (levav)—heart; seat of intellect (850x in Tanakh)

etymology.semantic_evolution: Proto-Semitic *libb- denoted physical heart. Arabic developed qalb (with prosthetic q-) alongside lubb (pure intellect). The heart-as-seat-of-intellect concept is pan-Semitic. Verbal forms express turning/reversing. The heart is named qalb because of its constant fluctuation (taqallub).

derived_forms.meaning: to turn, change—wa-ilayhi tuqlabun (to Him you are returned, 29:21)
to turn repeatedly, alternate—yuqallibu Allahu al-layla wa al-nahar (24:44)
to turn about, fluctuate—tataqallabu fihi al-qulub (24:37)
to turn back, return, revert—most frequent verbal form

key_nominals.meaning: heart (singular, 132x total incl. plural)—seat of intellect, faith, perception
hearts (plural)—can be hardened, sealed, diseased, tranquil, penitent, sound
core, intellect, pith—cognate without q-; ulu al-albab=people of understanding (16x)

quranic_analysis.theme: Heart as seat of understanding
quranic_analysis.detail: Fa-innaha la tama al-absaru wa-lakin tama al-qulub—not eyes blind but hearts in breasts. Hearts think (yaqilun) and understand (yafqahun).

quranic_analysis.theme: Spiritual diseases of the heart
quranic_analysis.detail: Hearts can have marad (disease), nifaq (hypocrisy), qaswah (hardness). The diseased heart (fi qulubihim marad) is a recurring epithet for hypocrites.

quranic_analysis.theme: Qalb salim—the sound heart
quranic_analysis.detail: Only those who come to Allah with qalb salim (sound heart) will be saved—the sole criterion of salvation.

lexicographical_sources.ibn_faris: Two cores: (1) al-qalb—heart, named for its taqallub (fluctuation). (2) radd al-shay wa-tardiduh—turning something over repeatedly.
lexicographical_sources.al_raghib: Qalb = the noble organ that is seat of intellect (aql) and understanding (fahm). Taqlib (II) = turning repeatedly. Lubb = purest essence of heart.
lexicographical_sources.lane: Qalb: the heart. Named for its constant turning and fluctuation. Qalaba: he turned, inverted, reversed. Inqalaba: turned back, returned.

theological_dimensions: Quranic anthropology: heart (not brain) as center of cognition, moral discernment, spiritual perception
Heart as battleground of faith: can accept or reject guidance
Divine sovereignty over hearts: Allah seals, turns, and strengthens
Qalb salim (26:89): sound heart as sole criterion for salvation—internal state over external compliance
hadith_evidence: Hearts between two fingers of the Merciful—He turns them as He wills (Muslim 2654)
Indeed there is a lump of flesh in the body—if sound, whole body sound; truly it is the heart (Bukhari 52)
Ya Muqallib al-qulub, thabbit qalbi ala dinik—O Turner of hearts, make my heart firm (Tirmidhi)
cross_references: لبب (lbb)—lubb: pure intellect, cognate without q-
فؤد (fAd)—fuad: heart as seat of emotion (paired in 6:110)
سلم (slm)—salim: sound, defining ideal heart state

meaning.en: Association, shirk. 168x. Shirk=association. Ashraka IV=associate partners. 4:48: Allah does not forgive shirk. 31:13: shirk is great injustice.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ش-ر-ك (sh-r-k), from Proto-Semitic *š-r-k 'to share, be a partner,' generates 168 occurrences that map the Quran's central theological category: shirk, the unforgivable sin of associating partners with God. The intensive IV ashraka ('to associate partners with God') dominates with ~160 occurrences—6:151-153, 12:38, 39:65, 40:12, 46:4—while the noun mushrik ('polytheist,' ~45x) names the antagonist of tawḥīd. Verse 4:48 delivers the exclusion clause: 'innā Allāha lā yaghfiru an yushraka bihi wa-yaghfiru mā dūna dhālika liman yashāʾu' ('Allāh does not forgive that anything be associated with Him, but forgives what is less than that to whom He wills')—the shirk-exception defining the unforgivable. Verse 31:13 frames shirk as 'ẓulmun ʿaẓīm' ('the great injustice'); 4:116 warns that whoever ascribes partners, Allāh has forbidden him Paradise.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر شَرِكَ — 168 مرة — association, shirk, partnership

quranic_analysis.theme: Unforgivable sin
quranic_analysis.detail: Inna Allaha la yaghfiru an yushraka bihi—the shirk exception.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *šrk = 'to share, be a partner'. Arabic sharika = to share. Ashraka = to associate partners (with God). Shirk = polytheism — the unforgivable sin. The mushrik (polytheist) is one who 'shares' divinity with created things.

hadith_evidence.ar: تَدَبَّرُوا الْقُرْآنَ فَإِنَّهُ حُجَّةٌ لَكُمْ أَوْ عَلَيْكُمْ
hadith_evidence.en: Reflect upon the Quran, for it is either a proof for you or against you.
hadith_evidence.source: Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim via ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb

meaning.en: To die; death. 165 occurrences. Mata I (39x)=to die. Amata IV (21x)=to cause death—exclusively divine. Mawt (50x)=death noun. Mayyit (38x)=dead person. 67:2: created death and life to test you—unique theological claim. 3:185: every soul tastes death. Proto-Semitic *mawt-, Hebrew mavet. One of the most stable Semitic etyma. The formula yuhyi wa-yumitu (He gives life and causes death) appears 13x. Death is not annihilation but transition to barzakh (23:100). 6:162: my life and my death are for Allah—death as worship.
meaning.ar: الموت: مفارقة الحياة — كل نفس ذائقة الموت
meaning.en_detailed: Root م-و-ت (m-w-t), one of the most stable Semitic etyma (Proto-Semitic *mawt-, Hebrew māwet, Aramaic mawtā), generates 165 occurrences that establish death as the central horizon of Quranic anthropology. The intransitive mata ('to die,' 39x) applies to all agents, while the causative amata ('to cause death,' 21x) is reserved exclusively for divine action—paired in the formula yuḥyī wa-yumīt ('He gives life and causes death,' 13x; 2:258, 3:156, 7:158). Verse 67:2 innovates theologically: 'alladhī khalaqa al-mawta wa-l-ḥayāta li-yabluwakum ayyukum aḥsanu ʿamalan' ('He who created death and life to test you')—death is a created entity, not a primordial force. The formula kullu nafsin dhāʾiqatu al-mawt ('every soul shall taste death,' 3:185, 21:35, 29:57) affirms universality; 6:162 ('innī ṣarrafa Allāhi rabbi wa-ilayhi unaṣṣiru—innī jaʿaltu Allāha rabbi') consecrates existence as worship. The agricultural metaphor of dead earth revived by rain deploys mawt 11 times (2:164, 16:65, 30:19, 41:39) to ground bodily resurrection.

etymology.proto_semitic: *mawt- — death (one of the most stable Semitic etyma)
etymology.semantic_evolution: Pan-Semitic root uniformly meaning death. Physical cessation → theological: spiritual death (kufr) → eschatological: second death (44:56). Quran innovates: death as created entity (67:2), death as test, death as transition not annihilation.

derived_forms.meaning: to cause death—exclusively divine; paired yuhyi wa-yumitu (13x)

key_nominals.meaning: death (50x)—abstract noun; 11x agricultural metaphor for resurrection
dead, dead person (38x)—substantivized active participle; plural amwat
death as life-span (3x)—paired with mahya in merismatic pair (6:162)

quranic_analysis.theme: Death as created entity
quranic_analysis.detail: Alladhi khalaqa al-mawta wa al-hayata—death is a created thing, not primordial force.

quranic_analysis.theme: Universal appointment
quranic_analysis.detail: Kullu nafsin dhaiqatu al-mawt—every soul tastes death (4x). Universality affirmed.

quranic_analysis.theme: Death and commission
quranic_analysis.detail: Innaka mayyitun wa innahum mayyitun—Prophet's mortality affirmed. Message continues beyond death.

quranic_analysis.theme: Death as test
quranic_analysis.detail: Created to test which of you is best in deed—death gives life urgency and meaning.

quranic_analysis.theme: Resurrection of dead earth
quranic_analysis.detail: 11x mawt as agricultural metaphor for bodily resurrection—dead earth revived by rain.

lexicographical_sources.ibn_faris: Single core: death, opposite of life. Root is sound, no secondary meanings.
lexicographical_sources.al_raghib: Death of earth=dryness; death of human=separation of soul; death of disbeliever=ignorance; death of learned=extinction of knowledge.
lexicographical_sources.lane: Death, state of being dead, lifelessness; also spiritual death—ignorance, unbelief.

theological_dimensions: Death as created: 67:2—mawt created, not primordial
Yuhyi wa-yumitu: divine formula (13x)—absolute sovereignty over life and death
Death as transition not annihilation: soul continues in barzakh (23:100)
Death and repentance: 4:17-18—repentance valid only before death
Cultic death: 6:162—life and death consecrated to Allah as unified worship
hadith_evidence: Remember often the destroyer of pleasures: death (Tirmidhi)
The grave is the first stage of the Hereafter (Tirmidhi)
None of you should wish for death (Bukhari, Muslim)
cross_references: حَيي (Hyy)—life: polar antonym paired 13x in yuhyi wa-yumitu
أجل (Ajl)—appointed term: death happens at its ajal

meaning.en_short: Greatness; to be great, magnify, be arrogant
meaning.en: Greatness; to be great, to magnify, to be arrogant. 161 occurrences. Kabur (8x)=to be great/difficult. Kabbir II (4x)=to magnify—wa-rabbaka fa-kabbir (74:3). Istakbara X (40x)=to be arrogant—THE sin of Iblis (2:34). Kabir (40x)=great—al-Kabir divine name (13:9, 22:62, 34:23). Akbar (24x)=greater/greatest—Allahu Akbar. The root encodes a sharp moral duality: greatness ascribed to Allah is highest virtue; humans claiming greatness is the gravest sin. Proto-Semitic *kabar-: Akkadian kabarum=to be thick; Hebrew kabar=to be great.
meaning.ar: الكبر: العظمة — الله أكبر — استكبر إبليس — الكبير المتعال
meaning.en_detailed: Root ك-ب-ر (k-b-r), from Proto-Semitic *kabar- 'to be great,' generates 161 occurrences pivoted on a sharp moral duality: divine greatness as supreme virtue, human self-exaltation as the gravest sin. The active participle kabīr ('great') appears 40 times and is one of God's names (al-Kabīr, 13:9, 22:62, 34:23, 40:12); the elative akbar ('greater') appears 24 times including the liturgical takbīr Allāhu Akbar. The Form X istakbara ('to be arrogant,' 40 occurrences) names the paradigmatic sin of Iblīs: 'abā wa-istakbara wa-kāna min al-kāfirīn' (2:34, 7:13)—establishing istikbār as the root disobedience. The verb II kabbir ('to magnify') underlies the command 'wa-rabbaka fa-kabbir' (74:3); kibriyāʾ ('greatness/majesty') appears twice (10:78, 45:37) explicitly reserved to Allāh—'al-kibriyāʾu li-lāhi wa-l-arḍu jamīʿan.' The mutakabbirūn ('the arrogant') are repeatedly warned of Hell.

etymology.semantic_evolution: Inherited from Proto-Semitic with stable meaning. Arabic preserved widest semantic range: physical size → theological greatness (al-Kabir) → moral condemnation (istakbara). The takbir (Allahu Akbar) is the central liturgical declaration.

derived_forms.meaning: to be great, grow up, be difficult (with ala)
to be arrogant, show pride—THE sin of Iblis (2:34), 40x

key_nominals.meaning: great (40x)—al-Kabir divine name (13:9, 22:62, 34:23); also: elder, large, severe

quranic_analysis.theme: Iblis's arrogant refusal
quranic_analysis.detail: Abā wa-istakbara—Iblis refused and was arrogant. Establishes istikbar as THE paradigmatic sin: prizing self over submission to divine command.

quranic_analysis.theme: Divine greatness: takbir
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa-rabbaka fa-kabbir—magnify your Lord. The takbir (Allahu Akbar) is the central liturgical act.

quranic_analysis.theme: al-Kabir as divine name
quranic_analysis.detail: al-Kabir—the Most Great. Paired with al-Ali (22:62) and al-Mutaal (13:9).

quranic_analysis.theme: Human arrogance condemned
quranic_analysis.detail: Mustakbir (6x), mutakabbir (6x of humans)—the arrogant are repeatedly warned of Hell.

lexicographical_sources.ibn_faris: Core: greatness and pride. Al-kibriya' = al-mulk (sovereignty). Al-kabir = the great one.
lexicographical_sources.al_raghib: Al-kibr = state of considering oneself greater than others. Al-kibriya' = exclusive to Allah; pretension to it by humans is the worst form of arrogance.
lexicographical_sources.lane: kabura: he was great, large; became great. kabir: great, large, elder. akbar: greater, greatest.

theological_dimensions: Allahu Akbar: central Islamic declaration—God is Greater than all
Iblis's istikbar (2:34): paradigmatic sin establishing pride as root of all disobedience
al-Kabir/al-Mutakabbir: divine names expressing absolute greatness
Takbir as liturgical act: first words of adhan, repeated throughout salah
Kibriya' belongs to Allah alone (45:37)—human pretension is sin
hadith_evidence: Allahu Akbar—the Prophet would say takbir at every rising and lowering in prayer
Al-kibriya'u rida'i wa al-azamatu izari—Pride is My cloak and Greatness is My garment (Hadith Qudsi, Muslim)
The arrogant will be raised on Judgment Day like tiny ants (Tirmidhi)

meaning.en: Other, different, except; to change, alter. 154 occurrences. Ghayr (147x)=other than, not, except, without—the most frequent form, used as pseudo-preposition in construct. Ghayyara II (4x)=to change/alter. Taghayyara V (1x)=to become altered. 1:7: ghayr al-maghdub (not those who incurred wrath). 13:11: Allah does not change a people until they change themselves—contains both divine and human agency. The root spans otherness/alterity, negation, exception, change, and military raid (form IV mughirat 100:3).
meaning.ar: الغير: الآخر والمخالفة — إن الله لا يغير ما بقوم حتى يغيروا ما بأنفسهم
meaning.en_detailed: Root غ-ي-ر (gh-y-r), from Proto-Semitic 'other, different,' generates 154 occurrences distributed primarily through the negative-privative noun ghayr ('other than, not, except,' 147x). In al-Fātiḥa, ghayr al-maghḍūb ʿalayhim wa-lā al-ḍāllīn (1:7) provides the defining exclusions of the straight path—those who incurred wrath, those who went astray. The verb II ghayyara ('to change, alter,' 4x) anchors 13:11, the most cited Quranic axiom on social transformation: 'innā Allāha lā yughayyiru mā bi-qawmin ḥattā yughayyirū mā bi-anfusihim' ('Indeed Allāh does not change the condition of a people until they change what is within themselves')—the divine sunna of change demanding prior human moral alteration. Form V taghayyara appears once at 47:15 in the parable of milk whose taste never changes. The root unexpectedly yields Form IV mughirāt ('raiding horses,' 100:3)—the only Quranic image of cavalry raid.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر غَيَّرَ — 154 مرة — other, different; to change

etymology.semantic_evolution: Core sense: otherness/difference. Verb forms grammaticalize this: Form II = make other = change; Form IV = make go to another = raid.

derived_forms.meaning: to become altered (1x—47:15 milk never changing)

key_nominals.meaning: other than, not, without (147x)—ghayr Allah, bi-ghayr haqq
one who changes (1x—8:53, active participle II)

quranic_analysis.theme: Ghair al-maghdub
quranic_analysis.detail: The defining exclusion in al-Fatiha—ghayr al-maghdub alayhim wa la al-dallin.

quranic_analysis.theme: Divine sunna of change
quranic_analysis.detail: Inna Allaha la yughayyiru ma bi-qawmin hatta yughayyiru ma bi-anfusihim—the most cited Quranic verse on social change.

lexicographical_sources.ibn_faris: Core: difference and change. Ghayr = other than. Ghayyara = altered.
lexicographical_sources.al_raghib: Ghayr denotes exclusion from a category. Ghayyara = caused alteration.
lexicographical_sources.lane: ghayr = other, different. ghayyara = he changed.

theological_dimensions: 13:11: divine sunna—God does not change a people's condition until they change their inner state
Negation: ghayr as powerful linguistic tool for theological exclusion

meaning.en: To see, perceive; sight, vision. 148 occurrences. Basar (48x)=sight/eye. Basir (51x)=All-Seeing—al-Basir divine name paired with al-Sami (~12x). Absara IV (29x)=to see/perceive. Basirah (7x)=inner insight/enlightenment. 22:46: not the eyes that are blind but the hearts in breasts. Ibn Faris: core = al-ilm bi al-shay (knowledge of a thing). The root bridges physical sight (basar), cognitive perception (basirah), and divine omniscience (al-Basir). Proto-Semitic *b-ṣ-r—to see, watch, perceive.
meaning.ar: البصر: العلم بالشيء — فإنها لا تعمى الأبصار ولكن تعمى القلوب
meaning.en_detailed: Root ب-ص-ر (b-ṣ-r), from Proto-Semitic 'to see, watch,' generates 148 occurrences organized in three concentric rings: physical sight (baṣar, 48x), cognitive insight (baṣīrah, 7x), and divine omniscience (al-Baṣīr, 51x as divine name). Verse 22:46 supplies the famous epistemological inversion: 'fa-innaha lā taʿmā al-abṣāru wa-lakin taʿmā al-qulūbu' ('not the eyes are blind, but the hearts in the breasts are')—the heart, not the eye, is the organ of true perception. The divine name al-Baṣīr is constantly paired with al-Samīʿ (~24x; 4:58, 22:61, 31:28) to express comprehensive divine awareness; 6:103 sharpens the paradox: 'lā tudrikuhu al-abṣāru wa-huwa yudriku al-abṣāra' ('Vision perceives Him not, but He perceives all vision'). The ethical command to 'lower the gaze' (ghuddū min abṣārihim, 24:30-31) makes baṣar a moral category, while the rhetorical question 'hal yastawī al-aʿmā wa-l-baṣīr' (6:50, 13:16, 35:19, 40:58) drives the blind-vs-seeing contrast.

etymology.semantic_evolution: Proto-Semitic visual perception → Arabic developed three concentric rings: (1) physical—basar=eye/sight (48x), (2) cognitive—basirah=insight/proof (7x), (3) divine—al-Basir as Allah omniscient perception (51x).

key_nominals.meaning: one who sees (4x); mubsirah = giving visibility (3x)

quranic_analysis.theme: Not eyes but hearts blind
quranic_analysis.detail: Fa-innaha la tama al-absaru wa-lakin tama al-qulub—the signature verse. Physical eyes (absar) not the issue; spiritual perception in the heart.

quranic_analysis.theme: al-Basir: divine omniscience
quranic_analysis.detail: al-Sami al-Basir—the paired divine attribute. Allah hears and sees all comprehensively.

quranic_analysis.theme: Lower your gaze
quranic_analysis.detail: Qul li-al-muminin yaghuddu min absarihim—the famous modesty verse.

quranic_analysis.theme: Blind vs seeing
quranic_analysis.detail: Hal yastawi al-ama wa al-basir—is the blind equal to the seeing? Repeated rhetorical question.

lexicographical_sources.ibn_faris: Core = al-ilm bi al-shay (knowledge of a thing). Sight is the primary vehicle for acquiring knowledge.
lexicographical_sources.al_raghib: Basar = physical eye that sees; basirah = inner eye that perceives truth. The physical and spiritual are two registers of one faculty.
lexicographical_sources.lane: al-basaru = al-ilmu (sight = knowledge). Basara: he saw, knew. Basir: seeing, knowing.

theological_dimensions: al-Basir as divine name: one of the most frequent attributes after al-Rahman, al-Rahim, al-Aziz, al-Hakim
Eye-heart epistemology: 22:46 negates physical sight primacy—true sight is in the heart
Six paired with al-Sami: comprehensive divine awareness—nothing escapes
Faculties as trust: sight/hearing/heart are divine gifts to be used righteously
6:103: Vision perceives Him not—divine transcendence beyond visual perception
hadith_evidence: Allah is not one-eyed but al-Masih al-Dajjal is one-eyed (Bukhari)—establishing divine visual perfection
Lowering the gaze as prescribed by 24:30—the cornerstone of Islamic modesty ethics
cross_references: عمى (Emy)—blindness: antonym; hal yastawi al-ama wa al-basir
رأى (rAy)—to see: most common see verb (327x)

meaning.en: Sign, verse, miracle. 382 occurrences—noun only. Ayah/ayat (382x)=the most frequent Quranic self-designation. Three meanings: Quranic verse, cosmic sign, prophetic miracle. 41:53: We will show them Our signs in the horizons and in themselves. Proto-Semitic *awayat- (sign/token), Hebrew ot, Aramaic ata. Ibn Faris: al-alamah—the sign, mark. Distributed across 59 surahs.
meaning.en_detailed: Root آ-ي-ة (ʾ-y-h), with the noun form āyah / āyāt ('sign, verse'), generates 382 occurrences—the Quran's most frequent self-designation, distributed across 59 surahs. Three concentric meanings interlock: Quranic verse (2:99 'āyāt al-kitāb'), cosmic sign (2:164 'in khalqi al-samāwāti wa-l-arḍi wa-khtilāfi al-layli wa-l-nahāri la-āyātin li-ulī al-albāb'), and prophetic miracle (7:158, 'qul innamā anā nadhīrun mubīn'). Verse 41:53 summarizes: 'sa-nurīhim āyātinā fī al-āfāqi wa-fī anfusihim ḥattā yatabayyana lahum annahu al-ḥaqq' ('We will show them Our signs in the horizons and within themselves until it becomes clear to them that it is the truth')—āyāt as the totality of divine self-disclosure. The root derives from Proto-Semitic *ʾ-y 'which, what?'—cognate with Hebrew ʾē ('where?') and Ge'ez ʾay ('which?'); the noun āyah retains etymological memory of pointing, indicating.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic interrogative particle. In Arabic, ayy functions as both interrogative and conditional — 'whichever'. Quranic usage: 'whichever way you turn, there is the face of Allah' (2:115).

quranic_analysis.theme: Cosmic signs
quranic_analysis.detail: Creation, night/day alternation—ayat for those who reflect.

quranic_analysis.theme: Quranic verses
quranic_analysis.detail: Ayat al-kitab—the Quran most frequent self-designation.

theological_dimensions: Ayat as divine self-disclosure
Cosmic epistemology: signs in horizons and selves (41:53)

hadith_evidence.ar: تَدَبَّرُوا الْقُرْآنَ فَإِنَّهُ حُجَّةٌ لَكُمْ أَوْ عَلَيْكُمْ
hadith_evidence.en: Reflect upon the Quran, for it is either a proof for you or against you.
hadith_evidence.source: Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim via ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb

meaning.en: Earth, land. 461 occurrences—most frequent geographical term. Ard (461x, noun only). Proto-Semitic *ʔarṣ́-, Hebrew erets. 84 surahs. Always feminine. Paired with samawat (~200x). Creation in six days (7:54). Vicegerency (2:30). Earth replaced on Judgment Day (14:48).
meaning.en_detailed: Root أ-ر-ض (ʾ-r-ḍ), the feminine noun arḍ ('earth, land'), from Proto-Semitic *ʾarṣ́-, generates 461 occurrences—the most frequent geographical term in the Quran, distributed across 84 surahs and constantly paired with samāwāt (~200x). The pairing frames cosmic theology: 7:54 'khalaqa al-samāwāti wa-l-arḍa fī sittati ayyāmin' opens the cosmogonic formula; 2:30 'innī jāʿilun fī al-arḍi khalīfatan' establishes human vicegerency over the earth. Eschatologically, 14:48 declares 'yawma tubaddalu al-arḍu ghayra al-arḍi wa-l-samāwātu wa-barazū li-Allāhi al-wāḥidi al-qahhār' ('the Day the earth will be replaced by another earth, and the heavens [also]')—cosmic transformation. The arḍ is also a vessel of divine signs (3:190, 13:3, 16:65) and a stage for moral testing (67:15). Cognate with Hebrew ʾereṣ and Akkadian erṣetu, the Quranic arḍ spans earth-as-soil, earth-as-territory, and earth-as-cosmic-order.

quranic_analysis.theme: Creation heavens and earth
quranic_analysis.detail: Khalaqa al-samawati wa al-arda fi sittati ayyam.

quranic_analysis.theme: Vicegerency
quranic_analysis.detail: Inni jailun fi al-ardi khalifatan—human stewardship.

quranic_analysis.theme: Earth replaced
quranic_analysis.detail: Yawma tubaddalu al-ardu ghayra al-ardi—cosmic transformation.

theological_dimensions: Heavens and earth: most frequent noun pair—divine sovereignty
Khilafa: human stewardship of earth

hadith_evidence.ar: تَدَبَّرُوا الْقُرْآنَ فَإِنَّهُ حُجَّةٌ لَكُمْ أَوْ عَلَيْكُمْ
hadith_evidence.en: Reflect upon the Quran, for it is either a proof for you or against you.
hadith_evidence.source: Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim via ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb

meaning.en: Heaven, sky; name. 381x. Sama'=sky (310x). Ism=name (39x). Sab'a samawat=seven heavens. Proto-Semitic *shamay-, Hebrew shamayim.
meaning.en_detailed: Root س-م-و (s-m-w), from Proto-Semitic *š-m-y 'to be high,' generates 381 occurrences centered on samāʾ ('sky/heaven,' 310x) and its plural samāwāt ('heavens,' ~190x), with the homophonous ism ('name,' ~25x) deriving from the same root via 'to mark/highlight.' The formula sabʿa samāwāt ('seven heavens') appears 7 times (2:29, 41:12, 65:12, 67:3, 71:15, 78:12, 9:87), each heaven layered (ṭibāqan, 67:3) above the earth—the Quran's stratified cosmic architecture. 21:30 sets the cosmogonic baseline: 'a-wa-lam yaraw kayfa nubdī al-arḍa—lammaʾū fī al-mashīʿi—wa-l-samāʾa banaynāhā bi-aydīn—inna al-samāʾāti wa-l-arḍa kānā ratqan fa-fatqnāhumā' ('the heavens and earth were a joined entity, and We split them apart'). The samāwāt are doorways to revelation (97:1-4, the night of qadr) and the locus of angels' descent.

quranic_analysis.theme: Seven heavens
quranic_analysis.detail: Allah created seven heavens in layers (tibaqan).

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *šmy = 'to be high → sky/heaven'. The Quranic samāwāt (seven heavens) are the cosmic architecture pointing to divine power. The ism (name) may derive from the same root via wasama = to mark (a 'high' mark of identification).

hadith_evidence.ar: حُفَّتِ الْجَنَّةُ بِالْمَكَارِهِ وَحُفَّتِ النَّارُ بِالشَّهَوَاتِ
hadith_evidence.en: Paradise is surrounded by hardships and Hell is surrounded by desires.

meaning.en: To protect, guard, safeguard; God-consciousness, piety. 258 occurrences. Ittaqa VIII (166x)=to be God-conscious—the most common form. Waqa I (16x)=to protect/shield. Taqwa (17x)=piety—the best provision (2:197). Muttaqin (49x)=the God-conscious—primary audience of Quran (2:2). 49:13: most noble is most righteous (atqa). Ibn Faris: core = al-hifz wa al-siyana (protection and safeguarding). The imperative ittaqu (fear Allah/be conscious) recurs ~40x. The root spans physical protection (16:81 garments) to the highest spiritual station of God-consciousness.
meaning.ar: التقوى: وقاية النفس من العذاب — إن أكرمكم عند الله أتقاكم
meaning.en_detailed: Root و-ق-ي (w-q-y), from Proto-Semitic *waqay- 'to protect, guard,' generates 258 occurrences that constitute the Quran's most comprehensive term for Islamic piety: taqwā ('God-consciousness, fear of God'). The Form VIII ittaqā ('to guard oneself through obedience') dominates with ~200 occurrences, including the ~40-fold refrain ittaqu Allāh ('be conscious of Allāh')—the most frequent Quranic imperative. The verbal noun taqwā (~50x) is foundational: 2:2 announces the Qurʾān as 'hudan li-l-muttaqīn' ('guidance for the God-conscious'); 2:197 calls taqwā 'khayru al-zādi' ('the best provision for the journey'); 49:13 makes it the supreme criterion of nobility: 'innā akramakum ʿinda Allāhi atqākum' ('the most noble of you before God is the most God-conscious'). The verb waqā ('to protect,' 10x) names both physical preservation (16:81 'garments that protect you from heat') and the famous 2:201 supplication 'rabbanā ātinā... wa-qinā ʿadhāba al-nār.'

etymology.semantic_evolution: Proto-Semitic 'protect' → Arabic developed into central theological term: ittaqa (guard oneself through obedience) → taqwa (the state of God-consciousness). Quranic innovation: physical protection verb → most comprehensive term for Islamic piety.

derived_forms.meaning: to fear God, be pious, guard oneself

quranic_analysis.theme: Taqwa as audience qualifier
quranic_analysis.detail: Dhalika al-kitab... hudan li-al-muttaqin—Quran is guidance for those possessing taqwa.

quranic_analysis.theme: Taqwa as criterion of nobility
quranic_analysis.detail: Inna akramakum inda Allahi atqakum—supreme criterion: not race/lineage but God-consciousness.

quranic_analysis.theme: Taqwa as best provision
quranic_analysis.detail: Fa-inna khayra al-zadi al-taqwa—spiritual sustenance for life's journey.

quranic_analysis.theme: Waqina: the most recited supplication
quranic_analysis.detail: Rabbana atina fi al-dunya hasanah... wa-qina adhaba al-nar—protection from Fire.

quranic_analysis.theme: Ittaqullah refrain
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa-ittaqullah—be conscious of Allah—the most frequent Quranic imperative.

lexicographical_sources.ibn_faris: Single core: al-hifz wa al-siyana (protection and safeguarding). All derived forms return to this.
lexicographical_sources.al_raghib: Taqwa = making the self reside in protection (wiqayah) from what is feared. The muttaqi is one who makes himself in wiqayah from punishment through obedience.
lexicographical_sources.lane: Waqa = he protected, guarded. Ittaqa = he guarded himself, was pious. Taqwa = fear of God, piety.

theological_dimensions: Taqwa: comprehensive Islamic virtue—God-consciousness motivating righteous action
Mutttaqin as primary Quranic audience (2:2): taqwa prerequisite for guidance
Atqa criterion (49:13): taqwa transcends all worldly distinctions
Taqwa as provision (2:197): spiritual sustenance for life's journey
Ittaqullah refrain (~40x): the most frequent divine command
hadith_evidence: Al-taqwa hahuna—Taqwa is here (pointing to heart, 3x) (Muslim)
Ittaqu Allah haqqa tuqatih—Fear Allah as He should be feared (3:102)
The most common cause of entering Paradise: taqwa and good character (Tirmidhi)
cross_references: خوف (xwf)—fear: taqwa is proactive righteousness, not mere terror
إيمان (Amn)—faith: taqwa is practical outworking of faith

meaning.en: Last, end; Hereafter. 250x. Al-Akhir (155x nominal: last/Hereafter), Akhar (70x: other)=Hereafter. Al-Akhir=divine name (57:3). Akhar (~130x)=other. Akhkhara II=delay.
meaning.en_detailed: Root أ-خ-ر (ʾ-kh-r), from Proto-Semitic *ʾ-kh-r 'to be behind, after,' generates 250 occurrences that establish the Quranic temporality of dunyā-vs-ākhira ('this-world vs. Hereafter'). The noun al-ākhira ('the Hereafter,' 115x) names 'the last' or 'later' life, structurally contrasted with al-dunyā ('the nearer'). The juxtaposition organizes Quranic ethics: 2:86 'alladhīna ishtaraw al-ḥayāta al-dunyā bi-l-ākhira' ('those who bought the life of this world at the price of the Hereafter'); 4:77 'al-ḥayātu al-dunyā laysat illā ʿibāratun' ('the life of this world is but a passing enjoyment'); 57:20 'al-ḥayātu al-dunyā laysat illā laʿiban wa-laḥwan' ('the life of this world is only play and diversion'). The divine name al-Akhir ('the Last,' 57:3) pairs with al-Awwal ('the First')—'Huwa al-Awwalu wa-l-Akhiru wa-l-Ẓāhiru wa-l-Bāṭinu'—expressing divine eternity encompassing all temporal sequence.

quranic_analysis.theme: Al-Akhir divine name
quranic_analysis.detail: Huwa al-Awwal wa al-Akhir—He is the First and the Last.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *ʾḫr = 'to be behind, after'. The Quranic ākhirah (the Last, the Hereafter) is the ultimate temporal horizon — what comes 'after' this world. The binary dunyā (the nearer) vs ākhirah (the later) structures Quranic temporality.

hadith_evidence.ar: تَدَبَّرُوا الْقُرْآنَ فَإِنَّهُ حُجَّةٌ لَكُمْ أَوْ عَلَيْكُمْ

meaning.en: After; distance. 235x. Ba'da=after (199x). Ba'id=far. 70:6-7: they see it as far, We see it as near. Antonym: qarib.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ب-ع-د (b-ʿ-d), from Proto-Semitic *b-ʿ-d 'to be far, distant,' generates 235 occurrences distributed between temporal 'after' (baʿd, 199x) and spatial 'far' (baʿīd, 25x). Verses 70:6-7 supply a striking epistemological paradox: 'innahum yarawnahu baʿīdan wa-narāhu qarībā' ('they see it [the Hour] as far off, but We see it as near')—the human perception of eschatological distance contradicted by divine immediacy. Verse 23:36 contains the disbelievers' mockery: 'wa-qālū a-idhā madhnā fī al-turābi a-innā la-fī khalqin jadīd—bal hum bi-liqāʾi rabbihim kāfirūn—wa-qālū hayyālaka hādhā yawmu al-dīn / abīdan mā nuʿad'—baʿīd as taunt of impossibility. The verbal forms baʿuda ('to be distant,' 2x) and the imprecation buʿd ('away!,' 7x, e.g., 11:60 'buʿḍan li-l-qawmi al-ẓālimīn') show the negative pole. The opposite qarīb ('near') frames the entire eschatological horizon.

quranic_analysis.theme: Perceived vs real distance
quranic_analysis.detail: Innahum yarawnahu ba'idan wa-narahu qariban—epistemological paradox.

key_nominals.meaning: far, distant (25x)—70:6-7 they see it as far

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *bʿd = 'to be far, distant'. Arabic baʿuda = to be far. Baʿd = after (temporal distance). The Quranic baʿīd (distant) describes eschatological remoteness — 'far, far is what you are promised' (23:36 — the disbelievers' mockery). The proximity to God's mercy vs distance from it is a recurring theme.

hadith_evidence.en: Reflect upon the Quran, for it is either a proof for you or against you.
hadith_evidence.source: Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim via ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb

meaning.en: Path, way, road. 176 occurrences—noun only, no verbal forms in Quran. Sabil (176x)=way/path. Sabil Allah (~68x)=the way of Allah—the most frequent usage: spending, striving, fighting in God's cause. Ibn al-sabil=wayfarer (8x)—Quranic category of charity recipients. Sawaa al-sabil=the middle/straight way (5x). Sabil al-ghayy=path of error (7:146). Sabr al-rashad=path of right guidance (40:29, 40:38). Broken plural subul occurs 8x. Cognate with Syriac šəbīlā, Hebrew šəbīl (path). Fa'il pattern = well-trodden way. Frequently contrasted: sadda an sabil Allah (hindered from God's way) and dalla an sabil (strayed from the way).
meaning.ar: السبيل: الطريق — وقتلوا في سبيل الله — والذين جاهدوا فينا لنهدينهم سبلنا
meaning.en_detailed: Root س-ب-ل (s-b-l), the noun sabīl ('path, way') borrowed from Aramaic/Syriac šəbīlā, generates 176 Quranic occurrences with no verbal forms—the word names a 'well-trodden way' extended metaphorically to divine and moral paths. The construction sabīl Allāh ('the way of God,' ~68x) is the most frequent: 2:154 'wa-lā taqulū li-man yuqṭalu fī sabīli Allāhi amwātun bal aḥyāʾun' ('those killed in God's way are not dead but alive'); 2:195 'wa-anfusahum fī sabīli Allāh' ('spending themselves in God's way'); 9:20 'alladhīna āmanū wa-hājarū wa-jāhadū fī sabīli Allāh' ('those who strove in God's way'). The phrase ibn al-sabīl ('wayfarer, traveler,' 8x; 2:177, 9:60, 17:26) names a Quranic category of charity recipients. The plural subul ('paths') appears 8x—5:16 'subul al-salām' ('ways of peace'); 29:69 promises 'those who strive in Us, We will guide them to Our paths (subulanā).'

etymology.semantic_evolution: Borrowed from Aramaic/Syriac šəbīlā (path). Arabic adopted as fa'il pattern noun with the physical sense of 'well-trodden way' and extended it to the theological concept of 'God's path/way'.

key_nominals.meaning: way, path (176x)—sabil Allah (~68x); also: method, manner, means
ways, paths (8x broken plural)—subulana (our ways, 14:12); subul al-salam (ways of peace, 5:16)
wayfarer, traveler (8x)—lit. son of the road; entitled to charity

quranic_analysis.theme: Sabil Allah: the way of God
quranic_analysis.detail: Fi sabil Allah—in the way of Allah. Encompasses jihad, spending for God's cause, and the path of faith. The most frequent Quranic designation for religious path.

quranic_analysis.theme: Hindered from God's way
quranic_analysis.detail: Sadda an sabil Allah—hindered/blocked from Allah's way. Common accusation against disbelievers.

quranic_analysis.theme: Ibn al-Sabil: wayfarer
quranic_analysis.detail: Wayfarer as Quranic category of charity recipients—those cut off from home and resources.

quranic_analysis.theme: Sawaa al-sabil: the middle way
quranic_analysis.detail: The balanced, straight, middle path—equivalent to al-sirat al-mustaqim.

lexicographical_sources.ibn_faris: s-b-l: a path and a flowing. Sabil = al-tariq (the way). The path that is well-trodden and clearly visible.
lexicographical_sources.al_raghib: Sabil = the path that is clear and easy. Metaphorically used for the path of truth and the path of falsehood.
lexicographical_sources.lane: sabil = a way, path, road. Al-sabil = the road. Sabil Allah = the way of Allah (religious warfare, jihad, etc.).

theological_dimensions: Sabil Allah as central theological metaphor: the way of God encompasses all righteous striving
Subul al-salam (5:16): ways of peace—divine guidance leads to manifold paths of peace
Ibn al-Sabil: institutionalized charity for displaced travelers—social justice mandate
Plural subul: God's ways are multiple—those who strive will be guided to Our ways (29:69)
hadith_evidence: Al-sadaqatu fi sabil Allah—Charity in the way of Allah multiplies 700-fold (Bukhari)
Ribat fi sabil Allah—Guarding the frontier in God's way is better than the world and what it contains (Bukhari)
Man khala min jihadin fi sabil Allah—Whoever dies without striving in God's way or intending it, dies on a branch of hypocrisy (Muslim)
cross_references: هدى (hdy)—guidance: subul al-salam as guidance paths
ضلل (Dll)—error: sabil al-ghayy vs sabil al-rashad

meaning.en: Evil, bad, ugly; harm, distress. 167 occurrences across 12 derived forms. Saa I (30x)=to be evil/grieve—opposite of nima. Su (50x)=evil/harm—al-nafs al-ammarah bi al-su (12:53). Sayyiat (36x pl.)=evil deeds—hasanat erase sayyiat (11:114). Sawat (5x)=shame/private parts (Fall narrative). Ibn Faris: core=ugliness and evil. Proto-Semitic *s--w. Key theological: the soul commands evil, good deeds erase bad. Opposites: hasan, khayr.
meaning.en_detailed: Root س-و-أ (s-w-ʾ), from Proto-Semitic *s-ʾ-w 'to be evil, ugly,' generates 167 occurrences across 12 derived forms—spanning ethical evil, physical harm, and the primal shame of the Fall narrative. The Form I saʾa ('to be evil, grieve,' 30x) names the opposite of niʿma: 16:60 declares that 'the evil (saʾ) of what you describe outweighs the good.' The verbal noun sūʾ ('evil, harm,' 50x) names what 'the soul commanding evil' (al-nafs al-āmmārah bi-l-sūʾ, 12:53) prompts—Joseph's diagnostic of human concupiscence. The plural sayyiʾāt ('evil deeds,' 36x) is redeemed through its opposite: 11:114 'innā al-ḥasanāti yudhhibna al-sayyiʾāt' ('good deeds erase evil deeds')—the formula of ethical transformation by counterweight. The dual form sawʾāt ('shame, private parts,' 5x) names the primal covering after Adam's lapse (20:121). The contrast sayyiʾah-vs-ḥasanah structures the Quranic moral ledger, where recompense follows: 6:160 'man jāʾa bi-l-ḥasanati fa-lahu ʿashru amthālihā wa-man jāʾa bi-l-sayyiʾati fa-lā yujzā illā mithlahā.'

key_nominals.meaning: evil deed (22x sg., 36x pl.)—hasanat erase sayyiat (11:114)
shame, private parts (5x pl. saw'at)—Fall narrative

quranic_analysis.theme: Good deeds erase evil
quranic_analysis.detail: Inna al-hasanati yudhhibna al-sayyiat—the redemptive power of good actions.

theological_dimensions: Al-nafs al-ammarah bi al-su: the soul commands evil (12:53)
Hasanat erase sayyiat: ethical transformation formula
Divine recompense: tenfold good, evil only its like

hadith_evidence.ar: لَا ضَرَرَ وَلَا ضِرَارَ
hadith_evidence.en: There shall be no harm nor reciprocating harm.

meaning.en: First, beginning, foremost. 170 occurrences across 4 branches. Awwal (82x)=first—al-Awwal divine name (57:3). Uli (45x)=possessors of—ulu al-albab (men of understanding). Al (26x)=family of—Al Firawn, Al Ibrahim. Tawil (17x)=interpretation—dream interpretation in Surah Yusuf (12:6-101) and doctrine of mutashabihat (3:7). Ibn Faris: core=precedence and beginning. Proto-Semitic *-w-l.
meaning.en_detailed: Root أ-و-ل (ʾ-w-l), from Proto-Semitic 'to precede, be first,' generates 170 occurrences distributed across four semantic branches: temporal priority (awwal, 'first'), family/kinship (āl, 'family of'), possession/attribution (ulū, 'possessors of'), and hermeneutics (taʾwīl, 'interpretation, ultimate meaning'). The divine name al-Awwal ('the First') appears at 57:3 paired with al-Akhir, al-Ẓāhir, al-Bāṭin: 'Huwa al-Awwalu wa-l-Akhiru wa-l-Ẓāhiru wa-l-Bāṭinu wa-huwa bi-kulli shayʾin ʿalīm'—the four names expressing divine encompassment of all temporal and ontological modalities. The noun āl ('family of') names the recurring Quranic constructions: āl Firʿawn ('Pharaoh's house,' ~25x), āl Ibrāhīm, āl Yaʿqūb. The form ulū al-albāb ('possessors of intellect/understanding,' 16x), ulū al-aʿyān ('people of vision'), ulū al-ʿilm ('those who know') name the addressed elite. The taʾwīl ('interpretation,' 17x) names the hermeneutic work: 3:7 'wa-mā yaʿlamu taʾwīla hu illā Allāh' (none knows its taʾwīl except Allāh); Surah Yūsuf revolves on dream interpretation (12:6, 12:21, 12:36, 12:44, 12:100-101).

quranic_analysis.theme: al-Awwal as divine name
quranic_analysis.detail: Huwa al-Awwal wa al-Akhir—He is the First and the Last. Paired with al-Akhir, al-Zahir, al-Batin.

theological_dimensions: al-Awwal: divine name—God precedes all creation and endures after all
Tawil: key exegetical concept—none knows mutashabihat interpretation except Allah (3:7)

meaning.en: Many, much, abundance. 167 occurrences. Kathir (63x)=many/much. Akthar (80x)=more/most—the dominant form. Akthar al-nas la yalamun (most people do not know)—recurring Quranic refrain. Kaththara II (1x)=to multiply. Kawthar (1x, 108:1)=abundance (Surah al-Kawthar). Takathur (2x)=mutual multiplication/ rivalry—alhakum al-takathur (102:1). Verb forms: kathura I (2x), kaththara II (1x), akthara IV (2x), istakthara X (3x).
meaning.en_detailed: Root ك-ث-ر (k-th-r), from Proto-Semitic 'to be many,' generates 167 occurrences across the adjectival kathīr ('many/much,' 63x), the elative akthar ('more/most,' 80x), and the substantive kawthar ('abundance'). The dominant formula akthar al-nās ('most people') recurs with striking predicates: 12:103, 12:106, 16:38, 16:83, 27:73, 30:6, 30:8, 34:36, 36:7—each declaring what 'most people' do not know, do not believe, do not understand, are ungrateful for. The recurring refrain 'wa-lākinna akthara al-nāsi lā yaʿlamūn / lā yuʾminūn / lā yashkurūn' is the Quran's sociological verdict: the majority live in epistemological distance from truth. Surah al-Takāthur (102) addresses the rivalrous multiplication of wealth and children (al-hākum al-takāthur) as spiritual distraction—'numbered will be the visits to graves' (2x). The unique proper noun al-Kawthar (108:1, 'the abundance') promises divine plenitude against apparent diminishment—a single word defining Paradise's superabundance.

quranic_analysis.theme: Most people do not know/believe
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa-lakinna akthara al-nasi la yalamun—recurring refrain emphasizing human heedlessness.

quranic_analysis.theme: Takathur: rivalry in abundance
quranic_analysis.detail: Alhakum al-takathur—distracted by rivalry in multiplying wealth/children until you visit the graves.

theological_dimensions: Akthar al-nas: most people ungrateful, heedless—epistemological distance from truth
Takathur: materialism as spiritual distraction
Kawthar: divine abundance as ultimate blessing

meaning.en: Like, similar; example, parable, statue. 169 occurrences. Mathal (88x)=example/parable. daraba mathalan = strike an example (~30x). Mithl (75x)=like/similar. nothing is like Him (42:11). Tamathil (2x)=statues. Ibn Faris: core=likeness. Hebrew cognate: mashal (proverb). Quranic parables: spider, mosquito, fly, good tree.
meaning.en_detailed: Root م-ث-ل (m-th-l), with the principal noun mathal ('example, parable,' 88x) and mithl ('like, similar,' 75x), generates 169 occurrences—constituting the Quran's signature rhetorical mode. The verb ḍaraba mathalan ('to strike a parable') introduces Quranic analogy ~30 times: the spider's web (29:41, 'the frailest of dwellings'), the mosquito and fly (2:26 'innā Allāha lā yastahyī an yaḍriba mathalan mā baʿūḍatan fa-mā fawqahā'), the good word as a good tree (14:24-26), the rain that revives dead earth (2:164, 16:65). Verse 42:11 establishes the negative theological pinnacle: 'laysa ka-mithlihi shayʾun' ('nothing is like Him')—the root underwriting divine transcendence: all created things serve as simile; God exceeds them infinitely. The plural tamāthīl ('statues,' 2x) names the idols carved as likenesses (34:13 'yaʿmalūna lahu mā yashāʾu min tamāthīl')—the parable form inverted into false representation.

quranic_analysis.theme: Quranic Parables
quranic_analysis.detail: Primary rhetorical device—spider web, good tree, mosquito.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *mwl = 'to incline → to have wealth'. The Arabic māl originally meant 'that which inclines the heart' — wealth as temptation. The Aramaic māmōnā entered Greek and Latin as 'Mammon' — the personification of wealth. The Quran treats māl as a divine trust and test.

meaning.en: Some, part, portion. 158x. Ba'd (157x)=some/part. opposite of kull (all). Ba'dukum li-ba'din = some of you to others (reciprocal/mutual). Ba'udah (1x)=mosquito (2:26). 2:85: do you believe in part of the Book and reject part?
meaning.en_detailed: Root ب-ع-ض (b-ʿ-ḍ), from Proto-Semitic *b-ʿ-d 'to be part,' generates 158 occurrences centered on baʿḍ ('some, part, portion')—the universal grammatical and conceptual operator of partition. The construction baʿḍukum li-baʿḍin ('some of you [against/for] others') structures social relationships: 2:36 'wa-qulnā uhbitū baʿḍukum li-baʿḍin ʿaduwwun' ('We said, Go down, some of you to others as enemies'); 6:52, 9:101, 24:32, 49:13—each mapping social, marital, communal, and economic relations. The sharply ethical use at 2:85 condemns selective belief: 'afa-tuʾminūna bi-baʿḍi al-kitābi wa-takfurūna bi-baʿḍin' ('do you believe in part of the Book and disbelieve in part?')—partition of faith into compatible and incompatible portions. The reciprocal mutuality of baʿḍ...baʿḍ echoes the brotherhood formula of 49:10. The unique noun baʿīḍah ('mosquito,' 2:26) ironically invokes 'a part' as the smallest creature used in Quranic parable.

quranic_analysis.theme: Reciprocal construction
quranic_analysis.detail: Ba'dukum li-ba'din aduwwun—mutual enmity.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *bʿd = 'to be far'. Baʿuda = to be distant. Baʿd = after. The dunyā (nearer) vs the baʿīd (far) — the two temporal horizons.

meaning.en: Below, besides, other than. 144x. Duna = besides/below. Min dun Allah = besides Allah (~50x). Taking protectors besides Allah—primary Quranic critique of shirk.
meaning.en_detailed: Root د-و-ن (d-w-n), functioning primarily as the preposition dūn ('below, besides, other than, less than'), generates 144 occurrences and serves as the Quran's central linguistic formula for idolatry. The construction min dūni Allāh ('besides Allah,' ~50 occurrences) is the dominant polemical target: 2:23 'wa-in kuntum fī raybin mimmā nazzalnā ʿalā ʿabdinā fa-ʾtū bi-sūratin min mithlihi wa-dʿū shuhadāʾakum min dūni Allāh' ('if you doubt what We revealed, produce a surah like it and call your witnesses besides Allah'); 2:107 'wa-taqūlūna tubnā li-Allāh mā lā yanfaʿunā wa-lā yaḍurru nā—laqad jaʾakum Allāhu bi-jināhi—in'afū Allāh yaghfir lakum' (in the broader argument about what one attributes to Allāh); 2:165 'wa-min al-nāsi man yaʿkhudu min dūni Allāhi andāḍan yuḥibbūnahum ka-ḥubbi Allāh' ('some take equals to God, loving them as God is loved'). The preposition names the entire ontological subordination that shirk enacts.

key_nominals.m: besides, other than; less than; before

quranic_analysis.theme: Min dun Allah
quranic_analysis.detail: The most frequent construction—denounces taking helpers besides God.

derived_forms.meaning: besides, other than; less than; before

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *dwn = 'to be low, inferior'. Arabic dūn functions as a preposition = 'below, less than, besides, without'. The Quranic 'min dūni Allāh' (besides/below Allah) is the linguistic formula for idolatry — placing something dūn (lower than) God.

meaning.en: Meeting, encounter; to cast, throw. 146x. Liqa' = meeting—liqa' Allah = meeting God (key eschatological concept, ~20x). Alqa IV = to cast/throw—alqa al-sam' (cast hearing), alqa al-Ruh (cast the Spirit). Talaqqa V = to receive. 29:5: whoever hopes for meeting Allah—the term is coming. 2:37: Adam received words from his Lord (talaqqa).
meaning.en_detailed: Root ل-ق-ي (l-q-y), from Proto-Semitic *l-q-y 'to meet, encounter,' generates 146 occurrences centered on liqāʾ Allāh ('meeting with God') as the supreme eschatological category. The phrase liqāʾ Allāh (and variants liqāʾī, liqāʾan) appears ~20 times, distinguishing believers from disbelievers: 29:5 'man kāna yarjū liqāʾa Allāh—fa-inna ajala Allāhi la-ʾātin' ('whoever hopes for the meeting with God—God's term is surely coming'); 6:31 'wa-annī ilā Allāhi muqallibukum wa-muwallīkum wa-ʿalayhi taqūlūn—Allāha laqad jaʾakum bi-jināhin'; 10:7 'idhā nubshirū fīhi liqāʾ Allāh' (wait until they meet God—taunting the believers). The verbal forms spread across the semantic field: Form I laqiya ('to meet,' 100x), talaqqā ('to receive,' 15x—2:37 'talaqqā Ādamu min rabbihi kalimāt' Adam received words from his Lord), alqā IV ('to cast/throw,' 7:117 'wa-nulqī ʿalayhim isrā'). The dual semantic range—meeting and casting—frames revelation as Allah 'casting' the Spirit on the Prophet.

quranic_analysis.theme: Meeting Allah
quranic_analysis.detail: Liqa' Allah—hope for or denial of meeting God distinguishes believers from disbelievers.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *lqy = 'to meet, encounter'. The Quranic liqāʾ Allāh (meeting with God) is the ultimate eschatological event — the encounter with one's Lord on the Day of Judgment. This gives 'meeting' profound theological weight.

meaning.en: God, deity; Allah. 2851 occurrences—the most frequent word in the Quran. Allah (2699x)—the supreme proper name of God. Ilah (147x)=deity, god—la ilaha illa Allah (no deity except Allah). The etymology is debated: contraction of al-ilah (the deity), or from Syrian alaha. The word encompasses all divine attributes. The Shahada centers on this root: ashhadu an la ilaha illa Allah. Allah is al-Rahman, al-Rahim, al-Malik, al-Quddus, and all 99 Names.
meaning.en_detailed: Root أ-ل-ه (ʾ-l-h), from Proto-Semitic *ʾ-l-h 'god, deity,' generates 2851 occurrences—the most frequent word in the Quran and the central term of Quranic theology. The proper noun Allāh ('God,' 2697x) is the supreme name; ilāh ('deity,' 147x) names any god; allāhumma is the vocative (5x). The shahādah formula lā ilāha illā Allāh ('no deity except Allāh')—built entirely on this root—anchors tawḥīd: 37:35 'idhā qulū lā ilāha illā antu subḥānak' ('when they said, no god but You, glory be to You'); 47:19 'fa-ʿlam annahu lā ilāha illā Allāh wa-staghfir li-dhanbika' ('know that there is no deity but Allāh'). The divine names cluster: al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm, al-Malik al-Quddūs, al-Salām al-Muʾmin—all adjectives of Allāh. The name may derive from al-ilāh ('the god') contracted, or from Syrian alāhā; the alif-lām is integral and not the article. The root's cognates include Hebrew ʾElōah and Aramaic ʾAlāhā; Arabic alone has reserved Allāh as the proper name of the One God.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر أَلِهَ — 2851 مرة — الإله المعبود، الاسم الأعظم لله تعالى

quranic_analysis.theme: Tawhid: la ilaha illa Allah
quranic_analysis.detail: The central Quranic declaration—no deity except Allah.

quranic_analysis.theme: Allah as Creator, Sustainer, Judge
quranic_analysis.detail: Comprehensive divine sovereignty—every attribute returns to Allah.

theological_dimensions: Tawhid: the absolute oneness of Allah—foundation of Islam
al-Asma' al-Husna: the 99 Most Beautiful Names
La ilaha illa Allah: the kalimah of faith

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *ʾlh = 'god, deity'. Arabic Allāh = the One God (al-ilāh contracted). Ilāh = any deity. The ʾalif-lām of Allāh is integral to the name — it cannot be stripped. Compare Hebrew ʾElōah (singular of ʾElōhīm) and Aramaic ʾAlāhā. The Quranic shahādah: 'lā ilāha illā Allāh' — negation of all ilāh followed by affirmation of Allāh alone.

hadith_evidence.ar: تَدَبَّرُوا الْقُرْآنَ فَإِنَّهُ حُجَّةٌ لَكُمْ أَوْ عَلَيْكُمْ
hadith_evidence.en: Reflect upon the Quran, for it is either a proof for you or against you.
hadith_evidence.source: Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim via ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb

meaning.en_short: Blessing, favor, bliss; to bestow favor
meaning.en: Blessing, favor, bliss. 140x. Ni'mah (40x)=blessing/favor. An'ama IV (39x)=to bestow favor—an'amta alayhim (1:7). Na'im (30x)=bliss (of Paradise). 93:11: wa amma bi-ni'mati rabbika fa-haddith—proclaim your Lord's blessing. 1:7: the path of those You have blessed. The root spans divine favor, gratitude response, and Paradise bliss.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ن-ع-م (n-ʿ-m), from Proto-Semitic *n-ʿ-m 'to be soft, pleasant,' generates 140 occurrences organized around divine favor (niʿma), the bestowal of favor (anʿama), and eschatological bliss (naʿīm). The verb IV anʿama ('to bestow favor,' 39x) is most frequent, anchoring al-Fātiḥa's path formula: 'iḥdinā al-ṣirāṭa al-mustaqīm / ṣirāṭa alladhīna anʿamta ʿalayhim ghayri al-maghḍūb ʿalayhim wa-lā al-ḍāllīn' (1:6-7, 'the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favor'). 14:34 declares the inexhaustible favor: 'wa-in taʿuddū niʿmata Allāhi lā tuḥṣūhā' ('if you enumerate Allāh's blessings, you cannot count them'). The noun naʿīm ('bliss,' 17x) names Paradise's positive content: 9:21, 10:9, 22:5, 35:35, 52:17-18, 56:12-18—paired with eating, drinking, enjoying. The declarative 'wa-ammā bi-niʿmati rabbika fa-haddith' (93:11, 'but proclaim the blessing of your Lord') transforms gratitude into speech.

quranic_analysis.theme: Divine blessings
quranic_analysis.detail: An'amta alayhim—those upon whom Allah has bestowed favor. The straight path belongs to the blessed.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *nʿm = 'to be soft, pleasant → blessed'. Niʿmah = blessing, favor. Naʿīm = bliss, delight (Paradise). Anʿama = to bestow favor. 'If you count the blessings (niʿam) of Allah, you cannot enumerate them' (14:34).

hadith_evidence.ar: تَدَبَّرُوا الْقُرْآنَ فَإِنَّهُ حُجَّةٌ لَكُمْ أَوْ عَلَيْكُمْ
hadith_evidence.en: Reflect upon the Quran, for it is either a proof for you or against you.
hadith_evidence.source: Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim via ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb

meaning.en: To ask, question, request. 129x. Sa'ala I = to ask. Yas'alunaka (~15x) = they ask you—formulaic Quranic pattern introducing legal/moral rulings. Su'al = question. Masa'il = questions/requests. 2:189: they ask you about the new moons (yas'alunaka ani al-ahillah). 17:85: they ask you about the Spirit. 17:23: do not say uff to parents—and if one or both reach old age, do not repel them.
meaning.en_detailed: Root س-أ-ل (s-ʾ-l), from Proto-Semitic *š-ʾ-l 'to ask, request,' generates 129 occurrences centered on the formula yasʾalūnaka ('they ask you, O Prophet')—the Quran's standard rhetorical-introductive device for legal-moral rulings. The formula appears ~15 times: 2:189 'yasʾalūnaka ʿani al-ahilla' ('they ask you about the new moons'); 2:215 'yasʾalūnaka mādhā yunfiqūn' ('they ask you what they should spend'); 2:217, 2:219, 2:220, 2:222, 5:4, 8:1, 17:85 'yasʾalūnaka ʿani al-rūḥ' ('they ask you about the Spirit'); 20:105, 79:42—each pivoting a divine response. The verb saʾala ('to ask,' 100x) ranges from neutral inquiry to the restrictive 'wa-lā tasʾalū ʿan ashyāʾa in tubda lakum tasuʾkum' ('do not ask about matters that, if made clear, would distress you,' 5:101). The Day of Judgment is yawm al-masʾalah (the Day of Questioning, 77:8).

quranic_analysis.theme: Yas'alunaka formula
quranic_analysis.detail: They ask you O Prophet—the standard formula introducing divine legal/moral responses.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *šʾl = 'to ask, request'. Stable meaning across Semitic. In the Quran, suʾāl encompasses both legitimate inquiry and forbidden questioning of divine wisdom. The Day of Judgment is the day of questioning (masʾalah).

hadith_evidence.ar: تَدَبَّرُوا الْقُرْآنَ فَإِنَّهُ حُجَّةٌ لَكُمْ أَوْ عَلَيْكُمْ
hadith_evidence.en: Reflect upon the Quran, for it is either a proof for you or against you.
hadith_evidence.source: Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim via ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb

meaning.en: Nearness; this world. 133x. Dunya (~115x) = this world—the nearer/lower life, contrasted with al-akhirah. Dana I = to be near, draw close. Adna IV = to bring near—al-sama' al-dunya (the lowest heaven). 57:20: the life of this world is but play and diversion. 2:86: those who bought this world over the Hereafter.
meaning.en_detailed: Root د-ن-و (d-n-w), from Proto-Semitic *d-n-w 'to be near, approach,' generates 133 occurrences centered on the foundational Quranic contrast: al-dunyā ('the nearer life, this world,' ~115x) versus al-ākhira ('the farther, the Hereafter'). The elative comparative dunyā (originally 'nearer' in time) becomes the noun of 'this-worldly life': 2:86 'alladhīna ishtaraw al-ḥayāta al-dunyā' ('those who bought the life of this world'); 4:77 'wa-taqūlūna matā hādhā al-waʿdu in kuntum ṣādiqīn—qul inna al-dunyā qalīlun wa-l-ākhiratu khayrun li-man ittaqā'; 57:20 'al-ḥayātu al-dunyā laysat illā laʿibun wa-laḥwun' ('the life of this world is only play and diversion'); 87:16-17 'innaka fī al-dunyā la-taqḍū amalan wa-lākinna al-ākhirata khayrun wa-abqā' ('you traverse stages in this world, but the Hereafter is better and more lasting'). The Form IV adnā ('nearer/lower,' 30x) includes 'al-samāʾ al-dunyā' (the lowest heaven, 37:6).

quranic_analysis.theme: Dunya vs Akhirah
quranic_analysis.detail: The fundamental Quranic contrast—the nearer life is temporary; the Hereafter is better and more lasting.

theological_dimensions: Dunya as deception: al-hayat al-dunya = the lower, deceptive life
The Hereafter is better: wa al-akhiratu khayrun wa abqa

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *dnw = 'to be near, approach'. Danā = to draw near. Dunyā = the nearer life (this world). 'The dunyā is the prison of the believer and the paradise of the disbeliever' (ḥadīth) — the 'nearer' vs the 'farther' (ākhirah).

hadith_evidence.ar: تَدَبَّرُوا الْقُرْآنَ فَإِنَّهُ حُجَّةٌ لَكُمْ أَوْ عَلَيْكُمْ
hadith_evidence.en: Reflect upon the Quran, for it is either a proof for you or against you.
hadith_evidence.source: Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim via ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb

meaning.en: Obedience, willingness. 129x. Ta'a = obedience. Ata'a IV = to obey—ati'u Allaha wa ati'u al-Rasul (4:59, obey Allah and the Messenger). Tatawwa'a V = to volunteer/willingly. Taw'an wa karhan = willingly or unwillingly (3:83, 13:15, 41:11). 4:59: the foundational verse of Islamic political theology—obedience hierarchy.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ط-و-ع (ṭ-w-ʿ), from Proto-Semitic *ṭ-w-ʿ 'to obey, be willing,' generates 129 occurrences distributed between obedience (ṭāʿa, Form I), capacity (isṭāʿa, Form X), and willing submission (ṭawʿan, adverb). The verb IV aṭāʿa ('to obey') dominates the obedience discourse: 4:59 'aṭīʿū Allāha wa-aṭīʿū al-Rasūla wa-ulī al-amri minkum' ('obey God, and obey the Messenger, and those in authority among you')—the foundational verse of Islamic political theology, establishing the obedience hierarchy. The combination ṭawʿan wa-karhan ('willingly or unwillingly,' 3:83, 13:15, 41:11) describes universal submission: 'all creation submitted to Him in ṭawʿ wa-karh.' Form X isṭāʿa ('to be able,' 40x) extends to capability: 18:67 'lā isṭāṭaʿū li-ḥamlihā' ('they were not able to bear it'). The hadith-anointed limit 'lā ṭāʿata li-makhluqin fī maʿṣiyati al-khāliq' safeguards ṭāʿa against absolutization.

quranic_analysis.theme: Obey Allah and the Messenger
quranic_analysis.detail: Ati'u Allaha wa ati'u al-Rasul—the recurring command establishing obedience hierarchy.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *ṭwʿ = 'to obey, be willing'. Ṭāʿa = to obey. Isṭāʿa = to be able. Ṭāʿah = obedience. The Quranic 'There is no obedience (ṭāʿah) to a creature in disobedience to the Creator' (ḥadīth) — the limits of obedience.

hadith_evidence.ar: أَكْثِرُوا ذِكْرَ هَادِمِ اللَّذَّاتِ — الْمَوْتِ
hadith_evidence.en: Increase remembrance of the destroyer of pleasures — death.

meaning.en: Warning, warner. 130x. Nadhir (44x)=warner—the Prophet sent as nadhir (warner) and bashir (bearer of good news). Andhara IV (44x)=to warn. Mundhar (16x)=one who warns. 35:23: you are only a warner (nadhir). The Prophet's core function: to warn of divine punishment for those who reject.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ن-ذ-ر (n-dh-r), from Proto-Semitic *n-dh-r 'to vow, consecrate, warn,' generates 130 occurrences centered on the Prophet as nadhīr ('warner')—paired with bashīr ('bearer of good tidings'). The Form IV andhara ('to warn,' 44x) and the active participle nadhīr ('warner,' 44x) are dominant: 35:23 'innamā anta nadhīr li-l-ʿālamīn' ('you are only a warner to all the world'); 2:119 'innā arsalnāka ḥaqqan bashīran wa-nadhīran' ('We sent you as bearer of good tidings and warner'); 13:7 'innamā anta mundhir wa-li-kulli qawmin hādīn' ('you are only a warner, and each people has its guide'); 67:26 'innamā anta mundhirun li-man yakhshāhu' ('I am only a warner to those who fear Him'). The parallel pair nadhīr/bashīr names the two-fold prophetic function—reward and punishment, glad tidings and warning. The noun mundhir ('one who warns,' 16x) is a frequent designation of the Prophet and prior messengers (Yūnus 10:2, Hūd 11:2, Ibrāhīm 15:11, Nūḥ 71:2).

quranic_analysis.theme: The Prophet as Warner
quranic_analysis.detail: Innama anta nadhir—you are only a warner. The Prophet warns but does not compel.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *nẓr = 'to watch, guard → to look'. The original sense of vigilant watching softened into visual perception. The Arabic manẓar (view, scene) and minẓār (telescope, modern) extend the visual sense. The Quranic naẓar encompasses physical seeing, intellectual consideration (a-fa-lā yanẓurūna), and eschatological waiting (fa-ntaẓirū).

hadith_evidence.ar: تَدَبَّرُوا الْقُرْآنَ فَإِنَّهُ حُجَّةٌ لَكُمْ أَوْ عَلَيْكُمْ
hadith_evidence.en: Reflect upon the Quran, for it is either a proof for you or against you.
hadith_evidence.source: Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim via ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb

meaning.en: To gather, collect, assemble. 129x. Jama'a I = to gather. Yawm al-Jam' = the Day of Assembly (64:9). Ajma'u IV = to gather/agree—fa-ajmi'u amrakum (10:71). Ijtama'a VIII = to come together. 2:148: wherever you are, Allah will bring you all together (jami'an). Resurrection as divine gathering of all creation.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ج-م-ع (j-m-ʿ), from Proto-Semitic *j-m-ʿ 'to gather, collect,' generates 129 occurrences organized around yawm al-jamʿ ('the Day of Gathering'), the eschatological assembly of all creation before God. 64:9 'yawma al-jamʿ dhālika yawmu al-tagābun' ('the Day of Gathering—that is the Day of Mutual Loss and Gain'); 42:7 'wa-idhā lam taʾtihim bi-āyatin qālū la-wa lawlā ijtabaytahā—qul innamā atbaʿu mimmā yūḥā ilayya min rabbi—this Qur'an guides to the straightest way' names the Day. The verb jamaʿa ('to gather') is most frequent: 2:148 'wa-li-kulli wijhatin huwa muwallīhā—wa-lā tasūḥū al-arḍa—fa-min ayyi shamlin yuwallajū fa-thumma wa-jjihū—and Allāh would never make your faith in vain' (in the broader context of 'inn Allāh la-jāmiʿu al-munāfiqīn,' 4:141). The Form IV ajmaʿa ('to be unanimous, resolve'), VIII ijtamaʿa ('to assemble') cover human collective action.

quranic_analysis.theme: Day of Assembly
quranic_analysis.detail: Yawm al-Jam'—the Day when all humanity is gathered for judgment.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *ǧmʿ = 'to gather, collect'. Jamaʿa = to gather. Jamʿ = gathering, total. Yawm al-Jamʿ = the Day of Gathering (Judgment). 'Say: Allah gives you life, then causes you to die, then He will gather you (yajmaʿukum) for the Day of Resurrection' (45:26).

hadith_evidence.ar: تَدَبَّرُوا الْقُرْآنَ فَإِنَّهُ حُجَّةٌ لَكُمْ أَوْ عَلَيْكُمْ
