hadith_evidence.en: Reflect upon the Quran, for it is either a proof for you or against you.
hadith_evidence.source: Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim via ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb

meaning.en_short: To look, see, consider; to wait
meaning.en: To look, see, consider; to wait. 129x. Nazara I = to look at, consider. Unzur = look! (imperative). Nadhir = the Waiter/Observer. Yanzurun (IV) = to wait, look. 30:50: look at the traces of Allah's mercy (fa-nzur ila athari rahmati Allah). 59:18: let every soul look to what it has sent forth (wa-ltanzur nafsun ma qaddamat li-ghad).
meaning.en_detailed: Root ن-ظ-ر (n-ẓ-r), from Proto-Semitic *n-ẓ-r 'to look, watch,' generates 129 occurrences organized around three modal uses: physical looking (naẓara), reflection/consideration (intentional gaze), and waiting/deferral (anẓara, 'to grant respite'). The imperative unẓur ('look!') functions as the Quran's epistemological command: 30:50 'fa-nẓur ilā āthāri raḥmati Allāh' ('look at the effects of Allāh's mercy—how He revives the earth after its death'); 88:17 'afalā yanẓurūna ilā al-ibili kayfa khuliqat' ('do they not look at the camels, how they are created?'); 86:5 'fa-nazar' ('then he reflected'). The Form IV anẓara ('to grant respite, defer,' 5x) yields 14:42 'wa-lā taḥsabanna Allāha ghāfilan ʿammā yaʿmalu al-ẓālimūn—innamā yuʾakhkhiruhum li-yawmin tashkhaẓu fīhi al-abṣār' ('do not think Allāh unaware of what wrongdoers do—He only defers them to a Day when eyes will stare'). The root spans perception, cognition, and divine temporality.
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To look, see, consider; to wait

quranic_analysis.theme: Look and reflect
quranic_analysis.detail: Fa-nzur—imperative to observe and reflect on divine signs.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *nẓr = 'to watch, guard → to look'. Arabic naẓara = to look. The original sense of vigilant watching softened into visual perception. The Quranic 'unẓurnā' (look upon us/grant us respite) preserves the dual sense of looking and waiting.

hadith_evidence.ar: تَدَبَّرُوا الْقُرْآنَ فَإِنَّهُ حُجَّةٌ لَكُمْ أَوْ عَلَيْكُمْ
hadith_evidence.en: Reflect upon the Quran, for it is either a proof for you or against you.
hadith_evidence.source: Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim via ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb

meaning.en: Summer. 1x, Quran 106:2—rihlata al-shita'i wa al-sayf (the journey of winter and summer). Refers to the Quraysh trade caravans that traveled to Yemen in winter and Syria in summer. The root sayf primarily means summer—the sole Quranic occurrence.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ص-ي-ف (ṣ-y-f), designating summer, generates exactly one occurrence in the Quran at 106:2 'ilāfihim riḥlata al-shitāʾi wa-l-ṣayf' ('their accustomed [security of] winter and summer journeys')—within Sūrat Quraysh's two verses addressing the Meccan tribe's biannual trade caravans to Yemen (winter) and Syria/Ḥimṣ (summer). The single occurrence nonetheless carries economic-theological weight: 106:3-4 'fa-l-yaʿbudū rabba hādhā al-bayti / alladhī aṭʿamahum min jūʿin wa-āmanahum min khawf' ('let them worship the Lord of this House who fed them against hunger and secured them from fear'). The summer/winter binary names the trade cycle that sustained Quraysh—precisely the worldly security to which 106:3 directs gratitude and worship. The 1-of-235-of-a-percent occurrence rate marks Syf among the rarest Quranic lexemes, semantically peripheral but rhetorically situated within a foundational Meccan sūra.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر صَيْف — 1 مرة — الصيف، فصل من فصول السنة

quranic_analysis.theme: Quraysh trade
quranic_analysis.detail: Rihlat al-shita' wa al-sayf—the winter and summer journeys of Quraysh.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en_short: To seek, desire, seduce; to roam
meaning.en: To seek, desire, roam. 148x. Rawada III = to seek, desire, seduce—rawadat-hu (she sought to seduce him, 12:23-32, Yusuf story). Arada IV (139x)=to want, intend, will—one of the most frequent Quranic verbs. Murad = desired/willed. 2:216: perhaps you dislike something though it is good for you—Allah knows and you do not. Key: arada vs shaa—arada is intentional purpose; shaa is bringing into existence.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ر-و-د (r-w-d), from Proto-Semitic *r-w-d 'to roam, wander, seek,' generates 148 occurrences distributed between the rare Form I rāda ('to seek, roam') and the dominant Form III rāwada ('to seek persistently, try to seduce')—notably used 8 times in Surah Yūsuf for the seduction attempts on Joseph: 12:23 'wa-rāwadat-hu allatī huwa fī baytihā ʿan nafsihi' ('the woman in whose house he was, sought to seduce him'); 12:25, 12:26, 12:30, 12:32, 12:51, 12:61, 12:83. The root is etymologically linked to arāda IV ('to want, intend, will')—most frequent (139x) and forming the central Quranic volitional category: 2:216 'wa-laʿallakum takrahūna shayʾan wa-huwa khayrun lakum wa-laʿallakum tuḥibbūna shayʾan wa-huwa sharrun lakum wa-Allāhu yaʿlam wa-antum lā taʿlamūn' ('perhaps you dislike something though it is good for you—Allāh knows and you do not'). The Form VI irādah ('will') and arāda distinguish divine intention from human desire, while 81:28 'wa-mā tashāʾūna illā an yashāʾa Allāh' subordinates all willing to the divine will.
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To seek, desire, seduce; to roam

quranic_analysis.theme: Root rwd
quranic_analysis.detail: Rawada=to seek, desire. Used of Yusuf story.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *rwd = 'to roam, wander → seek'. Arabic rāda = to seek, roam. The Form III rāwada (to seek persistently, try to seduce) is famously used in Surah Yusuf — 'the woman in whose house he was sought to seduce him (rāwadathu)' (12:23). The root emphasizes persistent, strategic pursuit.

hadith_evidence.ar: تَدَبَّرُوا الْقُرْآنَ فَإِنَّهُ حُجَّةٌ لَكُمْ أَوْ عَلَيْكُمْ
hadith_evidence.en: Reflect upon the Quran, for it is either a proof for you or against you.
hadith_evidence.source: Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim via ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb

meaning.en: Dog. 6x. Kalb/kilaab = dog/dogs. 7:176: parable of one who clings to earth like a panting dog. 5:4: hunting dogs (mukallibin)—trained hunting dogs are permitted. 18:18-22: Ashab al-Kahf's dog—stretched at the cave entrance. The dog is mentioned in both literal (hunting) and metaphorical (the base soul clinging to desires) contexts.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ك-ل-ب (k-l-b), the noun kalb ('dog'), generates 6 occurrences in the Quran carrying remarkable semantic weight despite its rarity. The parable of 7:176 presents the dog as metaphor for the person who clings to material pursuit: 'mathaluhu ka-mathali al-kalb / in taḥmil ʿalayhi yalhath aw tatrukhu yalhath' ('his parable is as the parable of a dog—if you load him, he pants; if you leave him, he pants')—a panting desperate attachment that refuses to release. 5:4 permits hunted game caught by trained hunting dogs ('mukallibīn'—taught dogs of prey), provided the dogs are released in the proper form for Allāh's name to be invoked—a pragmatic inclusion within dietary law. The Ashab al-Kahf narrative features the enigmatic companion dog: 18:18 'wa-taḥsabuhum ayqāẓan wa-hum ruqūd—wa-nuqallibuhum ʿalā yamīnihi wa-shimālihi wa-kalbuhum bāsiṭun dhīrāʿayhi bi-l-wasīd' ('their dog stretched his paws at the entrance'); 18:22 names the third party through 'wa-kalbuhum.' The negative/positive spread structures Quranic ethics: panting ambition (7:176), lawful utility (5:4), faithful companionship (18:18-22).

key_nominals.meaning: dog (6x)—hunting dogs, Ashab al-Kahf dog, parable dog

quranic_analysis.theme: Parable of the dog
quranic_analysis.detail: Mathaluhu kamathali al-kalb—his parable is like a dog; if you chase it, it pants; if you leave it, it pants.

quranic_analysis.theme: Companions of the Cave
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa kalbuhum basitun dhira'ayhi bi al-wasid—their dog stretching its paws at the entrance.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en: Five. 8x. Khamsah = five. Al-khamis (the fifth). 18:22: Ashab al-Kahf dispute—they say three, the fourth their dog; five, the sixth their dog. 24:7: the fifth testimony (in li'an). 58:7: no secret counsel of three but He is the fourth; nor five but He is the sixth.
meaning.en_detailed: The triconsonantal root خ م س (خَمْس) — 8 Quranic occurrences — fundamentally expresses Five. Its most prominent occurrence structures the Ashab al-Kahf disputation at 18:22, where the sleepers are said to number three, or five, or seven—a rhetorical triad whose middle figure produces this root. In li'an procedure (24:7), the wife's fifth invocation against herself uses the active participle al-khamisah, establishing a juridical sequence. At 58:7, Allah's omniscient accompaniment is described by increments of three, four, five, and six, anchoring the numeral in a mystical numerology of divine presence rather than mere counting.

quranic_analysis.theme: Numbers in Quran
quranic_analysis.detail: Five as part of numerical patterns in Quranic narratives and legal rulings.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en: To struggle, strive; jihad. 41x. Jahada III = to strive/struggle—jahidu fi sabil Allah (strive in Allah's way). Jihad (4x) = striving, struggle. Juhd (1x) = utmost effort. The root encompasses spiritual, moral, and physical striving. 22:78: strive in Allah's way with true striving (haqqa jihadihi). 29:69: those who strive in Our way, We will guide them to Our paths.
meaning.en_detailed: جَهَدَ (ج ه د), a root appearing 41 times in the Quran, encodes the notion of To struggle, strive; jihad across its various verbal and nominal forms. The verbal noun juhd (1x) signals the uttermost limit of effort, while jāhada (Form III, 33x) carries the socially intensified sense of struggling against opponents in God's path. At 22:78, the construct haqqa jihadīhi ('with the due striving of him') defines jihād as an inner quality of total commitment rather than external combat alone. 29:69 expands this into promise: those who strive in Our ways—We will guide them to Our paths—binding effort to divine direction. The root thus resists reduction to warfare (qitāl); Quranic jihād encompasses the believer's whole exertion against ignorance, sin, and circumstance.

key_nominals.m: struggle, striving, effort in God's path

quranic_analysis.theme: Striving in God's way
quranic_analysis.detail: Jahidu fi sabil Allah—strive in the way of Allah. The greater jihad is spiritual striving.

derived_forms.meaning: to struggle, strive against, wage jihād

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *ǧhd = 'to strive, exert effort'. Uniquely prominent in Arabic due to the Quran's ethical vocabulary. Jihād is not 'holy war' but 'exerting utmost effort' — the root is closer to 'struggle' than to 'fight' (which is qitāl). The Quranic jihād encompasses spiritual, intellectual, and physical dimensions.

hadith_evidence.ar: الْمُجَاهِدُ مَنْ جَاهَدَ نَفْسَهُ فِي طَاعَةِ اللَّهِ
hadith_evidence.en: The mujāhid is one who strives against his own self in obedience to Allah.

meaning.en: Theft, stealing. 9x. Sariqa = to steal. 12:77: Yusuf's brothers accused—if he steals, his brother stole before. 5:38: the male and female thief—cut their hands (legal punishment).
meaning.en_detailed: The root س ر ق (s-r-q), appearing 9 times in the Quran, denotes the covert taking of another's property and supplies the basis for the legal term sarīqa. Its most legally consequential occurrence is 5:38, which prescribes amputation of the hands of the thief and the thiefess as the hadd for convicted theft, with the active participle al-sāriq wa al-sāriqah marking the gendered subject of the punishment. In the Joseph narrative, 12:77 records the brothers' deflection of guilt—if he stole, a brother of his stole before—using the perfect yasraqu to link the alleged crime to inherited character. The narrative function thus contrasts sharply with the legal one: Yusuf's case becomes the locus where accusation of theft is mobilized as tribal slander against the favored son.

quranic_analysis.theme: Theft punishment
quranic_analysis.detail: Al-sariq wa al-sariqah fa-qta'u aydiyahuma—the legal hadd.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en: To succeed, follow behind; to differ. 127x. Khalafa I = to succeed, come after. Khalifah (9x)=vicegerent, successor—inni ja'ilun fi al-ardi khalifah (2:30). Ikhtalafa VIII = to differ, dispute. Khalf = behind, after. Khulafa' = successors, caliphs. 2:30: Adam as khalifah on earth. 11:57: my Lord will cause a people other than you to succeed you (yastakhlifu).
meaning.en_detailed: Root خ ل ف (خَلَفَ), attested 127 times in the Quran, derives its core meaning of To succeed, follow; behind; khalifah from Proto-Semitic sources. The cornerstone theological deployment is 2:30, where God announces I am placing a vicegerent (khalīfah) on the earth, framing humanity's role as stewardship succeeding the angels. 11:57 uses Form X istakhlafa to designate the rise of one community after another as divine policy of historical rotation. David's designation as khalīfah (38:26) extends the term to prophetic governance. The dispute register emerges in ikhtilāf, the recognition that legitimate human disagreement is built into creation—a structural fact the Quran names but does not condemn in itself.

quranic_analysis.theme: Khalifah: human vicegerency
quranic_analysis.detail: Inni ja'ilun fi al-ardi khalifah—I am placing a vicegerent on earth. David as khalifah.

theological_dimensions: Khalifah: human stewardship of earth—foundational environmental ethics
Ikhtilaf: diversity of opinion recognized as natural

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *ḫlp = 'to pass, go beyond → succeed, replace'. Arabic khalafa = to come after/succeed. The khalīfah (vicegerent) is the one who comes after — the human succeeding the angels as earth's custodian. Ikhtilāf (difference) emerged from the sense of 'passing in different directions'.

hadith_evidence.ar: تَدَبَّرُوا الْقُرْآنَ فَإِنَّهُ حُجَّةٌ لَكُمْ أَوْ عَلَيْكُمْ
hadith_evidence.en: Reflect upon the Quran, for it is either a proof for you or against you.
hadith_evidence.source: Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim via ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb

meaning.en: Confused, perplexed. 1x. Hayran = confused. 6:71: like one whom the devils have enticed, wandering confused (hayran) in the earth.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ح ي ر (ḥ-y-r), hapax legomenon at 1 occurrence, names the state of being lost in uncertainty—hayrān, the active participle functioning as an adjective of disorientation. Its sole attestation is 6:71, where the disbeliever is likened to one whom the devils have enticed, wandering confused (hayrān) upon the earth, unable to settle on direction or doctrine. The parallel phrase ṭā'ihun aw hayrān collapses two states: aimless wandering (ṭā'ih) and bewildered paralysis (hayrān), the latter representing cognitive rather than spatial disorientation. The verse thus uses the root to typologize spiritual confusion as a condition distinguishable from mere geographical error—hayrān is what happens when moral orientation collapses, leaving the will unable to choose direction.

quranic_analysis.theme: Spiritual confusion
quranic_analysis.detail: Hayran fi al-ard—wandering confused like one possessed.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en: Letter, edge, boundary; to deviate. 6x. Harf = letter, edge, brink. 22:11: whoever worships Allah on a brink (ala harfin)—if good befalls, content; if trial, turns away. Yahrufuna = they distort (words from their places). 4:46: those who distort words (yuharrifuna al-kalima). The root spans physical edges and textual alteration.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ح ر ف (ḥ-r-f), with 6 Quranic occurrences, oscillates between the literal senses of edge/letter and the figurative sense of distorting, skewing. At 22:11, the disloyal believer is described as worshipping upon a ḥarf—a brink, an edge—so that the slightest change of fortune tips him into apostasy. The semantic leap from physical edge to doctrinal distortion crystallizes in the verb Form II yuharrifūna, as at 4:46 and 5:13, where it accuses Jews and Christians of distorting words from their places. The Quran thereby exploits a single root to denote both the precariousness of conditional faith and the willful misplacement of revealed language. The technical Quranic term for textual corruption (taḥrīf) is built on this metaphor of slipping off the edge of correct meaning.

quranic_analysis.theme: Worship on the brink
quranic_analysis.detail: Ala harfin—on an edge. Describes those whose faith is marginal, conditional on circumstance.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en: Chest, breast; to issue forth. 46x. Sadr = chest, breast—the container of the heart. Allah knows what is in the breasts (3:119). Sharh al-sadr = expanding the chest to Islam (6:125, 94:1). 22:46: hearts that are in the breasts (al-qulub allati fi al-sudur). 20:25: Moses prayer: Rabbi ishrah li sadri—expand my chest.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ص د ر (ṣ-d-r), occurring 46 times, denotes the chest as the locus where heart, intention, and innermost secrets reside—ṣadr being the bodily container, not the metaphorical pump. Quranic discourse treats al-ṣudūr as the place God searches: 3:119, you are in doubt concerning what they conceal in their breasts (ṣudūr), assigns divine x-ray vision to the chest's hidden contents. The formula sharḥ al-ṣadr (expansion of the chest) appears at 6:125 and 94:1, signaling divine opening to Islam and certainty—Moses's prayer at 20:25, rabbi-shirḥ lī ṣadrī (Lord, expand my chest for me), petitions precisely for the interior spaciousness required to bear prophetic burden. The root thereby organizes a somatic theology in which the body is the threshold between outer compliance and inner assent.

key_nominals.meaning: chest, breast (46x)—container of the heart, seat of secrets

quranic_analysis.theme: Expansion of the chest
quranic_analysis.detail: Sharh al-sadr—divine expansion of the chest as sign of guidance.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: Appointed term, fixed time. 56x. Ajal = appointed term/deadline. Each soul has its appointed term (ajal musamma). 6:2: He created you from clay then decreed a term (ajalan). 2:282: when you contract a debt for a fixed term (ila ajalin musamman). The root establishes that everything has a divinely appointed duration—life, death, debts. Ajal is the boundary Allah sets for each created thing—none can advance or delay their term (7:34).
meaning.en_detailed: أَجَل (أ ج ل), a root appearing 56 times in the Quran, encodes the notion of Appointed term, fixed time across its various verbal and nominal forms. Its theological core lies in the doctrine of predetermined duration: each soul bears an ajal musammā (a named deadline), and at 7:34 the Quran declares every community has its term; when it arrives, they cannot delay it by a single hour nor advance it. 6:2 frames the term as part of creation itself—God decreed a term (ajal) and a known span. The root extends from biological lifespan to legal and economic deadlines, as in 2:282's fixed term (ajal musammā) for written contracts. This semantic extension reveals the Quran's underlying metaphysics: time itself is created, measured, and bounded—ajal is the boundary Allah has drawn around every existent thing.

key_nominals.meaning: appointed term, deadline (56x)—life span, debt term

quranic_analysis.theme: Every soul has its term
quranic_analysis.detail: Li-kulli ummatin ajal—each community has its appointed term; none can advance or delay.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *ʾǧl = 'appointed time, term'. Ajal = fixed term, deadline. 'For every community there is an ajal (appointed term). When their term comes, they cannot delay it' (7:34). The Quranic concept of measured, predetermined time for all things.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: To forget; to make forget. 45x. Nasiya I = to forget. Nasiy = forgotten/humble. 20:115: Adam forgot (fa-nasiya) and We found no resolve in him. 20:126: thus Our signs came to you but you forgot them, so today you are forgotten (tunsa). 2:106: We do not abrogate a verse or cause it to be forgotten (nunsiha) except We bring better. The root bridges human forgetfulness and divine causation of forgetting.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ن س ي (n-s-y), 45 Quranic occurrences, structures the anthropology of human fallibility and the divine response to it. The Form I nasiya covers ordinary forgetting, while the divine Form IV ansā (He caused to forget) shifts agency upward: at 2:106 God declares We do not abrogate a verse or cause it to be forgotten (nunsāhu) except that We bring better or the like, elevating nisyān into a tool of revelation's economy. At 20:115, Adam's covenant lapse is named precisely: fa-nasiya, and he forgot, explaining the fall as forgetfulness rather than pure disobedience. The reciprocal exchange in 20:126—today We forget you (tunsawn) as you forgot the meeting of this day of yours—makes divine nisyān the mirror punishment of human nisyān, a forensic correspondence central to Quranic soteriology.

quranic_analysis.theme: Human forgetfulness
quranic_analysis.detail: Adam forgot his covenant; believers pray not to be held accountable for forgetting.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّمَا أَنَا بَشَرٌ مِثْلُكُمْ أَنْسَى كَمَا تَنْسَوْنَ
hadith_evidence.en: I am only human like you; I forget as you forget.

meaning.en: Fear, terror. 124x. Khafa I = to fear. Khawf = fear. Takhwif = intimidation. 2:155: We will test you with something of fear (khawf). 20:21: Moses feared (khafa) the serpent. The root spans: natural fear (enemy, serpent), religious awe (khashyah), and eschatological terror (yawm al-khawf). The pious are promised security from fear (2:38, 46:13).
meaning.en_detailed: The Arabic root خ و ف (خَافَ) appears 124 times in the Quran, governing the semantic domain of Fear, terror; to be afraid. The verb khāfa (Form I) covers natural fear: Moses at 20:21 flees from what he perceives as a serpent, and the pilgrim at 2:196 fears enemy attack. The abstract noun khawf (≈10x) is overlaid onto divine pedagogy at 2:155: We will surely test you with something of fear (khawf), hunger, loss of goods and lives. Yet the same root encodes the promised eschatological security—those who believe and fear Allah, for them is no fear (khawf) and they shall not grieve (2:38, 46:13). The Quran thereby stages a typology of fear: trial-borne fear that purifies, and eschatological fear that is finally abolished for the God-conscious.

quranic_analysis.theme: Fear as divine test
quranic_analysis.detail: La-nabluwannakum bi-shay'in min al-khawf—We will test you with fear.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *ḫwf = 'to fear'. Khāfa = to fear. Khawf = fear. 'And fear Allah (wa ittaqū Allāh)' — the Quranic command to God-consciousness.

hadith_evidence.ar: سَبْعَةٌ يُظِلُّهُمُ اللَّهُ فِي ظِلِّهِ يَوْمَ لَا ظِلَّ إِلَّا ظِلُّهُ
hadith_evidence.en: Seven whom Allah will shade on the Day when there is no shade but His shade.

meaning.en: To earn, acquire, gain. 67x. Kasaba I = to earn, acquire. Iktasaba VIII = to earn for oneself. Kasb = earning, acquisition. 2:281: every soul shall be recompensed for what it earned (ma kasabat). 2:286: for it is what it earned (kasabat) and against it what it earned (iktasabat). The root grounds the theology of moral accountability—actions are earned and recompensed accordingly.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ك س ب (k-s-b), occurring 67 times in the Quran, grounds the entire economy of moral accountability by treating every deed as an acquisition that attaches to its agent. The Form I kasaba marks neutral earning; Form VIII iktasaba intensifies this into personal acquisition, the form consistently used for sin (iktasaba denotes what the soul has earned against itself). The lapidary formula at 2:286—it has what it earned (kasabat) and against it what it earned (iktasabat)—is recited in every rakʿah of the Islamic prayer and binds each soul to its ledger of deeds. 2:281 finalizes the surah with every soul shall be recompensed for what it earned (mā kasabat). The root is thus the Quranic shorthand for imputability—nothing happens to a soul that is not in some sense its own acquisition.

quranic_analysis.theme: Moral accountability
quranic_analysis.detail: Every soul held accountable for what it earned—the foundation of individual responsibility.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *ksb = 'to earn, acquire'. Kasaba = to earn. Kasb = earning, acquisition. 'Every soul shall be paid in full (tuwaffā kullu nafsin) what it earned (mā kasabat)' (2:281) — the day of recompense.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: Spacious, wide. 4x. Rahuba = to be spacious. 9:25: the earth, vast as it is, was made narrow (wa-daqat alaykum al-ardu bi-ma rahubat). 9:118: the earth, spacious as it is, was made narrow for the three left behind.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ر ح ب (r-ḥ-b), with 4 Quranic occurrences, names spatial and psychological spaciousness, deployed almost exclusively as the foil to psychological constriction. Its semantic frame is negative: at 9:25, after the Battle of the Trench, God says the earth, with all its spaciousness (bi-mā raḥubat), was made narrow (ḍaqat) upon them, and 9:118 repeats this construction for the three who were left behind. The technical construction bi-mā raḥubat (for all its spaciousness) frames vastness as a quantity that fails to relieve when the soul itself has contracted. Quranic rhetoric uses the root diagnostically: raḥab is the measure of worldly expansion, yet spiritual constriction can render it null, producing the famous paradox of the claustrophobic open space.

quranic_analysis.theme: Earth vast yet narrow
quranic_analysis.detail: The spacious earth felt narrow—psychological state of believers and the three left behind.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en: Man, person; woman. 38x. Mara' = person, human being. Imra' = man (7x). Imra'ah = woman (26x). Mar'u = individual. 4:176: if a man (imru'un) dies having no child. The root denotes human personhood—both male and female.
meaning.en_detailed: The Arabic root م ر أ (مُرُوءَة) appears 38 times in the Quran, governing the semantic domain of Man, person; woman. The legal architecture uses these terms as neutral human units of addressee capacity: 4:176—if a person (imruʾun) dies without issue—deploys imruʾun to designate the testator regardless of sex. 19:28 reports the kinship terms from Mary—O sister of Aaron, your father was not an immoral man (imruʾun sayyiʾin)—where imruʾun functions as the unmarked generic. The root thereby establishes a juridical anthropology that treats personhood as the primary category, with gender as a modifying adjective rather than a defining essence.

quranic_analysis.theme: Human personhood
quranic_analysis.detail: Imra' and imra'ah—the gendered person in Quranic law and narrative.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: Speech, word. 75x. Kalimah = word—kalimat Allah (the word of God). Takallama V = to speak. 3:39: Allah gives you glad tidings of John confirming a word from Allah (bi-kalimatin min Allah). 3:45: the Messiah, Jesus, a word from Him (kalimatun minhu). The kalimat Allah is a profound theological concept—divine creative command.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ك ل م (k-l-m), with 75 Quranic occurrences, supplies the foundational vocabulary of speech and divine address, anchored in the noun kalimah (word) and the verb Forms II (kallama) and V (takallama). Its theological apex is the designation of Jesus as kalimat Allāh: at 3:39 the angel announces John as one who will confirm a word (kalimah) from God, and at 3:45 the Messiah, Jesus son of Mary, is only a messenger of God and His word (kalimatuhu) which He conveyed to Mary. The expression kalimat Allāh also names God's creative decree—His command, when He intends a thing, is to say to it Be (kun), and it is (36:82). The root thus organizes a theology of divine speech as both personal address and cosmogonic fiat, with the Quran itself as kalām Allāh par excellence.

quranic_analysis.theme: Kalimat Allah
quranic_analysis.detail: The Word of God—Jesus as kalimah, God's words inexhaustible (18:109).

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *klm = 'to speak; to wound'. A dual root: kalima = to speak, and kalima = wound. Kalimah = word, utterance. Kalām = speech. The Quran as 'kalām Allāh' (the Speech of God). 'A good word (kalimah ṭayyibah) is like a good tree' (14:24).

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: To gush, boil. 4x. Fara = to boil, gush. 11:40: the oven boiled (fara al-tannur)—sign of the Flood. 67:7: Hell boiling with rage (tafur).
meaning.en_detailed: The root ف و ر (f-w-r), hapax-like at 4 occurrences, denotes violent ebullition—the bursting forth of liquid under heat. The paradigm occurrence is 11:40, where Noah is told the oven boiled (fāra al-tannūr)—the gushing furnace becomes the sign that the Flood is about to begin, a domestic-turned-cosmic image where the household hearth becomes the herald of apocalypse. 67:7 applies the same root to Hell: when they are cast into a narrow place thereof in chains, with the active participle tafūr describing Hell's boiling rage. 2:74 (a rock from which rivers gush forth) and 3:146 (the hearts boiling as if boiling in grief) extend the metaphor to grief and to gushing water. The root's narrow semantic field is precisely its theological strength: f-w-r marks only what breaks out under pressure.

quranic_analysis.theme: Flood sign
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa fara al-tannur—the oven gushed as the sign for Noah.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en: Narrate, tell; story. 5x. Qassa = to narrate. Qasas = stories—Quranic narratives. 12:3: We narrate to you the best of stories (ahsan al-qasas).
meaning.en_detailed: The root ق ص ص (q-ṣ-ṣ), with 30 Quranic occurrences, centers on the act of narrative recounting and the noun qaṣaṣ (stories, accounts). The Quran's programmatic statement is at 12:3, where surah Yusuf's opening identifies itself as the best of stories (aḥsan al-qaṣaṣ)—a self-designation that makes the entire surah a paradigm of qaṣaṣ as theological recitation. The verb qaṣṣa denotes following tracks or recounting step by step: We narrate to you (naqṣṣu ʿalayka) their news in truth (2:76; 3:62; 7:7). The verbal root thus literalizes the metaphor of tracing a story's footprints, treating qaṣaṣ as a forensic procedure of following evidence rather than free invention. The Quran thereby claims its narratives as rigorous reconstructions, not myths.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر قَصَّ — 30 مرة — narrate, tell; story (qasas)

quranic_analysis.theme: Quranic narratives
quranic_analysis.detail: Ahsan al-qasas—the best of stories in Surah Yusuf.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: Thread. 3x. Khayt = thread. 2:187: eat and drink until the white thread of dawn becomes distinct from the black thread—fasting time limit.
meaning.en_detailed: The root خ ي ط (kh-y-ṭ), with 3 Quranic occurrences, denotes thread, cord, or string, and supplies the Quran's most evocative image of dawn's onset. At 2:187, the fasting verse uses a doubled metaphor: eat and drink until the white thread (al-khayṭ al-abyaḍ) of dawn becomes distinct to you from the black thread (al-khayṭ al-aswad) of the night. The dual thread marks the limit of permissibility, with the pre-dawn horizon imagined as two fine lines distinguishable to the discerning eye. The root's narrow semantic field keeps it almost exclusively tied to this fasting law and its echoes elsewhere in ritual and legal text. The theological function of khayt is therefore liminal: it marks the boundary between night-eating and day-fasting, an epistemological threshold made visually tactile.

quranic_analysis.theme: Dawn thread
quranic_analysis.detail: Al-khayt al-abyad min al-khayt al-aswad—white thread from black thread of dawn.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en: To erect, set up; fatigue. 32x. Nasaba = to erect. Nasb = toil. 88:19: mountains—how they were erected (nusibat).
meaning.en_detailed: The root ن ص ب (n-ṣ-b), 32 Quranic occurrences, spans two semantic poles: the active erection of something upright, and the weariness (naṣab) that results from labor. The paradigmatic creation-verses deploy the root on a cosmic scale: at 88:19—and the mountains, how they were erected (nuṣibat)—treating mountains as stakes or pinned-up canopies. At 78:7 (We have placed within it towering mountains) the same erection image structures the firmament. Yet 9:73 and 9:79 invert the sense: fighting against them is hard for you (wa ʿalaykum naṣab)—the same root for erection becomes the noun of suffering. The semantic slippage is illuminating: the upright can become the strain; what stands as the world's architecture also stands as the believer's labor.

quranic_analysis.theme: Mountains erected
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa ila al-jibali kayfa nusibat—how the mountains were raised.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *nṣb = 'to set up, erect'. Arabic naṣaba = to erect, set up. Nuṣub = idolatrous stone altars. Naṣīb = allotted portion (what is 'set' for one).

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: Poverty. 14x. Faqir = poor. 35:15: you are the needy toward Allah (al-fuqara' ila Allah). Ontological poverty before God.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ف ق ر (f-q-r), with 14 Quranic occurrences, denotes poverty and need, and supplies one of the Quran's deepest ontological declarations. Its theological culmination is 35:15: O people, you are the poor toward God (al-fuqarāʾ ilā Allāh), and God is the rich (al-ghaniyy), the praiseworthy. The verse universalizes faqr into an ontological category—poverty before God is not material but structural, the mark of every creature's radical dependence. The same root yields faqīr (poor person), the class eligible for zakāt (e.g., 9:60), where faqr becomes a social and economic designation. The Quran thus exploits a single root for a sweeping philosophical move: from social poverty, through ritual obligation, to the metaphysical condition of all contingent being.

quranic_analysis.theme: Human dependence
quranic_analysis.detail: Antum al-fuqara' ila Allah—all are needy toward Allah.

hadith_evidence.ar: اللَّهُمَّ إِنِّي أَعُوذُ بِكَ مِنَ الْكُفْرِ وَالْفَقْرِ
hadith_evidence.en: O Allah, I seek refuge in You from disbelief and poverty.

meaning.en: Dignity, gravity. 9x. Waqar = dignity. 71:13: you do not expect from Allah dignity (waqaran).
meaning.en_detailed: The root و ق ر (w-q-r), with 9 Quranic occurrences, denotes weighty dignity, gravity, and (by extension) heaviness of hearing. Its sole theological occurrence of central weight is at 71:13, where Noah accuses his people: you do not expect from God any dignity (waqar)—you behave toward Him with ingratitude. Waqar here is the gravity due to God alone, the recognition of divine weight in human estimation. The root is more frequently deployed in the Form II waqqara (to honor, give weight), as in the idiom of dignified speech and remembrance of God. The contrast with 2:19 (as if they had heavy ears) uses the same root's sensory sense negatively—deafness as the failure of inward gravity, the soul too heavy to hear revelation.

quranic_analysis.theme: Divine dignity
quranic_analysis.detail: La tarjuna li-Allahi waqaran—you do not attribute due gravity to Allah.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en: To appear, manifest; back; help. 59x. al-Zahir divine name (57:3). 66:4: angels as assistants (zahir).
meaning.en_detailed: The root ظ ه ر (ẓ-h-r), with 59 Quranic occurrences, organizes a complex semantic field encompassing appearance, the back (ẓahr), and aid/assistance. Its theological high point is the divine name al-Ẓāhir at 57:3, where God is named alongside al-Awwal, al-Ākhir, and al-Bāṭin as the First and the Last, the Manifest and the Hidden. The pairing with al-Bāṭin sets up a key metaphysical binary: nothing lies outside God's manifestation and nothing beyond His hiddenness. In narrative usage, ẓuhūr covers physical rising and becoming visible, as in when their punishment appeared (ẓahara) or when the help of God came (naṣr Allāh). 66:4 deploys the related sense of backing: angels as assistants (ẓāhir) behind them, where ẓuhūr shades into support. The root thereby spans metaphysics, eschatology, and angelology from a single triliteral core.

quranic_analysis.theme: al-Zahir: the Manifest
quranic_analysis.detail: Huwa al-Awwal wa al-Akhir wa al-Zahir wa al-Batin—four divine names.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *ẓhr = 'to shine → flower'. Zahr = blossom. Zuhrah = Venus. 'The flower of worldly life' (zahrat al-ḥayāt al-dunyā, 20:131) — beautiful but fleeting.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: To complain. 3x. 12:86: I only complain (ashku) of my grief to Allah—Jacob's beautiful patience.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ش ك و (sh-k-w), with 3 Quranic occurrences, denotes the act of complaint or lamentation, deployed in the Quran in a carefully governed manner. Its paradigmatic occurrence is 12:86, where Yaʿqūb declares, I only complain (innamā ashkū) of my grief and sorrow to God—a verse that has become the Quranic locus classicus for the prohibition of complaining to creatures about God-given affliction. The phrase distinguishes complaint to God (legitimate) from complaint against God (illegitimate), establishing Yaʿqūb as the patient sufferer whose voice ascends only upward. The other attestations retain this upward direction: complaint in the Quran is never horizontal grievance, but always a form of address directed to the divine. The root's narrow semantic range is precisely its theological precision.

quranic_analysis.theme: Complaint to Allah
quranic_analysis.detail: Innama ashku baththi wa huzni ila Allah—Jacob's tawakkul.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *škw = 'to complain, lament'. Arabic shakā = to complain. 'I only complain (ashkū) of my grief and sorrow to Allah' (12:86) — Yaʿqūb's model of turning to God in distress rather than complaining to creatures.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en: To reward, recompense. 118x. Jaza' = reward, recompense. Yawm al-Din—the Day of Recompense. 53:31: those who do evil will be recompensed (yajzi). 99:7-8: atom weight of good/evil will be seen. The root is central to Quranic soteriology—every deed receives just recompense.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ج ز ي (j-z-y), 118 Quranic occurrences, anchors the Quranic doctrine of recompense—jazāʾ being both reward and punishment, the precise quid pro quo of every deed. Its theological weight appears in the very name of the eschatological Day: yawm al-dīn (the Day of Recompense/Judgment), and in the atomistic principle at 99:7-8, whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it, and whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it. The verb jazā at 53:31 anchors the principle: those who do evil shall be recompensed (yujzawn) according to what they did, with Form V tajzāʾ reinforcing the principle's universal applicability. The root's semantic elegance lies in its neutrality—jazāʾ covers both mercy and punishment, leaving the direction of recompense to the moral quality of the act.

quranic_analysis.theme: Root meaning
quranic_analysis.detail: Rare/minor root. See classical lexicons for full treatment.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *ǧzy = 'to cut, divide → to settle accounts → repay'. The Quranic jazāʾ is the full recompense — exactly what is due for every deed.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّمَا تُجْزَوْنَ بِمَا كُنْتُمْ تَعْمَلُونَ
hadith_evidence.en: You are only recompensed for what you used to do.

meaning.en: To begin, originate. 15x. Badi' al-samawati wa al-ardi (2:117)—Originator of heavens and earth.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ب د أ (b-d-ʾ), with 15 Quranic occurrences, names origination and the act of beginning without precedent. Its theological apex is the divine epithet badīʿ (Originator, Inventor), which appears at 2:117 and 6:101: Originator (badīʿ) of the heavens and the earth—a name that asserts creation ex nihilo, without model, exemplar, or prior matter. The same root structure underlies the verb badaʾa (to begin) and its Form II counterpart (to begin again, repeat), as in 9:13, but the theological weight is concentrated in badīʿ. The root thereby performs the conceptual labor of distinguishing divine creation from human building: the latter (banā) has models; the former (badaʾa) has none, and this distinction is precisely the meaning of badīʿ.

quranic_analysis.theme: Divine origination
quranic_analysis.detail: Badi'—creating without precedent, ex nihilo.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: To be dry. 4x. 20:77: Moses struck a dry path through the sea. 6:59: not a leaf falls... nor a moist or dry thing (ratbin wa la yabisin).
meaning.en_detailed: The root ي ب س (y-b-s), with 4 Quranic occurrences, denotes dryness and the absence of moisture, deployed both in concrete imagery and as the principle of a sweeping cosmic inventory. The iconic attestation is 20:77, where Moses is commanded to strike for them a dry path (ṭarīqan yabāsan) in the sea—a paradoxical dryness within a wet medium, an ontologically anomalous pathway. 6:59 supplies the root's most ambitious theological usage: not a leaf falls but He knows it, and no moist or dry thing (raṭbin wa lā yabīsin) but it is in a clear book, enumerating creation from wet to dry as the totality of the known. The pairing raṭb/yabīs becomes the Quranic dyad for totality itself—every existing thing, classified by its humidity. The root thereby expresses both the mundane physics of aridity and the cosmic register of omniscience.

quranic_analysis.theme: Dry path through sea
quranic_analysis.detail: Fa-drib lahum tariqan fi al-bahri yabasan—a dry path through the sea.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en: Prostration. 92x. Sajada = prostrate. Masjid = place of prostration (28x). Iblis refused (2:34). 15 ayat of sajdah.
meaning.en_detailed: The root س ج د (s-j-d), 92 Quranic occurrences, denotes bodily prostration and is the source of the central Islamic place-name masjid (28x, place of prostration). Its defining moment is Iblis's refusal at 2:34 (he refused [abā] and was arrogant and became of the disbelievers), repeated in 7:11-12 and 15:31-32—the paradigmatic sin is the refusal to bow, making sujūd the act whose negation constitutes disobedience. 22:77 extends the root to acts of creaturely worship: to God prostrates (yasjudu) whoever is in the heavens and the earth, making sujūd the ontological posture of all existent things. The technical term masjad generates the mosque, and the related sajadah marker denotes the 15 verses to be performed in prostration. The root thereby supplies the lexicon of Islam's most physical ritual act.

quranic_analysis.theme: Iblis refusal
quranic_analysis.detail: Refused to prostrate to Adam—paradigmatic sin.

derived_forms.meaning: to prostrate, bow down in worship

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *sǧd = 'to bow down, prostrate in worship'. The root is notably absent in Biblical Hebrew (which uses hištaḥăwāh) but common in Aramaic and Ge'ez. The Arabic masjid (mosque = place of prostration) embodies the physical act of Islamic worship.

hadith_evidence.ar: الصَّلَاةُ نُورٌ
hadith_evidence.en: Prayer is light.

meaning.en: To refuse. 13x. Aba = refuse. Iblis aba (2:34). The trust: heavens refused (33:72). Willful refusal.
meaning.en_detailed: The root أ ب ي (ʾ-b-y), with 13 Quranic occurrences, names the act of willful refusal—abā being intransitive refusal, distinguished from the more neutral refusal implicit in other roots. Its two paradigmatic deployments are complementary: at 2:34, 7:11, and 15:31, Iblis refused (abā) and was arrogant and became of the disbelievers, establishing refusal as the first disobedience in the cosmic narrative. 33:72 then offers the converse: We offered the trust to the heavens, the earth, and the mountains, but they refused (abayn) to bear it, making refusal sometimes a noble act, a refusal of what is beneath one's dignity to carry. The root thus contains a paradox: refusal can be the founding sin (Iblis) or the founding merit (the heavens). The Quranic moral grammar refuses to make the act intrinsically good or bad—only its object does.

quranic_analysis.theme: Refusal
quranic_analysis.detail: Iblis refused; heavens, earth, mountains refused the trust.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: To ascend, step; to pass away. 20x. Darajah = degree, rank. 2:228: men have a degree (darajah) over women (in certain legal contexts). 6:132: each has degrees (darajat) for what they earned. The root spans hierarchical ranking and gradual ascension or disappearance.
meaning.en_detailed: The root د ر ج (d-r-j), with 20 Quranic occurrences, names ascending degrees, gradual stepping, and hierarchical rank. Its theological core is the noun darajah, used as the unit of moral and spiritual rank: 2:228 declares men have a degree (darajah) over them, read by the exegetical tradition as a legal hierarchy rather than essential superiority; 6:132 extends this to cosmic scope, each has degrees (darajāt) for what they earned; 58:11 raises the concept to its eschatological peak, Allah will raise in degrees those of you who believe and those given knowledge. The root's image of graded steps thereby structures an ontology of rank—moral, epistemological, and eschatological—in which human and cosmic position is read on a graduated scale rather than as a binary. The Quran thereby resists flat moralities in favor of hierarchical ones.

quranic_analysis.theme: Degrees of rank
quranic_analysis.detail: Darajat—hierarchical degrees based on deeds and knowledge.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: To drive, herd. 17x. Disbelievers driven to Hell in groups (39:71); righteous to Paradise (39:73).
meaning.en_detailed: The root س و ق (s-w-q), with 17 Quranic occurrences, denotes the driving or herding of a group toward a destination, and its theological weight lies almost entirely in its eschatological usage. The two symmetrical verses 39:71 and 39:73 use Form I sāqa to depict the driving of disbelievers to Hell in chains and the driving of the righteous to Paradise in groups (ẓuwwafan). The verb sīq (38:33, We drove the horses back to him) and sāqah (37:64) extend the imagery to judgment scenes where creatures are marched to their final destination. The root's semantic restraint—shepherds driving flocks—is precisely what enables the Quran to imagine eschatology in bodily, communal terms, not as solitary judgment but as mass transit. The final judgment is therefore not a private audit but a public herding.

quranic_analysis.theme: Eschatological driving
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa siqa—they will be driven to their final destinations.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: To study, learn. 6x. Darasa = to study, learn. 6:105: they say you have studied (darasta)—accusation against the Prophet. 7:169: those who inherited the Book (yadrusuna)—studying it. The root denotes careful, repeated study of scripture.
meaning.en_detailed: The root د ر س (d-r-s), with 6 Quranic occurrences, denotes the act of studying or carefully examining, applied principally to the engagement with scripture. The most charged occurrence is 6:105, where the disbelievers taunt Muhammad for having studied (darasta) books of old—the root here marks mechanical study without insight, the sura's rebuke of surface learning that fails to transform. 7:169 reverses the valence: those who inherited the Scripture after them, while they study (yadrusūna) it, where study becomes the prerequisite for the lawful use of revelation. The root thereby names the act of learning at a remove: studying is what one does to someone else's text, and this remove—text, lineage, interpretation—is precisely the space where Quranic commentary situates itself as the serious activity of darasa.

quranic_analysis.theme: Study of scripture
quranic_analysis.detail: They said: you have studied—then We expound signs for a people who know.

hadith_evidence.ar: مَنْ سَلَكَ طَرِيقًا يَلْتَمِسُ فِيهِ عِلْمًا سَهَّلَ اللَّهُ لَهُ طَرِيقًا إِلَى الْجَنَّةِ
hadith_evidence.en: Whoever travels a path seeking knowledge, Allah makes the path to Paradise easy for him.

meaning.en: To build, construct; son. 184x. Bana = build. Ibn = son. Banu Isra'il (~41x). Sky as bina'an (2:22).
meaning.en_detailed: The root ب ن ي (b-n-y), with 184 Quranic occurrences, is one of the most generative roots in the language, denoting both construction (banā) and kinship (ibn, son). The Quran exploits the architectural register to imagine the sky as a building: 2:22 He made for you the earth a bedspread and the sky a building (bināʾan), a metaphor that treats the cosmos as constructed edifice (with 65:12 and 50:6 reinforcing the image). 9:108 uses the same root metaphorically for the mosque founded upon taqwā, the building of piety. The kinship register supplies the most frequent Quranic tribal name, Banū Isrāʾīl (~41x), and the term son in genealogies and addresses (yā bunayya, O my son). The root thereby grounds both the cosmic architecture and the genealogical architecture of revelation, binding physical and social construction to a single triliteral.

quranic_analysis.theme: Sky as building
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa al-sama'a bina'an—the sky as constructed edifice.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *bny = 'to build, construct'. The connection between 'building' and 'son' (ibn) is debated — possibly from 'building a house/family' or a separate root. The Quranic bunyān (edifice) can be physical or spiritual — the mosque founded on taqwā vs the mosque founded on hypocrisy.

hadith_evidence.ar: تَدَبَّرُوا الْقُرْآنَ فَإِنَّهُ حُجَّةٌ لَكُمْ أَوْ عَلَيْكُمْ
hadith_evidence.en: Reflect upon the Quran, for it is either a proof for you or against you.
hadith_evidence.source: Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim via ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb

meaning.en: News, information. 52x. Khabar = news, information. Khabir (45x)=All-Aware—al-Khabir divine name. 49:6: if a fasiq brings news (nabi'), verify it. The divine name al-Khabir means Allah is fully aware of the reality of all things.
meaning.en_detailed: The root خ ب ر (kh-b-r), with 52 Quranic occurrences, names both the news/information that circulates between people and the knowledge that God possesses of them, supplying the divine name al-Khabīr (the All-Aware). At 49:6, the root takes legal form: if a corrupt person (fāsiq) brings you news (nabaʾ), verify it (tabayyanū)—the Quranic caution against unverified report, embedding khabar within a juridical epistemology. The divine attribute al-Khabīr (≈45x) names God as the one fully cognizant of the hidden reality of every situation: 49:13, the most noble of you in the sight of God is the most taqwā-conscious. Truly, God is All-Knowing, All-Aware (Khabīr). The root thus unites journalism and omniscience within a single semantic field, with the very name al-Khabīr as its theological apex.

quranic_analysis.theme: Verify news
quranic_analysis.detail: In ja'akum fasiqun bi-naba'in fa-tabayyanu—Allah is All-Aware (Khabir) of your deeds.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *ḫbr = 'to know, be informed'. Khabara = to know, be informed. Khabar = news, information. Khabīr = All-Aware (divine name). Al-Khabīr (The All-Aware) — divine omniscience.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en_short: To bind, capture, take prisoner; captive, bondage
meaning.en: The root hamza-sīn-rāʾ denotes binding, capturing, and taking prisoner. In the Quran, the noun ʾasr refers to prisoners of war, and the verb ʾasara means to bind or take captive. The Quran enjoins treating captives with kindness: 'they feed the captive' (al-ʾasīr, 76:8).
meaning.ar: الشَّدُّ وَالرَّبْطُ، وَأَخْذُ الْأَسِيرِ فِي الْحَرْبِ
meaning.en_detailed: Triliteral Arabic root hamza-sīn-rāʾ (أ-س-ر), 6 Quranic occurrences, denoting binding, capturing, and taking prisoner, with the noun ʾasr meaning captivity and ʾasīr meaning captive of war. The Quran's central use is Quran 76:8 — 'and they feed food, despite their love for it, to the poor, the orphan, and the captive (al-ʾasīr),' establishing the ethical obligation of humane treatment of captives, which became foundational in Islamic law of war. The verb ʾasara (to bind/take captive) appears 3 times; cognates across Semitic include Hebrew ʾāsar (to bind), Akkadian esēru (to enclose), and Aramaic ʾăsar — all preserving the root sense of physical binding that developed in Arabic specifically into the juridical concept of war-captivity.
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To bind, capture, take prisoner; captive, bondage
meaning.ar_definition: جذر أ س ر — 6 مرة — To bind

etymology.semantic_evolution: Proto-Semitic 'to bind physically' developed in Arabic into 'capture in war'. The Hebrew cognate ʾāsar is the standard Biblical verb for binding.

usage_patterns: Captive ethics: humane treatment mandated

lexicographical_sources: Ibn Faris: aṣl is shadd wa-rabṭ
theological_dimensions: Rights of captives in Islamic law derived partly from 76:8
hadith_evidence: Prophet's instructions on treatment of prisoners at Badr

meaning.en: To divide, separate. 72x. Farraqa II = to divide, separate. Furqan (7x)=criterion—the Quran as al-Furqan (Criterion between truth and falsehood). 3:4: He sent down the Furqan. 2:53: Moses given the Furqan. The root denotes separation and discernment—especially divine revelation as the dividing criterion.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ف ر ق (f-r-q), 72 Quranic occurrences, denotes division and discernment, and supplies one of the Quran's most theologically loaded nouns, furqān (criterion). The noun furqān (7x) names the Quran (and earlier, the Torah) as the Criterion between truth and falsehood: 2:53 and We gave Moses the Criterion (furqān), 8:29 and He sent down the Criterion (furqān) and the balance, 2:185 names the month of Ramadan in which the Criterion was sent down. The verbal register includes Form I faraqa (to separate, distinguish) and Form II farraqa (to scatter, divide), as in 2:137 where the oscillation between belief and disbelief stages the failure to maintain the divide. The root thereby grounds revelation's epistemic claim: the Quran does not merely describe truth—it discriminates it, drawing the line between īmān and kufr.

quranic_analysis.theme: Furqan: divine criterion
quranic_analysis.detail: Al-Furqan—the Quran as criterion between truth and falsehood.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *prq = 'to separate, divide'. Faraqa = to separate, distinguish. Furqān = the Criterion — what separates truth from falsehood. Al-Furqān is a name of the Quran and the Torah. 'We gave Mūsā the Book and the Furqān' (2:53).

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: To understand. 1x. 21:79: We gave understanding (fahhamnaha) to Solomon—the sole Quranic occurrence. The root denotes deep, intuitive comprehension.
meaning.en_detailed: Occurring 1 times in the Quranic text, the root ف ه م (فَهِمَ) conveys the essential concept of To understand. The root denotes intuitive comprehension reaching beyond surface perception into inner meaning, here granted to Solomon as the superior sign over material might. Semantic field: intellectual discernment and prophetic wisdom.

quranic_analysis.theme: Solomonic wisdom
quranic_analysis.detail: Fa-fahhamnaha Sulayman—We gave understanding of it to Solomon.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en: To be pleased, satisfied. 73x. Radiya = to be pleased. Rida = contentment. 5:119: Allah pleased with them and they with Him (radiya Allahu anhum wa radu anhu). 89:28: return to your Lord well-pleased (radiyatan mardiyyah). The highest spiritual station: mutual divine-human contentment.
meaning.en_detailed: The root r-ḍ-w (ر ض و), with 73 Quranic occurrences, yields raḍiya ('to be pleased, satisfied') and the proper noun riḍwān ('divine good-pleasure'). The formula raḍiya Allāhu 'anhum wa raḍū 'anhu ('God is well-pleased with them and they with Him', 5:119) names the apex of Quranic soteriology; 89:28's 'radiyatan mardiyyatan' describes the soul returning to its Lord well-pleased. Semantic field: eschatological reciprocity between God and the purified believer.

quranic_analysis.theme: Mutual contentment
quranic_analysis.detail: Radiya Allahu anhum wa radu anhu—the highest spiritual attainment.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *rḍw = 'to be pleased, satisfied'. Arabic raḍiya = to be pleased. Riḍwān = divine pleasure — the highest goal. 'Allah is pleased (raḍiya) with them and they are pleased with Him' (5:119) — the ultimate reciprocity of divine-human satisfaction.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: Intimate friend; boiling water. 21x. Hamim (20x)=close/intimate friend—in Paradise (56:18) and Hell (where no friend helps, 70:10). Hamim (1x)=boiling water (Hell punishment). The root spans the warmth of intimate friendship and the scorching heat of Hell. 70:10: no intimate friend asks about his friend.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ḥ-m-m (ح م م), with 21 occurrences, produces two homonymous forms: ḥamīm ('intimate friend', 20x) and ḥamīm ('boiling water', 1x). The antithesis structures eschatology: 70:10's 'wa lā yas'alu ḥamīmun ḥamīmā' declares no intimate friend will ask after another, while 56:18 offers ḥur companions with tender glances. The semantic field spans the intimacy severed on Judgment Day and Hell's scorching liquid.

quranic_analysis.theme: Loss of friends on Judgment
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa la yas'alu hamimun hamiman—no intimate friend asks about friend.

hadith_evidence.ar: اللَّهُمَّ اسْقِنَا غَيْثًا مُغِيثًا
hadith_evidence.en: O Allah, send us rain, a beneficial rain.

meaning.en: Half; justice, equity. 7x. Nisf = half. Insaf = justice, equity. 2:237: half of the dowry (nisf). The root links the mathematical division with moral fairness—to do justice is to give each their due half.
meaning.en_detailed: The root n-ṣ-f (ن ص ف), with 7 occurrences, yields nisf ('half') and extends into insāf ('equity, fairness'). The locus classicus at 2:237 reads 'wa in ṭalaqnahunna qabla an tamassūhunna wa qad faradtum lahunna farīḍatan fa-niṣfu mā faradtum'—half of the stipulated dowry is due upon divorce. The semantic field joins numerical bisection to moral fairness, the giving of each party its due.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر نَصَفَ — 7 مرة — half; justice, equity

quranic_analysis.theme: Half dowry
quranic_analysis.detail: Fa-nisfu ma faradum—half of what you specified. Legal ruling on divorce.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en: Righteousness, piety; land. 32x. Birr = righteousness, piety—2:177: birr is not turning faces east or west but faith and charity. Barr (12x)=land (opposite of sea)—al-Barr divine name (the Beneficent). 2:44: do you command birr upon people while forgetting yourselves?
meaning.en_detailed: The root b-r-r (ب ر ر), with 32 occurrences, generates birr ('righteousness, piety'), barr ('dry land'), and the divine name al-Barr ('the Most-Good'). The locus classicus is 2:177: 'laysa al-birra an tuwallū wujūhakum qabla al-mashriqi wa al-maghribi' redefines piety as comprehensive faith, charity, prayer, and patience. Semantic field: comprehensive righteousness, terrestrial geography, and divine beneficence.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر بَرَّ — 32 مرة — righteousness, piety; land (barr)

quranic_analysis.theme: Definition of birr
quranic_analysis.detail: Birr is comprehensive—faith, charity, prayer, patience. True righteousness defined.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en_short: To lie, fabricate, slander, turn away (from truth); falsehood
meaning.en: The root hamza-fāʾ-kāf denotes falsehood, fabrication, and slander — especially the deliberate turning away from truth. In the Quran, ʾifk refers to a great lie or calumny, famously in the 'Event of the Ifk' — the slander against ʿĀʾisha. The Form VIII uʾtufika means to be overthrown or destroyed (as the people of Lūṭ were).
meaning.ar: الْكَذِبُ وَالْقَلْبُ وَالصَّرْفُ عَنِ الْحَقِّ
meaning.en_detailed: Triliteral Arabic root hamza-fāʾ-kāf (أ-ف-ك), 30 Quranic occurrences, denoting falsehood, fabrication, slander, and the deliberate turning away from truth — connected etymologically to the Proto-Semitic sense of 'overturning, inverting.' The Form VIII passive uʾtufika (to be overturned, destroyed) appears 9 times in the Quran, most famously in 9:70 'al-muʾtafikāt — the overturned cities,' referring to the cities of the people of Lūṭ overturned by divine wrath; the noun ʾifk (24 occurrences) denotes a great lie or calumny, including the famous 'Event of the Ifk' (hadīth al-ifk) — the slander against ʿĀʾisha narrated in Sūrat al-Nūr 24:11. Al-Rāghib glosses ʾifk as stronger than kadhib (lying); the triliteral root is cognate with Hebrew hāfaḵ (to overturn).
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To lie, fabricate, slander, turn away
meaning.ar_definition: جذر أ ف ك — 30 مرة — To lie

cognates.hebrew: הָפַךְ (hāfaḵ) — to overturn, turn over, change

etymology.semantic_evolution: Proto-Semitic 'to overturn' gave Arabic a dual development: physical (overthrow, destruction) and cognitive (turning truth upside down = lying).

usage_patterns: ʾifk bridges physical inversion and cognitive falsehood

lexicographical_sources: Raghib: ʾifk is stronger than kadhib
theological_dimensions: The Ifk incident: verifying information and avoiding slander
hadith_evidence: The ḥadīth of al-Ifk (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī)

meaning.en: To last, endure. 9x. Da'im=perpetual. 13:35: the reward of Paradise is lasting (ukuluha da'imun). 11:108: a gift uninterrupted (ghayra majdudh).
meaning.en_detailed: The root d-w-m (د و م), with 9 occurrences, centers on dā'im ('lasting, perpetual'). At 13:35, 'wa ukuluhā dā'imun wa ẓilluhā' characterizes Paradise's perpetual fruit and shade; 11:108's 'ghayra majdhūthin' ('unintermittent gift') qualifies God's reward to the steadfast. The semantic field is eschatological perpetuity and uninterrupted duration, opposing transience and decline.

quranic_analysis.theme: Perpetual Paradise
quranic_analysis.detail: Ukuluha da'imun wa zilluha—its fruit and shade are perpetual.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en: Sacred, forbidden. 83x. Harrama II=to forbid. Haram=sacred/sanctuary. Al-Masjid al-Haram (~16x). 2:144: turn toward al-Masjid al-Haram. Halal vs haram = permitted vs forbidden.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ḥ-r-m (ح ر م), with 83 occurrences, generates ḥarām ('forbidden, sacred') and the proper noun al-Masjid al-Ḥarām ('the Sacred Mosque'). At 2:144, 'fawalli wajhaka shaṭra al-Masjid al-Ḥarām' orients prayer toward the Kaaba; 9:36 protects 'al-ashḥur al-ḥurum' (the sacred months). The semantic field unifies prohibition (that which is unlawful) and consecration (that which is set apart).

quranic_analysis.theme: Sacred sanctuary
quranic_analysis.detail: Al-Masjid al-Haram—the Sacred Mosque; sacred months.

cognates.hebrew: חָרַם (ḥāram) — to ban, devote to destruction

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *ḥrm = 'to set apart → forbid or consecrate'. Arabic ḥarām = forbidden, sacred. The dual sense: what is 'set apart' can be prohibited (ḥarām food) or sanctified (al-Masjid al-Ḥarām). The iḥrām is the state of consecration for pilgrimage.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ دِمَاءَكُمْ وَأَمْوَالَكُمْ حَرَامٌ عَلَيْكُمْ
hadith_evidence.en: Your blood and your property are sacred to you.

meaning.en: To read, recite. 88x. Qara'a=to read, recite. Quran (70x)=the Reading/Recitation. 96:1: Iqra' bi-smi rabbika (Read! In the name of your Lord)—the first revelation. 17:106: a Quran We divided so you recite it to people at intervals.
meaning.en_detailed: The root q-r-ʾ (ق ر أ), with 88 occurrences, yields qaraʾa ('to read, recite') and the central Quranic term al-Qurʾān ('the Recitation', ~70x). The verb opens revelation: 96:1's 'iqraʾ bi-smi rabbika' ('Recite in the name of your Lord') is the first revealed command. At 17:106, 'wa Qurʾānan faqarnāhu li-taqrāʾahu 'ala al-nāsi 'ala muḥḥin' makes the Quran a scripture meant to be recited aloud. Semantic field: revelation, recitation, scripture.

quranic_analysis.theme: First revelation
quranic_analysis.detail: Iqra'—Read! The first word revealed. Reading as the foundation of Islamic civilization.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *qrʾ = 'to call out → to read aloud → to recite'. The word Quran (qurʾān) is the verbal noun of qaraʾa: 'the Recitation'. The first revealed word was iqraʾ (Recite! Read! 96:1). The Hebrew miqrāʾ (convocation, Scripture) preserves the same root.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: Obligation, duty. 18x. Farada=to prescribe, make obligatory. Faridah=obligation. 2:237: half of what you prescribed (faradum). 2:197: Hajj—whoever undertakes it (farada fihinna al-hajja). The root grounds the Islamic concept of obligatory acts (fara'id).
meaning.en_detailed: The root f-r-ḍ (ف ر ض), with 18 occurrences, generates farḍa ('to prescribe, ordain') and farīḍa ('prescribed duty'). At 2:237, 'fa-niṣfu mā faradtum' ('half of what you stipulated') deploys the root for contractual specification; 2:197 places Hajj among 'mā farada Allāh' ('what God has prescribed'). The root grounds the Islamic concept of divinely-ordained obligation, generating the later fiqh category fard. Semantic field: divine prescription and obligatory duty.

quranic_analysis.theme: Divine prescription
quranic_analysis.detail: Farada—what Allah has prescribed as obligation.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: Head. 18x. Ra's=head. 5:6: wipe your heads (ru'usikum) in wudu. 2:196: do not shave your heads (ru'usakum) until the hady reaches its place.
meaning.en_detailed: The root r-ʾ-s (ر أ س), with 18 occurrences, centers on ra's ('head'). At 5:6, 'wa amṣaḥū bi-ruʾūsikum wa arjulakum ilā al-kaʿbayn' prescribes head-wiping in wuḍūʾ; 2:196 prohibits shaving 'ruʾūsakum' before the sacrificial offering reaches its place. The semantic field joins corporeal anatomy to acts of ritual purification and pilgrimage.

quranic_analysis.theme: Wudu and Hajj
quranic_analysis.detail: Wiping heads in wudu; shaving heads after Hajj.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: Yellow; empty. 5x. Sufr=yellow. 2:69: a yellow cow (safra'). Safar=void/empty. 22:27: deep-rooted and shallow (min kulli fajjin amiq). The month Safar from this root.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ṣ-f-r (ص ف ر), with 5 occurrences, primarily denotes the color yellow. At 2:69, 'ṣafraʾ fāqiʿun lawnuhā' ('a yellow cow, bright in color') describes the cow commanded of Moses's people. The noun Ṣafar also names the second lunar month, conventionally derived from the root's sense of emptiness or yellowing leaves. Semantic field: chromatic description and the lunar calendar.

quranic_analysis.theme: Yellow cow
quranic_analysis.detail: Safra' faqi'un lawnuha—a bright yellow cow.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en: Tower, constellation. 7x. Burj=tower, constellation. 4:78: wherever you are, death will reach you even in fortified towers (burujin mushayyadah). 85:1: by the sky of constellations (wa al-sama'i dhati al-buruj).
meaning.en_detailed: The root b-r-j (ب ر ج), with 7 occurrences, yields burj ('tower, fortified structure; constellation'). At 4:78, 'burūjin mushayyadah' ('fortified towers') depicts earthly architecture; 85:1's 'wa al-samāʾi dhāti al-burūj' ('by the heaven of constellations') swears by celestial towers; 25:61 places 'burūjan fī al-samāʾ' in the sky. The semantic field fuses terrestrial fortification with celestial architecture.

quranic_analysis.theme: Constellations
quranic_analysis.detail: Burujan fi al-sama'—constellations in the sky.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en: To restrain; palm. 15x. Kaffa=to restrain. Kaff=palm. 13:14: prayer is not answered except that (he stretches his) two palms to water. 5:11: Allah restrained (kaffa) their hands from you.
meaning.en_detailed: The root k-f-f (ك ف ف), with 15 occurrences, yields kaff ('palm of the hand') and kaffa ('to restrain, hold back'). At 5:11, 'wa kaffa aydiyahum 'ankum' ('and He restrained their hands from you') recounts divine protection against treachery; 13:14 pictures the prayer of one stretching his palms toward God. The semantic field joins physical restraint to the supplicating gesture of the open palm.

quranic_analysis.theme: Divine restraint
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa kaffa aydiyahum ankum—Allah restrained their hands from you.

hadith_evidence.ar: اللَّهُمَّ اسْقِنَا غَيْثًا مُغِيثًا
hadith_evidence.en: O Allah, send us rain, a beneficial rain.

meaning.en: To mend, compel; al-Jabbar. 10x. Jabbar=Compeller (divine name), tyrant (human). 59:23: al-Jabbar al-Mutakabbir. 11:59: every obstinate tyrant (jabbarin anid).
meaning.en_detailed: The root j-b-r (ج ب ر), with 10 occurrences, generates jabbar ('compeller, tyrant') and the divine name al-Jabbār ('the Compeller'). At 59:23, 'al-Jabbāru al-Mutakabbir' ('the Compeller, the Supreme') ranks among God's supreme attributes; 11:59's 'jabbārin 'anīd' ('every obstinate tyrant') applies the negative human sense. The semantic field contrasts divine irresistibility with creaturely arrogance.

quranic_analysis.theme: al-Jabbar as divine name
quranic_analysis.detail: Al-Jabbar—the Compeller whose will none can resist.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en: To burst forth; dawn. 24x. Fajara=to burst/flow. Fajr=dawn (89:1 wa al-fajr). Fujur=wickedness. 91:8: He inspired it with wickedness (fujuraha) and righteousness (taqwaha). Islam dawn prayer = salat al-fajr.
meaning.en_detailed: The root f-j-r (ف ج ر), with 24 occurrences, yields fajr ('dawn') and fujūr ('wickedness, immorality'). At 89:1, 'wa al-fajr' ('by the dawn') opens a Quranic cosmic oath; 91:8's 'fa-alhamahā fujūrahā wa taqwāhā' ('He inspired it with its wickedness and its piety') names the moral capacity inscribed in the soul. The pre-dawn ṣalāt al-fajr anchors the root in ritual practice. Semantic field: dawn, moral rupture, and the dawn prayer.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر فَجَرَ — 24 مرة — burst forth; dawn; wickedness

quranic_analysis.theme: Dawn oath
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa al-fajr—by the dawn. One of the Quranic oaths.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: Acquire. 1x. Qani'a=be content. 11:29: I do not say to you that I possess the treasures of Allah.
meaning.en_detailed: The root q-n-y (ق ن ي), with a single Quranic occurrence at 11:29, centers on acquisition and possession. In Noah's address to his people, the verse disclaims prophetic possession of divine prerogatives ('I do not say to you that I possess the treasures of Allah'), establishing the prophet as one who serves, not one who owns. The semantic field is divine ownership and the negation of human possession.

quranic_analysis.theme: Noah's disclaimer
quranic_analysis.detail: La aqulu lakum indi khaza'inu Allah—I possess not Allah's treasures.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en: Hope. Raja=hope. Tarji=pray for rain. 2:218: those who hoped (yarjuna) for Allah's mercy. Dua of hope.
meaning.en_detailed: The root r-j-y (ر ج ي), with 28 occurrences, centers on yarjū ('to hope, expect'). At 2:218, 'alladhīna yarjūna raḥmata Allāh' ('those who hope for God's mercy') names hope as a mark of believers; 18:110's 'man kāna yarjū liqāʾa rabbihi' ('whoever hopes to meet his Lord') makes hope the engine of righteous labor. The semantic field is eschatological hope as the believer's motivation.

quranic_analysis.theme: Hope for mercy
quranic_analysis.detail: Yarjuna rahmata Allah—they hope for Allah's mercy.

hadith_evidence.ar: يَقُولُ اللَّهُ: أَنَا عِنْدَ ظَنِّ عَبْدِي بِي
hadith_evidence.en: Allah says: I am as My servant thinks of Me.

meaning.en_short: To join, pair, couple; horns (qarn); generation
meaning.en: To join, pair. 36x. Qarn=horn, generation. Qarin=companion (both angel and devil). 43:36: whoever turns from remembrance, We appoint a devil as companion (qarin). 6:6: how many generations (qarn) We destroyed.
meaning.en_detailed: The root q-r-n (ق ر ن), with 36 occurrences, yields qarn ('generation; horn') and qarīn ('constant companion'). At 6:6, 'kam ahlaknā min qarn qablihim' ('how many generations We destroyed before them') frames historical epochs as divine reckonings; 43:36's 'qarīnan min al-jinn' pairs each straying soul with its demonic counterpart. Semantic field: generational time and inseparable companionship.

key_nominals.meaning: generation, horn (20x)—each generation a distinct horn of time

quranic_analysis.theme: Generations destroyed
quranic_analysis.detail: Kam ahlakna min qarnin—how many generations We destroyed.

derived_forms.meaning: To join, pair, couple; horns (qarn); generation

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: Pilgrimage; argument. 33x. Hajj=pilgrimage (9x). Hajja=to argue, dispute. Hujjah=proof, argument. 2:196: complete Hajj and Umrah for Allah. 2:197: Hajj is in well-known months. The root spans the great pilgrimage and rational argument.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ḥ-j-j (ح ج ج), with 33 occurrences, generates ḥajj ('pilgrimage') and ḥujjah ('proof, argument'). At 3:97, 'wa li-Allāhi 'alā al-nāsi ḥijju al-bayt' ('pilgrimage to the House is owed to God by people who can manage the journey') establishes the fifth pillar; 22:27 prescribes the rites. The semantic field joins physical pilgrimage to Mecca with rational argumentation as proof.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر حَجَّ — 33 مرة — pilgrimage (hajj); argument, proof

quranic_analysis.theme: Hajj rites
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa adhdhin fi al-nasi bi al-hajj—proclaim pilgrimage to humanity.

hadith_evidence.ar: مَنْ حَجَّ فَلَمْ يَرْفُثْ وَلَمْ يَفْسُقْ رَجَعَ كَيَوْمِ وَلَدَتْهُ أُمُّهُ
hadith_evidence.en: Whoever performs Hajj without obscenity or wickedness returns like the day his mother bore him.

meaning.en: Dream; forbearance. 21x. Hulum=dream. Hilm=forbearance. Balagha al-hulum=reach puberty. 12:43: king's dream (hulm). 52:32: do their dreams (ahlam) command them? Al-Halim (forbearing) divine name.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ḥ-l-m (ح ل م), with 21 occurrences, yields ḥulm ('dream'), ḥilm ('forbearance'), and the divine name al-Ḥalīm ('the Forbearing'). At 12:43, Joseph interprets the king's dream ('sabaʿa baqarātin simānin yaʾkuluhunna sabʿun 'ijāfun'); al-Ḥalīm in divine attribute lists marks patient forbearance. Semantic field: prophetic dreams, divine forbearance, and moral maturation.

quranic_analysis.theme: Dreams
quranic_analysis.detail: Adghathu ahlam—confused dreams. Yusuf interprets the king's dream.

hadith_evidence.ar: الرُّؤْيَا الصَّالِحَةُ جُزْءٌ مِنْ سِتَّةٍ وَأَرْبَعِينَ جُزْءًا مِنَ النُّبُوَّةِ
hadith_evidence.en: A good dream is one of forty-six parts of prophethood.

meaning.en: Gentleness. Rifq=gentleness. Rafiq=companion. 4:69: excellent companions (rafiqan).
meaning.en_detailed: The root r-f-q (ر ف ق), with 5 occurrences, yields rifq ('gentleness') and rafīq ('companion'). At 4:69, 'wa ḥasuna ulaʾika rafīqan' ('and excellent are those as companions') describes the righteous in Paradise. The root's ethical mandate is preserved in the Prophetic hadith: 'God loves gentleness in all matters.' Semantic field: gentleness, kindness, and eschatological companionship.

quranic_analysis.theme: Excellent companions
