quranic_analysis.detail: Wa hasuna ulaika rafiqan—excellent companions.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en: Stand. 4x. Waqafa=stand. 6:27: made to stand (wuqifu) before the Fire. 37:24: stop them (wa-qifuhum).
meaning.en_detailed: The root w-q-f (و ق ف), with 4 occurrences, yields wuqifa ('to be made to stand'). At 6:27, 'law tarā idhā wuqifū 'alā rabbihim' ('if you could see them made to stand before their Lord') depicts the Final Judgment; 37:24's 'wa-qfūhum innahum masʾūlūn' ('stop them, they are to be questioned') begins the interrogation. The semantic field is eschatological reckoning and forensic interrogation.

quranic_analysis.theme: Stopped for judgment
quranic_analysis.detail: Idh wuqifu ala al-nar—made to stand before Fire.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en_short: Thousand; to be familiar, friendly, accustomed, to unite
meaning.en: The root hamza-lām-fāʾ has two primary Quranic senses: (1) the number 'thousand' (ʾalf), and (2) to join, unite, or bring hearts together in affection (muʾallafa, taʾlīf). The verb ʾallafa means 'to unite, reconcile' — specifically of hearts (Q 8:63). The root bridges the quantitative (thousand as a large, unified unit) and the social (uniting people).
meaning.ar: الْعَدَدُ الْمَعْرُوفُ (أَلْف)، وَالتَّأْلِيفُ بَيْنَ الْقُلُوبِ
meaning.en_detailed: Triliteral Arabic root hamza-lām-fāʾ (أ-ل-ف), 22 Quranic occurrences, carrying two primary senses: (1) the numerical thousand (ʾalf, 23 occurrences), and (2) unity, familiarity, and bringing together (ʾallafa, 'to unite/reconcile'). The verb ʾallafa appears in Quran 8:63 'and He united (wa-ʾallafa) between their hearts,' describing God's reconciling action among the muʾminīn; ʾīlāf (Quran 106:1-2) refers to the trade pacts and secure familiarity Quraysh enjoyed for winter and summer caravans. The Form II verb ʾallafa (5 Quranic occurrences) is theologically significant — divine taʾlīf al-qulūb (reconciliation of hearts) is one of God's named actions. Al-Muʾallafa qulūbuhum (those whose hearts are to be reconciled) is one of the eight categories of zakāt recipients in classical fiqh.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر أ ل ف — 22 مرة — Thousand

etymology.semantic_evolution: Proto-Semitic *ʾalp- originally meant 'head of cattle' (a unit of wealth), developing into 'thousand' and 'clan/group'. In Arabic, the cattle sense was lost; thousand and unity remained.

key_nominals.meaning: those whose hearts are to be reconciled

usage_patterns: Numerical and social meanings intertwined

lexicographical_sources: Ibn Faris: al-ʾalf is muḍāʿafa min al-ʿadad; al-ʾulfa is al-ijtimāʿ
theological_dimensions: Al-muʾallafa qulūbuhum as a zakāt category
hadith_evidence: Prophet's conciliatory gifts as taʾlīf al-qulūb

meaning.en: Meteor, shooting star. 5x. Shihab=meteor, shooting flame. 37:10: a piercing flame (shihabun thaqib) chases them—jinn trying to eavesdrop on heaven are pelted with meteors. 15:18: a clear flame (shihabun mubin). The root denotes bright, piercing light.
meaning.en_detailed: The root sh-h-b (ش ه ب), with 5 occurrences, yields shihāb ('flaming meteor, shooting star'). At 37:10, 'innahu shihābun thāqib' ('it is a piercing flame') describes the meteors hurled at jinn attempting to eavesdrop on heaven; 15:18's 'shihābun mubīn' reinforces the cosmic barrier. The semantic field is celestial antipersonnel fire guarding the unseen from lower creation.

quranic_analysis.theme: Jinn and meteors
quranic_analysis.detail: Shihabun—meteors chasing jinn from eavesdropping on heavenly discourse.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en_short: To swear an oath; to strive, exert effort; to fail, fall short
meaning.en: The root hamza-lām-wāw has a complex semantic range: (1) to swear or make an earnest oath, (2) to spare no effort (mā ʾalā — 'he did not fail to'), and (3) effort, strength. The Quranic usage emphasizes oath-making and the negative mā ʾalā ('he did not omit').
meaning.ar: الْحَلِفُ وَالْقَسَمُ، وَالْجُهْدُ وَالِاسْتِطَاعَةُ
meaning.en_detailed: Triliteral Arabic root hamza-lām-wāw (أ-ل-و), 37 Quranic occurrences, with a complex semantic range spanning oath-making, striving/effort, and failing/omitting — bound together by the binding, committing force of an oath. The most distinctive Quranic usage is the phrase mā ʾalaw (ما ألوا — 'they spared no effort') at 3:118 in rebuke of the munāfiqūn: 'they spare no effort (mā ʾalaw khabālan) to do mischief'; al-Ṭabarī glosses ʾalā as 'to be remiss/fall short' used only in the negative. The noun ʾaliyya (solemn oath/pledge) appears once (Quran 22:5 in the context of divine decree); Quranic oath-ethics (cf. 24:22 forbidding use of oaths to evade good deeds) emerges from this root's semantic center.
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To swear an oath; to strive, exert effort; to fail, fall short
meaning.ar_definition: جذر أ ل و — 37 مرة — To swear an oath

etymology.semantic_evolution: The binding nature of an oath ties the senses together: an oath is a binding commitment; striving binds one to effort.

derived_forms.meaning: to fail, fall short (only in negation)

usage_patterns: Oath-taking and effort

lexicographical_sources: Ibn Faris: al-ʾalw is taqṣīr and ḥilf
theological_dimensions: Oath ethics: not using oaths to avoid good deeds (24:22)
hadith_evidence: Prohibition of excessive oaths

meaning.en: To ride, mount. 15x. Rakiba=ride. 11:41: board (irkabu) the ark. 43:12: that you may ride (li-tastawu) on them. The root spans boarding ships and riding animals.
meaning.en_detailed: The root r-k-b (ر ك ب), with 15 occurrences, centers on rakiba ('to ride, board, mount'). At 11:41, 'irka' fīhā bi-smi Allāhi majrāhā wa mursāhā' ('board it; in God's name is its course and mooring') commands boarding Noah's ark; 43:12's 'li-tastawū 'ala ẓuhūrihā thumma taẓkurū niʿmata rabbikum' pictures humans riding God's created conveyances. Semantic field: transport, conveyance, and mount.

quranic_analysis.theme: Boarding the ark
quranic_analysis.detail: Irkabu fiha bi-smi Allahi majraha—board in Allah's name.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: Reward, wage. 108x. Ajr=reward, wage. 2:262: their reward (ajruhum) is with their Lord. The root is central to Quranic soteriology—divine reward for righteous deeds. Believers receive ajr without reckoning (3:37 repeated 3x).
meaning.en_detailed: The root ʾ-j-r (أ ج ر), with 108 Quranic occurrences, yields ajr ('wage, reward'). At 2:262, 'inn Allāha lā yaḍliqu ajra al-muḥsinīn' ('God does not waste the reward of the doers of good') declares the principle; 3:37's 'wa aṭyabta ajran' closes the annunciation to Zechariah. The root bridges economic wage and eschatological recompense, central to Quranic soteriology. Semantic field: reward, recompense, and fair exchange.

quranic_analysis.theme: Divine reward
quranic_analysis.detail: Ajruhum inda rabbihim—their reward is with their Lord.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *ʾǧr = 'to hire for wages → to reward'. The Quranic ajr is both the wage earned by labor and the reward granted by divine grace. The shift from contractual wage to eschatological reward reflects the transformation of economic into theological vocabulary.

hadith_evidence.ar: تَدَبَّرُوا الْقُرْآنَ فَإِنَّهُ حُجَّةٌ لَكُمْ أَوْ عَلَيْكُمْ
hadith_evidence.en: Reflect upon the Quran, for it is either a proof for you or against you.
hadith_evidence.source: Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim via ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb

meaning.en_short: Female, feminine; to make feminine; softness, gentleness
meaning.en: The root hamza-nūn-thāʾ denotes the female sex and femininity. In the Quran, it appears in biological contexts, in the critique of pre-Islamic female infanticide, and in the theological statement that God creates male and female (53:45).
meaning.ar: ضِدُّ الذَّكَرِ، وَاللِّينُ وَالسُّهُولَةُ
meaning.en_detailed: Triliteral Arabic root hamza-nūn-thāʾ (أ-ن-ث), 30 Quranic occurrences, designating the female sex (ʾunthā, ʾināth) — the biological and grammatical category of femininity, with related senses of softness and delicacy. The noun ʾunthā (female) appears 24 times; key verses include 53:45 'and that He creates the pairs, male (dhakar) and female (ʾunthā),' affirming divine creation of gender duality; 16:58-59 rebuking the pre-Islamic practice of female infanticide ('and when the female child buried alive is asked for what crime she was killed'); 81:8-9 'when the female (ʾunthā) buried alive is asked,' elevating the buried girl to eschatological questioner. The Form IV ʾānatha (to bear a female) appears once (42:49); al-Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ and Ibn Faris note the pairing with dhakar (male) as a primary Quranic gender distinction.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر أ ن ث — 30 مرة — Female

etymology.semantic_evolution: Proto-Semitic *ʾunṯ-at- 'female' gave Arabic ʾunthā preserving original /n/ and /ṯ/. Hebrew and Aramaic show assimilation *ʾinṯat > ʾiššā.

derived_forms.meaning: to give birth to a female

usage_patterns: Biological and social female identity

lexicographical_sources: Ibn Faris: al-ʾunthā is khilāf al-dhakar
theological_dimensions: Quranic elevation of the female: the buried girl will be asked for what crime she was killed
hadith_evidence: 'Whoever raises three daughters... will enter Paradise'

meaning.en: To make, craft. 20x. Sana'a=make, manufacture. 11:37: make (isna') the ark under Our eyes. 27:88: the mountains you think solid (suni'a)—Allah's craftsmanship (sun' Allah).
meaning.en_detailed: The root ṣ-n-ʿ (ص ن ع), with 20 occurrences, yields ṣana'a ('to make, manufacture') and ṣun' ('workmanship'). At 27:88, 'ṣun'a Allāhi alladhī atqana kulla shay'' ('the workmanship of God, who has perfected everything') describes divine craftsmanship; 11:37's 'iṣnaʿ al-fulka taḥtā aʿyūninā' ('make the ark under Our eyes') commands Noah's craft. Semantic field: skilled making and divine craftsmanship.

quranic_analysis.theme: Divine craftsmanship
quranic_analysis.detail: Sun'a Allahi alladhi atqana kulla shay—Allah's perfect craftsmanship.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en_short: To return; to converse; houris of Paradise
meaning.en: To return; conversation; houris. 13x. Hawariyun=disciples (of Jesus). Hur=maidens of Paradise with dark eyes (44:54, 52:20). Muhawarah=conversation (58:1). 18:37: questioning in dialogue.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ḥ-w-r (ح و ر), with 13 occurrences, generates ḥūr ('wide-eyed maidens of Paradise', 4x) and ḥawāriyyūn ('disciples of Jesus', 5x). At 44:54, 'kadhālika wa zawwajnahum bi-ḥūrin 'īn' ('thus, and We paired them with fair-eyed maidens') describes Paradise; 3:52 introduces Jesus's Ḥawāriyyīn disciples. The semantic field fuses celestial companionship with earthly discipleship.
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To return; to converse; houris of Paradise

quranic_analysis.theme: Disciples of Jesus
quranic_analysis.detail: Hawariyyun—the close disciples who believed in Jesus.

derived_forms.meaning: To return; to converse; houris of Paradise

hadith_evidence.ar: حُفَّتِ الْجَنَّةُ بِالْمَكَارِهِ وَحُفَّتِ النَّارُ بِالشَّهَوَاتِ
hadith_evidence.en: Paradise is surrounded by hardships and Hell is surrounded by desires.

meaning.en: To emigrate; forsake. 31x. Hajara=emigrate. Hijrah=emigration. Muhajirun=emigrants (those who left Makkah for Madinah). 2:218: those who believed and emigrated (hajaru) and strove in Allah's way.
meaning.en_detailed: The root h-j-r (ه ج ر), with 31 occurrences, centers on hajara ('to emigrate, abandon') and muhājirūn ('emigrants'). At 2:218, 'alladhīna āmanū wa hājarū wa jāhadū fī sabīli Allāh' ('those who believed and emigrated and struggled in God's way') defines the early Muslim community; 9:100 credits 'al-muhājirūn wa al-ansār' with foundational loyalty. Semantic field: emigration, loyalty, religious migration.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر هَجَرَ — 31 مرة — emigrate (hijrah); to forsake

key_nominals.meaning: emigration (not noun in Quran but muhajirun is frequent)
emigrant—the Makkan Muslims who migrated to Madinah

quranic_analysis.theme: The Emigrants
quranic_analysis.detail: Al-muhajirun—the first rank of believers.

hadith_evidence.ar: الْمُهَاجِرُ مَنْ هَجَرَ مَا نَهَى اللَّهُ عَنْهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The emigrant is one who abandons what Allah has forbidden.

meaning.en: Month. 21x. Shahr=month. 2:185: the month of Ramadan (shahru ramadan). 2:194: the sacred month (al-shahru al-haramu). 9:36: the number of months with Allah is twelve. The root also means to make known, publicize—a month is a well-known division of time.
meaning.en_detailed: The root sh-h-r (ش ه ر), with 21 occurrences, centers on shahr ('month') and its divine reckoning. At 2:185, 'shahru Ramaḍāna alladhī unzila fīhi al-Qurʾān' ('the month of Ramadan in which the Quran was revealed') names the fasting month; 9:36's 'iddata al-shuhūri 'inda Allāhi thnā 'ashar shahran' fixes the lunar calendar at twelve. Semantic field: lunar time, sacred months, revelatory chronology.

quranic_analysis.theme: Ramadan month
quranic_analysis.detail: Shahru ramadana alladhi unzila fihi al-qur'an—the month of Quran.

hadith_evidence.ar: مَنْ سَلَكَ طَرِيقًا يَلْتَمِسُ فِيهِ عِلْمًا سَهَّلَ اللَّهُ لَهُ طَرِيقًا إِلَى الْجَنَّةِ
hadith_evidence.en: Whoever travels a path seeking knowledge, Allah makes the path to Paradise easy for him.

meaning.en_short: To approach, come near (in time); proper time, maturity, ripeness
meaning.en: The root hamza-nūn-yāʾ denotes the approach of time — seasonableness, ripeness, and maturity. The Quranic noun ʾinā means 'time, proper season'; the verb ʾanā means 'it is time, it has approached'. The root conveys reaching an appointed moment: fruits ripe, water hot (ʾāniya), a meal whose time has come.
meaning.ar: بُلُوغُ الْوَقْتِ الْمُقَدَّرِ، وَالنُّضْجُ وَالْإِدْرَاكُ
meaning.en_detailed: Triliteral Arabic root hamza-nūn-yāʾ (أ-ن-ي), 36 Quranic occurrences, denoting the approach of time — seasonableness, ripeness, and the proper moment for something to reach completion. The verb ʾanā (it is time, it has ripened/approached) appears 6 times; the noun ʾinan (proper time/maturity) once; the adjective ʾāniya (boiling hot, intensely heated) twice. Key verses include 57:16 'Has not the time come (alam yaʾni) for those who believe that their hearts should humble themselves to the remembrance of God,' a famous call to spiritual urgency; 88:5 'in boiling water (māʾin ʾānin)' describing the seething Hell-water; al-Rāghib glosses ʾinā as 'the full ripeness of a thing at its proper moment,' distinguishing it from simple time-markers.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر أ ن ي — 36 مرة — To approach

etymology.semantic_evolution: Proto-Semitic 'time/season' developed into Arabic with a focus on ripeness and proper timing. The verb ʾanā specifically means 'the right time has come'.

derived_forms.meaning: to approach, come near; it is time

usage_patterns: Time and ripeness/heating

lexicographical_sources: Raghib: ʾinā is the full ripeness of a thing at its proper moment
theological_dimensions: 57:16 as a call to spiritual urgency — the time for heartfelt devotion is NOW
hadith_evidence: ʾAnāh (deliberateness) praised: 'Deliberateness is from God'

meaning.en_short: To seek refuge; there is no escape
meaning.en: To seek refuge. 1x. 18:58: they will find no escape (maw'ilan) from it. The sole Quranic occurrence—no escape from divine punishment.
meaning.en_detailed: The root w-ʾ-l (و أ ل), with a single Quranic attestation at 18:58, gives maw'il ('place of escape, refuge'). The verse closes the parable of the arrogant city: 'wa lam yajid min dūnihi maw'ilā' ('and they will find no refuge besides Him'). The semantic field is divine sovereignty and the negation of human escape from God's decree.
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To seek refuge; there is no escape

quranic_analysis.theme: No escape
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa lam yajidu min dunihi maw'ilan—they find no refuge besides Him.

derived_forms.meaning: To seek refuge; there is no escape

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en: Speed, haste. 30x. Sari'=swift. 2:203: hasten (Asri'u) in remembrance of Allah. 6:57: I follow only what is revealed to me (inna Allaha sari'u al-hisab—swift in account).
meaning.en_detailed: The root s-r-ʿ (س ر ع), with 23 occurrences, generates sarīʿ ('swift, rapid'). At 6:57, 'inn Allāha sarīʿu al-ḥisāb' ('God is swift in reckoning') declares the suddenness of divine accounting; 2:202, 3:19, and 5:4 repeat the formula in varied contexts. The semantic field is divine swiftness, the hastening to good deeds, and eschatological urgency.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر سَرُعَ — 23 مرة — speed, haste; to hasten

quranic_analysis.theme: Swift reckoning
quranic_analysis.detail: Inna Allaha sari'u al-hisab—Allah is swift in account.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: Severe, strong. 102x. Shadid=severe, strong. 2:165: wa alladhina amanu ashaddu hubban li-Allah (believers are stronger in love for Allah). Shadid al-'adhab (severe in punishment).
meaning.en_detailed: The root sh-d-d (ش د د), with 102 occurrences, generates shadda ('to bind, strengthen'), shadīd ('severe, intense'), and the elative ashadd ('more intense'). At 2:165, 'wa alladhīna āmanū ashaddu ḥubban li-Allāh' ('believers are stronger in love for God') contrasts divine love with worldly attachment. Compounds like shadīdu al-'iqāb ('severe in punishment') and shadīdu al-ḥisāb ('severe in reckoning') define divine attributes. Semantic field: severity, strength, and intensification.

quranic_analysis.theme: Strength of faith
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa alladhina amanu ashaddu hubban li-Allah—stronger love for Allah.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *šdd = 'to bind, make firm'. Arabic shadda = to bind, tighten, strengthen. Shadīd = severe, intense. The Quran uses shadīd for the severity of divine punishment and the intensity of human love — 'their love for [idols] is intense (shadīdan) like the love for Allah' (2:165).

hadith_evidence.ar: تَدَبَّرُوا الْقُرْآنَ فَإِنَّهُ حُجَّةٌ لَكُمْ أَوْ عَلَيْكُمْ
hadith_evidence.en: Reflect upon the Quran, for it is either a proof for you or against you.
hadith_evidence.source: Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim via ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb

meaning.en: Family, people. 100x. Ahl=family, people. Ahl al-kitab=People of the Book. Ahl al-bayt=household of Prophet (33:33). Ahl al-qur'a=villagers. 20:132: command your family (ahlaka) to pray.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ʾ-h-l (أ ه ل), with 127 occurrences—the most attested kinship term in the Quran—centers on ahl ('family, household, people'). The distinctive compounds include ahl al-bayt ('people of the house', 33:33) and ahl al-kitāb ('People of the Book', ~31x) designating Jews and Christians as prior recipients of revelation. At 20:132, 'wa'mur ahlaka bi al-ṣalāh' ('command your family to pray') launches prophetic responsibility. Semantic field: kinship, communal belonging, religious identity.

quranic_analysis.theme: Ahl al-Kitab
quranic_analysis.detail: People of the Book—Jews and Christians as recipients of prior revelation.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *ʾhl = 'tent → family, household'. The original meaning 'tent' shifted metonymically to 'tent-dwellers' → 'family, people'. The Arabic ahl is the community of belonging: ahl al-bayt (the Prophet's household), ahl al-kitāb (People of the Book). The Hebrew ʾōhel preserves the original material sense of 'tent'.

hadith_evidence.ar: تَدَبَّرُوا الْقُرْآنَ فَإِنَّهُ حُجَّةٌ لَكُمْ أَوْ عَلَيْكُمْ
hadith_evidence.en: Reflect upon the Quran, for it is either a proof for you or against you.
hadith_evidence.source: Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim via ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb

meaning.en: Daytime; river. 113x. Nahar=daytime (57x). Nahr=rivers (56x). 2:164: alternation of night and day (al-layli wa al-nahari). 47:15: rivers (anhaar) of water, milk, wine, honey in Paradise.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ن-ه-ر appears 113x in the Quran, distributed across two principal nominals: nahār (daytime, 57x) and anhār (rivers, 54x), with the verbal root itself rare. The semantic field unites the diurnal light of day with the flowing waters of Paradise; 2:164 places 'the alternation of night and day (ikhtilāf al-layli wa al-nahāri)' among God's greatest signs for those who reflect, while 47:15 depicts the anjār of Paradise as flowing with water, milk, wine, and honey—the promise of eternal abundance. 3:190 invokes the same alternation as a proof of fitra and reason. The etymological base *nhr ('to flow') underlies both meanings: daylight as flowing brightness against the darkness, rivers as flowing water—an eschatological bridge between the cosmic order of this world and the promised reward of the next.

quranic_analysis.theme: Alternation of night/day
quranic_analysis.detail: Ikhtilaf al-layli wa al-nahari—one of the great signs of God.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *nhr = 'to flow → river'. The Quranic nahār (day) and nahr (river) derive from the same root — the day as 'flowing light'. The rivers of Paradise (anhār) are a promise of eternal abundance.

hadith_evidence.ar: تَدَبَّرُوا الْقُرْآنَ فَإِنَّهُ حُجَّةٌ لَكُمْ أَوْ عَلَيْكُمْ
hadith_evidence.en: Reflect upon the Quran, for it is either a proof for you or against you.
hadith_evidence.source: Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim via ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb

meaning.en: Eternity. 87x. Khalid=eternal. Khaliduna fiha=abiding in it forever (repeated ~45x for Paradise and Hell). Mukhallad=eternal. 104:3: he thinks his wealth will make him eternal (akhladahu). The root marks endless duration in the afterlife.
meaning.en_detailed: Root خ-ل-د appears 87x, governing the Quranic vocabulary of eternal duration in the afterlife. Khalada = to abide forever; the formulaic khālidīna fīhā abadan ('abiding therein forever') recurs roughly forty-five times, distributed equally between Paradise (2:25; 4:57) and Hell (9:22; 98:8), making it one of the most frequently repeated Quranic phrases. The IV form akhlada surfaces pointedly in 104:3—'he thinks his wealth has made him eternal (akhladahu)'—capturing the delusive materialist worldview that the root elsewhere condemns; 87:13–17 reverses the picture by resting the blessed 'on couches lined (muttaki'īn)'. Al-khālidūn is the Quranic designation for the everlasting residents of both final abodes, with khuld denoting Paradise itself (25:15).
meaning.ar_definition: جذر خَلَدَ — 87 مرة — eternity; to abide forever

quranic_analysis.theme: Eternal abode
quranic_analysis.detail: Khalidina fiha abadan—abiding therein forever. Paradise and Hell both eternal.

derived_forms.meaning: to make eternal; to incline toward earth

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *ḫld = 'to last, remain, endure'. Arabic khalada = to remain forever. Khuld = eternity. The Quranic khālidūn (those who abide forever) describes both the residents of Paradise and Hell — the finality of the afterlife. 'Abiding therein forever (khālidīna fīhā)' — the definitive Quranic phrase for eternal destiny.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: Spouse, pair. 84x. Zawj=spouse, pair. 4:1: created you from one soul and made from it its mate (zawjaha). 36:36: created all things in pairs (azwaj). The root spans marriage, gender complementarity, and cosmic duality.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ز-و-ج appears 81x, its central nominal zawj fusing the meanings of spouse and pair across conjugal, biological, and cosmological registers. 4:1 declares God 'created you from one soul and made from it its mate (zawjahā)'; 36:36 widens the design to all creation: 'of every thing We created pairs (zawjayn) lest you reflect'; 51:49 reiterates 'and of all things We created pairs (azwāj)'. The verb zāwaja (III) names the reciprocal pairing in marriage; tazwīj names the act of pairing off. The root thus spans conjugal union, male–female complementarity as the basis of human kinship, and the cosmic duality that structures all created reality—the antithesis of shirk and odd-numbered associationism.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر زَوَّجَ — 81 مرة — spouse, pair; to marry

quranic_analysis.theme: Creation in pairs
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa min kulli shay'in khalaqna zawjayn—from everything We created pairs.

hadith_evidence.ar: النِّكَاحُ مِنْ سُنَّتِي فَمَنْ لَمْ يَعْمَلْ بِسُنَّتِي فَلَيْسَ مِنِّي
hadith_evidence.en: Marriage is part of my Sunnah; whoever does not follow my Sunnah is not of me.

meaning.en: Gratitude. 75x. Shakara=thank. Shakur=grateful—al-Shakur divine name. Shukr=gratitude. 2:152: remember Me and I will remember you; be grateful to Me (ushkuru li) and do not be ungrateful. 14:7: if you are grateful (la-in shakartum), I will increase you.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ش-ك-ر appears 75x, its semantic field centered on gratitude as the human response to divine blessing. Shakara = to thank, shukr = gratitude, shakūr = the intensely grateful. Al-Shakūr is a divine name (4:147), teaching that God accepts and abundantly rewards the servant's small thanks. 2:152 enjoins 'be grateful to Me (ushkurū lī) and do not be ungrateful'; 14:7 establishes the covenantal economy: 'if you are grateful (la-in shakartum), I will increase you (la-azīdannakum)'; 16:18 notes that 'if you count the favors of Allah, you cannot enumerate them'; 27:40 records the grateful supplication of Solomon. Shukr triggers divine increase; kufr seals it; the verb thus names both the cognitive recognition and the volitional response.

quranic_analysis.theme: Gratitude and increase
quranic_analysis.detail: La-in shakartum la-azidannakum—gratitude brings divine increase.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *škr = 'to recognize benefit → to be grateful'. The Quranic shukr is the human response to divine niʿmah (blessing): gratitude. Al-Shakūr (The Ever-Grateful) is a divine name — God 'thanks' the servant by rewarding abundantly.

hadith_evidence.ar: مَنْ لَا يَشْكُرِ النَّاسَ لَا يَشْكُرِ اللَّهَ
hadith_evidence.en: Whoever does not thank people does not thank Allah.

meaning.en: To bend, fold; exception. 67x. Thaniya=second (2x). Istathna=except. 68:18: they made no exception (la yastathnun—without saying in sha Allah). 2:282: witnesses—two men (ithnani).
meaning.en_detailed: Root ث-ن-ي appears 29x, its semantic range spanning the numeral ithnān (two, dual), the verb thanā (to bend, turn), and the reflexive istathnā (to make an exception). 68:18 critiques the Meccan disbelievers who promise sacrifice 'and make no exception (wa lā yastathnūn)'—i.e. those who fail to say in shā' Allāh before any vow or future-tense declaration; 2:282 prescribes 'two (ithnayn) men' as witnesses in financial contracts, doubling the testimony as a guard against falsehood. 17:31 forbids killing children 'for fear of poverty (imlāq)'—the same root's verbal sense describing inward turning. The istithnā' is the Quranic etiquette of epistemic humility before the divine will, expressed in the ubiquitous in shā' Allāh.

quranic_analysis.theme: In sha Allah exception
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa la yastathnun—they did not say in sha Allah.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *ṯny = 'to fold, turn'. Thanā = to fold, turn away. Ithnān = two. Yathnūna = they bend/turn away. 'They turn away (yathnūna) from the remembrance of Allah' — the neglect of dhikr.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: Patience, perseverance. 103x. Sabara=be patient. Sabr=patience. Al-Sabur=divine name (the Patient). 2:153: seek help through patience (sabr) and prayer. 2:155: give glad tidings to the patient (al-sabirin). 3:200: be patient (isbiru) and excel in patience (sabiru).
meaning.en_detailed: Root ص-ب-ر appears 103x, the most concentrated Quranic vocabulary of endurance and steadfastness. Ṣabr = patience, ṣabbār = exceedingly patient (intensive), al-Ṣabūr is a divine name. 2:153 commands 'seek help through patience (ṣabr) and prayer'; 2:155 promises 'glad tidings to the patient (al-ṣābirīn)' through trials of fear, hunger, loss of goods and life; 3:200 escalates the demand: 'be patient (iṣbirū) and vie in patience (ṣābirū)'; 8:46 grounds it theologically: 'Allah is with the patient (innā Allāha ma'a al-ṣābirīn)'; 103:3 inscribes patience as the mark of the righteous. Ṣabr denotes both passive endurance and active perseverance, encompassing every mode of holding firm under trial—a key Quranic virtue binding worship to ethics.

quranic_analysis.theme: Patience in trial
quranic_analysis.detail: Inna Allaha ma'a al-sabirin—Allah is with the patient. Glad tidings to the patient.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *ṣbr = 'to bind, tie → be firm, patient'. Ṣabr = binding the soul to endurance. 'iṣbirū wa ṣābirū' (3:200) — individual and communal perseverance.

hadith_evidence.ar: عَجَبًا لِأَمْرِ الْمُؤْمِنِ إِنَّ أَمْرَهُ كُلَّهُ خَيْرٌ
hadith_evidence.en: How wonderful is the affair of the believer — all of it is good.

meaning.en_short: To seek shelter, take refuge, betake oneself; shelter, abode
meaning.en: The root hamza-wāw-yāʾ denotes seeking shelter, refuge, and finding a dwelling place. In the Quran, it is used for physical shelter (the youth of the Cave), for emotional comfort, and for divine protection. The Form IV verb ʾāwā means 'to give shelter, host, protect'. Maʾwan denotes a place of refuge — often used for Paradise.
meaning.ar: الرُّجُوعُ إِلَى الْمَكَانِ وَالِانْضِمَامُ إِلَيْهِ لِلْحِفْظِ وَالْحِمَايَةِ
meaning.en_detailed: Triliteral Arabic root hamza-wāw-yāʾ (أ-و-ي), 36 Quranic occurrences, denoting seeking shelter, refuge, and a dwelling-place of protection — both for the one who seeks and (in Form IV) for the one who grants shelter. The Form I verb ʾawā (to seek shelter) appears 18 times; the Form IV ʾāwā (to give shelter/host) 8 times. Central verses include 18:10 'when the youths sought refuge (awā al-fityatu) in the Cave,' narrating the People of the Cave; 93:6 'Did He not find you an orphan and give you shelter (fa-ʾāwā),' of God's care for the orphaned Prophet; the noun maʾwā (shelter/refuge, 17 occurrences) refers both to earthly abodes and, eschatologically, to the 'abode of peace' (dār al-salām) — Paradise.
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To seek shelter, take refuge, betake oneself; shelter, abode
meaning.ar_definition: جذر أ و ي — 36 مرة — To seek shelter

cognates.hebrew: אוה — to desire, designate as dwelling

etymology.semantic_evolution: From 'dwelling' in Proto-Semitic, Arabic developed the nuance of seeking shelter for protection. Maʾwan preserves original dwelling sense.

usage_patterns: Physical and spiritual shelter

lexicographical_sources: Ibn Faris: al-ʾawy is al-rujūʿ ilā al-makān
theological_dimensions: God as Al-Muʾwī — the One who shelters the orphan
hadith_evidence: Reward of sheltering the orphan and traveler

meaning.en: Mountain. 41x. Jabal=mountain. 7:143: when Moses saw the mountain crumble (jabalan dakkan). 2:74: stones from which rivers burst—and some fears Allah. Mountains as signs of divine power—stabilizing earth and sites of revelation.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ج-ب-ل appears 41x, governing the Quranic vocabulary of mountains as cosmic structures. Jabal = mountain; jibāl (pl.) marks the earth's stabilizers. 7:143 records the Sinai theophany: when Moses' Lord manifested to the mountain 'it crumbled (jabalan dakkan)'; 13:3 declares 'He placed firm mountains (rawāsiya) lest the earth shake with you'; 21:30 affirms 'We placed therein firm mountains (rawāsiya) above it'; 33:72 famously records that 'We offered the trust (al-amānah) to the heavens, earth, and mountains (jibāl)—but they refused to bear it, and man bore it.' 16:68 contrasts bee-revelation with the mountain analogy. The root signifies the geological weight and moral gravity of created forms, mountains as both cosmological pillars and ethical loci.

quranic_analysis.theme: Mountains as signs
quranic_analysis.detail: Al-jibal—mountains as stabilizers of earth and sites of theophany.

hadith_evidence.ar: الْمُؤْمِنُ يَأْكُلُ فِي مِعًى وَاحِدٍ وَالْكَافِرُ يَأْكُلُ فِي سَبْعَةِ أَمْعَاءٍ
hadith_evidence.en: The believer eats in one intestine and the disbeliever eats in seven intestines.

meaning.en: To replace, substitute. 44x. Baddala II=replace, change. Ibdal IV=substitute. 2:108: whoever exchanges (yabaddal) faith for disbelief—he has strayed. 16:101: We substitute (baddalna) a verse in place of another.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ب-د-ل appears 44x, governing the Quranic vocabulary of replacement, exchange, and substitution. Baddala (II) = to exchange; the noun tabdīl marks divine substitution. 2:108 condemns 'whoever exchanges (yubaddilu) faith for disbelief'; 16:101 records the Meccan controversy: 'when We substitute (baddalnā) a verse in place of another'—the basis for the classical doctrine of naskh (abrogation); 14:28 promises 'Allah substitutes (yubaddilu) evil deeds with good'; 4:56 warns disbelievers of repeated skin-substitution in Hell; 24:55 promises that 'Allah will substitute (yubaddilu) for them a righteous people.' The root spans covenantal repudiation, juridical abrogation, and eschatological recompense—always foregrounding divine agency behind every replacement.

quranic_analysis.theme: Divine substitution
quranic_analysis.detail: Baddala—exchange, substitution. Quranic abrogation as divine replacement.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ اللَّهَ لَا يُغَيِّرُ مَا بِقَوْمٍ حَتَّى يُغَيِّرُوا مَا بِأَنْفُسِهِمْ
hadith_evidence.en: Allah does not change the condition of a people until they change what is in themselves.

meaning.en_short: To shorten; castle; to lower gaze
meaning.en: To shorten; castle; lower. 11x. Qasr=shorten. Qasr=castle/palace. Aqsara IV=desist. 4:101: shorten (taqsuru) prayer during travel. 7:202: their companions—they draw them not to desist (la yuqdirun).
meaning.en_detailed: Root ق-ص-ر appears 11x, unifying the senses of shortening, restraining, and palatial construction across ritual, ethical, and eschatological registers. 4:101 establishes the juridical ruling: 'when you travel, no blame upon you to shorten (taqṣirū) the prayer'; 24:31 commands the believing women 'to lower (yaqṣidna) their gaze (baṣar) and guard their modesty'; 7:202 notes the shayṭān's companions 'do not desist (lā yuqṣirūn)' from leading their charges astray; 25:10 contrasts the 'qṣūr (castles)' of the Hereafter with the unrewarding earthly architecture of the disbelievers; 33:53 commands the Prophet 'enter the houses through their doors.' The root spans ritual shortening in travel, ethical restraint of the gaze, and architectural qaṣr—palatial rewards of the Hereafter, joining bodily discipline in this world to palatial reward in the next.
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To shorten; castle; to lower gaze

quranic_analysis.theme: Shortening prayer
quranic_analysis.detail: Fa-laysa alaykum junahun an taqsuru min al-salat—no blame to shorten prayer while traveling.

derived_forms.meaning: To shorten; castle; to lower gaze

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: Consultation. 4x. Shura=consultation. 42:38: their affairs are decided by consultation among them (amruhum shura baynahum). 2:233: consultation about weaning. The root grounds Islamic principle of collective deliberation.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ش-و-ر appears 4x, generating the Quranic principle of al-shūrā (mutual consultation). 42:38, the verse that names the surah itself, defines the believing community as those 'whose affairs are decided by consultation among them (amruhum shūra baynahum) and who spend of what We have provided them'; 2:233 directs that the weaning of infants be settled by mutual consultation between parents; 3:159 commands the Prophet himself: 'consult them (fa-shāwirhum) in the matter, and when you have determined, rely on Allah.' Sūra 42 is named al-Shūrā for this principle. Shūrā grounds the Islamic norm of collective deliberation before decision—a value binding communal life.

quranic_analysis.theme: Shura principle
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa amruhum shura baynahum—their affairs are decided by mutual consultation.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en: Forelock. 4x. Nasiyah=forelock. 96:15-16: We will seize you by the forelock (al-nasiyah)—a lying, sinful forelock. The forelock as seat of destiny—seized in divine punishment.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ن-ص-ي appears 4x in the noun nasīyah (forelock, front of the head), the locus of subjection in Quranic eschatology. 96:15–16 announces the divine threat: 'We will seize him by the forelock (al-nasīyah)—a lying, sinful forelock (kadhdhābat khaṭīyah)'; 11:56 generalizes the principle: 'no living creature is there but He holds it by its forelock'; 55:41 names the forelocks and feet as the two seizing-points of the sinners on the Day of Judgment. The forelock marks the seized sinner dragged before divine judgment, an image drawn from the Arab custom of seizing an enemy or prisoner by the front hair—an indelible mark of mastery.

quranic_analysis.theme: Seizing the forelock
quranic_analysis.detail: La-nasfa'an bi al-nasiyah—We will seize by the forelock. Symbol of subjection.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *nšy = 'to forget'. Nasiya = to forget. Insān (human) possibly from the same root — the forgetting creature. 'Adam forgot (nasiya) and We found no resolve in him' (20:115).

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en: Forehead. 1x. 21:98: you and what you worship will be fuel for Hellfire—and you will be thrust face-first (jibah) upon it. The sole occurrence.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ج-ب-ه appears 1x, in the noun jabha (forehead) and its plural jibāh. 21:98 pronounces upon the idolaters and their gods: 'you and what you worship besides Allah are fuel for Hellfire, to which you will come (la-aṣlabuhum)—face-first (jibāh).' The single occurrence stages a stark contrast with the sujūd (prostration) of the Muslim, who bends forehead-to-earth in submission before God; the idolater's forehead instead meets Hellfire in humiliation—a vivid image of inversion, where the posture of submission is answered by the posture of contempt and assault. The verb jabaha also gives jabābira (ruthless tyrants), though the verbal root is absent from the Quran. The lexical rarity concentrates the meaning entirely in this one image of damnation.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر جَبَهَ — 1 مرة — forehead; to confront

quranic_analysis.theme: Face-first into Hell
quranic_analysis.detail: Hadhihi jahannamu allati kuntum tu'adun—aslabuha—face-first entry into Hell.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en_short: To seek, desire; to transgress, oppress
meaning.en: To seek; to transgress. 96x. Bagha=seek, demand, transgress, oppress. Ibtagha=seek. 42:27: if Allah expanded provision, they would rebel (la-baghaw) on earth. 49:9: if one party oppresses (tabghi) the other, fight the oppressor. The root bridges seeking and oppression.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ب-غ-ي appears 96x, its semantic field bridging desire (ibtighā') and transgression (baghy). 42:27 diagnoses the moral hazard: 'if Allah expanded provision for His servants, they would rebel (la-baghaw) on earth'; 49:9 lays the communal remedy: 'if two parties of believers fight, make peace; if one party oppresses (baghat) the other, fight the oppressor (allatī tabghī)'; 2:190 establishes the universal principle: 'do not transgress (wa lā ta'tadū)—Allah loves not the transgressors (al-bāghīn)'; 7:33 forbids declaring unlawful what Allah made lawful (tut'abawwa'a ma'ahum baghyan); 4:32 affirms that 'men have a share (naṣīb) of what they earn.' The root exposes the bridge from desire to excess to oppression.
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To seek, desire; to transgress, oppress

quranic_analysis.theme: Fighting oppression
quranic_analysis.detail: Fa-in baghat ihdahuma ala al-ukhra fa-qatilu allati tabghi—fight the transgressing party.

derived_forms.meaning: to desire, seek; to transgress, oppress

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *bġy = 'to seek, desire'. baghā = to seek; to transgress. Seeking can become excess → oppression. 'lā tabghū — Allah loves not the transgressors' (2:190).

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: To draw out, extract. 3x. Salla=draw out. 20:12: remove (fa-khla') your sandals—you are in the sacred valley of Tuwa.
meaning.en_detailed: Root س-ل-ل appears 3x, governing the gentle extraction of one thing from another. The most celebrated occurrence is 20:12, when God addresses Moses at Sinai: 'remove (fa-khla') your sandals—you are in the sacred valley of Ṭuwā (al-wādi al-muqaddas)'; the Form VIII variant khala'a retains the sense of stripping off, the inverse of wearing. The remaining occurrences reinforce the image of bodily preparation for divine encounter. The root marks removal of the profane from sacred encounter—a preparation for theophany whose corollary is the believer's removal of worldly barriers to divine address, even at the level of clothing. The sibilant gentleness of the root contrasts with violent derivatives from other roots that mark forced extraction.

quranic_analysis.theme: Sacred ground
quranic_analysis.detail: Fa-khla' na'layka—remove your sandals in the sacred valley.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en: To fabricate, invent. 60x. Iftara VIII=to fabricate against Allah—a grave sin. 6:93: who is more unjust than one who fabricates (iftara) against Allah a lie? 3:94: whoever fabricates (iftara) against Allah falsehood—they are the wrongdoers.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ف-ر-ي appears 60x, dominated by Form VIII iftara (to fabricate, forge). 6:93 indicts the worst oppressor: 'who is more unjust (aẓlamu) than one who fabricates (iftarā) against Allah a lie (kadhiban)?'; 3:94 repeats the charge: 'whoever fabricates (iftarā) against Allah falsehood, then they are the wrongdoers (al-ẓālimūn)'; 10:37 defends the Quran's inimitable character: 'this could not have been fabricated by other than Allah'; 7:89 records the hypothetical boast: 'we had fabricated (la-if'taraynā) lies against Allah else.' The semantic metaphor is cutting away from truth (farā = to cut, as in ripping cloth), producing falsehood as fabric torn from reality.

key_nominals.meaning: fabrication, false invention—iftira' ala Allah (against Allah)

quranic_analysis.theme: Iftira against Allah
quranic_analysis.detail: Man azlamu mimman iftara ala Allahi kadhiban—who is more unjust than one fabricating lies against Allah?

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *pry = 'to cut, split → to fabricate (cutting away from truth)'. Farā = to cut; to invent falsely. Iftarā = to fabricate lies. 'Who is more unjust than one who fabricates (iftarā) a lie against Allah?' (6:21).

hadith_evidence.ar: إِيَّاكُمْ وَالْكَذِبَ فَإِنَّ الْكَذِبَ يَهْدِي إِلَى الْفُجُورِ
hadith_evidence.en: Beware of lying, for lying leads to wickedness.

meaning.en: Psalms. 3x. Zabur=Psalms of David. 4:163: We gave David the Psalms (zaburan). Distinct from zbr as iron fragment.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ز-ب-ر appears 11x in the Quran, but its central nominal zabūr (Psalms) dominates the scriptural reference. 4:163 records: 'We gave David the Psalms (wa ātaynā Dāwūda zabūran) after the Reminder (al-dhikr)'; 17:55 situates David and Solomon as recipients of divine knowledge and given grace over many believing servants; 21:105 declares 'We have written in the Zabūr after the reminder (al-dhikr) that My righteous servants will inherit the earth.' The root denotes writing or inscription; the Zabūr is the revealed book of David, distinct from the Torah (tawrāh), Gospel (injīl), and Furqān. The verb zubara occurs in 25:5 to describe the gathering of mushrikūn.

quranic_analysis.theme: Psalms given to David
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa atayna Dawuda zaburan—We gave David the Psalms.

hadith_evidence.ar: الْيَدُ الْعُلْيَا خَيْرٌ مِنَ الْيَدِ السُّفْلَى
hadith_evidence.en: The upper hand is better than the lower hand.

meaning.en: To understand deeply. 20x. Faqiha=comprehend. Tafaqquh=deep learning. 9:122: a group should devote to tafaqquh fi al-din (deep understanding of religion). 6:98: We have detailed the signs for people who understand (yafqahun).
meaning.en_detailed: Root ف-ق-ه appears 20x, governing the Quranic vocabulary of deep understanding. Faqiha = to comprehend; tafaqquh = to seek deep understanding; fiqh = the resulting comprehension. 9:122 establishes the scholarly vocation: 'let a group devote to tafaqquh fī al-dīn (deep understanding of religion) and warn their people'; 6:98 declares 'We have detailed the signs for a people who comprehend (yafqahūn)'; 4:78 affirms: 'had they referred it to Allah and the Messenger, those who interpret would know'; 2:242 enjoins reflection. Fiqh in the Quran is not bare knowing (ʿilm) but cognitive penetration of meaning, the foundation of independent legal reasoning (ijtihād) that the Quran itself authorizes.

quranic_analysis.theme: Deep understanding
quranic_analysis.detail: Li-yatafaqqahu fi al-din—to gain deep understanding of religion. Foundation of Islamic scholarship.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: Forever, eternity. 28x. Abadan=forever, never. 2:95: they will never (abadan) wish for death. 72:23: Hellfire forever (abadan). 4:57: abiding therein forever (khalidina fiha abadan). Contrasted with khalid—abad is unconditioned duration.
meaning.en_detailed: Root أ-ب-د appears 28x, its central nominal abadan denoting unconditioned eternity. 2:95 reports the Jahiliyyah mentality: 'they will never (lā abadan) wish for death because of what their hands have sent ahead'; 4:57 intensifies with 'abiding therein forever (khālidīna fīhā abadan)'; 72:23 pronounces upon the disbelievers: 'they will not be relieved from the Fire—never (lā abadan)'; 33:65 declares 'no doubt about it—Allah does not wrong, abadan'; 9:83 limits earthly glories: 'enjoyment is little, then Hell will be their eternal home.' Abadan marks duration without terminus; paired with khālid, the doubling reinforces unconditional permanence and underscores the theological unidirectionality of the afterlife.

quranic_analysis.theme: Eternal duration
quranic_analysis.detail: Khalidina fiha abadan—abiding eternally. Doubled with khalid for emphasis.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: Thin. 1x. Raqqa=be thin. 2:74: your hearts hardened like stones or even harder.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ر-ق-ق appears 1x in the Quran, denoting thinness, fineness, or tenderness of substance. Its sole Quranic occurrence stands in implicit contrast with the Quranic vocabulary of heart-hardening (qaswa, 2:74: 'then your hearts hardened (qasat) after that—they are like stones or even harder in hardness'); the r-q-q root names the prior state of tenderness that hardened hearts have lost. The rare root marks the delicacy of conscience that, once lost, requires the prophetic remedy of softening (taḥannun) and remembrance (dhikr). Linguistically it is cognate with the parchment (raqq) on which texts were inscribed, evoking the fine surface that absorbs and preserves writing—the heart as writable parchment.

quranic_analysis.theme: Hardened hearts
quranic_analysis.detail: Qasat qulubukum—your hearts hardened.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en: Gesture. 1x. Ramaza=gesture. 3:41: your sign is three days not speaking except by gestures (ramzan)—Zakariya.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ر-م-ز appears 1x in the noun ramz (a gesture, bodily sign). 3:41 records Zakariya's sign: 'your sign is that you will not speak to people for three days except by gesture (illā ramzan)'—a silent dhikr confirming the angelic announcement of a son in old age; the prophet's bodily motion becomes the only speech permitted. The root names the bodily, non-verbal communication that stands in for articulate speech; its single Quranic use marks the prophet's three-day abstention from speech, during which his body alone gave praise—an extreme form of shukr. The root contrasts with kināya (allusion) and ishāra (pointing), both more articulate forms of non-verbal address.

quranic_analysis.theme: Zakariya's sign
quranic_analysis.detail: Illa ramzan—except by gesture.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en: Nearness. Zulfa=nearness. 11:114: prayer at the two ends of day and in approaches of the night (zulafan min al-layl).
meaning.en_detailed: Root ز-ل-ف appears 10x, its central nominal zulfa denoting temporal approach or nearness. 11:114 establishes the prayer-schedule: 'perform prayer at the two ends of day and in approaches of the night (zulafan min al-layl)—good deeds remove evil'; 73:20 supports the same routine: 'pray as much as is easy for you'; 30:17-18 commands 'glorify Allah when you reach evening and morning'; 39:9 marks the night-prayer of the devout 'prostrating and standing (sujjadan wa qiyāman)'; 40:7 declares 'those who carry the Throne (ḥamalat al-'arshi) and those around it glorify their Lord.' The root spans temporal approach (night-watches) and eschatological drawing-near (al-muqrabūn), uniting daily discipline with eternal proximity.

quranic_analysis.theme: Prayer timing
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa zulafan min al-layl—in approaches of the night.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en: Emerge. 13x. Baraza=appear. 14:21: they will emerge (barazu) before Allah on Judgment Day.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ب-ر-ز appears 9x, governing the Quranic vocabulary of emergence into visibility. Baraza = to emerge, come forth. 14:21 announces the eschatological scene: 'they will emerge (barazū) before Allah, all together (jamī'an)—on the Day when no soul will be wronged in anything'; 4:109 notes that whoever offends against his soul 'you will find every soul—whatever it had done—presented (yūra'ūna)'; 18:48 records 'they will be presented before your Lord in rows (ṣufufan)'; 67:13 warns against secret plotting between two or more, 'He knows the secret and the more hidden.' The root marks the unmasking of what was hidden, especially before divine judgment—a key eschatological motif.

quranic_analysis.theme: Emergence on Judgment
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa barazu li-Allahi jami'an—they emerge before Allah.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en: To split; hardship. 28x. Shaqqa=split, make difficult. Shiqaq=dissension. 90:11: he has not attempted the steep path (al-aqabah)—figurative of difficulty. 41:11: the heaven was split (fatara). 2:108: whoever opposes (yushaqiq) the Messenger.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ش-ق-ق appears 28x, its semantic field bridging physical splitting and moral disunion. Shaqqa = to split; shiqāq = discord, schism; 'aqabah = a steep pass. 2:108 indicts 'whoever opposes (yushāqiqu) the Messenger after guidance is clear'; 90:11 marks the moral challenge: 'he has not attempted the steep path (al-'aqabah)'; 41:11–12 records the cosmological: 'the heaven was split (fatara) and became as rose-petals'; 80:26 assigns the opening (shaqq) of the soil to God; 4:130 warns that 'if you divorce, Allah will substitute (yubaddilu)'. The root unites cosmological fissure with human dissension, exposing the correspondence between cosmic rupture and communal schism.

quranic_analysis.theme: Opposing the Messenger
quranic_analysis.detail: Man yushaqiqi al-rasula—whoever opposes the Messenger after guidance is clear.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: Grey hair. 3x. Shayb=grey hair. 19:4: my head has flared with grey hair (ishta'ala al-ra'su shayban)—Zakariya's old age prayer. 73:17: a Day that will make children grey-haired (shiban).
meaning.en_detailed: Root ش-ي-ب appears 3x, its central nominal shayb (grey hair) marking the threshold of mortal time. 19:4 records Zakariya's lament: 'my head has flared with grey hair (wa ishta'ala al-ra'su shayban), and I have never been unblessed in supplication to You, my Lord'—old age as the prophet's plea for an heir; 73:17 describes the Day of Judgment: 'a Day that will make children grey-haired (shīban)'; 22:5 mentions the stages of human creation culminating in 'weak old age (shaykhatan)'. Grey hair marks the closing of life's first half and the urgency of preparing for the next—the figure of Zakariya stands as the exemplar of late-life petition.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر شَابَ — 3 مرة — grey hair, old age

quranic_analysis.theme: Zakariya's prayer
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa ishta'ala al-ra'su shayban—my head blazed with grey hair, old age desperate for a heir.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en: To deviate, disobey. 54x. Fasaqa=deviate from command. Fasiq=sinner, deviant. Fisq=transgression. 49:6: if a fasiq brings news, verify it. 2:99: none reject Our signs except the deviant (al-fasiqun). The root describes departure from divine obedience.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ف-س-ق appears 54x, its semantic field centered on moral departure from divine command. Fasaqa = to deviate, fāsiq = the deviant one, fisq = transgression. 49:6 establishes the communal principle: 'if a fāsiq brings news (fāsiqun bi-naba'in), verify it (fa-tabayyanū) lest you harm a people in ignorance'; 2:99 generalizes: 'none reject Our signs except the fāsiqūn'; 5:3 includes the fisq pericope among unlawful meats (munkhaniqah, mawqūdhah, mutaraddiyyah, naṭīḥah); 65:1 connects fisq to wrongful divorce; 6:121 condemns those who 'eat up ribā (usury).' The fāsiq is the morally unreliable person whose testimony demands verification, classed with those who reject signs and stray from obedience.

key_nominals.meaning: deviant, disobedient one—verify news from a fasiq (49:6)

quranic_analysis.theme: Verify fasiq news
quranic_analysis.detail: In ja'akum fasiqun bi-naba'in fa-tabayyanu—due diligence before acting on news.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *psq = 'to split, go out → be immoral'. Fasaqa = to depart from obedience, be immoral. Fisq = immorality, transgression. 'Those who are immoral (fāsiqūn) among you' — the Quranic categorization of moral deviance.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: People, mankind. 241x. Nas=people, humanity. Al-nas (definite) appears 241x—one of the most frequent Quranic words. 114:1: Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind (rabbi al-nas). 4:1: O mankind (ya ayyuha al-nas), fear your Lord. From root meaning to be sociable, to move, to sway.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ن-و-س appears 241x in the noun nās (people, mankind), one of the most frequent Quranic words and the universal collective address of revelation. 4:1 opens: 'O mankind (yā ayyuhā al-nās), fear your Lord who created you from one soul and made from it its mate'; 114:1–3 frames the final sūrah: 'say: I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind (rabbi al-nās), the King of mankind (maliki al-nās), the God of mankind (ilāhi al-nās)'; 49:13 affirms 'We made you peoples and tribes (shu'ūban wa qabā'il) that you may know one another.' Nās is the collective humanity addressed by every prophet—the species summoned to single worship.

quranic_analysis.theme: O mankind address
quranic_analysis.detail: Ya ayyuha al-nas—the universal address to all humanity.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *nš = 'mankind'. Arabic nās (from *ʾunās) is the generic term for humanity in the Quran. Insān (from the same root) is the individual human. The nās are the collective addressees of prophetic messages — 'O mankind! (yā ayyuhā al-nās)'. The root is possibly connected to nasiya = to forget (humans as the forgetting species).

hadith_evidence.ar: تَدَبَّرُوا الْقُرْآنَ فَإِنَّهُ حُجَّةٌ لَكُمْ أَوْ عَلَيْكُمْ
hadith_evidence.en: Reflect upon the Quran, for it is either a proof for you or against you.
hadith_evidence.source: Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim via ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb

meaning.en_short: To spread, disperse, scatter, broadcast; to proclaim widely
meaning.en: The root bāʾ-thāʾ-thāʾ denotes scattering, dispersing, and spreading abroad. In the Quran, the Form I verb baththa means 'to spread, scatter, disperse' — used of creatures scattered over the earth, of grain broadcast over fields, and of news propagated. The noun bathth can also mean grief or distress — as if one's sorrows are scattered and only God can contain them.
meaning.ar: التَّفْرِيقُ وَالنَّشْرُ وَالْبَثُّ — تَفَرُّقُ الشَّيْءِ فِي الْأَرْضِ
meaning.en_detailed: Triliteral Arabic geminate root bāʾ-thāʾ-thāʾ (ب-ث-ث), 9 Quranic occurrences, denoting scattering, dispersing, and spreading abroad — both the act of active dispersion and, in extended usage, the scattered state of grief or distress. The Form I verb baththa (to scatter/disperse) appears 6 times; the noun bathth (scattering, also grief) 12 times; the Form VII inbaththa (to become scattered) once, in 101:4 'like scattered moths (ka-l-farāshi al-mabthūth).' Key verses include 2:164 'and He scattered (wa-baththa) therein of every creature,' a foundational theological statement on divine populating of the earth; 12:86 'he complains (baththa) of grief to God,' describing Yaʿqūb's emotion; 30:19 'He brings forth the living from the dead and scatters (yubathththu) the dead from the living,' pairing divine scattering with its converse gathering.
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To spread, disperse, scatter, broadcast; to proclaim widely
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ب ث ث — 9 مرة — To spread

etymology.semantic_evolution: Proto-Semitic 'scatter/disperse' preserved in Arabic baththa with the specific nuance of active, intentional scattering.

usage_patterns: Scattering of creatures and emotions

lexicographical_sources: Ibn Faris: al-bathth is tafrīq al-shayʾ
theological_dimensions: Bathth as divine action: God alone scatters and gathers creation

hadith_evidence.ar: اهْدِنَا الصِّرَاطَ الْمُسْتَقِيمَ
hadith_evidence.en: Guide us to the straight path.

meaning.en_short: Miserliness, stinginess, avarice; to withhold grudgingly
meaning.en: The root bāʾ-khāʾ-lām denotes stinginess and miserliness. In the Quran, bukhl is consistently condemned, especially when what is withheld is from God (zakāt, charity). The verb bakhila means 'he was miserly'. Associated with nifāq (hypocrisy), as hypocrites are described as stingy with their wealth for God's cause.
meaning.ar: ضِدُّ الْجُودِ وَالْكَرَمِ — مَنْعُ الْمَالِ مَعَ الْقُدْرَةِ
meaning.en_detailed: Triliteral Arabic root bāʾ-khāʾ-lām (ب-خ-ل), 12 Quranic occurrences, denoting miserliness, stinginess, and grudging withholding — the archetypal Arabic term for avarice, the opposite of jūd (generosity) and sakhāʾ (munificence). The Form I verb bakhila (to be miserly) appears 7 times; the noun bukhl (miserliness) 5 times. Key verses include 47:38 'and whoever withholds (wa-man yabkhal), he only withholds from himself — God is the Rich and you are the poor,' locating bukhl as self-defeating against God's self-sufficiency; 4:37 condemning those who are themselves miserly AND enjoin miserliness on others (compounding sin); al-Rāghib defines bukhl as 'withholding what should be given,' linking the concept to violations of zakāt and to the moral failing of the munāfiqūn.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ب خ ل — 12 مرة — Miserliness

etymology.semantic_evolution: Arabic bukhl is the archetypal word for miserliness across classical Arabic. Connects emotional withholding with the concrete act of keeping wealth.

derived_forms.key_verse: 47:38 وَمَن يَبۡخَلۡ فَإِنَّمَا يَبۡخَلُ عَن نَّفۡسِهِۦ

usage_patterns: Bukhl as moral failing linked to hypocrisy

lexicographical_sources: Raghib: bukhl is withholding what should be given
theological_dimensions: Bukhl as antithesis of ṣadaqa and ʾīthār; God as Al-Ghanī vs human stinginess
hadith_evidence: 'Beware of bukhl, for it destroyed those before you'

meaning.en: Harvest. 2x. Jana=pick. 55:54: fruits near, easy to reach.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ج-ن-ي appears 2x in the verb janā (to harvest, pick fruit). 55:54 celebrates Paradise: 'and the fruits of both gardens are near (dānin), easy to reach (qanīṭin)'; the verb describes the effortless plucking of eternal harvest—fruit that bends toward the hand without stretch of arm. 6:141 enjoins the believer against wastefulness: 'and do not waste (lā tusrif) by extravagance'. The root marks the agricultural reward of patient cultivation—metaphorically transferred to the eschatological picking of Paradise-fruits whose ease stands in contrast to the labor of this world's tillage. The rare occurrence concentrates the root in the sensory abundance of Sūrat al-Raḥmān.

quranic_analysis.theme: Paradise fruits
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa jana al-jannatayni danin—fruits of both gardens near.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en: Nullified, worthless. 16x. Habita=deeds become worthless/nulled. 2:217: whoever dies as disbeliever—their deeds are worthless (habitat a'maluhum). 3:22: their deeds nullified in this world and the Hereafter. The root denotes the theological erasure of deeds through disbelief.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ح-ب-ط appears 16x in the verb ḥabiṭa, whose theological force is the voiding and nullification of deeds through disbelief or apostasy. 2:217 establishes the principle: 'whoever turns back from his religion and dies as a disbeliever—their deeds are worthless (ḥabiṭat a'māluhum) in this world and the Hereafter'; 3:22 reiterates: 'those who disbelieve—their deeds are nullified (ḥabiṭat a'māluhum) and they will be dwellers of the Fire'; 6:88 contrasts: 'We will not cause to be lost (lā nuḍī'u) the reward of those who do good'; 9:69 declares the munāfiqūn's deeds 'like a mirage (sarāb).' The root marks the annihilation of moral capital at the moment of faith's collapse.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر حَبِطَ — 16 مرة — void, nullified, worthless

quranic_analysis.theme: Deeds nullified
quranic_analysis.detail: Habitat a'maluhum—their deeds become worthless through kufr.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: To precede; ancient; foot. 48x. Qaddama II=send ahead (of deeds). Qadam=foot. Qadim=ancient, prior. 2:110: what you send ahead (tuqaddimu) for yourselves. The root links temporal priority, eschatological preparation, and physical footing.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ق-د-م appears 48x, its semantic field spanning precedence, sending-forward, and physical footing. Qaddama (II) = to send ahead; qadam = foot; qadīm = ancient, prior. 2:110 establishes the eschatological principle: 'whatever you send ahead (tuqaddimū) for your souls of good, you will find it with Allah'; 3:147 urges 'racing in good works (sābiqū ilā al-khayrāt)'; 14:24 affirms 'good word (kalimah ṭayyibah) is like a good tree, firm-rooted (rāsikh)'; 2:250 records David's prayer 'make firm our feet (thabbit aqdamnā)'; 17:13 compares 'each person's record (kitāb) hung about his neck.' The root unites temporal priority, eschatological preparation, and physical stability—footing as destiny.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر قَدِمَ — 48 مرة — precede; ancient; foot

quranic_analysis.theme: Sending ahead for Hereafter
quranic_analysis.detail: Ma tuqaddimu li-anfusikum—what you send ahead for your souls.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en_short: To create ex nihilo; to be innocent, absolved, vindicated
meaning.en: The root bāʾ-rāʾ-hamza has two primary Quranic senses: (1) to create, bring into existence from nothing (baraʾa) — used exclusively for divine creation, and (2) to be innocent, free from guilt, absolved (barāʾa). The two senses are connected: God creates by bringing something forth 'free' from prior matter, and exoneration makes one 'free' from accusation. The noun barāʾa (Surah 9 is called Sūrat al-Barāʾa) means a declaration of disavowal or absolution.
meaning.ar: الْخَلْقُ مِنَ الْعَدَمِ، وَالتَّبْرِئَةُ مِنَ الذَّنْبِ، وَالْإِعْلَانُ بِالْبَرَاءَةِ
meaning.en_detailed: Triliteral Arabic root bāʾ-rāʾ-hamza (ب-ر-أ), 31 Quranic occurrences, with two principal semantic fields: (1) to create, bring into existence ex nihilo (baraʾa) — used exclusively of divine creation, parallel to Hebrew bārāʾ in Genesis 1:1 — and (2) to be innocent, free from guilt, absolved (barīʾ, barāʾa). The noun barāʾa (declaration of immunity/innocence) appears 3 times, including at the head of Quran 9:1 'barāʾa min Allāh wa-rasūlihi' (a declaration of immunity from God and His Messenger) — hence Sūrat al-Barāʾa (also al-Tawba). The divine name al-Bāriʾ (the Creator) appears 3 times, most fully in 59:24 alongside al-Khāliq (Creator) and al-Muṣawwir (Fashioner); Form II barraʾa (to declare innocent) appears 7 times, including 24:26 'God declared her innocent (barraʾahā Allāh) of what they said,' of Maryam.
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To create ex nihilo; to be innocent, absolved, vindicated
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ب ر أ — 31 مرة — To create ex nihilo

etymology.proto_semitic: *baraʾ- (to create, shape; to be clear, free)
etymology.semantic_evolution: Proto-Semitic *baraʾ- 'to create/shape' gave Hebrew bārāʾ — the standard Biblical verb for divine creation (Genesis 1:1). Arabic preserved both the creation sense and developed the separate sense of 'innocence/freedom'.

derived_forms.meaning: to be innocent, free from, absolved

usage_patterns: Divine creation (ex nihilo) distinguished from khalaqa (creation with measure)
Legal absolution from contractual obligation

lexicographical_sources: Ibn Faris: barāʾ includes khalq and tabriʾa; Raghib links both to 'freeing from deficiency'
theological_dimensions: Al-Bāriʾ as divine name: creates without precedent or model; distinct from Al-Khāliq (who proportions) and Al-Muṣawwir (who gives form)
hadith_evidence: Barāʾa in Sūrat al-Tawba as the declaration of disavowal — abrogation of treaties

meaning.en: To strengthen, support. 11x. Ayyada II=strengthen, support. 2:87: We gave Jesus clear proofs and strengthened him (ayyadnahu) with the Holy Spirit. 58:22: those—He has strengthened them (ayyadahum) with a spirit from Him.
meaning.en_detailed: Root أ-ي-د appears 11x in the verb ayyada (II: to strengthen, support, confirm). 2:87 records of Moses: 'We gave Moses clear proofs (al-bayyināt) and strengthened him (ayyadnāhu) with the Holy Spirit (rūḥ al-qudus)'; 2:253 extends the same to Jesus: 'We gave him clear signs and strengthened him (ayyadnāhu) with the Holy Spirit'; 5:110 names the disciples: 'when I strengthened (ayyaytukum) the disciples'; 58:22 promises the believers: 'those whom Allah has strengthened (ayyadahum) with a spirit from Him'; 41:30 affirms 'those who said: our Lord is Allah—then stood firm (istaqāmū)—the angels will descend upon them.' Ayyada marks divine reinforcement of prophetic mission and steadfast faith.

quranic_analysis.theme: Strengthened by Holy Spirit
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa ayyadnahu bi-ruhi al-qudus—confirmed with the Holy Spirit.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: Blame. Lamama=to blame. 14:22: so do not blame me (la talumuni) but blame yourselves. The root of self-recrimination.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ل-ي-م appears 14x, governing the Quranic vocabulary of blame and self-reproach. Lāma = to blame; al-lawwāmah = the self-blaming soul. 14:22 records the conversation of Hell's residents with their chiefs: 'do not blame me (lā talūmūnī) but blame yourselves (wa lumū anfusakum)—why do you call upon me for help when you have disbelieved?'; 75:2 swears 'by the self-blaming soul (al-nafs al-lawwāmah)'; 89:22 returns the soul 'repenting (al-nafs al-lawwāma)'; 24:6 records the lām curse formula in the law of qadhf. The root centers moral self-reproach as a sign of conscience yet alive—the lawwāmah stands between the ammārah and the muṭmaʾinnah.

quranic_analysis.theme: Self-blame
quranic_analysis.detail: Fa-la talumuni wa lumu anfusakum—blame not me but yourselves.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en_short: Blessing, abundance, divine favor; firmness, stability
meaning.en: The root bāʾ-rāʾ-kāf denotes blessing (baraka), abundance, and divine favor that increases and endures. Baraka is the immanent, enduring goodness bestowed by God — not merely material blessing but a spiritual increase that multiplies and persists. Also used for the act of kneeling (baraka al-baʿīr — the camel knelt), perhaps reflecting the steadfastness of blessing. The Qur'anic usage focuses on divine blessing (bāraka, tabāraka) and the blessed status of people, places, and objects.
meaning.ar: النَّمَاءُ وَالزِّيَادَةُ وَالدَّوَامُ — الْخَيْرُ الْإِلٰهِيُّ الثَّابِتُ
meaning.en_detailed: Triliteral Arabic root bāʾ-rāʾ-kāf (ب-ر-ك), 32 Quranic occurrences, denoting blessing (baraka), abundance, and enduring divine favor that multiplies and persists — connected etymologically to the kneeling of a camel at a watering place (a sign of settled abundance). The Form III bāraka (to bless) appears 9 times; the Form VI tabāraka (to be blessed, exalted) appears 9 times exclusively of God; the noun baraka (blessing) 3 times; the active participle mubārak (blessed) 7 times. Key verses include 67:1 'tabāraka alladhī bi-yadihi al-mulk' — 'Blessed (tabāraka) is He in whose hand is dominion,' a foundational theological statement reserving ultimate blessing exclusively to God; 17:1 'the blessed (mubārak) mosque' (al-Masjid al-Aqṣā); 7:137 'and We blessed (bāraknā) therein' of the land made holy. Al-Rāghib defines baraka as thubūt al-khayr al-ilāhī (the establishment of divine goodness).
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ب ر ك — 32 مرة — Blessing

etymology.semantic_evolution: Proto-Semitic 'to kneel' (a camel kneeling at a water source = abundance) gave the abstract sense of 'blessing/abundance'. Hebrew bārāḵ is the standard Biblical verb for blessing (e.g., the priestly blessing). Arabic baraka is blessing that endures and multiplies.

derived_forms.meaning: to be blessed, exalted, glorified (exclusively of God)

usage_patterns: Baraka as a divine attribute: only God is inherently blessed and the source of all blessing
Sacred geography: mubārak places carry enduring divine favor

lexicographical_sources: Raghib: baraka is thubūt al-khayr al-ilāhī (the stability of divine goodness); Ibn Faris notes both uprightness and blessing
theological_dimensions: Tabāraka as a theologically exclusive term — only God is tabāraka; creation receives baraka from Him
hadith_evidence: Prophet Muhammad's prayer for baraka in food, time, and community; 'O Allah, bless us in our Shaʿbān and Ramaḍān'

meaning.en: Oath. 3x. Qasam=oath. 56:75: I swear by the positions of the stars.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ق-س-م appears 33x, its semantic field spanning division (taqsim) and swearing (qasam). The Meccan sūras in particular open with divine oaths structured by this root. 56:75 declares 'I swear (uqsimu) by the positions of the stars (mawāqi'i al-nujūm)—it is indeed a tremendous oath (la-qasamun)'; 75:1–2 combines two oaths: 'by the Day of Resurrection and the self-blaming soul'; 89:3 adds 'by the even and the odd (al-witr wa al-shaf')'; 70:40 names 'the Lord of the easts (rabb al-mashāriqi) and the wests'; 53:1 swears 'by the star when it descends.' The divine qasam grounds creation as oath-worthy testimony to its Maker.

quranic_analysis.theme: Divine oaths
quranic_analysis.detail: Fa-la uqsimu bi-mawaqi'i al-nujumi—I swear by star positions.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: To pay, deliver. 6x. Adda II=pay, render. 2:283: let him who is trusted fulfill (yu'addi) his trust. 3:75: if entrusted with a qintar he will return it (yu'addihi). Amanah=trust.
meaning.en_detailed: Root أ-د-ي appears 6x in the verb addā (II: to pay, deliver, render). 2:283 commands: 'let him who is entrusted (u'tumina) fulfill (fa-l-yu'addī) his trust (amānatahu)'; 3:75 notes the surprising case of a People of the Book entrusted with a qinṭār of gold who 'will return it (yu'addīhi)'—yet expected to defraud; 4:58 establishes the universal rule: 'Allah commands you to render (tu'addū) trusts to their owners'; 4:5 commands 'give (wa ātū) the feeble-minded their property'; 13:22 affirms 'those who are patient and seek the face of their Lord (wajhi rabbihim).' Adā' is faithful delivery, the opposite of betrayal, and the test of trustworthiness in the moral economy.

quranic_analysis.theme: Fulfilling trusts
quranic_analysis.detail: Fa-l-yu'addi alladhi u'tumina amanatahu—let the entrusted fulfill his trust.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en: Evening. 1x. Masa'=evening. 40:46: exposed to Fire morning and evening (ghuduwwan wa ashiyyan).
meaning.en_detailed: مَسَى (م س و), a root appearing 1 times in the Quran, encodes the notion of Evening (masa') across its various verbal and nominal forms. In 40:46 the disbelievers of Pharaoh's people are described as being exposed to the Fire ‘morning and evening’ (ghuduwwan wa-ashiyyan), framing eternity as an endless cycle of temporal experience in which each dawn and dusk is recapitulated in torment. The verbal noun مساء thus marks the liminal transition from day to night, paired with غدو (morning) to articulate the diurnal rhythm of eschatological punishment. Classical lexicons distinguish مساء from عشاء (evening-twilight proper), with the former covering the broader late-afternoon to nightfall span.

quranic_analysis.theme: Morning and evening
quranic_analysis.detail: Al-naru yu'radu alayha ghuduwwan wa ashiyyan—Fire exposed morning and evening.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en_short: To spread, expand, extend; to make ample, spacious; to be open-handed
meaning.en: The root bāʾ-sīn-ṭāʾ denotes spreading, extending, and expanding — both physically (laying something flat, unfolding) and metaphorically (generosity, opening one's hand in giving). In the Quran, it describes God 'spreading' the earth (basṭ), stretching out one's hands in supplication or in threat, and God 'expanding' or 'constricting' provision (yabsuṭu al-rizq). The passive participle mabsūṭ means 'spread out, extended, open'.
meaning.ar: نَشْرُ الشَّيْءِ وَمَدُّهُ وَتَوْسِعَتُهُ — ضِدُّ الْقَبْضِ
meaning.en_detailed: Triliteral Arabic root bāʾ-sīn-ṭāʾ (ب-س-ط), 25 Quranic occurrences, denoting spreading, extending, and expanding — both literally (laying flat, unfolding) and metaphorically (extending provision, stretching the hand). The Form I verb basaṭa (to spread/extend) appears 11 times; the Form IV ʾabsaṭa (to stretch out) 2 times; the noun basṭa (ampleness, abundance) 3 times. Key verses include 13:26 'God extends (yabsuṭu) provision for whom He wills and restricts (yaqḍiru),' the foundational statement of divine economic sovereignty pairing basṭ with qabḍ (constriction); 5:28 'if you stretch out (basṭa) your hand to kill me, I will not stretch out mine,' Qābīl's refusal of violence against his brother Hābīl; al-Bayḍāwī glosses basṭ al-yad (stretching the hand) as gestures of supplication, threat, or generosity.
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To spread, expand, extend; to make ample, spacious; to be open
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ب س ط — 25 مرة — To spread

etymology.semantic_evolution: Proto-Semitic 'spread/extend' gave Arabic basṭ with specific Quranic applications: divine expansion of provision, stretching of hands, and the spreading out of the earth.

derived_forms.key_verse: 13:26 ٱللَّهُ يَبۡسُطُ ٱلرِّزۡقَ — God expands provision

derived_forms.meaning: to be spread out, become extended

usage_patterns: Basṭ al-rizq: divine expansion of provision
Basṭ al-yad: hand gestures — supplication, threat, generosity

lexicographical_sources: Ibn Faris: al-basṭ is nashr al-shayʾ wa-madduhu; opposite of qabḍ
theological_dimensions: God's active role in economic distribution: He 'spreads out' provision — basṭ is a divine action of grace
hadith_evidence: The Prophet was described as absaṭ al-nās kaffan — the most generous of people

meaning.en: Bury alive. 4x. Wa'ada=bury alive. 81:8: the buried girl (al-maw'udatu) asked for what sin she was killed.
meaning.en_detailed: The root و-أ-د (w-ʾ-d), attested once in the Quran, denotes the pre-Islamic Arabian practice of burying newborn girls alive (وأد waʿd), positioned by revelation among the supreme moral abominations. In 81:8, the apocalyptic interrogative is posed: ‘when the buried girl (الموؤودة al-mawʿūdah) is asked for what sin she was killed’—a powerful inversion that puts the society which executed the victim on trial rather than the infant. The root’s semantic field is tightly circumscribed to infanticide, with the passive participle موؤودة designating the buried child, almost exclusively female. Quranic rhetoric thus transforms waʿd from a tribal norm into an eschatological indictment, where the voiceless victim herself becomes the accuser on the Day of Judgment.

quranic_analysis.theme: Infanticide abolished
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa idha al-maw'udatu su'ilat—buried girl asked.
