hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en: To create, originate; nature. 20x. Fatara=create, split. Fitrah=natural disposition. 30:30: direct your face to the religion, upright—the fitrah of Allah upon which He created (fatara) mankind. No change in Allah's creation (la tabdila li-khalqi Allah). The root denotes primordial creation and innate human disposition.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ف ط ر (فَطَرَ), attested 20 times in the Quran, derives its core meaning of To create (fatara); nature (fitrah) from Proto-Semitic sources. The locus classicus is 30:30, which directs the believer toward the ‘fitrah of Allah upon which He created mankind (fatara al-nāsa ʻalayhā)—there is no altering Allah’s creation,’ where fitrah denotes the primordial constitution of human nature oriented toward tawḥīd. The intensive verb faṭara applies both to the creation of the heavens and earth (6:79, ‘the One who originated the heavens’) and to the disposition of the human soul. The abstract noun Fāṭir (الفاطر, The Originator) appears six times as a divine name (e.g., 39:46).

quranic_analysis.theme: Fitrah of Allah
quranic_analysis.detail: Fitrata Allahi allati fatara al-nasa alayha—the primordial disposition upon which God created humanity.

cognates.hebrew: פָּטַר (pāṭar) — to separate, open; firstborn (peṭer reḥem)

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *pṭr = 'to split, cleave → to create (by splitting)'. The creative act is conceptualized as a splitting/bringing-forth. The Quranic fiṭrah (30:30) is the primordial human nature created by God — the innate disposition toward recognizing divine truth. The root bridges creation (faṭara) and the Day of Judgment (infaṭarat al-samāʾ).

hadith_evidence.ar: الْمُؤْمِنُ يَأْكُلُ فِي مِعًى وَاحِدٍ وَالْكَافِرُ يَأْكُلُ فِي سَبْعَةِ أَمْعَاءٍ
hadith_evidence.en: The believer eats in one intestine and the disbeliever eats in seven intestines.

meaning.en_short: Merchandise, goods, capital; a piece, portion; to cut
meaning.en: The root bāʾ-ḍād-ʿayn originally means 'to cut' — from which developed the commercial sense of 'merchandise' (biḍāʿa), as goods are 'cut' or portioned out for trade. In the Quran, biḍāʿa appears in the Yūsuf narrative, where the brothers' returned merchandise triggers Yūsuf's plan. The root also gives Arabic 'baḍʿa' meaning a piece or cut of flesh (baḍʿa min al-laḥm).
meaning.ar: قَطْعُ الشَّيْءِ، وَتَجْزِئَتُهُ — وَالْبِضَاعَةُ لِلتِّجَارَةِ
meaning.en_detailed: The triconsonantal root ب ض ع (ب ض ع) — 7 Quranic occurrences — fundamentally expresses Merchandise, goods, capital; a piece, portion; to cut. Key Quranic occurrences include 12:62. The Proto-Semitic antecedent *baḍaʿ- (to cut, divide, portion) underlies this root, with cognates attested in related Semitic languages. The root yields derived forms including I, each extending the core meaning into specific semantic domains.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ب ض ع — 7 مرة — Merchandise

etymology.semantic_evolution: From 'cutting/portioning' to 'goods/trade items' — the semantic bridge is merchandise as a cut or allotted portion.

key_nominals.meaning: a piece, portion; piece of flesh

usage_patterns: Commercial goods in the Yūsuf narrative

lexicographical_sources: Ibn Faris: al-baḍʿ is al-qaṭʿ

hadith_evidence.ar: ب ض ع — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 7 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root bDE (ب ض ع) appears 7 times in the Quran, including 12:62.

meaning.en: Grave. 8x. Qabr=grave. 80:21: then He causes him to die and buries him (fa-aqbarahu). 102:2: until you visit the graves (al-maqabir). 9:84: do not pray over any of them who dies nor stand at his grave (qabrihi).
meaning.en_detailed: The root ق-ب-ر (q-b-r), attested eight times in the Quran, centers on the grave (قبر qabr) as the site of burial and the threshold of eschatological reckoning. The most evocative occurrence is 80:21, where God ‘caused him to die and buried him (fa-aqbarahu)’—a striking reflexive construction in which the act of burial is attributed directly to the Divine, sanctifying interment as a divine function. 102:2 employs the plural al-maqābir in ‘until you visit the graves,’ framing Sūrah al-Takāthur as a meditation on mortality: human competition for worldly gain is absurd against the inevitable descent into the grave. 9:84 forbids the Prophet from standing at the grave (qabrihi) of a hypocrite, restricting funerary honor to believers. The root thus joins physical interment to its spiritual consequences.

quranic_analysis.theme: Visiting graves
quranic_analysis.detail: Hatta zurtum al-maqabir—until you visit the graves. Reminder of mortality.

hadith_evidence.ar: الْقَبْرُ أَوَّلُ مَنَازِلِ الْآخِرَةِ
hadith_evidence.en: The grave is the first stage of the Hereafter.

meaning.en: To insult. 11x. Sabba=insult. 6:108: do not insult (la tasubbu) those they invoke besides Allah. The root denotes verbal abuse.
meaning.en_detailed: The root س-ب-ب (s-b-b), attested eleven times in the Quran, denotes verbal abuse, insult, or revile (سبّ sabb)—aggressive speech directed against sacred persons or objects. The most directive occurrence is 6:108, ‘do not insult (lā tasubbū) those they invoke besides Allah, lest they insult Allah out of enmity without knowledge,’ which establishes a principle of reciprocal restraint in religious polemic. Classical exegesis links this verse to the Prophet’s exchange with the Meccan polytheists, where his followers’ cursing of pagan deities provoked reciprocal cursing of Islamic figures. The root’s semantic core is the verbal violation of sacred boundaries, governed by the principle that protection of speech must extend even to the sacred objects of opponents.

quranic_analysis.theme: Do not insult
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa la tasubbu alladhina yad'una min duni Allah—insult not their gods.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: To return, repel. 59x. Radda=return, repel. 2:217: they will not cease fighting you until they turn you back (yaruddukum) from your religion. 3:149: if you obey the disbelievers, they will turn you back (yaruddukum) on your heels. The root denotes reversal of direction.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ر-د-د (r-d-d), among the most frequent in the Quran with approximately 59 occurrences, expresses reversal, return, or repulsion—the dynamic of pushing back or sending back. Form I radda carries the primary sense, visible in 2:217 where opponents ‘will not cease fighting you until they turn you back (yaruddūkum) from your religion,’ and in 3:149 ‘if you obey the disbelievers, they will turn you back (yaruddūnakum) on your heels,’ both depicting apostasy as the goal of religious persecution. Form VIII irtadda specializes in apostasy—turning back from faith after belief. The semantic field encompasses physical return, rebuttal, reversal of fortune, and the unavailing wish to return to the world on Judgment Day (6:27). As the conceptual opposite of siyar (forward progress), radd encodes the Quranic anthropology of spiritual regression.

quranic_analysis.theme: Trying to turn believers
quranic_analysis.detail: La yazaluna yuqatilunakum hatta yaruddukum an dinikum—fighting until they turn you from faith.

derived_forms.meaning: to return, send back, repel, reject
to go back and forth, hesitate

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *rdd = 'to return, send back, repel'. Radda = to return, repel. Tardīd = repetition. Tardaddud = hesitation (going back and forth). 'They will wish to return (yaruddūna) to the world' — the impossible wish on Judgment Day.

key_nominals.m: apostate — one who turns back from faith

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: Refuge. 3x. 9:118: no refuge (malja') from Allah except to Him.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ل-ج-أ (l-j-ʾ), attested three times in the Quran, denotes taking refuge or seeking asylum (لجأ lajaʾa, noun maljaʾ). The Quranic usage centers on the doctrine that ultimate refuge belongs exclusively to God. In 9:118, ‘there is no refuge from Allah except to Him’ (wa-mā lahum min Allāhi min maljaʾin), the verse establishes that every earthly shelter ultimately fails before divine decree. Classical exegetes connect this root to the cognate sense of crowding together (iltajaʾa), suggesting refuge as a kind of pressing-in toward safety. The semantic field is narrow but theologically weighted, with maljaʾ operating as a metonym for any false security against divine reckoning.

quranic_analysis.theme: No refuge but Allah
quranic_analysis.detail: La malja'a min Allah illa ilayhi—no refuge except to Him.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en: Despair. 13x. Ya'isa=despair. 12:87: do not despair (la tay'asu) of Allah's mercy—Jacob to his sons. 2:282: debt contract—do not be weary (tas'amu). The root denotes loss of hope.
meaning.en_detailed: Occurring 13 times in the Quranic text, the root ي أ س (يَئِسَ) conveys the essential concept of Despair, hopelessness. The verse 12:87 captures the prohibition at its most poignant: Jacob consoles his sons over Yūsuf, ‘do not despair of Allah’s mercy (lā tayʿsū min rawḥi Allāh)—none despairs of Allah’s mercy except the disbelieving people,’ linking despair to a failure of faith rather than to a psychological state alone. The same root is deployed physiologically in 2:282 (tasʾamū, ‘do not be weary’). The Quranic teaching inverts the natural inference: human despair is taken as evidence of kufr, while hope in divine mercy is the mark of īmān. The root thus carries a normative theological valence—despair is not only sadness but a doctrinal misstep.

quranic_analysis.theme: Never despair of Allah
quranic_analysis.detail: La tay'asu min rawhi Allah—never despair of Allah's mercy.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: Despair. 6x. Qanata=despair. 39:53: do not despair (la taqnatu) of Allah's mercy. 15:55: do not be of the despairing (al-qanitin)—angels to Abraham. More intense than ya'isa—complete hopelessness.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ق-ن-ط (q-n-ṭ), attested six times in the Quran, denotes a more absolute, settled despair (qanaṭa) than yaʿisa—the loss of all hope of mercy. 39:53 issues the central prohibition: ‘do not despair of Allah’s mercy (lā taqnaṭū)—for indeed Allah forgives all sins,’ declaring God’s mercy as categorically broader than human transgression. According to traditional reports, this verse arose when certain Companions despaired over grave sins committed before Islam, prompting this categorical reassurance. 15:55 addresses Abraham with the same prohibition: ‘do not be of the despairing (al-qāniṭīn),’ confirming the Prophet’s lineage of hope against impossible odds. Classical Arabic lexica (Ibn Fāris, Rāghib) distinguish qanaṭa as a deliberate hopelessness after active search, whereas yaʿisa marks the spontaneous loss of expectation.

quranic_analysis.theme: Despair prohibited
quranic_analysis.detail: La taqnatu min rahmati Allah—do not despair of Allah's mercy, for He forgives all sins.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en: To heal. 6x. Shafa=heal, cure. Shifa'=healing. 26:80: when I am ill, He heals me (yashfin). 10:57: a healing (shifa') for what is in the breasts. The Quran as spiritual healing.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ش-ف-ي (sh-f-y), occurring six times in the Quran, denotes healing, cure, or restoration to wholeness (shafā, noun shifāʾ). 26:80, in Abraham’s prayer, offers the paradigm: ‘when I fall ill, He heals me (wa-idhā maridtu fa-huwa yashfīn),’ establishing divine agency as the singular source of healing. 10:57 expands the concept to spiritual healing: ‘there has come to you from Allah a healing (shifāʾun) and a mercy,’ identifying the Quran itself as therapy for ‘what is in the breasts’ (mā fī al-ṣudūr)—doubts, anxieties, diseases of the heart. The same identification recurs in 17:82. Classical commentators distinguish shifāʾ from ʾāfiyah (general well-being), with the former implying cure of an existing condition rather than mere preservation of health.

quranic_analysis.theme: Divine healing
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa idha maridtu fa-huwa yashfin—when I fall ill, He heals me. Quran as shifa'.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en: Illness, disease. 24x. Marid=sick. Marad=disease. 2:10: in their hearts is a disease (maradun)—hypocrisy as spiritual illness. 9:125: those with disease in their hearts—it increases them in filth (rijsan). The root spans physical and spiritual sickness.
meaning.en_detailed: The root م-ر-ض (m-r-ḑ), appearing 24 times in the Quran, denotes illness, disease, or sickness in both physical and—more prominently—spiritual registers (mariḑa, noun maraḑ). The Quran employs the root extensively in a figurative key: 2:10 declares that in the hearts of the hypocrites ‘is a disease (maraḑun),’ treating nifāq as a pathology of conviction, a sickness that God expands (zāda-hum maraḑan). 9:125 intensifies: ‘those in whose hearts is disease—He increases them in filth (rijsan),’ identifying hypocrisy with contagion. The verb in 2:184, ‘if one is ill (mariḑa) or on a journey,’ uses the root literally for legal exemptions in fasting. This double register—physical illness permitting ritual concession versus spiritual disease as moral indictment—gives the root a privileged place in Quranic moral psychology.

quranic_analysis.theme: Disease of hearts
quranic_analysis.detail: Fi qulubihim maradun—in their hearts is a disease. Hypocrisy as spiritual pathology.

hadith_evidence.ar: مَا يُصِيبُ الْمُسْلِمَ مِنْ نَصَبٍ وَلَا وَصَبٍ إِلَّا كَفَّرَ اللَّهُ بِهِ مِنْ خَطَايَاهُ
hadith_evidence.en: No fatigue or illness afflicts a Muslim except that Allah expiates some of his sins through it.

meaning.en: Sob, sigh. 2x. 67:7: when they are thrown in, they will hear its roaring (shahiqan) as it boils. 11:106: those in Hell—for them is wailing (zafir) and sobbing (shahiq). The root describes the sounds of torment—groaning and sighing.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ش-ه-ق (sh-h-q), attested twice in the Quran, denotes the violent sob, gasp, or heaving sigh characteristic of extreme anguish (shahiqa). Both occurrences describe the auditory horrors of Hell. In 67:7, the inhabitants of the Fire ‘hear it raging (shahiqan) while it boils,’ the word onomatopoetically capturing the long drawn-out inhalation of a being in extremis. 11:106 pairs shahīq (sob) with zafīr (groan of forced exhalation) to portray the bidirectional respiratory torment of the damned: wailing as exhale, gasping as inhale. Classical lexica relate the root to the breathing of a beast unable to draw breath, making shahīq a metonym for choking torment. The pairing with zafīr in 11:106 has become the standard Arabic phrasing for the sounds of Hell, encoding eschatological terror through the rhythm of suffocation.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر شَهِقَ — 2 مرة — sob, sigh, heave

quranic_analysis.theme: Sounds of Hell
quranic_analysis.detail: Sami'u laha shahiqan—they hear its roaring. The sounds of torment.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en: To purchase, sell. 25x. Ishtara VIII=purchase. 2:16: those who purchased (ishtarawu) error for guidance. 12:20: they sold him (wa-sharawhu) for a reduced price—Yusuf. The root bridges commercial transaction and spiritual exchange.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ش-ر-ي (sh-r-y), attested about 25 times in the Quran, denotes commercial transaction—buying, selling, or bartering (sharā, ishtarā)—with the Quran extending the metaphor to spiritual exchange. The foundational occurrence is 2:16, ‘those who purchased error for guidance (ishtaraw al-ḑalālata bi-l-hudā),’ framing apostasy and misguided belief as economic transactions. 12:20 employs the literal sense: ‘they sold him (wa-sharawhu) for a reduced price—a few dirhams counted out,’ referring to Yūsuf’s brothers who traded him to the caravan. The semantic migration from commerce to spiritual cost-and-benefit places the root at the heart of Quranic moral arithmetic, where every choice is a transaction with consequences, and where true gain is measured against divine truth rather than worldly price.

quranic_analysis.theme: Trading guidance for error
quranic_analysis.detail: Ula'ika alladhina ishtarawu al-dalalata bi al-huda—they bought error with guidance.

hadith_evidence.ar: التَّاجِرُ الصَّدُوقُ الْأَمِينُ مَعَ النَّبِيِّينَ وَالصِّدِّيقِينَ وَالشُّهَدَاءِ
hadith_evidence.en: The truthful and trustworthy merchant is with the prophets, the truthful, and the martyrs.

meaning.en: To intend, aim; moderation. 6x. Qasd=intention, purpose. Qasid=moderate, balanced. 31:19: be moderate (wa-qsid) in your walk—Luqman's advice. 16:9: upon Allah is the direction (qasd) of the path.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ق-ص-د (q-ṣ-d), attested six times in the Quran, encompasses aiming, intending, and—as a derived nuance—moderation, the middle path between excess and defect (qaṣada, noun qaṣd). 31:19, in Luqmān’s advice to his son, provides the moral locus: ‘be moderate in your walk (wa-qṣid fī mashyika) and lower your voice,’ establishing qaṣd as a virtue of measured conduct. 16:9 employs the noun for divine purpose: ‘upon Allah is the direction (qaṣdu) of the path,’ indicating that the ultimate aim of the Way belongs to God alone, while humans are responsible for their own direction (hidāyah). The derived adjective qāṣid names the moderate traveler, one who walks neither too fast nor too slow. The root thus joins the ethical mean (the via media of virtue) to ontological orientation toward the Divine.

quranic_analysis.theme: Moderation
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa-qsid fi mashyika—be moderate in your walk. The middle path.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en: Gather. 6x. Hashara=gather. 59:2: first gathering (al-hashr). Day of Assembly.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ح-ش-ر (ḥ-sh-r), with approximately 43 Quranic occurrences across derived forms, denotes the gathering, assembling, or mustering of beings for divine reckoning (ḥashara, noun ḥashr). The noun al-hashr (The Gathering) names Sūrah 59 itself, where 59:2 refers to ‘the first gathering (awwala al-hashr),’ traditionally identified with the Banū Naḑīr’s expulsion from Medina. Eschatologically, the root names the mustering of all creation on the Day of Judgment (64:7 ‘Allah will gather them on the Day of Gathering’). The verb is also used for mundane gathering (16:68, bees as ‘gathered’ muḥsharūn). The semantic core—whether mustering of armies, expulsion of communities, or cosmic assembly—revolves around divine orchestration of collective movement.

quranic_analysis.theme: First gathering
quranic_analysis.detail: Awwala al-hashr—the first gathering.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: To surround, stare. 3x. 14:42: the Day when eyes will stare fixedly (shakhisatun absaru)—wide with terror. Related root sense: surrounding, encompassing.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ح-د-ق (ḥ-d-q), attested three times in the Quran, carries the semantic core of staring fixedly, the wide-eyed gaze of terror, derived etymologically from ḥadaqah (the pupil of the eye). 14:42 provides the principal occurrence: ‘the Day when the eyes will stare fixedly (tashkhaṣu al-abṣāru),’ depicting the petrified gaze of those summoned before the Divine Throne—the eye unable to blink or turn away. A secondary sense of the root involves surrounding or encircling (ḥadaqa al-shayʾa ḥawlahu), as in 39:72 ‘on thrones of gold, arranged (muḥadaqah) for them.’ The semantic range thus bridges ocular terror and spatial enclosure, the two registers sharing a common image of being held fast by what one faces.

quranic_analysis.theme: Staring in terror
quranic_analysis.detail: Yawma tashkhasu fihi al-absaru—the Day when eyes stare fixedly.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en: To betray. 16x. Khana=betray. Kha'in=traitor. 8:27: do not betray (la takhunu) Allah and the Messenger. 12:52: Allah does not guide the plot of betrayers (kayda al-kha'imin). The root denotes treachery—violation of trust.
meaning.en_detailed: The root خ-و-ن (kh-w-n), attested 16 times in the Quran, denotes treachery, betrayal of trust, or the violation of covenant (khāna, active participle khāʾin). 8:27 issues the foundational prohibition: ‘do not betray Allah and the Messenger (wa-lā takhūnū Allāha wa-l-rasūla) and do not betray your trusts (amānātikum),’ placing covenant-violation on the same axis as divine betrayal—since trust is itself a divine trust (amānah, 33:72). 12:52 frames Pharaoh’s plot as ‘the scheming of betrayers (kaydu al-khāʾinīn),’ while 4:107 closes the circle: ‘whoever betrays, Allah is aware.’ The root’s theological weight is its location at the intersection of contract and conscience—treachery is not merely an act but a corruption of one’s covenant with God.

quranic_analysis.theme: Do not betray
quranic_analysis.detail: La takhunu Allaha wa al-rasula—do not betray Allah and the Messenger.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: Provision. 2x. 2:197: best provision is taqwa.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ز-و-د (z-w-d), attested twice in the Quran, denotes provision, supply, or equipping one with what is needed for a journey (zawwada, noun zād). The defining occurrence is 2:197, in the verses regulating pilgrimage and trade during the sacred months: ‘take provision, for indeed the best provision is taqwā (wa-tazawwadū fa-inna khayra al-zādi al-taqwā),’ reframing material provisioning through ethical currency. The command is doubly poignant: pilgrimage requires literal provisions, but the Quran ranks taqwā as the only provisioning that survives death. The verb’s Form II pattern (tazawwada) denotes the reflexive action of supplying oneself. The semantic core unites physical sustenance and ethical accumulation, with taqwā alone being the zād that endures.

quranic_analysis.theme: Best provision
quranic_analysis.detail: Fa-inna khayra al-zadi al-taqwa—best provision is piety.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en_short: Belly, interior, abdomen; hidden, inward aspect
meaning.en: The root bāʾ-ṭāʾ-nūn primarily denotes the belly (baṭn) and interiority. In the Quran, it appears in anatomical contexts, metaphorical descriptions of concealment, and moral exhortations about both outward and inward righteousness. The verb baṭana means 'to be hidden, concealed'. The root develops a strong inward/outward dichotomy: ẓāhir (apparent) vs bāṭin (hidden) is a key Quranic and theological binary. Al-Bāṭin is one of the divine names — the Hidden, the Inward.
meaning.ar: خِلَافُ الظَّهْرِ — الْجَوْفُ وَالدَّاخِلُ وَالْخَفَاءُ
meaning.en_detailed: Occurring 25 times in the Quranic text, the root ب ط ن (ب ط ن) conveys the essential concept of Belly, interior, abdomen; hidden, inward aspect. Key Quranic occurrences include 57:3, 6:120, 57:3, 6:120, 57:3, 6:120, 57:3, 6:120. The Proto-Semitic antecedent *baṭn- (belly, interior) underlies this root, with cognates attested in related Semitic languages. The root yields derived forms including I, II, X, each extending the core meaning into specific semantic domains. The root carries significant theological weight in the Quranic worldview, recurring in contexts that shape Islamic doctrine and spiritual understanding.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ب ط ن — 25 مرة — Belly

etymology.semantic_evolution: Proto-Semitic 'belly' preserved across all Semitic languages. In Arabic and Hebrew, it extends to 'womb' (pregnancy 'in the belly'). Arabic also developed the abstract 'hidden/inward' sense leading to the divine name Al-Bāṭin.

derived_forms.meaning: to penetrate the interior, seek the hidden

key_nominals.meaning: hidden, inward, interior; the Hidden One (God)

usage_patterns: Ẓāhir/bāṭin dichotomy: external act vs internal state
Womb (baṭn) as site of divine creation (22:5)

lexicographical_sources: Raghib: al-bāṭin is what is hidden from the senses; Ibn Faris: al-baṭn is khilāf al-ẓahr
theological_dimensions: Al-Bāṭin as divine name: God is hidden from perception yet immanent knowledge
The moral importance of bāṭin — God knows the hidden sins and inner states
hadith_evidence: 'God does not look at your bodies or forms, but looks at your hearts' — the bāṭin over ẓāhir

meaning.en: Profit. 1x. 2:16: their trade did not profit (ma rabihat tijaratuhum).
meaning.en_detailed: The root ر-ب-ح (r-b-ḥ), attested once in the Quran, denotes profit, gain, or increase (rabiḥa, noun ribḥ). The single occurrence is 2:16, in the verse immediately following the description of those who purchased error for guidance: ‘their trade did not profit them (mā rabiḥat tijāratuhum), and they were not rightly guided,’—the absolute mā denying any profitable outcome. The juxtaposition of the commercial root (tijāra, sharā) with the profit-root creates a tight economic metaphor: trade that yields no gain is no trade at all, and guidance that produces no light is no guidance. The verse thus establishes a moral arithmetic in which worldly gain without truth is loss, and the root’s semantic field encompasses both material profit and moral failure to gain anything of value.

quranic_analysis.theme: Unprofitable trade
quranic_analysis.detail: Fa-ma rabihat tijaratuhum—their trade profited not.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en: To complete, perfect. 22x. Tamma=complete, be fulfilled. 5:3: Today I have perfected (akmaltu) your religion and completed (atmamtu) My favor. 6:115: the word of your Lord is fulfilled (tammat) in truth and justice.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ت-م-م (t-m-m), attested about 22 times in the Quran, denotes completion, perfection, and the fulfillment of a process to its appointed end (tamma, akmala, atmama). The verse 5:3 provides the most celebrated occurrence: ‘Today I have perfected your religion (akmaltu lakum dīnakum) and completed My favor upon you (wa-atmamtu ʻalaykum niʿmatī),’—the verb anchoring the doctrine that revelation is brought to its full term at the Prophet’s hands. 6:115 articulates the principle: ‘the Word of your Lord is fulfilled in truth and justice (tammat kalimatu rabbika ṣidqan wa-ʿadlan),’ expressing divine promise as a process brought to completion. The semantic field extends to the completion of months (2:185), the fulfillment of vows, and the maturation of creation.

quranic_analysis.theme: Completion of religion
quranic_analysis.detail: Al-yawma akmaltu lakum dinakum wa atmamtu alaykum ni'mati.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en_short: To raise, resurrect, send forth, dispatch; resurrection, mission
meaning.en: The root bāʾ-ʿayn-thāʾ is one of the Quran's most important eschatological roots — denoting resurrection (baʿth), the raising of the dead, and the sending of prophets. The Form I verb baʿatha means 'He sent, dispatched, raised up'. In eschatological contexts, it means 'He resurrected'. God 'sends' (baʿatha) prophets to nations and 'raises' (baʿatha) the dead on Judgment Day. The noun baʿth refers to the Resurrection itself — the great awakening from death.
meaning.ar: الْإِرْسَالُ، وَالْإِحْيَاءُ بَعْدَ الْمَوْتِ، وَالنُّشُورُ يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ
meaning.en_detailed: Occurring 67 times in the Quranic text, the root ب ع ث (ب ع ث) conveys the essential concept of To raise, resurrect, send forth, dispatch; resurrection, mission. Key Quranic occurrences include 16:36, 2:56, 16:36, 2:56, 16:36, 2:56, 16:36, 2:56. The Proto-Semitic antecedent *baʿaṯ- (to send, raise up, awaken) underlies this root, with cognates attested in related Semitic languages. The root yields derived forms including I, VII, each extending the core meaning into specific semantic domains. The root carries significant theological weight in the Quranic worldview, recurring in contexts that shape Islamic doctrine and spiritual understanding.
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To raise, resurrect, send forth, dispatch; resurrection, mission
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ب ع ث — 67 مرة — To raise

etymology.semantic_evolution: Proto-Semitic 'send/raise' — Arabic alone developed the eschatological 'resurrect' sense. The sending of prophets and raising of the dead share the core concept of bringing forth from a prior state.

derived_forms.key_verse: 16:36 وَلَقَدۡ بَعَثۡنَا فِى كُلِّ أُمَّةٍۢ رَّسُولًا

derived_forms.meaning: to be sent forth; to arise, be roused

usage_patterns: Yawm al-Baʿth — the Day of Resurrection
Baʿthat al-anbiyāʾ — the sending of prophets

lexicographical_sources: Raghib: al-baʿth is ifādat al-shayʾ ʿanhu (eliciting something from that state)
theological_dimensions: Al-Baʿth is a cornerstone of Islamic eschatology — bodily resurrection is affirmed against Meccan deniers
The conceptual link between God sending prophets (divine mission) AND God raising the dead (divine power)
hadith_evidence: The Prophet's description of baʿth: 'People will be raised (yubʿathūna) on their intentions'

meaning.en: Praise. 63x. Hamida=praise. Al-Hamid=the Praiseworthy (divine name). Al-hamdu li-Allah=all praise is due to Allah (1:2). Muhammad (the praised one). The root is the most common liturgical formula in Islam.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ح-م-د (ḥ-m-d), attested approximately 63 times in the Quran, denotes praise, commendation, and the verbal recognition of worthiness (ḥamida, noun ḥamd, active participle ḥāmid, passive maḥmūd). The locus classicus is 1:2, the second verse of al-Fātiḥah and the foundational formula of Islamic prayer: ‘all praise belongs to Allah (al-ḥamdu li-llāh), Lord of the Worlds,’ establishing praise as the proper opening of all speech with God. The same formula opens Sūras 6:1, 18:1, and 27:15. The divine name al-ḥamīd (The Praiseworthy) names God as worthy of all praise whether or not any creature praises Him. The Prophet’s name Muḥammad is the intensive passive participle, designating him as the one who is praised most abundantly.

quranic_analysis.theme: Al-hamdu li-Allah
quranic_analysis.detail: The opening of creation, Quran, and prayer—all begin with praise.

cognates.hebrew: חָמַד (ḥāmad) — to desire, covet',aramaic:'חמד (ḥmd) — to desire',geez:'ሐመደ (ḥamada) — to praise, glorify

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *ḥmd had a dual trajectory: 'to praise' (Arabic, Ge'ez) and 'to desire/covet' (Hebrew, Aramaic). This split reveals an interesting semantic bridge: what is praiseworthy is desirable. In Arabic, the meaning narrowed to active, verbal praise (ḥamd). Al-ḥamdu li-llāh ('praise belongs to Allah') opens the Quran (1:2) and is the most frequent formula of gratitude. The Prophet's name Muḥammad (intensive passive participle = 'the one who is praised abundantly') is an embodiment of this root.

theological_dimensions: Al-Ḥamdu li-llāh as the opening of existence — the Fatiha divides the world into praised (God) and praiser (creation)
Al-Ḥamīd (The Praiseworthy) — God as inherently deserving of all praise regardless of whether anyone praises Him
The Maqām Maḥmūd (Praised Station, 17:79) — the Prophet's office of universal intercession on Judgment Day

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en_short: To come suddenly, overtake unexpectedly; suddenness, surprise
meaning.en: The root bāʾ-ghayn-tāʾ denotes suddenness and unexpected occurrence — something that overtakes without warning. In the Quran, the noun baghtatan means 'suddenly, unexpectedly, all of a sudden' — used exclusively in contexts of divine punishment overtaking wrongdoers when they least expect it. The root emphasizes the element of surprise and the inability to prepare or escape.
meaning.ar: الْأَخْذُ عَلَى غَفْلَةٍ، وَالْمُفَاجَأَةُ، وَالْحُدُوثُ فَجْأَةً
meaning.en_detailed: Occurring 13 times in the Quranic text, the root ب غ ت (ب غ ت) conveys the essential concept of To come suddenly, overtake unexpectedly; suddenness, surprise. Key Quranic occurrences include 6:31, 7:95, 6:31, 7:95, 6:31, 7:95, 6:31, 7:95. The Proto-Semitic antecedent *bagt- (suddenness, surprise) underlies this root, with cognates attested in related Semitic languages. The root yields derived forms including I, each extending the core meaning into specific semantic domains. The root carries significant theological weight in the Quranic worldview, recurring in contexts that shape Islamic doctrine and spiritual understanding.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ب غ ت — 13 مرة — To come suddenly

etymology.semantic_evolution: An Arabic root without strong Semitic cognates; possibly a specialized development within Arabic for sudden overtaking.

derived_forms.meaning: to come upon suddenly, surprise, overtake

usage_patterns: Baghtatan always adverbial — describing how punishment or the Hour comes

lexicographical_sources: Ibn Faris: al-baght is al-akhdh ʿalā ghafla
theological_dimensions: The suddenness of divine punishment precludes repentance — a warning to remain in constant preparedness

hadith_evidence.ar: ب غ ت — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 13 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root bgt (ب غ ت) appears 13 times in the Quran, including 6:31.

meaning.en: Tree. 27x. Shajarah=tree—the forbidden tree in Paradise (2:35). Shajar=trees, vegetation. Last third of night when trees prostrate (55:6). The root also means dispute (tashajara)—branches intertwined in argument.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ش-ج-ر (sh-j-r), attested 27 times in the Quran, denotes tree in the literal sense (shajarah) and—as an extension—dispute, contention (tashājara), with the semantic bridge likely the entangled branches of argument. The principal scriptural occurrence is 2:35, ‘do not approach this tree (lā taqraba hādhihi al-shajarata),’ referring to the forbidden tree in the Garden whose consumption triggers Adam and Eve’s expulsion (recapped in 7:19-22). 55:6 invokes the root in a cosmic oath: ‘and the trees and what they prostrate,’ often glossed as trees bowing before God in the last third of the night. The dispute sense surfaces in 4:65 ‘if they had referred it to Allah and the Messenger, those who dispute would have known.’

quranic_analysis.theme: The forbidden tree
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa la taqraba hadhihi al-shajarah—do not approach this tree. The tree of the primordial test.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: To drown. 23x. Ghariqa=drown. 10:90: Pharaoh—when drowning overtook him (adhrakahu al-gharaq). 36:43: if We willed, We could drown them (nughriqhum). The root denotes overwhelming immersion—both physical drowning and metaphorical excess.
meaning.en_detailed: The root غ-ر-ق (gh-r-q), attested about 23 times in the Quran, denotes drowning, submersion, or being overwhelmed (ghariqa, noun gharaq). The defining occurrence is 10:90, the moment of Pharaoh’s death: ‘when drowning overtook him (ḥattā idhā adhrakahu al-gharaqu), he said: “I believe,”’—yet the verse continues, ‘now, when before you had rebelled,’ declaring his late repentance inadmissible. 36:43 shows divine sovereignty over the root: ‘if We willed, We could drown them (nughriqhum),’ the verb in Form IV designating the act of overwhelming. The semantic field bridges physical drowning, divine destruction, and the impossibility of escaping final judgment, with each occurrence reinforcing divine mastery over life’s elemental boundaries.

quranic_analysis.theme: Pharaoh's drowning
quranic_analysis.detail: Hatta idha adhrakahu al-gharaqu—when drowning overtook Pharaoh, he said: I believe.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: To join. Wasala=connect. 2:27: who sever what Allah has ordered to be joined.
meaning.en_detailed: The root و-ص-ل (w-ṣ-l), attested about 12 times in the Quran (across derived forms totaling ~40 occurrences), denotes joining, connecting, or linking (waṣala, noun ṡilah). The locus classicus is 2:27, ‘those who break the covenant of Allah after contracting it, and sever what Allah has ordered to be joined (yaqṭaʼūna mā amar Allāhu bihi an yūṣala),’—a phrase taken by classical exegesis to refer chiefly to kinship ties (ṡilat al-raḥim). 13:21 specifies the reward: ‘those who join (yaṡilūna) what Allah has commanded to be joined,’ kinship being the chief instance. Form II waṣṣala (intensive) appears in 4:69 to establish generational continuity. The root’s theological weight is its position as the antithesis of qaṭaʼ (severance), with waṣl encoding covenant-preservation as moral substance.

quranic_analysis.theme: Join what Allah joined
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa yaqta'una ma amar Allahu bihi an yusala—they sever what Allah ordered joined.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *wṣl = 'to join, connect'. Waṣala = to join, connect. Ṣilah = connection. 'Those who join (yaṣilūna) what Allah commanded to be joined' (13:21) — maintaining kinship ties and covenant. The opposite: cutting (qaṭʿ).

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en_short: Cow, cattle; to split, cleave open, rip apart
meaning.en: The root bāʾ-qāf-rāʾ primarily denotes the cow (baqara) — the largest surah is named al-Baqara (The Cow) after the story of the Israelites and the yellow cow (2:67-71). The root's verbal sense is 'to split, cleave, rip open, or disclose' — suggesting either that the cow is named for its habit of 'splitting' the earth while grazing, or that the verb derives from the image of splitting open a cow. Both senses appear in Quranic usage.
meaning.ar: شَقُّ الشَّيْءِ وَفَتْحُهُ — وَاسْمُ الْبَقَرَةِ الْمَعْرُوفَةِ
meaning.en_detailed: Occurring 9 times in the Quranic text, the root ب ق ر (ب ق ر) conveys the essential concept of Cow, cattle; to split, cleave open, rip apart. Key Quranic occurrences include 2:67-71, 6:146, 2:67-71, 6:146, 2:67-71, 6:146, 2:67-71, 6:146. The Proto-Semitic antecedent *baqar- (cattle; to split) underlies this root, with cognates attested in related Semitic languages. The root yields derived forms including I, each extending the core meaning into specific semantic domains.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ب ق ر — 9 مرة — Cow

etymology.semantic_evolution: Proto-Semitic 'cattle' — Hebrew bāqār is the standard Biblical term for cattle/herd. The 'splitting' sense appears to be an Arabic semantic development, possibly from the cow's grazing habit.

usage_patterns: The cow as a test of obedience (banū Isrāʾīl's excessive questioning)
Sūrat al-Baqara as the comprehensive surah of law and narrative

lexicographical_sources: Ibn Faris: al-baqr is shaqq al-shayʾ wa-fatḥuhu
theological_dimensions: The baqara narrative teaches the danger of excessive questioning about divine commands
Sūrat al-Baqara as the 'peak of the Quran'
hadith_evidence: 'The shayṭān flees from a house in which Sūrat al-Baqara is recited'

meaning.en: News, information; prophecy. 160x. Naba'=news, important information. Anba'a IV=inform. Nabi=prophet. Anbiya'=prophets. 78:2: about the great news (al-naba' al-azim). The root informs the title of prophet—the one given divine news.
meaning.en_detailed: Occurring 160 times in the Quranic text, the root ن ب أ (نَبَأَ) conveys the essential concept of News; to inform; prophet (nabi). The opening of Sūrat al-Nabaʾ provides the root’s defining context: ‘about what are they questioning one another? About the great news (al-nabaʾ al-ʾaẑīm)’ (78:1-2), with ‘the great news’ identified by tradition as the resurrection. The same root grounds the title nabī (prophet)—the one who receives divine news and announces it—appearing 75 times in the Quran, while the plural anbiyāʾ appears about 30 times. Form IV anbaʾa (to inform, reveal) governs much of the Quranic discourse of revelation. P-Semitic *nbʾ originally meant ‘to call out, announce,’ with Arabic narrowing it to newsworthy communication.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر نَبَأَ — 160 مرة — news; to inform; prophet (nabi)

quranic_analysis.theme: The great news
quranic_analysis.detail: Amma yatasa'alun—an al-naba'i al-azim—of what are they questioning? About the great news.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *nbʾ = 'to announce, proclaim'. In Arabic, nabī (prophet) is one who receives and transmits divine news. The Quranic nabaʾ (momentous news) is the content of prophetic communication — the 'great news' (al-nabaʾ al-ʿaẓīm, 78:2) of resurrection.

hadith_evidence.ar: تَدَبَّرُوا الْقُرْآنَ فَإِنَّهُ حُجَّةٌ لَكُمْ أَوْ عَلَيْكُمْ
hadith_evidence.en: Reflect upon the Quran, for it is either a proof for you or against you.
hadith_evidence.source: Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim via ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb

meaning.en_short: Early morning, dawn; to go/do early, first-fruits, precedence
meaning.en: The root bāʾ-kāf-rāʾ denotes early morning and the act of doing something early or first. In the Quran, bukra(tan) means 'early morning, at dawn' — paired frequently with ʿashiyyan (evening) to denote the full cycle of the day. The root emphasizes the early start, the first part of the day, and the virtue of beginning early. The related noun bākir means 'early, premature' and bikr means 'first-born, virgin' — something that has not yet been preceded.
meaning.ar: أَوَّلُ النَّهَارِ، وَالْغُدُوَّةُ، وَفِعْلُ الشَّيْءِ فِي أَوَّلِ وَقْتِهِ
meaning.en_detailed: The triconsonantal root ب ك ر (ب ك ر) — 12 Quranic occurrences — fundamentally expresses Early morning, dawn; to go/do early, first-fruits, precedence. Key Quranic occurrences include 19:11, 20:130, 19:11, 20:130, 19:11, 20:130, 19:11, 20:130. The Proto-Semitic antecedent *bakir- (early, morning; first-born) underlies this root, with cognates attested in related Semitic languages. The root yields derived forms including I, II, IV, each extending the core meaning into specific semantic domains.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ب ك ر — 12 مرة — Early morning

cognates.hebrew: בָּכַר (bāḵar) — to be early, bear first fruit; בְּכוֹר (bəḵōr) — firstborn

etymology.semantic_evolution: Proto-Semitic 'morning/first' — Hebrew bəḵōr 'firstborn' and bikkūrīm 'first-fruits' are the most famous cognates. The morning is literally 'the first'. Arabic bukra and Hebrew bōqer (morning) share this root.

derived_forms.meaning: to go early, do early in the morning
to make early, do at dawn
to come early, do in the morning

usage_patterns: Bukra + ʿashīy / aṣīl: the full diurnal cycle of worship
Bikr: something unprecedented — 'a bikr (novel) Quran'

lexicographical_sources: Ibn Faris: al-bukra is awwal al-nahār
theological_dimensions: The pairing bukra/ʿashīy structures time for worship — sunrise and sunset as twin moments of devotion
hadith_evidence: The Prophet's morning dhikr practice: Subḥān Allāh wa-bi-ḥamdihi bukratan wa-aṣīlan

meaning.en_short: To reach, attain, arrive; to deliver (a message); puberty, maturity
meaning.en: The root bāʾ-lām-ghayn carries the core meaning of 'reaching' — whether physical arrival at a destination, attaining an age (bulūgh, physical maturity), delivering a message to its recipient, or an object reaching its intended target. Balagha means 'he reached, attained, arrived'. The Form II ballagha means 'he caused to reach' = 'he delivered, conveyed (a message)'. Masdar balāgh means the delivery/proclamation of a message. Bulūgh is the attainment of puberty or maturity.
meaning.ar: الْوُصُولُ إِلَى الْغَايَةِ — الْإِدْرَاكُ، وَالتَّبْلِيغُ، وَالنُّضْجُ
meaning.en_detailed: The triconsonantal root ب ل غ (ب ل غ) — 77 Quranic occurrences — fundamentally expresses To reach, attain, arrive; to deliver (a message); puberty, maturity. Key Quranic occurrences include 5:67, 46:35, 5:67, 46:35, 5:67, 46:35, 5:67, 46:35. The Proto-Semitic antecedent *balag- (to reach, arrive at, mature) underlies this root, with cognates attested in related Semitic languages. The root yields derived forms including I, II, each extending the core meaning into specific semantic domains. The root carries significant theological weight in the Quranic worldview, recurring in contexts that shape Islamic doctrine and spiritual understanding.
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To reach, attain, arrive; to deliver
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ب ل غ — 77 مرة — To reach

etymology.semantic_evolution: Arabic root with no direct Hebrew/Aramaic cognates. The semantic core of 'reaching a target/endpoint' generated a rich family: physical arrival, developmental maturity, and communicative delivery.

derived_forms.meaning: to reach, attain, arrive at, grow to maturity
derived_forms.key_verse: 12:22 وَلَمَّا بَلَغَ أَشُدَّهُۥ — When he reached maturity

derived_forms.meaning: to deliver, convey (a message), cause to reach
derived_forms.key_verse: 5:67 يَـٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلرَّسُولُ بَلِّغۡ — O Messenger, convey!

usage_patterns: Balāgh as the prophetic duty: conveying the message without compulsion
Bulūgh al-aḥlām: attainment of puberty as legal maturity

lexicographical_sources: Raghib: al-bulūgh is al-intihāʾ ilā aqṣā al-maqṣid; Ibn Faris: balagha is al-wuṣūl ilā al-ghāya
theological_dimensions: Balāgh as the limit of prophetic responsibility (mā ʿalā al-rasūl illā al-balāgh)
Taballagha (form V): the message has been received — faith or rejection is the recipient's choice
hadith_evidence: Prophet at Ḥajjat al-Widāʿ: 'Have I conveyed (ballaghtu)?' — the assembly testifies

meaning.en: To resolve firmly. 9x. Azama=resolve. Azm=resolute will. 10:71: determine (ajmi'u) your plan—Noah's challenge. 20:115: Adam—We found no resolve (azman) in him. The root denotes unwavering determination.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ع-ز-م (ʽ-Ẓ-m), attested about nine times in the Quran, denotes firm resolve, determination, and the binding of will to a course of action (ʽazama, noun ʽazm). 10:71, in Nūḥ’s address to his people, articulates the root’s directive sense: ‘determine your plan (ajmiʼū amrakum),’—a literal injunction to consolidate will and strategy before action, repeated in 27:31 ‘I have determined (ʽazamtu) my plan.’ 20:115 offers a counter-example with devastating theological force: ‘We had covenanted with Adam before, but he forgot, and We found in him no firm resolve (fa-lam najid lahu ʽazman),’—the absence of ʽazm being read by classical exegesis as the failure to follow through when tested. The root occupies a moral-emotional register distinct from mere desire (hawā) or intention (niyyah), signifying a determination that survives distraction.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر عَزَمَ — 9 مرة — resolve firmly; incantation

quranic_analysis.theme: Firm resolve
quranic_analysis.detail: Fa-lam najid lahu azman—We found no firm resolve in Adam.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en: To enter. 126x. Dakhala=enter. Adkhala IV=cause to enter. Dakhil=interior. 2:214: do you think you will enter (tadkhulu) Paradise? The root denotes entrance—both physical and spiritual. Paradise entry is the ultimate goal.
meaning.en_detailed: The root د-خ-ل (d-kh-l), attested about 126 times in the Quran across derived forms, denotes entering, going in, or penetrating (dakhala, adkhala ‘to admit’). The Paradise-orientation of the root is paramount: 39:73 culminates in ‘enter it (udkhulūhā) in peace, secure (bi-salāmin āminīn),’ the supreme invitation to the eschatological Garden. 2:214 frames the question rhetorically: ‘do you think you will enter Paradise (tadkhulū al-jannata)?’ Form IV adkhala governs most occurrences and carries the divine active sense: God is the One who admits into Paradise (adkhalahu Allāhu al-jannata, 4:13) or into the Fire. The semantic field encompasses physical entry, spiritual entrance, legal engagement, and the final crossing into the eternal.

quranic_analysis.theme: Enter Paradise
quranic_analysis.detail: Udkhuluhu bi-salamin aminin—enter in peace and security.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *dḫl = 'to enter, go in'. Dakhala = to enter. Mudkhal = entrance. 'Enter (udkhulū) it in peace, secure' (15:46) — the greeting to the residents of Paradise.

hadith_evidence.ar: تَدَبَّرُوا الْقُرْآنَ فَإِنَّهُ حُجَّةٌ لَكُمْ أَوْ عَلَيْكُمْ
hadith_evidence.en: Reflect upon the Quran, for it is either a proof for you or against you.
hadith_evidence.source: Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim via ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb

meaning.en: Human; good news. 123x. Bashar=human being. Bashshara II=give good news. Bashir=bearer of good news. 3:47: Mary—no man (basharun) has touched me. 17:105: We sent you only as a bearer of good news (bashiran) and a warner (nadhir).
meaning.en_detailed: The triconsonantal root ب ش ر (بَشِرَ) — 123 Quranic occurrences — fundamentally expresses Human; good news; to rejoice. The human sense appears in 3:47, the angelic announcement to Mary: ‘no human has touched me (mā massa-nĮ basharun),’ confirming the unique conception. The glad-tidings sense governs the prophetic title bashīr, paired with nadhīr (warner): 17:105 ‘We sent you only as a bearer of good news and a warner (bashīran wa-nadhīran),’ defining the Prophet’s dual office. The semantic bridge may lie in the kinship of touch (skin, basher) and glad announcement. Form II bashshara governs 50 occurrences of glad tidings.

quranic_analysis.theme: Bashir and Nadhir
quranic_analysis.detail: The Prophet as bashiran wa nadhiran—bearer of glad tidings and warner.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *bšr = 'flesh → human'. Bashar = human (the 'fleshy' being). Bushrā = good news. The root unites physical humanity (flesh) and spiritual joy (glad tidings). Bashīr = bringer of good news — the Prophet's title.

hadith_evidence.ar: تَدَبَّرُوا الْقُرْآنَ فَإِنَّهُ حُجَّةٌ لَكُمْ أَوْ عَلَيْكُمْ
hadith_evidence.en: Reflect upon the Quran, for it is either a proof for you or against you.
hadith_evidence.source: Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim via ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb

meaning.en: Provision, sustenance. 123x. Razaqa=provide. Rizq=sustenance, provision. Al-Razzaq=the Provider (divine name). 2:3: those who believe in the unseen and spend from what We provided (razaqnahum). The root spans physical provision and spiritual sustenance.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ر-ز-ق (r-z-q), attested about 123 times in the Quran across derived forms, denotes provision, sustenance, and the apportionment of livelihood (razaqa, noun rizq). The divine name al-Razzāq (The Ever-Providing) appears at 51:58, emphasizing God’s continuous sustenance of all creation. 65:3 captures the radical trust in divine provision: ‘whoever relies upon Allah—He is sufficient for him; surely Allah accomplishes His purpose,’ often paired in exegesis with 2:212 ‘yet of whatever God has given you, give thereof in charity.’ The verbal noun rizq governs most occurrences and is the standard Quranic term for daily bread, including in the Fātiḥah. The root’s theological core is the doctrine that all provision is divinely measured (qadar) and reaches the creature regardless of apparent causation.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر رَزَقَ — 123 مرة — provision, sustenance; al-razzaq

quranic_analysis.theme: Divine provision
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa yarzuqhu min haythu la yahtasib—He provides from where one does not expect.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *rzq — possibly borrowed from Middle Persian rōzīg (daily bread, sustenance). The Quranic rizq is a central theological concept: all provision comes from God, measured and apportioned. The divine name al-Razzāq (The Ever-Providing) emphasizes God's continuous sustenance of all creation.

hadith_evidence.ar: تَدَبَّرُوا الْقُرْآنَ فَإِنَّهُ حُجَّةٌ لَكُمْ أَوْ عَلَيْكُمْ
hadith_evidence.en: Reflect upon the Quran, for it is either a proof for you or against you.
hadith_evidence.source: Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim via ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb

meaning.en: Hand. 120x. Yad=hand(s). Bayna yaday=before, in front of (lit. between hands). 2:97: confirming what was before it (ma bayna yadayhi). 5:64: both His hands (yadahu) are stretched out. The hand as symbol of power, agency, and presence.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ي-د-ي (y-d-y), centered on the noun yad (hand), is among the most frequent in the Quran with about 120 occurrences, encoding agency, power, possession, and presence. The idiom bayna yaday (‘between the two hands,’ i.e., before, in front of) governs about 50 occurrences, as in 2:97 ‘confirming what was before it (mā bayna yadayhi)’—the Quran’s self-positioning vis-à-vis previous revelation. The hand as divine symbol appears in 5:64 ‘both His hands are stretched out (yaduhu mabsūṭatān),’ debated in classical theology as either literal divine corporeality or, more commonly, divine generosity (jad, munificent giving). 48:10 is the covenant verse: ‘the hand of Allah is over their hands,’ identifying human swearing under the Prophet’s standard with divine ratification.

quranic_analysis.theme: Bayna yadayhi
quranic_analysis.detail: Musaddiqan li-ma bayna yadayhi—confirming what came before it.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *yd = 'hand'. Yad = hand, power, assistance. 'The hand (yad) of Allah is over their hands' (48:10). Bayna yaday = before/presence of. The hand as the organ of power and agency.

hadith_evidence.ar: تَدَبَّرُوا الْقُرْآنَ فَإِنَّهُ حُجَّةٌ لَكُمْ أَوْ عَلَيْكُمْ
hadith_evidence.en: Reflect upon the Quran, for it is either a proof for you or against you.
hadith_evidence.source: Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim via ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb

meaning.en_short: To test, try, afflict; to wear out, decay; to be patient in trial
meaning.en: The root bāʾ-lām-wāw has two primary Quranic senses: (1) to test, try, prove, or afflict (iblāʾ, balāʾ, ibtilāʾ) — God testing humans with good and evil, and (2) to wear out, become worn, decay (balā) — particularly of garments or bones. The two senses are connected: trial 'wears out' the one tested, and the result of a test 'exposes' or 'shows' what was hidden (as old garments show wear). Balāʾ can mean both 'trial' and 'blessing/favor' — since both prosperity and hardship test.
meaning.ar: الِاخْتِبَارُ وَالِامْتِحَانُ — وَالْفَنَاءُ وَالْبِلَى
meaning.en_detailed: Occurring 38 times in the Quranic text, the root ب ل و (ب ل و) conveys the essential concept of To test, try, afflict; to wear out, decay; to be patient in trial. Key Quranic occurrences include 67:2, 2:155, 67:2, 2:155, 67:2, 2:155, 67:2, 2:155. The Proto-Semitic antecedent *balay- (to wear out, decay; to test) underlies this root, with cognates attested in related Semitic languages. The root yields derived forms including I, II, IV, each extending the core meaning into specific semantic domains. The root carries significant theological weight in the Quranic worldview, recurring in contexts that shape Islamic doctrine and spiritual understanding.
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To test, try, afflict; to wear out, decay; to be patient in trial
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ب ل و — 38 مرة — To test

cognates.hebrew: בָּלָה (bālā) — to wear out, decay; בָּלַה (bālā) — to terrify (?)

etymology.semantic_evolution: Proto-Semitic 'wear out/decay' — Hebrew bālā means 'to wear out' (of garments). Arabic developed the 'test' sense from the idea that testing wears down the tested, or that a test reveals what's underneath (like wear reveals material).

derived_forms.key_verse: 2:155 وَلَنَبْلُوَنَّكُم — We will surely test you

derived_forms.meaning: to cause to wear out; to confer blessing/grace
derived_forms.key_verse: ʿan yublā — that He may test

derived_forms.meaning: to test, try, put to trial

key_nominals.meaning: test, trial, affliction; also: blessing, favor

usage_patterns: Ibtilāʾ as the purpose of creation: life as a test
Balāʾ as ambivalent: can be good (blessing) or bad (affliction)

lexicographical_sources: Raghib: al-balāʾ includes both niʿma (blessing) and shidda (hardship) as means of testing
theological_dimensions: Al-Ibtilāʾ theology: this life is dār ibtilāʾ (abode of testing); the afterlife is dār jazāʾ (abode of recompense)
hadith_evidence: 'How wonderful is the affair of the believer: all of it is khayr... if prosperity comes he is grateful, and if adversity comes he is patient'

meaning.en: Might, honor. 119x. Aziz=mighty, honored, dear. Al-Aziz=the Almighty (divine name, ~92x). Izzah=honor, might. 4:139: all might (al-izzah) belongs to Allah. 63:8: izzatu li-Allahi wa li-rasulihi wa li-al-mu'minin. The root denotes irresistible power, dignity, and preciousness.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ع-ز-ز (ʽ-Ẓ-Ẓ), attested about 119 times in the Quran, centers on might, strength, preciousness, and irresistible power (ʽazza, ʽazīz mighty, honored, ʿizzah honor, might). The divine name al-ʽAzīz (The Almighty) is among the most frequent in the Quran, occurring approximately 92 times, alongside al-Ṭakīm. 4:139 grounds the root in absolute theological claim: ‘all might belongs to Allah (fa-inna al-ʿizzata li-Allāhi jamīʿan),’ denying any share of absolute honor to other beings. 63:8 specifies: ‘yet might belongs to Allah, His Messenger, and the believers (ʿizzatun li-Allāhi wa-li-rasūlihi wa-li-l-muʿminīn),’ distributing honor along the divine-human axis. The root encodes Quranic theology’s anchoring of all true honor in God, with ʽazīz connoting both power and the rarity that makes something precious.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر عَزَّ — 119 مرة — might, honor; al-aziz (the almighty)

quranic_analysis.theme: All might belongs to Allah
quranic_analysis.detail: Fa-inna al-izzata li-Allahi jami'an—all honor belongs to Allah.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *ʿzz = 'to be strong, mighty'. Arabic ʿazīz (Mighty, All-Powerful) is one of the most frequent divine names (99x in Quran). The root connotes both strength and rarity — what is ʿazīz is precious because it is rare. God is ʿAzīz because His power is unique and unrivalled.

hadith_evidence.ar: تَدَبَّرُوا الْقُرْآنَ فَإِنَّهُ حُجَّةٌ لَكُمْ أَوْ عَلَيْكُمْ
hadith_evidence.en: Reflect upon the Quran, for it is either a proof for you or against you.
hadith_evidence.source: Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim via ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb

meaning.en: Father. 117x. Ab=father. Aba'=forefathers. 2:133: the God of your fathers (aba'ika) Ibrahim, Ismail, Ishaq. 12:4: Yusuf said to his father (abihi). The root spans paternal relationship and ancestral tradition.
meaning.en_detailed: The root أ-ب-و (ʾ-b-w), centered on the noun ab (father), is attested approximately 117 times in the Quran across derived forms, spanning biological fatherhood and ancestral or authoritative forebears. The plural ābāʾ (fathers, forefathers) governs many occurrences, as in 2:133 ‘the God of your fathers (ābāʿika) Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac,’—the ancestral patriarchs to whom the Muslim ummah traces its lineage. 33:5 establishes the legal importance of patrilineal identity: ‘call them by their fathers (bi-ābāʿihim),’ affirming that lineage is fixed by biological paternity rather than tribal claim. 2:170 dramatizes ancestral authority as the typical pitfall: ‘rather we follow what we found our fathers upon.’ P-Semitic *ʾb ‘father’ is attested across Hebrew (ʾāv), Aramaic, Geʼez, and Akkadian, anchoring patrilineal kinship in the Semitic world.

quranic_analysis.theme: Following forefathers
quranic_analysis.detail: Bal nattabi'u ma alfayna alayhi aba'ana—we follow what we found our fathers upon.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *ʾb = 'father'. Arabic ab = father. The dual sense of biological father and ancestral/authoritative father. 'Call them by their fathers (ābāʾihim)' (33:5) — the importance of patrilineal identity.

hadith_evidence.ar: الْجَنَّةُ تَحْتَ أَقْدَامِ الْأُمَّهَاتِ
hadith_evidence.en: Paradise lies under the feet of mothers.

meaning.en: To write. Satara=write lines. Mustatar=recorded. 68:1: Nun. By the pen and what they inscribe (yasturuna). The root of sacred inscription.
meaning.en_detailed: The root س-ط-ر (s-ṭ-r), attested about 16 times in the Quran across derived forms, denotes writing in lines, inscribing, or recording (saṭara, noun siṭr, line of writing). The most celebrated occurrence is the opening oath of Sūrah al-Qalam: ‘Nūn. By the pen and what they inscribe (wa-l-qalami wa-mā yasṭurūn)’ (68:1), placing writing at the origin of revelation—ink, line, and inscription as the very conditions of Quranic reality. The root thus grounds a Quranic theology of scripture: divine speech is preserved in lines (ṣuṭūr) and ‘recorded’ (mustaṭar) books (e.g., 54:53 ‘and everything they did is in the sijīn, mustaṭar’). 22:70 employs the verb for cosmic writing: ‘it is all in a record (mustaṭar),’—the universe itself as text. The semantic core is line-by-line inscription, the elementary act of textual preservation.

quranic_analysis.theme: By the pen
quranic_analysis.detail: Nun wa al-qalami wa ma yasturun—Nun, by the pen and what they inscribe.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *sṭr = 'to write in lines'. Arabic saṭara / istaṭara = to write. The Quran's opening oath 'Nūn. By the pen and what they inscribe (yasṭurūn)' (68:1) places writing at the origin of revelation. The saṭr (line of writing) is the unit of sacred text.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: To eat, consume. 109x. Akala=eat. Ukul=food, fruit. 2:35: eat (kula) freely from it—Adam in Paradise. 2:168: eat (kulu) of what is lawful and good on earth. Consumption as divine permission.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ʾ-k-l (أ ك ل) denotes consumption, ingestion, and devouring across physical and figurative registers, occurring 109 times in the Quran. The form akala covers both literal eating — 'eat (kulū) of what is lawful and good on the earth' (2:168) — and metaphorical consumption such as the devouring of inheritance unjustly (4:10) or the consuming effect of usury (2:275). The noun akl designates food, fruit, and fodder, while ʾukal functions as the verbal noun for the act of eating itself. The root also anchors the theological category of rizq (provision), framing all lawful eating as participation in divine sustenance rather than autonomous acquisition. Cognate with Hebrew ʾākal and Akkadian akālu, the root is among the most stable across Semitic, preserving a basic food-action sense while extending in Quranic usage into ethical and eschatological domains.

quranic_analysis.theme: Eat what is lawful
quranic_analysis.detail: Kulu mimma fi al-ardi halalan tayyiban—eat what is lawful and good.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *ʾkl = 'to eat, consume'. One of the most stable roots across Semitic. The Quran uses it for physical consumption (eating lawful food) and metaphorical consumption (devouring usury, consuming inheritance unjustly). The akh (brother, from *ʾḫw) is NOT from this root — a common confusion.

hadith_evidence.ar: الْمُؤْمِنُ يَأْكُلُ فِي مِعًى وَاحِدٍ وَالْكَافِرُ يَأْكُلُ فِي سَبْعَةِ أَمْعَاءٍ
hadith_evidence.en: The believer eats in one intestine and the disbeliever eats in seven intestines.

meaning.en: To do, act. 108x. Fa'ala=do, act. Af'al=deeds. 2:85: do you believe in part and reject part (afatu'minuna)? The root denotes general action—distinguished from amal (intentional craft).
meaning.en_detailed: The root f-ʿ-l (ف ع ل) is the paradigmatic Arabic root for action, doing, and performance, attested 108 times in the Quran. Its primary form faʿala covers both divine and human deeds — 'whatever Allah wills (yashāʾ), He does (yafʿalu)' (85:16) and 'they used to do (yafʿalūna) what they were forbidden' (16:112). The form IV afʿala adds a causative sense ('to make someone do'), while the noun fiʿl (deed, action) is the technical term for the unit of moral reckoning, distinct from ʿamal (continuous work). The verbal noun al-afʿāl (the deeds) recurs in eschatological contexts where humans are recompensed according to their fiʿl (3:30, 9:94). Because grammarians use fa-ʿa-la as the template for triliteral morphology, the root carries a meta-linguistic weight: it names the very paradigm by which Arabic verbs are conjugated.

quranic_analysis.theme: Actions and accountability
quranic_analysis.detail: Ma yaf'alu Allahu bi-adhabikum—what would Allah do with your punishment if you are grateful?

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *pʿl = 'to do, act'. Arabic faʿala = to do — the paradigmatic verb. The grammarians use fa-ʿa-la as the template for all triliteral verbs. The Quranic fiʿl (action) is what the human is held accountable for.

hadith_evidence.ar: تَدَبَّرُوا الْقُرْآنَ فَإِنَّهُ حُجَّةٌ لَكُمْ أَوْ عَلَيْكُمْ
hadith_evidence.en: Reflect upon the Quran, for it is either a proof for you or against you.
hadith_evidence.source: Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim via ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb

meaning.en: To intercede. Shafa'ah=intercession. 2:48: no intercession accepted without permission.
meaning.en_detailed: The root sh-f-ʿ (ش ف ع) denotes intercession, advocacy, and the addition of one unit to another, occurring 31 times in the Quran. The verb shafaʿa means to intercede or to add an even number, while shafāʿ is the pair, and shafaʿah the act of intercession — strictly regulated in Quranic theology. At 2:255 the famous Throne Verse declares that no intercession is valid 'except by His permission,' and 2:48 states that no ransom or intercession will be accepted from those who disbelieve. The same root applies to paired creation — 'He created you from a single soul, then made from it its mate (zawjahā)' uses the pairing sense — and to the dual-day concept of yawm al-shafaʿah. The cognate Hebrew shāphat and the related noun shafīʿ (intercessor) anchor an entire theological vocabulary around mediated access to the divine.

quranic_analysis.theme: Intercession
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa la tuqbal minha shafa'ah—no intercession accepted.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: Excellence, favor. 104x. Fadl=excellence, grace, bounty. Faddala II=prefer, favor. 4:32: Allah has favored (faddala) some of you over others. 2:253: some messengers We favored (faddalna) over others.
meaning.en_detailed: The root f-ḍ-l (ف ض ل) expresses excellence, superabundance, and grace, occurring 104 times in the Quran. The base faḍala means to exceed or remain over, while the intensive form II faḍḍala means to prefer or favor — 'Allah has favored some of you over others in provision' (4:32). The noun faḍl (bounty, grace) names divine favor itself: 'that is the bounty of Allah; He gives it to whom He wills' (62:4). At 2:253 'those messengers We favored (faḍḍalnā) some over others' specifies a hierarchy within prophecy, while faḍīlah denotes a moral virtue and mufaḍḍal connotes excellence. The root interweaves creation, ethics, and eschatology: God's faḍl is the cause of human merit, and on the Day of Judgment 'the bounty (faḍl) of Allah' becomes the only secure currency. Distinct from niʿmah (specific blessing), faḍl denotes unearned superabundance.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر فَضَّلَ — 104 مرة — excellence, favor; to prefer (fadl)

quranic_analysis.theme: Divine favor
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa Allahu faddala ba'dakum ala ba'd—Allah favored some over others in provision.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *fḍl = 'to exceed, surpass → be excellent'. Faḍala = to exceed. Faḍl = bounty, grace, excess. 'That is the bounty (faḍl) of Allah; He gives it to whom He wills' (62:4). Faḍīlah = virtue, excellence.

hadith_evidence.ar: تَدَبَّرُوا الْقُرْآنَ فَإِنَّهُ حُجَّةٌ لَكُمْ أَوْ عَلَيْكُمْ
hadith_evidence.en: Reflect upon the Quran, for it is either a proof for you or against you.
hadith_evidence.source: Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim via ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb

meaning.en: To return. 104x. Raja'a=return. Marji'=return place. 2:46: those who know they will return (raj'un) to their Lord. 2:156: inna li-Allahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un—we belong to Allah and to Him we return.
meaning.en_detailed: The root r-j-ʿ (ر ج ع) denotes return, turning back, and reversal, occurring 104 times in the Quran. The verb rajaʿa covers physical return — 'then to that which is lower shall they return (yarjiʿūn)' (95:5) — and metaphysical return to God, enshrined in the formula 'inna li-llāhi wa inna ilayhi rājiʿūn — we belong to Allah and to Him we return' (2:156). The noun marjaʿ names the place or moment of return — 'the return of all is to Me' (3:28) — and rujūʿ the abstract act. The causative form IV arjaʿa implies divine orchestration of return, as in 'if We give him a taste of mercy after adversity has touched him' (41:50). The root is structurally tied to maʿād (place of return) and to eschatology: every human rajaʿa to his Lord, and every created thing moves through cycles of departure and return.

quranic_analysis.theme: Return to Allah
quranic_analysis.detail: Inna li-Allahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un—the formula of istirja'.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *rǧʿ = 'to return, go back'. Arabic rajaʿa = to return. The Quranic rujūʿ is central — all return to God. 'Innā li-llāh wa innā ilayhi rājiʿūn' (2:156). Marjiʿ = place of return — the final destination of all beings.

hadith_evidence.ar: تَدَبَّرُوا الْقُرْآنَ فَإِنَّهُ حُجَّةٌ لَكُمْ أَوْ عَلَيْكُمْ
hadith_evidence.en: Reflect upon the Quran, for it is either a proof for you or against you.
hadith_evidence.source: Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim via ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb

meaning.en_short: Door, gate, entrance; chapter, section, category
meaning.en: The noun bab means door, gate, entrance. In the Quran, it appears in plural abwab (gates of Paradise, gates of Hell). Post-Quranically, bab became the standard term for 'chapter' of a book.
meaning.ar: المدخل والمنفذ
meaning.en_detailed: ب و ب (ب و ب), a root appearing 27 times in the Quran, encodes the notion of Door, gate, entrance; chapter, section, category across its various verbal and nominal forms. Key Quranic occurrences include 38:50. The Proto-Semitic antecedent *bab- (door) underlies this root, with cognates attested in related Semitic languages.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ب و ب — 27 مرة — Door

etymology.semantic_evolution: Proto-Semitic door/gate via Akkadian babu. Entered Arabic pre-Islamically.

usage_patterns: Gates as eschatological thresholds

lexicographical_sources: Ibn Faris: al-bab is madkhal al-dar
theological_dimensions: Gates of Paradise as threshold imagery
hadith_evidence: I am the city of knowledge and Ali is its gate

meaning.en: Grant. 65x. Wahaba=bestow. 3:38: grant me (hab li) from Yourself good offspring.
meaning.en_detailed: The root w-h-b (و ه ب) signifies bestowal, grant, and unconditional giving, occurring 25 times in the Quran. The verb wahaba names the sovereign act of divine grant, especially of offspring — 'My Lord, grant me (hab li) from Yourself righteous offspring' (3:38), the prayer of Zakariyyā. At 19:19 the angel announces to Maryam that God has granted her a pure son, and 3:8 records the supplication 'our Lord, let not our hearts deviate after You have guided us and grant us from Yourself mercy.' The intensive form wahhāb ('the Ever-Bestowing') is one of the divine names, applied to God five times (e.g., 38:9). The noun hibat denotes the gift as object, while hawb denotes a specific bestowal. Distinct from ʿaṭā (to give in answer) and nafaqa (to spend), wahaba presupposes an initiator who gives without transactional exchange — the paradigm of divine sovereignty over creation.

quranic_analysis.theme: Divine grant
quranic_analysis.detail: Hab li min ladunka dhurriyyatan tayyibah—grant me good offspring.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: Ruined. 2x. 9:109: building on crumbling bank (jurufin harin) of a cliff.
meaning.en_detailed: The root kh-r-b (خ ر ب) signifies ruin, desolation, and the structural collapse of a place or institution, occurring 2 times in the Quran. The verbal noun kharāb denotes the ruinous state, while the active participle khārib names an agent who brings ruin. The single Quranic nominal instance appears in the parable of 9:109: 'whoever sold this life for the next — he found the one he sought, and God does not let go to waste the reward of the believers.' The cognate root of this kind is paired with harīb in the phrase 'ʿalā shafā jurufin hārin — on the brink of a crumbling cliff' (9:109), where hār (devastated, crumbling) describes earth falling from a bank. This root anchors the semantic field of wasteland and the ruinous consequence of misdeeds, paralleling Hebrew ḥārab (to be dry, desolate) and giving Arabic the common noun kharāʾ (devastation).

quranic_analysis.theme: Crumbling foundation
quranic_analysis.detail: Ala shafa jurufin harin—on brink of crumbling bank.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en: To give birth; child. 102x. Walada=give birth. Walad=child, offspring. 112:3: He neither begets (yalid) nor is begotten (yulad)—divine transcendence. 19:35: it is not for Allah to take a son (waladan). The root affirms divine uniqueness through negation of procreation.
meaning.en_detailed: The root w-l-d (و ل د) denotes procreation, parentage, and lineage, occurring 102 times in the Quran. The verb walada means to give birth or beget, while walad denotes the child or offspring — distinct from ibn (son within lineage) and ṣabī (young child). The most concentrated theological usage negates divine procreation: 'He neither begets nor is begotten (lam yalid wa lam yūlad)' (112:3), the definitive disavowal of pagan claims to divine offspring. The active participle wālid names the parent (especially the father) — 'his parents (wālidāhu) and his brother and sister' (24:61) — and the feminine walīdah the mother. At 19:35 the Quraysh formula 'it is not for God to take a son (waladan)' frames Christ's sonship as incompatible with divine transcendence. Cognate with Hebrew yālad and Akkadian walādu, the root binds together the domestic, genealogical, and christological domains in Quranic discourse.

quranic_analysis.theme: Divine transcendence
quranic_analysis.detail: Lam yalid wa lam yulad—He begets not nor is He begotten.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *wld = 'to bear children'. The Quranic walad (child) is both blessing and test. The divine attribute 'lam yalid wa lam yūlad' (He begets not, nor is He begotten, 112:3) negates pagan concepts of divine progeny.

hadith_evidence.ar: الْيَدُ الْعُلْيَا خَيْرٌ مِنَ الْيَدِ السُّفْلَى
hadith_evidence.en: The upper hand is better than the lower hand.

meaning.en: Religion, debt; judgment. 101x. Din=religion, judgment, debt. 1:4: Maliki yawm al-din (Master of the Day of Judgment). 3:19: inna al-dina inda Allahi al-Islam. 109:6: to you your religion (dinukum) and to me mine. The root spans obligation, recompense, and faith.
meaning.en_detailed: The root d-y-n (د ي ن) carries the broad semantic field of obligation, judgment, recompense, and religion, occurring 101 times in the Quran. The noun dīn names religion in its fullest sense — including judgment ('Master of the Day of Judgment, māliki yawm al-dīn,' 1:4) and way of life — and encompasses the system of repayment and accountability. At 3:19 the defining verse states 'the religion (dīn) with Allah is Islam (submission),' while 109:6 commands disassociation: 'to you your religion (dīnukum) and to me mine.' The active participle dayyān (judge, reckoner) appears once in the Quran (1:4, in variant reading) and is one of God's names in Islamic theology. The root originally connoted 'to owe' or 'to be indebted,' and this foundational sense persists in the Quranic muktadīn meaning those who are accountable. The semantic journey from debt to judgment to religion maps the expansion of an economic term into an entire civilizational concept.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر دَانَ — 101 مرة — religion, debt; judgment (din)

quranic_analysis.theme: al-Din: the true religion
quranic_analysis.detail: Inna al-dina inda Allahi al-Islam—the religion with Allah is submission.

derived_forms.meaning: to be indebted; to profess religion; to judge

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *dyn = 'to judge → religion'. The Quranic dīn is the comprehensive term: judgment, religion, debt, recompense. The semantic field unites moral obligation (debt), divine judgment, and religious practice — all forms of 'being bound' to God.

hadith_evidence.ar: تَدَبَّرُوا الْقُرْآنَ فَإِنَّهُ حُجَّةٌ لَكُمْ أَوْ عَلَيْكُمْ
hadith_evidence.en: Reflect upon the Quran, for it is either a proof for you or against you.
hadith_evidence.source: Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim via ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb

meaning.en_short: To urinate; concern, attention, state of mind
meaning.en: Two senses: (1) urine/urination (bawl), and (2) the noun bal meaning 'state, condition, mind' — fa-ma baluhum (what is the matter with them?).
meaning.ar: البول والحال والبال
meaning.en_detailed: Occurring 4 times in the Quranic text, the root ب و ل (ب و ل) conveys the essential concept of To urinate; concern, attention, state of mind. Key Quranic occurrences include 47:32. The Proto-Semitic antecedent *bawl-/*bal- (urine; mind) underlies this root, with cognates attested in related Semitic languages.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ب و ل — 4 مرة — To urinate

etymology.semantic_evolution: Two roots converged: *bawl- urine and *bal- mind/attention.

usage_patterns: Bal as interrogative marker: ma bal = what is the case of...

lexicographical_sources: Ibn Faris: two separate roots
theological_dimensions: Ma bal as Quranic rhetorical device

hadith_evidence.ar: ب و ل — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 4 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root bwl (ب و ل) appears 4 times in the Quran, including 47:32.

meaning.en: Brother. 96x. Akh=brother. 33:5: call them by their fathers—that is more just. Your brothers (ikhwanukum) in religion. 49:10: believers are but brothers (ikhwah).
meaning.en_detailed: The root ʾ-kh-w (أ خ و) names the sibling relationship, occurring 96 times in the Quran. The noun akh denotes the brother, with ukht the sister and ikhwat or ikhwān the brothers collectively. The Quran uses biological brotherhood for narrative purposes — Yūsuf and his brothers (12:7–11), Hārūn as Mūsā's brother and spokesman (19:53, 20:42), and the two sons of Adam (5:27–30).
