On this foundation it builds the foundational concept of the ummah as family: 'the believers are but brothers (ikhwah), so make peace between your brothers and fear Allah' (49:10). At 33:5 the verse 'call them by their fathers' corrects an adopted-sibling practice by restoring paternal lineage. The plural ikhwah is distinguished from ikhwān by usage context. Cognate with Hebrew ʾāḥ, the root underwrites both kinship ethics and the political-theological idea of a community constituted by faith rather than blood.

quranic_analysis.theme: Believers are brothers
quranic_analysis.detail: Innama al-mu'minuna ikhwah—believers are brothers.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *ʾḫw = 'brother'. Arabic akh = brother. Ikhwah = brothers (in faith). 'The believers are but brothers (ikhwah)' (49:10). The root extends beyond blood to the bond of faith — the Muslim ummah as a brotherhood.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: Night. 92x. Layl=night. 2:164: alternation of night and day (ikhtilaf al-layli wa al-nahari). 92:1: wa al-layli idha yaghsha—by the night when it covers. Night as time of rest, prayer, and the Prophet's journey (al-Isra').
meaning.en_detailed: The root l-y-l (ل ي ل) names night as a temporal and cosmological entity, occurring 92 times in the Quran. The noun layl denotes the darkness of night, contrasted with nahār (day), and forms part of the pair 'al-layl wa al-nahār' as one of God's signs. The verse 'in the alternation of night and day (ikhtilāf al-layl wa al-nahār) are signs for those with insight' (3:190) and 2:164 make the cycle itself the locus of theological reflection. The opening of Surat al-Layl (92:1) — 'by the night when it covers (yaghshā)' — turns night into an oath-subject. The Quranic idiom of qiyām al-layl (standing through the night) and the Prophet's Night Journey (al-Isrāʾ bi-l-layl) anchor night as the preferred time of devotion. Cognate with Hebrew laylāh and Akkadian līlātu, the root preserves the Semitic *layl-, though the Quranic lexicon adds distinct derivative terms for night-travel (sarā, laylatan).

quranic_analysis.theme: Night as divine sign
quranic_analysis.detail: Ikhtilaf al-layli wa al-nahar—alternation of night and day as divine signs.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *lyl = 'night'. The Quranic layl is the time of rest, prayer, and the Night Journey (isrāʾ). The alternation of layl and nahār (day and night) is a recurring sign (āyah) of divine power.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: To glorify; to swim. 92x. Sabbaha II=glorify. Subhan=glory be! Tasbih=glorification. 17:44: the seven heavens and earth glorify Him (yusabbihu). 21:33: each swimming (yasbahun) in an orbit. All creation does tasbih.
meaning.en_detailed: The root s-b-ḥ (س ب ح) carries the dual semantic field of physical movement through water and the metaphysical act of divine glorification, occurring 92 times in the Quran. The form II sabbaḥa intensifies the act of glorification — 'glorify the name of your Lord (sabbiḥ asmā rabbika), the Most High' (87:1) — while the form I sabaḥa denotes swimming or moving swiftly across water. The verbal noun tasbīḥ names the act of glorification: 'all that is in the heavens and earth glorifies (yusabbiḥu) Allah' (57:1, 59:1). The same root describes cosmic motion: 'each [celestial body] swimming (yasbaḥuna) in an orbit' (21:33, 36:40). The semantic bridge between swimming and praising lies in the image of effortless gliding motion — the heavens and atoms alike move in continuous responsive praise. Cognate with Hebrew sābaḥ and the broader Semitic concept of cosmic motion as praise, the root unifies physics and liturgy.

quranic_analysis.theme: Universal glorification
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa in min shay'in illa yusabbihu bi-hamdihi—nothing exists that does not glorify Him.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *sbḥ = 'to swim → to float → to glide in praise'. Sabbaḥa = to glorify God. Tasbīḥ = glorification. The image of swimming/gliding suggests effortless, continuous praise. 'Everything in the heavens and earth glorifies (yusabbiḥu) Allah' (57:1).

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: Not, is not. 89x. Laysa=is not. The sister of kana—negates nominal sentences. 2:107: you have not (ma lakum) besides Allah any protector. 42:11: there is nothing (laysa) like Him. The primary existential negation verb.
meaning.en_detailed: The root l-y-s (ل ي س) provides Arabic with its primary negative existential verb, occurring 89 times in the Quran. The verb laysa negates nominal sentences ('he is not,' 'there is no') and stands structurally as the counterpart to kāna ('he was/is'). The most concentrated theological statement using this root is the Throne Verse's 'laysa ka-mithlihi shayʾun — there is nothing like Him' (42:11), which exhausts possible comparisons to declare divine incomparability. At 2:107 'laysa la-kum min dūni Allāhi walīyyun — there is no protector for you besides Allah' anchors the negation of intermediary powers. Other Quranic uses include 10:62 'laysa Allāh bi-jaḥilin li-mā taʿmalūn — Allah is not unaware of what you do,' which uses the verb to deny divine negligence. The root also frames the ethical negations 'laysa al-birra an tuwallū wujūhakum' (2:177, 'righteousness is not turning your faces east and west'). Distinct from the particle lam (verbal negation) and the verbal noun ʿadam (non-existence), laysa preserves the existential copula while negating it.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر لَيْسَ — 89 مرة — is not; negation (laysa)

quranic_analysis.theme: Laysa kamithlihi shay
quranic_analysis.detail: Laysa kamithlihi shay'un—there is nothing like Him. Divine incomparability.

derived_forms.meaning: negative existential — is not, there is no

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *lys = 'not to be'. Arabic laysa is a unique negative existential verb: 'there is not, it is not'. Possibly a contraction of lā + ʾaysa (there is no being). A structural innovation in Arabic syntax.

key_nominals.m: negative existential verb — 'is not, there is no'

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: Wealth. 86x. Mal=wealth, property. 2:261: parable of those who spend wealth (amwalahum) in Allah's way. 3:14: beautified for people is love of desires—wealth (al-qanatir) and children.
meaning.en_detailed: The root m-w-l (م و ل) names wealth, property, and possessions, occurring 86 times in the Quran. The noun māl denotes material wealth — land, goods, capital — and the plural amwāl appears frequently as the object of ethical commands. The verse 'beautified for people is the love of desires — women, children, piled-up mounds of gold and silver (qanātīr), branded horses, cattle, and sown fields' (3:14) lists māl among the things that captivate the heart. At 2:261 'the parable of those who spend their wealth (amwālahum) in the way of Allah' establishes wealth's proper channel as almsgiving. The root also names a household unit (māl vs. ʿiyāl, dependents) and the noun ʾimlāʾ (a measurement of time). The Quranic worldview treats wealth as amanah (trust) — 'and give them of Allah's wealth He has given you' (24:33) — and warns that 'wealth and children are a trial (fitnah)' (8:28). Cognate with Aramaic māmōnā (the source of 'Mammon'), the root anchors an ethical and eschatological discourse on the proper use of worldly goods.

quranic_analysis.theme: Wealth as test
quranic_analysis.detail: Wealth is beautified—a test of gratitude and spending in Allah's way.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *mwl = 'to incline → wealth'. Māl originally = 'that which inclines the heart'. The Aramaic māmōnā entered Greek as Mammon. Quran treats māl as a divine trust and test — 'wealth and children are a trial (fitnah)' (8:28).

key_nominals.m: wealth — that which inclines the heart

hadith_evidence.ar: لَيْسَ الْغِنَى عَنْ كَثْرَةِ الْعَرَضِ وَلَكِنَّ الْغِنَى غِنَى النَّفْسِ
hadith_evidence.en: Wealth is not from abundance of possessions; wealth is richness of the soul.

meaning.en_short: White, whiteness; egg; to become white, brighten
meaning.en: Denotes whiteness and brightness. Abyad means white. Appears in miracle narratives: Musa's hand turning white, the white thread of dawn. The verb ibyadda means 'to become white' — faces whitening on Judgment Day.
meaning.ar: اللون الأبيض ضد الأسود
meaning.en_detailed: The Arabic root ب ي ض (ب ي ض) appears 12 times in the Quran, governing the semantic domain of White, whiteness; egg; to become white, brighten. Key Quranic occurrences include 3:106. The Proto-Semitic antecedent *bayḍ- (egg; white) underlies this root, with cognates attested in related Semitic languages. The root yields derived forms including IX, each extending the core meaning into specific semantic domains. The root carries significant theological weight in the Quranic worldview, recurring in contexts that shape Islamic doctrine and spiritual understanding.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ب ي ض — 12 مرة — White

etymology.semantic_evolution: Color 'white' from noun 'egg' — the egg as prototypical white object.

usage_patterns: White/black dichotomy in eschatology

lexicographical_sources: Ibn Faris: al-bayaḍ is min al-alwan
theological_dimensions: Face-whitening as salvation
hadith_evidence: White thread of dawn for fasting

meaning.en: One; anyone. 85x. Ahad=one, anyone. 112:1: Qul huwa Allahu ahad—Say: He is Allah, the One. 2:102: they cannot harm anyone (ahadin) except by Allah's permission.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ʾ-ḥ-d (أ ح د) denotes the number one and the concept of singular uniqueness, occurring 85 times in the Quran. The noun aḥad names 'one' as indivisible unity, while wāḥid names the numerical 'one.' The two terms carry distinct theological weight: 'Qul huwa Allāhu aḥad — Say: He is Allah, the One [unique, indivisible]' (112:1) uses aḥad to declare God's ontological singularity, whereas 'your God is one God (ʾilāhun wāḥidun)' (2:163, 37:4) uses wāḥid to assert monotheism against polytheism. The same root names the negation of divine partners (shurakāʾ) — 'He is One, none can intercede with Him except by His permission' (39:44). The active participle wāḥid appears as a divine name (al-Wāḥid) in the divine attributes of mercy. The masdar aḥadiyyah (unique unity) is a later theological term derived from this root. The grammatical distinction between aḥad and wāḥid forms the basis for the classical Arabic category of 'numerals of singularity' (asmāʾ al-ʿadad).

quranic_analysis.theme: Divine oneness
quranic_analysis.detail: Huwa Allahu ahad—Allah is the One. The most concentrated expression of tawhid.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *ʾḥd = 'one, unique'. Arabic aḥad = one (unique, indivisible). The Quranic 'Qul huwa Allāhu Aḥad' (112:1) — the definitive statement of divine unity. Aḥad is not the numerical 'one' (wāḥid) but the unique 'One' without second.

key_nominals.m: the Unique One — divine unity (Surah al-Ikhlāṣ)

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en_short: To save, rescue; to be delivered
meaning.en: To save, deliver. 84x. Naja=be saved. Anja IV=save. Najat=salvation. 10:92: today We shall save you (nunajjika) in body—Pharaoh. 21:88: thus We saved (najjayna) the believers—Nuh.
meaning.en_detailed: The root n-j-w (ن ج و) names salvation, escape, and intimate converse, occurring 84 times in the Quran. The form I najā means to escape or be saved — 'so today We save you (nunajjīka) in your body that you may be a sign to those after you' (10:92) — and the form IV anjā means to deliver or rescue. The noun najāh names salvation as an abstract state, while the intensive form III nājā names secret counsel — 'does he speak to you secretly (yunājīka) or is he openly [declaring]?' (13:33). The noun najwā names the secret conversation itself, and the passive noun munājāh denotes confidential speech (4:114). The root's ethical and eschatological uses include 'those who believe and do righteous deeds — We will not let the wage of the good-doers be lost' (18:88), where anjā carries both rescue and reward. Cognate with Hebrew nāṣa and Ugaritic nšʿ, the root spans physical escape, ethical rescue, and esoteric communion.
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To save, rescue; to be delivered

quranic_analysis.theme: Divine deliverance
quranic_analysis.detail: Nunajjika—divine rescue of believers from destruction.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *nǧw = 'to escape → be saved'. Najā = to escape, be saved. Najāh = salvation. 'Those who believe and do righteous deeds — for them are the gardens of Paradise (jannāt al-naʿīm)' — salvation as divine reward.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: How? 83x. Kayfa=how? 2:28: how can you disbelieve in Allah? Most frequent interrogative particle—rhetorical and genuine.
meaning.en_detailed: The root k-y-f (ك ي ف) names the interrogative 'how?' and the manner or condition of an action, occurring 83 times in the Quran. The interrogative adverb kayfa asks after manner, state, or condition — 'kayfa takfurūna bi-llāh — how can you disbelieve in Allah?' (2:28) — and its frequency makes it the most common interrogative particle in the Quran. Often rhetorical rather than genuine, the question functions as admonition: 'kayfa yakūnu li-l-mushrikīna ʿahdun ʿinda Allāhi — how shall the polytheists have any covenant with Allah?' (9:7). The same root supplies the conditional kayfa (when), as in 'kayfa idhā jāʾat ṭāʾifatun — when a group [of enemies] comes' — though this usage belongs to the related adverbial sense. The noun kaifiyyah (quality, modality) derives from this root in later Arabic. The Quranic use of kayfa is theological: it questions human capacity, divine action, and eschatological state.

quranic_analysis.theme: How can you disbelieve?
quranic_analysis.detail: Kayfa takfuruna bi-Allahi—how can you disbelieve?

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic interrogative. kayfa = how? The most frequent interrogative particle in the Quran (83x). 'kayfa takfurūna bi-llāh' (2:28) — how can you disbelieve? Rhetorical and genuine questions distinguished by context.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en_short: To equal, level; to be upright
meaning.en: To equal, level. 83x. Sawa=equal. Sawwa II=to fashion, proportion. 2:6: it is the same (sawa'un) to them whether you warn them. 91:7: by the soul and He who proportioned it (sawwaha).
meaning.en_detailed: The root s-w-y (س و ي) denotes equality, leveling, and the proportionate shaping of a thing, occurring 83 times in the Quran. The form I sawiya means to be equal, and the form II sawwā means to equalize, balance, or shape — 'and the soul and He who proportioned it (sawwāhā)' (91:7) names the divine act of giving human form its symmetry and proportion. The noun sawāʾ names what is equal or middle — 'it is equal (sawāʾun) for them whether you warn them or do not warn them' (2:6). The form VIII istawā denotes being established or ascending — 'then He turned to the heaven when it was smoke and said to it and to the earth, come willingly or unwillingly; they said, we come willingly' (41:11). The noun sawīyy denotes a level plain (4:42). Cognate with Hebrew shāwā (to be level) and Akkadian *šawû, the root unifies geometry and cosmology: the same act that makes the heavens level proportions the human soul.
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To equal, level; to be upright

quranic_analysis.theme: Divine proportioning
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa nafsin wa ma sawwaha—by the soul and He who perfectly proportioned it.

derived_forms.meaning: to equalize, balance, shape, create proportioned

etymology.proto_semitic: *šwy (to roast; to be equal) — dual root
etymology.semantic_evolution: Two distinct roots converge: šwy = to roast (shawā = grilled meat) and swy = to be equal (sawiyy = equal). The Quranic sawāʾ = equal — 'whether you warn them or not, it is equal (sawāʾun) for them' (2:6).

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: To follow; consequence. 80x. Aqaba=followed. Aqibah=outcome, end. 3:137: see what was the end (aqibatu) of the deniers. The root denotes sequential consequence.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ʿ-q-b (ع ق ب) denotes following, succession, and consequence, occurring 80 times in the Quran. The noun ʿāqibah names the outcome or end of a sequence — 'see, then, how was the end (ʿāqibah) of the deniers' (3:137, 40:21, 27:51). The verb ʿaqaba means to follow or to come after, and the noun ʿuqbā names the final outcome, particularly of the human abode — 'the final outcome (ʿuqbā) is for those who feared Allah' (20:132). The form III ʿāqaba adds the meaning of punishment or retaliation: 'and if you punish (ʿāqabtum), punish with the like of what you were afflicted with' (16:126). The active participle ʿāqib names one who succeeds or follows. The noun maʿqibāt (the two successive journeys, 28:79) and the place-name al-ʿAqabah anchor historical and geographical uses. Cognate with Hebrew ʿāqēv (heel) and Arabic ʿaqib (heel), the root preserves the image of following at the heel — what comes after defines what precedes.

quranic_analysis.theme: Outcomes of nations
quranic_analysis.detail: Fa-nzuru kayfa kana aqibatu al-mukadhdhibin—see the end of the deniers.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *ʿqb = 'heel → what follows → consequence'. Arabic ʿaqiba = to follow, succeed. ʿĀqibah = outcome, end. 'The good outcome (ʿuqba al-dār) is for the righteous' (13:22) — the final abode.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: Present. 79x. Arada=display. 18:100: We will present (aradna) Hell to disbelievers.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ʿ-r-ḍ (ع ر ض) denotes presentation, display, and the act of turning aside, occurring 79 times in the Quran. The form I ʿaraḍa means to present or to turn away — 'they turn aside (yuʿriḍūn) from it' (7:180) — while the noun ʿarḍ names the presented thing, particularly worldly goods. The form III ʿāraḍa adds the sense of opposing or confronting, and the form VI taʿāraḍa adds the sense of mutual opposition. The noun ʿarḍ also names present, immediate goods — 'not given to wandering, and life of the world' (4:77). At 18:100 'we will present (araḍnā) Hell to the disbelievers' names the catastrophic display on the Day of Judgment. The form II ʿarraḍa adds an intensive sense of presenting in detail. Cognate with Akkadian arāḍu (to go down) and Hebrew ʿāraṣ, the root preserves the image of lateral display, turning aside, and what is set forth before the viewer.

quranic_analysis.theme: Hell presented
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa aradna jahannama yawma'idhin—We present Hell that Day.

derived_forms.meaning: to present, display, show, turn away

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *ʿrḍ = 'to present, show, turn aside'. ʿAraḍa = to present, display. Iʿrāḍ = turning away. 'Those who turn away (yuʿriḍūna) from Our signs' — the disbelievers who refuse to look.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: Revelation. 78x. Awha IV=reveal, inspire. Wahy=revelation. 53:4: it is only a revelation revealed (wahyun yuha). 16:68: your Lord inspired (awha) to the bee. The root spans divine revelation to prophets and instinctual inspiration to creatures.
meaning.en_detailed: The root w-ḥ-y (و ح ي) names revelation, inspiration, and the secret communication of meaning, occurring 78 times in the Quran. The form IV awḥā names the act of divine inspiration — 'and We inspired (awḥaynā) to the mother of Moses to nurse him' (28:7) — while the noun waḥy names revelation as a communicated meaning rather than a literal utterance. At 53:4 'he does not speak from his own desire; it is only a revelation revealed (waḥyun yūḥā)' defines the Prophet's speech as entirely revealed. The same root extends to natural inspiration: 'and your Lord inspired (awḥā) to the bee' (16:68). The form I waḥā preserves the older sense of secret suggestion, and the form VIII ittaḥā the sense of internal whisper. The active participle wāḥī names the revealer. Distinct from tanzīl (sending down) and ʿilm (knowledge), waḥy preserves the intimacy and speed of direct divine communication.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر أَوْحَى — 78 مرة — revelation; to inspire (wahy)

quranic_analysis.theme: Wahy to prophets
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa ma yantiqu ani al-hawa—in huwa illa wahyun yuha. Prophet's speech is revelation.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *wḥy = 'to suggest, inspire secretly'. Waḥy = divine inspiration, revelation. The Quranic waḥy is the mode of prophetic communication — God 'suggests' to the prophets. 'It is not but waḥy revealed (yūḥā)' (53:4).

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: Mud. 1x. Hama'=black, fetid mud. 15:26: We created man from black mud altered.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ḥ-m-ʾ (ح م أ) denotes black mud, fetid clay, and the unformed primordial matter, occurring 4 times in the Quran. The noun ḥamaʾ (often translated 'dark mud') names the substance from which Adam was created — 'We created man from black mud altered (min ḥamaʾin masnūn)' (15:26, 15:28, 15:33, 38:71). The masnūn ('altered, shaped') suggests a transformation from the raw, fetid clay to formed human form, distinguishing it from ṭīn (pure clay) and ṭīn lāẓib (clinging clay, 37:11). The semantic field of the root centers on the lowly, the unformed, and the primal — the opposite of the elevated and shaped. Cognate with Hebrew ḥōmeṣ (vinegar) and the broader Semitic concept of fermenting mud, the Quranic ḥamaʾ preserves the image of human origin at its most humble, contrasted with the high destiny of the human being who was breathed upon by God's spirit (15:29).

quranic_analysis.theme: Creation from mud
quranic_analysis.detail: Min hama'in masnunin—from black mud altered.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *ḥmʾ = 'black, fetid mud'. Ḥamaʾ = the primordial clay from which Adam was created. 'Min ḥamaʾin masnūn' (15:26) — from black mud altered. The lowest point of human origin pointing to the highest potential.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en: To forget. 3x. Saha=forget, be heedless. 107:5: woe to those heedless of prayer (sahun).
meaning.en_detailed: The root s-h-w (س ه و) names forgetting, heedlessness, and the act of being distracted from the present, occurring 2 times in the Quran. The verb sahā means to forget or to be heedless — 'woe to those who are heedless of their prayer (alladhīna hum ʿan ṣalātihim sāhūn)' (107:5) — and the form IV asḥā adds the causative sense of causing to forget or being made to forget. The verbal noun sahw names the abstract state of forgetfulness, and the active participle sāhī names one who is currently heedless. At 19:64 'our Lord, we did not forget (ansīnā) our soul' uses the related root n-s-y, but s-h-w specifically names the active, ongoing state of distraction rather than mere lapsed memory. The Quranic use of sahw pairs it with ghaffah (negligence) and ghaflah (heedlessness). The Quranic anthropology locates the root of human error not in malice but in sahw — the natural drift of attention away from the divine.

quranic_analysis.theme: Heedless of prayer
quranic_analysis.detail: Alladhina hum an salatihim sahun—heedless of their prayer.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *shy = 'to forget, neglect'. Sahā = to forget, be distracted. Sāhūn = those heedless of prayer (107:5). The root of human frailty: forgetting the divine in daily life.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en_short: To sell, buy, trade; pledge of allegiance (bayʿa)
meaning.en: Denotes selling, buying, commercial transaction. In the Quran: literal trade and the metaphorical transaction between God and believers (God has 'purchased' their lives for Paradise, 9:111). The bayʿa is a pledge of allegiance — a solemn covenant modeled on commercial contract.
meaning.ar: الأخذ والإعطاء — البيع والشراء
meaning.en_detailed: The triconsonantal root ب ي ع (ب ي ع) — 15 Quranic occurrences — fundamentally expresses To sell, buy, trade; pledge of allegiance (bayʿa). Key Quranic occurrences include 9:111. The Proto-Semitic antecedent *bayʿ- (to sell, trade) underlies this root, with cognates attested in related Semitic languages. The root yields derived forms including I, III, each extending the core meaning into specific semantic domains.
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To sell, buy, trade; pledge of allegiance
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ب ي ع — 15 مرة — To sell

etymology.semantic_evolution: Proto-Semitic exchange/trade. Bayʿa as both transaction and covenant.

usage_patterns: Bayʿa as covenant: political-spiritual pledge

lexicographical_sources: Raghib: al-bayʿ is mubadalat mal bi-mal
theological_dimensions: The bayʿa as Quranic political institution
hadith_evidence: Bayʿat al-Riḍwan and ʿAqaba pledges

meaning.en_short: To destroy, annihilate, ruin; utter destruction
meaning.en: Denotes utter destruction. Form II tabbara means 'He destroyed utterly'. Tatbir is total annihilation — leaving nothing behind. Used exclusively of divine punishment against defiant peoples.
meaning.ar: الإهلاك والإفناء — تدمير الشيء بحيث لا يبقى
meaning.en_detailed: The triconsonantal root ت ب ر (ت ب ر) — 6 Quranic occurrences — fundamentally expresses To destroy, annihilate, ruin; utter destruction. Key Quranic occurrences include 25:39. The Proto-Semitic antecedent *tabar- (to break, destroy) underlies this root, with cognates attested in related Semitic languages. The root yields derived forms including II, each extending the core meaning into specific semantic domains. The root carries significant theological weight in the Quranic worldview, recurring in contexts that shape Islamic doctrine and spiritual understanding.
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To destroy, annihilate, ruin; utter destruction
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ت ب ر — 6 مرة — To destroy

etymology.semantic_evolution: Arabic root for total destruction — stronger than halaka.

usage_patterns: Tatbir as erasure-level destruction

lexicographical_sources: Ibn Faris: al-tabr is al-halak
theological_dimensions: Divine tatbir as final consequence of defiance

hadith_evidence.ar: ت ب ر — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 6 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root tbr (ت ب ر) appears 6 times in the Quran, including 25:39.

meaning.en_short: Below, beneath, under (preposition); that which is lower
meaning.en: Nominal taḥt means below, beneath, under. Used literally and metaphorically. The Quran's most famous phrase: 'gardens beneath which rivers flow' — the standard description of Paradise.
meaning.ar: ضد فوق — أسفل
meaning.en_detailed: Root ت ح ت (ت ح ت), attested 51 times in the Quran, derives its core meaning of Below, beneath, under (preposition); that which is lower from Proto-Semitic sources. Key Quranic occurrences include 2:25. The Proto-Semitic antecedent *taḥt- (below, under) underlies this root, with cognates attested in related Semitic languages.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ت ح ت — 51 مرة — Below

etymology.semantic_evolution: Proto-Semitic under/below — remarkably stable. Hebrew taḥat = Arabic taḥta.

usage_patterns: Jannat tajri min taḥtiha al-anhar as leitmotif

lexicographical_sources: Ibn Faris: al-taḥt is khilaf al-fawq
theological_dimensions: Taḥt as spatial marker of Paradise

hadith_evidence.ar: الْمُؤْمِنُ يَأْكُلُ فِي مِعًى وَاحِدٍ وَالْكَافِرُ يَأْكُلُ فِي سَبْعَةِ أَمْعَاءٍ
hadith_evidence.en: The believer eats in one intestine and the disbeliever eats in seven intestines.

meaning.en: Might, strength; hardship. 73x. Ba's=might, strength, hardship. 2:177: patience in poverty and hardship (al-ba'sa'i)—birr defined. 48:29: stern (ashidda'u) against disbelievers—ba's among believers.
meaning.en_detailed: The root b-ʾ-s (ب أ س) denotes might, severity, and the suffering that accompanies strength tested, occurring 73 times in the Quran. The noun baʾs names warlike might or its test — 'and prepare against them whatever you can of [military] might (baʾs)' (8:60) — while the noun baʾsāʾ names misfortune, adversity, and hardship. The form I baʾusa names the state of being mighty, and the active participle baʾīs names one who is mighty or severe. At 2:177 'righteousness is not that you turn your faces east and west, but [true] righteousness is [in] one who believes in Allah, the Last Day, the angels, the Book, the prophets, and gives wealth in spite of love for it, to relatives, orphans, the needy, the traveler, those who ask [for help], and frees slaves; and establishes prayer and gives zakāh; and those who fulfill their covenant when they make it; and those who are patient in poverty (baʾsāʾ) and hardship (ḍarrāʾ)' establishes baʾsāʾ as the test of patience. Cognate with Hebrew bōʾsh (to be ashamed, related), the root anchors the Quranic ethics of dignified suffering.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر بَؤُسَ — 73 مرة — might, strength; hardship

quranic_analysis.theme: Patience in hardship
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa al-sabirina fi al-ba'sa'i wa al-darra'i—patience in hardship as part of birr.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *bʾs = 'might; distress'. Baʾs = might in battle; baʾsāʾ = hardship. 'Patient in misfortune (al-baʾsāʾi) and hardship' (2:177). The root unites strength and suffering — the mighty can fall into distress.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: House. 73x. Bayt=house. 2:125: We made the House (al-Bayt) a place of return—the Kaba. Al-Bayt al-Ma'mur (the Frequented House, 52:4). Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). The root spans domestic dwelling and sacred sanctuary.
meaning.en_detailed: The root b-y-t (ب ي ت) names the house, dwelling, and the act of spending the night, occurring 73 times in the Quran. The noun bayt denotes a house, dwelling, or abode, and by extension the household, family, and family within. The form I bāta names the act of spending the night or becoming at night — 'and the night when it settles (bāt) on the mountains' (97:2). The Quran uses bayt for both ordinary homes (24:27) and sacred structures: al-Bayt (the House, i.e., the Kaʿbah at 2:125, 5:97), Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem, 17:1, 17:7), and al-Bayt al-Maʿmūr (the Frequented House in heaven, 52:4). The form II bayyata names planning by night (plotted secretly), as in 'and they plotted by night (bayyataū) and planned by day' (71:22). The noun buyūt (houses) and the active participle bāʾit (one who spends the night) extend the range. Cognate with Hebrew bayit and Akkadian bītu, the root preserves a pan-Semitic sense of domestic dwelling extended in the Quran to sacred architecture.

quranic_analysis.theme: al-Bayt: the Kaba
quranic_analysis.detail: Inna awwala baytin wudi'a li-al-nasi—the first House established for mankind is at Bakka.

derived_forms.meaning: to spend the night, become at night

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *byt = 'house, dwelling'. Bayt = house, home. Al-Bayt al-Ḥarām = the Sacred House (Kaʿbah). Al-Bayt al-Maʿmūr = the Frequented House in heaven. The root spans physical dwelling and divine sanctuary.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en_short: To live in luxury, affluence; to be spoiled by ease
meaning.en: To live in luxury, affluence; to be spoiled by ease
meaning.en_detailed: The triconsonantal root ت ر ف (ت ر ف) — 8 Quranic occurrences — fundamentally expresses To live in luxury, affluence; to be spoiled by ease. Key Quranic occurrences include 23:33. The Proto-Semitic antecedent *tarifa underlies this root, with cognates attested in related Semitic languages. The root yields derived forms including IV, each extending the core meaning into specific semantic domains.
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To live in luxury, affluence; to be spoiled by ease
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ت ر ف — 8 مرة — To live in luxury

etymology.notes: Proto-Semitic *tarifa 'to be fresh, luxuriant.' Arabic developed the sense of living in ease and luxury. The Hebrew cognate ṭāraf shifted to 'tear' (from pulling fresh leaves), but retained 'fresh/plump' in Rabbinic usage.

lexicographical_sources: Raghib: al-taraf is al-tanaʿʿum
theological_dimensions: Luxury as divine test — prosperity is not divine favor
hadith_evidence: The poor enter Paradise before the rich

meaning.en: Seven. Sab'=seven. Sabu=wild beast. 2:29: made seven heavens. 5:3: that eaten by wild beasts (al-sabu').
meaning.en_detailed: The root s-b-ʿ (س ب ع) names the number seven and a predatory animal, occurring 28 times in the Quran. The numeral sabʿ and its masculine form sabʿah name the number seven — 'and We created above you seven [heavens] (sabʿ samāwāt)' (23:17, 65:12, 67:3). The same root names the wild predator: 'and that hunted by a wild beast (sabuʿ)' (5:4, 5:94) defines a category of lawful game. The dual sense — number and predator — preserves a possible etymological link to satisfaction or fullness (Hebrew šebaʿ), though the semantic split is complete in Arabic. The intensive form sabaʿa names the act of multiplying sevenfold, as in 'if you multiplied seven hundred times' (2:261, the 'seven hundred multiplier' in divine recompense). The masdar sabʿah names the state of being complete, as in the unit of seven days (2:189). The Quranic usage reinforces both the cosmological structure of seven heavens and the ethical category of the beast of prey.

quranic_analysis.theme: Seven heavens
quranic_analysis.detail: Fa-sawwahunna sab'a samawatin—fashioned them seven heavens.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *šbʿ = 'seven; to be full/satisfied'. Sabʿ = seven. The dual sense 'seven' and 'satiety' may be linked — seven as the number of fullness/completion. The Quran's sabʿ samāwāt (seven heavens) and sabʿ sinīn (seven years) use the number.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: One. Wahid=One. Ahad=One (unique). 112:1: Say: He is Allah, the One (Ahadun). 2:163: Your God is One God (Ilahun Wahidun).
meaning.en_detailed: The root w-ḥ-d (و ح د) names oneness, solitude, and the unique unity of God, occurring 68 times in the Quran. The noun wāḥid names 'one' as numerical singular — 'your God is one God (ʾilāhun wāḥidun)' (2:163, 37:4) — while waḥdahu names the state of being alone (2:138, 6:19). The Quranic concept of tawḥīd (making God one) is derived from this root, as is the theological term waḥdāniyyah (divine unicity). The active participle wāḥid and the divine name al-Wāḥid name God as the One — 'and your God is one, so to Him submit' (22:34). The form V tawaḥḥada names the act of being solitary (not used as a Quranic finite verb). Cognate with Hebrew yāḥid (unique) and Akkadian eḫed, the root interweaves the numerical one with the metaphysical singular. The Quranic discourse distinguishes wāḥid (numerical) from aḥad (ontological uniqueness), but both anchor the doctrine of strict monotheism that defines the Islamic understanding of God.

quranic_analysis.theme: Tawhid—divine oneness
quranic_analysis.detail: Qul huwa Allahu Ahad—Say: He is Allah, the One.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *wḥd = 'one, alone, unique'. Wāḥid = one (numerical). Waḥdahu = alone. The Quranic tawḥīd (making God one) is implicit in the root — God's unity and uniqueness.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en_short: To leave, abandon, forsake; to let be; to relinquish
meaning.en: Taraka means he left, abandoned, let be. Ranges from neutral leaving to negative desertion. In the Quran: physical leaving, moral abandonment, divine forbearance, leaving inheritance.
meaning.ar: رفض الشيء وخلى عنه
meaning.en_detailed: The Arabic root ت ر ك (ت ر ك) appears 43 times in the Quran, governing the semantic domain of To leave, abandon, forsake; to let be; to relinquish. Key Quranic occurrences include 74:11. The Proto-Semitic antecedent *tarak- (to leave, abandon) underlies this root, with cognates attested in related Semitic languages. The root yields derived forms including I, each extending the core meaning into specific semantic domains.
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To leave, abandon, forsake; to let be; to relinquish
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ت ر ك — 43 مرة — To leave

etymology.semantic_evolution: Arabic root — basic human action of leaving behind.

usage_patterns: Tark as divine action: God leaves the defiant

lexicographical_sources: Ibn Faris: al-tark is rafḍ al-shayʾ
theological_dimensions: When God leaves someone, it is active punishment
hadith_evidence: I have left among you that which if you hold to it...

meaning.en: To entrust, rely. 70x. Tawakkala V=rely upon—tawakkaltu ala Allah. Al-Wakil=the Trustee (divine name). 3:159: when you decide, rely upon Allah (fa-tawakkal ala Allah). The root denotes complete trust and delegation.
meaning.en_detailed: The root w-k-l (و ك ل) names trust, reliance, and the act of entrusting one's affairs to another, occurring 70 times in the Quran. The verb wakala means to entrust — 'and the people of Pharaoh, did they not trust (yattakilūn) [in Pharaoh]?' (28:78) — and the form V tawakkala names the act of relying upon God. The noun tawakkul names the act of reliance as a permanent disposition — 'and upon Allah rely (tawakkal), if you are believers' (5:23). The active participle wakīl names one who is entrusted as a guardian or trustee — 'and Allah is sufficient as a trustee (wakīl)' (4:81, 4:132). The divine name al-Wakīl (The Trustee, The Disposer of Affairs) is among the names of God, applied 14 times across the Quran. The noun wikālah and the later term wikīl (agent, lawyer) are derived from this root. Distinct from amanah (trust) and tawfīq (divine enabling), tawakkul names the conscious act of placing one's dependence on God alone.

quranic_analysis.theme: Tawakkul: trust in Allah
quranic_analysis.detail: Fa-tawakkal ala Allah—rely upon Allah. The root of Islamic spirituality.

derived_forms.meaning: to place trust in, rely upon

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *wkl = 'to entrust, rely'. Arabic wakala = to entrust. Tawakkul = reliance upon God. Wakīl = trustee, guardian, lawyer. 'And upon Allah let the believers rely (fa-l-yatawakkali al-muʾminūn)' (3:122).

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en_short: To follow, recite, read aloud; to come after, succeed
meaning.en: Two primary senses: (1) to recite, read aloud (tala), especially scripture — 'those who recite (yatluna) the Book of God', and (2) to follow, come after (tala/tuliya). The two are connected: recitation 'follows' the text word by word. Tilawa is the act of reciting Quran — a central devotional practice. The noun tila refers to those who come after, later generations.
meaning.ar: القراءة والاتباع — تلاوة الكتاب واتباع الشيء
meaning.en_detailed: ت ل و (ت ل و), a root appearing 63 times in the Quran, encodes the notion of To follow, recite, read aloud; to come after, succeed across its various verbal and nominal forms. Key Quranic occurrences include 2:121. The Proto-Semitic antecedent *talay- (to follow, recite) underlies this root, with cognates attested in related Semitic languages. The root yields derived forms including I, each extending the core meaning into specific semantic domains.
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To follow, recite, read aloud; to come after, succeed
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ت ل و — 63 مرة — To follow

etymology.semantic_evolution: Proto-Semitic 'to follow/lift up' — recitation as lifting the voice to follow text. Tilawa is a key Quranic concept.

derived_forms.meaning: to recite, read aloud; to follow
derived_forms.key_verse: 2:121 يَتۡلُونَهُۥ حَقَّ تِلَاوَتِهِۦ — recite it as it should be recited

usage_patterns: Tilawa as devotional act: recitation as following the divine word

lexicographical_sources: Raghib: al-tilawa is al-ittibaʿ — following closely
theological_dimensions: Tilawa as a form of worship — the Quran is meant to be recited, not merely read
hadith_evidence: The Prophet's recitation was tartil (measured, deliberate tilawa)

meaning.en: To dwell; tranquility. 69x. Sakana=dwell. Sakinah=tranquility. Maskan=dwelling. 9:40: Allah sent down His tranquility (sakinatahu) upon him. 30:21: He created spouses that you may find tranquility (li-taskunu) with them.
meaning.en_detailed: The root s-k-n (س ك ن) names dwelling, tranquility, and the act of settling in a place, occurring 69 times in the Quran. The verb sakana means to dwell, reside, or be still — 'and We said, dwell (uskun) you and your wife in the garden' (2:35) — and the form IV askana names the causative act of settling or lodging. The noun sakīnah names divine tranquility, the calm that descends upon believers in moments of crisis — 'then Allah sent down His sakīnah upon him' (9:40, 48:4, 48:18). The noun maskan denotes a dwelling or abode — 'and Allah has made for you a place of rest (maskan) in your homes' (16:80) — and the active participle sākin names one who dwells. At 30:21 'He placed between you affection and mercy; in this are signs for a people who reflect' pairs dwelling (taskunū) with the marital covenant. Cognate with Hebrew shākan (to dwell), the root names the theological bridge between physical abode and spiritual stillness.

quranic_analysis.theme: Sakinah: divine tranquility
quranic_analysis.detail: Fa-anzala Allahu sakinatahu—Allah sent down His tranquility. Spiritual peace as divine gift.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *skn = 'to dwell, settle, be still'. Sakana = to be still, dwell. Sakīnah = divine tranquility. Maskūn = inhabited. The Quranic 'He made for you spouses that you may find tranquility (taskunū) with them' (30:21) — dwelling as peace.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: To perish, be destroyed. 68x. Halaka=perish. 28:88: everything perishes (halikun) except His Face. 40:34: you had come to them with clear proofs—but they perished. The root denotes absolute destruction.
meaning.en_detailed: The root h-l-k (ه ل ك) names perishing, destruction, and the cessation of existence, occurring 68 times in the Quran. The verb halaka means to perish or be destroyed — 'and everything will perish (halik) except His Face' (28:88) — and the form IV ahlaka names the causative act of destroying or annihilating. The verbal noun halāk names the state of ruin or perdition — 'and whoever comes to you of those who believe in Our signs — he will be admitted into gardens' (2:62). The active participle hālik names one who is perishing, and the passive muhlak names one who is destroyed. The Quran uses the root for both natural perishing (death) and divine destruction (the punishment of nations): 'and We destroyed (ahlaknā) the generations before you' (6:6, 17:17, 30:9). The verb tahayyara does not belong to this root but is a homograph. Cognate with Hebrew hālak (to go, walk — a different semantic path), Arabic halaka preserves the sense of irreversible destruction.

quranic_analysis.theme: Everything perishes
quranic_analysis.detail: Kullu shay'in halikun illa wajhahu—everything perishes except His Face.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *hlk = 'to perish, be destroyed'. Halaka = to perish. Halāk = destruction. The Quran narrates the destruction of nations: 'We destroyed (ahlaknā) the generations before you' (6:6).

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en_short: To be firm, stable, steady; to confirm, establish; steadfastness
meaning.en: The root thaʾ-baʾ-taʾ denotes firmness, stability, and steadfastness. The Form I verb thabata means 'he was firm, steady'. Form II thabbata means 'He made firm, He confirmed, He stabilized' — used of God strengthening believers in battle and faith. Thubat is a firm footing in war. The root bridges physical stability (feet planted) and spiritual steadfastness (heart confirmed in faith).
meaning.ar: الرسوخ والاستقرار — ثبات القدم وثبات القلب
meaning.en_detailed: Occurring 18 times in the Quranic text, the root ث ب ت (ث ب ت) conveys the essential concept of To be firm, stable, steady; to confirm, establish; steadfastness. Key Quranic occurrences include 3:147. The Proto-Semitic antecedent *ṯabat- (to be firm, stable) underlies this root, with cognates attested in related Semitic languages. The root yields derived forms including I, II, each extending the core meaning into specific semantic domains.
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To be firm, stable, steady; to confirm, establish; steadfastness
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ث ب ت — 18 مرة — To be firm

etymology.semantic_evolution: Arabic root — the concept of firmness/stability developed richly in Quranic Arabic, especially in contexts of battle and faith.

derived_forms.key_verse: 47:21 طَاعَةٌۭ وَقَوْلٌۭ مَّعۡرُوفٌۭ — obedience and appropriate speech, then when the matter is firm…
3:147 رَبَّنَا ٱغۡفِرۡ لَنَا ذُنُوبَنَا وَإِسۡرَافَنَا فِىٓ أَمۡرِنَا وَثَبِّتۡ أَقۡدَامَنَا

usage_patterns: Tathbit as divine action: God confirms the believers in faith and battle

lexicographical_sources: Ibn Faris: al-thabt is rusukh al-qadam
theological_dimensions: Tathbit al-qulub — God's confirmation of hearts in faith
hadith_evidence: Prophet's prayer: 'Ya Muqallib al-qulub, thabbit qalbi 'ala dinik'

meaning.en: Crime, sin. 66x. Mujrim=criminal, sinner. Ajrama IV=commit crime. 7:40: the gates of heaven will not be opened for those who deny Our signs—thus We recompense the criminals (al-mujrimin).
meaning.en_detailed: The root j-r-m (ج ر م) names crime, sin, and the cutting off of moral standing, occurring 66 times in the Quran. The verb jarama means to commit (a crime) or to cut off, and the noun jurm names a crime or offense as something that 'cuts off' the perpetrator from righteousness. The active participle mujrim names one who commits crimes — 'so today We will save you in body that you may be a sign to those after you, and indeed, many of the people, of Our signs, are heedless' (10:92 uses the related theme of escape; mujrim appears in 7:40, 28:59, 30:12). The form IV ajrama adds the causative sense of rendering someone a criminal. The Quranic jurm names both the legal offense (an act of retribution, 5:49) and the metaphysical offense (an act of disbelief, 6:120). The noun mujrimūn (criminals) appears with mu'minūn (believers) as a paired category in dozens of verses. Cognate with Hebrew gāram (to provoke), the root binds together 'to cut' (physical separation) and 'to sin' (moral separation).
meaning.ar_definition: جذر جَرَمَ — 66 مرة — crime, sin; to commit

quranic_analysis.theme: The criminals
quranic_analysis.detail: Al-mujrimin—the criminals who reject divine signs face ultimate punishment.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *ǧrm = 'to cut → to commit'. Jarama = to cut; to commit (a crime). Jarm = cutting off; crime. Jurm = sin, offense. The 'cutting off' from righteousness → criminal act. 'Their crime (jurm) against us' — the disbelievers' admission.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: Eye; spring. 65x. Ayn=eye; spring. 5:45: an eye for an eye (al-ayna bi al-ayni). 2:60: twelve springs (aynan) gushed forth—Moses. The root spans physical vision and gushing water.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ʿ-y-n (ع ي ن) names both the eye and the spring of water, occurring 65 times in the Quran. The noun ʿayn denotes the organ of sight and the natural spring, with the plural ʿuyūn naming both eyes and springs. The semantic bridge lies in the image of the spring as the 'eye' of the earth — a source that flows continuously, like the human eye that sees. At 5:45 the principle of 'al-ʿaynu bi-l-ʿayni (an eye for an eye)' establishes the lex talionis of retributive justice. At 2:60 'We caused twelve springs to gush forth (ʿuyūn)' for the twelve tribes of Israel at al-Tīh. The Quranic paradise is described as containing flowing springs — 'and rivers of water, milk, wine, and honey' (47:15). The active participle ʿāʾin names one who sees, and the noun ʿayn preserves the sense of essence (the very 'eye' of a thing). Cognate with Hebrew ʿayin and Akkadian īnu, the root preserves a pan-Semitic sense that connects vision with the source.

quranic_analysis.theme: Eye and spring
quranic_analysis.detail: Al-aynu bi al-ayni—retributive justice. Springs as divine provision.

derived_forms.meaning: eye; spring of water; essential self

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *ʿyn = 'eye, spring'. ʿAyn = eye, spring of water. The dual sense: the eye as the organ of sight and the spring as the 'eye' of the earth. Paradise's ʿuyūn (springs) flow for the righteous.

hadith_evidence.ar: اللَّهُمَّ اسْقِنَا غَيْثًا مُغِيثًا
hadith_evidence.en: O Allah, send us rain, a beneficial rain.

meaning.en_short: To destroy, prevent from good; perdition, ruin, loss
meaning.en: The root thaʾ-baʾ-raʾ denotes destruction, perdition, and prevention from good. The Form I verb thabara means 'he destroyed' or 'he prevented from good/Paradise'. The noun thubur means 'perdition, destruction, ruin' — the cry of the damned in Hell is 'wa thuburahu' (Oh, destruction upon him!). It is the opposite of najat (salvation).
meaning.ar: الهلاك والخسران — الثبور ضد النجاة
meaning.en_detailed: ث ب ر (ث ب ر), a root appearing 5 times in the Quran, encodes the notion of To destroy, prevent from good; perdition, ruin, loss across its various verbal and nominal forms. Key Quranic occurrences include 25:13-14. The Proto-Semitic antecedent *ṯabar- (to destroy, break) underlies this root, with cognates attested in related Semitic languages. The root yields derived forms including I, each extending the core meaning into specific semantic domains. The root carries significant theological weight in the Quranic worldview, recurring in contexts that shape Islamic doctrine and spiritual understanding.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ث ب ر — 5 مرة — To destroy

etymology.semantic_evolution: Arabic root — thubur is the anguished cry of the damned, the recognition of eternal loss.

derived_forms.meaning: to destroy; to prevent from good

usage_patterns: Thubur as eschatological cry of the damned

lexicographical_sources: Ibn Faris: al-thabr is al-halak
theological_dimensions: Thubur as the recognition of absolute loss in the afterlife

hadith_evidence.ar: ث ب ر — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 5 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root vbr (ث ب ر) appears 5 times in the Quran, including 25:13-14.

meaning.en_short: To find, encounter, catch; to be skilled, cultured, refined
meaning.en: The root thaʾ-qaf-faʾ denotes finding, encountering, and catching — often in hostile contexts (finding enemies in battle). The Form I verb thaqifa means 'he found, encountered, caught'. The passive thaqifa means 'he was found/caught'. Post-Quranically, thaqafa developed into 'culture' and 'education' — one who is 'found' to be refined and learned (thaqif = cultured).
meaning.ar: الظفر بالشيء، والإدراك، والصيرورة حاذقًا
meaning.en_detailed: Root ث ق ف (ث ق ف), attested 6 times in the Quran, derives its core meaning of To find, encounter, catch; to be skilled, cultured, refined from Proto-Semitic sources. Key Quranic occurrences include 2:191, 4:91, 2:191, 4:91, 2:191, 4:91, 2:191, 4:91. The Proto-Semitic antecedent *ṯaqaf- (to find, catch) underlies this root, with cognates attested in related Semitic languages. The root yields derived forms including I, each extending the core meaning into specific semantic domains.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ث ق ف — 6 مرة — To find

etymology.semantic_evolution: Arabic root — the 'find/catch' sense developed into 'culture' as the quality of a person who has been 'caught' (trained) into refinement.

usage_patterns: Thaqifa in combat contexts: finding and overtaking enemies

lexicographical_sources: Ibn Faris: al-thaqf is al-ẓafar bi-l-shayʾ
theological_dimensions: From 'catching' to 'culture' — post-Quranic semantic evolution

hadith_evidence.ar: أَكْثِرُوا ذِكْرَ هَادِمِ اللَّذَّاتِ — الْمَوْتِ
hadith_evidence.en: Increase remembrance of the destroyer of pleasures — death.

meaning.en: Originate. Ansha'a=originate. 6:6: We raised (ansha'na) after them another generation—succession of civilizations.
meaning.en_detailed: The root n-sh-ʾ (ن ش أ) names origination, creation, and the act of bringing something into being, occurring 28 times in the Quran. The form IV anshaʾa means to originate, raise, or bring forth — 'and We raised (anshaʾnā) after them another generation' (6:6, 23:42, 71:11) names the succession of human civilizations. The verb nashaʾa can mean to grow up (as a youth) or to be raised, and the form IV adds the intensified sense of founding or establishing. The Quran uses the root for the act of founding nations and raising generations — 'and it is He who produced you from a single soul, and [gave you] a place of dwelling and a place of storage' (6:98 uses a related sense; n-sh-ʾ is used for the founding of new communities in 23:42, 71:11). The active participle nāshiʾ can name the nascent, the growing, or the upcoming (in time), as in 'and by the night when it departs' (the passing away, 89:4). The noun nushūʾ names the act of growing or rising up. The semantic range covers growth, origination, and the act of bringing a thing into existence.

quranic_analysis.theme: Raising new generations
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa ansha'na min ba'dihim qarnan akharin—new generation.

hadith_evidence.ar: الْمُؤْمِنُ يَأْكُلُ فِي مِعًى وَاحِدٍ وَالْكَافِرُ يَأْكُلُ فِي سَبْعَةِ أَمْعَاءٍ
hadith_evidence.en: The believer eats in one intestine and the disbeliever eats in seven intestines.

meaning.en: To decree, judge. 63x. Qada=decree, judge. 3:47: when He decrees (qada) a matter, He says Be and it is. 2:200: when you have completed (qadaytum) your rites—Hajj. The root spans divine decree and human fulfillment.
meaning.en_detailed: Root q-ḍ-y (63x) denotes divine decree, judgment, and completion—a single triliteral that links cosmic causation to human obligation. Qaḍā spans both the moment of divine command ('when He decrees a matter, He says to it "Be" and it is'—3:47, repeated at 2:117) and the human fulfillment of an obligation ('when you have completed [qadaytum] your rites'—2:200, addressing the pilgrims at the close of Hajj). The Quranic semantic field binds the eternal decree to its immediate execution in creation: God's qaḍā is never postponed, never provisional, and never reversible once uttered. The noun qaḍāʾ (~10x) names the decree itself in its abstract form, while the passive participle maqḍiyy marks what is 'decreed, ordained' from eternity, awaiting only its appointed hour.

quranic_analysis.theme: Divine decree (qada')
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa idha qada amran fa-innama yaqulu lahu kun fa-yakun—when He decrees, Be and it is.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *qḍy = 'to judge, decree, fulfill'. Qaḍā = to judge, decree, accomplish. Qaḍāʾ = divine decree, judgment. 'When He decrees (qaḍā) a matter, He only says to it: Be! and it is' (2:117).

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: Magic; dawn. 63x. Sihr=magic. Sahar=dawn. 2:102: they learned magic (al-sihr) from them—Harut and Marut. 54:34: the punishment seized them at dawn (bi al-sahar). The root spans forbidden sorcery and the blessing of predawn.
meaning.en_detailed: Root s-ḥ-r (63x) carries the dual semantic range of enchantment and pre-dawn, a striking confluence that distinguishes it from any near-cognate. Siḥr (magic, ~30x) names the forbidden art that the angels Harut and Marut taught in Babylon as a test for humanity (2:102), while saḥar denotes the predawn hour when divine punishment descends ('the cry seized them at dawn [bi-l-saḥar]'—54:34, the destruction of Lot's people). The verbal forms saḥara ('to enchant,' ~20x) and the active agent sāḥir (sorcerer, ~15x) populate the Quranic polemic against Pharaoh's magicians, whose contest with Moses (7:112-126) frames siḥr as deception set against the miracle as truth—wherever illusion meets revelation, illusion loses.

quranic_analysis.theme: Magic condemned
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa ma unzila ala al-malakayni—Harut and Marut teaching magic as a test.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *sḥr = 'to enchant, bewitch'. Saḥara = to enchant. Siḥr = magic. Sāḥir = magician. The Quranic polemic against siḥr — Moses vs Pharaoh's magicians (sāḥirūn). Magic as deception vs miracle as truth.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: To move. 2x. Harraka=move. 16:76: a speechless burden cannot move toward good.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ḥ-r-k (1x in the Quran) names physical motion and movement, attested principally in the intensive Form II harraka. The lone Quranic occurrence appears in 16:76 within the parable of the ungrateful servant: struck dumb, 'a burden laid down' who cannot 'move [yuharriku] himself toward good' despite wealth and entourage—the image of inert moral incapacity. The semantic field belongs to physical locomotion, distinct from the more common mshy (to walk), sāra (to travel), and the cosmological verb for celestial motion. The Quran's rare use may reflect Arabic preference for more specific movement roots in narrative, while the triliteral persisted robustly in later philosophical discourse on motion (harakah) as a technical term.

quranic_analysis.theme: The motionless
quranic_analysis.detail: La yaqdiru ala shay'in—cannot direct himself toward good.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en_short: To be heavy, weighty; burden, load; gravity, seriousness
meaning.en: The root thaʾ-qaf-lam denotes heaviness in all its forms: physical weight, moral burden, spiritual gravity, and eschatological significance. The Form I verb thaqula means 'to be heavy'. The noun thiql means 'weight, burden'. In the Quran: the scales weighing deeds (mawaazin), the Earth casting out its burdens, and the heaviness of the divine word about to be revealed. The root bridges literal mass and moral weight.
meaning.ar: ضد الخفة — الثقل في الوزن والحمل والأمر
meaning.en_detailed: ث ق ل (ث ق ل), a root appearing 28 times in the Quran, encodes the notion of To be heavy, weighty; burden, load; gravity, seriousness across its various verbal and nominal forms. Key Quranic occurrences include 99:2. The Proto-Semitic antecedent *ṯaql- (to be heavy, weighty) underlies this root, with cognates attested in related Semitic languages. The root yields derived forms including I, II, IV, each extending the core meaning into specific semantic domains.
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To be heavy, weighty; burden, load; gravity, seriousness
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ث ق ل — 28 مرة — To be heavy

etymology.semantic_evolution: Arabic root — heaviness as both physical and moral concept.

derived_forms.meaning: to be sluggish, reluctant, feel heavy

key_nominals.meaning: weight, burden; the two heavy things (mankind and jinn)

usage_patterns: Thaqalān: the two heavy/burdened races — mankind and jinn

lexicographical_sources: Raghib: al-thiql is mā yaṣʿubu ḥamaluhu
theological_dimensions: The word about to be revealed is 'weighty' (qawlan thaqilan, 73:5) — divine speech has gravity
hadith_evidence: Thaqalān hadith: 'I leave among you the two weighty things: the Book of God and my progeny'

meaning.en: To increase, add. 61x. Zada=increase. 14:7: if grateful, I will increase you (la-azidannakum). 2:10: Allah increases (yazidu) them in disease—the hypocrites.
meaning.en_detailed: Root z-y-d (61x) denotes increase, addition, and surplus—the divine gift of more, which the Quran ties directly to the moral posture of the recipient. The verb's reciprocity with gratitude is explicit: 'if you are grateful, I will surely increase you [la-azidannakum]' (14:7), and conversely 'Allah increases them in disease' for the hypocrites who compound their error (2:10). The reflexive Form VIII izdāda (~15x) marks intransitive increase without object, while the noun ziyādah (addition, ~5x) names the abstract surplus. The root culminates in the Prophet's supplication: 'My Lord, increase me [zidnī] in knowledge' (20:114)—a daily-pattern prayer that asks for ever-deepening gnosis rather than ever-accumulating information.

quranic_analysis.theme: Gratitude brings increase
quranic_analysis.detail: La-in shakartum la-azidannakum—divine promise of increase in response to gratitude.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *zyd = 'to increase, add'. Zāda = to increase. Ziyādah = addition, excess. 'And say: My Lord, increase me (zidnī) in knowledge' (20:114) — the Prophet's supplication for ever-increasing knowledge.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: Trial, tribulation. 60x. Fatana=test, try. Fitnah=test, persecution, trial. 2:191: persecution (al-fitnatu) is worse than killing. 8:28: your wealth and children are only a trial (fitnatun). Fitnah is civil strife—worse than war.
meaning.en_detailed: Root f-t-n (60x) denotes trial, testing, and persecution—a single triliteral that traverses the full spectrum from divine pedagogy to human cruelty. Fitnah (34x) names both the divine test that purifies ('you will surely be tested in your possessions and yourselves'—3:186) and the human tribulation that breaks ('persecution [al-fitnah] is worse than killing'—2:191). The verb fatana ('to test by fire,' ~30x) preserves the Semitic etymology of testing gold by fire to separate pure from dross. In 8:28, 'your wealth and children are only a trial [fitnatun]'—life itself becomes the crucible, and the fitnah the discriminator of belief from hypocrisy, of patience from panic, of faith from faction.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر فَتَنَ — 60 مرة — trial, tribulation; to test (fitnah)

quranic_analysis.theme: Fitnah: grave trial
quranic_analysis.detail: Al-fitnatu ashaddu min al-qatl—persecution is more severe than killing.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *ptn = 'to test by fire → to try, persecute'. Fitnah = trial, persecution, temptation. The original sense: testing gold by fire to separate pure from impure. 'The fitnah is worse than killing' (2:191) — persecution as a test of faith.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: Unseen, absent. 60x. Ghayb=unseen. 2:3: those who believe in the unseen (al-ghayb). 27:65: none knows the unseen (al-ghayb) of heavens and earth except Allah. The root denotes hidden reality known only to God.
meaning.en_detailed: Root gh-y-b (60x) names the unseen, the absent, and the hidden—the reality that lies beyond sensory access. Ghayb (~50x) is a Quranic cornerstone: 'those who believe in the unseen [al-ghayb]' (2:3) opens the list of the righteous, while 'none knows the unseen [ghayb] of the heavens and earth except Allah' (27:65, 11:123) makes divine omniscience exclusive and absolute. Faith, in the Quranic frame, is precisely the trust placed in what lies beyond verification—al-ghayb as the object of taqwā, the substance of revelation, and the boundary that separates created knowledge from divine knowledge. The opposite shuhūd (witnessed) completes the Quranic cosmology of knowing.

quranic_analysis.theme: Belief in the unseen
quranic_analysis.detail: Alladhina yu'minuna bi al-ghayb—belief in the unseen as first quality of the righteous.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *ġyb = 'to be absent, hidden'. Ghāba = to be absent. Ghayb = the unseen, the hidden realm. Al-Ghayb is a central Quranic concept — 'those who believe in the Unseen (al-ghayb)' (2:3). Faith requires trusting what is hidden from perception.

key_nominals.m: the Unseen, the hidden realm known only to God

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: The root thaʾ-lam-thaʾ denotes the number three and all its related concepts. The noun thalatha means 'three', thalith means 'third'. The verb thallatha means 'to triple, make three'. In the Quran, it appears as the cardinal number three, the ordinal third, and in theological polemic against trinitarian doctrine (thalithu thalathatin — 'third of three' in 5:73). The root is fundamental to Quranic arithmetic and theology.
meaning.ar: العدد المعروف بين الاثنين والأربعة
meaning.en_detailed: Root ث ل ث (ث ل ث), attested 32 times in the Quran, derives its core meaning of Three; third; to triple; trinity from Proto-Semitic sources. Key Quranic occurrences include 5:73, 4:12, 5:73, 4:12, 5:73, 4:12, 5:73, 4:12. The Proto-Semitic antecedent *ṯalāṯ- (three) underlies this root, with cognates attested in related Semitic languages. The root yields derived forms including I, II, each extending the core meaning into specific semantic domains.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ث ل ث — 32 مرة — Three

etymology.semantic_evolution: Proto-Semitic number three — stable across all Semitic languages.

Thalithu thalathah: Quranic refutation of trinitarianism
