hadith_evidence.en: The root vlv (ث ل ث) appears 32 times in the Quran, including 5:73.

meaning.en_short: Fruit, produce; to bear fruit, be productive, yield
meaning.en: The root thaʾ-mim-raʾ denotes fruit (thamar) and the process of fruiting and yielding produce. In the Quran, thamarat means 'fruits' — used literally of agricultural produce and metaphorically of the fruits of one's deeds. The verb athmara (Form IV) means 'it bore fruit'. The root emphasizes the result, yield, and benefit of something — the productive outcome of labor, faith, or divine blessing.
meaning.ar: حَمْلُ الشَّجَرِ — الثَّمَرُ وَالنَّتَاجُ
meaning.en_detailed: The triconsonantal root ث م ر (ث م ر) — 24 Quranic occurrences — fundamentally expresses Fruit, produce; to bear fruit, be productive, yield. Key Quranic occurrences include 6:141, 2:155, 6:141, 2:155, 6:141, 2:155, 6:141, 2:155. The Proto-Semitic antecedent *ṯamar- (fruit, produce) underlies this root, with cognates attested in related Semitic languages. The root yields derived forms including I, IV, each extending the core meaning into specific semantic domains.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ث م ر — 24 مرة — Fruit

etymology.semantic_evolution: Arabic root — fruit as the tangible result of a process, bridging agriculture and ethics.

usage_patterns: Fruits as divine provision and sign of God's bounty

lexicographical_sources: Ibn Faris: al-thamar is ḥaml al-shajar
theological_dimensions: Fruit-bearing as a metaphor for the results of faith and righteous deeds

hadith_evidence.ar: ث م ر — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 24 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root vmr (ث م ر) appears 24 times in the Quran, including 6:141.

meaning.en_short: Price, value, cost; eighth; to price, value
meaning.en: The root thaʾ-mim-nun has two primary senses: (1) price, value, or cost (thaman) — what is paid in exchange for something, and (2) the number eight/eighth (thamaniya, thamin). In the Quran, thaman appears in commercial contexts — things sold 'for a small price' (thamanan qalilan), i.e., selling divine truth for worldly gain. The number eight appears in the creation narrative (eight pairs of cattle) and in eschatology (eight angels bearing the Throne).
meaning.ar: قِيمَةُ الشَّيْءِ وَعِوَضُهُ — وَالْعَدَدُ بَعْدَ السَّبْعَةِ
meaning.en_detailed: ث م ن (ث م ن), a root appearing 19 times in the Quran, encodes the notion of Price, value, cost; eighth; to price, value across its various verbal and nominal forms. Key Quranic occurrences include 2:41, 69:17, 2:41, 69:17, 2:41, 69:17, 2:41, 69:17. The Proto-Semitic antecedent *ṯaman- (price; eight) underlies this root, with cognates attested in related Semitic languages. The root yields derived forms including I, each extending the core meaning into specific semantic domains. The root carries significant theological weight in the Quranic worldview, recurring in contexts that shape Islamic doctrine and spiritual understanding.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ث م ن — 19 مرة — Price

etymology.semantic_evolution: Arabic root — price/eight dual sense. The number eight may relate to a base-4 counting system.

derived_forms.meaning: to price, value; to be expensive

usage_patterns: Thaman as value exchanged — spiritual vs material transaction

lexicographical_sources: Ibn Faris: al-thaman is ʿiwad al-shayʾ
theological_dimensions: Selling divine signs for a small price: the ultimate bad bargain

hadith_evidence.ar: ث م ن — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 19 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root vmn (ث م ن) appears 19 times in the Quran, including 2:41.

meaning.en_short: To strike; to set forth (a parable)
meaning.en: To strike; set forth. 58x. Daraba=strike, coin, set forth. 2:26: Allah is not ashamed to set forth (yadriba) a parable. 57:13: a wall will be set up (duriba) between them—Paradise and Hell. The root spans physical striking and rhetorical exemplification.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ḍ-r-b (58x) centers on striking, with the Quran's distinctive semantic extension to rhetorical exemplification that defines much Quranic style. The verb's most iconic use: 'Allah is not ashamed to set forth [yadriba] a parable' (2:26) and 'He sets forth for you a parable [mathalan]' (14:24). Daraba thus spans physical striking, traveling (ḍarb fī al-arḍ), coinage (ḍarb al-dirham), separation ('a wall will be set up [ḍuriba] between them'—57:13), and the iconic ḍaraba mathalan ('to strike an example'). The verbal noun ḍarb (5x) names type and kind by metonymy. The 58 occurrences make this one of the Quran's most semantically loaded triliterals, a single root uniting hand and metaphor.

quranic_analysis.theme: Daraba mathalan
quranic_analysis.detail: Yadribu Allahu al-amthala—Allah sets forth parables. The central Quranic rhetorical device.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *ḍrb = 'to strike, beat'. Uniquely prominent in Arabic. The Quran innovated the semantic extension 'ḍaraba mathalan' (to set forth an example/parable) — a striking metaphor that 'strikes' the mind. The root also covers physical striking, travel (ḍarb fī al-arḍ), and coinage (ḍarb al-darāhim).

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: To wade. Khada=wade, plunge. 4:140: when you hear Allah's verses rejected—do not sit with them until they engage in other talk (yakhudu fi hadithin ghayrih).
meaning.en_detailed: Root kh-w-ḍ (12x) means to wade or plunge into a fluid medium, used both literally and metaphorically in the Quran. The central Quranic usage in 4:140 commands believers, upon hearing the verses mocked, to 'not sit with them until they plunge [yakhūḍū] into other talk [ḥadīth ghayrih]'—avoiding complicity in blasphemy by withdrawing before the conversation turns. The verbal image is that of wading through water: immersion in discourse, not mere verbal exchange. The same root names the navigating of ships ('when they ride in ships, they supplicate Allah, sincere to Him in faith'—29:65). The semantic field extends from literal wading to the active engagement with risky speech—wading as both physical passage and moral hazard.

quranic_analysis.theme: Avoid vain talk
quranic_analysis.detail: Hatta yakhudu fi hadithin ghayrihi—until they wade into other talk.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: Thawab means reward, recompense for deeds. Also means garment — that which 'returns' to cover the body. The verb thaba means 'he returned'. In the Quran: reward for good deeds and the 'garments' of Paradise (thiyab).
meaning.ar: الثواب والجزاء، واللباس الذي يعود على البدن
meaning.en_detailed: Occurring 28 times in the Quranic text, the root ث و ب (ث و ب) conveys the essential concept of Reward, recompense; garment; to return. Key Quranic occurrences include 3:145, 18:31, 3:145, 18:31, 3:145, 18:31, 3:145, 18:31. The Proto-Semitic antecedent *ṯawb- (to return; garment) underlies this root, with cognates attested in related Semitic languages. The root yields derived forms including I, IV, X, each extending the core meaning into specific semantic domains. The root carries significant theological weight in the Quranic worldview, recurring in contexts that shape Islamic doctrine and spiritual understanding.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ث و ب — 28 مرة — Reward

etymology.semantic_evolution: Reward as that which 'returns' to the doer. Garment as that which 'returns' to cover.

usage_patterns: Reward as return on investment of deeds

lexicographical_sources: Raghib: al-thawāb is mā yarjiʿu ʿalā al-ʿabd min jazāʾ ʿamalihi
theological_dimensions: Thawāb as eschatological concept

hadith_evidence.ar: ث و ب — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 28 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root vwb (ث و ب) appears 28 times in the Quran, including 3:145.

meaning.en: To forbid. 56x. Naha=forbid. Nahy munkar=forbidding wrong. 16:90: Allah commands justice and forbids (yanha) indecency and wrongdoing. The antonym of amr (command)—the amr/nahy binary is foundational to Islamic ethics.
meaning.en_detailed: Root n-h-y (56x) denotes prohibition, restraint, and abstention—the structural counterpart of amr (command) in the Quranic ethical binary. The Quran makes the pairing explicit: 'Allah commands justice and forbids [yanhā] indecency and wrongdoing [al-fahshā'a wa al-munkar]' (16:90). The Form VIII intahā ('to desist, reach the limit,' ~15x) marks the boundary action—ceasing at the threshold—and yields the noun muntahā ('the utmost limit,' ~5x), used of both spatial and temporal endpoints ('the limit of the night'—the dawn). Al-amr bi-l-ma'rūf wa-l-nahy 'an al-munkar (commanding right, forbidding wrong) becomes a foundational communal duty in the Quranic polity, the twin limbs of public ethical action.

quranic_analysis.theme: Commanding right, forbidding wrong
quranic_analysis.detail: Yanha ani al-fahsha'i wa al-munkar—He forbids indecency and wrongdoing.

derived_forms.meaning: to cease, desist, come to an end

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *nhy = 'to forbid, prohibit, restrain'. Nahā = to forbid. Nahy = prohibition. Al-Nāhī = the Forbidder. 'He forbids (yanhā) indecency and wrong' (16:90). The nahy ʿan al-munkar (forbidding evil) is a communal obligation.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en_short: To stir up, excite, arouse; to rebel
meaning.en: Verbs: athāra (Form IV) means 'he stirred up, raised, provoked'. Typically used for raising dust, provoking rebellion, or stirring up conflict. Rare in Quran but significant in narrative contexts (the golden calf story).
meaning.ar: إثارة الشيء وهيجانه
meaning.en_detailed: Root ث و ر (ث و ر), attested 5 times in the Quran, derives its core meaning of To stir up, excite, arouse; to rebel from Proto-Semitic sources. Key Quranic occurrences include 2:71. The Proto-Semitic antecedent *ṯawr- (to stir, excite) underlies this root, with cognates attested in related Semitic languages. The root yields derived forms including IV, each extending the core meaning into specific semantic domains.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ث و ر — 5 مرة — To stir up

etymology.semantic_evolution: From 'stirring up' (dust, emotions) — related to the noun thawr (bull) which stirs up dust when charging?

derived_forms.key_verse: 2:71 تُثِيرُ ٱلۡأَرۡضَ — stirring up the earth

usage_patterns: Stirring up the earth (plowing) as the opposite of the sacrificial cow

lexicographical_sources: Ibn Faris: al-thawr is hayajān al-shayʾ

hadith_evidence.ar: ث و ر — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 5 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root vwr (ث و ر) appears 5 times in the Quran, including 2:71.

meaning.en: Weakness. 52x. Da'ufa=be weak. Da'if=weak. 4:28: mankind was created weak (da'ifan). 8:66: if there are a hundred patient, they overcome two hundred. The root acknowledges human frailty and compensates through divine support.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ḍ-'-f (52x) names weakness, frailty, and diminution, with a secondary semantic branch meaning 'to double' (ḍi'f) that points to an older root-meaning of redundancy or folding. The Quran acknowledges human frailty as constitutive: 'mankind was created weak [ḍa'īfan]' (4:28), but compensates through divine support—'if there are a hundred patient among you, they overcome two hundred by Allah's permission' (8:66). The Quranic pattern: from ḍa'f (weakness) to quwwah (strength) is the arc of divine empowerment, reversing the human constitution (30:54). The root belongs to a moral-spiritual vocabulary rather than a physical one—weakness as an epistemological category, not merely a bodily state.

quranic_analysis.theme: Human weakness
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa khuliqa al-insanu da'ifan—mankind was created weak.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *ḍʿf = 'to be weak'. Ḍaʿufa = to be weak. Ḍaʿf = weakness. Ḍiʿf = double, twice. 'He created you from weakness (ḍaʿf), then made you strong' — human frailty and divine empowerment.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: Sea. 42x. Bahr=sea. Bahr=singular, Bihar=plural. 2:50: We parted the sea (al-bahr). Two seas sweet and salty.
meaning.en_detailed: Root b-ḥ-r (42x) denotes the sea or large body of water, paralleling Hebrew yām and Geez bāḥr—cognates that confirm an ancient Semitic maritime lexicon. The Quran's marine imagery includes the parting of the sea for Moses' people ('We parted the sea [al-baḥr] for you'—2:50) and the famous cosmography of two seas ('He released the two seas [al-baḥrayn] to meet, yet between them is a barrier they do not cross'—55:19-20). The plural biḥār extends to all large waters, while the Quran deploys the sea as a site of both divine power (saving the believer) and human peril (drowning the disbeliever)—a moral geography of the deep that maps heaven's favor and wrath onto the world's waters.

quranic_analysis.theme: Parting of the sea
quranic_analysis.detail: Fa-faraqna bikum al-bahra—We parted the sea for you.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *bḥr = 'sea, ocean'. Baḥr = sea. 'Two seas (baḥrayn) meet but do not mix' (55:19-20) — the Quranic marine metaphor.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: Mathwan means dwelling place, abode, or resting place. The verb thawā means 'he stayed, dwelt'. Used in the Quran for dwellings in this world and the next — both Paradise and Hell as eternal abodes. Mathwā al-mutakabbirīn (the abode of the arrogant) is Hell.
meaning.ar: الإقامة والمكث في المكان
meaning.en_detailed: Root ث و ي (ث و ي), attested 14 times in the Quran, derives its core meaning of To dwell, stay, abide, remain from Proto-Semitic sources. Key Quranic occurrences include 12:21, 3:151, 12:21, 3:151, 12:21, 3:151, 12:21, 3:151. The Proto-Semitic antecedent *ṯaway- (to dwell, stay) underlies this root, with cognates attested in related Semitic languages. The root yields derived forms including I, IV, each extending the core meaning into specific semantic domains. The root carries significant theological weight in the Quranic worldview, recurring in contexts that shape Islamic doctrine and spiritual understanding.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ث و ي — 14 مرة — To dwell

etymology.semantic_evolution: Dwelling/staying — the noun mathwan is the standard Quranic term for eternal abode in the afterlife.

usage_patterns: Mathwā as eschatological destination — both Paradise and Hell

lexicographical_sources: Raghib: al-mathwā is mawḍiʿ al-ʾiqāma
theological_dimensions: Mathwā al-mutakabbirīn — the abode of the arrogant

hadith_evidence.ar: ث و ي — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 14 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root vwy (ث و ي) appears 14 times in the Quran, including 12:21.

meaning.en: Jaḥīm is one of the primary Quranic names for Hell — the blazing, intensely hot fire. From the root meaning 'to be intensely hot'. Unlike nār (general fire), jaḥīm specifically denotes the raging, consuming fire of Hell. It appears 26 times, always in eschatological contexts.
meaning.ar: النار الشديدة التأجج — اسم من أسماء جهنم
meaning.en_detailed: The Arabic root ج ح م (ج ح م) appears 26 times in the Quran, governing the semantic domain of Blazing fire, Hell-fire; intense heat. Key Quranic occurrences include 2:119, 37:163, 2:119, 37:163, 2:119, 37:163, 2:119, 37:163. The Proto-Semitic antecedent *jaḥīm- (blazing heat) underlies this root, with cognates attested in related Semitic languages. The root carries significant theological weight in the Quranic worldview, recurring in contexts that shape Islamic doctrine and spiritual understanding.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ج ح م — 26 مرة — Blazing fire

etymology.semantic_evolution: Intense heat → specifically Hell-fire. One of seven Quranic names for Hell (with jahannam, saʿīr, saqar, ḥuṭama, hāwiya, laẓā).

hadith_evidence.en: Save yourselves from the Fire, even with half a date.

meaning.en_short: To be new; seriousness, effort; ancestor, grandfather
meaning.en: Jadd has three senses: (1) newness (jadīd — new, as in new creation), (2) seriousness, effort, diligence (jidd), and (3) grandfather, ancestor, majesty. Quran: 'They say: what, when we are bones and dust, will we be a new creation (khalqan jadīdan)?'
meaning.ar: الجِدَّة ضِدُّ الْقِدَمِ، وَالْجِدُّ الِاجْتِهَادُ، وَالْجَدُّ أَبُو الْأَبِ
meaning.en_detailed: The Arabic root ج د د (ج د د) appears 10 times in the Quran, governing the semantic domain of To be new; seriousness, effort; ancestor, grandfather. Key Quranic occurrences include 17:49, 13:5, 17:49, 13:5, 17:49, 13:5, 17:49, 13:5. The Proto-Semitic antecedent *jadd- (new; fortune; grandfather) underlies this root, with cognates attested in related Semitic languages.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ج د د — 10 مرة — To be new

etymology.semantic_evolution: Three homonymous roots converged: jadīd 'new', jadd 'grandfather/fortune', jidd 'seriousness'.

usage_patterns: Khalq jadīd as Quranic rebuttal to deniers of resurrection

lexicographical_sources: Ibn Faris: al-jidd is al-ʿaẓama wa-l-ḥaẓẓ
theological_dimensions: Jadīd al-khalq — the re-creation of humans is a central Quranic theological argument

hadith_evidence.ar: الْجَنَّةُ تَحْتَ أَقْدَامِ الْأُمَّهَاتِ
hadith_evidence.en: Paradise lies under the feet of mothers.

meaning.en: To reason. 49x. Aqala=reason, understand. 2:164: signs for a people who reason (ya'qilun). The root grounds the Quranic call to rational reflection—faith is not blind but reasoned.
meaning.en_detailed: Root '-q-l (49x) denotes reason and understanding, with the underlying Semitic image of 'binding' or 'restraining' (as one hobbles a camel by the leg) from which the intellect takes its name—the faculty that binds the passions. The Quran addresses its rational call repeatedly: 'signs for a people who reason [ya'qilūn]' (2:164) makes the exercise of intellect a precondition for receiving revelation, paired with tadabbur (rumination), tafakkur (contemplation), and dhikr (remembrance). The Form VIII i'taqala shifts the meaning to physical detention, but the Quranic usage remains centered on the active intellect—'aql as the instrument of moral and rational discernment, the faculty by which revelation meets the soul.

quranic_analysis.theme: People who reason
quranic_analysis.detail: La-ayatin li-qawmin ya'qilun—signs for a people who use their intellect.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *ʿql = 'to bind, hobble (a camel)' → 'to restrain → to reason'. The ʿaql (intellect) is etymologically the faculty that 'binds' the passions and restrains the self from folly. Arabic developed this into a rich philosophical vocabulary: the ʿaql as the instrument of moral and rational discernment.

hadith_evidence.ar: مَا رَأَيْتُ مِنْ نَاقِصَاتِ عَقْلٍ وَدِينٍ
hadith_evidence.en: I have not seen any deficient in intellect and religion [more than women].

meaning.en: Few. 8x. Qalla=be few. Qalil=few. 2:249: how many a small company (fi'atun qalilah) has overcome a large company.
meaning.en_detailed: Root q-l-l (76x) names fewness, littleness, and paucity. The Quran turns quantity into a moral argument: 'how often a small company [fi'atun qalīlah] has overcome a large company by permission of Allah' (2:249)—a divine preferential option for the qualitative over the quantitative. The adjective qalīl appears in divine self-statements: 'few of My servants are grateful' (34:13) and 'a few of them would have believed' (11:40). The opposite noun kathīr ('many') is more frequent in the Quran, but q-l-l carries the theological weight of choosing value over mass—the seed versus the chaff, the remnant over the crowd, the elite of belief over the multitude of custom.

quranic_analysis.theme: Small company victorious
quranic_analysis.detail: Kam min fi'atin qalilatin ghalabat—how often a small company overcame.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en_short: To flow, run, move swiftly; to be current, valid
meaning.en: Jarā means 'it flowed, ran'. Used of water flowing, ships sailing, the sun and moon 'running' in their courses, and metaphorically of affairs proceeding. Jāriya is a flowing stream; al-jawārī are the ships that run upon the sea. The root also gives the legal term jārī (current, valid).
meaning.ar: الجَرَيَانُ — سَيَلَانُ الْمَاءِ وَانْسِيَابُ السُّفُنِ
meaning.en_detailed: ج ر ي (ج ر ي), a root appearing 64 times in the Quran, encodes the notion of To flow, run, move swiftly; to be current, valid across its various verbal and nominal forms. Key Quranic occurrences include 14:33, 17:66, 14:33, 17:66, 14:33, 17:66, 14:33, 17:66. The Proto-Semitic antecedent *jaray- (to flow, run) underlies this root, with cognates attested in related Semitic languages. The root yields derived forms including I, II, IV, each extending the core meaning into specific semantic domains.
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To flow, run, move swiftly; to be current, valid
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ج ر ي — 64 مرة — To flow

etymology.semantic_evolution: Flow/run — applied to water, celestial bodies, ships, and legal validity.

derived_forms.key_verse: 14:33 ٱلشَّمۡسَ وَٱلۡقَمَرَ — sun and moon running

usage_patterns: Celestial bodies 'running' in their orbits as sign of divine order

lexicographical_sources: Raghib: al-jary is al-murūr al-sarīʿ
theological_dimensions: Jarayān of sun and moon as proof of divine regulation

hadith_evidence.ar: ج ر ي — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 64 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root jry (ج ر ي) appears 64 times in the Quran, including 14:33.

meaning.en: To preserve, protect. 44x. Hafiza=preserve, guard. Al-Hafiz=the Preserver (divine name). 15:9: We have sent down the Reminder and We will certainly preserve it (la-hafizun). Quran's divine protection.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ḥ-f-ẓ (44x) names preservation, guardianship, and protection. The Quran's most cited occurrence grounds its own textual integrity: 'We have sent down the Reminder [al-dhikr], and We will surely preserve it [la-ḥāfiẓūn]' (15:9)—the divine promise that sustains Quranic transmission across fourteen centuries. The divine name al-Ḥafīẓ (the Preserver) and the active participle ḥāfiẓ (guardian, 3:102) extend the field to angelic protection. The verb ḥafiẓa also names human guarding—of prayer (2:238, 'guard strictly your prayers'), of trusts (4:58), and of one's tongue against loose speech. The root spans both divine preservation and human moral vigilance, both the kept and the keeper.

quranic_analysis.theme: Preservation of Quran
quranic_analysis.detail: Inna nahnu nazzalna al-dhikra wa inna lahu la-hafizun—We preserve the Reminder.

hadith_evidence.ar: احْفَظِ اللَّهَ يَحْفَظْكَ
hadith_evidence.en: Preserve Allah and He will preserve you.

meaning.en_short: Skin, hide; to flog, whip; leather
meaning.en: Jild means skin or hide. The verb jalada means 'he flogged, whipped'. In the Quran: the ḥadd punishment of flogging for adultery (24:2). Also used for the 'skins' of the damned in Hell which are renewed as they burn (4:56).
meaning.ar: الجلد — الجِلْدُ، وَالْجَلْدُ ضَرْبُ الْجِلْدِ
meaning.en_detailed: Root ج ل د (ج ل د), attested 13 times in the Quran, derives its core meaning of Skin, hide; to flog, whip; leather from Proto-Semitic sources. Key Quranic occurrences include 24:2, 4:56, 24:2, 4:56, 24:2, 4:56, 24:2, 4:56. The Proto-Semitic antecedent *jald- (skin, hide) underlies this root, with cognates attested in related Semitic languages. The root yields derived forms including I, each extending the core meaning into specific semantic domains. The root carries significant theological weight in the Quranic worldview, recurring in contexts that shape Islamic doctrine and spiritual understanding.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ج ل د — 13 مرة — Skin

etymology.semantic_evolution: Skin/hide — the verb 'to flog' derives from striking the skin.

derived_forms.key_verse: 24:2 فَٱجۡلِدُوا۟ كُلَّ وَٰحِدٍۢ مِّنۡهُمَا مِا۟ئَةَ جَلۡدَةٍۢ

usage_patterns: Jalada as prescribed corporal punishment

lexicographical_sources: Ibn Faris: al-jald is al-ṣawt ʿalā al-jild
theological_dimensions: The ḥadd of jalada for zinā

hadith_evidence.ar: الْمُؤْمِنُ يَأْكُلُ فِي مِعًى وَاحِدٍ وَالْكَافِرُ يَأْكُلُ فِي سَبْعَةِ أَمْعَاءٍ
hadith_evidence.en: The believer eats in one intestine and the disbeliever eats in seven intestines.

meaning.en: Joy; secret. 44x. Surur=joy. Sirr=secret. 32:17: no soul knows what is hidden (ukhfiya) for them of joy (qurrati a'yun)—Paradise. The root spans hidden pleasure and confidential matters.
meaning.en_detailed: Root s-r-r (44x) spans the polar fields of concealed joy and concealed speech—an unusual semantic convergence in a single triliteral. The verbal noun sirr ('secret') and the plural asrār describe confidential matters and private consultations, while the cognate surūr names joy in its concealed, intimate register. The Quranic climax occurs in 32:17: 'no soul knows what has been hidden [ukhfiya] for them of [cooling] joy [qur'rat a'yun]'—paradise as the realm where joy exceeds all disclosure, where pleasure is too precious for tongues. The root's two senses unite around the privacy of what is most precious: the secret shared only with God, the joy reserved for the sightless beatific vision.

quranic_analysis.theme: Paradise joy
quranic_analysis.detail: Fala ta'lamu nafsun ma ukhfiya lahum min qurrati a'yun—hidden joys of Paradise.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en_short: To be loud, public, open; to proclaim aloud
meaning.en: Jahara means 'he spoke aloud, proclaimed publicly'. Jahr is the opposite of sirr (secret). The Quran emphasizes that God knows both what is secret and what is public (al-jahr wa-l-sirr, al-jahr wa mā yukhfūn). Form III jāhara means 'to confront openly, to be brazen'.
meaning.ar: ضد السر — الْإِعْلَانُ وَرَفْعُ الصَّوْتِ
meaning.en_detailed: Root ج ه ر (ج ه ر), attested 16 times in the Quran, derives its core meaning of To be loud, public, open; to proclaim aloud from Proto-Semitic sources. Key Quranic occurrences include 6:3, 71:8, 6:3, 71:8, 6:3, 71:8, 6:3, 71:8. The Proto-Semitic antecedent *jahr- (to be loud, open) underlies this root, with cognates attested in related Semitic languages. The root yields derived forms including I, III, each extending the core meaning into specific semantic domains. The root carries significant theological weight in the Quranic worldview, recurring in contexts that shape Islamic doctrine and spiritual understanding.
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To be loud, public, open; to proclaim aloud
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ج ه ر — 16 مرة — To be loud

etymology.semantic_evolution: Loudness/openness — the opposite of secrecy. God's knowledge encompasses both.

derived_forms.key_verse: 6:3 يَعْلَمُ سِرَّكُمْ وَجَهْرَكُمْ — He knows your secret and your open
71:8 ثُمَّ إِنِّى دَعَوۡتُهُمۡ جِهَارًۭا — then I called them openly

lexicographical_sources: Raghib: al-jahr is ẓuhūr al-shayʾ li-l-ḥāssa
theological_dimensions: God's knowledge of both secret and open as proof of omniscience

hadith_evidence.ar: ج ه ر — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 16 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root jhr (ج ه ر) appears 16 times in the Quran, including 6:3.

meaning.en: Night-blind. 3x. Asha=night-blind. 43:36: whoever turns away from remembrance of the Most Merciful—We assign a devil to him, so he is his companion.
meaning.en_detailed: Root '-sh-w (14x) refers to evening, twilight, and dimness of sight—the liminal hours when the sun declines and the day yields to night. The noun 'ashā' names the evening meal or supper, while the verbal sense 'ashiya relates to dimness of vision (the night-blind, a'shā). The Quranic usages cluster around temporal markers of prayer and devotion ('from midday [al-ḍuḥā] until the night's darkness [ghasaq al-layl]'—contrast with the evening prayer times of Maghrib and 'Ishā'). The semantic field of dusk encompasses both literal evening and the metaphorical dimness of perception ('upon their hearts is a covering and in their ears is deafness'—2:18). Dimness as a state of partial sight and partial faith.

quranic_analysis.theme: Devil as companion
quranic_analysis.detail: Nuqayyid lahu shaytanan fa-huwa lahu qarin—We assign a devil to him.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: Path. 45x. Sirat=path. Al-Sirat al-Mustaqim=the Straight Path. 1:6: ihdina al-sirata al-mustaqim—guide us to the straight path. The most recited supplication in Islam.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ṣ-r-ṭ (45x) names the path, road, or way, with the Quranic near-universal in the phrase al-ṣirāṭ al-mustaqīm (the straight path). The opening of Al-Fatiha enshrines it: 'guide us to the straight path [ihdinā al-ṣirāṭ al-mustaqīm]' (1:6)—a supplication repeated at least seventeen times daily in Islamic prayer, repeated by every Muslim from the cradle to the grave. The straight path becomes the central Quranic metaphor for correct religion: a route demanding directional clarity amid spiritual wandering. The plural ṣirāṭāt ('multiple paths') marks those who 'split their religion into sects' (6:159)—the straight path as the unifier, the many paths as the dividers. To be on the path is to be oriented; to leave it is to be lost.

quranic_analysis.theme: The Straight Path
quranic_analysis.detail: Ihdina al-sirata al-mustaqim—guide us to the straight path. Daily prayer.

hadith_evidence.ar: اهْدِنَا الصِّرَاطَ الْمُسْتَقِيمَ
hadith_evidence.en: Guide us to the straight path.

meaning.en: Fill. Mala'=chiefs. 7:60: the chiefs (al-mala') said.
meaning.en_detailed: Root m-l-w (10x) names fullness and, by semantic extension, the elite assembly. The verbal root means 'to fill' (mala'a al-inā'a: to fill the vessel); the cognate noun mala' refers to the chiefs, notables, or ruling council of a community—the 'filled' ranks of leadership whose seats are full of wealth and authority. The Quran deploys mala' as a sociological constant: 'the chiefs [al-mala'] of his people said' (7:60) introduces Noah's opposition, the same phrase recurring with Pharaoh's court (7:103, 109), Abraham's critics (21:63), and other prophet-narratives. The mala' are recurrently the obstruction to prophetic message, the 'filled' elite guarding their interests against the emptied message of God.

quranic_analysis.theme: Chiefs oppose prophets
quranic_analysis.detail: Qala al-mala'u min qawmihi—the chiefs said.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en_short: To deviate, oppress, tyrannize; injustice, tyranny
meaning.en: Jāra means 'he deviated, acted unjustly, oppressed'. Jawr is injustice, tyranny, and deviation from the right path. Also means 'neighbor' (jār) — originally 'one who has deviated from his own place to dwell nearby' (or 'one whom you must not oppress'). In the Quran, used for deviation from truth and for protection-seeking neighbors.
meaning.ar: الْمَيْلُ عَنِ الْحَقِّ — الظُّلْمُ وَالْجَوْرُ
meaning.en_detailed: Occurring 13 times in the Quranic text, the root ج و ر (ج و ر) conveys the essential concept of To deviate, oppress, tyrannize; injustice, tyranny. Key Quranic occurrences include 23:88, 8:48, 23:88, 8:48, 23:88, 8:48, 23:88, 8:48. The Proto-Semitic antecedent *jawr- (to turn aside; neighbor) underlies this root, with cognates attested in related Semitic languages. The root yields derived forms including I, IV, each extending the core meaning into specific semantic domains.
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To deviate, oppress, tyrannize; injustice, tyranny
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ج و ر — 13 مرة — To deviate

cognates.hebrew: גור (gūr) — to sojourn, dwell as stranger

etymology.semantic_evolution: Deviation from proper path → injustice. The neighbor (jār) is one who turns aside to dwell near you.

usage_patterns: Jawr as oppression — deviation from justice

lexicographical_sources: Ibn Faris: al-jawr is al-mayl ʿan al-ṭarīq
theological_dimensions: Al-Mujīr — God as the ultimate Protector who grants refuge

hadith_evidence.ar: ج و ر — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 13 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root jwr (ج و ر) appears 13 times in the Quran, including 23:88.

meaning.en_short: To come, bring, arrive; to commit, perpetrate
meaning.en: Jāʾa is one of the most frequent Quranic verbs (278 occurrences). Means 'he came, he brought, he arrived'. Used for physical arrival, bringing news or revelation, and committing an act (jāʾa bi — 'he came with' = 'he perpetrated'). The Quran frequently uses 'qad jāʾakum' (there has come to you) to introduce divine messages.
meaning.ar: الْمَجِيءُ — الْإِتْيَانُ وَالْوُصُولُ
meaning.en_detailed: The Arabic root ج ي أ (ج ي أ) appears 278 times in the Quran, governing the semantic domain of To come, bring, arrive; to commit, perpetrate. Key Quranic occurrences include 2:89, 19:27, 2:89, 19:27, 2:89, 19:27, 2:89, 19:27. The Proto-Semitic antecedent *jayʾ- (to come, arrive) underlies this root, with cognates attested in related Semitic languages. The root yields derived forms including I, each extending the core meaning into specific semantic domains. The root carries significant theological weight in the Quranic worldview, recurring in contexts that shape Islamic doctrine and spiritual understanding.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ج ي أ — 278 مرة — To come

etymology.semantic_evolution: Proto-Semitic 'to come' — one of the most basic motion verbs across Semitic languages.

derived_forms.key_verse: 2:89 وَلَمَّا جَآءَهُمۡ كِتَـٰبٌۭ — when there came to them a Book

usage_patterns: Qad jāʾakum as Quranic formula introducing divine messages

lexicographical_sources: Ibn Faris: al-jayʾ is al-intihāʾ ilā al-makān
theological_dimensions: Jāʾa bi — to bring/perpetrate: both literal bringing and moral commission

hadith_evidence.ar: ج ي أ — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 278 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root jyA (ج ي أ) appears 278 times in the Quran, including 2:89.

meaning.en: To plot. 43x. Makara=plot, scheme. 3:54: they plotted and Allah plotted (wa makaru wa makara Allah)—and Allah is the best of plotters. The root denotes strategic planning—both human and divine.
meaning.en_detailed: Root m-k-r (43x) denotes plotting, scheming, and strategic deception. The Quran applies the verb equally to human and divine action: 'they schemed and Allah schemed [wa makarū wa makara Allāh], and Allah is the best of plotters [khayru al-mākirīn]' (3:54)—the divine counter-plot is the active undoing of evil designs. The verbal noun makr names the stratagem itself, distinct from kayd (cunning stratagem) in its deliberative planning. The root belongs to a constellation of deception terms including khāda'a (outright deception), ḥāla'a (trickery), and ghība (absentee stratagem). All are ultimately subject to divine mastery—human plot folded into divine plot, the small scheme absorbed into the larger design.

quranic_analysis.theme: Divine counter-plotting
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa makaru wa makara Allah—they schemed and Allah schemed. Divine strategy.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: Deny. 12x. 27:14: they rejected (jahadu) though their souls were convinced.
meaning.en_detailed: Root j-ḥ-d (12x) names willful rejection, denial in the face of evidence. Unlike kufr (general disbelief), jahada is the active concealment of acknowledged truth: 'they rejected it [jahadū bihā] while their souls were convinced of it [wa-stayqanatha anfusuhum]' (27:14)—the trope of Pharaoh's magicians after witnessing the miracle, who 'believed in their hearts' yet denied outwardly. The root belongs to a constellation including jāhada (to strive) and juhd (effort, capacity)—though classical lexicographers separate jahdā from jāhadā, the denial sense is the Quranic characteristic. The root denotes the worst form of disbelief: knowing yet denying, witnessing yet rejecting, the heart convicted and the tongue in rebellion.

quranic_analysis.theme: Willful rejection
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa jahadu biha wa-stayqanatha anfusuhum—rejected though convinced.

hadith_evidence.ar: مَنْ سَلَكَ طَرِيقًا يَلْتَمِسُ فِيهِ عِلْمًا سَهَّلَ اللَّهُ لَهُ طَرِيقًا إِلَى الْجَنَّةِ
hadith_evidence.en: Whoever travels a path seeking knowledge, Allah makes the path to Paradise easy for him.

meaning.en: Sadness, grief. 42x. Hazina=be sad. Huzn=grief. 2:38: whoever follows My guidance—no fear upon them nor shall they grieve (la yahzanun). The righteous are promised freedom from grief.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ḥ-z-n (42x) names grief, sadness, and sorrow—the inner weight that bends the heart down toward earth. The Quran's foundational promise to the righteous is 'no fear upon them, nor shall they grieve [wa lā hum yaḥzanūn]' (2:38)—the negation pairs fearlessness with grieflessness for those on guidance. The verbal noun ḥuzn names the grief itself; the active ḥazīn names the sorrowful one ('do not make me among the grieved'—7:150, Moses' prayer against Pharaoh). The root also grounds the eschatological contrast: the dwellers of paradise will be delivered from all ḥuzn (35:34), while the disbelievers carry grief both in this world and the next—a sorrow with no terminus for the latter.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر حَزِنَ — 42 مرة — sadness, grief; to grieve

quranic_analysis.theme: No grief for the righteous
quranic_analysis.detail: La khawfun alayhim wa la hum yahzanun—no fear, no grief for those who follow guidance.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: Spend. Anfaqa=spend. Nifaq=hypocrisy. Hypocrite exits religion as from a tunnel.
meaning.en_detailed: Root n-f-q (111x) spans spending (Form IV anfaqa, ~70x) and hypocrisy (Form VIII infaqa, hidden) under a single semantic image. The bridge is the root's primary sense: 'going out' or 'emerging' from a tunnel (nafaq)—the hypocrite exits faith secretly, just as one spends wealth outwardly through a passage. The Quran reserves its longest sustained polemic (Surah al-Munāfiqūn) for the munāfiqūn (hypocrites, ~30x) whose interior disbelief contradicts their public profession. Anfaqa commands expenditure 'in the way of Allah' (2:195); nifāq names the spiritual bankruptcy of those who spend without faith—the outward passage of money without the inward passage of conviction, the tunnel with light at neither end.

quranic_analysis.theme: Hypocrisy
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa min al-nasi man yaqulu amanna—some say we believe.

cognates.hebrew: נָפַק (nāpaq) — Aramaic loan: to go out, emerge

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *npq = 'to go out, exit'. Arabic nifāq (hypocrisy) derives from the metaphor of going out/exiting — the hypocrite exits faith through a back tunnel (nafaq). The spending sense (anfaqa) also relates to 'putting out' wealth. The root encapsulates the drama of interior sincerity vs exterior pretense.

hadith_evidence.ar: تَدَبَّرُوا الْقُرْآنَ فَإِنَّهُ حُجَّةٌ لَكُمْ أَوْ عَلَيْكُمْ
hadith_evidence.en: Reflect upon the Quran, for it is either a proof for you or against you.
hadith_evidence.source: Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim via ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb

meaning.en: Ḥubb means love, affection, and deep attachment. The verb aḥabba means 'he loved'. In the Quran, God's love for believers and their love for God is a central theme. The root also means 'grain, seed' (ḥabb) — something precious and foundational. Al-ḥabīb is the beloved.
meaning.ar: الْوُدُّ وَالْمَحَبَّةُ — وَالْحَبُّ الْحُبُوبُ كَالْقَمْحِ وَالشَّعِيرِ
meaning.en_detailed: Occurring 95 times in the Quranic text, the root ح ب ب (ح ب ب) conveys the essential concept of Love, affection; grain, seed; beloved. Key Quranic occurrences include 3:31, 2:165, 3:31, 2:165, 3:31, 2:165, 3:31, 2:165. The Proto-Semitic antecedent *ḥabb- (love; grain) underlies this root, with cognates attested in related Semitic languages. The root yields derived forms including I, IV, X, each extending the core meaning into specific semantic domains. The root carries significant theological weight in the Quranic worldview, recurring in contexts that shape Islamic doctrine and spiritual understanding.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ح ب ب — 95 مرة — Love

etymology.semantic_evolution: Proto-Semitic: love and grain share the same root — grain as that which is 'loved' or cherished as life-sustaining.

usage_patterns: Muḥabbat Allāh — divine love as central Quranic theme

lexicographical_sources: Raghib: al-ḥubb is irādat mā tarāhu aw taẓunnuhu khayran
theological_dimensions: Ḥubb Allāh as the highest form of love — surpassing all worldly attachments
hadith_evidence: Ḥadīth: 'None of you truly believes until I am more beloved (aḥabba) to him than his father, his child, and all of mankind'

meaning.en: Ḥabl means rope, cord, or bond. In the Quran: 'ḥabl Allāh' (the rope of God) = the covenant with God, the Quran, or the means of connection to God. The root also means 'pregnancy' (ḥabal, ḥublā) — the bond between mother and fetus. Both senses share the core meaning of 'connection, binding'.
meaning.ar: الرِّبَاطُ وَالْحَبْلُ — وَالْحَمْلُ امْتِلَاءُ الْبَطْنِ
meaning.en_detailed: The Arabic root ح ب ل (ح ب ل) appears 7 times in the Quran, governing the semantic domain of Rope, cord; pregnancy. Key Quranic occurrences include 3:103, 3:112, 3:103, 3:112, 3:103, 3:112, 3:103, 3:112. The Proto-Semitic antecedent *ḥabl- (rope, bond) underlies this root, with cognates attested in related Semitic languages.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ح ب ل — 7 مرة — Rope

etymology.semantic_evolution: Proto-Semitic 'rope/cord' — used literally for physical rope and metaphorically for covenant bond.

usage_patterns: Ḥabl Allāh as the covenant/connection with God — interpreted as Quran, Islam, or the community

lexicographical_sources: Ibn Faris: al-ḥabl is al-rabt
theological_dimensions: The rope of God as unifying bond of the Muslim community
hadith_evidence: Ḥadīth: 'The Quran is the rope of God (ḥabl Allāh)'

meaning.en_short: To hinder, block; to turn away
meaning.en: To hinder, block. 42x. Sadda=hinder, block, turn away. 2:217: whoever hinders (yasuddu) from Allah's way. The root denotes active obstruction—especially from the path of God.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ṣ-d-d (42x) names obstruction, hindrance, and turning away. The verb sadda marks active resistance to truth: 'whoever hinders [yasuddu] from Allah's way' (2:217) places obstruction among the gravest sins, paired in 8:34 with setting up barriers to the sacred mosque in Mecca. The cognate ṣadīd names an iron-barrier (the barrier of Hellfire—57:19), and masadd denotes a barrier or obstruction. The root belongs to a constellation of opposition alongside 'adā (hostility), ʿaṣā (rebellion), and ʿaraḍa (to obstruct by interposition). Sadd is the active blocking—'turning away' someone from the path of God by threat, ridicule, or force, a sociology of obstruction that the Quran names and condemns.
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To hinder, block; to turn away

quranic_analysis.theme: Hindering from Allah's way
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa saddun an sabili Allah—hindering from Allah's path is among the worst sins.

derived_forms.meaning: To hinder, block; to turn away

hadith_evidence.ar: اهْدِنَا الصِّرَاطَ الْمُسْتَقِيمَ
hadith_evidence.en: Guide us to the straight path.

meaning.en_short: Stone, rock; to prevent, restrain; al-Ḥijr (rocky tract)
meaning.en: The root denotes prevention, restraint, and stone. Ḥajara means 'he prevented, restrained'. Ḥijr is a barrier or stone enclosure. Al-Ḥijr is the rocky dwelling of Thamūd (Surah 15). The intellect is called ḥijr because it restrains one from folly.
meaning.ar: المنع والحجر — والحجر الصخرة
meaning.en_detailed: The Arabic root ح ج ر (ح ج ر) appears 21 times in the Quran, governing the semantic domain of Stone, rock; to prevent, restrain; al-Ḥijr (rocky tract). Key Quranic occurrences include 15:80, 89:5, 15:80, 89:5, 15:80, 89:5, 15:80, 89:5. The Proto-Semitic antecedent *ḥijr- (enclosure, stone) underlies this root, with cognates attested in related Semitic languages.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ح ج ر — 21 مرة — Stone

etymology.semantic_evolution: Stone as barrier → prevention/restraint. Enclosure as protected space.

key_nominals.meaning: barrier, enclosure, stone; intellect that restrains

usage_patterns: Ḥijr as intellect: that which prevents from wrongdoing

lexicographical_sources: Ibn Faris: al-ḥajr is al-manʿ wa-l-taḍyīq
theological_dimensions: Al-Ḥijr as archaeological site of divine punishment

hadith_evidence.ar: اللَّهُمَّ اسْقِنَا غَيْثًا مُغِيثًا
hadith_evidence.en: O Allah, send us rain, a beneficial rain.

meaning.en: To answer. 43x. Ajaba IV=answer, respond. Istajaba X=respond, answer prayer. 2:186: I answer (ujibu) the call of the supplicant. The root denotes responsive communication—divine and human.
meaning.en_detailed: Root j-w-b (43x) names answering, responding, and the responsive reply. The Quranic climax of the root is the divine promise: 'I answer [ujību] the call of the supplicant [du'ā'a al-dā'] when he calls upon Me' (2:186)—the most concentrated expression of divine responsiveness in scripture, opening the famous 'verse of response' (āyat al-istijāba). Forms IV (ajāba) and X (istajāba) extend to responsive obedience: 'those who respond to Allah and the Messenger after being wounded' (3:172). The noun jawāb covers human reply; the root pairs with du'ā' (supplication) to construct the covenant of prayer and response that grounds Islamic piety—call and answer, ask and receive.

quranic_analysis.theme: Divine response to prayer
quranic_analysis.detail: Ujibu da'wata al-da'i—I answer the supplication of the supplicant.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en_short: To happen, occur, be new; event, occurrence; to narrate
meaning.en: Ḥadatha means 'it happened, occurred, came into being'. Ḥadīth means 'event, occurrence; speech, narrative; Prophetic tradition'. Muḥdath means 'newly originated, innovated'. The Quran refers to itself as 'the best ḥadīth' (39:23).
meaning.ar: الحدوث بعد أن لم يكن — والحديث الخبر
meaning.en_detailed: Occurring 36 times in the Quranic text, the root ح د ث (ح د ث) conveys the essential concept of To happen, occur, be new; event, occurrence; to narrate. Key Quranic occurrences include 39:23, 93:11, 39:23, 93:11, 39:23, 93:11, 39:23, 93:11. The Proto-Semitic antecedent *ḥadaṯ- (to be new, happen) underlies this root, with cognates attested in related Semitic languages. The root yields derived forms including I, II, IV, each extending the core meaning into specific semantic domains.
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To happen, occur, be new; event, occurrence; to narrate
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ح د ث — 36 مرة — To happen

etymology.semantic_evolution: New occurrence → narrative about what occurred. Ḥadīth bridges 'event' and 'account of event'.

derived_forms.meaning: to happen, occur, come to be

usage_patterns: Ḥadīth as divine speech and later Prophetic tradition

lexicographical_sources: Raghib: al-ḥadath is kull ḥādith — everything that occurs
theological_dimensions: The Quran as aḥsan al-ḥadīth — the supreme narrative

hadith_evidence.ar: ح د ث — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 36 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root Hdv (ح د ث) appears 36 times in the Quran, including 39:23.

meaning.en: Food; to eat. 48x. Ta'ama=eat. Ta'am=food. 2:61: one kind of food (ta'amin wahidin)—Israelites. 2:173: forbidden foods. The root spans consumption and dietary law.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ṭ-'m (48x) names food, eating, and tasting—the entire semantic field of consumption. The Quran deploys the noun ṭa'ām in both dietary law ('forbidden to you are [the following] foods [al-mayta, blood, pork]…'—2:173) and in parable ('you were upon the brink of a pit of fire, and He saved you from it'—3:103 sets up the demand for 'one kind of food [ṭa'āmin wāḥidin]' in 2:61). The verbal sense encompasses literal consumption and figurative 'tasting' of consequences ('let them taste [yaḍūqū] what they wrought'—3:106). The root grounds the halal/haram boundary at the table and the epistemology of consequence—what enters the mouth determines the soul, what is tasted determines the heart.

quranic_analysis.theme: Dietary law
quranic_analysis.detail: Hurrimat alaykum al-maytatu—forbidden foods enumerated.

hadith_evidence.ar: الْمُؤْمِنُ يَأْكُلُ فِي مِعًى وَاحِدٍ وَالْكَافِرُ يَأْكُلُ فِي سَبْعَةِ أَمْعَاءٍ
hadith_evidence.en: The believer eats in one intestine and the disbeliever eats in seven intestines.

meaning.en: Reverent fear. 48x. Khashiya=fear with awe. 35:28: only the knowledgeable among His servants fear (yakhsha) Allah. The root denotes fear born of knowledge—khashyah is the fear of those who truly know God.
meaning.en_detailed: Root kh-sh-y (48x) names reverent fear, awe, and the trembling that arises from true knowledge of divine majesty. Khashyah is distinguished from khawf (ordinary fear) by its cognitive ground: 'only the knowledgeable among His servants fear [yakhshā] Allah' (35:28)—fear as the proper response to recognizing the divine, not to worldly threat. The verbal noun khashyah appears in contexts of recitation ('when they hear what was revealed, you would see their eyes overflow with tears'—5:83) and pilgrimage ('whom neither trading nor commerce diverts from the remembrance of Allah'—24:37). The root denotes fear informed by ma'rifah, trembling rooted in intimacy rather than terror, the awe of the lover more than the dread of the slave.

quranic_analysis.theme: Fear born of knowledge
quranic_analysis.detail: Innama yakhsha Allaha min ibadihi al-ulama'—only the knowledgeable truly fear Allah.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en_short: Limit, boundary; iron; sharp; to restrict
meaning.en: Ḥadd means limit, boundary, and edge. In the Quran: 'These are the limits (ḥudūd) of God' — the boundaries of divine law. The verb ḥadda means 'he restricted, prevented'. Ḥadīd means 'iron' — the sharp, cutting metal. The root bridges legal boundaries, physical edges, and the sharpness of iron.
meaning.ar: المنع والفصل بين شيئين — والحديد
meaning.en_detailed: Root ح د د (ح د د), attested 25 times in the Quran, derives its core meaning of Limit, boundary; iron; sharp; to restrict from Proto-Semitic sources. Key Quranic occurrences include 2:187, 57:25, 2:187, 57:25, 2:187, 57:25, 2:187, 57:25. The Proto-Semitic antecedent *ḥadd- (sharp; boundary) underlies this root, with cognates attested in related Semitic languages. The root yields derived forms including I, III, each extending the core meaning into specific semantic domains. The root carries significant theological weight in the Quranic worldview, recurring in contexts that shape Islamic doctrine and spiritual understanding.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ح د د — 25 مرة — Limit

etymology.semantic_evolution: Sharp edge → boundary. Iron (ḥadīd) as the sharp metal that cuts and defines boundaries.

usage_patterns: Ḥudūd Allāh as divine legal boundaries

lexicographical_sources: Ibn Faris: al-ḥadd is al-faṣl bayna shayʾayn
theological_dimensions: Ḥudūd Allāh as the outer boundaries of the permissible

hadith_evidence.ar: ح د د — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 25 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root Hdd (ح د د) appears 25 times in the Quran, including 2:187.

meaning.en: Wonder. 26x. 37:12: but you wonder (ajibta) while they mock.
meaning.en_detailed: Root '-j-b (27x) names wonder, marvel, and admiration, often paired with mockery in the Quranic frame. 'But you wonder [ajibta] while they mock [yaskharūn]' (37:12) introduces the disbelievers' response to the Prophet's message: a stance of aesthetic astonishment that performs skepticism—'they marvel [ya'jabūn] that a warner from among themselves has come to them' (38:4, 64:6). The active form 'ajibahu ('he marveled at him') and the passive 'ujība bihi ('he is wondered at') extend the field. Wonder in the Quran is rarely neutral; it tends toward either faith (at God's signs in creation) or contempt (at the message). To marvel rightly is to worship; to marvel wrongly is to mock.

quranic_analysis.theme: You wonder, they mock
quranic_analysis.detail: Bal ajibta wa yaskharun—you wonder while they mock.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en_short: Curse, damnation; to expel from mercy
meaning.en: Curse, damnation. 41x. La'ana=curse. 2:88: Allah has cursed them (la'anahum) for their disbelief. 33:57: those who harm Allah and His Messenger—Allah has cursed them in this world and the Hereafter.
meaning.en_detailed: Root l-'-n (41x) names curse, damnation, and expulsion from divine mercy. The verb la'ana marks God's active repudiation: 'Allah has cursed them [la'ahum] for their disbelief [kufr]' (2:88) and 'those who harm Allah and His Messenger—Allah has cursed them in this world and the Hereafter' (33:57). The active al-la'īn names the cursed one ('upon them is the curse of Allah and the angels and the people altogether'—2:159, against those who hide the truth); the masdar la'n names the curse itself. The root extends to human cursing (la'ana) but the Quran reserves the term principally for divine malediction, distinguishing it from human imprecation by its cosmic scope and unfailing execution.

quranic_analysis.theme: Divine curse
quranic_analysis.detail: La'anahum Allah—Allah cursed them. Expulsion from divine mercy.

derived_forms.meaning: Curse, damnation; to expel from mercy

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: Ḥaraj means narrowness, distress, embarrassment, and critical difficulty. In the Quran: 'He has not placed upon you in religion any difficulty (ḥaraj)' — a foundational principle of Islamic jurisprudence. The root denotes constriction of space, mind, or spirit.
meaning.ar: الضيق والشدة — الحرج في المكان والنفس
meaning.en_detailed: The Arabic root ح ر ج (ح ر ج) appears 15 times in the Quran, governing the semantic domain of Narrowness, distress, difficulty; critical. Key Quranic occurrences include 22:78, 6:125, 22:78, 6:125, 22:78, 6:125, 22:78, 6:125. The Proto-Semitic antecedent *ḥaraj- (narrowness) underlies this root, with cognates attested in related Semitic languages.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ح ر ج — 15 مرة — Narrowness

etymology.semantic_evolution: Narrowness → difficulty and distress. Used for both physical constriction and mental anguish.

usage_patterns: Nafy al-ḥaraj: the Quranic principle that God does not impose impossible hardship

lexicographical_sources: Raghib: al-ḥaraj is al-ḍīq
theological_dimensions: Lā ḥaraj as a foundational principle of Islamic legal theory — removing difficulty

hadith_evidence.ar: ح ر ج — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 15 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root Hrj (ح ر ج) appears 15 times in the Quran, including 22:78.

meaning.en: Success. 40x. Aflaha IV=succeed. Muflih=successful. 23:1: certainly the believers have succeeded (aflaha). 2:5: those are on guidance and they are the successful (al-muflihun). The root denotes ultimate success—falah.
meaning.en_detailed: Root f-l-ḥ (40x) names success, prosperity, and the ultimate flourishing that transcends worldly gain or commercial profit. The Quran's opening pronouncement in the Mu'minūn: 'certainly the believers have succeeded [qad aflaha al-mu'minūn]' (23:1) makes falah a metaphysical category, not material wealth. The active participle mufliḥūn (those who prosper) names the eschatological victors: 'they are on guidance from their Lord, and they are the successful [al-mufliḥūn]' (2:5). The root grounds the Quranic contrast between dunya's fleeting gain and ākhira's enduring falah, with the Friday prayer at 62:10 promising that 'haste to good works' is the path to mufliḥūn. Success, in Quranic terms, is arrival rather than acquisition, the reaching of God rather than the hoarding of means.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر فَلَحَ — 40 مرة — success, prosperity; to succeed

quranic_analysis.theme: True success
quranic_analysis.detail: Qad aflaha al-mu'minun—certainly the believers have succeeded.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en_short: Free (not slave); heat, hot; to free, liberate
meaning.en: Ḥurr means free (not enslaved). Ḥarr means heat, hot. Ḥarūr is intense heat. The root spans freedom (social status) and heat (temperature). Some lexicographers connect them: a free person is 'hot-blooded', not cold/servile. In the Quran: freeing slaves (taḥrīr) and the 'companions of the Fire' in scorching heat.
meaning.ar: ضد العبد — الحرارة
meaning.en_detailed: The Arabic root ح ر ر (ح ر ر) appears 15 times in the Quran, governing the semantic domain of Free (not slave); heat, hot; to free, liberate. Key Quranic occurrences include 4:92, 9:81, 4:92, 9:81, 4:92, 9:81, 4:92, 9:81. The Proto-Semitic antecedent *ḥurr- (free; heat) underlies this root, with cognates attested in related Semitic languages. The root yields derived forms including II, IV, each extending the core meaning into specific semantic domains.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ح ر ر — 15 مرة — Free (not slave)

etymology.semantic_evolution: Freedom and heat share a root — perhaps from the idea of free-born having 'hot blood' vs servile cold.

usage_patterns: Taḥrīr as Quranic institution of emancipation

lexicographical_sources: Ibn Faris: al-ḥurr is khilāf al-ʿabd
theological_dimensions: Taḥrīr raqaba as expiation — linking spiritual purification to social liberation

hadith_evidence.ar: الْمُؤْمِنُ يَأْكُلُ فِي مِعًى وَاحِدٍ وَالْكَافِرُ يَأْكُلُ فِي سَبْعَةِ أَمْعَاءٍ
hadith_evidence.en: The believer eats in one intestine and the disbeliever eats in seven intestines.

meaning.en: Life. Hayy=Living. 2:255: Al-Hayy al-Qayyum—the Living, the Sustainer.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ḥ-y-y (184x) names life, living, and vitality in the broadest metaphysical sense—the triliteral of existence itself. The divine name al-Ḥayy (the Living) is enshrined in Ayat al-Kursi: 'Allah—there is no deity except Him, the Ever-Living [al-Ḥayy], the Self-Sustaining [al-Qayyūm]' (2:255). The verbal forms extend from physical life (ḥayāt, ~70x) to spiritual vitality ('whoever kills a soul… it is as if he had slain mankind entirely'—5:32) to eschatological resurrection ('how can you disbelieve in Allah when you were dead and He gave you life'—2:28). Form X istaḥyā ('to be bashful, ashamed,' ~10x) and Form II ḥayyā ('to greet,' ~5x) belong to the same root—one triliteral encompassing being itself.

quranic_analysis.theme: Al-Hayy al-Qayyum
quranic_analysis.detail: Allahu la ilaha illa huwa al-Hayyu al-Qayyum.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *ḥyw = 'to live, be alive'. Ḥayāt = life. Al-Ḥayy = The Living (divine name). 'The life of this world (al-ḥayāt al-dunyā) is only amusement and play' (6:32). The root of existence itself.

hadith_evidence.ar: تَدَبَّرُوا الْقُرْآنَ فَإِنَّهُ حُجَّةٌ لَكُمْ أَوْ عَلَيْكُمْ
hadith_evidence.en: Reflect upon the Quran, for it is either a proof for you or against you.
hadith_evidence.source: Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim via ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb

meaning.en_short: To regret, grieve; to expose, uncover; fatigue
meaning.en: Ḥasira means 'he regretted, grieved, was remorseful'. Ḥasra is intense regret and grief — the emotion of the damned on Judgment Day when they realize what they have lost. Also means 'to become tired, fatigued' and 'to uncover, expose' (ḥasara ʿan — he uncovered). The Quranic 'yā ḥasratā' (Oh, my regret!) is the archetypal eschatological lament.
meaning.ar: الندم والشدة — والحسرة أعلى درجات الندم
meaning.en_detailed: Occurring 12 times in the Quranic text, the root ح س ر (ح س ر) conveys the essential concept of To regret, grieve; to expose, uncover; fatigue. Key Quranic occurrences include 36:30, 2:167, 36:30, 2:167, 36:30, 2:167, 36:30, 2:167. The Proto-Semitic antecedent *ḥasar- (to regret; to expose) underlies this root, with cognates attested in related Semitic languages. The root yields derived forms including I, II, VII, each extending the core meaning into specific semantic domains. The root carries significant theological weight in the Quranic worldview, recurring in contexts that shape Islamic doctrine and spiritual understanding.
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To regret, grieve; to expose, uncover; fatigue
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ح س ر — 12 مرة — To regret

etymology.semantic_evolution: Regret as that which 'exposes' one's true state of loss. Ḥasra is the Quranic cry of eschatological remorse.

usage_patterns: Yā ḥasratā as eschatological cry — the definitive moment of regret

lexicographical_sources: Raghib: al-ḥasra is al-ghamm ʿalā mā fāt
theological_dimensions: Ḥasra as the highest degree of regret — irreversible loss

In the Quran: God has 'counted' (aḥṣā) everything, and on Judgment Day every deed will be 'counted'. Used for divine omniscience and eschatological accounting.

Those 'without a share (ḥaẓẓ) in the Hereafter' have traded their spiritual portion for worldly gain. The root emphasizes the idea of allotted destiny — one's ḥaẓẓ is predetermined.

meaning.en: To open; victory. 38x. Fataha=open. Fath=victory, opening. 48:1: We have given you a clear victory (fathan mubinan). 7:96: We would open (la-fatahna) upon them blessings from heaven and earth.
meaning.en_detailed: Root f-t-ḥ (38x) names opening and—distinctively in the Quran—victory. 'Indeed We have given you a clear victory [fathan mubīnan]' (48:1) makes fath a technical term for divine assistance that opens new horizons: the surah is named al-Fath for the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah, which tradition names 'the clear victory' despite its surface compromise. The verbal fataha spans literal opening ('We opened the gates of heaven with pouring water'—54:11, in the Noah narrative), legal judgment ('My Lord, judge [iḥtukum] between them in truth'—27:78 contrast), and the cosmic opening of blessed provision ('We would open upon them blessings [la-fatahnā 'alayhim barakāt]'—7:96). Fath as both event and opening, decision and door.

quranic_analysis.theme: Clear victory
quranic_analysis.detail: Inna fatahna laka fathan mubinan—We have granted you a clear victory.

meaning.en_short: To swear an oath; to ally, confederate
meaning.en: Ḥalafa means 'he swore, he made an oath'. Ḥilf is an oath, treaty, or confederation — the pre-Islamic institution of tribal alliance. The Quran regulates oath-taking: do not take your oaths (aymān) as deception. The root also gives 'to ally' — two parties swearing mutual loyalty.

meaning.en_detailed: The Arabic root ح ل ف (ح ل ف) appears 13 times in the Quran, governing the semantic domain of To swear an oath; to ally, confederate. Key Quranic occurrences include 5:89. The Proto-Semitic antecedent بني underlies this root, with cognates attested in related Semitic languages. The root yields derived forms including I, III, X, each extending the core meaning into specific semantic domains.

meaning.en_short: To untie, solve, make lawful; to descend, alight
meaning.en: Ḥalla means 'he untied, solved, made lawful'. Ḥalāl is the lawful, permitted — the opposite of ḥarām. The root also means 'to descend, alight, dwell' (ḥalla bi-l-makān, maḥall). The two senses connect: what is 'untied' (freed from restriction) is ḥalāl; and a traveler 'alights' at a destination and unties their pack.
meaning.ar: نقيض الحرام — الحل ضد العقد، والنزول
meaning.en_detailed: The triconsonantal root ح ل ل (ح ل ل) — 51 Quranic occurrences — fundamentally expresses To untie, solve, make lawful; to descend, alight. Key Quranic occurrences include 2:275, 2:196, 2:275, 2:196, 2:275, 2:196, 2:275, 2:196. The Proto-Semitic antecedent *ḥall- (to untie; dwell) underlies this root, with cognates attested in related Semitic languages. The root yields derived forms including I, II, IV, each extending the core meaning into specific semantic domains.
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To untie, solve, make lawful; to descend, alight
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ح ل ل — 51 مرة — To untie

etymology.semantic_evolution: Untie → make lawful. Dwell → alight. The common thread: release from constriction.

derived_forms.meaning: to untie, solve; to descend, alight, dwell

usage_patterns: Ḥalāl/ḥarām as fundamental Islamic legal binary
