The active participle jund (and collective junud) names the regiment; the noun carries, alongside its military sense, the connotation of the divine "army of unseen forces." The Quranic typology distinguishes the earthly jund (mulk) from the celestial jund (malakut). Classical Sufi manuals treat junud Allah as the ranks of divine servants, both angelic and human, who submit to His command.

quranic_analysis.theme: Armies of Allah
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa li-Allahi junudu al-samawati wa al-ardi—to Allah belong armies of heavens and earth.

hadith_evidence.ar: أَكْثِرُوا ذِكْرَ هَادِمِ اللَّذَّاتِ — الْمَوْتِ
hadith_evidence.en: Increase remembrance of the destroyer of pleasures — death.

meaning.en: War. 3x. 2:279: be warned of war (harb) from Allah—against usury.
meaning.en_detailed: The root Ha-ra-ba (H r b, 11 occurrences) expresses war, plunder, and the hostile breach of peace. The Quranic legal locus is 2:279 fa-in lam tafEalu fa-dhanu bi-Harbin mina Allahi wa rasulihi, "if you do not [refrain from usury], then know that there is war (Harb) from Allah and His Messenger"--a verse equating riba with open belligerence against the divine order. The verb Haraba (Form III) names the militant opposition (9:73 kaffat akhfa alladhina kafaru wa-hum junudun mujtamiEun, "those who disbelieve and oppose [Allah]"). The nominal Harb names the war itself. Classical exegesis derives the root's meaning from the tribal concept of predatory incursion (H-r-b as raiding); the cognates in Hebrew (Herev, sword), Aramaic (Hrb, sword/destruction), and GeEez (Haraba, plunder) confirm the semantic field of violent aggression. The Quranic metaphor of Harb mina Allah is the sharpest available; it parallels the Harb al-shimal in pre-Islamic poetry where the soul itself becomes a battlefield.

quranic_analysis.theme: War from Allah
quranic_analysis.detail: Fa'dhanu bi-harbin min Allah—war from Allah.

cognates.hebrew: חֶרֶב (ḥerev) — sword; חָרַב (ḥārav) — to be desolate

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *ḥrb = 'to destroy, plunder → war'. Arabic ḥarb = war. The Quran warns usurers of 'war (ḥarb) from Allah and His Messenger' (2:279).

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: Dammara means 'he destroyed, demolished, annihilated'. Tadmīr is utter destruction — used in the Quran for the annihilation of past nations that defied God's messengers. The root conveys irreversible, total destruction as divine punishment.
meaning.ar: التدمير — إهلاك الشيء بحيث لا يبقى له أثر
meaning.en_detailed: The root d-m-r (د م ر), with 10 occurrences, denotes total, irreversible destruction (tadmīr, dammara). Its defining verse is 17:16 'idhā aradnā an nuhlika ahlahā dammarnāhā tadmīran' — when We intend to destroy a town, We annihilate it utterly — applied to past communities like those of Lūṭ and the routed confederates. Al-Rāghib glosses al-tadmīr as al-halāk al-kullī (complete ruin), and the root signals destruction as divine judgment that leaves no remnant for restoration or return.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر د م ر — 10 مرة — To destroy

etymology.semantic_evolution: Destruction → total annihilation. Tadmīr is the obliteration of defiant nations.

derived_forms.key_verse: 17:16 دَمَّرۡنَـٰهَا تَدۡمِيرًۭا — We destroyed it completely

theological_dimensions: Raghib: al-tadmīr is al-halāk al-kullī

hadith_evidence.ar: د م ر — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 10 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root dmr (د م ر) appears 10 times in the Quran, including 17:16.

meaning.en: Dam means blood. In the Quran: prohibited food includes 'poured forth blood' (daman masfūḥan). Also the life-blood as sacred — the prohibition of murder. The root is one of the most ancient Semitic words for blood.
meaning.ar: الدم — السائل الأحمر المعروف
meaning.en_detailed: The root d-m-w (د م و), with 10 occurrences, names blood (dam) — one of the oldest and most stable Proto-Semitic roots, cognate with Hebrew dām. The Quranic prohibitions operate on two axes: 6:145 forbids 'al-dama al-masfūḥ' (flowing/poured-forth blood) as food, while 5:32 places the unlawful killing of a soul ('la-taʿa lamu al-nafsa al-dam') on par with slaying all humanity. The root underwrites both dietary law and the sanctity of life, treating blood as the visible carrier of the nafs that divine law protects.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر د م و — 10 مرة — Blood

etymology.semantic_evolution: One of the oldest Semitic roots — dam preserved identically across languages. Blood as life-force and prohibited food.

lexicographical_sources: The sanctity of blood in Islamic law
theological_dimensions: Ibn Faris: al-dam maʿrūf

hadith_evidence.ar: د م و — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 10 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root dmw (د م و) appears 10 times in the Quran, including 6:145.

meaning.en: Raʾfa means compassion, mercy, tenderness. Al-raʾūf is the Most Compassionate — a divine name. The root denotes tender, affectionate mercy — distinct from raḥma (general mercy). In the Quran, God is Raʾūf (with believers) and believers are described as 'compassionate (ruḥamāʾ) among themselves'.
meaning.ar: الرحمة والشفقة — الرأفة أرق من الرحمة
meaning.en_detailed: The root r-ʾ-f (ر أ ف), with 13 occurrences, denotes tender, intimate compassion (raʾfa) — finer and more particular than raḥma. It produces one of God's paired beautiful names, al-Raʾūf, joined in the divine attribute formula 'Raʾūf Raḥīm' (e.g., 2:143); 57:27 records that God placed 'raʾfa wa-raḥma' in the hearts of the Ḥawāriyyūn toward ʿĪsā. Al-Rāghib defines al-raʾfa as raḥma khāṣṣa (a special, focused mercy), distinguishing the delicate affection of the root from the expansive mercy of r-ḥ-m.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ر أ ف — 13 مرة — Compassion

etymology.semantic_evolution: Compassion → tender mercy. Raʾfa as affectionate, intimate compassion vs general raḥma.

theological_dimensions: Raghib: al-raʾfa is raḥma khāṣṣa — a more specific, tender mercy

hadith_evidence.ar: ر أ ف — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 13 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root rAf (ر أ ف) appears 13 times in the Quran, including 57:27.

meaning.en_short: To wait, watch, lie in wait; to delay
meaning.en: Tarabbasa means 'he waited, watched, lay in wait'. In the Quran: hypocrites 'wait' (yatarabbaṣu) for misfortune to befall believers. Tarabbuṣ is the waiting of the malicious — biding one's time for harm. Also used neutrally for the waiting period of a widow (ʿidda).
meaning.ar: الانتظار والترقب — التربص الانتظار مدة
meaning.en_detailed: The root r-b-ṣ (ر ب ص), with 17 occurrences, conveys watchful waiting, expectant observation, or lying in wait (tarabbuṣ, tarabbaṣa). It carries both legitimate and sinister registers: 2:228 'wa-l-muṭallaqātu yatarabbaṣna bi-anfusihinna thalātha qurūʾ' institutes the ʿidda waiting period for divorced women, while 9:98 describes hypocrites 'yatarabbaṣūna bikum' (lying in wait for you). Ibn Fāris defines al-tarabbuṣ as al-intiẓār, and the root's moral valence is determined entirely by the waiter's intent — patient obedience or hostile vigil.
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To wait, watch, lie in wait; to delay
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ر ب ص — 17 مرة — To wait

etymology.semantic_evolution: Waiting → watching. Tarabbuṣ as expectant waiting — positive or negative depending on intent.

derived_forms.meaning: to wait, watch, lie in wait; to delay
derived_forms.key_verse: 2:228 وَٱلۡمُطَلَّقَـٰتُ يَتَرَبَّصۡنَ — divorced women shall wait

theological_dimensions: Ibn Faris: al-tarabbuṣ is al-intiẓār

hadith_evidence.ar: إِيَّاكُمْ وَالْكَذِبَ فَإِنَّ الْكَذِبَ يَهْدِي إِلَى الْفُجُورِ
hadith_evidence.en: Beware of lying, for lying leads to wickedness.

meaning.en_short: Four, fourth; spring; dwelling; to pasture
meaning.en: Arbaʿ means four, fourth. Rubʿ is one-fourth — important in inheritance law. Also means dwelling (rabʿ) — a four-sided enclosure — and spring pasturage (rabīʿ). In the Quran: the number four appears in bird miracle of Ibrāhīm, four witnesses for adultery, four months of sacred truce.
meaning.ar: العدد المعروف بين الثلاثة والخمسة
meaning.en_detailed: The root r-b-ʿ (ر ب ع), with 22 occurrences, denotes four (arbaʿ), one-fourth (rubʿ), and the related spatial and pastoral senses of dwelling (rabʿ) and spring-pasture (rabīʿ). Key usages: 2:260 (Ibrāhīm's four birds), 4:12 'wa-lakum niṣfun mimmā taraka azwājukum in lam yakun lahunna waladun fa-in kāna lahunna waladun falakumu al-rubuʿ' (one-fourth inheritance to husbands), and 4:15 (four witnesses for liwāṭ). Proto-Semitic ʾarbaʿ- (Hebrew arbaʿ) is stable across Semitic languages; in inheritance law rubʿ is the canonical spousal share when children exist.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ر ب ع — 22 مرة — Four

etymology.semantic_evolution: Proto-Semitic number four — stable across all Semitic languages.

theological_dimensions: Ibn Faris: al-arbaʿ is al-ʿadad al-maʿrūf

hadith_evidence.ar: ر ب ع — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 22 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root rbE (ر ب ع) appears 22 times in the Quran, including 2:226.

meaning.en: Rujz means filth, abomination, punishment, or plague. In the Quran: the rujz sent upon Firʿawn's people (plagues), and 'shun the rujz of idols' (idolatry as spiritual filth). The root denotes something defiling — both physically (disease) and spiritually (idolatry).
meaning.ar: القذر والعذاب — والرجز العذاب والوثن
meaning.en_detailed: The root r-j-z (ر ج ز), with 10 occurrences, signifies filth, abomination, punishment, or plague (rujz). The root unites physical and spiritual defilement: 7:134 'wa-lammā waqaʿa ʿalayhimu al-rujz' describes the plagues sent upon Pharaoh's people, while 74:5 'wa-rjuna' commands avoidance of the rujz of idols, treating idolatry as spiritual pollution. Al-Rāghib glosses al-rujz as al-ʿadhāb wa-l-qadhar (punishment and uncleanness), so the root holds together the divine chastisements and the moral filth that provokes them.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ر ج ز — 10 مرة — Filth

etymology.semantic_evolution: Filth → punishment. Rujz as defilement that brings divine wrath.

theological_dimensions: Raghib: al-rujz is al-ʿadhāb wa-l-qadhar

hadith_evidence.ar: ر ج ز — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 10 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root rjz (ر ج ز) appears 10 times in the Quran, including 74:5.

meaning.en_short: Foot, leg; man (rajul); to go on foot
meaning.en: Rajul means man — a human male. Rijl means foot, leg. The root denotes bipedal movement — to go on foot. The man (rajul) is named for walking on two feet. In the Quran: 'And when you travel (ḍarabtum) in the earth, there is no blame on you to shorten prayer' — foot travel.
meaning.ar: الرجل — الذكر من بني آدم، والرجل القدم
meaning.en_detailed: The root r-j-l (ر ج ل), with 73 occurrences, names both the human male (rajul) and the foot/leg (rijl) — the man etymologically named for his bipedal gait (rajul mushtaqq min al-rijl, per Ibn Fāris). The foot-sense dominates wuḍūʾ law in 5:6 'fa-ighsilū wujūhakum wa-aydiyakum ilā al-marāfiq wa-imsahū bi-ruʾūsikum wa-arjulakum ilā al-kaʿbayn'; the human-male sense anchors legal testimony in 2:282 'wa-istashhidū shahīdayn min rijālikum'. Hebrew regel preserves the foot sense; Arabic uniquely derives rajul from rijl, grounding human dignity in upright walking.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ر ج ل — 73 مرة — Foot

etymology.semantic_evolution: Foot → man. The human male named for bipedal locomotion. Hebrew regel preserves the foot sense.

theological_dimensions: Ibn Faris: al-rajul is mushtaqq min al-rijl — man named for walking

hadith_evidence.ar: ر ج ل — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 73 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root rjl (ر ج ل) appears 73 times in the Quran, including 5:6.

meaning.en: Satan. 88x. 2:36: Satan caused them to slip from Paradise.
meaning.en_detailed: The root shin-Ta-nun ($Tn, 88 occurrences) expresses distance and enmity, yielding the noun al-shayTan--the eternal adversary of humanity. The Quranic chief occurrence is 2:36 fa-azallahuma al-shayTanu Eanha fa-akhrajahuma mimma kana fi-hi, "Satan caused them both to slip from [Paradise] and brought them out of what they were in"--naming the root's primary function in the primal narrative. The plural shayatin appears 20 times (2:102 wa ittaqu fitnatan la tuSibanna alladhina Zalamu minkum khaSSatan wa-dEamū anna Allaha shadidu al-Eiqab). The related form iblis (the singular chief Satan) appears 11 times, etymologically derived from ablasa (to despair). Classical scholars (Razi, Qurtubi) trace the root's semantic force from shaTana (to be distant from mercy), and contrast shayTan with malāEika (angels, those near Allah); the two terms together mark the cosmic moral typology. The active participle shayTani names whatever is of the satanic nature (6:112 dhālika annahu kana shayTani yunazzilu dhalika).

quranic_analysis.theme: Satan's deception
quranic_analysis.detail: Fa-azallahuma al-shaytanu—Satan made them slip.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *šṭn = 'to be distant, hostile'. The Arabic Shayṭān derives from shaṭana = to be far (from mercy). The Hebrew śāṭān is the 'adversary' — the prosecuting angel in Job. The Quranic Shayṭān is the eternal enemy (ʿaduwwun mubīn) of humanity.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en_short: To stone, pelt; to curse, revile; conjecture
meaning.en: Rajama means 'he stoned, pelted'. Rajm is stoning (capital punishment) and also 'conjecture' (rajm bi-l-ghayb) — throwing out guesses. In the Quran: Ibrāhīm threatened with 'stoning' (la-arjumannaka); the deniers 'guess at the unseen' (rajman bi-l-ghayb). The root bridges physical pelting with verbal assault and intellectual guesswork.
meaning.ar: الرمي بالحجارة — والرجم القول بالظن
meaning.en_detailed: The root r-j-m (ر ج م), with 14 occurrences, unites three 'throwing' senses: literal stoning (al-rajm bi-l-ḥijāra), verbal abuse, and intellectual conjecture. 18:22 condemns those who say 'rajman bi-l-ghayb' (guessing at the unseen), and 19:46 records the patriarch ʿĀzar's threat 'la-arjumannaka' (I will surely stone you) — verbal assault clothed in physical imagery. Al-Rāghib glosses al-rajm as al-ramy bi-l-ḥijāra, metaphorically al-ramy bi-l-ẓann, so the root links stone-pelting, cursing, and unfounded speculation as instances of ungrounded 'throwing.'
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To stone, pelt; to curse, revile; conjecture
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ر ج م — 14 مرة — To stone

etymology.semantic_evolution: Stoning → pelting → conjecturing. All involve 'throwing' — stones, curses, or guesses.

derived_forms.meaning: to stone, pelt; to curse, revile; to guess
derived_forms.key_verse: 18:22 رَجۡمًۢا بِٱلۡغَيۡبِ — guessing at the unseen

theological_dimensions: Raghib: al-rajm is al-ramy bi-l-ḥijāra — and metaphorically, ramy bi-l-ẓann

hadith_evidence.ar: ر ج م — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 14 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root rjm (ر ج م) appears 14 times in the Quran, including 18:22.

meaning.en_short: To fall, perish, be destroyed; to ruin
meaning.en: Radā means 'he perished, fell into ruin'. Tardiya is causing to fall — throwing into destruction. In the Quran: 'He will fall (taraddā) into the Pit'. The root denotes falling from height into destruction — both literal (falling into a pit) and spiritual (falling into Hell).
meaning.ar: الهلاك والسقوط — والردى الهلاك
meaning.en_detailed: The root r-d-y (ر د ي), with 6 occurrences, denotes perishing, falling into ruin, or being destroyed (radā, taraddā). Its defining verse is 92:11 'wa-mā yughnī ʿanhu māluhū idhā taraddā' (his wealth will not avail him when he falls — into ruin), which strikes at the futility of material accumulation before death; 7:150 'taraddaytum baʿda Allāh' records the Sinaiites' relapse. Ibn Fāris defines al-radā as al-halāk; the physical image of falling becomes a moral and eschatological metaphor for irreparable loss.
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To fall, perish, be destroyed; to ruin
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ر د ي — 6 مرة — To fall

etymology.semantic_evolution: Falling → perishing. Physical fall as metaphor for spiritual ruin.

derived_forms.meaning: to cause to fall, throw into destruction
to fall, tumble; to be destroyed
derived_forms.key_verse: 92:11 وَمَا يُغۡنِى عَنۡهُ مَالُهُۥٓ إِذَا تَرَدَّىٰٓ

theological_dimensions: Ibn Faris: al-radā is al-halāk

hadith_evidence.ar: ر د ي — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 6 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root rdy (ر د ي) appears 6 times in the Quran, including 92:11.

meaning.en_short: To be anchored, fixed, firm; to establish (mountains)
meaning.en: Arsā means 'he anchored, fixed firmly'. Rawāsī are the firmly-anchored mountains — one of the Quran's most frequent nature images. The mountains are 'cast' (alqā) into the earth as stabilizers (rawāsī) to prevent it from shaking. The root denotes immovable stability.
meaning.ar: الإرساء — الثبات والاستقرار، والرواسي الجبال الثوابت
meaning.en_detailed: The root r-s-w (ر س و), with 14 occurrences, denotes anchoring, fixing firmly, and stabilization (irsāʾ, rawāsī). The Quranic doctrine of mountains as earth-stabilizers is anchored in 13:3 'wa-hwa alladhī madda al-arḍa wa-jaʿala fīhā rawāsiya' and 79:32 'wa-l-jibāla arsāhā' (the mountains He anchored). Al-Rāghib defines al-irsāʾ as al-tathbīt al-shadīd (intense fixing), and the root underwrites a distinctive cosmological theology: mountains are 'anchors' thrown into the earth to prevent it from shaking underfoot, a ʿaǧab (intellect-engaging sign) of cosmic engineering.
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To be anchored, fixed, firm; to establish
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ر س و — 14 مرة — To be anchored

etymology.semantic_evolution: Anchoring → stabilizing. Rawāsī as the anchoring mountains that hold the earth steady.

derived_forms.meaning: to anchor, fix firmly, make stable
derived_forms.key_verse: 79:32 وَٱلۡجِبَالَ أَرۡسَىٰهَا — and the mountains He anchored

theological_dimensions: Raghib: al-irsāʾ is al-tathbīt al-shadīd

hadith_evidence.ar: ر س و — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 14 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root rsw (ر س و) appears 14 times in the Quran, including 79:32.

meaning.en_short: To watch, observe, lie in wait; ambush
meaning.en: Raṣada means 'he watched, observed, lay in wait'. Mirṣād is an ambush — a place of watchful waiting. In the Quran: 'Indeed your Lord is in an ambush (la-bi-l-mirṣād)' (89:14) — God observes and waits, ready to hold to account. The root denotes vigilant, purposeful watching.
meaning.ar: الترقب والمراقبة — والمرصد مكان الرصد
meaning.en_detailed: The root r-ṣ-d (ر ص د), with 6 occurrences, names watchful observation, ambush, and lurking surveillance (raṣada, mirṣād). Its peak verse, 89:14 'inna rabbaka la-bi-l-mirṣād' (indeed your Lord is at the ambush), declares God's cosmic observation post — every human act falls within divine surveillance. Al-Rāghib defines al-raṣd as al-tarqīb (watchful waiting), and the root governs both human ambushes (martial and moral) and God's unblinking vigil over every soul's deeds.
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To watch, observe, lie in wait; ambush
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ر ص د — 6 مرة — To watch

etymology.semantic_evolution: Watching → ambush. Mirṣād as divine observation post — God watches all.

derived_forms.meaning: to watch, observe, lie in wait
to set up an ambush, lie in wait
to watch carefully, be on the lookout

theological_dimensions: Raghib: al-raṣd is al-tarqīb li-l-shayʾ

hadith_evidence.ar: إِيَّاكُمْ وَالْكَذِبَ فَإِنَّ الْكَذِبَ يَهْدِي إِلَى الْفُجُورِ
hadith_evidence.en: Beware of lying, for lying leads to wickedness.

meaning.en: To run. 4x. 2:190: do not transgress (la ta'tadu).
meaning.en_detailed: The root Eayn-dal-waw (E d w, 106 occurrences across all forms) expresses running, exceeding limits, and the adversarial breach of bounds. Its primary Quranic ethical locus is 2:190 wa qatilu fi sabili Allahi alladhina yuqatilunakum wa la taEtadu, "fight in the way of Allah those who fight you but do not transgress (taEtadu)"--the verse that establishes the principle of proportionate response. The noun Eaduw (enemy) carries the root's stronger meaning of one who runs against; the related Eudwan (transgression) names the unjustified breach. Classical jurists treat Eudwan as a legal category distinct from jihad: Eudwan is the breach of law by one's own hands, jihad is the regulated defense of the community. The masdar al-Eudwan names the violation in the abstract; the active Eadinun names the violator (5:87 la taEtadu innAllaha la yuHibbu al-muEadinin, "do not transgress, for Allah does not love the transgressors"). The same root yields Eidah (menstruation) in extended usage through the concept of "running" of menstrual blood, but that connection is etymologically secondary.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر عَدَا — 106 مرة — run; exceed limits

quranic_analysis.theme: No transgression
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa la ta'tadu—do not transgress.

hadith_evidence.ar: تَدَبَّرُوا الْقُرْآنَ فَإِنَّهُ حُجَّةٌ لَكُمْ أَوْ عَلَيْكُمْ
hadith_evidence.en: Reflect upon the Quran, for it is either a proof for you or against you.
hadith_evidence.source: Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim via ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb

meaning.en: Arḍaʿat means 'she suckled'. Raḍāʿ is breastfeeding — the natural bond between mother and infant. In the Quran: 'The mothers shall suckle (yurḍiʿna) their children for two complete years' (2:233). The root also establishes foster-relationships (raḍāʿa) with the same legal implications as blood kinship.
meaning.ar: الإرضاع — مص الثدي للبن
meaning.en_detailed: The root r-ḍ-ʿ (ر ض ع), with 11 occurrences, denotes suckling, breastfeeding, and the foster-kinship that nursing establishes. 2:233 'wa-l-wālidātu yurḍiʿna awlādahunna ḥawlayn kāmilayn' prescribes two full years of lactation and notes that mothers shall be compensated through their husbands; 4:23 lists foster-mothers ('ummahātukumu al-lātī arḍaʿnakum') among the unmarriageable (maḥārim). Ibn Fāris glosses al-raḍāʿ as mass al-thady (sucking of the breast), and the root's juristic reach extends raḍāʿa into a fully regulated kinship tie with mahram status.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ر ض ع — 11 مرة — To suckle

etymology.semantic_evolution: Suckling → foster-kinship. Raḍāʿa as a legally recognized family bond.

theological_dimensions: Ibn Faris: al-raḍāʿ is mass al-thady

hadith_evidence.ar: ر ض ع — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 11 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root rDE (ر ض ع) appears 11 times in the Quran, including 2:233.

meaning.en_short: To pasture, tend (flocks); to observe, guard
meaning.en: Raʿā means 'he pastured, tended (flocks)'. Riʿāya is care, guardianship, and observation. In the Quran: the Prophet is 'a shepherd (rāʿin) over you'. The root bridges the pastoral (tending sheep) and the governmental (tending people). Rāʿinā (راعنا) also appears as a word the Jews twisted into an insult.
meaning.ar: الرعي — حفظ الماشية، والمراعاة الحفظ والصون
meaning.en_detailed: The root r-ʿ-y (ر ع ي), with 10 occurrences, denotes pasturing, tending, guarding, and mindful care (raʿā, rāʿin). The shepherd-leader metaphor dominates: a later rabbāniyya verse (57:27) speaks of shepherds over God's flock; 2:104 corrects the addressees' use of 'rāʿinā' (observe us/tend us) — easily twisted into abuse — with 'unẓurnā' (look at us). Al-Rāghib defines al-raʿy as ḥifẓ al-māshiya (guarding of livestock), and the root encapsulates the prophetic model of leadership as vigilant, attentive pastoring of the believing community.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ر ع ي — 10 مرة — To pasture

etymology.semantic_evolution: Pasturing → tending → guarding. The shepherd as archetype of the leader. Hebrew rāʿā is identical.

derived_forms.meaning: to observe, heed, take care of
to allow to pasture, give grazing
to observe mutually, watch over one another

theological_dimensions: Raghib: al-raʿy is ḥifẓ al-māshiya — the shepherd metaphor for leadership

hadith_evidence.ar: ر ع ي — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 10 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root rEy (ر ع ي) appears 10 times in the Quran, including 4:46.

meaning.en_short: To desire, wish; to turn away from (auto-antonym)
meaning.en: Raghiba means 'he desired, wished, longed for'. But the root is an auto-antonym: 'raghiba ʿan' means 'he turned away from, disdained'. In the Quran: 'They desire (yarghabūna) the life of this world' — both positive and negative forms appear. The root captures the ambivalence of human desire.
meaning.ar: الحرص على الشيء — والرغبة ضده: الرغبة عن الشيء أي الزهد فيه
meaning.en_detailed: The root r-gh-b (ر غ ب), with 8 occurrences, is a striking auto-antonym: raghiba alone means 'to desire intensely,' while raghiba ʿan means 'to turn away from with disdain.' The Quran exploits both senses: 9:59 'law annahum raḍū mā ātāhum Allāhu wa-rasūluhu wa-qālū ḥasbunā Allāhu yʾutīnā Allāhu min faḍlihi wa-rasūluhu innā ilā Allāhi rāghibūn' uses the positive sense, while 9:120 'mā kāna li-ahli al-Madīna wa-man ḥawlahum mina al-aʿrābi an yatakhallafū ʿan rasūli Allāhi wa-lā yarghabū ʿan anfusihim' uses the negative. Al-Rāghib defines al-raghba as al-irāda al-shadīda; the root thus holds together the Quranic tension between pursuing dunya and renouncing it.
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To desire, wish; to turn away from
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ر غ ب — 8 مرة — To desire

etymology.semantic_evolution: Desiring → also turning away. The ambivalence of human want — what we desire we may also come to disdain.

derived_forms.meaning: to desire, wish, long for; to turn away, disdain
derived_forms.key_verse: 9:59 وَرَغِبُوا۟ — they desire; 9:120 يَرۡغَبُوا۟ — they turn away

theological_dimensions: Raghib: al-raghba is al-irāda al-shadīda

hadith_evidence.ar: اهْدِنَا الصِّرَاطَ الْمُسْتَقِيمَ
hadith_evidence.en: Guide us to the straight path.

meaning.en: Rakaʿa means 'he bowed, knelt' — the ritual bowing (rukūʿ) that is an integral part of ṣalāh. In the Quran: 'Bow (irkaʿū) with those who bow'. The rukūʿ is the physical gesture of submission that defines prayer — the body bowing as the heart submits.
meaning.ar: الانحناء — الركوع خفض الرأس في الصلاة
meaning.en_detailed: The root r-k-ʿ (ر ك ع), with 13 occurrences, names the ritual bowing (rukūʿ) integral to Islamic prayer. 2:43 'wa-aqīmu al-ṣalā wa-ātū al-zakā wa-rkaʿū maʿa al-rākiʿīn' (bow with those who bow) makes congregational rukūʿ a defining feature of ṣalāh; 77:48 describes the righteous 'rākiʿīn' before their Lord. Al-Rāghib defines al-rukūʿ as inḥināʾ al-jasad (the body's bowing), so the root marries physical gesture with interior humility — the body bending as the soul submits, paired with sujūd as the architecture of Islamic worship.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ر ك ع — 13 مرة — To bow

etymology.semantic_evolution: Bowing → the physical gesture of Islamic prayer. Rukūʿ as embodied submission.

derived_forms.key_verse: 2:43 وَٱرۡكَعُوا۟ مَعَ ٱلرَّٰكِعِينَ — bow with those who bow

theological_dimensions: Raghib: al-rukūʿ is inḥināʾ al-jasad — the body's bow

hadith_evidence.ar: الصَّلَاةُ نُورٌ
hadith_evidence.en: Prayer is light.

meaning.en: Rahiba means 'he feared, was awed'. Rahba is fear, awe, or terror — both reverential fear of God and worldly terror. In a positive sense, ruhbān are monks — those who devote their lives to reverential fear of God. In the Quran: ruhbān are mentioned alongside qissīsīn (priests) as devout religious figures, but rahbāniyya (monasticism) is criticized as a human innovation.
meaning.ar: الخوف والفزع — والرهبانية الانقطاع للعبادة
meaning.en_detailed: The root r-h-b (ر ه ب), with 12 occurrences, signifies fear, reverent awe, and (in extended use) monastic withdrawal. The root's chief contrast appears in 57:27: 'wa-jaʿalnā fī qulūbi alladhīna ittabaʿūhu raʾfa wa-raḥma wa-rahbāniyata btadaʿūhā mā katabnāhā ʿalayhim' — God placed compassion and mercy in the disciples' hearts, but they invented rahbāniyya (monasticism), which He had not prescribed. 8:60 'turhibūna bihi ʿaduwwa Allāh' sanctions fear as legitimate military deterrence. Al-Rāghib defines al-rahba as khawf maʿa taḥarruz wa-iḥtirāz (fear with guarding); the root spans reverential awe of God, worldly terror, and the ascetic withdrawal critiqued as innovation.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ر ه ب — 12 مرة — Fear

etymology.semantic_evolution: Fear → awe → monastic devotion. Ruhbān as those who fear God; rahbāniyya as excessive withdrawal.

derived_forms.meaning: to fear, be afraid, be awed

theological_dimensions: Raghib: al-rahba is khawf maʿa taḥarruz wa-iḥtirāz

hadith_evidence.ar: ر ه ب — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 12 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root rhb (ر ه ب) appears 12 times in the Quran, including 57:27.

meaning.en_short: To overwhelm, cover, overtake (of punishment or harm)
meaning.en: Rahiqa means 'it overtook, overwhelmed, covered'. In the Quran: 'They feared that their master would overtake (yarhaqahumā) them with evil' and 'a boy who would overwhelm (yarhaquhumā) his parents with rebellion'. The root denotes being overtaken by something inescapable — punishment, evil, or rebellion.
meaning.ar: الغشيان والإحاطة — رهقه الأمر غشيه وقهره
meaning.en_detailed: The root r-h-q (ر ه ق), with 10 occurrences, denotes overwhelming, overtaking, or covering — something inescapable catching up and enveloping a person. 18:80 contains its most discussed instance, in al-Khiḍr's explanation: 'wa-kān abūhumā ṣāliḥan fa-khashinā an yurhiqahumā ṭughyānan wa-kufran' (we feared he would overwhelm them both with rebellion and ingratitude). Al-Rāghib defines al-rahaq as lughūb al-shayʾ bi-l-shayʾ — a thing overtaking another till it covers it; the root thus depicts the pressure of evil, rebellion, or punishment that bears down on a soul from which there is no escape.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ر ه ق — 10 مرة — To overwhelm

etymology.semantic_evolution: Overwhelming → being overtaken. Something that catches up and envelops one.

derived_forms.key_verse: 18:80 فَخَشِينَآ أَن يُرۡهِقَهُمَا — feared he would overwhelm them

theological_dimensions: Raghib: al-rahaq is lughūb al-shayʾ bi-l-shayʾ — catching up and enveloping

hadith_evidence.ar: ر ه ق — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 10 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root rhq (ر ه ق) appears 10 times in the Quran, including 18:80.

meaning.en: Zaraʿa means 'he sowed, cultivated'. Zarʿ is crops, agriculture — the basic human activity of farming that God uses as a metaphor for resurrection: the dead earth revived by rain. 'Have you seen what you sow (taḥruthūn)? Is it you who cause it to grow, or are We the Grower?' (56:63-64).
meaning.ar: الزرع — إلقاء البذر في الأرض، والحرث
meaning.en_detailed: The root z-r-ʿ (ز ر ع), with 14 occurrences, denotes sowing, cultivating, and the resulting crops (zarʿ, zaraʿa). It becomes the Quran's central agricultural metaphor for divine creative power: 56:63-64 'a-fa-raʾaytum mā taḥruthūn, a-antum tankhurūnahu am naḥnu al-nāhirūn' (have you seen what you sow? is it you who cause it to grow, or are We the Growers?) — a parable extending directly to resurrection of the dead. Hebrew cognate zeraʿ means 'seed/offspring,' and al-Rāghib defines al-zarʿ as inbāt al-arḍ (the sprouting of the earth); the root bridges agriculture, human generation, and God's exclusive causality in bringing life from barren ground.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ز ر ع — 14 مرة — To sow

etymology.semantic_evolution: Sowing → agriculture. Hebrew zeraʿ means 'seed, offspring'. The agricultural metaphor for resurrection.

derived_forms.key_verse: 56:63 أَفَرَءَيۡتُم مَّا تَحۡرُثُونَ — have you seen what you sow?

derived_forms.meaning: to cause to grow; to give crops

theological_dimensions: Raghib: al-zarʿ is inbāt al-arḍ

hadith_evidence.ar: ز ر ع — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 14 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root zrE (ز ر ع) appears 14 times in the Quran, including 56:63-64.

meaning.en: Justice. 25x. Qist=justice, equity. Aqsata IV=act justly. 4:3: if you fear you cannot be just (ta'dilu)—polygamy regulation. 5:8: be just (i'dilu)—that is closer to righteousness.
meaning.en_detailed: The root qaf-sin-TaE (q s T, 25 occurrences) conveys equity, justice, and the act of giving to each what is due. Its ethical locus classicus is 5:8 wa la yajrimannakum shanaEānu qawmin Eala an la taEdilu i'dilu huwa aqrabu li al-taqwa, "let not hatred of any people cause you to be unjust; be just (i'dilu)--that is closer to taqwa." The related noun qisT names the equitable measure (4:135 ya ayyuha alladhina amanu kunu qawwamīn bi al-qisTi shuhadaE lillahi, "O you who believe, be maintainers of justice as witnesses for Allah"). The Form IV aqsata covers both acting justly and (in legal usage) the deviation from it--classical jurists note this bifurcation, where the affirmative sense prevails in ethical passages (4:3 wa in khiftum alla taEdilu fawahidatan, "if you fear you cannot deal justly, then [marry] one [wife]"). The day of judgment is the great qisT (yawm al-qisT); the divine attribute al-Muqsit names the Just.

quranic_analysis.theme: Stand for justice
quranic_analysis.detail: I'dilu huwa aqrabu li al-taqwa—justice is closest to piety.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: Cling. 6x. Alaq=congealed blood. 96:2: He created man from a clinging clot (alaq).
meaning.en_detailed: The root Eayn-lam-qaf (E l q, 7 occurrences) expresses hanging, clinging, and the coagulated clot--the latter being its chief Quranic application. Its primary occurrence is the inaugural revelation of the Quran: 96:1-2 iqraE bi-smi rabbika alladhi khalaq, khalaqa al-insana min Ealaq, "read in the name of your Lord who created--created man from a clinging clot (Ealaq)." The noun Ealaq names both the biological state of the congealed blood-clot clinging to the uterine wall and the abstract state of anything that clings (correlated with the verb Ealiqa, "to be attached"). The Quranic sequence names the stages of embryological development (22:5 yaqumu, "and you see the earth dry, but when We send down water upon it, it stirs and swells"; cf. the nufqa-then-Ealaqa progression). Classical Islamic medicine (Ibn al-Nafis, al-Razi) debated whether the Ealaq of 96:2 implied a vegetative soul-stage; the standard lexical meaning covers both clingings and clot. The word's reading as a name of the divine attribute (al-Ealiq, "The Hanger" or "The Clinger") is rare in orthodox kalam.

quranic_analysis.theme: Creation from clot
quranic_analysis.detail: Khalaqa al-insana min alaq—created man from a clot.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en: Zaʿama means 'he claimed, alleged, asserted' — often with the implication that the claim is false or unsubstantiated. Zaʿīm is one who makes claims. In the Quran: 'They claim (zaʿama) that there is no resurrection' — zaʿama is the verb of false assertion. The root carries the connotation of speaking without warrant.
meaning.ar: القول بغير حق — والزعم ادعاء العلم بلا برهان
meaning.en_detailed: The root z-ʿ-m (ز ع م), with 17 occurrences, denotes claiming, alleging, or asserting — typically without warrant. Its most theologically charged instance is 64:7 'zaʿama alladhīna kafarū annahum lan yubʿathū' (those who disbelieve claim they will never be resurrected); 6:137 similarly records their 'zaʿm' that God has forbidden certain foods. Al-Rāghib defines al-zaʿm as al-qawl fīmā lā ṣiḥḥata lahu (saying what has no validity), so zaʿīm is properly a 'claimant' rather than a 'leader' — the root always carries the implication that the assertion is unsupported by evidence or knowledge.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ز ع م — 17 مرة — To claim

etymology.semantic_evolution: Claiming → false assertion. Zaʿama implies speaking without evidence or authority.

derived_forms.key_verse: 64:7 زَعَمَ ٱلَّذِينَ كَفَرُوٓا۟ — those who disbelieve claim

theological_dimensions: Raghib: al-zaʿm is al-qawl fīmā lā ṣiḥḥata lahu

hadith_evidence.ar: إِيَّاكُمْ وَالْكَذِبَ فَإِنَّ الْكَذِبَ يَهْدِي إِلَى الْفُجُورِ
hadith_evidence.en: Beware of lying, for lying leads to wickedness.

meaning.en: Help. 2x. A'ana=assist. 5:2: assist one another (ta'awanu) in righteousness and piety.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ع و ن (عَاوَنَ), attested 11 times in the Quran, derives its core meaning of To help, assist from Proto-Semitic sources. Its dominant Qurʾanic deployment is in the famous exhortation of 5:2, wa-taʿāwanū ʿalā al-birri wa al-taqwā 'cooperate with one another in righteousness and piety (taqwā)', which establishes mutual assistance in moral and religious obligation as a foundational communal ethic. The Form VI taʿāwana (mutual cooperation) presupposes the active subject's free choice, distinguishing legitimate collaborative virtue from any coerced or sinful alliance, and is paired antithetically in the verse with ʿalā al-ithm wa al-ʿudwān ('sin and transgression'), a prohibition the same root-system anchors.

quranic_analysis.theme: Cooperate in righteousness
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa ta'awanu ala al-birri wa al-taqwa—assist in piety.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: Right. Sawaba=be correct. Musibah=calamity. 4:79: whatever calamity (musibah) befalls you—from yourself.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ص-و-ب carries the semantic core of 'hitting the target, being correct, hitting upon' (sawābun = right aim), from which both 'righteousness/soundness' and the negative 'calamity' (musībah = that which befalls, from the sense of 'descending upon') develop. Occurring some seventy-seven times across the Qurʾān, it appears in 4:79 in the affirmation that 'whatever good befalls you (musībatun) is from God' (wa-mā asābaka min musībatin...), framing earthly trials as appointments of divine decree. The same root-family yields the verb asāba (to befall/afflict) and the nomen musībah, which classical tafsīr (Zamakhsharī, al-Rāzī) traces to the descent of fate upon the soul.

quranic_analysis.theme: Calamity
quranic_analysis.detail: Ma asabaka min hasanatin fa-min Allah—good from Allah.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِذَا اجْتَهَدَ الْحَاكِمُ فَأَصَابَ فَلَهُ أَجْرَانِ
hadith_evidence.en: When the judge strives and is correct, he receives two rewards.

meaning.en: Give drink. 12x. Saqa=give drink. 28:24: he watered (saqa) for them—Musa at Madyan's well.
meaning.en_detailed: The triconsonantal root س ق ي (سَقَى) — 25 Quranic occurrences — fundamentally expresses To give drink, water. Its most narrative-emphatic occurrence is 28:24, fa-saqā lahumā 'he watered their flocks for them', describing Mūsā's service at the well of Madyan, an act whose reciprocity initiates his marriage to Shuʿayb's daughter. The same root covers divine drinking in 76:21 (sawāb) and the future bliss of paradise, while the Form II sawwā ('to make drink abundantly') and noun siqā ('watering') extend the semantic field; classical lexicographers link saqā to flow (saqyan) and distinguish it from ʿaṭā (rain-giving).

quranic_analysis.theme: Musa at the well
quranic_analysis.detail: Fa-saqa lahuma—he watered for them.

hadith_evidence.ar: الْيَدُ الْعُلْيَا خَيْرٌ مِنَ الْيَدِ السُّفْلَى
hadith_evidence.en: The upper hand is better than the lower hand.

hadith_evidence.ar: كُلُّ مُسْكِرٍ حَرَامٌ
hadith_evidence.en: Every intoxicant is forbidden.

hadith_evidence.ar: اللَّهُمَّ اسْقِنَا غَيْثًا مُغِيثًا
hadith_evidence.en: O Allah, send us rain, a beneficial rain.

meaning.en: Zakā means 'it grew, increased, was pure'. Zakkā means 'he purified, cleansed, caused to grow'. Zakāt is the obligatory alms — that which purifies wealth and causes it to grow. The root bridges ritual purity, spiritual growth, and financial obligation. Tazkiya is self-purification — the soul's growth through cleansing.
meaning.ar: النماء والطهارة — الزكاة تطهير المال وتنميته
meaning.en_detailed: The root z-k-w (ز ك و), with 59 occurrences, fuses two semantic cores — purity (ṭahāra) and growth (namāʾ) — most famously in zakāt, the obligatory alms that purifies wealth and causes it to grow. 91:9-10 'qad aflaḥa man zakkāhā wa-qad khāba man dassāhā' (successful is he who purifies the soul; he has failed who corrupts it) makes tazkiyat al-nafs the supreme ethical project; 9:103 'wa-min amwālihim ṣadaqatun tuṭahhiruhum wa-tuzakkīhim' gives zakāt's double function — to cleanse and to grow. Al-Rāghib defines al-zakāt as al-namāʾ wa-l-ṭahāra; Hebrew zākā preserves the purity sense. The root binds ritual, moral, and economic purification into a single semantic field.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ز ك و — 59 مرة — To purify

etymology.semantic_evolution: Purity → growth. Hebrew zākā means 'to be pure, innocent'. Arabic developed the growth sense — purity leads to increase.

derived_forms.meaning: to grow, increase; to be pure
derived_forms.key_verse: 24:21 وَلَوۡلَا فَضۡلُ ٱللَّهِ عَلَيۡكُمۡ وَرَحۡمَتُهُۥ مَا زَكَىٰ مِنكُم

derived_forms.meaning: to purify, cleanse, make grow; to give zakāt
derived_forms.key_verse: 91:9 قَدۡ أَفۡلَحَ مَن زَكَّىٰهَا — successful is he who purifies it

theological_dimensions: Raghib: al-zakāt is al-namāʾ wa-l-ṭahāra

hadith_evidence.ar: مَا نَقَصَتْ صَدَقَةٌ مِنْ مَالٍ
hadith_evidence.en: Charity does not decrease wealth.

meaning.en: Doubt. 21x. Rayb=doubt. 2:2: that Book in which there is no doubt (la rayba fihi).
meaning.en_detailed: The root ر-ي-ب yields the nomen rayb ('doubt, suspicion, uncertainty'), cognate with Akkadian raʾbu and bearing the semantic core of 'trembling, vacillation'. Occurring approximately thirty-six times in the Qurʾān, it most famously anchors the opening of Sūrat al-Baqarah: dhālika al-kitābu lā rayba fīh, 'this Book, in which there is no doubt (lā rayba)', an emphatic negation that establishes the Qurʾān's epistemic certainty against the metaphysical doubt propagated by the munāfiqūn. The verbal form rāba and the active participle murīb occur in contexts of misguidance (e.g., 3:9; 9:45; 24:50), and classical tafsīr distinguishes rayb (subjective doubt) from shakk (objective doubt) as a matter of inner spiritual unsettlement rather than reasoned uncertainty.

quranic_analysis.theme: No doubt in Quran
quranic_analysis.detail: La rayba fihi—no doubt in it.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en_short: To slip, stumble, err; slippery place
meaning.en: Zalla means 'he slipped, stumbled, erred'. Zalal is an error, a slip, a moral stumble. In the Quran: 'After God saved you, you slipped (zalal)' — the moral stumble of the believers. The root denotes a sudden loss of footing — both physical and moral.
meaning.ar: الزلل — السقوط والخطأ بعد الاستقامة
meaning.en_detailed: The root z-l-l (ز ل ل), with 4 occurrences, denotes slipping, stumbling, and (metaphorically) erring after prior rightness. 3:155 'idh taqūlūna ʿalā Allāhi mā lā taʿlamūn ... an tazilla qadamun baʿda thawbuhā' (lest a foot slip after its standing firm) comments on the believers' wavering after Uḥud; 2:209 'thumma kāna ʿaqibata alladhīna āsawū al-sūʾā an kadhdhabū' follows 'wa-law tarā iz wazlaja alladhina ẓalamū fī ghamarāti al-mawti' patterns of moral collapse. Al-Rāghib defines al-zalal as al-khaṭaʾ baʿda al-ṣawāb (mistake after rightness); the root captures the fragility of uprightness and the sudden loss of footing, both physical and spiritual.
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To slip, stumble, err; slippery place
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ز ل ل — 4 مرة — To slip

etymology.semantic_evolution: Slipping → erring. A sudden loss of moral or physical footing.

derived_forms.meaning: to slip, stumble, err, make a mistake
derived_forms.key_verse: 3:155 فَتَزِلَّ قَدَمُۢ — lest a foot should slip

theological_dimensions: Raghib: al-zalal is al-khaṭaʾ baʿda al-ṣawāb

hadith_evidence.ar: ز ل ل — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 4 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root zll (ز ل ل) appears 4 times in the Quran, including 3:155.

meaning.en: Zahaqa means 'it vanished, perished, was destroyed'. Quran's most decisive verse: 'Truth has come and falsehood has vanished (zahaqa al-bāṭil)' (17:81). The root denotes the inherent impermanence of falsehood before truth.
meaning.ar: زهق الباطل أي بطل واضمحل
meaning.en_detailed: The root z-h-q (ز ه ق), with 5 occurrences, names the vanishing, perishing, or being driven out of falsehood and corrupt souls. Its defining verse is 17:81 'wa-qul jāʾa al-ḥaqq wa-zahaqa al-bāṭil' (truth has come and falsehood has vanished) — a Quranic axiom of metaphysical triumph. Form IV ʾazhaqa extends the sense to driving souls out at death (cf. 6:61 and the chain of zalzal-nafs imagery). Al-Rāghib defines al-zuhūq as al-buṭlān (vanity, invalidity), so the root expresses not just perishing but the inherent ontological fragility of falsehood when confronted with divine truth.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ز ه ق — 5 مرة — To vanish

etymology.semantic_evolution: Sudden dissipation → vanishing of falsehood. Zuhūq al-bāṭil as Quranic axiom.

derived_forms.meaning: to cause to perish; to drive out (soul)

lexicographical_sources: Raghib: al-zuhūq is al-buṭlān

hadith_evidence.ar: إِيَّاكُمْ وَالْكَذِبَ فَإِنَّ الْكَذِبَ يَهْدِي إِلَى الْفُجُورِ
hadith_evidence.en: Beware of lying, for lying leads to wickedness.

meaning.en_short: To cease, depart, be removed; to separate
meaning.en: Zāla means 'it ceased, departed, was removed'. Lā yazālu means 'it does not cease, it continues'. In the Quran: God holds the heavens lest they cease (tazūlā) — the stability of creation as ongoing divine preservation.
meaning.ar: زال الشيء فارق وانعدم
meaning.en_detailed: The root z-y-l (ز ي ل), with 10 occurrences, denotes ceasing, departing, passing away (zāla, zawāl, ʾazāla). 35:41 'inn Allāha yumsiku al-samāwāti wa-l-arḍa an tazūlā' (God holds the heavens and earth lest they cease) makes divine preservation the sole guarantee of cosmic stability; the negative phrasing 'lā yazāl' (it does not cease) yields the rhetorical sense of permanence and continuity. Ibn Fāris defines al-zawāl as al-dhahāb (going away); the root thus pairs with the divine act of holding (imsāk) to articulate a theology of sustained creation that would collapse without ongoing divine support.
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To cease, depart, be removed; to separate
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ز ي ل — 10 مرة — To cease

etymology.semantic_evolution: Cessation → removal. The negative lā yazāl means permanent continuation.

lexicographical_sources: Ibn Faris: al-zawāl is al-dhahāb

hadith_evidence.ar: ز ي ل — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 10 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root zyl (ز ي ل) appears 10 times in the Quran, including 35:41.

meaning.en: Green. 8x. Akhdar=green. 18:31: green garments of silk. 6:99: green vegetation (khadiran).
meaning.en_detailed: The root خ-ض-ر denotes the quality of 'greenness, verdure, freshness' (khaḍr), producing the nominal khaḍir/akhḍar ('green') in roughly eight Qurʾanic occurrences. It figures prominently in 18:31, yalbasuna thiyāban khudran min sundus, where the inhabitants of paradise are described as 'wearing green garments of silk', the chromatic register of barzakhī and eschatological felicity in classical tafsīr, paired with istabraq (heavy brocade) to mark the double-textured apparel of the saved. The same root appears in 6:99 (wa-huwa alladhī anzala mina al-samāʾi māʾan fa-akhrajnā bihi nabāta kulli shayʾin akhḍara) describing the verdant vegetation that bursts forth from rain as evidence of divine power, while 55:76 names the green cushions of paradise as a paradisiacal material image. Classical Arabic lexicographers (Ibn Manẓūr, Lisān al-ʿArab) connect khaḍr to the freshness of living plants in contrast to the dryness of yābis.

quranic_analysis.theme: Green in Paradise
quranic_analysis.detail: Yalbasuna thiyaban khudran—wearing green garments of silk.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en: Ship; orbit. 25x. Fulk=ship. Falak=orbit. 2:164: ships (al-fulk) sailing the sea. 36:40: each swimming in its orbit (falak).
meaning.en_detailed: The root ف-ل-ك centers on a circular motion, yielding two related nominals: fulk ('ship', from its cleaving of water in a curving wake) and falak ('orbit, celestial sphere, the arch of heaven'). Occurring approximately twenty-five times, it appears in the magnal signs of 2:164, fīhi al-fulku tajrī fī al-baḥri, 'ships that run through the sea', paired later in the same verse with the celestial falak of the sun and moon. Sūrat Yāʾ Sīn 36:40, kullun fī falakin yasbahūn, asserts that 'each [celestial body] swims in an orbit', an extraordinary pre-Copernican cosmological formulation. Classical tafsīr (Ṭabarī, Qurṭubī) records philological debate over whether falak denotes the orb itself or the path of its rotation, both senses present in the lexicon.

quranic_analysis.theme: Ships and orbits
quranic_analysis.detail: Al-fulk—ships and celestial orbits as divine signs.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: Find. 109x. Wajada=find. 93:8: He found you (wajadaka) poor and enriched you.
meaning.en_detailed: The Arabic root و ج د (وَجَدَ) appears 107 times in the Quran, governing the semantic domain of To find; to be passionate (wajd). Its thematic signature is 93:8, wa-wajadaka ḍāllan fa-hadā, 'He found you astray and guided you', followed by the triadic formulation 'He found you poor and enriched you, found you fearful and made you secure' (wa-wajadaka ʿāʾilan fa-aghnā; wa-wajadaka khāʾifan fa-amnaka), each clause marking divine salvific initiative responding to a human state. The Quranic verb is overwhelmingly concrete (finding, encountering), but the root later generated the Sufi technical term wajd ('ecstatic finding of God') and the philosophical nomen wujūd ('existence, being'), neither of which carries Quranic attestation; classical tafsīr roots these developments in 5:119 (fa-law anna wajadahu ṣābiran) where dhahabī sense prevails.

quranic_analysis.theme: He found you and enriched
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa wajadaka a'ilan fa-aghna—found you poor and enriched.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *wǧd = 'to find, come upon'. The root developed a rich Sufi vocabulary: wajd (ecstatic finding of God), wujūd (existence — the 'finding' of being). The Quranic wajada is primarily concrete: finding, discovering, encountering. Philosophical wujūd (existence) is a post-Quranic development from the same root.

hadith_evidence.ar: تَدَبَّرُوا الْقُرْآنَ فَإِنَّهُ حُجَّةٌ لَكُمْ أَوْ عَلَيْكُمْ
hadith_evidence.en: Reflect upon the Quran, for it is either a proof for you or against you.
hadith_evidence.source: Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim via ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb

meaning.en: Zayyana means 'he adorned, beautified'. Tazyīn is beautification — both divine (God's beautification of creation) and satanic (Satan's beautification of evil in human eyes). The root is central to Quranic moral psychology: evil is 'made fair-seeming' (zuyyina) to disbelievers.
meaning.ar: التحسين والتزيين — جعل الشيء ذا زينة
meaning.en_detailed: The root z-y-n (ز ي ن), with 46 occurrences, names adornment, beautification, and (often) deceptive embellishment (zayyana, zīna). The root bifurcates between divine and satanic beautification: 7:32 'wa-mā lakaum lā tunkhūna fī zīnati Allāhi' defends God's adornment as legitimate, while 4:119 records Iblīs vowing 'la-uzayyinanna lahum fī al-arḍi' (I will surely make evil fair-seeming to them). 27:4 'wa-la-qad zayyannā al-samāʾa al-dunyā bi-maṣābīḥ' extends beautification to the cosmic order. Al-Rāghib defines al-tazyīn as al-taḥsīn (making fair-seeming); the root undergirds the Quranic moral psychology in which good and evil alike require 'fair-seemingness' — but only one source is truthful.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ز ي ن — 46 مرة — To adorn

etymology.semantic_evolution: Adornment → beautification. The moral psychology of tazyīn — good made beautiful by God, evil by Satan.

lexicographical_sources: Raghib: al-tazyīn is al-taḥsīn

hadith_evidence.ar: ز ي ن — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 46 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root zyn (ز ي ن) appears 46 times in the Quran, including 4:119.

meaning.en: Sitta means six. Sādis means sixth. The number six in the Quran: the six days of creation, and the six foundational beliefs (belief in God, angels, books, messengers, Last Day, and divine decree). Sūdus is one-sixth — an inheritance fraction.
meaning.ar: العدد بين الخمسة والسبعة
meaning.en_detailed: The root s-t-t (س ت ت), with 8 occurrences, denotes the number six (sitta), sixth (sādis), and one-sixth (sudus). It appears in two key registers: cosmology, 7:54 'inna rabbakumu Allāhu alladhī khalaqa al-samāwāti wa-l-arḍa fī sittati ayyāmin' (your Lord created the heavens and earth in six days); and inheritance law, 4:11-12 sudus (one-sixth shares for parents, grandparents). Proto-Semitic *šidṯ- (Hebrew šeš) preserves the number across Semitic languages; the six days of creation become a Quranic anchor for cosmogony and a basis for legal reasoning by numerical analogy.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر س ت ت — 8 مرة — Six

etymology.semantic_evolution: Proto-Semitic number six. Stable across all Semitic languages.

hadith_evidence.ar: س ت ت — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 8 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root stt (س ت ت) appears 8 times in the Quran, including 7:54.

meaning.en: Sijn means prison — a place of confinement. The verb sajana means 'he imprisoned'. In the Quran: Yūsuf preferred prison to sin (12:33), and Firʿawn threatened Mūsā with imprisonment. The root denotes forcible confinement.
meaning.ar: الحبس — السجن مكان الحبس
meaning.en_detailed: The root s-j-n (س ج ن), with 12 occurrences, names prison (sijn) and imprisonment (sajana). Its most memorable use is Yūsuf's prayer in 12:33 'Allāhumma inna al-sijn aḥabbu ilayya mimmā yadʿūnanī ilayh' (Lord, prison is more beloved to me than what they call me to) — a moral choice of confinement over sin; 26:29 'la-ʾaṣinnannaka' records Pharaoh's threat to imprison Mūsā. Ibn Fāris defines al-sijn as al-ḥabs (detention); the root encapsulates a Quranic theme that legitimate suffering can be embraced when it preserves chastity, faith, or moral independence.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر س ج ن — 12 مرة — Prison

etymology.semantic_evolution: Confinement → prison. The Yūsuf story makes sijn a symbol of moral choice over temptation.

lexicographical_sources: Ibn Faris: al-sijn is al-ḥabs

hadith_evidence.ar: س ج ن — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 12 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root sjn (س ج ن) appears 12 times in the Quran, including 12:33.

meaning.en: Saḥaba means 'he dragged, pulled along'. In the Quran: the damned will be 'dragged (yusḥabūna) into the Fire on their faces' — the image of humiliating, forcible dragging to Hell. The root conveys forced motion against one's will.
meaning.ar: السحب — الجر على الوجه
meaning.en_detailed: The root s-ḥ-b (س ح ب), with 11 occurrences, signifies dragging, drawing, or pulling along — typically by force and against will. The Quran's stark eschatological images cluster here: 40:71 'idh yusḥabūna fī al-nāri ʿalā wujūhihim' (when they are dragged into the Fire upon their faces); 54:48 'yawma yusḥabūna fī al-nāri ʿalā wujūhihim'. Ibn Fāris defines al-saḥb as jarr al-shayʾ (the dragging of a thing), and the root's lexical force — being hauled face-down — becomes a vivid reversal of human dignity in the barzakh scenes of punishment.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر س ح ب — 11 مرة — To drag

etymology.semantic_evolution: Dragging → forcible humiliation. The damned dragged to their fate.

lexicographical_sources: Ibn Faris: al-saḥb is jarr al-shayʾ

hadith_evidence.ar: س ح ب — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 11 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root sHb (س ح ب) appears 11 times in the Quran, including 40:71.

meaning.en: Neck. 3x. Unuq=neck. 17:13: every man's fate fastened to his neck (unuqihi). 40:71: shackles on their necks (a'naq). The neck as symbol of destiny and punishment.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ع-ن-ق denotes the 'neck' (ʿunuq), and by synecdochic extension, the chain, shackle, or yoking instrument affixed to it; it occurs in roughly nine Qurʾanic forms. The most lexically arresting occurrence is 17:13, wa-kullu insānin alzamnāhu ṭāʾirahu fī ʿunuqihi, 'every human We have fastened his fate to his neck', a striking image in which the neck becomes the tablet of destiny and accountability is inscribed upon the body itself, reinforcing the verse's preceding warning against killing children for fear of poverty. The plural aʿnāq (necks) appears in 40:71 (yuq'alu fī al-aʿnāqi ṣawālimu) describing the shackling of the transgressors, while ḥadīd al-ʿunuq in 36:8 characterises the chained sinners of hell with iron fetters. Classical tafsīr (Ṭabarī, Zamakhsharī) notes that the neck imagery signals servitude and subjection to one's deeds.

quranic_analysis.theme: Fate on the neck
quranic_analysis.detail: Tairahu fi unuqihi—his fate fastened to his neck.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en_short: To mock, ridicule; to subjugate, make subservient
meaning.en: Sakhira has two distinct senses: (1) to mock, ridicule (sakhira min), and (2) to subjugate, make subservient (sakhkhara). In the Quran, the deniers mock (yaskharūna) the believers, while God 'subjugated' (sakhkhara) the cosmos for human benefit. The root spans the negative (mockery) and the positive (divine subjugation for service).
meaning.ar: الاستهزاء — والتسخير جعل الشيء مسخرا
meaning.en_detailed: The triconsonantal root س خ ر (س خ ر) — 42 Quranic occurrences — fundamentally expresses To mock, ridicule; to subjugate, make subservient. ., 2:212 — 'they mock [yaskharūna] those who believe'); sakhkhara (Form II, ~20 occurrences) means 'to subjugate, make subservient,' used almost exclusively of God's taskhīr of the cosmos for human benefit (45:13 — 'He has subjugated [sakhkhara] for you all that is in the heavens and earth'). Raghib al-Iṣfahānī carefully distinguishes the condemned human mockery (sukhrī) from the blessed divine subjugation (taskhīr), the latter being a recurring motif of Qurʾanic cosmology. The nominal musakhkhar ('subjugated,' 4 occurrences) and is taskhara (Form X, 'to seek to mock,' 2 occurrences) extend the semantic range, while istaskhara in 83:30 ('and when they passed by them they would exchange mocking glances') captures the insolent laugh of the damned at the righteous.
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To mock, ridicule; to subjugate, make subservient
meaning.ar_definition: جذر س خ ر — 42 مرة — To mock

etymology.semantic_evolution: Mockery → subjugation. Two distinct senses: human mockery (condemned) and divine taskhīr (blessing).

derived_forms.meaning: to seek to mock; to be mocked

lexicographical_sources: Raghib distinguishes the two senses carefully

hadith_evidence.ar: س خ ر — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 42 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root sxr (س خ ر) appears 42 times in the Quran, including 45:13.

meaning.en: To live; build. 24x. Amara=live long. Imran=civilization. Isti'mar=to settle. 11:61: He produced you from the earth and settled you (ista'marakum) therein.
meaning.en_detailed: Occurring 24 times in the Quranic text, the root ع م ر (عَمُرَ) conveys the essential concept of To live long; to build (umran). Occurring approximately twenty-four times in the Qurʾān, its theological centre is 11:61, wa-istiʿmara-kum fīhā 'He settled you / commissioned you to inhabit the earth', where the Form X istiʿmara combines habitation with cultivation, an act of divine trust (amānah) that Ibn Khaldūn later converted into the foundation of his ʿilm al-ʿumrān ('science of civilization'). The verbal ʿāmara appears in contexts of long life (2:96; 29:14) while the Form IV aʿmara ('to grant long life') appears in 26:18 (wa-aʿmaranā fīkum mā kāna ʿumruhu taflan, 'how long among you we lived'), the prophet Noah's retort to his people.

quranic_analysis.theme: Settlement of earth
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa ista'marakum fiha—He settled you on earth.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *ʿmr = 'to dwell, inhabit → to live long → to flourish'. Classical Arabic developed the concept of ʿumrān (civilization) — the flourishing of human society through habitation, cultivation, and governance. Ibn Khaldun later built his entire philosophy of history around this concept.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en_short: To exceed bounds, be excessive, prodigal
meaning.en: Asrafa means 'he exceeded bounds, was excessive, prodigal'. Isrāf is extravagance, waste, and transgression of limits. In the Quran: 'Do not be excessive (tusrifū) in killing', 'God does not love the extravagant (al-musrifīn)'. The root denotes crossing divinely-set boundaries, especially in consumption and violence.
meaning.ar: تجاوز الحد — والإسراف مجاوزة القصد
meaning.en_detailed: Occurring 23 times in the Quranic text, the root س ر ف (س ر ف) conveys the essential concept of To exceed bounds, be excessive, prodigal. Occurring 23 times, the root is overwhelmingly deployed via the IV form asrafa ('he was excessive, wasteful'), e.g., 6:141 — 'eat of its fruit... but do not be excessive [lā tusrifū],' and 7:31 — 'eat and drink, but do not be excessive' — articulating the Qurʾanic ethic of wasaṭiyya (moderation). Raghib glosses isrāf as mujāwazat al-ḥadd ('transgression of the limit'), locating its moral force in the crossing of divinely prescribed boundaries rather than mere quantitative excess. God is explicitly said not to love the musrifīn (6:141; 7:31), and the root's three nominal attestations (isrāf, 2 occurrences; musrif, 3) consistently condemn violation of limits in consumption, slaughter, and bloodshed.
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To exceed bounds, be excessive, prodigal
meaning.ar_definition: جذر س ر ف — 23 مرة — To exceed bounds

etymology.semantic_evolution: Exceeding → extravagance. Isrāf as transgression of the divine limit.

derived_forms.meaning: to exceed bounds, be excessive, wasteful
derived_forms.key_verse: 6:141 وَلَا تُسۡرِفُوٓا۟ — do not be excessive

lexicographical_sources: Raghib: al-isrāf is mujāwazat al-ḥadd

hadith_evidence.ar: س ر ف — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 23 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root srf (س ر ف) appears 23 times in the Quran, including 6:141.

meaning.en_short: To unveil, expose; journey, travel; book, scripture
meaning.en: Safara means 'he unveiled, exposed'. Safar is a journey (exposing oneself to the road). Sifr is a book or scripture (that which unveils knowledge). In the Quran: 'By the dawn when it breathes/uncovers (asfara)' and 'scriptures (ṣuḥuf) purified'. The root bridges uncovering, traveling, and writing — all forms of revelation.
meaning.ar: الكشف والإظهار — والسفر السير، والسفر الكتاب
meaning.en_detailed: Occurring 12 times in the Quranic text, the root س ف ر (س ف ر) conveys the essential concept of To unveil, expose; journey, travel; book, scripture. Occurring 12 times, the root's most striking Qurʾanic instance is the Qurʾānic hapax of Form IV asfara in 74:34 ('by the dawn when it brightens / uncovers'), where the verb conjoins the rising of light with the removal of darkness. Ibn Faris glosses al-safar as 'al-kashf' (unveiling), while the cognate Hebrew sefer ('book, scroll') preserves the Semitic sense of writing as revelation of meaning. Safar ('journey') appears twice, and the plural sufaraʾ in 80:15 refers to the noble angelic scribes (safara) in God's hands — agents of cosmic record-keeping. The root thus unites physical movement, epistemic disclosure, and scriptural fixation.
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To unveil, expose; journey, travel; book, scripture
meaning.ar_definition: جذر س ف ر — 12 مرة — To unveil

etymology.semantic_evolution: Unveiling → journey → book. Hebrew sefer means 'book, scroll' — that which reveals knowledge. Arabic safar preserves all three senses.

derived_forms.meaning: to become bright, dawn; to unveil

lexicographical_sources: Ibn Faris: al-safr is al-kashf

hadith_evidence.ar: السَّفَرُ قِطْعَةٌ مِنَ الْعَذَابِ
hadith_evidence.en: Travel is a portion of torment.

meaning.en: Ignorance. 24x. Jahila=be ignorant. Jahl=ignorance. Jahiliyyah=pre-Islamic ignorance. 2:67: I seek refuge from being among the ignorant (al-jahilin). 49:6: lest you harm a people in ignorance (bi-jahalah).
meaning.en_detailed: The Arabic root ج ه ل (جَهِلَ) appears 24 times in the Quran, governing the semantic domain of Ignorance; to be ignorant. Its normative horizon is the ethical condemnation in 49:6, fa-tusība qawman bi-jahālatin, 'lest you afflict a people in ignorance', warning believers against unmindful harm in dealing with criminal intelligence and litigation, and 2:67 (aʿūdhu billāhi an akūna mina al-jāhilīn), the prayer of refuge from ignorance. The same root famously gives rise to the nomen jāhiliyyah ('the state of pre-Islamic ignorance'), itself a Quranic construction (3:154; 5:50; 33:33; 48:26) that classical exegesis (Ibn Kathīr, Ibn Taymiyyah) interprets not as a chronological epoch but as an enduring moral disposition of unguided passion.

quranic_analysis.theme: Avoid ignorant harm
quranic_analysis.detail: Fa-tusibu qawman bi-jahalatin—lest you harm people in ignorance.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: Safiha means 'he was foolish, ignorant, light-minded'. Safah is folly, foolishness — the opposite of wisdom (ḥikma). In the Quran: 'Who would turn away from the religion of Abraham except one who fools himself (man safiha nafsahu)?' (2:130). The root denotes lack of sound judgment.
meaning.ar: الحمق والجهل — السفه ضد الحلم
meaning.en_detailed: س ف ه (س ف ه), a root appearing 11 times in the Quran, encodes the notion of To be foolish, ignorant, frivolous across its various verbal and nominal forms. Occurring 11 times, the root's defining verse is 2:130: 'who would turn away from the religion of Abraham except one who fools himself [man safiha nafsahu]?' — introducing the reflexive construction that becomes paradigmatic. The active participle safīh ('fool, frivolous person,' 8 occurrences) is frequently paired with the blind and deaf as a description of spiritual incapacity (e.g., 7:66, 'a people who were fools [safīhūn]'); the abstract safah appears 5 times. Crucially, the Qurʾān locates the root's moral gravity not in cognitive deficiency but in willful rejection — safah against the self.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر س ف ه — 11 مرة — To be foolish

etymology.semantic_evolution: Foolishness → lack of wisdom. Safah as the moral-intellectual failure to recognize truth.

derived_forms.meaning: to be foolish, ignorant; to fool oneself
derived_forms.key_verse: 2:130 مَن سَفِهَ نَفۡسَهُۥ — who fools himself

derived_forms.meaning: to deem foolish, treat as ignorant

lexicographical_sources: Raghib: al-safah is khiffat al-ʿaql

hadith_evidence.ar: س ف ه — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 11 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root sfh (س ف ه) appears 11 times in the Quran, including 2:130.

meaning.en: Sulṭān means authority, power, dominion, and also proof or evidence that establishes authority. In the Quran: Firʿawn claimed 'kingdom (sulṭān) of Egypt', while the deniers are challenged to 'bring your proof (sulṭānakum)'. The root bridges political power and logical authority — both require sulṭān.
meaning.ar: القدرة والتسلط — والسلطان الحجة والبرهان
meaning.en_detailed: Root س ل ط (س ل ط), attested 39 times in the Quran, derives its core meaning of Authority, power, dominion; sulṭān (proof, authority) from Proto-Semitic sources. Occurring 39 times, sulṭān is the Qurʾānic term for what entitles a claim: Firʿawn boasts of sulṭān in Egypt (43:51), Iblīs concedes to Adam 'I had no authority [sulṭān] over you' (14:22), and Mūsā is sent with 'Our signs and a clear authority [sulṭānan mubīn]' (40:23). Raghib defines al-sulṭān as 'al-qudra wa-l-ḥujja' ('power and proof'), capturing the dual sense. The cognate Hebrew šālaṭ ('to rule') confirms the political semantic core, while the Qurʾānic extension to evidentiary force makes sulṭān the standard term in the jihād verses where the deniers are challenged to 'bring their proof' (e.g., 2:91, 27:71).
meaning.ar_definition: جذر س ل ط — 39 مرة — Authority

etymology.semantic_evolution: Power → proof. Hebrew šālaṭ means 'to rule'. Arabic developed the dual sense: political power AND logical proof.

derived_forms.meaning: to give power over, make dominant

lexicographical_sources: Raghib: al-sulṭān is al-qudra wa-l-ḥujja

hadith_evidence.ar: س ل ط — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 39 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root slT (س ل ط) appears 39 times in the Quran, including 14:22.

meaning.en_short: To travel, follow a path; to insert, enter
meaning.en: Salaka means 'he traveled, followed a path, entered'. Maslak is a path or way. In the Quran: God 'makes the springs flow (salaka) in the earth', and 'He makes the night enter (yūliju) into the day'. The root denotes moving along a designated path.
meaning.ar: سلوك الطريق — السير فيه
meaning.en_detailed: The triconsonantal root س ل ك (س ل ك) — 12 Quranic occurrences — fundamentally expresses To travel, follow a path; to insert, enter. Occurring 12 times, the root is most strikingly used in 26:200 — 'thus We cause it [the Qurʾān] to enter [salaknāhu] into the hearts of the criminals' — using entry into the heart as the metaphor for reception of revelation. In 18:61, the fish 'took its way [salaka] into the sea,' and in 27:18 the ants' path is described via the same root. Ibn Faris glosses al-salk as nufūdh al-shayʾ ('penetration of a thing'); the nominal maslak ('path, way') is unattested in the Qurʾān but conceptually completes the root's vocabulary. The semantic core is consistently traversal or insertion — moving along a known route.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر س ل ك — 12 مرة — To travel

etymology.semantic_evolution: Path → traveling → inserting. Salaka implies following a designated course.

derived_forms.meaning: to travel, follow a path; to insert, cause to enter

lexicographical_sources: Ibn Faris: al-salk is nufūdh al-shayʾ

hadith_evidence.ar: السَّفَرُ قِطْعَةٌ مِنَ الْعَذَابِ
hadith_evidence.en: Travel is a portion of torment.

hadith_evidence.ar: اهْدِنَا الصِّرَاطَ الْمُسْتَقِيمَ
hadith_evidence.en: Guide us to the straight path.

meaning.en_short: To establish, prescribe; way, practice; tooth; age
meaning.en: To establish, prescribe; way, practice; tooth; age
meaning.en_detailed: The triconsonantal root س ن ن (س ن ن) — 21 Quranic occurrences — fundamentally expresses To establish, prescribe; way, practice; tooth; age. 'the established way of God'). With 21 total root occurrences, sunna names the divine pattern of dealing with past communities — destroying transgressors and rewarding the faithful — and constitutes the Qurʾānic ground for the doctrine of historical causality in salvation history. The secondary nominal sinn means both 'tooth' (1 occurrence) and 'age,' and the root's semantic evolution flows from the abstract sense of a hardened, established custom to a normative theological concept. The hadith literature's sunna of the Prophet is the human mirroring of this divine sunna.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر س ن ن — 21 مرة — To establish

etymology.semantic_evolution: Established way → sunna. The divinely ordained pattern of dealing with past nations.

hadith_evidence.ar: اهْدِنَا الصِّرَاطَ الْمُسْتَقِيمَ
hadith_evidence.en: Guide us to the straight path.

meaning.en: To occur, fall. 24x. Waqa'a=happen, fall. 56:1: when the Event (al-Waqi'ah) occurs—the inevitable Judgment. 69:15: on that Day the Event (al-Waqi'ah) will occur.
meaning.en_detailed: The root و-ق-ع carries the semantic core of 'falling down, happening, befalling', and yields the active verb waqaʿa ('to occur, happen, fall') and the nomen wāqiʿah ('event, calamity, the falling-down'). Occurring some twenty-four times in the Qurʾān, its most semantically charged use is the title of Sūrat al-Wāqiʿah ('The Inevitable Event'), where 56:1 declares idhā waqaʿati al-wāqiʿah, 'when the inevitable event occurs', an eschatological marker of unconditioned certainty (the same root supplies lay waqiʿah 'no escape from the happening'). Classical tafsīr (Ṭabarī, Zamakhsharī) notes that wāqiʿah here means both 'what will happen' and 'what must happen', a verbal noun of compulsion that subsumes within it all lesser calamities.

quranic_analysis.theme: The Inevitable Event
quranic_analysis.detail: Idha waqa'ati al-waqi'ah—when the Inevitable Event occurs.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en_short: Black; to be master, lord; to prevail
meaning.en: Black; to be master, lord; to prevail
meaning.en_detailed: Occurring 10 times in the Quranic text, the root س و د (س و د) conveys the essential concept of Black; to be master, lord; to prevail. ., the dark night) and a parallel sense cluster around 'mastery, lordship' (sāda, 'to be master'). Occurring 10 times, the most theologically significant nominal is sayyid ('master, lord, chief,' 2 occurrences), applied honorifically in 3:39 to Zakariyyā's son Yaḥyā and in 12:25 to the Egyptian master of Yūsuf ('the master of the house [sayyidaha]'). The etymological link between blackness and mastery is debated but may derive from the visual metaphor of the dominant figure as 'the one before whom others become black' (i.e., shadowy). The root's semantic range thus covers chromatic darkness and hierarchical preeminence, with no Qurʾānic Form I verbal of sāda attested despite the noun's prominence.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر س و د — 10 مرة — Black

etymology.semantic_evolution: Blackness → mastery. Sayyid (master) from same root — perhaps the master as leader of the 'black' masses?

hadith_evidence.ar: س و د — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 10 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root swd (س و د) appears 10 times in the Quran, including 3:39.

meaning.en: To wear; confuse. 23x. Labisa=wear. Labasa=confuse, mix. 2:42: do not mix (talbisu) truth with falsehood. 7:26: clothing of righteousness (libasu al-taqwa) is best.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ل-ب-س is semantically bipartite in the Qurʾān: it signifies both 'to put on, wear' (libās) and 'to confound, mix, obscure' (talbīs). With roughly twenty-three occurrences, the second sense governs the foundational prohibition of 2:42, wa-lā talbisū al-ḥaqqa bi-l-bāṭili, 'do not confound the truth with falsehood', a verb-form (Form II, intensive) that captures the deliberate concealment of truth under untruth. The clothing sense, by contrast, generates one of the Qurʾān's most celebrated metaphors in 7:26, libāsu al-taqwā, 'the clothing of righteousness/piety', declared khayr ('best') over material garments, a move classical Sufi tafsīr (Qušayrī, Rūzbihān Baqlī) seizes upon to interiorize the entire concept of dress.

quranic_analysis.theme: Clothing of righteousness
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa libasu al-taqwa dhalika khayrun—clothing of piety is best.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: Ascend. 3x. Araja=ascend. Ma'arij=ascents. 70:3: from Allah, Lord of the ascents (al-ma'arij).
meaning.en_detailed: Occurring 9 times in the Quranic text, the root ع ر ج (عَرَجَ) conveys the essential concept of To ascend; lame. Occurring nine times, it frames the heavens as a vertically structured cosmos in 70:3, mina Allāhi dhi al-maʿārij, 'from God, Lord of the ascents', a phrase whose plural noun implies a ladder-like architecture of creation. The verbal form ʿurijat ('shall be raised') punctuates the scenes of eschatological judgment (e.g., 4:153; 6:15; 17:93), while 43:33 (law kāna li al-arḍi jamiʿan wa-mithlahū maʿahu la-ftadawa bihi) describes the ungrateful Meccan rejection; the same root underlies muʿarrajūn ('those raised', 56:34), the inverts of paradise on elevated couches.

quranic_analysis.theme: Lord of Ascents
quranic_analysis.detail: Mina Allahi dhi al-ma'arij—from Allah, Lord of Ascents.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en: Wall, enclosure; to climb, ascend
meaning.en_detailed: س و ر (س و ر), a root appearing 17 times in the Quran, encodes the notion of Wall, enclosure; to climb, ascend across its various verbal and nominal forms. Its most theologically dramatic appearance is 57:13 — 'a wall [sūr] will be erected between them; on its inner side is mercy, on its outer side is punishment' — the parenetic barrier (sometimes identified with the wall of Yaʾjūj and Maʾjūj, Gog and Magog) separating the People of the Right Hand from the People of the Left. With 17 total root occurrences, the semantic field links physical enclosure to moral delimitation: the wall as boundary between righteous and damned, between outer and inner community, between legitimate and intrusive access. The verbal root preserves the idea of climbing over as a metaphor for trespass.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر س و ر — 17 مرة — Wall

etymology.semantic_evolution: Wall → climbing. Sūr as protective enclosure; tasawwur as scaling or mental ascent.

hadith_evidence.ar: س و ر — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 17 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root swr (س و ر) appears 17 times in the Quran, including 57:13.

meaning.en_short: Hour, moment; sāʿa (the Hour, Day of Judgment)
meaning.en: Hour, moment; sāʿa (the Hour, Day of Judgment)
meaning.en_detailed: Occurring 49 times in the Quranic text, the root س و ع (س و ع) conveys the essential concept of Hour, moment; sāʿa (the Hour, Day of Judgment). Al-sāʿa is consistently the imminent, sudden, and terrifying transition: 6:31 announces that 'the Hour will come upon them suddenly,' 22:1 warns of 'the earthquake of the Hour,' and 79:42–46 asks 'what will make you know what the Hour is?' (the famous sāʿa-mā-idhrāhā question). Occurring 49 times, the root has no Qurʾānic verbal Form I, depending entirely on the nominal sāʿa and its participial and adjectival extensions. The semantic evolution from simple 'moment' to the apocalyptic Hour reflects the Qurʾānic worldview in which all of history is gathered into one decisive instant of divine judgment.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر س و ع — 49 مرة — Hour

etymology.semantic_evolution: Moment → the eschatological Hour. Al-Sāʿa is the Quran's most dramatic temporal marker — the final moment of cosmic transition.

hadith_evidence.ar: س و ع — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 49 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root swE (س و ع) appears 49 times in the Quran, including 6:31.

meaning.en_short: To brand, mark; to offer for sale; pasturage
meaning.en: To brand, mark; to offer for sale; pasturage
meaning.en_detailed: س و م (س و م), a root appearing 15 times in the Quran, encodes the notion of To brand, mark; to offer for sale; pasturage across its various verbal and nominal forms.
