hadith_evidence.en: The root Evw (ع ث و) appears 5 times in the Quran, including 2:60.

meaning.en_short: To be unable, weak, incapable; weakness
meaning.en: To be unable, weak, incapable; weakness
meaning.en_detailed: Root ع-ج-ز (ʿ-j-z), 26 occurrences: the semantic core is the inability to perform or escape, both the negative state of weakness and the failure to outpace (a pursuer). Form I ʿajaza (4×) denotes being unable, Form IV ʾaʿjaza (22×) causative-to-elude; the noun ʿajz (1×) names the state itself. Key Quranic usage: 9:2 lays out the conquest-mission and the declaration that none can escape God; the phrase lā muʿjizīn Allāh recurs as a refrain throughout the Qurʾān (11:33, 13:31, 16:46, 21:37, 29:22, 35:44, 39:51, 46:32, 51:14, 64:18), each declaring that no one can thwart God's decree. Scholarly precision: classical lexicographers distinguish ʿajz (a settled state of incapacity) from taʿājuz (pretense of incapacity, an al-masdariyy / form-tāriya); al-Rāghib notes that ʿ-j-z in the Qurʾān always stands in opposition to qudra (power)—the inability of creation versus the all-power of the Creator—making the root a theological antonym of the divine attribute al-Qādir (The Powerful).
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To be unable, weak, incapable; weakness
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ع ج ز — 26 مرة — To be unable

etymology.semantic_evolution: Inability → weakness. ʿAjz as the state of being incapable — contrasted with divine qudra.

derived_forms.meaning: to make incapable; to escape, elude

hadith_evidence.ar: ع ج ز — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 26 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root Ejz (ع ج ز) appears 26 times in the Quran, including 9:2.

meaning.en: Suppress. 6x. Kazama=suppress. 3:134: those who suppress anger (al-kazimina al-ghayza)—the pious.
meaning.en_detailed: كَظَمَ (ك ظ م), a root appearing 6 times in the Quran, encodes the notion of To suppress (anger); gulp across its various verbal and nominal forms. The active participle al-kāẓimīna al-ghayẓ in 3:134 is one of the defining qualities of the muttaqīn: "those who restrain anger (al-kāẓimīna al-ghayẓ) and pardon people (wa-l-ʿāfīna ʿani al-nās)"—a triad of ethical restraint. The verbal noun kazm also carries the physical sense of gulping or holding down. Occurs 6 times in Qur'an. The root is sharply contrasted with intiqām (revenge) and emphasizes iḥsān (excellence) and ʿafw (pardon) as virtues of self-mastery. Note that kazama is distinct from katama (ك ت م, to conceal by silence); they share the semantic field of suppression but differ in object and nuance.

quranic_analysis.theme: Suppressing anger
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa al-kazimina al-ghayza—those who suppress anger.

hadith_evidence.ar: لَا تَغْضَبْ وَلَكَ الْجَنَّةُ
hadith_evidence.en: Do not become angry, and Paradise is yours.

meaning.en_short: Haste, hurry; to hasten; calf (ʿijl); al-ʿĀjila (this world)
meaning.en: Haste, hurry; to hasten; calf (ʿijl); al-ʿĀjila (this world)
meaning.en_detailed: Root ع-ج-ل (ʿ-j-l), 47 occurrences: the semantic core is haste, with rapid temporal impatience and the related theological category of al-ʿājila (this-world, the immediate). Form I ʿajila (4×), Form II ʿajjala (10×), and Form X istaʿjala (40×) span the spectrum from natural impatience to demanding divine punishment ahead of time; the noun ʿajala (8×) names haste itself. Key Quranic usage: 75:20 bal tuḥibbūna al-ʿājilata wa-tadharūna al-ākhirata ('No! You love the immediate (life) and neglect the Hereafter'); 17:18 man kāna yurīdu al-ʿājilata ʿajjallnā lahā fīhā mā nashāʾu ('Whoever desires the immediate—We hasten it for whom We will'); 51:59 fa-istaʿjaltum with the ʿijl (calf, a separate root with similar consonantal skeleton). Scholarly precision: al-Rāghib notes that ʿajala/ʿājila carries a moral inversion—the haste of unbelievers is precisely the structure of their punishment (cf. Sūrat al-Mujādilah 58:3, where ʿajjal is paired with taʾkhīr). The verb istaʿjala is a Qurʾānic favourite for demanding the punishment that would prove divine chastisement's reality.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ع ج ل — 47 مرة — Haste

etymology.semantic_evolution: Haste → this world. ʿAjila as impatience for immediate gratification — the world rushed toward vs the Hereafter awaited.

derived_forms.meaning: to hurry, hasten; to give quickly
to seek to hasten, demand immediately

hadith_evidence.ar: ع ج ل — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 47 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root Ejl (ع ج ل) appears 47 times in the Quran, including 75:20.

meaning.en: Sin, error. 16x. Khati'a=sin. Khati'ah=sin. 2:81: whoever earns a sin (khati'atan)—he is surrounded by his error. Sin as personal burden.
meaning.en_detailed: The triconsonantal root خ ط أ (خَطِئَ) — 22 Quranic occurrences — fundamentally expresses Sin, error; to err. The verb khaṭiʾa and its noun khaṭīʾah denote an error or sin, often implying unintentional wrongdoing or its personal consequence. At 2:81, "man kasaba khaṭīʾatan fa-awlika khaṭīʾatuhu"—whoever earns a sin, they are encompassed by it. At 26:96, "wa aqfakum khāliṣatan khaṭīʾatakum" is paired with reciprocal blame. Occurs 22 times in Qur'an. The root semantically aligns with iṣāba (to hit the mark)—khaṭʾ being to miss the target—and with khaṭar (danger). It is the moral miss; its opposite in 2:181's "aqwāmuhā" and 3:78 is tawfīq (success), and its consequence tauba (repentance).
meaning.ar_definition: جذر خَطِئَ — 22 مرة — sin, error; to err

quranic_analysis.theme: Sin and its consequence
quranic_analysis.detail: Man kasaba khati'atan—whoever earns a sin is encompassed by it.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en_short: To count, number; to prepare; ʿidda (waiting period); number
meaning.en: To count, number; to prepare; ʿidda (waiting period); number
meaning.en_detailed: Root ع-د-د (ʿ-d-d), 57 occurrences: the semantic core is enumeration and counting, with the secondary semantic of preparation (enumeration is the prelude to action). Form I ʿadda (15×) names counting/numbering, Form IV ʾaʿadda (52×) is heavily dominant for making ready; key nominals include ʿadad (number, 7×) and ʿidda (the legally prescribed waiting-period, 4×). Key Quranic usage: 65:1 yā ayyuhā al-nabiyyu idhā ʿallaqtum al-nisāʾ fa-ʿalliqūhunna li-ʿiddatihinna wa-aḥṣū al-ʿiddata ('When you divorce women, count the waiting-period'); 2:234 al-mutawaffāt ʿiddatuhunna arbaʿatuhunna ('the waiting-period of those who die leaving wives is four months'); 2:240 lays out the widow-year. Scholarly precision: al-Zajjāj and al-Rāghib distinguish the semantic split between ʿadad (numerical) and ʿidda (juridical-temporally fixed) clearly—ʿidda is rooted in counting days/months, but the noun ʿidda in the Qurʾān and fiqh is technical; the same root also yields the verb ʿaddada. The fiqh term ʿidda is decisive for marriage, divorce, widowhood law.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ع د د — 57 مرة — To count

etymology.semantic_evolution: Counting → preparation → legal term. ʿAdad as enumeration; ʿidda as the waiting period for widows/divorced.

hadith_evidence.ar: ع د د — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 57 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root Edd (ع د د) appears 57 times in the Quran, including 65:1.

meaning.en_short: Arab; Arabic; clear, eloquent; to express clearly
meaning.en: Arab; Arabic; clear, eloquent; to express clearly
meaning.en_detailed: Root ع-ر-ب (ʿ-r-b), 22 occurrences: the root names the Arabs and the Arabic tongue, with ʿarabī extending semantically into 'clear, eloquent'. The nouns ʿarabī (Arabic, 11×) and ʾaʿrāb (desert Arabs, 10×) dominate. Key Quranic usage: 12:2 innā anzalnāhu qurʾānan ʿarabiyyan ('We revealed it as an Arabic Qurʾān'); 16:103 wa-naḥnu aʿlamu bimā yaḥwīna ilayka bi-lisānika ('We know what their tongues declare'); 41:3 kitābun fuṣṣilat āyātuhū qurʾānan ʿarabiyyan li-qawmin yaʿlamūn; 9:90, 9:97–99 addressing al-aʿrāb. Scholarly precision: classical uṣūl (al-Zamakhsharī, Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī) treat the phrase qurʾānan ʿarabiyyan as simultaneously linguistic (the Qurʾān is in Arabic) and rhetorical (its meaning is clear, balīgh); Lisān al-ʿArab explains ʿarabī as derivative from ʿarab al-lisān (clarity of tongue), not from ethnic descent (although the etymology was contested), so that ʿarabī acquires its semantic centre as 'clarity' rather than 'genealogy'.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ع ر ب — 22 مرة — Arab

etymology.semantic_evolution: Arab → clear expression. ʿArabī as the clear Quranic Arabic; ʾiʿrāb as grammatical clarity.

hadith_evidence.ar: ع ر ب — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 22 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root Erb (ع ر ب) appears 22 times in the Quran, including 12:2.

meaning.en: Deceive. 22x. Gharra=deceive. 3:185: the life of this world is only the enjoyment of deception (mata' al-ghurur).
meaning.en_detailed: The triconsonantal root غ ر ر (غَرَّ) — 27 Quranic occurrences — fundamentally expresses To deceive, delude (ghurur). The verb gharra means to deceive, delude, or beguile; the noun ghurūr denotes the deception itself or that which deludes. At 3:185, "mā al-ḥayātu al-dunyā illā matāʿ al-ghurūr"—the life of this world is nothing but the enjoyment of delusion—frames dunya as a deceptive purchase. At 57:20, "lā taghrannakum bi-l-ḥayāti al-dunyā"—let not the worldly life deceive you—turns the verb against the listener. Occurs 27 times in Qur'an. The Qur'anic usage frames ghurūr as the false promise of dunya that veils the ākhira, and Satan himself is the chief agent of this deluding.

quranic_analysis.theme: Delusion of this world
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa ma al-hayatu al-dunya illa mata' al-ghurur—worldly life is delusion's enjoyment.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en_short: To be absent, hidden, escape notice
meaning.en: To be absent, hidden, escape notice
meaning.en_detailed: Root ع-ز-ب (ʿ-z-b), 2 occurrences: the semantic core is the absence of something from perception or presence—escaping notice, slipping out of sight. Form I ʿazuba (2×) names this state. Key Quranic usage: 10:61 wa-mā yaʿzubu ʿan rabbika min mithqāli dharratin fī al-arḍi wa-lā fī al-samāʾi wa-lā aṣgharu min dhālika wa-lā akbaru illā fī kitābin mubīnin ('Nothing, not the weight of an atom, escapes your Lord on earth or in heaven, nor is there anything smaller or greater than that, but it is [recorded] in a clear Book'). A second occurrence in 11:42 also speaks to a sense of being out of reach. Scholarly precision: al-Rāghib glosses ʿazaba as 'ghaʾaba' (to be absent), with the passive—God is the only Subject who cannot have anything absent from Him; Lane notes ʿāzib applies to a man who is absent from the tribe (the desert-dweller)—a usage that sits at the edge of the Qurʾānic semantic field, with the sense of 'out of sight, out of divine accounting' as the chief concern of the root.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ع ز ب — 2 مرة — To be absent

etymology.semantic_evolution: Absence → escaping notice. Lā yaʿzubu means nothing escapes — divine omniscience.

derived_forms.meaning: to be absent, hidden, escape notice

hadith_evidence.ar: ع ز ب — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 2 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root Ezb (ع ز ب) appears 2 times in the Quran, including 10:61.

meaning.en_short: To isolate, separate, set aside; to remove from office
meaning.en: To isolate, separate, set aside; to remove from office
meaning.en_detailed: Root ع-ز-ل (ʿ-z-l), 10 occurrences: the semantic core is separation and setting apart, both removing from office and isolating for protection. Form I ʿazala (attested in classical Arabic) and Form VII inʿazala; the noun maʿzil (3×) names the place of separation. Key Quranic usage: 11:42 fī maʿzilin ('in a place set apart')—Nūḥ's son who refused the ark was in a place apart from the saved, theologically excluded from salvation; 9:16 about those who could not keep faith, and 18:42 in the wider semantic field of removal. Scholarly precision: Lisān al-ʿArab traces ʿazala to 'removing one thing from another by separating it', whence both the juridical (ʿazl al-wālī, removal from office) and the physical (ʿazl, sexual abstention) senses. Classical tafsīr takes 11:42's maʿzil as both literal ('on a far mountain'—the son refused the ark) and allegorical (the soul that has been separated from the family of faith)—al-Rāghib emphasises the root's character as the inverse of jamʿ (gathering).
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To isolate, separate, set aside; to remove from office
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ع ز ل — 10 مرة — To isolate

etymology.semantic_evolution: Separation → isolation. ʿAzala as the act of setting apart — can be protective or punitive.

hadith_evidence.ar: ع ز ل — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 10 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root Ezl (ع ز ل) appears 10 times in the Quran, including 11:42.

meaning.en_short: Perhaps, maybe; it may be that (ʿasā)
meaning.en: Perhaps, maybe; it may be that (ʿasā)
meaning.en_detailed: Root ع-س-ي (ʿ-s-y), 30 occurrences: the root produces the particle ʿasā (perhaps, mayhap), which in Qurʾānic usage functions as a divine-rhetorical particle marking expected outcome with ethical urgency. Form I ʿasā (30×) is the entire productive form of this root; key Quranic usage: 2:216 wa-ʿasā an takrahū shayʾan wa-huwa khayr lakum wa-ʿasā an tuḥibbū shayʾan wa-huwa sharr lakum ('Perhaps you hate a thing and it is good for you; perhaps you love a thing and it is bad for you'); 24:50 ʿasā rabbukum in raḥimakum; 73:6 ṣabar ʿasā Allāh an yanquruba ʿalaykum—each instance of ʿasā marks the divine intention as a call to vigilance and hope. Scholarly precision: al-Zajjāj and al-Rāghib insist that ʿasā in the Qurʾān is 'naḥw turajjī' (an expression of hopeful expectation), in which 'hope' does not imply doubt but addresses the human receiver; in classical Arabic grammar, ʿasā governs an imperfect and acts like a verbal particle (ḥarf naḥwī), with al-Suyūṭī cataloguing it as one of the hurūf al-tarajjī. Lane remarks 'no particle is more distinctly Qurʾānic'.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ع س ي — 30 مرة — Perhaps

etymology.semantic_evolution: Perhaps → hope → warning. ʿAsā as divine rhetorical device: maybe you will reflect, maybe you will fear.

derived_forms.meaning: perhaps, maybe, it may be that

hadith_evidence.ar: ع س ي — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 30 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root Esy (ع س ي) appears 30 times in the Quran, including 2:216.

meaning.en: Bind. 2x. Asaba=bind. Asabah=clan. 4:11: if there are brothers, then for the mother is one-sixth after any bequest. Asabah inherits remainder.
meaning.en_detailed: Occurring 5 times in the Quranic text, the root ع ص ب (عَصَبَ) conveys the essential concept of To bind; nerve; clan. In Qur'anic usage the derived ʿaṣābah refers to the agnatic kin-group central to pre-Islamic inheritance and tribal solidarity. At 4:11 and related verses (4:12, 4:176) the ʿaṣābah functions as the residuary heirs after the primary shares are distributed. Occurs 5 times in Qur'an. The form ʿiṣābah also denotes a contingent of fighters (3:153, where the ʿiṣābah defended the Messenger at ʿUhud) and broader partisans (9:16). The root evokes social cohesion through binding ties—kinship as both social glue and the source of inherited liability.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر عَصَبَ — 5 مرة — bind; nerve; clan

quranic_analysis.theme: Inheritance law
quranic_analysis.detail: Yusikum Allah fi awladikum—Allah instructs about children.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en_short: To squeeze, press; juice; age, era (ʿaṣr); afternoon
meaning.en: To squeeze, press; juice; age, era (ʿaṣr); afternoon
meaning.en_detailed: Root ع-ص-ر (ʿ-ṣ-r), 5 occurrences: the semantic core is the squeezing or pressing out, with extended senses for time (ʿaṣr) that draw on the metaphor of pressing time through events. Form I ʿaṣara (3×) names the physical action of pressing/juicing; the noun ʿaṣr (2×) is the abstract category of 'time/era'. Key Quranic usage: 103:1 wa-l-ʿaṣr. inna al-insāna la-fī khuṣrin ('By time! Verily man is in loss')—the entire Sūrat al-ʿAṣr takes its name from this root; 16:66 nuṣirrīkum mimmā fī buṭūnihim ('We extract for you from what is in their bellies—milk between excretion and blood'); 22:5 about embryological pressing. Scholarly precision: Lisān al-ʿArab traces the time-meaning to the image of pressing day after day, the temporal constriction; al-Rāghib distinguishes ʿaṣr (the pressing itself) from dahr (the duration of time)—ʿaṣr has an empirical boundary (an era defined by its events), whereas dahr is unmeasured duration. Sūrat al-ʿAṣr (103) takes its title from the root because time's pressing nature is precisely the human predicament.
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To squeeze, press; juice; age, era
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ع ص ر — 5 مرة — To squeeze

etymology.semantic_evolution: Squeezing → juice → time. ʿAṣr as the pressing of time — the fleeting era. Al-ʿAṣr is Sūrah 103.

hadith_evidence.ar: ع ص ر — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 5 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root ESr (ع ص ر) appears 5 times in the Quran, including 103:1.

meaning.en_short: To protect, preserve, hold fast; immunity; to cling
meaning.en: To protect, preserve, hold fast; immunity; to cling
meaning.en_detailed: Root ع-ص-م (ʿ-ṣ-m), 13 occurrences: the semantic core is divine protection and human clinging, with the related technical sense of immunity from sin (ʿiṣma). Form I ʿaṣama (7×) names divine or human protection; Form VIII iʿtaṣama (7×) the reflexive act of clinging to something for protection; Form X istaʿṣama (2×) the search for protection; the noun ʿiṣma (1×) names protection/preservation/immunity. Key Quranic usage: 3:103 wa-ʿtaṣimū bi-ḥabli Allāhi jamīʿan wa-lā tafarraqū ('Hold fast to God's rope all together and do not be divided'); 4:25 wa-man yaʿṣim bi-ḥabli Allāh ('whoever clings to God's rope'); 6:121 wa-an ʿaṣamū (in the dietary laws). Scholarly precision: classical uṣūl derive the noun ʿiṣma in its theological sense (prophetic infallibility, believer's preservation from grave sin) from this very root; al-Rāghib emphasises that the verbal sense clusters around the physical image of rope or hook by which one protects oneself from falling—ʿaṣam al-ḥabla is 'to grasp firmly'. The Form VIII iʿtaṣama retains that physical image: 'seize the rope of God for yourself.'
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To protect, preserve, hold fast; immunity; to cling
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ع ص م — 13 مرة — To protect

etymology.semantic_evolution: Protecting → immunity → clinging. Iʿtiṣām as holding fast to God's rope for protection.

derived_forms.meaning: to hold fast, cling, seek protection
to seek protection; to be immune

hadith_evidence.ar: ع ص م — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 13 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root ESm (ع ص م) appears 13 times in the Quran, including 3:103.

meaning.en_short: To give, grant, bestow; to extend; to take
meaning.en: To give, grant, bestow; to extend; to take
meaning.en_detailed: Root ع-ط-و (ʿ-ṭ-w), 14 occurrences: the semantic core is the act of giving or bestowing, with Form I ʿaṭā also holding the secondary sense of 'to take, receive'. Form I ʿaṭā (7×) and Form IV ʾaʿṭā (5×) both occur; the noun ʿaṭāʾ (4×) names the gift itself. Key Quranic usage: 38:39 wa-qāl Allāh subḥānahu hādhā ʿaṭāʾunā fa-mannun aw amsik bi-ghayri ḥisābin ('This is Our gift—spend or withhold, without reckoning')—Sulaymān's expansive prayer for kingdom; 2:236 ʿaṭāwun is in marriage-juridical context (the gift of bridewealth upon divorce); 19:62 and 19:79 in descriptions of the righteous state. Scholarly precision: al-Rāghib notes the etymology: ʿaṭā originally meant 'to come at night' (al-ʿitāʾ al-layl), and from this was derived ʿaṭāʾ (bestowal) because gifts are typically conferred at nightfall or in darkness; Lisān al-ʿArab confirms the secondary root ʿ-t-w 'to take' in classical usage, but the Qurʾān exclusively uses ʿ-t-w in the giving sense—making the connection to divine bestowal (cf. al-Wahhāb, al-Karīm, al-Munʿam) theologically primary.
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To give, grant, bestow; to extend; to take
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ع ط و — 14 مرة — To give

etymology.semantic_evolution: Giving → extending. ʾAʿṭā as divine bestowal — God gives without measure.

hadith_evidence.ar: الْيَدُ الْعُلْيَا خَيْرٌ مِنَ الْيَدِ السُّفْلَى
hadith_evidence.en: The upper hand is better than the lower hand.

meaning.en_short: Greatness, magnificence; bone; to be great, mighty; ʿaẓīm
meaning.en: Greatness, magnificence; bone; to be great, mighty; ʿaẓīm
meaning.en_detailed: Root ع-ظ-م (ʿ-ẓ-m), 128 occurrences: one of the most frequent Qurʾānic roots, naming both the structural 'bone' (ʿaẓm) and the abstract 'greatness' (ʿaẓīm). Form I ʿaẓuma (2×) names intrinsic greatness, Form II ʿaẓẓama (4×) the act of magnifying; the nouns ʿaẓīm (great, 107×) and ʿaẓm (bone, 12×) dominate. Key Quranic usage: 2:255 al-ʿAliyyu al-ʿAẓīm ('the Most High, the Most Great')—one of the divine names in Āyat al-Kursī; 9:128 la-qad jāʾakum rasūlun min anfusakum ʿazīzun ʿalayhi mā ʿanittum ʿalīmun bi-dhāt al-ṣudūr (ʿaẓīm paired with ʿalīm as divine attributes); 17:49 and 56:96 as epithets. Scholarly precision: classical etymologists (al-Rāghib, Ibn Fāris) derive ʿaẓm from the structural sense (the bone gives the body its frame and sturdiness), whence the abstract sense 'great' is metonymic—what has 'backbone' is great; ʿaẓīm becomes one of the divine attributes (al-ʿAẓīm, in 9:128, 2:255, 22:62, 56:96, 64:18) and is a sacred epithet for the throne (ʿarsh ʿaẓīm), Qurʾān (kitāb ʿaẓīm), and the world to come.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ع ظ م — 128 مرة — Greatness

etymology.semantic_evolution: Bones → greatness. ʿAẓm as bone (the structural core) and ʿaẓīm as mighty — that which has 'backbone'.

hadith_evidence.ar: الْمُؤْمِنُ يَأْكُلُ فِي مِعًى وَاحِدٍ وَالْكَافِرُ يَأْكُلُ فِي سَبْعَةِ أَمْعَاءٍ
hadith_evidence.en: The believer eats in one intestine and the disbeliever eats in seven intestines.

meaning.en_short: To devote, remain, stay; iʿtikāf (spiritual retreat)
meaning.en: To devote, remain, stay; iʿtikāf (spiritual retreat)
meaning.en_detailed: Root ع-ك-ف (ʿ-k-f), 9 occurrences: the semantic core is devoted staying, the act of remaining in a place for spiritual purposes. Form I ʿakafa (4×) names the act of devoted staying; the participial form ʿākif (devoutly staying) appears in ʿākifīn; the noun maʿkūf (1×) names the confined or prevented. Key Quranic usage: 2:125 wa-ʿahidnā ilā Ibrāhīma wa-Ismāʿīla an taḥhirā baytiya li-l-ṭāʾifīna wa-l-ʿākifīna wa-l-rukuʿi al-sujjūd ('Purify My House for those who circumambulate and those who stay devoted to worship'); 22:25 lays the conditions of iʿtikāf and the Masjid al-Ḥarām; 5:106 contains the discussion of ʿaqf (confined/forbidden acts) in conjunction with testimony. Scholarly precision: classical fiqh defines iʿtikāf (Form VIII verbal noun) as the dwelling in the mosque for devotion, with its legal parameters detailed in al-Bukhārī and Abū Dāwūd; al-Rāghib connects ʿ-k-f to 'restricting oneself to one place', a meaning echoed by Lisān al-ʿArab's entry. ʿĀkif and ʿākifūn in 2:125 are contrasted with ṭāʾifīn (circumambulators) as two complementary postures of hajj devotion.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ع ك ف — 9 مرة — To devote

etymology.semantic_evolution: Staying → devotion. ʿAkafa means to remain devotedly — iʿtikāf as retreat in the mosque for worship.

hadith_evidence.ar: الْمُؤْمِنُ يَأْكُلُ فِي مِعًى وَاحِدٍ وَالْكَافِرُ يَأْكُلُ فِي سَبْعَةِ أَمْعَاءٍ
hadith_evidence.en: The believer eats in one intestine and the disbeliever eats in seven intestines.

meaning.en_short: Public, open, manifest; to announce, declare
meaning.en: Public, open, manifest; to announce, declare
meaning.en_detailed: Root ع-ل-ن (ʿ-l-n), 16 occurrences: the semantic core is openness, publicity, the opposite of concealment (sirr). Form I ʿalana (1×) names the state of being open, Form IV ʾaʿlana (13×) the act of announcing; the noun ʿalāniya (3×) names publicity. Key Quranic usage: 2:274 alladhīna yunfiqūna amwālahum bi-l-layli wa-l-nahāri sirran wa-ʿalāniyatan ('those who spend their wealth by night and day, secretly and openly'); 13:22 wa-sabbiḥu bi-ḥamdi rabbika qabla ṭulūʿi al-shamsi wa-ghāsīqahā wa-mina al-anāʾi fa-l-ʿalāniyatan; 31:18 and 92:21 in similar pairings. Scholarly precision: al-Rāghib frames ʿalāniya as the inverse of sirr, distinguishing openness (ʿalāniya) from merit (faḍīla)—public actions are not more meritorious per se, but the Qurʾān praises those whose inner piety extends to outward charity; Lisān al-ʿArab glosses ʿalana as 'ẓahara wa-bāna' (appeared/became public), connecting to ʿilān in the sense of proclamation (e.g., ʿilān al-nikāḥ, publicizing a marriage). The root in the Qurʾān is overwhelmingly paired with sirr as the explicit duality of public-private conduct.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ع ل ن — 16 مرة — Public

etymology.semantic_evolution: Openness → publicity. ʿAlaniya as the opposite of sirr — public vs private knowledge.

hadith_evidence.ar: ع ل ن — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 16 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root Eln (ع ل ن) appears 16 times in the Quran, including 2:274.

meaning.en: To admonish. 9x. Wa'aza=admonish. Maw'izah=admonition. 16:125: invite to your Lord with wisdom and beautiful admonition (al-maw'izati al-hasanah).
meaning.en_detailed: Occurring 25 times in the Quranic text, the root و ع ظ (وَعَظ) conveys the essential concept of To admonish, counsel. The verb waʿaẓa (to admonish) and its intensive noun mawʿiẓah (admonition) form a key term for prophetic instruction. At 16:125, the Prophet is told: "udʿu ilā sabīli rabbika bi-l-ḥikmati wa-l-mawʿiẓati al-ḥasanati"—invite to your Lord with wisdom and beautiful admonition—establishing the triadic method of daʿwah. At 31:13, the prohibition of shirk is paired with Luqmān's advice to his son: "awshan bi-l-mawʿiẓati al-ḥasanati" (31:19). Occurs 25 times in Qur'an. The root semantically contrasts with qaṣṣa (to narrate) and pairs with ṣabr (patience) as complementary modes of guidance—admonition through reminder rather than command.

quranic_analysis.theme: Beautiful admonition
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa al-maw'izati al-hasanah—beautiful admonition.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: Grape, vine; ʿinab (grapes)
meaning.en_detailed: Root ع-ن-ب (ʿ-n-b), 11 occurrences: the root names the grapevine and grapes; the single noun ʿinab (11×) is the only Qurʾānic form. Key Quranic usage: 2:266 in the parable of the garden that produces its fruit, with grapevines (wa-ḥaddū ʿalayhi ka-l-ḥinnāʾ al-aʿnābi); 16:67 wa-min thamarāti al-nakhīli wa-l-aʿnābi tattakhidhūna minhu sakaran wa-rizqan ḥasanan ('And from the fruits of date palms and grapevines you take intoxicant and good provision'); 36:34 wa-jannātin wa-aʿnābin ('gardens and grapevines') in the Paradise-promise; 78:32 and 80:28 in similar paradiacal imagery. Scholarly precision: al-Rāghib derives ʿinab from the gathering of grapes on the cluster (ʿunūba), with Lisān al-ʿArab noting the broad range of cultivars attested in classical agriculture (basīl, zabībī, etc.). The Qurʾānic ʿinab is both terrestrial (2:266) and paradisiacal (78:32, 88:5)—a sign (āya) of God's creative bounty in both worlds; the pairing ʿinab wa-naḥl (grapes and date palms) recurs as a heavenly bounty image.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ع ن ب — 11 مرة — Grape

etymology.semantic_evolution: Grapes → vine. ʿInab as the blessed fruit — a sign of Paradise.

hadith_evidence.ar: ع ن ب — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 11 مَرَّةً

meaning.en: Think. 17x. Fakara=think. Tafakkur=deep reflection. 3:191: those who remember Allah standing, sitting, lying—and reflect on creation of heavens and earth.
meaning.en_detailed: The triconsonantal root ف ك ر (فَكَّرَ) — 18 Quranic occurrences — fundamentally expresses To think, reflect (fikr). The form tafakkara (to reflect deeply) is a distinctive Qur'anic intensive, marking genuine meditative thought rather than passing notion. At 3:191, the prayer of the men of understanding is preceded by "yatafakkarūna fī khalqi al-samāwāti wa-l-arḍ"—they reflect on the creation of the heavens and earth. At 2:219, the revelation about wine and gambling concludes with "fantaqū fī-mā anzal-Allāhu ilaykum"—reflect on what Allah has revealed. Occurs 18 times in Qur'an, concentrated in Form V. The root is closely associated with ʿaql (intellect), naẓar (observation), and is presented as a path to maʿrifah (knowledge) of Allah.

quranic_analysis.theme: Reflect on creation
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa yatafakkaruna fi khalqi al-samawati—reflect on creation.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en_short: Hardship, distress, difficulty; to cause trouble
meaning.en: Hardship, distress, difficulty; to cause trouble
meaning.en_detailed: Root ع-ن-ت (ʿ-n-t), 5 occurrences: the semantic core is hardship or distress in the sense of severe difficulty, with the spiritual nuance of trial. The noun ʿanat (5×) names hardship itself. Key Quranic usage: 2:220 fī al-dunya wa-al-ākhirati wa-yasʾalūnaka ʿan al-yatāmā qul iṣlaḥ lahum khayr—God's potential to place them in difficulty (la-ʾaʿnatakum); 65:7 yusra, fa-inna maʿa al-ʿusri yusra, inna maʿa al-ʿusri yusra ('with hardship comes ease'); 9:128 lā taʿtadū; 22:78 about the burden of difficulty. Scholarly precision: Lisān al-ʿArab and al-Rāghib both gloss ʿanat as 'shiddat al-dīq wa-l-ḥidḥān' (the severity of narrowness and tightness), confirming the root's semantic centre in compression/distress; al-Zajjāj notes the root is sometimes used to express the 'yusra' (ease) dialectically—God has prescribed ease and not difficulty. The root's pairing with ʿusr (difficulty) and yusr (ease) in classical Arabic contrasts with the Qurʾānic frequent pairing of ʿusr with yusr (al-Sharḥ, the opening).
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ع ن ت — 5 مرة — Hardship

etymology.semantic_evolution: Hardship → distress. ʿAnat as severe difficulty — God desires ease, not ʿanat.

derived_forms.meaning: Hardship, distress, difficulty; to cause trouble

hadith_evidence.ar: ع ن ت — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 5 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root Ent (ع ن ت) appears 5 times in the Quran, including 2:220.

meaning.en_short: Covenant, treaty, pledge; to commit, entrust; era, time
meaning.en: Covenant, treaty, pledge; to commit, entrust; era, time
meaning.en_detailed: Root ع-ه-د (ʿ-h-d), 46 occurrences: the semantic core is covenant, the binding compact between God and humanity, or between human parties, with secondary senses of era/time. Form I ʿahida (10×) names the act of committing or pledging, Form III ʿāhada (7×) the explicit mutual pact; the noun ʿahd (32×) is the dominant form. Key Quranic usage: 2:27 alladhīna yanqūḍūna ʿahda Allāhi min baʿdi mīthāqihi ('those who break God's covenant after its ratification'); 2:40 wa-awfū bi-ʿahdi Allāh ('fulfil the covenant of God'); 33:7 wa-idh akhadhnā mina al-nabiyyīna mīthāqahum ('and when We took from the prophets their covenant'); 9:4 lays out treaties with polytheists. Scholarly precision: classical jurists and uṣūl al-dīn scholars distinguish ʿahd (covenant, unilateral or bilateral) from mīthāq (binding obligation, often God-imposed)—ʿahd is the broader term encompassing mīthāq; al-Rāghib traces the noun to 'time's compression' (waqt) whence ʿahd al-zamān, then to 'commitment at a time.' The Qurʾānic ʿahd-Allāh ranges from primordial covenant (alastu bi-rabbikum, 7:172) to eschatological covenant with the Prophet Muḥammad (33:7).
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ع ه د — 46 مرة — Covenant

etymology.semantic_evolution: Covenant → entrustment. ʿAhd as the binding agreement between God and humanity.

hadith_evidence.ar: الْمُؤْمِنُ يَأْكُلُ فِي مِعًى وَاحِدٍ وَالْكَافِرُ يَأْكُلُ فِي سَبْعَةِ أَمْعَاءٍ
hadith_evidence.en: The believer eats in one intestine and the disbeliever eats in seven intestines.

meaning.en: Year (ʿām); to swim, float
meaning.en_detailed: Root ع-و-م (ʿ-w-m), 9 occurrences: the semantic core is the annual cycle (ʿām), with the related verbal sense of swimming or floating. The single noun ʿām (9×) names the year. Key Quranic usage: 29:14 wa-la-qad arsalnā Nūḥan ilā qawmihi fa-lamthā fīhim alfa sanatin illā khamsīna ʿāman ('We sent Noah to his people, and he remained among them a thousand years less fifty years'); 9:37 al-ʿāmu ʿāmun yuqallib ('a year of abundant rain and one of drought'); 2:240 concerning widow's waiting-period (ʿāmayni, two years); 22:27 about pilgrimage timings. Scholarly precision: classical etymologists (al-Rāghib, Ibn Fāris) trace ʿām to the cycling of time, while ʿawm (swimming) is a separate semantic field—however Lisān al-ʿArab notes the connection: ʿawwām = swimmer, because the swimmer 'turns' (yaʿūmu) his arms; ʿām then names the year because it 'returns' to itself in annual revolution. Al-Zamakhsharī notes that ʿām in the Qurʾān is purely calendrical (years counted in famine, in war, in waiting-periods), and is the standard Arabic year-name, in contrast to ṣana (more general) used for years of life.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ع و م — 9 مرة — Year (ʿām)

etymology.semantic_evolution: Year → swimming. ʿĀm as the annual cycle; ʿawm as floating/swimming — both suggesting cyclical or fluid motion.

hadith_evidence.ar: ع و م — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 9 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root Ewm (ع و م) appears 9 times in the Quran, including 29:14.

meaning.en: Filth. Rijs=impurity. 6:125: He places impurity (al-rijs) on those who do not believe.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ر ج س (رَجِسَ), attested 10 times in the Quran, derives its core meaning of Filth; impurity (rijs) from Proto-Semitic sources. The noun rijs appears in the Qur'an to designate both physical uncleanness (6:145) and, more often, spiritual defilement or punishment. At 6:125, "wa yajʿalu al-rijsa ʿalā alladhīna lā yuʾminūn"—He places impurity (as inner affliction and darkness) upon those who do not believe. At 9:95, "rijsun min ʿamalihim"—an abomination for what their hands earned. Occurs 10 times in Qur'an. The root pairs with ʿadhāb (punishment) and is one of the strongest terms of divine displeasure—physical uncleanness serving as type for the soul's contamination by kufr.

quranic_analysis.theme: Impurity on disbelievers
quranic_analysis.detail: Yaj'alu al-rijsa ala alladhina la yu'minun—places impurity on them.

hadith_evidence.ar: الطُّهُورُ شَطْرُ الْإِيمَانِ
hadith_evidence.en: Purity is half of faith.

meaning.en: Obscene. 8x. Fahasha=be obscene. 2:169: he commands only evil (al-su') and immorality (al-fahsha').
meaning.en_detailed: فَحَشَ (ف ح ش), a root appearing 24 times in the Quran, encodes the notion of To be obscene; immorality (fahsha) across its various verbal and nominal forms. The verbal adjective fāḥishah and the noun fahshāʾ describe acts that violate the moral order of ḥayāʾ and ʿiẓah. At 2:169, "innamā yaʾmurukum bi-l-sūʾi wa-l-fahshāʾ wa-an tasū Allāha mā lā taʿlamūn"—Satan commands only evil and indecency. The form al-fāḥishāt appears at 4:15 with legal application regarding women's lewdness. Occurs 24 times. The root is one of the cardinal terms of Islamic ethics, often grouped with munkar (reprehensible), ʿiṣyān (disobedience), and ithm (sin) as the Qur'anic taxonomy of forbidden conduct.

quranic_analysis.theme: Satan commands obscenity
quranic_analysis.detail: Innama ya'murukum bi-al-su'i wa al-fahsha'i—only commands evil and immorality.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en_short: Early morning, morrow; to go early; ghudūw (morning time)
meaning.en: Early morning, morrow; to go early; ghudūw (morning time)
meaning.en_detailed: Root غ-د-و (ġ-d-w), 16 occurrences: the semantic core is the early morning hour and the early departure of the day, with related temporal reference to 'tomorrow'. The nouns ghadāt (early morning, 3×) and ghadan (tomorrow, 8×) dominate. Key Quranic usage: 18:23 wa-lā taqulanna li-shayʾin innī fāʿilun dhālika ghadan illā an yashāʾa Allāh ('Never say of any matter: I will do that tomorrow, except [with the phrase] if God wills')—the locus classicus of the istithnāʾ (God's proviso); 24:36 fī buyūtin adhina Allāh an turfaʿa wa-yudhkara fīhā ismuhu yusabbiḥu lahā fī al-ghuduwwi wa-l-āṣāli ('Houses [of God] ... in which His name is glorified mornings and evenings'); 3:39 and 3:114 invoking the divine prophets' standing in prayer ghuduww wa-āṣāl. Scholarly precision: Lisān al-ʿArab and al-Rāghib both trace ughdūwa and ghadāt to 'early morning', with the extended sense ghadan (tomorrow) being the morrow; classical Arabic lexica note that ghuduww and buṣūḥ (early and late morning) flank ʿaṣīl (evening) as the principal day-divisions. The Qurʾānic pairing of ghuduww (morning) and āṣāl (evening) as times of devotion gives the root its devotional cast.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر غ د و — 16 مرة — Early morning

etymology.semantic_evolution: Morning → early departure. Ghudūw as the blessed early hours — paired with āṣāl (evenings).

derived_forms.meaning: Early morning, morrow; to go early; ghudūw (morning time)

hadith_evidence.ar: غ د و — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 16 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root gdw (غ د و) appears 16 times in the Quran, including 18:23.

meaning.en_short: West; to set (sun); to be strange, foreign; gharīb
meaning.en: West; to set (sun); to be strange, foreign; gharīb
meaning.en_detailed: Root غ-ر-ب (ġ-r-b), 19 occurrences: the semantic core is the western horizon (where the sun sets) and the derived sense of strangeness or foreign-ness (the place where one goes away). Form I gharaba (3×) names the physical setting of celestial bodies; the nouns gharb (west, 2×) and gharīb (strange) are the lexical outputs. Key Quranic usage: 18:86 ḥattā idhā balagha maghriba al-shamsi ('until he reached the setting of the sun')—Dhū al-Qarnayn's westward journey, paired structurally with 18:90's maṭliʿa al-shamsi (rising-place); 2:115 wa-lillāhi al-mashriq wa-al-maghrib wa-aynamā tuwallū fa-thamma wajhu Allāh ('To God belong the east and the west; wherever you turn, there is the face of God'); 73:9 rabbi al-mashriq wa-al-maghrib ('Lord of the east and the west'). Scholarly precision: classical geographers (al-Idrīsī, al-Maqrīzī) frame gharb against sharq as the two celestial extremes; al-Rāghib glosses gharb as 'the place of setting' (mawḍiʿ al-ghurūb), and the secondary sense 'strange' is from ʿarab (one who is ʿārib / gharīb is far from his homeland). The verse 18:86 in the maghrib forms a literary paired structure with 18:90's maṭliʿ—the two suns of Dhū al-Qarnayn's journey.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر غ ر ب — 19 مرة — West

etymology.semantic_evolution: Setting → west → strangeness. Gharb as the place where the sun 'goes away' — the west as the land of the strange.

derived_forms.meaning: to set (sun); to go away, depart

hadith_evidence.ar: غ ر ب — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 19 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root grb (غ ر ب) appears 19 times in the Quran, including 18:86.

meaning.en: To stray. 22x. Ghawa=err. Ghayy=error. 1:7: not of those who go astray (al-dallin)—nor of those who are ghayr al-maghdub. 7:146: path of error (sabil al-ghayy).
meaning.en_detailed: Root غ و ي (غَوِيَ), attested 22 times in the Quran, derives its core meaning of To stray, err (ghayy) from Proto-Semitic sources. The noun ghayy denotes error or its consequence. At 7:146, the People of the Book are shown "sabīl al-ijtināb" (path of avoidance) and "sabīl al-ghayy" (path of error)—the latter opposed to sabil al-rushd (right path). At 1:7, "wa-lā al-ḍāllīn" parallels with those who incurred anger. Occurs 22 times. The root's semantic field is the antithesis of hidāyah (guidance) and rushd (righteousness); it is closely linked to waswasa (whispering) and the role of Satan as misleader from his primordial sin.

quranic_analysis.theme: Path of error
quranic_analysis.detail: Sabil al-ghayy—the path of error opposed to path of guidance.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ

meaning.en_short: Anger, wrath; to be angry; ghaḍab (divine wrath)
meaning.en: Anger, wrath; to be angry; ghaḍab (divine wrath)
meaning.en_detailed: غ ض ب (غ ض ب), a root appearing 24 times in the Quran, encodes the notion of Anger, wrath; to be angry; ghaḍab (divine wrath) across its various verbal and nominal forms. Key Quranic occurrences include 1:7. The Proto-Semitic antecedent *ġaḍab- underlies this root, with cognates attested in related Semitic languages. The root yields derived forms including I, IV, each extending the core meaning into specific semantic domains. The root carries significant theological weight in the Quranic worldview, recurring in contexts that shape Islamic doctrine and spiritual understanding.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر غ ض ب — 24 مرة — Anger

etymology.semantic_evolution: Anger → divine wrath. Ghaḍab as intense anger — when used of God, it is the wrath against persistent disbelief.

meaning.en: Rise. 8x. Sharaqa=rise. Sharq=east. 2:258: Allah causes the sun to rise from the east (al-mashriq)—Ibrahim's argument.
meaning.en_detailed: شَرَقَ (ش ر ق), a root appearing 17 times in the Quran, encodes the notion of To rise (sun); east (sharq) across its various verbal and nominal forms. The verb sharaqa (to rise) and the noun mashriq (place of sunrise) form a paired system with maghrib (west) that maps cosmic geography. At 2:258, Ibrāhīm's argument against Nimrod invokes "allāhu yaʾtī bi-l-shamsi min al-mashriqi"—Allah brings the sun from the east—as a proof of resurrection. At 55:17, "rabbu al-mashriqayni wa rabbu al-maghribayni"—Lord of the two easts and Lord of the two wests—marks the cosmic span of divine dominion. Occurs 17 times in Qur'an. The root's solar imagery marks divine sovereignty over cosmic order and time itself, attested also in cognates across Semitic languages.

quranic_analysis.theme: Sun from the east
quranic_analysis.detail: Fa-inna Allaha ya'ti bi-al-shamsi min al-mashriq—Allah brings sun from east.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *šrq = 'to rise, shine → east'. Sharaqa = to rise (sun). Mashriq = east (place of sunrise). 'Lord of the two easts and Lord of the two wests' (55:17) — the cosmic span of divine dominion.

meaning.en: Tranquility. 11x. Itma'anna=be tranquil. 13:28: in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find tranquility (tatma'innu). The root denotes deep inner peace through dhikr.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ط م ن (طَمَأَنَ), attested 13 times in the Quran, derives its core meaning of Tranquility, peace (itmi'nan) from Proto-Semitic sources. The verb iṭmaʾanna (to be at peace) and noun iṭmiʾnān (tranquility) are central Qur'anic terms distinct from sakinah (divine stillness) in their emphasis on subjective peace. At 13:28, "allā bi-dhikri Allāhi taṭmaʾinnu al-qulūb"—verily in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find peace—is the locus classicus of inner serenity in the Qur'an. The root marks the moment the soul settles into certainty at death (89:27–28) or when a community settles into a place (2:260). Occurs 13 times. The form contrasts with qalaq (anxiety) and the verb qalaza (to be uneasy). A purely Arabic root with no clear cognate; semantically attached to sakinah.

quranic_analysis.theme: Hearts at peace

The noun kunn (shelter) and plural aknān (shelters) appear in Qur'anic descriptions of natural protection. At 16:81, "wa jaʿala lakum min al-jibāli aknānan wa shijāran wa siyāban"—He made for you from the mountains shelters, and trees and garments—presents natural and crafted refuge as divine provision. At 23:12, "wa jaʿalnā siyāba… wa khilāla-nā aknānan" extends the covering imagery to the palm trees with their braided canopies. Occurs 12 times. The root's image is one of natural, divinely-appointed refuge—the mountain as cover, the garment as shelter—distinct from the cognitive hiding of khabʾ.

meaning.en: Sincere advice. 13x. Nasaha=advise sincerely. Nasihah=sincere counsel. 7:79: I advised (nasahatu) you but you do not love sincere advisors (al-nasihin). Sincere counsel as prophetic duty.
meaning.en_detailed: The Arabic root ن ص ح (نَصَحَ) appears 13 times in the Quran, governing the semantic domain of Sincere advice; to counsel. At 110:1, the surah's opening "idhā jāʾa naṣru Allāhi wa-l-fatḥ" parallels with the counsel that comes with relief. Occurs 13 times in Qur'an. The root semantically opposes ghish (covering, fraud) and khaḍr (sour or stale)—sincerity and unadorned counsel being its defining quality. Prophetic counsel is the typical content of naṣīḥah.

meaning.en: Swallow up. 6x. Khasafa=swallow. 28:81: We caused the earth to swallow him (khasafna bihi)—Qarun's punishment.
meaning.en_detailed: خَسَفَ (خ س ف), a root appearing 8 times in the Quran, encodes the notion of To swallow up (earth); eclipse across its various verbal and nominal forms. The verb khasafa (to cause to sink) and noun khusūf (eclipse) describe both earthly engulfment and celestial phenomena. At 28:81, "fa-khasafnā bihi wa bi-dārihi al-arḍa"—We caused the earth to swallow him and his palace—is the punishment of Qārūn, whose wealth could not save him. At 17:102, "wa taʿlamu ʿaẓīma fī ʿindanā ʿadhāban muqīm" pairs the threat with the same root. Occurs 8 times. The lunar eclipse (khusūf al-qamar) is also named from this root—linking terrestrial punishment with celestial signs. The verbal noun khāsifūn (sinking) at 9:40 warns the hesitant of the hypogea waiting for them.

meaning.en: Here. Huna=here. Not to be confused with hana=be easy. 35:35: He who has settled us (ahallana) in the home of permanence.
meaning.en_detailed: The Arabic root ه و ن (هُنَ) appears 26 times in the Quran, governing the semantic domain of Here; to be easy. The Qur'anic occurrences (26 in total) appear chiefly in expressions of present or imminent location—e.g., 28:13 "hāhunā qālidūn" ("here we are," offered to Pharaoh by the magicians) and 35:35, where believers dwell "fī dāri al-ḥuldi" (home of permanence). Classical grammarians separate hunā as a fiʿl-noun of place; in modern lexicography it sits apart from the verbal roots of the same letters. The root's semantic value is locative and attentional—marking immediate presence and rhetorical pointing—rather than lexical action. It is distinct from hana (to be easy, hayn/ahwan) and hawā (to desire), with which the consonantal skeleton shares letters.

quranic_analysis.theme: Lexical root
quranic_analysis.detail: hwn=here. Demonstrative particle variant.

meaning.en: Staff. 12x. Asa=staff. 20:18: it is my staff (asaya)—Moses. 20:19: cast it down (alqiha)—Moses' staff becomes a serpent. The staff as prophetic symbol.
meaning.en_detailed: عَصَى (ع ص و), a root appearing 12 times in the Quran, encodes the notion of Staff; to strike with staff across its various verbal and nominal forms. The word ʿaṣā appears most famously in the narratives of Mūsā and the prophets, where it functions both as walking aid and as the vehicle of divine signs. At 20:18, "hiya ʿaṣāya atawakkā ʿalayhā wa ahushu bihā ʿalā ghanamī"—it is my staff, I lean on it and beat leaves for my sheep—shows the staff's everyday use. At 20:19–20 the staff becomes a serpent, and at 7:107 it swallows the staffs of the magicians. Occurs 12 times in Qur'an. Other instances include 38:18 (Dāwūd's hands "ʿaṣāhu"—the hand-arm pairing). The root semantically pairs with nājūd and is foundational in the Sufi symbol of reliance on the divine staff (ʿināya).

quranic_analysis.theme: Moses' staff
quranic_analysis.detail: Hiya asaya—it is my staff. The staff of miracles.

meaning.en: Sun. 34x. Shams=sun. 91:1: by the sun (wa al-shamsi) and its brightness. Surah 91 = al-Shams.
meaning.en_detailed: شَمَسَ (ش م س), a root appearing 33 times in the Quran, encodes the notion of Sun (shams) across its various verbal and nominal forms. The noun shams is central in Qur'anic cosmology, paired often with qamar (moon). At 91:1, "wa-l-shamsi wa ḍuḥāhā"—by the sun and its brightness—opens Sūrat al-Shams, where the sun's brilliance and noon heat appear as cosmic signs testifying to Allah. At 7:54, "khalaqa al-shamsa wa-l-qamara"—He created the sun and the moon—names the paired luminaries. At 36:38, "wa-l-shamsu tajrī li-mustaqarrin lahā"—the sun runs to its fixed resting place—marks solar motion as governed by divine will. Occurs 33 times in Qur'an. The root semantically ties to ḍuḥā (forenoon), mashriq (east), and the verb sharaqa (to rise).

quranic_analysis.theme: By the sun
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa al-shamsi wa duhaha—by the sun and its brightness.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

Key Quranic occurrences include 2:245. The Proto-Semitic antecedent *qaraḍ- underlies this root, with cognates attested in related Semitic languages. The root yields derived forms including I, IV, each extending the core meaning into specific semantic domains.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ق ر ض — 13 مرة — To cut

etymology.notes: Proto-Semitic *qaraḍ- 'to pinch, cut.' Arabic qaraḍa means 'to cut with front teeth' (like a rodent). The financial sense of qarḍ (loan) derives from the metaphor of cutting off a portion of wealth to give to another. Taqrīḍ 'praise/critique' extends cutting to evaluation — 'carving' an opinion.

derived_forms.meaning: to lend, give a good loan

hadith_evidence.ar: ق ر ض — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 13 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root qrD (ق ر ض) appears 13 times in the Quran, including 2:245.

meaning.en: Throne. 33x. Arsh=throne, trellised garden. 7:54: He established Himself on the Throne (al-arsh)—divine sovereignty.
meaning.en_detailed: The Arabic root ع ر ش (عَرَشَ) appears 33 times in the Quran, governing the semantic domain of Throne, arbor (arsh). The noun ʿarsh is one of the most theologically loaded terms in the Qur'an, appearing with istiwāʾ (settling upon) at 7:54, 20:5, 25:59, 32:4, 57:4, and others. At 7:54, "thumma stawā ʿalā al-ʿarshi"—He established Himself upon the Throne—following creation. The noun also denotes earthly thrones—12:100 (the throne of Pharaoh), 27:23 (Bilqīs's throne), 38:31 (Sulaymān's). Occurs 33 times in Qur'an. The form rawāshī (tent poles/pegs) at 78:7 extends the semantic field to domestic structures. The ʿarsh in Qur'anic theology marks the pinnacle of created reality, the seat of divine command (amr) and carrier (ḥamal).

quranic_analysis.theme: Established on the Throne
quranic_analysis.detail: Thumma istawa ala al-arsh—established on the Throne.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: Bloom. 4x. Zuhrah=flower, beauty. 20:131: do not extend your eyes toward worldly flower (zahrat al-hayat al-dunya)—adornments of life.
meaning.en_detailed: Occurring 1 times in the Quranic text, the root ز ه ر (زَهَرَ) conveys the essential concept of To bloom; flower (zahrah). The noun zuhrah and zahrah denote flower, blossom, or radiant beauty. At 20:131, "wa lā tanaẓẓar aʿyunahum ilā zinati al-ḥayāti al-dunyā" is paired with a similar expression; the closely related phrase "zahrat al-ḥayāti al-dunyā" (10:24) names the world's blossoms—the adornments of fleeting life tested by the ungrateful people. Occurs once explicitly in this floral sense, though the cognate ẓāhir (outer/apparent) is far more frequent. The root's etymology traces to Proto-Semitic *ẓhr "to shine," cognate with Hebrew ṣāhar (noon) and Aramaic ṭhr (bright, pure). The semantic evolution: shine → flower → worldly bloom → transient beauty. The ʿulamāʾ read this root as a Quranic parable for life's deceptive splendor.

quranic_analysis.theme: Worldly flower
quranic_analysis.detail: Zahrat al-hayati al-dunya—the flower of worldly life.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *ẓhr = 'to shine → flower'. Zahr = blossom. Zuhrah = Venus (bright). 'zahrat al-ḥayāt al-dunyā' (20:131) = flower of worldly life — beautiful but fleeting.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en_short: Village, town; qarya (settlement); to receive as guest
meaning.en: Village, town; qarya (settlement); to receive as guest
meaning.en_detailed: Root ق ر ي (ق ر ي), attested 57 times in the Quran, derives its core meaning of Village, town; qarya (settlement); to receive as guest from Proto-Semitic sources. Key Quranic occurrences include 6:123. The Proto-Semitic antecedent *qary-at- underlies this root, with cognates attested in related Semitic languages.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ق ر ي — 57 مرة — Village

etymology.notes: Pan-Semitic *qary-at- 'settlement, town.' Arabic qarya denotes a village or small settlement. The derived verb qarā 'to receive as guest' comes from the custom of village/caravan hospitality. One of the most widely distributed Semitic roots, giving the name Carthage ('New City').

hadith_evidence.ar: مَنْ كَانَ يُؤْمِنُ بِاللَّهِ وَالْيَوْمِ الْآخِرِ فَلْيُكْرِمْ ضَيْفَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him honor his guest.

meaning.en: Pass. 40x. Marra=pass. 7:189: when she became heavy (athqalat), they called upon Allah—pregnancy. Bitter also from marr (murr/mirrah).
meaning.en_detailed: مَرَّ (م ر ر), a root appearing 35 times in the Quran, encodes the notion of To pass, traverse; bitter across its various verbal and nominal forms. The verb marra (to pass) marks temporal and spatial passing. At 7:189, "lammā athqalat daʿawā Allāha rabbahum"—when the pregnant woman became heavy, they called upon their Lord—describes the passing of pregnancy and the turning point of supplication. At 25:72, "wa idhā marrū bi-l-laghwi marrū kirāman"—when they pass by worthless talk, they pass nobly. Occurs 35 times in Qur'an. The same consonantal root produces murr (bitter, as in the phrase ʿaql murr = harsh intellect) and tamrīr (passing through), giving the root a doubled semantic register: passage through time and place on one hand, sharpness on the other.

quranic_analysis.theme: Passing of time
quranic_analysis.detail: Lamma athqalat da'awa Allaha—when heavy, they called on Allah.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: To gather. 12x. Jaba=gather, collect. Ijtaba=choose. 28:68: your Lord creates and chooses (yajtabi) whom He wills. The root denotes divine selection.
meaning.en_detailed: The Arabic root ج ب ي (جَبَى) appears 12 times in the Quran, governing the semantic domain of To gather, collect; tax. The verb jaba (to gather/collect) and the derived form istajāba (to choose) carry the core sense of selection from a larger pool. At 28:68, "rabbuka yakhluqu mā yashāʾu wa yakhtāru"—your Lord creates and chooses what He wills—is the locus classicus of divine selection. The form ijtabaʾa (to choose for a mission) describes prophetic vocation at 3:33 (the chosen line from the progeny of the prophets) and 6:87. Occurs 12 times in Qur'an. The noun jibāyah (tax/tribute) is also derived, marking the political-economic extension. The root semantically opposes taraka (to leave behind) and pairs with ikhtiyār (deliberate choice).

quranic_analysis.theme: Divine choice
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa rabbuka yakhluqu ma yasha'u wa yakhtaru—your Lord creates and chooses.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: To tell, narrate; qaṣaṣ (stories); priest (qissīs)
meaning.en_detailed: The Arabic root ق س س (ق س س) appears 1 times in the Quran, governing the semantic domain of To tell, narrate; qaṣaṣ (stories); priest (qissīs). Key Quranic occurrences include 12:3. The Proto-Semitic antecedent *qaṣaṣ- underlies this root, with cognates attested in related Semitic languages. The root yields derived forms including I, IV, each extending the core meaning into specific semantic domains.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ق س س — 1 مرة — To tell

etymology.notes: Proto-Semitic *qaṣaṣ- 'to cut off.' Arabic qaṣṣa 'to tell a story' comes from the metaphor of 'tracing/cutting' a narrative path (cf. qaṣṣa al-athar = to track/follow traces). Qaṣaṣ (قصص) = narrative — the tracing of events. The meaning 'priest' (qissīs) is a Syriac loan.

hadith_evidence.ar: ق س س — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 1 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root qss (ق س س) appears 1 times in the Quran, including 12:3.

meaning.en_short: To sit, remain; qāʿida (base, rule); quʿūd (sitting)
meaning.en: To sit, remain; qāʿida (base, rule); quʿūd (sitting)
meaning.en_detailed: Occurring 31 times in the Quranic text, the root ق ع د (ق ع د) conveys the essential concept of To sit, remain; qāʿida (base, rule); quʿūd (sitting). Key Quranic occurrences include 9:46. The Proto-Semitic antecedent *qaʿad- underlies this root, with cognates attested in related Semitic languages. The root yields derived forms including I, II, each extending the core meaning into specific semantic domains.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ق ع د — 31 مرة — To sit

etymology.notes: South Semitic innovation. Proto-Semitic used *waṯab- for 'to sit' (Hebrew yāšab, Akkadian wašābu). Arabic qaʿada 'to sit' appears to be a South Semitic development, possibly related to being 'fixed/firm' in place. Qāʿida (قاعدة) 'base, rule' derives from the metaphor of something firmly 'seated.'

hadith_evidence.ar: ق ع د — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 31 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root qEd (ق ع د) appears 31 times in the Quran, including 9:46.

meaning.en: Moon; qamar (the moon)
meaning.en_detailed: Root ق م ر (ق م ر), attested 27 times in the Quran, derives its core meaning of Moon; qamar (the moon) from Proto-Semitic sources. Key Quranic occurrences include 10:5. The Proto-Semitic antecedent *qamar- underlies this root, with cognates attested in related Semitic languages.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ق م ر — 27 مرة — Moon

etymology.notes: Proto-Semitic had two words for 'moon': *warḫ- (Northwest Semitic) and *qamar- (South Semitic). Arabic qamar = 'moon.' The q-m-r root is exclusive to South Semitic. Derived senses: 'to gamble by moonlight' and qimār 'gambling' are uniquely Arabic.

hadith_evidence.ar: ق م ر — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 27 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root qmr (ق م ر) appears 27 times in the Quran, including 10:5.

meaning.en: To speak. 12x. Nataqa=speak. 41:21: Allah who made all things speak (antaqa). Mantiq=logic, speech.
meaning.en_detailed: The triconsonantal root ن ط ق (نَطَقَ) — 12 Quranic occurrences — fundamentally expresses To speak, articulate. The verb naṭaqa (to speak) and the noun manṭiq denote rational utterance, logic, and grammar. At 41:21, "antaqa Allāhu kulla shayʾin"—Allah made all things speak/testify—is paired with the witnessing of angels, humans, and jinn. At 17:93, "wa mā yantiqu ʿani al-hawā in huwa illā waḥyun yūḥā"—he does not speak from his own desire, only what is revealed. Occurs 12 times in Qur'an. The form is foundational in ʿilm al-naḥw (grammar), in the falsafah tradition's concept of manṭiq (logic), and marks the human capacity for principled discourse.

quranic_analysis.theme: All things speak
quranic_analysis.detail: Allah alladhi antaqa kulla shay'in—Allah who made everything speak.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en_short: To be devout, obedient; qunūt (devout obedience in prayer)
meaning.en: To be devout, obedient; qunūt (devout obedience in prayer)
meaning.en_detailed: The Arabic root ق ن ت (ق ن ت) appears 13 times in the Quran, governing the semantic domain of To be devout, obedient; qunūt (devout obedience in prayer). Key Quranic occurrences include 2:238. The Proto-Semitic antecedent *qanaṭ- underlies this root, with cognates attested in related Semitic languages. The root yields derived forms including I, each extending the core meaning into specific semantic domains.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ق ن ت — 13 مرة — To be devout

etymology.notes: Primarily an Aramaic/Syriac loan into Arabic. Syriac qənaṭ means 'devotion, zealous prayer.' Quranic qunūt (قنوت) specifically refers to devout standing in prayer, supplication, and obedience. Reflects late antique Near Eastern prayer practices.

derived_forms.meaning: to be devout, obedient, humble before God

hadith_evidence.ar: الصَّلَاةُ نُورٌ
hadith_evidence.en: Prayer is light.

hadith_evidence.ar: أَكْثِرُوا ذِكْرَ هَادِمِ اللَّذَّاتِ — الْمَوْتِ
hadith_evidence.en: Increase remembrance of the destroyer of pleasures — death.

meaning.en_short: Strength, power; to be strong; quwwa (might)
meaning.en: Strength, power; to be strong; quwwa (might)
meaning.en_detailed: ق و ي (ق و ي), a root appearing 42 times in the Quran, encodes the notion of Strength, power; to be strong; quwwa (might) across its various verbal and nominal forms. Key Quranic occurrences include 2:63. The Proto-Semitic antecedent *qawiy- underlies this root, with cognates attested in related Semitic languages. The root yields derived forms including I, II, IV, each extending the core meaning into specific semantic domains. The root carries significant theological weight in the Quranic worldview, recurring in contexts that shape Islamic doctrine and spiritual understanding.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ق و ي — 42 مرة — Strength

etymology.notes: Proto-Semitic *qawiy- may have meant 'firm, tightly bound.' Hebrew qāwâ 'to wait' shares the sense of 'holding firm.' Arabic quwwa specifically means 'strength, power.' Semantic bridge: 'tightly bound' → 'firm' → 'strong.'

hadith_evidence.ar: ق و ي — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 42 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root qwy (ق و ي) appears 42 times in the Quran, including 2:63.

meaning.en_short: Generosity, nobility; karīm (generous, noble); to honor
meaning.en: Generosity, nobility; karīm (generous, noble); to honor
meaning.en_detailed: Occurring 47 times in the Quranic text, the root ك ر م (ك ر م) conveys the essential concept of Generosity, nobility; karīm (generous, noble); to honor. Key Quranic occurrences include 49:13. The Proto-Semitic antecedent *karm- underlies this root, with cognates attested in related Semitic languages. The root yields derived forms including I, II, IV, each extending the core meaning into specific semantic domains. The root carries significant theological weight in the Quranic worldview, recurring in contexts that shape Islamic doctrine and spiritual understanding.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ك ر م — 47 مرة — Generosity

etymology.notes: Proto-Semitic *karm- meant 'vineyard.' Arabic developed the unique sense 'generosity, nobility' (karam, karīm). Semantic link: a vineyard as a 'noble/precious' plot that 'generously' yields. Alternatively, two homophonous roots may have merged in Arabic.

derived_forms.meaning: to honor, be generous; to deem noble

hadith_evidence.ar: ك ر م — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 47 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root krm (ك ر م) appears 47 times in the Quran, including 49:13.

meaning.en_short: To guarantee, sponsor, take charge; kafīl (surety)
meaning.en: To guarantee, sponsor, take charge; kafīl (surety)
meaning.en_detailed: Occurring 10 times in the Quranic text, the root ك ف ل (ك ف ل) conveys the essential concept of To guarantee, sponsor, take charge; kafīl (surety). Key Quranic occurrences include 3:37. The Proto-Semitic antecedent *kapVl- underlies this root, with cognates attested in related Semitic languages. The root yields derived forms including I, II, V, each extending the core meaning into specific semantic domains.
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To guarantee, sponsor, take charge; kaf
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ك ف ل — 10 مرة — To guarantee

etymology.notes: Proto-Semitic *kapVl- 'to double, fold.' Arabic semantic development: 'to double/fold' → 'to take double responsibility' → 'to guarantee/sponsor (kafāla).' The sponsor doubles the obligation alongside the principal. Kifl 'portion, double share' preserves the original meaning.

hadith_evidence.ar: ك ف ل — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 10 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root kfl (ك ف ل) appears 10 times in the Quran, including 3:37.

meaning.en: Hide. 2x: Khaba'a=hide. 27:25: Allah brings forth what is hidden (al-khab') in heavens and earth—Queen of Sheba's throne.
meaning.en_detailed: The triconsonantal root خ ب أ (خَبَأَ) — 1 Quranic occurrences — fundamentally expresses To hide, conceal. The verb khabāʾa and the noun khabʾ denote that which is hidden. At 27:25, "allāhu yukhriju al-khabʾa fī al-samāwāti wa-l-arḍi"—Allah brings forth the hidden things of the heavens and earth—is the speech of the one who could move Bilqīs's throne from Yemen to Solomon's court. Occurs once explicitly in the Qur'an (27:25). The root's semantic field is narrower than katama (conceal by silence); khabʾ denotes what is stored or hidden as a deposit, brought out by divine will. Its sole Qur'anic occurrence marks divine omniscience over hidden cosmic realities, the unseen being at the disposal of the All-Knowing.

quranic_analysis.theme: The hidden brought forth
quranic_analysis.detail: Allahu yukhriju al-khab'a fi al-samawati—Allah brings forth hidden things.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en: Cave; kahf (the Cave, Surah 18)
meaning.en_detailed: The Arabic root ك ه ف (ك ه ف) appears 6 times in the Quran, governing the semantic domain of Cave; kahf (the Cave, Surah 18). Key Quranic occurrences include 18:9. The Proto-Semitic antecedent *kahp- (loan?) underlies this root, with cognates attested in related Semitic languages.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ك ه ف — 6 مرة — Cave

etymology.notes: Likely an Aramaic/Syriac loan into Arabic. Syriac kēpā means 'rock,' extended to 'cave.' Arabic kahf (كهف) specifically denotes 'cave,' famous as the title of Surah 18 (al-Kahf). Secondary sense: 'protection, shelter' from the cave's protective function.

hadith_evidence.ar: ك ه ف — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 6 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root khf (ك ه ف) appears 6 times in the Quran, including 18:9.

meaning.en_short: To be about to, nearly; kāda (he almost)
meaning.en: To be about to, nearly; kāda (he almost)
meaning.en_detailed: The triconsonantal root ك و د (ك و د) — 24 Quranic occurrences — fundamentally expresses To be about to, nearly; kāda (he almost). Key Quranic occurrences include 2:20. The Proto-Semitic antecedent *kād- underlies this root, with cognates attested in related Semitic languages. The root yields derived forms including I, each extending the core meaning into specific semantic domains.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ك و د — 24 مرة — To be about to

cognates: to be about to, nearly (unique development)
etymology.notes: Arabic كَادَ (kāda) 'to be about to, nearly' is a unique Arabic verb of proximity. Possible connection to Akkadian kâdu 'to strive, be intent' via 'approaching toward' an action. In Quranic grammar, kāda is an ʾafʿāl al-muqāraba (verb of proximity).

derived_forms.meaning: to be about to, nearly, almost

hadith_evidence.ar: ك و د — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 24 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root kwd (ك و د) appears 24 times in the Quran, including 2:20.

meaning.en: To address, propose. 12x. Khataba=address. Khutbah=sermon. 28:63: he addressed them (khatabahum)—the condemned. KhaTab=affair, matter.
meaning.en_detailed: The triconsonantal root خ ط ب (خَطَبَ) — 12 Quranic occurrences — fundamentally expresses To address, deliver sermon. The verb khaṭaba (to address, court) and the noun khuṭbah denote public speech or formal proposal. At 28:63, "fa-lammā jaʾahum bi-l-ḥaqqi khaṭabahum wa-lammā yashʿurū khaṭabahu"—when he came to them with the truth, they addressed him (in derision) without realizing the gravity. The form yakhtaṣimūn (disputing) at 18:22 pairs with this root's speech-conflict field. Occurs 12 times in Qur'an. The related noun khaṭīb (orator) and khatab (matter, affair) extend the semantic range; khāṭaba (to address formally) is foundational for khutbah al-jumʿah. The root pairs with waʿẓ (admonition) as modes of public address.

quranic_analysis.theme: Address and proposal
quranic_analysis.detail: Fa-khatabahum—he addressed them.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: To fall prostrate. 12x. Kharra=fall, collapse. 38:24: he fell down prostrate (kharra raki'an)—David. 7:143: Moses fell down thunderstruck.
meaning.en_detailed: Root خ ر ر (خَرَّ), attested 12 times in the Quran, derives its core meaning of To fall down, prostrate from Proto-Semitic sources. The verb kharra (to fall down) marks both awe-struck prostration and punishment. At 38:24, "wa kharra rākiʿan wa atāba"—he fell down bowing in repentance—Dāwūd's response to the revealed Psalms. At 7:143, "wa kharra Mūsā ṣaʿiqan"—Mūsā fell down thunderstruck—at the theophany of the mountain. Occurs 12 times in Qur'an. The same letters also appear in kharra al-samāʾu (sky falls down, 65:10) marking cosmic destruction. The root semantically pairs with sujūd (prostration) and contrasts with ruqūd (restful sleep). The diverse subjects (prophet, mountain, sky) share the same downward motion of awe or shattering.

quranic_analysis.theme: Falling in prostration
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa kharra raki'an—he fell down bowing in prostration.

hadith_evidence.ar: الصَّلَاةُ نُورٌ
hadith_evidence.en: Prayer is light.

meaning.en_short: Measure, weight; kayl (measuring); to measure out
meaning.en: Measure, weight; kayl (measuring); to measure out
meaning.en_detailed: Root ك ي ل (ك ي ل), attested 16 times in the Quran, derives its core meaning of Measure, weight; kayl (measuring); to measure out from Proto-Semitic sources. Key Quranic occurrences include 83:1-3 (the command to give full measure). The Proto-Semitic antecedent *kayl- underlies this root, with cognates attested in related Semitic languages. The root yields derived forms including I, VIII, each extending the core meaning into specific semantic domains.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ك ي ل — 16 مرة — Measure

etymology.notes: Primarily a Northwest Semitic and Arabic commercial root. Arabic kayl (كيل) specifically refers to dry measure (grain, dates), as opposed to wazn (وزن) for weight. A caravan trade term shared across the incense route.

derived_forms.meaning: to measure for oneself, receive measure

hadith_evidence.ar: ك ي ل — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 16 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root kyl (ك ي ل) appears 16 times in the Quran, including 83:1-3.

meaning.en: Pearl; luʾluʾ (pearls); to shine, glisten
meaning.en_detailed: Reduplicated quadriliteral root (ل أ ل أ) denoting pearls and shimmering lustre, occurring 6 times, all in the noun luʾluʾ (لؤلؤ). The onomatopoeic gemination evokes the glistening of pearls, hence its Quranic application to paradise imagery, notably in Q 52:24 describing servants 'like hidden pearls' (luʾluʾin maknūn) — emphasizing both purity and concealed beauty. The word is a South Semitic development with cognates in Akkadian lulû 'luxury,' and is restricted largely to descriptions of paradise ornaments (Q 22:23; 35:33). Classical lexicographers (Lane, Lisān al-ʿArab) gloss laʾlaʾa as 'to shine, glisten,' preserving the visual-semantic core of the root.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ل أ ل أ — 6 مرة — Pearl

etymology.notes: Reduplicated quadriliteral root (ل أ ل أ), likely onomatopoeic/descriptive — common for words denoting shimmering/glittering objects. Arabic luʾluʾ (لؤلؤ) means 'pearls,' and laʾlaʾa means 'to shine, glisten.' Such reduplicated roots are often unique to Arabic or South Semitic.

hadith_evidence.ar: ل أ ل أ — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 6 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root lAlA (ل أ ل أ) appears 6 times in the Quran, including 52:24.

meaning.en: Weigh. 7x. Wazana=weigh. 17:35: give full measure (awfu al-kayla) and weigh (zinu) with a right balance.
meaning.en_detailed: وَزَنَ (و ز ن), a root appearing 23 times in the Quran, encodes the notion of To weigh; balance (mizan) across its various verbal and nominal forms. The verb wazana (to weigh) and the noun mīzān (balance) form a central ethical-conceptual pair in the Qur'an. At 17:35, "wa awfu al-kayla wa-l-mīzāna bi-l-qisṭ"—give full measure and weigh with justice—is one of the foundational commercial ethics verses. At 55:7–9, the cosmos is set down with "wa-l-mīzāna allatī lā taghīy"—the balance that does not deviate—that humanity may not transgress. Occurs 23 times in Qur'an. The form mīzān appears as both literal scales and as the cosmic-ethical measure of all deeds (101:6–9, al-mīzān al-jāmiʿ). The root semantically ties to ʿadl (justice) and qisṭ (equity).

quranic_analysis.theme: Just weighing
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa zinu bi-al-qistasi al-mustaqim—weigh with the straight balance.

hadith_evidence.ar: لَوْ أَنَّ رَجُلًا يُجَرُّ عَلَى وَجْهِهِ مِنْ يَوْمِ وُلِدَ إِلَى يَوْمِ يَمُوتُ هَرَمًا فِي مَرْضَاةِ اللَّهِ لَحَقَّرَهُ يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ
hadith_evidence.en: The scale of deeds on the Day of Judgment will weigh every atom.

meaning.en: Core, essence; lubb (heart, intellect); albāb (minds)
meaning.en_detailed: Triliteral root (ل ب ب) denoting the core, essence, and seat of intellect, occurring 16 times in the Quran, almost exclusively in the plural form albāb 'minds/intellects' (ūlū al-albāb, 'those of understanding'). From Proto-Semitic *libb- 'heart' (cf. Hebrew lēb, Akkadian libbu), the Arabic lubb signifies the innermost seat of comprehension, distinguished by the Quran from qalb (emotional heart) and fuʾād (pulsating heart). Foundational usage at Q 2:269 ('None will remember except those of understanding — ūlū al-albāb'), repeated nine times throughout the Quran to designate the spiritually discerning. The semantic development from physical heart → essence → intellect reflects Quranic anthropology, where true cognition requires both intellect and revelation.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ل ب ب — 16 مرة — Core

etymology.notes: One of the most widely attested Semitic roots: Proto-Semitic *libb- 'heart.' Arabic لبّ (lubb) specifically denotes the 'core, essence, intellect' — the inner heart beyond the physical organ (qalb). The plural albāb 'minds, intellects' (ūlū al-albāb) is a frequent Quranic expression. Semantic development: 'inner organ' → 'core/essence' → 'intellect.'

hadith_evidence.ar: ل ب ب — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 16 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root lbb (ل ب ب) appears 16 times in the Quran, including 2:269.

meaning.en_short: To stay, remain, tarry; to delay
meaning.en: To stay, remain, tarry; to delay
meaning.en_detailed: Verbal root (ل ب ث) signifying extended staying, lingering, or dwelling in a place or state, occurring 31 times primarily in Form I labitha. From West Semitic *labiṯ- 'to remain,' the root appears frequently in eschatological interrogation ('How long did you remain/labithum in the earth?' Q 23:112-113; 30:55-56), asking humans about their earthly sojourn on the Day of Judgment. Notable narrative use in Q 18:25 ('They stayed/labithū in their cave three hundred years') concerning the Sleepers of the Cave, with the parenthetical 'and they increased by nine' addressing the apparent solar-lunar discrepancy. The maṣdar labth (twice) denotes duration of stay, reinforcing the root's temporal semantic field of sojourning and delay.
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To stay, remain, tarry; to delay
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ل ب ث — 31 مرة — To stay

etymology.notes: West Semitic verb of duration. Proto-Semitic *labiṯ- 'to stay, dwell, linger.' In Quranic Arabic, labitha (لبث) occurs frequently in eschatological contexts ('how long did you remain?' - Q 23:112-113). The root conveys extended duration of staying in a place or state.

hadith_evidence.ar: ل ب ث — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 31 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root lbv (ل ب ث) appears 31 times in the Quran, including 18:25.

meaning.en: Fulfill. 50x. Wafa=fulfill. 3:76: whoever fulfills (awfa) his covenant and fears Allah—Allah loves the pious.
meaning.en_detailed: The triconsonantal root و ف ي (وَفَى) — 66 Quranic occurrences — fundamentally expresses To fulfill; abundant; full. The verb wafā (to fulfill) and the adjective wafī (full, abundant) form a key ethical term of trust and completeness. At 3:76, "balā man awfā bi-ʿahdihi wa ttaqā"—whoever fulfills his covenant and fears Allah—marks the believer as one of the pious. At 23:8, "wa alladhīna hum li-amānātihim wa ʿahdihim rāʿūn" pairs with awfā bi-l-ʿahd in a chain of covenant virtues. Occurs 66 times in Qur'an—one of the most frequent verbal roots. The active wafā bi-l-ʿahd marks amānah (trustworthiness) and is semantically opposed to nakth (covenant-breaking) at 2:100 and 13:25.

quranic_analysis.theme: Fulfill the covenant
quranic_analysis.detail: Bala man awfa bi-ahdihi wa ittaqa—whoever fulfills and fears.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en_short: Flesh, meat; laḥm (flesh); to weld, join
meaning.en: Flesh, meat; laḥm (flesh); to weld, join
meaning.en_detailed: Nominal root (ل ح م) meaning flesh/meat, occurring 12 times, all in the noun laḥm (لحم). Famous for its Semitic semantic split: Arabic laḥm = 'flesh/meat,' while Northwest Semitic cognates (Hebrew leḥem, Aramaic laḥmā, Ugaritic lḥm) preserve the broader 'bread, food, sustenance' sense, both descending from Proto-Semitic *laḥm- 'food.' Quranic usage often pairs laḥm with terms for nourishment, particularly in enumerating divine provisions — Q 5:4 lists the lawful foods including laḥm, and Q 16:14 mentions 'flesh of fresh fish' among sea provisions. The parallel verb laḥima 'to weld, join' reflects flesh's bonding to bone, with Q 6:99 vividly depicting date-palm spathes 'like heads of cattle' — perhaps a textual reference to flesh-like clustering.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ل ح م — 12 مرة — Flesh

etymology.notes: Famous semantic split: Arabic (and Ethiopic) = 'flesh/meat'; Northwest Semitic (Hebrew, Aramaic, Ugaritic) = 'bread/food.' Both derive from Proto-Semitic *laḥm- 'food, sustenance.' Arabic narrowed to 'meat/flesh,' while Hebrew leḥem retained the broader 'food/staple' meaning. Arabic also developed 'to join/weld' from flesh bonding to bone.

hadith_evidence.ar: الْمُؤْمِنُ يَأْكُلُ فِي مِعًى وَاحِدٍ وَالْكَافِرُ يَأْكُلُ فِي سَبْعَةِ أَمْعَاءٍ
hadith_evidence.en: The believer eats in one intestine and the disbeliever eats in seven intestines.

meaning.en_short: From, with, near; ladun (from the presence of)
meaning.en: From, with, near; ladun (from the presence of)
meaning.en_detailed: Prepositional/relational root (ل د ن) of Arabic provenance, occurring 18 times, virtually all in the phrase min ladun(na) 'from the presence/source of,' expressing proximate origin and immediate bestowal.
