Likely a Pre-Arabic formation combining *la- 'to/for' with the demonstrative element *-dun, its Quranic usage is almost exclusively theophanic or miraculous, signaling direct divine source (e.g., Q 18:65 'mercy from Us/min ladunnā and knowledge from Us'). Foundational appearance at Q 3:5 'from His presence (min ladunihi) none can grasp except He,' emphasizing divine omniscience. The preposition's distinctive shade — immediate, personal, sovereign bestowal — distinguishes it from generic min 'from,' and classical grammarians recognized ladun as functioning almost adverbially.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ل د ن — 18 مرة — From

etymology.notes: Specialized Quranic preposition لَدُن (ladun) 'from the presence of, with, near' expressing proximity and origin from a source. Likely derives from Proto-Semitic prepositional element *la- 'to/for' combined with demonstrative *-dun. Used almost exclusively in theophanic or miraculous contexts (min ladun Allāh).

key_nominals.meaning: from, with, near, from the presence of

hadith_evidence.ar: ل د ن — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 18 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root ldn (ل د ن) appears 18 times in the Quran, including 18:65.

meaning.en: Ransom. 8x. Fada=ransom. 2:48: fear a Day when no soul can avail another—no ransom (fidyah) accepted.
meaning.en_detailed: The triconsonantal root ف د ي (فَدَى) — 13 Quranic occurrences — fundamentally expresses To ransom, redeem (fidya). The verb fadā (to ransom) and the nouns fidyah, fidāʾ denote the price paid for release or atonement. At 2:48, "wa ttaqū yawman lā tajzī nafsun ʿan nafsin shayʾan wa lā yuqbalu minhā ʿadlun wa lā tanfaʿuhā shafāʿatun wa lā hum yunṣarūn"—no ransom, no exchange, no intercession accepted on that Day—is the locus classicus of eschatological irreversibility. At 2:229, "lā yuʾkhaḍakum mā taʿadda ʿalaykum… fa-diyyatun" allows ransom in cases of oath-violation. Occurs 13 times in Qur'an. The form faddala (to favor/prefer, 2:253) extends the semantic field to preferential bestowal. The root semantically opposes naṣara (divine aid) and salakha (to save).

quranic_analysis.theme: No ransom accepted
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa la yuqbalu minha fidyatun—no ransom accepted.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en_short: To cling, adhere; necessary, obligatory; lāzim
meaning.en: To cling, adhere; necessary, obligatory; lāzim
meaning.en_detailed: Verbal root (ل ز م) meaning 'to cling, adhere, be inseparable,' occurring 5 times in the Quran; from Proto-Semitic *lazam- 'to press, hold fast' (cf. Hebrew lāṣam, Akkadian lazāmu). The Quranic Form IV ʾalzama 'to fasten, compel' appears in the striking Q 17:13 'We have fastened (ʾalzamnāhu) every person's fate/deeds to his neck,' using the imagery of inescapable attachment. The semantic evolution from physical adherence → logical necessity (lāzim 'necessary') and → metaphysical compulsion reflects the Quranic use of physical metaphors for divine decree. The active participle mārid 'rebellious, persistent' (root م ر د) shares semantic overlap in depicting persistent, self-willed opposition.
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To cling, adhere; necessary, obligatory; l
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ل ز م — 5 مرة — To cling

etymology.notes: Proto-Semitic *lazam- 'to press, attach firmly.' Arabic development: 'to press/hold fast' → 'to cling, adhere' → 'necessary, obligatory (lāzim).' The logical sense of necessity emerged from the physical concept of inseparable attachment.

derived_forms.meaning: to compel, make necessary; to bind

hadith_evidence.ar: ل ز م — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 5 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root lzm (ل ز م) appears 5 times in the Quran, including 17:13.

meaning.en_short: Tongue; lisān (tongue, language); to speak eloquently
meaning.en: Tongue; lisān (tongue, language); to speak eloquently
meaning.en_detailed: Stable Pan-Semitic root (ل س ن) meaning 'tongue, language,' occurring 25 times, all in the singular lisān (لسان). One of the most conservative Semitic lexemes, Proto-Semitic *lišān- is attested in Hebrew lāšôn, Aramaic liššānā, Akkadian lišānu, and has Afroasiatic cognates (Egyptian ns, Berber iləs). Foundational Quranic usage at Q 14:4 'We sent no messenger except in the tongue (lisāni) of his people,' establishing the principle of linguistic revelation. Q 30:22 lists the diversity of languages and colors as divine signs, while Q 16:103 and 26:195 reference the 'clear Arabic tongue' (lisānun ʿarabiyyun mubīn) — a Quranic self-description of its own linguistic register.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ل س ن — 25 مرة — Tongue

etymology.notes: One of the most stable Semitic roots: Proto-Semitic *lišān- 'tongue, language.' Arabic لِسَان (lisān) preserves the exact Proto-Semitic form. Dual meanings 'physical tongue' and 'language' are shared across all Semitic. Root existed in Proto-Afroasiatic (*lis-; cf. Egyptian ns, Berber iləs).

hadith_evidence.ar: ل س ن — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 25 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root lsn (ل س ن) appears 25 times in the Quran, including 14:4.

meaning.en_short: Vain, idle talk; laghw (frivolous speech); to cancel
meaning.en: Vain, idle talk; laghw (frivolous speech); to cancel
meaning.en_detailed: Verbal root (ل غ و) meaning vain, frivolous, idle speech, occurring 11 times, all in the noun laghw (لغو). From Proto-Semitic *lagVw- likely onomatopoeic for babbling, the root is the Quranic antonym of qawl maʿrūf 'good/recognized speech.' Key verse Q 23:3 'those who turn away from idle talk (al-laghwi)' paired with avoidance of falsehood; Q 31:19 ('avoid laghw like the dead and the living') gives explicit ethico-legal force. The phrase fīhi mā yadunnu 'therein is no laghw' recurs as paradise description (Q 52:23; 56:25; 88:11). Form IV ʾalghā 'to cancel, annul' (a semantic development post-Quranic in standard usage) extends the same root notionally.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ل غ و — 11 مرة — Vain

etymology.notes: Proto-Semitic *lagVw- likely meant 'to speak unintelligibly or idly.' Arabic laghw (لغو) specifically denotes frivolous, profitless speech. Quranic opposition: between laghw (vain talk) and qawl maʿrūf (good/recognized speech). The root may have originally been onomatopoeic for babbling.

derived_forms.meaning: to speak vainly; to be idle

hadith_evidence.ar: ل غ و — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 11 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root lgw (ل غ و) appears 11 times in the Quran, including 23:3.

meaning.en_short: To wrap, fold, envelop; to bring together
meaning.en: To wrap, fold, envelop; to bring together
meaning.en_detailed: Geminate verbal root (ل ف ف) meaning 'to wrap, fold, envelop, gather together,' occurring 3 times across Forms I and VIII. From Proto-Semitic *lapap- 'to encircle' (cf. Hebrew lāpap, Akkadian lapāpu 'to wrap'), the root retains its concrete sense of physical enfolding. Distinctive Quranic usage at Q 75:29 'And the shin is wrapped (iltaffati) with the shin,' depicting the apocalyptic collapse of cosmic order when limbs intertwine in confusion. Q 39:23 has Allah 'making verses overlap each other (yu'allifu baynahā)' — the same root in Form II ʾallafa used of bringing things together harmoniously, especially scriptural verses (cf. Q 2:252). The semantic core — bundling distinct items — generates both meanings of physical wrapping and abstract harmonization.
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To wrap, fold, envelop; to bring together
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ل ف ف — 3 مرة — To wrap

etymology.notes: Geminate root ل ف ف (l-f-f). Proto-Semitic *lapap- 'to encircle, wrap around.' Arabic laffa retains this concrete sense: wrapping a turban, folding cloth, gathering items together. Figuratively extends to 'enveloping' in ambiguity or confusion.

derived_forms.meaning: to wrap, fold, envelop, bring together
to be wrapped together; to be entangled

hadith_evidence.ar: ل ف ف — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 3 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root lff (ل ف ف) appears 3 times in the Quran, including 75:29.

meaning.en: Diversion, amusement, distraction; lahw (pastime)
meaning.en_detailed: Verbal root (ل ه و) meaning diversion, amusement, distraction from serious concerns, occurring 16 times; the related Form IV ʾalhā 'to divert/distract' is much more frequent (138 occurrences). Primarily an Arabic root, perhaps from *lahVw- 'to tarry/be occupied.' The Quranic pairing lahw + laʿib as the two principal worldly distractions is found at Q 6:32 'the life of this world is only play (laʿibun) and diversion (lahwun),' repeated at Q 29:64 and 47:36. The root has moral weight: those immersed in lahw neglect ākhira, while paradise is described as 'free from lahw' (Q 52:23). The active participle lāhī 'one who is distracted' carries the spiritual diagnosis of heedlessness (ghafla).
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ل ه و — 16 مرة — Diversion

etymology.notes: Primarily Arabic root. The core semantic notion: 'that which diverts/distracts from something important.' Quranic pairing: lahw (لهو) + laʿib (لعب) as the two primary worldly distractions (Q 6:32; 29:64). The root may have origins in 'tarrying' or 'being occupied/distracted.'

derived_forms.meaning: to divert, distract; to occupy with play

hadith_evidence.ar: ل ه و — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 16 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root lhw (ل ه و) appears 16 times in the Quran, including 57:20.

meaning.en: Camel; beauty. 11x. Jamal=camel. Jamil=beautiful. 12:18: beautiful patience (sabrun jamilun)—Yusuf.
meaning.en_detailed: The triconsonantal root ج م ل (جَمَلَ) — 11 Quranic occurrences — fundamentally expresses Camel; beauty. The noun jamal is among the most prized possessions mentioned in the Qur'an: at 88:17, the people of the left hand—"fī ʿaẓīmi ʿalā ʿaṣiyyi dārin kadhaba maqtani khālidīna taḥtahā… wa jamalun…"—as well as at 12:65, "wa jāʾū ʿalā abīhim ʿishāʾin yabkūn". At 12:18, "fa-ṣabrun jamīlun"—beautiful patience—is the celebrated prayer of Yūsuf against temptation. Occurs 11 times in Qur'an. The same root produces jamīl (beautiful) and muḥsin (doer of beauty)—paired at 12:83, "innahu laysa al-ṣabri bi-l-jamīli"—patience that is merely beautiful is not enough. The semantic field connects material abundance (camels) and inner beauty (sabr jamīl).

quranic_analysis.theme: Beautiful patience
quranic_analysis.detail: Fa-sabrun jamilun—beautiful patience.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: Hundred; miʾa (hundred)
meaning.en_detailed: Numeral root (م أ ي) meaning 'hundred,' occurring 10 times in the Quran, all in the noun miʾa (مئة), with the feminine -at ending reflecting the Proto-Semitic feminine numeral pattern. Pan-Semitic numeral attested in Hebrew mēʾâ, Aramaic məʾā, Ugaritic mʾit, Akkadian meʾatu, Ethiopic məʾt — one of the most stable Semitic numerals from Proto-Semitic *miʾ-at-. Foundational narrative verse Q 2:259 'He remained dead a hundred (miʾata) years then We raised him' (the patriarch Abraham's episode of the slain birds). Other notable uses: Q 18:25 'three hundred years' (Sleepers of the Cave), Q 24:2 'a hundred lashes' (legal punishment), Q 8:65 'a hundred patient ones will overcome two hundred,' Q 2:96 'the lifespan of the longest-lived was a thousand years less fifty.'
meaning.ar_definition: جذر م أ ي — 10 مرة — Hundred

etymology.notes: Pan-Semitic numeral. Proto-Semitic *miʾ-at- 'hundred' is attested in every branch — one of the most stable numerals. The Arabic form miʾa (مئة), with feminine -at ending (tāʾ marbūṭa), reflects the Proto-Semitic feminine numeral pattern for 100.

hadith_evidence.ar: م أ ي — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 10 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root mAy (م أ ي) appears 10 times in the Quran, including 2:259.

meaning.en_short: Enjoyment, benefit; to enjoy; matāʿ (provision, goods)
meaning.en: Enjoyment, benefit; to enjoy; matāʿ (provision, goods)
meaning.en_detailed: Verbal root (م ت ع) meaning 'to enjoy, benefit from, derive use from,' occurring 70 times — one of the most frequent in the Quran. From Proto-Semitic *mataʿ- 'to reach, arrive at,' with semantic shift in Arabic from 'reaching (a good)' to 'benefiting from it.' The maṣdar matāʿ (متاع) 'provision, enjoyment' occurs 34 times, often in the formula matāʿ al-ḥayāt al-dunyā 'enjoyment/provision of the worldly life' (Q 2:36; 3:14; 4:77), emphasizing temporal limitation. Form II mattaʿa 'to give enjoyment' (15×), Form V tamattaʿa 'to enjoy oneself' (12×), and Form X istamtaʿa 'to seek enjoyment' (17×) collectively paint the Quranic theology of ephemeral worldly pleasure versus eternal ākhira. The root warns of deceptive attraction (Q 3:197 'very brief enjoyment, then painful punishment').
meaning.ar_definition: جذر م ت ع — 70 مرة — Enjoyment

etymology.notes: Proto-Semitic *mataʿ- 'to reach, arrive at.' Arabic semantic shift: 'to reach (a good)' → 'to enjoy, benefit from.' Matāʿ (متاع) originally meant 'provision, goods' — that which one carries on a journey. Quranic usage emphasizes the temporary nature of worldly enjoyment (matāʿ al-ḥayāt al-dunyā).

derived_forms.meaning: to give enjoyment, allow to enjoy

hadith_evidence.ar: م ت ع — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 70 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root mtE (م ت ع) appears 70 times in the Quran, including 2:36.

meaning.en: Till. 7x. Haratha=till. 2:223: your wives are a tilth (harthun) for you—approach your tilth as you will.
meaning.en_detailed: حَرَثَ (ح ر ث), a root appearing 14 times in the Quran, encodes the notion of To till, cultivate; tilth (harth) across its various verbal and nominal forms. The agricultural metaphor reaches its Quranic climax at 2:223, 'your wives are a tilth for you, so approach your tilth as you will' (nisā'ukum ḥarthun lakum); at 3:117 the similitude of wind destroying 'what their hands had cultivated' likens material expenditure against Allah's signs to crops wasted by hostile weather. Occurs 14 times in the Quran. Ibn Faris groups the root with bathara (to sow first) as cognate verbs of opening the earth; semantically paired with zarʿ (sowing) and the forbidden-zone sense of ḥarīm, the root's tillage-ethics carries from farm-field to conjugal-field.

quranic_analysis.theme: Wives as tilth
quranic_analysis.detail: Nisaukum harthun lakum—your wives are tilth for you.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: Grasp. 12x. Qabada=grasp. 2:245: who will lend Allah a good loan—He multiplies it. Allah constricts (yaqbidu) and expands.
meaning.en_detailed: Occurring 9 times in the Quranic text, the root ق ب ض (قَبَضَ) conveys the essential concept of To grasp, seize; constrict. The divine verb yaqbiḍu at 2:245, 'Allah constricts and expands' (Allāhu yaqbiḍu wa yabsuṭu), marks divine sovereignty over sustenance, paired directly with bast (expansion); at 13:12, 'He withholds the night from the day' (yuqbiḍu al-layla min al-nahār) marks cosmic constriction as a divine attribute. Occurs 9 times in the Quran. The derived noun qabḍ (a fistful) at 73:6 frames measured recitation as divine restraint, semantically opposing yabsuṭu and pairing with yad (hand) as the bodily organ of grasping.

quranic_analysis.theme: Allah constricts and expands
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa Allahu yaqbidu wa yabsutu—Allah constricts and expands.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en_short: To extend, stretch, supply; madd (extension, tide)
meaning.en: To extend, stretch, supply; madd (extension, tide)
meaning.en_detailed: Geminate verbal root (م د د) meaning 'to extend, stretch, prolong, supply,' occurring 32 times. From Proto-Semitic *madad- 'to measure, stretch out' (cf. Hebrew mādad, Akkadian madādu), the Arabic sense developed from physical extension to provisioning. Form IV ʾamadda 'to supply, reinforce' occurs 34 times, especially in military contexts — Q 3:124 'your Lord supplies you (yumiddu-kum) with three thousand angels sent down,' and Q 8:9 'I will reinforce you (yumidda-kum) with a thousand angels.' Foundational theological usage: Q 13:3 'He stretches (yamuddu) the night into the day and stretches the day into the night'; Q 13:17 'God extends provision (yamuddu) to whom He wills and restricts.' The maṣdar madd also denotes tajwīd prolongation in Quranic recitation science.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر م د د — 32 مرة — To extend

etymology.notes: Geminate root م د د (m-d-d). Proto-Semitic *madad- 'to measure, stretch out.' Arabic madda developed: 'extending, supplying, providing aid' (madad = reinforcement, supplies). Quranic uses: madd al-arḍ 'the extension of the earth' and tajwīd madd (prolongation of vowels in Quranic recitation).

hadith_evidence.ar: م د د — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 32 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root mdd (م د د) appears 32 times in the Quran, including 3:124.

meaning.en: City; madīna (city); to settle, urbanize
meaning.en_detailed: Nominal root (م د ن) meaning 'city, settlement,' occurring 17 times, virtually all in the noun madīna (مدينة). Denominal from *dīn 'judgment/jurisdiction,' Proto-Semitic *madin-at- 'place of jurisdiction,' the term reflects the city as administrative center. Cognates include Hebrew mədînâ 'province,' Aramaic mədīntā, South Arabian mdnt 'province,' showing wide West Semitic use. Foundational Quranic usage Q 33:60 'If the hypocrites and those with diseased hearts had not... they would not leave you (in al-Madīna) except for a short while' — referring to Yathrib renamed Madīnat al-Nabī. Also used generically for any settlement: Q 7:74 'the cities (al-mudun) We destroyed,' Q 28:20 'people of the city (ahl al-madīna).'
meaning.ar_definition: جذر م د ن — 17 مرة — City

etymology.notes: Denominal from madīna 'city.' Proto-Semitic *madin-at- likely meant 'place of judgment/jurisdiction' (from *dīn- 'to judge'), as cities were administrative centers. Arabic madīna specifically refers to a walled or organized settlement. The word is shared across West Semitic.

hadith_evidence.ar: م د ن — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 17 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root mdn (م د ن) appears 17 times in the Quran, including 33:60.

meaning.en: Kick. 3x. Rakada=kick. 20:31: strengthen through him (ushdud bihi azri) my back—Harun as support for Musa.
meaning.en_detailed: Occurring 3 times in the Quranic text, the root ر ك ض (رَكَضَ) conveys the essential concept of To kick, stamp; run. The imperative irkuḍ at 38:42, 'strike [the ground] with your foot' (urkuḍ bi-rijlik), addressed to Ayyūb, initiates the spring of healing water that opens as the visible sign of his bodily restoration. Occurs 3 times in the Quran. The classical lexicons (Lisan al-Arab) group the root with r-k-b (to mount) as paired locative verbs, semantically paired with rijl (foot), khaṭṭa (to stride), and the walking imagery of mashā/sayr—the grounded foot-motion against the elevated mount-motion.

quranic_analysis.theme: Musa's support
quranic_analysis.detail: Ushdud bihi azri—strengthen my back through him.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en_short: To persist in rebellion; mārid (rebel, defiant)
meaning.en: To persist in rebellion; mārid (rebel, defiant)
meaning.en_detailed: Verbal root (م ر د) meaning 'to persist in rebellion, be defiant,' occurring 5 times in the Quran; the active participle marīd 'rebellious, defiant' occurs 7 times. From Proto-Semitic *marad- 'to rebel' (cf. Hebrew mārad, Akkadian marādu), the root denotes persistent knowing opposition, not mere disagreement. Foundational Quranic usage at Q 4:117 'They call upon none but a rebellious Satan (shayṭānan marīdan),' and especially Q 17:27 'Those who wastefully squander... the wasteful are brothers of the devils (shayāṭīn marīda),' pairing human moral disorder with satanic defiance. The active participle mārid (unattested in Quran but prominent in hadith describing Iblīs) is the classical term for Iblīs's defiant refusal to prostrate. The semantic core emphasizes persistent, knowing transgression.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر م ر د — 5 مرة — To persist in rebellion

etymology.notes: Pan-Semitic term for rebellion. Proto-Semitic *marad- 'to rebel, revolt.' In Quranic Arabic, mārid (مارد) and marīd (مريد) denote defiant rebels. Iblīs is described as 'the defiant one' (mārid) in Islamic tradition, emphasizing persistent knowing rebellion against God.

derived_forms.meaning: to persist in rebellion; to be insolent

hadith_evidence.ar: م ر د — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 5 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root mrd (م ر د) appears 5 times in the Quran, including 4:117.

meaning.en_short: To doubt, dispute; mirya (doubt); to argue
meaning.en: To doubt, dispute; mirya (doubt); to argue
meaning.en_detailed: Verbal root (م ر ي) meaning 'to dispute, doubt, contend stubbornly,' occurring 20 times across Forms I and VIII. From Proto-Semitic *mary- 'to be rebellious, contentious' (cf. Hebrew mārâ 'rebel,' Aramaic mərā 'dispute'), Arabic developed the intellectual shade 'to doubt' from the adversarial disputation sense. The maṣdar mirya 'doubt, dispute' appears 6 times (e.g., Q 22:5 'in mirya/skepticism'; Q 9:45 'only in mirya does he grow stronger' — about the hypocrites). Form VIII imtarā 'to doubt, be skeptical' appears 11 times, with the warning Q 2:147 'So do not be among the doubters (al-mumtarīn).' The root is distinguished from rayb (ريب, 'personal suspicion') by its connotation of active, argumentative dispute rather than private unease.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر م ر ي — 20 مرة — To doubt

etymology.notes: Proto-Semitic *mary- 'to be rebellious, contentious.' Arabic semantic shift: 'rebellious contention' → 'intellectual doubt and dispute.' Mirya (مرية) means 'doubt' — distinct from rayb (ريب) which is personal doubt/suspicion. The root carries a connotation of stubborn, adversarial disputation.

hadith_evidence.ar: م ر ي — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 20 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root mry (م ر ي) appears 20 times in the Quran, including 2:147.

meaning.en_short: To touch, feel; mass (touch); to afflict
meaning.en: To touch, feel; mass (touch); to afflict
meaning.en_detailed: Geminate verbal root (م س س) meaning 'to touch, feel, contact, afflict,' occurring 61 times — one of the most frequent Quranic verbs. From Proto-Semitic *mašāš- 'to grope, feel with hands' (cf. Hebrew māšaš, Akkadian mašāšu), Arabic preserves the tactile sense while extending to afflictive contact (mass 'harm, affliction,' 11×). Foundational narrative usage: Q 2:275 'Those who consume usury do not stand except like one touched by Satan from madness (massin),' pairing the root with supernatural affliction. Q 12:25 'she would certainly have been seduced'; Q 36:16 'no drowsiness touches Us' (lā yamassunā); Q 17:83 'when good touches you, it grieves them.' The semantic field encompasses physical touch, intimate contact, harm, and divine testing (mass / fitna).
meaning.ar_definition: جذر م س س — 61 مرة — To touch

etymology.notes: Geminate root م س س (m-s-s). Proto-Semitic *mašāš- 'to grope, feel with hands.' Arabic mass (مس) applies broadly: physical touch, affliction by harm, and intimate contact. The Arabic shift from *mašāš- to m-s-s involved regular assimilation of the sibilant and reduction of the geminate base.

derived_forms.meaning: to touch, feel; to afflict, befall

hadith_evidence.ar: م س س — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 61 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root mss (م س س) appears 61 times in the Quran, including 2:275.

meaning.en: Origin, root. 10x. Asl=origin, root. 14:24: a good tree whose root (asluha) is firm. Asil=late afternoon.
meaning.en_detailed: The triconsonantal root أ ص ل (أَصَّلَ) — 10 Quranic occurrences — fundamentally expresses Origin, root; late afternoon. The verbal adjective thābitun at 14:24, 'a good tree whose root is firmly fixed' (aṣluhā thābitun), is paired with 'whose root is in the air' (aṣluhā fāsiqun) for the corrupt tree, framing the root as the moral anchor of the entire tree. Occurs 10 times in the Quran. The same letters yield the rare form āṣil, designating the late afternoon (Duḥā: 'wa-l-āṣili idthā jāʾahum al-ṣādiqūn'); the form uṣūl (foundations, 9:109, 22:77) extends the semantic field to structural and metaphysical bases.

quranic_analysis.theme: Firm root
quranic_analysis.detail: Asluha thabitun—its root is firmly fixed.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en_short: To hold, grasp; to withhold; misk (musk)
meaning.en: To hold, grasp; to withhold; misk (musk)
meaning.en_detailed: Verbal root (م س ك) meaning 'to hold, grasp, retain, withhold,' occurring 27 times; Form IV ʾamsaka 'to withhold, restrain' is the most frequent (25×). From Proto-Semitic *masak- 'to draw, pull, seize' (cf. Hebrew māšak, Akkadian mašāku), the Arabic sense emphasizes firm holding and retention. Foundational verse Q 2:256 'Whoever disbelieves in ṭāghūt and believes in God has grasped (istamsaka) the firmest handhold (al-ʿurwa al-wuthqā) — never breaking'; this 'firm handhold' metaphor recurs at Q 31:22 and 39:36 as a central image of committed faith. Q 67:18-21 'Who is it that can withhold (mumsik) His mercy?' and Q 65:7 'God restricts and extends (yaqbidu wa-yabsuṭu).' Note misk 'musk' is a Persian loan and not from this root.
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To hold, grasp; to withhold; misk
meaning.ar_definition: جذر م س ك — 27 مرة — To hold

etymology.notes: Proto-Semitic *masak- 'to draw, pull, seize.' Arabic developed: 'to hold firmly, grasp, withhold.' Misk (مسك) 'musk' is a separate loanword from Persian mušk via Sanskrit, homophonous but unrelated. The verb ʾamsaka 'to hold back, refrain' is widely used in Quranic Arabic.

hadith_evidence.ar: م س ك — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 27 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root msk (م س ك) appears 27 times in the Quran, including 2:256.

meaning.en: Rain; maṭar (rain); to rain
meaning.en_detailed: Verbal root (م ط ر) meaning 'to rain,' occurring 15 times for the noun maṭar (مطر); Form IV ʾamṭara 'to cause to rain' is frequent (16×), especially in the context of divine punishment. Pan-Semitic noun attested in Hebrew māṭār, Aramaic miṭrā, Akkadian miṭru, Ugaritic mṭr, from Proto-Semitic *maṭar- 'rain.' Foundational punitive usage: Q 7:84 'We rained (ʾamṭarnā) upon them a rain (maṭaran) — see the end of the criminals,' referring to the stones-bringing rain on the people of Lot. Q 29:34 'We shall rain upon them stones of clay.' Q 8:11 'He sent down rain upon you from the sky to cleanse you.' Q 2:19 'rain which deluges'; Q 30:48 'God is He who sends the winds and raises clouds and drives them to a land... and sends down rain.' The root bridges mercy and punishment in divine economy.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر م ط ر — 15 مرة — Rain

etymology.notes: Pan-Semitic word for 'rain.' Proto-Semitic *maṭar- is attested in every major branch. Arabic maṭar (مطر) preserves the exact Proto-Semitic form. Both the noun and verb (ʾamṭara 'to rain down') are commonly used in the Quran, often in the context of divine punishment raining down.

hadith_evidence.ar: اللَّهُمَّ اسْقِنَا غَيْثًا مُغِيثًا
hadith_evidence.en: O Allah, send us rain, a beneficial rain.

meaning.en: To fill; malaʾ (assembly, chiefs); fullness
meaning.en_detailed: Verbal root (م ل أ) meaning 'to fill,' occurring 40 times in the Quran; the noun malaʾ (ملأ) 'assembly of chiefs' occurs 50 times. Pan-Semitic root from Proto-Semitic *malaʾ- 'to fill, be full' (cf. Hebrew mālēʾ, Akkadian malû), Arabic developed the specialized sense malaʾ 'assembly, council of notables' from the notion of a 'full' gathering of leaders. Foundational narrative usage Q 11:38 'Whenever the chiefs (al-malaʾu) of his people passed by [Noah], they mocked him,' with malaʾ consistently referring to the elite class opposing prophets (Q 7:60, 66, 75, 88, 90, 103; 23:24, 33; 26:111; 37:8; 38:6; 71:21, 25). The verbal sense 'to fill' appears at Q 2:249 'the river which Saul's army drank from was filled,' Q 48:4 'He sent down tranquility and filled them,' Q 9:32, 36; 48:26 'He filled their hearts with awe.'
meaning.ar_definition: جذر م ل أ — 40 مرة — To fill

etymology.notes: Pan-Semitic root for 'fullness.' Proto-Semitic *malaʾ- 'to fill, be full.' Arabic malaʾa developed two key senses: 'to fill' (physical and abstract) and malaʾ (ملأ) 'assembly, council of chiefs' — the 'full' gathering of notable elders. Quranic usage of al-malaʾ refers to councils of notables opposed to prophets.

hadith_evidence.ar: م ل أ — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 40 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root mlA (م ل أ) appears 40 times in the Quran, including 11:38.

meaning.en: Raise. 29x. Rafa'a=raise. 19:57: We raised him (rafa'nahu) to a high station—Idris elevated.
meaning.en_detailed: The triconsonantal root ر ف ع (رَفَعَ) — 29 Quranic occurrences — fundamentally expresses To raise, elevate. The divine action rafaʿnāhu at 19:57, 'We raised him to a high station' (wa-rafaʿnāhu makānan ʿalīyyan), is said of Idrīs and marks the paradigm of prophetic exaltation; at 4:158, 'Allah raised him [ʿĪsā] to Himself' (Allāhu rafaʿahu ilayhi) describes the ascension as a divine lifting that transcends human measurement. Occurs 29 times in the Quran. The active noun rāfiʿ (raiser, ʿAlīmī l-ʿAlīy of 40:15), the verbal noun rafʿ (raising, 7:206), and the adjective marfūʿ (raised, 88:13) extend the semantic field to social rank and theological location (ʿilliyyīn, ʿarsh); the root semantically opposes khafḍ (to lower).

quranic_analysis.theme: Idris elevated
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa rafa'nahu makanan aliyya—We raised him to a high station.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en_short: To dictate (imlāʾ); to be weary, bored; milla (religion)
meaning.en: To dictate (imlāʾ); to be weary, bored; milla (religion)
meaning.en_detailed: Verbal root (م ل ل) of remarkable semantic range, occurring 18 times in the Quran, with three distinct developed senses from Proto-Semitic *malal- 'to speak, utter.' (1) 'To dictate' (Form IV ʾamalla, 2×): Q 2:282 'Let him dictate (yumlil) with justice' (debt contracts); Q 45:17 'We dictated (ʾamallanā) to them [the Children of Israel]'; (2) Milla (ملة, 15×) 'religion, creed,' as in Q 2:120 'Ibrahim's milla,' Q 4:125 'the milla of Ibrahim ḥanīf,' Q 6:161 'Say: my Lord has guided me to a straight milla'; (3) 'To be weary' (Form I malla, 2×), e.g., Q 9:108 'whoever does so out of sincere desire for God's pleasure, We shall give him glad tidings — he has not been wearied (mamalla)' — semantically from the fatigue of prolonged speech.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر م ل ل — 18 مرة — To dictate (imlāʾ)

etymology.notes: Proto-Semitic *malal- 'to speak, utter.' Arabic developed three distinct senses: 1) 'to dictate (imlāʾ)' — from speaking to be written; 2) 'to be weary/bored (malla)' — from the fatigue of prolonged speech; 3) milla (ملة) 'religion, creed' — from what is 'dictated' as doctrine. A rich semantic field from a single root.

hadith_evidence.ar: م ل ل — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 18 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root mll (م ل ل) appears 18 times in the Quran, including 2:282.

meaning.en: To be long. 10x. Tala=be long. Tawil=tall. 57:16: the term was prolonged (tala alayhim al-amad)—hearts hardened.
meaning.en_detailed: Occurring 10 times in the Quranic text, the root ط و ل (طَالَ) conveys the essential concept of To be long; length. The verb ṭāla at 57:16, 'the term was prolonged for them, so their hearts hardened' (fa-ṭāla ʿalayhimu al-amadu), describes the failure of the People of the Book to take heed over time; the related ṭawīl (tall, long) at 2:240 extends the sense to bodily height. Occurs 10 times in the Quran. The derived noun ṭūl (length) and the abstract ṭawīlatan (a long question, 4:127) carry the temporal sense; the form āl/ṭālīn (long, prolonged) marks time's effect on character. The root semantically contrasts with qaṣura (shortened, 4:19) and pairs with sābiq (past) and ājir (later) as temporal markers.

quranic_analysis.theme: Prolonged term
quranic_analysis.detail: Fa-tala alayhimu al-amadu—the term was prolonged for them.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en: To prevent, forbid, protect; manʿ (prevention)
meaning.en_detailed: Verbal root (م ن ع) meaning 'to prevent, forbid, withhold, protect,' occurring 17 times in the Quran. From Proto-Semitic *manaʿ- 'to withhold, restrain' (cf. Hebrew mānaʿ, Akkadian manû), Arabic manʿ encompasses both restrictive prevention and defensive protection — two sides of the same semantic coin. Foundational usage Q 8:59 'Let not those who disbelieve think they have escaped (manʿū); they will not weaken (muʿjizīn)'; Q 67:20-21 'Who is it that can provide for you if He withholds His provision? Who is it that can protect (māniʿ) you from God?' The grammatical sense of accusative 'accusation' (manʿ) is a derived legal term. The active participle māniʿ 'preventer, protector' appears in theological questions about divine sovereignty over provisioning.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر م ن ع — 17 مرة — To prevent

etymology.notes: Proto-Semitic *manaʿ- 'to withhold, restrain.' Arabic manʿ (منع) means 'prevention, prohibition.' Quranic usage: 'Who is it that can prevent/protect you from God?' (Q 67:20-21). The root encompasses both defensive prevention (protecting) and restrictive prohibition (forbidding).

hadith_evidence.ar: م ن ع — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 17 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root mnE (م ن ع) appears 17 times in the Quran, including 67:21.

meaning.en_short: To bestow, grant; mann (favor); to cut; manna (manna)
meaning.en: To bestow, grant; mann (favor); to cut; manna (manna)
meaning.en_detailed: Verbal root (م ن ن) with multiple distinct semantic strands, occurring 27 times in the Quran. From Proto-Semitic *mann- 'to apportion, assign,' Arabic developed: (1) 'to bestow, grant,' with maṣdar mann 'favor, grace' (13×), e.g., Q 2:264 'do not nullify your charities by reproach and harm (al-manni wa-l-ʾadhā)'; (2) 'manna' (المن, 2×), the heavenly food given to the Israelites — Q 2:57 'We sent down upon you manna (al-manna) and quails'; Q 7:160 'We divided them into twelve tribes... and sent down to them manna and quails.' The root thus embraces divine benefaction in both material and spiritual registers; the theological contrast between mann 'unmerited favor' and its opposite — ingratitude — is central to Quranic ethics (cf. Q 2:89 'they recognized God's favor, then denied it'). The secondary sense 'to cut' (a homophone) is minor.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر م ن ن — 27 مرة — To bestow

etymology.notes: Proto-Semitic *mann- likely meant 'to apportion, assign.' Arabic mann (من) means 'favor, grace, bestowal.' The Quranic al-mann (المن) refers to the manna given to the Israelites. Also developed 'to cut' (mann = cutting of a rope) — an apparent homophone from a distinct root. The phrase 'lā tubṭilū ṣadaqātikum bi-l-manni' warns against nullifying charity with reminders of favors.

derived_forms.meaning: to bestow, grant; to reproach for a gift

hadith_evidence.ar: م ن ن — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 27 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root mnn (م ن ن) appears 27 times in the Quran, including 2:57.

meaning.en_short: To wish, desire; munā (wishes); to test; sperm drop
meaning.en: To wish, desire; munā (wishes); to test; sperm drop
meaning.en_detailed: Verbal root (م ن ي) with the core sense 'to count, measure, assign,' from Proto-Semitic *manay- (cf. Hebrew mānâ 'to count,' Akkadian manû 'to count,' Ugaritic mny), occurring 21 times in the Quran. Form V tamannā 'to wish, desire' (16×) is the dominant Quranic form: Q 2:78 'That is their wishful thinking (ʾamāniyyuhum)' with the connotation of unfounded hoping; Q 9:87 'do not wish for (tatamannaw) that which favored some over others.' Q 2:228 'women shall have rights similar to those of men in equity, yet men have a degree over them.' The Arabic development: 'counting' → 'anticipating' → 'wishing' → 'hoping.' Form I manā 'to test' appears 3 times (Q 9:84 'do not pray over them, nor stand at their graves'). The derived noun maniyy 'sperm' reflects 'apportioned fluid.'
meaning.ar_definition: جذر م ن ي — 21 مرة — To wish

etymology.notes: Proto-Semitic *manay- 'to count, number, assign.' Arabic developed multiple senses: 1) 'to wish, desire (tamannā)' — from 'counting on' an outcome; 2) 'to test, try' — from 'measuring'; 3) maniyy 'sperm drop' — from the notion of 'apportioned' fluid; 4) munā 'wishes, hopes.' The counting/measuring core meaning is preserved in all branches.

hadith_evidence.ar: م ن ي — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 21 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root mny (م ن ي) appears 21 times in the Quran, including 2:78.

meaning.en_short: To spread, make smooth, prepare; mahd (cradle, bed)
meaning.en: To spread, make smooth, prepare; mahd (cradle, bed)
meaning.en_detailed: Verbal root (م ه د) meaning 'to spread, make smooth, prepare a level surface,' occurring 16 times in the Quran; the maṣdar mahd 'cradle, bed' appears 7 times. From Proto-Semitic *mahad- 'to spread, level' (cf. Hebrew māhad 'to spread,' Akkadian mahādu), the Arabic mahd emphasizes the prepared, smoothed surface of a resting place. Foundational usage Q 20:53 'He who made the earth a bed (mahdan) for you and caused to grow therein paths and means of livelihood'; Q 71:19 'And God made the earth a spread (mahādan) for you.' Q 3:46 'He will speak to the people from the cradle (al-mahdi) and in maturity' — about Jesus. The semantic core — spreading smooth for rest — yields both literal cradle/bed and the figurative 'preparing the way,' as in the divine tamhīd 'preparation' of outcomes.
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To spread, make smooth, prepare; mahd
meaning.ar_definition: جذر م ه د — 16 مرة — To spread

etymology.notes: Proto-Semitic *mahad- 'to spread, level, make smooth.' Arabic mahd (مهد) specifically means 'cradle, bed' — a spread-out resting place. Quranic usage: 'He who made the earth a bed/cradle for you' (mahdan; Q 20:53). The sense of preparation (tamhīd) derives from 'smoothing the way.'

hadith_evidence.ar: م ه د — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 16 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root mhd (م ه د) appears 16 times in the Quran, including 3:46.

meaning.en: Water; māʾ (water)
meaning.en_detailed: Nominal root (م و ه) — the proto-root *māy/*māʾ 'water,' occurring 63 times in the Quran in the noun māʾ (ماء). One of the most stable and ancient Semitic lexemes: Proto-Semitic *māy- attested in Hebrew mayim (with dual -im), Aramaic mayyā, Ugaritic my, Akkadian mû, Ethiopic māy — and reconstructible to Proto-Afroasiatic *maʾ- (cf. Egyptian nmw). Foundational Quranic usage Q 21:30 'We made from water (al-māʾi) every living thing,' the scriptural anchor for the primordial role of water in creation. Q 25:53 'He released the two seas, meeting each other, between them a barrier they do not transgress'; Q 56:68-70 'have you reflected on the water you drink? Was it you who sent it down... or were We the sender?' Q 30:24 'of the cattle there are eight pairs... He sends down rain from the sky.'
meaning.ar_definition: جذر م و ه — 63 مرة — Water

etymology.notes: Pan-Semitic word for 'water.' Proto-Semitic *māy-/*māʾ- 'water' is one of the most stable and ancient Semitic lexemes. Arabic māʾ (ماء) preserves the Proto-Semitic form with the glottal stop. The dual mayāni and plural miyāh show the original weak radical pattern. One of the few Semitic words with a Proto-Afroasiatic reconstruction (*maʾ- 'water').

hadith_evidence.ar: اللَّهُمَّ اسْقِنَا غَيْثًا مُغِيثًا
hadith_evidence.en: O Allah, send us rain, a beneficial rain.

meaning.en: Spirit. 21x. Ruh=spirit. 17:85: they ask about the spirit (al-ruh)—say: the spirit is by command of my Lord.
meaning.en_detailed: The triconsonantal root ر و ح (رُوحَ) — 57 Quranic occurrences — fundamentally expresses Spirit, soul (ruh). The interrogative at 17:85, 'they ask you about the rūḥ—say: the rūḥ is by command of my Lord' (al-rūḥu min amri rabbi), marks the spirit as a divine mystery withheld from human grasp; at 58:22, 'He sent down the spirit of tranquility into the hearts of the believers' marks divine sakinah. Occurs 57 times in the Quran. The root semantically pairs with raʾāḥa (to go in the evening) on the everyday plane and with malaʾika (angels) and nabī (prophet) on the metaphysical plane—the Holy Spirit (rūḥ al-qudus) being identified with Jibrīl in classical commentaries.

quranic_analysis.theme: The Spirit
quranic_analysis.detail: Quli al-ruhu min amri rabbi—the spirit is by command of my Lord.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: To grow, sprout; nabāt (plants, vegetation)
meaning.en_detailed: Verbal root (ن ب ت) meaning 'to grow, sprout, germinate,' occurring 26 times in the Quran; the maṣdar nabāt 'plants, vegetation' appears 4 times. From Proto-Semitic *nabat- 'to sprout, grow' (cf. Hebrew nābaṭ, Aramaic nəbaṭ, Ethiopic nabṭ 'vegetation'), the root is primarily botanical. Foundational Quranic usage Q 71:17 'And God has caused you to grow from the earth as plants (nabātan),' with the verb ʾanbata. Q 3:37 'He made her [Mary's mother] grow (ʾanbatahā) a good growth (nabātan ḥasanan)' — the divine nurturing of Mary; Q 6:99 'And He it is who sends down rain from the sky, then We cause to grow (nunbitu) through it every kind of vegetation (nabātin).' Q 18:45 'the example of the worldly life is like rain We sent down, then the vegetation (nabātu) of the earth mingles with it,' using the root for eschatological decay as well.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ن ب ت — 26 مرة — To grow

etymology.notes: Proto-Semitic *nabat- 'to sprout, grow (of plants).' Arabic nabāt (نبات) means 'plants, vegetation.' Quranic usage: 'And God causes you to grow from the earth as plants' (Q 71:17). The root is primarily used for botanical growth, extending metaphorically to the growth of children.

hadith_evidence.ar: ن ب ت — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 26 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root nbt (ن ب ت) appears 26 times in the Quran, including 3:37.

meaning.en_short: Star; najm (star); to appear gradually; installment
meaning.en: Star; najm (star); to appear gradually; installment
meaning.en_detailed: Nominal root (ن ج م) meaning 'star,' occurring 13 times in the noun najm (نجم), from Proto-Semitic *najm- (attested in Aramaic najmā, Ethiopic najm; cf. Arabic kawkab for planets). The name of Sūrat 53 (Sūrat al-Najm), opening with Q 53:1 'By the star (al-najmi) when it descends (ḥinā yahūq)' — the descending referring to the setting or piercing through the firmament in the Prophet's Night Journey. Q 86:3 'By the piercing star (al-najmu al-thāqib)'; Q 56:75 'I swear by the setting-places of the stars'; Q 37:88 refers to stars being 'among the greatest signs.' The verbal stem najama 'to appear gradually, emerge' is the basis of the noun nujūm 'installments,' as in Q 25:32 'the disbelievers said: why was the Quran not sent down all at once? Thus do We reveal it in installments (nujūman),' applying stellar emergence to Quranic progressive revelation.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ن ج م — 13 مرة — Star

etymology.notes: Primarily South Semitic and Aramaic word for 'star.' Arabic najm (نجم) specifically means a bright visible star (as opposed to kawkab 'planet'). Quranic usage: 'By the star when it sets' (Q 53:1 — Surat al-Najm). Extended to 'appearing gradually' as stars emerge and to 'installment' (nujūman) for the gradual revelation of the Quran.

hadith_evidence.ar: ن ج م — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 13 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root njm (ن ج م) appears 13 times in the Quran, including 53:1.

meaning.en_short: Palm tree; nakhl (date palms); to sift, select
meaning.en: Palm tree; nakhl (date palms); to sift, select
meaning.en_detailed: Nominal root (ن خ ل) meaning 'palm tree' (especially date palm), occurring 20 times in the noun nakhl (نخل); a secondary verbal sense 'to sift, select' is a homophonic development. The root (n-kh-l) has cognates in Aramaic naḥlā 'palm tree,' Ethiopic naḫl 'palm,' though Hebrew nāḥal means 'wadi' (a homograph). Foundational Quranic usage Q 20:71 'I will surely cut off your hands and feet on alternate sides, then I will crucify you on the trunks of palm trees (al-nakhli)' — Pharaoh's threat against the magicians. Q 16:67 'from the fruits of date-palms and grapes you make intoxicants and good provision'; Q 36:34 'and we have made therein gardens of date-palms (nakhlin) and grapes'; Q 80:29 'We brought forth therein gardens and grain and splendid palm trees (nakhlin)' — all testifying to divine provision in agricultural bounty.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ن خ ل — 20 مرة — Palm tree

etymology.notes: The root ن خ ل (n-kh-l) has two distinct meanings in Arabic: 1) 'palm tree' (nakhl = date palms) — the older sense; 2) 'to sift, select' — a transferred sense from the process of sifting dates or possibly a homophone. Nakhl is a key Quranic plant, frequently mentioned alongside olives and grapes as signs of God's provision.

hadith_evidence.ar: الْيَدُ الْعُلْيَا خَيْرٌ مِنَ الْيَدِ السُّفْلَى
hadith_evidence.en: The upper hand is better than the lower hand.

meaning.en: To be holy. 10x. Quddus=Most Holy (divine name). 59:23: al-Malik al-Quddus. Ruh al-Qudus=Holy Spirit.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ق د س (قَدُسَ), attested 10 times in the Quran, derives its core meaning of Holiness, purity; al-Quddus from Proto-Semitic sources. The name al-Quddus appears at 59:23 in the divine-name sequence paired with al-Salām, al-Muʾmin, al-Muhaymin, al-ʿAzīz, al-Jabbār, al-Mutakabbir; the derived Rūḥ al-Quds (Holy Spirit) appears at 2:87, 5:110, and 16:102. Occurs 10 times in the Quran. The form quds (holy, sacred) appears in the compounds al-Arḍ al-Muqaddasah (the Holy Land, 5:21) and Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). The root semantically pairs with ṭāhir (pure), mutahhar (purified), and salīm (sound), and contrasts with najis (impure) and rijs (filth).
meaning.ar_definition: جذر قَدُسَ — 10 مرة — holiness, purity; al-quddus

quranic_analysis.theme: Most Holy
quranic_analysis.detail: Al-Quddus—the Most Holy. One of the 99 Names.

hadith_evidence.ar: الطُّهُورُ شَطْرُ الْإِيمَانِ
hadith_evidence.en: Purity is half of faith.

meaning.en: To overpower. 10x. Qahara=subdue. Al-Qahhar=the Subduer (divine name). 12:39: Allah the One, the Subduer (al-Wahid al-Qahhar).
meaning.en_detailed: The triconsonantal root ق ه ر (قَهَرَ) — 10 Quranic occurrences — fundamentally expresses To overpower; al-Qahhar. The name al-Qahhār appears at 12:39, 'Allah, the One, the Subduer' (Allāhu al-Wāḥidu al-Qahhāru), and at 13:16 paired with al-Wāḥid al-Qahhār in a paradigmatic divine-name sequence; at 38:65, 'the Subduer over all His servants' (al-Qahhāru fawqa ʿibādihi) closes the divine-name chain. Occurs 10 times in the Quran. The active participle qāhirūn (subduers, 4:34) names a social rank within marriage discourse, an extended use of the root's relational subjugation; semantically the root pairs with jabbār (compeller), ʿazīz (mighty), and mutakabbir (supreme).

quranic_analysis.theme: The Subduer
quranic_analysis.detail: Allahu al-Wahidu al-Qahharu—Allah, the One, the Subduer.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en_short: To call, summon; nidāʾ (call); nadī (council, gathering)
meaning.en: To call, summon; nidāʾ (call); nadī (council, gathering)
meaning.en_detailed: Verbal root (ن د و) meaning 'to call, summon,' occurring 53 times across Forms I, III, and VI; from Proto-Semitic *nadaw- (cf. Aramaic nədaʾ 'to call,' Akkadian nadû 'to throw'). The Quranic Form III nādā 'to call out loudly' occurs 25 times, often in eschatological context: Q 28:62-65 'the day He will call you (yunādī-kum)'; Q 41:44 'if the disbelievers were not disputing with it...'; the intercessional ḥawḍ (Pool) and divine call (nidāʾ) on the Day of Resurrection. Q 2:171 'The parable of those who disbelieve is like one who cries (yanʿiqu) to cattle — they hear only a call (duʿāʾan) and a cry (nidāʾan).' The noun nidāʾ 'call, summons' appears 5 times; nadī 'council, assembly' appears 2 times (Q 19:73 'in the form of a council'; Q 38:6 'the chiefs (al-malaʾu) of his people').
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ن د و — 53 مرة — To call

etymology.notes: Proto-Semitic *nadaw- likely meant 'to impel, cast forth.' Arabic developed the specialized sense 'to call, summon (nādā).' Nidāʾ (نداء) 'call, proclamation' is a frequent Quranic term, especially for the divine call. Nadī (ندي) and nadwa (ندوة) 'council, gathering' derive from the notion of 'calling people together.'

derived_forms.meaning: to call one another, cry out mutually

hadith_evidence.ar: ن د و — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 53 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root ndw (ن د و) appears 53 times in the Quran, including 2:171.

meaning.en_short: To pull out, remove; to snatch; nizāʿ (conflict, pulling)
meaning.en: To pull out, remove; to snatch; nizāʿ (conflict, pulling)
meaning.en_detailed: Verbal root (ن ز ع) meaning 'to pull out, remove, extract; to snatch,' occurring 20 times in the Quran across Forms I, III, and VI; from Proto-Semitic *nazaʿ- 'to pull out' (cf. Aramaic nəzaʿ 'to extract'). Form VI tanāzaʿa 'to dispute, wrangle, contend' (8×) extends the physical pulling into social antagonism: Q 8:46 'obey God and His Messenger, and do not dispute (tanāzaʿū) lest you lose heart.' Q 2:197 'do not dispute (tanāzaʿū) about the rites of Hajj.' The maṣdar nizāʿ 'dispute, conflict' (2×) at Q 26:9 'and verily in this is a sign, but most of them are not believers'; the verbal Form I nazaʿa (8×) at Q 12:80 'he turned away from them and said: how great is my grief for Joseph'; Q 79:16 'and Moses said: rather than [be delayed], we have hastened to You, our Lord.'
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To pull out, remove; to snatch; niz
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ن ز ع — 20 مرة — To pull out

etymology.notes: Proto-Semitic *nazaʿ- 'to pull out, extract.' Arabic nazaʿa (نزع) specifically means 'to pull out, remove forcefully.' Nizāʿ (نزاع) 'conflict, strife' derives from the notion of people 'pulling' in opposite directions. Quranic usage: 'Those who dispute/pull against the signs of God' (Q 40:4).

hadith_evidence.ar: ن ز ع — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 20 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root nzE (ن ز ع) appears 20 times in the Quran, including 50:26.

meaning.en_short: Vulture; nasr (vulture, eagle); to aid, help (distinct from naṣr)
meaning.en: Vulture; nasr (vulture, eagle); to aid, help (distinct from naṣr)
meaning.en_detailed: Nominal/onomastic root (ن س ر) meaning 'vulture, eagle,' occurring once in the Quran (Q 71:23) as the name of a pre-Islamic Arabian idol. From Proto-Semitic *našr- 'eagle, vulture' (cf. Hebrew nešer, Akkadian našru, Ugaritic nšr), the root is Pan-Semitic for large birds of prey. Quranic usage Q 71:23 (in Sūrat Nūḥ): 'And they said: do not abandon your gods, do not abandon Wadd, Suwāʿ, Yaghūth, Yaʿūq, and Nasr,' listing five major pagan deities of Noah's people (per traditional reading). This verse is the source for the classical hadith that the Hour will not come until no one on earth remembers these names. Crucially distinct from the Arabic root n-ṣ-r 'to help/aid' (whence naṣr 'victory'); the two roots are homophones and frequently confused in non-specialist literature.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ن س ر — 1 مرة — Vulture

etymology.notes: Pan-Semitic word for a large bird of prey. Proto-Semitic *našr- 'eagle, vulture.' Arabic nasr (نسر) specifically denotes 'vulture' or 'eagle.' Quranic usage: The idol Nasr (mentioned in Q 71:23 as one of the gods of Noah's people). Note: This is distinct from the Arabic root ن ص ر (n-ṣ-r) 'to help, aid' — a common confusion in etymological study.

hadith_evidence.ar: ن س ر — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 1 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root nsr (ن س ر) appears 1 times in the Quran, including 71:23.

meaning.en: Lightning. 6x. Baraqa=flash. 2:20: the lightning (al-barqu) almost snatches their sight—hypocrites in darkness.
meaning.en_detailed: Occurring 6 times in the Quranic text, the root ب ر ق (بَرَقَ) conveys the essential concept of To flash; lightning (barq). The phrase yakādu al-barq yakhṭafu abṣārahum at 2:20, 'lightning almost snatches away their sight,' describes the paralyzing visual assault on the hypocrites; at 13:12, 'He shows you lightning, [giving] fear and hope' (yurīkum al-barq khawfan wa ṭamaʿan) frames lightning as a paired sign of dread and desire. Occurs 6 times in the Quran. The verbal noun bāriq (shining, 2:74; 24:43) names the luminous edge of the cloud; the root semantically pairs with raʿd (thunder) and ṣawʿ (lightning-bolt) in the meteorological triad.

quranic_analysis.theme: Lightning and darkness
quranic_analysis.detail: Yakadu al-barqu yakhtafu absarahum—lightning almost snatches sight.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en: Low. 10x. Safala=be low. Asfal=lowest. 95:5: lowest of the low (asfala safilin).
meaning.en_detailed: Root س ف ل (سَفُلَ), attested 10 times in the Quran, derives its core meaning of Low, lowest from Proto-Semitic sources. The elative phrase asfal safilīn at 95:5, 'the lowest of the low' (asfala sāfilīn), describes the lowest eschatological pit reserved for those who deny the divine signs, paired with aʿlā ʿalīyīn above; at 37:98, 'they found therein the lowest of the people' (asfala al-nās) names a community's moral and spiritual degradation. Occurs 10 times in the Quran. The root semantically contrasts with ʿuluw (high, elevated) and irtifāʿ (elevation); the elative pattern a-f-ʿal marks the most extreme of the same root, here intensifying the depth of the abyss.

quranic_analysis.theme: Lowest state
quranic_analysis.detail: Asfala safilin—the lowest of the low.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en_short: Women; nisāʾ (women, plural of imraʾa); to forget
meaning.en: Women; nisāʾ (women, plural of imraʾa); to forget
meaning.en_detailed: Nominal root (ن س و) functioning uniquely in Arabic as the irregular (suppletive) plural of imraʾa 'woman,' with nisāʾ (نساء) occurring 59 times in the Quran. The Proto-Semitic root for 'woman' is *ʾinṯ-at- (cf. Hebrew ʾiššâ, Aramaic ʾittəṯā, Akkadian aššatu), making Arabic nisāʾ an areal/Arabic-specific plural formation. The verb form nasiya 'to forget' is a homophone from a distinct root, though classical Arabic etymologists (and Ibn Qutayba) speculate about folk-etymological connections. Foundational usage Q 3:14 'Beautified for mankind is love of desires: women (al-nisāʾi), children, accumulated heaps of gold and silver, horses of mark, cattle and crops' — the classical locus of al-nisāʾ in Quranic anthropology. Q 4:34 — the famous 'awliyāʾ verse'; Q 33:35 the list of believing men and women; Q 24:31 modesty injunctions. The noun is one of the most semantically charged Quranic terms for social legislation.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ن س و — 59 مرة — Women

etymology.notes: Proto-Semitic *ʾinṯ-at- 'woman, female' is the primary Semitic root. Arabic nisāʾ (نساء) 'women' is the suppletive plural of imraʾa (امرأة). The root ن س و (n-s-w) for 'women' is unique to Arabic; the verb nasiya 'to forget' from the same root letters is likely a homophone from a distinct root. The association between 'women' and a root with n-s-y letters is distinctive to Arabic.

hadith_evidence.ar: ن س و — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 59 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root nsw (ن س و) appears 59 times in the Quran, including 3:14.

meaning.en_short: Drop of fluid; nuṭfa (sperm drop, germ cell)
meaning.en: Drop of fluid; nuṭfa (sperm drop, germ cell)
meaning.en_detailed: Core semantic: 'nuṭfa (نطفة)' — a drop of fluid, specifically the sperm-drop or germ cell from which human life begins; derived from the root ن ط ف (n-ṭ-f), occurring 12 times in the Quran, all in the singular form nuṭfa. Quranic usage centers on the biological origin of man: 'He created man from a sperm-drop (nuṭfa)' (Q 16:4, 36:77, 75:37, 80:19) and the progression 'then a clinging clot, then a lump of flesh' (alaq, muḍgha) as stages of embryogenesis (Q 23:13-14). Etymologically the root *naṭaf- 'to drip, drop' is pan-Semitic (Heb. nāṭap, Akk. naṭāpu), preserving the imagery of a pure, small liquid droplet. Scholarly precision: the Quranic nuṭfa refers to the mingled male and female gametic fluid (nuṭfat amshāj, Q 76:2) — a deliberately non-mechanistic, sign-bearing concept of origins.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ن ط ف — 12 مرة — Drop of fluid

etymology.notes: Proto-Semitic *naṭaf- 'to drop, drip.' Arabic nuṭfa (نطفة) specifically denotes 'a drop of fluid, sperm drop.' Quranic usage: 'He created man from a sperm-drop (nuṭfa)' (Q 16:4; 75:37). The root also covers 'pure/clear water' and metaphorically 'gem, pearl' — from the clarity of a pure drop.

key_nominals.meaning: drop of fluid; sperm drop, germ cell

hadith_evidence.ar: ن ط ف — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 12 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root nTf (ن ط ف) appears 12 times in the Quran, including 80:19.

meaning.en_short: To flee, disperse; to go forth (for battle); nafar (group)
meaning.en: To flee, disperse; to go forth (for battle); nafar (group)
meaning.en_detailed: Core semantic: 'nafara (نفر)' — to flee, disperse, or go forth (especially for battle or mobilization), with the nominal nafar meaning 'a group, band'; from the root ن ف ر (n-f-r), occurring 18 times across Forms I, II, and X. Quranic usage frames nafir as communal mobilization: 'The believers should not go forth (yanfirū) all together' (Q 9:122) regulates expeditionary duty, while 'If a party from every expedition remained behind, they could devote themselves to religious knowledge and warn their people when they return' (Q 9:122) describes the proper balance. The derived Form X istanfara 'to mobilize, call to arms' (Q 4:71) depicts mustering for jihād. Etymologically the root *napar- 'to break forth, burst out' connects Hebrew nāpar 'to sprout' and Akkadian napāru — the original image of breaking out giving rise to both 'fleeing in panic' and 'mobilizing in force.'
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To flee, disperse; to go forth
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ن ف ر — 18 مرة — To flee

etymology.notes: Proto-Semitic *napar- 'to break forth, burst out.' Arabic nafara (نفر) developed: 'to flee, disperse' and 'to go forth (for battle or pilgrimage).' Nafar (نفر) means 'a group of people' — those who go forth together. Quranic nafīr (نفير) refers to mobilization for battle.

derived_forms.meaning: to flee, disperse; to go forth, mobilize
to drive away, cause to flee

hadith_evidence.ar: ن ف ر — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 18 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root nfr (ن ف ر) appears 18 times in the Quran, including 9:122.

meaning.en_short: Benefit, use; to benefit; nafʿ (benefit, profit)
meaning.en: Benefit, use; to benefit; nafʿ (benefit, profit)
meaning.en_detailed: Core semantic: 'nafaʿa (نفع)' — to benefit, avail, be useful, with the nominal nafʿ 'benefit, profit, advantage'; from the root ن ف ع (n-f-ʿ), occurring 50 times, the great majority in Form I. Quranic usage is decisive in evaluating beliefs and actions: 'They learned what harms them and does not benefit (yānfaʿuhum) them' (Q 2:102) denounces sorcery; 'Those who believe and do righteous deeds — their Lord guides them by their faith; rivers will flow beneath them in gardens of bliss' contrasts with the powerless intercessors 'who can avail you (yanfaʿū) nothing' (Q 6:70). The negative interrogative 'what will benefit you (mā yanfaʿukum)' on the Day of Judgment (Q 75:9) is a recurring rhetorical pivot. Distinct from nafaq 'spending' despite superficial similarity; the root privileges tangible, lasting utility.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ن ف ع — 50 مرة — Benefit

etymology.notes: Primarily West Semitic root for 'benefit, usefulness.' Arabic nafʿ (نفع) means 'benefit, profit, usefulness.' Quranic opposition: between mā yanfaʿu 'what benefits' and mā lā yanfaʿu 'what does not benefit' — a key criterion for evaluating actions and beliefs. Note: Arabic distinguishes نفع (nafʿ, benefit) from نفق (nafaqa, spending).

hadith_evidence.ar: ن ف ع — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 50 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root nfE (ن ف ع) appears 50 times in the Quran, including 2:102.

meaning.en: To decrease, diminish; nuqṣān (loss, reduction)
meaning.en_detailed: Core semantic: 'naqaṣa (نقص)' — to decrease, diminish, reduce; with nuqṣān 'loss, diminution' and naqṣ 'deficiency'; from the root ن ق ص (n-q-ṣ), occurring 10 times in Form I. Quranic usage spans theological and commercial registers: 'We will not decrease (lā naqṣu) anything from the Book' (Q 6:59) affirms divine omniscience and the integrity of fate; 'Then He reduces (nanquṣu) the land from its edges' (Q 13:41) depicts the abasement of disbelieving communities. Legal-commercial uses warn against fraudulent reduction ('Do not diminish (lā taqṣū) people's goods,' implicit in market-place ethics). Etymologically the root *naqaṣ- 'to cut off, chip away' is pan-Semitic (Heb. nāqaṣ, Akk. naqāṣu) — the concrete image of chipping away from a whole generating both physical and moral senses of loss.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ن ق ص — 10 مرة — To decrease

etymology.notes: Proto-Semitic *naqaṣ- 'to cut off, chip away.' Arabic naqaṣa (نقص) 'to decrease, diminish, reduce.' Nuqṣān (نقصان) 'loss, reduction.' Quranic usage: 'We will not decrease/diminish anything from the Book' (Q 6:59). Often used in commercial/legal contexts for shortchanging and reduction.

hadith_evidence.ar: ن ق ص — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 10 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root nqS (ن ق ص) appears 10 times in the Quran, including 13:41.

meaning.en_short: To take revenge, punish; niqma (vengeance, punishment)
meaning.en: To take revenge, punish; niqma (vengeance, punishment)
meaning.en_detailed: Core semantic: 'naqama / intaqama' — to take revenge, avenge, punish; niqma 'vengeance, punishment'; muntaqim 'Avenger' (a divine name); from the root ن ق م (n-q-m), occurring 17 times across Forms I and VIII. Quranic usage applies the root overwhelmingly to divine retribution: 'And God is Mighty, Possessor of Vengeance' (Dhū Intiqām, Q 3:4; cf. 5:95, 39:37) anchors God's sovereign response to wrongdoing; 'Thus is the seizure of your Lord when He seizes the towns while they are wronging' (Q 11:102) presents niqma as cosmic justice. Form VIII intaqama dominates the Quranic distribution (13 of 17 occurrences), emphasizing God's active, complete retribution. Etymologically pan-Semitic *naqam- 'to avenge' (Heb. nāqam, Akk. naqāmu) preserves a single inherited semantic core of justified retaliation.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ن ق م — 17 مرة — To take revenge

etymology.notes: Pan-Semitic root for 'vengeance, retribution.' Proto-Semitic *naqam- 'to avenge.' Arabic naqama (نقم) means 'to take revenge, punish, resent.' Niqma (نقمة) 'vengeance, punishment.' Quranic usage: 'They resented nothing from them except that they believed in God' (Q 85:8). Often used for divine punishment.

hadith_evidence.ar: ن ق م — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 17 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root nqm (ن ق م) appears 17 times in the Quran, including 3:4.

meaning.en_short: Marriage; to marry; nikāḥ (marriage contract, intercourse)
meaning.en: Marriage; to marry; nikāḥ (marriage contract, intercourse)
meaning.en_detailed: Core semantic: 'nakaḥa (نكح)' — to marry, enter into marriage (contract and consummation); nikāḥ 'marriage, wedlock'; from the root ن ك ح (n-k-ḥ), occurring 23 times across Forms I and IV. Quranic usage shapes Islamic marriage law: 'Marry (ankiḥū) the unmarried among you' (Q 24:32) is the central command; 'And when you divorce women and they have reached their term, do not prevent them from remarrying (an yankiḥna) their husbands' (Q 2:232) regulates post-divorce remarriage; 'Forbidden to you are… married women except those whom your right hands possess' (Q 4:24) treats nikāḥ as the lawful frame for sexual union. Form IV ʾankaḥa 'to give in marriage, marry off' governs parental and guardian duty. Etymologically West Semitic (Aramaic nəkaḥ, Ethiopic nakaḥa 'to have intercourse'); a rare Semitic root for marriage as covenant.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ن ك ح — 23 مرة — Marriage

etymology.notes: Primarily West Semitic root for 'marriage, sexual intercourse.' Arabic nakaḥa (نكح) specifically denotes the marriage contract and consummation. Nikāḥ (نكاح) is the Quranic term for the marriage bond. The root appears in Quranic legal passages on marriage, divorce, and remarriage.

hadith_evidence.ar: النِّكَاحُ مِنْ سُنَّتِي فَمَنْ لَمْ يَعْمَلْ بِسُنَّتِي فَلَيْسَ مِنِّي
hadith_evidence.en: Marriage is part of my Sunnah; whoever does not follow my Sunnah is not of me.

meaning.en_short: To punish, make an example; shackle, fetter; to hinder
meaning.en: To punish, make an example; shackle, fetter; to hinder
meaning.en_detailed: Core semantic: 'nakala / nakkala' — to punish, make an example, deter; nakāl 'exemplary punishment, deterrent'; from the root ن ك ل (n-k-l), occurring 5 times, predominantly as the nominal nakāl (4 times). Quranic usage frames nakāl as God's pedagogic punishment for disobedient communities: 'We made it a deterrent (nakālan) for their time and for later generations' (Q 2:66) makes the punishment of the Sabbath-breakers a cautionary exemplar; 'And they shall taste the evil consequences of their deeds' (Q 39:26) and similar verses treat nakāl as warning-sign rather than mere penalty. The sense of 'shackle/fetter' (nukl) is secondary, from the restraints used in punitive execution. Etymologically the root *nakal- 'to be crafty, to smite' (Heb. nākal, Akk. nakālu) has specialized in Arabic to deterrent punishment.
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To punish, make an example; shackle, fetter; to hinder
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ن ك ل — 5 مرة — To punish

etymology.notes: Proto-Semitic *nakal- 'to be crafty, to smite/punish.' Arabic nakala (نكل) developed: 'to punish, make an example of, deter.' Nakāl (نكال) 'exemplary punishment' in Quranic usage: 'a deterrent punishment from God' (Q 5:38). The sense of 'shackle/fetter' derives from the physical restraints used in punishment.

hadith_evidence.ar: ن ك ل — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 5 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root nkl (ن ك ل) appears 5 times in the Quran, including 2:66.

meaning.en: Crookedness. 9x. Iwaj=crookedness. 39:28: Arabic Quran without any crookedness (iwaj).
meaning.en_detailed: The Arabic root ع و ج (عَوِجَ) appears 9 times in the Quran, governing the semantic domain of Crookedness; deviation. The negative descriptive at 39:28, 'a Quran in Arabic, without any crookedness' (Qurʾānan ʿarabiyyan ghayra dhī ʿiwajin), marks the Quran's linguistic and theological coherence as one of its proofs; the same noun ʿiwaj appears at 3:71 paired with the warning to the People of the Book 'not to swerve' and at 18:1 alongside 'straightened.' Occurs 9 times in the Quran. The root semantically contrasts with qawwām (straight, just), qist (equity), and iqāmat (to set upright); the verbal noun iwāj (crookedness, 11:88) marks the failure of Yūsuf's brothers' counsel.

quranic_analysis.theme: Without crookedness
quranic_analysis.detail: Qur'anan arabiyyan ghayra dhi iwajin—Quran without any crookedness.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en: To obtain, attain, reach; nayl (attainment)
meaning.en_detailed: Core semantic: 'nāla (نال)' — to obtain, attain, reach (often after effort); nayl 'attainment, achievement'; from the root ن ي ل (n-y-l), occurring 12 times in Form I. Quranic usage marks successful reach after striving: 'You will not attain (lan tanālū) righteousness (al-birr) until you spend from what you love' (Q 3:92) sets spendthrift charity as the threshold of piety; 'If good touches you, it grieves them; if evil befalls you (aṣābahu), they rejoice' (Q 3:120, using nāla in related context) marks the contingent character of human fortune. The verbal nāla connotes achievement won through trial. Etymologically a West Semitic root (Aramaic nəyal 'to obtain') with limited Arabic development focused on the active, volitional sense of attainment.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ن ي ل — 12 مرة — To obtain

etymology.notes: Likely a West Semitic root for 'attaining, obtaining.' Arabic nāla (نال) 'to obtain, attain, reach.' Nayl (نيل) 'attainment, acquisition.' The root primarily conveys successful achievement after effort. Quranic usage: 'You will not attain righteousness until you spend from what you love' (Q 3:92).

hadith_evidence.ar: ن ي ل — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 12 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root nyl (ن ي ل) appears 12 times in the Quran, including 3:120.

meaning.en: Measure. 132x. Qadara=measure. 2:236: bestow on them a provision according to what is reasonable (al-mut'atu bi-al-ma'ruf)—on the wealthy according to his capacity (qadaru).
meaning.en_detailed: قَدَرَ (ق د ر), a root appearing 132 times in the Quran, encodes the notion of To measure, decree (qadr) across its various verbal and nominal forms. The divine name al-Qadīr (All-Powerful) and the noun qadr (measure, decree, destiny) interlock: at 97:1–3, Laylat al-Qadr (the Night of Decree/Power) unites both senses; at 54:49, 'We have decreed everything in measure' (kullu shayʾin khalaqnāhu bi-qadrin) marks cosmic order as measured creation. Occurs 132 times in the Quran. The form qaddara (Form II) at 41:10, 'He measured it out (fa-qaddarahu) and guided [it],' marks the precision of cosmic estimation; the nouns taqdīr (predestination) and muqaddar (decreed, 41:41) extend the field. The semantic path runs from physical measure to cosmic decree to divine omnipotence.

quranic_analysis.theme: Divine measure
quranic_analysis.detail: Matta'uhunna ala al-musi'i qadaruhu—provision according to capacity.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *qdr = 'to measure, compute → to have power'. Arabic qadara = to measure, decree. Qadr = measure, destiny. Qadīr = All-Powerful. The semantic path: one who measures/controls has power. The Quran's Laylat al-Qadr (Night of Power/Decree) unites the senses of divine power and divine measurement.

hadith_evidence.ar: تَدَبَّرُوا الْقُرْآنَ فَإِنَّهُ حُجَّةٌ لَكُمْ أَوْ عَلَيْكُمْ
hadith_evidence.en: Reflect upon the Quran, for it is either a proof for you or against you.
hadith_evidence.source: Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim via ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb

meaning.en: Mockery, ridicule; to mock; huzūʾ (derision)
meaning.en_detailed: Core semantic: 'haziʾa / istahzaʾa' — to mock, ridicule, deride; huzuʾ 'mockery, derision'; from the root ه ز أ (h-z-ʾ), occurring 34 times, all in the nominal huzuʾ or the Form X mustahziʾūn. Quranic usage is overwhelmingly eschatological and condemnatory: disbelievers mock prophets and divine signs in this life and will be mocked in turn — 'God does not shy away from using the parable of a mosquito' (Q 2:26, immediately after verses on istihzāʾ); 'Do not make your oaths a means of deceit, lest one community become more numerous than another; God only tests you by this' (Q 16:94 and 2:14: 'we are only mocking'); the verb mustahziʾūn is reserved for active scorn. Etymologically primarily Arabic (Aramaic həzaʾ 'to mock'), the root carries strong pejorative weight absent from milder 'to laugh' roots.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ه ز أ — 34 مرة — Mockery

etymology.notes: Primarily Arabic root for 'mockery, ridicule.' Arabic hazuʾa (هزأ) and istahzaʾa (استهزأ) 'to mock, ridicule.' Huzuʾ (هزؤ) and huzūʾ (هزوء) 'mockery, derision.' Quranic usage: frequently in the context of disbelievers mocking prophets and divine signs. The root denotes an active, scornful mockery.

hadith_evidence.ar: ه ز أ — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 34 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root hzA (ه ز أ) appears 34 times in the Quran, including 2:14.

meaning.en: To burn. 9x. Haraqa=burn. 20:97: I will surely burn it (la-nuharriqannahu)—golden calf.
meaning.en_detailed: Occurring 9 times in the Quranic text, the root ح ر ق (حَرَقَ) conveys the essential concept of To burn. The vow at 20:97, 'I will burn it to ashes' (la-nuḥarriqannahu), is said by Mūsā of the golden calf, indicating not only its destruction but its annihilation as a sign; at 36:50 the form mukhallaṣīn marks those 'taken' by burning into eschatological punishment. Occurs 9 times in the Quran. The verbal noun ḥarīq (burning, 9:63) describes the fire of hell in this-worldly metaphor. The root semantically pairs with ḥarq (fire), ʿadhdhaba (to punish by burning), and nar (fire); it is distinct from the pre-Islamic homograph ḥaraqa (to earn), which the Quran explicitly rejects.

quranic_analysis.theme: Burning the calf
quranic_analysis.detail: La-nuharriqannahu—I will burn it to ashes.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en_short: Jews; hūd; to be Jewish; to repent, turn back
meaning.en: Jews; hūd; to be Jewish; to repent, turn back
meaning.en_detailed: Core semantic: 'hūd (هود)' — Jews; alladhīna hādū 'those who be(became) Jewish'; with secondary senses 'to repent, turn back'; from the root ه و د (h-w-d), occurring 21 times. The noun hūd is the Arabic ethnonym for Jews, ultimately a borrowing from Hebrew/Aramaic yəhûdî 'Jew, Judean' (from yəhûdâ 'Judah'). Quranic usage identifies Jewish communities as recipients of prior scripture: 'Those who believe, and those who are Jews (alladhīna hādū), and the Christians, and the Sabeans — whoever believes in God and the Last Day and does righteous deeds' (Q 2:62, 5:69) sets up the salvation-dialogue across revealed communities. The dual meaning 'to be Jewish / to repent' is etymologically distinct but homonymous in Arabic; the verb hāda is reserved in the Quran for the Jewish sense. The proper name Hūd (Q 7:65-72, 11:50-60) is the prophet sent to ʿĀd.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ه و د — 21 مرة — Jews

etymology.notes: Arabic ه و د (h-w-d) for 'Jews' (hūd; yahūd) is derived from Hebrew/Aramaic yəhûdî 'Jew, Judean' (from yəhûdâ 'Judah'). The Arabic root developed: hāda 'to be/become Jewish' and the adjective hūdī 'Jewish.' Quranic usage: 'Those who believe, and those who are Jews...' (Q 2:62). The alternative meaning 'to repent' is a separate development.

derived_forms.meaning: to be Jewish; to repent, turn back

hadith_evidence.ar: التَّائِبُ مِنَ الذَّنْبِ كَمَنْ لَا ذَنْبَ لَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The one who repents from sin is like one who has no sin.

meaning.en_short: To be equal; match; to incline
meaning.en: Equal. Kuf'=match, equal. 112:4: nor is there any equal (kufuwan) to Him.
meaning.en_detailed: كَفَأَ (ك ف أ), a root appearing 1 times in the Quran, encodes the notion of To be equal; match; to incline across its various verbal and nominal forms. The denial at 112:4, 'nor is there to Him any equal' (wa-lam yakun lahu kufuwan aḥadun), closes the surah of pure divine unity with the negation of any counterpart; this single Quranic occurrence of the abstract noun kufʾ is one of the most concentrated theological statements in the Quran, framing tawḥīd as the absence of any second. Occurs 1 time in the Quran. The semantic field stands in stark opposition to sharik (partner), mithl (equal), and ṣāḥib (companion)—the divine uniqueness being defined by the absolute absence of any parallel or match.
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To be equal; match; to incline

quranic_analysis.theme: No equal to Allah
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa lam yakun lahu kufuwan ahad—no equal to Him.

derived_forms.meaning: To be equal; match; to incline

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en_short: Trust, confidence; to trust; wathīqa (document); firm
meaning.en: Trust, confidence; to trust; wathīqa (document); firm
meaning.en_detailed: Core semantic: 'wathiqa (وثق)' — to be firm, solid, trustworthy; mīthāq 'covenant, solemn pact' (the central Quranic term); wathāq 'bond, fetter'; wathīqa 'document'; from the root و ث ق (w-th-q), occurring 34 times. Quranic usage centers on divine covenants: 'And [recall] when We took from the prophets their covenant (mīthāqahum) and from you [Muhammad] and from Noah and Abraham and Moses and Jesus' (Q 33:7) — the divine mīthāq with the prophets is the Quran's master covenant concept; 'And remember the favor of God upon you and the covenant (mīthāq) which He made with you when you said, "We hear and obey"' (Q 2:63) frames the Sinai mīthāq with the Children of Israel. The semantic field extends from physical firmness → trust → written covenant → legal document. Etymologically West Semitic *waṯiq- 'firm, trustworthy' (Heb. yāṯēq, Aramaic wəṯaq).
meaning.ar_definition: جذر و ث ق — 34 مرة — Trust

etymology.notes: Primarily West Semitic root for 'trust, firmness, confidence.' Arabic wathiqa (وثق) 'to trust, have confidence.' Wathīqa (وثيقة) 'document, bond, covenant' — a written guarantee. Mīthāq (ميثاق) 'covenant' is a central Quranic term for the divine covenant with humanity and prophets. The semantic field spans: physical firmness → trust → covenant.

hadith_evidence.ar: و ث ق — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 34 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root wvq (و ث ق) appears 34 times in the Quran, including 2:63.

meaning.en: Face, countenance; direction; wajh (face, aspect)
meaning.en_detailed: Core semantic: 'wajh (وجه)' — face, countenance, direction, aspect; jiha 'side, direction'; from the root و ج ه (w-j-h), occurring 78 times, the great majority as the noun wajh. Quranic usage is theologically central: 'To God belongs the east and the west; wherever you turn (tuwallū), there is the face of God (wajh Allāh)' (Q 2:115) — the foundational verse making wajh Allāh an omnipresent, non-spatial divine aspect; 'The face of your Lord, Majestic and Honor-bearing, remains' (Q 55:27) makes the divine wajh the only eternally abiding reality. 'Those who fulfill the covenant of God and do not break the contract' (Q 13:20) — the people of piety sell their lives seeking God's 'face.' The semantic shift from physical face to divine aspect via abstraction is one of the Quran's most important theological moves.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر و ج ه — 78 مرة — Face

etymology.notes: Primarily Arabic and Aramaic root for 'face, direction.' Arabic wajh (وجه) 'face, aspect, direction.' Jiha (جهة) 'direction, side.' Quranic usage: 'Wherever you turn, there is the face of God' (wajh Allāh; Q 2:115). The root developed rich theological meanings: wajh Allāh 'the countenance of God' and the concept of orientation (tawajjuh).

hadith_evidence.ar: و ج ه — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 78 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root wjh (و ج ه) appears 78 times in the Quran, including 2:115.
