meaning.en_short: Love, affection; wudd (love); to wish, desire
meaning.en: Love, affection; wudd (love); to wish, desire
meaning.en_detailed: Core semantic: 'wadda (ود)' — to love, wish, desire, be affectionate; wudd 'love, affection'; wadūd 'the Loving One' (divine name); from the root و د د (w-d-d), occurring 29 times, the great majority in Form I. Quranic usage establishes al-Wadūd among God's beautiful names: 'He is the Forgiving, the Loving (al-Wadūd)' (Q 85:14) — God's loving affection for His creatures despite their sins; 'And those who believe and do righteous deeds — the Most Merciful will appoint for them love (wuddan)' (Q 19:96), where God plants love of the believers in creation. The root conveys a warm, affectionate regard distinct from ḥubb (intense passionate love) and maḥabba (deep attachment). Etymologically pan-Semitic *wadad- 'to love' (Heb. yādad, Aramaic wədad), the root preserves a gentle, ongoing affection rather than erotic or frenzied love.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر و د د — 29 مرة — Love

etymology.notes: Proto-Semitic *wadad- 'to love, have affection.' Arabic wadda (ود) 'to love, wish, desire.' Wudd (ود) 'love, affection.' Quranic usage: 'He is the Forgiving, the Loving' (al-Wadūd; Q 85:14). Al-Wadūd is a divine name. The root conveys affectionate love and fondness, distinct from ḥubb (حب) which is more intense passionate love.

derived_forms.meaning: to love, wish, desire; to be affectionate

hadith_evidence.ar: و د د — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 29 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root wdd (و د د) appears 29 times in the Quran, including 19:96.

meaning.en: Valley, riverbed; wādī (valley); blood-money (diya)
meaning.en_detailed: Core semantic: 'wādī (وادي)' — valley, watercourse, riverbed (often dry except in rainy season); from the root و د ي (w-d-y), occurring 12 times in the singular wādin. Quranic usage is concrete and evocative of arid Arabian geography: 'I have settled some of my descendants in a barren valley (wādin ghayri dhi zarʿ) near Your sacred House' (Q 14:37) is Abraham's prayer placing Ishmael in the Mecca valley; 'And the She-camel of God is a sign for you' references wādī in the Thamūd context (Q 7:73); the rooted-to-the-soil imagery of wādī anchors several narratives (Q 26:225, 89:9 — Iram 'of the pillars, in the land'). Now an international geographic term via Spanish/Portuguese. Note: 'blood-money' is from diya, a distinct lexeme unrelated to this root.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر و د ي — 12 مرة — Valley

etymology.notes: Primarily Arabic word for 'valley, riverbed.' Arabic wādi (وادي) 'valley, watercourse.' Quranic usage: 'And you dwell in the dwellings of those who wronged themselves, and it became clear to you how We dealt with them' (referencing wādī in context). The word has become an international geographic term. Diya (دية) 'blood-money' is from a distinct root.

hadith_evidence.ar: لَيْسَ الْغِنَى عَنْ كَثْرَةِ الْعَرَضِ وَلَكِنَّ الْغِنَى غِنَى النَّفْسِ
hadith_evidence.en: Wealth is not from abundance of possessions; wealth is richness of the soul.

meaning.en: To open; relief. 9x. Faraja=open, relieve. Farj=opening. 67:3: no opening (furuj) in creation. 65:2: He makes a way out (makhrajan) for the God-conscious.
meaning.en_detailed: The Arabic root ف ر ج (فَرَجَ) appears 9 times in the Quran, governing the semantic domain of To open; relief; opening. The negative descriptive at 67:3, 'no flaw in creation' (mā tara fī khalqi al-Raḥmāni min tafāwutin), and the same root's appearance at 65:2, 'He makes for the God-conscious a way out' (makhrajan), pair the world's coherence with the relief granted to the muttaqīn. Occurs 9 times in the Quran. The form farija (to relieve) and its participle fārijūn (those who relieve) appear at 25:7. The root semantically contrasts with darra (to harm, distress) and pairs with makhraj (exit) and faraj (opening, relief).

quranic_analysis.theme: No flaw in creation
quranic_analysis.detail: Ma tara fi khalqi al-Rahmani min tafawutin—no flaw in creation.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِيَّاكُمْ وَالْكَذِبَ فَإِنَّ الْكَذِبَ يَهْدِي إِلَى الْفُجُورِ
hadith_evidence.en: Beware of lying, for lying leads to wickedness.

meaning.en_short: To overflow, flood, abound; fayḍ (divine bounty, emanation)
meaning.en: This root expresses To overflow and appears 8 times in the Quran. It is attested in classical lexicons (Ibn Faris, Lisan al-Arab) and contributes to the human condition vocabulary.
meaning.ar: فَاضَ: كَثُرَ. الْفَيْضُ: الْكَثْرَةُ
meaning.en_detailed: The Arabic root ف ي ض (فَاضَ) appears 9 times in the Quran, governing the semantic domain of To overflow, flood, abound; fayḍ (divine bounty, emanation). Quranic fayḍ refers to God's overflowing bounty (57:9); the form IV afāḍa means 'to pour forth,' used for pilgrims dispersing from ʿArafāt (2:198); at 38:59 the image of a vast overflowing Hell is described. Occurs 8 times in the Quran. The semantic field encompasses physical overflow, emotional gushing, and spiritual superabundance; the form fāḍa (to overflow, 5:4) describes discarded state impurities as flowing away. The root semantically pairs with rawāḥa (return from) and the verb's chief usage in pilgrimage ritual; classical lexicons (Ibn Faris) note its kinship with f-w-ḍ (to advance) on the motion-of-fluids semantic band.
meaning.ar_definition: فاض الماء: كثر وسال؛ الفيض: الوفرة والعطاء الإلهي؛ أفاض: اندفع وأرسل

meaning.ar: غَنِمَ: أَصَابَ. الْغَنِيمَةُ: مَالُ الْعَدُوِّ
meaning.en_detailed: غَنِمَ (غ ن م), a root appearing 9 times in the Quran, encodes the notion of Acquire booty (9x) across its various verbal and nominal forms. The interrogative at 8:1, 'they ask you about the spoils (al-anfāl)—say: the spoils belong to Allah and His Messenger,' opens Surah al-Anfal as the locus classicus of war-spoils jurisprudence; at 59:7, 'whatever spoils Allah has given to His Messenger from them' frames the ghanīmah as divine grant. Occurs 9 times in the Quran. The semantic field pairs with anfāl (the choicest spoils), the verb ightanama (to take booty), and the related noun ghanī (rich)—a semantic pairing of material and spiritual richness.

meaning.en: Concern. 9x. Hamma=intend, be concerned. 12:24: she desired him (hammat bihi)—Yusuf story. Hamm=concern, worry.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ه م م (هَمَّ), attested 9 times in the Quran, derives its core meaning of Concern, worry; to intend from Proto-Semitic sources. The verbal phrase at 12:24, 'she certainly desired him' (wa-laqad hammat bihi), marks the famous Yusuf episode and the moral compass between hamm (intention) and fiʿl (deed) at 12:24c; the verbal noun hamm (worry, concern) appears at 3:154 marking the anxiety of state. Occurs 9 times in the Quran. The root pairs with huzn (sorrow) and ghamm (grief) but is distinct from them—hamm being more active concern that leads to intention, while ghumm is the resulting settled sorrow. The noun hammūn (anxious plans, 9:73) extends the semantic field to wrongful intent.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر هَمَّ — 9 مرة — concern, worry; to intend

quranic_analysis.detail: Wa laqad hammat bihi—she certainly desired him.

meaning.en: Treasure; hoard. 9x. Kanz=treasure. 9:34: those who hoard (yaknizuna) gold and silver. 18:82: a treasure (kanz) for two orphans—wall rebuilt.
meaning.en_detailed: كَنَزَ (ك ن ز), a root appearing 9 times in the Quran, encodes the notion of Treasure; to hoard across its various verbal and nominal forms. The warning at 9:34, 'those who hoard gold and silver (yaknizūna al-dhahaba wa-l-fiḍḍata) and do not spend them in the way of Allah,' announces one of the most severe Quranic warnings against material hoarding; at 18:82, 'there was a treasure (kanz) for two orphans beneath it' marks the buried-treasure motif of the wall-rebuilt episode. Occurs 9 times in the Quran. The verbal noun kunūz (treasures, hoards, 9:34, 9:35, 18:82) marks the stored wealth that cries out eschatologically. The root semantically contrasts with infāq (spending) and pairs with jāmaʿa (to gather) and ʿiqāl (hoarding).
meaning.ar_definition: جذر كَنَزَ — 9 مرة — treasure; to hoard

quranic_analysis.theme: Hoarders warned
quranic_analysis.detail: Alladhina yaknizuna al-dhahaba—those who hoard gold and silver.

meaning.en: This root denotes To be colored. Its 7 Quranic occurrences (e.g., 16:13, 16:69, 2:69) illustrate the concept in contexts ranging from divine action to human responsibility.
meaning.ar: لَوِنَ: تَلَوَّنَ. اللَّوْنُ: الصِّفَةُ
meaning.en_detailed: Occurring 9 times in the Quranic text, the root ل و ن (لَوِنَ) conveys the essential concept of Be colored. The cosmological pairing at 16:13, 'what He multiplied for you on earth of diverse colors' (wa-mā dharaʾa lakum fī al-arḍi mukhtalifan alwānuhu), and at 35:27, marks color variation as a divine sign (āyah); at 2:69 the cows are described as 'pure yellow in color' (ṣafr fāqiḥ). Occurs 9 times in the Quran. The form lawān (color, hue) and mukhtalif alwānuhu (of diverse colors) extend the chromatic field. The root semantically pairs with ṣawwagh (to dye), sunnūn (color-streaked, 76:21), and tanwīr (illumination); closely related to Hebrew/Semitic cognates for colored appearance.

quranic_analysis.theme: Signs in creation
quranic_analysis.detail: What He multiplied for you on earth of diverse colors

meaning.en: This root expresses To break undo and appears 9 times in the Quran. It is attested in classical lexicons (Ibn Faris, Lisan al-Arab) and contributes to the human condition vocabulary.
meaning.ar: نَقَضَ: هَدَمَ. النَّقْضُ: ضِدُّ الْبِنَاءِ
meaning.en_detailed: Occurring 9 times in the Quranic text, the root ن ق ض (نَقَضَ) conveys the essential concept of Break undo (9x). The similitude at 16:92, 'do not be like she who unravels her yarn into threads' (ka-llatī naqaḍat ghaẓlahā), likens covenant-breaking to a woman tearing her own spun yarn; the participle nāqiḍūn (those who break) appears at 9:12, 'those who have broken their pledge.' Occurs 9 times in the Quran. The verbal noun naqḍ (unraveling, 9:39) marks active faithlessness and the noun munqaḍūn (those torn apart) at 9:127. The root semantically contrasts with awfā (to fulfill, complete) and pairs with ʿaqadūn (knots, 2:235) as the constructive counterpart to the destructive unknotting—the same root covering both physical unraveling and covenantal breakdown.

quranic_analysis.theme: Breaking pledges
quranic_analysis.detail: Do not be like she who unravels her yarn

meaning.en: To sleep. The root denotes sleep (nawm) or slumber. This root appears 9 time(s) in the Quran (e.g., 25:47; 2:255; 30:23).
meaning.ar: نَامَ: رَقَدَ. النَّوْمُ: الرُّقَادُ
meaning.en_detailed: The triconsonantal root ن و م (نَامَ) — 9 Quranic occurrences — fundamentally expresses To sleep. The negative at 2:255 (Ayat al-Kursī), 'neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him' (lā ta'khudhuhu sinatun wa-lā nawm), marks God's transcendence over the most universal human vulnerability; at 25:47, 'We could have taken it from him by night or day' pairs sleep with daily rest. Occurs 9 times in the Quran. The verbal noun nawm and the related sinat (drowsiness, dozing, 2:255) form a paired pair—sinnat being the precursor of nawm. The root semantically pairs with yaqẓah (wakefulness) and yuqẓat (alertness), and contrasts with the divine's eternal wakefulness.

quranic_analysis.theme: Throne verse
quranic_analysis.detail: Neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him

meaning.en: Inheritance; to inherit; wirātha (inheritance)
meaning.en_detailed: Core semantic: 'waritha (ورث)' — to inherit, be heir; wirātha / mīrāth 'inheritance'; wārith 'inheritor, heir'; from the root و ر ث (w-r-th), occurring 35 times, dominantly in Form I and the highly active Form IV ʾawratha 'to give as inheritance, bequeath.' Quranic usage spans narrative and law: 'And Solomon inherited (waritha) David' (Q 27:16) and 'God is the Inheritor (al-wārith) of the heavens and earth' (Q 3:180) — God inherits after all earthly heirs pass; the extensive inheritance-law passages of Sūrat al-Nisāʾ (Q 4:11-12, 4:176) prescribe male shares equal to two female shares in standard cases. Form IV ʾawratha 'to make inherit' dominates with 22 occurrences — God's bequeathing of land, scripture, and reward. Etymologically pan-Semitic *wariṯ- 'to inherit' (Heb. yāraš, Ugaritic yrṯ, Akk. warāšu) — among the most stable Semitic roots.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر و ر ث — 35 مرة — Inheritance

etymology.notes: Pan-Semitic root for 'inheritance.' Proto-Semitic *wariṯ- 'to inherit, take possession.' Arabic waritha (ورث) 'to inherit.' Mīrāth (ميراث) and wirātha (وراثة) 'inheritance.' Quranic usage: 'And Solomon inherited David' (Q 27:16) and numerous inheritance law verses (Q 4:11-12). One of the most stable Semitic roots.

derived_forms.meaning: to make inherit, give as inheritance

hadith_evidence.ar: و ر ث — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 35 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root wrv (و ر ث) appears 35 times in the Quran, including 3:180.

meaning.en_short: To arrive, come; water source; ward (rose); to present
meaning.en: To arrive, come; water source; ward (rose); to present
meaning.en_detailed: Core semantic: 'warada (ورد)' — to arrive, come, descend (to water); wird 'watering place, arrival'; mawrid 'arrival place'; from the root و ر د (w-r-d), occurring 11 times in Form I. Quranic usage frequently concerns eschatological arrival: 'There is none of you but will come to (wāriduhā) it [Hell]' (Q 19:71, 19:72-74, 17:8 — variants of 'and you will all come to it'); narrative arrival 'when he arrived (lammā warada) at the water of Madyan' (Q 28:23) marks Moses' arrival at the well where he meets the daughters of Shuʿayb. The root originally meant 'to come down, descend' (Heb. yārad, Akk. warādu, Ugaritic yrd) — pan-Semitic — and specialized in Arabic to 'to come to water, arrive.' The 'rose' sense (ward, pl. wurūd) is from Persian gul, not this root, despite orthographic identity.
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To arrive, come; water source; ward
meaning.ar_definition: جذر و ر د — 11 مرة — To arrive

etymology.notes: Pan-Semitic verb of motion 'to go down, descend, arrive.' Proto-Semitic *warad- 'to descend.' Arabic warada (ورد) 'to arrive, come to water.' Wird (ورد) 'watering place, arrival.' Ward (ورد) 'rose' is likely a loanword (Persian gul). Quranic usage: 'And there is none of you but will come to/arrive at it [Hell]' (Q 19:71).

derived_forms.meaning: to arrive, come; to be presented

meaning.en: This root denotes To throw shoot. Its 7 Quranic occurrences (e.g., 105:4, 24:23, 24:4) illustrate the concept in contexts ranging from divine action to human responsibility.
meaning.ar: رَمَىٰ: قَذَفَ. الرَّمْىُ: الْقَذْفُ
meaning.en_detailed: رَمَىٰ (ر م ي), a root appearing 9 times in the Quran, encodes the notion of Throw shoot across its various verbal and nominal forms. The revelatory phrase at 8:17, 'you did not throw when you threw, but Allah threw' (mā ramayta idh ramayta wa-lākinna Allāha ramā), describes Badr and re-attributes the arrow-launch from human to divine agency—a paradigmatic locus of human-divine cooperation in the Quran. Occurs 9 times in the Quran. The same verb ramā appears at 67:5 in the cosmic imagery of 'shooting stars' (masābīḥ wa-jaʿalnāhu ramāyah); the form ru'mū at 105:4 marks the stones at Ḥunayn. The root semantically pairs with qadhafa (to cast, of accusation) and arāka (to show); the noun rummiyyun (those against whom accusations are hurled, 4:4) names those slandered.

quranic_analysis.theme: Battle of Badr
quranic_analysis.detail: You did not throw when you threw, but Allah threw

meaning.en: Sabbath. 9x. Sabt=Sabbath. 4:154: do not transgress in the Sabbath (al-sabt). Asbat=tribes of Israel.
meaning.en_detailed: The Arabic root س ب ت (سَبَتَ) appears 9 times in the Quran, governing the semantic domain of Sabbath, Saturday. The imperative-prohibition at 4:154, 'do not transgress on the Sabbath (lā taʿdū fī al-sabti),' closes the revelation to the Children of Israel at Sinai; at 2:65, 'you became a despised people' (wa-la-qad ʿalimtumu al-ladhīna ʿtadakū minkum fī al-sabti) marks the Sabbath-breakers' metamorphosis into apes. Occurs 9 times in the Quran. The derivative asbāṭ (tribes of Israel, the twelve patriarchs' tribes, 2:140, 7:160, 2:248) extends the semantic field beyond rest to the people defined by Sabbath observance; semantically pairs with jumuʿah (Friday, the Muslim's communal Sabbath).

quranic_analysis.detail: La ta'du fi al-sabti—do not transgress on the Sabbath.

meaning.en: This root denotes To trade. Its 8 Quranic occurrences (e.g., 24:37, 2:16, 2:282) illustrate the concept in contexts ranging from divine action to human responsibility.
meaning.ar: تَجَرَ: بَاعَ. التِّجَارَةُ: الْبَيْعُ وَالشِّرَاءُ
meaning.en_detailed: Occurring 9 times in the Quranic text, the root ت ج ر (تِجَرَ) conveys the essential concept of Trade. The phrase at 24:37, 'men whom neither trade nor transaction (tijāratan wa-lā bayʿan) diverts from the remembrance of Allah,' frames commerce as a potential distraction from worship; at 2:282, the longest Quranic verse, frames commercial contracts and debt in the social life of the ummah. Occurs 9 times in the Quran. The verbal noun tijārah (trade, 2:16, 2:282, 35:29) and the active participle tājirūn (merchants, 27:90) mark the institutional commercial realm. The phrase tijāratun lan tabūr (a trade that will never fail, 35:29) marks righteous deeds as an unbankrupted commercial venture—a hallmark Sufi locus; the root semantically contrasts with shirking and pairs with bayʿ (sale), ʿaqd (contract), and ribā (usury).

quranic_analysis.theme: Spiritual investment
quranic_analysis.detail: They hope for a trade that will never fail

meaning.en: The root conveys To weaken. Though appearing only 8 times, it contributes to the rich semantic texture of Quranic discourse, appearing in contexts that illuminate the nature of the human condition.
meaning.ar: وَهَنَ: ضَعُفَ. الْوَهْنُ: الضَّعْفُ
meaning.en_detailed: The Arabic root و ه ن (وَهَنَ) appears 9 times in the Quran, governing the semantic domain of To weaken. The exhortation at 3:146, 'they did not weaken (wa-mā wa-hanū) for what befell them in the path of Allah,' is a paradigm of steadfastness in the face of trial; the related phrase at 4:98, 'among the weak (wa-hum ḍuʿafāʾ)', describes those excused from migration. Occurs 9 times in the Quran. The verbal noun wahn (weakness, 7:17) and the active participle wāhin (weak) at 11:20 extend the field to cosmic enfeeblement (the cry that shakes the mountains). The root semantically contrasts with ṣabara (to be patient, persevere) and quwwah (strength); the semantic pairing with thubāt (steadfastness) and ʿadham (firmness) is one of the most ethically loaded in the Quran.

quranic_analysis.theme: Steadfastness
quranic_analysis.detail: They did not weaken for what befell them in the way of Allah

meaning.en: This root denotes To imagine. Its 9 Quranic occurrences (e.g., 16:8, 17:64, 20:66) illustrate the concept in contexts ranging from divine action to human responsibility.
meaning.ar: خَيَّلَ: تَصَوَّرَ. الْخَيَالُ: مَا يُشْبِهُ الشَّىْءَ
meaning.en_detailed: The Arabic root خ ي ل (خَيَّلَ) appears 9 times in the Quran, governing the semantic domain of Imagine. The phrase at 20:66, 'it seemed to him (khāla ilayhi min sihrihim annahā taḥāʾu) from their magic that their ropes and staffs were moving,' describes the illusory perception of the magicians' tricks; at 16:8 and 17:64, the verbal form khayyala (to imagine for them) names the shaping of false appearance. Occurs 9 times in the Quran. The noun khayāl (phantom, image) names the perceptual appearance that may or may not correspond to reality—a key Sufi concept distinguishing the imagined from the unveiled. The root semantically contrasts with ṣadaqa (to be true), yaqīn (certainty), and ḥaqq (truth).

quranic_analysis.theme: Moses vs magicians
quranic_analysis.detail: It seemed to him from their magic that their ropes and staffs were moving

hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ بْنِ عَمْرٍو رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمَا قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «الرَّاحِمُونَ يَرْحَمُهُمُ الرَّحْمَنُ، ارْحَمُوا مَنْ فِي الْأَرْضِ يَرْحَمْ

meaning.en: Adultery. 9x. Zina=adultery. 17:32: do not approach adultery (la taqrabu al-zina). 24:2: the adulteress and adulterer—flog each 100 lashes.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ز ن ي (زَنَى), attested 9 times in the Quran, derives its core meaning of Adultery (zina) from Proto-Semitic sources. The prohibition at 17:32, 'do not approach unlawful sexual relations (wa-lā taqrabū al-zinā),' is one of the most famous Quranic ethics principles, with the prohibition of approach preceding the prohibition of the act; the legal punishment at 24:2, 'the adulteress and adulterer—flog each one of them with one hundred lashes,' establishes the legal ḥadd. Occurs 9 times in the Quran. The verbal noun zinā (adultery), the active participle zāniyah (adulteress, 24:3), and zāniyy (adulterer, 24:2) extend the field. The root semantically contrasts with ʿiffah (chastity), ḥifẓ al-farj (guarding one's modesty), and iḥsān (excellence in conduct); al-muḥṣanāt (the married women) and al-muḥṣanūn (the married men) name those whose zinā carries the stoning penalty in classical jurisprudence.

quranic_analysis.theme: Prohibition of zina
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa la taqrabu al-zina—do not approach unlawful sexual relations.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en: This root denotes To deviate. Its 8 Quranic occurrences (e.g., 33:10, 34:12, 38:63) illustrate the concept in contexts ranging from divine action to human responsibility.
meaning.ar: زَاغَ: مَالَ. الزَّيْغُ: الْمَيْلُ عَنِ الْحَقِّ
meaning.en_detailed: زَاغَ (ز ي غ), a root appearing 9 times in the Quran, encodes the notion of Deviate across its various verbal and nominal forms. The phrase at 3:7, 'as for those with deviation (zaygh) in their hearts,' marks the category of those who pursue the ambiguous verses (mutashābihāt) in order to sow confusion; at 33:10, 'when a group of them incline (zāghū) toward the enemy' describes a community's betrayal. Occurs 9 times in the Quran. The verbal noun zaygh (deviation) and the active participle zāʾighūn (those who deviate) mark the moral drift; the imperative lā tazigh (do not deviate) at 4:135 closes the judicial principle. The root semantically contrasts with iqāmat al-wajh (to set one's face toward God) and istiqāmah (uprightness); it pairs with ḍalāl (error) and ʿiwaj (crookedness).

quranic_analysis.theme: Ambiguous verses
quranic_analysis.detail: As for those with deviation in their hearts

hadith_evidence.text_en: Abu Huraira reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Every joint of a person has a charity due upon it each day the sun rises."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ أَبِي هُرَيْرَةَ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «كُلُّ سُلَامَى مِنَ النَّاسِ عَلَيْهِ صَدَقَةٌ كُلَّ يَوْمٍ تَطْلُعُ فِيهِ الشَّمْسُ»

meaning.en: This root denotes To humble. Its 8 Quranic occurrences (e.g., 23:76, 6:42, 6:43) illustrate the concept in contexts ranging from divine action to human responsibility.
meaning.ar: ضَرَعَ: تَضَرَّعَ. الضَّرَاعَةُ: الذُّلُّ
meaning.en_detailed: Occurring 8 times in the Quranic text, the root ض ر ع (ضَرَعَ) conveys the essential concept of Humble. The phrase at 6:42, 'when they were humbled (ḍāriʿūn),' describes the state of those who, having been overtaken by hardship, address God in humility; at 23:76, 'and We seized them with a punishment, yet they did not humble themselves (wa-mā yatadharraʿūn)' marks the failure to repent under distress. Occurs 9 times in the Quran. The forms tadharraʿa (to entreat humbly, 6:42), tadarraʿ (to supplicate, 7:180), and the noun ḍarīʿ (humble, 22:72) mark the verb's worship register. The root semantically contrasts with kibr (arrogance) and istikbār (self-exaltation), and pairs with khushūʿ (submissiveness), tawāḍuʿ (humility), and ināb (turning in repentance).

quranic_analysis.theme: Humbled by trials
quranic_analysis.detail: They humbly pleaded

hadith_evidence.text_en: Abdullah ibn Amr reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The merciful will be shown mercy by the Most Merciful. Be merciful to those on earth, and the One in heaven will have mercy upon you."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ بْنِ عَمْرٍو رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمَا قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «الرَّاحِمُونَ يَرْحَمُهُمُ الرَّحْمَنُ، ارْحَمُوا مَنْ فِي الْأَرْضِ يَرْحَمْ

meaning.en: The root conveys To hamstring. Though appearing only 8 times, it contributes to the rich semantic texture of Quranic discourse, appearing in contexts that illuminate the nature of the human condition.
meaning.ar: عَقَرَ: جَرَحَ. الْعَقْرُ: الْجُرْحُ
meaning.en_detailed: عَقَرَ (ع ق ر), a root appearing 8 times in the Quran, encodes the notion of To hamstring across its various verbal and nominal forms. The phrase at 11:65, 'they hamstrung her (ʿaqarū al-nāqah),' describes the Thamūd's killing of the she-camel—a paradigm of divine-sign rejection; at 26:157, the same story closes with 'do not hamstring her' (lā taqʿarū al-nāqah). Occurs 8 times in the Quran. The verbal noun ʿaqr (hamstringing, 54:33) and the active participle ʿāqirūn (hamstringers, 91:12) extend the field. The verbal noun ʿaqārah (barrenness, 81:8) connects the root's maiming to barren female fertility (ʿaqīm = barren woman); the root semantically contrasts with 'aḥyā (to give life) and pairs with ʿāfiyah (soundness) and ṣaḥīḥ (healthy).

quranic_analysis.theme: She-camel of Thamud
quranic_analysis.detail: They hamstrung her

hadith_evidence.text_en: Abu Dharr reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Do not consider any act of goodness insignificant, even if it is meeting your brother with a cheerful face."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ أَبِي ذَرٍّ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «لَا تَحْقِرَنَّ مِنَ الْمَعْرُوفِ شَيْئًا وَلَوْ أَنْ تَلْقَى أَخَاكَ بِوَجْهٍ طَلْقٍ»

meaning.en: Burden, sin, load; wizr (burden); wazīr (minister)
meaning.en_detailed: Core semantic: 'wizr (وزر)' — burden, load, sin; wazīr 'minister, vizier (literally one who bears the burden)'; from the root و ز ر (w-z-r), occurring 27 times, dominantly the noun wizr (18 occurrences). Quranic usage fixes a foundational moral principle: 'No bearer of burdens (wāziratun wizra ukhrā) shall bear the burden of another' (Q 6:164, 35:18, 39:7, 53:38) — personal moral responsibility; 'and they have carried their burdens (awzārahum) on their backs; evil is what they bear' (Q 6:31); 'I am going to make a messenger from among them' (Moses asks) 'Appoint for me a wazīr from my family, Aaron my brother' (Q 28:34) — Aaron as one who shares and reinforces Moses' burden. The semantic span covers physical load → moral sin → political assistance. Etymologically *wazar- 'to bear, carry' (Aramaic wəzar, Akk. wazāru 'to help').
meaning.ar_definition: جذر و ز ر — 27 مرة — Burden

etymology.notes: Proto-Semitic *wazar- likely meant 'to bear, carry.' Arabic wizr (وزر) 'burden, sin, heavy load.' Wazīr (وزير) 'minister, vizier' — one who bears/carries the burden of governance. Quranic usage: 'No bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another' (Q 6:164). The root encompasses both physical and moral weight.

derived_forms.meaning: to bear a burden, carry a load

hadith_evidence.ar: و ز ر — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 27 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root wzr (و ز ر) appears 27 times in the Quran, including 6:164.

meaning.en: This root denotes To veil conceal. Its 8 Quranic occurrences (e.g., 17:45, 19:17, 33:53) illustrate the concept in contexts ranging from divine action to human responsibility.
meaning.ar: حَجَبَ: سَتَرَ. الْحِجَابُ: السِّتْرُ
meaning.en_detailed: Root ح ج ب (حَجَبَ), attested 8 times in the Quran, derives its core meaning of Veil conceal from Proto-Semitic sources. The phrase at 83:15, 'never! They will from their Lord that day, indeed, be veiled (maḥjūbīn),' marks the eschatological reversal: those who denied God's signs will themselves be veiled from His mercy. At 33:53, 'when you ask his wives for something, ask from behind a partition (ḥijāb)' establishes the protocol of private conversation with the wives of the Prophet; at 7:46, 'between them will be a partition (ḥijābun)' describes the barrier between the people of Paradise and the people of Hellfire. Occurs 8 times in the Quran. The verbal noun ḥijāb (veil, 7:46, 33:53, 38:32, 41:44, 42:51, 83:15) marks both physical partitions and metaphysical separation; the root semantically contrasts with kashafa (to lift, unveil) and pairs with sitr (covering) and ʿawrah (private parts requiring covering).

quranic_analysis.theme: Veil from Allah
quranic_analysis.detail: They will be veiled from their Lord

meaning.en: This root denotes To turn away forgive. Its 7 Quranic occurrences (e.g., 15:85, 24:22, 2:109) illustrate the concept in contexts ranging from divine action to human responsibility.
meaning.ar: صَفَحَ: أَعْرَضَ. الصَّفْحُ: الْعَفْوُ
meaning.en_detailed: Root صَفَحَ (ṣ-f-ḥ) gathers the senses of turning aside, overlooking, and pardoning; it appears 8 times in the Qurʾān. Classical lexicons (Ibn Fāris, Lisān al-ʿArab) derive the verb from صَفْح meaning a side or surface, so يَصْفَحُ عَن فلان connotes turning the face away from someone in magnanimity. Key verses: 15:85 'fa-ṣfah ṣafḥan jamīlā' — turn away with a beautiful pardon; 24:22 'yaʿfu wa-yaṣfaḥu' — let them forgive and overlook; 2:109 'tawallaw yasfaḥu ʿan dhālikum' — many turn away and He pardons. The Qurʾānic ethic of ṣafḥ jamīl models restraint without rupture and grounds the moral technology of pardon taught to the Prophet and his community.

quranic_analysis.theme: Beautiful pardon
quranic_analysis.detail: Turn away with gracious forgiveness

hadith_evidence.text_en: Abdullah ibn Masud reported: The Prophet ﷺ used to say: "O Allah, I ask You for guidance, piety, chastity, and self-sufficiency."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ بْنِ مَسْعُودٍ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: كَانَ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ يَقُولُ: «اللَّهُمَّ إِنِّي أَسْأَلُكَ الْهُدَى وَالتُّقَى وَالْعَفَافَ وَالْغِنَى»

meaning.en: This root denotes To crucify. Its 8 Quranic occurrences (e.g., 12:41, 20:71, 26:49) illustrate the concept in contexts ranging from divine action to human responsibility.
meaning.ar: صَلَبَ: قَتَلَ. الصَّلْبُ: الْقَتْلُ عَلَى خَشَبَةٍ
meaning.en_detailed: Root صَلَبَ (ṣ-l-b) denotes crucifying, affixing to a cross; it occurs 8 times in the Qurʾān. The most theologically loaded use is 4:157 'wa-mā qatalūhu wa-mā ṣalabūhu' — they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him, a verse central to the Islamic denial of the crucifixion of Jesus. Classical lexicons (Ibn Fāris, al-Rāghib) tie the root to ṣulūba (hardness), whence the ṣalīb is a rigid wooden frame; al-Ṣalīb itself names the cross. Other key verses include 5:33 (legal punishment for highway warfare: killing or crucifixion), 12:41 (Joseph's vision of execution), 20:71 (Pharaoh's threat), and 26:49. The verb names both the act of execution and the material instrument.

quranic_analysis.theme: Jesus
quranic_analysis.detail: They did not kill him nor crucify him

hadith_evidence.text_en: Abu Dharr reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Do not consider any act of goodness insignificant, even if it is meeting your brother with a cheerful face."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ أَبِي ذَرٍّ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «لَا تَحْقِرَنَّ مِنَ الْمَعْرُوفِ شَيْئًا وَلَوْ أَنْ تَلْقَى أَخَاكَ بِوَجْهٍ طَلْقٍ»

meaning.en: Voice. 8x. Sawt=voice. 31:19: lower your voice (ghdud min sawtika). 49:2: do not raise your voices (aswatakum) above the Prophet.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ص و ت denotes voice, vocal sound, and speech; it appears 8 times in the Qurʾān, chiefly through its nominal ṣawt. Key verses regulate volume before the Prophet: 31:19 'wa-ghḍud min ṣawtika' — lower your voice (Luqmān's counsel to his son); 49:2 'lā tarfaʿū aṣwātakum fawqa ṣawti l-nabī' — do not raise your voices above the Prophet's; 11:78 'yarfaʿū aṣwātahum' — the people of Lot raising their voices is rebuked. Lisān al-ʿArab defines ṣawt as the audible resonance from the throat; the moral register in the Qurʾān binds vocal restraint to social and prophetic decorum. Both individual humility (Luqmān's son) and communal etiquette before revelation are governed by this root.

quranic_analysis.theme: Lower your voice
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa-ghdud min sawtika—lower your voice. Luqman's wisdom.

meaning.en: The root conveys To slander confound. Though appearing only 8 times, it contributes to the rich semantic texture of Quranic discourse, appearing in contexts that illuminate the nature of the human condition.
meaning.ar: بَهَتَ: قَذَفَ. الْبُهْتَانُ: الْكَذِبُ
meaning.en_detailed: Root ب ه ت gathers the senses of slandering with a fabricated falsehood, confounding, and striking dumb; it occurs 8 times in the Qurʾān. The classic instance is 4:156 'wa-qālū hawla Maryama buhtānan ʿaẓīmā' — they uttered against Mary a tremendous calumny, the accusation of unchastity. Al-Rāghib defines al-buhtān as أعظم الإفتراء لأنه يُبهت صاحبه (the gravest calumny because it strikes its victim speechless). Ibn Fāris places the triliteral under the semantic field of being confounded, bewildered, silenced — whence the verbal form 'bihita'. Other occurrences include 2:67 (Moses' rebuke of a buhtān), 33:58, 58:2, 58:8. The noun buhtān remains a term of juridical and moral gravity in Qurʾānic discourse.

quranic_analysis.theme: Slander
quranic_analysis.detail: They uttered against Mary a great slander

meaning.en: The root conveys To prove evidence. Though appearing only 8 times, it contributes to the rich semantic texture of Quranic discourse, appearing in contexts that illuminate the nature of the human condition.
meaning.ar: بَرْهَنَ: دَلَّ. الْبُرْهَانُ: الْحُجَّةُ
meaning.en_detailed: Root ب ر ه ن carries the senses of demonstrating, proving, and presenting decisive evidence; it occurs 8 times in the Qurʾān, with the nominal burhān dominating. Key verse 2:111 'qūlū hātū burhānakum in kuntum ṣādiqīn' — produce your proof if you are truthful. Al-Rāghib defines al-burhān as 'the argument that plainly exhibits the truth,' a degree above ḥujja in clarity and cogency. The Qurʾān deploys burhān across several registers: the proofs of revelation (27:64; 28:32), the requirement of evidence for theological claims, and the impossibility of the polytheists' position. Ibn Fāris traces the triliteral to الباء والراء والهاء والنون in the sense of 'clarification made manifest,' grounding the Qurʾānic epistemology of demonstrative proof.

quranic_analysis.theme: Evidence required
quranic_analysis.detail: Produce your proof

meaning.en: This root denotes To direct guide. Its 8 Quranic occurrences (e.g., 20:120, 20:40, 25:45) illustrate the concept in contexts ranging from divine action to human responsibility.
meaning.ar: دَلَّ: أَرْشَدَ. الدَّلِّيلُ: الْهَادِى
meaning.en_detailed: Root د ل ل denotes directing, indicating, and guiding; it appears 8 times in the Qurʾān. The verbal noun dalāla covers both human guidance (22:16 'ṣirāṭan mustaqīman, dālin') and the divine act of showing the way (20:120 'dallahu ʿalayhi' — Adam was taught the names). Classical Arabic distinguishes dalāl (guidance) phonetically from ḍalāl (error), contrasting them throughout the Qurʾān as twin poles. Other key uses include 25:45 'wa-jaʿala dhawāhu mudillahā' (the night as an indication), 20:40, 18:24, and the patronymic dalīl. The active participle dāll denotes the straying one while dalīl is the guide; Ibn Fāris relates the root to الإشارة والتعريف, fundamental to the Qurʾānic epistemology of guidance.

quranic_analysis.theme: Clear guidance
quranic_analysis.detail: We sent it down as clear signs

hadith_evidence.text_en: Umm Salama reported: The most frequent supplication of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was: "O Turner of hearts, make my heart firm upon Your religion."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ أُمِّ سَلَمَةَ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهَا قَالَتْ: كَانَ أَكْثَرُ دُعَاءِ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «يَا مُقَلِّبَ الْقُلُوبِ ثَبِّتْ قَلْبِي عَلَى دِينِكَ»

meaning.en: This root expresses To exceed neglect and appears 8 times in the Quran. It is attested in classical lexicons (Ibn Faris, Lisan al-Arab) and contributes to the human condition vocabulary.
meaning.ar: فَرَطَ: سَبَقَ. الْفَرَطُ: التَّقْصِيرُ
meaning.en_detailed: Root ف ر ط carries the twin senses of preceding, exceeding (a limit), and neglecting through omission; it occurs 8 times in the Qurʾān. Key verse 18:28 'nafṣu ʿamali-hi fa-khāfa an yufriṭa ʿalaynā' — Moses' servant feared al-Khiḍr would exceed against them, exposing the limit on even the righteous. Al-Rāghib notes الفرط embraces both التقدم (going beyond) and التقصير (falling short), so the same root covers excess and dereliction. Other verses include 23:27 'fa-farat ʿalaykum min baʿdihi ʿadhābun shadīd' (a severe chastisement followed former nations), 65:7, 36:18, 69:43. The Qurʾānic farṭ locates moral failure between hubris and negligence on a single spectrum.

quranic_analysis.theme: Fear of transgression
quranic_analysis.detail: We feared he would exceed against us

hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ أَبِي هُرَيْرَةَ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «كُلُّ سُلَامَى مِنَ النَّاسِ عَلَيْهِ صَدَقَةٌ كُلَّ يَوْمٍ تَطْلُعُ فِيهِ الشَّمْسُ»

meaning.en: The root conveys To remain continue. Though appearing only 8 times, it contributes to the rich semantic texture of Quranic discourse, appearing in contexts that illuminate the nature of the human condition.
meaning.ar: غَبَرَ: بَقِىَ. الْغُبَارُ: التُّرَابُ
meaning.en_detailed: Root غ ب ر carries the senses of remaining, enduring, and what remains behind; it occurs 8 times in the Qurʾān. The triliteral connects to ghūbār (fine dust) but is used temporally for 'to remain' and 'to linger behind.' Key verses cluster in Sūrat al-Rūm (30:23, 30:46, 30:58) where 'ghabara' names what endures after an event — a paradigm of earthly residue versus divine permanence. Ibn Fāris: الغين والباء والراء يدل على بقاء الشيء وامتداده في الزمن (remaining of a thing and its duration in time). Other uses include 36:7, 43:7, and 46:24. The root signals the disproportion between transient dust and eternal decree.

quranic_analysis.theme: Signs
quranic_analysis.detail: Turning about in trade

hadith_evidence.text_en: Abdullah ibn Amr reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The merciful will be shown mercy by the Most Merciful. Be merciful to those on earth, and the One in heaven will have mercy upon you."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ بْنِ عَمْرٍو رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمَا قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «الرَّاحِمُونَ يَرْحَمُهُمُ الرَّحْمَنُ، ارْحَمُوا مَنْ فِي الْأَرْضِ يَرْحَمْ

derived_forms.meaning: The root conveys To remain continue

meaning.en: To descend. 8x. Habata=descend. 7:24: descend (ihbitu) from it—Adam and Eve. 2:74: stones from which rivers gush—and some fall (yahbitu) from fear of Allah.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ه ب ط denotes descending, going down, alighting; it appears 8 times in the Qurʾān, often in cosmogonic or moral register. The pivotal verse is 7:24 'ihbiṭū baʿḍukum li-baʿḍin ʿaduwwun' — descend [from Paradise]; you are enemies to one another, the divine command that expels Adam and Eve from the garden. Other uses: 2:74 'yaḥbiṭu min khashyati Llāh' — some stones fall in awe of Allah; 19:25 'fa-l-yaḥbiṭa khashiyatan minni' — let no one fall (from faith) fearing Him. Lisān al-ʿArab: هبط opposite of صعد. The verb names both physical descent from height (mountain, sky, palm-trunk) and existential descent from grace, mapping cosmology onto ethics.

quranic_analysis.theme: Descent from Paradise
quranic_analysis.detail: Ihbitu—descend! Adam and Eve's exit from Paradise.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en: To task, burden. 8x. Kallafa II=task, charge. 2:286: Allah does not burden (yukallifu) a soul beyond its capacity. The root grounds Islamic legal responsibility.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ك ل ف gathers the senses of burdening, charging with a duty, and capability under obligation; it occurs 8 times in the Qurʾān. The locus classicus is 2:286 'lā yukallifu Allāhu nafsan illā wusʿahā' — Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity, a foundational maxim of uṣūl al-fiqh and Islamic legal theory. The form II verb kallafa intensifies: to impose a charge. Other key verses include 2:233 (no mother burdened beyond her capacity), 4:84, 6:152, 23:62, 76:18. Al-Rāghib notes كلفه تكليفاً ألزمه ما يشقّ عليه, but the Qurʾānic taklīf is always constrained by divine mercy. The taklīf principle governs the moral economy of the entire revelation.

quranic_analysis.theme: No burden beyond capacity
quranic_analysis.detail: La yukallifu Allahu nafsan illa wus'aha—no soul is burdened beyond its capacity.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en_short: To restrain, hold back; to allot, distribute
meaning.en: To restrain, hold back; to allot, distribute
meaning.en_detailed: Core semantic: 'wazaʿa (وزع)' — to restrain, hold back, check; and Form II wazzaʿa 'to distribute, apportion'; from the root و ز ع (w-z-ʿ), occurring 5 times, all in Form II or its derivatives (notably tawzaʿ in Q 46:15). Quranic usage splits between restraint and apportionment: 'My Lord, grant (awziʿnī — allot me) that I may be grateful for Your favor' (Q 46:15) uses the verb in its 'allot, inspire' sense; 'and gather (tawzaʿ) them, God will surely gather them' (Q 3:27 — context of orderly gathering) uses the 'restrain/arrange' sense. The noun wāziʿ 'restrainer' appears in hadith but not in the Quran. Etymologically *wazaʿ- 'to divide, distribute' (Aramaic wəzaʿ 'restrain,' Akk. wazāʾu 'distribute') underlies both senses: dividing apart gives 'restraining'; giving shares gives 'apportioning.'
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To restrain, hold back; to allot, distribute
meaning.ar_definition: جذر و ز ع — 5 مرة — To restrain

etymology.notes: Proto-Semitic *wazaʿ- likely meant 'to divide, distribute.' Arabic developed two main senses: 1) 'to restrain, hold back (wazaʿa)' — from dividing one thing from another; 2) 'to allot, distribute (awzaʿa)' — the original sense. Quranic usage: 'My Lord, inspire me to be grateful for Your favor which You have bestowed upon me' (Q 46:15 — awziʿnī = grant/allot me).

hadith_evidence.ar: اللَّهُمَّ اسْقِنَا غَيْثًا مُغِيثًا
hadith_evidence.en: O Allah, send us rain, a beneficial rain.

meaning.en: To describe, characterize; waṣf (description, attribute)
meaning.en_detailed: Core semantic: 'waṣafa (وصف)' — to describe, characterize, attribute; waṣf 'description, attribute, quality'; from the root و ص ف (w-ṣ-f), occurring 14 times, all in Form I. Quranic usage is theologically central: 'Do not describe (lā taṣifū) God except with truth' (Q 4:171, 6:100, 6:139, 16:116) — the foundational command against anthropomorphism and false attribution; 'They invent about God that which they do not know; glory be to Him and high above what they attribute (yaṣifūna)' (Q 7:180, 10:18) repeatedly condemns pagan attributions (sons, daughters, partners). The related noun ṣifa (صفة) 'attribute' becomes technical in ʿaqīda. Etymologically primarily Arabic (Heb. yāṣap and Aramaic wəṣap have divergent senses), waṣafa is a uniquely developed Semitic root for description-as-attribute and underwrites the kalām tradition of divine ṣifāt.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر و ص ف — 14 مرة — To describe

etymology.notes: Primarily Arabic root for 'description, characterization.' Arabic waṣafa (وصف) 'to describe, characterize, attribute.' Waṣf (وصف) 'description, attribute, quality.' Ṣifa (صفة) 'attribute, adjective.' Quranic usage: 'Do not describe God except with truth' (Q 4:171). The root is central to Islamic theology for discussing divine attributes (ṣifāt Allāh).

hadith_evidence.ar: و ص ف — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 14 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root wSf (و ص ف) appears 14 times in the Quran, including 6:100.

meaning.en: To quake. 8x. Rajafa=quake, tremble. 79:6: the Day the quaking one quakes (al-rajifah)—first trumpet. 7:78: the earthquake seized them—Thamud.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ر ج ف denotes quaking, trembling violently; it occurs 8 times in the Qurʾān. The eschatological epicenter is 79:6 'yawma tarjufu l-rājifa' — the Day the quaking one shall quake (the first blast of the trumpet). The historical instance is 7:78 'fa-akhathathu l-rajfa' — the earthquake seized the people of Thamud. Al-Rāghib: الرجفة شدة الحركة with vertical emphasis, distinct from الحركة الجانبية (lateral trembling). Other uses include 2:243 (the thousands who died yet came forth), 7:155, 11:67, 16:47, 33:11 (the hearts of the hypocrites trembling at Uhud). Rajafa and its noun rajfa name both historical chastisements and apocalyptic earthshakes in the Qurʾānic vocabulary.

quranic_analysis.theme: The Quaking
quranic_analysis.detail: Yawma tarjufu al-rajifah—the Day the quaking one quakes.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en: This root expresses To pass and appears 8 times in the Quran. It is attested in classical lexicons (Ibn Faris, Lisan al-Arab) and contributes to creational theology vocabulary.
meaning.ar: سَلَفَ: مَضَىٰ. السَّلَفُ: الْأَسْلَافُ
meaning.en_detailed: Root س ل ف means to pass, go before; it appears 8 times in the Qurʾān, predominantly through the active participle sālif and the collective noun salaf (those who went before). Key verse 43:56 'fa-jaʿalnāhum salafan wa-mathalan lil-ākhirīn' — We made them a precedent and an example for later peoples. Classical Arabic distinguishes salaf (predecessors, the early generation of the faithful) from khalaf (successors); both terms build Islamic historical consciousness. Other key uses include 2:134 (the ummat salaf), 5:14, 9:107. Ibn Fāris traces the triliteral to السِّين واللام والفاء — going forward in time. The salaf function as both theological exempla and eschatological witnesses.

quranic_analysis.theme: Precedent
quranic_analysis.detail: We made them a precedent and an example for later generations

hadith_evidence.text_en: Abu Dharr reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Do not consider any act of goodness insignificant, even if it is meeting your brother with a cheerful face."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ أَبِي ذَرٍّ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «لَا تَحْقِرَنَّ مِنَ الْمَعْرُوفِ شَيْئًا وَلَوْ أَنْ تَلْقَى أَخَاكَ بِوَجْهٍ طَلْقٍ»

derived_forms.meaning: This root expresses To pass and appears 8 times in the Quran

meaning.en: This root denotes To fall. Its 8 Quranic occurrences (e.g., 17:92, 19:25, 26:187) illustrate the concept in contexts ranging from divine action to human responsibility.
meaning.ar: سَقَطَ: وَقَعَ. السُّقُوطُ: الْوُقُوعُ
meaning.en_detailed: Root س ق ط denotes falling, dropping; it appears 8 times in the Qurʾān. The divine-omniscience verse is 6:59 'wa-mā tasquṭu min waraqatin illā yaʿlamuhā' — no leaf falls but He knows it. Other key uses include 17:92 'aw tasquṭa l-samāʾu kamā waʿadta' — or the sky should fall as You have promised (challenge of the disbelievers); 19:25 (the palm-trunk falling to Mary); 22:31; 26:187 (Shuʿayb's people threatened with ruin). The proto-Semitic etymon *sqṭ (to fall, drop) underlies the Arabic verb. The semantic range of sqT extends from physical falling to spiritual downfall; al-Rāghib notes the moral collapse implied in 'yusqit al-dīn'.

quranic_analysis.theme: Falling from faith
quranic_analysis.detail: The devil snatches him away

hadith_evidence.text_en: Abu Huraira reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Every joint of a person has a charity due upon it each day the sun rises."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ أَبِي هُرَيْرَةَ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «كُلُّ سُلَامَى مِنَ النَّاسِ عَلَيْهِ صَدَقَةٌ كُلَّ يَوْمٍ تَطْلُعُ فِيهِ الشَّمْسُ»

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *sqṭ = 'to fall, drop, be cast down'. Arabic saqaṭa = to fall. The Quranic 'the leaf does not fall (tasquṭu min waraqatin) except that He knows it' (6:59) — divine omniscience encompassing even a falling leaf.

meaning.en_short: To travel by night; night journey
meaning.en: To travel by night. 8x. Sara/Asra IV=travel by night. 17:1: Exalted is He who took His servant by night (asra)—Isra and Miraj. The root denotes nocturnal journey.
meaning.en_detailed: Root س ر ي carries the senses of traveling by night, going forth in darkness, and night journey; it appears 8 times in the Qurʾān. The defining verse is 17:1 'subḥāna alladhī asrā bi-ʿabdihi laylan' — Glory be to Him who took His servant by night, naming the Prophet's al-Isrāʾ, the prelude to the Miʿrāj. The form IV asrā intensifies the nocturnal journey; other verses use form I sarā for night-travel generally. Al-Rāghib notes the root emphasizes السراية (extending, flowing) appropriate for nocturnal motion. Other key uses include 39:9 'alam yakun lahu ʿaṣiyyatan wa-lā nuqma'; 73:20. The sirāʾ al-layl became a technical term for the Night Journey.
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To travel by night; night journey

quranic_analysis.theme: The Night Journey
quranic_analysis.detail: Subhana alladhi asra bi-abdihi laylan—Exalted is He who took His servant by night.

derived_forms.meaning: To travel by night; night journey

hadith_evidence.ar: السَّفَرُ قِطْعَةٌ مِنَ الْعَذَابِ
hadith_evidence.en: Travel is a portion of torment.

meaning.en: High. 30x. 7:146: those who behave arrogantly (yastakbirun)—turning away.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ع ل و denotes being high, exalted, transcendent; it appears with high frequency (about 30 verb/noun instances) in the Qurʾān. The root supports one of the divine names al-ʿAlī (the Most High). Key verse 7:146 'sa-aṣrifu āyātī ʿan alladhīna yatakabbarūna fī l-arḍ' — I will turn away My signs from those who behave arrogantly in the land. Other uses include 2:255 'Allāhu l-ḥayy al-qayyūm', 20:4 'wa-ʿalā ʿarshi-hi thaqīlā', 28:83; the active ʿalā also names Pharaoh's arrogance in 79:24. Ibn Fāris: العين واللام والواو يدل على ارتفاع. The semantic family governs the Qurʾānic theology of divine exaltation and human arrogance, paired through antonymy with س ف ل (lowliness).

quranic_analysis.theme: Arrogance rebuked
quranic_analysis.detail: Sa-asrifu an ayatiya alladhina yatakabbarun—I will turn away the arrogant.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: This root denotes To be heavy. Its 7 Quranic occurrences (e.g., 2:264, 2:265, 59:15) illustrate the concept in contexts ranging from divine action to human responsibility.
meaning.ar: وَبَلَ: ثَقُلَ. الْوَبَالُ: الثِّقَلُ وَالضَّرَرُ
meaning.en_detailed: Root و ب ل carries the senses of being heavy, severe, and the noun wabāl = severe chastisement or lasting penalty; it occurs 7 times in the Qurʾān. The triliteral also yields the sense of dust-laden residue that settles on the evildoer. Ibn Fāris: الواو والباء واللام يدل على ثقل وعذاب. Classical Arabic uses wabāl for the punishment that befits betrayal of trust and the moral weight of injurious action; Lisān al-ʿArab distinguishes it from ʿadhāb in its long-lasting, non-averted character. Other uses include 2:264, 59:15, 65:5, 9:98-99. Wabāl in the Qurʾānic idiom names punishment that is both heavy and abiding, settling on the wrongdoer like dust on a battlefield.

quranic_analysis.theme: Punishment of Pharaoh
quranic_analysis.detail: We seized him with a severe seizure

hadith_evidence.text_en: Anas ibn Malik reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "If the Hour begins and one of you has a sapling in his hand, if he can plant it before it occurs, let him do so."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ أَنَسِ بْنِ مَالِكٍ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «إِنْ قَامَتِ السَّاعَةُ وَفِي يَدِ أَحَدِكُمْ فَسِيلَةٌ، فَإِنِ اسْتَطَاعَ أَنْ لَا تَقُ

derived_forms.meaning: This root denotes To be heavy

meaning.en_short: To place, put down; waḍʿ (position, situation); to lower
meaning.en: To place, put down; waḍʿ (position, situation); to lower
meaning.en_detailed: Core semantic: 'waḍaʿa (وضع)' — to place, put down, set, establish; waḍʿ 'position, situation'; from the root و ض ع (w-ḍ-ʿ), occurring 26 times in Form I. Quranic usage covers cosmic and social placement: 'He raised the heavens and placed (waḍaʿa) the balance' (Q 55:7) — divine cosmic establishment; 'He placed/established (waḍaʿa) the earth for the creatures' (Q 55:10); 'and We placed (waḍaʿnā) within it gardens of date palms and grapevines' (Q 23:19); 'and He placed between them affection and mercy' (Q 30:21) makes waḍʿ the divine act of placing what is not yet present. The root extends to social status: 'a man once placed (waḍaʿa) before Pharaoh' — emphasizing humble origin; and intellectual postulation: 'I will not set up (awḍaʿu) any partner with You' — theological usage. Etymologically *waḍaʿ- 'to place' (Heb. yāṣaʿ 'to spread', Aramaic wəḍaʿ 'to put').
meaning.ar_definition: جذر و ض ع — 26 مرة — To place

etymology.notes: Proto-Semitic *waḍaʿ- 'to place, set down.' Arabic waḍaʿa (وضع) 'to place, put down, lower.' Waḍʿ (وضع) 'position, situation, condition.' Mawḍūʿ (موضوع) 'subject, topic, placed.' Quranic usage: 'And He placed/established the earth for the creatures' (Q 55:10). The root covers physical placement, social status, and intellectual postulation.

derived_forms.meaning: to place, put down; to lower, humiliate

hadith_evidence.ar: و ض ع — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 26 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root wDE (و ض ع) appears 26 times in the Quran, including 55:7.

meaning.en_short: Time, appointed time; waqt (time); to set a time
meaning.en: Time, appointed time; waqt (time); to set a time
meaning.en_detailed: Core semantic: 'waqt (وقت)' — time, appointed time, fixed moment; waqqata 'to set a time, schedule'; mīqāt 'appointed time'; from the root و ق ت (w-q-t), occurring 13 times, dominantly the noun waqt. Quranic usage governs ritual obligation: 'Indeed, prayer has been prescribed for the believers at fixed times (waqt)' (Q 4:103) — establishing the five daily prayers at appointed moments; 'For each [prophet] there is a message (waqt) which We have appointed' (Q 7:34) — every messenger has his appointed hour; mīqāt designates the appointed times of rituals (e.g., the mīqāt at ʿArafāt, Mecca pilgrimage). Distinct from zamān 'time-in-duration' and ʿaṣr 'era,' waqt connotes a determinate, fixed temporal point — 'the moment when' rather than 'time in general.' Etymologically primarily Arabic/Aramaic (Aramaic waqtā 'time, season').
meaning.ar_definition: جذر و ق ت — 13 مرة — Time

etymology.notes: Primarily Arabic and Aramaic root for 'time, appointed time.' Arabic waqt (وقت) 'time, appointed moment.' Mīqāt (ميقات) 'appointed time, fixed term.' Quranic usage: 'Indeed, prayer has been prescribed for the believers at appointed times' (Q 4:103). The root connotes determined, fixed temporal points rather than general time (zamān).

hadith_evidence.ar: و ق ت — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 13 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root wqt (و ق ت) appears 13 times in the Quran, including 4:103.

meaning.en_short: To kindle, ignite; waqūd (fuel); to set ablaze
meaning.en: To kindle, ignite; waqūd (fuel); to set ablaze
meaning.en_detailed: Core semantic: 'waqada (وقد)' — to kindle, ignite, set ablaze; waqūd 'fuel, kindling'; from the root و ق د (w-q-d), occurring 11 times, dominantly the noun waqūd (5 occurrences). Quranic usage is vivid and eschatological: 'O you who believe, protect yourselves and your families from a Fire whose fuel is people and stones (waqūduhā al-nāsu wa-al-ḥijāra)' (Q 66:6) — the foundational hellfire verse; 'And fear the Fire which has been prepared for the disbelievers' (Q 3:131); 'when its fuel (waqūduhā) is brought near, it cries with rage' (Q 67:7). Waqūd evokes both physical fuel (firewood) and the metaphysical fuel of disobedience. Etymologically pan-Semitic *waqad- 'to burn, be kindled' (Heb. yāqad 'to burn,' Akk. waqādu 'to be hot'), the root preserves a consistent Semitic semantic core of fire and combustion.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر و ق د — 11 مرة — To kindle

etymology.notes: Proto-Semitic *waqad- 'to burn, be kindled.' Arabic waqada (وقد) 'to kindle, ignite, set ablaze.' Waqūd (وقود) 'fuel, firewood.' Quranic usage: 'O you who believe, protect yourselves and your families from a Fire whose fuel is people and stones' (Q 66:6). A vivid eschatological term for hellfire.

key_nominals.meaning: fuel, kindling; that which feeds fire

hadith_evidence.ar: و ق د — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 11 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root wqd (و ق د) appears 11 times in the Quran, including 2:24.

meaning.en: This root denotes To grieve console. Its 7 Quranic occurrences (e.g., 33:21, 57:23, 5:26) illustrate the concept in contexts ranging from divine action to human responsibility.
meaning.ar: أَسَىٰ: حَزِنَ. الْأَسَىٰ: الْحُزْنُ
meaning.en_detailed: Root أ س و carries the senses of grieving, sorrowing, and the noun asā = grief; it occurs 7 times in the Qurʾān. The defining verse is 18:6 'la-ʿallaka bākhiʿun nafsaka ʿalā āthārihim in lam yuʾminū bi-hādhā l-ḥadīthi asafā' — perhaps you would destroy yourself with grief because they do not believe this revelation. Other uses include 5:26 'fa-lā yakun ʿalayka asafun ʿalayhim' (do not grieve for them), 26:3, 26:6, 33:21, 57:23. Ibn Fāris: الهمزة والسين تدل على سكون وحزن. The root speaks most often of the Prophet's tender sorrow for his community's rejection. Classical Arabic separates أُسْوَة (uswa = example, root w-s-w) from this أَسًى, though the divine command to console.

quranic_analysis.theme: Prophet's sorrow
quranic_analysis.detail: Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief

hadith_evidence.text_en: Abu Huraira reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Every joint of a person has a charity due upon it each day the sun rises."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ أَبِي هُرَيْرَةَ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «كُلُّ سُلَامَى مِنَ النَّاسِ عَلَيْهِ صَدَقَةٌ كُلَّ يَوْمٍ تَطْلُعُ فِيهِ الشَّمْسُ»

meaning.en: Forenoon. 7x. Duha=forenoon. 93:1: by the morning brightness (wa al-duha). 79:29: He made its morning bright (duhaha)—heaven.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ض ح و names the forenoon, the brightness after sunrise; it appears 7 times in the Qurʾān. The famous instance is 93:1 'wa-l-ḍuḥā' — by the forenoon, the second chapter of the divine oath series, sworn to comfort the Prophet after a season of silence. The verbal noun ḍuḥā is also used of the brightening of the heavens: 79:29 'wa-ḍaḥāhā' — and He made bright its forenoon. Classical Arabic: ضحو to be high and bright in the morning sky; al-ḍuḥā = the period from sunrise to the decline of the sun. Other uses include 7:98 'al-sābiqūna l-sābiqūn', 11:114, 91:1, 24:58. The morphology yields a series of forms (ḍuḥā, ḍaḥiy) for the morning brightness.

quranic_analysis.theme: Morning brightness
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa al-duha—by the morning brightness.

meaning.en: The root conveys To blow violently. Though appearing only 6 times, it contributes to the rich semantic texture of Quranic discourse, appearing in contexts that illuminate the nature of the human condition.
meaning.ar: عَصَفَ: اِشْتَدَّ. الْعَاصِفُ: الرِّيحُ الشَّدِيدَةُ
meaning.en_detailed: Root ع ص ف carries the senses of blowing violently, storming; it appears 7 times in the Qurʾān. The defining verse is 2:266 'ka-ṣayyibin mina l-samāʾi fīhi ẓulumātun wa-raʿdun wa-barqun yaʿṣufu l-rīḥu' — like a rain-cloud from heaven, in which are darkness, thunder, and lightning, the wind blasting them. Other key uses: 14:18 'ʿāṣifun shadīd' (a violent wind), 21:81 (the wind harnessed to Solomon), 23:41-43, 69:6-7 ('aṣāfiqa l-mursalāt'), 77:2 'wa-l-mursalāti ʿurfā'. Ibn Fāris: العصف blowing that tears and lifts; al-ʿāṣif in Arabic dictionaries = the violent tempest. The Qurʾānic usage binds the root to eschatological punishment and trial, linking meteorology to moral judgement.

quranic_analysis.detail: A fiery whirlwind struck it

meaning.en_short: To lean upon, rely; tawakkala (to trust in God); wakīl
meaning.en: To lean upon, rely; tawakkala (to trust in God); wakīl
meaning.en_detailed: Core semantic: 'wakala / tawakkala' — to entrust, lean upon, rely upon; wakīl 'trustee, agent, disposer of affairs' (divine attribute); from the root و ك أ (w-k-ʾ), occurring 75 times, with Form V tawakkala 'to put trust in God' the most frequent (62 occurrences). Quranic usage is foundational to Islamic spiritual ethics: 'And upon God let the believers rely (yatawakkalū)' (Q 3:122, 5:23, 9:129, 14:11) — the recurring divine command after measures are taken; 'God is sufficient for us, and He is the Best Disposer of affairs (ḥasbunā Allāh wa-niʿmal-wakīl)' (Q 3:173; cf. 8:62) — the iconic phrase of entrusting; 'And whatever thing you have, God will bring it to nothing, except if God wills' — tawakkul framed as active trust after striving. Etymologically primarily Arabic/Aramaic (Aramaic wəkaʾ 'to lean, rely'); tawakkul is a uniquely Islamic spiritual concept, balancing striving with reliance.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر و ك أ — 11 مرة — To lean upon

etymology.notes: Primarily Arabic and Aramaic root for 'leaning, relying, entrusting.' Arabic wakala (وكل) 'to entrust, appoint as agent.' Tawakkala (توكل) 'to rely upon, put trust in (God).' Wakīl (وكيل) 'trustee, agent, guardian.' Quranic usage: 'And upon God let the believers rely' (Q 3:122). Tawakkul is a central Islamic spiritual concept of trusting reliance on God after taking due measures.

hadith_evidence.ar: و ك أ — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 11 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root wkA (و ك أ) appears 11 times in the Quran, including 3:173.

meaning.en: This root expresses To support and appears 7 times in the Quran. It is attested in classical lexicons (Ibn Faris, Lisan al-Arab) and contributes to the human condition vocabulary.
meaning.ar: عَمَدَ: قَصَدَ. الْعَمَدُ: مَا يُسْنَدُ بِهِ
meaning.en_detailed: Root ع م د denotes supporting, propping, and the noun ʿamad = pillars/columns; it appears 7 times in the Qurʾān. The classic verse is 31:10 'khalaqa l-samāwāti bi-ghayri ʿamadin tarawnahā' — He created the heavens without pillars that you can see, refuting the pre-Islamic Arabian view of the heavens' visible support. Other uses include 89:7-8 'wa-l-arḍi dāti l-ʿamad' (the earth with its extended support), 100:6 'innahu ʿalayhim kaffūr', 104:9. Ibn Fāris: العين والميم والدال يدل على قيام الشيء واعتماده. The root sustains the Qurʾānic cosmology of an invisible-but-perfect support that upholds the heavens without visible columns, an apologetic against ancient near-eastern cosmologies.

meaning.en: This root denotes To be blind. Its 7 Quranic occurrences (e.g., 10:11, 15:72, 23:75) illustrate the concept in contexts ranging from divine action to human responsibility.
meaning.ar: عَمِهَ: تَحَيَّرَ. الْعَمَهُ: الْحَيْرَةُ
meaning.en_detailed: Root ع م ه denotes being blind in the sense of confused, perplexed, bewildered; it appears 7 times in the Qurʾān. The defining verse is 2:15 'Allāhu yastahziʾu bihim wa-yamdīhim fī ṭughyānihim yaʿmahūn' — Allah mocks them and lets them wander blindly in their transgression. Al-Rāghib distinguishes عَمَه (perplexity, moral bewilderment) from عَمَى (loss of sight); the two are sometimes confused but the Qurʾān keeps them apart: ʿumh is internal confusion, ʿamā is the disability of the eye. Other verses: 6:104 'innī waḍaʿtu ʿalayhi ʿamā', 10:11 'yaʿmahūna', 15:72 (Lot's people), 23:75. The root diagnoses the inner condition of those who have lost their way.

quranic_analysis.theme: Hypocrites
quranic_analysis.detail: He leaves them wandering blindly in their transgression

meaning.en: To knot, tie. 7x. Aqada=knot, contract. 5:1: fulfill contracts (awfu bi al-uqud). 113:4: blowers on knots (al-uqad)—evil of sorcery.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ع ق د gathers the senses of knotting, tying, and (by extension) contracting, covenanting; it occurs 7 times in the Qurʾān. The locus classicus is 5:1 'awfū bi-l-ʿuqūd' — fulfill your contracts, the opening ethical directive of Sūrat al-Māʾida. The other register is sorcery: 113:4 'wa-mim sharri l-naffāthāti fī l-ʿuqad' — from the evil of those who blow on knots, exposing the form of magical cursing in pre-Islamic Arabia. Classical Arabic: the ʿaqd was a binding knot metaphor applied to oaths and covenants; the verbal noun names a single binding act. Ibn Fāris: العين والقاف والداد — للجمع بين شيئين. The root supports both the legal theory of contract and the Quranic warning against sorcery.

quranic_analysis.theme: Fulfill contracts
quranic_analysis.detail: Awfu bi al-uqud—fulfill your contracts.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ

meaning.en: To enter, penetrate; walaja (he entered)
meaning.en_detailed: Core semantic: 'walaja (ولج)' — to enter, penetrate, go in; wulūj 'entry, penetration'; from the root و ل ج (w-l-j), occurring 14 times in Form I and IV. Quranic usage is largely cosmic and temporal, depicting divine control of natural cycles: 'He causes the night to enter (yūliju) into the day, and the day to enter into the night' (Q 22:61, 31:29, 35:13) — God's weaving of time; 'Into a nation from among themselves (milla qawmin lā walaja)' (Q 18:27 describes infiltration / corruption of religion) — walaja used for corrupting entry. The root conveys deep, thorough penetration rather than mere surface entry. Etymologically primarily Arabic/Aramaic (Aramaic wəlaj 'to enter'), walaja is a relatively rare Semitic root specialized to the image of penetration and the merging of one thing into another.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر و ل ج — 14 مرة — To enter

etymology.notes: Primarily Arabic and Aramaic root for 'entering, penetrating.' Arabic walaja (ولج) 'to enter, penetrate deeply.' Quranic usage: 'He causes the night to enter into the day and the day to enter into the night' (Q 22:61). The root conveys deep, thorough penetration, often for natural cycles and divine action.

hadith_evidence.ar: و ل ج — وَرَدَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 14 مَرَّةً
hadith_evidence.en: The root wlj (و ل ج) appears 14 times in the Quran, including 3:27.

meaning.en_short: Certainty; to be certain; yaqīn (absolute certainty)
meaning.en: Certainty; to be certain; yaqīn (absolute certainty)
meaning.en_detailed: Core semantic: 'yaqina / ʾayqana' — to be certain, know with certainty; yaqīn 'absolute certainty, certitude' (often glossed as 'the most certain knowledge'); from the root ي ق ن (y-q-n), occurring 28 times across Forms I and IV. Quranic usage is foundational to epistemology and eschatology: 'And worship your Lord until there comes to you certainty (al-yaqīn)' (Q 15:99) — commentators universally read al-yaqīn here as death itself, marking the term of earthly worship; 'Knowledge (ʿilm) is not given to you except a little' (Q 17:85); 'Indeed, this is in the scrolls — the scrolls of Abraham and Moses' (Q 87:18-19) — yaqīn as the highest epistemic state; 'and worship Him, and put your trust (wa-tawakkal) in Him'; 'Indeed, the hour is surely coming — but I keep it almost hidden' (Q 20:15). The triliteral yaqīn uniquely denotes absolute certitude beyond zann (conjecture) and beyond ẓann rajīh (strong probability). Etymologically primarily Arabic/Aramaic (Aramaic yəqin 'to be certain').
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ي ق ن — 28 مرة — Certainty

etymology.notes: Primarily Arabic root for 'certainty, certitude.' Arabic yaqina (يقن) 'to be certain, have certainty.' Yaqīn (يقين) 'absolute certainty, certitude.' Quranic usage: 'And worship your Lord until certainty comes to you' (al-yaqīn = death; Q 15:99). The root denotes the highest degree of knowledge — beyond doubt, beyond probability.

derived_forms.meaning: to be certain, know with certainty

hadith_evidence.en: The root yqn (ي ق ن) appears 28 times in the Quran, including 15:99.

meaning.en: To originate. 7x. Bada'a=originate. Badi'=Originator (2:117). Bid'ah=innovation. Allah as absolute Originator of creation.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ب د ع carries the senses of originating, inventing, creating without precedent; it occurs 4 times in the Qurʾān. The classic verse is 2:117 'badīʿu l-samāwāti wa-l-arḍi' — Originator of the heavens and the earth, one of the divine names (al-Badīʿ). Al-Rāghib: البدع اختراع الشيء على غير مثال سبق (to invent a thing without preceding example), whence the noun bidʿa (innovation). Other uses: 6:101 'badīʿu l-samāwāti wa-l-arḍi', 10:3, 27:64 'am man yabdaʾu l-khalqa thumma yuʿīduhu'. The root is rare but carries heavy theological weight: it names God's unique creative act, distinguishing His agency from all secondary causation. Ibn Fāris places the triliteral under innovation and creation.

quranic_analysis.theme: Originator
quranic_analysis.detail: Badi'u al-samawati wa al-ardi—Originator of heavens and earth.

hadith_evidence.ar: الْمُؤْمِنُ يَأْكُلُ فِي مِعًى وَاحِدٍ وَالْكَافِرُ يَأْكُلُ فِي سَبْعَةِ أَمْعَاءٍ
hadith_evidence.en: The believer eats in one intestine and the disbeliever eats in seven intestines.

meaning.en: The root conveys To be a husband. Though appearing only 5 times, it contributes to the rich semantic texture of Quranic discourse, appearing in contexts that illuminate the nature of the human condition.
meaning.ar: بَعَلَ: زَوَّجَ. الْبَعْلُ: الزَّوْجُ
meaning.en_detailed: Root ب ع ل denotes being a husband, the noun ba'l = husband (in the context of marriage); it appears 7 times in the Qurʾān. The defining verse is 4:128 'in khāfat min baʿlihā shūzhan aw iʿrāḍan' — if a woman fears ill-treatment or desertion from her husband. Classical Arabic distinguishes ba'l (husband, with legal rights over a wife) from zawj (spouse, neutral) and from ba'ala (to send forth); the ba'l carries juridical weight. Other uses include 2:228 (the wife's rights, her ba'l being like a partner), 4:4 (mahr entitlements), 4:12, 11:72 (Sarah and her ba'l Abraham), 24:31. Ibn Fāris: الباء والعين واللام — للسيد والمرجع. The root is reserved in the Qurʾān for the matrimonial partner.

quranic_analysis.theme: Marriage
quranic_analysis.detail: If a woman fears ill-treatment from her husband

hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ أَبِي ذَرٍّ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «لَا تَحْقِرَنَّ مِنَ الْمَعْرُوفِ شَيْئًا وَلَوْ أَنْ تَلْقَى أَخَاكَ بِوَجْهٍ طَلْقٍ»

meaning.en: To weep. 7x. Baka=weep. 12:84: his eyes whitened from grief—Jacob weeping for Yusuf. 44:29: heaven and earth did not weep for Pharaoh.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ب ك ي means to weep, to cry; it appears 7 times in the Qurʾān. The classic instance is 12:84 'wa-byaddat ʿaynāhu min al-ḥuzni fa-huwa kaẓīm' — his (Jacob's) eyes whitened from grief; he was a man of bitter complaint, the picture of lifelong weeping for Joseph. The eschatological contrast is 44:29 'lam yabki ʿalayhimā al-samāʾu wa-l-arḍu' — neither heaven nor earth wept for the unjust. Other verses: 5:31 (Cain's remorse after killing Abel), 12:16 (Joseph's brothers' false weeping before their father), 17:109, 19:58, 28:18. Al-Rāghib: البكاء إفراز العين دموعا عند الحزن. The Qurʾānic bkī is reserved for grief that overflows into tears, often tied to prophetic sorrow.

quranic_analysis.theme: Jacob's tears
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa abyaddat aynahu min al-huzni—his eyes whitened from grief.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ

meaning.en: This root expresses To cheat defraud and appears 7 times in the Quran. It is attested in classical lexicons (Ibn Faris, Lisan al-Arab) and contributes to the human condition vocabulary.
meaning.ar: بَخِسَ: نَقَصَ. الْبَخْسُ: النَّقْصُ
meaning.en_detailed: Root ب خ س carries the senses of cheating, defrauding, diminishing in measure; it appears 7 times in the Qurʾān. The classic verse is 11:85 'wa-lā tabkhasū l-nāsa ashyāʾahum' — and do not defraud people of their due, the closing admonition in Shuʿayb's address to Midian, anchoring a sustained Qurʾānic polemic against commercial injustice. Al-Rāghib: بخسه حقّه نقصه إياه; bakhs = decrease, diminution. Other verses include 2:42 'wa-lā talbisū l-ḥaqqa bi-l-bāṭili', 4:32 (inheritance justice), 7:85, 26:181-183 'wa-lā tabkhasū l-mīzāna', 6:152 'wa-lā tabkhasū l-mawāzīna'. The bakhs in commerce is the unjust reduction; in theology it is the privative withholding of truth, making the root a moral diagnostic of measure and right.

quranic_analysis.theme: Justice
quranic_analysis.detail: Do not defraud people of their things

hadith_evidence.text_en: Abdullah ibn Amr reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The just will be with Allah on pulpits of light."

meaning.en: To crush, level. 7x. Dakka=crush, pummel. 7:143: He made the mountain crumble (dakkan)—Moses at Sinai. 89:21: earth pounded to powder (dakkan dakkan).
meaning.en_detailed: Root د ك ك carries the senses of crushing, smashing flat, leveling; it appears 7 times in the Qurʾān. The classic instance is 7:143 'wa-jaʿalahu dakkan khaṣṣafan' — He made the mountain (Sinai) level as ground at Moses' vision, the moment when the mountain crumbled under theophany. The eschatological application is 89:21 'ka-l-dakki dakka' — like a single crash, the earth's total levelling at the Resurrection. Other uses: 11:67 (the cry striking the unjust), 21:30 'wa-l-arḍu baʿda dhālika daḥāhā', 39:69 'wa-nufikha fī l-ṣūri fa-ṣaʿiqa man fī l-samāwāti', 54:14 'tamarrū marra'. The morphological pattern Fa''ala (geminate doubled) intensifies the crushing force. Ibn Fāris: الدك الكسر الشديد, the violent total breaking.

quranic_analysis.theme: Mountain crumbled
quranic_analysis.detail: Ja'alahu dakkan—He made it crumble to dust.

meaning.en: The root conveys To return. Though appearing only 6 times, it contributes to the rich semantic texture of Quranic discourse, appearing in contexts that illuminate the nature of the human condition.
meaning.ar: فَاءَ: رَجَعَ. الْفَىْءُ: الظِّلُّ بَعْدَ الزَّوَالِ
meaning.en_detailed: Root ف ي أ carries the senses of returning, coming back, turning; it appears 7 times in the Qurʾān. The defining verse is 49:11 'wa-in lam yatubu fa-ūlāʾika hum al-ẓālimūn' — if they do not repent, they are the wrongdoers, where the root frames the call to return to God. The verb fāʾa and its form tafāʾa govern the Qurʾānic doctrine of repentance as returning (tawba). Other key uses include 2:226 'wa-lā taḥillū l-nisāʾ', 4:135 'wa-in yatawallaw yuʿrid ʿan baʿḍ', 9:74, 9:125, 58:3. Al-Rāghib: الفَىْء الرجوع وأصله رجوع الظلّ بعد الزوال. The root governs the Qurʾānic doctrine of return, grounding the divine-human dynamic of repentance.

quranic_analysis.theme: Repentance
quranic_analysis.detail: If they do not repent, they are the wrongdoers

meaning.ar: غَرَفَ: أَخَذَ. الْغَرْفُ: الْأَخْذُ بِالْيَدِ

meaning.en: To be a camel. The root denotes a she-camel (naqah). This root appears 7 time(s) in the Quran (e.g., 11:64; 17:59; 26:155).
meaning.ar: نَاقَ: بَعُرَ. النَّاقَةُ: الْأُنْثَىٰ مِنَ الْإِبِلِ
meaning.en_detailed: The nominal root nūn-wāw-qāf (ن و ق), occurring 7 times in the Quran exclusively in the feminine plural form nāqat (she-camel), centers on the she-camel as a divinely designated sign. The most prominent Quranic instance is Ṣāliḥ's she-camel (nāqat Allāh) sent to Thamūd (7:73, 11:64, 17:59), whose hamstringing brought divine destruction. The root's restricted Quranic usage — always feminine plural and always in the context of prophetic validation — marks it as a specialized theophanic lexeme rather than a general zoological term. Cognates in other Semitic languages include Hebrew nāqâ (female) and Akkadian nāqu (to cry out), though the Arabic specialization to the she-camel is distinctive to the Arabian milieu.

meaning.en: To aim, intend; tayammum (dry ablution); yamm (sea)
meaning.en_detailed: Core semantic: 'yamm (يم)' — sea, large body of water (often specifically 'the sea' as a vast water); tayammum 'dry ablution, to aim at, intend'; from the root ي م م (y-m-m), occurring 11 times. Quranic usage centers on Pharaonic setting and ritual law: 'We inspired the mother of Moses: "Nurse him; and when you fear for him, cast him into the river/sea (al-yamm)"' (Q 28:7, 28:10) — al-yamm here is the Nile (used as 'sea'); 'And when they met, the companions of Pharaoh said: "Indeed, we are about to be overcome"' (Q 26:61); the Pharaoh drowned in al-yamm. Tayammum 'dry ablution' (Q 4:43, 5:6) is from the same root via 'aiming/intending toward clean earth.' Etymologically pan-Semitic *yamm- 'sea' (Heb. yām, Ugaritic ym, Ethiopic yamm), the root is among the most stable for the concept of 'sea' across Semitic.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ي م م — 11 مرة — To aim

etymology.notes: Pan-Semitic word for 'sea, large body of water.' Proto-Semitic *yamm- 'sea.' Arabic yamm (يم) specifically denotes 'sea, ocean, large river.' Quranic usage: 'So We inspired to the mother of Moses: Nurse him; and when you fear for him, cast him into the river/sea (al-yamm)' (Q 28:7). Tayammum (تيمم) 'dry ablution' — derived from 'aiming/intending' rather than from yamm — is from this same root but a different semantic development.

derived_forms.meaning: to aim, intend; to perform dry ablution
