meaning.en_short: Right hand; oath; blessing; yamīn (right, oath); to bless
meaning.en: Right hand; oath; blessing; yamīn (right, oath); to bless
meaning.en_detailed: Core semantic: 'yamīn (يمين)' — right hand, right side; oath, covenant; yumn 'blessing, good fortune'; maymana 'right flank'; from the root ي م ن (y-m-n), occurring 71 times, almost exclusively as the noun yamīn. Quranic usage is foundational to eschatology and legal oaths: 'And the companions of the right — what are the companions of the right?' (aṣḥāb al-yamīn; Q 56:8-9, 56:27, 56:38, 56:90-91) — the blessed inhabitants of paradise, set against aṣḥāb al-shimāl 'the companions of the left' who fare badly; 'And I do not acquit myself; indeed, the soul is a persistent enjoiner of evil except those on whom my Lord has mercy' (Q 12:53); 'you who believe, fulfill your contracts (al-ʿuqūd)' (Q 5:1) — yamīn in oath-bearing uses; 'And the sun runs [on its fixed course] toward its resting place' (Q 36:38) references yawm yamīn. Etymologically pan-Semitic *yamin- 'right hand' (Heb. yāmîn, Ugaritic ymn, Akk. imnu), with the semantic link between 'right hand' and 'oath' universal across Semitic.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر ي م ن — 71 مرة — Right hand

etymology.notes: Pan-Semitic word for 'right hand/side.' Proto-Semitic *yamin- 'right hand, right side.' Arabic yamīn (يمين) 'right hand, oath, blessing.' Quranic usage: 'And the companions of the right — what are the companions of the right?' (aṣḥāb al-yamīn; Q 56:27). The link between 'right hand' and 'oath' comes from the ancient practice of raising or clasping the right hand when swearing an oath. Yumn 'blessing, good fortune' shares the same root, as the right side was considered auspicious throughout Semitic cultures.

derived_forms.meaning: to bless; to go to the right

meaning.en: To perceive, to know, to be aware of; poetry; hair. The root bridges sensory perception, aesthetic expression, and bodily form in a striking semantic triad. Quranic usage prominently critiques poetry in favor of prophetic revelation: 'And the poets — only the misguides follow them' (26:224), while exempting 'those who believe and do righteous deeds' (26:227). The noun shaʿr (hair) extends the root into bodily imagery, and the verb shaʿara marks intuitive awareness — a knowledge closer to feeling than to analytic cognition.
meaning.en_detailed: Core semantic: 'shaʿara (شعر)' — to perceive, know, be aware of; shiʿr 'poetry'; shaʿr 'hair'; from the root ش ع ر (sh-ʿ-r), occurring 40 times. Quranic usage is most prominent in the foundational polemic against poetry: 'And the poets — only the misguides follow them; have you not seen that they go astray in every valley and say what they do not do?' (Q 26:224-226) — defining shiʿr negatively except for the prophetic exception (Q 26:227); 'He [the Prophet] did not teach him [the poet] poetry (shiʿr); it is not appropriate for him'; 'Hud said: do not make excuses; we know what you conceal and what you declare'; 'of those who believed and did not mix their belief with injustice' (Q 6:82). The semantic core of shaʿr is 'perception/awareness' (compare Arab. waṣfa for the awareness that comes through hair-touching skin sensations), from which both 'poetry' (the heightened awareness of the poet) and 'hair' (the perceptible body-covering) develop. Etymologically Arabic root with limited cognates.

meaning.en: To resemble, to be similar; to be ambiguous. The root governs the Quran's foundational negative theology: 'There is nothing like unto Him' (42:11), establishing absolute divine transcendence through the denial of similitude. The passive voice shubbiha (it was made to appear similar) appears in contexts of confusion and misperception, while tashābaha marks the ambiguity of certain Quranic verses. The root thus spans both the theological assertion of God's uniqueness and the hermeneutical challenge of interpretive ambiguity.
meaning.en_detailed: Core semantic: 'shabaha (شبه)' — to resemble, be similar, be ambiguous; shibh / shabah 'likeness, resemblance, ambiguity'; from the root ش ب ه (sh-b-h), occurring 12 times. Quranic usage centers on similarity and likeness claims: 'There is nothing like unto Him (laysa ka-mithlihi shayʾ), and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing' (Q 42:11) — the foundational negative theology; 'Then We made you a middle way (wa-lladhīna kafarū bi-āyātina hum al-ḥizb al-shayṭān)' — the verse of comparison; 'Or do they say: "He invented a lie about God"? If God willed, He would seal your heart' (Q 42:24) — the mushabbihāt (anthropomorphist) and mujassimah position rejected. The root carries both neutral similarity and theological danger (tashbīh). The verbal noun shubha 'doubtful matter' appears in fiqh. Etymologically Arabic root with limited cognates; primarily used in Islamic theological discourse.

meaning.en: To fear, to be anxious; to have compassion; the twilight glow. The root unites the psychological state of anxious concern with the crepuscular phenomenon of the afterglow at sunset — perhaps because both signal transitions and liminal states. Quranic usage centers on the eschatological fear that should accompany the awareness of divine judgment, and the shafaq (redness after sunset) as a temporal marker for prayer and the onset of night.
meaning.en_detailed: Core semantic: 'shafaqa (شفق)' — to fear, pity, be anxious; ishrāq 'sunrise glow'; shafaq 'afterglow, twilight' (the redness after sunset); from the root ش ف ق (sh-f-q), occurring 11 times. Quranic usage is concentrated in two adjacent verses: 'And from after Isha until dawn — the recitation of the night vigil; indeed, the night vigil was ever a powerful means of ascent and a fitting time for remembrance' (Q 73:20 context); 'And [He is] the one who takes away the shafaq' (the afterglow of sunset) — and turns the night into rest, and the sun and moon into reckoning (Q 6:96 — 'and the sun and the moon [are] signs for you'); 'He [the angel] has mastery over them and watches over them by night and day' — fearing for those under his care (Q 72:27); 'And [recall] when those who disbelieved plotted against you to imprison you or kill you or expel you [from Makkah]' (Q 8:30). The dual semantic of fear-of-God and twilight-glow is rare and beautiful; etymologically Arabic with limited cognates.

meaning.en: The brink, the edge, the verge — typically of destruction. A rare but potent noun occurring only twice in the Quran (9:109, 9:35), always in eschatological contexts describing those who stand at the very precipice of a yawning pit of fire. The root conveys the existential precariousness of those who have rejected divine guidance: suspended between safety and catastrophe, at the edge of irreversible ruin.
meaning.en_detailed: Core semantic: 'shafā (شفا)' — brink, edge, verge (typically of a chasm or destruction); from the root ش ف و (sh-f-w), occurring 2 times, in the closely related phrase 'the brink of a yawning pit (shawāʾin min hufrin)' / 'a fire whose fuel is people and stones' (Q 9:109, 9:35). Quranic usage is exclusively eschatological: 'Whoever turns away from My remembrance — his shall be a straitened life, and We shall raise him blind on the Day of Resurrection' — the warning against deliberate distance from divine guidance leaves the soul on the brink; 'and you have indeed destroyed your souls' (Q 2:54, 7:160) and the more extended 'they were on the brink of a vast pit (wa-hum ʿalā shafā ḥuf ratin min al-nār)' (Q 9:109) describes the peril of the munāfiqūn hovering over the fire's edge. The word is concrete in image but morally elevated — destruction is one slip away. Etymologically Arabic root.

meaning.en: This root expresses To hate and appears 5 times in the Quran. It is attested in classical lexicons (Ibn Faris, Lisan al-Arab) and contributes to the human condition vocabulary.
meaning.ar: مَقَتَ: كَرِهَ. الْمَقْتُ: شِدَّةُ الْبُغْضِ
meaning.en_detailed: مَقَتَ (م ق ت), a root appearing 6 times in the Quran, encodes the notion of Hate (5x) across its various verbal and nominal forms. Its five Quranic occurrences include the striking declaration at 40:10 that Allah's hatred (maqt) of disbelievers after their profession of faith is greater than their hatred of themselves—a semantic intensification linking divine and human maqt in eschatological reckoning. Lexicographers distinguish maqtu from karāha (mild dislike) and bughd (active hatred) by its quality of absolute and irreversible repudiation, characteristic of divine judgment.

meaning.en: To mingle. 6x. Maraja=mingle, let loose. 55:19-20: He let loose (maraja) the two seas meeting—between them a barrier. The root denotes dynamic mixing.
meaning.en_detailed: The root m-r-j in Ibn Faris's taxonomy conveys mixing, flowing, and unrestrained movement (maraja al-shay': khalṭahu wa arsalahu), capturing both the dynamic commingling and the freedom from constraint. Quranic usage centers on the famous cosmological image at 55:19–20 where God released the two seas that meet yet remain separated by a barzakh, demonstrating the root's dual semantic of mingling and letting loose. In moral discourse the derived phrase maraja al-shayṭān denotes the incitement of disorder—a semantic extension from unrestrained physical flow to chaos of conduct, hence the root's fitness for depicting unchecked passions.

meaning.en: This root expresses To incline and appears 3 times in the Quran. It is attested in classical lexicons (Ibn Faris, Lisan al-Arab) and contributes to the human condition vocabulary.
meaning.ar: مَالَ: عَدَلَ. الْمَيْلُ: الْعُدُولُ
meaning.en_detailed: The root m-y-l semantically denotes inclination, deviation, and leaning (māla ʿanhu: ʿadala), with the noun mayl and the active participle mā'il covering both physical tilt and figurative bias. Its Quranic usage at 4:129 instructs believers not to incline completely toward one wife in matters of equal treatment, where the cognate tamilī conveys unjust emotional preference requiring divine correction. Classical grammarians note that this verb in form I inherently suggests directional movement away from equilibrium, distinguishing it from the spatial root m-w-l (turn away decisively) which signifies complete departure from a prior state.

meaning.en: The root conveys To flee. Though appearing only 6 times, it contributes to the rich semantic texture of Quranic discourse, appearing in contexts that illuminate the nature of the human condition.
meaning.ar: نَدَّ: نَفَرَ. النَّدُّ: ضِدٌّ وَعَدُوٌّ
meaning.en_detailed: The doubled-middle root n-d-d conveys fleeing, scattering, and straying (nadda: nafara wa sharaḍa), carrying connotations of sudden departure and outright apostasy. At 2:22, the warning against making rivals (andād) to Allah involves a paronomastic play on the root, where nidd (counterpart, rival) evokes the essence of straying from monotheism into which a competing loyalty has carried the soul. The intensified form nadda implies swift and complete defection, semantically distinct from the more general ʿadā (run) or dāra (turn around in place).

meaning.en: The root conveys To incite provoke. Though appearing only 4 times, it contributes to the rich semantic texture of Quranic discourse, appearing in contexts that illuminate the nature of the human condition.
meaning.ar: نَزَغَ: حَرَّضَ. النَّزْغُ: الْإِفْسَادُ
meaning.en_detailed: The root n-z-g in classical lexicography denotes incitement, provocation, and the injection of discord (nazagha: ḥarraḍa wa afsada), particularly of whispers that sow enmity between people. Its Quranic occurrences center on the famous istiʿādha at 7:200—'idhā nazagha al-shayṭānu nazghan' ('if a provocation from Satan should incite you')—where the masdar nazgh captures the subtle instigation that contrasts with the more overt assault of waṣwasa. Lexicographers observe the root's military connotation of skirmishing forces that harass the flanks, hence its fitness for satanic whisperings that disturb the peace of the soul without engaging it openly.

meaning.en: This root denotes To leap bound. Its 6 Quranic occurrences (e.g., 12:18, 12:25, 12:26) illustrate the concept in contexts ranging from divine action to human responsibility.
meaning.ar: قَمَصَ: نَزَا. الْقَمْصُ: الْوَثْبُ
meaning.en_detailed: The root q-m-ṣ denotes violent leaping, bounding, and the convulsive struggle of a recumbent creature (qamaṣa: waṭaba wa qafaza), most often used of animals kicking out against their riders or handlers. Quranic usage includes 12:18 where the brothers bring Joseph's shirt with false blood, and contexts where qamaṣa depicts aggressive resistance against constraint or authority. The semantic field is kinetic and defiant, implying a violent motion against imposed control, which classical lexicographers distinguish from the more neutral waṭaba (leap) by its connotation of resistance.

meaning.en: Right guidance. 6x. Rushd=right guidance, maturity. 2:256: right guidance is distinct from error (al-rushdu min al-ghayy). No compulsion in religion.
meaning.en_detailed: The root r-sh-d denotes soundness, integrity, and proper guidance (al-rushdu: al-istiqāmatu ʿalā al-ṭarīqi al-mustaqīm), semantically opposed to ghayy (error and deviation) as two ontologically distinct trajectories. At 2:256 the famous declaration qad tabayyana al-rushdu mina al-ghayyi distinguishes guidance from misguidance as two clear paths, providing the theological foundation for 'there is no compulsion in religion.' The verbal noun rushd often pairs in classical usage with nubūwa (prophethood) and balāgh (mature discernment), forming the canonical triad of awareness, message-delivery, and adult competence in matters of faith.

quranic_analysis.theme: Guidance clear from error
quranic_analysis.detail: Qad tabayyana al-rushdu mina al-ghayyi—guidance is clear from error.

meaning.en: To desire, to crave, to have appetite. The root anchors a Quranic moral anthropology in which the appetitive soul (shahawāt) is neither condemned outright nor celebrated uncritically, but recognized as a divinely created drive that must be disciplined: 'Beautified for people is the love of desires' (3:14). The root names the psychological infrastructure of worldly attraction — women, children, wealth, livestock — that the believer must subordinate to higher spiritual aims.
meaning.en_detailed: Core semantic: 'shahā (شها)' — to desire, crave, have appetite; shahwa 'appetite, desire, lust'; mashhada 'object of desire'; from the root ش ه و (sh-h-w), occurring 13 times. Quranic usage anchors a moral anthropology in which the appetitive soul is a site of divine command: 'Beautified for people is the love of desires (shahawāt) — of women and children and hoarded heaps of gold and silver and branded horses and cattle and tillage' (Q 3:14) — the famous enumeration of worldly shahawāt; 'And those who guard their private parts except from their wives or those whom their right hands possess; indeed, they are not to be blamed — but whoever seeks beyond that (ibtghāʾa dhālika fahūlāʾa hum al-ʿādilūn)' (Q 23:5-7); 'We have made whatever is on the earth an adornment for it that We may test them as to which of them is best in conduct' (Q 18:7); 'the soul of the evil-doer is ever demanding (li-lladhīna kafarū ʿalayhim hīna al-nifāq)'; 'and We presented to him the example of the two sons of Adam' (Q 5:30). The root is central to Sufi ethics of mujāhada against the commanding nafs. Etymologically Arabic root.

etymology.notes: Arabic Quranic root.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ

meaning.en: To block. 6x. Sadda=block. 18:95: I will make a rampart (saddan) between you—Dhu al-Qarnayn. The root denotes barrier and obstruction.
meaning.en_detailed: The root s-d-d in classical Arabic denotes blocking, closing, and shutting (sadda al-shay': aghlaqahu), with the masdar sadd referring to a barrier, dam, or obstruction. Quranic usage at 18:95 features Dhū al-Qarnayn's construction of a mighty barrier (saddan) between Gog and Magog, employing a baked iron and molten copper interlayer that demonstrates human cooperation with divine permission. The substantive sadīd also denotes clotted blood in Quranic usage (e.g., 14:16), linking the root's sense of blockage to physiological obstruction in scenes of eschatological torment.

quranic_analysis.theme: Dhu al-Qarnayn's barrier
quranic_analysis.detail: Aj'al baynakum wa baynahum radman—I will make a barrier.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en: Doubt, uncertainty, skepticism. The root names the epistemic state opposed to certainty (yaqīn) and faith (īmān), appearing in foundational Quranic polemics against those who waver between truth and falsehood. The Quran presents shakk as the antithesis of the knowledge that comes through revelation: 'Those who were given the Scripture did not differ except after knowledge had come to them' (3:19). The root thus defines the boundary between conviction and vacillation.
meaning.en_detailed: Core semantic: 'shakka (شك)' — to doubt, be uncertain; shakk 'doubt'; shakīk 'of dubious origin'; from the root ش ك ك (sh-k-k), occurring 15 times. Quranic usage is foundational to faith-knowledge dichotomy: 'Indeed, the religion in the sight of God is Islam; and those who were given the Scripture did not differ except after knowledge had come to them, out of mutual jealousy (wa-mā khtalafa alladhīna ʾūtū al-kitāba illā min baʿdi mā jāʾahumu al-ʿilm baghyan baynahum)' (Q 3:19; contrast with Q 2:147 'al-ṣābiqūna al-awwalūn min al-muhājirīn wa-l-anṣār wa-lladhīna ittabaʿūhum bi-iḥsānin radiya Allāhu ʿanhum'); 'And those who believe are uncertain (wa-in takthurū al-shayṭānu)' — the call to certainty of revelation: 'And [recall] when Abraham was tried by his Lord with words and he fulfilled them; He said: indeed I will make you a leader (imāman) for the people' (Q 2:124 — where shakk is forbidden about this); 'And whoever is in doubt about the Hour — surely it will come upon them' (Q 22:55). The verb shakka 'to doubt' stands opposed to ʾayqana 'to be certain'; both share the conceptual field of epistemic certainty. Etymologically Arabic root with limited cognates, but the verb 'to pierce' (shakka 'to pierce, stab' = concrete physical sense) is primary in classical Arabic, with doubt the figurative extension.

etymology.notes: Arabic Quranic root.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: This root denotes To be covered. Its 6 Quranic occurrences (e.g., 2:191, 33:61, 3:112) illustrate the concept in contexts ranging from divine action to human responsibility.
meaning.ar: غَلِفَ: غَطَّىٰ. الْغِلَافُ: الْغِطَاءُ
meaning.en_detailed: The root gh-l-f in Ibn Faris's Maqāyīs al-Lughah conveys covering, wrapping, and envelopment (ghalufa: ghashshāhu), with the derived noun ghilāf referring to a covering, sheath, or rind. The famous Quranic phrase at 2:88—'qulūbunā ghulafun' ('our hearts are wrapped')—is the polemical remark of certain Jews against Muhammad's message, employing the plural participle ghulaf to denote hearts sealed against understanding revelation. Lexicographers note that this root pairs naturally with qalb (heart) to imply willful sealing against divine address, distinguishing it from physical covering by its connotation of volitional resistance to truth.

quranic_analysis.theme: Covered hearts
quranic_analysis.detail: Our hearts are wrapped

hadith_evidence.text_en: Abu Huraira reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Every joint of a person has a charity due upon it each day the sun rises."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ أَبِي هُرَيْرَةَ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «كُلُّ سُلَامَى مِنَ النَّاسِ عَلَيْهِ صَدَقَةٌ كُلَّ يَوْمٍ تَطْلُعُ فِيهِ الشَّمْسُ»

derived_forms.meaning: This root denotes To be covered

meaning.en: The root conveys To tread. Though appearing only 5 times, it contributes to the rich semantic texture of Quranic discourse, appearing in contexts that illuminate the nature of the human condition.
meaning.ar: وَطِئَ: دَاسَ. الْوَطْءُ: الدَّوْسُ
meaning.en_detailed: The root w-ṭ-ʾ in classical Arabic denotes treading, trampling, and sexual intercourse (waṭiʾa: dāsa), with watʾ in Quranic Arabic encompassing both literal stepping and marital union. The Quranic usage at 73:6 draws on the metaphorical sense of 'treading firmly' in night vigil prayer: innā nāshiʾati al-layli hiya ashaddu watʾan wa aqwamu qīlan—the night's devotion being more impacting (watʾan) and more upright in speech for the soul. The root appears in classical legal vocabulary as the standard term for consummating marriage (waṭiʾa al-zawja), preserving its double semantic field of physical stepping and intimate encounter.

quranic_analysis.theme: Night prayer
quranic_analysis.detail: The night vigil is more impactful

hadith_evidence.text_en: Abdullah ibn Amr reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The merciful will be shown mercy by the Most Merciful. Be merciful to those on earth, and the One in heaven will have mercy upon you."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ بْنِ عَمْرٍو رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمَا قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «الرَّاحِمُونَ يَرْحَمُهُمُ الرَّحْمَنُ، ارْحَمُوا مَنْ فِي الْأَرْضِ يَرْحَمْ

meaning.en: This root expresses To mix and appears 6 times in the Quran. It is attested in classical lexicons (Ibn Faris, Lisan al-Arab) and contributes to the human condition vocabulary.
meaning.ar: خَلَطَ: مَزَجَ. الْخَلْطُ: الْمَزْجُ
meaning.en_detailed: The root kh-l-ṭ denotes mixing, blending, and confusing (khalaṭa: mazaża), with the derived form mukhlaṭ contrasting with mufarriq (separated, distinguished). Quranic usage at 38:28—'aʿantaqimu kunta al-muʾminīna wa al-mujrimīna' style rhetoric where shunning ethical mixture is fundamental—employs the semantic field of mixing to refute the moral conflation of the unjust and the just. The verbal noun khalṭ also appears in classical legal usage for fraudulent mixing (especially of impure substances with pure ones), and in the Quranic warning at 2:220 the related mukhliṭātīn preserves this ethical boundary-marking sense.

quranic_analysis.theme: Justice
quranic_analysis.detail: Shall We treat believers like corrupters?

hadith_evidence.text_en: Abu Dharr reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Do not consider any act of goodness insignificant, even if it is meeting your brother with a cheerful face."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ أَبِي ذَرٍّ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «لَا تَحْقِرَنَّ مِنَ الْمَعْرُوفِ شَيْئًا وَلَوْ أَنْ تَلْقَى أَخَاكَ بِوَجْهٍ طَلْقٍ»

meaning.en: This root expresses To drive away and appears 5 times in the Quran. It is attested in classical lexicons (Ibn Faris, Lisan al-Arab) and contributes to the human condition vocabulary.
meaning.ar: زَجَرَ: نَهَىٰ. الزَّجْرُ: الْمَنْعُ
meaning.en_detailed: The root z-j-r denotes driving away, restraining by force, and rebuke (zajara: nahā wa ṣarafa), carrying connotations of forceful repulsion distinct from the gentler nahy. Its Quranic occurrence at 37:2 in the opening of Sūrat al-Ṣāffāt—'fa al-ṣāffāti ṣaffan fa al-zājirāti zajrā' ('by those ranged in ranks, driving fiercely')—describes the angels who drive away the demons from overhearing revelation. The semantic triad of dafʿ (repelling), zajr (forceful restraint), and waʿz (warning) is essential in classical Quranic tafsīr for distinguishing gradations of divine and angelic interdiction.

quranic_analysis.theme: Angels
quranic_analysis.detail: By those who drive away

hadith_evidence.text_en: Umm Salama reported: The most frequent supplication of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was: "O Turner of hearts, make my heart firm upon Your religion."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ أُمِّ سَلَمَةَ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهَا قَالَتْ: كَانَ أَكْثَرُ دُعَاءِ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «يَا مُقَلِّبَ الْقُلُوبِ ثَبِّتْ قَلْبِي عَلَى دِينِكَ»

derived_forms.meaning: This root expresses To drive away and appears 5 times in the Quran

meaning.en: Earthquake. 6x. Zalzala=shake violently. 99:1: when the earth is shaken (zulzilat) with its earthquake (zilzalaha). Surah al-Zalzalah.
meaning.en_detailed: The doubled root z-l-z-l is an intensified form of z-l-l (to shake) that denotes violent or repeated quaking (zalzala: ḥarrakahu taḥrīkan shadīdan), conveying the dramatic, repeated motion of earthquake rather than a single tremor. Sūrat al-Zalzalah (Quran 99) takes its name from the root's first-occurrence formulation, 'idhā zulzilati al-arḍu zilzālahā' ('when the earth is shaken with its final shaking')—a hendiadys emphasizing both the event and its intensity. The masdar zilzāl is virtually unique to eschatological discourse in the Quran, depicting the prelude to the Day of Judgment when the earth discloses its burdens.

quranic_analysis.theme: The earthquake
quranic_analysis.detail: Idha zulzilati al-ardu zilzalaha—when the earth is shaken.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en: This root denotes To visit. Its 6 Quranic occurrences (e.g., 102:2, 18:17, 22:30) illustrate the concept in contexts ranging from divine action to human responsibility.
meaning.ar: زَارَ: قَصَدَ. الزِّيَارَةُ: الْقَصْدُ
meaning.en_detailed: The root z-w-r in classical Arabic carries a polysemous semantic field including visiting, falsehood, and turning aside, with zāra meaning to visit or draw near (zāra: qaṣada wa atā), and the masdar ziyārah preserving the connotation of intentional approach. At 102:2 the verb zurtumu (the interrogative 'until you visit the graves') employs zāra in its most concrete meaning of visiting or reaching a place. The related form zūr (falsehood, lie) at 25:72 reveals the root's additional semantic range, while tazāwara at 18:17 depicts the sun inclining from the cave—a derived sense of deviation or veering that classical lexicographers integrate within the same triliteral field.

quranic_analysis.theme: Righteous
quranic_analysis.detail: They do not bear false witness

meaning.en: This root denotes To be stingy miserly. Its 4 Quranic occurrences (e.g., 33:19, 4:128, 59:9) illustrate the concept in contexts ranging from divine action to human responsibility.
meaning.ar: شَحِحَ: بَخِلَ. الشُّحُّ: الْبُخْلُ الشَّدِيدُ
meaning.en_detailed: The root sh-ḥ-ḥ in classical Arabic denotes extreme stinginess and tight-fistedness (al-shuḥḥu: al-bukhlu al-shadīdu al-mutashaddidu), a more intensive and ingrained form than bukhl alone. The Quran employs the root in a striking paradox at 59:9—'wa man yūqa shuḥḥa nafsihi fa ulāʾika humu al-mufliḥūn' ('whoever is protected from the stinginess of his own soul, they are the successful')—where the passive shuḥḥa denotes a person sealed within their greed. The lexicographical tradition distinguishes shuḥḥ as the ingrained disposition toward miserliness while bukhl may be situational or acquired, preserving the root's lexical intensity.

quranic_analysis.theme: Success
quranic_analysis.detail: Whoever is protected from his own stinginess

meaning.en: This root expresses To deviate and appears 3 times in the Quran. It is attested in classical lexicons (Ibn Faris, Lisan al-Arab) and contributes to the human condition vocabulary.
meaning.ar: شَطَرَ: نَحَا. الشَّطْرُ: النِّصْفُ
meaning.en_detailed: The root sh-ṭ-r in classical Arabic denotes the half or side of a thing (al-shaṭru: al-niṣf), with the derived form shāṭara meaning to incline toward one side and shāṭirūn often paired with directional intent. At 2:144 the divine command 'fa-walli wajhaka shaṭra al-masjidi al-ḥarām' ('turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque') employs shaṭar to mean 'in the direction of,' encompassing orientation rather than mere directional leaning. This verse, foundational to the Qiblah change from Jerusalem to Makkah, makes the root central to Islamic ritual orientation and the legal concept of istiqbāl.

quranic_analysis.theme: Qiblah
quranic_analysis.detail: Turn your face toward al-Masjid al-Haram

hadith_evidence.text_en: Ali reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to me: "Say: O Allah, guide me and direct me."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ عَلِيٍّ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: قَالَ لِي رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «قُلِ: اللَّهُمَّ اهْدِنِي وَسَدِّدْنِي»

derived_forms.meaning: This root expresses To deviate and appears 3 times in the Quran

meaning.en: To legislate. 5x. Shara'a=legislate, prescribe. Shir'ah=law. 42:13: He has legislated (shara'a) for you the religion. The root of Islamic law (shari'ah).
meaning.en_detailed: The root sh-r-ʿ denotes beginning, initiating, and establishing a clear path (sharaʿa al-shayʾ: badaʾahu wa awḍaḥa ṭarīqahu), with the derived shirʿah and the famous shāriʿah preserving the meaning of a divinely prescribed way. At 42:13 the verb sharaʿa carries its fullest legislative sense: 'sharaʿa lakum mina al-dīni mā waṣṣā bihi Nūḥan' ('He has prescribed for you of the religion what He enjoined upon Noah'), establishing the paradigm of prophetic legislation that links each successive community. The word sharīʿah became the foundational term for Islamic sacred law, denoting the divinely legislated path of salvation preserved through prophetic transmission.

quranic_analysis.theme: Divine legislation
quranic_analysis.detail: Shara'a lakum mina al-dini—He legislated religion for you.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en: The root conveys To expand explain. Though appearing only 5 times, it contributes to the rich semantic texture of Quranic discourse, appearing in contexts that illuminate the nature of the human condition.
meaning.ar: شَرَحَ: فَسَّرَ. الشَّرْحُ: التَّفْسِيرُ
meaning.en_detailed: The root sh-r-ḥ denotes expansion, opening up, and explanation (sharaḥa: fataḥa wa wassaʿa), with the verbal noun sharḥ covering both physical expansion and explanatory elucidation. The famous opening of Sūrat al-Sharḥ (94:1)—'a-lam nashraḥ laka ṣadrak' ('Did We not expand your breast for you?')—employs sharaḥa in the corporeal sense of opening the chest to enable spiritual receptivity and prophetic mission. The pairing of sharḥ al-ṣadr (expansion of the breast) with ḍīq al-ṣadr (constriction) became the standard Quranic vocabulary for the spiritual states of ease and distress, also drawn upon in the basmala context.

quranic_analysis.theme: Comfort
quranic_analysis.detail: Did We not expand your chest?

meaning.en: The root conveys To scatter separate. Though appearing only 5 times, it contributes to the rich semantic texture of Quranic discourse, appearing in contexts that illuminate the nature of the human condition.
meaning.ar: شَتَّ: تَفَرَّقَ. الشَّتُّ: الِافْتِرَاقُ
meaning.en_detailed: The root sh-t-t in Ibn Faris's analysis signifies separation and dispersion (shatta al-shayʾ: farraqahu wa baddadahu), capturing the idea of fragmenting what was once unified into scattered factions. At 59:14 the famous phrase 'qulūbuhum shuttā' ('their hearts are divided') uses the plural participle to denote hearts scattered into opposing factions, a classical diagnosis of religious hypocrisy and tribal factionalism. The semantic field of shatā distinguishes from the spatial tafarruq through its emphasis on disorganized or hostile fragmentation rather than simple geographic dispersal.

quranic_analysis.theme: Disunity
quranic_analysis.detail: Their hearts are divided

meaning.en: To intend. Root denotes intention (amm), leading, or imam. This root appears 5 time(s) in the Quran (e.g., 17:18; 17:22; 68:49).
meaning.ar: أَمَّ: قَصَدَ. الْإِمَامُ: الْقَائِدُ
meaning.en_detailed: The root ʾ-m-m denotes leading, heading toward, and intention (ʾamma al-qawm: taqaddamahum), with the active participle imām being the most semantically loaded form in the Quranic vocabulary. At 2:124 the covenant with Abraham culminates in 'innī jāʿiluka li-l-nāsi imāman' ('I will make you an imam for the people'), where imām signifies both leader and exemplar of the divine way. The derivatives umma (community) and umm (mother) preserve the root's core sense of gathering around a leading principle, while the verb ʾamāna (he headed toward) retains the directional impetus of the triliteral.

quranic_analysis.theme: Abraham
quranic_analysis.detail: I will make you a leader for the people

hadith_evidence.text_en: Abdullah ibn Masud reported: The Prophet ﷺ used to say: "O Allah, I ask You for guidance, piety, chastity, and self-sufficiency."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ بْنِ مَسْعُودٍ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: كَانَ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ يَقُولُ: «اللَّهُمَّ إِنِّي أَسْأَلُكَ الْهُدَى وَالتُّقَى وَالْعَفَافَ وَالْغِنَى»

meaning.en: To encompass, to include comprehensively; the north. The root connects spatial direction (shamāl, the north wind or northern direction) with the abstract concept of comprehensive inclusion (shumūl). Quranic usage in 18:18 describes the People of the Cave being turned to the right and the left (north), while classical lexicography links shumūl to divine all-encompassing knowledge and power — God's attributes enfold all things without exclusion.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ش م ل (شَمِل), attested 12 times in the Quran, derives its core meaning of To encompass, include; north from Proto-Semitic sources. Occurring 12 times in the Qurʾān, it appears in the directional sense at 18:18 ('وَنُقَلِّبُهُمْ ذَاتَ الْيَمِينِ وَذَاتِ الشَّمَالِ') describing the People of the Cave turned right and left. Classical lexicographical tradition (Lisān al-ʿArab of Ibn Manẓūr) connects شُمُول to إِحَاطَة (comprehensiveness), a concept employed theologically to denote God's all-encompassing mercy and knowledge, with form X اِسْتَشْمَلَ extending the meaning to self-enwrapping in a garment.

etymology.notes: Arabic Quranic root.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: The root conveys To dwell. Though appearing only 5 times, it contributes to the rich semantic texture of Quranic discourse, appearing in contexts that illuminate the nature of the human condition.
meaning.ar: أَرِكَ: أَقَامَ. الْأَرِيكَةُ: السَّرِيرُ
meaning.en_detailed: The root ʾ-r-k in classical Arabic centers on the noun ʾarīka (or ʾarāʾik, plural), denoting an elevated throne, cushioned seat, or reclining couch (ʾarīkatun: sarīrun muttakaʾun ʿalayhi). At 18:31 the verse describing the gardens of the righteous—'wa arāʾika ʿalāḥā yatabawwaʾūn' ('upon which they recline on couches')—employs this root for the cushions of Paradise, evoking rest and dignified repose. The cognate verb form arika is rarer but retains the sense of stable, settled repose, distinct from the transient sitting of daʾūfa or the standing of wāqif.

quranic_analysis.theme: Paradise
quranic_analysis.detail: Reclining therein on couches

meaning.en: This root expresses To grieve regret and appears 5 times in the Quran. It is attested in classical lexicons (Ibn Faris, Lisan al-Arab) and contributes to the human condition vocabulary.
meaning.ar: أَسِفَ: حَزِنَ. الْأَسَفُ: الْحُزْنُ
meaning.en_detailed: The root ʾ-s-f in classical Arabic signifies intense grief compounded with moral concern or anger (ʾasifa: ḥazina wa ghaḍiba), a stronger affective state than ḥuzn (grief) alone. At 7:150 the retrospective on Moses' return from Mount Sinai after the calf-worship—the form appearing with Moses' cry: 'innī ʾasiftu ʿalākum' ('I was grieved with you')—the verb ʾasafa captures both sorrow and indignation at his people's lapse. Lexicographers distinguish ʾasaf from ḥuzn by the former's active component of moral concern or righteous anger, marking it as grief that issues in action.

quranic_analysis.theme: Moses' grief
quranic_analysis.detail: He said: My Lord, forgive me and my brother

hadith_evidence.text_en: Abdullah ibn Amr reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The merciful will be shown mercy by the Most Merciful. Be merciful to those on earth, and the One in heaven will have mercy upon you."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ بْنِ عَمْرٍو رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمَا قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «الرَّاحِمُونَ يَرْحَمُهُمُ الرَّحْمَنُ، ارْحَمُوا مَنْ فِي الْأَرْضِ يَرْحَمْ

meaning.en: To be wretched, miserable, unfortunate. The root defines one pole of the Quran's eschatological binary: the shaqī (wretched) stands opposite the saʿīd (felicitous) on the Day of Judgment (11:105-106). 20:2 affirms that the Quran was not revealed to cause the Prophet distress: 'We have not sent down the Quran to you that you be distressed.' The root thus names the final state of those who rejected divine guidance, while also emphasizing that revelation itself is not a source of misery but of mercy.
meaning.en_detailed: Occurring 12 times in the Quranic text, the root ش ق و (شَقِي) conveys the essential concept of To be wretched, miserable. Occurring 12 times, the verb شَقِيَ appears in striking contrastive contexts such as 11:105-106 ('فَمِنْهُمْ شَقِيٌّ وَسَعِيدٌ'), dividing humanity into the wretched and the felicitous on the Day of Judgment, and 20:2 ('مَا أَنزَلْنَا عَلَيْكَ الْقُرْآنَ لِتَشْقَىٰ'), affirming the Prophet was not sent to suffer. Classical exegesis (al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī) glosses شَقَاء as encompassing both the privation of good (in ʿālam al-dharr) and the suffering of the Hereafter, with form VIII اِشْتَقَى intensifying the meaning.

etymology.notes: Arabic Quranic root.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: This root expresses To be difficult and appears 5 times in the Quran. It is attested in classical lexicons (Ibn Faris, Lisan al-Arab) and contributes to the human condition vocabulary.
meaning.ar: عَسَرَ: ضَاقَ. الْعُسْرَةُ: الْفَقْرُ
meaning.en_detailed: The root ʿ-s-r denotes hardship, difficulty, and constraint (ʿasara: ḍāqa wa ishtadda), with ʿusr being the masdar for a state of difficulty or constriction. Quranic usage at 65:7 forms part of the famous prophetic formula 'maʿa al-ʿusri yusran' ('with hardship comes ease'), repeated twice for emphasis in the context of divorce and waiting periods. The root appears alongside its antonym yusr (ease) to articulate the divine principle of compensatory facilitation, fundamental to the Qur'anic theology of divine mercy within affliction.

quranic_analysis.theme: Relief
quranic_analysis.detail: Allah will bring ease after hardship

hadith_evidence.text_en: Abu Huraira reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Every joint of a person has a charity due upon it each day the sun rises."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ أَبِي هُرَيْرَةَ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «كُلُّ سُلَامَى مِنَ النَّاسِ عَلَيْهِ صَدَقَةٌ كُلَّ يَوْمٍ تَطْلُعُ فِيهِ الشَّمْسُ»

meaning.en: To encompass. Root denotes encompassing ('umum), or uncle. This root appears 3 time(s) in the Quran (e.g., 24:61; 33:50; 4:23).
meaning.ar: عَمَّ: شَمِلَ. الْعُيُوبُ الْعَامَّةُ
meaning.en_detailed: The root ʿ-m-m in classical lexicography signifies encompassing, totality, and inclusion (ʿamma: shamala wa aḥāṭa), with the active participle ʿāmm denoting what is universal or all-inclusive. The divine attribute al-Wāsiʿ (the All-Encompassing) at 6:133 ('wa Allāhu al-Wāsiʿu ʿalīm') draws on this root's semantic field, expressing the comprehensive reach of divine knowledge and encompassing power. The derived noun ʿamm (paternal uncle) likely preserves the root's sense of relatedness or family-wide scope, while the verbal noun ʿumūm denotes universality as in ʿumūm al-khalq (all of creation).

quranic_analysis.theme: Divine attributes
quranic_analysis.detail: He is the All-Encompassing, All-Knowing

hadith_evidence.text_en: Abdullah ibn Amr reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The merciful will be shown mercy by the Most Merciful. Be merciful to those on earth, and the One in heaven will have mercy upon you."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ بْنِ عَمْرٍو رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمَا قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «الرَّاحِمُونَ يَرْحَمُهُمُ الرَّحْمَنُ، ارْحَمُوا مَنْ فِي الْأَرْضِ يَرْحَمْ

meaning.en: To drink, to imbibe; a beverage; to absorb. The root encompasses the physical act of drinking and its extended figurative senses of absorption and participation. Quranic usage ranges from Saul's test of his troops at the river (2:249) to the righteous drinking from sealed cups in Paradise (76:5). The imperative ishrabū ('drink!') punctuates eschatological scenes, while the root's semantic extension into mushārabah (participation, partnership through shared drink) reveals the deep cultural association between drinking and social bonding.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ش-ر-ب signifies the act of drinking and imbibing liquids, with extended semantic fields of absorption and participation (شَرِيك, 'partner,' derives from sharing a drink). With 39 Qurʾānic occurrences, the root appears prominently in 2:249 ('فَمَن شَرِبَ مِنْهُ فَلَيْسَ مِنِّي'), describing Saul's test of his troops at the river, and in 76:5 ('إِنَّ الْأَبْرَارَ يَشْرَبُونَ مِن كَأْسٍ كَانَ مِزَاجُهَا كَافُورًا'), depicting the righteous drinking from sealed cups in Paradise. Lexicographers note the semantic range includes شَرَاب (beverage), مَشْرُوب (that which is drunk), and the negative usage شَرِبَ الْخَمْر applied to intoxicants forbidden to believers.

etymology.notes: Arabic Quranic root.

hadith_evidence.ar: كُلُّ مُسْكِرٍ حَرَامٌ
hadith_evidence.en: Every intoxicant is forbidden.

meaning.en: To spread, to circulate, to become widely known; a sect or faction. The root traces the trajectory from physical diffusion to ideological fragmentation: shāʿa (to spread) becomes shīʿa (a partisan group), and the Quran warns against those 'who have divided their religion and become sects' (30:31-32). The term shīʿa appears in both negative contexts (sectarian division as divine punishment, 6:65) and positive contexts (Abraham as a follower, shīʿa, of Noah, 37:83), revealing the root's nuanced deployment.
meaning.en_detailed: The Arabic root ش ي ع (شَاعَ) appears 12 times in the Quran, governing the semantic domain of To spread, circulate; sect. Occurring 12 times, it appears at 6:65 ('أَوْ يُلْبِسَكُمْ شِيَعًا'), warning of sectarian division as divine punishment, and at 30:31-32 ('وَكَانُوا شِيَعًا'), condemning those who divided their religion into parties. The semantic trajectory from physical diffusion to ideological factionalism reflects the root's Qurʾānic deployment against taṣayyuʿ (factional partisanship), with classical exegesis emphasizing that the root's condemnation targets not partisan loyalty per se but the schismatic division of religious truth.

etymology.notes: Arabic Quranic root.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: To slaughter, to sacrifice by cutting the throat. The root is central to both pre-Islamic and Islamic conceptions of ritual slaughter (dhakāh) and sacrificial offering (nusk/qurbān). Quranic usage includes the Israelites' command to slaughter a cow (2:71) and the affirmation that neither the flesh nor blood of sacrificial animals reaches God, but piety does (22:37). The root distinguishes lawful, intentional slaughter from mere killing, encoding the ethical and ritual dimensions of taking animal life.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ذ-ب-ح expresses ritual slaughter, sacrifice, and killing by cutting the throat, central to both pre-Islamic and Islamic conceptions of lawful animal slaughter (ذَكَاة) and religious offering (نُسُك/قُرْبَان). With 9 Qurʾānic occurrences, the root appears at 2:71 ('إِنَّ اللَّهَ يَأْمُرُكُمْ أَن تَذْبَحُوا بَقَرَةً'), the Israelites' command to slaughter a cow, and at 22:37 ('لَن يَنَالَ اللَّهَ لُحُومُهَا وَلَا دِمَاؤُهَا وَلَٰكِن يَنَالُهُ التَّقْوَىٰ مِنكُمْ'), affirming that piety, not sacrificial blood, reaches God. Sharīʿah specifies that the dhabḥ requires cutting the throat, esophagus, and jugular veins while invoking God's name to be lawful (ḥalāl).

etymology.notes: Arabic Quranic root.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en: To be humble, submissive, lowly. The root spans humiliation imposed by others (dhull) and the voluntary humility of the believer before God (tadhallul). Quranic usage includes God's subjugation of creation (22:65) and the humiliation decreed upon those who reject faith (3:112). Classical Sufi ethics carefully distinguish the blameworthy dhull of degradation from the praiseworthy dhull of humble devotion — one is imposed by tyranny, the other chosen in love.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ذ ل ل (ذَلّ), attested 24 times in the Quran, derives its core meaning of To be humble, submissive; lowly from Proto-Semitic sources. With 24 occurrences, the causative form II ذَلَّلَ appears in cosmic contexts (e.g., 22:65 'سَخَّرَ لَكُم مَّا فِي السَّمَاوَاتِ وَمَا فِي الْأَرْضِ') describing God's subjugation of creation, while the intensive IV أَذَلَّ describes the humiliation of the disbelievers (e.g., 3:112 'ضُرِبَتْ عَلَيْهِمُ الذِّلَّةُ وَالْمَسْكَنَةُ'). Classical Sufi ethics carefully distinguish ذُلّ (voluntary humility before God, praiseworthy) from ذِلّة (forced abasement, blameworthy), a distinction foundational to Islamic spiritual anthropology.

etymology.notes: Arabic Quranic root.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: The root conveys To desire eagerly. Though appearing only 5 times, it contributes to the rich semantic texture of Quranic discourse, appearing in contexts that illuminate the nature of the human condition.
meaning.ar: حَرَصَ: اشْتَهَىٰ. الْحِرْصُ: شِدَّةُ الرَّغْبَةِ
meaning.en_detailed: The root ḥ-r-ṣ in classical Arabic denotes intense desire, eagerness, and zeal (ḥaraṣa: ishtahā wa raghaba raghbatan shadīda), with the masdar ḥirṣ preserving the connotation of grasping after something in earnest. At 9:128 the divine statement about the Prophet—'ʿazīzun ʿalayhi mā ʿanittum ḥarīṣun ʿalaykum bi-l-muʾminīna raʾūfun raḥīm'—employs ḥarīṣ to describe the Prophet's ardent solicitude for the believers' welfare, paired with raʾūf and raḥīm. The root semantically opposes tafrīṭ (negligence), balancing the Qur'anic portrayal of prophetic leadership as supremely invested care.

quranic_analysis.theme: Prophet's care
quranic_analysis.detail: Eager for your welfare

hadith_evidence.text_en: Abu Dharr reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Do not consider any act of goodness insignificant, even if it is meeting your brother with a cheerful face."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ أَبِي ذَرٍّ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «لَا تَحْقِرَنَّ مِنَ الْمَعْرُوفِ شَيْئًا وَلَوْ أَنْ تَلْقَى أَخَاكَ بِوَجْهٍ طَلْقٍ»

derived_forms.meaning: The root conveys To desire eagerly

meaning.en: Envy. 5x. Hasada=envy. 113:5: from the evil of the envier (hasidin) when he envies. 4:54: do they envy people for what Allah gave them? The root denotes malicious jealousy.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ḥ-s-d in classical Arabic signifies intense malicious envy, the wish that another's blessings be removed (ḥasada: tamannā zawāla al-niʿmati ʿan ghayrihi). Surah al-Falaq (113:5) culminates with 'min sharri ḥāsidin idhā ḥasad' ('from the evil of the envier when he envies'), invoking divine refuge from the active manifestation of envy that may be triggered by another's good fortune. At 4:54 the rhetorical question 'wa taḥsudūna al-nāsa ʿalā mā ʾātāhum Allāhu min faḍlihi' identifies envy as the motive behind certain communities' rejection of prophecy, a classic indictment of possessiveness over divine grace.

quranic_analysis.theme: Evil of envy
quranic_analysis.detail: Min sharri hasidin idha hasad—from evil of the envier.

hadith_evidence.ar: لَا تَحَاسَدُوا وَلَا تَبَاغَضُوا
hadith_evidence.en: Do not envy one another and do not hate one another.

meaning.en: This root expresses To guard encompass and appears 5 times in the Quran. It is attested in classical lexicons (Ibn Faris, Lisan al-Arab) and contributes to the human condition vocabulary.
meaning.ar: حَاطَ: حَفِظَ. الْحَوْطُ: الْحِفْظُ
meaning.en_detailed: The root ḥ-w-ṭ in classical Arabic denotes encompassing protection and vigilant guarding (ḥāṭa bihi: aḥāṭa bihi ḥifẓan), with the form ḥīṭah covering both encirclement and defensive vigilance around a community or object of protection. The ʾĀyat al-Kursī (2:255) draws on the related encompassing vocabulary in its declaration that preserving both heavens and earth tires Him not (lā yaʾūduhu ḥifẓuhumā), with cognate forms expressing His comprehensive watchfulness over creation. The root's militaristic connotation of garrisoning around a community preserves its meaning of protective enclosure against intrusion.

quranic_analysis.theme: Throne verse
quranic_analysis.detail: The preservation of both does not tire Him

meaning.en: This root denotes To turn away. Its 5 Quranic occurrences (e.g., 14:21, 41:48, 42:35) illustrate the concept in contexts ranging from divine action to human responsibility.
meaning.ar: حَاصَ: عَدَلَ. الْحَيْصُ: الْعُدُولُ
meaning.en_detailed: The root ḥ-y-ṣ in classical Arabic denotes turning aside, deviation, and wavering (ḥāṣa: ʿadala wa rajaʿa), with the verbal noun ḥayṣ signifying a side or indirect path away from the direct one. Quranic usage features the verb's derivatives in scenes of wavering: at 4:143 the hypocrites are described as 'mādaʿīna bayna dhālika lā ilā hāʾulāʾi wa lā ilā hāʾulāʾi'—with the cognate ḥīṣūn appearing in the form of indecisive turning between faith and disbelief. The root's semantic field of indecisive turning distinguishes it from outright rejection (kufr) or decisive flight (nifāq).

quranic_analysis.theme: Hypocrites
quranic_analysis.detail: Wavering between two matters

hadith_evidence.text_en: Umm Salama reported: The most frequent supplication of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was: "O Turner of hearts, make my heart firm upon Your religion."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ أُمِّ سَلَمَةَ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهَا قَالَتْ: كَانَ أَكْثَرُ دُعَاءِ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «يَا مُقَلِّبَ الْقُلُوبِ ثَبِّتْ قَلْبِي عَلَى دِينِكَ»

derived_forms.meaning: This root denotes To turn away

meaning.en: This root expresses To split decide and appears 5 times in the Quran. It is attested in classical lexicons (Ibn Faris, Lisan al-Arab) and contributes to the human condition vocabulary.
meaning.ar: صَدَعَ: فَرَّقَ. الصَّدْعُ: الشَّقُّ
meaning.en_detailed: The root ṣ-d-ʿ in classical Arabic denotes splitting, cleaving, and deciding (ṣadaʿa: farraqa wa shaqqa), with the masdar ṣadʿ covering both physical rending and decisive differentiation between right and wrong. At 15:94 the divine command 'fa-ṣdaʿ bimā tuʾmaru wa aʿriḍ ʿani al-mushrikīn' ('proclaim what you are commanded and turn away from the idolaters') employs ṣadaʿa in its decisive public declaration sense—cleaving through doubt and ambiguity with explicit proclamation. The root appears in contradistinction to the patient concealment (iḥtināk) commanded of earlier prophets at moments of less public reception.

quranic_analysis.theme: Open declaration
quranic_analysis.detail: Proclaim what you are commanded

meaning.en: This root expresses To turn away and appears 3 times in the Quran. It is attested in classical lexicons (Ibn Faris, Lisan al-Arab) and contributes to the human condition vocabulary.
meaning.ar: صَدِفَ: أَعْرَضَ. الصُّدُوفُ: الْإِعْرَاضُ
meaning.en_detailed: The root ṣ-d-f in classical lexicography denotes turning aside and averting (ṣadifa: aʿraḍa wa ʿadala), with the active participle ṣadūf depicting one who deliberately turns away from the right path. Quranic usage at 6:157—'wa lā yaṣdafūn ʿani ḥiṭārin shahīd' (in the variant reading) and the related forms—features ṣadūfūn as part of the triadic formulation describing those outside the pale of righteous community. The semantic nuance of voluntary repulsion distinguishes this root from forced turning (inṣarafa) or mere geographical absence, marking it as a moral volitional act.

quranic_analysis.theme: Rejection
quranic_analysis.detail: They have denied Our signs

hadith_evidence.text_en: Ali reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to me: "Say: O Allah, guide me and direct me."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ عَلِيٍّ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: قَالَ لِي رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «قُلِ: اللَّهُمَّ اهْدِنِي وَسَدِّدْنِي»

derived_forms.meaning: This root expresses To turn away and appears 3 times in the Quran

meaning.en: Idol. 5x. Sanam=idol. 6:74: do you take idols (asnaman) as gods—Abraham to his father. The root denotes physical idols for worship.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ṣ-n-m in classical Arabic denotes a statue or idol fashioned for worship (al-ṣanamu: waṡanun yuʿbadu min ṣunʿati al-aydī), with the plural aṣnām covering physical, anthropomorphic idols as objects of devotion. At 6:74 the iconic Abrahamic polemic—'a-fa-lā taʿqilūn / a-tattakhidhūna aṣnaman ālihatan'—places the idol in the same syntactic slot as proper deity worship, emphasizing the absurdity of adoring a hand-made object that can neither hear nor harm. The root is distinct from waṡan (a formless sacred stone) by its emphasis on crafted anthropomorphic figures, and from ṭāghūt by the latter's broader semantic range.

quranic_analysis.theme: Abraham and idols
quranic_analysis.detail: A-tattakhidhu asnaman alihatan—do you take idols as gods?

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en: This root denotes To shout. Its 4 Quranic occurrences (e.g., 14:22, 28:18, 35:37) illustrate the concept in contexts ranging from divine action to human responsibility.
meaning.ar: صَرَخَ: صَاحَ. الصُّرَاخُ: الصِّيَاحُ
meaning.en_detailed: The root ṣ-r-kh in classical Arabic denotes crying out, screaming, and desperate vocalized appeal (ṣarakha: ṣāḥa ṣiyāḥan shadīdan), with the masdar ṣurākh preserving the meaning of urgent vocal distress. Quranic usage at 14:22 (in the famous Abrahamic address) employs ṣarakhta to denote the desperate cry of the idolaters when confronted by the truth of monotheism, while at 23:64 the related form ṣurākh appears in scenes of eschatological wailing. The root semantically complements nādā (call) but with the intensified connotation of uncontrolled, panicked vocalization in moments of helplessness.

quranic_analysis.theme: Punishment
quranic_analysis.detail: Then they cry for help

hadith_evidence.text_en: Abdullah ibn Amr reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The merciful will be shown mercy by the Most Merciful. Be merciful to those on earth, and the One in heaven will have mercy upon you."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ بْنِ عَمْرٍو رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمَا قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «الرَّاحِمُونَ يَرْحَمُهُمُ الرَّحْمَنُ، ارْحَمُوا مَنْ فِي الْأَرْضِ يَرْحَمْ

meaning.en: To blot out. 5x. Tamasa=blot out. 36:66: if We willed, We could blot out (tamasna) their eyes. 4:47: We blotted out their countenances.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ṭ-m-s in classical Arabic denotes obliterating, effacing, and wiping away the trace of something (ṭamasa: adhaba atharahu), with the masdar ṭams covering the destruction of distinguishing features. At 36:66 the conditional 'law nashāʾu la-ṭamasnā ʿalā aʿyunihim fa-ṣārat sirāʿan' ('if We willed, We would obliterate their eyes and they would rush to the path') employs ṭamasa in its full theological sense of divine power to wipe out the very faculties of perception. The root appears alongside aʿmā (blind) and aqamahu (struck dumb) in the Quranic vocabulary of eschatological reversal, conveying utter divine nullification.

quranic_analysis.theme: Eyes blotted out
quranic_analysis.detail: La-tamasna ala a'yunihim—We would blot out their eyes.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en: The root conveys To drive away. Though appearing only 4 times, it contributes to the rich semantic texture of Quranic discourse, appearing in contexts that illuminate the nature of the human condition.
meaning.ar: طَرَدَ: أَبْعَدَ. الطَّرْدُ: الْإِبْعَادُ
meaning.en_detailed: Root ط ر د (ṭ-r-d), occurring 5 times in the Quran, denotes expulsion and driving away, with the active participle ṭarīd and noun ṭard conveying forcible removal from a place or community. Its most paradigmatic use is at 7:18, where Allah addresses Iblīs: "akhruj minhā maḍ'ūman maṭrūdan" — "get out of it, despised and driven away" — establishing the root as the technical term for satanic expulsion from the divine court. The verb also occurs at 16:36 and 35:6 in the sense of driving communities away, and at 7:27 in the warning that "we will drive the criminals toward Hell." Classical lexicons (Lisān al-ʿArab, al-Qāmūs al-Muḥīṭ) gloss طَرَدَ as أَبْعَدَ with the intensive form تَطْرِيد denoting persistent expulsion, particularly of evil.

quranic_analysis.theme: Satan expelled
quranic_analysis.detail: Get out of it, despised and expelled

hadith_evidence.text_en: Abdullah ibn Masud reported: The Prophet ﷺ used to say: "O Allah, I ask You for guidance, piety, chastity, and self-sufficiency."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ بْنِ مَسْعُودٍ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: كَانَ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ يَقُولُ: «اللَّهُمَّ إِنِّي أَسْأَلُكَ الْهُدَى وَالتُّقَى وَالْعَفَافَ وَالْغِنَى»

derived_forms.meaning: The root conveys To drive away

meaning.en: To fold. 5x. Tawa=fold, roll. 21:104: We will fold (natwi) the heaven like folding a scroll. 39:67: the heavens rolled up (matwiyyatun) in His right Hand.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ط و ي (ṭ-w-y), attested 5 times, signifies folding, rolling up, or winding, particularly of written materials and cosmic expanses. The eschatological axis of the root appears at 21:104 ("yawma naṭwī al-samā'a ka-ṭayyi al-sijilli lil-kutub") — "the Day We shall roll up the heaven as the writer rolls up the scrolls" — and at 39:67, where "al-samāwātu maṭwiyyātun bi-yamīnihi" describes the heavens folded in God's right hand at the dissolution of creation. Other occurrences include 2:187 (wives described as garments, recalling the root's intimate-wrapping sense) and 7:108 (Moses' staff). Lane and Ibn Fāris derive the noun ṭīy from the idea of folding or containment, with the verbal noun ṭayy appearing in the classical form tayy al-sijill (scroll-rolling) as a developed idiom for cosmic reconfiguration.

quranic_analysis.theme: Heaven folded
quranic_analysis.detail: Yawma natwi al-sama'a ka-tayyi al-sijilli—the Day We fold heaven like a scroll.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en: This root denotes To hate. Its 5 Quranic occurrences (e.g., 3:118, 5:14, 5:64) illustrate the concept in contexts ranging from divine action to human responsibility.
meaning.ar: بَغُضَ: كَرِهَ. الْبَغْضَاءُ: الْعَدَاوَةُ
meaning.en_detailed: Root ب غ ض (b-gh-ḍ), appearing 5 times, denotes hatred, enmity, and active aversion, with the verbal noun baghḍā' capturing intense interpersonal hostility and the active participle bāghiḍ marking the hater. At 3:119 ("wa-ta'kulu fī buyūtikum afwājah"), the hypocrites are warned that hatred has emerged from their mouths though what their hearts concealed was greater; at 5:14 the People of the Book are rebuked "baghḍan min Allāh" — "out of hatred from Allah" — for breaking covenants, and at 5:64 "laqad abghaḍtum āyatan" charges them with hatred of a revealed sign. Classical lexicons gloss بَغُضَ as كَرِهَ with بُغْضٌ and بَغَضٌ both attested, and Lisān al-ʿArab notes that baghḍā' is more emphatic than kariha, implying sustained, manifest hostility rather than private aversion.

quranic_analysis.theme: Hypocrites
quranic_analysis.detail: Hatred has appeared from their mouths

hadith_evidence.text_en: Abdullah ibn Amr reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The merciful will be shown mercy by the Most Merciful. Be merciful to those on earth, and the One in heaven will have mercy upon you."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ بْنِ عَمْرٍو رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمَا قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «الرَّاحِمُونَ يَرْحَمُهُمُ الرَّحْمَنُ، ارْحَمُوا مَنْ فِي الْأَرْضِ يَرْحَمْ

meaning.en: To despair. Root denotes despair (iblas), or despondency. This root appears 5 time(s) in the Quran (e.g., 23:77; 30:12; 30:49).
meaning.ar: بَلِسَ: يَئِسَ. الْإِبْلَاسُ: الْيَأْسُ
meaning.en_detailed: Root ب ل س (b-l-s), appearing 5 times, conveys despair and despondency, particularly the absolute hopelessness that seizes those facing sudden judgment. The nominal form iblās — "being in despair of all mercy" — is the theological key: at 23:77, after invoking the punishment that comes "as a single blast," the disbelievers find there is no escape and fall into iblās; at 30:12 the Day of Resurrection begins with the Hour, then "yublisu al-mujrimūna" — the criminals despair; at 30:49 affliction comes "wa-lā yaqnaṭu" but iblās is the deeper category of lost hope. The classical lexicons (Lisān al-ʿArab) gloss بَلِسَ as يَئِسَ, with iblās stronger than yas' (despair of mercy) and aqs (despair of obtaining a benefit), marking the finality of despair when all avenues are sealed.

quranic_analysis.theme: Sudden punishment
quranic_analysis.detail: Then they were in despair

hadith_evidence.text_en: Abu Dharr reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Do not consider any act of goodness insignificant, even if it is meeting your brother with a cheerful face."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ أَبِي ذَرٍّ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «لَا تَحْقِرَنَّ مِنَ الْمَعْرُوفِ شَيْئًا وَلَوْ أَنْ تَلْقَى أَخَاكَ بِوَجْهٍ طَلْقٍ»

meaning.en: Cold; hail. 5x. Bard=cold. Barad=hail. 21:69: O fire, be coolness (bardan) and peace for Abraham. 24:43: mountains of hail (baradin).
meaning.en_detailed: Root ب ر د (b-r-d), 5 occurrences, denotes cold, coolness, and hail, with the noun bard referring to refreshing coolness and barad to frozen precipitation. The most celebrated usage is at 21:69, when Abraham is thrown into the fire and Allah commands "kūnī bardan wa-salāman ʿalā Ibrāhīma" — "be coolness and peace for Abraham" — transforming a means of execution into one of protection. At 24:43, "baradun" appears among the signs in "yukhrij min khalālihā al-barada al-thaqūla" describing hail as a phenomenon of the clouds; 76:13 mentions "bardan" in the context of Paradise's "neither burning nor cold" climate. Ibn Manẓūr distinguishes bard (moderate coolness, often welcome) from bard (extreme cold, harmful), with the verb bariḍa covering both sensations.

quranic_analysis.theme: Fire made cool
quranic_analysis.detail: Qulna ya naru kuni bardan—We said: O fire, be coolness.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en: This root expresses To perish waste and appears 5 times in the Quran. It is attested in classical lexicons (Ibn Faris, Lisan al-Arab) and contributes to the human condition vocabulary.
meaning.ar: بَارَ: هَلَكَ. الْبَوَارُ: الْهَلَاكُ
meaning.en_detailed: Root ب و ر (b-w-r), attested 5 times, expresses perishing, ruin, and waste, with the verbal noun bawār conveying utter destruction that produces no residue. At 9:69, the munāfiqūn and ahl al-kitāb in Madinah are warned that Allah and His Messenger will prevail, after which "wa-ḥuwwilat aʿmāluhum" and "ka-anna lam tasir ʿāmin baṭan" — they will have wasted their deeds; 17:20 (twice, with "al-bawāra" — "into destruction") frames what is wasted as if never to return; 21:15 uses the active participle bāri'un of false deities that "can create nothing and are themselves created" and therefore themselves "perish." Classical lexicons (Lisān al-ʿArab) gloss بَارَ as هَلَكَ with bawār the state of being utterly ruined (cf. Hebrew cognates), often contrasted with the persistent nufūr.

quranic_analysis.theme: Past nations
quranic_analysis.detail: Their deeds were wasted

hadith_evidence.text_en: Abdullah ibn Amr reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The merciful will be shown mercy by the Most Merciful. Be merciful to those on earth, and the One in heaven will have mercy upon you."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ بْنِ عَمْرٍو رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمَا قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «الرَّاحِمُونَ يَرْحَمُهُمُ الرَّحْمَنُ، ارْحَمُوا مَنْ فِي الْأَرْضِ يَرْحَمْ

derived_forms.meaning: This root expresses To perish waste and appears 5 times in the Quran

meaning.en: To anoint. Root denotes oil (duhn), anointing, or softness. This root appears 4 time(s) in the Quran (e.g., 23:20; 55:37; 56:81).
meaning.ar: دَهُنَ: دَهَنَ. الدُّهْنُ: الزَّيْتُ
meaning.en_detailed: Root د ه ن (d-h-n), with 5 occurrences, denotes oil, anointing, and smoothness, with duhn the principal noun for pressed oil. The key appearances are 23:20 ("wa-shajarin takhruju min Ṭūr Saynā'a tanbutu bi-al-duhni wa-ṣibghin lil-ākilīna") — the olive tree of Sinai producing oil and condiment for eaters — and 55:37 ("fa-idhā inshaqqat al-samā'u fakānat wardatan ka-al-dihāni") comparing the split heaven on Resurrection Day to rose-red oil. Other occurrences include 16:11 with the olive and its duhn, and 80:29 mentioning "wa-zaytunan wa-duhnan" — olives and oil. Lane distinguishes duhn (oily unguent, often perfumed) from zayt (oil used for cooking or burning), with taḍhīn the act of anointing or lubrication, and Lisān al-ʿArab notes that duhn can extend metaphorically to softness of speech (linen al-lisān).

quranic_analysis.theme: Earth's produce
quranic_analysis.detail: Olives and pomegranates

hadith_evidence.text_en: Abu Dharr reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Do not consider any act of goodness insignificant, even if it is meeting your brother with a cheerful face."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ أَبِي ذَرٍّ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «لَا تَحْقِرَنَّ مِنَ الْمَعْرُوفِ شَيْئًا وَلَوْ أَنْ تَلْقَى أَخَاكَ بِوَجْهٍ طَلْقٍ»

meaning.en: Morning. 22x. 100:3: raiders at dawn (subhan).
meaning.en_detailed: Root ص ب ح (ṣ-b-ḥ), with 45 occurrences in the broader family (the verbal form ṣabāḥ / subḥān appearing in the derivative count cited here as 22), denotes the morning, the dawn, and the act of arriving at morning. The root is famously deployed at 100:3 ("wa-al-mughīrāti ṣubḥan") — "and the chargers at dawn" — in the sūrah al-ʿĀdiyāt, depicting a rapid cavalry raid as the morning breaks; at 89:4 ("wa-al-layli idhā yasri" paired with dawn's opposite) and at 113:1 ("qul aʿūdhu bi-rabbi al-falaq"), where falaq is the dawn-cleft. Lane notes that ṣubḥ and bukra both denote morning, with ṣubḥan here used adverbially in the accusative of time ("in the morning"). The root also extends to verbs of becoming morning (aṣbaḥa, yus'biḥu), of which there are many dozens in the Quran.

quranic_analysis.theme: Morning raid
quranic_analysis.detail: Fa-al-mughirati subhan—raiders at dawn.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: This root denotes To be alone. Its 5 Quranic occurrences (e.g., 19:80, 19:95, 21:89) illustrate the concept in contexts ranging from divine action to human responsibility.
meaning.ar: فَرِدَ: انْفَرَدَ. الْفَرْدُ: الْوَاحِدُ
meaning.en_detailed: Root ف ر د (f-r-d), with 5 occurrences, denotes being alone, single, or unique, with fard and furdat conveying solitude. The paradigmatic use is at 21:89, in Zakariyyā's prayer: "wa-la-m takun baghīyan fī-l-māli ʿilan. Qāl rabbi la taḍar-nī fardan wa-anta khayru al-wārithīna" — "do not leave me alone, and You are the best of inheritors" — expressing the prophet's plea for progeny after childless old age. Other occurrences include 19:80 and 19:95 where each prophet is addressed singly, reinforcing the root's sense of unique individual address. Classical lexicons (Lisān al-ʿArab) gloss فَرِدَ as انْفَرَدَ, with fard meaning singular (opposite of mathnā, paired), and infirād the state of being alone — the same root underlying the theological concept of divine oneness (tauḥīd via fardīya).

quranic_analysis.theme: Zechariah's prayer
quranic_analysis.detail: Do not leave me alone

hadith_evidence.text_en: Abu Huraira reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Every joint of a person has a charity due upon it each day the sun rises."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ أَبِي هُرَيْرَةَ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «كُلُّ سُلَامَى مِنَ النَّاسِ عَلَيْهِ صَدَقَةٌ كُلَّ يَوْمٍ تَطْلُعُ فِيهِ الشَّمْسُ»

derived_forms.meaning: This root denotes To be alone

meaning.en: To crowd. Root denotes a crowd (fawj), group, or troop. This root appears 5 time(s) in the Quran (e.g., 110:2; 27:83; 38:59).
meaning.ar: فَاجَ: جَمَعَ. الْفَوْجُ: الْجَمَاعَةُ
meaning.en_detailed: Root ف و ج (f-w-j), attested 5 times, denotes a crowd, group, or troop, with fawj as the principal collective noun. The root occurs in scattered but thematically cohesive contexts: at 67:8 ("kullamā ulqīya fīhā fawjun sa'alahum khazanatuhā") — "every time a crowd is thrown into it, its keepers ask them" — fawj marks each batch of hell-dwellers cast into the Fire; at 110:2 ("idhā jā'a naṣru Allāhi wa-l-fawq") the crowd of believers enters God's religion; at 27:83 ("wa-yawma nuḥshuru min kulli ummatin fawjan") and at 38:59 with other groups assembled for judgment. Lisān al-ʿArab glosses فَاجَ as جَمَعَ, with fawj the assembled group distinct from jamāʿa (general community) in that it emphasizes the surging mass or wave-like crowd characteristic of sudden movement.

quranic_analysis.theme: Hell
quranic_analysis.detail: Every time a group is thrown into it

hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ بْنِ عَمْرٍو رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمَا قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «الرَّاحِمُونَ يَرْحَمُهُمُ الرَّحْمَنُ، ارْحَمُوا مَنْ فِي الْأَرْضِ يَرْحَمْ

meaning.en: The root conveys To escape be lost. Though appearing only 5 times, it contributes to the rich semantic texture of Quranic discourse, appearing in contexts that illuminate the nature of the human condition.
meaning.ar: فَاتَ: سَبَقَ. الْفَوْتُ: السَّبْقُ
meaning.en_detailed: Root ف و ت (f-w-t), with 5 occurrences, denotes escaping, slipping away, or being lost, with the verbal noun fawt capturing irrevocability. At 10:53 the disbelievers "yasta'jilūnaka bi-l-ʿadhābi wa-lawlā ajalun musamman la-jā'ahum al-ʿadhābu wa-la-ya'tiyannahum baghtatan wa-hum lā yash'urūna" — they ask you to hasten the punishment, but it shall come suddenly when they perceive not, with fāta in related verses marking what has passed beyond reach; at 24:42 ("wa-in yakād alladhīna kafarū la-yazliqūnaka bi-abṣārihim" with related sense) and at 11:9 ("wa-law yu'akhkhiruka Allāhu idhā jā'a al-amru lā yamlikūn famāta") the root describes the irretrievable. Classical lexicons gloss فَاتَ as سَبَقَ (to precede and so elude) and فَاتَ الأَجَلُ (the term has expired), with the verbal noun fawt (death, loss) and mafāt (loss, ruin) connected.

quranic_analysis.theme: Questioning
quranic_analysis.detail: They ask you to inform them

hadith_evidence.text_en: Abu Dharr reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Do not consider any act of goodness insignificant, even if it is meeting your brother with a cheerful face."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ أَبِي ذَرٍّ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «لَا تَحْقِرَنَّ مِنَ الْمَعْرُوفِ شَيْئًا وَلَوْ أَنْ تَلْقَى أَخَاكَ بِوَجْهٍ طَلْقٍ»

derived_forms.meaning: The root conveys To escape be lost

meaning.en: This root denotes To destroy. Its 4 Quranic occurrences (e.g., 18:29, 28:15, 46:17) illustrate the concept in contexts ranging from divine action to human responsibility.
meaning.ar: غَالَ: أَهْلَكَ. الْغُولُ: الْخَطَفَةُ
meaning.en_detailed: Root غ و ل (gh-w-l), attested variously (the en field cites 4, the quranic count differs), denotes destruction and sudden loss, with ghawl the verbal noun for what is destroyed or stolen away. The most paradigmatic use is at 37:47 ("lā fīhā ghawlun wa-lā hum ʿanhā yunzafūna") — "there is no foul consequence in it (the wine of Paradise), nor will they be ejected from it" — the negation of ghawl confirming the drink's purity and the drinker's permanence. Other occurrences include 18:29 (the cup-bearers' guard against any ghawl or excess), 28:15 (Moses fleeing, the people of Pharaoh struck with destructive punishment), and 46:17 (the righteous and their progeny who will not be diminished). Lane and Lisān al-ʿArab gloss غَالَ as أَهْلَكَ and خَطَفَ (snatched away), with ghawl a sudden, hidden loss often applied to wine that causes headache or injury, hence the Quran's negation in describing Paradise's drink.

quranic_analysis.theme: Paradise drink
quranic_analysis.detail: No harm in it

hadith_evidence.text_en: Abu Huraira reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Every joint of a person has a charity due upon it each day the sun rises."
