meaning.en: Crescent moon; to praise. 5x. Hillal=crescent moon. 2:189: they ask about the new moons (al-ahillah). Tahallala=to praise—la ilaha illa Allah.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ه ل ل (h-l-l), with 5 occurrences, denotes the crescent moon and the act of praising (notably via the talhīl 'lā ilāha illā Allāh'), with ahilla (plural of hilāl) being the new crescents. At 2:189 ("yas'alūnaka ʿani al-ahillati qul hiya mawāqītu li-l-nāsi wa-l-ḥajji") — "they ask you about the new crescents; say, they are timings for the people and the pilgrimage" — the root establishes lunar time-keeping for worship. Other occurrences include the talhīl sense in 24:36 (sabbīḥ lahu, subḥān Allāh, declaring God's purity) and 76:26 ("wa-min al-layli fa-sabbiḥhu wa-adhbāri al-nujūm" — "from the night and at the fading of the stars") and the well-known hadith prohibition against fasting on the yawm al-shakk (day of doubt). Lane distinguishes hilāl (the slender crescent, visible from sunset) from hilāl used of the first two or three nights of the month, when the new moon rises.

quranic_analysis.theme: New moons
quranic_analysis.detail: Yas'alunaka ani al-ahillati—they ask about new moons.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en: To shake. 5x. Hazza=shake. 19:25: shake (huzzi) the trunk of the palm tree—Maryam. 3:152: He shook them (hazzakum) until—Uhud.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ه ز ز (h-z-z), with 5 occurrences, denotes shaking, agitation, and disturbance, with the doubled middle radical emphasizing intensity. The most celebrated use is at 19:25 ("wa-huzzī ilayki bi-jiḍḥi al-nakhlati tusāqiṭ ʿalayki ruṭaban junayyā") — "and shake toward you the trunk of the palm tree; it will drop ripe dates upon you" — the angel Jibrīl's instruction to Maryam in childbirth. Other occurrences include 3:152, where Allah reminds the believers at Uḥud: "wa-la-qad ʿasākum qarīḥun laqad ʿasākum ba'dahu l-ladhīna ʿalaykum wa-hum hazza-kum" — "He shook you with a blow" — at the battle's tumultuous reversal; 16:47 ("lam yazilzāl bi-l-khayri"); 17:92 (challenging to topple heaven); and 21:18 (men and jinn unable to pierce God's scheme). Lisān al-ʿArab glosses هَزَّ as حَرَّكَ, with the doubled radical marking intense, sudden motion.

quranic_analysis.theme: Shake the palm
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa huzzi ilayki bi-jidh'i al-nakhlati—shake the trunk of the palm.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en: This root denotes To reveal. Its 5 Quranic occurrences (e.g., 59:3, 7:143, 7:187) illustrate the concept in contexts ranging from divine action to human responsibility.
meaning.ar: جَلَا: أَظْهَرَ. التَّجْلِيَةُ: الْإِيضَاحُ
meaning.en_detailed: Root ج ل و (j-l-w), with 5 occurrences, denotes revealing, unveiling, and manifesting, with tajallī (theophanic unveiling) the famous derived form in Sufi theology. At 7:143 ("wa-lammā jā'a Mūsā li-mīqātinā wa-kallama-hu rabbi qul rabbi ar-nī anẓur ilayka qāla lan tarānī wa-lākinin unẓur ilā al-jibali fa-in istaqarra maqāma-hu fa-sawfa tarānī") — Moses asks to see Allah, who responds by unveiling (yatajallā) to the mountain; the mountain crumbles and Moses falls unconscious — the root captures the divine self-disclosure. At 7:187 the Hour's revelation to humans is questioned, and at 59:3 ("law ākharunā ilā ajalin qarībin") the root appears in the sense of making clear. Ibn Fāris and Lane gloss جَلَا as أَظْهَرَ, with tajallī the theological term (Q 7:143) for divine unveiling, distinct from ẓuhūr (mere appearance) in its overwhelming character.

quranic_analysis.theme: Question about Hour
quranic_analysis.detail: An asker asked for a punishment to occur

hadith_evidence.text_en: Abu Dharr reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Do not consider any act of goodness insignificant, even if it is meeting your brother with a cheerful face."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ أَبِي ذَرٍّ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «لَا تَحْقِرَنَّ مِنَ الْمَعْرُوفِ شَيْئًا وَلَوْ أَنْ تَلْقَى أَخَاكَ بِوَجْهٍ طَلْقٍ»

meaning.en: To blame, to censure, to dispraise. The root stands as the direct antonym to ḥamd (praise), with the active participle dhamīm naming one who is blameworthy and the verbal noun madhamma designating the state of being censured. With only 5 Quranic occurrences — reflecting the Quran's preference for active ethical exhortation over mere dispraise — the root appears in contrasting the praiseworthy and the blameworthy, and in warning against earning divine reproach through hypocrisy.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ذ-م-م expresses blame, censure, and dispraise, standing as the antonymic counterpart to ح-م-د (praise), with the active participle ذَمِيم and verbal noun مَذَمَّة denoting the state of being censured. With only 5 Qurʾānic occurrences—a fact reflecting the Qurʾān's preference for active ethical framing over mere dispraise—the root appears in contexts contrasting the praiseworthy and the blameworthy, and warning against earning divine reproach through hypocrisy or betrayal. Classical lexicographers (al-Zajjāj, Ibn Fāris) note that ذَمّ implies lasting or constitutive blame, distinct from the momentary لَوْم (transient rebuke), with ذَامَّ (form III) carrying reciprocal censure.

etymology.notes: Arabic Quranic root.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en: To be hungry. Root denotes hunger (ju'). This root appears 5 time(s) in the Quran (e.g., 106:4; 16:112; 20:118).
meaning.ar: جَاعَ: جَاعَ. الْجُوعُ: الْحَاجَةُ
meaning.en_detailed: Root ج و ع (j-w-'), with 5 occurrences, denotes hunger, with jūʿ the noun for the state of being hungry. The root is theologically deployed: at 106:4 ("wa-waṣṣalnāhu bi-say'in ya'kulu-hu wa-l-jūʿa") — "and We appointed him (Quraysh's messenger) to suffer hunger" — in the sūrah al-Fīl's aftermath context, hunger is paired with fear as divine protection. At 88:7 ("lā yuṭ'imu wa-lā yughnī min jūʿin") — "neither nourishing nor of any avail against hunger" — describes the dafīʿ of the hell-dweller, and at 20:118 ("wa-in ta'ūḥ fī al-arḍi fa-laysa lakum al-jūʿu fīhi al-makhāṣu") hunger as the cost of earth-dwelling. The verb jā'a (form I) means "to be hungry," and Lane glosses جَاعَ as أَصَابَهُ الْجُوعُ, with jīʿ also attested for hunger's onset.

quranic_analysis.theme: Hell food
quranic_analysis.detail: Neither nourishing nor relieving hunger

hadith_evidence.text_en: Abdullah ibn Amr reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The merciful will be shown mercy by the Most Merciful. Be merciful to those on earth, and the One in heaven will have mercy upon you."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ بْنِ عَمْرٍو رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمَا قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «الرَّاحِمُونَ يَرْحَمُهُمُ الرَّحْمَنُ، ارْحَمُوا مَنْ فِي الْأَرْضِ يَرْحَمْ

meaning.en: The root conveys To pass. Though appearing only 5 times, it contributes to the rich semantic texture of Quranic discourse, appearing in contexts that illuminate the nature of the human condition.
meaning.ar: جَازَ: عَبَرَ. الْجَوَازُ: الْإِذْنُ
meaning.en_detailed: Root ج و ز (j-w-z), with 5 occurrences, denotes passing through, crossing, and transiting, with the verbal noun jawāz (license) and jāz (bridge). At 9:17 ("mā kāna li-l-mushrikīna an yaʿmuru masājida Allāhi shāhidīna ʿalā anfusihim bi-l-kufri ulā'ika ḥabiṭat aʿmāluhum wa-fī al-nāri hum khālidūna") — preceded by the prohibition that "the polytheists shall not maintain the mosques of Allah" — and at 4:114 ("wa-man yashfiʿ shafā'atan ḥasanatan yakun lahu naṣīb minhā" with jawāz in the sense of entitlement); also at 27:57 (the spider's web as the "weakest of houses") and 28:22 (Moses at Midian's well). Lisān al-ʿArab glosses جَازَ as عَبَرَ and سَلَكَ, with jawāz the act of lawful passing or permission (e.g., customs permit).

quranic_analysis.theme: Mosque entry
quranic_analysis.detail: It is not for the polytheists

hadith_evidence.text_en: Abu Dharr reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Do not consider any act of goodness insignificant, even if it is meeting your brother with a cheerful face."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ أَبِي ذَرٍّ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «لَا تَحْقِرَنَّ مِنَ الْمَعْرُوفِ شَيْئًا وَلَوْ أَنْ تَلْقَى أَخَاكَ بِوَجْهٍ طَلْقٍ»

meaning.en: To complete. 5x. Kamala=be complete. 5:3: today I have perfected (akmaltu) your religion. The root denotes fullness and perfection.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ك م ل (k-m-l), with 5 occurrences, denotes completeness, perfection, and totality, with the verbal noun kamāl and the active participle kāmil marking wholeness. The paradigmatic occurrence is at 5:3 ("al-yawma akmaltu lakum dīnakum wa-atmamtu ʿalaykum niʿmatī wa-raḍītu lakumu al-islāma dīnan") — "today I have perfected your religion and completed My favor upon you, and I have chosen Islam as your religion" — the verse of perfection, traditionally associated with ʿĀshūrāʾ and the Farewell Pilgrimage. Other occurrences include the active participle kāmil in 6:155 (perfect balance in the scales) and 12:6 and 12:96 (Joseph's vision and the dream as kāmil). Lisān al-ʿArab and Lane gloss كَمَلَ as تَمَّ, with ikmāl stronger (completion that has no remainder) and tamām its near-synonym in some constructions.

quranic_analysis.theme: Religion perfected
quranic_analysis.detail: Al-yawma akmaltu lakum dinakum—today I perfected your religion.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en: Eclipse; fragment. 5x. Kisaf=fragment. 34:9: pieces (kisafan) of the sky fall. 75:8: moon eclipsed (khasafa)—related sense.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ك س ف (k-s-f), with 5 occurrences, denotes eclipse and the falling of fragments, with kusūf and kisaf both attested. At 34:9 ("fa-ṣadda Allāhu ʿanhum wa-nazzalnā ʿalayhim kisafan min al-samā'i") — "so Allah turned away from them, and We dropped upon them fragments from the sky" — the punishment sent upon the Sabaʾ or against Pharaoh's people. At 81:2 ("wa-idhā al-nujūmu inkadarat") and at 75:8 ("wa-jumuʿati al-shamsu wa-l-qamar" with related form khusūf in eclipse), the root connects to cosmic disorder. Lisān al-ʿArab distinguishes kisaf (fragments broken off, as of cloud, stone, or sky) from kusūf (eclipse, specifically lunar or solar obscuration), with the verb kasafa meaning to tear away or strip a piece.

quranic_analysis.theme: Sky fragments
quranic_analysis.detail: Nusqit alayhim kisafan min al-sama'i—We drop fragments from the sky.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en: The root conveys To clothe. Though appearing only 5 times, it contributes to the rich semantic texture of Quranic discourse, appearing in contexts that illuminate the nature of the human condition.
meaning.ar: كَسَا: لَبِسَ. الْكِسْوَةُ: اللِّبَاسُ
meaning.en_detailed: Root ك س و (k-s-w), with 5 occurrences, denotes clothing, covering, and enveloping, with kiswa the noun for a garment (the Kiswa being the cloth of the Kaʿbah). At 2:197 ("wa-ṭāwirūka bi-l-arbaʿīna laylatan — wa-kisāwatu al-taqwā khayrun — wa-ta'āwunū ʿalā al-birri wa-l-taqwā") — "but righteousness is the best clothing" — the metaphor compares taqwā to a garment (libās) and kisā'a. Other occurrences include 7:26 (Adam and his wife given raiment of the Garden to cover nakedness), 7:27 (the children's clothing), and the verb in passives for clothing as endowment. Lisān al-ʿArab glosses كَسَا as لَبِسَ and أَلْبَسَ, with kiswa the visible garment and kisā'a (clothing, mantle) used for royal covering, both related to the idea of envelopment.

quranic_analysis.theme: Hajj
quranic_analysis.detail: The garment of righteousness

hadith_evidence.text_en: Abu Dharr reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Do not consider any act of goodness insignificant, even if it is meeting your brother with a cheerful face."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ أَبِي ذَرٍّ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «لَا تَحْقِرَنَّ مِنَ الْمَعْرُوفِ شَيْئًا وَلَوْ أَنْ تَلْقَى أَخَاكَ بِوَجْهٍ طَلْقٍ»

meaning.en: Star. 5x. Kawkab=star, planet. 6:76: when he saw a star (kawkaban)—Abraham's celestial contemplation. 24:35: like a pearl-like star (kawkabun durriyyun).
meaning.en_detailed: Root ك و ك ب (k-w-k-b), with 5 occurrences, denotes a star, planet, or celestial body, with kawkab the principal noun. At 6:76 ("fa-lammā rā'a kawkaban qāla hādhā rabbī fa-lammā afala qāla lā uḥibbu al-āfilīna") — "when Abraham saw a star, he said, 'This is my Lord.' But when it set, he said, 'I do not love those that set'" — the root opens the story of Abraham's disavowal of celestial worship in the sūrah al-Anʿām. At 24:35, the famous āyat al-nūr (light verse) describes divine light "ka-misḥātin fīhā miṣbāḥun al-misḥāḥu fī zujājatīn al-zujājatu ka-annahā kawkabun durriyyun yūqadu min shajaratin mubārakatin zaytūnatin" — "like a brilliant star" (lit., "a pearl-like planet") — for the radiant olive-fed lamp. Lane notes kawkab can refer to any luminous celestial body, including planets and distinguished stars, distinct from najm (star in general) and shams/qamar (sun/moon).

quranic_analysis.theme: Abraham's star
quranic_analysis.detail: Fa-lamma ra'a kawkaban—when he saw a star.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en: This root denotes To touch. Its 5 Quranic occurrences (e.g., 4:43, 57:13, 5:6) illustrate the concept in contexts ranging from divine action to human responsibility.
meaning.ar: لَمَسَ: مَسَّ. اللَّمْسُ: الْمَسُّ
meaning.en_detailed: Root ل م س (l-m-s), with 5 occurrences, denotes touching, contact, and tactile perception, with lams the verbal noun for the act of touching. At 4:43 ("aw lamastumu al-nisā'a") — "or you have touched women" — the legal term for sexual contact (a juridical cause for wuḍūʾ), sometimes interpreted as a euphemism (Lane gives this as a softened form of jimāʿ). At 57:13 ("wa-tarā al-mujrimīna yawma'idhin muqarranīna fī al-asfād. Sāriqahum wa-jū'uhum wa-lamsuhum") — "bound together in fetters, their faces, and the Fire" — lams appears as a noun for what they burned and what they touched. Lisān al-ʿArab distinguishes lams (touching without penetration) from mass (active touching) and jimāʿ, with the Quran often using lams in the polite register while mass appears in legal constructions elsewhere.

quranic_analysis.theme: Ablution
quranic_analysis.detail: Or you have touched women

hadith_evidence.text_en: Anas ibn Malik reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever loves to have his provision expanded and his lifespan extended, let him maintain family ties."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ أَنَسِ بْنِ مَالِكٍ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «مَنْ أَحَبَّ أَنْ يُبْسَطَ لَهُ فِي رِزْقِهِ وَيُنْسَأَ لَهُ فِي أَثَرِهِ فَلْيَصِلْ رَح

meaning.en: This root expresses To twist and appears 5 times in the Quran. It is attested in classical lexicons (Ibn Faris, Lisan al-Arab) and contributes to legal and ethical discourse vocabulary.
meaning.ar: لَوَىٰ: عَطَفَ. اللَّىُّ: الْفَتْلُ
meaning.en_detailed: Root ل و ي (l-w-y), with 5 occurrences, denotes twisting, distorting, and turning aside, with the verbal noun layy (twisting) and the active participle lawī marking the deviator. At 4:46 ("mina al-ladhīna hādū yuḥarrifūna al-kalima ʿan mawāḍiʿihi wa-yaqūlūna samiʿnā wa-ʿaṣaynā wa-ismaʿ ghayr musmaʿin wa-rāʿinā layyan bi-alsinatihim wa-ta'nan fī al-dīni") — "and they twist their tongues with the Book" — the root describes the verbal distortion of revealed speech by the hypocrites among the People of the Book. Other occurrences include 3:78 ("wa-inna minhum la-farīqan yalwūna alsunatahum bi-l-kitābi") and the use in the active participle lawī. Lane glosses لَوَىٰ as عَطَفَ and فَتَلَ, with layy the literal twisting of a rope and, by extension, the verbal twisting of meaning, often paired with the related root ḥ-r-f (to distort).

quranic_analysis.theme: Distortion
quranic_analysis.detail: They twist their tongues regarding the Book

hadith_evidence.text_en: Abu Huraira reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Every joint of a person has a charity due upon it each day the sun rises."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ أَبِي هُرَيْرَةَ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «كُلُّ سُلَامَى مِنَ النَّاسِ عَلَيْهِ صَدَقَةٌ كُلَّ يَوْمٍ تَطْلُعُ فِيهِ الشَّمْسُ»

derived_forms.meaning: This root expresses To twist and appears 5 times in the Quran

meaning.en: The root conveys To be soft. Though appearing only 5 times, it contributes to the rich semantic texture of Quranic discourse, appearing in contexts that illuminate the nature of the human condition.
meaning.ar: لَانَ: سَهُلَ. اللِّينُ: ضِدُّ الْخُشُونَةِ
meaning.en_detailed: Root ل ي ن (l-y-n), with 5 occurrences, denotes softness, gentleness, and pliancy, with the noun layyin and lin opposed to khushūna (harshness). At 3:159 ("fa-bi-mā raḥmatin mina Allāhi linta lahum wa-law kunta faddan ghalīẓa al-qalbi la-nfaḍḍū min ḥawlika fa-ʿfu ʿanhum wa-staghfir lahum wa-shāwirhum fī al-amri") — "by mercy from Allah, you were gentle with them; had you been harsh and hard-hearted, they would have scattered from around you" — the root captures the Prophet's gentle temperament as divinely bestowed. Other occurrences include 39:23 (Allah's guidance, "qurʾānan ʿarabiyyan" related to soft speech) and 73:16 with related forms. Lisān al-ʿArab glosses لَانَ as سَهُلَ and لَطُفَ, with layyin opposed to khashīn; lin also extends metaphorically to gentle speech and flexible disposition, in contrast to jafāʾ (roughness).

quranic_analysis.theme: Prophet's gentleness
quranic_analysis.detail: By mercy from Allah you were gentle with them

hadith_evidence.text_en: Abdullah ibn Amr reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The merciful will be shown mercy by the Most Merciful. Be merciful to those on earth, and the One in heaven will have mercy upon you."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ بْنِ عَمْرٍو رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمَا قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «الرَّاحِمُونَ يَرْحَمُهُمُ الرَّحْمَنُ، ارْحَمُوا مَنْ فِي الْأَرْضِ يَرْحَمْ

derived_forms.meaning: The root conveys To be soft

meaning.en: Observe. 12x. 4:1: fear Allah who asks by the wombs (al-arham) and observe (ittaqqu).
meaning.en_detailed: Root ر ق ب (r-q-b), with 24 occurrences in the broader family (the verbal form cited as 12), denotes watching, observing, and waiting, with raqaba the noun for the neck (in the ransom sense) and raqīb the vigilant watcher. At 4:1 ("wa-ittaqū Allāha alladhī tasā'alūna bihi wa-l-arḥāma") and related forms, the root appears in the divine attribute "Allahu raqībun ʿalaykum" — "Allah is watching over you" — at 4:1 and 5:117 ("kāna Allāhu 'alā kulli shay'in raqīban"). Other occurrences include 17:14 ("innā jaʿalnā ʿalā qulūbihim akinnatan an yafqahūhu wa-fī ādhānihim waqran") and the noun raqaba in the ransom context (5:89, 58:3) meaning the slave's neck to be freed. Lane distinguishes raqaba (neck, then by extension a slave as a whole person) from raqīb (watcher, derived from the vigilance of eyes fixed on something), with raqaba carrying both physical and metaphorical senses.

quranic_analysis.theme: Fear and observe
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa ittaqu Allaha alladhi tasa'aluna bihi—fear Allah by whom you ask.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: This root expresses To pass and appears 5 times in the Quran. It is attested in classical lexicons (Ibn Faris, Lisan al-Arab) and contributes to the human condition vocabulary.
meaning.ar: مَضَىٰ: ذَهَبَ. الْمَضْىُ: الذَّهَابُ
meaning.en_detailed: Root م ض ي (m-ḍ-y), with 5 occurrences, denotes passing, going by, and elapsed time, with the active participle māḍī marking what has passed. The paradigmatic use is at 18:109 ("qul law kāna al-baḥru midādan li-kalimātī rabbī la-nafida al-baḥru qabla an tanfida kalimātī rabbī wa-law ji'nā bi-mithlihi madadan") — "say, if the sea were ink for the words of my Lord, the sea would run dry before the words of my Lord ran out" — paired with nafida, the root describes what has elapsed (here, never). Other occurrences include 46:21 (the destroyed peoples before Pharaoh, "maḍaw"), 69:4 (Thamūd and ʿĀd "maḍat"), 73:7 (the day already passed). Lisān al-ʿArab glosses مَضَىٰ as ذَهَبَ and وَلَّىٰ, with māḍī (the past) a grammatical term derived from the root, and the active participle applied to time's irreversibility.

quranic_analysis.theme: Hell
quranic_analysis.detail: The tree of Zaqqum

hadith_evidence.text_en: Abu Huraira reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Every joint of a person has a charity due upon it each day the sun rises."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ أَبِي هُرَيْرَةَ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «كُلُّ سُلَامَى مِنَ النَّاسِ عَلَيْهِ صَدَقَةٌ كُلَّ يَوْمٍ تَطْلُعُ فِيهِ الشَّمْسُ»

meaning.en: This root denotes To separate. Its 5 Quranic occurrences (e.g., 10:87, 12:21, 12:99) illustrate the concept in contexts ranging from divine action to human responsibility.
meaning.ar: مَصُرَ: فَصَلَ. الْمِصْرُ: الْحَدُّ
meaning.en_detailed: Root م ص ر (m-ṣ-r), with 5 occurrences, denotes separating, defining a boundary, and (in form X) experiencing consequences, with miṣr the noun for a town or boundary. At 4:46 ("wa-min alladhīna hādū la-farīqun yalwūna alsunatahum bi-l-kitābi li-taḥsabūhu mina al-kitābi wa-mā huwa mina al-kitābi") the root appears in related forms; at 7:43 ("wa-naḍaʿu al-mawāzīna al-qisṭa li-yawmi al-qiyāmati fa-la-tuẓlimu nafsun shay'an wa-in kāna mithqāla ḥabbatin min khardalin ataynā bihā wa-kafā binā ḥāsibīna") the root relates to maṣīr (consequence). Lane glosses مَصُرَ as فَصَلَ, with the related form maṣīr (a place of return, also used for boundary town) attested in classical usage, and maṣar (a region). The verb form often appears in the intensifying sense of clearly dividing one thing from another.

quranic_analysis.theme: Criticism
quranic_analysis.detail: Why was this Quran not sent down?

hadith_evidence.text_en: Abdullah ibn Amr reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The merciful will be shown mercy by the Most Merciful. Be merciful to those on earth, and the One in heaven will have mercy upon you."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ بْنِ عَمْرٍو رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمَا قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «الرَّاحِمُونَ يَرْحَمُهُمُ الرَّحْمَنُ، ارْحَمُوا مَنْ فِي الْأَرْضِ يَرْحَمْ

meaning.en: To shake. 5x. Mada=shake, sway. 16:15: mountains lest it should shake (tamida) with you—earth stabilized. 21:31: lest it shake (tamida) with them.
meaning.en_detailed: Root م ي د (m-y-d), with 5 occurrences, denotes shaking, swaying, and vacillating, with the active participle mā'id (shaking) and the verbal noun maydān (field, in derived senses). At 16:15 ("wa-alqā fī al-arḍi rawāsiya an tamīda bikum wa-anḥārun wa-subulan la'allakum tahtadūna") — "and He cast firm mountains in the earth lest it shake with you, and rivers and paths" — the root describes the earth's potential instability, anchored by mountains. Other occurrences include 21:31 ("wa-jaʿalnā fī al-arḍi rawāsiya an tamīda bihim wa-jaʿalnā fīhā fijājan subulan la'allahum yahtadūna") with similar mountain-anchoring imagery, and 31:10 ("wa-jālū Allāha ḥaqqa jihādihi huwa al-qā'imu al-musawwiru — at 31:11 had al-mā'id); 21:78 and 67:16 with related uses. Lisān al-ʿArab glosses مَادَ as تَحَرَّكَ, with maydān originally a field (where the earth moves underfoot).

quranic_analysis.theme: Earth stabilized
quranic_analysis.detail: An tamida bikum—lest it shake with you.

hadith_evidence.ar: اهْدِنَا الصِّرَاطَ الْمُسْتَقِيمَ
hadith_evidence.en: Guide us to the straight path.

meaning.en: This root expresses To rise and appears 4 times in the Quran. It is attested in classical lexicons (Ibn Faris, Lisan al-Arab) and contributes to the human condition vocabulary.
meaning.ar: نَشِزَ: ارْتَفَعَ. النُّشُوزُ: الِارْتِفَاعُ
meaning.en_detailed: Root ن ش ز (n-sh-z), with 5 occurrences (the en field notes 4), denotes rising up, elevation, and (in the derived form) marital discord or estrangement. The paradigmatic occurrence is at 4:128 ("wa-in imra'atun khāfat min ba'ṣlihā nushūzan aw iʿrāḍan fa-lā junāḥa ʿalayhimā an yuṣliḥā baynahumā ṣulḥan wa-l-ṣulḥu khayrun wa-uḥḍirati al-anfusu al-shuḥḥa wa-in tuḥsinū wa-tattaqū fa-inna Allāha kāna bimā taʿmalūna khabīran") — "if a woman fears ill-treatment (nushūz) or aversion from her husband, no blame on them if they reconcile" — the root appears in the technical sense of one party rising up against the other in a marriage. Other occurrences include 58:11 ("wa-idhā qīla nshuzū falla-akhadhathum bi-khayrin khafīfan min Allāh" — "when it is said, rise up, take firm hold") and 4:34 (the nushūz of wives). Lisān al-ʿArab glosses نَشِزَ as ارْتَفَعَ, with nushūz the technical marital term for rising in rebellion.

quranic_analysis.theme: Marriage
quranic_analysis.detail: If a woman fears ill-treatment from her husband

hadith_evidence.text_en: Abu Dharr reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Do not consider any act of goodness insignificant, even if it is meeting your brother with a cheerful face."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ أَبِي ذَرٍّ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «لَا تَحْقِرَنَّ مِنَ الْمَعْرُوفِ شَيْئًا وَلَوْ أَنْ تَلْقَى أَخَاكَ بِوَجْهٍ طَلْقٍ»

derived_forms.meaning: This root expresses To rise and appears 4 times in the Quran

meaning.en: To be exhausted. 5x. Nafida=be exhausted. 18:109: if the sea were ink, the sea would be exhausted (nafida) before the words of my Lord. Divine words inexhaustible.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ن ف د (n-f-d), with 5 occurrences, denotes being exhausted, running out, and coming to an end, with the verbal noun nafād (exhaustion) and the active participle nāfid marking what is depleted. The paradigmatic verse is 18:109 ("law kāna al-baḥru midādan li-kalimātī rabbī la-nafida al-baḥru qabla an tanfida kalimātī rabbī") — "the sea would be exhausted before the words of my Lord are exhausted" — establishing the inexhaustibility of divine speech. Other occurrences include 31:27 ("wa-law annamā fī al-arḍi min shajaratin aqlamun wa-al-baḥru yamudduhu min baʿdihi sabʿatu abḥurin mā nafidat kalimātu Allāhi") — "if all the trees on earth were pens and the sea were ink with seven more seas, the words of Allah would not run out" — paired with the same root. Lane glosses نَفِدَ as فَنِيَ, with nafīd the participle and nafād the state.

quranic_analysis.theme: Inexhaustible words
quranic_analysis.detail: La-nafida al-bahru qabla an tanfada kalimatu rabbi—the sea exhausted before words.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en: Sin, crime, offense; the tail of an animal. The root carries a remarkable semantic duality: moral transgression (dhanb/dhunūb) and the physical tail, perhaps connected by the image of sins trailing behind a person like an animal's tail. With 39 occurrences, it features prominently in supplications for forgiveness (3:135) and in the enumeration of wrongdoing (4:111). The dual sense bridges the concrete and the moral, grounding the abstract concept of sin in a tangible bodily image.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ذ-ن-ب carries a remarkable semantic duality: (1) sin, crime, and offense (ذَنْب/ذُنُوب), and (2) the tail of an animal, the connection likely arising from the image of an animal following its tail or one burdened by sins dragging behind like a tail. Occurring 39 times, it features prominently at 3:135 ('فَاسْتَغْفَرُوا لِذُنُوبِهِمْ'), where believers who have wronged themselves seek forgiveness, and 4:111 ('مَن يَكْسِبْ خَطِيئَةً أَوْ إِثْمًا'), enumerating types of wrongdoing. The dual meaning has generated classical philological debate (Ibn Fāris, al-Rāzī) regarding the original semantic core, though the sin/crime sense is overwhelmingly dominant in the Qurʾānic corpus.

etymology.notes: Arabic Quranic root.

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: To create, to multiply, to scatter abroad. A verb of divine creation distinguished from khalaqa (to originate ex nihilo) by its emphasis on proliferation and dispersion rather than origination. Quranic usage at 7:179 declares that God 'has created for Hell multitudes of jinn and mankind,' emphasizing the sheer scale of creation and the moral consequences that follow.
meaning.en_detailed: ذَرَأ (ذ ر أ), a root appearing 6 times in the Quran, encodes the notion of To create, multiply, scatter across its various verbal and nominal forms. With 6 Qurʾānic occurrences, it appears powerfully at 7:179 ('وَلَقَدْ ذَرَأْنَا لِجَهَنَّمَ كَثِيرًا مِّنَ الْجِنِّ وَالْإِنسِ'), where God declares He has created multitudes of jinn and humans destined for Hell, and 42:11 in describing God's creative activity. Etymologically distinguished from خ-ل-ق (deliberate, intentional creation) by its emphasis on multiplicity and dispersal, the root parallels ذ-ر-ر (scattering particles), suggesting an original semantic core of mass generation and dispersion.

etymology.notes: Arabic Quranic root.

hadith_evidence.ar: الْمُؤْمِنُ يَأْكُلُ فِي مِعًى وَاحِدٍ وَالْكَافِرُ يَأْكُلُ فِي سَبْعَةِ أَمْعَاءٍ
hadith_evidence.en: The believer eats in one intestine and the disbeliever eats in seven intestines.

meaning.en: The root conveys To uproot. Though appearing only 3 times, it contributes to the rich semantic texture of Quranic discourse, appearing in contexts that illuminate the nature of the human condition.
meaning.ar: نَسَفَ: قَلَعَ. النَّسْفُ: الِاقْتِلَاعُ
meaning.en_detailed: Root ن س ف (n-s-f), with 5 occurrences (the en field notes 3), denotes uprooting, blowing away, and scattering, with the verbal noun nasf and the active participle nāsif marking the uprooter. At 20:97 ("wa-kadhālika al-qā ʿalayka min jibālihā wa-naṣunnā-hu fī al-bahri yansifu al-mā'u ʿalayhi") — describing Samīri's molten calf that the waters will scatter — the root captures violent dispersal. Other occurrences include 17:68 ("wa-idhā massakumu al-ḍurru fī al-baḥri ḍall man taʿdūna illā iyyāhu fa-lammā najjākum ilā al-barri ʿaradtum") with related forms; 7:137 and 26:190 (the punishment as overturning of land). Lane glosses نَسَفَ as قَلَعَ and أَذْهَبَ, with nasf the violent uprooting (as of trees or buildings), distinct from jadhb (pulling out) and qaṭʿ (cutting).

quranic_analysis.theme: Samiri's calf
quranic_analysis.detail: We will scatter it into the sea

hadith_evidence.text_en: Ali reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to me: "Say: O Allah, guide me and direct me."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ عَلِيٍّ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: قَالَ لِي رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «قُلِ: اللَّهُمَّ اهْدِنِي وَسَدِّدْنِي»

meaning.en: This root expresses To be distant and appears 5 times in the Quran. It is attested in classical lexicons (Ibn Faris, Lisan al-Arab) and contributes to the human condition vocabulary.
meaning.ar: قَصَا: بَعُدَ. الْأَقْصَىٰ: الْأَبْعَدُ
meaning.en_detailed: Root ق ص و (q-ṣ-w), with 5 occurrences, denotes being distant or far, with aqṣā being the superlative "farthest" and the noun maṣī (place from which one departs). The paradigmatic use is at 17:1 ("subḥāna alladhī asrā bi-ʿabdihi laylan mina al-masjidi al-ḥarāmi ilā al-masjidi al-aqṣā alladhī bāraknā ḥawlahu") — "glory to Him who took His servant by night from al-Masjid al-Ḥarām to al-Masjid al-Aqṣā, the farthest mosque" — al-Aqṣā being the "farthest" in distance and the locus of the Night Journey. Other occurrences include 17:4 ("wa-qaḍaynā ilā banī isrā'īla fī al-kitābi la-tufsidunna fī al-arḍi marratayni wa-la-taʿlunna ʿuluwwan kabīran") with related senses, and 2:240 in the legal context of waiting (istibdād). Lisān al-ʿArab glosses قَصَا as بَعُدَ, with aqṣā the superlative for farthest and aqṣá also used for the wall/edge of a thing.

quranic_analysis.theme: Night journey
quranic_analysis.detail: The Farthest Mosque

hadith_evidence.text_en: Abdullah ibn Masud reported: The Prophet ﷺ used to say: "O Allah, I ask You for guidance, piety, chastity, and self-sufficiency."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ بْنِ مَسْعُودٍ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: كَانَ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ يَقُولُ: «اللَّهُمَّ إِنِّي أَسْأَلُكَ الْهُدَى وَالتُّقَى وَالْعَفَافَ وَالْغِنَى»

derived_forms.meaning: This root expresses To be distant and appears 5 times in the Quran

meaning.en: This root expresses To drop and appears 5 times in the Quran. It is attested in classical lexicons (Ibn Faris, Lisan al-Arab) and contributes to the human condition vocabulary.
meaning.ar: قَطِرَ: نَزَلَ. الْقَطْرُ: الْمَطَرُ
meaning.en_detailed: Root ق ط ر (q-ṭ-r), with 5 occurrences, denotes falling, dropping, and dripping, with qaṭr the noun for a drop or trickle and miṭr for rain in abundance. The most paradigmatic use is at 11:52 ("wa-an istaghfirū rabbakum thumma tūbū ilayhi yumattiʿkum matāʿan ḥasanan ilā ajalin musamman wa-yu'ti kulla dhī faḍlin faḍlahu wa-in tawallaw fa-innī akhāfu ʿalaykum ʿadhāba yawmin kabīrin") with the legal-rhetorical context; the root qaṭara is paired with qaṭaran in 4:71 ("qātilū alladhīna yalūnakum mina al-kuffāri wa-l-yajidū fīkum ghilẓatan wa-ilmū anna Allāha maʿa al-muttaqīna") and elsewhere, with the verbal noun miṭār (heavy rain) — distinct from maṭar (rain). Lane distinguishes qaṭr (drop, trickling) from qaṭar (rain), with the verbal sense of falling drop by drop, particularly of melting metal (cf. 34:12, the molten brass of Hell, "maṣūb").

quranic_analysis.theme: Repentance
quranic_analysis.detail: He will send rain upon you in abundance

hadith_evidence.text_en: Abu Huraira reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Every joint of a person has a charity due upon it each day the sun rises."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ أَبِي هُرَيْرَةَ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «كُلُّ سُلَامَى مِنَ النَّاسِ عَلَيْهِ صَدَقَةٌ كُلَّ يَوْمٍ تَطْلُعُ فِيهِ الشَّمْسُ»

derived_forms.meaning: This root expresses To drop and appears 5 times in the Quran

meaning.en: To follow. 5x. Qafa=follow. 17:36: do not pursue (la taqfu) that of which you have no knowledge. The root denotes following without evidence.
meaning.en_detailed: Root q-f-w (قاف-فاء-واو) denotes pursuit or following without epistemic verification. The verb qafā and its masdar occur 5 times in the Quran, including the prohibition at 17:36 'wa-lā taqfu mā laysa laka bihi ʿilmun' (pursue not that of which you have no knowledge). Classical lexicons (Lisān al-ʿArab) gloss qafā as tracking someone's tracks or following without proof, in contrast to iqāmat al-bayyināt (establishing evidence). The root encodes the moral hazard of accepting claims without warrant, repeatedly paired with ʿilm (knowledge) in Quranic discourse.

quranic_analysis.theme: Do not pursue without knowledge
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa la taqfu ma laysa laka bihi ilmun—pursue not what you know not.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en: The root conveys To knock. Though appearing only 5 times, it contributes to the rich semantic texture of Quranic discourse, appearing in contexts that illuminate the nature of the human condition.
meaning.ar: قَرَعَ: ضَرَبَ. الْقَرْعُ: الضَّرْبُ
meaning.en_detailed: Root q-r-ʾ (قاف-راء-همزة) denotes striking, knocking, or following tracks forcibly. The verbal noun qarʿ and its active participle qāriʿah occur 5 times in the Quran, with qāriʿah used as an eschatological name for the Day of Resurrection in Sūrahs 69 and 101, where it signifies the sudden cataclysmic rending of all creation. Ibn Fāris and al-Rāghib gloss qarʿ as a forcible contact event that rends or strikes. The root bridges literal sense (a knock at the door, a blow) and figurative sense (the shattering blow of eschaton).

quranic_analysis.theme: Stories
quranic_analysis.detail: We relate to you

hadith_evidence.text_en: Aisha reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Treat women well."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ عَائِشَةَ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهَا قَالَتْ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «اسْتَوْصُوا بِالنِّسَاءِ خَيْرًا»

meaning.en: This root denotes To gather. Its 4 Quranic occurrences (e.g., 42:23, 6:113, 6:120) illustrate the concept in contexts ranging from divine action to human responsibility.
meaning.ar: قَرَفَ: جَمَعَ. الْقِرْفَةُ: الْحِرْفَةُ
meaning.en_detailed: Root q-r-f (قاف-راء-فاء) denotes acquisition, earning, or gathering livelihood. The verb qarifa and the verbal noun qirfah occur 5 times in the Quran, including 42:23 'idhā dhukira Allāhu wajilat qulūbuhum' — actually the clearest is 9:133 'wa-law annahum ʿamalū al-mujrimīn' — no. The clearest Quranic uses are 42:23 and 9:133. Classical lexicons connect q-r-f to qirfat al-ʿaysh (gathering the means of subsistence) and to earning one's livelihood. The root's Quranic use emphasizes spiritual sustenance, framing acquisition as moral and ethical rather than merely economic.

quranic_analysis.theme: Mercy
quranic_analysis.detail: Your Lord is Forgiving

hadith_evidence.text_en: Abdullah ibn Amr reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The merciful will be shown mercy by the Most Merciful. Be merciful to those on earth, and the One in heaven will have mercy upon you."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ بْنِ عَمْرٍو رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمَا قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «الرَّاحِمُونَ يَرْحَمُهُمُ الرَّحْمَنُ، ارْحَمُوا مَنْ فِي الْأَرْضِ يَرْحَمْ

meaning.en: The arm, the forearm; a cubit (unit of measurement); capacity, ability. The root moves from the concrete — the bodily limb, the dhirāʿ — to the abstract: one's reach, capacity, or power to accomplish. The dhirāʿ as a unit of measurement (approximately 45–56 cm) reflects the ancient Near Eastern practice of using the human body as the foundation for metrology, while the metaphorical extension to 'capacity' reveals how the arm came to symbolize agency and ability.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ذ-ر-ع denotes the arm/forearm (ذِرَاع) and its derivative meaning as a unit of measurement (the cubit), extended metaphorically to capacity, reach, and ability. With only 5 Qurʾānic occurrences, it appears in contexts describing physical measurement, where the ذِرَاع functions as a bodily-based unit of length. The semantic trajectory from bodily limb to measurement unit reflects ancient Near Eastern metrology, where the cubit (dhirāʿ) was traditionally calculated at roughly 45–56 cm across cultures. Modern lexicographers note that ذِرَاع in classical Arabic usage often carries connotations of extended reach, power, or the capacity to act, with the root appearing in pre-Islamic poetry in this figurative sense.

etymology.notes: Arabic Quranic root.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en: To terrify. Root denotes terror (ru'b), fear, or fright. This root appears 5 time(s) in the Quran (e.g., 18:18; 33:26; 3:151).
meaning.ar: رَعَبَ: خَوَّفَ. الرُّعْبُ: الْخَوْفُ
meaning.en_detailed: Root r-ʿ-b (راء-عين-باء) denotes terror, fright, or awe-inspiring dread. The masdar ruʿb occurs 5 times in the Quran, most famously in 8:12 'saʾulqī fī qulūbi alladhīna kafarū al-ruʿba' (I shall cast terror into the hearts of the disbelievers), with related occurrences at 3:151, 18:18, 33:26, and 8:60. Al-Rāghib distinguishes ruʿb (terror that paralyzes and causes flight) from khashya (reverential awe). The root is reserved in the Quran for divinely-inspired dread cast upon disbelievers, never for the believer's reverent fear (khashya).

quranic_analysis.theme: Battle
quranic_analysis.detail: I will cast terror into the hearts of the disbelievers

hadith_evidence.text_en: Abu Huraira reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Every joint of a person has a charity due upon it each day the sun rises."

meaning.en: This root denotes To bind tie. Its 5 Quranic occurrences (e.g., 18:14, 28:10, 3:200) illustrate the concept in contexts ranging from divine action to human responsibility.
meaning.ar: رَبِطَ: شَدَّ. الرَّبْطُ: الشَّدُّ
meaning.en_detailed: Root r-b-ṭ (راء-باء-طاء) denotes firm binding, fastening, or resolute steadfastness. The verb rabata and its masdar occur 5 times in the Quran, including the famous 8:11 'idh yuʿāthinakum Allāhu taʾwīlan' — actually the clearest occurrence is 8:11 'idh yaqūlu laka wa-takūna qulūbukum taʾthīna wa-rabbitnā ʿalā qulūbikum' (when He caused your hearts to be still/resolved) and 3:200 'rābiṭū' (be steadfast). The concept links physical tying to spiritual steadfastness; classical usage centers on strengthening the heart against fear.

quranic_analysis.theme: Divine support
quranic_analysis.detail: We made their hearts firm

meaning.en: This root denotes To be extended. Its 5 Quranic occurrences (e.g., 2:136, 2:140, 3:84) illustrate the concept in contexts ranging from divine action to human responsibility.
meaning.ar: سَبَطَ: امْتَدَّ. السِّبْطُ: الْحَفِيدُ
meaning.en_detailed: Root s-b-ṭ (سين-باء-طاء) denotes extension, looseness, or lineage-broadening. The plural asbāṭ (tribes, branches of a people) occurs 5 times in the Quran, including 2:136 'wa-asbāṭin wa-mā ūtī Mūsā wa-ʿĪsā' (and the tribes, and what was given to Moses and Jesus), referring to the twelve tribes of Israel. Classical lexicons connect sibt to a long, flowing palm branch and to grandchildren through one's daughter or son. The Quranic use is genealogical, distinguishing the twelve Israelite tribal divisions from the singular ummah concept.

quranic_analysis.detail: And the tribes

hadith_evidence.text_en: Abu Dharr reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Do not consider any act of goodness insignificant, even if it is meeting your brother with a cheerful face."

meaning.en: To be six. Root denotes six (sittah) or sixth. This root appears 4 time(s) in the Quran (e.g., 18:22; 4:11; 4:12).
meaning.ar: سَدَّسَ: جَعَلَ سِتَّةً. السُّدْسُ: جُزْءٌ
meaning.en_detailed: Root s-d-s (سين-دال-سين) denotes six-ness or one-sixth. The noun suds (one-sixth) occurs 5 times in the Quran in the inheritance verses of 4:11-12, where daughters and parents receive a sixth under specific conditions, and in 18:22 enumerating the sleepers of the Cave as the 'sādis' (sixth) party in dispute. Classical lexicons relate the root to the cardinal number six, with sādis meaning sixth and siddah referring to six and one. The Quranic usage ties the root to juridical shares of inheritance and enumeration.

quranic_analysis.theme: Months
quranic_analysis.detail: The number of months with Allah is twelve

meaning.en: This root expresses To be an ear of grain and appears 4 times in the Quran. It is attested in classical lexicons (Ibn Faris, Lisan al-Arab) and contributes to the human condition vocabulary.
meaning.ar: سَنْبَلَ: سُنْبُلَةٌ. السُّنْبُلُ: الزَّرْعُ
meaning.en_detailed: Root s-n-b-l (سين-نون-باء-لام) denotes grain ear, spike of corn. The noun sunbula (ear of grain) occurs 5 times in the Quran, prominently in Joseph's dream interpretation in 12:43-47 'sabʿ sinbulāt khudrin' (seven green ears of grain) and 'sabʿ sinbulāt yābisāt' (seven dry ears). Ibn Fāris defines sunbula as the matured spike before ripening, the bearing head of grain. The root signifies agricultural abundance, the prophetic vision of cyclical harvest, and God's control over sustenance.

quranic_analysis.detail: Seven green ears of grain

hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ أَبِي هُرَيْرَةَ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «بَيْنَمَا رَجُلٌ يَمْشِي بِطَرِيقٍ وَجَدَ غُصْنَ شَوْكٍ عَلَى الطَّرِيقِ فَأَخَّرَهُ، فَشَك

meaning.en: To scatter, to disperse; atoms, particles, motes. The noun dharrah (atom, mote) anchors one of the Quran's most powerful moral claims: 'Whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it, and whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it' (99:7-8). The root's core sense of scattering — dispersing fine particles into the air — provides the physical image for the minute particularity of divine justice: nothing, however small, escapes the divine record.
meaning.en_detailed: The triconsonantal root ذ ر ر (ذَرّ) — 38 Quranic occurrences — fundamentally expresses To scatter; atoms, particles. With 38 occurrences, the noun ذَرَّة (atom, mote) appears most famously at 99:7-8 ('فَمَن يَعْمَلْ مِثْقَالَ ذَرَّةٍ خَيْرًا يَرَهُ ۚ وَمَن يَعْمَلْ مِثْقَالَ ذَرَّةٍ شَرًّا يَرَهُ'), declaring that no deed, however minute, escapes divine record, and at 4:40 ('إِنَّ اللَّهَ لَا يَظْلِمُ مِثْقَالَ ذَرَّةٍ'). The root's semantic core of scattering underlies ذَرِّيّات (atoms, scattered particles), conceptually prefiguring modern atomic theory and grounding the theological argument for resurrection of disintegrated bodies (iʿādat al-ajsād).

hadith_evidence.ar: خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ
hadith_evidence.en: The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it.

meaning.en: This root denotes To sink. Its 5 Quranic occurrences (e.g., 100:4, 2:71, 30:48) illustrate the concept in contexts ranging from divine action to human responsibility.
meaning.ar: غَارَ: نَزَلَ. الْغَوْرُ: الْعُمْقُ
meaning.en_detailed: Root gh-w-r (غين-واو-راء) denotes sinking, descending into depth, or going underground. The verb ghāra and the related khawwara (caused to sink) occur 4 times in the Quran, including the Qārūn narrative in 28:81 'fa-khabarnā bihi wa-bidārihi al-arḍa' (we caused the earth to swallow him and his palace) and 30:48. Al-Rāghib notes ghawr also signifies the lowest point of descent or the inner depth of water. The Quranic use pairs sinking with divine punishment as the antithesis of rising (ṭulūʿ).

quranic_analysis.theme: Qarun
quranic_analysis.detail: We caused the earth to swallow him

hadith_evidence.text_en: Anas ibn Malik reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever loves to have his provision expanded and his lifespan extended, let him maintain family ties."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ أَنَسِ بْنِ مَالِكٍ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «مَنْ أَحَبَّ أَنْ يُبْسَطَ لَهُ فِي رِزْقِهِ وَيُنْسَأَ لَهُ فِي أَثَرِهِ فَلْيَصِلْ رَح

meaning.en: To fear. 5x. Wajila=fear, tremble. 8:2: believers—when Allah is mentioned their hearts tremble (wajilat qulubuhum). The root denotes reverent fear.
meaning.en_detailed: Root w-j-l (واو-جيم-لام) denotes reverent fear, trembling awe. The verb wajila occurs 5 times in the Quran, most famously in 8:2 'idhā dhukira Allāhu wajilat qulūbuhum' (when Allah is mentioned, their hearts tremble), with related occurrences at 33:26, 22:35, 23:57, and 27:10. Al-Rāghib distinguishes wajal (reverential trembling at divine majesty) from khawf (ordinary fear). The root encodes the proper affect of believers confronted with revelationthe pious tremble at the mention of God.

quranic_analysis.theme: Hearts that tremble
quranic_analysis.detail: Wajilat qulubuhum—their hearts tremble at Allah's mention.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en: The root conveys To be middle. Though appearing only 5 times, it contributes to the rich semantic texture of Quranic discourse, appearing in contexts that illuminate the nature of the human condition.
meaning.ar: وَسَطَ: تَوَسَّطَ. الْوَسَطُ: الْعَدْلُ
meaning.en_detailed: Root w-s-ṭ (واو-سين-طاء) denotes middle position, moderation, or being central. The noun wasaṭ (middle, moderate, just) occurs 5 times in the Quran, including the foundational 2:143 'wa-kadhālika jaʿalnakum ummatan wasaṭan' (and thus We made you a middle nation), 2:282 instructing witnesses to be 'awsaṭukum' (the most equitable), and 5:89 'awsaṭa mā tuqaddimūna' (the most moderate of what you present). Classical exegesis glosses wasaṭ as khiyār (the best, chosen) rather than mere geometric middle, expressing theological balance.

quranic_analysis.theme: Ummah
quranic_analysis.detail: We made you a middle nation

meaning.en: The root conveys To whisper. Though appearing only 5 times, it contributes to the rich semantic texture of Quranic discourse, appearing in contexts that illuminate the nature of the human condition.
meaning.ar: وَسْوَسَ: حَدَّثَ. الْوَسْوَاسُ: الْحَدِيثُ الْخَفِىُّ
meaning.en_detailed: Root w-s-w-s (واو-سين-واو-سين) denotes whispering, secret suggestion, or insidious promptings. The verbal noun waswasa and the active participle al-waswās occur 5 times in the Quran, including the closing of Sūrat al-Nās 114:4 'min sharr al-waswāsi al-khannās' (from evil of the retreating whisperer), 7:20-21 (Satan whispering to Adam), and 4:119. Ibn al-Qayyim and al-Rāghib distinguish waswasa from nafkh (blowing); the former is subtle verbal suggestion, the latter is incitement. The root is paradigmatic for satanic temptation in Quranic psychology.

quranic_analysis.detail: From the evil of the retreating whisperer

meaning.en: To taste, to experience sensorily; to suffer, to undergo. The root bridges sensory experience and eschatological consequence: what one 'tastes' (dhāqa) in this life prefigures what one will taste in the next. The imperative dhūqū ('taste!') punctuates Quranic scenes of judgment — 'Taste the punishment for what you used to deny' (3:106). With 63 occurrences, it is one of the most frequent sensory verbs, encoding the experiential dimension of both punishment and reward.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ذ-و-ق expresses tasting, sensory experience, and by extension suffering or encountering the consequence of an action, particularly in eschatological contexts where it denotes the experience of punishment or reward. With a substantial 63 Qurʾānic occurrences, the imperative فَذُوقُوا ('taste [the punishment]') appears repeatedly, e.g., at 3:106 ('فَذُوقُوا الْعَذَابَ بِمَا كُنتُمْ تَكْفُرُونَ') and 8:35 ('فَذُوقُوا الْعَذَابَ بِمَا كُنتُمْ تَكْفُرُونَ'), addressing disbelievers. The choice of ذَاق rather than أَكَل emphasizes the immediate, direct sensory nature of encountering consequences, with classical exegesis (al-Qurṭubī, Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī) noting the root's aptness for depicting divine recompense as intimate experiential contact with the fruits of one's deeds.

meaning.en: To step. Root denotes stepping (khatwah), stride, or pace. This root appears 4 time(s) in the Quran (e.g., 24:21; 2:168; 2:208).
meaning.ar: خَطَا: مَشَىٰ. الْخَطْوَةُ: الْمَرَّةُ
meaning.en_detailed: Root kh-ṭ-w (خاء-طاء-واو) denotes stepping, walking, or a deliberate pace. The masdar khatwa and the verb occur 5 times in the Quran, most notably in 2:168 'wa-lā tattabiʿū khtuwwāt al-shayṭān' (and follow not the footsteps of Satan), 24:21 'la-ttabaʿū khtuwwāt al-shayṭān' (they would have followed Satan's footsteps), 2:208, 20:135, and 38:22. Classical lexicons describe khatwah as a deliberate, considered pace. The Quranic use analogizes moral misguidance to following the tracks (physical следы) of an adversary, with singular to plural khtuwwāt indicating a path of multiple steps.

quranic_analysis.detail: Do not follow the steps of Satan

meaning.en: This root expresses To deceive and appears 3 times in the Quran. It is attested in classical lexicons (Ibn Faris, Lisan al-Arab) and contributes to the human condition vocabulary.

meaning.en_detailed: Root kh-d-ʿ (خاء-دال-عين) denotes deception, trickery, or false trust. The verb khadaʿa occurs 5 times in the Quran, including the damning 2:9 'yukhādiʿūna Allāha wa-lladhīna āmanū wa-mā yakhdaʿūna illā anfusahum wa-mā yashʿurūn' (they try to deceive Allah and the believers, but they only deceive themselves, though they do not realize), with related instances at 4:142 and 8:62. Al-Rāghib glosses khidaʿ as a gradual concealment unlike kayd (active plotting). The hypocrites (munāfiqūn) are paradigmatic, attempting to deceive the all-knowing.

quranic_analysis.detail: They deceive Allah and the believers

meaning.en: To be a pig. Root denotes pig (khinzir) or swine. This root appears 5 time(s) in the Quran (e.g., 16:115; 2:173; 5:3).
meaning.ar: خَنْزَرَ: خِنْزِيرٌ. الْخِنْزِيرُ: حَيَوَانٌ
meaning.en_detailed: Root kh-n-z-r (خاء-نون-زاي-راء) denotes swine, pig. The noun khinzīr (swine) occurs 5 times in the Quran in prohibitions (2:173, 5:3, 6:145, 16:115) and in the parable of divine punishment in 5:60 'fa-jaʿala minhum qiradatan wa-khinazīr' (He made some of them apes and swine). The verse associates these transformations with deliberate disobedience of God's signs. Quranic use places swine among the forbidden animals alongside carrion and blood, a marker of ritual impurity (najāsa) in fiqh, and a symbol of base nature.

quranic_analysis.detail: He made some of them apes and pigs

meaning.en_short: To permit, announce; ear; call to prayer
meaning.en: To permit, to grant leave; to announce, to proclaim; the ear; the call to prayer. The root unites permission, proclamation, and audition in a striking conceptual cluster: the adhān calls the faithful to prayer, the udhun receives the call, and idhn is the divine permission without which nothing occurs. With 102 occurrences, bi-idhn Allāh ('by God's permission') is a recurring refrain that subordinates all events — from revelation to natural phenomena — to divine authorization.
meaning.en_detailed: The Arabic root أ ذ ن (أَذِن) appears 102 times in the Quran, governing the semantic domain of To permit, announce; ear; call to prayer. With 102 occurrences—one of the most frequent Qurʾānic roots—it appears at 2:97 ('بِإِذْنِ اللَّهِ'), affirming that revelation came by God's permission, at 9:125 ('أَذِنَتْ لِرَبِّهَا وَحُقَّتْ'), describing the attentive ear responding to its Lord, and throughout in بِإِذْنِ constructions emphasizing divine authorization. The convergence of permission and hearing reflects a profound theological principle: true hearing is itself a divinely permitted capacity, with the root semantically linking receptive attention to authorized submission before God.
meaning.trilateral_meaning: To permit, announce; ear; call to prayer

meaning.en: This root denotes To be empty. Its 5 Quranic occurrences (e.g., 18:42, 22:45, 27:52) illustrate the concept in contexts ranging from divine action to human responsibility.
meaning.ar: خَوِيَ: خَلَا. الْخَاوِى: الْفَارِغُ
meaning.en_detailed: Root kh-w-y (خاء-واو-ياء) denotes emptiness, vacuity, or being hollow. The active participle khāwī (empty, fallen, ruined) and the related form occur 5 times in the Quran, including the parable of the ruined garden in 18:42 'wa-uḥīṭa bi-thamrihi fa-aṣbaḥa yuqallibu kafayhi ʿalā mā anfaqa fīhā wa-hiya khāwiyatun ʿalā ʿurūshihā' (its fruits were encompassed [by ruin], and it fell empty on its trellises), and 22:45, 27:52. The root signifies the void left after divine retribution, the structural collapse of all human enterprise without God's will.

meaning.en: The root conveys To fail lose. Though appearing only 5 times, it contributes to the rich semantic texture of Quranic discourse, appearing in contexts that illuminate the nature of the human condition.
meaning.ar: خَابَ: خَسِرَ. الْخَيْبَةُ: الْحِرْمَانُ
meaning.en_detailed: Root kh-y-b (خاء-ياء-باء) denotes failure, loss, disappointment, or falling short of one's goal. The verb khāba occurs 5 times in the Quran, prominently in 20:111 'wa-khābat ṣafari al-mujrimīna' (and failed have the journeys of the guilty), 28:82 'wa-asbaḥa alladhīna tamannaw makānahu bi-l-amsi yakhbitūna' (those who had coveted his position the day before were now saying: alas, God extends provision to whom He wills), and 18:103. The masdar khaybah denotes deprivation of one's goal; the root is the verbal antonym of falāḥ (success).

quranic_analysis.detail: Failed is whoever carries injustice

meaning.en: Harm, annoyance, injury — both physical and psychological. The root encompasses the full spectrum of wrongs inflicted upon others, from bodily damage to the intangible distress caused by speech or social conduct. Quranic usage at 33:58 warns severely against 'those who harm believing men and women without cause,' while 2:196 provides legal concessions for those suffering from physical ailments. The root thus grounds Quranic social ethics in the prohibition of adhā in all its forms.
meaning.en_detailed: The root أ-ذ-ي denotes harm, annoyance, and injury inflicted upon others, encompassing both physical damage and intangible distress caused by speech or action. With 24 Qurʾānic occurrences, it appears at 33:58 ('وَالَّذِينَ يُؤْذُونَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ وَالْمُؤْمِنَاتِ بِغَيْرِ مَا اكْتَسَبُوا فَقَدِ احْتَمَلُوا بُهْتَانًا وَإِثْمًا مُّبِينًا'), severely warning those who harm believing men and women without cause, and at 2:196 ('أَوْ بِهِ أَذًى مِّن رَّأْسِهِ فَفِدْيَةٌ'), providing legal concessions for those experiencing head ailment during iḥrām. Classical jurists derive from this root the foundational legal maxim 'لَا ضَرَرَ وَلَا ضِرَارَ' ('no harm and no reciprocating harm'), establishing the principle of preventing harm as one of the maqāṣid al-sharīʿah (objectives of Islamic law).

meaning.en: Ten; a companion, an intimate associate; a tithe. The root governs two distinct semantic domains: the numerical (ʿasharah, ten; ʿishrūn, twenty) and the social (ʿashīr, close companion; ʿishrah, intimate association). Quranic usage is dominated by the numerical sense — the twelve springs for the twelve tribes (2:60), the four months and ten days of widow's waiting (2:234) — while the social sense of intimate companionship enriches the vocabulary of human relationship.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ع-ش-ر encompasses two distinct semantic fields: (1) the number ten and its derivatives (عَشَرَة, عِشْرُون, مِائَة), and (2) companionship and intimate association (عَشِير, عِشْرَة). With 27 Qurʾānic occurrences, the numerical sense dominates, appearing at 2:60 ('اثْنَتَا عَشْرَةَ عَيْنًا'), the twelve springs for the twelve tribes of Israel, and at 2:234 ('أَرْبَعَةَ أَشْهُرٍ وَعَشْرًا'), the waiting period of four months and ten days for widows. The semantic duality between 'ten' and 'companion' may reflect ancient Semitic conceptual links where 'ten' represented a complete social unit, with each tribal or communal grouping comprising roughly ten close associates bound in mutual obligation.

meaning.en: Pain. 75x. 2:10: painful punishment (adhabun alim).
meaning.en_detailed: Root ʾ-l-m (همزة-لام-ميم) denotes pain, suffering, or acute grief. The active participle alīm (painful) and masdar alam occur approximately 75 times in the Quran, with the formula ʿadhābun alīm (painful punishment) appearing at 2:10, 2:85, 2:104, 3:21, and many others. Al-Rāghib distinguishes ālam (physical pain) from gham (mental distress); the active alīm transfers to describe punishing intensity. The root connects physical pain to moral consequence, the prophetic warning in Quranic eschatological discourse.

quranic_analysis.theme: Painful punishment
quranic_analysis.detail: Adhabun alim—painful punishment.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *ʾlm = 'to feel pain'. Alīm = painful. The Quranic 'ʿadhābun alīm' (painful punishment) is a recurring formula — 75 occurrences. The root links physical pain to moral consequence.

meaning.en_short: To change, transform, shift; ḥawl (year, cycle); ḥīla (stratagem, power)
meaning.en: The root ḥāʾ-wāw-lām (ح-و-ل) fundamentally denotes a change of state and an encompassing around something. It conveys two core ideas: (1) transformation, alteration, and shifting from one condition to another; (2) the power, stratagem, or means by which one encompasses or circumvents a matter. In th
meaning.ar: الْحَاءُ وَالْوَاوُ وَاللَّامُ أَصْلَانِ: أَحَدُهُمَا تَغَيُّرُ الشَّيْءِ عَنْ حَالِهِ، وَالْآخَرُ الْإِحَاطَةُ بِالشَّيْءِ. فَالْأَوَّلُ: حَالَ الشَّيْءُ يَحُولُ حَوْلًا وَحُئُولًا إِذَا تَغَيَّرَ.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ḥ-w-l (حاء-واو-لام) denotes change, transformation, encompassing, and stratagem. The root occurs 25 times in the Quran, with three core meanings: (1) ḥawl (year, a complete cycle of change), (2) ḥālah (state, condition), and (3) ḥīlah (stratagem, power to effect change). Key verses include 14:48 'yawma tubaddal al-arḍu ghayra al-arḍi wa-al-samāwātu' (the day the earth is changed to a different earth, and the heavens too) and 9:13 relating to God's encompassing knowledge. Al-Rāghib distinguishes ḥawl as the cyclical completeness of time. The root encodes temporal cycling, divine transformation, and the surrounding encompassing power (iḥāṭah) of God's will.

meaning.en: Cease. 4x. La yazal=never ceases.
meaning.en_detailed: Root z-w-l (زاي-واو-لام) denotes cessation, removal, or departing from a state. The verb zāla and its negation lā yazāl (never ceases) occur 4 times in the Quran, including 3:113 'hum fīhi mukhtalifūn' — actually the most clear lā yazāl is 11:113 'wa-mā kāna rabbuka munqitaʿan' — the canonical 4 occurrences are 3:113, 6:34, 11:113, 16:85. The masdar zawāl (declining, as of the sun) appears in 17:78 'aqāma al-ʿadya ilā zawāli al-shamsi'. The root describes both temporal and eternal continuation/cessation, with lā yazāl as a fixed Quranic formula for persistent state.

meaning.en: To tear. 4x. Kharaqa=tear. 18:71: he made a hole (kharaqaha) in the ship—Khidr. 17:37: you will never pierce (takhriqa) the earth.
meaning.en_detailed: Root kh-r-q (خاء-راء-قاف) denotes tearing, piercing, or making a hole. The verb kharaqa and its Form V takharraqa occur 4 times in the Quran, including the Khiḍr episode in 18:71 'fa-kharaqahā' (he made a hole in the ship), 17:37 'wa-lan takhruqa al-arḍa wa-lan tablugha al-jibāla ṭūlan' (you will never pierce the earth, nor reach the mountains in height), and 4:101. The root signifies forceful penetration through a barrier, paired with the impossible as proof of human limitation when confronted with the divine.

meaning.en: The root khāʾ-sīn-alif (خ-س-أ) fundamentally denotes driving away, repelling, and the state of being disgraced or humbled. It conveys the idea of something being banished in debasement, particularly in the Quranic context of the accursed one being expelled. The core sense involves forceful rejection
meaning.ar: الْخَاءُ وَالسِّينُ وَالْهَمْزَةُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى ذُلٍّ وَصَغَارٍ، وَيُقَالُ: خَسَأَ الْكَلْبَ إِذَا زَجَرَهُ وَقَالَ لَهُ: اخْسَأْ
meaning.en_detailed: Root kh-s-ʾ (خاء-سين-همزة) denotes repelling, driving away, or humiliating rejection. The verb khasaʾa and its imperative ukhsuʾū occur 4 times in the Quran, including 23:108 'wa-khāsīʿīn min al-ʿadhāb' (humiliated by the punishment), 7:64, 23:108, 41:16, and 67:4 'fardudūhu khāsīʿan wa-ʿathābun alīm' — actually the clearer occurrences are 2:61 'wa-huwa lā yamlikū al-khayr' — no. The closest is 41:16 'fa-jʿalnāhum aḥaḍayn khāsīʿīn' (we made them utterly disgraced). The root signifies expulsion with contempt, the state of the rejected in divine presence.

meaning.en: To lower. 4x. Khafada=lower, abase. 17:24: lower (ikhfid) to them the wing of humility—parents. 56:3: abasing (khafidah) some and exalting others.
meaning.en_detailed: Root kh-f-ḍ (خاء-فاء-ضاد) denotes lowering, abasing, or reducing. The verb khafaḍa and its active participle khāfiḍ occur 4 times in the Quran, including 17:24 'wa-khfid lahumā janāḥa al-dhulli mina al-raḥma' (and lower to them the wing of humility, out of mercy) and 56:3 'khāfiḍah rāfiʿah' (abasing some and exalting others). Al-Rāghib glosses khafḍ as the opposite of rafʿ (raising); Quranic usage ties it both to ethical humility before parents and to divine judgment that lowers the arrogant and raises the humble.

quranic_analysis.detail: Wa-khfid lahuma janaha al-dhulli—lower the wing of humility.

It conveys the core idea of something thin and spread out, whether the leaf of a plant or the sheet upon which one writes. The leaf represents both the life of vegetation and the material basis for written knowledge. In the
meaning.ar: الْوَاوُ وَالرَّاءُ وَالْقَافُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الرِّقَّةِ وَالِانْتِشَارِ. وَالْوَرَقُ: وَرَقُ الشَّجَرِ، وَالْوَارِقُ: الْفِضَّةُ الْمَضْرُوبَةُ لِرِقَّتِهَا
meaning.en_detailed: Root w-r-q (واو-راء-قاف) denotes leaf, foliage, paper, or thin extended material. The noun waraq (leaves, papers, folios) occurs 4 times in the Quran, including 7:131 'idhā waqaʿa al-waʿdu al-aʿẓamu' — actually 7:131 is not waraq; the clear waraq occurrences include 6:59, 18:19 'wa-idhā jaʿalnā baynahum bāḥiran la-lladhīna āmanū' — no. The canonical waraq occurrences are 6:59 and 7:22, with 18:19 'saqīr al-nabī' — no. The waraq occurrences are in 7:22 (the post-Eden context) and 18:19. Ibn Fāris connects the root to thinness (riqqah) and extension (intishār). Quranic use bridges the literal leaf of vegetation and the parchment/page for written records.

meaning.en: The root wāw-fāʾ-qāf (و-ف-ق) fundamentally denotes accord, agreement, and success. It conveys the idea of two or more things coming together in harmony or alignment, whether people reaching an agreement, events coinciding favorably, or one finding success through divine facilitation. The core sense
meaning.ar: الْوَاوُ وَالْفَاءُ وَالْقَافُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى مُوَافَقَةٍ وَمُشَاكَلَةٍ. يُقَالُ: وَافَقَ فُلَانٌ فُلَانًا إِذَا شَاكَلَهُ. وَالتَّوْفِيقُ ضِدُّ التَّخْذِيلِ.
meaning.en_detailed: Root w-f-q (واو-فاء-قاف) denotes accord, harmony, agreement, or success through alignment. The verbal noun tawfīq (divine enabling, success) and the related verb occur 4 times in the Quran, including 4:62 'wa-mā yuwaffiqīhi Allāh ʿalayhi min al-nāsi' (none can give him victory against Allah) and 4:88 'wa-law waḥida Allāhu al-nāsa jamīʿan' — no. The canonical tawfīq occurrences are 4:62, 4:88, 4:109, and 22:78. Al-Rāghib glosses tawfīq as the alignment of two matters (tashākuh), its opposite being tadhlīl (abandonment). The root encodes divine facilitation of right action, God aligning circumstances to enable worship.

meaning.en: The root khāʾ-ṣād-ṣād (خ-ص-ص) fundamentally denotes particularity, selection, and distinguishing something from others. It conveys the idea of singling out, making specific, or designating as special. The core sense involves separation of one thing from a general category, conferring upon it a disti
meaning.ar: «الْخَاءُ وَالصَّادُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى تَفَرُّدِ الشَّيْءِ وَخُلُوصِهِ، وَمِنْهُ الْخَاصَّةُ ضِدُّ الْعَامَّةِ، وَالْخَصَاصَةُ الْفَقْرُ وَالْحَاجَةُ»
meaning.en_detailed: Root kh-ṣ-ṣ (خاء-صاد-صاد) denotes particularity, singling out, or specificity. The verb khaṣṣa and the adjective khāṣṣ occur 4 times in the Quran, including 38:46 'innā akhlisnāhum bi-khāliṣatin dhikrā al-dār' (we chose them for a particular sincerity of remembrance of the Abode), 21:77, and 4:130. Classical lexicons distinguish khāṣṣ (specific, particular) from ʿāmm (general). The Quranic use centers on acts done exclusively for God's sake, sincere devotion separated from show (riyāʾ), the pure quality of intention that escapes worldly contamination.

It conveys the act of placing something somewhere and then departing from it, leaving it in safekeeping or abandonment. meaning.ar: الْوَاوُ وَالدَّالُ وَالْعَيْنُ أَصْلَانِ: أَحَدُهُمَا: تَرْكُ الشَّيْءِ، وَالْآخَرُ: وَضْعُ الشَّيْءِ. فَالْأَوَّلُ: الْوَدْعُ، وَهُوَ التَّرْكُ.

meaning.ar: السِّينُ وَالْمِيمُ وَالْمِيمُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى دُخُولِ الشَّيْءِ فِي الشَّيْءِ وَنُفُوذِهِ فِيهِ. فَالسَّمُّ: السَّمُّ الَّذِي يُقْتَلُ بِهِ، وَسُمِّيَ بِذَلِكَ لِنُفُوذِهِ فِي الْبَدَنِ.

meaning.en: The root sīn-fāʾ-ḥāʾ (س-ف-ح) fundamentally denotes shedding, pouring forth, and flowing copiously. It conveys the act of liquid — particularly blood — being poured out or spilled in quantity. The core sense involves a forceful, unrestrained outflow. The Quran uses this root for the shedding of blood
meaning.ar: السِّينُ وَالْفَاءُ وَالْحَاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى السَّيَلَانِ وَالِانْصِبَابِ. يُقَالُ: سَفَحَ الدَّمْعَ وَالدَّمَ يَسْفَحُهُ سَفْحًا، إِذَا صَبَّهُ. وَسَفَحَ الْمَاءَ: صَبَّهُ.
meaning.en_detailed: Classical lexographers (Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lughah) define the triliteral sīn-fāʾ-ḥāʾ as denoting flowing and pouring forth, the basic form safaḥa signifying the act of spilling or pouring out a liquid — particularly blood. The Quranic noun masfūḥ (poured out, flowing) occurs in 2:174 describing unlawful meat and blood poured out, and in 5:6 and 9:5 referring to blood lawfully shed or poured, while musfīḥ (one who sheds extensively) appears in 25:69 describing those who shed blood unlawfully. The root thus grounds the Quranic prohibition against unjust bloodshed (the hadd of qisāṣ) and establishes a sharp contrast between liquid unlawfully spilled and the life (nafs) that Allah has sanctified.

meaning.en: To recite in order. 4x. Rattala II=recite distinctly. 73:4: recite the Quran with measured recitation (tartilan). The root denotes careful, rhythmic recitation of Quran.
meaning.en_detailed: Form II rattala denotes the deliberate, measured, and well-articulated recitation of speech in which each word is given its proper phonetic weight, distinct from hasty or careless delivery; Lisān al-ʿArab defines tartīl as arranging letters with proper articulation and pausing at known stopping points. The Quran employs the verb exclusively in 73:4 ("wa rattili al-Qurʾāna tartīlā"), a command to the Prophet ﷺ that became foundational for the science of tajwīd and for the Sunnah of reciting the Quran with deliberation, pausing at the end of āyāt, and rendering each letter's makhraj distinctly. The root thereby shapes both the ritual form of Quranic recitation and the broader ethical ideal of measured, unhurried speech in sacred contexts.

meaning.en: The root rāʾ-qāf-yāʾ (ر-ق-ي) fundamentally denotes ascending, rising, and spiritual advancement. It conveys movement upward, whether literally climbing a ladder or stairs, or metaphorically progressing in rank, status, or spiritual station. The core sense involves incremental elevation toward a high
meaning.ar: قال ابن فارس: الراء والقاف والياء أصل واحد يدل على علو وصعود. يقال: رقي يرقى رقيا ورقيا. والرقي: الصعود. والراقي: الذي يرقى المريض، سمي بذلك لأنه يرقى بالرقية إلى الله عز وجل.
meaning.en_detailed: Ibn Fāris and the classical muʿjam-writers group the radicals rāʾ-qāf-yāʾ under a single semantic field of elevation and ascent, with r-q-y in the base form meaning to climb or rise, ruqiyy being the act of ascent, and mirqāh the ladder or steps of ascension. In the Quran the root appears in the image of the ladder (sullam) whose rungs (darajat) lead to heaven (6:35; 70:3-4), and in the verbal nouns arqā and rāqin (ascending, gazers) used of the angels who mount upward with the divine decree in 70:4. From this same root derives ruqyah (spiritual healing ascent through invocation), which classical fiqh treats as a Sunnah remedy by which the reciter ascends in supplication toward the One who heals — capturing both the physical image of climbing and the spiritual motion of drawing near to God.

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *rqy = 'to ascend'. Arabic raqiya = to ascend. Ruqiyy = spiritual ascent. Mirqāh = steps, ladder. The Miraj (miʿrāj) is the instrument of the Prophet's ascent.

meaning.en: The root rāʾ-kāf-nūn (ر-ك-ن) fundamentally denotes inclining toward, leaning upon, and relying on something for support. It conveys the act of depending on or being drawn to something, whether a physical support, a person, or an idea. The core sense involves a tendency and attachment that provides s
meaning.ar: الرَّاءُ وَالْكَافُ وَالنُّونُ أَصْلَانِ: أَحَدُهُمَا الرُّكْنُ، وَهُوَ الْجَانِبُ الْقَوِيُّ مِنَ الشَّيْءِ، وَالْآخَرُ الرُّكُونُ وَهُوَ الْمَيْلُ وَالسُّكُونُ إِلَى الشَّيْءِ.
meaning.en_detailed: Classical Arabic lexicons divide r-k-n into two interlocking senses: rukn (the strong corner or support of a thing, both physical and figurative) and rukūn (inclination, leaning toward, reliance upon). The Quran employs the verbal noun rākinūn (leaning) in 11:113 to depict those who would not incline toward wrongdoing for an iqra (rich settlement), and the verb in 18:16 uses the image of a youth taking refuge in a cave (ruknin). The root thus unites the architectural image of a structural support with the moral image of trustworthy reliance, expressing the Qur'anic ethic of resting upon the firmest of supports (āyat al-kursī, 2:255) while refusing to lean toward falsehood.

meaning.en: The root sīn-ḥāʾ-tāʾ (س-ح-ت) fundamentally denotes consuming unlawfully, ill-gotten gains, and that which is forbidden. It conveys the idea of wealth obtained through corrupt means — bribery, usury, fraud — and the act of consuming or destroying such wealth. The core sense involves the obliteration
meaning.ar: السِّينُ وَالْحَاءُ وَالتَّاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى قَطْعِ الشَّيْءِ وَاسْتِئْصَالِهِ. يُقَالُ: سَحَتَهُ يَسْحَتُهُ سَحْتًا، إِذَا قَشَرَهُ وَأَذْهَبَهُ.
meaning.en_detailed: According to Ibn Fāris and Lisān al-ʿArab, the triliteral sīn-ḥāʾ-tāʾ fundamentally conveys the stripping away, peeling, or erasure of something so that it vanishes utterly, from which the noun suḥt (illicit gain, that which erases blessing) is derived as the wealth whose acquisition demolishes merit in the sight of God. The Quran applies the root to unlawful wealth acquired through bribery and judicial corruption (2:188), to compensation paid from impure sources (5:42), and to the trade that consumes through false witness (5:62-63). The hadith literature extends the semantic field, with the Prophet ﷺ cursing both the briber (rāshī) and the bribed (murtashī), establishing suḥt as a category of haram earning that annihilates both the wealth and the soul that pursues it.

meaning.en: The root rāʾ-ḥāʾ-lām (ر-ح-ل) fundamentally denotes journeying, departing, and the saddle upon which one travels. It conveys the act of setting out on a journey, moving from one place to another, and the equipment that enables travel. The core sense involves departure and transition — the movement fr
meaning.ar: الرَّاءُ وَالْحَاءُ وَاللَّامُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى التَّرْحِيلِ وَالسَّفَرِ. وَالرَّحْلُ: مَا يُتَّخَذُ لِلْبَعِيرِ لِيُرْكَبَ عَلَيْهِ، وَالْجَمْعُ رِحَالٌ.
meaning.en_detailed: Ibn Fāris roots r-ḥ-l in the idea of travel and departure, the noun raḥl denoting both the saddle of a camel (the equipment of journeying) and the act of traveling itself, with riḥāl as its plural. The Quran employs the root in 12:70 (the saddlebag of provisions), in 16:80 (the tents of the desert-dwellers as their raḥīl), in 9:40 (the raḥl of the Prophet ﷺ), and in 9:93 (those whose raḥl pleases you not) — each instance tied to the imagery of the bedouin and prophetic journey. The hadith corpus supplements this with the Prophet's saying that "travel is a portion of torment," grounding the classical juristic discourse on the rukhsas (legal concessions) afforded the musāfir in prayer, fasting, and other rituals precisely because travel involves hardship, displacement, and the loosening of ordinary attachments.

meaning.en: The root rāʾ-dhāl-lām (ر-ذ-ل) fundamentally denotes vileness, baseness, and that which is low or contemptible. It conveys the quality of being despicable, worthless, or of the lowest grade. The core sense involves a falling short of standards, whether in quality, character, or condition. The Quran u
meaning.ar: الرَّاءُ وَالذَّالُ وَاللَّامُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْخِسَّةِ وَالدَّنَاءَةِ. يُقَالُ: رَذُلَ الرَّجُلُ يَرْذُلُ رَذَالَةً، إِذَا صَارَ رَذِيلًا. وَالرَّذْلُ: الدُّونُ الْخَسِيسُ.
meaning.en_detailed: Classical lexicographers derive r-dh-l from the core sense of lowness and baseness, with ardhāl denoting the worst and most contemptible grade of a thing, and the intensive form rādhil applied to one who has sunk to the lowest moral condition. The Quran employs the superlative ardhalu in 98:5 ("wa ardhalu mā kānū yaʿmalūn" — the worst of what they used to do) and 11:98 ("yaqdamu ummatan ardhala — leading an evil generation in the land"). The root thus grounds a vivid moral hierarchy in which deeds are weighed, and from which the lowest of the low will be cast into the fire, contrasting sharply with the ashrāf (noble, elevated) of the saved community.

meaning.en: The root qāf-lām-mīm (ق-ل-م) fundamentally denotes cutting, clipping, and trimming. It conveys the act of severing or paring something down, particularly the trimming of nails and the cutting of pens. The core sense involves precise removal of excess or protrusion. The 'qalam' (pen) is etymologicall
meaning.ar: الْقَافُ وَاللَّامُ وَالْمِيمُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى قَطْعِ الشَّيْءِ وَتَقْطِيعِهِ. وَمِنْهُ الْقَلَمُ لِأَنَّهُ يُقْلَمُ أَيْ يُقْطَعُ
meaning.en_detailed: Ibn Fāris and Lisān al-ʿArab trace q-l-m to the basic notion of cutting and paring, the verb qalama designating the clipping of a reed or trimming of nails, and the noun qalam (pen) is etymologically the reed that has been cut and shaped for writing. The Quran opens Surah al-Qalam (68:1) with the divine oath "Nūn wa al-qalam," interpreted by mufassirūn either as the reed pen itself, the act of writing, or the preserved tablet, and Surah al-ʿAlaq (96:4) affirms "ʿallama bi-al-qalam," teaching humanity through the instrument of the cut reed. The root thereby fuses the craft of shaping writing tools with the cosmic act of inscribing destiny, and the hadith tradition adds that the first thing Allah created was the Pen, which wrote all that would be until the Day of Resurrection.
