meaning.en: To copy; abrogate. 4x. Nasakha=copy, abrogate. 2:106: We do not abrogate (nansakh) a verse—divine replacement. The root grounds the doctrine of abrogation.
meaning.en_detailed: Classical Arabic roots n-s-kh in two complementary senses — physical copying or transcribing (a manuscript is a nuskhah), and the abrogation of one ruling by another (naskh al-āyah) — both grounded in the image of one thing taking the place of another so that the original is displaced. The Quran presents the doctrine of abrogation most explicitly in 2:106 ("mā nansakh min āyatin aw nunsihā naʾti bi-khayrin minhā aw mithlihā"), where the Divine prerogative of abrogating, forgetting, or replacing verses is asserted, and in 7:154 referring to the alwāḥ (tablets) inscribed with divine guidance. Classical uṣūl al-fiqh developed this root into the entire discipline of al-nāsikh wa al-mansūkh (the abrogating and the abrogated), distinguishing between abrogation of recitation (al-tilāwah) and of ruling (al-ḥukm), while simultaneously preserving the doctrine that the Quran's textual transmission is itself an act of divine copying from the Lawḥ Maḥfūẓ.
meaning.ar_definition: جذر نَسَخَ — 4 مرة — copy; to abrogate

meaning.en: The root nūn-sīn-lām (ن-س-ل) fundamentally denotes offspring, progeny, and the act of reproduction. It conveys the idea of successive generations emerging from predecessors, whether humans, animals, or even ideas. The core sense involves the separation and continuation of something from its source,
meaning.ar: النُّونُ وَالسِّينُ وَاللَّامُ أَصْلَانِ: أَحَدُهُمَا الْخُرُوجُ وَالِانْفِصَالُ، وَالْآخَرُ السُّرْعَةُ.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ن س ل (نسل), attested 4 times in the Quran, derives its core meaning of Offspring, progeny, and the a from Proto-Semitic sources. The Quran employs the noun nasl and the verb nasala in 7:172 ("wa idh akhtha rabbuka min Banī Ādama min ẓuhūrihim dhurrīyatihum wa ashhadahum ʿalā anfusihim — He took from the loins of the children of Adam their progeny as witnesses"), and in 13:8 and 35:11 (Allah creates and brings forth progeny, no female conceives or gives birth without His knowledge). The root thereby grounds the Quranic theology of human lineage as both biological emergence and divinely witnessed descent, with the Sunnah's command to multiply ("tadabbakhu wa tanāsalū") extending this creative succession into the realm of moral responsibility before God.

meaning.en: The root nūn-fāʾ-lām (ن-ف-ل) fundamentally denotes something extra, supererogatory, and beyond what is obligatory. It conveys the idea of an addition, supplement, or gift that is not required but given out of generosity. The core sense involves abundance and increase beyond the expected measure. In
meaning.ar: النُّونُ وَالْفَاءُ وَاللَّامُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الزِّيَادَةِ. يُقَالُ: نَفَلَ يَنْفُلُ نَفْلًا إِذَا أَعْطَى زِيَادَةً.
meaning.en_detailed: Ibn Fāris derives n-f-l from the core sense of increase and addition beyond what is required, with nafl denoting what is given over and above the obligatory (farḍ), and the verbal noun nawāfil (plural of nāfilah) designating supererogatory acts of devotion or voluntary gifts. The Quran uses the verb in 9:79 ("wa inn tuwallaw yaʿtika Allāhu ʿadhāban alīman" followed by "wal-man tāba wa ʿamila ṣāliḥan fa-llāhu yataqabbubu minhu — and whoever turns in repentance and does righteousness, God accepts from him"), where nafl/nawāfil structure the principle of divine reward that exceeds strict obligation. Classical fiqh builds upon this root an entire category of worship: the Sunnah rawātib (regular non-obligatory prayers), voluntary fasting, and sadaqah are all nawāfil that draw the servant nearer to God while affirming that He repays good with good beyond all measure.

meaning.en: The root nūn-qāf-rāʾ (ن-ق-ر) fundamentally denotes pecking, tapping, and scrutinizing with precision. It conveys the act of striking something with a pointed object, like a bird pecking at a seed, and by extension, the careful examination or investigation of minutiae. The core sense involves a focus
meaning.ar: قال ابن فارس: (نقر) النون والقاف والراء أصل واحد يدل على ضرب الشيء بالشيء يترك فيه أثرًا. من ذلك نقر الطائر الحبّ ينقره بمنقاره، ونقر الرجل الشيء بإصبعه. والنقرة: الحفرة في الأرض.
meaning.en_detailed: Classical lexographers trace n-q-r to the image of striking or piercing with a pointed object so as to leave a small mark or cavity — the bird pecking (nāqir) at a seed with its beak, or the finger tapping to make a naqrah (small depression). In the Quran the root appears in the striking image of 6:95 ("inna Allāha fāliq al-ḥabbi wa al-nawā"), and in 21:47 ("wa naḍaʿu al-mawāzīna al-qista li-yawmi al-qiyāmah"), but its most concentrated theological use is in 3:191 ("rabbanā mā khalaqta hādhā bāṭilan"), with the verb yaqūr applied to the breaking of bone, and in the famous hadith on the takwīn of deeds. The root thereby grounds the Quranic contrast between the apparent triviality of a deed (the size of a naqrah, an atom's weight) and its eternal weight before God, an image that anchors the doctrine of weighing deeds on the Day of Judgment.

meaning.en: To carve. 4x. Nahata=carve, sculpt. 26:149: you carve houses out of mountains (tanhituna)—Thamud. 7:74: carving houses from mountains.
meaning.en_detailed: نَحَتَ (ن ح ت), a root appearing 4 times in the Quran, encodes the notion of To carve, sculpt across its various verbal and nominal forms. The Quran applies the verb in 7:74 and 26:149 to the people of Thamūd ("wa taḥtūnūna min al-jibāli buyūtan — you carve houses out of the mountains"), an image of architectural skill born of both prosperity and hubris, for which they were destroyed. The root thereby anchors a recurring Quranic motif in which the arts of construction and ornamentation, when pursued without taqwā, become signs of moral decadence preceding divine punishment — the dwellings carved into the rock standing as mute monuments to a vanished people.

meaning.en: Distinguish. 4x. 8:37: Allah may separate wicked from good.
meaning.en_detailed: The quadrilateral/form II mayyaza denotes the act of discriminating, distinguishing, or separating one thing from another according to a clear criterion, from the same root that yields tamyīz (the grammatical concept of specification) and imtiyāz (distinction in rank). The Quran employs the verb in 8:37 ("li-yamīza Allāhu al-khabītha min al-ṭayyib — that Allah may separate the wicked from the good") and 3:179 ("ḥattā yamīza Allāhu al-mukhliṣīna mina al-munāfiqīn"), where the active form (subject Allāh) presents divine discrimination as the ultimate moral sorting that human judgment cannot accomplish. The root thereby grounds the Quranic doctrine that only Allah possesses the absolute knowledge to distinguish sincere profession from hypocrisy, faith from disbelief, and the hidden impurity of hearts from their outward appearance.

quranic_analysis.theme: Divine discrimination
quranic_analysis.detail: Li-yamiza Allahu al-khabitha—Allah separates the wicked.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en: The root mīm-zāy-qāf (م-ز-ق) fundamentally denotes tearing apart, shredding, and dispersing. It conveys the act of ripping something into pieces and scattering those pieces so that reunification becomes impossible. The core sense involves violent fragmentation and dispersal. The Quran uses this root
meaning.ar: مَزَقَ: الْمِيمُ وَالزَّاءُ وَالْقَافُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى التَّمْزِيقِ وَالتَّفْرِقَةِ. وَمَزَقَ الثَّوْبَ: شَقَّهُ. وَمَزَّقَهُ: فَرَّقَهُ.
meaning.en_detailed: Classical Arabic m-z-q denotes the violent tearing apart of a thing into pieces that are then scattered so as to preclude reunion, distinguished from shaqqa (splitting along a seam) and qaṭṭaʿa (cutting into segments). The Quran employs the verb in 34:19 ("fa-qaḍāhu Allāhu mā madhā ilā laylin wa l-nahāri — and they will not be able to ward off His decree"), and most vividly in 19:25 ("wa mrurū khawāṣan — no, pass by it ruined") alongside 19:90 where the skies are nearly rent (tataqṭaʿu) for them, and in 25:34 describing the scattering of the wicked in hell. The root thus grounds a recurring Quranic eschatology of irreversible dispersal, in which unity is shattered and assemblies torn apart — whether by God's decree at death or at the Day when mountains are like carded wool and the guilty are dragged by their forelocks into the Fire.

meaning.en: Ewe. 4x. Na'jah=ewe. 38:23: this is my brother—he has 99 ewes and I have one ewe (na'jah). David's parable of the rich man.
meaning.en_detailed: The noun naʿjah (plural naʿj, niʿāj) denotes a ewe, a mature female sheep, and classical dictionaries distinguish it from a sheep in general (shāh, ghanam) and from a young female (kharūf). The Quran employs the word exclusively within David's parable in 38:23, where one disputant says of his companion, "hādhā akhī lahu tisʿun wa tisʿūna na'jatan wa li-na'jatan wāḥidah — this is my brother; he has ninety-nine ewes and I have one ewe, yet he says, 'Entrust her to me,' and he overwhelms me in speech." The parable is a juridical test for David's prophetic wisdom (the judgment being that the claimant's claim to forcibly take the single ewe from the rightful owner is unjust), and it illustrates the use of a humble pastoral image to teach the ethical principle that the stronger party must not expropriate the property of the weaker, even by one unit.

quranic_analysis.theme: David's parable
quranic_analysis.detail: Tis'un wa tis'una na'jatan—ninety-nine ewes.

meaning.en: Glory. 4x. Majid=glorious. 11:73: He is Praiseworthy, Glorious (Hamidun Majid). 85:15: Lord of the Throne, Glorious (al-Majid).
meaning.en_detailed: Classical Arabic m-j-d combines the senses of glory, nobility, and generous bestowal, the intensive form majīd signifying that which is at once most noble in essence and most generous in giving. In the Quran the root yields the divine epithet al-Majīd (the All-Glorious, the Most Noble), which appears in 11:73 ("innahu hamīdun majīd — He is Praiseworthy, Glorious") applied to Allah, and in 85:15 ("dhū al-ʿarshi al-majīd — the Lord of the Glorious Throne"), both within passages that emphasize divine majesty, magnificence, and uncircumscribed bounty. The root thus anchors a Quranic theology in which God's majesty is inseparable from His liberality: the One whose throne is gloriously elevated is the same One whose grace descends in measureless generosity upon His servants.

quranic_analysis.theme: Glorious Lord
quranic_analysis.detail: Innahu Hamidun Majidun—He is Praiseworthy, Glorious.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ

meaning.en: The root mīm-sīn-ḥāʾ (م-س-ح) fundamentally denotes wiping, anointing, and passing the hand over a surface. It conveys the act of stroking or rubbing something lightly, whether in ritual purification (masḥ over socks or the head), anointing with oil, or surveying land. The core sense involves contact
meaning.ar: (مَسَحَ) الْمِيمُ وَالسِّينُ وَالْحَاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى إِمْرَارِ الْيَدِ عَلَى الشَّيْءِ، سَوَاءٌ كَانَ لِتَنْظِيفٍ أَوْ تَبَرُّكٍ. وَمِنْهُ الْمَسْحُ عَلَى الرَّأْسِ وَالْخُفَّيْنِ.
meaning.en_detailed: Occurring 4 times in the Quranic text, the root م س ح (مسح) conveys the essential concept of Wiping, anointing, and passin. The Quran uses the verb in 5:6 ("wamsḥū bi-ruʾūsikum — and wipe over your heads"), establishing the licit mode of ritual purification, and in 4:43 ("fa-tamassḥū bi-al-ṭīn — then touch (i.e., wipe with) earth") referring to tayammum (dry ablution when water is unavailable), and in 7:195 the verb masaka describes the hand reaching out. The root thereby grounds both a major fiqhi chapter on the conditions and duration of valid wiping, and the principle that the divine law accommodates the condition of the traveler and the sick by permitting lighter modes of cleansing when full ritual washing is impossible.

hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ حُذَيْفَةَ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «إِنَّ الدَّجَّالَ أَعْوَرُ، مَمْسُوحُ الْعَيْنِ الْيُسْرَى»

meaning.en: The root mīm-hāʾ-nūn (م-ه-ن) fundamentally denotes service, profession, and humble labor. It conveys the idea of work that one does habitually as a means of livelihood, often associated with manual or menial tasks. The core sense involves the deliberate engagement in work, particularly that which is
meaning.ar: (مَهَنَ) الْمِيمُ وَالْهَاءُ وَالنُّونُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى ضَعْفٍ وَحَقَارَةٍ. وَالْمَهِينُ: الْحَقِيرُ الضَّعِيفُ. وَمِنْهُ الْمَاءُ الْمَهِينُ: الْقَلِيلُ الْحَقِيرُ.
meaning.en_detailed: Classical Arabic m-h-n yields two contrasting but related semantic fields in the Lisān and Tāj al-ʿArūs: mihnah (trial, affliction, severe testing) and mihn (skilled profession, disciplined craftsmanship), both suggesting a sustained engagement that humbles or refines the practitioner. The Quran employs the root in 67:11 referring to the trial of the people of Pharaoh and their torment, and in the divine address 76:4 ("wa la-qad kunnā qabla dhalika fī sadrin ḍāyiqin — and We had before been in a state of narrowness") plus 77:20 ("a-fara-aytumu al-māʾa alladhī tashrabūn — have you considered the water you drink") where the phrase "al-māʾ al-muhīn" denotes the humble, lowly water that serves but cannot lift itself. The root thus ties the dignity of disciplined service to the humble realities of creaturely need: the servant who endures trial and the servant who works skillfully both occupy the same lexical field of endurance before God.

hadith_evidence.text_en: Abu Huraira reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him honor his guest."

meaning.en: To defame. 4x. Lamaza=defame. 104:1: woe to every slanderer (humazah) and backbiter (lumazah)—Surah al-Humazah. The root denotes malicious defamation.
meaning.en_detailed: لَمَزَ (ل م ز), a root appearing 4 times in the Quran, encodes the notion of To defame, slander across its various verbal and nominal forms. The Quran employs the noun al-lumazah (the backbiting fault-finder) in 104:1 ("waylun li-kulli humazatin lumazah — woe to every slandering backbiter"), a surah devoted to condemning those who disparage others while believing themselves prosperous, and the root thereby grounds a major chapter of ʿaqīdah and akhlāq on the prohibition of contemptuous speech that wounds the dignity of a fellow Muslim. The Quranic ethic reaches beyond private morality into social critique: such a person counts, records, mocks, and oppresses, unaware that every word is written and weighed.

quranic_analysis.theme: Woe to slanderers
quranic_analysis.detail: Waylun li-kulli humazatin lumazah—woe to every slanderer.

meaning.en: The root lām-jīm-jīm (ل-ج-ج) fundamentally denotes persistence, obstinacy, and the deep, fathomless sea. It conveys two interconnected ideas: (1) stubborn insistence on a course of action, refusing to relent; (2) the vast, deep ocean that seems endless. The core sense involves something vast and uny
meaning.ar: اللَّامُ وَالْجِيمُ وَالْجِيمُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْمُوَالَاةِ وَاللُّزُومِ. مِنْ ذَلِكَ الْإِلْجَاجُ، وَهُوَ الْإِلْحَاحُ. وَاللُّجَّةُ: كَثْرَةُ الْمَاءِ وَتَرَاكُمُهُ.
meaning.en_detailed: Ibn Fāris derives l-j-j from two senses that share the underlying image of depth and persistence: lujjah (the deep, fathomless sea) and iljāj (stubborn insistence, pressing on without relenting). The Quran applies the root to both images: 25:53 ("wa huwa alladhī maraja al-baḥrayni hādhā ʿadhbun furātun wa hādhā milḥun ujāj — and it is He who merged the two seas, this one sweet and this one bitter and salty") using ujjāj for the bitter sea that overwhelms the palate, and 51:11 describing the drowned people of Lot (al-lajjīn) whose course of persistence in sin ended beneath the deep. The root thereby links the moral image of stubborn insistence to the cosmic image of the unfathomable sea — both domains where human measure is overwhelmed — and 31:27 affirms that "all speech" (al-kalām) cannot exhaust God's knowledge, just as the sea cannot be drained.

meaning.en_short: A cup, goblet, or drinking ve
meaning.en: The root kāf-wāw-bāʾ (ك-و-ب) fundamentally denotes a cup, goblet, or drinking vessel. It conveys the idea of a round, brimless container used for beverages, distinct from a 'kaʾs' (a filled cup). The core sense involves a vessel of hospitality and pleasure. In the Quran, 'akwāb' (cups) are among the
meaning.ar: الكَوْبُ: إناءُ الشَّرابِ، والجمعُ أكْوابٌ. قال ابنُ فارس: الكافُ والواوُ والباءُ أصلٌ واحدٌ يدلُّ على إناءٍ يُشْرَبُ فيه.
meaning.en_detailed: Classical Arabic k-w-b designates a rounded drinking vessel, often without a handle and typically used for wine or aromatic drinks in contexts of refined hospitality; the plural akwāb is the more common Quranic form, while kāʾs denotes a filled cup and ibriq a jug. The Quran lists akwāb among the furnishings of Paradise in 56:18 ("akwābin mawḍūḥah — goblets placed in position"), 37:45 ("yuqālu lahā wa kaʾsun dhayq — a cup of mingled drink will be passed to them") with the surrounding context of khawāṣir and ʿīnān, 76:15 ("akwābin wadqāl — set before them goblets and vessels of silver"), and 78:34 ("akwāban jāwiyah — goblets placed in array"). The root thus anchors an entire Quranic imagery of celestial hospitality in which the elect are served from vessels whose very shape signals purity, refinement, and an unending banquet that contrasts with the filth (ghislīn) of the rejected.

hadith_evidence.text_en: Ibn Abbas reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "In Paradise are things that no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no heart has conceived."

meaning.en: Distress. 4x. 21:76: rescued from great distress (al-karb).
meaning.en_detailed: The triconsonantal root ك ر ب (كَرَبَ) — 4 Quranic occurrences — fundamentally expresses Distress, anguish. The Quran employs al-karb al-ʿaẓīm (great distress) in 21:76 ("wa najjaynāhu mina al-karbi al-ʿaẓīm") in the story of David and Solomon, where David's just judgment over the ewe parable is followed by his prayer and Solomon's gift of wisdom, and in 21:77 and 2:45 referring to the distress of those who turn away from remembrance and who are laden with burdens. The root thereby grounds a major dimension of prophetic spirituality: the karb is not merely psychological distress but a state of existential pressure that only God can relieve, and the Quran presents Divine response to genuine karb as a sign of mercy, exemplified in 21:76 where the prophets are rescued and given both insight and sagacity.

quranic_analysis.theme: Rescued from distress
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa najjaynahu min al-karbi al-azim—rescued from great distress.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ
hadith_evidence.en: Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.

meaning.en: The root lām-mīm-mīm (ل-م-م) fundamentally denotes gathering, collecting, and approaching closely. It conveys the idea of things being brought together, assembled, or coming near to something. The core sense involves proximity and aggregation. In the Quran, 'lamam' refers to minor sins or fleeting f
meaning.ar: اللَّامُ وَالْمِيمُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْجَمْعِ وَالضَّمِّ. مِنْ ذَلِكَ لَمَمْتُ الشَّيْءَ أَلُمُّهُ لَمًّا إِذَا جَمَعْتَهُ وَضَمَمْتَ بَعْضَهُ إِلَى بَعْضٍ.
meaning.en_detailed: Classical Arabic l-m-m combines the senses of gathering, brushing close, and being almost upon a thing without fully arriving — the noun lamam denoting either a near approach or the small sins that brush the soul without dominating it. The Quran employs this latter sense in 53:32 ("wa alladhīna ijtanabū kabīra al-ithm wa al-fawāḥisha illā l-lamam — those who avoid the greater sins and indecencies, save for lamam"), where classical tafsīr distinguishes lamam from persistent major sins, treating it as fleeting lapses or minor faults. The hadith literature adds that "Allah has overlooked for my nation what their souls whisper so long as they do not speak of it or act upon it" (Bukhārī, Muslim), rooting the doctrine of divine forbearance in this same idea of the fleeting brush that does not consolidate into a settled state of sin.

meaning.en: Body. 4x. Jasad=body, corpse. 38:34: We placed on his throne a body (jasadan)—Solomon's test. 7:148: the calf—a mere body that lows.
meaning.en_detailed: جَسَدَ (ج س د), a root appearing 4 times in the Quran, encodes the notion of Body, corpse across its various verbal and nominal forms. The Quran employs the word in 38:34 ("wa alqaynā ʿalā kursiyyihi jasadan — and We cast upon his throne a jasad") within the trial of Solomon, where the body that occupied his throne either died or was a demon forced to take Solomon's form, and in 7:148 describing the golden calf as "jasadan lahu khuwārun — a body that lows," contrasted by Moses with the living Lord who hears and sees. The root thereby marks a crucial Quranic opposition: the mere body or form, however impressive, is not alive before God unless it is animated by the spirit (rūḥ) and the soul (nafs) that He alone breathes.

quranic_analysis.theme: Solomon's test
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa alqayna ala kursiyyihi jasadan—a body on his throne.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ

meaning.en: The root jīm-rāʾ-ḥāʾ (ج-ر-ح) fundamentally denotes wounding, injuring, and acquiring. It conveys two interconnected meanings: (1) the act of cutting or injuring the body, causing a visible wound; (2) the earning or acquisition of something — whether good deeds or sins — through one's actions. The co
meaning.ar: الْجِيمُ وَالرَّاءُ وَالْحَاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْقَطْعِ وَالْكَسْرِ. وَمِنْهُ الْجُرْحُ، وَهُوَ الْقَطْعُ فِي الْجَسَدِ.
meaning.en_detailed: Classical Arabic j-r-ḥ fuses two semantic fields Ibn Fāris groups together as 'cutting and breaking': jarḥ (a wound, an incision in the body, especially one inflicted by a sword) and kasb (acquisition, the act of earning one's portion through action). The Quran uses the root primarily in the acquisitional sense in 9:14, 9:24, and 9:111 in the contrast between those who "jarḥū fī sabil Allāh" (strive through action in God's path) and those who merely claim faith, while 2:60 and other verses use jarḥ for literal wounds in the context of retaliation (qisāṣ). The root thus grounds both the legal doctrine of equal retaliation for wounds ("al-jarḥ bi-al-qisāṣ") and the moral doctrine that humans acquire, through every action, exactly what they have chosen for the hereafter — both senses bound together by the image of the soul being wounded or earned according to its deeds.

meaning.en_short: A wall, enclosure, and that w
meaning.en: The root jīm-dāl-rāʾ (ج-د-ر) fundamentally denotes a wall, enclosure, and that which is fitting or worthy. It conveys two primary ideas: (1) the physical structure of a wall that encloses and protects; (2) the quality of being suitable, appropriate, or deserving of something. The core sense involves
meaning.ar: الْجِيمُ وَالدَّالُ وَالرَّاءُ أَصْلَانِ: أَحَدُهُمَا الْجِدَارُ، وَالْآخَرُ الْجَدَارَةُ وَهِيَ الِاسْتِحْقَاقُ. يُقَالُ: هُوَ جَدِيرٌ بِكَذَا أَيْ خَلِيقٌ وَمُسْتَحِقٌّ.
meaning.en_detailed: Classical Arabic j-d-r yields two complementary senses Ibn Fāris distinguishes: jadīr (a wall, the enclosing structure of a building) and jadārah (suitability, worthiness — as in jadīr, deserving). The Quran employs jadīr in the singular at 18:82 and 18:77 (the wall that the righteous youth Dhū al-Qarnayn rebuilt over the orphaned people's treasure), in the plural jidārin at 18:21 describing the wall of the cave, and in 59:14 ("law naḥnu ʿalayna la-mā ʿalā al-jidāri aw ḥiṭānan — if they had been against us, they would not have been able to hold against a wall or barricade"). The hadith "akrimū akhākum" and other ethical applications use the derived sense of deserving, while the physical image of the rebuilt wall — restored without payment, without betrayal of the trust — illustrates the Quranic ideal of protecting the vulnerable who cannot yet reward protection.

meaning.en: The root ghayn-yāʾ-thāʾ (غ-ي-ث) fundamentally denotes rain, aid, and divine succor. It conveys the idea of life-giving water sent from the heavens and, by extension, any help or relief that arrives when desperately needed. The core sense involves rescue from hardship through an external beneficent f
meaning.ar: الغَيْثُ: المَطَرُ، والغَوْثُ: الإغاثَةُ، والغِيَاثُ: الإغاثَةُ، والاسْتِغاثَةُ: طَلَبُ الغَوْثِ
meaning.en_detailed: Classical Arabic gh-y-th denotes rain that comes to relieve drought, and by extension any succor or aid that arrives at the moment of greatest need — the same root yielding ghawth (rescue, succor), istighātha (cry for help), and maghīth (responder). The Quran applies the root most often to the literal rain that revives the dead earth after drought: 6:6, 27:58-60 ("wa anzalnā mina al-muʿṣirāti māʾan fīhi jibālun min māʾin — and We sent down from the rain-clouds water in torrents"), 4:32, and 7:57 ("wa Allāhu anzala mina al-samāʾi māʾan fa-aḥyā bihi al-arḍa baʿda mawtihā — He sent down water from the sky and quickened the earth after its death"). The root thereby grounds one of the most powerful Quranic natural signs — water as divine gift, and analogically the rain of mercy that revives the soul of the believer when faith has become dry.

meaning.en: The root hāʾ-yāʾ-hamza (ه-ي-أ) fundamentally denotes preparation, readiness, and shaping something into proper form. It conveys the act of arranging, organizing, and making something suitable for its intended purpose. The core sense involves the transition from disorder to order, from potential to a
meaning.ar: الْهَاءُ وَالْيَاءُ وَالْهَمْزَةُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى إِصْلَاحِ الشَّيْءِ وَتَهْيِئَتِهِ. يُقَالُ: هَيَّأْتُ الشَّيْءَ تَهْيِئَةً، إِذَا أَصْلَحْتَهُ وَجَعَلْتَهُ عَلَى هَيْئَةٍ.
meaning.en_detailed: Classical Arabic h-y-ʾ denotes the act of preparing, arranging, or shaping something so that it becomes fit for its intended purpose, the verb hayyiʾa (Form II) meaning to dispose, and the noun hayʾah the resulting form or shape. The Quran uses the verb primarily in the divine or angelic voice: in 18:81 commanding that the corrupt city of Dhu al-Qarnayn's exploiters be readied for its punishment ("ḥattā idhā nazzalnā ʿalayhi ṭāghūta — until We brought against them a war-cry"), and in 81:18 ("wa al-layli idhā ʿasʿasā"), the imperative and active of this root grounding the idea that every phenomenon has been precisely shaped and readied by God. Theologically, the root teaches that nothing in creation is haphazard — every event, every soul, every worldly preparation has its preordained form — and that human responsibility lies in shaping the soul (tahayyuʾ) to receive the divine decree when it comes.

The Quran applies the verb to the ritual bath of the deceased before burial in 5:31 ("khafīfan dhālika dayman aw thawban — light that al-mayta washed"), to the washing of the idol-garments in 37:41 ("wa ḥīrin mājiʾin — and a blazing fire"), and to the unending flow of ghislīn in the pit of Hell (69:36, "wa la-ṭaʿāmu illā min ghislīn — and no food except from ghislīn"), which denotes the purulent exudate of those in the Fire. meaning.en: The root ghayn-mīm-rāʾ (غ-م-ر) fundamentally denotes submerging, overwhelming, and the inexperience of youth. It conveys three interconnected ideas: (1) water that covers and overwhelms, flooding over something; (2) the generosity that overflows, giving abundantly; (3) the raw, untested nature of a
meaning.ar: الْغَيْنُ وَالْمِيمُ وَالرَّاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى التَّغْطِيَةِ. مِنْ ذَلِكَ الْغَمْرَةُ: الشِّدَّةُ تُغَطِّي الْإِنْسَانَ. وَالْغَمَرَاتُ: شَدَائِدُ الْمَوْتِ.
meaning.en_detailed: Classical Arabic gh-m-r combines three closely related senses Ibn Fāris describes as 'covering and overwhelming': ghamrah (a deluge that overwhelms), ghamarāt (the throes of death or the overmastering calamities), and ghamar (a young, untrained bird that has not yet learned). The Quran employs the plural ghamarāt in 6:93 ("wa la-qad ʿalimta anna l-insāna la-yughmā — you know indeed that the human soul is overwhelmed"), and the singular in the image of youth untrained in 22:5 ("wa tara al-arḍa hāmiʾatan — and you see the earth black with vegetation"), but the most concentrated theological use is in 6:93 and 79:1 ("wa al-nāziʿāti gharaqā — by those who pluck out violently") plus the hadith on the "deluge of death." The root thus connects three Quranic themes: the cosmic flood that overwhelms the wicked (Nūḥ, the people of ʿĀd), the death-throes that overwhelm the soul in its final hour, and the untrained novice whose soul is still open and in need of formation.

meaning.en: To lower. 4x. Ghadda=lower. 24:30: tell believing men to lower their gaze (yaghuddu min absarihim). 24:31: tell believing women. The root of modesty.
meaning.en_detailed: The triconsonantal root غ ض ض (غَضَّ) — 4 Quranic occurrences — fundamentally expresses To lower (gaze). The Quran employs the imperative form yaghudḍū twice in 24:30-31 ("qul li-al-muʾminīna yaghudḍū min abṣārihim wa yaḥfaẓū furūjahum — tell the believing men to lower their gaze and guard their private parts; and tell the believing women to lower their gaze and guard their private parts"), establishing the dual foundation of ʿaqīdah and akhlāq: the eye is the gateway to the heart, and the disciplined lowering of vision is the first outward sign of inner taqwā. The root thereby grounds a major chapter of Islamic ethics on the relationship between sight and chastity, with the hadith "the gaze is a poisoned arrow of Satan" reinforcing the Quranic principle that the chastened eye precedes the chastened soul.

meaning.en: Darkness. 4x. Ghasaq=darkness. 17:78: establish prayer until the darkness of night (ghasaqi al-layl). 113:3: from the evil of darkness (ghasiqin) when it settles.
meaning.en_detailed: Classical Arabic gh-s-q denotes the darkness of night as it deepens and settles — particularly the late-night blackness, the verbal noun ghasaq sometimes glossed as the inky darkness that descends between the dusk and the dawn. The Quran employs ghasaq al-layl in 17:78 ("aqimi al-ṣalāta li-dulūki al-shamsi ilā ghasaqi al-layl — establish prayer from the decline of the sun until the darkness of night"), defining the temporal boundary of the daily ritual structure, and the active participle gāsiq in 113:3 ("min sharri ghāsiqin idhā waqab — from the evil of darkness when it settles"), used in the protective invocation of Surah al-Falaq. The root thereby grounds two complementary Quranic images: the lawful, ordained darkness that frames the nightly prayer and the protective remembrance of God, and the threatening darkness (ghasiq) from which the believer seeks refuge in God's own name — for the night is both veil of divine mercy and matrix of unseen harm.

meaning.en: To excuse, to accept an apology; virginity, intactness. The root spans the social practice of offering and accepting excuses (maʿādhīr) and the physical state of untouched purity. Quranic usage at 75:15 declares that even if one 'offers all excuses' on the Day of Judgment, they will not be accepted, while legal contexts discuss the legitimacy of excuses in discharging religious obligations. The theological extension emphasizes that God alone is the ultimate excuser and acceptor of sincere repentance.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ع ذ ر (عَذَر), attested 12 times in the Quran, derives its core meaning of Excuse, apology; virginity from Proto-Semitic sources. With 12 Qurʾānic occurrences, the plural مَعَاذِير (excuses) appears at 75:15 ('وَلَوْ أَلْقَىٰ مَعَاذِيرَهُ'), declaring that even if one offers all one's excuses, they will not be accepted on the Day of Judgment, and in legal contexts discussing those who offer false excuses. The theological use of the root extends to excusing believers of obligations when legitimate cause exists (العُذر), with the classical meaning of 'virginity' tied to the metaphor of physical intactness paralleling moral purity.

meaning.en: To seek refuge, to take shelter, to appeal for protection. The root is central to the Quranic vocabulary of divine protection: aʿūdhu ('I seek refuge') opens the two protective sūras (113, 114), and istaʿidh ('seek refuge') is counseled whenever satanic suggestion arises (7:200). The root names the believer's reflex of turning to God for shelter against evil — a spiritual act so fundamental it frames the daily experience of threat and the corresponding recourse to divine guardianship.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ع-و-ذ conveys seeking refuge, protection, and shelter, central to the Qurʾānic invocations of divine protection against evil and misfortune. With 17 occurrences, the first-person singular أَعُوذُ ('I seek refuge') appears in the two protective sūras 113:1 ('قُلْ أَعُوذُ بِرَبِّ الْفَلَقِ') and 114:1 ('قُلْ أَعُوذُ بِرَبِّ النَّاسِ'), as well as throughout the imperative اِسْتَعِذْ بِاللَّهِ (e.g., 7:200 'وَإِمَّا يَنزَغَنَّكَ مِنَ الشَّيْطَانِ نَزْغٌ فَاسْتَعِذْ بِاللَّهِ'). The root's semantic core of flight to sanctuary is realized in Islamic ritual through the taʿawwudh formula preceding Qurʾānic recitation, and undergirds the broader theological principle that all genuine refuge (iʿādha) is found only in God.

meaning.en: To live, to exist biologically; livelihood, sustenance, the means of life. The root captures both the fact of being alive and the material conditions that sustain life. Quranic usage affirms God's provision of maʿāyish — diverse means of subsistence on earth (7:10) — while warning that turning from divine remembrance yields maʿīshah ḍankā, a straitened, constricted life (20:124). The root thus links biological survival to spiritual orientation.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ع-ي-ش denotes life and livelihood/sustenance, capturing both biological existence and the material means by which life is sustained. With 8 Qurʾānic occurrences, the plural مَعَايِش (livelihoods) appears at 7:10 ('وَجَعَلْنَا لَكُمْ فِيهَا مَعَايِشَ'), affirming God's provision of diverse means of subsistence on earth, while the singular مَعِيشَة occurs at 20:124 ('فَإِنَّ لَهُ مَعِيشَةً ضَنكًا'), warning that turning from divine remembrance yields a straitened life. The semantic relationship between ʿaysh (life) and maʿīsha (livelihood) reflects a Qurʾānic anthropology in which true life encompasses both spiritual orientation and material provision, with the latter inseparable from the former as divinely ordained sustenance.

meaning.en: To seize violently, to strike with force, to overpower. The root denotes sudden, forceful seizure — the kind of violent grasp that overwhelms resistance instantaneously. Quranic usage characterizes the tyrannical behavior of past nations: 'When you strike, you strike as tyrants' (26:130), describing the people of Lot. The root names the mode of action characteristic of oppressors who rely on brute force rather than justice.
meaning.en_detailed: بَطَش (ب ط ش), a root appearing 10 times in the Quran, encodes the notion of To seize violently, strike across its various verbal and nominal forms. With 10 Qurʾānic occurrences, it appears at 26:130 ('وَإِذَا بَطَشْتُم بَطَشْتُمْ جَبَّارِينَ'), characterizing the people of Lot as striking tyrannously, and at 28:19 ('فَلَمَّا أَنْ أَرَادَ أَن يَبْطِشَ بِالَّذِي هُوَ عَدُوٌّ لَّهُمَا'), describing Moses' attempt to strike the Egyptian oppressor. The root's semantic core of sudden forceful seizure is theologically extended to God's own 'taking' (بَطْشَة اللَّه), as at 7:155 ('لَهُمْ عَذَابٌ أَلِيمٌ بِمَا كَانُوا يَسْتَكْبِرُونَ'), emphasizing divine omnipotence expressed through overwhelming intervention against the wicked.

meaning.en: The reduplicated quadriliteral S-l-S-l (ص-ل-ص-ل) denotes ringing, clinking clay. In the Quran (55:14), man is created from SalSāl (صلصال) — sounding clay, describing the material stage before the spirit was breathed in. Ibn Faris notes the onomatopoeic quality: the sound of dry clay striking clay.
meaning.ar: صلصل: جَذْرٌ قُرْآنِيٌّ يَدُلُّ عَلَى مَفْهُومٍ فِي الْقُرْآنِ الْكَرِيمِ.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ص-ل-ص-ل, an onomatopoetic reduplicated quadrilateral denoting ringing, clinking clay (occurs 4x in the Quran). Its chief deployment is the creation narrative at 15:26, 15:28, 15:33, and 55:14, where man is created from صلصال (ṣalṣāl, sounding clay) — describing the material substrate of Adam before the spirit was breathed in. Ibn Fāris notes the onomatopoeic quality (the sound of dry clay striking clay), distinguishing it from طين (ṭīn, moist clay) and حَمَإ مَسْنُون (ḥamaʾ masnūn, dark fetid mud). The root belongs to a small set of Quranic quadrilaterals whose semantic force is mimetic rather than derivational.

meaning.en: The quadriliteral q-n-T-r (ق-ن-ط-ر) denotes heaps of wealth, great riches. A loanword from Aramaic qanṭrā or ultimately Latin centenarium. In the Quran (3:14, 4:20, 3:14), it describes accumulated gold and silver that distract from worship. Muqanṭarah (مقنطرة) = stored up in heaps.
meaning.ar: قنطر: جَذْرٌ قُرْآنِيٌّ يَدُلُّ عَلَى مَفْهُومٍ فِي الْقُرْآنِ الْكَرِيمِ.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ق-ن-ط-ر, a quadrilateral denoting heaps of accumulated wealth and great hoards (occurs 4x in the Quran), likely a loanword from Aramaic qanṭarā or Latin centenarium. Its principal Quranic uses are 3:14 (ʿindahū qinṭārun min dhahabin, 'with him a hundred-weight of gold') and 4:20, with the adjectival muqanṭarah ('heaped up, stored in abundance') in 3:14 describing hoarded gold and silver. The Quran consistently frames قنطار as a worldly enticement (ẓīna) that competes with remembrance of Allah rather than as a blessing in itself — the greedy believer is warned that such wealth will not deliver on the Day of Judgment.

meaning.en: The quadriliteral z-x-r-f (ز-خ-ر-ف) conveys ornamentation, gold decoration. Al-Raghib describes it as "beautification with gold." In the Quran (6:112, 10:24, 17:93, 43:35), it describes worldly adornment that deceives, contrasted with lasting spiritual truth.

meaning.en_detailed: Root ز-خ-ر-ف, a quadrilateral denoting gaudy ornamentation, gilding, and seductive beautification (occurs 4x in the Quran). Its Quranic uses are 6:112 (zukhrufa al-qawl, 'adorned speech that misleads'), 10:24 (the worldly life likened to rain whose produce amazes the disbelievers), 17:93, and 43:35 (gilded adornment rejected). Al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī defines it as beautification through gold; the Quran consistently contrasts زخرف with the lasting truth of divine revelation, marking worldly ornament as deceptive and ephemeral.

Classical usage (Ibn Fāris) frames the root as 'to drive forward and impel'; the Quran deploys it for the meteorological propulsion of clouds, rendering wind an instrument of divine governance over the atmosphere.

meaning.en: Foam. 3x. Zabad=foam. 13:17: the flood carries foam (zabadan) rising—parable of truth and falsehood. The foam vanishes but what benefits remains.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ز-ب-د, a triliteral denoting foam, scum, and the froth that rises from agitated liquids (occurs 3x in the Quran). Its most striking usage is 13:17 (zabadan rābiyan) — the foam rising from a torrent as a parable of falsehood, vanishing while the beneficial substance remains for people; 34:12 and 13:17 (reprise) deploy the cognate for the dross separated from molten ore. The Quranic image is that of base and pure elements being partitioned — a recurring parable of truth and falsehood.

Ibn Fāris defines the root as 'to lower and quiet' — Quranic usage renders it the controlled, measured expression of reverence or secrecy.

It conveys the act of hitting something with force and the consequent disoriented, unsteady movement. The core sense involves loss of control and stability. The Quran uses this root in the powerful p

meaning.en_detailed: Root خ-ب-ت, a triliteral denoting abating, subsiding, and becoming quiet or humble (occurs 3x in the Quran). hadith_evidence.text_en: Abu Huraira reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The best of you is the best to his family, and I am the best of you to my family."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ أَبِي هُرَيْرَةَ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «خَيْرُكُمْ خَيْرُكُمْ لِأَهْلِهِ، وَأَنَا خَيْرُكُمْ لِأَهْلِي»

meaning.en: Idol. 3x. 29:17: you worship idols (awthanan) besides Allah.
meaning.en_detailed: Root و-ث-ن, a triliteral denoting an idol, graven image, and stone-statue worshipped in lieu of God (occurs 3x in the Quran). Its occurrences are 29:17 and 29:25 in the plural awthān within the critique of the ʿābidīn al-awthān ('idol-worshippers'), and 21:57-59 in Abraham's polemic against the idols his people worship besides Allah. The Quranic awthān are consistently framed as the null alternatives to the worship of the One God, and Abraham's mocking of the idols (21:63) is paradigmatic of prophetic engagement with tāghūt.

quranic_analysis.theme: Idols worshiped
quranic_analysis.detail: Innama ta'buduna min duni Allahi awthanan—you worship idols.

hadith_evidence.ar: إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ

meaning.en: The root khāʾ-dhāl-lām (خ-ذ-ل) fundamentally denotes forsaking, abandoning, and failing to support when support is needed. It conveys the act of withdrawing help at a critical moment, leaving someone isolated and vulnerable. The core sense involves betrayal through desertion — the failure of an ally
meaning.ar: «الْخَاءُ وَالذَّالُ وَاللَّامُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى تَرْكِ النَّصْرِ وَالْإِعَانَةِ. يُقَالُ: خَذَلَهُ يَخْذُلُهُ خَذْلًا وَخِذْلَانًا، إِذَا تَرَكَ نَصْرَهُ وَخَذَلَ عَنْهُ أَصْحَابُهُ.»
meaning.en_detailed: Root خ-ذ-ل, a triliteral denoting forsaking, abandoning support, and failing to come to the aid of an ally (occurs 3x in the Quran). Its uses are 3:144 (wa in yanshuri'llāhu yanshurkum, 'if Allah helps you, none can overcome you'), 8:30, and 73:11, all concerning divine takhyīḍ — Allah's abandonment or support. Ibn Fāris defines the root as 'to abandon support and aid'; the Quranic emphasis is on divine abandonment being the most feared consequence of sin, as when the Prophet warns that Allah may withdraw His favor from a people.

meaning.en: The root wāw-jīm-sīn (و-ج-س) fundamentally denotes sensing, perceiving inwardly, and the hidden flutter of fear. It conveys the subtle, instinctive detection of something — often danger — that arises within the heart before the mind fully registers it. The core sense involves an intuitive, pre-cogni
meaning.ar: الْوَاوُ وَالْجِيمُ وَالسِّينُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْحِسِّ وَالْخَوْفِ الْخَفِيِّ. يُقَالُ: أَوْجَسَ الرَّجُلُ، إِذَا أَضْمَرَ الْخَوْفَ فِي نَفْسِهِ
meaning.en_detailed: Root و-ج-س, a triliteral denoting a subtle inner stirring, instinctive perception, and the hidden flutter of fear (occurs 3x in the Quran). All three occurrences — 3:154, 8:2, and 9:125 — describe āwajaṣat fī nafsihī, the instinctive apprehension in the Prophet's companions during the battles of Uḥud and after the Tabūk expedition. Classical usage (Ibn Fāris) frames it as 'hidden perception' — the Quran uses it for the pre-rational detection of threat that precedes deliberation.

meaning.en: The root thāʾ-lām-lām (ث-ل-ل) fundamentally denotes ruin, destruction, and the crumbling of what was once solid. It conveys the utter demolition and collapse of a structure or the devastation of a people. The core sense involves a complete breaking down — not just damage, but total ruin. This root a
meaning.ar: الثَّاءُ وَاللَّامُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى جَمَاعَةٍ مِنَ النَّاسِ، وَيُقَالُ: ثُلَّةٌ مِنَ النَّاسِ أَيْ جَمَاعَةٌ كَثِيرَةٌ
meaning.en_detailed: Root ث-ل-ل, a triliteral fundamentally denoting a group or party of people (occurs 3x in the Quran). Its occurrences — 11:100, 17:5, and 25:38 — use thulāl, the desolate remains of past generations who once stood as a multitude. Classical meaning (Ibn Fāris) is thullatun min al-nās, 'a gathering of people'; the sense of ruin is the secondary semantic of 'what remains of a destroyed community'. The Quran deploys it to mark the post-destruction emptiness of cities once populous.

meaning.en_short: A peg, stake, and that which
meaning.en: The root wāw-tāʾ-dāl (و-ت-د) fundamentally denotes a peg, stake, and that which is driven firmly into the ground for anchorage. It conveys the idea of securing something by fixing it in place, providing stability and support. The core sense involves firmness and permanence. The Quran uses 'awtād' (p
meaning.ar: الْوَاوُ وَالتَّاءُ وَالدَّالُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى ثَبَاتٍ وَشِدَّةٍ. مِنْ ذَلِكَ الْوَتِدُ، وَهُوَ مَا يُوتَدُ فِي الْأَرْضِ مِنْ خَشَبٍ أَوْ حَدِيدٍ.
meaning.en_detailed: Root و-ت-د, a triliteral denoting a peg, stake, or iron rod driven into the ground for anchorage (occurs 3x in the Quran). Its occurrences are 38:12 (Iblīs's boast to be superior to Adam and his awtādin), 78:7 (wa jʿalnā fīhā rawāsiya shākhiḍātin wa jaʿalnā lahum fīhā furujan, 'and We placed therein firm mountains and gave them shelter'), and 89:1 (the cosmic oath over al-fajr). Classical usage (Ibn Fāris) frames the root as 'firmness and strength'; the Quranic awtād is both literal fastening and metaphor for the apparently unshakeable that collapses before Allah.

meaning.en: The root wāw-tāʾ-rāʾ (و-ت-ر) fundamentally denotes odd number, singular, and that which stands alone without a pair. It conveys the state of being unmatched, unprecedented, or occurring at intervals. The core sense involves individuality and unevenness. The Quran swears by 'al-watr' — the odd, the s
meaning.ar: الْوَاوُ وَالتَّاءُ وَالرَّاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى انْفِرَادٍ مِنَ الْأَشْيَاءِ. يُقَالُ: وَتْرٌ وَوِتْرٌ، وَهُوَ الْفَرْدُ. وَالْإِيتَارُ: إِفْرَادُ الشَّيْءِ.
meaning.en_detailed: Root و-ت-ر, a triliteral denoting being odd, singular, and unmatched (occurs 3x in the Quran). Its most striking usage is 89:3 (wa al-shafʿi wa al-watri) — the cosmic oath 'by the even and the odd' — alongside the divine attribute Allah as al-Witr (6:46, 13:16) and the witr prayer. P-Semitic *wtr 'to be single, odd' underlies the Arabic sense; the Quran elevates oddness/uniqueness into a divine attribute, since He is singular without a pair.

hadith_evidence.text_en: Abdullah ibn Amr reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The merciful will be shown mercy by the Most Merciful. Be merciful to those on earth, and the One in heaven will have mercy upon you."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ بْنِ عَمْرٍو رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمَا قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «الرَّاحِمُونَ يَرْحَمُهُمُ الرَّحْمَنُ، ارْحَمُوا مَنْ فِي الْأَرْضِ يَرْحَمْ

etymology.semantic_evolution: P-Semitic *wtr = 'to be single, odd'. Arabic watr = odd number. Witr = the odd-numbered prayer. 'By the even and the odd (wa al-shafʿi wa al-watri)' (89:3) — cosmic oath.

meaning.en: To be palatable. 3x. Sagha=be easy to swallow. 16:66: pure milk, easy to swallow (sa'ighan) for drinkers—the cow parable.
meaning.en_detailed: Root س-و-غ, a triliteral denoting being palatable, easy to swallow, and agreeable to the body (occurs 3x in the Quran). Its principal usage is 16:66 (labānan khalisan sāighan li'l-shāribīn) — 'pure milk, easy to swallow for those who drink' — the climactic detail of the cow-parable. Classical meaning extends to what the system accepts without reluctance (sāghat al-ṭaʿām, 'the food was agreeable to swallow'); the Quran deploys it for nourishment that slips easily down the throat as a sign of divine care in the produce of the cattle.

quranic_analysis.theme: Pure milk
quranic_analysis.detail: Labanan khalisan sa'ighan—pure milk, pleasant to swallow.

meaning.en: The root sīn-yāʾ-ḥāʾ (س-ي-ح) fundamentally denotes flowing, traveling, and moving freely through the land. It conveys the idea of water flowing across the earth's surface and, by extension, the spiritual practice of wandering the land in devotion and reflection. The core sense involves unbounded, pu
meaning.ar: السِّينُ وَالْيَاءُ وَالْحَاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الذَّهَابِ فِي الْأَرْضِ. يُقَالُ: سَاحَ يَسِيحُ سَيْحًا وَسِيَاحَةً، إِذَا ذَهَبَ فِي الْأَرْضِ
meaning.en_detailed: Root س-ي-ح, a triliteral denoting flowing, traveling, and moving freely through the land (occurs 3x in the Quran). Its occurrences include 2:240 (wa al-sāʾiḥātu al-sayḥ 'alayhi in muttuwa huwa akhkhaluhum), 9:112, and 66:5 in the legal context of waiting periods and devotional wandering. Ibn Fāris defines the root as 'to go forth in the earth'; in Quranic usage sāḥa and the cognate sāʾiḥāt describe those who traverse the land for remembrance and as a lifeway of faith.

meaning.en: The root sīn-ṭāʾ-rāʾ (س-ط-ر) fundamentally denotes a line, row, and the act of writing. It conveys the structuring of information into ordered lines — whether written lines on a page, aligned trees in an orchard, or narratives set in sequence. The core sense involves deliberate arrangement and inscr
meaning.ar: قال ابن فارس في مقاييس اللغة: السين والتاء والراء أصل واحد يدل على تغطية الشيء وستره. يقال: سترت الشيء أستره ستراً، إذا غطيته. والستر: ما يستر به.
meaning.en_detailed: Root س-ط-ر (with ṭāʾ), a triliteral denoting a line, row, and the act of writing — distinct from the homograph س-ت-ر with tāʾ meaning covering (occurs 3x in the Quran). Its principal occurrence is 36:12 (satr qabla dhālika fī al-ṣuḥufi al-ūlā) — 'inscribed in former scriptures' — alongside 6:7 and 6:112. Classical meaning (Ibn Fāris) is 'arranged lines' — of letters, or rows of palm trees (suṭūr al-nakhl); the root governs the act of inscribing with deliberate order, of writing things down row upon row.

meaning.en: To strip. 3x. Salakha=strip. 36:37: We strip (naslakhu) the day from the night—emergence of daylight. The root denotes peeling away.
meaning.en_detailed: Root س-ل-خ, a triliteral denoting stripping, peeling, and removing a covering layer (occurs 3x in the Quran). Its principal occurrence is 36:37 (wa āyatan lahum al-laylu naslakh minhu al-nahāra) — 'a sign for them is the night, from which We strip the day' — a vivid image of light displacing darkness. Classical meaning is 'to peel off a skin or covering'; the Quran deploys it for the cosmic removal of one state to reveal another — a recurring typology of divine unveiling.

quranic_analysis.detail: Naslakhu minhu al-nahar—We strip day from night.

It conveys the gradual process by which sorrow, worry, or attachment fades from the heart, replaced by what brings comfort and peace. The core sense involves the healing passage of time and the
meaning.ar: (سَلَا) السِّينُ وَاللَّامُ وَالْحَرْفُ الْمُعْتَلُّ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى ذَهَابِ الْحُزْنِ وَالْهَمِّ. يُقَالُ سَلَوْتُ عَنْهُ أَسْلُو سُلُوًّا، إِذَا ذَهَبَ حُزْنُكَ عَنْهُ.
meaning.en_detailed: Root س-ل-و, a triliteral denoting forgetting, consoling, and the gradual fading of grief or attachment from the heart (occurs 3x in the Quran). Its principal occurrences are 12:13 and 12:18 (ta-salawaynī) — Jacob's sons telling him, 'If he [Joseph] is taken, you will be among the losers' — paired with the cognate salawayn in 7:180. Classical meaning (Ibn Fāris) is 'the departure of grief and anxiety from oneself'; the Quran deploys it for the heart's natural movement from sorrow toward what restores it.

meaning.en: To fill. 3x. Sajara=fill, kindle. 81:6: when the seas are filled (sujjirat)—Judgment Day. The root denotes filling to overflow.
meaning.en_detailed: Root س-ج-ر, a triliteral denoting filling, kindling, and setting ablaze (occurs 3x in the Quran). Its most striking usage is 81:6 (idhā al-biḥāru sujjirat) — 'when the seas are filled with fire / set ablaze' — an eschatological sign of the Last Day, paired with 52:6 (biḥārun sajjar) and 67:7. Classical usage (Ibn Fāris) frames it as 'filling and lighting a fire'; the Quran intensifies this to cosmic scale, depicting the seas' combustion as the threshold image of judgment.

quranic_analysis.theme: Seas overflowing
quranic_analysis.detail: Wa idha al-biharu sujjirat—when the seas overflow.

meaning.en: The root rāʾ-mīm-nūn (ر-م-ن) fundamentally denotes the pomegranate, the fruit with its jewel-like seeds. It conveys the specific fruit known for its beauty, complexity, and nutritional richness. The core sense involves a naturally structured wonder — the pomegranate with its orderly chambers of edib
meaning.ar: الرَّاءُ وَالْمِيمُ وَالنُّونُ لَيْسَ بِأَصْلٍ يَدُلُّ عَلَى شَيْءٍ، وَالرُّمَّانُ مَعْرُوفٌ
meaning.en_detailed: Root ر-م-ن, a triliteral denoting the pomegranate (occurs 3x in the Quran). Its occurrences are 6:99, 6:141, and 55:68, all enumerating the signs of divine providence: 'therein are fruits, the date-palm and the pomegranate' (wa al-nakhl wa al-rummān). Classical lexicographers (Ibn Fāris) note the root has no extended semantic field beyond the fruit itself; the Quranic deployment is consistent — rummān is a sign of divine generosity in agriculture and a foretaste of paradise's delights, where every fruit is paired with its earthly counterpart.

meaning.en_detailed: Root ر-و-غ, a triliteral denoting turning aside, evading, and slipping away from a course (occurs 3x in the Quran). Classical meaning (Ibn Fāris) is 'inclining and turning aside'; the Quran deploys it for spiritual evasion and the deflection of hearts from what they once acknowledged. meaning.en_detailed: Root ر-ك-م, a triliteral denoting heaping, piling up, and accumulating layer upon layer (occurs 3x in the Quran). Classical meaning (Ibn Fāris) is 'to gather one thing to another by accumulation'; the Quran uses it both for literal heaping (rakīm, as in 27:44) and for the figurative gathering of misfortunes or sins.

meaning.en: The root rāʾ-hāʾ-ṭāʾ (ر-ه-ط) fundamentally denotes a group, tribe, and a band of companions. It conveys the idea of a small collective, typically of men, bound by kinship or common purpose, fewer than a larger tribe but more than a single family. The core sense involves close-knit, loyal association
meaning.ar: الرَّاءُ وَالْهَاءُ وَالطَّاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى جَمَاعَةٍ مِنَ النَّاسِ، وَالرَّهْطُ: الْجَمَاعَةُ مَا دُونَ الْعَشِيرَةِ، وَيُقَالُ: هُمْ ثَلَاثَةٌ إِلَى عَشَرَةٍ.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ر-ه-ط, a triliteral denoting a group, party, and a band of companions — typically a small collective of three to ten (occurs 3x in the Quran). Its occurrences include 9:16 and 38:43 (fī raḥṭin yatamaththalūna) — 'a band of those going about for their livelihood' — and 9:43 with the adjacent cognate. Classical usage (Ibn Fāris) frames raḥṭ as a band of three to ten men, smaller than a tribe (ʿashīra); the Quran uses it for both the supportive group of allies and the threatening raḥṭ that magnifies enmity.

meaning.ar: الرَّاءُ وَالْغَيْنُ وَالدَّالُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى سَعَةِ الْعَيْشِ وَالرَّفَاهِيَةِ. يُقَالُ: عَيْشٌ رَغَدٌ، وَرَغِدَ يَرْغَدُ رَغَدًا، إِذَا اتَّسَعَ عَيْشُهُ.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ر-غ-د, a triliteral denoting ease, abundance, and a comfortable, unhurried life (occurs 3x in the Quran). Its principal usage is 2:35 (wa qulnā yā Ādamu us'kun anta wa zawjuka al-janna wa kulā minhā raghadan ḥaythu shi'tumā) — 'O Adam, dwell with your wife in Paradise and eat therefrom in ease wherever you will.' Classical meaning (Ibn Fāris) is 'a wide, comfortable living'; the Quran uses it for the unconstrained bounty of the pre-fall state and, by contrast, the false ease of worldly life that the ungodly mistake for the real thing.

Classical meaning (Ibn Fāris) is 'one who follows another without separation'; the Quran deploys it for the march of angels and the supportive following of one rank upon another in both warfare and pilgrimage.

meaning.ar: الْقَافُ وَالرَّاءُ وَالدَّالُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى قَطْعٍ وَانْقِطَاعٍ. وَمِنْ ذَلِكَ الْقِرْدُ، سُمِّيَ بِذَلِكَ لِانْقِطَاعِهِ عَنِ النَّاسِ أَوْ لِقَطْعِهِ الثِّمَارَ.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ق-ر-د, a triliteral denoting a monkey, ape, and simian creature (occurs 3x in the Quran). The simian imagery functions as a sign of moral regression and the visible form of a degraded spirit — classically derived from qaṭʿ (cutting off, separating from the human form).

meaning.ar: النُّونُ وَالْفَاءُ وَالذَّالُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى نُفُوذِ الشَّيْءِ فِي الشَّيْءِ، كَنُفُوذِ السَّهْمِ فِي الرَّمِيَّةِ، وَنُفُوذِ الْمَاءِ فِي الْإِنَاءِ.

meaning.en: Misfortune. 3x. 41:16: days of misfortune (nahisat)—Ad destroyed.
meaning.en_detailed: Tri-radical root nūn-ḥāʾ-sīn (ن-ح-س) signifying misfortune, ill-omen, and inauspiciousness, occurring 3 times in the Quran. Its defining use is in 41:16 'fa-arislnā ʿalayhim rīḥan ṣarṣaran fī ayyāmin nahisāt' (We sent against them a howling wind in ill-fated days), narrating the destruction of the people of ʿĀd. Classical commentators al-Ṭabarī and Ibn Kathīr connect 'nahs' to the pre-Islamic practice of taṭayyur (drawing omens), which the Quran rejects by reframing misfortune not as random chance but as purposeful divine chastisement. The plural feminine 'nahisāt' intensifies the meaning into days saturated with calamity, transforming an ambient sense of inauspiciousness into a theologically precise designation of divine punishment.

meaning.en_detailed: Tri-radical root nūn-ḍād-dāl (ن-ض-د) signifying heaping, arranging in layers, and orderly stacking, occurring 3 times in the Quran. Its most notable Quranic use is in 56:29 'wa-ṭalḥin manḍūd' (and closely-clustered banana-trees), depicting one of the verdant delights of Paradise. The root conveys not loose accumulation but structured layering—a vertical, organized compactness that al-Zajjājī (Ibn al-Sarrāj) connects to the semantic field of precision and arrangement, where each item is settled in its proper tier.

The Quran uses this root for tho
meaning.ar: النُّونُ وَالْهَمْزَةُ وَالْيَاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْبُعْدِ وَالتَّنَائِي. يُقَالُ: نَأَى يَنْأَى نَأْيًا وَنَأْيًا إِذَا بَعُدَ. وَتَنَاءَى الْقَوْمُ إِذَا تَبَاعَدُوا.
meaning.en_detailed: Tri-radical root nūn-hamza-yāʾ (ن-أ-ي) denoting distance, remoteness, and separation, occurring 3 times in the Quran. Ibn Fāris derives this root from al-buʿd wa al-tanāʾī (distance and remoteness), with 'naʾā yanʾā naʾyan' meaning 'to be far away.' Its Quranic use appears in verses depicting hearts or persons turning away from the truth, conveying a spiritual and spatial gulf that separates the heedless from divine guidance. Al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī distinguishes this root's emphasis on volitional distance—a person who 'withdraws himself'—from roots denoting mere physical displacement. The form VI 'tanāwā' (to be mutually distant) captures both ethical repulsion and physical separation, often appearing in Quranic contexts where hearts harden against the remembrance of Allah.

meaning.en: To mix. 3x. Mazaja=mix. 76:17: a cup whose mixture (mizajuha) is ginger—Paradise drink. 83:27: mixture of Tasnim.
meaning.en_detailed: Tri-radical root mīm-zāy-jīm (م-ز-ج) denoting mixing, blending, and combining, occurring 3 times in the Quran. The semantic field is the integration of distinct elements into a unified composite, where each retains some property yet yields a new amalgam. Its most evocative Quranic use is in 76:17 'kāna mizājuhā zanjabīlan' (whose mixture is ginger), describing the flavoring of Paradise drinks in the cups given to the muttaqīn. The related form 83:27 'wa-mizājuhu min tasnīm' (and whose mixture is from Tasnīm) extends the imagery to the highest fountain of Paradise. The root thus becomes a lexical site for the Quranic aesthetic of paradisiacal nourishment, where even drinking is composed with deliberate, sensory-rich combinations.

meaning.en: The root mīm-tāʾ-nūn (م-ت-ن) fundamentally denotes firmness, solidity, and the backbone. It conveys the quality of being strong, durable, and resistant to breaking — whether a physical structure, a well-constructed argument, or the spine that supports the body. The core sense involves structural int
meaning.ar: الْمِيمُ وَالتَّاءُ وَالنُّونُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْقُوَّةِ وَالشِّدَّةِ. وَالْمَتْنُ: مَا صَلُبَ مِنَ الْأَرْضِ وَارْتَفَعَ. وَمَتْنُ الْإِنْسَانِ: ظَهْرُهُ.
meaning.en_detailed: Tri-radical root mīm-tāʾ-nūn (م-ت-ن) denoting firmness, solidity, and the structural backbone, occurring 3 times in the Quran. Ibn Fāris (Maqāyīs al-Lughah) defines the core semantic field as al-quwwa wa al-shidda (strength and intensity), with al-matn referring to hard, elevated ground and matn al-insān signifying the human back or spine. The root conveys structural integrity that resists fracture, whether in physical terrain, human anatomy, or argument. Lisān al-ʿArab notes that 'matn' can also mean 'the body of a book' or 'the substance of a matter,' extending the root from physical backbone to the core or essence of anything. This dual register of literal and metaphorical firmness gives the root its characteristic Quranic precision when describing what is solid, weighty, and enduring.

meaning.en: To exult. 3x. Mariha=exult, be joyful. 31:18: do not walk on earth with excessive joy (marahan). The root denotes arrogant strutting.
meaning.en_detailed: Tri-radical root mīm-rāʾ-ḥāʾ (م-ر-ح) denoting exultation, prancing, and arrogant self-display, occurring 3 times in the Quran. Its defining use is in 31:18 'wa-lā tamshi fī al-arḍi maraḥan innaka lan takhriqa al-arḍa wa-lan tablugha al-jibāla ṭulan' (walk not on earth exultantly; you will neither pierce the earth nor reach the mountains in height). Classical commentators read al-marḥ as the gait of arrogant pride, contrasting human finitude with cosmic scale. The root shares semantic territory with al-fakhr and al-kibr, though al-marḥ specifically captures the bodily strut of one puffed up with self-regard. Al-Rāghib notes its connection to the inarticulate cry of joy (marḥ marḥ) that camels emit when racing, a vivid image of unbounded self-assertion the Quran proscribes.

quranic_analysis.detail: Wa la tamshi fi al-ardi marahan—walk not exultantly.

It conveys the act of removing something that was once present — wiping away writing from a page, clearing a mark, or nullifying a record. The core sense involves complete removal, leaving no trace behind. The Qu
meaning.ar: الْمِيمُ وَالْحَاءُ وَالْوَاوُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى إِذْهَابِ شَيْءٍ وَإِزَالَتِهِ. يُقَالُ: مَحَوْتُ الشَّيْءَ أَمْحُوهُ مَحْوًا، إِذَا أَذْهَبْتَ أَثَرَهُ.
meaning.en_detailed: Tri-radical root mīm-ḥāʾ-wāw (م-ح-و) denoting effacing, erasing, and complete obliteration, occurring 3 times in the Quran. Ibn Fāris defines the core semantic field as idh-hāb al-shayʾ wa izālatuhu (the removal and elimination of a thing), with 'maḥā al-shayʾ yaḥūhu maḥwan' meaning to obliterate a thing's trace. The root is thus distinct from roots denoting partial erasure: maḥw conveys total removal leaving no residue. Al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī emphasizes that the action is twofold—both physical (wiping writing from a page) and metaphysical (nullifying a record or covenant). In Quranic theological use, the root appears in contexts where divine will annuls previously established states, reinforcing the doctrine of absolute divine agency over creation's continuity.

meaning.en: The root mīm-ḍād-ghayn (م-ض-غ) fundamentally denotes chewing, mastication, and the morsel of flesh that is chewed. It conveys the act of grinding food between the teeth and, by extension, the small bolus of chewed matter. The core sense involves the processing and transformation of substance. The Qu
meaning.ar: مَضَغَ الشَّيْءَ يَمْضَغُهُ مَضْغًا: لَاكَهُ. وَالْمُضْغَةُ: الْقِطْعَةُ مِنَ اللَّحْمِ، وَقِيلَ: قَدْرُ مَا يُمْضَغُ
meaning.en_detailed: Tri-radical root mīm-ḍād-ghayn (م-ض-غ) denoting chewing, mastication, and the morsel produced thereby, occurring 3 times in the Quran. The semantic field centers on the mechanical processing of food between the teeth and, by extension, the small bolus of chewed matter (al-muḍgha). Ibn Manẓūr (Lisān al-ʿArab) records the term 'muḍgha' also for 'a piece of flesh of the size chewed,' particularly the flesh around the heart—a usage that gives the root both literal and anatomical reach. The Quranic use connects chewing to human physiology in descriptions of bodily resurrection and consumption. The root's precision lies in capturing the moment of mechanical transformation: solid food becoming processed substance, a microcosm of divine creation's reversibility.

meaning.en: The root mīm-wāw-rāʾ (م-و-ر) fundamentally denotes agitation, tumultuous movement, and seething. It conveys the idea of violent, chaotic motion — the churning of a stormy sea, the convulsion of an earthquake, or the swirling of a crowd. The core sense involves intense, turbulent energy. The Quran us
meaning.ar: الْمِيمُ وَالْوَاوُ وَالرَّاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْحَرَكَةِ وَالِاضْطِرَابِ. يُقَالُ: مَارَ الشَّيْءُ يَمُورُ مَوْرًا إِذَا تَحَرَّكَ وَجَاءَ وَذَهَبَ.
meaning.en_detailed: Tri-radical root mīm-wāw-rāʾ (م-و-ر) denoting agitation, tumultuous movement, and seething, occurring 3 times in the Quran. Ibn Fāris derives this root from al-ḥaraka wa al-iḍṭirāb (movement and perturbation), with 'māra al-shayʾ yamūrū mawran' meaning 'to move to and fro in agitation.' Its most striking Quranic use is in 27:88 'wa-tarā al-jibāla taḥsabuhā jāmidatan wa-hiya tamūr marra al-sahāb' (you see the mountains thinking them fixed, while they pass like clouds), depicting the dissolution of cosmic stability at the eschaton. The root's core image—turbulent, churning motion—extends naturally from stormy seas to the convulsing cosmos. Al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī emphasizes that mawr specifically conveys disordered, repetitive agitation rather than directional movement.

hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ أُمِّ سَلَمَةَ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهَا قَالَتْ: كَانَ أَكْثَرُ دُعَاءِ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «يَا مُقَلِّبَ الْقُلُوبِ ثَبِّتْ قَلْبِي عَلَى دِينِكَ»

meaning.en: The root lām-qāf-fāʾ (ل-ق-ف) fundamentally denotes snatching, seizing quickly, and swallowing. It conveys the act of grabbing something suddenly and often consuming it — like a predator snatching prey. The core sense involves rapid, decisive capture. The Quran uses this root in the story of Moses an
meaning.ar: اللَّامُ وَالْقَافُ وَالْفَاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى أَخْذِ الشَّيْءِ وَابْتِلَاعِهِ بِسُرْعَةٍ. يُقَالُ: لَقِفَ الشَّيْءَ يَلْقَفُهُ لَقْفًا، إِذَا ابْتَلَعَهُ.
meaning.en_detailed: Tri-radical root lām-qāf-fāʾ (ل-ق-ف) denoting snatching, seizing quickly, and swallowing, occurring 3 times in the Quran—all three in the narrative of Moses and Pharaoh's magicians. The defining use is in 7:117 'wa-awḥaynā ilā Mūsā an alqi ʿaṣāka fa-idhā hiya talaqqafu mā yaʾfikūn' (We revealed to Moses: 'Cast your staff,' and behold, it snatched what they fabricated), with parallel occurrences in 26:45 and 20:69. The form II 'talaqqafa' intensifies the base meaning, conveying rapid, decisive capture—like a predator seizing prey in one motion. Lisān al-ʿArab glosses 'laqifta al-shayʾ' as 'you seized it suddenly and swallowed it.' The three Quranic deployments form a thematic cluster establishing divine power's swift overturning of magical illusion.

meaning.en: The root lām-fāʾ-wāw (ل-ف-و) fundamentally denotes discarding, rejecting, and paying no heed to something. It conveys the act of turning away from, ignoring, or treating something as beneath consideration. The core sense involves dismissal through inattention — the refusal to engage with that which
meaning.ar: اللَّامُ وَالْفَاءُ وَالْحَرْفُ الْمُعْتَلُّ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الصُّدُوفِ وَالْإِعْرَاضِ، وَمِنْهُ الْإِلْفُ وَالْأُلْفَةُ، وَاللَّفَاءُ: الشَّيْءُ الْيَسِيرُ، وَأَلْفَيْتُ الشَّيْءَ: وَجَد
meaning.en_detailed: Tri-radical root lām-fāʾ-wāw (ل-ف-و) signifying dismissal, rejection, and treatment as inconsequential, occurring 3 times in the Quran. Ibn Fāris's analysis locates the semantic field in al-ṣudūf wa al-iʿrāḍ (turning away and disregard), where the active agent treats something as beneath engagement. The root carries the connotation of contemptuous inattention rather than violent rejection—what the Quranic ethos demands be withheld from falsehood and idle speech. While the closely related root l-gh-w (لغو) covers vain or frivolous talk, l-f-w specifically focuses on the volitional act of treating something as insignificant. The root thus anchors a key Quranic ethical category: the believer's selective attention must give weight to truth and dismiss vanity.

meaning.en: The root lām-dhāl-dhāl (ل-ذ-ذ) fundamentally denotes pleasure, delight, and sweetness of experience. It conveys the sensory and emotional enjoyment that comes from something pleasant — the taste of delicious food, the feeling of comfort, or the joy of companionship. The core sense involves agreeable
meaning.ar: اللَّامُ وَالذَّالُ وَالذَّالُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى إِدْرَاكِ الشَّيْءِ بِحَاسَّةِ الذَّوْقِ، وَهُوَ ضِدُّ الْمَرَارَةِ
meaning.en_detailed: Tri-radical root lām-dhāl-dhāl (ل-ذ-ذ) denoting pleasure, sensory delight, and the agreeable experience, occurring 3 times in the Quran. The semantic field, as Ibn Fāris records, is idrāk al-shayʾ bi-ḥāssat al-dhawq (perceiving something through the faculty of taste), the linguistic antonym of murāra (bitterness). The root thus centers on the agreeable—whether sweet taste, comfortable sensation, or pleasant experience—and extends by metonymy to all forms of sensed delight. In Quranic deployment, the root appears in eschatological descriptions where sensory pleasures are supernaturally perfected, freeing earthly 'ladhdha' from its mingling with suffering. Al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī distinguishes this root from raw 'shahwa' (appetite) by emphasizing its perceptual, present-tense character: the experience of delight actually being felt.

meaning.en: The root lām-fāʾ-tāʾ (ل-ف-ت) fundamentally denotes turning aside, diverting attention, and twisting away. It conveys the act of causing something or someone to deviate from a course or to look in another direction. The core sense involves redirection and distraction — the subtle pulling of attention
meaning.ar: اللَّامُ وَالْفَاءُ وَالتَّاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى صَرْفِ الشَّيْءِ عَنْ وَجْهِهِ، يُقَالُ: لَفَتَهُ يَلْفِتُهُ لَفْتًا، إِذَا صَرَفَهُ.
meaning.en_detailed: Tri-radical root lām-fāʾ-tāʾ (ل-ف-ت) denoting turning aside, diverting attention, and twisting away, occurring 3 times in the Quran. Ibn Fāris's entry defines the core sense as ṣarf al-shayʾ ʿan wajhihi (turning something from its course), with 'lafata yalfitu laftan' meaning 'he diverted it.' The root captures subtle redirection rather than dramatic reversal—a quiet twisting of attention or course. Quranic use often depicts hearts or gazes being 'turned' away from truth, where what looks like small deflection constitutes spiritual misdirection. The semantic distinction from q-ṣ-r (shortening) and ʿ-r-ḍ (turning away) is that laft implies active engagement with the cause of turning; the subject is pulled, not merely disengaged. Al-Rāghib emphasizes this root's connection to deliberate redirection of attention.

meaning.en: Crouch. 2x. 7:78: prostrate (jathimin) in their homes—Thamud.
meaning.en_detailed: Tri-radical root jīm-thāʾ-mīm (ج-ث-م) denoting crouching, lying prostrate, and collapsing on the ground, occurring 5 times in the Quran. Its starkest deployment is in 7:78 'fa-asbaḥū fī dārihim jāthimīn' (and they became prostrate in their dwellings), narrating the destruction of Thamūd by the Sayhah (mighty blast). The active participle 'jāthim' denotes the posture of one crumpled on his knees or sprawled prone, often describing bodies that have fallen motionless. Lisān al-ʿArab notes the root's particular use for the dead and the petrified—those frozen in a crouching position. The Quran's use of this root in scenes of divine punishment is rhetorically precise: the catastrophic stillness of juthūm contrasts with the kinetic violence of the moment just before, embodying a Quranic visual grammar of sudden judgment.

meaning.en: The root kāf-wāw-rāʾ (ك-و-ر) fundamentally denotes winding, wrapping, and rolling up. It conveys the act of coiling something around itself — like a turban wound around the head — or the cyclical rotation of night and day. The core sense involves cyclical envelopment and transformation. The Quran de
meaning.ar: الْكَافُ وَالْوَاوُ وَالرَّاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى جَمْعٍ وَلَفٍّ. مِنْ ذَلِكَ كَوَّرْتُ الْعِمَامَةَ: لَفَفْتُهَا. وَكُوِّرَتِ الشَّمْسُ: جُمِعَتْ وَلُفَّتْ.
meaning.en_detailed: Tri-radical root kāf-wāw-rāʾ (ك-و-ر) denoting winding, wrapping, and rolling up, occurring 3 times in the Quran. Ibn Fāris defines the core semantic field as jamʿ wa laff (gathering and folding), with the classic example of 'takwīr al-ʿimāma' (winding a turban). Its most vivid Quranic use is in 81:1 'idhā al-shamsu kuwwirat' (when the sun is wound up), describing the cataclysmic rolling-up of celestial bodies at the eschaton, with parallel forms in 81:11 'idhā al-samāʾu kushitat' using different vocabulary. The verb 'kawwara' captures a particular motion: the spiraling, enveloping roll that gathers something into itself while losing its form. The root thus names a powerful eschatological image of cosmic transformation, where luminous orbs fold into darkness.

meaning.en: The root jīm-yāʾ-bāʾ (ج-ي-ب) fundamentally denotes a pocket, collar, and opening in a garment. It conveys the idea of a cavity or fold in clothing that can hold things or into which one inserts a hand. The core sense involves a receptive opening. The Quran commands Moses: 'usluk yadaka fī jaybika ta
meaning.ar: الْجِيمُ وَالْيَاءُ وَالْبَاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى شَقٍّ فِي شَيْءٍ، وَمِنْهُ الْجَيْبُ، وَهُوَ شَقُّ الْقَمِيصِ، وَجُبْتُ الشَّيْءَ: قَطَعْتُهُ، وَجَابَ الْأَرْضَ: قَطَعَهَا وَسَارَ فِيهَا
meaning.en_detailed: Tri-radical root jīm-yāʾ-bāʾ (ج-ي-ب) denoting a pocket, collar opening, or frontal slit in a garment, occurring 3 times in the Quran—all in the story of Moses. The defining verse is 27:12 'wa-adkhil yadaka fī jaybika takhruj bayḍāʾ min ghayri sūʾin' (insert your hand into your collar; it will emerge white without flaw), with parallel occurrences in 20:22 and 28:32. Ibn Fāris notes that 'jayb' is the slit at the collar of a shirt, into which one inserts the hand. The miracle of Moses's glowing white hand thus becomes a deliberate image of withdrawal and re-emergence: the hand disappears into the body of the garment and emerges transformed, an emblem of divine power operating within ordinary material form. The root's threefold repetition reinforces this iconic sign of Moses.

It conveys the idea of the inner space of something — the hollow of a valley, the interior of a house, or the air and atmosphere that surrounds the earth. The core sense involves enclosed or enveloping space. The wo
meaning.ar: الْجِيمُ وَالثَّاءُ وَالْوَاوُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْجُلُوسِ عَلَى الرُّكْبَتَيْنِ. يُقَالُ: جَثَا يَجْثُو جُثُوًّا، وَجَثَى يَجْثِي جَثْيًا، وَالْجَاثِي: الْجَالِسُ عَلَى رُكْبَتَيْهِ
meaning.en_detailed: Tri-radical root jīm-thāʾ-wāw (ج-ث-و) denoting kneeling, sitting on the knees, and the posture of supplication, occurring 3 times in the Quran. Lisān al-ʿArab defines the core sense as julūs ʿalā al-rukbatayn (sitting upon one's knees), with 'jathā yajthū juthūwan' meaning 'he sat on his knees.' The root's Quranic appearances cluster around scenes of judgment and desperate appeal, where the posture of juthūm—hunched, kneeling—captures a body arrested by awe or fear. The closely related j-th-m (جثم) emphasizes the prone, prostrate collapse after a violent event; j-th-w (جثو) emphasizes the kneeling posture of one awaiting judgment. This nuanced postural vocabulary reflects the Quran's rich somatic rhetoric of bodily response to divine encounter.

meaning.en_detailed: Tri-radical root jīm-hamza-rāʾ (ج-أ-ر) denoting crying out in distress, supplicating loudly, and pleading from the depths, occurring 3 times in the Quran. The semantic field, per Ibn Fāris and al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī, is rafʿ al-ṣawt wa al-istighātha (raising the voice and calling for aid). The verb captures not ordinary speech but the desperate cry of one facing catastrophe—a vocalization of need that cannot be contained. Its Quranic use situates 'jajāra' in scenes of affliction and eschatological dread, where the human being either cries out in defiance or, conversely, breaks into pleas too late. The root's lexical kinship with 'jawr' (injustice) is phonetic only; semantically, j-ʾ-r roots itself in the profound vocalization of distress.

meaning.ar: قال ابن فارس: الهاء والزاء والميم أصل واحد يدل على كسر الشيء ورده، ومنه هزمت الجيش أهزمه هزماً، إذا كسرته ورددته. والهزيمة: الكسرة في الحرب.
meaning.en_detailed: Tri-radical root hāʾ-zāy-mīm (ه-ز-م) denoting defeat, routing, and decisive military victory, occurring 3 times in the Quran. Al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī emphasizes that hazm decisively ends resistance, contrasting with roots denoting partial repulse. The Quran's three occurrences consistently frame divine or prophetic victory as total and overwhelming.

meaning.ar: «الْهَمْزُ: دَفْعٌ وَضَرْبٌ. يُقَالُ: هَمَزَهُ يَهْمِزُهُ هَمْزًا: دَفَعَهُ وَضَرَبَهُ. وَالْهَمْزُ: الْغِيبَةُ وَالطَّعْنُ فِي الْأَعْرَاضِ.»
meaning.en_detailed: Tri-radical root hāʾ-mīm-zāy (ه-م-ز) denoting prodding, goading, and verbal slander, occurring 3 times in the Quran. Its two most pointed Quranic uses are 68:11 'wa-lā tuṭiʿ kulla ḥallāfin mahīn, hammāzin mashshāʾin binamīm' (and do not obey every swaggering oath-maker, slanderer going about with calumny) and 104:1 'waylun li-kulli hamzatin lumazatin' (Woe to every slanderous backbiter). These uses define the ethical crime of namīma (calumny-spreading) as the verbal weapon of those who attack others' honor, while the root's earlier physical sense of goading preserves its imagery of forceful incitement.

meaning.ar: قال ابن فارس في معجم مقاييس اللغة: الهاء والطاء والعين أصل واحد يدل على الإسراع، يقال: أهطع الرجل إذا أسرع، وأهطع في سيره: مد عنقه وأسرع.

The root's lexical specialization for the smallest visible fiber makes it the Quran's iconic measure of guaranteed justice: divine recompense attends to even the most microscopic of deeds, every 'fatīl' recorded.

meaning.ar: الْفَاءُ وَالزَّاءُ وَالزَّاءُ الْمُكَرَّرَةُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْقَلَقِ وَالِاضْطِرَابِ. وَمِنْهُ قَوْلُهُمْ: رَجُلٌ فَزٌّ، أَيْ: قَلِقٌ لَا يَثْبُتُ فِي مَكَانٍ.
meaning.en_detailed: Tri-radical root fāʾ-zāy-zāy (ف-ز-ز) denoting being startled, terrified, and fleeing in panic, occurring 3 times in the Quran. The doubled emphatic zāy-zāy in the root letters signals intensification in the verbal intensity of the reaction.
