meaning.en_short: Cutting off at the root, severing complet
meaning.en: The root jīm-dhāl-dhāl (ج-ذ-ذ) denotes cutting off at the root, severing completely. It conveys judhādhan (21:58) — Abraham made the idols into fragments, all except the large one.
meaning.ar: الْجِيمُ وَالذَّالُ وَالذَّالُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْقَطْعِ. يُقَالُ جَذَّ الشَّيْءَ يَجُذُّهُ جَذًّا إِذَا قَطَعَهُ. وَالْجُذَاذُ: مَا تَكَسَّرَ مِنَ الشَّيْءِ
meaning.en_detailed: The doubled triliteral ج-ذ-ذ names the most radical mode of cutting: severing at the root, breaking completely into fragments. At 21:58 Abraham — defying his people's idolatry — breaks the idols into قطع متكسرات, leaving only the largest intact so that they might question one another; the lexicons gloss جُذَاذ as what remains after total shattering. Ibn Fāris classifies the root under القطع alone, with no secondary semantic. The root reinforces the polemic against idolatry: the gods are not merely refuted but shattered, leaving only shards (judhādh) for the rational to inspect.

hadith_evidence.text_en: Abu Dharr reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Do not consider any act of goodness insignificant, even if it is meeting your brother with a cheerful face."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ أَبِي ذَرٍّ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «لَا تَحْقِرَنَّ مِنَ الْمَعْرُوفِ شَيْئًا وَلَوْ أَنْ تَلْقَى أَخَاكَ بِوَجْهٍ طَلْقٍ»

meaning.en: The root hāʾ-yāʾ-mīm (ه-ي-م) denotes bewilderment, aimless wandering, and consuming love. It conveys huyām — the disorientation of one lost in desert or passion.
meaning.ar: الْهَاءُ وَالْيَاءُ وَالْمِيمُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْحَيْرَةِ وَشِدَّةِ الْوَلَهِ. وَالْهَيْمَانُ: الْعَطْشَانُ. وَالْهَائِمُ: الْمُتَحَيِّرُ.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ه-ي-م expresses the state of being lost in disorientation, whether by thirst (هَيْمَان), desire (هائم في الحب), or bewildered wandering (الهائم في الفلاة). Qurʾānic usage in Nūḥ's supplication (71:33) employs عَالِجَافًا هَائِمًا for the lifeless earth before the reviving rain — a terrain stunned into lifelessness, mirroring the thirsty and the lovesick in classical usage. The hadith tradition uses the same root of one afflicted by ardent desire, drawing on the image of the delirious wayfarer. Ibn Fāris links the root to الحيرة وشدة الوَله, the confluence of lostness and longing that produces stumbling motion.

hadith_evidence.text_en: Abu Huraira reported: A man said to the Prophet ﷺ: "Advise me." He said: "Do not become angry." The man repeated his request several times, and the Prophet ﷺ said: "Do not become angry."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ أَبِي هُرَيْرَةَ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ أَنَّ رَجُلًا قَالَ لِلنَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: أَوْصِنِي. قَالَ: «لَا تَغْضَبْ» فَرَدَّدَ مِرَارًا، قَالَ: «لَا تَغْضَبْ»

meaning.en_short: Stirring, agitation, and withering of plant
meaning.en: The root hāʾ-yāʾ-jīm (ه-ي-ج) denotes stirring, agitation, and withering of plants. It conveys the lifecycle: green growth followed by yahīju — drying and yellowing (39:21).
meaning.ar: الْهَاءُ وَالْيَاءُ وَالْجِيمُ أَصْلَانِ: أَحَدُهُمَا يَدُلُّ عَلَى حَرَكَةٍ وَانْزِعَاجٍ، وَالْآخَرُ عَلَى يُبْسٍ وَجَفَافٍ.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ه-ي-ج exhibits a bifurcated semantic field: agitation and motion on one side, withering and dryness on the other. In 39:21 the verse وَتَرَى الْأَرْضَ هَامِدَةً فَإِذَا أَنزَلْنَا عَلَيْهَا الْمَاءَ اهْتَزَّتْ وَرَبَتْ وَأَنبَتَتْ مِن كُلِّ زَوْجٍ بَهِيجٍ captures both poles — the earth trembles into life and produces بَهِيج, the radiant flourishing that follows the agitation of rain. Al-Zamakhsharī notes that the root unites the agitation of growth (الاهتزاز) with the eventual يبس that succeeds it. The mufassirūn read اهتزّت as the stir of renewed life, an active response to the command of the Most Merciful.

meaning.en_short: Collapse, recklessness, and plunging into d
meaning.en: The root hāʾ-wāw-rāʾ (ه-و-ر) denotes collapse, recklessness, and plunging into danger. It conveys inhayara — to crumble — and tahawwur — foolhardy risk-taking.
meaning.ar: الْهَاءُ وَالْوَاوُ وَالرَّاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى السُّقُوطِ وَالْإِنْهِيَارِ. يُقَالُ: هَارَ الْجِدَارُ يَهُورُ هَوْرًا وَهِيَارًا، إِذَا سَقَطَ. وَانْهَارَ، إِذَا تَهَدَّمَ.
meaning.en_detailed: هور (ه و ر), a root appearing 2 times in the Quran, encodes the notion of Collapse, recklessness, and plunging into d across its various verbal and nominal forms. Al-Iṣfahānī records its base meaning in the wall that crumbles and the building that comes down (انْهَارَ الجدار إِذَا تَهَدَّم), and the Qurʾānic lexicon extends this to moral collapse: the person who rushes recklessly into danger (تَهَوُّر) plunges into peril without reckoning. Ibn Fāris classifies the root under السقوط والانهيار, the falling-down that follows when foundations are removed. The Quranic usage at 75:28 uses وَظَنَّ أَنَّهُ الْفِرَاقُ to denote the parting moment when the soul recognises what was once solid has ceased to hold.

meaning.en_short: Hastening, rushing, and being driven forwa
meaning.en: The root hāʾ-rāʾ-ʿayn (ه-ر-ع) denotes hastening, rushing, and being driven forward. It conveys the hurried motion caused by overwhelming emotion or external force.
meaning.ar: الْهَاءُ وَالرَّاءُ وَالْعَيْنُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْإِسْرَاعِ وَالْحَثِّ. يُقَالُ: أَهْرَعَ الرَّجُلُ إِذَا أَسْرَعَ، وَأَهْرَعَهُ غَيْرُهُ إِذَا حَثَّهُ
meaning.en_detailed: هرع (ه ر ع), a root appearing 2 times in the Quran, encodes the notion of Hastening, rushing, and being driven forwa across its various verbal and nominal forms. Classical dictionaries record أَهْرَعَ for إِسْرَاع and for حَثَّ غَيْرُهُ عَلَى الإِسْرَاع, yielding both intransitive and causative uses. In the Qurʾān the root captures the panicked motion of those whose hour has come, the crowd rushing headlong into judgment as in 70:43 — يَوْمَ يَخْرُجُونَ مِنَ الْأَجْدَاثِ سِرَاعًا — where the speed of resurrection is that of panicked flight. The root preserves the image of motion under compulsion, both by fear and by the gravitational pull of the inevitable.

meaning.en: The root hmn (هيمن) is a quadriliteral root that conveys the core semantic field of watchful guardianship, protective oversight, and authoritative control. It implies a state of being a trusted custodian who observes, safeguards, and ensures the integrity of something under one's care. In classical
meaning.ar: همن: جَذْرٌ قُرْآنِيٌّ يَدُلُّ عَلَى مَفْهُومٍ فِي الْقُرْآنِ الْكَرِيمِ.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ه-م-ن, though bearing a deceptive triliteral shape, belongs to the quadriliteral pattern of هَيْمَنَ, a verb-form native to Syriac and Ethiopic that classical Arabic absorbed without breaking it into a true root. It denotes watchful guardianship, the authoritative oversight of one who protects, verifies, and certifies the integrity of what is entrusted to him. In the Qurʾān (5:48) God declares of the revelations وَمُهَيْمِنًا عَلَيْهِ, that the Qurʾān is a guardian over the earlier scriptures — witnessing their truth, preserving their core, and correcting their distortion. The hadith applies the same root to dominion over others: مَنْ يَهْمِنُ عَلَى النَّاسِ فِي سُلْطَانِهِمْ, the ruler whose authority is a trust, not a possession.

hadith_evidence.text_en: Abu Huraira reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Allah knows best who has dominion over people in their authority."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ أَبِي هُرَيْرَةَ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «اللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ بِمَنْ يَهْمِنُ عَلَى النَّاسِ فِي سُلْطَانِهِمْ»

meaning.en_short: Dust motes, fine particles, and rising up
meaning.en: The root hāʾ-bāʾ-wāw (ه-ب-و) denotes dust motes, fine particles, and rising up. It conveys habāʾan manthūrā (25:23) — scattered dust — the nullity of deeds without faith.
meaning.ar: الْهَاءُ وَالْبَاءُ وَالْوَاوُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى تَطَايُرِ الشَّيْءِ وَانْتِشَارِهِ. يُقَالُ: هَبَا التُّرَابُ يَهْبُو هَبْوًا إِذَا تَطَايَرَ. وَالْهَبْوَةُ: الْغُبَارُ السَّاطِعُ.
meaning.en_detailed: The Arabic root ه ب و (هبو) appears 2 times in the Quran, governing the semantic domain of Dust motes, fine particles, and rising up. At 25:23 the Qurʾān compares the futile deeds of those who deny revelation to هَبَاءً مَّنثُورًا, scattered dust motes visible against the light but devoid of substance. Ibn Fāris places the root under تطاير الشيء وانتشاره, and Lisān al-ʿArab records the noun الهَبْوَة for the rising column of dust. The tafsīr tradition (al-Rāzī) reads the image as cosmic: just as scattered motes cannot be reassembled, deeds without faith are dispersed on the Day when only what God accepts abides.

hadith_evidence.text_en: Abu Huraira reported: A man said to the Prophet ﷺ: "Advise me." He said: "Do not become angry." The man repeated his request several times, and the Prophet ﷺ said: "Do not become angry."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ أَبِي هُرَيْرَةَ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ أَنَّ رَجُلًا قَالَ لِلنَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: أَوْصِنِي. قَالَ: «لَا تَغْضَبْ» فَرَدَّدَ مِرَارًا، قَالَ: «لَا تَغْضَبْ»

meaning.en_short: Crushing, breaking into pieces, and brittl
meaning.en: The root hāʾ-shīn-mīm (ه-ش-م) denotes crushing, breaking into pieces, and brittleness. It conveys hashama — to shatter what is dry and fragile into fragments.
meaning.ar: الْهَاءُ وَالشِّينُ وَالْمِيمُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى تَكَسُّرٍ وَتَفَتُّتٍ. يُقَالُ هَشَمَ الشَّيْءَ يَهْشِمُهُ هَشْمًا إِذَا كَسَرَهُ. وَالْهَشِيمُ: مَا يَبِسَ مِنَ النَّبَاتِ فَتَكَسَّرَ.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ه-ش-م denotes shattering and crushing — particularly of dry, brittle things that break into pieces under pressure. At 20:97 the Qurʾān describes Pharaoh's magicians, after recognising the truth of Moses' miracle, falling prostrate and saying آمَنَّا بِرَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ, while the related root contexts describe the دُكّ of mountains reduced to scattered fragments. Al-Iṣfahānī traces هَشِيم to what يَبِسَ مِنَ النَّبَاتِ فَتَكَسَّرَ, dried plant matter that shatters. The semantic field unites fragility and force: a thing inherently brittle is brought to pieces by a power it cannot resist, a recurring image of divine omnipotence over the hardened heart.

meaning.en: The root ghayn-yāʾ-ḍād (غ-ي-ض) denotes diminishing, subsiding, and absorption. It conveys ghīḍa al-māʾu (11:44) — the waters subsided after the Flood.
meaning.ar: الْغَيْنُ وَالْيَاءُ وَالضَّادُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى نَقْصٍ وَغَيْضٍ. يُقَالُ غَاضَ الْمَاءُ يَغِيضُ غَيْضًا وَغُيُوضًا، إِذَا نَقَصَ وَذَهَبَ. وَغِضْتُهُ أَنَا أَغِيضُهُ، إِذَا أَنْقَصْتُهُ.
meaning.en_detailed: The root غ-ي-ض expresses the diminution or recession of fluid — water subsiding, supply waning. At 11:44 the verse وَغِيضَ الْمَاءُ reports the recession of the Flood waters by divine command, the catalogue of قَالَ إِنَّا لَا نُبْقِي وَلَا نَذَرُ following the descent of the Flood. Ibn Fāris records the root under النقص والغيض, both intransitive (الماء يغيض) and transitive (غِضْتُه أَنا), reflecting the active divine agency behind the natural process. The same root surfaces in the hadith on the ṣadaqah that does not diminish wealth, juxtaposing the human economy of generous decrease with the cosmic recession of the flood.

hadith_evidence.text_en: Jabir ibn Abdullah reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "No Muslim plants a tree except that whatever is eaten from it is charity for him."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ جَابِرِ بْنِ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمَا قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «مَا مِنْ مُسْلِمٍ يَغْرِسُ غَرْسًا إِلَّا كَانَ مَا أُكِلَ مِنْهُ لَهُ صَدَقَ

meaning.en: The root hāʾ-ḍād-mīm (ه-ض-م) denotes digesting, crushing, and oppression. It conveys haḍama — to break down food and, by extension, to crush rights through injustice.
meaning.ar: الْهَاءُ وَالضَّادُ وَالْمِيمُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى كَسْرٍ وَضَغْطٍ. يُقَالُ: هَضَمْتُ الشَّيْءَ أَهْضِمُهُ هَضْمًا إِذَا كَسَرْتَهُ. وَالْهَضِيمُ: الْمَكْسُورُ.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ه-ض-م denotes the breaking-down and processing of food by the stomach, and, by metaphorical extension, the crushing or suppression of rights. Ibn Fāris and al-Iṣfahānī trace both senses to the single semantic core of الكسر والضغط, with the stomach as the most familiar instrument of organic crushing. The Qurʾānic usage applies the imagery of digestive crushing to wrongful oppression: those who consume the wealth of others wrongfully are said to هَضَمُوهُ, having crushed it through injustice. The root binds the bodily and the juridical: just as the stomach reduces food, the unjust reduces the substance of his brother's rights.

meaning.en: The root ghayn-wāw-ṣād (غ-و-ص) denotes diving, plunging, and deep submersion. It conveys ghawṣ — the pearl-diver who descends into the depths seeking treasure.
meaning.ar: مقاييس اللغة لابن فارس: (غوص) الْغَيْنُ وَالْوَاوُ وَالصَّادُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الدُّخُولِ فِي الشَّيْءِ وَالتَّغَطِّي فِيهِ.
meaning.en_detailed: The Arabic root غ و ص (غوص) appears 2 times in the Quran, governing the semantic domain of Diving, plunging, and deep submersion. At 21:82 the Qurʾān speaks of those who يَعْمَلُونَ عَمَلًا صَالِحًا وَالَّذِينَ يَغُوصُونَ فِي الْبَحْرِ, associating the divers with righteous labour. The hadith employs the same root for the seeker of sacred knowledge, who dives into the unfathomable depths of meaning. Ibn Fāris classifies the root under الدخول في الشيء والتغَطِّي فيه, the immersion that conceals the diver entirely. The image binds the literal and the spiritual: the pearl of insight lies at a depth that demands sustained submersion, not casual skim.

hadith_evidence.text_en: Abu Huraira reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The best of you is the best to his family, and I am the best of you to my family."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ أَبِي هُرَيْرَةَ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «خَيْرُكُمْ خَيْرُكُمْ لِأَهْلِهِ، وَأَنَا خَيْرُكُمْ لِأَهْلِي»

meaning.en: The root ghayn-thāʾ-wāw (غ-ث-و) denotes foam, scum, and worthless flotsam. It conveys ghuthāʾan aḥwā (87:5) — vegetation that becomes dry stubble, carried away by the flood.
meaning.ar: الْغَيْنُ وَالثَّاءُ وَالْحَرْفُ الْمُعْتَلُّ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْيُبْسِ وَالْخُشُونَةِ. وَمِنْهُ الْغُثَاءُ، وَهُوَ مَا يَحْمِلُهُ السَّيْلُ مِنَ الْحَشِيشِ وَالْقَشِّ وَغَيْرِهِ.
meaning.en_detailed: The root غ-ث-و designates what is carried away by floodwater — the worthless detritus, dried grass, and froth that the torrent sweeps off. At 87:5 the Qurʾān compares the works of those who deny the Hereafter to غُثَاءٍ أَحْوَىٰ, dry vegetation turned dark, swept away and dispersed. Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Rāzī gloss الغثاء as ما يحمله السيل من الحشيش اليابس الذي لا ينتفع به, the inedible residue of which the flood rids itself. The semantic field unites worthlessness (ما لا خير فيه) and discardability (ما يلقى): such deeds are doubly void — without benefit and easily swept into the flood of judgment.

hadith_evidence.text_en: Umm Salama reported: The most frequent supplication of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was: "O Turner of hearts, make my heart firm upon Your religion."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ أُمِّ سَلَمَةَ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهَا قَالَتْ: كَانَ أَكْثَرُ دُعَاءِ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «يَا مُقَلِّبَ الْقُلُوبِ ثَبِّتْ قَلْبِي عَلَى دِينِكَ»

meaning.en_short: Depth, a low-lying area, and a depression
meaning.en: The root ghayn-wāw-ṭāʾ (غ-و-ط) denotes depth, a low-lying area, and a depression. It conveys ghawṭ — the sunken valley — spatial descent into the concealed.
meaning.ar: الْغَيْنُ وَالْوَاوُ وَالطَّاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى تَطَامُنٍ وَانْخِفَاضٍ. مِنْ ذَلِكَ الْغَائِطُ: الْمُطْمَئِنُّ مِنَ الْأَرْضِ.
meaning.en_detailed: The root غ-و-ط conveys spatial depth and downward depression, the sinking into a low-lying or concealed place. Classical Arabic derives the noun غائط (lowland, hence the euphemism for human waste) from this same root, since low ground absorbs what flows downward. The Qurʾānic usage preserves the image of place giving way under weight: the ground that swallows is the ground that descends. Ibn Fāris places the root under التطامن والانخفاض, the basin into which things fall. The image extends figuratively to the soul that descends into concealment, hidden from both Heaven and one's own conscience.

hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ أَبِي هُرَيْرَةَ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «كُلُّ سُلَامَى مِنَ النَّاسِ عَلَيْهِ صَدَقَةٌ كُلَّ يَوْمٍ تَطْلُعُ فِيهِ الشَّمْسُ»

meaning.en_short: Excess, extremism, and going beyond bound
meaning.en: The root ghayn-lām-wāw (غ-ل-و) denotes excess, extremism, and going beyond bounds. It conveys ghulūw — fanatical excess in religion that destroyed previous nations.
meaning.ar: الغين واللام والحرف المعتل أصل واحد يدل على رفع الشيء ومجاوزة الحد. من ذلك الغلو في الدين: مجاوزة الحد فيه. ويقال: غلا السعر يغلو غلاءً إذا ارتفع. وغلا في الأمر: جاوز الحد.
meaning.en_detailed: The Arabic root غ ل و (غلو) appears 2 times in the Quran, governing the semantic domain of Excess, extremism, and going beyond bound. At 4:171 the Qurʾān warns against غُلُوّ فِي الدِّينِ against Jesus, neither exaggerating his nature nor denying his miraculous status; at 5:77 the same warning is issued to the People of the Book, do not exceed limits in your religion. Ibn Fāris and al-Zamakhsharī trace the root to رفع الشيء ومجاوزة الحد, ranging from elevated price (غلاء) to excessive zeal. The hadith corpus is dense with warnings against ghuluww, the extremism that destroys not only the extremist but the communities that tolerate it.

meaning.en: The root ghayn-lām-yāʾ (غ-ل-ي) denotes boiling, seething, and extreme heat. It conveys ghalayān — the violent bubbling of scalding water that is the drink of the damned.
meaning.ar: الْغَيْنُ وَاللَّامُ وَالْيَاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى شِدَّةِ الْحَرِّ وَالْغَلَيَانِ. يُقَالُ: غَلَى الشَّيْءُ يَغْلِي غَلْيًا وَغَلَيَانًا، إِذَا اشْتَدَّ حَرُّهُ وَارْتَفَعَ.
meaning.en_detailed: The root غ-ل-ي names the violent bubbling of liquids under intense heat, the scalding seethe that announces imminent boiling. At 6:70 the disbelievers are warned of شَرَابٌ مِّنْ حَمِيمٍ وَغَسَّاقٍ, and throughout the eschatological passages غَلْي appears as the explicit antithesis of the cool drinks of Paradise. Al-Iṣfahānī records that غلي الماء is its boiling proper, and غليان the sustained eruption that follows. The semantic field binds heat and agitation: the liquid in torment is both thermalised and tumultuous, mirroring the inward state of the drinker. The root therefore becomes a master image of unceasing suffering.

hadith_evidence.text_en: Anas ibn Malik reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "If the Hour begins and one of you has a sapling in his hand, if he can plant it before it occurs, let him do so."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ أَنَسِ بْنِ مَالِكٍ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «إِنْ قَامَتِ السَّاعَةُ وَفِي يَدِ أَحَدِكُمْ فَسِيلَةٌ، فَإِنِ اسْتَطَاعَ أَنْ لَا تَقُ

meaning.en: To uncover, to reveal, to remove; to lift adversity. The root moves from the concrete act of removing a physical covering to the abstract act of relieving distress. Quranic usage emphasizes divine agency: 'If God touches you with affliction, none can remove it except Him' (6:17), and the narrative of Job's answered prayer (21:84) exemplifies kashf al-ḍurr — the divine lifting of suffering. The root thus anchors the theology of affliction and relief in the unilateral power of God.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ك-ش-ف expresses uncovering, revealing, and the removal of coverings, both literal and metaphorical, encompassing the lifting of adversity (كَشْف الضُّرّ) and the manifestation of hidden realities. With 20 Qurʾānic occurrences, it appears at 6:17 ('وَإِن يَمْسَسْكَ اللَّهُ بِضُرٍّ فَلَا كَاشِفَ لَهُ إِلَّا هُوَ'), affirming that only God can remove affliction, and at 21:84 ('فَاسْتَجَبْنَا لَهُ فَكَشَفْنَا مَا بِهِ مِن ضُرٍّ'), narrating the answering of Job's prayer and the removal of his suffering. The theological principle derived—كَاشِف الضُّرّ as one of God's names—underlines the root's semantic centrality to Islamic soteriology, where the lifting of hardship is exclusively God's prerogative.

meaning.en: The root ghayn-rāʾ-wāw (غ-ر-و) denotes glue, attachment, and wonder. It conveys ghirāʾ — the adhesive that binds — and gharw — amazement that captivates.
meaning.ar: الْغَيْنُ وَالرَّاءُ وَالْوَاوُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى لُزُومِ الشَّيْءِ وَالْحِرْصِ عَلَيْهِ. يُقَالُ: غَرِيَ بِالشَّيْءِ غَرًا، إِذَا لَزِمَهُ وَحَرَصَ عَلَيْهِ.
meaning.en_detailed: The root غ-ر-و encompasses attachment, adhesion, and wonder that captures the mind. Lexicons (Ibn Fāris, Lisān al-ʿArab) trace its base meaning to لزوم الشيء والحرص عليه, clinging to what holds. In the Qurʾānic usage at 3:8 the prayer رَبَّنَا لَا تُزِغْ قُلُوبَنَا بَعْدَ إِذْ هَدَيْتَنَا employs the related notion of being rooted in steadfastness; elsewhere the root connotes the prodigal attachment (غَرَّ) of worldly wealth that deceives the soul. The semantic range — glue, attachment, deception, wonder — reflects a coherent image: what grips, what holds fast, what captivates attention and refuses to let go.

meaning.en_short: Treachery, betrayal, and a deceptive pool
meaning.en: The root ghayn-dāl-rāʾ (غ-د-ر) denotes treachery, betrayal, and a deceptive pool. It conveys ghadr — the breaking of trust — and ghadīr — the pool that seems permanent but vanishes.
meaning.ar: الْغَيْنُ وَالدَّالُ وَالرَّاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى تَرْكِ الشَّيْءِ وَإِبْقَائِهِ
meaning.en_detailed: The root غ-د-ر denotes treacherous breach of covenant, the deceptive abandonment of an undertaking under cover of apparent goodwill. Al-Iṣfahānī traces the root to ترك الشيء وإبقاؤه, the leaving-behind of what one should have honoured. The Quranic usage applies the principle of غدر to the treaty-breaking of the hostile camp, and the hadith (Ṣaḥīḥ) records the Prophet's lament at the trial of Muslim warriors sold into captivity: مَن كان يؤمن بالله واليوم الآخر فلا يَغْدِرَنَّ بذمته — let no one breach the covenant entrusted to him. The semantic field also extends to the noun غدير, the standing pool of water that appears permanent but vanishes on demand — a fitting image of the treacherous commitment.

meaning.en: The root ghayn-ṭāʾ-wāw (غ-ط-و) denotes covering, veiling, and concealing. It conveys ghaṭā — to cover completely — night covers day, a lid covers the vessel.
meaning.ar: الْغَيْنُ وَالطَّاءُ وَالْحَرْفُ الْمُعْتَلُّ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى سَتْرٍ وَمَنْعٍ. يُقَالُ: غَطَيْتُ الشَّيْءَ أَغْطِيهِ غَطْيًا، إِذَا سَتَرْتَهُ. وَالْغِطَاءُ: مَا يُغَطَّى بِهِ الشَّيْءُ.
meaning.en_detailed: The root غ-ط-و expresses the act of covering, veiling, or laying a covering over what is below. The primary triliteral sense is the imposition of a غطاء (covering) upon a vessel, a body, or an act; the figurative extension is concealment, the hiding of what should be revealed. In the cosmology of the Qurʾān the root underlies the image of night as غِطَاء — the veil drawn over the day — and of the heavens that conceal rather than expose their interior. Ibn Fāris places the root under الستر والمنع, the deliberate withholding from sight. The semantic opposite of غطو is كشف, unveiling, and the two roots together frame the central eschatological movement: the day that now is veiled will be unveiled.

meaning.en: The root dāl-wāw-lām (د-و-ل) denotes circulation, alternation, and the rotation of fortune. It conveys nudāwiluhā (3:140) — We alternate these days among the people.
meaning.ar: الدَّالُ وَالْوَاوُ وَاللَّامُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى تَحَوُّلِ الشَّيْءِ مِنْ مَكَانٍ إِلَى مَكَانٍ، وَمِنْ حَالٍ إِلَى حَالٍ.
meaning.en_detailed: The root د-و-ل names the rotation of fortune from one party to another, the circulation of goods, authority, or victory among the peoples. At 3:140 the Qurʾān addresses the Muslim community after the setback at Uḥud: وَتِلْكَ الْأَيَّامُ نُدَاوِلُهَا بَيْنَ النَّاسِ, declaring that the days of trial are rotated among peoples by divine wisdom. The Day itself, al-dawla, names both the alternation and the moment of its occurrence. The mufassirūn read the root as a warning against pride in victory and despair in defeat — both are positions on the dial of a single moving hand.

meaning.en: The root dāl-khāʾ-nūn (د-خ-ن) denotes smoke, vapor, and haze. It conveys dukhān (44:10) — the visible smoke that is a sign of the approaching Day.
meaning.ar: الدَّالُ وَالْخَاءُ وَالنُّونُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى مَا يَتَصَعَّدُ مِنَ النَّارِ وَغَيْرِهَا، وَيُقَالُ: دَخَنَتِ النَّارُ تَدْخُنُ دُخَانًا وَدَخِنًا.
meaning.en_detailed: The Arabic root د خ ن (دخن) appears 2 times in the Quran, governing the semantic domain of Smoke, vapor, and haze. At 44:10 the Qurʾān employs دُخَانٌ مُّبِينٌ as a sign of the approaching Hour, the sky that visibly divides into smoke. Ibn Fāris places the root under ما يتَصعَّد من النار, the rising column. Lexicons distinguish دُخان (thin smoke) from دُخَان (heavy, lingering). The semantic field unites materiality and metaphor: the air-borne product of fire is, in the end, the breath of a world whose foundations have been undone.

meaning.en: The root fāʾ-kāf-kāf (ف-ك-ك) denotes loosening, releasing, and dislocating. It conveys fakka — to untie a knot, free a captive, or separate what was joined.
meaning.ar: الْفَاءُ وَالْكَافُ وَالْكَافُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى فَتْحِ الشَّيْءِ وَحَلِّهِ. يُقَالُ: فَكَكْتُ الشَّيْءَ أَفُكُّهُ فَكًّا، إِذَا فَتَحْتَهُ وَحَلَلْتَهُ. وَفَكَكْتُ الرَّهْنَ: خَلَّصْتُهُ.
meaning.en_detailed: The doubled triliteral ف-ك-ك names the action of untying, loosening, or releasing what was bound. At 8:63 the Qurʾān reports God as فَكَّ أَيْدِيَهُمْ وَأَيْدِيَكُمْ عَنْهُمْ, He loosed their hands from yours (and yours from theirs) through divine intervention at the treaty of al-Ḥudaybiya; the same root names the فَكَاك of captives (ransom) and the فَكّ of knots. Al-Zamakhsharī traces the root to فَتْحُ الشيء وحَلّه, the undoing of a closure. The semantic range binds physical and abstract: to untie a knot, to ransom a captive, to dislocate a joint, to break a spell — all share the moment when what was held becomes free.

meaning.en_short: Tears, weeping, and the moisture of the ey
meaning.en: The root dāl-mīm-ʿayn (د-م-ع) denotes tears, weeping, and the moisture of the eye. It conveys damʿ (5:83) — eyes overflowing with tears upon hearing truth.
meaning.ar: الدَّالُ وَالْمِيمُ وَالْعَيْنُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى سَيَلَانِ شَيْءٍ، وَمِنْهُ الدَّمْعُ: مَاءُ الْعَيْنِ، وَالدَّمْعَةُ: الْقَطْرَةُ مِنْهُ، وَالدَّمْعُ: سَيَلَانُ الْعَيْنِ بِالدَّمْعِ.
meaning.en_detailed: The root د-م-ع designates the moisture of the eye and its flowing forth in weeping. The Qurʾānic usage at 5:83 places the image at the heart of spiritual response: وَتَسِيلُ مِنْ أَعْيُنِهِمُ الدَّمْعُ مِمَّا عَرَفُوا مِنَ الْحَقِّ, eyes flowing with tears because of what they recognised of the truth. Ibn Fāris traces the root to سَيَلَان الشيء, the flowing-of-anything, with the eye's tear as the prototype. The semantic field is bodily but cognitive: tears are the body's response to what the soul has received, the physical signal of an inward recognition. The hadith corpus values دمع as the visible sign of the humbled heart, distinguishing genuine compunction from mere outward display.

meaning.en_short: Time, eternity, and the long span of ages
meaning.en: The root dāl-hāʾ-rāʾ (د-ه-ر) denotes time, eternity, and the long span of ages. It conveys al-dahr (76:1) — Time itself — and the hadith: lā tasubbū al-dahr — do not curse time.
meaning.ar: الدَّالُ وَالْهَاءُ وَالرَّاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى مُدَّةٍ مِنَ الزَّمَانِ، وَيُقَالُ: الدَّهْرُ الزَّمَانُ الطَّوِيلُ، وَجَمْعُهُ دُهُورٌ.
meaning.en_detailed: دهر (د ه ر), a root appearing 2 times in the Quran, encodes the notion of Time, eternity, and the long span of ages across its various verbal and nominal forms. At 76:1 the Qurʾān opens سورة الإنسان with هَلْ أَتَىٰ عَلَى الْإِنسَانِ حِينٌ مِّنَ الدَّهْرِ لَمْ يَكُن شَيْئًا مَّذْكُورًا, Has there come upon man a period of time wherein he was not a thing remembered? Al-Zajjāj and the mufassirūn gloss الدهر here as a time-span so vast as to make man's existence a forgettable speck. The hadith records the Prophet's correction لَا تَسُبُّوا الدَّهْرَ, do not curse time — for time is but the operation of God upon His creatures. The semantic field unites the unfathomable and the immanent: duration through which the Eternal acts.

meaning.en: The root bāʾ-zāy-ghayn (ب-ز-غ) denotes rising, emerging, and the dawn. It conveys buzuūgh — the first appearance of the sun — the moment light breaks.
meaning.ar: الْبَاءُ وَالزَّاءُ وَالْغَيْنُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى طُلُوعِ الشَّيْءِ وَظُهُورِهِ. يُقَالُ: بَزَغَ الْقَمَرُ وَالشَّمْسُ إِذَا طَلَعَا.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ب-ز-غ names the act of emerging or breaking forth into visibility — particularly the first appearance of light. Lexicons record بَزَغَ الفجر as the first flush of dawn, بَزَغَت الشمس as the rising of the sun. The semantic field unites invisibility with the moment of irruption: the light was always there, but its breaking into the visible is the būzūgh. The hadith employs the root for the hour of judgment, when light itself will be displaced and the world of vision extinguished. The image extends to the soul: faith, like dawn, has a moment when its hidden presence becomes manifest visibility.

meaning.en: The root bāʾ-sīn-sīn (ب-س-س) denotes scattering, crumbling, and dry dust. It conveys bussati al-jibālu bassan (56:5) — the mountains will be crushed and scattered.
meaning.ar: الْبَاءُ وَالسِّينُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى تَفْتِيتِ الشَّيْءِ وَدَقِّهِ. يُقَالُ: بَسَسْتُ الشَّيْءَ أَبُسُّهُ بَسًّا إِذَا فَتَّتَّهُ وَدَقَقْتَهُ.
meaning.en_detailed: The doubled triliteral ب-س-س designates the scattering or crumbling of a thing into dry, fragmented pieces. At 56:5 the Qurʾān declares وَبُسَّتِ الْجِبَالُ بَسًّا — the mountains shall be crumbled into scattered dust. Ibn Fāris traces the root to تَفْتِيت الشيء ودَقّه, the reduction of what was whole into what is small. The semantic field unites dry substance and the breaking of it: the verb is regularly employed of dry twigs (البَسيس) crumbled by the hand. The Qurʾānic usage extends the image to cosmic destruction: what seemed immovable is reduced to a powder that scatters, and the scattered dust is the final testimony to a world dissolved.

meaning.en_short: Cutting off, severing, and exclusive devoti
meaning.en: The root bāʾ-tāʾ-lām (ب-ت-ل) denotes cutting off, severing, and exclusive devotion. It conveys tabattul (73:8) — devote yourself exclusively to Him, detached from all else.
meaning.ar: الْبَاءُ وَالتَّاءُ وَاللَّامُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْقَطْعِ. يُقَالُ: بَتَلْتُ الشَّيْءَ أَبْتُلُهُ بَتْلًا، إِذَا قَطَعْتَهُ.
meaning.en_detailed: The root b-t-l in its primary sense denotes severance and detachment. Its single Form V verbal noun in the Qurʾān, tabattul (73:8), is the classical lexeme for exclusive devotional orientation: ‘devote yourself exclusively to Him’ (wa-nabattil ilayhi tabattulan). Ibn Fāris groups all derivatives under the radical notion of qatʿ (cutting), and Lane notes that tabattula further connotes withdrawal from worldly attachments. As a Qurʾānic term, it marks the spiritual posture of turning wholly away from created beings toward God.

meaning.en_short: Killing oneself from grief, deep anguish
meaning.en: The root bāʾ-khāʾ-ʿayn (ب-خ-ع) denotes killing oneself from grief, deep anguish. It conveys bākhiʿun nafsaka (26:3) — perhaps you would kill yourself with grief that they will not believe.
meaning.ar: (بَخَعَ) الْبَاءُ وَالْخَاءُ وَالْعَيْنُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْإِهْلَاكِ وَالْقَتْلِ. يُقَالُ بَخَعَهُ أَيْ قَتَلَهُ. وَبَخَعَ نَفْسَهُ أَيْ قَتَلَهَا غَمًّا.
meaning.en_detailed: The Arabic root ب خ ع (بخع) appears 2 times in the Quran, governing the semantic domain of Killing oneself from grief, deep anguish. In 26:3 the active participle bākhiʿun modifies nafsaka, ‘killing yourself,’ portraying the Prophet's anguish over his people's rejection. Classical commentators such as al-Ṭabarī gloss it as qatlahā ghamman — slaying oneself from sorrow. The root thus preserves the idea of a person consumed by grief to the point of self-destruction.

meaning.en: The root bāʾ-sīn-rāʾ (ب-س-ر) denotes unripe dates, frowning, and hastiness. It conveys the fruit before ripening — hard and astringent — and the sour face of displeasure.
meaning.ar: الْبَاءُ وَالسِّينُ وَالرَّاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى شِدَّةٍ وَعُبُوسٍ. يُقَالُ: بَسَرَ وَجْهَهُ يَبْسُرُهُ بَسْرًا، إِذَا قَبَضَهُ وَكَلَحَهُ.
meaning.en_detailed: The root b-s-r clusters around the semantic field of hardness, astringency, and a sour or stern countenance. In 55:10 the bare earth (al-arḍ) is described as baṣīra, blackened and cracked under drought — the visual opposite of verdant freshness. Lane and Ibn Fāris connect this to basara, ‘to compress or contract the face,’ underlying the harsh, unripe quality of busr, the date before it ripens. The root thus conveys incipient, severe, and unfinished states.

hadith_evidence.text_en: Abu Dharr reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Do not consider any act of goodness insignificant, even if it is meeting your brother with a cheerful face."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ أَبِي ذَرٍّ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «لَا تَحْقِرَنَّ مِنَ الْمَعْرُوفِ شَيْئًا وَلَوْ أَنْ تَلْقَى أَخَاكَ بِوَجْهٍ طَلْقٍ»

meaning.en: The root bāʾ-sīn-lām (ب-س-ل) denotes being grim-faced, frowning, and accursed. It conveys the severe expression of one facing doom — the bāsūl — the fierce warrior.
meaning.ar: الْبَاءُ وَالسِّينُ وَاللَّامُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْمَرَارَةِ وَالشِّدَّةِ. فَالْبَسْلُ: الْحَرَامُ، وَالْبَسْلُ: الشِّدَّةُ، وَالْبَسْلُ: الْعُبُوسُ.
meaning.en_detailed: The root b-s-l expresses severity, bitterness, and a forbidding grimness. The Qurʾānic nominal basl (8:60) denotes the firm restraint or lethal force employed against enemies, paralleling ṭarad and siḥr in the same verse. Lisān al-ʿArab records three classical senses — the forbidden (ḥarām), severity, and a frowning grimace — all bound by a core notion of unbending harshness. Al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī classifies basl among terms for morally repugnant and austere states.

meaning.en: The root bāʾ-dāl-nūn (ب-د-ن) denotes the body, corpulence, and the sacrificial animal. It conveys al-budn (22:36) — the large-bodied sacrificial camels made symbols of Allah.
meaning.ar: الْبَاءُ وَالدَّالُ وَالنُّونُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الضَّخَامَةِ وَالْكِبَرِ. مِنْ ذَلِكَ الْبَدَنَةُ، وَهِيَ النَّاقَةُ الضَّخْمَةُ، وَالْجَمْعُ بُدْنٌ. وَالرَّجُلُ بَادِنٌ: ضَخْمُ الْبَدَنِ.
meaning.en_detailed: The root b-d-n centers on corpulence and substantial bodily presence. In 22:36 al-budn refers to the bulky sacrificial camels, identified by Abū ʿUbayda and other lexicographers as the fat, full-grown animals singled out for the ḥajj rites. The nominal badan for the human body is cognate to this sense of mass and bulk, and bādin describes a corpulent person. The root thus joins physical substance to ritual function, designating the visible, weighty body appropriate for consecration.

meaning.en: The root bāʾ-rāʾ-ṣād (ب-ر-ص) denotes leprosy, the white skin affliction. It conveys baraṣ (3:49) — the disease Jesus healed by divine permission, restoring skin and dignity.
meaning.ar: الْبَاءُ وَالرَّاءُ وَالصَّادُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْبَرَاءَةِ وَالِانْفِصَالِ. وَمِنْهُ الْبَرَصُ، وَهُوَ بَيَاضٌ يَظْهَرُ فِي الْجِلْدِ، كَأَنَّهُ تَبَرَّأَ مِنْ لَوْنِهِ الْأَصْلِيِّ.
meaning.en_detailed: The root b-r-ṣ signifies the leprous discoloration of the skin. Baraṣ in 3:49 and 5:110 names the condition healed by Jesus through divine permission, classed among the afflictions most feared in classical Arabia. Ibn Fāris connects the word to barāʾa in the sense of detachment, as the disease appears to have separated from the normal hue of the skin. Jurists used the term to establish purity-law (ṭahāra) rulings on those afflicted with conspicuous skin disease.

meaning.en_short: Insolence, ingratitude in prosperity, and w
meaning.en: The root bāʾ-ṭāʾ-rāʾ (ب-ط-ر) denotes insolence, ingratitude in prosperity, and wantonness. It conveys bāṭir — the person corrupted by abundance into reckless ingratitude.
meaning.ar: الْبَاءُ وَالطَّاءُ وَالرَّاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى دَهَشٍ وَعَجَبٍ وَتَجَاوُزِ حَدِّ الْقَصْدِ. يُقَالُ: بَطِرَ الرَّجُلُ بَطَرًا، إِذَا تَجَاوَزَ حَدَّ الْقَصْدِ فِي الْأَمْرِ وَدَهِشَ.
meaning.en_detailed: The root b-ṭ-r carries the sense of wanton transgression that arises from unearned abundance. In 2:15 and 7:146, the active participle bāṭirūn designates the people of Moses who, having witnessed the calf, persisted in insolence and ingratitude for the favors granted them. The classical lexicographers define baṭara as surpassing due measure in heedlessness or arrogance. The concept is closely tied to istikbār and forms part of the Qurʾānic vocabulary of disbelieving pride.

meaning.en: The root bāʾ-nūn-nūn (ب-ن-ن) denotes fingertips, the delicate extremities. It conveys banān (75:4) — Allah can proportion even the fingertips in resurrection.
meaning.ar: (بَنَنَ) الْبَاءُ وَالنُّونُ وَالنُّونُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى طَرَفِ الشَّيْءِ. مِنْ ذَلِكَ الْبَنَانُ، وَهِيَ أَطْرَافُ الْأَصَابِعِ. وَيُقَالُ: بَنَّنَ الرَّجُلُ إِذَا أَشَارَ بِبَنَانِهِ.
meaning.en_detailed: The root b-n-n denotes the tip or extremity, especially of the fingers. In 75:4, banān is paired with naqsh to express that even the unique pattern of human fingertips can be reassembled in resurrection. The word is attested in early Arabic poetry for the fingertips as instruments of pointing and indication, and taṣrīḥ ‘alā l-banān in the ḥadīth literature marks the deliberate gesture of swearing. The root thus connotes the fine, terminal extremities of the body.

meaning.en: The root ṭāʾ-rāʾ-wāw (ط-ر-و) denotes freshness, tenderness, and newness. It conveys ṭarāwa — the appealing softness of what is young and not yet hardened by time.
meaning.ar: مقاييس اللغة لابن فارس: (طَرَا) الطَّاءُ وَالرَّاءُ وَالْحَرْفُ الْمُعْتَلُّ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْحُدُوثِ وَالنَّضَارَةِ. يُقَالُ: طَرِيَ الشَّيْءُ يَطْرَى، إِذَا جَدَّ وَنَضُرَ.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ṭ-r-w signifies newness, freshness, and the supple quality of what has not hardened or aged. Lane records ṭarāʾ as the moisture and softness found in fresh meat, dates, and the like — the opposite of the yubūsa of old age. While rarely cited as a separate lemma, its derivatives surface in classical descriptions of newly arrived letters, fresh fruits, and the pleasing condition of youthful things. The semantic field emphasizes delicacy, suppleness, and recent origin.

meaning.en: The root ṭāʾ-mīm-thāʾ (ط-م-ث) denotes menstruation, the monthly cycle. It conveys ṭamth — the biological process unique to women, referenced in Quranic purity rulings.
meaning.ar: الطَّاءُ وَالْمِيمُ وَالثَّاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى مَسِّ الرَّجُلِ الْمَرْأَةَ، وَهُوَ الْجِمَاعُ. يُقَالُ: طَمَثَ الرَّجُلُ الْمَرْأَةَ يَطْمِثُهَا طَمْثًا، إِذَا افْتَرَعَهَا.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ṭ-m-th is reserved in the Qurʾān and ḥadīth for the unique biological state of menstruation, with all implications for purity and ritual exclusion. The active participle ṭāmiṭūn in 2:222 functions as a polite euphemism for menstruating women, paralleling other Qurʾānic terms for this condition. Ibn Fāris preserves an older gloss linking ṭamth to first contact, from which the specific sense of the menses is drawn. The term is integral to the fiqh of janaabah and the prohibitions on sexual intercourse during the cycle.

meaning.en_short: Camel dung, droppings, and animal excremen
meaning.en: The root bāʾ-ʿayn-rāʾ (ب-ع-ر) denotes camel dung, droppings, and animal excrement. It conveys the most base of animal refuse — what is cast off as worthless.
meaning.ar: الْبَاءُ وَالْعَيْنُ وَالرَّاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْبَعِيرِ، وَهُوَ الْجَمَلُ، وَالْأُنْثَى نَاقَةٌ. وَيُقَالُ بَعِيرٌ لِلذَّكَرِ وَالْأُنْثَى حَتَّى يَتَبَيَّنَ.
meaning.en_detailed: The root b-ʿ-r primarily denotes the camel and the particular qualities of its droppings, often invoked in matters of ṭahāra and of base things cast away. Classical lexica record baʿīr and baʿra in the senses of camel and camel-dung, the latter being the most notoriously foul of animal excretions in Bedouin estimation. The root underlines the lowliest by-products of an animal otherwise prized by the Arabs. Derivations often carry the connotation of what is foul, rejected, or expelled.

meaning.en: The root ṭāʾ-ʿayn-nūn (ط-ع-ن) denotes piercing, stabbing, and sharp criticism. It conveys ṭaʿana — to thrust a spear — and metaphorically, to wound with words.
meaning.ar: الطَّاءُ وَالْعَيْنُ وَالنُّونُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى خَرْقِ الشَّيْءِ وَثَقْبِهِ، يُقَالُ: طَعَنَهُ بِالرُّمْحِ يَطْعَنُهُ طَعْنًا.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ṭ-ʿ-n denotes the piercing thrust of a spear and, metaphorically, the sharp wounding of speech or criticism. Al-Iṣfahānī defines ṭaʿn as the act of breaching a body with a piercing instrument, distinguishing it from qaṣf and darb. In classical rhetoric, ṭaʿn al-ʿaqd signifies the laying open of a fault, and jurists distinguished ṭiʿn in testimony from kasr al-sariq. The root thus joins physical violence to the figure of verbal incision.

meaning.en_short: A twin, equivalent, and paired growth
meaning.en: The root ṣād-nūn-wāw (ص-ن-و) denotes a twin, equivalent, and paired growth. It conveys ṣinwān (13:4) — twin palm trees growing from the same root — complementary pairs.
meaning.ar: الصَّادُ وَالنُّونُ وَالْوَاوُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى ضَمِّ الشَّيْءِ إِلَى الشَّيْءِ، مِنْ ذَلِكَ الصِّنْوُ: الْغُصْنُ يَنْبُتُ مِنْ أَصْلِ الشَّجَرَةِ، وَالْجَمْعُ صِنْوَانٌ.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ṣ-n-w denotes equivalent or twin objects, particularly branches growing from a common root. In 13:4, ṣinwān (‘pairs of palm trees’) describes twin clusters that share a single base, joined in the botanical symmetry that betokens design. Lane glosses the noun as ‘a palm branch that issues from the same root as another.’ The root's semantic core is parity of origin, often extended in classical Arabic to peers, equals, and matched companions.

meaning.en_short: In-law relations, marriage kinship, and mel
meaning.en: The root ṣād-hāʾ-rāʾ (ص-ه-ر) denotes in-law relations, marriage kinship, and melting. It conveys ṣihr — the bonds created through matrimony — the fusion of families.
meaning.ar: الصَّادُ وَالْهَاءُ وَالرَّاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى خَلْطِ شَيْءٍ بِشَيْءٍ، وَمِنْهُ الصِّهْرُ: خَلْطُ النَّسَبِ بِالنَّسَبِ، وَالصَّهْرُ: إِذَابَةُ الشَّيْءِ.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ṣ-h-r carries the meanings of in-law relationship and the heat of melting. The Qurʾānic phrase ṣihrun waḥīd (4:23) forbids marriage to a man's mother-in-law and daughter-in-law, fixing the boundaries of affinal kinship. Ibn Fāris explains the etymology through the melting (taṣhīr) of fats, evoking the mixing of two substances — an apt metaphor for the mingling of two lineages through marriage. The root thus binds a specific kinship category to the image of two streams of blood becoming one.

meaning.en: The root ṣād-fāʾ-dāl (ص-ف-د) denotes binding, shackling, and iron fetters. It conveys al-aṣfād (14:49) — the chains that bind the damned — restraint and captivity.
meaning.ar: الصَّادُ وَالْفَاءُ وَالدَّالُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الشَّدِّ وَالْإِيثَاقِ. يُقَالُ: صَفَدْتُ الرَّجُلَ أَصْفِدُهُ صَفْدًا، إِذَا شَدَدْتَهُ بِالصَّفَادِ، وَهُوَ الْقَيْدُ.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ṣ-f-d denotes fettering, restraint, and the chains used to bind captives. In 14:49, aṣfād (chains, shackles) recurs alongside silāsila to describe the restraints prepared for the people of Pharaoh and the guilty. The basic sense of şafd in lexica is to bind or imprison, and Lisān al-ʿArab glosses ṣafād as a shackle (qayd). As a Qurʾānic symbol, it signifies the irreducible confinement of the doomed within the grip of divine justice.

meaning.en_short: A finger, digit, and that which points
meaning.en: The root ṣād-bāʾ-ʿayn (ص-ب-ع) denotes a finger, digit, and that which points. It conveys iṣbaʿ — the instrument of precise indication — the heart is between two fingers of the Most Merciful.
meaning.ar: الصَّادُ وَالْبَاءُ وَالْعَيْنُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى طَرَفٍ مِنَ الْأَطْرَافِ، وَالْإِصْبَعُ مِنْ ذَلِكَ، وَهِيَ طَرَفُ الْيَدِ وَالرِّجْلِ
meaning.en_detailed: The root ṣ-b-ʿ denotes the digits of the hand and, by extension, the act of pointing. Classical lexica define iṣbaʿ as the terminus of the hand, the limb used to indicate and signal precisely. The ḥadīth of the heart being between two Fingers of the Most Merciful (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, Kitāb al-Qadar) draws upon this exact pointing function to express divine mastery over inner states. The root thus centers on the fingertip as instrument of direction and indication.

meaning.en: The root ṣād-dāl-yāʾ (ص-د-ي) denotes echo, resonance, and thirst. It conveys ṣadā — the hollow reply from emptiness — the sound that returns because nothing fills the void.
meaning.ar: الصَّادُ وَالدَّالُ وَالْحَرْفُ الْمُعْتَلُّ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى مَيْلٍ وَعُدُولٍ. يُقَالُ: صَدَى يَصْدِي، إِذَا مَالَ.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ṣ-d-y denotes an echo, a resonance, and metaphorically the hollow thirst that consumes one for what one cannot reach. Al-Ṭabarī and the lexicographers gloss ṣadā in 13:31 as the empty answering-cry that does not profit its utterer, indicating the emptiness of words without content. The same root lies behind ṣady, severe thirst, by a metaphorical leap to the unfulfilled longing of the heart. It thus joins sonic emptiness to the deeper thirst of the soul.

hadith_evidence.text_en: Abu Dharr reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Do not consider any act of goodness insignificant, even if it is meeting your brother with a cheerful face."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ أَبِي ذَرٍّ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «لَا تَحْقِرَنَّ مِنَ الْمَعْرُوفِ شَيْئًا وَلَوْ أَنْ تَلْقَى أَخَاكَ بِوَجْهٍ طَلْقٍ»

meaning.en: The root ḥāʾ-wāw-dhāl (ح-و-ذ) denotes seizing, possessing, and taking control. It conveys ḥawdha — to drive forward assertively — to claim ownership and command.
meaning.ar: "الْحَاءُ وَالْوَاوُ وَالذَّالُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْحَوْزِ وَالْقَبْضِ وَالِاسْتِيلَاءِ"
meaning.en_detailed: The root ḥ-w-ḍ expresses the act of seizing, gathering in, and taking possession. Lane records ḥawḍ and ḥīḍa in the senses of driving together and grasping tightly, and the verbal noun ḥayḍa denotes a violent seizure. While the derivative verbs are rare in the Qurʾānic corpus, the root underlies a semantic field of forceful acquisition, control, and confinement. The notion of a determined, possessive grip recurs across its derivations in classical usage.

meaning.en_short: Inclining, leaning, and bending the ear
meaning.en: The root ṣād-ghayn-wāw (ص-غ-و) denotes inclining, leaning, and bending the ear. It conveys ṣagha — to tilt toward — the attentive lean of one who listens intently.
meaning.ar: الصَّادُ وَالْغَيْنُ وَالْحَرْفُ الْمُعْتَلُّ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْمَيْلِ وَالْعُدُولِ عَنِ الْحَقِّ. يُقَالُ: صَغَا يَصْغُو صَغْوًا وَصُغُوًّا، وَصَغِيَ يَصْغَى صَغًى، فَهُوَ صَاغٍ وَصَغٍ.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ṣ-gh-w denotes inclination, leaning, and the bending of the ear toward a sound. In 4:81 the imperative addressed to the waverers — 'will you incline toward God's covenant' — challenges those who turn aside from the Prophet's pact. Lisān al-ʿArab distinguishes ṣaghā and ṣaghī, the latter tending toward the lower rather than the higher object of listening. The root thus centers on the voluntary tilt of attention and conscience toward a chosen direction.

meaning.en: The root ḥāʾ-wāw-shīn (ح-و-ش) denotes gathering, collecting, and courtyard. It conveys ḥawsh — the enclosed space where animals and things are gathered.
meaning.ar: «الْحَاءُ وَالْوَاوُ وَالشِّينُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الضَّمِّ وَالْجَمْعِ. يُقَالُ: حَاشَ الْقَوْمُ إِذَا اجْتَمَعُوا، وَحَاشَ الْإِبِلَ يَحُوشُهَا إِذَا جَمَعَهَا وَسَاقَهَا.»
meaning.en_detailed: The root ḥ-w-sh clusters around the gathering of animals or persons into a single enclosed space. Lane and Lisān al-ʿArab define ḥawsh as a courtyard or pen, and ḥāsh as a man who collects or drives cattle. In its Qurʾānic deployment, the term underlies the concept of refuge or sanctuary (ḥīsh, ḥāshiyya), often denoting what is withdrawn or peripheral. The semantic core is collection into a bounded place, with secondary senses of withdrawal and protection.

meaning.en_short: A long period, an age, and a belt
meaning.en: The root ḥāʾ-qāf-bāʾ (ح-ق-ب) denotes a long period, an age, and a belt. It conveys aḥqāban (78:23) — ages upon ages — the vast stretches of time the damned will endure.
meaning.ar: الْحَاءُ وَالْقَافُ وَالْبَاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى مُضِيِّ الزَّمَانِ الطَّوِيلِ، وَيُقَالُ: حَقِبَ الشَّيْءُ إِذَا تَأَخَّرَ وَاحْتَبَسَ.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ḥ-q-b denotes a long duration, an age, and an encircling band or belt. In 78:23, aḥqāban — ‘ages upon ages’ — describes the successive millennia the denizens of Hell will abide, intensified by the plural form. Lisān al-ʿArab preserves the sense of ḥiqab, a long span of years uninterrupted by death, and ḥaqaba, the broad belt worn around the waist. The root thus conjoins vast temporality with the image of binding time to those who endure it.

meaning.en_short: Breaking an oath, perjury, and sin
meaning.en: The root ḥāʾ-nūn-thāʾ (ح-ن-ث) denotes breaking an oath, perjury, and sin. It conveys ḥinth (56:46) — the great sin of persisting in oath-breaking.
meaning.ar: قال ابن فارس في مقاييس اللغة: (حَنَثَ) الْحَاءُ وَالنُّونُ وَالثَّاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى انْعِطَافٍ وَمَيْلٍ. يُقَالُ حَنَثَ فِي يَمِينِهِ إِذَا مَالَ عَنْهَا وَلَمْ يَفِ بِهَا.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ḥ-n-th denotes the breaking of an oath or vow and, by extension, grave sin. In 56:46, ḥinṯ, qualifying an ‘azīman (great oath), underscores the magnitude of the sin of false swearing — set among the works of the people of the right hand who yet falter. Ibn Fāris derives the verb ḥanatha from a notion of twisting aside, hence departing from the binding vow. Lexical sources emphasize that ḥinṯ ranks among al-kabāʾir when coupled with deliberate falsehood.

meaning.en: The root ḥāʾ-jīm-zāy (ح-ج-ز) denotes withholding, separating, and the barrier. It conveys ḥajaza — to prevent two things from meeting — the partition that divides.
meaning.ar: قال ابن فارس: الحاء والجيم والزاء أصل واحد يدل على حاجز بين الشيئين. يقال: حجزت بينهما أحجز حجزاً، أي حلت بينهما. والحاجز: الحائل.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ḥ-j-z denotes the act of interposing a barrier between two things, hence also of withholding, separating, and protecting. Al-Rāghib and Ibn Fāris define ḥajaza as placing a ḥājiz (parting object) between persons or things, deriving ḥijāza (the protected interior of a house) from the same barrier-imagery. The root thus underlies concepts of partition, refuge, protection, and interdiction, with extensions into the legal language of stopping or preventing an act.

meaning.en: The root ḥāʾ-bāʾ-sīn (ح-ب-س) denotes confinement, detention, and endowment. It conveys ḥubs — to hold back from circulation — a prisoner or a perpetual charitable trust.
meaning.ar: الْحَاءُ وَالْبَاءُ وَالسِّينُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْمَنْعِ وَالْإِمْسَاكِ. يُقَالُ حَبَسْتُهُ أَحْبِسُهُ حَبْسًا، وَالْحَبْسُ ضِدُّ الْإِرْسَالِ.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ḥ-b-s centers on withholding, confinement, and the act of holding something back from circulation. Lane defines ḥabs as the opposite of irsāl — the act of binding, restraining, or retaining. In classical fiqh, ḥabs designates an endowed property whose revenues are perpetually devoted to a charitable cause, distinct from waqf proper in some schools. The root joins physical detention to the broader figure of sealing something within a fixed purpose.

meaning.en: The root ḥāʾ-ṭāʾ-bāʾ (ح-ط-ب) denotes firewood, fuel-gathering, and combustible material. It conveys ḥammālata al-ḥaṭab (111:4) — the wife of Abu Lahab, carrier of thorny firewood.
meaning.ar: الْحَاءُ وَالطَّاءُ وَالْبَاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى جَمْعِ شَيْءٍ وَضَمِّهِ. مِنْ ذَلِكَ الْحَطَبُ، وَهُوَ مَا يُجْمَعُ مِنَ الْيَابِسِ لِلْوَقُودِ.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ḥ-ṭ-b denotes firewood and the gathering of combustible matter. In 111:4, the epithet ḥammālata l-ḥaṭab applied to Abū Lahab's wife punishes her for the gossip she used to kindle against the Prophet — a fiery burden gathering fuel for the flames. Lisān al-ʿArab glosses ḥaṭab as dry branches collected for burning, and the verb ḥaṭaba as gathering such fuel. The root thus fuses collection, dry combustibility, and the image of a punitive fire.

meaning.en: The root ḥāʾ-ṭāʾ-ṭāʾ (ح-ط-ط) denotes lowering, putting down, and diminishing. It conveys ḥaṭṭa — to reduce a burden — and the Quranic plea: wa ḥuṭṭa khaṭāyānā — and put down our sins.
meaning.ar: الْحَاءُ وَالطَّاءُ وَالطَّاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى وَضْعِ الشَّيْءِ وَإِسْقَاطِهِ. يُقَالُ: حَطَّ الشَّيْءَ يَحُطُّهُ حَطًّا، إِذَا وَضَعَهُ وَأَسْقَطَهُ.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ḥ-ṭ-ṭ expresses the lowering, putting down, or reduction of a burden. In 2:58 and 7:161 the prayer wa-ḥuṭṭa khaṭāyānā (‘and put down our sins upon us’) is the plea of those who have borne an unsustainable weight — the doubled form suggesting both forgiveness and easing of consequence. Ibn Fāris defines ḥaṭṭ as the act of lowering or letting fall. The semantic core unifies descent, lightening, and the relieving of a load.

meaning.en_short: Being unable, weary, and falling short
meaning.en: The root ʿayn-yāʾ-yāʾ (ع-ي-ي) denotes being unable, weary, and falling short. It conveys ʿayy — the exhaustion of capacity — the tongue unable to express, the mind unable to grasp.
meaning.ar: الْعَيْنُ وَالْيَاءُ وَالْيَاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الضَّعْفِ وَالْإِعْيَاءِ، يُقَالُ: عَيِيَ الرَّجُلُ يَعْيَا عَيَاءً إِذَا تَعِبَ وَأَعْيَا.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ʿ-y-y denotes the exhaustion that renders one incapable of doing or saying more. In 28:33, Mūsā's plea ‘My chest straitens and my tongue does not hasten (yaʿyā) —‘ expresses the strain of inadequate speech before Pharaoh. Lisān al-ʿArab and Lane define ʿayāʾ as the tiredness of body or mind, with the verbal form ranging from physical fatigue to the utter failure of words. The root thus covers both corporeal weariness and expressive collapse.

meaning.en: The root ʿayn-yāʾ-lām (ع-ي-ل) denotes poverty, want, and many dependents. It conveys ʿayla — the burden of scarcity — having too little for those who depend on you.
meaning.ar: الْعَيْنُ وَالْيَاءُ وَاللَّامُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى ضِيقِ الْحَالِ وَكَثْرَةِ الْعِيَالِ. يُقَالُ: عَالَ الرَّجُلُ يَعِيلُ عَيْلَةً، إِذَا افْتَقَرَ.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ʿ-y-l centers on poverty and the burden of dependants. In 68:14, the accusative ghawwāsin ʿayyallan — ‘erring, very heedless’ — pairs al-Iṣfahānī's gloss of ʿayla with the wide-ranging responsibility of providing for others. Lane records the verbal form ʿāla as to grow poor with many dependents, and ʿīla as the crowd of those who cling to a man for subsistence. The semantic field unites scarcity with the social weight of dependents.

meaning.en: The root ʿayn-tāʾ-qāf (ع-ت-ق) denotes freedom, nobility, and antiquity. It conveys ʿitq — the liberation of a slave — and ʿatīq — the ancient, venerable, and noble.
meaning.ar: الْعَيْنُ وَالتَّاءُ وَالْقَافُ أَصْلَانِ: أَحَدُهُمَا الْقِدَمُ، وَالْآخَرُ الْعِتْقُ وَهُوَ الْحُرِّيَّةُ. فَالْأَوَّلُ: الْعَتِيقُ الْقَدِيمُ، وَالْعَاتِقُ الْقَدِيمُ.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ʿ-t-q holds two primary senses: emancipation from bondage and the venerability of age. In 90:13 the active participle ʿatīq, applied to the human soul, carries both ideas — the liberated soul, free from the chains of mortal attachment, and the venerable soul returned to its ancient origin. Lisān al-ʿArab preserves both branches: ʿitq as manumission, and ʿatīq as ancient and noble. The term lies at the heart of the ethical and theological discourse of freedom in Islam.

meaning.en: The root ʿayn-thāʾ-rāʾ (ع-ث-ر) denotes stumbling, tripping, and discovering unexpectedly. It conveys ʿathara — to lose footing — and the serendipitous discovery that comes from stumbling.
meaning.ar: الْعَيْنُ وَالثَّاءُ وَالرَّاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْأَثَرِ. وَالْعَثْرُ: الْوُقُوعُ عَلَى الشَّيْءِ. يُقَالُ عَثَرَ عَلَى الشَّيْءِ يَعْثُرُ عَثْرًا وَعُثُورًا: اطَّلَعَ عَلَيْهِ.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ʿ-th-r denotes the tripping of the foot and, by extension, the finding of something one was not actively seeking. In 18:21 the active participle ʿāṣirūn (yet knowing not how long they have tarried) is paired by al-Ṭabarī with ʿathara, the inadvertent discovery following a stumble. The same root underlies āthār (vestiges) and iʿtibār (drawing lessons from traces). The semantic core thus joins bodily stumbling to the deeper figure of finding meaning in what one chances upon.

meaning.en_short: Dragging roughly, seizing violently, and c
meaning.en: The root ʿayn-tāʾ-lām (ع-ت-ل) denotes dragging roughly, seizing violently, and coarseness. It conveys ʿutull (68:13) — the churlish brute — dragged to Hell by his forelock.
meaning.ar: الْعَيْنُ وَالتَّاءُ وَاللَّامُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى جَذْبٍ وَقَبْضٍ بِعُنْفٍ. وَمِنْهُ الْعَتْلُ: الْأَخْذُ بِالْجُمْعَةِ وَالْجَرُّ بِعُنْفٍ. وَالْعُتُلُّ: الْجَافِي الْغَلِيظُ.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ʿ-t-l denotes violent hauling and the brutality that accompanies it. In 68:13 the Qurʾān denounces as ʿutull a sinner denying the truth — a coarse, stubborn oppressor, destined to be dragged to Hell by his forelock. Lisān al-ʿArab explains ʿatl as seizing a man by his hair or tunic and dragging him, and ʿutull as the churlish lout who lacks discernment. The root thus fuses physical violence with the moral obtuseness of one who refuses to hear.

meaning.en: The root ʿayn-rāʾ-rāʾ (ع-ر-ر) denotes scabies, mange, and an affliction. It conveys ʿarra — the visible skin disease that mars — any distressing blemish.
meaning.ar: الْعَيْنُ وَالرَّاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى أَمْرٍ يَضُرُّ وَيَغُمُّ. مِنْ ذَلِكَ الْعَرُّ: الْجَرَبُ، وَالْعَرَّةُ: الشِّدَّةُ، وَالْعُرَّةُ: الْجُنُونُ.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ʿ-r-r connects to harming affliction, particularly the scabrous skin disease ʿarra, in classical Arabic a condition likened to scabies or mange. In 2:60 and 7:133 the phrase ‘you with no harm upon you (lā ʿarra ʿalaykum)’ contrasts well-being with the afflictions brought upon Pharaoh's people. Lisān al-ʿArab pairs ʿarra with jarab (scabies), ʿarra with shadīd (hardship), and ʿarra with junūn (madness). The semantic core is exposure to harm that visibly marks and humbles the afflicted.

meaning.en: The root ʿayn-jīm-fāʾ (ع-ج-ف) denotes leanness, emaciation, and extreme thinness. It conveys ʿijāf (12:43) — the lean cows of Joseph's dream — gaunt and skeletal.
meaning.ar: الْعَيْنُ وَالْجِيمُ وَالْفَاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْهُزَالِ وَالضَّعْفِ. يُقَالُ: عَجِفَ الْبَعِيرُ يَعْجَفُ عَجَفًا، فَهُوَ عَجِفٌ وَعَجْفَاءُ، وَالْجَمْعُ عِجَافٌ.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ʿ-j-f denotes leanness and the thinness that follows hunger, drought, or sustained affliction. In 12:43 the 'seven lean (ʿijāf) cows' of Joseph's dream stand as the classical Qurʾānic emblem of famine years succeeding abundance. Lisān al-ʿArab defines ʿajaf as the loss of flesh and moisture, with ʿijāf designating gaunt, emaciated beasts. The semantic field unites dryness, the loss of bodily fullness, and the gauntness that signals scarcity.

meaning.en_short: Colored wool, fluff, and carded fiber
meaning.en: The root ʿayn-hāʾ-nūn (ع-ه-ن) denotes colored wool, fluff, and carded fiber. It conveys al-ʿihn al-manfūsh (101:5) — mountains like carded wool on Judgment Day.
meaning.ar: الْعَيْنُ وَالْهَاءُ وَالنُّونُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى اللِّينِ وَالرَّخَاوَةِ، وَمِنْهُ الْعِهْنُ: الصُّوفُ، وَالْعِهْنَةُ: الْخَصْلَةُ مِنَ الصُّوفِ.
meaning.en_detailed: Arabic root ع-ه-ن (ʿayn-hāʾ-nūn), occurring 2 times in the Quran, denotes colored wool, carded fiber, and soft fluff. Its central usage is al-ʿihn al-manfūsh in 101:5, 'carded wool,' describing the mountains losing their solidity on the Day of Judgment — a powerful image of cosmic dissolution and the reversal of earthly permanence. Classical lexicographers (Ibn Fāris, Lisān al-ʿArab) relate it to softness and looseness, with al-ʿihna being a lock or tuft of wool. The metaphor evokes both fragility and dispersal, fitting the eschatological dissolution theme of Sūrat al-Qāriʿa.

meaning.en_short: Being bare, devoid, and without adornment
meaning.en: The root ʿayn-ṭāʾ-lām (ع-ط-ل) denotes being bare, devoid, and without adornment. It conveys ʿāṭil — a neck without a necklace — conspicuous absence.
meaning.ar: الْعَيْنُ وَالطَّاءُ وَاللَّامُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى خُلُوٍّ وَفَرَاغٍ. يُقَالُ: عَطِلَ الرَّجُلُ إِذَا خَلَا مِنَ الْحِلْيَةِ، وَعُطِّلَتِ الْإِبِلُ إِذَا تُرِكَتْ بِلَا رَاعٍ.
meaning.en_detailed: Arabic root ع-ط-ل (ʿayn-ṭāʾ-lām), occurring 2 times in the Quran, conveys being bare, devoid, and stripped of adornment, with the secondary sense of abandoned or unattended. The form ʿunuq ʿāṭil denotes a neck without its necklace — an image of conspicuous emptiness, used in references to the arrogant who cast off divine grace. Lexicographers derive it from emptiness and vacancy, contrasting the adorned state with one left bare. The root marks a thematic contrast between ornamentation (ḥily) and the desolation that follows rejection of the divine order.

meaning.en: The root ʿayn-bāʾ-thāʾ (ع-ب-ث) denotes play, frivolity, and purposelessness. It conveys ʿabath (23:115) — creation was not made in vain — every existence has profound purpose.
meaning.ar: الْعَيْنُ وَالْبَاءُ وَالثَّاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى فِعْلِ الشَّيْءِ لَا لِغَرَضٍ وَلَا لِمَنْفَعَةٍ، يُقَالُ: عَبِثَ يَعْبَثُ عَبَثًا، وَهُوَ اللَّعِبُ وَالْبَاطِلُ.
meaning.en_detailed: Arabic root ع-ب-ث (ʿayn-bāʾ-thāʾ), occurring 2 times in the Quran, denotes play, frivolity, and purposeless action. Its pivotal occurrence is ʿabathan in 23:115, 'Did you think We created you in vain (ʿabathan)?' — a foundational Quranic negation of existential futility. Ibn Fāris and al-Rāghib al-Aṣfahānī classify it under actions lacking purpose or benefit, distinguished from ludh (mere play) by its stronger connotation of meaninglessness. The root carries profound theological weight: every created being has a maqṣūd (purpose), and to deny this is to deny divine wisdom.

meaning.en: The root ʿayn-ḍād-lām (ع-ض-ل) denotes hindering, preventing, and muscular cramp. It conveys ʿaḍl (2:232) — preventing women from remarriage — forbidden in the Quran.
meaning.ar: الْعَيْنُ وَالضَّادُ وَاللَّامُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْمَنْعِ وَالتَّضْيِيقِ. يُقَالُ: عَضَلْتُهُ أَعْضِلُهُ عَضْلًا إِذَا مَنَعْتُهُ وَضَيَّقْتُ عَلَيْهِ
meaning.en_detailed: Arabic root ع-ض-ل (ʿayn-ḍād-lām), occurring 2 times in the Quran, denotes hindering, constraining, and preventing by force. Its central Quranic usage is in 2:232, prohibiting guardians from preventing women from remarrying (wa-lā taʿḍulūhunna) — a specific legal prohibition against obstructionist coercion. Classical dictionaries link the root to muscular constriction (ʿaḍal = muscle) and to tightening/restricting, giving the verbal sense of 'pressing someone into impossibility.' The Quran thus transforms a physical metaphor into a juridical principle safeguarding women's marital freedom.

meaning.en_short: Biting, gnawing, and holding with teeth
meaning.en: The root ʿayn-ḍād-ḍād (ع-ض-ض) denotes biting, gnawing, and holding with teeth. It conveys yaʿaḍḍa ʿalā yadayhi (25:27) — the wrongdoer biting his hands in regret on Judgment Day.
meaning.ar: الْعَيْنُ وَالضَّادُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى شِدَّةِ الْأَخْذِ بِالْأَسْنَانِ، ثُمَّ يُسْتَعَارُ فِي كُلِّ شِدَّةٍ وَغَيْظٍ.
meaning.en_detailed: Arabic root ع-ض-ض (ʿayn-ḍād-ḍād), occurring 2 times in the Quran, denotes biting, gnawing, and seizing with the teeth, with the extended metaphorical sense of intense regret and self-directed anguish. The form yaʿḍḍu ʿalā yadayhi (e.g., 25:27) depicts the wrongdoer biting his own hands in frustrated regret. Ibn Fāris traces this to the original meaning of forceful seizing by the teeth, then extended to any fierce grasping or angry frustration. The image powerfully expresses the futility of remorse once the moment of choice has passed.

meaning.en: The root ḍād-mīm-mīm (ض-م-م) denotes joining, attaching, and drawing together. It conveys ḍamma — to bring two things into contact and unite them.
meaning.ar: ضَمَّ الشَّيْءَ إِلَى الشَّيْءِ: جَمَعَهُ إِلَيْهِ وَأَلْصَقَهُ
meaning.en_detailed: Arabic root ض-م-م (ḍād-mīm-mīm), occurring 2 times in the Quran, denotes joining, attaching, and drawing things into close contact. The verbal form ḍamma signifies bringing two things together so they adhere, and the noun ḍimma denotes that which is taken under protection or trust. Classical usage extends it from physical joining (gathering garments, gathering children) to abstract attachment and consolidation. The root implies intimacy and bonding, the opposite of separation (farq), and grounds Quranic concepts of community cohesion and divine gathering.

meaning.en_short: Hidden malice, deep-seated hatred, and ra
meaning.en: The root ḍād-ghayn-nūn (ض-غ-ن) denotes hidden malice, deep-seated hatred, and rancor. It conveys ḍighn (7:43) — the grudge Allah removes from the hearts of Paradise dwellers.
meaning.ar: الضَّادُ وَالْغَيْنُ وَالنُّونُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى شَيْءٍ فِي الْقَلْبِ مِنْ عَدَاوَةٍ وَبَغْضَاءَ. يُقَالُ: ضَغَنَ عَلَيْهِ يَضْغَنُ ضَغَنًا، إِذَا أَضْمَرَ لَهُ الْعَدَاوَةَ.
meaning.en_detailed: Arabic root ض-غ-ن (ḍād-ghayn-nūn), occurring 2 times in the Quran, denotes concealed malice, deep-seated rancor, and hidden hatred. Its central occurrence is ḍighn in 7:43, 'And We will remove whatever rancor (ḍighn) is in their chests,' describing the purified hearts of the people of Paradise. Ibn Fāris and al-Rāghib define it as enmity concealed within the soul, distinguished from ghill (active grudge) by its inward, suppressed quality. The Quranic vision presents Paradise as a place where even the deepest traces of interpersonal grudges are extracted, leaving only pure fellowship.

meaning.en_short: Sighing, expressing grief, and the cry of
meaning.en: The root hamza-wāw-hāʾ (أ-و-ه) denotes sighing, expressing grief, and the cry of pain. It conveys awwāh (9:114) — Abraham was awwāh — sighing in compassion and grief for sinners.
meaning.ar: الْهَمْزَةُ وَالْوَاوُ وَالْهَاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى تَصَوُّتٍ وَحُزْنٍ.
meaning.en_detailed: Arabic root أ-و-ه (hamza-wāw-hāʾ), occurring 2 times in the Quran, denotes sighing, lamenting, and uttering cries of grief and supplication. Its form awwāh (9:114) is applied to Ibrāhīm, 'Indeed Abraham was awwāh (most compassionate and supplicating),' characterizing the prophet's tender-hearted response to human suffering and his abundant weeping. Classical lexicographers connect the root to a voice of pain or supplication (taṣawwut wa-ḥuzn). The Quranic usage elevates it from mere lamentation to the prophetic virtue of mercy (raḥma) intertwined with reverent fear (khashya).

meaning.en: The root hamza-thāʾ-thāʾ (أ-ث-ث) denotes furniture, household goods, and furnishings. It conveys athāth (19:74) — the material possessions that make a house a home.
meaning.ar: "الْهَمْزَةُ وَالثَّاءُ وَالثَّاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى كَثْرَةِ الشَّيْءِ وَعَدَدِهِ. مِنْ ذَلِكَ الْأَثَاثُ: مَتَاعُ الْبَيْتِ، وَالْجَمْعُ أُثُثٌ.
meaning.en_detailed: Arabic root أ-ث-ث (hamza-thāʾ-thāʾ), occurring 2 times in the Quran, denotes furniture, household goods, and material furnishings. The noun athāth refers to the apparatus and equipment of daily domestic life, mentioned in 19:74 ('furniture and goods [athāth]') as part of the worldly possessions that seduce and distract. The root also conveys abundance and quantity of items. The Quranic use presents athāth as the visible layer of material comfort, contrasting transitory worldly goods with the eternal ḥayāt khālida (lasting life).

meaning.en: To walk, to go on foot; to spread (of news, reports). The root's primary sense of ambulation extends metaphorically to the diffusion of information — just as a person walks across the earth, so news 'walks' through a community. Quranic usage ranges from the parable of hesitant hypocrites walking only when lightning flashes (2:20) to the prohibition of walking on the earth with arrogant self-conceit (17:37). The root thus encodes both physical movement and social circulation.
meaning.en_detailed: Occurring 23 times in the Quranic text, the root م ش ي (مَشَى) conveys the essential concept of To walk, go; to spread (news). With 23 Qurʾānic occurrences, the verb appears at 2:20 ('كُلَّمَا أَضَاءَ لَهُم مَّشَوْا فِيهِ وَإِذَا أَظْلَمَ عَلَيْهِمْ قَامُوا'), in the parable of lightning that briefly illuminates the path of hesitant hypocrites, and at 17:37 ('وَلَا تَمْشِ فِي الْأَرْضِ مَرَحًا'), prohibiting walking on earth with arrogant self-conceit. The root's semantic trajectory reflects the Qurʾānic ethical framing of locomotion as moral action, where even walking bears spiritual significance and the believer is called to walk (مَشْي) with humility upon the earth, conscious of divine presence.

meaning.en: The root hamza-mīm-wāw (أ-م-و) denotes a maidservant, female slave. It conveys ama — the bondwoman — distinct from free women in certain legal provisions.
meaning.ar: (أ م و) الْهَمْزَةُ وَالْمِيمُ وَالْوَاوُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْخِدْمَةِ وَالْعُبُودِيَّةِ. وَالْأَمَةُ: الْمَمْلُوكَةُ، وَالْجَمْعُ إِمَاءٌ.
meaning.en_detailed: Arabic root أ-م-و (hamza-mīm-wāw), occurring 2 times in the Quran, denotes a maidservant or female bondwoman, the counterpart of ʿabd for male slaves. The form ama/imāʾ designates women in bondage, who in pre-Islamic and early Islamic Arabia held a distinct legal status from free women (ḥurra). The Quran addresses them in specific legal contexts (e.g., marriage, modesty, manumission), elevating their dignity and recommending their liberation. Classical etymology derives the word from service and submission (khidma wa-ʿubūdiyya), and the root forms the basis for the Islamic jurisprudence of emancipation.

meaning.en: The root hamza-rāʾ-bāʾ (أ-ر-ب) denotes need, want, and cleverness. It conveys arab — a specific desire — and arīb — the wise, resourceful person who achieves goals.
meaning.ar: الْعَيْنُ وَالرَّاءُ وَالْبَاءُ أَصْلَانِ: أَحَدُهُمَا يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْبَيَانِ وَالْفَصَاحَةِ، وَالْآخَرُ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الطَّلَبِ وَالْإِرَادَةِ.
meaning.en_detailed: Arabic root أ-ر-ب (hamza-rāʾ-bāʾ), occurring 2 times in the Quran, denotes need, want, specific desire, and resourcefulness. The noun arab conveys a particular want, while the active participle arīb denotes the astute, discerning person who achieves objectives through cleverness. Ibn Fāris identifies two semantic cores: one of eloquent clarity (faṣāḥa), the other of desire and pursuit (ṭalab). The dual semantic register — both 'intelligent discernment' and 'specific need' — gives the root depth, connecting intellectual acuity with the fulfillment of wants.

meaning.en_short: An oath, covenant, and sacred bond
meaning.en: The root hamza-lām-lām (أ-ل-ل) denotes an oath, covenant, and sacred bond. It conveys ill — the solemn pact — and dhimma — the treaty (9:8-10) — the bonds that must not be broken.
meaning.ar: (إِلٌّ) الْهَمْزَةُ وَاللَّامُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى عَهْدٍ وَيَمِينٍ. وَالْإِلُّ: الْعَهْدُ وَالْيَمِينُ. وَالْإِلُّ: الْقَرَابَةُ. وَالْإِلُّ: الْحِلْفُ.
meaning.en_detailed: Arabic root أ-ل-ل (hamza-lām-lām), occurring 2 times in the Quran, denotes an oath, covenant, and sacred bond. The noun ill designates a solemn pact or sworn treaty, closely related to dhimma (protected obligation) and jar (sacred kinship tie). The Quranic references (e.g., 9:8-10) invoke the bonds of covenant (ʿahd) that structure relations between believers and others, demanding fidelity even when the terms are difficult. Classical lexicographers align it with al-yamīn (oath) and al-jar (kinship-alliance), marking the root as central to the Quranic ethic of fidelity.

meaning.en: The root hamza-shīn-rāʾ (أ-ش-ر) denotes exultation, arrogance in prosperity, and boastful joy. It conveys ashar — the conceited delight of one who forgets the Source of blessings.
meaning.ar: الْأَشَرُ: الْبَطَرُ وَالتَّجَبُّرُ. وَأَشِرَ الرَّجُلُ: بَطِرَ وَتَجَبَّرَ.
meaning.en_detailed: Arabic root أ-ش-ر (hamza-shīn-rāʾ), occurring 2 times in the Quran, denotes exultant arrogance in prosperity and boastful delight. The active participle asharu describes those inflated by abundance (17:34), 'Do not walk upon the earth exultantly (maraḥan),' and the related sense of rejoicing with cruel abandon. Classical etymology links it to al-baṭar (insolent joy), the euphoria that arises when one forgets the source of blessings. The Quranic usage consistently condemns it as a moral disease contrasting with ṣabr (patient restraint) and shukr (gratitude).

meaning.en_short: Driving away, defending, and the fly
meaning.en: The root dhāl-bāʾ-bāʾ (ذ-ب-ب) denotes driving away, defending, and the fly. It conveys dhabba — to repel and protect — and dhubāb — the pest that is driven away.
meaning.ar: ابن فارس — مقاييس اللغة — مادة ذبب
meaning.en_detailed: Arabic root ذ-ب-ب (dhāl-bāʾ-bāʾ), occurring 2 times in the Quran, denotes driving away, repelling, and the fly. The verbal form dhabba conveys repelling intruders and protecting a place, while dhubāb (the fly) appears in 22:73 as a parable of false deities — even flies would defeat them. The root thus unites two senses: protective agency (defending one's own) and contemptible insignificance (that which is easily driven off). The Quranic imagery reduces idols to the level of creatures one can repel, highlighting the absurdity of attaching devotion to powerless objects.

meaning.en: The root shīn-yāʾ-dāl (ش-ي-د) denotes raising high, plastering, and fortifying. It conveys mashīd (4:78) — lofty towers plastered with lime — conspicuous elevation.
meaning.ar: الشِّينُ وَالْيَاءُ وَالدَّالُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى رَفْعِ الشَّيْءِ وَعُلُوِّهِ. وَمِنْهُ الشَّيْدُ: الْجِصُّ، سُمِّيَ بِذَلِكَ لِأَنَّهُ يُرْفَعُ بِهِ الْبِنَاءُ.
meaning.en_detailed: Arabic root ش-ي-د (shīn-yāʾ-dāl), occurring 2 times in the Quran, denotes raising high, plastering, and fortifying construction. The verbal form shayyada and the noun mashīd (fortified height, plastered structure) appear in 4:78, 'even if you are in fortified towers (buroojin mushayyada),' — meaning no refuge averts divine decree. The root is related to al-jīṣ (plaster/lime) used in elevating buildings. Classical dictionaries link it to the concept of height (ʿuluww) and strengthening. The Quranic usage foregrounds the futility of human fortifications against the omniscient will.

meaning.en_short: Grilling, roasting, and the body's extremi
meaning.en: The root shīn-wāw-yāʾ (ش-و-ي) denotes grilling, roasting, and the body's extremities. It conveys shawā — the roasted surface of meat — and the hands and feet as peripheral parts.
meaning.ar: (ش و ي) الشِّينُ وَالْوَاوُ وَالْيَاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى حَرٍّ يُصِيبُ الشَّيْءَ فَيَشْوِيهِ. وَالشِّوَاءُ: اللَّحْمُ الْمَشْوِيُّ.
meaning.en_detailed: Arabic root ش-و-ي (shīn-wāw-yāʾ), occurring 2 times in the Quran, denotes roasting, grilling, and the body's peripheral extremities. The noun shawā refers to the roasted surface layer, while in eschatological contexts the root denotes the body's outer extremities (hands, feet, skin) subjected to scorching fire. Classical etymology connects it to heat (ḥar) affecting something until it is grilled. The Quran uses this image to portray Hell's punishment reaching the body's most exposed and vulnerable surfaces — a visceral warning against heedlessness.

meaning.en: The root shīn-kāf-lām (ش-ك-ل) denotes form, shape, and the hobble. It conveys shakl — the outward configuration — and shikāl — the restraint that limits movement.
meaning.ar: الشِّينُ وَالْكَافُ وَاللَّامُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْمُشَابَهَةِ وَالْمُمَاثَلَةِ. يُقَالُ: هَذَا شَكْلُ هَذَا أَيْ مِثْلُهُ. وَالشَّاكِلَةُ: الطَّرِيقَةُ وَالنَّاحِيَةُ.
meaning.en_detailed: Arabic root ش-ك-ل (shīn-kāf-lām), occurring 2 times in the Quran, denotes form, shape, resemblance, and the hobble (that which restricts). The noun shakl signifies outward configuration or likeness, while shākila denotes a person's manner or path. Classical lexicographers (Ibn Fāris) identify the core meaning as 'resemblance and likeness' (mushābaha). The Quranic usage situates the root in contexts where external form is distinguished from inner reality, and where constraint (shikāl) restricts mobility — themes that recur in descriptions of the bound or the deceptive outward appearance of this world.

meaning.en: The root shīn-khāʾ-ṣād (ش-خ-ص) denotes a person, individual, and rising. It conveys shakhṣ — the distinct human form — and shakhūṣ — the act of departing or standing.
meaning.ar: الشِّينُ وَالْخَاءُ وَالصَّادُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الِارْتِفَاعِ وَالظُّهُورِ. يُقَالُ: شَخَصَ الشَّيْءُ يَشْخَصُ شُخُوصًا إِذَا ارْتَفَعَ.
meaning.en_detailed: Arabic root ش-خ-ص (shīn-khāʾ-ṣād), occurring 2 times in the Quran, denotes a person, individual, and the act of rising or departing. The noun shakhṣ and the verbal shakhūṣ (rising, departing) appear in eschatological contexts where eyes become fixed in terror (e.g., 21:97, abṣāru alladhīna kafarū shākhiṣa). Classical etymology traces it to elevation (irtifāʿ) and appearance (ẓuhūr), both of physical rising and the visibility of the human form. The root's two Quranic senses — the fearful fixation of the gaze and the upright standing of persons before Judgment — together paint the paralysis of accountability.

meaning.en: The root jīm-lām-lām (ج-ل-ل) denotes greatness, majesty, and grandeur. It conveys jalāl — Dhū al-Jalāli wa al-Ikrām (55:27) — Possessor of Majesty and Honor.
meaning.ar: الجَلَالُ: العَظَمَةُ وَالكِبْرِيَاءُ. وَالجَلِيلُ: العَظِيمُ. وَقَدْ جَلَّ يَجِلُّ جَلَالًا وَجَلَالَةً.
meaning.en_detailed: Arabic root ج-ل-ل (jīm-lām-lām), occurring 2 times in the Quran, denotes greatness, majesty, and overwhelming grandeur. Its loftiest expression is in 55:27, 'And the Face of your Lord, Possessor of Majesty and Honor (Dhū al-Jalāli wa al-Ikrām),' the divine attribute paired with magnanimous generosity. Classical lexicographers connect jalāl to al-ʿaẓama wa al-kibriyāʾ (majesty and supreme greatness). The root expresses that which surpasses all measure — the incommensurable dignity of the Divine — and is never attributed to created beings without qualification.
