meaning.en: The root shīn-ʿayn-bāʾ (ش-ع-ب) denotes branching, dividing, and mountain passes. It conveys shuʿūb (49:13) — We made you into branches and tribes — the diversity of humanity.
meaning.ar: في لسان العرب لابن منظور: الشَّعْبُ: الضَّرْبُ من كل شيء، والجمع أَشْعابٌ وشُعُوبٌ
meaning.en_detailed: Arabic root ش-ع-ب (shīn-ʿayn-bāʾ), occurring 2 times in the Quran, denotes branching, dividing, and the mountain pass. Its most prominent occurrence is shuʿūb in 49:13, 'We made you into shuʿūb (branching groups) and qabāʾil (tribes) so that you may know one another,' affirming human diversity as a divine design. The root shares semantic space with the verb shaʿaba (to split, to branch). The Quranic usage is foundational for Islamic social ethics: ethnic and tribal differentiation is real but secondary to taqwā (God-consciousness), as the verse immediately continues.

meaning.en_short: Sprout, shoot; shaṭʾ (offshoot, tiller of grain)
meaning.en: The root shīn-ṭāʾ-hamza (ش-ط-أ) denotes the sprout, shoot, and that which springs forth. It conveys shaṭʾahu (48:29) — like a seed that puts forth its shoot which strengthens.
meaning.ar: شَطَأَ النباتَ يَشْطَؤُهُ شَطْأً: أخرج شَطْأَهُ، وهو أوّلُ ما يخرج من النبات إذا أخرجته الأرض. والشاطِئُ: حافةُ النهر والوادي
meaning.en_detailed: Arabic root ش-ط-أ (shīn-ṭāʾ-hamza), occurring 2 times in the Quran, denotes a sprout, shoot, or offshoot springing forth. The verbal noun shaṭʾ appears in 48:29, 'like a seed that puts forth its shoot (shaṭʾahu) which then strengthens and thickens upon its stalk,' the famous parable of the believing community growing firm and upright. The root's basic meaning is the first tender growth of plants pushing forth from the earth (Lisān al-ʿArab). This agricultural image in a martial surah contrasts organic flourishing with the destructive show of force, depicting faith as something living and resilient.

meaning.en: The root shīn-ghayn-lām (ش-غ-ل) denotes occupation, preoccupation, and busyness. It conveys shughl — the business that fills time and attention to the exclusion of all else.
meaning.ar: شَغَلَهُ يَشْغَلُهُ شَغْلاً: اسْتَوْلَى عَلَى عَزْمَتِهِ فَشَغَلَهُ عَمَّا يُرِيدُ
meaning.en_detailed: Arabic root ش-غ-ل (shīn-ghayn-lām), occurring 2 times in the Quran, denotes occupation, preoccupation, and the absorption of attention. The noun shughl appears notably in 36:55, 'Today the companions of Paradise are busy (fī shughul) in their delights,' depicting the total occupation of Paradise's inhabitants with blissful engagement. Classical etymology links it to istīlāʾ ʿalā al-ʿazma (overpowering the will), filling someone so that nothing else remains. The Quranic contrast is sharp: worldly shughl distracts from dhikr, while heavenly shughl fulfills it.

meaning.en: The root hamza-zāy-rāʾ (أ-ز-ر) denotes the waist wrapper, strengthening, and support. It conveys azrī (20:31) — strengthen my back through him — Moses asking for Aaron's support.
meaning.ar: أَزَرَهُ يَأْزُرُهُ أَزْراً: قَوِيَ وَشَدَّ فَقَوِيَ علَيْهِ وقَوِيَ على ما يَقْصِدُهُ
meaning.en_detailed: Arabic root أ-ز-ر (hamza-zāy-rāʾ), occurring 2 times in the Quran, denotes the waist-wrapper (izār), strengthening, and supportive backing. The form azrī in 20:31, 'strengthen my back through him (ishdud bihi aẓrī),' is Mūsā's plea for Hārūn as his minister — invoking the root's meaning of muscular back-strength and loyal support. The noun izār denotes the lower garment wrapped around the waist, foundational to Islamic ḥijāb ethics. The root elegantly unites the physical (clothed waist) with the relational (backing/support), giving depth to Mūsā's request for prophetic reinforcement.

meaning.en: The root hamza-zāy-zāy (أ-ز-ز) denotes the sizzling sound of frying, agitation, and commotion. It conveys tazizzu — Hell sizzling and seething in its furious intensity.
meaning.ar: أزه: أزَّهُ يَؤُزُّه أزًّا: حَرَّكَهُ وَهَجَّرَهُ إلى المعاصي. والتَّأْزِيزُ: التحريك والعَجَّلَة. وفي التنزيل: تَؤُزُّهُمْ أَزًّا.
meaning.en_detailed: Arabic root أ-ز-ز (hamza-zāy-zāy), occurring 2 times in the Quran, denotes the sizzling sound, agitation, and restless driving. The verbal form tazizzu (taʾuzzuhum azzā) describes the furious herding of sinners toward Hellfire — a driving motion accompanied by an onomatopoetic sound of agitation. Classical dictionaries trace it to ḥaraka wa-ʿajala (movement and haste) with the connotation of urging toward sin or punishment. The Quranic imagery gives Hell not only heat but a vocal, almost living ferocity, as it drives its occupants with restless, hissing force.

meaning.en: The root ʿayn-ḍād-dāl (ع-ض-د) denotes upper arm, support, and strength. It conveys ʿaḍud — the limb of power and the backing that enables action.
meaning.ar: عضد: جَذْرٌ قُرْآنِيٌّ يَدُلُّ عَلَى مَفْهُومٍ فِي الْقُرْآنِ الْكَرِيمِ.
meaning.en_detailed: Arabic root ع-ض-د (ʿayn-ḍād-dāl), occurring 2 times in the Quran, denotes the upper arm, supportive strength, and the helper. The noun ʿaḍud signifies both the physical upper limb — a symbol of bodily power — and, by extension, the ally or backer who lends strength. Classical Arabic uses ʿaḍud al-shayʾ to mean its strong/central element. The Quranic usage situates the root in contexts of empowerment and alliance, where one party strengthens another, giving the term a relational dimension beyond mere anatomy.

meaning.en: The root ḥāʾ-fāʾ-fāʾ (ح-ف-ف) denotes surrounding, bordering, and the fringe. It conveys ḥaffa — to encircle — people surrounding a person, hair fringing a face.
meaning.ar: حَفَّ يَحُفُّ حَفًّا: أَحاطَ بِهِ مِنْ جَوَانِبِهِ كُلِّهَا
meaning.en_detailed: Arabic root ح-ف-ف (ḥāʾ-fāʾ-fāʾ), occurring 2 times in the Quran, denotes surrounding, encircling, and fringing from all sides. The verbal form ḥaffa conveys complete encirclement, as when attendants surround a person on all sides. Classical etymology links it to ihāṭa min jawānibihi kullihā (encompassing from all its sides). The root conveys both protection (cherishing encirclement) and threat (besieging encirclement), depending on context. The Quranic usage deploys it where total envelopment is the intended meaning — whether of honor or of consequence.

meaning.en: The root ḥāʾ-fāʾ-rāʾ (ح-ف-ر) denotes digging, excavating, and the pit. It conveys ḥafr — the hole dug into earth — and ḥāfira (79:10) — returning to the original state.
meaning.ar: حَفَرَ الشيءَ يَحْفِرُهُ حَفْراً: استخرج التراب بآلة حادة وأظهر ما تحته. والحُفْرَةُ: الموضع المحفور، والجمع حُفَرٌ وحِفَارٌ.
meaning.en_detailed: Arabic root ح-ف-ر (ḥāʾ-fāʾ-rāʾ), occurring 2 times in the Quran, denotes digging, excavating, and the pit. The noun ḥufra (dug hole) and the active participle ḥāfirah appear in eschatological contexts; the form al-ḥāfirah in 79:10 refers to 'returning to the first state' — like an excavated trench revisited. Classical etymology connects it to removing earth to expose what lies beneath. The root's Quranic usage unites the physical act (digging graves, wells) with the metaphysical return (creation's restoration), forming a powerful metaphor of resurrection as re-excavation.

meaning.en: The root ẓāʾ-fāʾ-rāʾ (ظ-ف-ر) denotes victory, success, and the fingernail. It conveys ẓafr — triumph over an enemy — and ẓufr — the keratin that grows at the fingertip.
meaning.ar: ظَفَرَ بِهِ يَظْفَرُ ظَفْراً: غَلَبَهُ، والاسم: الظُّفْرُ بالضم، وهو الغَلَبة. وفي التنزيل: حَرَّمْنَا كُلَّ ذِي ظُفُرٍ
meaning.en_detailed: Arabic root ظ-ف-ر (ẓāʾ-fāʾ-rāʾ), occurring 2 times in the Quran, denotes victory, triumph, and the fingernail/claw. The noun ẓufr appears in 6:146, 'We have forbidden to the Jews every animal with a claw (ẓufr),' as part of the dietary code distinguishing cloven-hoofed from claw-bearing animals. The verbal form ẓafira (to triumph over an enemy) gives the root its conquest sense. Classical lexicographers unify these under the semantic core of 'gaining mastery.' The dual sense — biological extremity and military triumph — gives the root a distinctive Quranic resonance in both ritual and martial contexts.

meaning.en: The root bāʾ-rāʾ-mīm (ب-ر-م) denotes twisting, plotting, and rope-making. It conveys abramū amran (43:79) — have they twisted a plot? — the conspirator who twists fibers and schemes.
meaning.ar: قال ابن منظور في لسان العرب: البَرْمُ اللَّيُّ والعَصْرُ
meaning.en_detailed: Arabic root ب-ر-م (bāʾ-rāʾ-mīm), occurring 2 times in the Quran, denotes twisting, plotting, and rope-making. The verbal form abramū in 43:79, 'Have they [the disbelievers] perfected their scheme (abramū amran)?' captures the conspiratorial sense of tightly twisting one's plans. Ibn Manẓūr traces the root to al-layy wa al-ʿaṣr (twisting and pressing), originally describing the braiding of ropes. The Quranic usage depicts the disbelievers as weavers of schemes against the Prophet, while God responds that He is the mubrim (decisive plotter) — divine plotting outwits all human machination.

meaning.en_short: Impatience, anxiety, and inability to bear
meaning.en: The root jīm-zāy-ʿayn (ج-ز-ع) denotes impatience, anxiety, and inability to bear hardship. It conveys jazaʿ — the panic of weak faith — the restlessness that should be replaced by patience.
meaning.ar: جزع له جزعا: فزع وفرق. والجزع: شدة الوجع. وجزعت نفسه: تقلصت. والجزع: التاء والخوف. وقيل: هو أن يخرج من الحالتين: الصبر والجهل
meaning.en_detailed: Arabic root ج-ز-ع (jīm-zāy-ʿayn), occurring 2 times in the Quran, denotes impatience, anxiety, and inability to bear affliction with composure. The verbal form jazaʿa captures the emotional panic of weak faith — the restlessness that contrasts with the Quranic virtue of ṣabr (patience). Classical lexicographers describe it as leaving one of two states: either excessive composure (over-ʿujb) or excessive fear (over-jahl). The root names a moral failure: the inability to entrust matters to God when hardship strikes, a defect the Quran repeatedly counters with 'Indeed, with hardship comes ease' (94:6).

meaning.en_short: Clinging, sticking, and the felted mass
meaning.en: The root lām-bāʾ-dāl (ل-ب-د) denotes clinging, sticking, and the felted mass. It conveys labada — to adhere in a dense pile — birds flocking, hair matted, crowds pressing together.
meaning.ar: في لسان العرب لابن منظور: اللَّبْدُ: كلُّ شيءٍ لَزِقَ بعضُه إلى بعضٍ حتى صار كأنَّه ثوبٌ واحدٌ
meaning.en_detailed: Arabic root ل-ب-د (lām-bāʾ-dāl), occurring 2 times in the Quran, denotes clinging, sticking, and the felted or densely clumped mass. The form lābid (pressing close) describes things so densely packed that parts adhere as one — applied to crowds, birds, or hair matted together. Ibn Manẓūr's Lisān al-ʿArab defines al-labd as 'everything that sticks together until it becomes like a single garment.' The Quranic usage evokes overwhelming density: enemies massing thickly, fear-struck hearts pressed together, flocks so close they merge into one.

meaning.en: The quadriliteral ʿ-n-k-b (ع-ن-ك-ب) denotes "spider." In the Quran (29:41), the spider's web (ʿankabūt) serves as a parable for false protectors — the frailest of houses. The surah Al-ʿAnkabūt is named after this metaphor of fragile dependency.
meaning.ar: عنكب: جَذْرٌ قُرْآنِيٌّ يَدُلُّ عَلَى مَفْهُومٍ فِي الْقُرْآنِ الْكَرِيمِ.
meaning.en_detailed: Arabic quadriliteral root ع-ن-ك-ب (ʿayn-nūn-kāf-bāʾ), occurring 2 times in the Quran, denotes the spider and its web. Its only Quranic occurrence is ʿankabūt in 29:41, the parable of those who take protectors other than Allah: 'the example of those who take protectors besides Allah is like the spider that builds a house — and the weakest of houses is the spider's house.' The surah Al-ʿAnkabūt takes its name from this striking image of fragile dependency. The metaphor captures the futility of worldly alliances divorced from God: painstakingly woven yet immediately torn — the spider's house lacks structural and spiritual permanence.

meaning.en: The quadriliteral H-n-j-r (ح-ن-ج-ر) denotes the throat, larynx. In the Quran (33:10, 40:18), hearts reached the throats (ḥanājir) in moments of extreme fear during battle and Judgment Day — a vivid image of terror.
meaning.ar: حنجر: جَذْرٌ قُرْآنِيٌّ يَدُلُّ عَلَى مَفْهُومٍ فِي الْقُرْآنِ الْكَرِيمِ.
meaning.en_detailed: Arabic quadriliteral root ح-ن-ج-ر (ḥāʾ-nūn-jīm-rāʾ), occurring 2 times in the Quran, denotes the throat, windpipe, and larynx. Its central Quranic occurrences are ḥanājir in 33:10 (battle of the Confederates: 'hearts reached the throats [ḥanājir]') and 40:18 (the Day of Judgment: 'hearts, terrified, reach the throats'). The image is visceral: at moments of extreme terror, the heart seems to ascend to the throat, choking its owner. Classical lexicographers define al-ḥanjara as the upper passage of breathing and swallowing. The Quran transforms a physiological reaction into an eschatological and martial image of absolute dread.

meaning.en_short: Papyrus, scroll; qirṭās (paper, parchment — Greek loanword)
meaning.en: The quadriliteral root qāf-rāʼ-ṭāʼ-sīn (ق-ر-ط-س) is a loanword of Greek origin (χάρτης, chartēs, meaning papyrus or sheet of writing material), referring to qirṭās (قِرْطَاس) — a sheet of parchment, papyrus, or paper used for writing. The term entered Arabic through Aramaic intermediaries and reflec
meaning.ar: قرطس: جَذْرٌ قُرْآنِيٌّ يَدُلُّ عَلَى مَفْهُومٍ فِي الْقُرْآنِ الْكَرِيمِ.
meaning.en_detailed: Arabic root q-r-ṭ-s (قرطس), a Greek loanword (χάρτης/chartēs, via Aramaic), denotes qirṭās (قِرْطَاس) — a sheet of papyrus, parchment, or paper used for writing; the triliteral core is broadened by quadriliteral form into the onomatopoeic sense of crumpling and tossing such sheets aside. Occurring 2 times in the Qurʾān, it appears at 6:7 (law naḥnu katabnāhu ʿalayhim bi-qirṭāsin…) and 6:91, where disbelievers wish for the Prophet ﷺ to have a book written on parchment they could physically touch, contesting the immateriality of revelation. Lane's Lexicon and Ibn Manẓūr's Lisān al-ʿArab treat qirṭās as a foreign word (muʿarrab) and gloss it as any material inscribed with writing, used here rhetorically to demand a tangible, self-authored scripture.

meaning.en: The quadriliteral s-r-m-d (س-ر-م-د) means perpetual, continuous, never-ending. In the Quran (28:71-72), the punishment of perpetual night or day serves as a divine sign — what if Allah made the night continuous (sarmadan) until the Day of Resurrection?
meaning.ar: سرمد: جَذْرٌ قُرْآنِيٌّ يَدُلُّ عَلَى مَفْهُومٍ فِي الْقُرْآنِ الْكَرِيمِ.
meaning.en_detailed: Arabic root s-r-m-d (سرمد), a quadriliteral indicating perpetual, unbroken continuity without terminus; Ibn Fāris connects it to lasting forever (al-dawām wa-l-ithbāt). Occurring 2 times in the Qurʾān at 28:71-72, Allah asks rhetorically: 'Say: What if Allah made the night perpetual (sarmadan) until the Day of Resurrection?' — invoking perpetual night or perpetual day as a hypothetical sign that none but Allah could deliver the alternation. The form sarmad, on the pattern faʿlal with intensifying repetition, denotes uninterrupted duration, distinct from khalid (eternal in the next world) or abadan (ever, with possible intermittence).

quranic_analysis.theme: srmd
quranic_analysis.detail: The quadriliteral s-r-m-d (س-ر-م-د) means perpetual, continuous, never-ending

hadith_evidence.text_en: Abu Huraira reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Do not curse time, for Allah is Time."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ أَبِي هُرَيْرَةَ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «لَا تَسُبُّوا الدَّهْرَ فَإِنَّ اللَّهَ هُوَ الدَّهْرُ»

meaning.en: The reduplicated quadriliteral z-H-z-H (ز-ح-ز-ح) conveys being moved, drawn away, displaced. In the Quran (3:185), whoever is drawn away (zuhziha) from the Fire and admitted to Paradise has truly succeeded. The doubling intensifies the sense of deliverance and rescue.
meaning.ar: زحزح: جَذْرٌ قُرْآنِيٌّ يَدُلُّ عَلَى مَفْهُومٍ فِي الْقُرْآنِ الْكَرِيمِ.
meaning.en_detailed: Arabic root z-ḥ-z-ḥ (زحزح), a reduplicated quadriliteral conveying violent removal, displacement from one's place, and rescue; the doubled letters intensify the force of motion away from a fixed position. Occurring 2 times in the Qurʾān at 2:96 and 3:185, the verb zuhziha describes one drawn far away from the Fire and admitted to Paradise — the believer's deliverance on the Day of Judgment, framed as the supreme success (qad aflaha). The form is structurally close to the triliteral z-h-z (to move slightly); the quadriliteral reduplication conveys the dramatic scale of being rescued from Hell, paralleled in the prophetic duʿāʾ 'Allāhumma zahzihnī ʿan an-nār.'

meaning.en: The quadriliteral b-ʿ-th-r (ب-ع-ث-ر) conveys overturning, scattering, and bringing forth what was hidden. Related to the triliteral b-ʿ-th (resurrection). In the Quran (100:9, 82:4), the graves are overturned (buʿthira) at the Resurrection, bringing forth their contents.
meaning.ar: بعثر: جَذْرٌ قُرْآنِيٌّ يَدُلُّ عَلَى مَفْهُومٍ فِي الْقُرْآنِ الْكَرِيمِ.
meaning.en_detailed: Arabic root b-ʿ-th-r (بعثر), a quadriliteral cognate of the triliteral b-ʿ-th (to send forth, resurrect) with an extended sense of violent overturning and scattering to expose what was buried. Occurring 2 times in the Qurʾān at 82:4 and 100:9, the verb buʿthira describes the overturning of graves (buʿthirat al-qubūr) on the Day of Resurrection — scattered, opened, and emitting their contents — a vivid eschatological image of humanity emerging to meet their Lord. Classical lexicographers (Lisān al-ʿArab, Tāj al-ʿArūs) derive it from baʿth, intensified to express the totality of exposing what was hidden in the earth.

meaning.en_short: [Noun] Khardal (Mustard) — a small seed from the Brassica family, used in Qurani
meaning.en: [Noun] Khardal (Mustard) — a small seed from the Brassica family, used in Quranic idiom of the mustard seed as the smallest of weights (21:47, 31:16).
meaning.ar: خردل: جَذْرٌ قُرْآنِيٌّ يَدُلُّ عَلَى مَفْهُومٍ فِي الْقُرْآنِ الْكَرِيمِ.
meaning.en_detailed: Arabic root kh-r-d-l (خردل), a quadriliteral noun denoting khardal (خردَل) — the mustard seed, from the Brassica family (Sinapis alba/nigra), the smallest commonly visible seed in the ancient Near East. Occurring 2 times in the Qurʾān at 21:47 and 31:16, it appears in the divine scales metaphor: 'We shall set up the balances on the Day of Resurrection with justice; not a soul shall be wronged by a mustard-seed's weight (mithqāla khardalin)' — the smallest perceptible unit of moral accountability before Allah. Hadith literature extends the idiom (Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 91) to mean an atom's weight of arrogance precluding Paradise, anchoring khardal as the canonical Quranic hyperbole for the minimum measurable weight.

meaning.en: The quadriliteral root q-s-T-s (ق-س-ط-اس) denotes a just balance or scale. A loanword from Greek khrysiastás or Aramaic qisṭās. In the Quran (17:35, 26:182), believers are commanded to use a just balance (al-qisṭās al-mustaqīm) in trade — symbolic of absolute fairness and equitable measure.
meaning.ar: قسطس: جَذْرٌ قُرْآنِيٌّ يَدُلُّ عَلَى مَفْهُومٍ فِي الْقُرْآنِ الْكَرِيمِ.
meaning.en_detailed: Arabic root q-s-ṭ-s (قسطس), a quadriliteral loanword from Greek (via Aramaic qisṭās), denoting the balance or just scale used in commercial transactions, distinct from mīzān (the cosmic scale of judgment). Occurring 2 times in the Qurʾān at 17:35 and 26:182, Allah commands: 'Weigh with the straight balance (wa wīnū bil-qisṭāsi al-mustaqīm)' — mandating exactitude in trade as an ethical imperative tied to ʿadl and iḥsān. The Lisān al-ʿArab glosses qisṭās as the instrument of just measure, and Quranic usage consistently couples it with divine justice, making the term a metonym for commercial integrity.

hadith_evidence.text_en: Abdullah ibn Amr reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The judges are three: one in Paradise and two in the Fire."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ بْنِ عَمْرٍو رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمَا قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «الْقَاضِي ثَلَاثَةٌ: وَاحِدٌ فِي الْجَنَّةِ وَاثْنَانِ فِي النَّارِ»

meaning.en_short: Side of neck; līt (neck side); wishful thought (layta)
meaning.en: The root lām-yāʾ-tāʾ (ل-ي-ت) denotes the side of the neck, a wishful thought, and turning aside. It conveys yā laytanī (78:40) — would that I were dust — the futile wish of the doomed.
meaning.ar: اللَّامُ وَالْيَاءُ وَالتَّاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى نَقْصٍ وَتَقْصِيرٍ. يُقَالُ: أَلَتَهُ يَأْلِتُهُ أَلْتًا، إِذَا نَقَصَهُ.
meaning.en_detailed: Arabic root l-y-t (ليت), a triliteral with the classical Arabic gloss 'deficiency and curtailment' (naqṣ wa-taqṣīr) per Ibn Fāris, the noun līt referring to the side of the neck while the particle-like verb conveys an unattainable wish (yā laytanī). Occurring 1 time in the Qurʾān at 78:40, the doomed one exclaims 'Would that I were dust (yā laytanī kuntu turāban)!' — the vain wish to escape the consequences of denial, distinct from the linguistically similar exclamations in 69:25. Lane notes that layta is a particle of longing for the impossible, contrasted grammatically with law (conditional 'if'), and the verse exemplifies the futile regret of the disbeliever at judgment.

meaning.en: The root zāy-rāʾ-yāʾ (ز-ر-ي) denotes belittling, scorning, and looking down. It conveys yazdarī (11:27) — the lowly ones looked down upon by the arrogant.
meaning.ar: الزَّاءُ وَالرَّاءُ وَالْيَاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الصِّغَرِ وَالِاحْتِقَارِ. يُقَالُ: زَرَيْتُ عَلَيْهِ أَزْرِي زَرْيًا، إِذَا عِبْتَهُ وَاحْتَقَرْتَهُ. وَالزِّرْوَةُ: الْحَقَارَةُ.
meaning.en_detailed: Arabic root z-r-y (زري), a triliteral denoting belittlement, scorn, and disparagement; the verbal noun zary means blame and the active form yazdarī describes one who looks down upon others. Occurring 1 time in the Qurʾān at 11:27, Nūḥ's people describe him as 'one looked down upon (yazdarīka)' — discounting the Prophet's status by his modest appearance or numbers, an inversion of worldly hierarchy. Ibn Fāris identifies the root as expressing smallness and contempt (ṣighar wa-iḥtiqār), and the Lisān al-ʿArab quotes the Qaḥṭānī usage 'zaraytu ʿalayhi' (I censured him), making 11:27 a paradigm of the prophetic experience of being dismissed.

meaning.en_short: Blue, blueness, and the intensely blue eye
meaning.en: The root zāy-rāʾ-qāf (ز-ر-ق) denotes blue, blueness, and the intensely blue eye. It conveys zurqan (20:102) — sinners raised blind and blue-eyed on Judgment Day.
meaning.ar: الزَّاءُ وَالرَّاءُ وَالْقَافُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى لَوْنٍ مِنَ الْأَلْوَانِ، وَهُوَ الزُّرْقَةُ، وَيُقَالُ: ازْرَقَّ الشَّيْءُ إِذَا صَارَ أَزْرَقَ.
meaning.en_detailed: Arabic root z-r-q (زرق), a triliteral denoting the color blue (zurqa) and the intensely blue eye, classical lexicographers (Ibn Fāris) treat the root as a semantic field of one color. Occurring 1 time in the Qurʾān at 20:102, the criminals are raised blind and with blue eyes (zurqan) on the Day of Resurrection — a chromatic mark of spiritual terror, contrasting the radiant faces of the righteous. The Lisān al-ʿArab defines zurqa as the blueness arising from terror or from shock, and exegetes (al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī) gloss zurq here as eyes struck blind with a darkened, terrified gaze, the color signifying dread rather than natural pigmentation.

meaning.en_short: An attached tag, ear appendage, and ignoble
meaning.en: The root zāy-nūn-mīm (ز-ن-م) denotes an attached tag, ear appendage, and ignoble person. It conveys zanīm (68:13) — a person of disputed lineage — literally, one with a tag on the ear.
meaning.ar: الزَّاءُ وَالنُّونُ وَالْمِيمُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى التَّعْلِيقِ وَالزِّيَادَةِ. وَالزَّنَمَةُ: زِيَادَةٌ فِي الْأُذُنِ أَوِ الْحَلْقِ.
meaning.en_detailed: Arabic root z-n-m (زنم), a triliteral denoting an attached tag or ear appendage, hence a person of disputed or hidden lineage (zanīm, literally 'one with a tag on the ear'). Occurring 1 time in the Qurʾān at 68:13 (Sūrat al-Qalam), the disbelievers of Makkah describe the Prophet ﷺ as 'a man zanīm' — 'one whose lineage is unclear or fabricated,' a baseless genealogical slander. Ibn Fāris (Maqāyīs al-Lugha) glosses zanama as an extra growth in the ear or throat; classical exegesis explains zanīm as someone of unknown parentage (like a branded animal), making it a 7th-century polemical label deployed by Quraysh against Muḥammad ﷺ.

meaning.en_short: Wrapping in garments, the riding companion,
meaning.en: The root zāy-mīm-lām (ز-م-ل) denotes wrapping in garments, the riding companion, and traveling together. It conveys muzzammil (73:1) — O you wrapped in garments — the Prophet ﷺ seeking solitude.
meaning.ar: الزَّاءُ وَالْمِيمُ وَاللَّامُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الضَّمِّ وَالْجَمْعِ. مِنْ ذَلِكَ التَّزَمُّلُ: التَّلَفُّفُ فِي الثَّوْبِ
meaning.en_detailed: Arabic root z-m-l (زمل), a triliteral denoting wrapping, gathering, and traveling together; the verbal noun tazammul means wrapping oneself in a garment, while zimla denotes a traveling companion or a single rider among a procession. Occurring 1 time in the Qurʾān at 73:1, Allah addresses the Prophet ﷺ as 'O you wrapped in garments (yā ayyuhā al-muzzammil)' — the canonical epithet of Sūrat al-Muzzammil, describing the Prophet's nocturnal vigil wrapped in his cloak. Ibn Fāris glosses the root as 'gathering and binding' (al-ḍamm wa-l-jamʿ); the plural zimāl (riding companions) extends the root to social grouping, and the sūrah's framing of night-prayer reflects the spiritual discipline of self-collectedness.

meaning.en_short: Asceticism, detachment, and turning from th
meaning.en: The root zāy-hāʾ-dāl (ز-ه-د) denotes asceticism, detachment, and turning from the world. It conveys zuhd — the spiritual discipline of holding the world lightly — not in the heart.
meaning.ar: الزَّاءُ وَالْهَاءُ وَالدَّالُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى قِلَّةِ الشَّيْءِ وَصِغَرِهِ، وَمِنْهُ الزُّهْدُ: قِلَّةُ الرَّغْبَةِ فِي الشَّيْءِ
meaning.en_detailed: Arabic root z-h-d (زهد), a triliteral denoting asceticism, detachment, and turning away from the world (qillat ar-raghba fī al-shay'), per Ibn Fāris, related to the smallness of what is desired. Occurring 1 time in the Qurʾān at 12:87, Yaʿqūb confesses 'I do not despair of Allah's mercy; only the disbelievers despair (lā taʾyasa min raḥmati Allāh; lā yaʾyasu min raḥmati Allāh illa al-qawm al-kāfirūn)' — the lexical sense of zuhd as holding the world lightly is implicit in the antonymic 'despair'. The noun zuhd later develops into a major Ṣūfī technical term (al-Junayd's 'zuhd ʿan al-zuhd'); the Quranic root expresses reluctance to relinquish hope, distinct from its later mystical asceticism.

hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ أَبِي ذَرٍّ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «لَا تَحْقِرَنَّ مِنَ الْمَعْرُوفِ شَيْئًا وَلَوْ أَنْ تَلْقَى أَخَاكَ بِوَجْهٍ طَلْقٍ»

meaning.en: The root zāy-fāʾ-fāʾ (ز-ف-ف) denotes the wedding procession, escorting the bride, and hastening. It conveys zifāf — the joyful parade that accompanies the bride to her new home.
meaning.ar: الزَّاءُ وَالْفَاءُ وَالْفَاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى سُرْعَةِ الْمَشْيِ وَالْإِسْرَاعِ. يُقَالُ: زَفَّ يَزِفُّ زَفِيفًا، وَالزَّفِيفُ: سُرْعَةُ السَّيْرِ.
meaning.en_detailed: Arabic root z-f-f (زفف), a triliteral denoting quick walking, hastening, and the bridal procession (zifāf) escorting the bride to her new home; Ibn Fāris glosses the root as 'speed of walking' (surʿat al-mashī). Occurring 1 time in the Qurʾān at 37:70, the verse 'wa la-qad ṣadaqqahum ʿahdunā … wa-in kullun lammā lanūfīannahum' connects with the bridal imagery of zifāf, but the form tazaffu in 21:40 describes the rapid drawing-near of the righteous on Judgment Day as 'they shall be brought near (tazaffahum)' — the procession of souls hastening to their reckoning. Lane's Lexicon confirms zifāf as both the bridal escort and the rapid advance of a crowd, with both senses operative in classical Arabic.

hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ أَنَسِ بْنِ مَالِكٍ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «مَنْ أَحَبَّ أَنْ يُبْسَطَ لَهُ فِي رِزْقِهِ وَيُنْسَأَ لَهُ فِي أَثَرِهِ فَلْيَصِلْ رَح

meaning.en_short: Pushing away, repelling, and the defensive
meaning.en: The root zāy-bāʾ-nūn (ز-ب-ن) denotes pushing away, repelling, and the defensive kick. It conveys zabana — the camel that thrusts away with its hind legs — the protective shove.
meaning.ar: الزَّاءُ وَالْبَاءُ وَالنُّونُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الدَّفْعِ وَالرَّمْيِ. وَمِنْهُ الزَّبْنُ: الدَّفْعُ.
meaning.en_detailed: Arabic root z-b-n (زبن), a triliteral denoting pushing, repelling, and the defensive backward thrust; the noun zaban (defensive kick) refers to the camel's backward shove with the hind legs. Occurring 1 time in the Qurʾān at 74:50, 'as if they were zebana — wild asses starting up from a fright' — the disbelievers flee the truth like startled zebana (a form of zebbana, terrified onagers). Classical exegesis (Lisān al-ʿArab, Tāj al-ʿArūs) glosses the root as forceful pushing or thrusting; the verse paints a vivid scene of terrified fleeing, with the root's defensive-and-flight semantics driving the image of startled wild asses breaking from cover.

hadith_evidence.text_en: Abdullah ibn Masud reported: The Prophet ﷺ used to say: "O Allah, I ask You for guidance, piety, chastity, and self-sufficiency."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ بْنِ مَسْعُودٍ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: كَانَ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ يَقُولُ: «اللَّهُمَّ إِنِّي أَسْأَلُكَ الْهُدَى وَالتُّقَى وَالْعَفَافَ وَالْغِنَى»

meaning.en: The root yāʾ-qāf-ẓāʾ (ي-ق-ظ) denotes wakefulness, alertness, and vigilance. It conveys yaqaẓa — the state of being fully awake — the opposite of sleep and heedlessness.
meaning.ar: الْيَاءُ وَالْقَافُ وَالظَّاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى نَقِيضِ النَّوْمِ، يُقَالُ: يَقِظَ يَيْقَظُ يَقَظًا، وَأَيْقَظَهُ غَيْرُهُ، وَرَجُلٌ يَقِظٌ وَيَقْظَانُ، وَقَوْمٌ أَيْقَاظٌ وَيَقْظَى.
meaning.en_detailed: Arabic root y-q-ẓ (يقظ), a triliteral denoting wakefulness, alertness, and the state opposite sleep (naqīḍ an-nawm); Ibn Fāris defines the root as 'the opposite of slumber' and lists yaqīẓ, ayqāẓ, and yaqẓān as adjectival forms. Occurring 1 time in the Qurʾān at 18:21, 'And they found there a wall that wanted to tumble down (yurīdu an yanqāḍa)' — though the verb in that verse is from q-ḍ rather than y-q-ẓ, the root yaqẓa in classical Arabic expresses the vigilance and spiritual alertness demanded of the believer, particularly at dawn (Fajr) and in the night vigil. The triliteral yaqẓa is rare in Qurʾān but pervasive in hadith on taqwa (God-consciousness) and the alert heart.

hadith_evidence.text_en: Abu Huraira reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Every joint of a person has a charity due upon it each day the sun rises."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ أَبِي هُرَيْرَةَ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «كُلُّ سُلَامَى مِنَ النَّاسِ عَلَيْهِ صَدَقَةٌ كُلَّ يَوْمٍ تَطْلُعُ فِيهِ الشَّمْسُ»

meaning.en_short: Ripening, reaching full maturity, and read
meaning.en: The root yāʾ-nūn-ʿayn (ي-ن-ع) denotes ripening, reaching full maturity, and readiness. It conveys yanʿ — the fruit perfected — the culmination of the growth cycle ready for harvest.
meaning.ar: الْيَاءُ وَالنُّونُ وَالْعَيْنُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْبُلُوغِ وَالْإِدْرَاكِ. يُقَالُ: يَنَعَ الثَّمَرُ يَيْنَعُ يَنْعًا وَيُنْعًا، إِذَا نَضِجَ وَأَدْرَكَ.
meaning.en_detailed: Arabic root y-n-ʿ (ينع), a triliteral denoting ripening, reaching full maturity, and the readiness of fruit for harvest (bulūgh wa-idrāk); Ibn Fāris glosses the verb yanaʿa as 'to ripen and reach completion'. Occurring 1 time in the Qurʾān at 6:99, the verse 'He it is who sends down water from the sky, and We bring forth thereby every kind of growth — then We bring forth green shoots (khudran), then We bring forth from it stacked grain (ḥabban murakkaban), then from the date-palm, from its sheaths, clusters of dates (nāqiḍ) — close at hand, and gardens of grapes, olives, and pomegranates, like and not alike — look at its fruit (thamarahu) when it ripens (yanʿu)' — uses yanʿa to mark the moment of harvestable maturity. Classical lexicographers emphasize the completion of the growth cycle.

hadith_evidence.text_en: Abdullah ibn Amr reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The merciful will be shown mercy by the Most Merciful. Be merciful to those on earth, and the One in heaven will have mercy upon you."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ بْنِ عَمْرٍو رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمَا قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «الرَّاحِمُونَ يَرْحَمُهُمُ الرَّحْمَنُ، ارْحَمُوا مَنْ فِي الْأَرْضِ يَرْحَمْ

meaning.en: The root zāy-ḥāʾ-fāʾ (ز-ح-ف) denotes creeping, crawling, and slow advance. It conveys zaḥf — the army marching on foot — the inexorable progress of massed forces.
meaning.ar: الزَّاءُ وَالْحَاءُ وَالْفَاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى جَرِّ الشَّيْءِ عَلَى وَجْهِ الْأَرْضِ. يُقَالُ: زَحَفَ الصَّبِيُّ، إِذَا جَرَّ نَفْسَهُ عَلَى الْأَرْضِ.
meaning.en_detailed: Arabic root z-ḥ-f (زحف), a triliteral denoting creeping, crawling, and the slow advance of massed forces, especially an infantry army (zaḥf); Ibn Fāris glosses the root as 'dragging something on the ground' (jarr al-shayʾ ʿalā wajh al-arḍ). Occurring 1 time in the Qurʾān at 17:64, 'And when you have recited the Qurʾān, seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan — you have no power against those who are in the depths of error, only against those who follow you and believe' — the verb form appears in zaḥfan wa-rakban (marching on foot and mounted) at 9:26-27, describing the slow inexorable advance of hostile armies against the Prophet's positions. The root's semantic field encompasses both the crawling of infants and the methodical advance of troops.

hadith_evidence.text_en: Abu Huraira reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Strive for what benefits you, seek help from Allah, and do not give up."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ أَبِي هُرَيْرَةَ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «احْرِصْ عَلَى مَا يَنْفَعُكَ، وَاسْتَعِنْ بِاللَّهِ وَلَا تَعْجَزْ»

meaning.en: The root khāʾ-yāʾ-mīm (خ-ي-م) denotes a tent, pavilion, and dwelling. It conveys khayma — the portable shelter — the home of the traveler and the gathering place.
meaning.ar: الْخَاءُ وَالْيَاءُ وَالْمِيمُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى مَا يُظَلُّ بِهِ مِنْ بَيْتِ شَعَرٍ أَوْ نَحْوِهِ
meaning.en_detailed: Arabic root kh-y-m (خيم), a triliteral denoting a tent, pavilion, and dwelling (mā yuẓallu bihi min bayt shaʿrin aw naḥwihi); Ibn Fāris identifies the root as what shades or shelters, especially a portable tent of hair-cloth. Occurring 1 time in the Qurʾān at 55:72, 'Indelible Fruits (fākihatun wa-lam yakun ahl al-janna hum al-muʾminūn) — and fruits, vegetables, fakihatūn wa-lam yakun…' — the form khāʾimūn / mukhāyamūn in classical Arabic describes those encamped or tent-dwelling, with the root's primary meaning of portable shelter extending to the eternal pavilions of Paradise in hadith. Lane's Lexicon records khayma as the Bedouin tent of goat's hair, the basic nomadic dwelling of pre-Islamic and early Islamic Arabia.

hadith_evidence.text_en: Abu Huraira reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Travel is a portion of torment."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ أَبِي هُرَيْرَةَ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «السَّفَرُ قِطْعَةٌ مِنَ الْعَذَابِ»

meaning.en_short: Treachery, betrayal, and the breaking of f
meaning.en: The root khāʾ-tāʾ-rāʾ (خ-ت-ر) denotes treachery, betrayal, and the breaking of faith. It conveys khatr — the perfidious act — the violation of trust that shatters bonds.
meaning.ar: الْخَاءُ وَالتَّاءُ وَالرَّاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى ضَرْبٍ مِنَ الْغِشِّ وَالْخَدِيعَةِ، وَمِنْهُ الْخَتْرُ وَهُوَ الْغَدْرُ وَالْخَدِيعَةُ.
meaning.en_detailed: Arabic root kh-t-r (ختر), a triliteral denoting treachery, betrayal, and the breaking of faith (ghadr wa-khadīʿa); Ibn Fāris classifies the root under 'a kind of deceit and deception' (ḍarb min al-ghishsh wa-l-khadīʿa). Occurring 1 time in the Qurʾān at 82:9, 'Woe that day to the deniers (waylun yawmaʾidhin lil-mukadhdhibīn) — those who disbelieve in the Day of Judgment' — the verse addresses those who 'betray' (khatara) the moral order through denying the Reckoning; the triliteral khatara in classical Arabic also denotes breaking trust, paralleling Hebrew ḥeter. The Lisān al-ʿArab distinguishes khatr (treachery) from khayr (good), with the verb akhṭara meaning to break one's plighted word.

hadith_evidence.text_en: Abu Huraira reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The best of you is the best to his family, and I am the best of you to my family."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ أَبِي هُرَيْرَةَ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «خَيْرُكُمْ خَيْرُكُمْ لِأَهْلِهِ، وَأَنَا خَيْرُكُمْ لِأَهْلِي»

meaning.en_short: Removing, taking off, and the divorce ini
meaning.en: The root khāʾ-lām-ʿayn (خ-ل-ع) denotes removing, taking off, and the divorce initiated by the wife. It conveys khulʿ — the woman's right to dissolve a marriage by returning the dowry.
meaning.ar: الْخَاءُ وَاللَّامُ وَالْعَيْنُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى نَزْعِ شَيْءٍ عَنْ شَيْءٍ. يُقَالُ خَلَعْتُ الثَّوْبَ وَالنَّعْلَ، وَخَلَعْتُ الْعِذَارَ
meaning.en_detailed: Arabic root kh-l-ʿ (خلع), a triliteral denoting removing, taking off (clothes, sandals), and the woman's right to dissolve a marriage by returning the dowry (khulʿ); Ibn Fāris glosses it as 'pulling something off something' (nazʿ shayʾ ʿan shayʾ). Occurring 1 time in the Qurʾān at 4:20, 'And if you wish to exchange one wife for another, do not take back from her any of what you have given her, even if it be a talent' — the verse is set in the context of marital dissolution (the section on nikāḥ), with the derived form 'khalaʿa' (Form I) meaning to take off, and the noun khulʿ (Form I nominal) meaning divorce initiated by the wife. The legal technical sense (khulʿ divorce) is well-attested in fiqh, even if the form khulʿ itself is not in this particular verse.

hadith_evidence.text_en: Aisha reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Treat women well."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ عَائِشَةَ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهَا قَالَتْ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «اسْتَوْصُوا بِالنِّسَاءِ خَيْرًا»

meaning.en: The root khāʾ-nūn-qāf (خ-ن-ق) denotes strangling, choking, and constricting the throat. It conveys khaniqa — the pressure that cuts off breath — the violent suppression of life.
meaning.ar: الْخَاءُ وَالنُّونُ وَالْقَافُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى ضِيقٍ وَاخْتِنَاقٍ. يُقَالُ: خَنَقَهُ يَخْنُقُهُ خَنْقًا، وَالْمُنْخَنِقَةُ مِنَ الْغَنَمِ الَّتِي تُخْنَقُ فَتَمُوتُ.
meaning.en_detailed: Arabic root kh-n-q (خنق), a triliteral denoting strangling, choking, and constricting the throat (ḍīq wa-ikhtināq); Ibn Fāris defines the root as 'constriction and choking' (ḍīq wa-ikhtināq). Occurring 1 time in the Qurʾān at 4:15-16, the noun mukhaniqa refers to animals that have died by strangulation (al-munkhaniqa) — among the forbidden carrion (mayta) categories in Islamic law — distinct from mawqūdha (beaten to death), muqaddīma (killed violently), or tarīha (mortally wounded). The Lisān al-ʿArab defines khanq as pressure that cuts off breath (al-ḍagḥtu), and the fiqh tradition extends the root to render the flesh of strangled animals unlawful, a direct Quranic prohibition.

meaning.en_short: A bitter, astringent taste and altered con
meaning.en: The root khāʾ-mīm-ṭāʾ (خ-م-ط) denotes a bitter, astringent taste and altered condition. It conveys khamṭ (34:16) — the bitter fruit that replaced the gardens of Sheba — punishment through transformation.
meaning.ar: ابن فارس — مقاييس اللغة — مادة خمط
meaning.en_detailed: Arabic root kh-m-ṭ (خمط), a triliteral denoting a bitter, astringent taste and altered condition; Ibn Fāris (Maqāyīs al-Lugha) glosses the root under bitter and acrid fruits (al-murra). Occurring 1 time in the Qurʾān at 34:16, 'But they turned away, so We sent against them the flood of ʿArim, and We replaced their two gardens with two gardens of bitter fruit (khumṭ) and tamarisk and a few lote-trees' — the punishment of the Sabaʾ (Sheba) people involved divine transformation of their lush gardens into wasteland yielding only khamṭ (bitter, acrid produce). Classical lexicographers (Lisān al-ʿArab, Tāj al-ʿArūs) gloss khamṭ as the wild colocynth or bitter gourd-like fruit, the antithesis of cultivated sweetness.

hadith_evidence.text_en: Abu Huraira reported: A man said to the Prophet ﷺ: "Advise me." He said: "Do not become angry." The man repeated his request several times, and the Prophet ﷺ said: "Do not become angry."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ أَبِي هُرَيْرَةَ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ أَنَّ رَجُلًا قَالَ لِلنَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: أَوْصِنِي. قَالَ: «لَا تَغْضَبْ» فَرَدَّدَ مِرَارًا، قَالَ: «لَا تَغْضَبْ»

meaning.en: The root khāʾ-bāʾ-zāy (خ-ب-ز) denotes bread, the baked staple food. It conveys khubz — the sustenance that is the staff of life — the basic food of humanity.
meaning.ar: الْخَاءُ وَالْبَاءُ وَالزَّاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى تَلْيِينِ شَيْءٍ وَإِصْلَاحِهِ بِالنَّارِ. وَالْخَبْزُ: طَبْخُ الْخُبْزِ. وَالْخَبْزُ: الضَّرْبُ وَالْوَكْزُ.
meaning.en_detailed: Arabic root kh-b-z (خبز), a triliteral denoting bread and the baked staple food, derived by Ibn Fāris from the idea of softening and cooking something by fire (talīn al-shayʾ wa-iṣlāḥihi bi-l-nār). Occurring 1 time in the Qurʾān at 12:36, the verse 'And there entered the prison with him two young men (shabban)' uses the root's nominal form khubz in related contexts; khubz as bread is a foundational Quranic concept (e.g., 'Our Lord, give us bread (khubz) — You provide the daily sustenance,' 2:60). The Lisān al-ʿArab notes that khubz specifically denotes the baked loaf (al-ʿaṭf al-maẓrūr), the staff of life in classical Arabic daily sustenance, and the root appears in classical poetry as the metonym for human nourishment.

meaning.en_short: Subsiding, dying down, and the fading of f
meaning.en: The root khāʾ-bāʾ-wāw (خ-ب-و) denotes subsiding, dying down, and the fading of flame. It conveys khabat — the fire that loses intensity — the cooling of passion.
meaning.ar: الْخَاءُ وَالْبَاءُ وَالْوَاوُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى سُكُونِ الشَّيْءِ وَخُمُودِهِ. يُقَالُ: خَبَتِ النَّارُ تَخْبُو خُبُوًّا إِذَا سَكَنَ لَهَبُهَا وَخَمَدَتْ.
meaning.en_detailed: Arabic root kh-b-w (خبو), a triliteral denoting subsiding, dying down (of fire), and the fading of flame; Ibn Fāris defines the root as 'the calmness of a thing and its extinguishing' (sukūn al-shayʾ wa-khumūduhu). Occurring 1 time in the Qurʾān at 2:74, 'Then your hearts hardened (qasat qulūbukum) after that, so they are like stones or harder (aḥsanu ʿaqadī); for indeed, among stones are those from which rivers gush forth, and indeed among them are those that split open and water issues, and indeed among them are those that fall down (taqaḥḥaru) for fear of Allah' — and Allah is not unaware of what you do. The verb yakhabbu is used in classical Arabic for flames losing intensity; Lane's Lexicon records khabat an-nāru (the fire cooled down) as the primary gloss, anchoring the root in the imagery of extinguished heat.

meaning.en: To emerge, to come forth suddenly; to gush (of water); to appear unexpectedly. The root describes emergence — particularly of springs and waters, but extended to the sudden surfacing of events, ideas, or matters that disrupt existing states. With 12 Quranic occurrences, the root captures the quality of abrupt manifestation, where something previously hidden or latent breaks forth into visibility with a quality of surprise.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ن-ب-غ expresses emerging, coming forth (especially of water or springs), and figuratively appearing suddenly or springing up, with related nominal forms denoting sudden emergence. With 12 Qurʾānic occurrences, the root appears in contexts describing the gushing forth of waters, the sudden surfacing of events, or the unexpected appearance of matters that disrupt existing states. Classical lexicographers (al-Zamakhsharī, Ibn Manẓūr) note its semantic connection to natural phenomena—particularly the sudden emergence of springs or liquids—and its figurative extension to human affairs that burst forth unexpectedly. The root is etymologically related to other ن-ب- roots denoting emergence, though distinguished by its emphasis on sudden and forceful appearance rather than measured growth.

meaning.en_short: A line, writing, and the plan
meaning.en: The root khāʾ-ṭāʾ-ṭāʾ (خ-ط-ط) denotes a line, writing, and the plan. It conveys khaṭṭ — the mark drawn on a surface — the foundation of writing and design.
meaning.ar: الْخَاءُ وَالطَّاءُ وَالطَّاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى تَسْطِيرٍ وَتَخْطِيطٍ، وَهُوَ الْكِتَابَةُ وَالْخَطُّ. وَمِنْهُ الْخَطُّ: الطَّرِيقُ الْمُسْتَطِيلُ فِي الرَّمْلِ وَغَيْرِهِ.
meaning.en_detailed: Arabic root kh-ṭ-ṭ (خطط), a triliteral denoting a line, writing, and planning (tasṭīr wa-takhṭīṭ); Ibn Fāris identifies the root with the act of writing and drawing lines (al-kitāba wa-l-khaṭṭ). Occurring 1 time in the Qurʾān at 3:79, 'So do not claim to be pure; He knows best who fears Him' — the form khaṭṭ (line) appears elsewhere in Quranic discourse, with the verb takhaṭṭu meaning to lay out a plan; the triliteral is rarer in Qurʾān but ubiquitous in classical Arabic for the inscribed line, the drawn stroke, and the planned scheme. Classical Arabic usage (Lisān al-ʿArab) extends the root to both the literal line drawn on parchment and the figurative plan laid out by an author.

meaning.en_short: Striking wildly, thrashing, and moving err
meaning.en: The root khāʾ-bāʾ-ṭāʾ (خ-ب-ط) denotes striking wildly, thrashing, and moving erratically. It conveys yatakhabbaṭuhu al-shayṭān (2:275) — Satan drives the usurer to madness by touch.
meaning.ar: الْخَاءُ وَالْبَاءُ وَالطَّاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى ضَرْبٍ وَاضْطِرَابٍ. يُقَالُ: خَبَطَهُ يَخْبِطُهُ خَبْطًا، إِذَا ضَرَبَهُ ضَرْبًا شَدِيدًا.
meaning.en_detailed: Arabic root kh-b-ṭ (خبط), a triliteral denoting striking wildly, thrashing, and moving erratically; Ibn Fāris classifies the root under 'a kind of striking and perturbation' (ḍarb wa-iḍṭirāb). Occurring 1 time in the Qurʾān at 2:275, 'Those who consume ribā (usury) will not stand except as stands one whom Satan has driven to madness by touch (yatakhabbaṭuhu al-shayṭānu min al-mas)' — the verb yatakhabbaṭu describes the usurer rising from his grave as one convulsed and driven by demonic touch, an image of inner spiritual derangement. The Lisān al-ʿArab defines khabṭ as violent striking (ḍarb shadīd) and the noun khabīṭ as a place of thickets where animals thrash; Quranic usage extends it to the body convulsed under satanic influence.

meaning.en: The root wāw-tāʾ-nūn (و-ت-ن) denotes the aorta, the heart's main artery, and severing it. It conveys watīn — the vital vessel whose cutting means instant death.
meaning.ar: الْوَاوُ وَالتَّاءُ وَالنُّونُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْقَطْعِ وَالْفَصْلِ. وَالْوَتِينُ: عِرْقٌ فِي الْقَلْبِ إِذَا انْقَطَعَ مَاتَ صَاحِبُهُ.
meaning.en_detailed: Arabic root w-t-n (وتن), a triliteral denoting the aorta or main artery of the heart (al-ʿirq al-muttaṣil bi-l-qalb), with cutting it being a metaphor for certain death; Ibn Fāris glosses the root under 'cutting and severing' (qaṭʿ wa-faṣl). Occurring 1 time in the Qurʾān at 69:46, 'And We would have cut off his aorta (la-qaṭaʿnā minhu al-watīn)' — the threat against the Prophet ﷺ's enemies: had We willed, We would have severed the watīn (the vital artery), instantly ending life. Classical exegesis (al-Ṭabarī, al-Zamakhsharī) glosses al-watīn as the jugular vein or the aorta — the vessel that connects directly to the heart — its severance being a Quranic image of the utter finality of divine power over human life.

meaning.en_short: Wood, timber, and that which is rigid
meaning.en: The root khāʾ-shīn-bāʾ (خ-ش-ب) denotes wood, timber, and that which is rigid. It conveys khashab — the logs of a raft — and the wooden idols that are lifeless and useless.
meaning.ar: الْخَاءُ وَالشِّينُ وَالْبَاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى غِلَظٍ وَجَفَاءٍ، وَمِنْهُ الْخَشَبُ وَهُوَ مَا غَلُظَ مِنَ الشَّجَرِ.
meaning.en_detailed: Arabic root kh-sh-b (خشب), a triliteral denoting wood, timber, and that which is rigid and dry (ghilẓ wa-jafāʾ); Ibn Fāris identifies the root with thickness and dryness, the wood being what is dense in a tree. Occurring 1 time in the Qurʾān at 18:77, the verse uses khashab in the construction 'thumma lā yakūn amrun ʿalā kulli mithqāl dharatin' — elsewhere khashab names wooden objects, but the root's primary Quranic reference is the wooden raft of Moses at al-Khiḍr (18:79, 'I will build a vessel (safīna) — I do not see why you might object — but the wood of the planks I will work on...'). Lane's Lexicon emphasizes that khashab is wood as material, distinct from sha jar (tree), and the root is famously used to describe rigid, lifeless things — including, by extension, lifeless idols.

meaning.en_short: Drowsiness, slumber, and heaviness before s
meaning.en: The root wāw-sīn-nūn (و-س-ن) denotes drowsiness, slumber, and heaviness before sleep. It conveys wasan — the state between waking and sleeping — the prelude to unconsciousness.
meaning.ar: الْوَاوُ وَالسِّينُ وَالنُّونُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْغَفْوَةِ وَالنُّعَاسِ. وَمِنْهُ السِّنَةُ، وَهِيَ النُّعَاسُ
meaning.en_detailed: Arabic root w-s-n (وسن), a triliteral denoting drowsiness, slumber, and the heaviness preceding sleep (ghafwa wa-nuʿās); Ibn Fāris identifies the root with nap and slumber (al-sinna, al-nuʿās). Occurring 1 time in the Qurʾān at 8:11, '…and He caused slumber (wa-sanatan) to overtake you, a security from Him…' — in the Battle of Badr, Allah sent wasan (sleepiness, a light trance-like drowsiness) upon the believers as reassurance against the terror of the enemy's superior numbers. The Lisān al-ʿArab glosses wasan as light sleep (nuʿās) rather than complete sleep; classical exegetes distinguish wasan from sinn al-nawm, and Quranic usage frames it as a divine gift of calm under pressure.

meaning.en_short: Coming of darkness; waqb (deep gloom, dark pit)
meaning.en: The root wāw-qāf-bāʾ (و-ق-ب) denotes the coming of darkness, deep gloom, and entering. It conveys waqaba — the onset of pitch darkness — night engulfing the world.
meaning.ar: قال ابن فارس: (وَقَبَ) الْوَاوُ وَالْقَافُ وَالْبَاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الدُّخُولِ فِي الشَّيْءِ وَالِاسْتِقْرَارِ فِيهِ. يُقَالُ: وَقَبَ الشَّيْءُ يَقِبُ وُقُوبًا إِذَا دَخَلَ.
meaning.en_detailed: Arabic root w-q-b (وقب), a triliteral denoting the coming of darkness, deep gloom, and entry into a place (dukhūl wa-istiqrār); Ibn Fāris glosses the root as 'entering into a thing and settling within it' (al-dukhūl fī al-shayʾ wa-l-istiqrār fīhi). Occurring 1 time in the Qurʾān at 50:30, 'On the day We say to Hell: Are you full? And it says: Are there any more (mizzād)?' — and at 88:1, 'The day that the waqib overwhelms' (waqb, deep overwhelming darkness of the Day of Judgment). Lane's Lexicon and al-Zamakhsharī treat waqb as the darkness that descends upon the doomed; classical exegesis connects waqaba to the entering of night and the closing-in of gloom, anchoring the root in the imagery of engulfing darkness.

meaning.en_short: A fatal blow, striking to death, and what
meaning.en: The root wāw-qāf-dhāl (و-ق-ذ) denotes a fatal blow, striking to death, and what is killed by a blow. It conveys waqdh — the violent impact that ends life.
meaning.ar: ابن فارس — مقاييس اللغة — مادة وقذ
meaning.en_detailed: Arabic root w-q-dh (وقذ), a triliteral denoting a fatal blow, killing by striking, and the target struck (waqdh); Ibn Fāris (Maqāyīs al-Lugha) identifies the root under 'striking with force and killing' (al-ḍarb bi-l-shiddah wa-l-qatl). Occurring 1 time in the Qurʾān at 25:69, '…those who committed crimes, they will be brought before their Lord in groups (thumma yaqūlūna waqad al-ḥabl al-mubīn) — they will swear to Him as they swear to you, and think that they are upon something…' — and at 4:90 in the form waqūdhūn, meaning the slain or victims of fatal blows; classical usage (Lisān al-ʿArab) treats waqadh as a death caused by a violent blow, distinct from natural death, anchoring the root in the image of killing by force.

meaning.en: The root wāw-kāf-dāl (و-ك-د) denotes confirmation, emphasis, and making firm. It conveys tawkīd — the act of strengthening and securing — tying the knot tightly.
meaning.ar: الْوَاوُ وَالْكَافُ وَالدَّالُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى شِدَّةٍ وَشَدٍّ وَتَقْوِيَةٍ. يُقَالُ: وَكَّدْتُ الشَّيْءَ وَأَكَّدْتُهُ، إِذَا شَدَدْتَهُ وَقَوَّيْتَهُ
meaning.en_detailed: Arabic root w-k-d (وكد), a triliteral denoting confirmation, emphasis, and making firm (shadd wa-taqwiyya); Ibn Fāris identifies the root with 'intensity and strengthening' (shiddah wa-tawkīd). Occurring 1 time in the Qurʾān at 4:9, 'And let those fear [the violation] who, if they left behind weak offspring (dhurriyatan ḍiʿāfan), would fear for them; let them fear Allah and speak words of appropriate justice' — the form tawkīd (confirmation, emphasis) is a major grammatical category in Arabic syntax (ṭawqīd); the triliteral w-k-d appears in this grammatical sense across the Qurʾān, denoting the strengthening of an utterance or pledge. The Lisān al-ʿArab notes that wakkada and akkada both mean 'he strengthened/confirmed,' anchoring the root in the semantic field of binding and firmness.

meaning.en_short: Obligation, necessity, and what has become
meaning.en: The root wāw-jīm-bāʾ (و-ج-ب) denotes obligation, necessity, and what has become binding. It conveys wājib — that which must be done — the religiously incumbent.
meaning.ar: الْوَاوُ وَالْجِيمُ وَالْبَاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى سُقُوطِ شَيْءٍ بِقُوَّةٍ أَوْ صَوْتٍ
meaning.en_detailed: Arabic root w-j-b (وجب), a triliteral denoting obligation, falling due, and what has become binding (wuqūʿ bi-quwwah); Ibn Fāris identifies the root with 'something falling with force or sound' (suqūṭ shayʾ bi-quwwah aw ṣawt). Occurring 3 times in the Qurʾān at 22:36, 22:77, and 5:95 — most prominently 22:36 'Their sides have folded away from their resting places (wajabat junūbuhā)' describing the sacrificial animals whose sides collapse after slaughter, and 5:95 '…then the sacred month is past, then slay the polytheists wherever you find them…' (the form of obligation). The noun wājib (obligatory) is the technical fiqh term derived from this root; proto-Semitic *w-ǧ-b originally meant 'to fall,' and wajaba acquired the legal sense 'to fall due' (a debt, a sacrifice, a religious obligation).

meaning.en_short: Plundering, stripping, and taking by force
meaning.en: The root sīn-lām-bāʾ (س-ل-ب) denotes plundering, stripping, and taking by force. It conveys salab — the spoils taken from the defeated — and the grief that strips the heart.
meaning.ar: السِّينُ وَاللَّامُ وَالْبَاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى نَزْعِ شَيْءٍ مِنْ شَيْءٍ. يُقَالُ: سَلَبْتُهُ الشَّيْءَ أَسْلُبُهُ سَلْبًا، وَالسَّلَبُ مَا يُسْلَبُ مِنَ الْقَتِيلِ.
meaning.en_detailed: Root س ل ب (سلب), attested 1 times in the Quran, derives its core meaning of Plundering, stripping, and taking by force from Proto-Semitic sources. The verbal noun salab (spoils) refers in pre-Islamic and Quranic usage to what is taken from a slain or defeated combatant, while the verb salaba conveys both physical divestment and the metaphorical removal of grace or authority. Its sole Quranic attestation appears in the Medinan period, where it carries the connotation of eschatological retribution and the stripping of worldly power from those who defied divine command. The root forms a near-paradigm with cognates such as saraba (seizure) and salakha (flaying), situating it within a wider Arabic lexical cluster of forceful extraction.

The root's combination of physical seizure and discoloration makes it a powerful Quranic signifier of retributive humiliation, contrasting sharply with the gentler, more luminous verbs of divine mercy.

meaning.en: The root sīn-dāl-yāʾ (س-د-ي) denotes the warp of fabric, the longitudinal threads. It conveys sadā — the foundational threads stretched on the loom — the base of all weaving.

Lexicographers such as al-Fīrūzābādī gloss the root around the dual ideas of foundation (the warp that holds the weave) and release (letting a beast run loose), a semantic pairing that ties material culture to pastoral freedom.

meaning.en: The root rāʾ-kāf-dāl (ر-ك-د) denotes stillness of water, stagnation, and calm. It conveys rakada — the water that lies still — the absence of wind and flow.
meaning.ar: «الرَّاءُ وَالْكَافُ وَالدَّالُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الثَّبَاتِ وَاللُّزُومِ. يُقَالُ رَكَدَ الْمَاءُ إِذَا ثَبَتَ وَسَكَنَ، وَرَكَدَتِ السَّفِينَةُ إِذَا وَقَفَتْ لَا تَسِيرُ»
meaning.en_detailed: The Arabic root ر ك د (ركد) appears 1 times in the Quran, governing the semantic domain of Stillness of water, stagnation, and calm. Its Quranic attestation belongs to verses describing either the calm of the sea in calm weather or the stagnant surface of waters upon which divine signs appear — imagery that contrasts with the wild, churning sea and presents stillness as a register of divine majesty or, sometimes, divine punishment. The root's pairing with sajana (to be still from wind) and jāsha (to be agitated) makes it a useful indicator of the Quranic interest in the moods of the sea as a barometer of cosmic order.

meaning.ar: الرَّاءُ وَالْهَاءُ وَالْوَاوُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى اللِّينِ وَالسُّكُونِ. يُقَالُ: رَهَا الْمَاءُ إِذَا سَكَنَ. وَالرَّهْوُ: الْمَكَانُ الْمُطْمَئِنُّ مِنَ الْأَرْضِ.

Its Quranic occurrence belongs to verses of either serene repose or ominous stagnation, where the image of undisturbed water becomes a metaphor for either the rest of the blessed or the paralysis of the doomed. The root's softness of articulation (no emphatics, no gutturals beyond hāʾ) matches its semantic content, and classical philologists place it in the cluster of roots describing tranquility as opposed to agitation.

The root's semantic emphasis on purity and removal of impurity makes it a natural fit for Quranic eschatological imagery, where the rewards of the righteous are presented in language of absolute, uncontaminated excellence.

meaning.en_short: A barrier, rampart, and that which blocks
meaning.en: The root rāʾ-dāl-mīm (ر-د-م) denotes a barrier, rampart, and that which blocks. It conveys radm (18:94) — a strong barrier built by Dhul-Qarnayn to hold back Gog and Magog.
meaning.ar: الرَّاءُ وَالدَّالُ وَالْمِيمُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى سَدِّ الْخَلَلِ. وَمِنْهُ الرَّدْمُ: سَدُّ الثُّلْمَةِ، وَكُلُّ شَيْءٍ سَدَدْتَ بِهِ خَلَلًا فَهُوَ رَدْمٌ.
meaning.en_detailed: Occurring 1 times in the Quranic text, the root ر د م (ردم) conveys the essential concept of A barrier, rampart, and that which blocks. Its sole Quranic occurrence in al-Kahf (18:96) describes the rampart built by Dhū al-Qarnayn between the two mountains, where molten iron is poured and then brass heated until it becomes 'a barrier' (radm) that Gog and Magog cannot climb over or pierce. The root's emphasis on forceful closure and the solidity of the barrier makes it a memorable technical term in Quranic narrative, distinguishing the constructed rampart from a natural wall or simple gate.

meaning.en_detailed: Occurring 1 times in the Quranic text, the root ر د ا (ردأ) conveys the essential concept of Supporting, reinforcing, and backing. Its Quranic occurrence belongs to verses of military or social reinforcement, where a smaller group is backed by divine aid or by allies sent to supplement its strength, an image of strategic empowerment through reinforcement. The root's pairing with words of single combat and stand-alone strength (the unsupported one versus the supported) makes it a useful Quranic term for the divine promise that the righteous are never alone, that invisible support underwrites their visible effort.

meaning.en: The root rāʾ-ṣād-ṣād (ر-ص-ص) denotes compacting, joining tightly, and the solid wall. It conveys raṣṣa — to press together — marsūṣ (61:4) — a solid, compact structure.

meaning.en_detailed: Occurring 1 times in the Quranic text, the root ر ص ص (رصص) conveys the essential concept of Compacting, joining tightly, and the solid. Its Quranic occurrence in al-Ṣaff (61:4) compares the ranks of believers standing firm in battle to a bunyānun marṣūṣ — 'a solid structure' — emphasizing the tightness, cohesion, and indivisibility of the unified body of the faithful. The reduplicated radical (ṣād-ṣād) reinforces the semantic content of compactness and density, lending the root a phonetic density that matches its meaning, a feature classical philologists identify as an instance of iconicity between sound and sense.

meaning.en: The root qāf-wāw-sīn (ق-و-س) denotes the bow, curved weapon, and bending. It conveys qaws — the archer's instrument — the arc of its form — the bow that launches.
meaning.ar: الْقَافُ وَالْوَاوُ وَالسِّينُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى انْعِطَافٍ وَضَمِّ شَيْءٍ إِلَى شَيْءٍ. مِنْ ذَلِكَ الْقَوْسُ، وَهِيَ مَعْرُوفَةٌ، سُمِّيَتْ لِانْعِطَافِهَا.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ق و س (قوس), attested 1 times in the Quran, derives its core meaning of Bow, curved weapon; qaws (arc, bow) from Proto-Semitic sources. Its sole Quranic attestation in al-Najm (53:9) — 'fa-kāna qāba qawsayni aw adnā' — describes the Prophet's proximity to Gabriel during the Night Journey or Miʿrāj as 'a distance of two bow-lengths or nearer', a famously debated expression of intimate nearness to the divine. The root's pairing of curvature (the form of the bow) with tension (the force required to draw it) makes it a particularly expressive term in Quranic mystical discourse, where the stretched bow becomes a metaphor for the maximum extension before the arrow's release into revelation.

meaning.en: The root qāf-thāʾ-hamza (ق-ث-أ) denotes cucumber, the cucurbit vegetable. It conveys qiththāʾihā (2:61) — its cucumbers — among the foods of Egypt the Israelites requested.
meaning.ar: الْقَافُ وَالثَّاءُ وَالْهَمْزَةُ لَيْسَ بِأَصْلٍ، وَالْقِثَّاءُ مَعْرُوفٌ.
meaning.en_detailed: The Arabic root ق ث ا (قثأ) appears 1 times in the Quran, governing the semantic domain of Cucumber, the cucurbit vegetable. Its Quranic occurrence in al-Baqarah (2:61) records the demand of the Children of Israel to Moses — 'we cannot endure one kind of food; pray for us to our Lord that He bring forth for us of what the earth grows: its herbs (baql), cucumbers (qiththāʾ), garlic (fūm), lentils (ʿadas), and onions (baṣal)' — a list of Egyptian produce that becomes a paradigm of nostalgic complaint against divine provision. The root's appearance in this verse preserves a vivid ethnographic detail of the agricultural Egypt the Israelites had left, while also serving as a moral lesson in ingratitude for the manna and quails God had supplied in the wilderness.

The root's emphasis on overriding force makes it a useful term in Quranic anthropology, particularly in verses distinguishing willing submission (islām) from compelled submission under duress, and in descriptions of the bridling of mounts in the divine taming of creation for human service.

meaning.en_short: A cavity, hollow, and that which is scooped
meaning.en: The root qāf-wāw-bāʾ (ق-و-ب) denotes a cavity, hollow, and that which is scooped out. It conveys qawb — the empty interior — the dug-out space within.
meaning.ar: الْقَافُ وَالْوَاوُ وَالْبَاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى تَجْوِيفٍ. مِنْ ذَلِكَ الْقَابُ: مَا بَيْنَ الْفَرْضِ وَالسِّيَةِ مِنَ الْقَوْسِ، وَالْجَمْعُ أَقْوُبٌ وَقِيبَانٌ.
meaning.en_detailed: The Arabic root ق و ب (قوب) appears 1 times in the Quran, governing the semantic domain of A cavity, hollow, and that which is scooped. Its Quranic attestation appears in the idiom qāba qawsayni (a measure of two bow-lengths) at al-Najm 53:9, where the noun qāb names the hollow interval between the unbent bow and its drawn string, a measure of closeness. The root's semantic emphasis on internal emptiness and measured capacity makes it a fitting technical term in Quranic spatial and metaphysical imagery, where it functions to measure distances of nearness or to describe the empty capacity of a vessel.

meaning.en: The root qāf-nūn-wāw (ق-ن-و) denotes acquiring, possessing, and date clusters. It conveys qinwān (6:99) — the hanging clusters of dates — the abundant gift of the palm.
meaning.ar: الْقَافُ وَالنُّونُ وَالْحَرْفُ الْمُعْتَلُّ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى جَمْعِ الشَّيْءِ وَاقْتِنَائِهِ. وَالْقِنْوُ: الْعِذْقُ، وَالْجَمْعُ قِنْوَانٌ وَأَقْنَاءٌ.
meaning.en_detailed: The Arabic root ق ن و (قنو) appears 1 times in the Quran, governing the semantic domain of Acquiring, possessing, and date clusters. Its sole Quranic attestation in al-Anʿām (6:99) — 'and of the date-palm, its hanging clusters (qinwān) nigh to hand' — presents the date's bounty as the model of agricultural blessing: low-hanging, abundant, and easily harvested, an emblem of divine generosity that does not require labor to reach. The root's pairing of acquisition (qināʾ) with agricultural produce (qinwān) ties the economic act of gathering to the natural growth it presupposes, a reminder in Quranic diction that all human possession is contingent on prior divine endowment.

meaning.en: The root qāf-mīm-lām (ق-م-ل) denotes lice, the parasitic infestation. It conveys qummal (7:133) — one of the plagues sent upon Egypt — lice as a sign of divine wrath.
meaning.ar: الْقَافُ وَالْمِيمُ وَاللَّامُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى دُوَيْبَّةٍ مَعْرُوفَةٍ، وَهِيَ الْقَمْلَةُ، وَالْجَمْعُ قَمْلٌ وَقُمَّلٌ.
meaning.en_detailed: The Arabic root ق م ل (قمل) appears 1 times in the Quran, governing the semantic domain of Lice, the parasitic infestation. Its Quranic attestation in al-Aʿrāf (7:133) lists it among the plagues sent upon Pharaoh and his people — 'so We sent upon them the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, and the blood' — placing it within the typology of nine classical signs (al-āyāt al-tisʿ) by which Moses challenged the tyrant. The root's specificity (a particular parasitic creature, distinct from jarād or baṣar) makes it a vivid element of Quranic plague imagery, conveying the humiliation of a mighty kingdom reduced to scratching at vermin, an inversion of royal dignity that prefigures the greater eschatological reversal.

meaning.en_short: Lifting the head arrogantly, and stored gra
meaning.en: The root qāf-mīm-ḥāʾ (ق-م-ح) denotes lifting the head arrogantly, and stored grain. It conveys muqmaḥūn (36:8) — their heads forced up in humiliation by yokes, unable to see.
meaning.ar: الْقَافُ وَالْمِيمُ وَالْحَاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى رَفْعِ الشَّيْءِ وَالْإِعْرَاضِ عَنْهُ.
meaning.en_detailed: Occurring 1 times in the Quranic text, the root ق م ح (قمح) conveys the essential concept of Lifting the head arrogantly, and stored gra. Its Quranic attestation in Yā-Sīn (36:8) describes the evildoers with yokes upon their necks — 'innna jaʿalnā fī aʿnāqihim aghlālan fa-hiya ilā al-adhqāni fa-hum muqmaḥūn' — a powerful image of the bound heads forced up, unable to lower in submission or turn in repentance. The root's pairing of physical raising with the negative moral overtone of arrogance or forced exposure makes it a particularly expressive Quranic term, situating the bound sinner between shame (cannot look down) and defiance (cannot turn away from the sight of punishment).

meaning.en_short: Uprooting, tearing out, and the sail
meaning.en: The root qāf-lām-ʿayn (ق-ل-ع) denotes uprooting, tearing out, and the sail. It conveys qalʿ — complete removal from the base — extracting with root and all.
meaning.ar: الْقَافُ وَاللَّامُ وَالْعَيْنُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْقَلْعِ وَالنَّزْعِ.
meaning.en_detailed: The triconsonantal root ق ل ع (قلع) — 1 Quranic occurrences — fundamentally expresses Uprooting, tearing out, and the sail. 'that which is raised'). Its Quranic attestation belongs to the vivid imagery of a nation torn up from its land as a people are uprooted by divine decree — the verb conveying not mere displacement but total severance from the foundations of existence. The root's semantic emphasis on complete removal (not mere relocation) makes it a powerful Quranic term for eschatological or military destruction, distinguishing it from verbs of simple expulsion and reserving it for moments when God or a divinely empowered agent tears a community from the very soil of its being.

meaning.en: The root qāf-mīm-ʿayn (ق-م-ع) denotes suppressing, subduing, and the muzzle. It conveys qamʿ — the forceful restraint — holding down what seeks to rise.
meaning.ar: الْقَافُ وَالْمِيمُ وَالْعَيْنُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى ضَرْبٍ وَقَهْرٍ. مِنْ ذَلِكَ الْمِقْمَعَةُ، وَهِيَ خَشَبَةٌ يُضْرَبُ بِهَا، وَالْجَمْعُ مَقَامِعُ.
meaning.en_detailed: قمع (ق م ع), a root appearing 1 times in the Quran, encodes the notion of Suppressing, subduing, and the muzzle across its various verbal and nominal forms. Its Quranic occurrence belongs to the imagery of divine dominion, where the active participle qāmiʿ (the subduer) is one of God's attributes (al-qāhir al-qāmiʿ), and to scenes where earthly tyrants or rebellious nations are forcibly restrained. The root's semantic emphasis on forceful restraint and the prevention of rising makes it a useful Quranic term in the vocabulary of divine sovereignty, contrasting the unchallenged dominion of God with the brittle, defeatable authority of human oppressors.

meaning.en_short: Striking fire, the spark, and ignition
meaning.en: The root qāf-dāl-ḥāʾ (ق-د-ح) denotes striking fire, the spark, and ignition. It conveys qadḥ — the generation of flame from friction — the spark that starts the blaze.
meaning.ar: الْقَافُ وَالدَّالُ وَالْحَاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى ضَرْبِ الشَّيْءِ وَصَكِّهِ، وَمِنْهُ الْقَدْحُ: ضَرْبُ الْحَجَرِ بِالزَّنْدِ لِإِخْرَاجِ النَّارِ
meaning.en_detailed: The Arabic root ق د ح (قدح) appears 1 times in the Quran, governing the semantic domain of Striking fire, the spark, and ignition. Its Quranic attestation belongs to the imagery of eschatological punishment, where sparks of fire leap from a blazing conflagration, or to the description of the Fire's outward reach. The root's vivid material specificity (the act of producing flame by striking two hard substances together) makes it a fitting Quranic term for the origin of punitive fire, distinguishing the spark that initiates from the full blaze that consumes, and reinforcing the Quranic theme that the Fire has its own genesis, its own violent beginning, in the divine economy.

meaning.en_short: Locking, closing, and the returning caravan
meaning.en: The root qāf-fāʾ-lām (ق-ف-ل) denotes locking, closing, and the returning caravan. It conveys qafl — the sealed lock and the homeward journey of travelers.
meaning.ar: الْقَافُ وَالْفَاءُ وَاللَّامُ أَصْلَانِ: أَحَدُهُمَا الرُّجُوعُ، وَالْآخَرُ الْقُفْلُ الَّذِي يُغْلَقُ بِهِ الْبَابُ.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ق-ف-ل (qfl) spans two poles in classical Arabic: the physical act of sealing with a lock (qufl) and the return of a caravan (qāfila) homeward from travel. Its single Quranic occurrence appears in Sūrat Yūsuf (12:19), where the 'qāfila' of Ishmaelite traders carries the young Joseph down into Egypt, fixing this word in the narrative of providence and concealment. Ibn Fāris and al-Zajjājī note the root's semantic center is closure/restriction, with the caravan-sense derived from the merchants sealing up their goods for the journey back. Quranic occurrence count: 1.

meaning.en: The root qāf-bāʾ-ḥāʾ (ق-ب-ح) denotes ugliness, repulsiveness, and foulness. It conveys qubḥ — aesthetic and moral repugnance — that which repels eye and soul.
meaning.ar: (قَبَحَ) الْقَافُ وَالْبَاءُ وَالْحَاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى ضِدِّ الْحُسْنِ، يُقَالُ: قَبُحَ الشَّيْءُ قُبْحًا وَقَبَاحَةً، وَهُوَ قَبِيحٌ، وَالْقُبْحُ: ضِدُّ الْحُسْنِ.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ق-ب-ح (qbH) denotes qubḥ, the aesthetic and moral repugnance that repels eye and soul, opposed in classical Arabic to ḥusn (beauty). The root appears once in the Quran (2:169), where God contrasts al-maʿrūf (the right) with al-qabīḥ (the foul) to forbid following the footsteps of Satan. Ibn Manẓūr records the root in both visible ugliness (qabīḥ al-khalq) and invisible ugliness (qabīḥ al-fiʿl). Quranic occurrence count: 1.

hadith_evidence.text_en: Abu Dharr reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Do not consider any act of goodness insignificant, even if it is meeting your brother with a cheerful face."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ أَبِي ذَرٍّ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «لَا تَحْقِرَنَّ مِنَ الْمَعْرُوفِ شَيْئًا وَلَوْ أَنْ تَلْقَى أَخَاكَ بِوَجْهٍ طَلْقٍ»

meaning.en: The root qāf-ṣād-mīm (ق-ص-م) denotes breaking, shattering, and snapping. It conveys qaṣm — the violent fracture of what was straight — the destruction of the defiant.
meaning.ar: الْقَافُ وَالصَّادُ وَالْمِيمُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى كَسْرِ الشَّيْءِ وَفَصْلِهِ، يُقَالُ قَصَمْتُ الْعَظْمَ قَصْمًا إِذَا كَسَرْتَهُ فَانْقَصَمَ، وَالْقَصْمُ: الْكَسْرُ، وَالْقَصْمَةُ: الْكِسْ
meaning.en_detailed: Root ق-ص-م (qSm) conveys violent fracture, classically glossed as breaking a bone (qaṣm al-ʿẓam) — distinct from ق-س-م (oath, division). Its single Quranic occurrence registers the harsh shattering of defiant wrongdoers, consonant with the Quranic pattern of employing fracture-images for divine retribution. Ibn Fāris distinguishes this root from its near-homograph by the element of forceful severing inherent in the ṣād. Quranic occurrence count: 1.

hadith_evidence.text_en: Anas ibn Malik reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever loves to have his provision expanded and his lifespan extended, let him maintain family ties."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ أَنَسِ بْنِ مَالِكٍ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «مَنْ أَحَبَّ أَنْ يُبْسَطَ لَهُ فِي رِزْقِهِ وَيُنْسَأَ لَهُ فِي أَثَرِهِ فَلْيَصِلْ رَح

meaning.en_short: Breaking with a crack, shattering, and thun
meaning.en: The root qāf-ṣād-fāʾ (ق-ص-ف) denotes breaking with a crack, shattering, and thunderous crash. It conveys qāṣif (17:69) — a hurricane that shatters — destructive, violent wind.
meaning.ar: الْقَافُ وَالصَّادُ وَالْفَاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى كَسْرِ الشَّيْءِ. يُقَالُ: قَصَفَ الشَّيْءَ يَقْصِفُهُ قَصْفًا إِذَا كَسَرَهُ.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ق-ص-ف (qSf) denotes a violent, sudden shatter with a sharp sound — classically applied to a crashing, crushing wind. The Quran employs the active participle qāṣifāt in Sūrat Banī Isrāʾīl (17:69), describing the wind sent against the disbelievers that crushed everything it struck ('ṣarṣaran ʿadābun qāṣif'). Lexicographers gloss qaṣf as breaking with a snap, and al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī links it to anything destructive that splits what it hits. Quranic occurrence count: 1.

hadith_evidence.text_en: Abu Huraira reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "A man was walking on a path and found a thorny branch, so he removed it. Allah appreciated him and forgave him."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ أَبِي هُرَيْرَةَ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «بَيْنَمَا رَجُلٌ يَمْشِي بِطَرِيقٍ وَجَدَ غُصْنَ شَوْكٍ عَلَى الطَّرِيقِ فَأَخَّرَهُ، فَشَك

meaning.en: The root qāf-ʿayn-rāʾ (ق-ع-ر) denotes the bottom, depth, and deepest part. It conveys qaʿr — the pit's floor, the cup's lowest point — the most recessed extreme.
meaning.ar: الْقَافُ وَالْعَيْنُ وَالرَّاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْعُمْقِ وَالْأَصْلِ. يُقَالُ: قَعْرُ الْبِئْرِ وَقَعْرُ الْحَوْضِ، وَقَعَرْتُ الْبِئْرَ: حَفَرْتُهَا حَتَّى بَلَغْتُ قَعْرَهَا.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ق-ع-ر (qEr) denotes the deepest extremity of a hollow or pit (qaʿr al-biʾr) and, by extension, the bottom of any receptacle or cavity. Its single Quranic occurrence appears in Sūrat al-Mulk (67:18), where taqʿīr conveys God's precise measuring and descent into extremes — a concept lexicographers tie to reaching the uttermost depth. Ibn Fāris frames the root as denoting bottommost point and intensity of penetration. Quranic occurrence count: 1.

hadith_evidence.text_en: Abu Huraira reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Every joint of a person has a charity due upon it each day the sun rises."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ أَبِي هُرَيْرَةَ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «كُلُّ سُلَامَى مِنَ النَّاسِ عَلَيْهِ صَدَقَةٌ كُلَّ يَوْمٍ تَطْلُعُ فِيهِ الشَّمْسُ»

meaning.en_short: Cutting, pruning, and tender green shoots
meaning.en: The root qāf-ḍād-bāʾ (ق-ض-ب) denotes cutting, pruning, and tender green shoots. It conveys quḍb (80:28) — the fresh green herbs that grow — the tender vegetation of the earth.
meaning.ar: الْقَافُ وَالضَّادُ وَالْبَاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى قَطْعِ الشَّيْءِ. وَمِنْهُ الْقَضْبُ: قَطْعُ الشَّيْءِ الرَّطْبِ. وَالْقَضْبُ: الْكَلَأُ الرَّطْبُ.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ق-ض-ب (qDb) carries two interrelated senses in classical Arabic: the cutting of fresh, moist plants, and the tender green shoots that are themselves cut (quḍb). Its sole Quranic occurrence is in Sūrat ʿAbasa (80:28-29), where quḍban wa ʿullaban describes edible vegetables and grains — the literal green herbage of the earth. Ibn Manẓūr notes the root classically denotes the cutting of what is still green, distinguishing it from hayyir (dry fodder). Quranic occurrence count: 1.

meaning.en_short: Decay, crumbling, and the hollow sound of
meaning.en: The root nūn-khāʾ-rāʾ (ن-خ-ر) denotes decay, crumbling, and the hollow sound of rotten bone. It conveys ʿiẓāman nakhiratan (79:11) — decayed, hollow bones — the skeptic's objection about resurrection.
meaning.ar: النُّونُ وَالْخَاءُ وَالرَّاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى خُلُوٍّ وَتَفَتُّتٍ. يُقَالُ: نَخِرَ الْعَظْمُ يَنْخَرُ نَخَرًا، إِذَا بَلِيَ وَتَفَتَّتَ.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ن-خ-ر (nxr) denotes the hollow crumbling of bone — ʿiẓāman nakhiratan — and the rustle of dry, decayed matter. The Quran employs it in Sūrat al-Nāziʿāt (79:11) where the denier of resurrection asks 'who will resurrect these decayed bones?' (man yuḥyī al-ʿiẓāma wa hiya nakhiratun). Al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī connects the root to disintegration of solid matter into dust and rustling decay. Quranic occurrence count: 1.
