hadith_evidence.text_en: Ibn Abbas reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "There are two blessings which many people squander: health and free time."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ ابْنِ عَبَّاسٍ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمَا قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «نِعْمَتَانِ مَغْبُونٌ فِيهِمَا كَثِيرٌ مِنَ النَّاسِ: الصِّحَّةُ وَالْفَرَاغُ»

meaning.en_short: Intention, resolve, and the core of purpose
meaning.en: The root nūn-wāw-yāʾ (ن-و-ي) denotes intention, resolve, and the core of purpose. It conveys niyya — the inner determination that underlies every deed — actions are by intentions.
meaning.ar: النَّوَى: الْقَصْدُ. وَالنَّوَى: الْبُعْدُ. وَالنَّوَى: النَّوَاةُ مِنَ التَّمْرِ. وَكُلُّهَا مِنْ أَصْلٍ وَاحِدٍ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْبُعْدِ وَالْقَصْدِ
meaning.en_detailed: Root ن-و-ي (nwy) centers on niyya — the inner intention and resolve that directs an act toward its object, and secondarily on distance (buʿd). The Quranic form nūnū (or nawait) appears in the hadith-near register; the root's Quranic occurrence clusters around verse context where purpose and direction of will are at stake. Ibn Fāris glosses the three senses: distance, intention, and the date-stone (nawā) — all expressing 'that which is at the core or center.' Quranic occurrence count: 1.

meaning.en_short: Letter nūn; the great fish/whale; dhū al-nūn (Jonah)
meaning.en: The root nūn-wāw-nūn (ن-و-ن) denotes the letter nūn, the great fish/whale, and the inkpot. It conveys Dhū al-Nūn — Jonah, companion of the whale — and the inkpot of knowledge.
meaning.ar: النُّونُ: الْحُوتُ، وَالْجَمْعُ نِينَانٌ. وَالنُّونُ: الْحِبْرُ، وَالْجَمْعُ أَنْوَانٌ. وَيُقَالُ: نَانَ يَنُونُ نَوْنًا إِذَا تَأَخَّرَ. وَالنُّونُ: السَّيْفُ. وَالنُّونُ: الْقَلَمُ.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ن-و-ن (nwn) in classical Arabic denotes the whale/great fish (ḥūt), the inkwell (dawāt), and the letter nūn itself. The Quran employs it as 'Dhū al-Nūn' in Sūrat al-Anbiyāʾ (21:87) and as the sacred letter nūn opening Sūrat al-Qalam (68:1). Ibn Manẓūr notes the root's semantic cluster: the fish (whale), the ink (ḥibr), and the sword — all heavy, primary instruments. Quranic occurrence count: 1.

meaning.en_short: Rising with difficulty, bearing a burden,
meaning.en: The root nūn-wāw-hamza (ن-و-أ) denotes rising with difficulty, bearing a burden, and star-setting. It conveys nawʾ — the struggle of lifting weight and celestial navigation.
meaning.ar: (نَأَى) الْهَمْزَةُ وَالنُّونُ وَالْحَرْفُ الْمُعْتَلُّ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْبُعْدِ وَالتَّنَائِي. وَمِنْهُ النَّأْيُ: الْبُعْدُ.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ن-و-أ (nwA) — properly ن-أ-ي — denotes remoteness (buʿd), rising with effort, and the heavenly navigation of stars. The Quranic form appears in the phrase nawʾan, where 'we raised the heavens without pillars you can see' (31:10, with cognate root), but the root's distinct form in ʿArabī lexicons covers the strenuous lifting and celestial ascent. Ibn Fāris distinguishes this root from نو (intent) and نون (whale). Quranic occurrence count: 1.

meaning.en: The root nūn-wāw-ṣād (ن-و-ص) denotes avoiding, escaping, and seeking refuge. It conveys nawṣ — the desperate flight from danger — seeking a way out.
meaning.ar: (نَاصَ) النُّونُ وَالْوَاوُ وَالصَّادُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْهَرَبِ وَالتَّأَخُّرِ. يُقَالُ: نَاصَ يَنُوصُ نَوْصًا إِذَا تَأَخَّرَ وَهَرَبَ. وَالْمَنَاصُ: الْمَهْرَبُ.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ن-و-ص (nwS) means to flee, retreat, and seek escape — al-manāṣ is the place of refuge from which one evades danger. The Quran employs the noun form manāṣ in Sūrat Ṣād (38:3), where the transgressors have no refuge ('mā lahum min manāṣin'). Al-Zajjājī and al-Farrāʾ explain the root as signifying withdrawal and the desperate flight from a threatening situation. Quranic occurrence count: 1.

hadith_evidence.text_en: Abu Huraira reported: A man said to the Prophet ﷺ: "Advise me." He said: "Do not become angry." The man repeated his request several times, and the Prophet ﷺ said: "Do not become angry."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ أَبِي هُرَيْرَةَ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ أَنَّ رَجُلًا قَالَ لِلنَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: أَوْصِنِي. قَالَ: «لَا تَغْضَبْ» فَرَدَّدَ مِرَارًا، قَالَ: «لَا تَغْضَبْ»

meaning.en_short: Reaching for, grasping, and what is at han
meaning.en: The root nūn-wāw-shīn (ن-و-ش) denotes reaching for, grasping, and what is at hand. It conveys nawsha — reaching to seize the near — and the futility of reaching faith at death.
meaning.ar: النُّونُ وَالْوَاوُ وَالشِّينُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى تَنَاوُلِ شَيْءٍ مِنْ بَعِيدٍ، وَيُقَالُ: نَاشَ يَنُوشُ نَوْشًا إِذَا تَنَاوَلَ شَيْئًا مِنْ بَعِيدٍ، وَالتَّنَاوُشُ: التَّنَاوُلُ مِنْ بُعْ
meaning.en_detailed: Root ن-و-ش (nw$) denotes grasping from afar, reaching to seize what is at hand, and by extension the late, futile reaching for what one missed. The Quranic verb form yatanāwushūn appears in Sūrat al-Wāqiʿa (56:83), where the soul reaches forth to those who came before it — implying a striving toward the near at death's threshold. Ibn Fāris glosses tanāwush as the grasping of what is close after having lost what is far. Quranic occurrence count: 1.

meaning.en: The root nūn-qāf-ʿayn (ن-ق-ع) denotes soaking, steeping, and the pool. It conveys naqʿ — immersion in liquid and the standing water where things are steeped.
meaning.ar: النُّونُ وَالْقَافُ وَالْعَيْنُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى شَيْءٍ يَثُورُ وَيَنْتَشِرُ. مِنْ ذَلِكَ النَّقْعُ: الْغُبَارُ، يُقَالُ: نَقَعَ الْغُبَارُ يَنْقَعُ نَقْعًا إِذَا ثَارَ.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ن-ق-ع (nqE) carries senses of standing water where things are soaked (naqʿ) and the dust raised in battle. Its single Quranic occurrence appears in Sūrat Yā-Sīn (36:13) 'wa dalla maʿahum,' but the root's specific instance registers the agitation/raising of dust stirred up — in Ibn Fāris's framework, 'that which rises and spreads.' The semantic center oscillates between the standing pool and the billowing dust. Quranic occurrence count: 1.

hadith_evidence.text_en: Anas ibn Malik reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "If the Hour begins and one of you has a sapling in his hand, if he can plant it before it occurs, let him do so."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ أَنَسِ بْنِ مَالِكٍ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «إِنْ قَامَتِ السَّاعَةُ وَفِي يَدِ أَحَدِكُمْ فَسِيلَةٌ، فَإِنِ اسْتَطَاعَ أَنْ لَا تَقُ

meaning.en: The root nūn-kāf-dāl (ن-ك-د) denotes miserliness, scantiness, and giving grudgingly. It conveys nakad — the withholding of what should be given — the stingy, begrudging heart.
meaning.ar: النُّونُ وَالْكَافُ وَالدَّالُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى ضِيقٍ وَشِدَّةٍ وَعُسْرٍ. يُقَالُ: نَكِدَ يَنْكَدُ نَكَدًا، إِذَا عَسُرَ وَاشْتَدَّ. وَالْمَنْكُودُ: الَّذِي لَا يُعْطِي خَيْرًا.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ن-ك-د (nkd) denotes narrowness, hardship, and grudging withholding of good. The Quranic form mankūd (the grudging one) appears in Sūrat al-Takāthur (102:2), where 'the accumulators made you heedless until you reached the maqābir' — and the root emphasizes the withholding, miserly nature that refuses to give what it has. Ibn Manẓūr records the root as signifying tight-fistedness (shuḥḥ) and difficulty. Quranic occurrence count: 1.

hadith_evidence.text_en: Abu Huraira reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Every joint of a person has a charity due upon it each day the sun rises."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ أَبِي هُرَيْرَةَ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «كُلُّ سُلَامَى مِنَ النَّاسِ عَلَيْهِ صَدَقَةٌ كُلَّ يَوْمٍ تَطْلُعُ فِيهِ الشَّمْسُ»

meaning.en: The root nūn-mīm-mīm (ن-م-م) denotes tale-bearing, gossiping, and spreading secrets. It conveys namīma — the destructive act of carrying words to sow discord — a grave sin.
meaning.ar: النُّونُ وَالْمِيمُ وَالْمِيمُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى حَرَكَةٍ وَاخْتِفَاءٍ. وَالنَّمِيمَةُ: حِكَايَةُ الْكَلَامِ عَلَى وَجْهِ الْإِفْسَادِ.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ن-م-م (nmm) centers on namīma — the carrying of tales to sow discord between people, classically condemned as a grave moral sin. The Quran employs the root's derivation in the prohibition against spreading malicious reports; the classical locus is the hadith cursing the namīm. Al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī defines namīma as narrating speech with the intent of causing enmity between its hearers. Quranic occurrence count: 1.

hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ أَبِي هُرَيْرَةَ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «أَكْثِرُوا ذِكْرَ هَاذِمِ اللَّذَّاتِ» يَعْنِي الْمَوْتَ

meaning.en: The root nūn-jīm-sīn (ن-ج-س) denotes impurity, filth, and ritual uncleanness. It conveys najas — the state that precludes acts of worship requiring ritual purity.
meaning.ar: النُّونُ وَالْجِيمُ وَالسِّينُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى قَذَرٍ وَدَنَسٍ، وَمِنْهُ النَّجَسُ وَالنَّجَاسَةُ
meaning.en_detailed: Root ن-ج-س (njs) denotes najas/najāsa — physical filth and, more importantly in fiqh, ritual uncleanness that precludes valid prayer. The Quran uses the noun najis in the plural najas (8:11) where God 'sent down upon you tranquility from Himself' (semantically related verse) but the root's key occurrence is in 9:28 where the mushrikūn are described in a state of najāsa ritual contamination. Lexicographers gloss najis as that which contaminates and bars valid worship. Quranic occurrence count: 1.

hadith_evidence.text_en: Abdullah ibn Amr reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The merciful will be shown mercy by the Most Merciful. Be merciful to those on earth, and the One in heaven will have mercy upon you."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ بْنِ عَمْرٍو رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمَا قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «الرَّاحِمُونَ يَرْحَمُهُمُ الرَّحْمَنُ، ارْحَمُوا مَنْ فِي الْأَرْضِ يَرْحَمْ

meaning.en: The root nūn-jīm-dāl (ن-ج-د) denotes highland, plateau, and elevation. It conveys al-najdayn (90:10) — We guided him to the two highroads — the paths of good and evil.
meaning.ar: النُّونُ وَالْجِيمُ وَالدَّالُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الِارْتِفَاعِ وَالْغِلَظِ. فَالنَّجْدُ: الْأَرْضُ الْمُرْتَفِعَةُ الْغَلِيظَةُ. وَالنَّجْدُ: الطَّرِيقُ الْمُرْتَفِعُ الْوَاضِحُ.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ن-ج-د (njd) denotes the highland, the elevated plateau, and the clear, raised path. The Quran uses the dual form al-najdayn in Sūrat al-Balad (90:10): 'wa hadaynāhu al-najdayn' — 'We guided him to the two highroads,' meaning the two manifest paths of good and evil. Ibn Fāris glosses najd as the elevated, prominent ground and the conspicuous road. Quranic occurrence count: 1.

hadith_evidence.text_en: Umm Salama reported: The most frequent supplication of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was: "O Turner of hearts, make my heart firm upon Your religion."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ أُمِّ سَلَمَةَ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهَا قَالَتْ: كَانَ أَكْثَرُ دُعَاءِ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «يَا مُقَلِّبَ الْقُلُوبِ ثَبِّتْ قَلْبِي عَلَى دِينِكَ»

meaning.en_short: Shaking the head in mockery, wagging scor
meaning.en: The root nūn-ghayn-ḍād (ن-غ-ض) denotes shaking the head in mockery, wagging scornfully. It conveys yunghiḍūna ruʾūsahum (17:51) — they shake their heads at you in derision.
meaning.ar: النُّونُ وَالضَّادُ وَالدَّالُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى تَحْرِيكٍ وَاضْطِرَابٍ. يُقَالُ: نَضَدْتُ الشَّيْءَ أَنْضُدُهُ نَضْدًا إِذَا حَرَّكْتَهُ.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ن-غ-ض (ngD) denotes the shaking motion, particularly the wag of the head in mockery and disdain. The Quran employs the verb yunghiḍūn in Sūrat al-Isrāʾ (17:51): 'wa idhā raūka in yattakhidhūnaka illā huzuwan' (17:51) — the derisive head-shaking at the Prophet. Classical lexicographers note the root's association with contemptuous motion toward another. Quranic occurrence count: 1.

hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ أَبِي هُرَيْرَةَ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «خَيْرُكُمْ خَيْرُكُمْ لِأَهْلِهِ، وَأَنَا خَيْرُكُمْ لِأَهْلِي»

meaning.en_short: A clear path, manifest way, and methodology
meaning.en: The root nūn-hāʾ-jīm (ن-ه-ج) denotes a clear path, manifest way, and methodology. It conveys minhāj (5:48) — the clear course of right guidance set for each community.
meaning.ar: النُّونُ وَالْهَاءُ وَالْجِيمُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى وُضُوحِ الشَّيْءِ وَظُهُورِهِ. مِنْ ذَلِكَ النَّهْجُ: الطَّرِيقُ الْوَاضِحُ. وَالْمَنْهَجُ وَالْمِنْهَاجُ: الطَّرِيقُ الْوَاضِحُ.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ن-ه-ج (nhj) denotes a clear, manifest path (nahj, minhāj) — the visible road that can be followed without doubt. The Quran employs minhāj in Sūrat al-Māʾida (5:48): 'li-kulli jaʿalnā minka shirʿatan wa minhājan' — 'For each We have made a shirʿa and minhāj.' Al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī links the root to the disclosure of a route once obscure. Quranic occurrence count: 1.

hadith_evidence.text_en: Ali reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to me: "Say: O Allah, guide me and direct me."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ عَلِيٍّ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: قَالَ لِي رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «قُلِ: اللَّهُمَّ اهْدِنِي وَسَدِّدْنِي»

meaning.en_short: Blowing lightly with moisture, the whisper
meaning.en: The root nūn-fāʾ-thāʾ (ن-ف-ث) denotes blowing lightly with moisture, the whisper of magic. It conveys al-naffāthāt (113:4) — those who blow on knots — the sorceresses of pre-Islamic Arabia.
meaning.ar: النُّونُ وَالْفَاءُ وَالثَّاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى تَفَتُّحِ الشَّيْءِ وَانْتِشَارِهِ. مِنْ ذَلِكَ النَّفْثُ: وَهُوَ نَفْخُكَ بِرِيقِكَ، وَهُوَ أَقَلُّ مِنَ التَّفْلِ.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ن-ف-ث (nfv) means to blow lightly with moisture, particularly the whispered breath of a sorcerer or incantation. The Quran uses the active participle al-naffāthāt fī al-ʿuqad in Sūrat al-Falaq (113:4): 'wa min sharri al-naffāthāti fī al-ʿuqad' — 'from the evil of those who blow on knots,' referring to the female sorceresses of pre-Islamic Arabia. Ibn Fāris glosses nafth as gentle blowing with spittle, weaker than nafkha. Quranic occurrence count: 1.

hadith_evidence.text_en: Abu Dharr reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Do not consider any act of goodness insignificant, even if it is meeting your brother with a cheerful face."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ أَبِي ذَرٍّ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «لَا تَحْقِرَنَّ مِنَ الْمَعْرُوفِ شَيْئًا وَلَوْ أَنْ تَلْقَى أَخَاكَ بِوَجْهٍ طَلْقٍ»

meaning.en_short: Extracting, drawing forth, and springing wa
meaning.en: The root nūn-bāʾ-ṭāʾ (ن-ب-ط) denotes extracting, drawing forth, and springing water. It conveys nabṭ — the emergence of what was hidden — the discovery of truth through effort.
meaning.ar: النُّونُ وَالْبَاءُ وَالطَّاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى خُرُوجِ الشَّيْءِ مِنَ الشَّيْءِ. يُقَالُ: نَبَطَ الْمَاءُ يَنْبُطُ نَبْطًا إِذَا خَرَجَ مِنَ الْبِئْرِ.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ن-ب-ط (nbT) denotes water bursting forth from a well (nabaṭa al-māʾu yanbūṭu) and, by extension, the drawing out of something hidden into the open. Its single Quranic occurrence registers the springing forth of hidden essence; classical lexicographers tie the root to the gushing of water from a vein in the earth. Al-Zajjājī glosses nabṭ as the emergence of what was concealed beneath. Quranic occurrence count: 1.

meaning.en: The root nūn-bāʾ-zāy (ن-ب-ز) denotes a nickname, byname, and epithet. It conveys nabz — particularly the offensive nickname: wa lā tanābazū bi al-alqāb (49:11) — do not call each other by offensive names.
meaning.ar: النُّونُ وَالْبَاءُ وَالزَّاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى اللَّقَبِ السَّيِّئِ. يُقَالُ: نَبَزَهُ يَنْبِزُهُ نَبْزًا، إِذَا لَقَّبَهُ بِسُوءٍ. وَالنَّبَزُ: اللَّقَبُ الْقَبِيحُ.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ن-ب-ز (nbz) means to give someone a sobriquet, particularly a hostile or mocking nickname. The Quran forbids this directly in Sūrat al-Ḥujurāt (49:11): 'wa lā tanābazū bi-l-alqāb' — 'do not call one another by offensive epithets.' Ibn Manẓūr and al-Aṣmaʿī distinguish between harmless kunya (teknonym) and the aggressive nabz that humiliates. Quranic occurrence count: 1.

meaning.en_short: Goring, butting, and striking with horns
meaning.en: The root nūn-ṭāʾ-ḥāʾ (ن-ط-ح) denotes goring, butting, and striking with horns. It conveys naṭḥ — the characteristic attack of horned animals — the sudden violent impact.
meaning.ar: النُّونُ وَالطَّاءُ وَالْحَاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى ضَرْبٍ بِشَيْءٍ صُلْبٍ. وَالنَّطْحُ: ضَرْبُ الْكَبْشِ بِرَأْسِهِ. وَالنَّطِيحَةُ: الشَّاةُ الَّتِي نَطَحَتْهَا أُخْرَى فَمَاتَتْ.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ن-ط-ح (nTH) denotes the goring or butting of horned animals, the violent impact of one hard thing upon another. The Quranic form naṭīḥa (the gored animal) and the verbal form natakha appear in the law of ritual slaughtering, where naṭīḥa is the carcass of an animal killed by another's horns — discussed by jurists as not valid slaughter. Ibn Fāris glosses naṭḥ as striking with something hard at the head. Quranic occurrence count: 1.

meaning.en_short: Shepherd's cry; naʿq (harsh shouting, driving call)
meaning.en: The root nūn-ʿayn-qāf (ن-ع-ق) denotes the cry of a shepherd, shouting, and harsh calling. It conveys naʿq — the crude shout of a herder to his flock — unintelligible and crude (2:171).
meaning.ar: الْعَيْنُ وَالنُّونُ وَالْقَافُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى صَوْتٍ وَصِيَاحٍ. يُقَالُ: نَعَقَ الرَّاعِي بِغَنَمِهِ يَنْعِقُ نَعْقًا، إِذَا صَاحَ بِهَا.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ن-ع-ق (nEq) denotes the loud, sharp cry of a shepherd to his flock (naʿq al-rāʿī), and by extension any harsh, inarticulate shout. The Quran uses the verb form in Sūrat al-Baqara (2:171): 'mithla al-anʿāmi bal hum aḍall' paired with 'wa kāna yunʿiqu' describing the disbelievers' cry compared to a shepherd's unintelligible call. Ibn Fāris frames the root around the crassness of a voice addressed to animals. Quranic occurrence count: 1.

meaning.en_short: Slaughtering, the upper chest, and sacrific
meaning.en: The root nūn-ḥāʾ-rāʾ (ن-ح-ر) denotes slaughtering, the upper chest, and sacrifice. It conveys inḥar (108:2) — so pray to your Lord and sacrifice — the ritual slaughter of devotion.
meaning.ar: النُّونُ وَالْحَاءُ وَالرَّاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْحَلْقِ، وَمِنْهُ النَّحْرُ، وَهُوَ مَوْضِعُ الْقِلَادَةِ مِنَ الْحَلْقِ، وَيُقَالُ نَحَرَهُ أَيْ أَصَابَ نَحْرَهُ.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ن-ح-ر (nHr) denotes the upper chest/throat (naḥr) where the knife goes in sacrifice, and the ritual slaughter itself (naḥr, munāḥara). The Quran employs the verb form in Sūrat al-Kawthar (108:2): 'fa-ṣalli li-rabbika wa inḥar' — 'so pray to your Lord and sacrifice.' Al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī links the root to the throat-region (nuqratan al-ḥalq), distinguished from dhabaḥ (general slaughter). Quranic occurrence count: 1.

meaning.en_short: A vow, pledge, and fulfillment of one's ter
meaning.en: The root nūn-ḥāʾ-bāʾ (ن-ح-ب) denotes a vow, pledge, and fulfillment of one's term. It conveys naḥb — the solemn commitment — and the completion of one's appointed span.
meaning.ar: النُّونُ وَالْحَاءُ وَالْبَاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْوَعْدِ وَالْعَهْدِ. وَالنَّحْبُ: النَّذْرُ. وَقَالَ: قَضَى نَحْبَهُ: مَاتَ عَلَى وَفَاءِ نَذْرِهِ.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ن-ح-ب (nHb) denotes a solemn vow (nadhr) and the fulfillment of one's appointed term (naḥb). The Quran uses the verbal form qaḍā naḥbahu in Sūrat al-Aḥzāb (33:23) describing the believers of Badr: 'wa qaḍā naḥbahum,' meaning those who fulfilled their pledge unto death. Ibn Manẓūr and al-Aṣmaʿī gloss the root as the votary who completes his vow unto death. Quranic occurrence count: 1.

meaning.en: The root nūn-ḍād-khāʾ (ن-ض-خ) denotes sprinkling, spraying, and gentle gushing. It conveys naḍkh — water emerging in a fine spray — the fountains of Paradise.
meaning.ar: النُّونُ وَالضَّادُ وَالْخَاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى انْفِجَارِ الْمَاءِ وَانْدِفَاعِهِ
meaning.en_detailed: Root ن-ض-خ (nDx) denotes the gentle gushing or spraying of water (naḍkh al-māʾ) — water bursting forth in fine droplets. Its single Quranic occurrence registers the bursting of celestial water, classical lexicographers noting the root differs from nafth (gentle blowing) and fakhr (overflowing). Ibn Fāris frames it as the pressing out of liquid in a fine, pressurized spray. Quranic occurrence count: 1.

meaning.en_short: Ripening, maturing, and being fully cooked
meaning.en: The root nūn-ḍād-jīm (ن-ض-ج) denotes ripening, maturing, and being fully cooked. It conveys naḍj — the completion of a process — fruit at its peak, food perfectly prepared.
meaning.ar: النُّونُ وَالضَّادُ وَالْجِيمُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْإِدْرَاكِ وَالنُّضْجِ، يُقَالُ: نَضِجَ الثَّمَرُ إِذَا أَدْرَكَ، وَنَضِجَ اللَّحْمُ إِذَا اسْتَوَى عَلَى النَّارِ
meaning.en_detailed: Root ن-ض-ج (nDj) denotes ripening, maturing, and the perfect completion of a process — of fruit reaching ripeness, of food being fully cooked. Its single Quranic occurrence registers this imagery of maturation; classical usage distinguishes naḍj (full cooking/ripening) from raw insipid state. Al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī glosses naḍj as the attainment of a thing's prime (bulūghihi). Quranic occurrence count: 1.

Its single Quranic occurrence appears in Sūrat Yūsuf (12:65) where Yusuf's brothers, sent ahead to provision themselves with grain, become 'lā taʿlūnī' — the term mīra registers the food-stuffs they brought. Al-Zajjājī notes the root connotes supplies brought in for a city's needs. Quranic occurrence count: 1.

meaning.en: The root mīm-khāʾ-ḍād (م-خ-ض) denotes churning, shaking, and labor pains. It conveys makhḍ — the vigorous agitation of milk to produce butter and the convulsions of childbirth.
meaning.ar: الْمِيمُ وَالْخَاءُ وَالضَّادُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى حَرَكَةِ الشَّيْءِ وَاضْطِرَابِهِ. وَمِنْهُ الْمَخَاضُ، وَهُوَ وَجَعُ الْوِلَادَةِ عِنْدَ حَرَكَةِ الْوَلَدِ وَاضْطِرَابِهِ.
meaning.en_detailed: Root م-خ-ض (mxD) denotes churning, violent agitation, and the labor pangs (makhāḍ) of childbirth. Its single Quranic occurrence appears in Sūrat Fāṭir (35:33) where makhāḍ al-mawt registers the pangs of death approaching, paralleling the throes of birth. Al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī ties the root to the violent stirring that extracts the pure from the impure, as in churning milk. Quranic occurrence count: 1.

meaning.en: The root mīm-kāf-wāw (م-ك-و) denotes whistling, shrill noise, and bird-calls. It conveys mukāʾan wa taṣdiya (8:35) — the pagan practice of whistling and clapping at the Kaʿba.

meaning.en_detailed: Root م-ك-و (mkw) denotes the high-pitched whistling or shrill cry (mukāʾ), and, as used pejoratively, the silly whistling and clapping of the pagans. The Quran employs it in Sūrat al-Anfāl (8:35): 'mukāʾan wa taṣdiya' — describing the disbelievers' whistling and hand-clapping around the Kaʿba as vanity. Ibn Manẓūr notes the root exclusively denotes the whistling sound, often mocking. Quranic occurrence count: 1.

meaning.en: The root mīm-sīn-khāʾ (م-س-خ) denotes transformation, metamorphosis, and changing form. It conveys maskh — the divine punishment transforming sinners into apes and swine.
meaning.ar: 'الْمِيمُ وَالسِّينُ وَالْخَاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى تَغْيِيرِ الشَّيْءِ عَنْ صُورَتِهِ إِلَى صُورَةٍ أُخْرَى أَقْبَحَ.
meaning.en_detailed: Root م-س-خ (msx) denotes transformation from one form to another, usually into something lower (maskh) — classically applied to divine punishment transforming humans into apes and swine. The Quran uses the verbal form in Sūrat al-Baqara (2:65): 'fa-qulna lahum kūnū qiradatan khāsiʾīn' alongside 'maska' in 5:60 describing those whom God cursed into apes and swine. Al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī defines maskh as change of image to a worse form. Quranic occurrence count: 1.

meaning.en: The root mīm-ḥāʾ-lām (م-ح-ل) denotes drought, barrenness, and withholding of rain. It conveys maḥl — the severe dryness that threatens all life.
meaning.ar: الْمِيمُ وَالْحَاءُ وَاللَّامُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْمَكْرِ وَالْخَدِيعَةِ وَالْمُدَافَعَةِ. وَمِنْهُ الْمَحْلُ: الْمَكْرُ. وَالْمِحَالُ: الْمُكَابَرَةُ فِي الْخُصُومَةِ.
meaning.en_detailed: Root م-ح-ل (mHl) denotes drought, barrenness, and the severe withholding of rain (maḥl). Its single Quranic occurrence registers barrenness or drought as divine punishment or trial, classical Arabic linking it to qaḥt (famine) and ʿadam al-khayr. Ibn Fāris notes the root's semantic field includes drought of rain and, by extension, a barren season that threatens life. Quranic occurrence count: 1.

meaning.en: The root mīm-ʿayn-zāy (م-ع-ز) denotes goats, the caprine species. It conveys maʿz — the goat, valued for milk, meat, and hair, distinct from sheep.
meaning.ar: «مَيَزَ: الْمِيمُ وَالْيَاءُ وَالزَّاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْفَصْلِ وَالتَّمْيِيزِ بَيْنَ الشَّيْئَيْنِ»
meaning.en_detailed: The triconsonantal root م ع ز (معز) — 1 Quranic occurrences — fundamentally expresses Goats, the caprine species. Ibn Faris places the homograph m-y-z (in yāʾ) under faṣl wa-tamyīz (distinction and differentiation), and this root likewise preserves a sense of the goat as the small ruminant distinguished from sheep, valued for milk, hair, and the lean meat of the Arabian desert. Classical philologists record the Bedouin preference for maʿz over naʿm in arid stations, with the root serving in pre-Islamic poetry as the pastoral figure of endurance and modest provision. The verb māza (in yāʾ form) meaning to separate preserves the semantic genealogy of distinction that runs through the homographic root system, with the goat occupying the place of the most differentiated herd animal.

meaning.en: The root mīm-ṭāʾ-wāw (م-ط-و) denotes extending, stretching, and pulling taut. It conveys maṭw — elongation — drawing something to its full extension.
meaning.ar: الْمِيمُ وَالطَّاءُ وَالْوَاوُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى مَدِّ الشَّيْءِ وَبَسْطِهِ. وَمِنْهُ الْمَطْوُ: مَدُّ الْجِلْدِ وَغَيْرِهِ. وَالْمَطِيطَةُ: الْأَرْضُ الْبَعِيدَةُ.
meaning.en_detailed: The triconsonantal root م ط و (مطو) — 1 Quranic occurrences — fundamentally expresses Extending, stretching, and pulling taut. The Quranic form almaddu al-mattw in 'wa-l-arḍi wa-mā tahāwā' / 'wa-mā madda' describes the spreading expanse whose full interpretation classical commentators debate (the earth, the shadow, the breath, the rope), but all agree the root signals the deliberate longitudinal pull. Maṭīyah (the stretched leather) and matwa (the act of stretching) preserve the verbal action of pulling something taut, as in drying hides or stretching cloth. The cognate maṭṭa (to stretch, prolong) enters later Arabic with the same core meaning, and the semantic field aligns with the classical Arab's sensitivity to measured extension, with al-Rāghib noting that the root's specific sense distinguishes voluntary extension from the natural length of al-ṭūl.

meaning.en: The root mīm-ʿayn-yāʾ (م-ع-ي) denotes intestines, bowels, and digestive tract. It conveys amʿāʾ — the coiled internal organs that process sustenance.
meaning.ar: الْمِيمُ وَالْيَاءُ وَالْيَاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْحَيَاةِ وَالسَّيَلَانِ، وَالْمَاءُ هُوَ السَّائِلُ الَّذِي بِهِ حَيَاةُ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ
meaning.en_detailed: Occurring 1 times in the Quranic text, the root م ع ي (معي) conveys the essential concept of Intestines, bowels, and digestive tract. Al-Rāghib's reading places amʿāʾ as the locus of physical hunger and digestive processing, with the root's semantic genealogy connecting to the muʿāyāh (interior organs exposed in butchery). Classical lexicographers preserve the form maʿy as the place where life and flow converge — the body's inner tube. The hadith tradition retains the root in descriptions of intestinal distress (iḍṭirāb al-amʿāʾ), with the prophet's medicine acknowledging the bowels' role in health and disease, while the Quranic usage in 2:174 lists amʿāʾ among the forbidden substances (those not properly slaughtered or strangled) — the consumption of which carries juridical consequence.

meaning.en: The root mīm-shīn-jīm (م-ش-ج) denotes mixing, blending, and mingling fluids. It conveys amshāj (76:2) — We created man from a mixed drop — the union of male and female fluids.
meaning.ar: الْمِيمُ وَالشِّينُ وَالْجِيمُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْخَلْطِ وَالْمُزَاوَجَةِ. يُقَالُ: مَشَجْتُ الشَّيْءَ أَمْشُجُهُ مَشْجًا إِذَا خَلَطْتُهُ.
meaning.en_detailed: Occurring 1 times in the Quranic text, the root م ش ج (مشج) conveys the essential concept of Mixing, blending, and mingling fluids. The Quranic form amshāj in 'inna khalaqnā al-insāna min nuṭfatin amshāj' describes the mingled drop, classically read by al-Ṭabarī as the commingled male and female seminal fluids that together constitute the embryo, though some extend the meaning to include ancestral admixtures going back to Adam. Al-Rāghib restricts the technical sense to the immediate parental union, with the root's image preserving the unity-in-distinction of the contributing elements. The verb mashaja (to mix, to interweave) survives in medical and alchemical literature, while the noun mizāj (temperament, mixture) entered philosophical Arabic through translation movements. Modern Quranic philology affirms the embryological reading without excluding the broader biological sense, with the root preserving the theology of human creation through cooperation.

meaning.en_short: Seeking refuge, clinging to, and circumamb
meaning.en: The root lām-wāw-dhāl (ل-و-ذ) denotes seeking refuge, clinging to, and circumambulation. It conveys liwādh — pressing close for protection — the desperate seeking of shelter.
meaning.ar: قال ابن فارس في مقاييس اللغة: (ل و ذ) اللام والواو والذال أصل واحد يدل على الالتجاء والاستتار. يقال: لاذ به يلوذ لوذاً، إذا استتر به والتجأ إليه.
meaning.en_detailed: The Arabic root ل و ذ (لوذ) appears 1 times in the Quran, governing the semantic domain of Seeking refuge, clinging to, and circumamb.  Classical commentators note that the root preserves the imagery of a hunted creature taking cover, with liwādh being the protective embrace itself, the desperate seeking of sanctuary by the pursued. Al-Rāghib reads luwūdh as the action of the one who has no other refuge, with the divine response framed as the only ultimate shelter. The verb lādha yalūdhu preserves the sense of pressing close to a protector, while the root remains rare in the Quran but rhetorically powerful, capturing the human condition of vulnerability and the divine response of sanctuary.

meaning.en: The root lām-zāy-bāʾ (ل-ز-ب) denotes clinging, sticking, and necessary attachment. It conveys lāzib (37:11, 54:2) — a clinging clay that sticks fast and cannot be shaken off.
meaning.ar: اللَّامُ وَالزَّاءُ وَالْبَاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى لُزُوقِ الشَّيْءِ بِالشَّيْءِ. يُقَالُ: لَزِبَ الطِّينُ يَلْزَبُ لَزَبًا، إِذَا لَصِقَ. وَطِينٌ لَازِبٌ: لَاصِقٌ.
meaning.en_detailed: The Arabic root ل ز ب (لزب) appears 1 times in the Quran, governing the semantic domain of Clinging, sticking, and necessary attachmen. In 37:11 the clay of human creation is named as lāzib, while in 54:2 the mud in which the bases of Pharaoh's drowned army are gathered bears the same epithet — clay that will not detach, mud that holds fast. Al-Rāghib reads lāzib as what adheres by necessity rather than by accident, the earth that clings to the feet or the mud that holds what it has received. The root maintains the semantic field of binding, with classical Arabic preserving laẓūba (sticky thing) and lizāb (the adhering quality). The theological implication is that humanity is fashioned from the most earthly and persistent matter, with Pharaoh's army gathered in the same sticky mud that formed the first humans — a sign of creation from humble substance.

meaning.en: The root lām-qāf-ḥāʾ (ل-ق-ح) denotes pollination, fertilization, and impregnating wind. It conveys lawāqiḥ (15:22) — the fertilizing winds — carriers of life that the earth cannot generate alone.
meaning.ar: اللَّامُ وَالْقَافُ وَالْحَاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى إِلْقَاحِ الشَّيْءِ وَتَلْقِيحِهِ، وَهُوَ أَنْ يَجْعَلَ فِيهِ مَا يُثْمِرُ أَوْ يُنْتِجُ
meaning.en_detailed: Root ل ق ح (لقح), attested 1 times in the Quran, derives its core meaning of Pollination, fertilization, and impregnatin from Proto-Semitic sources. The Quranic plural lawāqiḥ in 'wa-arsalnā al-riyāḥ lawāqiḥ' names the impregnating winds that drive the clouds together to release rain, which the earth absorbs as the means of fertility. Classical commentators, especially al-Ṭabarī and al-Zamakhsharī, debated whether lawāqiḥ refers to the winds themselves or to the rains they carry, but all agree the root signals the male fertilizing agent — wind as celestial inseminator. The verb laqaḥa (to impregnate) and the active participle lāqiḥ preserve the imagery of organic impregnation in classical Arabic. The pairing of winds with rain in this verse establishes the root within the Quranic theology of cosmic cooperation, where celestial agents transmit divine generative power across the kingdom of the air.

meaning.en: The root lām-qāf-mīm (ل-ق-م) denotes a morsel, mouthful, and what is put in the mouth. It conveys luqma — the single bite — the portion consumed in one motion.
meaning.ar: اللَّامُ وَالْقَافُ وَالْمِيمُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْأَخْذِ وَالْبَلْعِ. يُقَالُ: لَقِمَ يَلْقَمُ لَقْمًا، وَالْتَقَمَ يَلْتَقِمُ، وَاللُّقْمَةُ مَا يُبْتَلَعُ.
meaning.en_detailed: The Arabic root ل ق م (لقم) appears 1 times in the Quran, governing the semantic domain of A morsel, mouthful, and what is put in the. 3:44), denotes the morsel or bite taken into the mouth — Ibn Faris places it under akhdh wa-balʿ (taking and swallowing), with luqma being the specific portion consumed in one motion. Classical Arabic distinguishes luqma (the lump, larger portion) from qarṣ (a small bite with the front teeth), with the verb laqima / iltaqama (to engulf, swallow up) extending the root into vivid imagery of swallowing — including Quranic usage describing what the earth swallows and the devouring of the sea. Al-Rāghib notes the root's semantic narrowing to 'putting into the mouth,' making it central to classical Arabic literature on table etiquette, where the prohibition against luqma-taking with the left hand derives from the sunnah's discipline of eating. The hadith condemning haste at meals ('lā yuhwīla ʾahadanahu al-ṭaʿām') alludes to the same root's negative connotations of uncontrolled ingestion.

meaning.en: The root lām-qāf-bāʾ (ل-ق-ب) denotes a title, nickname, and appellation. It conveys laqab — the honorific or descriptive name — do not call each other by offensive laqabs (49:11).
meaning.ar: (لَقَبٌ) اللَّامُ وَالْقَافُ وَالْبَاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى التَّنَابُزِ بِالْأَلْقَابِ، وَهُوَ التَّدَاعِي بِالْأَسْمَاءِ الَّتِي يُسْتَقْبَحُ أَنْ يُدْعَى بِهَا.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ل ق ب (لقب), attested 1 times in the Quran, derives its core meaning of A title, nickname, and appellation from Proto-Semitic sources. Classical Arabic distinguishes ism (proper name), laqab (cognomen/title — often honorific or satirical), and kunya (patronymic), with the laqab historically serving to mark lineages, professions, or defects. Al-Rāghib reads laqab as the appellation used to distinguish a person by praise or blame, with the Quranic prohibition specifically against the derogatory use, while neutral honorifics (al-Rashīd, al-Mahdī) remained acceptable. The hadith 'hal tasubbu fulānan? innahu la-hu' emphasizes the dangers of hostile naming. Modern Muslim name-ethics inherit from this verse the principle that offensive appellations, even jokingly used, carry moral weight, with the root serving as a witness against the dignity of the addressee.

meaning.en: The root lām-fāʾ-ẓāʾ (ل-ف-ظ) denotes uttering, pronouncing, and ejecting. It conveys lafẓ — verbal articulation — the word that leaves the tongue and enters the world.
meaning.ar: ابن فارس — مقاييس اللغة — مادة لفظ
meaning.en_detailed: Root ل ف ظ (لفظ), attested 1 times in the Quran, derives its core meaning of Uttering, pronouncing, and ejecting from Proto-Semitic sources. The Quranic form lufẓun in 'bal aqūlu lahum qawlan lafẓan / wa-qālā lā taqūlu lafẓan' preserves the root's sense of the spoken form of a word rather than its meaning, with the variant in Ibn Ishāq's reading of Ibrahim's hasty 'innī khāʾifun' as an utterance conveying more fear than the situation warranted. Classical commentators note that lafẓ in Quranic usage denotes the uttered word, with the root carrying the sense of a thing thrown out (cf. lafatha, to cast forth). The terminology of balāghah and uṣūl al-fiqh inherits from this root the technical distinction between lafẓ (the uttered word) and maʿnā (the meaning), while the hadith literature uses lafẓ in discussions of intention (niyyah) versus external pronunciation in matters of ṭahārah and prayer.

meaning.en: The root lām-hāʾ-mīm (ل-ه-م) denotes devouring, gulping, and swallowing greedily. It conveys iltihām — the voracious eating of a predator — consuming everything in sight.
meaning.ar: اللَّامُ وَالْهَاءُ وَالْمِيمُ أَصْلَانِ: أَحَدُهُمَا الْأَكْلُ بِشَرَاهَةٍ، وَالْآخَرُ إِلْقَاءُ شَيْءٍ فِي النَّفْسِ. فَالْأَوَّلُ: اللَّهْمُ، وَهُوَ الْأَكْلُ بِشَرَاهَةٍ.
meaning.en_detailed: The Arabic root ل ه م (لهم) appears 1 times in the Quran, governing the semantic domain of Devouring, gulping, and swallowing greedily. Al-Rāghib reads lahm in this sense as the shade of unquenchable hunger, the corporeal appetite at its most bestial, distinct from the homonymous lahm (flesh). The verbal noun luhm preserves the imagery of voracious eating, while the hadith disapproving of haste at meals ('la yaḥuwwala ʾahadanahu al-ṭaʿām') alludes to the same root's negative connotations of uncontrolled ingestion. Classical lexicographers distinguish the verbal form (voracity) sharply from the anatomical noun (flesh), with the active semantic field preserved in medical literature describing bestial eating disorders. The root's rarity in the Quran belies its rhetorical force when used — it names appetite at its most ugly.

meaning.en_short: Scorching, burning the face, and the blast
meaning.en: The root lām-fāʾ-ḥāʾ (ل-ف-ح) denotes scorching, burning the face, and the blast of fire. It conveys talfaḥu wujūhahum al-nār (23:104) — the Fire will scorch their faces black.
meaning.ar: «اللَّامُ وَالْفَاءُ وَالْحَاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى إِصَابَةِ النَّارِ وَحَرِّهَا، يُقَالُ: لَفَحَتْهُ النَّارُ تَلْفَحُهُ لَفْحًا، إِذَا أَصَابَتْ وَجْهَهُ بِحَرِّهَا»
meaning.en_detailed: The Arabic root ل ف ح (لفح) appears 1 times in the Quran, governing the semantic domain of Scorching, burning the face, and the blast. The Quranic active verb talfaḥu in 'talfaḥu wujūhahum al-nār' describes Hellfire burning the faces of the ungodly and turning them black — the form lufḥ naming the facial strike as the most dishonoring of all bodily assault. Al-Rāghib reads the root's special focus on the face as the locus of human dignity, with burning the face as the ultimate reversal of honor — what light and form once conveyed, fire now destroys. Classical Arabic preserves lafaḥa as the fire's first blow, while jadal and sūʿ denote the general burning. The verse's polemic against the ungodly finds its visual apex in this image of faces being scorched by divine fire, the punishment matching the sin of facial arrogance.

meaning.en_short: Blazing fire, fierce flame, and intense ign
meaning.en: The root lām-ẓāʾ-yāʾ (ل-ظ-ي) denotes blazing fire, fierce flame, and intense ignition. It conveys laẓā (70:15) — a name for Hell — the raging blaze that consumes all.
meaning.ar: اللَّامُ وَالظَّاءُ وَالْحَرْفُ الْمُعْتَلُّ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْتِهَابِ النَّارِ وَاشْتِدَادِ حَرِّهَا. وَمِنْهُ اللَّظَىٰ: نَارُ جَهَنَّمَ. وَتَلَظَّتِ النَّارُ: الْتَهَبَتْ.
meaning.en_detailed: The Arabic root ل ظ ي (لظي) appears 1 times in the Quran, governing the semantic domain of Blazing fire, fierce flame, and intense ign. The Quranic noun al-laẓā in 70:15 names one of the proper designations of Hell, alongside Jahannam, Saʿīr, Saqar, and Ḥuṭamah — the form laẓā capturing the open, flaring character of the flame, distinguished from the closed-in sūʿ and the roaring jahīm. Al-Rāghib reads laẓā as the fire of intense combustion whose flame is overt and flaring, without smoke. The verbal form talaẓẓā in 74:29 intensifies the root through the tafāʿul pattern ('wa-talaẓẓat al-nāru'), naming the fire that rages against its fuel. The hadith literature uses the root in descriptions of the heat of the Day of Judgment, with classical Arabic etymologies associating laẓā with the driest, hottest fire — the kind that flares openly into the air.

meaning.en_short: Beard, facial hair; liḥya (beard of chin and cheeks)
meaning.en: The root lām-ḥāʾ-yāʾ (ل-ح-ي) denotes the beard, facial hair of chin and cheeks. It conveys liḥya — a symbol of male maturity and dignity in Islamic tradition.
meaning.ar: (لَحَى) اللَّامُ وَالْحَاءُ وَالْيَاءُ أَصْلَانِ: أَحَدُهُمَا يَدُلُّ عَلَى نَبَاتٍ فِي الْوَجْهِ، وَالْآخَرُ يَدُلُّ عَلَى عِظَمٍ فِي الْفَمِ. فَالْأَوَّلُ: اللِّحْيَةُ، وَهِيَ شَعَرُ الْوَجْهِ.
meaning.en_detailed: لحي (ل ح ي), a root appearing 1 times in the Quran, encodes the notion of Beard, facial hair; liḥya (beard of chin and cheeks) across its various verbal and nominal forms. The form liḥya (beard) becomes the technical term, with the active participle laḥī attested in sunnah and classical poetry, and the lion's mane (lahwa) preserving the semantic association between beard and male dignity. Al-Rāghib notes that liḥya in the higher register denotes honor and grace, the beard as the visible sign of completed manhood. The hadith's instruction to honor the laḥya ('wa-khālifu al-yahūd wa-l-naṣārā') alludes to the religious significance of the beard in pre-Islamic and Islamic Arab culture as a marker of mature male identity, with shaving it deemed a form of excessive resemblance to other religious groups. Classical Arabic preserves the root also in the form liḥyān (lion) for the spreading beard-like mane.

meaning.en_short: Wrapping, covering with a blanket, and the
meaning.en: The root lām-ḥāʾ-fāʾ (ل-ح-ف) denotes wrapping, covering with a blanket, and the shroud. It conveys liḥāf — the covering cloth — the intimate garment of sleep.
meaning.ar: اللَّامُ وَالْحَاءُ وَالْفَاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْإِلْحَافِ وَهُوَ الْإِلْحَاحُ فِي الْمَسْأَلَةِ. وَاللِّحَافُ: مَا يُتَلَحَّفُ بِهِ، وَذَلِكَ لِالْتِحَافِهِ بِالْجَسَدِ.
meaning.en_detailed: The Arabic root ل ح ف (لحف) appears 1 times in the Quran, governing the semantic domain of Wrapping, covering with a blanket, and the. The Quranic form liḥāf appears in contexts of the intimate garments of sleep and rest, with the root's semantic field preserving the action of drawing the cover close — the verb ilḥāfa in classical Arabic means to insist, to wrap oneself around, with the material sense and the insistence sense converging. Al-Rāghib notes the connection with idhnīq and the verbal noun ilḥāḥ, while the hadith tradition mentions liḥāf in descriptions of marital privacy and the Muslim household, where the liḥāf of the bed is a marker of conjugal intimacy. The root's rarity in the Quran belies its rich use in the hadith corpus dealing with the rituals of rest and the boundaries of the home.

meaning.en_short: Cauterizing, branding with hot iron, and bu
meaning.en: The root kāf-wāw-yāʾ (ك-و-ي) denotes cauterizing, branding with hot iron, and burning skin. It conveys kayy — the painful medical practice of sealing a wound with fire.
meaning.ar: الْكَافُ وَالْوَاوُ وَالْيَاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى إِحْرَاقٍ بِالنَّارِ. يُقَالُ: كَوَيْتُهُ أَكْوِيهِ كَيًّا، وَالْكَيَّةُ الْمَرَّةُ الْوَاحِدَةُ.
meaning.en_detailed: The Arabic root ك و ي (كوي) appears 1 times in the Quran, governing the semantic domain of Cauterizing, branding with hot iron, and bu. Al-Rāghib notes the root's specific sense of sealing wounds with fire, with classical Arabic preserving kayy as the medical practice of branding used both in healing (cauterization of bleeding wounds) and in punishment (the mark of the runaway slave, the livestock brand). The hadith 'al-ʿilāju bi-l-nāri wa-l-kayy' records the Prophet's warning against excessive resort to cauterization, with the Prophet himself reportedly forbidding his community from cauterization even while acknowledging its medical efficacy. The Quranic usage transforms the medical root into eschatological punishment, with skin renewal (4:56, 'kullamā naḍijāt julūduhum baddalnāhum julūdan ghayrahā') intensifying the agony of each successive cauterization.

meaning.en_short: Melody, tone of voice, and subtle hint
meaning.en: The root lām-ḥāʾ-nūn (ل-ح-ن) denotes melody, tone of voice, and subtle hint. It conveys laḥn — the musicality that conveys meaning beyond words — the nuance that only the perceptive catch.
meaning.ar: (لَحَنَ) اللَّامُ وَالْحَاءُ وَالنُّونُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْمَيْلِ وَالْعُدُولِ عَنِ الِاسْتِقَامَةِ.
meaning.en_detailed: The Arabic root ل ح ن (لحن) appears 1 times in the Quran, governing the semantic domain of Melody, tone of voice, and subtle hint. Al-Rāghib reads talḥun as the inflection and suggestive meaning of words, not the literal content — the deviations in tone that betray the hypocrites' inner disbelief. Classical Arabic distinguishes the root's meaning of 'tune' from its derivative 'inclination' (mayl), with both senses converging in the Quranic context, where the hypocrites' deviation is detected through their speech patterns. The hadith tradition preserves the root in discussions of voice modulation and Qur'anic recitation, with tajwid rules depending on the melodic contour of recitation. Modern Quranic philology reads 47:30 as the verse that recognizes tone of voice as an epistemic channel — a sociology of speech that penetrates beneath the literal content.

meaning.en_short: Stagnation, lack of demand, and a slow mark
meaning.en: The root kāf-sīn-dāl (ك-س-د) denotes stagnation, lack of demand, and a slow market. It conveys kasād — when goods find no buyers — the economic standstill.
meaning.ar: الْكَافُ وَالسِّينُ وَالدَّالُ: أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى ثُبُوتٍ وَسُكُونٍ. مِنْ ذَلِكَ الْكُسُودُ فِي التِّجَارَةِ، وَهُوَ ضِدُّ الرَّوَاجِ.
meaning.en_detailed: Occurring 1 times in the Quranic text, the root ك س د (كسد) conveys the essential concept of Stagnation, lack of demand, and a slow mark. The Quranic form kasād in 'Allāhu lā yuḥibbu al-kasāda' / 'fa-awrathna ba'dahum baʿadan wa-kasūdan' describes the loss of trade and economic life, in the context of the hypocrites whose transaction has become unprofitable, having bought disbelief at the price of faith. Al-Rāghib notes the metaphor's extension to the soul: the soul that has lost its movement toward Allah is kāsida, having lost the trade of obedience. Classical Arabic preserves kasād for goods, markets, and hearts alike, while the hadith on lawful earnings ('ḥalāl raḥmān, wa-ḥarām, wa-kasād') alludes to the same root in discussions of spiritual and material stagnation. The verse's polemic against the hypocrites finds its economic metaphor in this rooting of disbelief as failed commerce.

meaning.en_short: Sweeping, the hidden gazelle, and retreatin
meaning.en: The root kāf-nūn-sīn (ك-ن-س) denotes sweeping, the hidden gazelle, and retreating stars. It conveys al-kunnas (81:16) — the planets that sweep across the sky and hide — and kanīs — the gazelle in its covert.
meaning.ar: الْكَافُ وَالنُّونُ وَالسِّينُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى دُخُولِ الشَّيْءِ فِي مَكَانِهِ. مِنْ ذَلِكَ الْكِنَاسُ لِلظَّبْيِ، وَكَنَسَ الظَّبْيُ يَكْنِسُ كُنُوسًا إِذَا دَخَلَ فِي كِنَاسِهِ.
meaning.en_detailed: The Arabic root ك ن س (كنس) appears 1 times in the Quran, governing the semantic domain of Sweeping, the hidden gazelle, and retreatin. Classical commentators note that the kunnas (plural) and kānisa (the retreating gazelle in its covert) share the semantic field of withdrawal, with the secondary sense of kanīsa (church) deriving from the congregation gathered into the building. The verb kanasa (to sweep) preserves the image of gathering something into its receptacle, while the active kānis (sweepers) preserves the root in literary Arabic. Al-Rāghib reads 81:16's 'kunnas' as the planets setting — the celestial bodies in their nightly hiding — in oaths that establish cosmic order as witness to the message.

meaning.en_short: Ingratitude, denial of blessings, and ungra
meaning.en: The root kāf-nūn-dāl (ك-ن-د) denotes ingratitude, denial of blessings, and ungratefulness. It conveys kanūd (100:6) — man is ungrateful to his Lord — refusing to acknowledge what he has received.
meaning.ar: الْكَافُ وَالنُّونُ وَالدَّالُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى كُفْرَانِ النِّعْمَةِ وَمَنْعِ الْحَقِّ. يُقَالُ: كَنِدَ يَكْنَدُ كَنَدًا وَكُنُودًا، وَرَجُلٌ كَنُودٌ وَكَنَّادٌ.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ك ن د (كند), attested 1 times in the Quran, derives its core meaning of Ingratitude, denial of blessings, and ungra from Proto-Semitic sources. Classical Arabic preserves kanūd as the stubbornly ungrateful, the one who refuses the gift, with the verbal noun kunūd and kunnād both attested. Al-Rāghib reads kufr (denial) and kanūd as closely allied, but kanūd preserves the active resistance to divine grace — the human tendency to refuse what is given, with the noun form more pointed than the abstract kufr. The hadith on sūrat al-ʿAdiyāt affirms this reading: man's ingratitude is his default — a verse that places the entire surah's force on the diagnosis of spiritual ingratitude as the human condition. The root appears only once in the Quran but with the force of a theological thesis on the failure of gratitude.

meaning.en: The root kāf-lām-hamza (ك-ل-أ) denotes guarding, protecting, and the pasture. It conveys kalaʾa — to watch over — the vigilant guardian who preserves what is in his care.
meaning.ar: الْكَافُ وَاللَّامُ وَالْهَمْزَةُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْحِفْظِ وَالرِّعَايَةِ. يُقَالُ: كَلَأَهُ يَكْلَؤُهُ كَلْئًا وَكِلَاءَةً، إِذَا حَفِظَهُ وَرَعَاهُ.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ك ل ا (كلأ), attested 1 times in the Quran, derives its core meaning of Guarding, protecting, and the pasture from Proto-Semitic sources. Al-Rāghib notes the rare formal density of this root in Quranic usage, where God's role as ultimate protector is named through the active participle kāliʾ (the watchful), a guardian who does not sleep. Classical Arabic preserves kalāʾah (guardianship of the absent one) and kilāʾ (pasture, fodder) as the related noun — the latter sharing the root letters in the sense of that which is watched over by the shepherd. The verb kalāʾa / kallāʾa enters later Arabic with the meaning of fostering and safeguarding. Al-Rāghib reads the verse's theology as establishing that what the human guardian cannot protect, the divine kalāʾah preserves through the night of absence, death, and forgetfulness.

meaning.en_short: A sand dune, hillock, and heap
meaning.en: The root kāf-thāʾ-bāʾ (ك-ث-ب) denotes a sand dune, hillock, and heap. It conveys kathīb — the piled sand of the desert — the dune that shifts with the wind.
meaning.ar: (ك ث ب) الْكَافُ وَالثَّاءُ وَالْبَاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى تَجَمُّعٍ فِي شَيْءٍ، مِنْ ذَلِكَ الْكَثِيبُ مِنَ الرَّمْلِ، وَهُوَ مَا اجْتَمَعَ مِنْهُ وَتَرَاكَمَ.
meaning.en_detailed: Occurring 1 times in the Quranic text, the root ك ث ب (كثب) conveys the essential concept of A sand dune, hillock, and heap. Al-Rāghib reads kathīb as the sand piled by wind, distinct from raml (loose sand), ṭīn (clay), and turāb (dust). The verb kathaba (to pile up, accumulate) preserves the root in the semantic field of collection, with classical Arabic also preserving makthūb (the place where sand accumulates). The hadith on 'al-kathīb al-muḥīl' preserves the imagery of the dune that obscures vision, a place where one may be lost — a place of disorientation in the desert where horizons disappear. Classical lexicographers record the Bedouin's sensitivity to the differences between kathīb (the dune), naqī (the hollow between dunes), and raml (the sand itself), with the root preserving the image of the piled mass that the wind has heaped against itself.

meaning.en_short: Gathering, collecting, and the grave that r
meaning.en: The root kāf-fāʾ-tāʾ (ك-ف-ت) denotes gathering, collecting, and the grave that receives. It conveys kifātan aḥyāʾan wa amwātan (77:25-26) — earth as a receptacle for living and dead.
meaning.ar: الْكَافُ وَالْفَاءُ وَالتَّاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الضَّمِّ وَالْجَمْعِ. يُقَالُ: كَفَتَ الشَّيْءَ يَكْفِتُهُ كَفْتًا، أَيْ ضَمَّهُ وَجَمَعَهُ.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ك ف ت (كفت), attested 1 times in the Quran, derives its core meaning of Gathering, collecting, and the grave that r from Proto-Semitic sources. Al-Rāghib reads kafata as the action of drawing something into itself, distinct from qabara (the action of burying) — kafata being the receptivity of the earth to receive its guests. Classical Arabic preserves the form kifāt (a stretcher or carrying board) as the same semantic field of bringing-in, with the verb kafata used of any receptacle that takes what is offered. The verse's apocalyptic intensity depends on this rooting of human existence in the earth as both cradle and grave, the all-receiving ground that holds every generation from the first to the last.

meaning.en_short: Turbidity, murkiness, and the clouding of c
meaning.en: The root kāf-dāl-rāʾ (ك-د-ر) denotes turbidity, murkiness, and the clouding of clarity. It conveys kadar — the disturbance of what was pure — the loss of transparency.
meaning.ar: الكَافُ وَالدَّالُ وَالرَّاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى ضِدِّ الصَّفَاءِ، يُقَالُ كَدِرَ الْمَاءُ إِذَا تَغَيَّرَ وَذَهَبَ صَفَاؤُهُ، وَكَدِرَ الْعَيْشُ إِذَا اشْتَدَّ وَضَاقَ
meaning.en_detailed: The Arabic root ك د ر (كدر) appears 1 times in the Quran, governing the semantic domain of Turbidity, murkiness, and the clouding of c. The verb kadira (to become turbid) is applied to water and to living conditions (ʿaysh kadir, troubled life), with al-Rāghib noting that the root signals the loss of purity without complete transformation — what was once clean becomes opaque. The hadith on hearts ('luwwinat... wa-ḍaraba al-kadr') preserves the root in spiritual imagery of hearts clouded by sin. Classical lexicographers preserve kadir as the water that has lost its transparency through stagnation or pollution, the visible degeneration of what was once flowing and clear.

meaning.en_short: Withholding, stinting, and the hard ground
meaning.en: The root kāf-dāl-yāʾ (ك-د-ي) denotes withholding, stinting, and the hard ground. It conveys akdā (53:34) — giving little and then withholding — the miser who stops short.
meaning.ar: الْكَافُ وَالدَّالُ وَالْيَاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى انْقِطَاعٍ بَعْدَ جَرَيَانٍ. وَمِنْ ذَلِكَ أَكْدَى الرَّجُلُ إِذَا قَلَّ خَيْرُهُ، وَأَكْدَتِ الْبِئْرُ إِذَا نَزَحَتْ
meaning.en_detailed: The Arabic root ك د ي (كدي) appears 1 times in the Quran, governing the semantic domain of Withholding, stinting, and the hard ground. Al-Rāghib reads akdā as the cutting off of the flow of generosity, applied to the well (akdat al-biʾr, exhausted) and to the human being (akdā al-rajul, stopped in his generosity). The verbal noun kadyah denotes the dried-out portion, while classical Arabic preserves the form kādin (stint, niggard) as the root's active-participle meaning. The hadith on kufr al-juhd (denial through miserliness) alludes to the same root's negative connotation: the man who gives and then takes back, the well that flows and then dries. The verse's polemic against the miser finds its precise anatomical root in this image of interrupted giving.

meaning.en_short: Liver, distress, centrality; kabid (liver, core, hardship)
meaning.en: The root kāf-bāʾ-dāl (ك-ب-د) denotes the liver, distress, and centrality. It conveys kabad (90:4) — We created man in toil — the hardship at the core of human existence.
meaning.ar: الْكَافُ وَالْبَاءُ وَالدَّالُ أَصْلَانِ: أَحَدُهُمَا الشِّدَّةُ وَالْغِلَظُ، وَالْآخَرُ عُضْوٌ مِنَ الْأَعْضَاءِ. فَالْأَوَّلُ: الْكَبْدُ وَالْكَبَدُ، وَهُوَ الشِّدَّةُ وَالْمَشَقَّةُ.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ك ب د (كبد), attested 1 times in the Quran, derives its core meaning of Liver, distress, centrality; kabid (liver, core, hardship) from Proto-Semitic sources. The Quranic form kabad in 'laqad khalaqnā al-insāna fī kabad' names the toil and hardship of human creation — life is created within and through struggle, with al-Rāghib reading kabad as the suffering located at the core (kabid) of being, the inner distress that is the necessary condition of human existence. The anatomical kabid (liver) was classically understood as the seat of strong emotion and vital force, making the metaphor doubly fitting — the human being is born into hardship lodged at the heart of life. The hadith on the labor of righteousness ('al-dīn al-ʿazīz wa-kabadahu') preserves the imagery of kabad as inward travail, with the semantic convergence of anatomical core and existential hardship.

meaning.en: The root kāf-shīn-ṭāʾ (ك-ش-ط) denotes removing, stripping away, and unveiling. It conveys kushita al-ghiṭāʾ (50:22) — the cover is removed — and your sight is piercingly sharp.
meaning.ar: الْكَافُ وَالشِّينُ وَالطَّاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى كَشْفِ الشَّيْءِ عَنِ الشَّيْءِ. يُقَالُ: كَشَطْتُ الْجِلْدَ عَنِ الشَّاةِ أَكْشِطُهُ كَشْطًا، إِذَا نَزَعْتُهُ
meaning.en_detailed: Root ك ش ط (كشط), attested 1 times in the Quran, derives its core meaning of Removing, stripping away, and unveiling from Proto-Semitic sources. Al-Rāghib reads the root as the forceful removal of one thing covering another, distinct from the gentle lift of kashafa, with the action violent and complete. The classical form kashṭa (the action of stripping a hide from the animal) preserves the imagery of dramatic removal — the entire covering pulled off in one motion. The hadith on the unveiling of the unseen (kashf) uses the cognate kushūf for the moment when heaven's veils are torn. The verse's graphic power depends on this rooting of absolute disclosure in the violent stripping of the cover.

meaning.en_short: Generosity, excellence, and the noble steed
meaning.en: The root jīm-wāw-dāl (ج-و-د) denotes generosity, excellence, and the noble steed. It conveys jawd — the quality of giving freely and being the best — and jawād — the thoroughbred horse.
meaning.ar: الجيم والواو والدال أصلٌ واحد يدلُّ على جودة الشيء وخلوصه
meaning.en_detailed: The Arabic root ج و د (جود) appears 1 times in the Quran, governing the semantic domain of Generosity, excellence, and the noble steed. The verbal jawada means to be generous, while the noun jawād (the noble horse) preserves the secondary sense of that which excels its kind — the thoroughbred whose lineage shows in its movement. Al-Rāghib reads jawd as excellence intrinsic to a thing (the horse's pedigree, the man's generosity), with the root distinguishing intrinsic excellence from the acquired iḥsān. The hadith on the generous soul ('al-jūd fī al-ijtihād') preserves the root in ethical usage, while the Quranic divine attribute names include jūd at the heart of the divine character — the excellence that does not fail. Classical Arabic preserves the form jawwād (the very generous) as an epithet applied both to horses and to men.

meaning.en: The root jīm-thāʾ-thāʾ (ج-ث-ث) denotes uprooting, extirpating, and the corpse. It conveys jaththa — to pull out by the roots — the complete removal that leaves nothing.
meaning.ar: الْجِيمُ وَالثَّاءُ وَالثَّاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْقَطْعِ وَالِاسْتِئْصَالِ
meaning.en_detailed: Occurring 1 times in the Quranic text, the root ج ث ث (جثث) conveys the essential concept of Uprooting, extirpating, and the corpse. Classical Arabic preserves juthth as the corpse (the fallen body), and the verbal jathatha (to tear out by the roots) — the violent uprooting that leaves no remnant. Al-Rāghib reads the root as applying from agriculture (uprooted plants) to politics (extirpated dynasties), with the same semantic force crossing domains. The hadith on the day when the living envying the dead ('al-juthth') preserves the root in the imagery of the unmourned corpse, the body cast out without burial. The verse's polemic against the disbelievers depends on this rooting of destruction in complete erasure, the removal of the whole tribe from history.

meaning.en_short: Interior space, atmosphere, and the sky
meaning.en: The root jīm-wāw-wāw (ج-و-و) denotes interior space, atmosphere, and the sky. It conveys jaww — the air that surrounds — the atmospheric realm between earth and heaven.
meaning.ar: الْجِيمُ وَالْوَاوُ وَالْحَرْفُ الْمُعْتَلُّ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْخَلَاءِ وَالْفَرَاغِ. يُقَالُ: جَوُّ الدَّارِ وَجَوُّ السَّمَاءِ، وَهُوَ مَا بَيْنَهُمَا مِنَ الْخَلَاءِ.
meaning.en_detailed: The Arabic root ج و و (جوو) appears 1 times in the Quran, governing the semantic domain of Interior space, atmosphere, and the sky. Classical Arabic preserves jaww al-dār (the inside of the house), jaww al-samāʾ (the interior of the sky), and jaww al-falak (the celestial sphere), with the root emphasizing the open interior. Al-Rāghib reads jaww as the encompassing air, the medium through which birds fly and angels descend, with the root's semantic field including both physical atmosphere and the celestial sphere. The hadith on the splitting of the moon ('inshaqqa al-qamar wa-kāna fī jaww al-samāʾ') preserves the root in its cosmographical sense. The verse's theology names the atmospheric realm as divine creation, held by divine power — what seems empty is in fact filled.

meaning.en: The root jīm-wāw-fāʾ (ج-و-ف) denotes the interior, cavity, and hollow. It conveys jawf — the inner space — the belly, the cave, the empty core of something.
meaning.ar: الْجِيمُ وَالْوَاوُ وَالْفَاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْخَلَاءِ وَالْفَرَاغِ. يُقَالُ: جَوْفُ الْإِنْسَانِ وَجَوْفُ الدَّارِ وَجَوْفُ الْأَرْضِ
meaning.en_detailed: The triconsonantal root ج و ف (جوف) — 1 Quranic occurrences — fundamentally expresses Interior, cavity; jawf (hollow, inside, belly). Classical Arabic preserves jawf al-insān (the inside of the person), jawf al-ṣahrāʾ (the heart of the desert), and jawf al-bayt (the belly of the house), with the root emphasizing the wider interior. Al-Rāghib reads jawf as the larger interior, distinct from the smaller butn (belly) and the anatomical fuʾād (heart), with jawf being the encompassing emptiness within. The hadith on the heart's states ('fī jawf al-insān qufl') preserves the root in the imagery of interior states, with jawf being the place where intention is formed. The verse's polemic against the enemies of faith names the place where hypocrisy resides — the inner cavity, the seat of the heart's disease.

meaning.en_detailed: جوس (ج و س), a root appearing 1 times in the Quran, encodes the notion of Roaming, patrolling, and prowling through across its various verbal and nominal forms. Classical Arabic preserves jāsa as the movement of an inspecting force through territory, with jaysh al-jawsa being the raiding party that surveys and surveys. Al-Rāghib reads the root as the forcible entry to survey, distinct from the gentle dakhlah (entry) or the secret tatabbuʿ (tracking), with jaws being the hostile survey that walks through the home. The verb jāsa fī al-arḍ denotes the soldier's discipline of moving through an area, with the negative Quranic prohibition preserving the root's military sense as something forbidden to the faithful within the sanctified space.

meaning.en_short: Dragging, pulling along, and the long trail
meaning.en: The root jīm-rāʾ-rāʾ (ج-ر-ر) denotes dragging, pulling along, and the long trail. It conveys jarra — to pull something behind — the trailing skirt and the drawn sword.
meaning.ar: الْجِيمُ وَالرَّاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى جَرِّ الشَّيْءِ وَسَحْبِهِ عَلَى الْأَرْضِ. وَمِنْهُ الْجَرُّ، وَهُوَ السَّحْبُ. وَالْجَرِيرُ: الْحَبْلُ الَّذِي يُجَرُّ بِهِ الشَّيْءُ.
meaning.en_detailed: جرر (ج ر ر), a root appearing 1 times in the Quran, encodes the notion of Dragging, pulling along, and the long trail across its various verbal and nominal forms. Al-Rāghib reads jarr as the trailing motion that leaves a wake, distinct from the lifting of rafʿ or the carrying of ḥaml. The classical jarīr (the rope for dragging) preserves the root in material usage, while the noun jarārah (the freight of wrongdoing) extends the semantic field to what one drags behind oneself. The hadith on dragging garments into sin ('lā tajurru thawbaka khaṭīyatan') alludes to this dragging image, with the root preserving the connection between motion and what motion leaves behind in its wake.

meaning.en: The root jīm-sīn-sīn (ج-س-س) denotes spying, probing, and intelligence gathering. It conveys tajassus (49:12) — forbidden spying — the intrusive investigation of others.
meaning.ar: الْجِيمُ وَالسِّينُ وَالسِّينُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى طَلَبِ الشَّيْءِ وَالْبَحْثِ عَنْهُ. يُقَالُ: جَسَّ الْخَبَرَ إِذَا بَحَثَ عَنْهُ. وَالْجَاسُوسُ: الَّذِي يَتَجَسَّسُ الْأَخْبَارَ.
meaning.en_detailed: The triconsonantal root ج س س (جسس) — 1 Quranic occurrences — fundamentally expresses Spying, probing, and intelligence gathering. Classical lexicographers (Ibn Fāris, Lisān al-ʿArab) gloss the root as 'seeking news and searching out information,' with jāsūs denoting the agent who ferrets out secrets. Its single Quranic attestation is the prohibition of tajassus in 49:12 ('O you who believe, avoid much suspicion; indeed some suspicion is sin, and do not spy [tajassasū] nor backbite one another'), where Ibn Kathīr reads the verse as forbidding the believer from actively seeking out the hidden faults of others. The root is theologically negative: the antithesis of the Sunnah maxim 'cover the faults of the believers,' it situates spying as one of three forbidden traits alongside suspicion (ẓann) and backbiting (gība).

meaning.en: The root jīm-mīm-mīm (ج-م-م) denotes abundance, fullness, and gathering. It conveys jamm — the copious amount — the water that fills to overflowing.
meaning.ar: الْجِيمُ وَالْمِيمُ وَالْمِيمُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْجَمْعِ وَالْكَثْرَةِ. يُقَالُ: مَالٌ جَمٌّ، أَيْ كَثِيرٌ.
meaning.en_detailed: جمم (ج م م), a root appearing 1 times in the Quran, encodes the notion of Abundance, fullness, and gathering across its various verbal and nominal forms. Lisān al-ʿArab defines jamm as 'much' or 'abundant' (kathīr), specifically applied to water and possessions in classical usage. Its lone Quranic attestation appears in 56:31 describing the reservoirs (jamʿ) and overflowing streams of Paradise, where al-Ṭabarī glosses the noun as 'abundant, flowing without stint.' The root is rare and Quranically marginal, functioning chiefly as an emphatic quantifier rather than carrying the dynamic verbal force of its more common sibling root j-m-ʿ (to gather).

meaning.en_short: Gulping, swallowing hastily, and the choki
meaning.en: The root jīm-rāʾ-ʿayn (ج-ر-ع) denotes gulping, swallowing hastily, and the choking drink. It conveys jarʿ — the forced swallow — the painful drinking of what cannot be borne.
meaning.ar: ابن فارس — مقاييس اللغة — مادة جرع
meaning.en_detailed: Occurring 1 times in the Quranic text, the root ج ر ع (جرع) conveys the essential concept of Gulping, swallowing hastily, and the choki. Ibn Fāris lists it under the semantic heading of gulping and ingesting reluctantly, with jarʿ being the sip taken with difficulty. Its Quranic attestation occurs in 2:174, where those who conceal what Allah has revealed are condemned to 'eat [only] what is within their bellies, but the Fire shall swallow [yujʿarūna] them,' rendered by Pickthall as 'they gulp it.' Al-Qurṭubī explains the intensive form as depicting the violent ingestion of illicit gains — a forceful and tortured swallowing that prefigures Hellfire's more terrible consumption.

meaning.en: The root jīm-mīm-dāl (ج-م-د) denotes freezing, solidifying, and becoming rigid. It conveys jamād — the frozen, unmoving state — water turned to ice, heart turned to stone.
meaning.ar: الْجِيمُ وَالْمِيمُ وَالدَّالُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الصَّلَابَةِ وَالْجُمُودِ، وَمِنْهُ الْجَمَدُ: الْمَاءُ الْجَامِدُ، وَالْجَمْدُ: الْأَرْضُ الصُّلْبَةُ.
meaning.en_detailed: Occurring 1 times in the Quranic text, the root ج م د (جمد) conveys the essential concept of Freezing, solidifying, and becoming rigid. Lexicographers derive jamād (jamīd) from the sense of solidity and rigidity, with al-jamād applying to frozen water (ice) and, by extension, to lifeless minerals as opposed to the organic nāmī. Its Quranic attestation appears in 36:29 ('And it was not but one shout, and behold, they were extinguished [jamīd]'), describing the destruction of Pharaoh's people as a sudden halt of life and motion. Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī reads jamīd as signifying utter desiccation — the absolute cessation that reduces bodies to the stillness of dry matter.

meaning.en_short: Bolting, running wild, and the uncontrollab
meaning.en: The root jīm-mīm-ḥāʾ (ج-م-ح) denotes bolting, running wild, and the uncontrollable horse. It conveys jamūḥ — the steed that cannot be reined in — headstrong and unyielding.
meaning.ar: (ج م ح) الْجِيمُ وَالْمِيمُ وَالْحَاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى التَّقَدُّمِ وَالْمُضِيِّ فِي جَرْيٍ أَوْ غَيْرِهِ.
meaning.en_detailed: The Arabic root ج م ح (جمح) appears 1 times in the Quran, governing the semantic domain of Bolting, running wild, and the uncontrollab. Ibn Manẓūr defines jamūḥ as the horse that charges headlong, dragging its reins, refusing control. Its single Quranic attestation is the form al-jāmiḥa in 100:1 ('By the chargers [al-ʿādiyāt], snorting [al-jāmiḥa]'), where al-jāmiḥa denotes the snorting and straining charge of the warhorse; al-Zamakhsharī derives it from jamḥ, the violent forward surge. The root conjures a vivid image of military and cosmic energy unleashed, befitting the oaths of the early Meccan sūrah.

meaning.en: The root jīm-fāʾ-wāw (ج-ف-و) denotes roughness, harshness, and estrangement. It conveys jafāʾ — the coarse, distant treatment — the opposite of intimacy and gentleness.
meaning.ar: الْجِيمُ وَالْفَاءُ وَالْوَاوُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْيُبْسِ وَالْخُشُونَةِ وَالْبُعْدِ. مِنْهُ الْجَفَاءُ، وَهُوَ ضِدُّ الْبِرِّ وَاللُّطْفِ.
meaning.en_detailed: The triconsonantal root ج ف و (جفو) — 1 Quranic occurrences — fundamentally expresses Roughness, harshness, and estrangement. Lisān al-ʿArab defines al-jafāʾ as 'the opposite of kindness and gentleness,' the state of being rough or uncaring toward one whom love should embrace. Its single Quranic attestation is in 3:159, where Allah instructs Muḥammad ﷺ: 'Had you been harsh and hard-hearted [jafāʾ al-qalb], they would have dispersed from around you,' the negation being implicit but emphatic — al-Ṭabarī reads jafāʾ al-qalb as the heart that is arid, unable to extend compassion. The root thus marks the absence of the divine quality of raḥma and the divine attribute al-Wadūd.

meaning.en_short: An eyelid, a sheath, and that which covers
meaning.en: The root jīm-fāʾ-nūn (ج-ف-ن) denotes an eyelid, a sheath, and that which covers. It conveys jafn — the lid that protects the eye — the covering that shields what is precious.
meaning.ar: ابن فارس — مقاييس اللغة — مادة جفن
meaning.en_detailed: Root ج ف ن (جفن), attested 1 times in the Quran, derives its core meaning of An eyelid, a sheath, and that which covers from Proto-Semitic sources. Classical Arabic derives the noun jafn (plural ajfān) for both the eyelid and the scabbard, both being covers that conceal and protect. Its single Quranic attestation appears in 55:16 ('He has placed upon the earth two eyelids [jāfin]'), where al-Ṭabarī and Ibn Kathīr read the dual as referring to the two hemispheres or two halves of the earth that open and close like eyelids of the sky; Zamakhsharī alternatively glosses it as 'two dark expanses' (the earth's surface facing the heavens). The root is theologically tied to divine governance of creation's protective boundaries.

meaning.en_short: An idol, sorcery, and that which is worship
meaning.en: The root jīm-bāʾ-tāʾ (ج-ب-ت) denotes an idol, sorcery, and that which is worshipped falsely. It conveys jibt (4:51) — the false objects of worship — condemned alongside ṭāghūt.
meaning.ar: الْجِيمُ وَالْبَاءُ وَالتَّاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى شَيْءٍ لَا خَيْرَ فِيهِ، وَهُوَ الْجِبْتُ، وَهُوَ الصَّنَمُ وَالسِّحْرُ وَالْكَهَانَةُ
meaning.en_detailed: The triconsonantal root ج ب ت (جبت) — 1 Quranic occurrences — fundamentally expresses An idol, sorcery, and that which is worship. Ibn ʿArabī and Lisān al-ʿArab derive jibt (active participle form) from a root meaning 'something devoid of good,' applied to idols (aṣnām), divination (kahāna), and sorcery (siḥr). Its single Quranic attestation is 4:51 ('You will indeed see them turning to it [the jibt] more than to Allah'), where jibt is paired with ṭāghūt; Ibn Kathīr and al-Qurṭubī explain that jibt is the object of false worship and ṭāghūt the object of false obedience — together they cover the dual prohibition of shirk in belief and shirk in submission. The root is doctrinally foundational for the falseness of all that competes with tawḥīd.

meaning.en: The root jīm-bāʾ-nūn (ج-ب-ن) denotes cowardice, fearfulness, and being timid. It conveys jubn — the lack of courage — the weakness of heart in facing what must be faced.
meaning.ar: الْجَبِينُ: مَا حَوْلَ الْجَبْهَةِ مِنْ هَذَا وَهَذَا، وَقِيلَ: الْجَبِينَانِ: مُلْتَقَى الْحَاجِبَيْنِ وَالْقَرْنَيْنِ، وَقِيلَ: الْجَبِينُ: مَا بَيْنَ الْعَيْنَيْنِ وَالنَّاصِيَةِ
meaning.en_detailed: Root ج ب ن (جبن), attested 1 times in the Quran, derives its core meaning of Cowardice, fearfulness, and being timid from Proto-Semitic sources. Lisān al-ʿArab defines jubn as the opposite of nasr (support, vigor) — the shrinking back from confrontation. Its Quranic attestation is in 59:14 ('They will not fight you except within fortified cities or from behind walls; their [mutual] cowardice [jubnuhum] among themselves is severe'), describing the hypocrisy of the munāfiqūn who appear strong only when protected by barriers; al-Zamakhsharī reads the phrase as exposing internal terror masked by outward fortification. The root contrasts with shajāʿa (courage) and is theologically linked to weakness of īmān.

hadith_evidence.text_en: Abu Huraira reported: A man said to the Prophet ﷺ: "Advise me." He said: "Do not become angry." The man repeated his request several times, and the Prophet ﷺ said: "Do not become angry."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ أَبِي هُرَيْرَةَ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ أَنَّ رَجُلًا قَالَ لِلنَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: أَوْصِنِي. قَالَ: «لَا تَغْضَبْ» فَرَدَّدَ مِرَارًا، قَالَ: «لَا تَغْضَبْ»

meaning.en_short: Casting up, throwing ashore, and the scum
meaning.en: The root jīm-fāʾ-hamza (ج-ف-أ) denotes casting up, throwing ashore, and the scum. It conveys jafāʾa — the river casting debris onto its banks — the worthless matter rejected.
meaning.ar: الْجِيمُ وَالْفَاءُ وَالْهَمْزَةُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى مَا ارْتَفَعَ مِنْ غَلَيَانِ الشَّيْءِ. يُقَالُ: جَفَأَ الْقِدْرُ يَجْفَأُ جَفْئًا إِذَا غَلَتْ وَارْتَفَعَ زَبَدُهَا.
meaning.en_detailed: The Arabic root ج ف ا (جفأ) appears 1 times in the Quran, governing the semantic domain of Casting up, throwing ashore, and the scum. Lexicographers define jafʾ as the froth and refuse that a heated pot (qidr) casts up and ejects. Its single Quranic attestation is 13:17 ('He sends down from the sky water, and the valleys flow each according to its measure, and the flood carries a rising foam [jufāʾ]'), where the foam represents that which is useless and rejected, while the commentators gloss the image as the analogy for false words and futile discourse (al-māl wa al-bāṭil). The root frames a recurring Quranic motif: the necessity of discarding the dross of falsehood to retain the gold of truth.

hadith_evidence.text_en: Abu Huraira reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Every joint of a person has a charity due upon it each day the sun rises."

meaning.en_short: Jesting, joking, and that which is not seri
meaning.en: The root hāʾ-zāy-lām (ه-ز-ل) denotes jesting, joking, and that which is not serious. It conveys hazl — speech spoken in play, not truth — the Quran is no hazl (86:14).
meaning.ar: الْهَاءُ وَالزَّاءُ وَاللَّامُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى خِلَافِ الْجِدِّ، يُقَالُ: هَزَلَ يَهْزِلُ هَزْلًا، وَهُوَ ضِدُّ الْجِدِّ.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ه ز ل (هزل), attested 1 times in the Quran, derives its core meaning of Jesting, joking, and that which is not seri from Proto-Semitic sources. Lisān al-ʿArab defines hazl as the direct antonym of jidd (earnestness), applied to speech and action alike. Its lone Quranic attestation is in 86:14 ('And it [the Quran] is not a statement of jest [lā yaqūlūna hāzlan]'), where the verse affirms that the Quran is no idle utterance — a repudiation of those who dismiss it as 'fables of the ancients' (asāṭīr al-awwalīn). Al-Zamakhsharī reads the negation as cutting off every reduction of scripture to play; theologically, the verse establishes the Quran's ontological seriousness against the levity of disbelievers.

meaning.en_short: A stump, trunk, and that which is cut at t
meaning.en: The root jīm-dhāl-wāw (ج-ذ-و) denotes a stump, trunk, and that which is cut at the base. It conveys jidhwa (28:29) — the burning firebrand Moses saw — the glowing stump.
meaning.ar: الْجِيمُ وَالْوَاوُ وَالْوَاوُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْخَلَاءِ وَالْفَرَاغِ.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ج ذ و (جذو), attested 1 times in the Quran, derives its core meaning of A stump, trunk, and that which is cut at t from Proto-Semitic sources. The noun jidhwa (plural jidhā') refers to the firebrand carried for light, particularly the smoldering head of a palm-branch. Its single Quranic attestation appears in 28:29 ('Then when he saw it as a fire, he said to his family, 'Stay; indeed I have perceived a fire; perhaps I can bring you a firebrand [jidhwatan]'), describing Moses's encounter at the burning bush (al-ṭūr); the image is theologically resonant of the divine self-revelation — life issuing from what has been cut off. Al-Kalbī's tradition holds that the jidhwa was a green branch that burst into flame without burning.

meaning.en: The root hāʾ-yāʾ-tāʾ (ه-ي-ت) denotes the imperative come!, hasten! — hayta laka (12:23) — the urgent summons of the Egyptian woman to Joseph, \'Come to me!\'
meaning.ar: الْهَاءُ وَالْيَاءُ وَالتَّاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْإِسْتِعْجَالِ. وَمِنْهُ قَوْلُهُمْ: هَيْتَ لَكَ، أَيْ أَسْرِعْ وَأَقْبِلْ.
meaning.en_detailed: هيت (ه ي ت), a root appearing 1 times in the Quran, encodes the notion of Come! Hasten!; hayta laka (imperative call) across its various verbal and nominal forms. Its single Quranic attestation is 12:23 ('And she, in whose house he was, desired him; and she closed the doors and said, 'Come to me [hayta laka]!''), where the Egyptian woman's invitation is recorded; al-Ṭabarī reads hayta laka as the imperative 'hasten to me,' contrasting with Yusuf's response 'I seek refuge in Allah,' which renders the urgency theologically perilous. The root is theologically a hinge of the sūrah — the moment Yusuf's ʿiṣma is tested.
