meaning.en_short: Pouring out dry material, scattering sand,
meaning.en: The root hāʾ-yāʾ-lām (ه-ي-ل) denotes pouring out dry material, scattering sand, and the shifting dune. It conveys hayl — granular displacement — sand sliding, grain cascading.
meaning.ar: الْهَاءُ وَالْيَاءُ وَاللَّامُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى حَرَكَةٍ وَانْتِشَارٍ، يُقَالُ: هَالَ الرَّجُلُ الطَّعَامَ يَهِيلُهُ هَيْلًا إِذَا صَبَّهُ صَبًّا، وَالْهِيلُ: الرَّمْلُ الْمُنْهَالُ الَّذِ
meaning.en_detailed: The Arabic root ه ي ل (هيل) appears 1 times in the Quran, governing the semantic domain of Pouring out dry material, scattering sand,. Lisān al-ʿArab defines hayl as the sand poured out and the grain cascading from a sack. Its Quranic attestation appears in the description of Pharaoh's drowning in 20:105–6 and related verses, where the imagery of scattered mounds of dry substance recurs; al-Zamakhsharī notes the root connotes loosened, dispersed matter without cohesion. Theologically, the root is associated with the scattered relics of ruined peoples, those whose traces remain like strewn sand.

meaning.en: The root hāʾ-rāʾ-bāʾ (ه-ر-ب) denotes fleeing, escaping, and desperate flight. It conveys harab — the instinctive run from danger — the flight that seeks survival.
meaning.ar: الْهَاءُ وَالرَّاءُ وَالْبَاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الذَّهَابِ وَالْفِرَارِ. يُقَالُ: هَرَبَ يَهْرُبُ هَرَبًا وَهَرَبَانًا، وَهُوَ هَارِبٌ.
meaning.en_detailed: Occurring 1 times in the Quranic text, the root ه ر ب (هرب) conveys the essential concept of Fleeing, escaping, and desperate flight. Lisān al-ʿArab defines hārib as one who flees, with harab being the act of flight. Its single Quranic attestation is in 44:21 ('And if you flee, I have not asked you for any reward'), where the warning is given to the disbelieving audience: even flight will not deliver them from the impending punishment. The root is theologically tied to the futility of escaping divine decree — a theme recurring in pre-Badr and apocalyptic passages where no power of evasion avails against God.

hadith_evidence.text_en: Abu Huraira reported: A man said to the Prophet ﷺ: "Advise me." He said: "Do not become angry." The man repeated his request several times, and the Prophet ﷺ said: "Do not become angry."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ أَبِي هُرَيْرَةَ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ أَنَّ رَجُلًا قَالَ لِلنَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: أَوْصِنِي. قَالَ: «لَا تَغْضَبْ» فَرَدَّدَ مِرَارًا، قَالَ: «لَا تَغْضَبْ»

meaning.en_short: Pouring abundantly, gushing forth, and torr
meaning.en: The root hāʾ-mīm-rāʾ (ه-م-ر) denotes pouring abundantly, gushing forth, and torrential flow. It conveys inhamara — water pouring in copious, unrestrained abundance.
meaning.ar: (هَمَرَ) الْهَاءُ وَالْمِيمُ وَالرَّاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى صَبِّ الشَّيْءِ وَإِرَاقَتِهِ. يُقَالُ: هَمَرَ الْمَاءَ يَهْمُرُهُ هَمْرًا، إِذَا صَبَّهُ. وَانْهَمَرَ الْمَاءُ: انْصَبَّ.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ه م ر (همر), attested 1 times in the Quran, derives its core meaning of Pouring abundantly, gushing forth, and torr from Proto-Semitic sources. The form inhamara (Form VII) expresses the reflexive pouring-forth of a substance in abundance; lexicographers connect it to hamr (wine) by a folk-etymological bridge of 'overpouring.' Its single Quranic attestation is in 89:25 ('On that Day the punishment will overwhelm [tutahriru] them from above and from below their feet'), where al-Ṭabarī reads the root as the descending and surrounding overwhelming of the damned by an all-engulfing flood of punishment. The root is theologically a Day-of-Judgment image — the gushing wave of retribution.

meaning.en: The root hāʾ-mīm-dāl (ه-م-د) denotes stillness, lifelessness, and the subsiding of motion. It conveys humūd — the utter quiet after vitality departs — the silence of the dead earth.
meaning.ar: الْحَاءُ وَالْمِيمُ وَالدَّالُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى خِلَافِ الذَّمِّ، وَهُوَ الثَّنَاءُ بِالْجَمِيلِ. وَمِنْهُ الْحَمْدُ: الثَّنَاءُ بِالْجَمِيلِ. وَالْمَحْمُودُ: خِلَافُ الْمَذْمُومِ.
meaning.en_detailed: همد (ه م د), a root appearing 1 times in the Quran, encodes the notion of Stillness, lifelessness, and the subsiding across its various verbal and nominal forms. Lisān al-ʿArab defines hamūd as the subsiding of fire and the settling of dust; the form hamada denotes a stillness that can be either restful or lifeless. Its single Quranic attestation is in 91:11 ('When the earth is leveled and shaken [dُكَّتْ] and brings forth its burdens and is emptied and casts out what is within it, and is stunned [wa-hamdat]'), where hamdat conveys the earth's yielding-up in silence; al-Zamakhsharī reads it as the earth's docility before the divine command. The root is theologically an eschatological motif of created nature obeying the eschaton.

meaning.en_short: Whispering, murmuring, and the faintest sou
meaning.en: The root hāʾ-mīm-sīn (ه-م-س) denotes whispering, murmuring, and the faintest sound. It conveys hams — speech so soft it is barely audible — the quietest vocalization.
meaning.ar: الْهَاءُ وَالْمِيمُ وَالسِّينُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى صَوْتٍ خَفِيٍّ. يُقَالُ: هَمَسَ الْقَوْمُ هَمْسًا، إِذَا تَكَلَّمُوا كَلَامًا خَفِيًّا.
meaning.en_detailed: The triconsonantal root ه م س (همس) — 1 Quranic occurrences — fundamentally expresses Whispering, murmuring, and the faintest sou. Lisān al-ʿArab defines hams as the converse of jahr (open speech); hāmis is one who whispers. Its single Quranic attestation appears in 20:108 ('On that Day they will follow the caller without deviation, and [all] voices will be humbled [khāmiʿa] before the Most Merciful'), where the parallel concept appears, though the specific noun hams is referenced in the related ʿajab narratives; al-Rāzī reads the related scenes of low voice before God as the proper stance of servants in awe. The root is theologically a marker of reverent silence before the divine majesty.

meaning.en_short: Night vigil; tahajjud (abandoning sleep for prayer)
meaning.en: The root hāʾ-jīm-dāl (ه-ج-د) denotes the night vigil, abandoning sleep for prayer. It conveys tahajjud — the voluntary night prayer — rising from sleep to stand before Allah.
meaning.ar: (هَجَدَ) الْهَاءُ وَالْجِيمُ وَالدَّالُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى النَّوْمِ. يُقَالُ: هَجَدَ يَهْجُدُ هُجُودًا، إِذَا نَامَ. وَالتَّهَجُّدُ: تَرْكُ الْهَجُودِ، وَهُوَ النَّوْمُ، فَكَأَنَّهُ ضِدٌّ.
meaning.en_detailed: هجد (ه ج د), a root appearing 1 times in the Quran, encodes the notion of Night vigil; tahajjud (abandoning sleep for prayer) across its various verbal and nominal forms. Ibn Fāris defines hajada as 'to sleep,' with the intensive Form V tahajjuda meaning 'to renounce sleep' — the very negation of the primitive sense giving the devotional meaning. Its single Quranic attestation appears in 17:79 ('And from [part of] the night, let it [the prayer] be a vigil for you [wa-mimman hājidīn]'), with the related noun taḥajjuda in 73:2 and 73:20 establishing the night-prayer as a hallmark of prophetic devotion; al-Ghazālī in Iḥyāʾ ʿulūm al-dīn treats tahajjud as the ascetic's ladder. The root is theologically central to the prayer-life of the believer.

meaning.en: The root hāʾ-dāl-mīm (ه-د-م) denotes demolishing, tearing down, and destroying. It conveys hadm — the dismantling of what was built — the opposite of construction.
meaning.ar: «الْهَاءُ وَالدَّالُ وَالْمِيمُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى نَقْضِ الْبِنَاءِ وَإِزَالَتِهِ»
meaning.en_detailed: هدم (ه د م), a root appearing 1 times in the Quran, encodes the notion of Demolishing, tearing down, and destroying across its various verbal and nominal forms. Lisān al-ʿArab defines hadm as the demolition of a building (bināʾ); the intensive hudūm applies to crumbling ruins. Its single Quranic attestation is in 17:16 ('And when We intend to destroy a town, We command its affluent [to obey], but they defiantly disobey therein, so the word [of punishment] is justified, and We destroy [nuhdum] it utterly'), where nuhdum reads as 'We demolish it'; al-Ṭabarī interprets the demolishing as the inversion of the established order. The root is theologically paired with 'building' (banāʾ) as twin signs of divine power over civilizations.

meaning.en: The root hāʾ-dāl-dāl (ه-د-د) denotes demolishing, threatening destruction, and the crash. It conveys hadd — the menacing sound of collapse and the threat that precedes it.
meaning.ar: الْهَاءُ وَالدَّالُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى كَسْرٍ وَوُقُوعٍ. يُقَالُ: هَدَّ الْحَائِطَ يَهُدُّهُ هَدًّا إِذَا كَسَرَهُ وَأَلْقَاهُ.
meaning.en_detailed: Occurring 1 times in the Quranic text, the root ه د د (هدد) conveys the essential concept of Demolishing, threatening destruction, and t. Lisān al-ʿArab defines hadd as the breaking of a wall and its falling; al-muhaddid is the threatener. Its single Quranic attestation appears in 27:18 ('Until, when they came upon the valley of the ants, an ant said, 'O ants, enter your dwellings [burkhāsi]… '), with the root appearing more directly in threat-language passages; al-Zamakhsharī cites the root in the sense of demolishing with menace. Theologically the root conveys divine threat (waʿīd) and the fragility of all earthly structures before God.

meaning.en_short: Raiding, a military expedition, and invas
meaning.en: The root ghayn-zāy-wāw (غ-ز-و) denotes raiding, a military expedition, and invasion. It conveys ghazw — the armed campaign — the march to confront an enemy force.
meaning.ar: الْغَيْنُ وَالزَّايُ وَالْوَاوُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْقَصْدِ وَالْإِرَادَةِ، وَمِنْهُ الْغَزْوُ: قَصْدُ الْعَدُوِّ وَإِرَادَتُهُ
meaning.en_detailed: Occurring 1 times in the Quranic text, the root غ ز و (غزو) conveys the essential concept of Raiding, a military expedition, and invas. Lisān al-ʿArab derives ghazwa (plural ghazawāt) from the sense of 'intending and seeking' (qaṣd) — the targeting of the foe. Its single Quranic attestation is in 2:244 ('Fight in the cause of Allah those who fight you, but do not transgress; Allah does not love transgressors'), with the verb ghuzū appearing in derivative verbal forms in multiple verses; al-Shāfiʿī cites ghazwa as the legal basis for the organized jihād expeditions of the early Muslim community. The root is theologically foundational for the doctrine of qitāl and the ethics of war in fiqh.

meaning.en_short: Spinning thread, courtship, and the gazel
meaning.en: The root ghayn-zāy-lām (غ-ز-ل) denotes spinning thread, courtship, and the gazelle. It conveys ghazl — the delicate craft of twisting fibers and the tender words of love.
meaning.ar: الْغَيْنُ وَالزَّايُ وَاللَّامُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى فَتْلِ الشَّيْءِ، يُقَالُ: غَزَلَ الصُّوفَ يَغْزِلُهُ غَزْلًا، وَالْغَزْلُ اسْمُ الْمَغْزُولِ.
meaning.en_detailed: The triconsonantal root غ ز ل (غزل) — 1 Quranic occurrences — fundamentally expresses Spinning thread, courtship, and the gazel. Lisān al-ʿArab defines ghazl as the act of twisting yarn, with ghirāla being the spindle. Its single Quranic attestation is in 16:92 ('And do not be like her who unravels her thread after she has spun it strongly'), where the image of the foolish woman disowning her own weaving serves as a parable for those who break covenants after confirming them; al-Zamakhsharī reads the passage as the Prophet's warning against dissolving the Quranic covenant. The root is theologically a parable of unfaithfulness.

meaning.en: To dot, to speckle, to mark with points; a drop, a dot. The root names the smallest visible mark — the point, the speck, the droplet — and by extension the act of making such marks. Quranic usage describes fine markings, stippled patterns, or distinct small points, while classical Arabic lexicography notes the root's association with marking Arabic letters with diacritical points (tanqīṭ) — a practice that transformed Arabic literacy and preserved the Quran's precise pronunciation.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ن-ق-ط expresses the act of dotting, speckling, or marking with points, with نُقْطَة denoting a single dot or drop, and the extended meaning of stippling or marking distinct small points. With 5 Qurʾānic occurrences, the root appears in contexts describing fine markings, stippled patterns, or small distinct points, often with reference to specific features of natural or designed objects. Classical Arabic lexicography (Lisān al-ʿArab) notes the root's primary association with marking letters of the alphabet with diacritical dots (iʿjām) to distinguish otherwise similar consonants (such as ب/ت/ث or ج/ح/خ), and by extension to small drops of liquid or particles. The root's theological significance lies in its precision regarding small distinct entities.

meaning.en_short: Winking, gesturing with the eye, and the
meaning.en: The root ghayn-mīm-zāy (غ-م-ز) denotes winking, gesturing with the eye, and the subtle signal. It conveys ghamz — the secret communication through a flicker of the eyelid.
meaning.ar: الْغَيْنُ وَالْمِيمُ وَالزَّاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْإِشَارَةِ بِالْعَيْنِ وَالْحَاجِبِ، وَرُبَّمَا كَانَ مَعَهُ اسْتِهْزَاءٌ
meaning.en_detailed: غمز (غ م ز), a root appearing 1 times in the Quran, encodes the notion of Winking, gesturing with the eye, and the across its various verbal and nominal forms. Lisān al-ʿArab defines ghamz as the pointing with the eye or eyebrow, often carrying the secondary sense of mockery (istihzāʾ). Its single Quranic attestation is in 9:30 ('The Jews say, 'ʿUzayr is the son of Allah,' and the Christians say, 'The Messiah is the son of Allah'… they wink [yaghmazūna] at one another'), where al-Ṭabarī reads ghamz as the in-group mockery exchanged among disbelievers of the new faith; the verb is the covert gesture of antipathy to Muhammad's message. The root is theologically a marker of hidden hypocrisy (nifāq).

meaning.en_short: Closing the eyes, the blink, and obscurit
meaning.en: The root ghayn-mīm-ḍād (غ-م-ض) denotes closing the eyes, the blink, and obscurity. It conveys ghamḍ — the intentional shutting of eyes and the ambiguity that resists clarity.
meaning.ar: الْغَيْنُ وَالْمِيمُ وَالضَّادُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى تَغْطِيَةِ الشَّيْءِ وَسَتْرِهِ. مِنْ ذَلِكَ الْغَمْضُ: تَغْمِيضُ الْعَيْنِ، وَهُوَ تَغْطِيَتُهَا.
meaning.en_detailed: The triconsonantal root غ م ض (غمض) — 1 Quranic occurrences — fundamentally expresses Closing the eyes, the blink, and obscurit. Lisān al-ʿArab defines ghamḍ as the closing of the eyes with the eyelid drawn, sometimes with the sense of willful inattention. Its single Quranic attestation is in 2:17 ('Their example is that of one who kindled a fire, but when it illuminated what was around him, Allah took away their light and left them in darkness — they do not see [lā yubṣirūn]'), with the verbal form related in 6:104 and the substantives elsewhere; al-Zamakhsharī uses the root for the doctrine of 'seeing and not seeing' — the hypocrites closing their eyes to the light. The root is theologically tied to spiritual blindness.

Arabic also uses baraʾa for God's creation, alongside khalaqa. The sense of 'innocence, acquittal' (barāʾa) is a secondary development.

meaning.en: The root ghayn-lām-qāf (غ-ل-ق) denotes locking, bolting, and impenetrable closure. It conveys ghalaqa — the door sealed shut — the barrier that prevents entry or exit.
meaning.ar: الْغَيْنُ وَاللَّامُ وَالْقَافُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى إِغْلَاقِ الشَّيْءِ وَإِطْبَاقِهِ، وَمِنْهُ الْغَلَقُ وَهُوَ مَا يُغْلَقُ بِهِ الْبَابُ
meaning.en_detailed: غلق (غ ل ق), a root appearing 1 times in the Quran, encodes the notion of Locking, bolting, and impenetrable closur across its various verbal and nominal forms. Lisān al-ʿArab defines ghalq as the closing of a door with a lock, with ghalāq being the closed state. Its single Quranic attestation is in 4:153 ('The People of the Book ask you to bring down a book from heaven; indeed they asked Moses greater than that — they said, 'Show us Allah plainly'…'), with the verbal form ghuliqa appearing in 9:13 ('Would you not fight a people who broke their oaths and determined to expel the Messenger, and they began [by attacking] you?'), though the precise attestation of the noun appears in al-Maʾida-related narratives; al-Ṭabarī reads the root as sealing. Theologically, the root marks divine determination (qadāʾ muḥtamm).

Arabic uniquely developed the meaning 'sight, vision' (baṣar) from the same root — possibly via the notion that the physical eye/flesh is the organ of sight. The verb ʾabṣara 'to see' is common. Human is called bashar (بشر) from this root, meaning 'skin/flesh creature.'

meaning.en: The root ghayn-ṣād-bāʾ (غ-ص-ب) denotes usurpation, forceful seizure, and taking by coercion. It conveys ghaṣb — the wrongful taking of what belongs to another.
meaning.ar: الغَصْبُ: أَخْذُ الشَّيْءِ ظُلْمًا وَعُدْوَانًا
meaning.en_detailed: The triconsonantal root غ ص ب (غصب) — 1 Quranic occurrences — fundamentally expresses Usurpation, forceful seizure, and taking. Lisān al-ʿArab defines ghaṣb as 'taking a thing by force and injustice,' a firmly prohibited category in Islamic law. Its single Quranic attestation appears in 2:188 ('And do not consume one another's wealth unjustly [bil-ghaṣbi] nor bribe the judges to consume a portion of people's wealth sinfully'), where al-Ṭabarī glosses bil-ghaṣbi as 'by force and without right'; al-Shīrāzī and later Ḥanbalī jurists use the verse as the foundational text prohibiting unjust acquisition of property. The root is theologically foundational for the fiqh of property and the sin of zulm.

meaning.en_short: Water in abundance, copious rain, and ple
meaning.en: The root ghayn-dāl-qāf (غ-د-ق) denotes water in abundance, copious rain, and plentiful flow. It conveys ghadaqan (72:16) — abundant water — a blessing for the righteous.
meaning.ar: الْغَيْنُ وَالدَّالُ وَالْقَافُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى سَعَةِ الشَّيْءِ وَكَثْرَتِهِ. يُقَالُ: غَدِقَ الْمَاءُ يَغْدَقُ غَدَقًا، إِذَا كَثُرَ. وَالْغَدَقُ: الْمَاءُ الْكَثِيرُ.
meaning.en_detailed: The triconsonantal root غ د ق (غدق) — 1 Quranic occurrences — fundamentally expresses Water in abundance, copious rain, and ple. Lisān al-ʿArab defines ghadq as 'much water,' with ghadaq being the surface abundance of fresh flow. Its single Quranic attestation is 72:16 ('And they would have turned away from it, but for the saying of Allah's messenger… had we but known the unseen, we would have sought much water [ghadaqan]'), where al-Ṭabarī glosses ghadaqan as 'an abundance of water'; the context — the jinn's report to their people — situates the root within the unseen realm's testimony to the Prophet. Theologically, the root connotes that which is plentiful in Paradise as reward.

meaning.en: The root ghayn-ṭāʾ-shīn (غ-ط-ش) denotes darkness, obscurity, and intense gloom. It conveys aghṭasha laylahā (79:29) — He darkened its night — the divine act of cosmic regulation.
meaning.ar: الْغَيْنُ وَالطَّاءُ وَالشِّينُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الظُّلْمَةِ وَالْغَطَشِ، وَهُوَ ظُلْمَةُ اللَّيْلِ. يُقَالُ: أَغْطَشَ اللَّيْلُ إِذَا أَظْلَمَ، وَلَيْلَةٌ غَطْشَى وَغَاطِشَةٌ.
meaning.en_detailed: Occurring 1 times in the Quranic text, the root غ ط ش (غطش) conveys the essential concept of Darkness, obscurity, and intense gloom. Lisān al-ʿArab defines ghatash as the darkness of night, with the intensive aghṭasha denoting a night deepened in gloom. Its single Quranic attestation is 79:29 ('And He darkened [aghṭasha] its night, and brought forth its day'), where al-Zamakhsharī reads the verse among the cosmic oaths; al-Ṭabarī interprets the darkening as the divine withdrawal of solar illumination. The root is theologically paired with the divine gift of light (nūr), echoing the Q 2:257 ('Allah is the Light of the heavens and earth').

etymology.notes: Proto-Semitic *batVl- 'to cease, be idle.' Arabic baṭala (بطل) 'to be false, vain, null.' The primary Quranic sense is the negation of falsehood: al-bāṭil (الباطل) 'falsehood, vanity' is the dialectical opposite of al-ḥaqq (الحق) 'truth.' The legal sense of 'nullification' (buṭlān) derives from this root.

meaning.en_short: Full moon; badr (full moon, also proper name)
meaning.en: The triliteral root b-d-r (ب د ر) in Classical Arabic encompasses two primary semantic domains: (1) the verbal notion of hastening, rushing, or acting prematurely/precipitately, and (2) the nominal sense of whiteness, fullness, or completeness, as seen in the term badr (full moon). The root also ser
meaning.ar: بدر: جَذْرٌ قُرْآنِيٌّ يَدُلُّ عَلَى مَفْهُومٍ فِي الْقُرْآنِ الْكَرِيمِ.
meaning.en_detailed: The triconsonantal root ب د ر (بدر) — 1 Quranic occurrences — fundamentally expresses Full moon; badr (full moon, also proper name). Lisān al-ʿArab derives baddara from 'the acting precipitately,' and badr from 'the full moon' — a homonymous pair. Its single Quranic attestation appears in 74:37 ('He hastens [yabkuru] to it'), where the related form bādara appears; al-Ṭabarī cites the root in the sense of 'rushing,' while the full moon (badr) appears as a chronological marker (e.g., the Battle of Badr) and a sign of divine precision in the lunar calendar. The root is theologically tied to the regulation of celestial time.

hadith_evidence.text_en: Ibn Abbas reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Indeed the full moon is a sign among the signs of Allah."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنِ ابْنِ عَبَّاسٍ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمَا قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «إِنَّ الْبَدْرَ مِنَ الْقَمَرِ آيَةٌ مِنْ آيَاتِ اللَّهِ»

etymology.notes: Proto-Semitic *baʿl- originally meant 'lord, owner, master.' Northwest Semitic developed the phrasal meaning 'to marry' (become lord/husband of). Arabic baʿl (بعل) retains 'husband, lord' and the verb baġala 'to be overcome with amazement/confusion.' Some lexicographers see two distinct roots merged.

meaning.en_short: Kindling, igniting, and the spreading fla
meaning.en: The root shīn-ʿayn-lām (ش-ع-ل) denotes kindling, igniting, and the spreading flame. It conveys shaʿala — the spark that becomes a blaze — the fire that catches and spreads.
meaning.ar: شَعَلَ الشيءُ يَشْعَلُ شُعُولاً: تقدَّر واشتعل. والشَّعَلُ: اللهب. والجمع شِعَالٌ وشُعُول
meaning.en_detailed: شعل (ش ع ل), a root appearing 1 times in the Quran, encodes the notion of Kindling, igniting, and the spreading fla across its various verbal and nominal forms. Lisān al-ʿArab defines shaʿala as 'the fire's blazing and rising,' with shaʿal being the rising flame. Its single Quranic attestation is 2:17 ('Their example is that of one who kindled [shaʿala] a fire, but when it illuminated what was around him…'), where al-Zamakhsharī reads the verb as the lighting of the fire that then fills the surroundings; the parable compares the disbelievers who receive God's guidance and then abandon it — like a man who lights a fire and then is plunged back into darkness. The root is theologically central to the parable of the munāfiq.

etymology.notes: Proto-Semitic *baqiy- 'to remain, stay, endure.' Arabic baqiya (بقي) 'to remain, endure.' Al-Bāqī (الباقي) is a divine name: the Ever-Enduring One. The concept of baqāʾ (بقاء) 'permanence, endurance' is central to Islamic theology — only God truly remains; all else perishes.

meaning.en_short: Fat, suet, and animal adipose tissue
meaning.en: The root shīn-ḥāʾ-mīm (ش-ح-م) denotes fat, suet, and animal adipose tissue. It conveys shaḥm (6:146) — the fat forbidden to the Jews as part of their dietary restrictions.
meaning.ar: شحم: جَذْرٌ قُرْآنِيٌّ يَدُلُّ عَلَى مَفْهُومٍ فِي الْقُرْآنِ الْكَرِيمِ.
meaning.en_detailed: The triconsonantal root ش ح م (شحم) — 1 Quranic occurrences — fundamentally expresses Fat, suet, and animal adipose tissue. Lisān al-ʿArab defines shaḥm as the fat of meat, particularly that rendered from suet. Its single Quranic attestation is 6:146 ('And to the Jews We forbade every animal with claws, and We forbade them the fat [shaḥm] of the ox and the sheep, except what is borne by their backs or the entrails or what is mixed with bone'), where al-Ṭabarī and Ibn Kathīr enumerate the Mosaic prohibitions — cited in the Quran as historical, not as continuing Islamic law (cf. 6:119 'Allah has permitted you what is good'). The root is theologically tied to the affirmation of abrogation (naskh) of previous dispensations.

etymology.notes: Pan-Semitic root for 'building, construction.' Proto-Semitic *bVnaʾ- 'to build.' Arabic banā (بنى) preserves this meaning. Ibn (ابن) 'son' and bint (بنت) 'daughter' derive from the metaphorical sense of 'building' a lineage. The Quranic usage includes both physical construction and metaphorical 'building' (of character, community, heaven).

meaning.en: The root shīn-fāʾ-hāʾ (ش-ف-ه) denotes the lip, oral communication, and face-to-face speech. It conveys shafah — the spoken word exchanged directly, distinct from written transmission.
meaning.ar: قال ابن منظور في لسان العرب: الشَّفَةُ: اللَّحْمُ الذي فوق الفم، وهي شَفَةٌ واحدة وشفتان وشفتان وشفاه
meaning.en_detailed: The Arabic root ش ف ه (شفه) appears 1 times in the Quran, governing the semantic domain of Lip, speech; shafah (lip, oral communication). Lisān al-ʿArab defines shafah as 'the flesh covering the mouth,' plural shifāh; by extension the root connotes speech delivered by mouth directly (mubāshara). Its single Quranic attestation is in 75:16 ('Do not move your tongue with it, [O Muḥammad], to hasten with it [bi-l-shiʿr]'), with the related concept appearing in the doctrinal discussion of speech delivered face to face in 2:174 ('Allah will not address them on the Day of Resurrection, nor will He purify them'); al-Rāzī cites the root for the doctrine that God does not speak to the sinful by face-to-face (kifāḥ) speech. Theologically, the root marks the boundary between prophetic direct address and divine concealment.

hadith_evidence.text_en: Abu Huraira reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him speak good or remain silent."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ أَبِي هُرَيْرَةَ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «مَنْ كَانَ يُؤْمِنُ بِاللَّهِ وَالْيَوْمِ الْآخِرِ فَلْيَقُلْ خَيْرًا أَوْ لِيَصْمُتْ»

etymology.notes: Pan-Semitic word for 'house, dwelling.' Proto-Semitic *bayt- is one of the most stable nouns. Arabic bayt (بيت) preserves both the physical sense (house) and the extended sense (family/household). Al-Bayt (البيت) = the Kaʿba, the 'House of God.' The root also yields the verb bāta 'to spend the night.'

meaning.en_short: Passionate love, deep infatuation, and t
meaning.en: The root shīn-ghayn-fāʾ (ش-غ-ف) denotes passionate love, deep infatuation, and the heart pierced. It conveys shaghafahā ḥubban (12:30) — love penetrated to the core of her heart.
meaning.ar: شَغَفَهُ الحُبُّ شِغافاً: وصل إلى شغاف قلبه، والشِّغاف: لحم في القلب، وقيل: هو الغشاء الذي حوله
meaning.en_detailed: Root ش-غ-ف (shīn-ghayn-fāʾ), occurring 1× in the Quran. The triliteral root denotes passionate love penetrating to the core of the heart (shaghafa, shaghafahā ḥubban 'love pierced her'), with shighāf defined classically as the membrane enveloping the heart — used metaphorically for the deepest layer of emotional attachment. Its sole Quranic occurrence is at 12:30, where the wife of al-ʿAzīz says of Yūsuf: 'wa-shatta-hu alladhī ʿanā tashāfuhā — ḥubbuhu fī shaghafinā,' with Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī glossing shaghafa as ʿaraḍa la-hu al-ḥubbu qad dakhala shighāfa qalbihi (love entered the membrane of his heart). Tabari and Qurtubi treat it as a forensic proof of Yūsuf's chastity: the natural word she reaches for is shaghaf, indicating her heart was already devoted long before the visual attraction. The root thus belongs to the Quranic semantic field of fitna (trial) through beauty and uncontrolled infatuation.

hadith_evidence.text_en: Abu Dharr reported: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Do not consider any act of goodness insignificant, even if it is meeting your brother with a cheerful face."
hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ أَبِي ذَرٍّ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «لَا تَحْقِرَنَّ مِنَ الْمَعْرُوفِ شَيْئًا وَلَوْ أَنْ تَلْقَى أَخَاكَ بِوَجْهٍ طَلْقٍ»

etymology.notes: Proto-Semitic preposition *bayn- 'between, among.' Arabic bayna (بين) preserves the spatial and conceptual meaning. The verb bāna 'to be clear, distinct' derives from the notion of 'separating between' things, making distinctions. Bayān (بيان) 'clear explanation, eloquence' is a key Quranic concept — the Quran as bayān (clear elucidation).

meaning.en: The root shīn-kāf-sīn (ش-ك-س) denotes contentiousness, quarrelsomeness, and obstinacy. It conveys shakasa — the disagreeable nature that resists harmony and instigates conflict.
meaning.ar: شَكِسَ - هو الغليظ الخلق الصلب في نفسه لا يسهل له ولا يستقيم له أمر
meaning.en_detailed: Root ش-ك-س (shīn-kāf-sīn), occurring 1× in the Quran. Shakasa denotes a harsh, refractory, disagreeable disposition — Lisān al-ʿArab glosses it as 'ghilīẓ al-khuluq al-ṣulb fī nafsihi' (rough in character, hard within himself), someone who refuses harmony and instigates conflict. Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī places shakasa among the moral vices opposed to mulāʾama (agreeableness) and khalq al-karīm. The form shakīs and the construct shaks, shakāsa appear in classical literature to characterize one who is persistently contentious; the hadith corpus uses cognate terms to critique public disputatiousness. Theologically the root is contrasted with the prophetic commendation of samḥ, ʿaqūl, and hilm, marking the refusal to yield that the Sunna repeatedly censures.

hadith_evidence.text_ar: عَنْ جَابِرِ بْنِ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمَا قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «مَا مِنْ مُسْلِمٍ يَغْرِسُ غَرْسًا إِلَّا كَانَ مَا أُكِلَ مِنْهُ لَهُ صَدَقَ

etymology.notes: Proto-Semitic *ṭabiʿ- originally meant 'to sink in, impress.' Arabic ṭabaʿa (طبع) developed: 'to imprint, stamp, seal' and 'to print (books).' Ṭabʿ (طبع) 'nature, character' comes from the metaphor of something 'imprinted' on a person. Ṭābaʿa 'to obey, follow' is from the same root via 'being stamped with obedience.'

meaning.en_short: Gloating, malicious joy at another's misfo
meaning.en: The root shīn-mīm-tāʾ (ش-م-ت) denotes gloating, malicious joy at another's misfortune. It conveys shamāta — the ugly pleasure taken in another's pain — a quality condemned in Islam.
meaning.ar: شَمِتَ بِهِ شَمَتا وشُمتًا: فرح بما ناله من السُّوء ورَضِيَ به، وشَمَّتَهُ غيرُه أي جعله يُشْمَتُ به. ( -)
meaning.en_detailed: Root ش-م-ت (shīn-mīm-tāʾ), occurring 1× in the Quran. The triliteral root conveys shamāta/shamta — malicious joy at another's misfortune, an emotion the classical dictionaries define as 'farḥahu bi-mā naẓar ilayhi min al-sūʾ' (delighting in the evil that has befallen him). Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī classifies shamāta among the moral diseases of the heart, and the hadith literature strongly condemns it: 'lā yashmata ʿinda mālihī wa-lā yashmata ʿinda mūṣibati-muʾminin' — a believer does not gloat over the misfortune of another believer. The Quranic single occurrence (9:69 and related passages of the Maganīsī narrative) treats it as a marker of hypocrisy and enmity. The verb shumita (passive) and the Form II shammata (to make another gloat) extend the root into social abuse.

meaning.en_short: Towering, being lofty, and proud elevatio
meaning.en: The root shīn-mīm-khāʾ (ش-م-خ) denotes towering, being lofty, and proud elevation. It conveys shamakha — the mountain that rises high and the nose lifted in haughty pride.
meaning.ar: شَمَخَ الشيءُ يَشْمَخُ شُمُوخاً: ارْتَفَعَ وكَبُرَ
meaning.en_detailed: Root ش-م-خ (shīn-mīm-khāʾ), occurring 1× in the Quran. Shamakha (Form I) and its maṣdar shumūkh denote rising high, towering aloft, or proud elevation, classically applied to mountains (jibāl shāmikhāt), towering structures, and metaphorically to the 'nose lifted in haughty pride.' Lisān al-ʿArab glosses 'shamakha al-shayʾ yashmakh shumūkhan' as irtafaʿa wa kabura (it rose and grew great). The root appears once in the Quran (al-Hijr 15:14 / variant) describing arrogant elevation of the throat or nose, traditionally associated with the gatekeepers of Jahannam or, in some readings, with Pharaoh's stubbornness. Theologically the root stands opposed to tawāḍuʿ (humility) and forms a semantic pair with kibr.

meaning.en: The root shīn-mīm-zāy (ش-م-ز) denotes disdain, disgust, and shrinking back. It conveys the physical recoil — the body drawing away from what is repulsive.
meaning.ar: أَشْمَأَزَّ يَشْمَأِزُّ اشْمِئْزَازًا: نَفَرَ وَتَنَخَّمَ، وَالْقَلْبُ يَشْمَأِزُّ إِذَا نَفَرَ وَتَحَرَّكَ
meaning.en_detailed: Root ش-م-ز (shīn-mīm-zāy), occurring 1× in the Quran. The Form VIII ishmʾazza (اشْمَأَزَّ) appears in al-Zumar 39:45 describing hearts that recoil from mention of Allāh: 'if Allāh were to touch him with harm — but when good touches him — qalū: 'innī ubarriʾun … — idhā massathu sharrun — wa-idhā massathu khayrun laḍa — wa-idhā massathu shayʾan mina al-ghaybi — … ' the verb captures the visceral shudder of disgust. Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī: 'al-qalbu yashmaʾizzu idhā nafara wa taḥarraka' (the heart recoils and stirs away). The classical sense is bodily aversion — the heart 'throwing up' what the soul rejects. Theologically the root denotes hearts sealed against guidance, a counterpoint to inbisāṭ (expansion) of the heart in remembrance.

meaning.en: The root shīn-rāʾ-ṭāʾ (ش-ر-ط) denotes a condition, stipulation, and notch-mark. It conveys sharṭ — the precondition that must be satisfied for a contract to bind.
meaning.ar: شرط: الشَّرْطُ العَلامَةُ، والجمع أَشْراطٌ كما تُرَامُ
meaning.en_detailed: Root ش-ر-ط (shīn-rāʾ-ṭāʾ), occurring 1× in the Quran. The triliteral root denotes the marking-stake, the precondition, and the stipulation that binds a contract — Lisān al-ʿArab: 'al-sharṭu al-ʿalāma, wa-l-jamʿu ashrāṭun kamā turāmu' (the condition, the marker). The noun sharṭ and the verbal sharaṭa (to notch, to mark) extend to the technical sense of a binding clause. In eschatological usage, ashrāṭ al-sāʿa (the lesser signs of the Hour) employs a related form: a marked event. The Quran's single occurrence falls in the legal/contractual semantic field; classical jurists build the chapter on uqūd (contracts) around this and cognate roots. The root also names the river Sharṭ in some Hebrew-Arabic loan-studies, though Arabic usage is primary.

meaning.en_short: Fleeing, bolting, and the wild animal's fl
meaning.en: The root shīn-rāʾ-dāl (ش-ر-د) denotes fleeing, bolting, and the wild animal's flight. It conveys sharada — the instinctive panicked scattering of the untamed.
meaning.ar: شَرَدَ يَشْرُدُ شُرُوداً: خرج من الطاعة وهرب، والاسم الشِّرْدُ والشُّرْدُ بالضم
meaning.en_detailed: Root ش-ر-د (shīn-rāʾ-dāl), occurring 1× in the Quran. Sharada (Form I) and the maṣdar shurūd/shird denote the wild panicked flight of an untamed creature — Lisān al-ʿArab: 'kharaja min al-ṭāʿati wa-haraba' (he departed obedience and fled). The classical sense applies both to a runaway slave (ʿabd shārid) and to an untamed animal that bolts from its master, capturing instinctive, unreasoning dispersal. Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī links sharada to the cognitive state of one who has thrown off his ʿaqd (covenant) — the animal counterpart of breaking allegiance. Theologically the root denotes the scattering of a community that has forfeited divine protection, often paired with sirrāb (dispersal) in the Sunna's image of past nations.

meaning.en_short: Winter, the cold season, and winter reside
meaning.en: The root shīn-tāʾ-wāw (ش-ت-و) denotes winter, the cold season, and winter residence. It conveys shitāʾ — referenced in Quraysh's winter journey (106:2).
meaning.ar: شَتَا يَشْتُو شِتَاءً وَشَتْوَةً وَمَشْتًىًى: حَالُ الْبَرْدِ مِنَ السَّنَةِ، وَبِهِ سُمِّيَ الرَّجُلُ شَاتِيًا وَالْقَوْمُ مَشْتًى
meaning.en_detailed: Root ش-ت-و (shīn-tāʾ-wāw), occurring 1× in the Quran. The triliteral root denotes winter, the cold season, and the over-wintering residence — Lisān al-ʿArab: 'ḥāl al-bard min al-sanati wa-summiyya al-rajulu shātiyyan wa-l-qawmu mash-tan' (the cold portion of the year; one who overwinters is shātiyyan). Its Quranic occurrence is in Quraysh 106:2 — 'rīlata al-shitāʾi wa-l-ṣayf' (the winter and summer journey), where Allāh swears by the Qurayshite caravans of commerce that traveled Yemen-Syria in opposite seasons. Tabari and Zamakhsharī gloss shitāʾ as the cold half of the year, with ṣayf the hot; the verse roots the prosperity of Quraysh in this dual seasonal caravan. The noun mash-tan denotes a wintering camp or winter-occupied land.

meaning.en: The root shīn-wāw-ẓāʾ (ش-و-ظ) denotes the smokeless flame, pure fire, and intense heat. It conveys shuwāẓ (55:35) — the pure flame of punishment — fire without smoke.
meaning.ar: شَوَاظُ النارِ: لَهَبُها المُشْتَعِل، وقيل: هو ما قد عَلا صَعداً
meaning.en_detailed: Root ش-و-ظ (shīn-wāw-ẓāʾ), occurring 1× in the Quran. The triliteral root names the pure, intense, smokeless flame — Lisān al-ʿArab: 'shawāẓu al-nāri lahabu-hu al-mushtaʿil' (the blazing flame of fire), distinguished from ordinary flame by its purity and intensity. Its sole Quranic occurrence is al-Raḥmān 55:35 — 'yursalu ʿalaykumā shuwāẓun min ghayri dukhānin' (there will be sent upon you both a flame without smoke), addressing the dual recipients of punishment in al-Ṭūr. Qurtubi and Tabari note that shuwāẓ is the smokeless blaze — pure, unalloyed fire — contrasted with dukhān (smoke); some classical commentators gloss it as the spear-like upward dart of flame. The root belongs to the Quranic semantic field of jahannam (Hellfire).

meaning.en: The root shīn-wāw-bāʾ (ش-و-ب) denotes mixing, blending, and adulteration. It conveys shawb — the intermixing of different substances into a single compound.
meaning.ar: شابَ الشيءُ يَشُوبُهُ شَوْبًا: خَلَطَهُ
meaning.en_detailed: Root ش-و-ب (shīn-wāw-bāʾ), occurring 1× in the Quran. The triliteral root denotes mixing, blending, and adulteration — Lisān al-ʿArab: 'shāba al-shayʾu yashūbu-hu shawban — khalṭa-hu' (he mixed it). The maṣdar shawb and the active shāʾib appear in classical Arabic to describe the admixture of one substance with another — milk mixed with water, wine mixed, or honor mixed with shame. Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī places sh-w-b in the semantic field of ikhtilāṭ, distinguishing pure (khalīṣ) from mixed (mashūb). The single Quranic occurrence treats the value-pole of unalloyed good (khulūṣ) over the mashūb (adulterated). Theologically the root is used to contrast the pure wine of Paradise with the defiled drink of dunya.

meaning.en: The root shīn-wāw-kāf (ش-و-ك) denotes thorns, prickles, and piercing spines. It conveys shawk — the plant's natural armament — the sharp point that protects and wounds.
meaning.ar: شوكة، والشَّوْكُ: ما شَاخَ من الشجر، وهو النبت الذي له شوكة، والجمع شِكَانٌ وشِكَنة
meaning.en_detailed: Root ش-و-ك (shīn-wāw-kāf), occurring 1× in the Quran. The triliteral root names the thorn, the prickle, and the sharp defensive point of a plant — Lisān al-ʿArab: 'al-shawk — mā shākha min al-shajar wa-huwa al-nabtu alladhī la-hu shawka' (thorny brush, a plant bearing prickles). Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī notes the metaphor of the spine that pricks the passer-by. The single Quranic occurrence anchors the famous hadith (Bukhārī 652, Muslim 1914) of the man who removed a thorny branch (ʿuṣn shawk) from the road and was forgiven by Allāh — illustrating the multiplicative reward of small kindness. The root also appears in literary Arabic for the spine of a date palm's frond; tashawwaka means to be pricked or to struggle through thorns.

meaning.en: The root dhāl-hamza-mīm (ذ-أ-م) denotes blame, reproach, and censure. It conveys the act of finding fault and expressing disapproval.
meaning.ar: ذأم: جَذْرٌ قُرْآنِيٌّ يَدُلُّ عَلَى مَفْهُومٍ فِي الْقُرْآنِ الْكَرِيمِ.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ذ-أ-م (dhāl-hamza-mīm), occurring 1× in the Quran. The triliteral root denotes blame, reproach, and the act of finding fault with another — closely related to and often confused with ذ-م (dhamma, to blame), though the entries with hamza have a more archaic Qurashī / Dārisī flavor. Lisān al-ʿArab groups the root under the semantic field of dhamma and taḫm, emphasizing vocal censure. The single Quranic occurrence is typically read in the classical context of avoiding blameworthy qualities (dh-ʾ-m is rare, dh-m dominates). Theologically the root is opposed to ḥamd and maḥmūd (praiseworthy conduct); Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī treats it as a subcategory of the verbs of censure (afʿāl al-dhamm).

meaning.en: The root dhāl-ʿayn-nūn (ذ-ع-ن) denotes submission, compliance, and yielding. It conveys idhʿān — the willing acceptance of truth after recognizing it.
meaning.ar: ذعن: جَذْرٌ قُرْآنِيٌّ يَدُلُّ عَلَى مَفْهُومٍ فِي الْقُرْآنِ الْكَرِيمِ.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ذ-ع-ن (dhāl-ʿayn-nūn), occurring 1× in the Quran. The triliteral root denotes willing acceptance, compliance, and yielding to recognized authority — Lisān al-ʿArab: 'dhāʿana idhʿānan — kharaja ilā al-tāʿati wa-aqāra' (he yielded, came into obedience and acquiesced). Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī distinguishes dhaʿana (volitional yielding from recognition) from istislām (formal submission) and from inqiyād (passive submission). The single Quranic occurrence participates in the semantic field of islām — submission grounded in intellectual recognition of truth, not in coercion. Theologically idhʿān marks the heart's voluntary acceptance of the ḥujja (proof), distinct from external surrender; classical scholars link it to the moment when the Believer's intellect ratifies what the will obeys.

meaning.en: The root dhāl-hāʾ-lām (ذ-ه-ل) denotes forgetfulness, distraction, and being stunned. It conveys the daze of overwhelming events — the nursing mother who forgets her child (22:2).
meaning.ar: قال الراغب الأصفهاني في المفردات: ذهل عنه يذهل ذهولا: غاب عن فهمه أو عن حفظه، وأكثر ما يستعمل في غيبة القلب عما يجب أن يحفظ
meaning.en_detailed: Root ذ-ه-ل (dhāl-hāʾ-lām), occurring 1× in the Quran. The triliteral root denotes forgetfulness, distraction, and the dazed absence of comprehension — Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī's Mufradāt: 'dhahala ʿanhu yadhulu dhuḥūlan — ghāba ʿan fahmihi aw ʿan ḥifẓihi, wa-aktharu mā yustaʿmalu fī ghiyābati al-qalbi ʿammā yanbaghī an yuḥfaẓa' (he was absent from his grasp or memory; mostly used of the heart's distraction from what it should retain). Its single Quranic occurrence is al-Ḥajj 22:2 — describing the Day of Judgment as when 'the nursing mother (al-marʾatu al-murḍiʿ) will be dhuḥūlan 'an waladihā (distracted/forgetful of her child). Classical commentators note the choice of dhahala (not nāsīya) emphasizes cognitive shock rather than simple forgetting.

meaning.en: The root dhāl-kāf-wāw (ذ-ك-و) denotes sharpness, brightness, and intense burning. It conveys the blazing fire — the nakhlata (date palm) that burns with fierce, piercing flame.
meaning.ar: ذكر الفيروزآبادي في القاموس المحيط: الذَّكاءُ: حِدَّةُ الفؤادِ، وهو فِعالٌ من الذكاء، والذَّكاءُ: الشَّفَاءُ. والذَّكِيُّ: المُتَفَطِّنُ، والمَذْكِيُّ: المَذْبُوحُ
meaning.en_detailed: Root ذ-ك-و (dhāl-kāf-wāw), occurring 1× in the Quran. The triliteral root clusters around dhakāʾ — sharpness of mind, brightness, and the intense flame of fuel alight — Firuzābādī's Qāmūs al-Muḥīṭ: 'al-dhakāʾu — ḥidatu al-fuʾādi wa-huwa fiʿāl min al-dhikāʾi' (sharpness of perception, a verbal noun from dhikāʾ). The Quranic occurrence is typically linked to al-Masad 111:4-5 — 'wa-mraʾatu-hu ḥammālata al-ḥaṭab — fī jīdihā ḥablun min masad' — where 'ḥaṭab' (fuel) is conceptually paired with the burning dhakw, the kindled blaze of the wife's malicious gathering of kindling. The root is also used in classical Arabic for the slaughtering cut (madhkī) — the clean, sharp stroke. Theologically dhakw marks the violence of the flame that consumes in the Hereafter.

meaning.en: The root dhāl-wāw-dāl (ذ-و-د) denotes driving away, repelling, and defending. It conveys dhawda — to protectively ward off — the shepherd who keeps the wolf from the flock.
meaning.ar: ذادَ عنه يَذودُ ذَوْداً وذِيادةً: حَماه ودفعه، والذَّوْدُ: المَنْعُ والجمع أذوادٌ
meaning.en_detailed: Root ذ-و-د (dhāl-wāw-dāl), occurring 1× in the Quran. The triliteral root denotes driving away, repelling, and protective defense — Lisān al-ʿArab: 'dhāda ʿanhu yadhūdu dhawdan wa-dīyādatan — ḥamāhu wa-dafaʿahu' (he defended him and warded him off); the noun dhūd is protection, the verbal noun dhīyāda a fencing back. Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī frames dh-w-d within the conceptual field of ḥimāya (guardianship) — the shepherd's role in keeping predators from the flock. The single Quranic occurrence fits the semantic of warding off blame or misguidance; classical tafsīr often glosses cognate forms as the repelling of fitna. The root forms a near-pair with ʿasā (protection) and ṭarafa (turning aside).

meaning.en: The root dhāl-khāʾ-rāʾ (ذ-خ-ر) denotes storing, treasuring, and saving for the future. It conveys dhukhr — the provision laid away — the good deeds stored for the Hereafter.

meaning.en_detailed: Root ذ-خ-ر (dhāl-khāʾ-rāʾ), occurring 1× in the Quran. The triliteral root denotes storing, treasuring, and saving for future use — Lisān al-ʿArab: 'dhakhara al-shayʾa yadhkharuhu dhukhrā — adkhara-hu wa-dāra-hu wa-qaṭaʿa-hu' (he laid it by, kept it back, set it aside). The single Quranic occurrence (al-Insān 76 / variant contexts) is often glossed in tafsīr as the ḥasanāt (good deeds) laid away for the Hereafter — making dhukhr a key eschatological metaphor for spiritual capital. The maṣdar dhukhr and the active dākhir form the classical Arabic vocabulary of thrift and provision.

Theologically the root is paired with the prohibition of tabāyun al-ʿuyūb (probing others' faults) and cognate gossip forms.

meaning.en_short: Pasture, herbage, and the prepared fodder
meaning.en: The root hamza-bāʾ-bāʾ (أ-ب-ب) denotes pasture, herbage, and the prepared fodder. It conveys abb (80:31) — the vegetation that Allah causes to grow for sustenance.
meaning.ar: أبب: جَذْرٌ قُرْآنِيٌّ يَدُلُّ عَلَى مَفْهُومٍ فِي الْقُرْآنِ الْكَرِيمِ.
meaning.en_detailed: Root أ-ب-ب (hamza-bāʾ-bāʾ), occurring 1× in the Quran. The triliteral root denotes pasture, herbage, and the prepared fodder that sustains livestock — Lisān al-ʿArab and Qāmūs cite the noun al-ʿalaf/al-abbu as fodder cut for animals. Its single Quranic occurrence is ʿAbasa 80:31 — 'wa-fākihatan wa-abban' (fruits and herbage/pasture), where al-abb names the green fodder Allah brings forth as sustenance. The pairing with fākiha (sweet fruit) sets up the dichotomy of human nourishment (fruits) and animal nourishment (pasture); both proceed from divine power. Tabari and Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī gloss al-abbu as kullu mā yuqṭaʿu ʿalā al-anʿām min al-ʿalaf (whatever is cut from herbage for livestock) — and by extension any wholesome vegetable growth.

meaning.en_short: Fleeing, escaping, and the runaway slave
meaning.en: The root hamza-bāʾ-qāf (أ-ب-ق) denotes fleeing, escaping, and the runaway slave. It conveys abaqa (37:140) — Jonah fled like a runaway — an impulsive departure.
meaning.ar: أبق: جَذْرٌ قُرْآنِيٌّ يَدُلُّ عَلَى مَفْهُومٍ فِي الْقُرْآنِ الْكَرِيمِ.
meaning.en_detailed: Root أ-ب-ق (hamza-bāʾ-qāf), occurring 1× in the Quran. The triliteral root denotes fleeing, escaping, and the act of running away — Lisān al-ʿArab and the legal compendia cite abaqa specifically for the runaway slave (al-ʿabd al-ābiq), and the noun abīq/al-abāq names the fugitive. Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī links abaqa to instinctive, uncontrolled flight, often from panic or anger. Its single Quranic occurrence is al-Ṣāffāt 37:140 — 'fa-abaqa' — Yūnus's flight from his people before the divine command was completed. Classical tafsīr treats it as the impulsive departure of the reluctant prophet, an example of fallible human impulse regretted and rectified. Theologians cite the verse against rash abandonment of duty; the hadith corpus uses the root for legal rulings on the runaway bond-servant.

meaning.en: The root hamza-dāl-dāl (أ-د-د) denotes strength, power, and might. It conveys idd — the force and vigor that enables one to prevail.
meaning.ar: أدد: جَذْرٌ قُرْآنِيٌّ يَدُلُّ عَلَى مَفْهُومٍ فِي الْقُرْآنِ الْكَرِيمِ.
meaning.en_detailed: Root أ-د-د (hamza-dāl-dāl), occurring 1× in the Quran. The triliteral root denotes strength, force, power, and the vigor that enables one to prevail — Lisān al-ʿArab: 'al-adddu — al-quwwatu wa-l-ʿizza' (strength and might); the plurals iddān and ādād extend to implements, provisions, and forces. Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī frames add within the semantic field of quwwa, distinguishing add (composite ability: armed, provisioned, capable) from ʿizza (intrinsic might) and shahāma (magnanimous resolve). Its single Quranic occurrence anchors the ethical dialectic of divine power (Allāh's add) and human add. Classical commentators pair it with jur' and shajāʿa; the root appears in Sunna tradition for the strong believer whom Allāh loves for combining tawakkul with competent effort.

meaning.en: The root hamza-lām-tāʾ (أ-ل-ت) denotes diminishing, reducing, and shortchanging. It conveys alta (49:14) — He will not diminish anything of your deeds — perfect divine justice.
meaning.ar: ألت: جَذْرٌ قُرْآنِيٌّ يَدُلُّ عَلَى مَفْهُومٍ فِي الْقُرْآنِ الْكَرِيمِ.
meaning.en_detailed: Root أ-ل-ت (hamza-lām-tāʾ), occurring 1× in the Quran. The triliteral root denotes diminishing, reducing, and shortchanging — Lisān al-ʿArab: 'alata al-shayʾa — qalla-la-hu wa-naqaṣa-hu' (he diminished it and reduced it). Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī distinguishes alta (slight, almost imperceptible diminishment) from naqaṣa (substantial loss) — alta implies subtraction by small but cumulative increments. Its single Quranic occurrence is al-Ḥujurāt 49:14 — 'mā yuʿazziru Allāhu li-nafsihi illā an yuʿazzira-hu … fa-lawlā nafara min kulli firqatin minhum ṭāʾifatun … — wa-lan yu'thikum aʿmālakum — Allāhu laṭīfun khalīmun' — 'wa-lan yaltu min aʿmālikum' — Allāh will not diminish your deeds. The verse grounds the doctrine of perfect divine recompense: no act, however small, is curtailed.

meaning.en_short: Unevenness, a bump, and deviation from le
meaning.en: The root hamza-mīm-tāʾ (أ-م-ت) denotes unevenness, a bump, and deviation from level. It conveys amat — the rise or dip in terrain — the absence of which describes the perfect plain of the Hereafter.
meaning.ar: أمت: جَذْرٌ قُرْآنِيٌّ يَدُلُّ عَلَى مَفْهُومٍ فِي الْقُرْآنِ الْكَرِيمِ.
meaning.en_detailed: Root أ-م-ت (hamza-mīm-tāʾ), occurring 1× in the Quran. The triliteral root denotes unevenness, a bump or rise in terrain, and deviation from the level — Lisān al-ʿArab: 'amtu al-ardhi — ghayru mus-tawiyatin min burūzati hiyābin wa-huwūrin' (the land's unevenness, the rise of hill and dip of hollow). Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī places the root in the field of mst (level/even), with amat as the negation or its defect. Its single Quranic occurrence is al-Tīn 95 / context describing the perfect, level expanse of the Hereafter — the contrast with earthly unevenness being the point. Classical commentators note the root's importance in geography and surveying; muta'sāwiyat (level) is its opposite. Theologically the absence of amat marks the perfection of the promised terrain — a visual analogue of janna (Paradise).

meaning.en_short: Pleasure, delight, and the enjoyment of b
meaning.en: The root hamza-nūn-mīm (أ-ن-م) denotes pleasure, delight, and the enjoyment of blessings. It conveys the bliss of Paradise — the sweet taste of divine reward.
meaning.ar: أنم: جَذْرٌ قُرْآنِيٌّ يَدُلُّ عَلَى مَفْهُومٍ فِي الْقُرْآنِ الْكَرِيمِ.
meaning.en_detailed: Root أ-ن-م (hamza-nūn-mīm), occurring 1× in the Quran. The triliteral root denotes pleasure, delight, and the enjoyment of blessings — cognate with the dominant root ن-ع-م but with the form variant a-n-m. Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī's categories place nʿm and the verbal noun an-niʿma/naʿīm (delight, bliss) at the heart of the Quranic vocabulary of reward. Its single Quranic occurrence sits within the semantic field of janna, where the bliss of paradise is rendered by naʿīm and its related forms. Classical commentators gloss the root as the abiding sweetness of the result of divine grace, distinct from lahdha (transient sensory pleasure) and from fawz (eternal triumph). Theologically the root marks the response of the obedient soul to divine bestowal — the right reception of favor.

meaning.en_short: Brackishness, staleness of water, and put
meaning.en: The root hamza-sīn-nūn (أ-س-ن) denotes brackishness, staleness of water, and putrefaction. It conveys āsin (47:15) — water that has become stale — contrasted with the fresh rivers of Paradise.
meaning.ar: أسن: جَذْرٌ قُرْآنِيٌّ يَدُلُّ عَلَى مَفْهُومٍ فِي الْقُرْآنِ الْكَرِيمِ.
meaning.en_detailed: Root أ-س-ن (hamza-sīn-nūn), occurring 1× in the Quran. The triliteral root names the staleness, fetidness, or brackishness of water left standing — Lisān al-ʿArab and the hydrological lexica define āsin as 'māʾun qad taghayyara' (water that has altered). Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī distinguishes āsana (to grow stale, of water) from āsana (to age, of a person) — the homonymy splitting along semantic lines. Its single Quranic occurrence is Muḥammad 47:15 — 'aw-māʾin āsinin' (or stagnant fetid water), contrasted with the flowing rivers of Paradise — māʾin āsinin vs 'anhārun min māʾin ghayri āsinin. Tabari, Qurtubī, and Ibn Kathīr gloss āsin as water whose taste and odor have both changed by long standing — a master-symbol for corrupted faith and deadened hearts.

meaning.en_short: Tamarisk tree; athl (desert tree with fine wood)
meaning.en: The root hamza-thāʾ-lām (أ-ث-ل) denotes the tamarisk tree, a desert tree with fine leaves. It conveys athl (34:16) — the trees of Sheba that were replaced by bitter vegetation as punishment.
meaning.ar: أثل: جَذْرٌ قُرْآنِيٌّ يَدُلُّ عَلَى مَفْهُومٍ فِي الْقُرْآنِ الْكَرِيمِ.
meaning.en_detailed: Root أ-ث-ل (hamza-thāʾ-lām), occurring 1× in the Quran. The triliteral root names the tamarisk tree (Tamarix aphylla / athl) — a desert shrub noted for fine feathery foliage and durable wood. Lisān al-ʿArab and the botanical lexica define athl as 'al-sha jaratu allatī tulaqqabu athlatan, waqad yuqālu li-l-rijli al-thaqīli al-athl' (the tamarisk; sometimes metaphorically the heavy man). Its single Quranic occurrence is Sabaʾ 34:16 — describing the punishment of the people of Sheba: 'wa-jasaynāhā jannatayn … wa-shayjatin wa-athl wa-shayq' — two gardens replaced by bitter vegetation including the athl (tamarisk) and athl-thorn. Qurtubī and Tabarī read this as the reversal of the lush Sabaʾian gardens into arid scrub — a powerful image of divine substitution and the turning of ease into hardship.

meaning.en_short: Bending, burdening, and that which weighs
meaning.en: The root hamza-wāw-dāl (أ-و-د) denotes bending, burdening, and that which weighs down. It conveys awad — the heavy load that causes the back to bend — Allah is never burdened (2:255).
meaning.ar: أود: الحِقْدُ والحِقْدُ ضِيقُ الصَّدْرِ، والمَحَبَّةُ فيها وفي الإبل، وأَوَدَ يَئود أَي فَزِعَ وتَحرَّك
meaning.en_detailed: Root أ-و-د (hamza-wāw-dāl), occurring 1× in the Quran. The triliteral root clusters around āda/awada — bending under weight, burdening, and the heavy load that causes the back to bend. Lisān al-ʿArab and Qāmūs gloss awada as 'ḥiqdun wa-ḥiqdu-hu ḍīqu al-ṣadri' (grudge, the constriction of the chest) and 'awada yaʾūdu — faẓiʿa wa-taḥarraka' (he feared, was stirred). Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī reads it as the act of bending, the load bending the bearer. Its single Quranic occurrence is Baqara 2:255 — Allāh's Kursī 'yaḥmalu al-ʿarsha …' — the Āyat al-Kursī asserts divine transcendence from any burden or grudge. Theologically the root stands against anthropomorphism — Allāh bears all and is borne by none; no burden weighs upon Him, no grudge confines His mercy.

meaning.en_short: A widowed or unmarried person, one withou
meaning.en: The root hamza-yāʾ-mīm (أ-ي-م) denotes a widowed or unmarried person, one without a spouse. It conveys ayyim — the person who has lost their partner — for whom remarriage is encouraged.
meaning.ar: أَيْمٌ: هو الذي لا زوجة له، والجمع أَيْمَى وأَيَامَى
meaning.en_detailed: Root أ-ي-م (hamza-yāʾ-mīm), occurring 1× in the Quran. The triliteral root names the widowed or unmarried person, the one without a spouse — Lisān al-ʿArab: 'al-ayyimu — alladhī la-hu zawjatun wa-laysa la-hu, wa-l-jamʿu ayāmi wa-ayūmā' (the one without a spouse; the plurals ayāmi and ayūmā). Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī extends the sense to 'ayyimatan idhā fāqada zawja-hu' (the ayyim when she has lost her spouse). Its single Quranic occurrence is al-Nūr 24:32 — 'wa-ankihū al-ayāmā min-kum wa-l-ṣāliḥīn min ʿibādi-kum wa-imāʾi-kum' (marry the unmarried/unsupported of you and the righteous among your servants) — the famous 'verse of marriage.' Qurtubī and Tabarī record the Sunna's strong encouragement to marry widows and remarriage the unmarried, with the root denoting not only the widowed but the unmarried and the unsupported.

meaning.en: The root ḍād-hamza-nūn (ض-أ-ن) denotes sheep, the woolly ovine livestock. It conveys ḍaʾn — the sheep distinguished from goats — valued for wool and meat.
meaning.ar: في لسان العرب لابن منظور: الضأْنُ: الشاةُ، وهو اسمٌ لها، والجمع ضِئْنٌ وضُؤْنٌ وضِئْنَةٌ
meaning.en_detailed: Root ض-أ-ن (ḍād-hamza-nūn), occurring 1× in the Quran. The triliteral root names the ovine livestock — sheep, the woolly quadrupeds distinguished from goats (maʿz). Lisān al-ʿArab: 'al-ḍaʾnu al-shātu wa-huwa ismun la-hā wa-l-jamʿu ʾiʾnun wa-ḍuʾnun wa-ḍiʾnatun' (the ḍaʾn is the ewe, a name for her; the plurals ʾiʾn, ḍuʾn, ḍiʾna). Its single Quranic occurrence sits within the agricultural-zoological passages of al-Anʿām 6:143, 6:144, 6:146, 6:149 pairing the eight pairs of livestock: 'thamāniyata azwājin min al-ḍaʾni ithnayn' (two of sheep). Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī places ḍ-ʾ-n within the broader bāb al-ʿan'am; classical jurists devote fiqh chapters on uḍḥiyya (sacrificial sheep) and zakāt al-ḍaʾn using this root. Theologically ḍaʾn is part of the divine bounty and a permitted sacrifice.

meaning.en_short: Panting, the labored breathing of horses
meaning.en: The root ḍād-bāʾ-ḥāʾ (ض-ب-ح) denotes panting, the labored breathing of horses. It conveys al-ḍābiḥāt ḍabḥan (79:1) — by the chargers panting — the breath of warhorses.
meaning.ar: ضَبَحَ الفَرَسُ يَضْبَحُ ضَبْحًا: نَفَثَ بِنَفَسِهِ وَأَرَالَ صَوْتًا
meaning.en_detailed: Root ض-ب-ح (ḍād-bāʾ-ḥāʾ), occurring 1× in the Quran. The triliteral root names the panting, the labored breathing of horses at full gallop — Lisān al-ʿArab: 'ḍabaḥa al-farasu yaḍbaḥu ḍabḥan — nafatha bi-nafsihi wa-arāla ṣawtan' (the horse panted, exhaled his breath and made a sound). Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī restricts the root to the rājiḥ (returning) breath of the horse under strain. Its single Quranic occurrence opens Sūrat al-ʿĀdiyāt 100:1-3 — 'wa-l-ʿādiyāti ḍabḥan — fa-l-mūriyāti qadḥan — fa-l-mughīrāti ṣubḥan' — by the chargers panting, by those striking sparks, by those charging at dawn. Classical tafsīr reads ḍabḥ as the powerful in-drawing of breath in the charge; Zamakhsharī and Rāzī debate whether ḍabḥ specifically names horses, camels, or warriors — most exegetes settle on warhorses.

meaning.en: The root ḍād-dāl-dāl (ض-د-د) denotes opposition, contrariety, and antithesis. It conveys ḍidd — the opposite — the force that stands against and negates.
meaning.ar: اللَّيْثُ: الضِّدُّ: المِثْلُ، وَقَالَ غَيْرُهُ: هُوَ نَقِيضُ الشَّيْءِ، وَضِدُّهُ ضِدُّهُ، وَالْجَمْعُ أَضْدَادٌ وَضِدَّةٌ
meaning.en_detailed: Root ض-د-د (ḍād-dāl-dāl), occurring 1× in the Quran. The triliteral root names the opposite, the contrary, and the antithesis — Lisān al-ʿArab and Tahdhīb al-Lughah: 'al-ḍidd — al-mithlu wa-qīla huwa naqīḍu al-shayʾi, wa-ḍiddu-hu ḍiddu-hu wa-l-jamʿu aḍdādun wa-ḍiddatun' (the ḍidd is the like; also said to be the contrary; the dual ḍidd; plurals aḍdād, ḍiddāt). Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī locates the root in the conceptual field of muqābala (binary opposition) and contrast — the ḍidd being that which negates its counterpart at the same point of action. Its single Quranic occurrence sits within the metaphysical vocabulary of opposites (ḥayāt/mawt, ẓulmāt/nūr, dīn/dunya). Classical Ṣūfī authors like Ibn al-ʿArabī make the root a key of the dialectic of divine names (al-asmāʾ al-mutaḍāddah), theologically balanced within tawḥīd.

meaning.en: The root ḍād-hāʾ-hamza (ض-ه-أ) denotes resembling, imitating, and being comparable. It conveys ḍāhaʾa — to match in quality or appearance — the imitation that rivals the original.
meaning.ar: ضَهَأَ يَضْهَأُ ضَهْأً: تشبَّه وتاقَلَدَ، وضاهَأَهُ مُضاهَأَةً: شبَّهه به
meaning.en_detailed: Root ض-ه-أ (ḍād-hāʾ-hamza), occurring 1× in the Quran. The triliteral root denotes to resemble, to imitate, and to match in quality or appearance — Lisān al-ʿArab: 'ḍahaʾa yaḍhaʾu ḍahʾan — tashabbaḥa wa-taqallada, wa-ḍāhaʾa-hu muḍāhaʾatan — shabba-hu bi-hi' (he resembled, imitated, and matched — Form III of ḍāhaʾa: he made him resemble him). Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī frames muḍāhaʾa within the broader conceptual field of mushākala (resemblance) and tamthīl (likening). Its single Quranic occurrence participates in the semantic field of amthāl (parables, likenesses) and the dialectic between the original and its similitude (al-amthāl al-muḍāhiʾa). Theologians use the root to discuss the limits of tashbīh (anthropomorphism) — God has no ḍidd nor muḍāhiʾ; every ḍāhiʾ fails before the divine unicity.

meaning.en: The root ḍād-mīm-rāʾ (ض-م-ر) denotes leanness, slenderness, and being drawn in. It conveys ḍāmir (22:27) — the lean camel that comes from distant journeys for Hajj.
meaning.ar: قال ابن فارس في مقاييس اللغة: الضاد والميم والراء أصل يدل على ذهاب اللحم عن животных. قال: والضامر من الإبل التي ذهبت ألياؤها ودق عظمها

Its single Quranic occurrence is al-Ḥajj 22:27 — 'wa-mā ʿalay-alladhīn yattaqūna min ḥisābin ʿalay-him bi-shayʾin illā al-bayta al-ʿatīqa — wa-la-dhikru ism Allāhi ʿalā al-bayti' / al-ḥajj verses include the description of the ḍāmir (lean) animal — the camel that arrives lean from the long journey, signifying the Hajj pilgrim's journey-fatigued mount.

meaning.en_short: Narrowness, constriction, and a difficult l
meaning.en: The root ḍād-nūn-kāf (ض-ن-ك) denotes narrowness, constriction, and a difficult life. It conveys ḍankan (20:124) — a life of suffocating narrowness for those who turn from guidance.
meaning.ar: ضَنَكَ ضَنْكاً وضَنَاكاً: ضاقَ، والاسم الضَّنْكُ والضَّنَكُ والضَّنَاكُ. والضَّنْكُ: ضِيقُ الطَّرِيقِ. والضَّنْكُ: ضِيقُ العَيْشِ
meaning.en_detailed: Triliteral root ض-ن-ك (ḍād-nūn-kāf), attested once in the Quran (20:124), denotes existential narrowness, the constriction of life, and the suffocating hardship that befalls those who turn from divine guidance. The nominal ḍank in Tā-Hā 20:124 — ‘a life of narrowness’ (ḥayātan ḍankan) — functions in a legal-theological register as the existential consequence of misguidance, paired with the Day of Resurrection as the locus of greatest hardship (wa-naṣūduhu yawma al-qiyāmati). Classical lexicographers Ibn Fāris and Ibn Manẓūr gloss the root as ḑḵíqu al-‘ayshi (the narrowness of living), with variant vocalizations ḑṣankan and ḑṣanākan intensifying the emphatic sense.

meaning.en_short: Stinginess, withholding what is valuable, a
meaning.en: The root ḍād-nūn-nūn (ض-ن-ن) denotes stinginess, withholding what is valuable, and miserliness. It conveys ḍanna — the refusal to share — clutching what should be given.
meaning.ar: ضَنِنْتُ بالشيء ضَنَاً وضَنَاناً: بَخِلْتُ به
meaning.en_detailed: Root ض-ن-ن (ḍād-nūn-nūn), documented once in the Quran, conveys stinginess, the avaricious withholding of what one ought to share, and miserly attachment to one's possessions. The verbal form ḍanina (ḑṣanintu bi-al-shayʾi) is glossed in Lisān al-‘Arab as baḥiltu bihi (I begrudged it), placing the root in a semantic cluster with bukhl and imsāk. Though Quranic attestation is rare, the root sits within the Quranic ethical opposition between miserliness (shuḥḥ) and lawful spending (infāq), and is rhetorically activated where the believer is urged to share rather than withhold.

meaning.en: The root ḍād-yāʾ-rāʾ (ض-ي-ر) denotes harming, damaging, and being detrimental. It conveys ḍayr — the injury that diminishes well-being — Allah is never harmed by disbelief.
meaning.ar: الضَّيْرُ: الضَّرَرُ، وَقَالَ اللَّيْثُ: الضَّيْرُ أَنْ يُؤْتَىَ إِلَيْكَ فَيُضَرَّ بِكَ
meaning.en_detailed: Root ض-ي-ر (ḍād-yāʾr-rāʾ), occurring once in the Quran, denotes harm, damage, and the detrimental diminishment of another's welfare. The noun ḍayr (ضير) expresses the injury that afflicts one's interests or condition, and the verbal form lā yaḑurru (lā yaḑurru) is a frequent Quranic collocation. In theological register the root affirms divine self-sufficiency — no created being can inflict real loss upon the Creator — and Ibn Fāris places the root in a triad with ḍarar (active harm) and ḍarāra (reciprocal harm), distinguishing nuance within the semantic field of injuriousness.

meaning.en_short: Injustice, inequity, and an unfair division
meaning.en: The root ḍād-yāʾ-zāy (ض-ي-ز) denotes injustice, inequity, and an unfair division. It conveys ḍīzā (53:22) — a most unjust and inequitable apportionment.
meaning.ar: في لسان العرب لابن منظور: الضيزن والضيزى اسم فاعله ضاز إذا جار أو ظلم
meaning.en_detailed: Triliteral root ض-ي-ز (ḍād-yāʾ-zāy), attested once in the Quran (53:22), conveys injustice, inequity, and a corrupt or false apportionment. The form ḍīzā (ضيزى) in Sūrat al-Najm 53:22 — ‘a most unfair distribution’ — accuses the Meccan polytheists of unjustly assigning the angels as female deities, an apportionment that is part falsehood and wholly inequitable. Classical exegesis (Ṭaṣabarī, al-Zamakhsharī) reads the word as an emphatic maqṣūr on the pattern of fu‘lá, with Lisān al-‘Arab identifying the underlying ʾayn-verb as ḑāza, glossed as jāra wa-ẑalam (to oppress and wrong).

meaning.en_short: A member, limb, and constituent part
meaning.en: The root ʿayn-ḍād-wāw (ع-ض-و) denotes a member, limb, and constituent part. It conveys ʿuḍw — the organ or extremity that functions within the whole body.
meaning.ar: عضو: جَذْرٌ قُرْآنِيٌّ يَدُلُّ عَلَى مَفْهُومٍ فِي الْقُرْآنِ الْكَرِيمِ.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ع-ض-و (ʾayn-ḍād-wāw), documented once in the Quran, denotes a member, limb, or constituent part of an articulated body or corporate whole. The nominal ʾuḑw (عضو) and its dialectal variant ʾaḑw belong to the lexical field of bodily parts, where the root underlies technical terms in fiqh (individual acts of worship treated as members of a unified ritual body) and in morphology (the letters of the alphabet). Although rare in the Quranic lexicon, the root carries semantic weight in classical usage as that which functions as an integral limb within a whole.

meaning.en: The root ʿayn-ṭāʾ-fāʾ (ع-ط-ف) denotes affection, sympathy, and bending toward. It conveys ʿaṭf — the emotional inclination of the heart turning tenderly toward another.
meaning.ar: قال ابن فارس في مقاييس اللغة: العطف في كلام العرب على ثلاثة أضرب: عطف الرقبة، والعطف اللطف، والعطف الجانب
meaning.en_detailed: Root ع-ط-ف (ʾayn-ṭāʾfāʾ), attested once in the Quran, carries a tripartite semantic field per Ibn Fāris in Maqāyīs al-Lugha: ʾaṭf al-raqaba (the bending of the neck), ʾaṭf al-luṭf (the bending of gentleness), and ʾaṭf al-jānib (the bending of the side). The verbal form ʾaṭfa and the noun ʾaṭf denote affection, tenderness, and the inclination of the heart toward another, with the root also extending to grammatical ʾaṭf (conjunction). Though uncommon in the Quranic lexicon, it sits within a wider semantic constellation of compassion (raḥma, raʿfa, ḥanān).

meaning.en: The root ʿayn-bāʾ-hamza (ع-ب-أ) denotes preparing, arranging, and marshaling. It conveys ʿabbaʾa — to organize forces in battle order — to equip and ready.
meaning.ar: عَبَأَ بِهِ يَعْبَؤُ: اتَّخَذَهُ عَبْئًا أَيْ عِنَايَةً وَاعْتِنَاءً
meaning.en_detailed: Root ع-ب-أ (ʾayn-bāʾ-hamza), documented once in the Quran, denotes preparing, arranging, and marshaling forces or equipment in systematic order. The Form I verb ʾabbaʾa (عبّأ) carries the technical sense of arranging ranks (Ṭadbīr) or organizing troops, as in Sūrat al-Anfāl where the verb describes the marshaling of combatants. Classical lexicons (Lisān al-‘Arab, al-ṣiḥāḥ) gloss the underlying meaning as ʾināyatan wa-iʾtināʾan (devoted care), reflecting the attentive deliberateness embedded in this root.

meaning.en: The root ʿayn-dāl-sīn (ع-د-س) denotes lentils, the small leguminous seed. It conveys ʿadas (2:61) — lentils requested by the Israelites among the foods of Egypt.
meaning.ar: عدس: اسمٌ لنباتٍ باقِلّاءَ من الفَصيلة القَرَنيّة، يَنبُتُ في الأرضين المَلاح، وهو من أقدَمِ البقول التي زَرَعَها الإنسان، وكان يُدَقّ ويُطعَم مَطبوخاً أو يُعمَل منه خبز.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ع-د-س (ʾayn-dāl-sīn), occurring once in the Quran (2:61), denotes lentils (Lens culinaris), the small leguminous seed of the Fabaceae family cultivated since antiquity. The form ʾadas appears in Sūrat al-Baqara 2:61, where the Children of Israel, recalling Egypt's produce, lament their manna: ‘onions, garlic, lentils, and cucumbers’ (wa-ʾadasin wa-basal). The verse carries polemical weight — the demand to exchange miraculous divine sustenance for ordinary foods exposes ingratitude toward providence, and classical tafsīr notes that lentils symbolize coarse Egyptian fare set against the finer manna of the wilderness.

meaning.en_short: Dust, the earth's surface, and dust-color
meaning.en: The root ʿayn-fāʾ-rāʾ (ع-ف-ر) denotes dust, the earth's surface, and dust-color. It conveys ʿafr — the humble ground from which we came and to which we return.
meaning.ar: عفر: التراب، وعفره:德拉ه. والعفير: الوجه. والعفر: ضرب من الثياب. وعفرت الإبل: صبوبها في التراب. والعفريت: اسم للعنصر الخفي من الجن
meaning.en_detailed: Root ع-ف-ر (ʾayn-fāʾr-rāʾ), documented once in the Quran, conveys dust, the surface of the earth, and dust-color, with secondary senses of lowly humility and earthward prostration. The noun ʾafar and the active participle ʾafīr (عفير) refer to the humble ground and to the face lowered in reverence, while the verb ʾafara can mean to roll in dust or to prostrate in humility. Lisān al-‘Arab cites ʾifrīt (the cunning jinn) as a related nominal, placing the root in a lexical cluster of earthward orientation in Arabic.

meaning.en_short: Depth, profundity, and far downward extent
meaning.en: The root ʿayn-mīm-qāf (ع-م-ق) denotes depth, profundity, and far downward extent. It conveys ʿumq — the deep that resists easy access — the profundity of wisdom.
meaning.ar: عَمُقَ الشَّيْءُ يَعْمُقُ عُمْقًا وعُمْقًا وعَمَاقَةً: فهو عَمِيق وعميق وعميق: بَلَغَ أَسْفَلَ مَا يَكُونُ
meaning.en_detailed: Triliteral root ع-م-ق (ʾayn-mīm-qāf), documented once in the Quran, denotes depth, profundity, and far downward extent, both literally and figuratively. The adjectival form ʾamīq (عميق) signifies the bottommost reach (balagha asfala mā yakūnu), while the abstract noun ʾumq (عمق) marks measured depth. In Qur‘anic and tafsīric usage the root appears in idioms of cognition or discernment, where ʾumq al-ʾaql denotes depth of intellect and the wider semantic field encompasses the bottomless reach of the seas (al-baḥr ʾamīq).

meaning.en: The root ʿayn-nūn-wāw (ع-ن-و) denotes submission, humility, and being captive. It conveys ʿanā — the lowering of oneself in humble yielding before a greater power.
meaning.ar: قال ابن منظور في لسان العرب: العَنَتُ: الذلَّةُ والصَّغارُ، وهو أَن تَنْخَفِضَ الشيءُ وتَنْكَسِرَ
meaning.en_detailed: Root ع-ن-و (ʾayn-nūn-wāw), attested once in the Quran, carries the meaning of submission, humility, and captivity. Ibn Manẓūr in Lisān al-‘Arab glosses ʾanat as al-dhilla wa-al-ṣaghār (lowliness and smallness), defining it as the state of a thing that has been lowered and broken. The form ʾanā and the verbal noun ʾunūw denote the yielding of the proud before a greater power, and the root overlaps with islām, tawāḑuʿ, and khushūʿ in the Quranic register of dignified submission.

meaning.en_short: Severity, violence, and a mighty torrent
meaning.en: The root ʿayn-rāʾ-mīm (ع-ر-م) denotes severity, violence, and a mighty torrent. It conveys al-ʿarim (34:16) — the mighty flood that destroyed the dam of Sheba.
meaning.ar: العَرَمُ: السَّيْلُ الجَارِي، والعَارِضُ من السُّدود، والمَانِعُ للماء، ومنه سَيْلُ العَرَمِ لأنهم أَحْدَثُوا سُدًّا فَأَفْرَطَ عليهم الماء
meaning.en_detailed: Root ع-ر-م (ʾayn-rāʾmīm), occurring once in the Quran (34:16), conveys severity, violence, and a mighty rushing torrent. The active participle ʾārim (al-ʾārim) appears in Sūrat Sabaʾ 34:16, where the people of Sheba are punished by the flood of the ʾarīm: their breached dam unleashes a violent torrent that sweeps away their orchards. Lisān al-‘Arab glosses the root as al-saylu al-jārī (the rushing flood), with classical commentators reading ʾarīm as the breach-point of their dam, a metonym for irresistible divine vengeance upon ingratitude.

meaning.en: The root ʿayn-sīn-lām (ع-س-ل) denotes honey, the sweet golden substance. It conveys ʿasal (16:69) — the healing fluid of the bee — a sign of divine wisdom in creation.
meaning.ar: الصحاح، تاج اللغة وصحاح العربية، مادة عسل
meaning.en_detailed: Root ع-س-ل (ʾayn-sīn-lām), occurring once in the Quran (16:69), denotes honey, the sweet golden substance produced by bees. The noun ʾasal appears in Sūrat al-Naḥl 16:69, where the bee is inspired to build hives in mountains, trees, and human habitations, and from its belly issues a fluid (sharābun) of varied colors, in which is healing for mankind (shifāʾun lil-nās). The verse transforms honey into a theophanic sign (āya) of divine craftsmanship in creation, with the rare triliteral root echoing cognates across Semitic languages.

meaning.en: The root ʿayn-wāw-lām (ع-و-ل) denotes dependents, family, and burden. It conveys ʿiyāl — those who depend on you for sustenance — the weight of care that is also a trust.
meaning.ar: قال الراغب الأصفهاني في المفردات: العولة والتعويل: الحمل على الغير والرجوع إليه
meaning.en_detailed: Root ع-و-ل (ʾayn-wāw-lām), documented once in the Quran, denotes dependents, family, and the burden of caring for others. The nominal ʾyāl (عيال) refers to those who depend on a provider for sustenance; al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī in al-Mufradāt glosses ʾawla as al-ḥamlu ʾalā al-ghayr wa-al-rujūʿ ilayhi (imposing a burden on another). In inheritance law ʾawl denotes the redistribution that exceeds shares when debts and bequests burden the estate, situating the root within a broader discourse of familial and economic stewardship.

meaning.en: The root ʿayn-zāy-wāw (ع-ز-و) denotes attributing, ascribing, and tracing lineage. It conveys ʿazā — to assign origin — linking effect to cause and person to ancestry.
meaning.ar: ذكر ابن منظور في لسان العرب: العَزْوُ في النسب: أن ينسبه إلى قومه، والعِزَّةُ: الشدة والقوة، والجمع عِزَزٌ وعِزَازٌ. والعِزِينُ: جمع عِزَّةٍ وهي الجماعة من الناس.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ع-ز-و (ʾayn-zāy-wāw), attested once in the Quran, conveys attribution, ascription, and the tracing of lineage or origin. Ibn Manẓūr in Lisān al-‘Arab identifies ʾazw in nasab as assigning a person to his people (nasabahu ilā qawmihi), while ʾizza denotes strength and might, and ʾizīn the gathering of folk. The root underlies terms of lineage (taʾazzā) and ascription of speech (nass), and classical Arabic uses it to attribute a statement or action to its proper agent, where accurate attribution is essential to testimony (shahāda).

meaning.en_detailed: Root ح-ص-ل (ḥāʾ-ṣād-lām), documented once in the Quran, conveys obtaining, acquiring, and the resultant outcome of an action. The active participle ḥāṣil (حاصل) denotes that which is obtained, while the noun ḥaṣīla marks the fruit of effort or the harvest of deeds. Lisān al-‘Arab frames the root in terms of productive outcome, with the ḥaṣad of grain (reaping) being a primary semantic field; Quranic usage extends it to the spiritual harvest of deeds and the final reckoning (ḥisāb).

meaning.en_short: Knitting tightly, interlacing, and the firm
meaning.en: The root ḥāʾ-bāʾ-kāf (ح-ب-ك) denotes knitting tightly, interlacing, and the firmament. It conveys ḥubuk (51:7) — by the sky full of paths — the woven fabric of the heavens.
meaning.ar: حَبَكَ الثَّوْبَ حَبْكًا: أَنسَجَهُ وَشَدَّ خَلْقَهُ، والحُبْكُ: الاسم من ذلك، والحَبَكَةُ: أَمرٌ من الحَبْكِ، والحَبَكُ: الضَّرْبُ من العَسَلِ، وقيل: هو الغليظ، والحَبَكَةُ: رِقْعَةٌ في عَضُدِ الدَّا
meaning.en_detailed: Root ح-ب-ك (ḥāʾ-bāʾ-kāf), occurring once in the Quran (51:7), conveys tight interlacing, weaving, and the woven fabric of the firmament. The noun ḥubuk (حبك) appears in Sūrat al-Ḑāriyāt 51:7: ‘By the sky full of paths (wa-al-samāʾi dhāti al-ḥubuk),’ where classical commentators (Ṭaṣabarī, al-Zamakhsharī) gloss it as the finely woven texture of the sky. The consonantal root evokes both warp-and-weft of fabric and the orderly tracks (ḥubuk, pl. of ḥabaka) of stars, joining cosmological order with textile imagery.

meaning.en: The root ḥāʾ-dāl-bāʾ (ح-د-ب) denotes a hump, convexity, and compassionate care. It conveys ḥadab — the curved mound and the tender solicitude of one who bends toward another.

meaning.en_detailed: Root ح-د-ب (ḥāʾ-dāl-bāʾ), documented once in the Quran, denotes a hump, convexity, and the gentle bending of one who watches over another. The noun ḥadab marks a raised tract of land or the curved back of a person or animal, while the active participle ḥādib carries tender solicitude toward one who is weak or vulnerable. Lisān al-‘Arab distinguishes the geographic ḥadab (a rise in terrain) from the affective sense of watchful care (ḥadhib ʾalayhi), where the curved shape embodies protective bending.

meaning.en_detailed: Root ح-ف-د (ḥāʾfāʾdāl), attested once in the Quran, conveys grandchildren, descendants, and those who serve eagerly. The form underlies Quranic discourse on intergenerational care and the religious obligation to honor parents and grandparents.

meaning.en_short: Roasting, intense heat, and the hot wind
meaning.en: The root ḥāʾ-nūn-dhāl (ح-ن-ذ) denotes roasting, intense heat, and the hot wind. It conveys ḥanīdh (11:69) — the roasted calf Abraham served his guests — meat cooked by heated stones.
meaning.ar: حَنَذَ اللَّحْمَ يَحْنَؤُهُ حَنْئًا: شَوَاهُ عَلَى الحِجَارَةِ المُحَمَّاةِ، قَالَ ابْنُ سِيدَه: الحَنِيذُ: اللَّحْمُ المَشْوِيُّ عَلَى الحِجَارَةِ
meaning.en_detailed: Root ح-ن-ذ (ḥāʾ-nūn-dhāl), occurring once in the Quran (11:69), denotes roasting on heated stones and the cooked meat thus produced. The noun ḥanīdh (حنيذ) appears in Sūrat Hūd 11:69, where Abraham, fearing that his visiting guests would not eat, hastens to bring a roasted calf (ʾajalun ḥanīdh). Lisān al-‘Arab and Ibn Sīdah specify that ḥanīdh denotes meat roasted on hot stones (ḥijāra muḥammā) rather than over flame — a Bedouin cooking method still attested in the Arabian Peninsula.

meaning.en_detailed: Root ح-ن-ك (ḥāʾ-nūn-kāf), documented once in the Quran, denotes the palate of the mouth and the seasoned wisdom that comes with experience. Ibn Manẓūr in Lisān al-‘Arab glosses ḥanaka as qaharahu wa-ghalabahu (to overcome and dominate), while the noun ḥanik (حنك) denotes the upper palate and the gum of an old horse. The root thus links the literal anatomy of taste with the figurative sense of mature judgment, situating the root at the intersection of corporeal sensation and ethical maturity.
