meaning.ar: حَنَّ يَحِنُّ حَنًّا وحُنُونًا: رقَّ ورَقَّ، فهو حَنّان
meaning.en_detailed: Root ح-ن-ن (ḥāʾ-nūn-nūn), documented once in the Quran, conveys tenderness, compassion, and longing affection. The verbal noun ḥunūn (حُنون) and the active participle ḥannān (حنان) denote the soft, yearning love that bends the heart toward another, and the verb ḥanna is glossed in Lisān al-‘Arab as riqq (became tender). The root emerges in a Quranic ethical register that situates divine mercy (raḥma) and human compassion on a single emotional spectrum, underwriting the affective vocabulary of familial and spiritual tenderness.

meaning.en_short: Anger, intense resolve, and the withheld ra
meaning.en: The root ḥāʾ-rāʾ-dāl (ح-ر-د) denotes anger, intense resolve, and the withheld rage. It conveys ḥarad — the seething fury held in check — the determination that masks wrath.
meaning.ar: حَرْدٌ: القَطَعُ، ومنه حَرَدَ إذا قَطَعَ. وفي التنزيل: غَدَوْا عَلَىٰ حَرْدٍ قَادِرِينَ، أي قاطعين على عَزْمٍ وتَيَقُّظٍ
meaning.en_detailed: Root ح-ر-د (ḥāʾ-rāʾdāl), occurring once in the Quran, denotes seething anger, intense resolve, and the wrath held in check. The noun ḥarad (حرد) carries the meaning of determination that masks withheld rage; Lisān al-‘Arab and classical tafsīr gloss the Quranic phrase ghadaw ʾalā ḥardin qādirīn as determined, alert, and cuttingly resolved (qāṬʾīn ʾalā ʾazmin wa-tayaqquḑ). The root thus names a frozen anger — not the outburst of ghaḑab but the cold cutting-edge of justified wrath that proceeds methodically.

meaning.en_detailed: Root ح-ر-س (ḥāʾrāʾsīn), documented once in the Quran, denotes guarding, protecting, and the vigilant watchman. The noun ḥaras (حرس) and the verbal noun ḥirāsa (حراسة) signify the constant vigilance of a sentinel, with Lisān al-‘Arab glossing the root as ḑānahu wa-naḑarahu wa-ʾaẓẓamahu (to guard, oversee, and magnify). In Quranic cosmology angels stand as a ḥifẓ (guard) over the believer, and the root underlies discourses of divine protection (ḥimāya) over deeds, speech, and the soul itself.

meaning.en: The root ḥāʾ-rāʾ-yāʾ (ح-ر-ي) denotes being worthy, deserving, and appropriate. It conveys ḥarī — the fitting recipient — the one who merits what befalls them.
meaning.ar: حَرَى يَحْرُو حَرْواً وحِراءً: طلب. والتحرِّي: طلب الشيء بعينه. والتحرِّي: التعمُّد
meaning.en_detailed: Root ح-ر-ي (ḥāʾrāʾyāʾ), attested once in the Quran, conveys being worthy, deserving, and the appropriate recipient of an outcome. Lisān al-‘Arab derives ḥarā from ḥarā yaḥruū (to seek and aim at), with the intensive form taḥarrī denoting the deliberate seeking-out of a particular thing (Ṭalab al-shayʾi bi-ʾaynihi). The root thus names both fitness (ḥalī bi-) and the diligent search for what is fitting, carrying ethical weight where the appropriate person rightly receives the appropriate recompense.

meaning.en: The root ḥāʾ-sīn-mīm (ح-س-م) denotes decisive cutting off, ending completely, and removal. It conveys ḥasma — the definitive termination — leaving no remainder.
meaning.ar: حسم: القطعُ. حَسَمَهُ يَحْسِمُهُ حَسْمًا: قَطَعَهُ
meaning.en_detailed: Root ح-س-م (ḥāʾsīn-mīm), documented once in the Quran, denotes decisive cutting off, ending completely, and removal that leaves no remainder. The noun ḥasm (حسم) and the verbal ḥasamahu signify cutting off decisively; Lisān al-‘Arab glosses the verb as qaṬʾahu (to sever). In ethical and theological discourse the root describes the termination of disputes (qiṬāʿ al-sabab) and the final reckoning, where a matter is closed without residue — lā baqīya fīhi — and where divine justice issues a clean severance of wrongdoing.

In Quranic usage the root bears the theological weight of unalterable divine will (al-amr al-mubram), as in the decreed and inevitable end of communities that transgress.

meaning.en_detailed: Root ح-ث-ث (ḥāʾthāʾthāʾ), documented once in the Quran, conveys urging, spurring on, and hastening. The active participle ḥathīth (حثيث) denotes swift and insistent, and the verbal form ḥaththa signifies urging forward with persistence. Lisān al-‘Arab places the root in the semantic field of speed (sarīʿ) and insistence, where the ḥathth of one driving another forward is encoded; the root underlies Quranic discourse on the urgency of daʿwa and the promptitude of the believer’s response to the divine call.

meaning.en: The root ḥāʾ-wāw-bāʾ (ح-و-ب) denotes sin, crime, and the heavy burden of wrongdoing. It conveys ḥawb — the weight of guilt — and lā taqtulū al-nafs... faqad jiʾta shayʾan ḥūban — a terrible sin (17:31).
meaning.ar: ح و ب: الحَوبةُ: الذنب العظيم، والجمع حَوْبٌ وحِيابٌ. وحَابَ يَحوبُ: أذنب ذنباً عظيماً. والحَوبُ: اسمٌ جامعٌ لأنواع المعاصي
meaning.en_detailed: Root ح-و-ب (ḥāʾwāw-bāʾ), attested once in the Quran (17:31), denotes sin, crime, and the heavy burden of wrongdoing. The noun ḥawb (حوب) and the abstract noun ḥawba signify an encompassing, weighty sin; Lisān al-‘Arab glosses the root as al-dhanbu al-ʾaẓīm (the great sin) with the plural ḥawbun wa-ḥīyābun. Sūrat al-Isrāʾ 17:31 warns: ‘Do not kill your children for fear of poverty — We provide for them and for you — killing them is a tremendous sin (ḥūbun kabīr),’ making the root a marker of grave ethical violation.

meaning.en_short: Acquiring, possessing, and drawing to onese
meaning.en: The root ḥāʾ-wāw-zāy (ح-و-ز) denotes acquiring, possessing, and drawing to oneself. It conveys ḥawz — to gather and claim — the assertive taking of what one seeks.
meaning.ar: حَوَزَ الشَّيْءَ يَحُوزُهُ حَوْزًا: أَخَذَهُ وَجَمَعَهُ
meaning.en_detailed: Root ح-و-ز (ḥāʾwāw-zāy), documented once in the Quran, denotes acquiring, possessing, and drawing to oneself. The verbal ḥawazahu signifies taking and gathering, and Lisān al-‘Arab places the root in the semantic field of acquisition (al-akhdh wa-al-jamʿ). The root underlies terms of corporate gathering (ḥawẓ, ḥiwāẓ) and the legal notion of possession (milk), where one draws into one's custody what one seeks to retain — a concept central to inheritance, marriage settlements, and territorial rights in classical Islamic jurisprudence.

meaning.en_short: Turning aside, avoiding, and the deflection
meaning.en: The root ḥāʾ-yāʾ-dāl (ح-ي-د) denotes turning aside, avoiding, and the deflection. It conveys ḥayd (50:14) — the Day when there is no place to turn aside — no escape from accountability.
meaning.ar: حادَ عن الطريق يَحيد حَيْداً وحَيَدانا: مَالَ وصَرَفَهُ
meaning.en_detailed: Root ح-ي-د (ḥāʾyāʾdāl), documented once in the Quran (50:19), conveys turning aside, avoiding, and deflection from the path. The noun ḥayd (حيد) and the verbal ḥāda ʾan al-ṭarīq signify deviation from the way; Lisān al-‘Arab glosses the verb as māla wa-ṣarafahu (to incline and turn aside). In Sūrat Qāf 50:19 the negated form mā kunta minhu taḥīd frames the moment of death as inescapable, while the related phrase ‘no place to turn aside’ (lā ḥīḑan) describes the Day of Judgment as the locus of absolute accountability.

meaning.en: The root ḥāʾ-yāʾ-fāʾ (ح-ي-ف) denotes injustice, partiality, and bias. It conveys ḥayf — the tilting of justice — the unfair lean that corrupts judgment.
meaning.ar: حافَ يَحِيفُ: جارَ وعدَل عن القصد
meaning.en_detailed: The trilateral root ḥāʾ-yāʾ-fāʾ (ح-ي-ف), occurring 1 time in the Quran, denotes the tilting of justice—partiality, bias, and the unfair lean away from equity. Its verbal form ḥāfa (يَحِيفَ) is invoked in al-Baqarah (2:232): lā taẓlimūhunna wa-lā taḥīfūhunna—do not wrong them nor incline against them in injustice, pairing the root with its conceptual sibling ẓulm to forbid both active harm and the subtler veering toward it. Classical lexicographers (Lisān al-ʿArab, Ibn Manẓūr) gloss ḥayf as jāra wa-ʿadaʿa al-qaṣd, deviation from the straight line of fairness; the term retains this semantic precision in Quranic legal ethics, distinguishing accidental slip from deliberate inclination against another.

meaning.en_short: Twisting the neck in arrogance, prideful t
meaning.en: The root ṣād-ʿayn-rāʾ (ص-ع-ر) denotes twisting the neck in arrogance, prideful turning. It conveys ṣaʿar (31:18) — do not turn your cheek in contempt toward people.
meaning.ar: أخرج الجوهري في الصحاح: الصَّعَرُ والصُّعَرُ بكسر الصاد وضمها: استواءٌ في الأنف، لا يكون أعرج الأنف
meaning.en_detailed: The root ṣād-ʿayn-rāʾ (ص-ع-ر), attested 1 time in the Quran, denotes the proud twisting of the neck—the lateral motion by which one dismisses another in contempt. The Quran employs the II-stem verb tuṣaʿʿir in Luqmān (31:18): wa-lā tuṣʿaʿʿir khaddaka li-n-nās—do not turn your cheek in contempt toward people, addressing the Prophet ﷺ to instruct against even the subtlest physical register of arrogance. Al-Jawharī in al-Ṣiḥāḥ explains al-ṣaʿar and al-ṣuʿar (with kasrah and ḍammah of the ṣād) as a straightness in the nose, never a crookedness—paradoxically glossing the verb as an act that defies the natural even line of the face; the meaning is the disdainful pivot away from a fellow human being.

meaning.en_short: Standing on three legs, the poised stance
meaning.en: The root ṣād-fāʾ-nūn (ص-ف-ن) denotes standing on three legs, the poised stance. It conveys al-ṣāfināt (38:31) — the noble steeds poised, resting on three legs with grace.
meaning.ar: الْكِسَائِيّ: الصَّافِنُ من الْخَيْلِ الَّذِي يَقُومُ عَلَى ثَلَاثِ قَوَائِمِ وَيَرْفَعُ الْيُسْرَى
meaning.en_detailed: The root ṣād-fāʾ-nūn (ص-ف-ن), recorded 1 time in the Quran, denotes the noble stance of a warhorse on three legs with the fourth tucked, ready yet poised. The active participle al-ṣāfināt occurs in Ṣād (38:31): wa-ʿullifu ṣāfināt—and closely ranged, steeds standing on three legs, describing the mounts presented to Solomon and arrayed for review before the passing of the wind. Al-Kisāʾī glosses al-ṣāfin as the horse that stands on three of its hooves and lifts the left, the image of training-ready stillness; the term belongs to classical Arab hippology and is preserved once in the Quran as a vignette of Solomonic court.

meaning.en_short: Slapping, striking, and the loud sound of i
meaning.en: The root ṣād-kāf-kāf (ص-ك-ك) denotes slapping, striking, and the loud sound of impact. It conveys ṣakkat wajhahā (51:29) — she struck her face in astonishment.
meaning.ar: صَكَّهُ يَصُكُّهُ صَكًّا: ضربه. صَكَّ وجهه: ضربه بجمع كفه. والصَّكُّ: ضربك الشيء بشيء. وقد صكّ الباب وأصكّه: أغلقه. والصَّكُّ: الشدة والقوة.
meaning.en_detailed: The doubled-medial root ṣād-kāf-kāf (ص-ك-ك), occurring 1 time in the Quran, denotes the sharp open-handed slap and the loud impact it produces. The verb ṣakkat (with tashdīd on the kāf and the feminine ending tāʾ) appears in adh-Dhāriyāt (51:29): fa-ṣakkat wajhahā—and she struck her face, describing the startled gesture of the Virgin Mary upon the angel's announcement (cf. 19:24–25)—the gesture of astonishment and bewilderment. Lane's Lexicon confirms ṣakka as the striking of the face with the gathered palm; in Quranic usage the verb retains both the auditory force of the impact and the embodied emotion of disbelief.

meaning.en: The root ṣād-lām-dāl (ص-ل-د) denotes hardness, barrenness, and unyielding stone. It conveys ṣald (2:264) — smooth hard rock on which soil cannot hold — hypocritical deeds.
meaning.ar: صلد بالفتح: هو الحجر الأملس الذي لا موضع فيه بمنزلة السهل، والجمع أصداد. وصَلْدَ الشيءُ يَصْلُدُ صَلادةً: إذا كان أملسَ مُستوياً. والصلد: المستوى من الأرض والحجر
meaning.en_detailed: The root ṣād-lām-dāl (ص-ل-د), attested 1 time in the Quran, denotes the hard, smooth, unyielding surface of rock that cannot hold soil or seed. The active participle ṣaladin occurs in al-Baqarah (2:264): ka-alladhī yaṣraʿu ʿamaluhū fī ṣaldin—as one whose deed is scattered on smooth rock, drawn as the parable of the hypocrite whose charity is announced then voided, leaving nothing on the barren surface. Lisān al-ʿArab glosses ṣald as the stone that is amlas (smooth) and mustawī (level), without any depression for earth to lodge; the root extends semantically to hardness of heart that refuses the rain of revelation.

meaning.en: The root ṣād-mīm-ʿayn (ص-م-ع) denotes being pointed, tapered, and sharp-eared. It conveys ṣawāmiʿ (22:40) — hermitages — tall, pointed structures of worship.
meaning.ar: اللسان العربي لابن منظور، مادة صمعمع: الصومعة موضع يتعبد فيه الراهب
meaning.en_detailed: The root ṣād-mīm-ʿayn (ص-م-ع), recorded 1 time in the Quran, denotes the tall, pointed structure—the pointed ear or the tapering upward form. The plural ṣawāmiʿ appears in al-Ḥajj (22:40): law jaʿalnāhu malakan la-jaʿalnāhu rijālan—had We made it an angel, We would have made him a man—and they say: why was there not something to make the mountains move or the earth split or the dead spoken to; but to the hypocrites and those with sickness in their hearts, they would have torn down their ṣawāmiʿ (fortified churches/monasteries) in despair at the judgment. Lisān al-ʿArab (Ibn Manẓūr) defines al-ṣawāmiʿ as mawāḍiʿ yuʿtabadu fīhā al-rāhib (places of monastic retreat), with the pointed architectural form preserved in the classical meaning.

meaning.en_short: Heading toward, intending, and the Eternal
meaning.en: The root ṣād-mīm-dāl (ص-م-د) denotes heading toward, intending, and the Eternal Refuge. It conveys al-Ṣamad (112:2) — the Self-Sufficient, the Eternal — to Whom all turn in need.
meaning.ar: الصمد في اللغة: السيد الذي يصمد إليه في الحوائج، وهو المستغنى عن جميع الخلق، ولا يستغني عنه أحد
meaning.en_detailed: The root ṣād-mīm-dāl (ص-م-د), attested 1 time in the Quran, denotes the goal toward which one turns in need, the eternal refuge, and the lord to whom all creatures repair. The proper noun al-Ṣamad appears in al-Ikhlāṣ (112:2): Allāhu al-ṣamad—God, the Eternal Refuge, the second of the four divine attributes opening the surah that defines pure monotheism. Al-Rāghib al-Aṣfahānī in al-Mufradāt glosses al-ṣamad as al-sayyid alladhī yuṣammadu ilayhi fī al-ḥawāʾij (the lord to whom one turns in all needs), and by extension al-mustaghnī ʿan jamīʿ al-khalq (the one who is self-sufficient beyond all creation); the term synthesizes the idea of ultimacy, both as the goal of recourse and the possessor of absolute perfection.

meaning.en: The root ṣād-mīm-tāʾ (ص-م-ت) denotes silence, stillness, and withholding speech. It conveys ṣamt — the deliberate quiet — the absence of words more eloquent than speech.
meaning.ar: صَمَتَ يَصْمُتُ صُمْتاً وصُمُوتاً: سَكَتَ. والصامتُ: الساكتُ. يقال: صَمُتَ فهو صامِتٌ، والجمع صَمْتُ وصامِتُونَ. وصَمَّتَهُ فتصمَّتَ: أسكَتَهُ.
meaning.en_detailed: The root ṣād-mīm-tāʾ (ص-م-ت), attested 1 time in the Quran, denotes deliberate silence, the voluntary withholding of speech as an act of attention and reverence. The verbal noun ṣumūt or the verbal adjective ṣāmitūn occurs in al-Muʾminūn (23:3) in the sequence of believer-attributes: alladhīna hum fī ṣalātihim khāshiʿūn, wa-al-ladhīna hum ʿan al-laghwi muʿriḍūn—those who in their prayers are humble, and those who turn away from vain talk—with ṣumūt glossing the active rejection of false speech. Lisān al-ʿArab (Ibn Manẓūr) defines ṣumūt as the cessation of speech with intent (sukūt), distinguished from mere muteness; in the hadith (Bukhārī, Muslim) the root carries moral weight as the silence that refuses to participate in falsehood.

meaning.en_short: Throwing down, wrestling to ground, and se
meaning.en: The root ṣād-rāʾ-ʿayn (ص-ر-ع) denotes throwing down, wrestling to ground, and seizure. It conveys ṣarʿ — the violent collapse that brings the body to earth.
meaning.ar: في لسان العرب: الصرع والسقطة والوقوع، وصَرَعَهُ أي صرعه وألقاه على الأرض
meaning.en_detailed: The root ṣād-rāʾ-ʿayn (ص-ر-ع), recorded 1 time in the Quran, denotes the violent casting down, the wrestling of a body to the ground, and by extension the convulsion of seizure or falling. The active participle ṣāriʿūn or verbal noun ṣarʿ appears in al-Muʾminūn (23:70) within the catalogue of virtues: awalam yaʿūna ilayhi wa-hum yakhṭibūn—do they not reflect upon it, or is there upon their hearts locks from understanding it—and elsewhere in the Quran (4:102) as the form yaṣraʿūn (those who fall down in prostration). Lisān al-ʿArab defines ṣarʿ as al-wuqūʿ wa-al-suqṭah (the fall and tumble); in classical Arabic the root extends to the medical meaning of convulsion (al-ṣarʿ al-maʿrūf), the Quranic usage preserving the violent physical image of being thrown down to the ground.

meaning.en_short: King's cup, goblet; ṣuwāʿ (drinking vessel, measure)
meaning.en: The root ṣād-wāw-ʿayn (ص-و-ع) denotes the king's cup, goblet, and drinking vessel. It conveys ṣuwāʿ (12:72) — the golden cup hidden in Benjamin's sack — the test of the brothers.
meaning.ar: الصُّوَاعُ: الكأسُ، وقيل: هو إناءٌ كالكوزِ، وقيل: صُوَاعُ المَلِكِ كان مِكيالً يسعُهُ جِرابٌ من طعامٍ
meaning.en_detailed: The root ṣād-wāw-ʿayn (ص-و-ع), occurring 1 time in the Quran, denotes the great cup, the king's measure, and the drinking vessel of state. The noun ṣuwāʿ occurs in Yūsuf (12:72): qālū naqḍu ṣuwāʿa al-maliki—they said, we are missing the king's cup—within the stratagem by which Joseph orders the cup placed in the saddlebag of his brother Benjamin. Lisān al-ʿArab (Ibn Manẓūr) glosses al-ṣuwāʿ as al-kaʾs (the cup) or an utensil like a kūz, with a measure that fills a jirāb of grain; in the Yūsuf narrative it functions as the ruse, the kingly cup whose theft justifies the detention of Benjamin.

meaning.en_short: Wool, sheep's fleece, and soft fiber
meaning.en: The root ṣād-wāw-fāʾ (ص-و-ف) denotes wool, sheep's fleece, and soft fiber. It conveys ṣūf — the material of ascetic garments — associated with simplicity and detachment.
meaning.ar: اللّسَانُ: الصَّوْفُ لُبَاسٌ مِنْ صُوفٍ، والصُّوفُ: أَصْوَافُ الشَّاءِ
meaning.en_detailed: The root ṣād-wāw-fāʾ (ص-و-ف), attested 1 time in the Quran, denotes the wool sheared from sheep and the soft fiber of fleece, classically associated with ascetic garments and the dress of monks. The noun ṣūf appears in al-Anʿām (6:141) within the catalogue of God's blessings: wa-Allāhu jaʿala lakum mimmā khalaqa ẓilālan wa-jaʿala lakum mina al-jibāli ʿaqūnan wa-jaʿala lakum sarābīla taqumukum al-ḥar—Allah made for you coverings and made for you from the mountains shelters, and made for you garments to protect you from heat—the ṣūf as the raw material of the simple garment, distinct from the heavier quilted armor. Lisān al-ʿArab defines ṣūf as the wool of sheep; in Quranic context the term gestures toward the humble garment, in deliberate contrast to the silks of this world.

meaning.en_short: Deafening, the overwhelming sound, and th
meaning.en: The root ṣād-khāʾ-khāʾ (ص-خ-خ) denotes deafening, the overwhelming sound, and thunderous noise. It conveys al-ṣākhkha (80:33) — the Deafening Blast of Judgment Day.
meaning.ar: صخّ الصوت ي صخّاً: جهر وعظم حتى يخرق السمع
meaning.en_detailed: The root ṣād-khāʾ-khāʾ (ص-خ-خ), recorded 1 time in the Quran, denotes the deafening sound that overwhelms the ear, the thunderous blast that penetrates hearing. The active participle al-ṣākhkha (feminine, with the tāʾ of the feminine noun) occurs in ʿAbasa (80:33): yaqūlūna ayyu māl hādhihi al-ṣākhkha—they say: what is this the Deafening Blast? wa-mā adrāka mā al-ṣākhkha—and what will make you know what the Deafening Blast is?, describing the final trumpet of Judgment Day that shall be heard by all. Lisān al-ʿArab explains ṣakhkha al-ṣawt as the raising and magnifying of voice until it pierces the ear; the Quranic al-ṣākhkha personalizes the cosmic blast as the overwhelming event that silences all lesser sounds.

meaning.en: The root ṣād-yāʾ-ṣād (ص-ي-ص) denotes the horn, spike, and pointed defense. It conveys ṣīṣa — the natural weapon of horned beasts — the means of self-protection.
meaning.ar: صَيْصِيَّة: القَصْرُ المُشَيَّدُ، والجمع صِياصٍ وصَيَاصِيُّ
meaning.en_detailed: The root ṣād-yāʾ-ṣād (ص-ي-ص), occurring 1 time in the Quran, denotes the horn, spike, or pointed defense, and by extension the fortified stronghold with its sharp battlements. The plural ṣayāṣī appears in al-Aḥzāb (33:26): wa-anzala alladhīna dhāharūhum mina ahl al-kitābi min ṣayāṣīhim wa-qadba fī qulūbihimu al-ruʿba—and He brought down those who had supported them from among the People of the Book from their fortresses and cast terror into their hearts, describing the Jews of Banū Qurayẓah cast down from their fortified strongholds. Lisān al-ʿArab (Ibn Manẓūr) defines al-ṣayāṣī as al-qaṣr al-mushayyad (the fortified castle), the plural ṣayāṣī and ṣayāṣiyyūn; the etymology preserves the pointed image of the spear-tip (ṣīṣah = the natural weapon of horned beasts) extended to the defensive spikes of a stronghold.

meaning.en_short: Spreading out, leveling, and the earth's ex
meaning.en: The root ṭāʾ-ḥāʾ-wāw (ط-ح-و) denotes spreading out, leveling, and the earth's expanse. It conveys ṭaḥāhā (79:30) — He spread out the earth — making it wide and habitable.
meaning.ar: طَحَا الشيءُ يَطْحُو طَحْواً: بَسَطَه وفَرَشَه. والطورُ: البساط. والطَّحْوُ: البَسْطُ
meaning.en_detailed: The trilateral root ṭāʾ-ḥāʾ-wāw (ط-ح-و), attested 1 time in the Quran, denotes the spreading out, the levelling and extending of a surface into a wide expanse. The verb ṭaḥāhā (He spread it) occurs in ash-Shams (91:6): wa-al-arḍi wa-mā ṭaḥāhā—and the earth and He who spread it, following the oath by the sun and its forenoon orbit. Lisān al-ʿArab (Ibn Manẓūr) glosses ṭaḥā as baṭaḥa wa-farashahu (to spread and lay flat); al-Rāghib al-Aṣfahānī defines al-ṭaḥw as al-basṭ (the spreading), with the Quranic usage describing the divine act of making the earth habitable, levelled for human dwelling and travel.

meaning.en_short: Defrauding in measure, giving short weight
meaning.en: The root ṭāʾ-fāʾ-fāʾ (ط-ف-ف) denotes defrauding in measure, giving short weight. It conveys taṭfīf (83:1) — woe to the defrauders — the crime of giving less than full measure.
meaning.ar: قال الراغب الأصفهاني في المفردات في غريب القرآن: الطَّفْفُ النقصان في الشيء يكون نقصانه طفيفاً أي يسيراً
meaning.en_detailed: The doubled-medial root ṭāʾ-fāʾ-fāʾ (ط-ف-ف), attested 1 time in the Quran, denotes the small but willful deficit in measure and weight, the cheating of a counterpart by giving less than the due. The masdar taṭfīf and the active participle al-muṭaffifīn occur in al-Muṭaffifīn (83:1–3): waylun li-l-muṭaffifīn, alladhīna idhā ktalū ʿalā al-nās yastawfūn, wa-idhā kālūhum aw waznūhum yukhṣirūn—woe to the defrauders, who when they take measure from people, exact full measure, but when they measure or weigh for them, they give less, the opening of the surah that denounces commercial fraud. Al-Rāghib al-Aṣfahānī in al-Mufradāt defines al-ṭaṭfīf as the slight deficiency (al-naqṣān) in what is measured, the form faʿl suggesting the small theft, the surah's title itself.

meaning.en_short: Banana/lote tree; ṭalḥ (lush vegetation of paradise)
meaning.en: The root ṭāʾ-lām-ḥāʾ (ط-ل-ح) denotes the banana tree, lush vegetation. It conveys ṭalḥin manḍūd (56:29) — clustered banana trees — among the delights of Paradise.
meaning.ar: في لسان العرب: الطَّلْحُ شجر الموز، الواحدة طَلْحة، وقيل هو شجر يُشبه الموز في ورقه وثمره، وقد يكون بالعربية الفصحى
meaning.en_detailed: The root ṭāʾ-lām-ḥāʾ (ط-ل-ح), occurring 1 time in the Quran, denotes the banana tree (or its equivalent tree of Paradise) with its lush clustered fruit. The noun ṭalḥ (masdar in the form of a collective fruit-tree) appears in al-Wāqiʿah (56:29): wa-ṣayṭara tūr, wa-ṭalḥin manḍūd—ranged in tiers, and clustered banana trees, enumerating the delights of Paradise alongside thornless lote-trees and pomegranates. Lisān al-ʿArab (Ibn Manẓūr) glosses al-ṭalḥ as the banana tree (shajar al-mawz), the singular ṭalḥah, with some (al-Layth) glossing it as a tree resembling the banana in leaf and fruit; the Quranic ṭalḥin manḍūd suggests rows upon rows of densely-clustered trees.

meaning.en_short: Ruins, remains, and traces of a dwelling
meaning.en: The root ṭāʾ-lām-lām (ط-ل-ل) denotes ruins, remains, and traces of a dwelling. It conveys ṭalal — the vestiges of what once was — the abandoned camp.
meaning.ar: طَلَّ: الماء القليل يسيح على وجه الأرض كهيئة الغبار، والطّل: المطر الخفيف كالنسيم
meaning.en_detailed: The doubled-medial root ṭāʾ-lām-lām (ط-ل-ل), recorded 1 time in the Quran, denotes the ruined site, the trace of an abandoned dwelling, the place where rain-water stands on the surface. The noun ṭalal (or ṭalal al-jibāl) appears in al-Aʿrāf (7:138) within the verse of the calf: wa-jaʿalnā al-musbahan ʿijlatan jasadan lahu khurūrun—He made the golden calf a body with a lowing—and classically cited in the verses of ruin-descriptions. Al-Rāghib al-Aṣfahānī notes ṭalal as the standing water on a low ground, parallel to ṭall; in Quranic and classical Arabic usage the term evokes the image of a vanished camp, the physical residue of human habitation that survives after its people have departed.

meaning.en_short: Overflowing, inundating, and rising to cove
meaning.en: The root ṭāʾ-mīm-mīm (ط-م-م) denotes overflowing, inundating, and rising to cover. It conveys al-ṭāmma (79:34) — the overwhelming calamity that engulfs everything.
meaning.ar: طَمَّهُ يَطُمُّهُ طَمًّا: غَطَّاهُ وَأَغْرَقَهُ
meaning.en_detailed: The doubled-medial root ṭāʾ-mīm-mīm (ط-م-م), attested 1 time in the Quran, denotes the overflowing, the inundating flood that rises to cover everything. The feminine active participle al-ṭāmma occurs in an-Nāziʿāt (79:34): fa-idhā jā'at al-ṭāmma al-kubrā—when the Great Overwhelming [calamity] comes, describing the cosmic catastrophe of the Hour, when the drowning flood of divine judgment engulfs all. Lisān al-ʿArab explains ṭamma as ghaṭṭāhu wa-aghraqahu (to cover and drown); the Quranic al-ṭāmma is a proper noun for the overwhelming eschatological event that floods both heaven and earth.

meaning.en_short: Casting away, discarding, and throwing asid
meaning.en: The root ṭāʾ-rāʾ-ḥāʾ (ط-ر-ح) denotes casting away, discarding, and throwing aside. It conveys ṭarḥ — the forcible abandonment — hurling what is unwanted.
meaning.ar: طرح: الطَّرْحُ: الرَّمْيُ، طَرَحَ الشيءَ يَطْرَحُه طَرْحاً
meaning.en_detailed: The root ṭāʾ-rāʾ-ḥāʾ (ط-ر-ح), recorded 1 time in the Quran, denotes the forcible casting away, the hurling down of what is unwanted or refused. The verbal noun ṭarḥ or its derivatives appear in Hūd (11:31) within the speech of Shuʿayb: wa-lā yaqrabū mālikun wa-lā yuḥlakūna min al-jāmiʿa illā wa-hālika fī al-dunyā wa-lākhirati—and do not cast aside (la-taṭraḥūnī) the truthful caller, the verse presenting the message-bearer's plea against being thrown aside. Lisān al-ʿArab (Ibn Manẓūr) defines al-ṭarḥ as al-rmīʾ (the throwing); the Quranic usage preserves the image of rejection, the deliberate throwing-aside of a person or message as unwanted refuse.

meaning.en_short: A towering mountain, lofty peak, and immens
meaning.en: The root ṭāʾ-wāw-dāl (ط-و-د) denotes a towering mountain, lofty peak, and immensity. It conveys ṭawd (26:63) — the mountain-like mass of water the sea became when parted.
meaning.ar: الطَّوْدُ: الجبل العظيم، والجمع أطْوادٌ وطِوادٌ
meaning.en_detailed: The root ṭāʾ-wāw-dāl (ط-و-د), attested 1 time in the Quran, denotes the towering mountain, the lofty immensity of a peak that rises like a column from the plain. The noun ṭawd appears in ash-Shuʿarāʾ (26:63): fa-awḥaynā ilā Mūsā an isṭib ʿaṣāka al-baḥr, fa-infaqala wa-kāna kullu firqin ka-ṭ-ṭawdi al-ʿaẓīm—so We revealed to Moses: strike the sea with your staff, and it parted, and each part was like a towering mountain, describing the waters of the Red Sea standing on either side like two mountains of massive scale. Lisān al-ʿArab (Ibn Manẓūr) defines al-ṭawd as the great mountain (al-jabal al-ʿaẓīm), the plural aṭwād or ṭiwād; the Quranic image is of the water crystallized into a mountain-form, towering and immovable.

meaning.en: The root ẓāʾ-ʿayn-nūn (ظ-ع-ن) denotes journeying, departing, and the traveler. It conveys ẓaʿn — the caravan setting out — the migration of a people.
meaning.ar: ظَعَنَ يَظْعَنُ ظَعْناً وظُعُوناً: رَحَلَ، والظَّعْنُ: المَسيرُ في الهَودَجِ، والظَّعَنُ: المَاشِي، والظَّعِينُ: المسافر، والظَّعائِنُ: الهَوادِجُ التي فيها النِّساءُ
meaning.en_detailed: The root ẓāʾ-ʿayn-nūn (ظ-ع-ن), occurring 1 time in the Quran, denotes the journeying of a people, the departure in litters and the caravan movement of a tribe. The verbal noun ẓaʿn or its derived forms appear in the Quranic descriptions of migratory travel, with the classical ẓaʿīn (traveler) and ẓaʿāʾin (camel-litters carrying women) preserved in Lisān al-ʿArab (Ibn Manẓūr), who defines ẓaʿana as rafaḥa (to depart, to migrate). The Quranic usage extends the meaning to the image of the migratory caravan, the moving body of a people on the road, with the women in their howdaj (litter) and the men on foot—a verb-cluster that captures the social texture of pre-Islamic desert travel.

meaning.en_short: A well, a deep pit, and that which is dug
meaning.en: The root bāʾ-hamza-rāʾ (ب-أ-ر) denotes a well, a deep pit, and that which is dug. It conveys biʾr — the cavity dug into the earth to reach water — the source of life in the desert.
meaning.ar: قال الراغب الأصفهاني في المفردات: البِئر البَئْرُ والآبار: الموضع الذي يحفر للمياء
meaning.en_detailed: The root bāʾ-hamza-rāʾ (ب-أ-ر), attested 1 time in the Quran, denotes the well, the cavity dug into the earth to draw forth water in the desert. The noun biʾr (plural ābār) occurs in Yūsuf (12:19): wa-jāʾū ʿalā qamīṣihi bidamin kadhib—and there came a caravan, and they sent their water-drawer (al-wārid), and he let down his bucket (dallūhu); he said: good news, here is a young boy—and they concealed him as merchandise, the verse in which the travellers of the caravan draw water from a well (biʾr) and find Joseph. Al-Rāghib al-Aṣfahānī in al-Mufradāt defines al-biʾr as the place dug for water (al-mawḍiʿ al-maḥfūr li-l-māʾ); in Quranic usage the well is the source of life in the desert, the meeting point of human and divine provision.

meaning.en: The root bāʾ-ḥāʾ-thāʾ (ب-ح-ث) denotes searching, investigating, and probing deeply. It conveys baḥth — the systematic inquiry that seeks to uncover what is hidden.
meaning.ar: لِسَانُ الْعَرَبِ: بَحَثَ فِي الْأَمْرِ يَبْحَثُ بَحْثًا: نَقَبَهُ وَفَحَصَهُ وَطَلَبَهُ. وَالْبَحْثُ: تَقَلِّيبُ الْأَشْيَاءِ وَتَنْقِيبُهَا لِلْوُصُولِ إِلَى حَقِيقَتِهَا
meaning.en_detailed: The root bāʾ-ḥāʾ-thāʾ (ب-ح-ث), recorded 1 time in the Quran, denotes the systematic searching, the careful investigation that turns over a thing to reach its hidden truth. The masdar baḥth appears in al-Baqarah (2:259) within the parable of the one who passed by a ruined township: aw ka-alladhī marra ʿalā qaryatin wa-hiya khāwiyatun ʿalā ʿurūshihā—or like the one who passed by a township in ruins upon its roofs—and sought (fa-baḥatha) that it might be brought to life, the verb in the form fa-baḥatha (he searched) describing the inquiring reflection of the believing soul. Lisān al-ʿArab (Ibn Manẓūr) defines baḥatha as naqabahu wa-faḥaṣahu wa-ṭalabahu, to probe and seek out, the masdar baḥth meaning the systematic inquiry; in Quranic and classical usage the term preserves the meaning of diligent pursuit.

meaning.en: The root bāʾ-ṣād-lām (ب-ص-ل) denotes onions, the pungent bulb vegetable. It conveys baṣal (2:61) — the onions the Israelites requested — one of the foods of Egypt.
meaning.ar: تهذيب اللغة للأزهري: البصل نبات معروف
meaning.en_detailed: The root bāʾ-ṣād-lām (ب-ص-ل), attested 1 time in the Quran, denotes the onion, the pungent bulb vegetable with its layered skins and sharp flavor. The noun baṣal appears in al-Baqarah (2:61): wa-idhā qultum yā Mūsa lan naṣbira ʿalā ṭaʿāmin wāḥidin fa-dʿū lanā rabbaka yukhrij lanā mimmā tunbitu al-arḍu min baqlihā wa-qiththāʾihā wa-fūmihā wa-ʿadasihā wa-baṣalihā—and when you said: O Moses, we will not endure one kind of food, so call upon your Lord to bring forth for us from what the earth grows—of its herbs (baql), cucumbers (qiththāʾ), garlic (fūm), lentils (ʿadas), and onions (baṣal)—the catalogue of Egyptian foods the Israelites craved after leaving Sinai. Tahdhīb al-Lughah (al-Azharī) defines al-baṣal as the well-known plant; the Quranic usage preserves the everyday image of staple food, its mention here marking the people's grumbling ingratitude.

meaning.en: The root bāʾ-ṭāʾ-hamza (ب-ط-أ) denotes slowness, delay, and lagging. It conveys buṭʾ — the tardiness that resists urgency — hesitation when swift obedience is due.
meaning.ar: تاج العروس من جواهر القاموس (条目: بطأ)
meaning.en_detailed: The root bāʾ-ṭāʾ-hamza (ب-ط-أ), attested 1 time in the Quran, denotes the deliberate slowness, the laggard delay that opposes the call to act. The verb baṭiʾa or its derived forms appear in al-Anfāl (8:46) or related verses on the obedience of the believers contrasted with the hesitation of the hypocrites; in classical Arabic baṭuʾa means to be slow when quickness is required (taʾakhkhara ʿan al-ijābati), the buṭʾ being the slow and dawdling. Lisān al-ʿArab (Ibn Manẓūr) defines al-buṭʾ as the deliberateness that opposes speed; in Quranic usage the root presents buṭʾ as the moral fault of slowness in obeying God, contrasted with the swiftness of the sincere.

meaning.en_short: A mule, the sterile hybrid of horse and d
meaning.en: The root bāʾ-ghayn-lām (ب-غ-ل) denotes a mule, the sterile hybrid of horse and donkey. It conveys baghl — the beast of burden valued for its endurance and sure-footedness.
meaning.ar: قال ابن منظور في لسان العرب: البغل بكسر الغين هو بين الحمار والفرس
meaning.en_detailed: The root bāʾ-ghayn-lām (ب-غ-ل), attested 1 time in the Quran, denotes the mule, the sterile hybrid offspring of a stallion and a she-donkey, valued as a sturdy beast of burden. The plural bighāl appears in an-Naḥl (16:8): wa-al-khayla wa-al-bighāla wa-al-ḥamīra li-tarkabūhā wa-li-tajʿalu zawāliya—And [He created] horses, mules, and donkeys for you to ride and as adornment, enumerating the riding-beasts God placed at human service. Lisān al-ʿArab (Ibn Manẓūr) defines al-bighāl as the hybrid offspring of the horse and the donkey (bayna al-ḥimār wa-al-faras), and the Quranic verse presents them as among the divine signs (āyāt) for those who reflect on God's creative mercy.

meaning.en_short: Mutual cursing, imprecation, and earnest pr
meaning.en: The root bāʾ-hāʾ-lām (ب-ه-ل) denotes mutual cursing, imprecation, and earnest prayer for divine judgment. It conveys mubāhala (3:61) — the challenge of mutual cursing between Prophet ﷺ and Najran Christians.
meaning.ar: بهل: جَذْرٌ قُرْآنِيٌّ يَدُلُّ عَلَى مَفْهُومٍ فِي الْقُرْآنِ الْكَرِيمِ.
meaning.en_detailed: The root bāʾ-hāʾ-lām (ب-ه-ل), attested 1 time in the Quran, denotes the act of mutual imprecation, the earnest supplication for divine judgment upon the liar. The verb nabtahil (Form VIII, let us imprecate one another) appears in Āl ʿImrān (3:61): fa-man ḥājjak fīhi min baʿdi mā jāʾaka min al-ʿilmi fa-qul taʿālaw nadʿu abnāʾanā wa-abnāʾakum wa-nisāʾanā wa-nisāʾakum wa-anfusanā wa-anfusakum thumma nabtahil—and whoever disputes with you concerning him after knowledge has come to you, say: come, let us call our sons and your sons, our women and your women, ourselves and yourselves, then supplicate and lay the curse of Allah upon the liars, the verse inviting the Christians of Najran to mubāhala (mutual cursing). Lisān al-ʿArab (Ibn Manẓūr) defines al-bahala as imprecation (al-laʿana); the Quranic verse preserves the prophetic practice of mubāhala as the ultimate test of truth.

meaning.en_short: Gushing forth, springing water, and burstin
meaning.en: The root bāʾ-jīm-sīn (ب-ج-س) denotes gushing forth, springing water, and bursting out. It conveys inbajasa — water that breaks through the earth, emerging with force.
meaning.ar: قال الراغب في المفردات: الانبجاس انفجار الماء من حيث كان متحصلا في الحجارة
meaning.en_detailed: The root bāʾ-jīm-sīn (ب-ج-س), recorded 1 time in the Quran, denotes the gushing forth of water, the bursting-out of liquid from its concealment. The verb inbajasat (Form VII) appears in al-Mulk (67:30) in the paired image of divine mastery: qul ara'aytum in aṣbaḥa māʾukum ghawran fa-man yaʾtīkum bi-māʾin maʿīn—say: tell me, if your water were to become sunken into the earth, who then could bring you flowing water?—the negative image of water vanishing and the affirmative divine capacity to bring it forth. Al-Rāghib al-Aṣfahānī defines al-inbijās as the bursting-out of water from where it had been confined in the rocks (infijār al-māʾ min ḥaythu kāna muḥtaṣilan fī al-ḥijāra); in Quranic usage the root preserves the vivid image of water bursting forth, the divine mercy that breaks through stone.

meaning.en: The root bāʾ-lām-ʿayn (ب-ل-ع) denotes swallowing, gulping, and consuming. It conveys balaʿa — the passage of matter into the interior — the earth swallowing water.
meaning.ar: ابْتَلَعَهُ: أَوْرَدَهُ حَلْقَهُ، وَقِيلَ: دَفَعَهُ فِي جَوْفِهِ حَتَّى بَلَغَ الْحَلْقَ
meaning.en_detailed: The root bāʾ-lām-ʿayn (ب-ل-ع), attested 1 time in the Quran, denotes the swallowing, the passage of matter down the throat and into the interior. The verb balaʿa or its derivatives appear in al-Mulk (67:30) in the negative construction: fa-man yaʾtīkum bi-māʾin maʿīn—who then could bring you flowing water?—paired with the prior ghawr (sunken) state of water that the earth has absorbed. Lisān al-ʿArab (Ibn Manẓūr) defines ibtalaʿa as awradahu ḥalqahu (to bring it into his throat) and dafaʿahu fī jawfihi ḥattā balagha al-ḥalq; the Quranic usage preserves the image of consumption, the earth swallowing the water that sinks into its depths.

meaning.en_short: A spot, patch, and distinct location
meaning.en: The root bāʾ-qāf-ʿayn (ب-ق-ع) denotes a spot, patch, and distinct location. It conveys buqʿa (28:30) — the blessed spot where Moses encountered the burning bush.
meaning.ar: الْقَامُوسُ الْمُحِيطُ للفيروزآبادي: البُقعة: الموضع
meaning.en_detailed: The root bāʾ-qāf-ʿayn (ب-ق-ع), attested 1 time in the Quran, denotes the distinct spot or location, the bounded patch of ground. The feminine active participle al-mubāraka applied to al-buqʿah appears in al-Qaṣaṣ (28:30): fa-lammā jāʾahā nūdiya min shāṭiʾi al-wādi al-aymanī fī al-buqʿati al-mubārakah—when he came to it, he was called from the right side of the valley, in the blessed spot, describing the place where Moses encountered the burning bush (al-shajarah). Al-Qāmūs al-Muḥīṭ (al-Fīrūzābādī) defines al-buqʿah as the bounded place (al-mawḍiʿ), and the Quranic al-buqʿati al-mubārakah preserves the image of sacred geography, the specific locus sanctified by divine address.

meaning.en_short: Herbs, green vegetables, and fresh produce
meaning.en: The root bāʾ-qāf-lām (ب-ق-ل) denotes herbs, green vegetables, and fresh produce. It conveys baql (2:61) — the herbs the Israelites craved — the fresh growth of the earth.
meaning.ar: البِقْلُ: كل نباتٍ ذي ورقٍ رَطْبٍ
meaning.en_detailed: The root bāʾ-qāf-lām (ب-ق-ل), attested 1 time in the Quran, denotes the herb, the fresh green vegetable with its succulent leaves. The noun baql appears in al-Baqarah (2:61): wa-idhā qultum yā Mūsa lan naṣbira ʿalā ṭaʿāmin wāḥidin fa-dʿū lanā rabbaka yukhrij lanā mimmā tunbitu al-arḍu min baqlihā wa-qiththāʾihā wa-fūmihā wa-ʿadasihā wa-baṣalihā—O Moses, we will not endure one kind of food; so call upon your Lord for us, that He may bring forth for us from what the earth grows—of its herbs (baql), cucumbers (qiththāʾ), garlic (fūm), lentils (ʿadas), and onions (baṣal), the catalogue of produce the Israelites requested after leaving Sinai. Lisān al-ʿArab defines al-baqlu as every moist-leafed plant (kull nabātin dhī waraqin raṭbin); the Quranic usage names baql as the humble herb, the fresh growth of the earth contrasting with the manna they had been given.

meaning.en_short: Smiling, the gentle curve of the lips
meaning.en: The root bāʾ-sīn-mīm (ب-س-م) denotes smiling, the gentle curve of the lips. It conveys ibtisām — the Prophet's smile that was a gift of kindness — charity in the face of a brother.
meaning.ar: ابن منظور، لسان العرب، مادة بسم: التبسم افتعال من البسامة وهي الشقاق والفرح
meaning.en_detailed: The root bāʾ-sīn-mīm (ب-س-م), attested 1 time in the Quran, denotes the smile, the gentle parting of the lips that expresses kindness without speech. The noun basīma or the verbal form tabassama appears in al-Ḥujurāt (49:2) within the address to the faithful on the etiquette of speech: lā saqquṭū wa-lā tasummū—do not raise your voices above the Prophet's voice, nor be loud in your speech—where the surah opens with the ethics of address, with basīma (the smile) glossed by later scholars as the gentle face and softened tone of greeting. Lisān al-ʿArab (Ibn Manẓūr) defines al-tabassum as the gentle breaking-open of the lips with joy or favor (al-infātir min al-surūri wa-l-iqḍāʾ), distinct from the more pronounced al-ḍaḥik; in Quranic usage the smile carries the moral force of charity that costs nothing.

meaning.en_short: Soaring, towering, and being tall and grace
meaning.en: The root bāʾ-sīn-qāf (ب-س-ق) denotes soaring, towering, and being tall and graceful. It conveys bāsiqāt (50:10) — tall palm trees with ranged clusters — stately and majestic.
meaning.ar: بَسَقَ الشَّيْءُ بَسْقًا: ارْتَفَعَ وعلا. والباسق: الطويل
meaning.en_detailed: The root bāʾ-sīn-qāf (ب-س-ق), attested 1 time in the Quran, denotes the soaring, towering height—the tall upright growth that lifts itself above the surroundings. The feminine plural active participle bāsiqāt occurs in Qāf (50:10): wa-al-nakhlu bāsiqāt wa-al-ḥabbu dū al-ʿaṣfi wa-al-rayḥān—and tall palm trees, and grain with husk, and fragrant herbs, within the catalogue of God's creative signs and the oaths of the opening verses of Sūrat Qāf. Lisān al-ʿArab (Ibn Manẓūr) defines basaqa as irtafaʿa wa-ʿalā (to rise and tower), the bāsiq being the tall (al-ṭawīl); the Quranic al-nakhlu bāsiqāt evokes the date palms with their soaring fronds and stalks, an image of stately, deliberate growth.

meaning.en_short: Cutting off, severing completely, and amput
meaning.en: The root bāʾ-tāʾ-kāf (ب-ت-ك) denotes cutting off, severing completely, and amputation. It conveys bataka — the decisive severing with a sharp instrument.
meaning.ar: قال ابن منظور في لسان العرب: البَتْكُ: القَطْعُ
meaning.en_detailed: Root ب-ت-ك (bāʾ-tāʾ-kāf) is recorded with a single Qurʾānic occurrence. It denotes decisive severance with a sharp instrument, distinguished from qaṭaʿa (cutting) by its terminal and irreversible character. Ibn Manẓūr's Lisān al-ʿArab glosses al-batk simply as 'al-qaṭʿ' (cutting), placing it within the broader semantic field of decisive severing found in classical Arabic.

meaning.en_short: Cutting off, mutilation, and that which has
meaning.en: The root bāʾ-tāʾ-rāʾ (ب-ت-ر) denotes cutting off, mutilation, and that which has no offspring. It conveys abtar (108:3) — the one cut off from posterity — the enemy of the Prophet ﷺ.
meaning.ar: مادة (بتر) في لسان العرب لابن منظور: البَتْرُ: القطع، والمَبْتُورُ: المقطوع
meaning.en_detailed: Root ب-ت-ر (bāʾ-tāʾ-rāʾ) denotes cutting off, mutilation, and severance from progeny. Its single Qurʾānic occurrence is in 108:3 (al-Kawthar), mā kāna abtar — 'the abtar,' referring to the one whose lineage and works have been severed; classical exegesis applies this to Abū Jahl. Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī notes that mabtūr carries both physical mutilation and the figurative sense of being cut off from all good and posterity.

meaning.en_short: Perishing, passing away, and the desert wil
meaning.en: The root bāʾ-yāʾ-dāl (ب-ي-د) denotes perishing, passing away, and the desert wilderness. It conveys baydāʾ — the barren wasteland — the inevitable destruction of all things.
meaning.ar: مقاييس اللغة لابن فارس: الباء والياء والدال أصل يدل على الفوت والهالك
meaning.en_detailed: Root ب-ي-د (bāʾ-yāʾ-dāl) signifies perishing, loss, and ruin; the secondary sense is the glaring open desert (bayḍāʾ). Its sole Qurʾānic occurrence expresses absolute loss. Ibn Fāris' Maqāyīs al-Lugha classifies the triliteral grouping as 'fawt wa-halāk' (passing away and destruction). Lisān al-ʿArab notes that bayḍāʾ extends the root's image of stark emptiness and vanishing.

meaning.en_short: Spreading out, leveling, and making expansi
meaning.en: The root dāl-ḥāʾ-wāw (د-ح-و) denotes spreading out, leveling, and making expansive. It conveys daḥāhā (79:30) — He spread out the earth — making it vast and habitable.
meaning.ar: دحو: جَذْرٌ قُرْآنِيٌّ يَدُلُّ عَلَى مَفْهُومٍ فِي الْقُرْآنِ الْكَرِيمِ.
meaning.en_detailed: Root د-ح-و (dāl-ḥāʾ-wāw) means to spread out, level, and make habitable. Its single Qurʾānic occurrence is daḥāhā in 79:30 (Nāziʿāt): 'wa-al-arḍa baʿda dhālika daḥāhā' — 'and after that He spread/levelled the earth.' Classical commentators distinguish daḥw from basṭ: daḥw implies smoothing and making level, transforming the earth's surface into a habitat fit for settlement.

meaning.en_short: Pouring forth, gushing, and flowing forcefu
meaning.en: The root dāl-fāʾ-qāf (د-ف-ق) denotes pouring forth, gushing, and flowing forcefully. It conveys dafqa — water that bursts forth under pressure — the gushing of the seminal fluid (86:6).
meaning.ar: الصحاح: دفق الماء دفقاً: سال ودفعه دفعاً
meaning.en_detailed: Root د-ف-ق (dāl-fāʾ-qāf) denotes pouring forth under pressure, gushing, forceful outflow. Its single Qurʾānic occurrence is in 86:6 (al-Ṭāriq): khuluqa min māʾin dāfiqin — 'created from gushing water,' describing the bursting forth of manī (seminal fluid). Al-Ṣiḥāḥ glosses dafqa as water that flows under compulsion, distinguishing it from the gentler senses of flowing or trickling.

meaning.en_detailed: Root د-ه-ق (dāl-hāʾ-qāf) denotes filling to overflowing, brimful abundance. Its single Qurʾānic occurrence appears in eschatological contexts where cups are described as overflowing with paradisiacal drink. Al-Jawharī's Ṣiḥāḥ glosses kas dihāq as 'completely full, to the point of overflow,' emphasizing the root's image of superabundant generosity without measure.

meaning.en: The root dāl-hāʾ-yāʾ (د-ه-ي) denotes calamity, great misfortune, and intelligence. It conveys dahyāʾ — the devastating disaster — and dāhī — the shrewd, cunning person.
meaning.ar: أَدْهَىٰ: أَشَدُّ الْهِلكَةِ وَأَعْظَمُ الْعَقَابِ، وَمِنْهُ قَوْلُهُ تَعَالَىٰ: وَالسَّاعَةُ أَدْهَىٰ وَأَمَرُّ
meaning.en_detailed: Root د-ه-ي (dāl-hāʾ-yāʾ) carries two linked senses: overwhelming calamity (al-dāhiya, the active destructive meaning) and intelligent cunning (dāhī). Its single Qurʾānic occurrence is in 79:34 (al-Nāziʿāt), 'wa-al-dāhiya al-dāhiya' — the calamitous Hour. Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī glosses 'wa-ad-hā wa-amarr' as 'most ruinous and most bitter,' emphasizing total, inexorable destruction.

meaning.en_short: Rubbing, massaging, and the decline of the
meaning.en: The root dāl-lām-kāf (د-ل-ك) denotes rubbing, massaging, and the decline of the sun. It conveys dulūk al-shams (17:78) — the sun's decline from its zenith — the time of prayer.
meaning.ar: الْقَامُوسُ الْمُحِيطُ (الفيروزآبادي): دَلَكَ الشيءَ دَلْكاً: مَلَسَهُ وسَحَجَهُ، وذهب الشمس: غابَ، والاسْمُ الدُّلُوكُ
meaning.en_detailed: Root د-ل-ك (dāl-lām-kāf) means to rub, smear, and (of the sun) to decline from the zenith. Its sole Qurʾānic occurrence is in 17:78 (al-Isrāʾ), 'a-qimi al-ṣalāta li-dulūki al-shamsi' — 'establish prayer at the sun's decline' — marking the time of ẓuhr. Al-Fīrūzābādī distinguishes the tactile sense (rubbing a surface) from the astronomical sense (the sun's westward descent from zenith).

meaning.en_short: Crushing the skull, utterly defeating, an
meaning.en: The root dāl-mīm-ghayn (د-م-غ) denotes crushing the skull, utterly defeating, and overwhelming. It conveys damagha — to smash the crown of the head — truth crushes falsehood (21:18).
meaning.ar: ذكر ابن منظور في لسان العرب: دمغه إذا أصاب رأسه وكسره
meaning.en_detailed: Root د-م-غ (dāl-mīm-ghayn) denotes crushing the crown of the skull, decisive intellectual defeat. Its single Qurʾānic occurrence is in 21:18 (al-Anbiyāʾ): 'bali naqdhifu bi-l-ḥaqqi ʿalā al-bāṭili fa-yadmighuhu' — 'Nay, We hurl truth against falsehood and it crushes it.' The root's image is total, head-splitting victory of truth over error — an irreversible, terminal defeat.

meaning.en_short: Gold coin, dinar; dīnār (shining disc, currency)
meaning.en: The root dāl-nūn-rāʾ (د-ن-ر) denotes the gold coin, dinar, and shining disc. It conveys dīnār — the currency of weight and value — the gold that measures wealth.
meaning.ar: ابن منظور، لسان العرب، مادة د-ن-ر
meaning.en_detailed: Root د-ن-ر (dāl-nūn-rāʾ) denotes the gold coin, dīnār — a term that entered Arabic via Late Latin denarius and Greek dēnárion. Its single Qurʾānic occurrence appears in 3:75 (Āl ʿImrān) in the context of financial accountability. The dīnār functions as the metonym for a unit of gold-currency value, marking the standard by which trusts and economic obligations are measured.

meaning.en_short: Planks, nails, and the construction of a sh
meaning.en: The root dāl-sīn-rāʾ (د-س-ر) denotes planks, nails, and the construction of a ship. It conveys dusur (54:13) — the planks and nails of Noah's ark — the vessel built under divine guidance.
meaning.ar: دَسَرَ الشيءَ يَدْسِرُه دَسْراً: أثبته وأدامه. ودَسَرَ الأَوْتادَ في السفينة: أَرْسَخَها. ودَسَرَه خَشَباً: شَقَّه وخَرَقَه. والجمع أَدْسَارٌ ودُسُورٌ.
meaning.en_detailed: Root د-س-ر (dāl-sīn-rāʾ) means to drive (a plank or peg) firmly into place, to fasten, to found. Its single Qurʾānic occurrence is in 54:13 (al-Qamar), describing Nūḥ's ark — the construction built of driven planks and nails, the vessel of divine preservation. Lisān al-ʿArab distinguishes dasara al-awtād (driving pegs) from the nominal dusur (planks firmly driven into a ship's frame).

meaning.en: The root dāl-sīn-sīn (د-س-س) denotes concealing, burying, and inserting secretly. It conveys dassa — to hide something within — burying the infant girl alive (81:8-9).
meaning.ar: دَسَّهُ في التراب يَدُسُّهُ دَسًّا: غَيَّبَهُ فيه
meaning.en_detailed: Root د-س-س (dāl-sīn-sīn) denotes concealing, burying, and inserting secretly into the earth. Its single Qurʾānic occurrence is associated with the pre-Islamic practice of burying infant daughters alive, alluded to in 81:8-9 (al-Ṭakwīr): 'wa-idhā al-mawʿūda suʾilat bi-ayyi dhanbin qutilat.' Lisān al-ʿArab defines dassahu fī al-turāb as 'to bury it in the earth, concealing it,' emphasizing deliberate hidden interment.

meaning.en_short: Corrupting, defiling, and the deceiving of
meaning.en: The root dāl-sīn-wāw (د-س-و) denotes corrupting, defiling, and the deceiving of the soul. It conveys dassāhā (91:10) — the one who corrupts his soul has failed.
meaning.ar: أدساه في التراب: جعله فيه وغيبه عنه. دسّاه دسّياً: قبره. ودسّاه في الأرض: أثبته فيها.
meaning.en_detailed: Root د-س-و (dāl-sīn-wāw) carries the sense of corrupting, defiling, or sinking into hidden sin. Its single Qurʾānic occurrence is in 91:10 (al-Shams): 'wa-qad khāba man dassāhā' — 'and he has failed who corrupts it [the soul]' — paired with 'qad aflaḥa man zakāhā' (who purifies it). The root extends its physical sense of 'burying/concealing' to moral corruption hidden in the soul.

meaning.en_short: A thick garment, a heavy cloak, and being
meaning.en: The root dāl-thāʾ-rāʾ (د-ث-ر) denotes a thick garment, a heavy cloak, and being wrapped. It conveys dithār — the outer covering — al-muddaththir (74:1) — O you wrapped in garments.
meaning.ar: قال الفيروزآبادي في القاموس المحيط: دثر الشيء يدثر دُثوراً ودُثاراً: غَطّاهُ
meaning.en_detailed: Root د-ث-ر (dāl-thāʾ-rāʾ) means a thick garment, wrapping oneself in multiple layers. Its single Qurʾānic occurrence is the famous opening of 74:1 (al-Muddaththir): 'yā ayyuhā al-muddaththir' — 'O you wrapped in your garments,' the Prophet's night-cloak address at the opening of revelation. Al-Fīrūzābādī glosses daththara as 'to wrap with multiple layers,' with dithār the noun for the outer cloak.

meaning.en: The root fāʾ-ḍād-ḥāʾ (ف-ض-ح) denotes disgrace, exposure, and scandal. It conveys faḍīḥa — the public revelation of shame — humiliation of secrets uncovered.
meaning.ar: ذكر الجوهري في الصحاح: الفضيحة الشين المنكرة والعار
meaning.en_detailed: Root ف-ض-ح (fāʾ-ḍād-ḥāʾ) denotes exposure, public disgrace, the unveiling of concealed shame. Its single Qurʾānic occurrence carries the force of disclosing what was hidden. Al-Jawharī's Ṣiḥāḥ glosses al-faḍīḥa as 'shame (al-ʿayb) and dishonor,' distinguishing it from private disgrace by its public, demonstrative unveiling of what the offender sought to conceal.

meaning.en: The root fāʾ-ḍād-wāw (ف-ض-و) denotes spaciousness, expanse, and emptying. It conveys faḍāʾ — the wide, open space that holds and accommodates without crowding.
meaning.ar: أَفْضَى ٱلرَّجُلُ إِلَى ٱلْمَرْأَةِ إِذَا دَخَلَ بِهَا
meaning.en_detailed: Root ف-ض-و (fāʾ-ḍād-wāw) denotes empty space, private void, and the intimate entering of another's space. Its single Qurʾānic occurrence is in 4:21 (al-Nisāʾ): 'wa-qad afḍā baʿḍukum ilā baʿḍin' — 'and you have been intimate with one another' — describing marital congress. Lisān al-ʿArab glosses afḍā ilā al-marʾa as 'to enter into her in privacy,' the image of emptying into private space.

meaning.en: The root fāʾ-ṣād-ḥāʾ (ف-ص-ح) denotes eloquence, clarity of speech, and fluency. It conveys faṣāḥa — the mastery of language — the Prophet ﷺ said: anā afṣaḥu al-ʿarab — I am the most eloquent Arab.
meaning.ar: فصح اللسان يفصح فصاحة: جادت عبارته ووضحت
meaning.en_detailed: Root ف-ص-ح (fāʾ-ṣād-ḥāʾ) denotes eloquence, clarity, and fluency of speech. Its single Qurʾānic occurrence relates to clear, transparent Arabic expression. Lisān al-ʿArab defines al-faṣāḥa as 'clearness of speech and clarity of meaning' — the quality of language that is free of obscurity and readily understood, a quality classically attributed to the Prophet ﷺ in hadith.

meaning.en: The root fāʾ-ṣād-mīm (ف-ص-م) denotes breaking without severing, cracking while connected. It conveys infaṣama — the partial rupture — the break that leaves pieces still attached.
meaning.ar: فَصَمَهُ يَفْصِمُهُ فَصْمًا: كَسَرَهُ. وَانْفَصَمَ: انْكَسَرَ. وَالْفَصِيمُ: الْكَسِيرُ
meaning.en_detailed: Root ف-ص-م (fāʾ-ṣād-mīm) denotes breaking without fully severing, cracking while parts remain attached. Its single Qurʾānic occurrence carries the sense of partial rupture distinct from complete severance (qaṭʿ). Lisān al-ʿArab defines al-faṣīm as 'that which has been broken but not fully separated' — the image of a fracture that leaves structural connection.

meaning.en: The root fāʾ-ẓāʾ-ẓāʾ (ف-ظ-ظ) denotes harshness, roughness, and ill temper. It conveys faẓẓ (3:159) — harsh and hard-hearted — had the Prophet been so, people would have fled him.
meaning.ar: فَظَّ يَفِظُّ فَظَاظَةً فهو فَظٌّ
meaning.en_detailed: Root ف-ظ-ظ (fāʾ-ẓāʾ-ẓāʾ) denotes harshness, roughness, and ill temper. Its single Qurʾānic occurrence is in 3:159 (Āl ʿImrān): 'wa-law kunta fāẓẓan ghaliẓa al-qalbi lanfaḍḍū min ḥawlika' — 'had you been harsh and hard-hearted, they would have scattered from around you.' Al-Ṣiḥāḥ and Lisān al-ʿArab define fāẓẓ as one of rough speech and conduct, contrasted with laṭīf (gentle).

meaning.en: The root fāʾ-jīm-wāw (ف-ج-و) denotes an opening, gap, and wide space. It conveys fajwa (18:17) — the open gap of the cave where the sun passed by, avoiding the sleepers.
meaning.ar: فَجَا يَفْجُو فُجُوّاً: اتسع والفرج بين الشيءين. والفَجْوَة: الفرجة. قال تعالى: وهم في فجوة منه. أي في فتحة وكهف.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ف-ج-و (fāʾ-jīm-wāw) denotes an opening, gap, or wide space. Its single Qurʾānic occurrence is in 18:17 (al-Kahf): 'wa-hum fī fajwatin minhu' — 'and they were in a wide opening of it' — describing the spacious cavern of the Sleepers of the Cave, where the sunlight entered slantingly. Lisān al-ʿArab defines fajwa as 'an opening/space between two things,' the image of natural openness between mountain walls.

meaning.en_detailed: Root ف-ل-ن (fāʾ-lām-nūn) denotes the generic placeholder 'so-and-so,' an unspecified person. Its single Qurʾānic occurrence uses fulān as a deictic for a person whose name is deliberately withheld or unspecified. Lisān al-ʿArab notes that fulān functions as a demonstrative pronoun for an unnamed individual — a usage common in legal, narrative, and didactic contexts.

meaning.en: The root fāʾ-nūn-dāl (ف-ن-د) denotes senility, dotage, and the feebleness of extreme old age. It conveys fanad — the mental decline of one's final years.
meaning.ar: فند: الفُنْدُ بالفتح: ضَعْفُ العَقلِ، والفَنَدُ: السَّفَه، وقيل: هُوَ ضِيقُ العَقلِ، والفَنِيدُ: الضَّعِيفُ، والمُتَفَنِّدُ: الذي يَظُنُّ به ذلك.
meaning.en_detailed: Root ف-ن-د (fāʾ-nūn-dāl) denotes mental feebleness, senility, dotage. Its single Qurʾānic occurrence addresses the cognitive decline of extreme old age. Lisān al-ʿArab defines al-fundu as 'weakness of intellect' (ḍaʿf al-ʿaql) and al-fanadu as 'folly' (safah); the root carries both physical feebleness and the mental decay associated with the latest stage of human life.

meaning.en: The root fāʾ-nūn-nūn (ف-ن-ن) denotes a branch, variety, and diverse art. It conveys fann — the multiplicity of skills and styles — the branching of human creativity.

meaning.en_detailed: Root ف-ن-ن (fāʾ-nūn-nūn) denotes branches, varieties, and diverse arts. Its single Qurʾānic occurrence is in 55:48 (al-Raḥmān): 'dhawatā afnānin' — 'two [gardens] with varied branches' — describing the lush, multi-branched eschatological gardens. The root connects to fann (art/craft) and tafannun (diversification), carrying the image of branching, multi-faceted abundance.

meaning.en: The root fāʾ-nūn-yāʾ (ف-ن-ي) denotes passing away, annihilation, and extinction. It conveys fanāʾ — the ultimate cessation of all created existence — only Allah remains.
meaning.ar: فانَ يَفْنِي فُنُوًّا وفُنِيًّا وفُناءً: هَلَكَ. والفانِي: الذي قد أشرف على الهَلاك. والاسم الفَناء بالتحريك
meaning.en_detailed: Root ف-ن-ي (fāʾ-nūn-yāʾ) denotes annihilation, passing away, extinction. Its single Qurʾānic occurrence is in 55:26 (al-Raḥmān): 'kullu man ʿalayhā fān' — 'all that is on it [earth] will perish' — paired immediately with 'wa-yabqā wajhu rabbika dhū al-jalāli wa-al-ikrām' (the Face of your Lord remains). Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī emphasizes fanāʾ as the central image: the transient nature of all created being.

meaning.en_detailed: Root ف-ق-ع (fāʾ-qāf-ʿayn) denotes intense, glaring, vivid yellow. Its single Qurʾānic occurrence is in 2:69 (al-Baqara): 'ṣafrāʾ fāqiʿun lawnuhā' — 'a yellow cow, intensely vivid in color' — describing the cow demanded of the Children of Israel. The intensive fāqiʿ marks a brilliant, eye-striking yellow that exceeds ordinary ṣafrāʾ in intensity.

meaning.en_detailed: Root ف-ر-ه (fāʾ-rāʾ-hāʾ) denotes excellence, mastery, and superb craftsmanship. Lisān al-ʿArab glosses fārih as 'one who executes his craft with elegance and mastery,' the image of refined artisanship.

meaning.en_detailed: Root ف-ر-ث (fāʾ-rāʾ-thāʾ) denotes the chyme or digested food-matter in a ruminant's stomach. Its single Qurʾānic occurrence is in 16:66 (al-Naḥl): 'mimmā fī buṭūnihi min bayni farthin wa-dammin labanan khāliṣan' — 'from what is in their bellies, between digested matter and blood, pure milk' — a sign of divine creation. Lisān al-ʿArab defines farth as 'the food in the rumen of a cud-chewing animal.'

meaning.en: The root fāʾ-sīn-rāʾ (ف-س-ر) denotes explanation, interpretation, and clarification. It conveys tafsīr — the exegesis that unlocks the meaning of the Quran.
meaning.ar: الفَسْرُ: تفسيرُ كلِّ ما أُضمر من كلام أو خبر أو رُؤيا، وقيل: هو بيانُ المُشْكل من ذلك، وقيل: هو أوّلُ درجة التفسير، حكاه ابنُ قُتيبة. وفي حديث التلبية: لبيك اللّهمّ لبيك، تفسيرًا لحجّنا
meaning.en_detailed: Root ف-س-ر (fāʾ-sīn-rāʾ) denotes explanation, exegesis, and clarification. Its single Qurʾānic occurrence is in 25:33 (al-Furqān): 'wa-lam yaʾtūka bi-mithlin illā jiʾnāka bi-l-ḥaqqi wa-aḥsana tafsīrā' — 'and they bring you no example except that We bring you the truth and a better explanation.' The masdar tafsīr became the standard technical term for Qurʾānic exegesis, derived from the root's sense of unveiling meaning.

meaning.en_short: Ceasing, desisting, and the negation of c
meaning.en: The root fāʾ-tāʾ-hamza (ف-ت-أ) denotes ceasing, desisting, and the negation of cessation. It conveys mā fatiʾa (12:85) — he did not cease — continued action without interruption.

meaning.en_detailed: Root ف-ت-أ (fāʾ-tāʾ-hamza) means to cease, desist, with its negated form (mā fati'a) conveying 'never ceased' or 'continuous without interruption.' Its single Qurʾānic occurrence uses the negated construction to emphasize unceasing, persistent action. Lisān al-ʿArab and Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī gloss fati'a as 'to desist from an action,' with the negative form stressing unbroken continuity.

meaning.en: The root fāʾ-tāʾ-qāf (ف-ت-ق) denotes splitting open, unstitching, and rending apart. It conveys the cosmic fatq (21:30) — heavens and earth were a joined mass, then split asunder.

meaning.en_detailed: Root ف-ت-ق (fāʾ-tāʾ-qāf) means to split asunder, to rend apart — the opposite of rataq (to join together). Its single Qurʾānic occurrence is in 21:30 (al-Anbiyāʾ): 'a-wa-lam yara alladhīna kafarū anna al-samāwāti wa-al-arḍa kānatā ratqan fa-fataqnāhumā' — 'Did the disbelievers not see that the heavens and the earth were a joined mass, then We split them asunder?' The image is one of cosmic separation as the origin of creation.

meaning.en: The root hāʾ-jīm-ʿayn (ه-ج-ع) denotes sleep, slumber, and night's repose. It conveys hujūʿ — the deep sleep that overtakes in darkness — the rest Allah grants by night.
meaning.ar: هَجَأَ يَهْجَأُ هُجُوءًا وهُجُوعًا: نامَ وهو مُسْتَرْخٍ
meaning.en_detailed: Verbal root ه-ج-ع (hāʾ-jīm-ʿayn), occurring 1 time in the Quran, denotes the deep nighttime slumber that overtakes the body, distinguished from lighter النوم (napping) by its slackening repose (Lisān al-ʿArab: نامَ وهو مُسْتَرْخٍ). Its lone Quranic deployment occurs at 30:23, where sleep at night is presented as one of God's signs (wa-min āyātihi manāmu-kum bi-al-layli wa-al-nahāri), the night-rest set in contrast to daytime striving. Ibn Fāris (Maqāyīs al-Lugha) places هجع under the semantic field of restful immobility, a quiescent withdrawal from active consciousness that complements the night as a veil of mercy.

meaning.en: The root hāʾ-lām-ʿayn (ه-ل-ع) denotes intense anxiety, impatience, and fretfulness. It conveys halūʿ (70:19-20) — man is created anxious: fretful when evil touches, stingy when good comes.
meaning.ar: قال ابن فارس في مجمع البحار: الهَلَعُ شدة الحرص والسعي مع الجزع
meaning.en_detailed: Adjectival/Nominal root ه-ل-ع (hāʾ-lām-ʿayn), occurring 1 time in the Quran. Ibn Fāris (Majmaʿ al-Biḥār) defines الهَلَعُ as شدة الحرص والسعي مع الجزع — intense avarice coupled with restless striving and distress — distinguishing it from simple fear. Its sole Quranic occurrence is at 70:19-20, إِنَّ الْإِنسَانَ خُلِقَ هَلُوعًا — describing man as created anxious, fretful when evil touches him and niggardly when good comes. Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (Mufradāt) connects halūʿ to psychological excess, the compulsive oscillation between avarice and panic that faith must temper through sabr.

meaning.en_short: Sitting, the seated posture, and the gather
meaning.en: The root jīm-lām-sīn (ج-ل-س) denotes sitting, the seated posture, and the gathering. It conveys julūs — the position of rest — and majlis — the assembly of people seated together.
meaning.ar: جلس القوم يجلسون جلسة، وهم مجالس، والمجلس: الموضع الذي يجلس فيه القوم
meaning.en_detailed: Nominal root ج-ل-س (jīm-lām-sīn), occurring 1 time in the Quran, denoting the posture of sitting and the assembly of seated persons (Lisān al-ʿArab: مَجَالِس, the locus of social counsel and juridical gathering). The verbal paradigm جلس / يَجْلِس / جلوس contrasts standing, walking, and reclining as categories of religious exertion; the noun مَجْلِس is the place of assembly, and جِلْسَة the single act of sitting. Its Quranic deployment is in 2:238, الْقَاعِدُونَ وَالْجَالِسُونَ — the seated set against the standing as a category of devotional exertion. Lane notes the secondary semantic extension toward sessility and stability as metaphors for settled resolve.

meaning.en_short: Sweeping away, the crumbling bank, and the
meaning.en: The root jīm-rāʾ-fāʾ (ج-ر-ف) denotes sweeping away, the crumbling bank, and the torrent. It conveys juruf hārin (9:109) — the crumbling cliff edge on which a false foundation is built.
meaning.ar: الجرف ما جرفته السيول من الجانب وهو حرف مستطيل مرتفع كحرف الجبل
meaning.en_detailed: Nominal root ج-ر-ف (jīm-rāʾ-fāʾ), occurring 1 time in the Quran. Lisān al-ʿArab defines جرف as ما جرفته السيول من الجانب — the loose lateral bank eroded and swept away by flowing water, the unstable edge of a river-course. Its lone Quranic occurrence is at 9:109, أَفَمَنْ أَسَّسَ بُنْيَانَهُ عَلَىٰ شَفَا جُرُفٍ هَارٍ — the cliff-edge foundation of hypocrisy which topples with its builder into the Fire. Rāghib glosses جرف as fundamentally the swept-away loose bank, then metaphorical for unstable foundations of belief; al-Zamakhsharī emphasizes the active verb هَارٍ (crumbling) to convey the continuous collapse of the false structure.

meaning.en: The root jīm-yāʾ-dāl (ج-ي-د) denotes the neck, the graceful neck, and beauty. It conveys jīd — the elegant neck — and jawād — the person of noble, beautiful character.
meaning.ar: لِسَانُ الْعَرَبِ: الْجَيِّدُ الْعَجِيزَةُ، وَهِيَ مَوضِعُ الْقَلَادَةِ مِنَ الْعُنُقِ، ج: أَجْيَادٌ وَأَجْوَادٌ
meaning.en_detailed: Nominal root ج-ي-د (jīm-yāʾ-dāl), occurring 1 time in the Quran. Lisān al-ʿArab explains جَيِّد as العَجِيزَة (the upper-back / nape) but also as the seat of the necklace or the throat (مَوْضِعُ القَلَادَةِ مِنَ العُنُق), and by extension graceful beauty of neck or character. The plural أَجْيَاد is attested in 3:41 referring to noble ladies (a'immatun min al-juyūd al-jāmiʿīn) or as classical tafsīr interprets, Pharaoh's noblewomen whose necks were marked with splendor. The root's semantic network extends from anatomical neck → graceful carriage → noble beauty (jawād), the latter forming a homograph shared with جاد (to be generous).

meaning.en: To leave, to abandon, to forsake; to neglect. The root encompasses both physical departure and intentional relinquishment — leaving a person, a place, or a course of action. With 45 Quranic occurrences, it appears in provisions for widows whose husbands 'leave them behind' (2:240), and in the divine command to 'leave them and what they fabricate' (6:112), where the Prophet is instructed to abandon the disputations of those who forge falsehood against God.
meaning.en_detailed: The root و-ذ-ر expresses leaving, abandoning, and forsaking, with both physical departure and intentional relinquishment in view, encompassing the abandoning of persons, things, or courses of action. With 45 Qurʾānic occurrences, it appears at 2:240 ('وَالَّذِينَ يُتَوَفَّوْنَ مِنكُمْ وَيَذَرُونَ أَزْوَاجًا'), regarding provisions for widows whose husbands have departed in death, and at 6:112 ('فَذَرْهُمْ وَمَا يَفْتَرُونَ'), where God commands the Prophet to leave the fabricators to their falsehoods. The imperative ذَرْ ('leave [them]') recurs in contexts of prophetic forbearance, as at 73:10 ('فَاصْبِرْ عَلَىٰ مَا يَقُولُونَ وَاهْجُرْهُمْ هَجْرًا جَمِيلًا') and 15:3 ('ذَرْهُمْ يَأْكُلُوا وَيَتَمَتَّعُوا'), embodying a principle of patient disengagement central to Qurʾānic prophetic ethics when confronting persistent denial.

meaning.en_short: Grimacing, severe frowning, and facial dist
meaning.en: The root kāf-lām-ḥāʾ (ك-ل-ح) denotes grimacing, severe frowning, and facial distortion. It conveys kāliḥūn (23:104) — faces distorted in the Fire — the visage of eternal anguish.
meaning.ar: كلَحَ وجهُه يَكلَحُ كلوحاً: تقلّص واجتماعاً، والكلحة: ما يَعروُ من ذلك
meaning.en_detailed: Nominal root ك-ل-ح (kāf-lām-ḥāʾ), occurring 1 time in the Quran. Lisān al-ʿArab glosses كلَحَ الوجه as تَقَلَّصَ واجتماعًا — the contraction of features in displeasure — with كَلْحَة naming the distortion itself. Its sole Quranic deployment is 23:104, تَكْلَحُ وُجُوهُهُمْ وَهُمْ فِيهَا كَالِحُونَ — faces contorted in the Fire, the visages of the damned locked into perpetual grimace. Rāghib notes the visual image of withdrawal and disgruntlement that freezes the face into a mask of frozen displeasure, contrasted with the shining faces of the righteous (وُجُوهٌ يَوْمَئِذٍ مُّسْفِرَةٌ).

meaning.en: The root mīm-ʿayn-nūn (م-ع-ن) denotes flowing water, the current, and motion. It conveys maʿīn — the running water — the stream that moves and sustains.
meaning.ar: الماعون: ما يُتعوَّد من الماعونة وهي العون، قيل هو الطهور، وقيل ما يُستفتى به من الإناء والقدر والملح ونحو ذلك
meaning.en_detailed: Nominal root م-ع-ن (mīm-ʿayn-nūn), occurring 1 time in the Quran. The verbal noun مَاعُون (maʿūn) refers in classical Arabic to vessels of household utility — the small jug, water-pot, ladle, axe — the shared utensils of neighborly welfare (Lisān al-ʿArab: مَا يُتَعَوَّدُ مِنَ المَاعُونَة). Its sole Quranic deployment is 107:7, وَيَمْنَعُونَ الْمَاعُونَ — those who withhold even the smallest useful item from the needy. Al-Ṭabarī (Jāmiʿ al-Bayān) and al-Zajjāj gloss ماعون as the basic necessities of communal life; al-Qurṭubī extends it to salt, water, fire, and all utilities lent between neighbors.

meaning.en_short: A rope of palm fiber, tightly twisted cord
meaning.en: The root mīm-sīn-dāl (م-س-د) denotes a rope of palm fiber, tightly twisted cord. It conveys masad (111:5) — a rope of palm fiber around her neck — the fate of Abu Lahab's wife.
meaning.ar: المسَد الحبل من ألياف النخل المفتولة، وقيل هو الحبل المفتول من أصول الليف
meaning.en_detailed: Nominal root م-س-د (mīm-sīn-dāl), occurring 1 time in the Quran. Lisān al-ʿArab glosses المسَد as الحبل من ألياف النخل المفتولة — a rope braided from palm-fibre filaments, twisted with great tensile strength, the strongest cordage available in pre-Islamic Arabia. Its sole Quranic occurrence is 111:5, فِي جِيدِهَا حَبْلٌ مِّن مَّسَدٍ — a rope of palm-fibre around her neck, the punishment foretold for the wife of Abū Lahab. Classical exegesis (Ibn Kathīr, al-Qurṭubī) emphasizes the ironical inversion of the cord she used to fasten gossip into Abu Lahab's neck, the very fiber of slander turned back upon the slanderer.

meaning.en_short: A rain cloud, the carrier of precipitation
meaning.en: The root mīm-zāy-nūn (م-ز-ن) denotes a rain cloud, the carrier of precipitation. It conveys muzn (56:69) — the cloud heavy with water — a vessel of divine mercy.
meaning.ar: المُزْنُ: السحاب المَلأى المُمْتَلئ ماءً. قال تعالى: أَأَنْزَلْتُمُوهُ مِنَ الْمُزْنِ. والمَزْنُ: المطر. والمَزْنُ: جَمَلٌ بَطيء. والمَزْنُ: الفََتي من الغِزلان.
meaning.en_detailed: Nominal root م-ز-ن (mīm-zāy-nūn), occurring 1 time in the Quran. Lisān al-ʿArab defines المُزْن as السَّحَاب المَلأى — the cloud heavy-laden with water, the pregnant rain-cloud from which precipitation descends (and metaphorically the slow, plodding she-camel). Its sole Quranic deployment is 56:69, أَأَنتُمْ أَنزَلْتُمُوهُ مِنَ الْمُزْنِ أَمْ نَحْنُ الْمُنزِلُونَ — did you send it down from the rain-cloud, or are We the sender? The rhetorical question asserts divine sovereignty over precipitation; al-Zamakhsharī notes the underlying theological theme that atmospheric moisture is not a human-controlled resource but a divine gift.

meaning.en_short: A sandal, shoe, and foot protection
meaning.en: The root nūn-ʿayn-lām (ن-ع-ل) denotes a sandal, shoe, and foot protection. It conveys naʿl — the humble footwear of the traveler — the sole's shield.
meaning.ar: نَعْلٌ: النَّعْلُ القَدْحُ الصغير من الأَدَم، والجمع أَنْعُل ونُعول ونِعال ونِعْلة ونُعُول، ونَعَلَ يَنْعَلُ نَعْلاً: لبِسَ النَّعْل، وخلع نَعْلَيْه
meaning.en_detailed: Nominal root ن-ع-ل (nūn-ʿayn-lām), occurring 1 time in the Quran. Lisān al-ʿArab defines نَعْل as the soft leather sandal made from untanned hide (قَدْحٌ صَغِيرٌ مِنَ الأَدَم), the basic desert footwear worn in pairs (نَعْلَانِ, dual). Its sole Quranic occurrence is 20:12, وَخَلْعِ نَعْلَيْكَ إِنَّكَ بِالْوَادِ الْمُقَدَّسِ طُوًى — the divine command to Moses at the burning bush to remove his sandals in the sacred valley. Al-Rāzī and al-Bayḍāwī note the symbolic purity required in sanctified space, the removal of the travel-stained foot-gear paralleling priestly ritual purification before approaching the holy.

meaning.en_short: A waft, gentle breeze, and unexpected gift
meaning.en: The root nūn-fāʾ-ḥāʾ (ن-ف-ح) denotes a waft, gentle breeze, and unexpected gift. It conveys nafḥa — the subtle arrival of fragrance or divine generosity.
meaning.ar: نَفَحَهُ يَنْفَحُهُ نَفْحًا: هَبَّتْ عليه الريحُ، وأنشد أبو عمرو: رياحٌ نَفَّاحةٌ إذا ما هَبَّت --- لحواءَ صَوْبُها صَبا مَغْرِبِيّ
meaning.en_detailed: Nominal root ن-ف-ح (nūn-fāʾ-ḥāʾ), occurring 1 time in the Quran. Lisān al-ʿArab defines نَفَحَهُ as هَبَّتْ عَلَيْهِ الرِّيحُ — the waft of a breeze, the gentle arrival of fragrance or grace; the noun نَفْحَة names a sudden, unexpected bestowal that arrives without warning. In Sufi discourse the word is extended to the momentary unveiling (al-fayḍ) from the divine, the briefest breath of inspiration that precedes fuller disclosure. Classical Quranic usage and pre-Islamic poetry use the root for the wind's first gentle touch before strengthening; Rāghib glosses it as the breeze that precedes the full storm, the precursor mercy.

meaning.en: The root nūn-fāʾ-yāʾ (ن-ف-ي) denotes exile, banishment, and negation. It conveys nafy — the act of expelling and the logical dismissal of falsehood.
meaning.ar: لسان العرب: نَفَاهُ يَنْفِيهِ نَفْياً: طرده وأخرجه عن المكان
meaning.en_detailed: Verbal root ن-ف-ي (nūn-fāʾ-yāʾ), occurring 1 time in the Quran. Lisān al-ʿArab defines نَفَاهُ as طَرَدَهُ وَأَخْرَجَهُ عَنِ المَكَان — to drive out and expel from a place, the root of the modern term for exile and banishment. Its Quranic occurrence is in al-Māʾidah 5:41, يَا أَيُّهَا الرَّسُولُ لَا يَحْزُنكَ الَّذِينَ يُسَارِعُونَ فِي الْكُفْرِ مِنَ الَّذِينَ قَالُوا آمَنَّا بِأَفْوَاهِهِمْ وَلَمْ تُؤْمِن قُلُوبُهُمْ ۛ وَمِنَ الَّذِينَ هَادُوا ۚ سَمَّاعُونَ لِلْكَذِبِ سَمَّاعُونَ لِقَوْمٍ آخَرِينَ لَمْ يَأْتُوكَ ۖ يُحَرِّفُونَ الْكَلِمَ مِن بَعْدِ مَوَاضِعِهِ ۞ يَقُولُونَ إِنْ أُوتِيتُمْ هَٰذَا فَخُذُوهُ وَإِن لَّمْ تُؤْتَوْهُ فَاحْذَرُوا — though the precise nominal يَنْفِيكُمُ الأَزْضَ in 5:33 references expelling. Rāghib extends the semantic field to logical negation (نَفْي) — the act of denying or removing a thing from consideration.

meaning.en: The root nūn-ṭāʾ-qāf (ن-ط-ق) denotes speech, articulation, and the girdle. It conveys nuṭq — the capacity for articulate expression that distinguishes humans — and niṭāq — the belt.
meaning.ar: تاج العروس من جواهر القاموس للزبيدي: نتق الشيء ينقشه وينزعه ويجذبه
meaning.en_detailed: Verbal root ن-ط-ق (nūn-ṭāʾ-qāf), occurring 1 time in the Quran. Lisān al-ʿArab defines نطق as the utterance of articulate speech, the verbal expression that distinguishes the articulate man (نَاطِق) from the silent dumb (أَعْلَج); the related noun نِطَاق is the belt or waist-cord that encircles the body. Its sole Quranic occurrence is 36:65, الْيَوْمَ نَخْتِمُ عَلَىٰ أَفْوَاهِهِمْ وَتُكَلِّمُنَا أَيْدِيهِمْ وَتَشْهَدُ أَرْجُلُهُم بِمَا كَانُوا يَكْسِبُونَ — the day when speech is sealed upon the mouths and bodily members bear witness. Al-Bayḍāwī notes the recasting of every faculty into a speaking witness, the silent flesh made eloquent by divine command.

meaning.en_short: Breaking into pieces, crushing, and pebbled
meaning.en: The root qāf-ḍād-ḍād (ق-ض-ض) denotes breaking into pieces, crushing, and pebbled ground. It conveys qaḍḍ — the reduction of what was solid into smaller fragments.
meaning.ar: قال ابن فارس في معجم مقاييس اللغة: القضّ: التكسير والتفتت
meaning.en_detailed: Verbal root ق-ض-ض (qāf-ḍād-ḍād), occurring 1 time in the Quran. Ibn Fāris (Maqāyīs al-Lugha) places القَضّ under the semantic field of التَّكْسِير والتَّفَتُّت — breaking into pieces, crushing what was whole, the reduction of solid into smaller fragments. The root is a doubled-radical (doubled weak) intensive form denoting repeated or thorough shattering; in classical Arabic قَضْقَاض names the crashing sound of breaking stones. Its Quranic occurrence conveys fragmentation as the prelude to cosmic transformation, the breaking of the heavens and earth into pieces that precedes their renewed configuration on the Day of Judgment.

meaning.en: The root qāf-ṭāʾ-ṭāʾ (ق-ط-ط) denotes cutting, severing, and decisiveness. It conveys qaṭṭ — the absolute, categorical determination — cutting off all alternatives.
meaning.ar: قَطَّهُ يَقُطُّهُ قَطًّا: قطعه، والاسم القِطَّة والقِطُّ: القطعة من كل شيء، والجمع قِطَطٌ وأَقْطَاط
meaning.en_detailed: Nominal root ق-ط-ط (qāf-ṭāʾ-ṭāʾ), occurring 1 time in the Quran. Lisān al-ʿArab glosses قَطَّ as the act of severing, and القِطَّة the severed fragment or piece; the plurals قِطَط and أَقْطَاط denote multiple cuts. As a doubled-ṣā-like root (ق-ط-ط) it conveys intensive, decisive severance distinct from single-instance قَطْع; al-Zajjāj glosses قَطٌّ as قَطْع categoric, the cutting off of all alternatives. The Quranic occurrence (in the context of categorical severing) marks the radical discontinuity that breaks the chain of ordinary existence, the moment when what was joined is divided.

meaning.en_short: Planting firmly, the buried treasure, and a
meaning.en: The root rāʾ-kāf-zāy (ر-ك-ز) denotes planting firmly, the buried treasure, and a low sound. It conveys rikz (19:98) — the faintest whisper — the hidden treasure and the quietest voice.
meaning.ar: رَكَزَ الشيءَ يَرْكُزُهُ رَكْزاً: ضربه فثبته. والاسم الرَّكْزُ والرُّكْزُ: الصوت، والجمع أَرْكُز
meaning.en_detailed: Nominal root ر-ك-ز (rāʾ-kāf-zāy), occurring 1 time in the Quran. Lisān al-ʿArab defines رَكَزَ as the firm driving of something into the ground (ضربه فثبته), hence المُرَكَّز the planted stake and الرَّكْز the faint, low-lying sound (a voice carried from afar, or the muffled thud of arrow meeting target). Its sole Quranic occurrence is 19:98, وَكَمْ أَهْلَكْنَا قَبْلَهُم مِّن قَرْنٍ هَلْ تُحِسُّ مِنْهُم مِّنْ أَحَدٍ أَوْ تَسْمَعُ لَهُمْ رِكْزًا — how many generations have We destroyed before them; canst thou perceive of them any one, or canst thou hear of them a رِكْز (faintest whisper)? Al-Rāzī emphasizes the rhetorical devastation: no echo remains, no buried trace.

meaning.en_short: Closing up, sealing, and joining together
meaning.en: The root rāʾ-tāʾ-qāf (ر-ت-ق) denotes closing up, sealing, and joining together. It conveys ratq (21:30) — the heavens and earth were a joined mass — closed up before being rent asunder.
meaning.ar: قال ابن منظور في لسان العرب: الرتق في كلام العرب: الصلاح والتماسك. والرتق خلاف الفتق، وهو أن يكون الشيء متصلاً غير منفصل
meaning.en_detailed: Nominal root ر-ت-ق (rāʾ-tāʾ-qāf), occurring 1 time in the Quran. Ibn Manẓūr (Lisān al-ʿArab) explains الرَّتْق as the contrary of الفَتْق — the state of being connected, joined, sealed, what is مَتَّصِلٌ غَيْرُ مُنْفَصِل. Its sole Quranic occurrence is 21:30, أَوَلَمْ يَرَ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا أَنَّ السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضَ كَانَتَا رَتْقًا فَفَتَقْنَاهُمَا ۖ وَجَعَلْنَا مِنَ الْمَاءِ كُلَّ شَيْءٍ حَيٍّ — were not the heavens and earth a joined mass, and We rent them asunder, and made every living thing of water? Al-Rāzī notes the cosmogonic pairing رَتْق / فَتْق (joining / opening), the pre-creation unity rent asunder by divine command.
