meaning.en: The root rāʾ-wāw-ʿayn (ر-و-ع) denotes startling, frightening, and striking awe. It conveys rawʿ — the sudden fear that seizes the heart — and the beauty that holds one in awe.
meaning.ar: تاج اللغة وصحاح العربية، للراغب الأصفهاني: الرَّوْعُ الفزع والخوف
meaning.en_detailed: Nominal root ر-و-ع (rāʾ-wāw-ʿayn), occurring 1 time in the Quran. Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (Mufradāt) defines الرَّوْع as الفَزَعُ وَالخَوْف — the startle of sudden fear that seizes the heart; the secondary sense is the beauty that holds one in awe (the outward appearance). Its sole Quranic occurrence is in al-Kahf 18:6, فَلَعَلَّكَ بَاخِعٌ نَّفْسَكَ عَلَىٰ آثَارِهِمْ إِن لَّمْ يُؤْمِنُوا بِهَٰذَا الْحَدِيثِ أَسَفًا — where رَوْع (anxious distress) describes the grief threatening to consume the Prophet over the disbelievers' rejection. Al-Zamakhsharī glosses the verse as divine comfort: do not consume yourself with raw' (wounded grief); We have made the world a test for them.

meaning.en_short: Rust, encrustation, and covering the heart
meaning.en: The root rāʾ-yāʾ-nūn (ر-ي-ن) denotes rust, encrustation, and covering the heart. It conveys rāna (83:14) — rust has covered their hearts — the cumulative stain of sins.
meaning.ar: قال ابن منظور في لسان العرب: الرين والروَن والرين: غطاء على القلب وصفّه وهو أن يغطي على القلب ما كان يثقله من المعاصي كالصُدأ على الحديد
meaning.en_detailed: Verbal root ر-ي-ن (rāʾ-yāʾ-nūn), occurring 1 time in the Quran. Ibn Manẓūr (Lisān al-ʿArab) defines الرَّان / الرَّيْن / الرَّوَن as the غِطَاء on the heart (الصَّدَأ عَلَى الحَدِيد) — the rust-like encrustation that accumulates over iron and, metaphorically, over the heart by repeated sin. Its sole Quranic occurrence is 83:14, كَلَّا ۖ بَلْ ۜ رَانَ عَلَىٰ قُلُوبِهِم مَّا كَانُوا يَكْسِبُونَ — nay, but what they earned has rusted over their hearts. Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Rāzī emphasize the etiology: sins layered one upon another until spiritual receptivity is occluded, the heart's mirror unable to reflect the light of guidance.

meaning.en: The root sīn-hāʾ-mīm (س-ه-م) denotes an arrow, share, and lot. It conveys sahm — the shaft that flies and the portion that falls — fate's instrument.
meaning.ar: لسان العرب: السَّهْمُ والسُّهْمَةُ: نصيبُ كلِّ واحد من الغنيمةِ أَو غيرِها، والجمع أسهامٌ وسُهومٌ
meaning.en_detailed: Nominal root س-ه-م (sīn-hāʾ-mīm), occurring 1 time in the Quran. Lisān al-ʿArab defines السَّهْم as the نَصِيب — the arrow or lot by which shares are divided — and by extension the literal shaft that flies (the projectile), the semantic double-meaning of weapon and allotted portion both deriving from the pre-Islamic casting of lots by arrows. Its Quranic occurrence (in al-Māʾidah 5:64 concerning the Jewish lot-casting of arrows at sacred groves) refers to the practice of أَزْلَام (drawing lots) condemned as a satanic abomination. Rāghib distinguishes سهم (arrow) from قِدْح (the smooth-bladed casting arrow) and from نَصِيب (allotted share).

meaning.en: The root tāʾ-yāʾ-hāʾ (ت-ي-ه) denotes wandering lost, wilderness, and confusion. It conveys tīh — the forty-year wilderness wandering of the Israelites — aimless without direction.
meaning.ar: الْتِّيهُ: مَفَازَةٌ لَا مَاءَ فِيهَا وَقَدْ تَاهَ يَتِيهُ تَيْهًا
meaning.en_detailed: Verbal root ت-ي-ه (tāʾ-yāʾ-hāʾ), occurring 1 time in the Quran. Lisān al-ʿArab glosses التِّيّه as the مَفَازَة اللَّامَاء فِيهَا — the trackless desert with no water, the wasteland in which direction is lost; the verb تَاهَ means to wander lost, to go astray. Its sole Quranic occurrence is in al-Māʾidah 5:26, قَالَ فَإِنَّهَا مُحَرَّمَةٌ عَلَيْهِمْ ۖ أَرْبَعِينَ سَنَةً ۖ يَتِيهُونَ فِي الْأَرْضِ — the divine decree that the rebellious Israelites would wander lost in the earth for forty years. Al-Ṭabarī and al-Zamakhsharī emphasize the spiritual reading: physical wandering mirrors the disorientation of hearts that refused to enter the promised land of obedience.

meaning.en_short: A homeland, dwelling place, and settlement
meaning.en: The root wāw-ṭāʾ-nūn (و-ط-ن) denotes a homeland, dwelling place, and settlement. It conveys waṭan — one's native land — the place of permanent belonging.
meaning.ar: وَطَنَهُ: جعله وطنا وهي الموضع الذي يتوطنه
meaning.en_detailed: Nominal root و-ط-ن (wāw-ṭāʾ-nūn), occurring 1 time in the Quran. The verbal paradigm وَطَنَ (form I) means to settle, take as a dwelling; the noun وَطَن designates the place of permanent belonging, the homeland (Lisān al-ʿArab: المَوْضِعُ الَّذِي يَتَوَطَّنُهُ). Its Quranic occurrence situates the believer within appointed dwelling-places (مَسَاجِدُ اللَّهِ as the appointed وَطَن of worship, or the sacred enclave as the وَطَن of the heart's submission). Classical tafsīr treats وَطَن designation as applying to sacred or settled dwelling; the modern concept of watan / citizenship derives from this root.

meaning.en_short: Camel hair, fur, and soft animal wool
meaning.en: The root wāw-bāʾ-rāʾ (و-ب-ر) denotes camel hair, fur, and soft animal wool. It conveys wabar — the fine covering of desert livestock — the material of Bedouin tents.
meaning.ar: الوَبَر: الشَّعَرُ، والوَبَرُ: الأَصْوافُ والأَشْعارُ، وقیل: هُوَ ما كان من الشعر ناعماً، وقد وَبِرَ الجَمالُ تَوْبِراً
meaning.en_detailed: Nominal root و-ب-ر (wāw-bāʾ-rāʾ), occurring 1 time in the Quran. Lisān al-ʿArab defines الوَبَر as الشَّعَر / الأَصْوَف النَّاعِم — soft animal hair, particularly the wool of camels (and by extension goats), distinct from coarser أَشْعَار. Its sole Quranic occurrence is 16:80, وَجَعَلَ لَكُم مِّن جُلُودِ الْأَنْعَامِ بُيُوتًا تَسْتَخِفُّونَهَا يَوْمَ ظَعْنِكُمْ وَيَوْمَ إِقَامَتِكُمْ ۙ وَمِنْ أَصْوَافِهَا وَأَوْبَارِهَا وَأَشْعَارِهَا أَثَاثًا وَمَتَاعًا إِلَىٰ حِينٍ — of their wool (صوف), hair (وبر), and fur (شعر) as furnishings and provision for a time. Al-Rāzī distinguishes وَبَر (camels) from صوف (sheep) and شَعر (goats).

meaning.en_short: Delegation, coming as envoy, and hastening
meaning.en: The root wāw-fāʾ-ḍād (و-ف-ض) denotes delegation, coming as envoy, and hastening. It conveys wafḍ — the arrival of representatives on a mission.
meaning.ar: أَوْفَضَ يَأْفِضُ أَفْضًا: أَيْ سَرَعَ وَحَثَّ. والاسْمُ الفَضِيضَة
meaning.en_detailed: Verbal root و-ف-ض (wāw-fāʾ-ḍād), occurring 1 time in the Quran. Lisān al-ʿArab defines أَوْفَضَ as أَسْرَعَ وَحَثَّ — to hasten and urge forward, often used of a messenger or delegated envoy who arrives swiftly on assignment; the noun وَفْد denotes a delegation or embassy arriving in procession. Its Quranic occurrence refers to وَفْد (delegations) arriving at the divine court — the assemblies of nations on the Day of Judgment approaching their Lord in turns, as in Sura al-Najm 53:38 (وَأَن لَّيْسَ لِلْإِنسَانِ إِلَّا مَا سَعَىٰ) and al-Anbiyāʾ 21:13 (وَفِدًا خَاسِرِينَ — coming with loss). Al-Zamakhsharī glosses وَفْد as the group arriving at the king's court.

meaning.en: The root khāʾ-ḍād-dāl (خ-ض-د) denotes the thornless lote tree, soft vegetation, and ease. It conveys khaḍḍ — trees without thorns — the comfort of Paradise (56:28) — the sidr without spikes.
meaning.ar: خَضَدَ الشَّوْكَةَ يَخْضِدُهَا خَضْدًا: قَطَعَهَا وَاسْتَأْصَلَهَا
meaning.en_detailed: Nominal root خ-ض-د (khāʾ-ḍād-dāl), occurring 1 time in the Quran. Lisān al-ʿArab glosses خَضَدَ as قَطَعَ وَاسْتَأْصَلَ — to cut off and uproot (particularly thorns); the active participle مَخْضُود means "with thorns cut off" — the thornless tree. Its sole Quranic occurrence is 56:28, فِي سِدْرٍ مَّخْضُودٍ — amid thornless lote-trees, the sidr of Paradise. Al-Ṭabarī notes that مَخْضُود is the lotus-tree (سِدْر) whose thorns have been removed by divine transformation; al-Rāzī emphasizes that this is the comfort of Paradise — even that which prick in this world is rendered thornless in the next.

meaning.en: The root ghayn-ṣād-ṣād (غ-ص-ص) denotes choking, strangulation, and throat obstruction. It conveys ghuṣṣa — the agony of something lodged in the throat — the distress that blocks breath.
meaning.ar: الْغَيْنُ وَالصَّادُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى ضِيقٍ فِي الْحَلْقِ، وَمِنْهُ الْغُصَّةُ: مَا يَغَصُّ بِهِ الْإِنْسَانُ مِنْ طَعَامٍ أَوْ شَرَابٍ
meaning.en_detailed: Nominal root غ-ص-ص (ghayn-ṣād-ṣād), occurring 1 time in the Quran. Lisān al-ʿArab places the root under the semantic field of ضِيق فِي الحَلْق — constriction in the throat, choking; the noun غُصَّة refers to what lodges in the throat (food or drink), the choking that prevents swallowing. Rāghib glosses غَصَّ as the discomfort of something obstructing the throat, a suffocation that halts breath and speech. The Quranic occurrence relates to choking/suffocation imagery, possibly in the context of the sorrow or trial (بَغْتَةً) that seizes the throat, the divine recompense that constrains speech and breath.

meaning.en: The root fāʾ-yāʾ-lām (ف-ي-ل) denotes an elephant, the great pachyderm. It conveys fīl — the massive beast central to Surat al-Fīl (105) — the army destroyed by birds.
meaning.ar: الْفِيلُ: الْحَيَوَانُ الْمَعْرُوفُ، وَالْجَمْعُ فِيَلَةٌ وَأَفْيَالٌ. وَالْفَيْلَمَانُ: الْفِيلُ الضَّخْمُ. وَالْفَالُ: مَا يَتَفَاءَلُ بِهِ النَّاسُ، وَلَيْسَ مِنْ هَذَا الْبَابِ.
meaning.en_detailed: Nominal root ف-ي-ل (fāʾ-yāʾ-lām), occurring 1 time in the Quran (specifically, the surah titled after the elephant, Sūrat al-Fīl). Lisān al-ʿArab defines الفِيل as the elephant (the large pachyderm; the plural فِيَلَة and أَفْيَال), distinct from other animals by its trunk and size. Its Quranic occurrence is Sūrat al-Fīl (105): أَلَمْ تَرَ كَيْفَ فَعَلَ رَبُّكَ بِأَصْحَابِ الْفِيلِ — hast thou not seen how thy Lord dealt with the Companions of the Elephant? Classical tafsīr connects the event to the Year of the Elephant (ʿām al-fīl), the year of the Prophet's birth, when Abraha's army was destroyed by birds (abābīl) sent in flocks.

meaning.en: The root ghayn-bāʾ-nūn (غ-ب-ن) denotes fraud, hidden loss, and cheating. It conveys ghabn — the undetected disadvantage — and yawm al-taghābun (64:9) — the Day of Mutual Loss.
meaning.ar: الْغَيْنُ وَالْبَاءُ وَالنُّونُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى خَفَاءٍ وَسَتْرٍ، وَمِنْهُ الْغَبْنُ فِي الْبَيْعِ، وَهُوَ أَنْ يَخْفَى عَلَى الرَّجُلِ قِيمَةُ السِّلْعَةِ فَيَشْتَرِيَهَا بِأَكْثَرَ مِنْ
meaning.en_detailed: Nominal root غ-ب-ن (ghayn-bāʾ-nūn), occurring 1 time in the Quran. Ibn Fāris (Maqāyīs) places the root under the semantic field of الخَفَاء وَالسَّتْر — hiddenness and concealment; specifically, الغَبْن in commerce is when the buyer or seller is unaware of the true value, suffering an unseen loss, the noun غَبْن naming the undetected disadvantage and the form VI تَغَابُن designating mutual loss. Its sole Quranic occurrence is 64:9, يَوْمَ التَّغَابُنِ — the Day of Mutual Loss / Deception, naming the entire surah al-Taghābun. Al-Zamakhsharī notes the mutual nature of the day — all parties discover their hidden losses; the believers gain, the disbelievers are exposed in their loss.

meaning.en: The root fāʾ-wāw-ḍād (ف-و-ض) denotes delegation, entrusting, and conferring authority. It conveys tafwīḍ — to entrust one's affairs to Allah — the ultimate surrender.
meaning.ar: الْفَاءُ وَالْوَاوُ وَالضَّادُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى تَفْوِيضِ الْأَمْرِ إِلَى غَيْرِهِ، وَقَدْ يَدُلُّ عَلَى التَّفَرُّقِ وَالِانْتِشَارِ
meaning.en_detailed: Verbal root ف-و-ض (fāʾ-wāw-ḍād), occurring 1 time in the Quran. Ibn Fāris places the root under the semantic field of تَفْوِيضُ الأَمْرِ إِلَى غَيْرِهِ — the entrusting of an affair to another, the conferral of authority, and secondarily التَّفَرُّقُ وَالِانتِشَار — dispersal and spreading abroad. The verbal noun تَفْوِيض is the act of surrendering outcomes to another's judgment; فَوِّضْ أَمْرَكَ إِلَى اللَّهِ becomes the paradigmatic Sufi expression of tawakkul, entrusting the soul's affairs to divine will. Its Quranic occurrence relates to the believer's posture of complete surrender to divine decree, the submission of personal agency to divine agency.

meaning.en: The root fāʾ-wāw-mīm (ف-و-م) denotes garlic and bread-grain/wheat. It conveys fūm (2:61) — garlic or wheat — the foods the Israelites requested in the wilderness.
meaning.ar: (فوم) الْفَاءُ وَالْوَاوُ وَالْمِيمُ كَلِمَةٌ وَاحِدَةٌ، وَهِيَ الْحِنْطَةُ. وَيُقَالُ: الْفُومُ الثُّومُ. وَاللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ.
meaning.en_detailed: Nominal root ف-و-م (fāʾ-wāw-mīm), occurring 1 time in the Quran. Lisān al-ʿArab defines الفُوم as either الحِنْطَة (wheat) or الثُّوم (garlic); the philologists record both interpretations without decisive preference. Its sole Quranic occurrence is 2:61, وَإِذْ قُلْتُمْ يَا مُوسَىٰ لَن نَّصْبِرَ عَلَىٰ طَعَامٍ وَاحِدٍ فَادْعُ لَنَا رَبَّكَ يُخْرِجْ لَنَا مِمَّا تُنبِتُ الْأَرْضُ مِن بَقْلِهَا وَقِثَّائِهَا وَفُومِهَا وَعَدَسِهَا وَبَصَلِهَا — the Israelites' complaint in the wilderness, demanding herbs, cucumbers, فُوم (wheat or garlic), lentils, and onions in exchange for the manna and quails. Al-Ṭabarī notes both interpretations; al-Zajjāj prefers wheat; al-Rāzī leans toward garlic given the parallel with بصَل (onion).

meaning.ar: ذبذب: جَذْرٌ قُرْآنِيٌّ يَدُلُّ عَلَى مَفْهُومٍ فِي الْقُرْآنِ الْكَرِيمِ.
meaning.en_detailed: Quadriliteral reduplicative root ذ-ب-ذ-ب (thāʾ-bāʾ-thāʾ-bāʾ), occurring 1 time in the Quran. The reduplication of the bivalent consonants phonetically enacts the semantic oscillation it denotes — the wavering, vacillation, the being torn between two opposing states; the verbal noun ذَبْذَبَة expresses the motion of a pendulum, the to-and-fro indecision. Its sole Quranic occurrence is 4:143, مُّذَبْذَبِينَ بَيْنَ ذَٰلِكَ لَآ إِلَىٰ هَٰؤُلَاءِ وَلَآ إِلَىٰ هَٰؤُلَاءِ — waverers between this and that, belonging neither to the believers nor to the disbelievers. Al-Rāzī and al-Zamakhsharī note the image of a person suspended between two poles, the spiritual no-man's-land of the hypocrites (مُنَافِقُون).

The noun ʿabqarīy appears in Quran 55:23 as a description of the wondrous furnishing and carpets of Paradise: 'and ʿabqarīy ḥisān' (cushions of peerless beauty), where lexicographers gloss it as something surpassing all workmanship. The root is otherwise rare outside the Quran and classical poetry, with classical hadith usage preserved in the phrase al-ʿabqarī min al-ʿilm (the masterly one in knowledge).

meaning.en_detailed: Arabic quadriliteral root qāf-ṭāʾ-mīm-rāʾ (ق-ط-م-ر), 1 Quranic occurrence, designating the qiṭmīr (قِطْمِير) — the extraordinarily thin, translucent membrane enveloping the date-stone inside the date fruit — used as a powerful Quranic metaphor for absolute insignificance and powerlessness. The term appears in Quran 35:13 in a rebuke of those who invoke deities besides God: 'those you call upon besides Him own not even a qiṭmīr (mā yamlikūna min qiṭmīr),' meaning that the false gods possess nothing whatsoever, not even the most microscopic of things. Al-Ṭabarī and Lisān al-ʿArab specify qiṭmīr as the fine inner pellicle of the date-stone, the smallest possible visible thing, paralleling Hebrew qitmor.

meaning.ar: سردق: جَذْرٌ قُرْآنِيٌّ يَدُلُّ عَلَى مَفْهُومٍ فِي الْقُرْآنِ الْكَرِيمِ.
meaning.en_detailed: Arabic quadriliteral root sīn-rāʾ-dāl-qāf (س-ر-د-ق), 1 Quranic occurrence, a borrowing of Middle Persian srādag (royal tent, pavilion, enclosure), designating the surādiq — a curving wall of tent-cloth encircling a royal pavilion or its metaphorical extension as encompassing barrier. The noun surādiq appears in Quran 18:29 in the description of Hell's torments for the wrongdoers: 'We have prepared for the wrongdoers a Fire whose pavilion (surādiq) encompasses them' — the image of a vast encircling wall of flame. meaning.en_detailed: Arabic quadriliteral root zāy-mīm-hāʾ-rāʾ (ز-م-ه-ر), 1 Quranic occurrence, designating zamharīr (زَمْهَرِير) — intense, biting, freezing cold, representing the polar opposite of scorching heat in the spectrum of extreme temperatures. The adjective qamṭarīr appears in Quran 76:10 in the speech of the righteous fearing God: 'Indeed we fear from our Lord a day of frowning and distressful grimness (yawman ʿabūsan qamṭarīrā),' describing the terrifying harshness of the Day of Judgment. The noun rafraf appears in Quran 55:76 in the description of the righteous reclining in Paradise: 'reclining on green cushions (rafrafin khuḍrin) and ʿabqarīy ḥisān,' where rafraf specifies the plump green cushions and ʿabqarīy the patterned spread or carpet beneath them. In the Quran, it appears in the plural form al-Aḥqāf (الأحقاف), the name of Surah 46, which refers to the sand dunes region where the prophet Hūd was sent to the people of ʿĀd. meaning.en_detailed: Triliteral Arabic root ḥāʾ-qāf-fāʾ (ح-ق-ف), 1 Quranic occurrence, denoting the ḥaqf — a curved sand dune or winding tract of sand, the kind found in extended dunes-regions of the Arabian desert. The noun al-Aḥqāf (الأحقاف), the plural form, gives its name to Sūrat al-Aḥqāf (Quran 46), with the central verse 46:21 reading: 'And mention, [O Muḥammad], the brother of ʿĀd when he warned his people in [the region of] al-Aḥqāf,' referring to the prophetic mission of Hūd to the people of ʿĀd. Ibn ʿAbbās and the mufassirūn (al-Ṭabarī) identified al-Aḥqāf with the sand-dune regions of al-Shiḥr (southern Arabia) where the vanished ʿĀd once lived.

meaning.en: The quadriliteral root H-D-H-D (ه-د-ه-د) denotes the hoopoe bird (Upupa epops), a distinctive crested bird known in Arabic folklore. In the Quran, the hoopoe appears in the story of Prophet Solomon (Sulaymān), serving as a scout who brings news of the kingdom of Sheba and its queen Bilqīs. The bird

meaning.en_detailed: Quadriliteral reduplicative Arabic root hāʾ-dāl-hāʾ-dāl (ه-د-ه-د), 1 Quranic occurrence, designating the hudhud — the hoopoe bird (Upupa epops), a distinctive crested species whose name is onomatopoetic of its call. The noun hudhud appears in the Sūrat al-Naml narrative of Prophet Sulaymān (Quran 27:20-28), where Sulaymān inspects his assembled troops of birds and questions the absent hudhud, who later returns with intelligence about the kingdom of Sheba and its queen Bilqīs. The reduplicative form iconically mimics the bird's characteristic 'hud-hud-hud' call; classical hadith forbade the killing of the hoopoe (Sunan Abī Dāwūd 5267), suggesting its recognized religious-cultural status.

Classical grammarians differ on its derivation — some analyze it

meaning.en_detailed: Triliteral Arabic root lām-wāw-tāʾ (ل-و-ت), 1 Quranic occurrence, in this root's singular Quranic use associated with the rare negative particle lāta — meaning 'not at all,' 'not,' or 'there is no,' where grammarians debate whether the tāʾ is original or a suffix. The word appears in Quran 38:3 in the accusative construction: 'but there was no time for escape (wa-lāta ḥīna manāṣin),' where Sībawayh and al-Khalīl analyze lāta as laisa (not), with the tāʾ either a particle of emphatic negation or a taltala (phonetic intensifier). Al-Ṭabarī's tafsīr preserves Ibn ʿAbbās's gloss 'laysa ḥīna firārin' (not the time for fleeing), confirming the negative sense; al-Zamakhsharī notes its parallel structure to laysa in classical Arabic grammar.

The noun al-majūs appears in Quran 22:17 in the legal-liturgical verse listing religious communities whose legal status God will judge on the Last Day: 'Indeed, those who believed, those who were Jews, the Sabians, the Christians, the Magians, and the polytheists — indeed, God will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection' (al-majūsa wa-alladhīna ashrakū). Lisān al-ʿArab traces the term through Middle Persian maguš, Magi; Islamic law later extended to Magians the protected status (dhimmī) accorded People of the Book, per several āthār.

meaning.en: The quadriliteral root KH-R-Ṭ-M (خ-ر-ط-م) denotes the snout or trunk, particularly of an elephant or pig. In the Quran, it appears in Surah Al-Qalam (68:16) as a vivid metaphorical expression: ‘We will brand him upon the snout’ (سَنَسِمُهُ عَلَى الْخُرْطُومِ). This refers to a prominent disbeliever

meaning.en_detailed: Quadriliteral Arabic root khāʾ-rāʾ-ṭāʾ-mīm (خ-ر-ط-م), 1 Quranic occurrence, designating the khurṭūm — the snout, trunk, or muzzle of an animal, particularly the prominent proboscis of an elephant or pig. The noun al-khurṭūm appears in Quran 68:16 in the prophetic threat against a particular leading disbeliever of Quraysh: 'We will brand him upon the snout (sanasimuhu ʿalā al-khurṭūm),' glossed by tafsīr as a mark of public humiliation affixed to the most visible and protruding feature of the face. Ibn ʿAbbās's reports identify the referent as al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra; al-Rāghib and Lisān al-ʿArab derive khurṭūm from kharṭama (to seize with the snout), with the quadriliteral structure perhaps originally onomatopoetic.
